title: Clinical Case
description: A clinical case-based question bank developed from the course sheets and teaching materials prepared by Dr. Abdulrahman Al-Juaiki. Questions are organized by medical system, topic and linked clinical case to support structured clinical reasoning and examination preparation.
attribution: Based on Dr. Abdulrahman Al-Juaiki's course sheets and the supplied Clinical Case Markdown banks.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which statement best defines a seizure?

options.label: A
options.text: A transient occurrence of symptoms or signs due to abnormal electrical activity in the brain

options.label: B
options.text: Any involuntary limb movement during sleep

options.label: C
options.text: Any episode of fever associated with irritability

options.label: D
options.text: A permanent loss of motor function caused by a structural brain lesion

options.label: E
options.text: A prolonged state of unconsciousness caused by hypoglycaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: A transient occurrence of symptoms or signs due to abnormal electrical activity in the brain
questions.initialExplanation: A seizure is a transient clinical event caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. It may manifest with motor, sensory, autonomic, behavioural or consciousness changes, or a combination of these.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the definition given.
- B. Incorrect. Involuntary movement during sleep is not necessarily epileptic; normal sleep movements and other paroxysmal disorders may mimic seizures.
- C. Incorrect. Fever and irritability alone do not define a seizure.
- D. Incorrect. A seizure is transient and does not by itself mean permanent motor loss.
- E. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia can provoke a seizure, but seizures have many causes and are not defined by prolonged unconsciousness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Seizure: transient symptoms/signs due to abnormal brain electrical activity.
- Manifestations may be motor, sensory, autonomic, behavioural/psychic or mixed.
- Convulsion refers specifically to involuntary muscular contraction (a motor manifestation); not every seizure is convulsive.
- Febrile convulsion is the commonest cause of childhood convulsions.

questions.stem: Which child meets standard definition of a febrile seizure?

options.label: A
options.text: A 4-month-old infant with fever and a seizure due to bacterial meningitis

options.label: B
options.text: A 5-year-old child with a seizure caused by severe hypoglycaemia

options.label: C
options.text: A 9-year-old child with a seizure during fever and a known brain tumour

options.label: D
options.text: A 3-year-old child with a seizure during fever, with no CNS infection and an identified extracranial infection

options.label: E
options.text: A 2-year-old child with recurrent afebrile seizures

questions.correctAnswerText: A 3-year-old child with a seizure during fever, with no CNS infection and an identified extracranial infection
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe febrile convulsion as a seizure associated with fever in a child aged approximately 6 months to 6 years, without CNS infection. The fever source is usually outside the CNS, such as URTI, UTI, gastroenteritis or pneumonia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The child is younger than the age range, and meningitis excludes the diagnosis of a simple febrile seizure.
- B. Incorrect. A metabolic provocation such as hypoglycaemia is an alternative cause of seizure and should be corrected; it is not classified as a simple febrile seizure.
- C. Incorrect. The child is older than standard age range and has a structural intracranial cause.
- D. Correct. The age is within the stated range and there is fever without CNS infection.
- E. Incorrect. Recurrent unprovoked seizures suggest epilepsy, not febrile convulsion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Febrile seizure: age 6 months to 6 years.
- Fever is present, but CNS infection is absent.
- Common fever sources: URTI, UTI, gastroenteritis and pneumonia.
- A seizure with meningitis/encephalitis must not be labelled a simple febrile seizure.

questions.stem: Which statement about the epidemiology of febrile seizures is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: They affect almost children in routine care and not usually recur

options.label: B
options.text: They occur in approximately 2-4% of children and recur in about 30-40%

options.label: D
options.text: They occur in children with a family history of epilepsy

options.label: E
options.text: They are limited to children older than 10 years

questions.correctAnswerText: They occur in approximately 2-4% of children and recur in about 30-40%
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives an incidence of approximately 2-4% of children and recurrence in approximately 30-40%. A genetic predisposition is noted, and febrile seizures are slightly more common in boys.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Febrile seizures affect a minority of children and recurrence is possible.
- B. Correct. These are the epidemiological estimates stated in the source.
- C. Incorrect. It is recognized a slight male predominance.
- D. Incorrect. A family history increases risk but is not required for a febrile seizure to occur.
- E. Incorrect. standard age range is approximately 6 months to 6 years.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Incidence: approximately 2-4%.
- Recurrence: approximately 30-40%.
- Slight male predominance.
- Genetic predisposition is relevant but not obligatory.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 7 minutes during a febrile illness. It is the only seizure in 24 hours, and the neurological examination is normal after recovery. How is this event classified?

options.label: A
options.text: Complex febrile seizure because it occurred with fever

questions.correctAnswerText: Simple febrile seizure
questions.initialExplanation: A simple febrile seizure is generalized, lasts less than 15 minutes, occurs only once within 24 hours and is not followed by a focal neurological deficit. This event meets all these criteria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fever is part of the definition of a febrile seizure and does not itself make it complex.
- B. Correct. The event is generalized, shorter than 15 minutes, single in 24 hours and has no residual focal deficit.
- C. Incorrect. The seizure occurred during fever.
- D. Incorrect. A 7-minute febrile seizure is not classified as status epilepticus 's simple/complex distinction; ongoing convulsive seizures beyond 5 minutes nevertheless require emergency treatment.
- E. Incorrect. There is no focal onset or evidence of recurrent unprovoked seizures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Simple febrile seizure: generalized, <15 minutes, one in 24 hours, no postictal focal neurological deficit.
- Simple febrile seizures do not cause brain damage in the otherwise healthy child.
- A simple febrile seizure does not usually require routine EEG or brain CT.
- Treat an ongoing seizure promptly according to the pediatric seizure emergency pathway.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old develops a focal seizure lasting 18 minutes during a febrile illness and has transient right-sided weakness afterwards. Which classification is most appropriate?
questions.correctAnswerText: Complex febrile seizure
questions.initialExplanation: A febrile seizure is complex if it is focal, lasts more than 15 minutes, recurs within 24 hours, or is followed by a postictal neurological deficit. This child has more than one complex feature.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Breath-holding spells are typically triggered by crying or pain and are not epileptic seizures.
- B. Incorrect. Absence seizures are brief episodes of impaired awareness without this focal motor/postictal pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Rolandic epilepsy causes focal seizures, often during sleep, but the association with fever and prolonged focal event supports complex febrile seizure.
- D. Correct. Focality, duration >15 minutes and postictal weakness are features of a complex febrile seizure.
- E. Incorrect. The seizure is focal, prolonged and followed by a neurological deficit.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Complex febrile seizure: focal, >15 minutes, recurrent in 24 hours and/or postictal focal deficit.
- Simple febrile seizure: generalized, <15 minutes, single in 24 hours and no focal deficit.
- Complex febrile seizures are associated with a higher subsequent epilepsy risk than simple febrile seizures.
- A focal neurological deficit after a seizure requires careful assessment and follow-up.

questions.stem: Which factor is listed as a major predictor of recurrence of febrile seizures?

options.label: A
options.text: High fever of 40.5°C or above at seizure onset

options.label: B
options.text: First febrile seizure after 5 years of age

options.label: C
options.text: Absence of a family history of febrile seizures

options.label: D
options.text: Age below 1 year at the first febrile seizure

options.label: E
options.text: A long febrile illness lasting more than 24 hours before the seizure

questions.correctAnswerText: Age below 1 year at the first febrile seizure
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include younger age (especially under 1 year), a short duration of illness before the seizure and a lower temperature at the time of seizure among major recurrence risk factors. Family history of febrile seizures/epilepsy and complex features are listed as minor factors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Recognized features include a lower temperature at the time of seizure as increasing recurrence risk.
- B. Incorrect. A first event after the usual febrile seizure age range is less typical.
- C. Incorrect. A positive family history is a risk factor; absence of family history is not.
- D. Correct. Younger age, particularly below 1 year, is a major recurrence risk factor.
- E. Incorrect. A seizure occurring early in the febrile illness, before prolonged fever, increases recurrence risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Major recurrence risks: age <1 year, seizure early in the febrile illness and lower temperature at the time of seizure.
- Minor risks: family history of febrile seizures/epilepsy, complex seizure, daycare, male sex and lower serum sodium.
- Clinical descriptions include genetic predisposition and rapidly rising temperature as relevant to pathophysiology.
- Do not use recurrence risk factors to diagnose epilepsy.

questions.stem: A child is brought to the emergency department while actively convulsing with fever. What is the first priority?

options.label: A
options.text: Perform lumbar puncture during the convulsion

options.label: B
options.text: Give an oral antipyretic while the child is unconscious

options.label: C
options.text: Stabilize airway, breathing and circulation, position safely and check glucose

options.label: D
options.text: Perform a CT brain scan immediately

options.label: E
options.text: Obtain an EEG before giving treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Stabilize airway, breathing and circulation, position safely and check glucose
questions.initialExplanation: An actively convulsing child requires emergency ABC management. Clinical descriptions include placing the child in the lateral position, clearing the airway if required, monitoring, providing oxygen, assessing circulation, obtaining IV access where possible and checking reversible metabolic causes such as hypoglycaemia and hypocalcaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lumbar puncture is not performed during an unstable active convulsion and is considered only after stabilization when clinically indicated.
- B. Incorrect. Oral medication is unsafe in an unconscious or actively convulsing child because of aspiration risk.
- C. Correct. ABC stabilization and immediate assessment for reversible causes are the priorities.
- D. Incorrect. CT is not the first step in an actively convulsing child; stabilize first and image only when indicated.
- E. Incorrect. EEG must not delay stabilization and seizure termination.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Active seizure: ABC first.
- Place the child laterally when feasible; protect from injury and do not restrain the limbs or put objects in the mouth.
- Give oxygen/monitoring and check bedside glucose.
- Correct hypoglycaemia or hypocalcaemia when present.
- Do not delay seizure termination for investigations.

questions.stem: A child continues to have a generalized convulsion after initial ABC stabilization. Which drug class is used first to terminate the ongoing seizure?
questions.correctAnswerText: Benzodiazepine
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include IV diazepam or lorazepam as initial anticonvulsant treatment for a child with ongoing convulsions. If IV access is unavailable, buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam are alternatives described. Exact dosing and repetition must follow the current emergency protocol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ethosuximide is used for typical absence epilepsy, not emergency convulsive seizure termination.
- B. Correct. Benzodiazepines are first-line acute treatment for an ongoing convulsive seizure.
- C. Incorrect. Valproate may be used for selected epilepsy syndromes as maintenance therapy; it is not the initial route/class described for immediate seizure termination in this pathway.
- D. Incorrect. Antipsychotics do not terminate epileptic convulsions and may worsen clinical management.
- E. Incorrect. Carbamazepine is used for selected focal epilepsies, not as the first rescue drug for an ongoing generalized convulsion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- First-line acute therapy for ongoing convulsive seizure: benzodiazepine.
- Routes may include IV/IO lorazepam or diazepam; buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam if vascular access is not available, according to protocol.
- Avoid repeated excessive benzodiazepine doses because of respiratory depression.
- If the seizure persists, escalate promptly using the local pediatric status epilepticus pathway.

questions.stem: A child remains in convulsive status despite appropriately administered benzodiazepine doses. What is the next management principle?

options.label: A
options.text: Escalate to a second-line antiseizure medication such as phenytoin or phenobarbital, while preparing senior/airway support

options.label: B
options.text: Stop monitoring and allow the child to sleep

options.label: D
options.text: Perform routine lumbar puncture before further seizure treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Escalate to a second-line antiseizure medication such as phenytoin or phenobarbital, while preparing senior/airway support
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include loading and maintenance treatment with phenytoin or phenobarbital when the child continues to convulse after benzodiazepine treatment. Persistent seizure activity requires senior help and early anaesthetic/ICU involvement, with airway and ventilation support if necessary.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the escalation approach described.
- B. Incorrect. Ongoing convulsive status is a medical emergency and requires continued treatment and monitoring.
- C. Incorrect. Resolution of fever does not terminate ongoing status epilepticus.
- D. Incorrect. Investigations must not delay status treatment; LP is considered only after stabilization and when indicated.
- E. Incorrect. Ethosuximide is for absence seizures and is not rescue therapy for convulsive status.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Persistent convulsion after benzodiazepine: second-line antiseizure medication and senior support.
- Prepare for airway management, anaesthesia and ICU care if seizures persist.
- Monitor respiratory status, circulation, glucose and electrolytes.
- Do not delay seizure treatment for CT, EEG or lumbar puncture.
- Exact drug sequence, doses and infusion rates must follow the current local pediatric status epilepticus protocol.

questions.stem: A child has recovered fully after a single simple febrile seizure. The examination is normal and there are no features suggesting CNS infection. Which statement about investigations is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Brain MRI is required before discharge

options.label: B
options.text: Routine long-term antiseizure medication is required

options.label: C
options.text: Routine CT brain and EEG are not indicated in a typical simple febrile seizure

options.label: D
options.text: A lumbar puncture is mandatory in children in routine care with fever and a seizure

options.label: E
options.text: Routine CT brain and EEG are required in each simple febrile seizure

questions.correctAnswerText: Routine CT brain and EEG are not indicated in a typical simple febrile seizure
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that CT brain and EEG are not indicated for simple febrile convulsions. Investigations should be directed toward the source of fever and clinical concern for meningitis or another underlying disorder. Lumbar puncture is considered when CNS infection is suspected, not routinely in every simple febrile seizure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. MRI is not routinely required after a typical simple febrile seizure with full recovery and a normal examination.
- B. Incorrect. Long-term prophylactic antiseizure medication is not routinely recommended because adverse effects outweigh the benefit for most children.
- C. Correct. This matches standard guidance.
- D. Incorrect. LP is not mandatory for every febrile seizure; it depends on age, clinical appearance, immunization status and suspicion of CNS infection.
- E. Incorrect. Routine neuroimaging and EEG do not improve management of a typical simple febrile seizure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Simple febrile seizure: no routine EEG or CT brain.
- Assess the cause of fever and look for evidence of meningitis/encephalitis.
- LP is reserved for clinical indications suggesting CNS infection; it must not be performed in an unstable child or when contraindications are present.
- Provide parental reassurance and return precautions.

cases.title: A child has recurrent unprovoked episodes of abnormal movements
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child has had two unprovoked episodes of abnormal neurological activity separated by several weeks. There is no fever, acute infection, hypoglycaemia or electrolyte disturbance at either presentation. The clinician evaluates the episodes as possible epilepsy.

questions.stem: Which definition of epilepsy is used?

options.label: A
options.text: Any seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes

options.label: C
options.text: Any brief episode of syncope with limb jerking

options.label: D
options.text: Two or more recurrent unprovoked seizures

options.label: E
options.text: A single seizure occurring during fever

questions.correctAnswerText: Two or more recurrent unprovoked seizures
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe epilepsy as recurrent (two or more) unprovoked seizures. A seizure due to an acute provoking cause such as fever, hypoglycaemia or an electrolyte disturbance is not automatically epilepsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A prolonged seizure may meet a status epilepticus definition but does not alone establish epilepsy.
- B. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia is an acute provoking cause and must be corrected.
- C. Incorrect. Syncope with brief jerking can mimic a seizure but is not necessarily epileptic.
- D. Correct. This is the definition stated in the source.
- E. Incorrect. A seizure associated with fever in the appropriate age range and without CNS infection is a febrile seizure, not epilepsy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Epilepsy: recurrent unprovoked seizures (≥2 ).
- Separate acute symptomatic seizures from epilepsy.
- Status epilepticus is defined by prolonged seizure activity or repeated seizures without recovery.
- standard guidance reports an approximate prevalence of 0.5% in children.

questions.stem: A child has continuous generalized convulsive activity for 7 minutes. Which statement best reflects the operational definition of convulsive status epilepticus?

options.label: A
options.text: It begins after 30 minutes of convulsions

options.label: B
options.text: It is diagnosed after three separate seizures in one month

options.label: C
options.text: It requires a normal level of consciousness between seizures

options.label: D
options.text: It begins when a convulsive seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, requiring emergency treatment

options.label: E
options.text: It is defined by any seizure lasting more than 15 seconds

questions.correctAnswerText: It begins when a convulsive seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, requiring emergency treatment
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance includes the historical 30-minute definition but also notes the newer operational threshold of 5 minutes or more. Treatment should begin at 5 minutes because a seizure continuing beyond this point is less likely to stop spontaneously and requires emergency management.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Thirty minutes is the older definition; it is unsafe to wait this long before treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Status epilepticus is defined by duration or recurrent seizures without recovery, not by monthly frequency.
- C. Incorrect. Repeated seizures without regaining consciousness can also constitute status epilepticus.
- D. Correct. The operational treatment threshold is 5 minutes.
- E. Incorrect. A brief seizure is not status epilepticus based on duration alone.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Older definition: ≥30 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery over 30 minutes.
- Operational treatment threshold: convulsive seizure ≥5 minutes.
- Treat promptly with ABC support and the local status epilepticus algorithm.
- Refractory status persists despite an adequate benzodiazepine and an appropriate second-line antiseizure medication.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes focal from generalized seizures?

options.label: A
options.text: Generalized seizures arise from the cerebellum

options.label: B
options.text: Focal seizures arise from a network in one cerebral hemisphere, whereas generalized seizures involve both hemispheres from onset

options.label: C
options.text: Focal seizures are typically bilateral and symmetrical

options.label: D
options.text: Generalized seizures typically begin with an aura

options.label: E
options.text: Focal seizures typically cause complete loss of consciousness

questions.correctAnswerText: Focal seizures arise from a network in one cerebral hemisphere, whereas generalized seizures involve both hemispheres from onset
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance classifies focal seizures as arising from one hemisphere and generalized seizures as involving both hemispheres from onset. Focal seizures may occur with preserved or impaired consciousness and may secondarily generalize.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Generalized seizures involve bilateral cerebral networks and are not restricted to the cerebellum.
- B. Correct. This is the basic anatomical distinction.
- C. Incorrect. Focal seizures may produce unilateral motor or sensory manifestations.
- D. Incorrect. Generalized seizures usually have no warning/aura 's description.
- E. Incorrect. Focal aware seizures occur with preserved consciousness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Focal seizure: onset in one hemisphere; may have an aura and may or may not impair awareness.
- Generalized seizure: both hemispheres involved from onset; often bilateral and symmetrical.
- Focal seizure with secondary generalization progresses from focal onset to bilateral tonic-clonic activity.
- A detailed witness history helps identify focal onset.

questions.stem: A child reports a sudden unpleasant smell immediately before a seizure with impaired awareness and lip smacking. Which seizure origin is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Temporal lobe
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance associates temporal lobe seizures with auditory or sensory phenomena such as smell or taste. An unpleasant smell may be an olfactory aura, followed by impaired awareness and automatisms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Parietal seizures may produce contralateral altered sensation or dysaesthesia.
- B. Incorrect. The cerebellum coordinates movement and is not the typical origin of an epileptic olfactory aura.
- C. Incorrect. The described aura and automatisms are typical of a focal cerebral seizure, not an isolated brainstem event.
- D. Correct. Olfactory or gustatory aura is associated with temporal lobe seizure onset.
- E. Incorrect. Occipital seizures commonly produce positive or negative visual phenomena.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Frontal lobe: motor phenomena.
- Temporal lobe: auditory, olfactory or gustatory phenomena; automatisms may occur.
- Occipital lobe: visual phenomena.
- Parietal lobe: contralateral altered sensation/dysaesthesia.
- The aura can reflect the site of focal seizure onset.

cases.title: A school-aged child has sudden staring episodes
cases.vignette: A 8-year-old child is reported by the teacher to stop speaking abruptly, stare for several seconds and then resume the activity without confusion. The episodes occur many times each day. There is no warning and no postictal sleepiness.

questions.stem: Which seizure type is most likely?

options.label: C
options.text: Focal motor seizure with secondary generalization

questions.correctAnswerText: Typical absence seizure
questions.initialExplanation: Typical absence seizures are brief episodes of impaired awareness with abrupt onset and termination, usually lasting 5-30 seconds. They may occur many times a day without an aura or postictal phase.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Tonic-clonic seizures involve loss of consciousness and rhythmic convulsions followed by a postictal phase.
- B. Correct. Brief staring, frequent daily episodes and immediate recovery are characteristic.
- C. Incorrect. Focal seizures may have an aura, focal manifestations or a longer postictal period.
- D. Incorrect. Myoclonic seizures produce brief jerking movements rather than isolated staring.
- E. Incorrect. Atonic seizures cause sudden loss of muscle tone and falls/head drops.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typical absence: sudden brief impairment of awareness, usually 5-30 seconds.
- Abrupt onset and termination; no aura and no postictal phase.
- May occur many times a day and interfere with school performance.
- Development is often otherwise normal.

questions.stem: Which EEG finding is characteristic of typical childhood absence epilepsy?

options.label: B
options.text: Focal temporal slowing without epileptiform discharges

options.label: D
options.text: Bilaterally synchronous generalized spike-and-wave discharges at approximately 3 Hz

questions.correctAnswerText: Bilaterally synchronous generalized spike-and-wave discharges at approximately 3 Hz
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include fast generalized spike-and-wave activity of approximately 3-4 Hz, bilaterally synchronous, during typical absence seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Burst suppression may be seen in severe encephalopathy or other severe epileptic states, not typical absence epilepsy.
- B. Incorrect. A focal temporal abnormality does not describe the classic generalized absence EEG.
- C. Incorrect. Hypsarrhythmia is associated with infantile spasms (West syndrome).
- D. Correct. Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave activity is the classic EEG pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Centrotemporal spikes are associated with benign Rolandic epilepsy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typical absence EEG: generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave (standard guidance gives approximately 3-4 Hz).
- Hyperventilation may provoke an absence seizure.
- Ethosuximide is listed as the drug of choice for typical absence seizures.
- Prognosis is generally good; many children remit during adolescence.

questions.stem: A child suddenly drops to the floor because of a brief loss of muscle tone. Which seizure type best explains this event?
questions.correctAnswerText: Atonic seizure
questions.initialExplanation: Atonic seizures cause a transient loss of muscle tone, resulting in a sudden fall or head drop. They may be associated with myoclonic jerks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Sudden loss of tone and falling are characteristic of atonic seizures.
- B. Incorrect. Focal sensory seizures cause abnormal sensation rather than sudden generalized loss of tone.
- C. Incorrect. Myoclonic seizures cause brief shock-like jerks rather than loss of tone.
- D. Incorrect. Absence seizures cause brief impaired awareness without loss of postural tone in the typical form.
- E. Incorrect. Tonic seizures cause sustained stiffening or rigid posturing.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Myoclonic seizure: brief, shock-like jerking of limbs, neck or trunk.
- Atonic seizure: sudden loss of tone, often causing falls or head drops.
- Tonic seizure: sustained increase in tone/rigid posturing.
- Identify injury risk in children with recurrent atonic seizures.

cases.title: An infant has clusters of brief flexor spasms after waking
cases.vignette: A 7-month-old infant develops repeated brief episodes of neck, trunk and limb flexion, followed by extension/abduction of the arms. The spasms occur in clusters, especially on waking. Parents initially thought the infant had colic. Developmental progress has slowed.

questions.stem: Which epilepsy syndrome is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Infantile spasms (West syndrome)
questions.initialExplanation: Infantile spasms are brief flexor, extensor or mixed contractions of the neck, trunk and limbs, often occurring in clusters around waking or sleep transitions. standard guidance places the usual age between 3 and 12 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lennox-Gastaut usually presents later in early childhood with multiple seizure types and developmental impairment.
- B. Correct. The age, clustered spasms and developmental concern are typical of West syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy typically begins in adolescence, often with morning myoclonic jerks.
- D. Incorrect. Childhood absence epilepsy occurs in school-aged children and presents with brief staring spells.
- E. Incorrect. Rolandic epilepsy is a childhood focal epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, often during sleep.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- West syndrome: infantile spasms, usually 3-12 months.
- Spasms may be flexor, extensor or mixed and occur in clusters, often on waking.
- Developmental delay or regression is an important associated feature.
- It may be mistaken for colic or normal infant movements.

questions.stem: Which EEG pattern is characteristic of infantile spasms?

options.label: D
options.text: Normal EEG in most affected infants

options.label: E
options.text: Hypsarrhythmia: chaotic high-voltage slow waves with multifocal epileptiform activity

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypsarrhythmia: chaotic high-voltage slow waves with multifocal epileptiform activity
questions.initialExplanation: Hypsarrhythmia is the characteristic EEG pattern associated with West syndrome. It consists of a chaotic, high-voltage background with multifocal epileptiform activity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is the typical EEG pattern of childhood absence epilepsy.
- B. Incorrect. Centrotemporal spikes suggest benign Rolandic epilepsy.
- C. Incorrect. A single focal occipital spike does not describe hypsarrhythmia.
- D. Incorrect. EEG is a key investigation and is often markedly abnormal.
- E. Correct. Hypsarrhythmia is the classic EEG finding in infantile spasms.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infantile spasms → hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
- Common examples include vigabatrin, ACTH and corticosteroids as treatments.
- Tuberous sclerosis is an important associated cause; vigabatrin is especially relevant in TSC-associated infantile spasms.
- Symptomatic infantile spasms often have a poorer developmental prognosis than idiopathic cases.

questions.stem: An infant with tuberous sclerosis develops infantile spasms. Which medication is specifically listed as a treatment for infantile spasms?
questions.correctAnswerText: Vigabatrin
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include vigabatrin, ACTH and corticosteroids as treatments for infantile spasms. Vigabatrin is especially associated with treatment of spasms in children with tuberous sclerosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Gabapentin is not the standard treatment for infantile spasms in this standard guidance.
- B. Correct. Vigabatrin is listed for infantile spasms and is particularly relevant in tuberous sclerosis.
- C. Incorrect. Ethosuximide is used for typical absence epilepsy.
- D. Incorrect. Carbamazepine is used for selected focal epilepsies and is not the treatment listed for West syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Clobazam may be used in some seizure contexts but is not the specific first treatment listed for infantile spasms here.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infantile spasms: vigabatrin, ACTH or corticosteroids.
- Tuberous sclerosis is an important secondary cause.
- Early recognition and urgent specialist treatment are essential because ongoing spasms may worsen developmental outcome.
- Treatment choice and monitoring should follow a pediatric epilepsy specialist protocol.

cases.title: A child has focal seizures during sleep with facial movements
cases.vignette: A 8-year-old child has brief seizures during sleep, with twitching of one side of the face and abnormal sensations around the tongue. Awareness is usually preserved. The child is otherwise developing normally.

questions.stem: Which epilepsy syndrome is most likely?

options.label: E
options.text: Benign focal epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (Rolandic epilepsy)

questions.correctAnswerText: Benign focal epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (Rolandic epilepsy)
questions.initialExplanation: Benign Rolandic epilepsy commonly occurs in children aged approximately 4-10 years. It causes focal seizures during sleep or focal symptoms involving the tongue and face, often with preserved awareness. The EEG shows centrotemporal spikes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy usually begins in adolescence with myoclonic jerks, often after waking.
- B. Incorrect. Absence epilepsy causes brief episodes of impaired awareness without focal facial sensory symptoms.
- C. Incorrect. Lennox-Gastaut is associated with multiple seizure types, developmental impairment and poor response to medication.
- D. Incorrect. Infantile spasms occur in infancy and produce clustered flexor/extensor spasms.
- E. Correct. The age, sleep-related facial symptoms and preserved awareness are characteristic.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rolandic epilepsy: age 4-10 years, often sleep-related, focal facial/tongue symptoms.
- Awareness is usually preserved.
- EEG: centrotemporal spikes.
- Generally benign, often remits during adolescence; some children may not require long-term antiseizure treatment.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: It is caused exclusively by fever

options.label: B
options.text: It presents around 1-3 years with multiple seizure types and often underlying brain injury or malformation

options.label: C
options.text: It begins in infancy with isolated absence seizures and normal development

options.label: D
options.text: It is a benign focal epilepsy that remits by adolescence

options.label: E
options.text: It is characterized by morning myoclonic jerks in otherwise healthy teenagers

questions.correctAnswerText: It presents around 1-3 years with multiple seizure types and often underlying brain injury or malformation
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include Lennox-Gastaut syndrome as beginning around 1-3 years, with multiple seizure types such as atonic, tonic and atypical absence seizures. Many children have an underlying brain injury or malformation, respond poorly to antiseizure medication and have neurodevelopmental difficulties.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lennox-Gastaut is an epilepsy syndrome, not a febrile seizure disorder.
- B. Correct. This is the syndrome description in the source.
- C. Incorrect. Lennox-Gastaut is not an isolated absence syndrome and usually involves multiple seizure types.
- D. Incorrect. This describes the generally benign course of Rolandic epilepsy.
- E. Incorrect. Morning myoclonic jerks in adolescence suggest juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lennox-Gastaut: onset around 1-3 years.
- Multiple seizure types: tonic, atonic and atypical absence.
- Often associated with underlying brain injury/malformation.
- Poor response to antiseizure medication and neurodevelopmental/behavioural impairment are common.

cases.title: A teenager has morning jerks after waking
cases.vignette: A 15-year-old adolescent experiences sudden brief jerks of both arms shortly after waking. The jerks may cause objects to be dropped. The adolescent has also had one generalized tonic-clonic seizure. School performance and baseline cognition are normal.

questions.stem: Which epilepsy syndrome is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
questions.initialExplanation: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy commonly presents in adolescence with myoclonic jerks, often shortly after waking. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures and sometimes absence seizures may also occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Childhood absence epilepsy causes brief staring spells rather than prominent morning myoclonic jerks.
- B. Incorrect. West syndrome presents in infancy with clustered spasms and hypsarrhythmia.
- C. Incorrect. Rolandic epilepsy usually occurs in younger children with focal facial/oral symptoms, often during sleep.
- D. Correct. Morning myoclonic jerks in an adolescent with otherwise preserved learning are typical of JME.
- E. Incorrect. Lennox-Gastaut usually begins in early childhood with multiple seizure types and developmental impairment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- JME: adolescent onset, myoclonic jerks often shortly after waking.
- Generalized tonic-clonic seizures and absence seizures may coexist.
- Learning is often unimpaired.
- Treatment is usually effective, but Clinical guidance notes that long-term treatment is often required and remission is less likely.

questions.stem: Which investigation is considered the investigation of choice in the evaluation of epilepsy?

options.label: D
options.text: Lumbar puncture in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: EEG
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include EEG as the investigation of choice for epilepsy. A normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy; prolonged or ambulatory EEG may be required when the diagnosis remains uncertain.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Skull X-ray does not assess epileptic electrical activity.
- B. Correct. EEG supports seizure classification and may identify an epilepsy syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. CK is used in the assessment of muscle disease such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- D. Incorrect. LP is indicated only when CNS infection or another specific diagnosis is suspected.
- E. Incorrect. Echocardiography evaluates cardiac structure and function.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EEG is the investigation of choice.
- A normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy.
- Consider 24-hour ambulatory/video EEG when needed.
- MRI/CT is used when a structural cause is suspected or the clinical picture warrants imaging.
- Metabolic studies may be indicated with developmental regression, fasting/feeding-related seizures or other suggestive features.

questions.stem: A child with seizures has developmental regression and episodes that occur when fasting. Which additional investigations are particularly relevant?

options.label: A
options.text: No further investigations because EEG is normal

options.label: B
options.text: Sweat chloride testing in each case

options.label: C
options.text: Metabolic investigations, alongside appropriate neuroimaging and genetic assessment

questions.correctAnswerText: Metabolic investigations, alongside appropriate neuroimaging and genetic assessment
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance indicates metabolic investigations when seizures are associated with developmental arrest/regression or feeds/fasting. Genetic testing is increasingly useful in intractable epilepsy with developmental delay or epileptic encephalopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy or an underlying metabolic disorder.
- B. Incorrect. Sweat chloride investigates cystic fibrosis and is not a routine seizure workup.
- C. Correct. Regression and fasting-related seizures raise concern for metabolic or genetic causes.
- D. Incorrect. Bone marrow biopsy is not part of the routine evaluation of epilepsy.
- E. Incorrect. Ankle radiographs do not investigate this neurological presentation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- History and eyewitness description remain central to diagnosis.
- EEG helps classify seizures but may be normal between events.
- Imaging assesses structural lesions.
- Developmental regression, fasting-related events or feed-related seizures should prompt metabolic/genetic evaluation.
- Tailor tests to the clinical pattern rather than ordering every investigation in every child.

questions.stem: Which treatment principle is preferred when a child requires maintenance antiseizure medication?

options.label: A
options.text: Start several antiseizure drugs simultaneously in children in routine care

options.label: B
options.text: Stop medication suddenly once the child feels better

options.label: C
options.text: Avoid discussing adverse effects with the family

options.label: D
options.text: Change medication each week regardless of seizure control

options.label: E
options.text: Use monotherapy at the lowest effective dose with regular follow-up and monitoring for adverse effects

questions.correctAnswerText: Use monotherapy at the lowest effective dose with regular follow-up and monitoring for adverse effects
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes choosing an antiseizure drug appropriate for the seizure type, using monotherapy at the minimum dose that controls seizures without unacceptable adverse effects. Parent education and regular follow-up are essential.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Polytherapy increases adverse-effect burden and is not the starting principle for most children.
- B. Incorrect. Antiseizure medication should not be stopped abruptly because seizures may recur or worsen.
- C. Incorrect. Families should understand adverse effects, administration and safety advice.
- D. Incorrect. Frequent unnecessary medication changes undermine seizure control and adherence.
- E. Correct. This is the treatment goal described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Choose the drug according to seizure type/epilepsy syndrome.
- Aim for monotherapy at the lowest effective dose.
- Explain adverse effects and the importance of adherence.
- Do not stop antiseizure medication suddenly.
- Physical activity is not automatically prohibited, but specific risks (e.g. swimming) require supervision and safety planning.

questions.stem: A child with epilepsy has been seizure-free for 2 years. Which statement best reflects the approach described?

options.label: A
options.text: Consider withdrawal after 2 seizure-free years in selected children; juvenile absence and myoclonic epilepsy usually need longer treatment

options.label: B
options.text: A normal EEG alone is sufficient to stop medication abruptly

options.label: C
options.text: Medication must typically continue for life in children in routine care

options.label: D
options.text: most antiseizure drugs must be stopped immediately at 2 years

options.label: E
options.text: Medication should be replaced with prophylactic antibiotics

questions.correctAnswerText: Consider withdrawal after 2 seizure-free years in selected children; juvenile absence and myoclonic epilepsy usually need longer treatment
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that antiseizure medication may be discontinued after 2 years without seizures in selected children, but treatment is usually continued indefinitely in juvenile absence epilepsy and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Withdrawal should be individualized and gradual under specialist supervision.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This reflects standard guidance's distinction between selected seizure-free children and syndromes with a higher relapse tendency.
- B. Incorrect. A normal EEG alone does not determine safe withdrawal, and abrupt cessation is unsafe.
- C. Incorrect. Lifelong therapy is not required for every child with epilepsy.
- D. Incorrect. Medication is not stopped automatically or abruptly.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not replace antiseizure medication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider withdrawal only after an individualized seizure-free period and specialist review.
- standard guidance mentions 2 years seizure-free as a point at which withdrawal may be considered.
- JAE and JME commonly require prolonged/ongoing treatment.
- Taper medication gradually; never stop abruptly.

questions.stem: A child with focal epilepsy is being considered for medication. Which drug is listed as a first-line option for focal seizures?
questions.correctAnswerText: Carbamazepine
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include carbamazepine as the drug of choice for partial/focal seizures. The later drug table also includes lamotrigine and other options depending on the child and epilepsy syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ethosuximide is used for typical absence seizures.
- B. Incorrect. ACTH is used in the treatment of infantile spasms.
- C. Incorrect. Vigabatrin is listed for infantile spasms.
- D. Incorrect. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis, not epilepsy.
- E. Correct. Carbamazepine is listed for focal/partial seizures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Focal/partial seizure: carbamazepine is listed as DOC.
- Typical absence: ethosuximide.
- Infantile spasms: vigabatrin, ACTH or corticosteroids.
- Select medication according to syndrome and current specialist guidance; a drug suitable for one seizure type may worsen another.

questions.stem: A child taking sodium valproate develops weight gain and hair loss. Which statement about this medication is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is associated with nausea and vomiting

options.label: C
options.text: It may cause weight gain, hair loss and rarely idiosyncratic liver failure; it is also teratogenic

options.label: D
options.text: It causes selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibition

options.label: E
options.text: It commonly causes severe visual-field restriction

questions.correctAnswerText: It may cause weight gain, hair loss and rarely idiosyncratic liver failure; it is also teratogenic
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include weight gain, hair loss, teratogenicity and rare idiosyncratic liver failure as important adverse effects of valproate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Nausea and vomiting are listed with ethosuximide.
- B. Incorrect. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as pyridostigmine are used for myasthenia gravis.
- C. Correct. These are the adverse effects listed for valproate.
- D. Incorrect. Atomoxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor used in ADHD.
- E. Incorrect. Visual-field restriction is associated with vigabatrin.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Valproate: weight gain, hair loss, teratogenic risk and rare liver failure.
- Carbamazepine: rash, ataxia and hepatic enzyme induction.
- Lamotrigine: rash, insomnia and ataxia.
- Ethosuximide: nausea/vomiting.
- Levetiracetam: irritability.
- Vigabatrin: visual-field restriction.

cases.title: A child has prolonged convulsions despite initial emergency treatment
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child presents with ongoing generalized convulsions. The seizure does not stop after an initial benzodiazepine and an appropriate second-line antiseizure medication. The emergency team prepares senior, anaesthetic and intensive care support.

questions.stem: Which definition best describes refractory status epilepticus?

options.label: A
options.text: A seizure that stops spontaneously within 1 minute

options.label: B
options.text: A febrile seizure lasting less than 5 minutes

options.label: C
options.text: A brief staring spell with immediate recovery

options.label: D
options.text: Two unprovoked seizures separated by several years

options.label: E
options.text: Seizures persisting despite an adequate initial benzodiazepine and a second appropriate antiseizure medication

questions.correctAnswerText: Seizures persisting despite an adequate initial benzodiazepine and a second appropriate antiseizure medication
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe refractory status epilepticus as clinical or electrographic seizures that persist despite an adequate dose of an initial benzodiazepine and a second appropriate antiseizure medication.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A seizure stopping quickly does not meet the definition.
- B. Incorrect. A brief febrile seizure does not meet status criteria.
- C. Incorrect. This is more typical of an absence seizure.
- D. Incorrect. This may meet the definition of epilepsy, not refractory status.
- E. Correct. This is the definition in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Refractory status: ongoing clinical/electrographic seizure despite benzodiazepine plus a second appropriate antiseizure drug.
- Requires senior and anaesthetic/ICU involvement.
- Assess airway, breathing, circulation, glucose and reversible causes continuously.
- Continuous EEG may be required to assess ongoing electrographic seizure activity.

questions.stem: A child remains in status epilepticus for more than 24 hours despite continuous IV anaesthetic infusion. Which term is used?
questions.correctAnswerText: Super-refractory status epilepticus
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe super-refractory status epilepticus as status that persists or recurs after more than 24 hours of continuous IV anaesthetic therapy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the definition stated.
- B. Incorrect. Rolandic epilepsy is a generally benign focal epilepsy of childhood.
- C. Incorrect. Absence epilepsy causes brief episodes of impaired awareness.
- D. Incorrect. Recurrent focal epilepsy does not describe status persisting despite anaesthesia.
- E. Incorrect. Simple febrile seizure is a brief febrile event with no CNS infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Refractory status: persists after adequate benzodiazepine and second-line medication.
- Super-refractory status: persists or recurs after >24 hours of continuous IV anaesthetic therapy.
- Requires specialist neurocritical care, continuous monitoring and EEG-guided treatment.
- Treat underlying causes and prevent systemic complications.

cases.title: A toddler turns blue after becoming upset
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old becomes upset when a toy is taken away. The child cries, holds the breath at the end of expiration, becomes blue around the lips and briefly loses consciousness. The episode resolves spontaneously and the child rapidly returns to normal. Neurological examination is normal.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cyanotic breath-holding spell
questions.initialExplanation: Cyanotic breath-holding attacks are common in toddlers, usually between 6 months and 5 years. They are often triggered by upset or crying, followed by breath-holding in expiration, cyanosis and occasionally brief loss of consciousness. Recovery is rapid.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A generalized tonic-clonic seizure is not typically triggered by crying and breath-holding in this sequence.
- B. Incorrect. Meningitis causes systemic illness and neurological/meningeal features rather than isolated stereotyped breath-holding spells.
- C. Incorrect. The child recovers rapidly and spontaneously; this is not cardiac arrest.
- D. Correct. The emotional trigger, expiratory breath-holding, cyanosis and rapid recovery are characteristic.
- E. Incorrect. Absence seizures are brief episodes of impaired awareness without a preceding emotional trigger or cyanosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cyanotic breath-holding spell: common form, usually triggered by upset/crying.
- Child holds breath in expiration, becomes blue and may briefly lose consciousness.
- Usually occurs from 6 months to 5 years and resolves spontaneously by around 5 years.
- EEG is usually normal; reassurance and behavioural strategies are central.

questions.stem: A 20-month-old briefly becomes pale and loses consciousness immediately after a minor painful injury. Which mechanism best explains a pallid breath-holding spell?

options.label: C
options.text: Reflex vagal activation causing cardiac bradycardia

questions.correctAnswerText: Reflex vagal activation causing cardiac bradycardia
questions.initialExplanation: Pallid breath-holding spells are less common and are usually triggered by pain or a minor injury. A vagal reflex causes bradycardia, pallor and sometimes brief loss of consciousness.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The brief event immediately after pain is not typical of fasting hypoglycaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Raised intracranial pressure causes a different, more persistent pattern of neurological symptoms.
- C. Correct. This is the mechanism described.
- D. Incorrect. The trigger and rapid recovery suggest a reflex anoxic/pallid spell rather than epilepsy.
- E. Incorrect. Meningitis does not typically cause isolated pain-triggered pallor with immediate recovery.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pallid breath-holding spell: less common than cyanotic type.
- Trigger: pain or minor trauma.
- Mechanism: vagal reflex → bradycardia → pallor/brief loss of consciousness.
- EEG is generally normal and the condition is usually self-limiting.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old faints after standing for a long time in a hot, crowded room. The child has a brief period of limb jerking but regains consciousness quickly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Vasovagal syncope
questions.initialExplanation: Vasovagal syncope may be triggered by a hot/stuffy environment, prolonged standing or fear. Brief clonic movements can occur during syncope and do not necessarily indicate epilepsy. Recovery is usually spontaneous.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lennox-Gastaut is an epilepsy syndrome with multiple seizure types, usually beginning in early childhood.
- B. Correct. The trigger, brief faint and rapid recovery are typical of vasovagal syncope.
- C. Incorrect. Infantile spasms occur in infancy in clusters and are associated with developmental concerns.
- D. Incorrect. CNS infection causes systemic illness and persistent neurological findings.
- E. Incorrect. The clear vasovagal trigger and rapid recovery favour syncope rather than focal epilepsy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Syncope may be triggered by heat, prolonged standing, fear or pain.
- Brief clonic movements may occur during cerebral hypoperfusion.
- Rapid spontaneous recovery favours syncope.
- Consider cardiac arrhythmia when there is exertional syncope, palpitations, family history of sudden death or an abnormal ECG.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has recurrent brief episodes of vertigo lasting several minutes, sometimes with nystagmus and falling. Neurological examination is normal between episodes. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood
questions.initialExplanation: Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood is characterized by recurrent brief episodes of vertigo, dizziness, nystagmus or falling, with a normal CNS examination between episodes. Attacks often resolve spontaneously and usually need no specific treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A brainstem tumour usually causes progressive or persistent neurological signs.
- B. Incorrect. Meningitis usually causes fever, systemic illness and meningeal irritation.
- C. Incorrect. Tonic-clonic seizures cause loss of consciousness and convulsions rather than isolated recurrent vertigo.
- D. Incorrect. Cerebellar stroke generally causes acute persistent ataxia rather than recurrent self-limited episodes over time.
- E. Correct. The episodic vertigo, nystagmus and normal interval examination are typical.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Benign paroxysmal vertigo: recurrent brief vertigo, dizziness, nystagmus or falls.
- Neurological examination is normal between attacks.
- Episodes resolve spontaneously.
- Keep a broad differential if symptoms become persistent or focal neurological signs appear.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl has episodes of shaking that are not stereotyped. There is no cyanosis, tongue biting, urinary incontinence or injury. EEG is normal. Which statement best reflects standard guidance's approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Consider a non-epileptic/pseudo-seizure presentation after excluding medical causes; psychological assessment may be required

options.label: B
options.text: Diagnose meningitis despite no systemic or neurological features

options.label: C
options.text: Start lifelong antiseizure medication without further assessment

options.label: D
options.text: Diagnose epilepsy solely because the child shakes

questions.correctAnswerText: Consider a non-epileptic/pseudo-seizure presentation after excluding medical causes; psychological assessment may be required
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include pseudo-seizures as more common in girls over 10 years, often with atypical events, no cyanosis, incontinence, injury or tongue biting, and a normal EEG. Diagnosis is by exclusion and psychological assessment/support is important. In modern practice, functional seizures should be diagnosed positively where possible, not dismissed as merely psychological.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This reflects the differential and diagnostic approach.
- B. Incorrect. There are no features in this vignette to support meningitis.
- C. Incorrect. Antiseizure medication is not indicated for functional seizures unless coexisting epilepsy is present.
- D. Incorrect. Shaking alone does not establish an epileptic seizure.
- E. Incorrect. Lennox-Gastaut is a childhood epilepsy syndrome with characteristic seizure types and EEG/developmental features.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider non-epileptic/functional seizures when episodes are atypical.
- A normal routine EEG alone does not exclude epilepsy; diagnosis requires clinical assessment and appropriate video-EEG when needed.
- Exclude physiological causes such as syncope, arrhythmia, metabolic abnormalities and sleep disorders.
- Psychological support and a clear, non-stigmatizing explanation are important.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl has recurrent episodes of tonic posturing with copulatory movements, followed by flushing and sweating. Consciousness is preserved, neurological examination is normal and EEG is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Infantile gratification disorder (childhood masturbation)
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include infantile gratification disorder in young girls, typically between 2 months and 3 years. Episodes may include tonic posturing and rhythmic movements followed by flushing and perspiration, with preserved consciousness and a normal neurological examination/EEG.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A focal autonomic seizure may cause autonomic symptoms, but the described pattern and preserved awareness are typical of gratification behaviour.
- B. Incorrect. Ataxia causes impaired coordination, not episodic tonic posturing with gratification movements.
- C. Incorrect. Infantile spasms cause clustered flexor/extensor spasms in infants and are associated with EEG abnormalities.
- D. Correct. The characteristic semiology and normal neurological findings support a gratification behaviour.
- E. Incorrect. Generalized epilepsy would not be expected to preserve awareness with this stereotyped behavioural context.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infantile gratification disorder may mimic seizures.
- Consciousness is preserved; neurological examination and EEG are usually normal.
- Clinical descriptions include spontaneous resolution by around 3 years.
- Avoid unnecessary antiseizure medication; reassure caregivers and assess for other causes if the pattern is atypical.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has a triad of nystagmus, head tilt and head nodding. MRI brain and EEG are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Spasmus nutans
questions.initialExplanation: Spasmus nutans is characterized by a triad of nystagmus, head tilt/torticollis and head nodding. Clinical guidance notes that MRI and EEG are usually normal and that the condition often resolves before 5 years of age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness, ptosis and bulbar symptoms.
- B. Incorrect. Infantile spasms present with clusters of flexor/extensor spasms and an abnormal EEG.
- C. Incorrect. Hydrocephalus causes progressive head enlargement and raised intracranial pressure.
- D. Correct. This is the classic triad.
- E. Incorrect. Tuberous sclerosis may cause seizures, hypomelanotic macules and intracranial lesions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Spasmus nutans: nystagmus + head tilt + head nodding.
- MRI and EEG are usually normal.
- Often resolves before 5 years.
- Atypical findings or persistent/progressive nystagmus still warrant ophthalmic and neurological evaluation.

cases.title: A young infant presents with fever, poor feeding and lethargy
cases.vignette: A 7-week-old infant is brought with fever, poor feeding, vomiting and increasing lethargy. The infant is irritable when handled and has a tense, bulging anterior fontanelle. Urgent assessment and treatment are arranged.

questions.stem: What is the definition of meningitis?

options.label: C
options.text: Inflammation of the meninges covering the brain

options.label: E
options.text: Abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles

questions.correctAnswerText: Inflammation of the meninges covering the brain
questions.initialExplanation: Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord. It may be bacterial, viral, tuberculous or due to other uncommon causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Inflammation of peripheral nerves is a neuropathy, such as Guillain-Barre syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Anterior horn cell degeneration occurs in conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy and poliomyelitis.
- C. Correct. This is the definition.
- D. Incorrect. Inflammation of the brain parenchyma is encephalitis.
- E. Incorrect. This describes hydrocephalus.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Meningitis: inflammation of the meninges.
- Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency with significant mortality and neurological morbidity.
- Viral meningitis is often self-limiting, depending on the organism and clinical context.
- Differentiate meningitis from encephalitis, which involves brain parenchyma and often causes altered behaviour, consciousness or seizures.

questions.stem: Which organism group is most relevant when considering bacterial meningitis in a young infant?

options.label: C
options.text: Group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes

questions.correctAnswerText: Group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include Group B Streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria monocytogenes among important pathogens in young infants/neonates. The likely organisms vary with age and local epidemiology.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These viruses cause gastroenteritis, not typical bacterial meningitis.
- B. Incorrect. Fungal meningitis occurs in selected immunocompromised patients but is not the standard pathogen group.
- C. Correct. These are important neonatal/young infant bacterial meningitis pathogens.
- D. Incorrect. These are not the principal organisms listed for young infant bacterial meningitis.
- E. Incorrect. Malaria may cause neurological disease but is not a typical bacterial meningitis organism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Young infant pathogens listed: GBS, E. coli and Listeria.
- In older children, consider meningococcus, pneumococcus and Hib (depending on immunization status).
- Organism distribution is age-dependent and should be interpreted with local antimicrobial resistance data.
- Start empirical treatment promptly in suspected bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: Which is a recognized risk factor for childhood meningitis?

options.label: B
options.text: Normal immunization and no underlying condition

questions.correctAnswerText: Lack of specific immunization
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include poverty/overcrowding, lack of specific immunization, meningomyelocele/meningocele, VP shunt and immunodeficiency among meningitis risk factors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Myopia does not increase meningitis risk.
- B. Incorrect. This is not a risk factor.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital dermal melanocytosis is a benign skin finding.
- D. Incorrect. Physiological jaundice does not predispose to meningitis.
- E. Correct. Incomplete vaccination increases risk of infections such as Hib and pneumococcal disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Risks: overcrowding, incomplete immunization, neural tube defects, VP shunt and immunodeficiency.
- Complement deficiency predisposes particularly to meningococcal infection.
- Asplenia/splenic dysfunction (e.g. sickle cell disease) increases risk of encapsulated organisms.
- T-cell defects and acquired immunodeficiency increase risk of opportunistic infection.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant with meningitis has fever, poor feeding, irritability, vomiting and a bulging fontanelle, but no clear neck stiffness. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Meningitis causes focal limb weakness in infants

options.label: C
options.text: The symptoms establish epilepsy rather than meningitis

options.label: D
options.text: Infants often have non-specific systemic manifestations, and meningeal signs may be absent or difficult to elicit

options.label: E
options.text: Meningitis is unlikely because neck stiffness must typically be present

questions.correctAnswerText: Infants often have non-specific systemic manifestations, and meningeal signs may be absent or difficult to elicit
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is that infants and young children with an open anterior fontanelle may present with non-specific features such as fever, poor feeding, irritability, vomiting, diarrhoea, lethargy, mottling and a bulging/tense fontanelle. Classic meningeal signs may be absent or unreliable.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Infant meningitis commonly causes systemic and non-specific symptoms.
- B. Incorrect. A bulging fontanelle may be a sign of raised intracranial pressure and can occur in meningitis.
- C. Incorrect. The systemic illness and bulging fontanelle support CNS infection, not primary epilepsy.
- D. Correct. This is the key age-related clinical distinction.
- E. Incorrect. Neck stiffness may be absent in infants and young children.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infants: fever, poor feeding, irritability, vomiting/diarrhoea, lethargy, mottling and bulging fontanelle.
- Older children: headache, photophobia, neck stiffness and more specific neurological symptoms.
- Absence of neck stiffness does not exclude meningitis in an infant.
- Assess consciousness, perfusion, fontanelle, seizures and signs of raised ICP.

questions.stem: Which finding is a positive Kernig sign?

options.label: A
options.text: Pain on passive extension of the knee when the hip and knee are flexed

options.label: B
options.text: A tremor that stops when the limb is held

options.label: C
options.text: A head circumference above the 97th centile

options.label: D
options.text: Reflex flexion of the hips and knees when the neck is flexed

questions.correctAnswerText: Pain on passive extension of the knee when the hip and knee are flexed
questions.initialExplanation: Kernig sign is elicited with the patient supine and the hip and knee flexed. Pain or resistance during passive knee extension is considered a positive sign of meningeal irritation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This describes Kernig sign.
- B. Incorrect. This feature helps distinguish jitteriness from seizure activity.
- C. Incorrect. This is macrocephaly.
- D. Incorrect. This describes Brudzinski sign.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests facial nerve weakness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Kernig sign: pain/resistance on passive knee extension with hip flexed.
- Brudzinski sign: passive neck flexion causes reflex flexion of hips and knees.
- Neck stiffness may occur in other severe conditions such as tonsillitis, upper-lobe pneumonia or cervical lymphadenopathy.
- No single meningeal sign is sufficiently sensitive to exclude meningitis when absent.

questions.stem: A child with suspected meningitis is in shock, has reduced consciousness and signs of raised intracranial pressure. What is the safest approach to lumbar puncture?

options.label: A
options.text: Delay antibiotics until CSF culture becomes positive

options.label: B
options.text: Withhold lumbar puncture while unstable or raised ICP is suspected; obtain cultures and start IV antibiotics urgently

options.label: C
options.text: Discharge if neck stiffness is absent

options.label: D
options.text: Perform LP after giving an oral antipyretic

questions.correctAnswerText: Withhold lumbar puncture while unstable or raised ICP is suspected; obtain cultures and start IV antibiotics urgently
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include cardiorespiratory instability, signs of raised intracranial pressure, coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia, focal neurological signs and local infection at the LP site as contraindications or reasons to defer lumbar puncture. Antibiotics must not be delayed when LP is unsafe.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Delaying antibiotics in suspected bacterial meningitis increases morbidity and mortality.
- B. Correct. Stabilize first, defer LP when unsafe and give urgent empirical therapy.
- C. Incorrect. Absence of neck stiffness does not exclude meningitis, particularly in infants.
- D. Incorrect. An antipyretic does not make LP safe in a child with shock or raised ICP.
- E. Incorrect. LP in an unstable child may precipitate deterioration and must not delay resuscitation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Defer LP in cardiorespiratory instability/shock or concerning signs of raised ICP.
- Other concerns: coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia, focal neurological signs and infection at the puncture site.
- Obtain blood cultures promptly where feasible, but do not delay antibiotics.
- Reassess the need and safety of LP after stabilization.

questions.stem: Which CSF pattern is most consistent with untreated bacterial meningitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Clear CSF, lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal protein and normal glucose in each case

options.label: B
options.text: CSF with isolated red cells and no inflammatory response

options.label: C
options.text: Low protein, high glucose and no white cells

options.label: D
options.text: Turbid CSF, neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein and low glucose

options.label: E
options.text: Clear CSF, normal cells, normal protein and normal glucose

questions.correctAnswerText: Turbid CSF, neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein and low glucose
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include bacterial meningitis as typically having turbid CSF, a high white-cell count predominantly neutrophils, elevated protein, low glucose and a positive Gram stain/culture in many cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This pattern is more typical of viral meningitis, although viral CSF findings can vary.
- B. Incorrect. Isolated red cells may reflect a traumatic tap or haemorrhage and do not describe typical bacterial meningitis.
- C. Incorrect. This pattern does not support bacterial meningitis.
- D. Correct. This is the typical bacterial CSF pattern.
- E. Incorrect. This is closer to normal CSF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bacterial CSF: high WBC (mainly neutrophils), high protein, low glucose, often turbid.
- Viral CSF: usually lymphocytic, normal or mildly increased protein and usually normal glucose.
- TB meningitis: lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein and low glucose; appearance may be clear or turbid.
- Interpret CSF in context of age, prior antibiotics and blood glucose.

questions.stem: A child has suspected meningitis after receiving oral antibiotics for several days. CSF shows marked pleocytosis, but bacterial culture is negative. Which explanation is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: The CSF sample must be normal

options.label: B
options.text: Partial antibiotic treatment may sterilize the culture while CSF inflammation persists

options.label: C
options.text: Antibiotics typically cause a high CSF glucose

options.label: D
options.text: A negative culture excludes bacterial meningitis

options.label: E
options.text: The child definitely has absence epilepsy

questions.correctAnswerText: Partial antibiotic treatment may sterilize the culture while CSF inflammation persists
questions.initialExplanation: This is explained that prior oral antibiotic treatment can make CSF cultures negative despite persistent CSF white-cell elevation. Rapid antigen testing and PCR may help identify the organism. If bacterial meningitis remains clinically suspected, a full appropriate treatment course is required.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. CSF may show significant pleocytosis despite a negative culture.
- B. Correct. Partial treatment can reduce culture yield without resolving CNS inflammation.
- C. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not consistently increase CSF glucose; bacterial meningitis typically lowers CSF glucose.
- D. Incorrect. A negative culture after antibiotics does not exclude bacterial meningitis.
- E. Incorrect. Epilepsy does not explain inflammatory CSF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prior antibiotics can produce culture-negative bacterial meningitis.
- Marked CSF pleocytosis may persist.
- Rapid antigen tests and PCR may help identify the organism.
- Treat clinically suspected bacterial meningitis adequately even when culture is negative after partial treatment.

questions.stem: Which empirical antibiotic approach is described for suspected bacterial meningitis in a child younger than 3 months?

options.label: B
options.text: IV ampicillin plus gentamicin, or an ampicillin-based regimen with a third-generation cephalosporin as indicated

options.label: E
options.text: No antibiotics until the causative organism is cultured

questions.correctAnswerText: IV ampicillin plus gentamicin, or an ampicillin-based regimen with a third-generation cephalosporin as indicated
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include IV ampicillin plus gentamicin as a first-line empirical option for infants under 3 months, with an ampicillin plus third-generation cephalosporin option also described. Empirical therapy must follow current local neonatal/young-infant meningitis guidance and local resistance patterns.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Topical therapy cannot treat CNS infection.
- B. Correct. This matches the age-based empirical options listed in the source.
- C. Incorrect. Oral amoxicillin alone is not adequate empirical treatment for suspected bacterial meningitis in a young infant.
- D. Incorrect. Oral azithromycin alone does not provide appropriate empirical coverage.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics must not be delayed while awaiting culture results.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Under 3 months: Common examples include IV ampicillin plus gentamicin or an ampicillin plus third-generation cephalosporin regimen.
- Treatment is IV, urgent and age/pathogen dependent.
- Exact drug choice and dosing must follow current local guidelines and renal function.
- Obtain cultures first if this can be done without delaying treatment.

questions.stem: Which complication is identified as the most common long-term sequela of childhood bacterial meningitis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sensorineural hearing loss
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include sensorineural hearing loss as the most common long-term sequela of meningitis, particularly following pneumococcal and Hib infection, due to inflammatory injury to cochlear hair cells.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the commonest long-term complication stated in the source.
- B. Incorrect. Cataract is a congenital ocular condition and not the common long-term meningitis complication.
- C. Incorrect. Myopia is not the characteristic major sequela of bacterial meningitis.
- D. Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome is not the commonest neurological sequela.
- E. Incorrect. Clubfoot is an orthopaedic deformity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hearing loss is the commonest long-term sequela highlighted.
- Other late effects: epilepsy, visual/speech disturbance, intellectual/learning disability and cerebral palsy.
- Early hearing assessment and developmental follow-up are important after meningitis.

questions.stem: A child with suspected tuberculous meningitis has CSF lymphocytosis, markedly raised protein and low glucose. Which CSF pattern is most consistent with standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Neutrophilic pleocytosis, low protein and high glucose

options.label: B
options.text: Normal white-cell count, normal protein and high glucose

options.label: C
options.text: Isolated red cells with normal protein

options.label: D
options.text: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein and low glucose

options.label: E
options.text: No white cells with very low protein

questions.correctAnswerText: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein and low glucose
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include TB meningitis as typically having high CSF white cells predominantly lymphocytes, high protein and low glucose. The appearance may be clear, turbid or viscous.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Neutrophilic pleocytosis is more characteristic of acute bacterial meningitis.
- B. Incorrect. Normal CSF findings do not support TB meningitis.
- C. Incorrect. Isolated red cells may reflect a traumatic tap or haemorrhage.
- D. Correct. This is the typical CSF pattern described for TB meningitis.
- E. Incorrect. TB meningitis usually produces an inflammatory CSF response and elevated protein.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TB meningitis: lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose.
- CSF appearance may be clear or turbid/viscous.
