- Consider TB in subacute presentation and relevant exposure/risk context.
- A negative initial test does not always exclude TB; specialist-directed microbiological testing may be needed.

questions.stem: Which feature is most typical of uncomplicated viral meningitis compared with bacterial meningitis?

options.label: A
options.text: CSF culture is positive for bacteria in most cases

options.label: B
options.text: CSF typically has a positive Gram stain

options.label: C
options.text: CSF usually has lymphocytic pleocytosis, with normal or mildly increased protein and usually normal glucose

options.label: D
options.text: CSF typically has very low glucose and predominantly neutrophils

questions.correctAnswerText: CSF usually has lymphocytic pleocytosis, with normal or mildly increased protein and usually normal glucose
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include viral meningitis as usually aseptic and self-limiting. CSF is typically clear with lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal or mildly raised protein and usually normal glucose, although some viruses may lower CSF glucose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bacterial culture is generally negative in viral meningitis.
- B. Incorrect. A positive Gram stain supports bacterial infection, not uncomplicated viral meningitis.
- C. Correct. This is the typical viral CSF pattern.
- D. Incorrect. Neutrophilic pleocytosis and low glucose are more typical of bacterial meningitis.
- E. Incorrect. Viral CSF is often clear.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral meningitis: usually clear CSF, lymphocytes, normal/mildly high protein and usually normal glucose.
- Enteroviruses are an important cause.
- Viral meningitis is often self-limiting, but clinical status and organism matter.
- Do not assume viral disease in a sick child until bacterial meningitis has been appropriately considered.

questions.stem: A child with bacterial meningitis deteriorates with shock, purpura, thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy. Which severe complication is classically associated with meningococcal sepsis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include DIC and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome among complications of bacterial meningitis/meningococcal sepsis. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome involves severe sepsis with adrenal haemorrhage and shock.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy.
- B. Incorrect. Crigler-Najjar is a bilirubin conjugation disorder.
- C. Correct. This is the classic association with fulminant meningococcal sepsis.
- D. Incorrect. West syndrome is an infantile epilepsy syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Sturge-Weber is a neurocutaneous syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Meningococcal sepsis may progress rapidly to septic shock.
- Petechial/purpuric rash, poor perfusion and hypotension are emergency signs.
- DIC and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome are life-threatening complications.
- Immediate resuscitation and IV antibiotics are essential.

questions.stem: A child with bacterial meningitis develops hyponatraemia due to syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). Which management principle is emphasized?

options.label: B
options.text: Careful fluid restriction with monitoring of fluid balance and electrolytes

options.label: C
options.text: Stop most monitoring once antibiotics are started

options.label: E
options.text: Give insulin to reduce sodium loss

questions.correctAnswerText: Careful fluid restriction with monitoring of fluid balance and electrolytes
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include SIADH as a complication of meningitis and recommends fluid restriction to reduce the risk of worsening hyponatraemia. Fluid management must be individualized to the child's perfusion and current pediatric meningitis protocol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Excess hypotonic fluid can worsen dilutional hyponatraemia.
- B. Correct. Fluid restriction and close monitoring are the principles described.
- C. Incorrect. Vital signs, fluid balance, electrolytes and neurological status require ongoing monitoring.
- D. Incorrect. Unrestricted water intake may worsen SIADH.
- E. Incorrect. Insulin has no role in treating SIADH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SIADH may complicate meningitis.
- Monitor sodium, fluid input/output, weight and neurological status.
- Avoid excessive free water; follow a careful fluid plan.
- Fluid restriction must not compromise resuscitation in a child with shock.

cases.title: A previously healthy child develops fever and a rapidly spreading purpuric rash
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child develops sudden high fever, irritability and a toxic appearance. Within hours, widespread petechiae and purpura appear. Capillary refill is delayed, the pulse is rapid and blood pressure is falling.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern is most concerning for meningococcal septicaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Recurrent brief staring spells with immediate recovery

options.label: B
options.text: High fever, toxic appearance, petechial/purpuric rash and rapidly developing shock

options.label: C
options.text: Chronic headache with no fever and normal examination

options.label: D
options.text: Isolated chronic limb weakness without systemic symptoms

options.label: E
options.text: Mild fever, isolated rhinorrhoea and normal perfusion

questions.correctAnswerText: High fever, toxic appearance, petechial/purpuric rash and rapidly developing shock
questions.initialExplanation: Meningococcal septicaemia may present with high-grade fever, irritability, a very toxic appearance and a rapidly progressive petechial/purpuric rash. Shock may develop within hours, with poor perfusion, delayed capillary refill, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion or coma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are more consistent with absence seizures.
- B. Correct. This is the classic emergency presentation described.
- C. Incorrect. This is not an acute septic presentation.
- D. Incorrect. Chronic isolated weakness does not fit acute meningococcal sepsis.
- E. Incorrect. A mild upper respiratory infection with normal perfusion does not suggest meningococcal sepsis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Meningococcal disease can cause meningitis, rapidly progressive sepsis or both.
- Look for petechial/purpuric rash, toxic appearance and shock.
- Deterioration can occur within hours even in a previously healthy child.
- Treat immediately; do not wait for rash progression or confirmatory tests.

questions.stem: A febrile child has a widespread non-blanching purpuric rash and signs of shock. What is the immediate management priority?

options.label: C
options.text: ABC resuscitation, urgent IV/IO access and immediate empirical parenteral third-generation cephalosporin, with ICU-level support as required

options.label: D
options.text: Wait for lumbar puncture and culture confirmation before giving antibiotics

options.label: E
options.text: Give antipyretic and reassess the next day

questions.correctAnswerText: ABC resuscitation, urgent IV/IO access and immediate empirical parenteral third-generation cephalosporin, with ICU-level support as required
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is immediate ABC management, urgent empirical antibiotics (e.g. IV ceftriaxone), ICU management when required, isolation/notification and prophylaxis for contacts. Prehospital parenteral antibiotics may be given according to emergency protocols when transfer is urgent.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. EEG does not treat sepsis and must not delay resuscitation.
- B. Incorrect. Oral treatment is inadequate for septic shock.
- C. Correct. Prompt resuscitation and antibiotics are essential in suspected meningococcal sepsis.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics must not be delayed for LP or culture confirmation in an unstable child.
- E. Incorrect. Antipyretic alone is dangerously inadequate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Suspected meningococcal sepsis: immediate ABC and senior/critical-care help.
- Give urgent parenteral empirical antibiotics.
- Manage shock and organ dysfunction in an appropriate resuscitation/PICU setting.
- Isolate, notify public health/infection-control teams and arrange contact prophylaxis according to guidance.
- Do not delay treatment for LP, imaging or microbiology.

questions.stem: Which contact-management measure is described after meningococcal meningitis or invasive Hib infection?

options.label: A
options.text: Give close contacts prophylaxis (e.g., rifampicin or ciprofloxacin) to eradicate carriage, following public-health guidance

options.label: B
options.text: Routine lumbar puncture for most contacts

options.label: D
options.text: No action is needed for household contacts

options.label: E
options.text: Long-term antiseizure medication for close contacts

questions.correctAnswerText: Give close contacts prophylaxis (e.g., rifampicin or ciprofloxacin) to eradicate carriage, following public-health guidance
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include rifampicin or ciprofloxacin prophylaxis for household contacts of meningococcal meningitis and Hib infection to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage. The exact agent and eligibility should follow current local public-health guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the contact-prophylaxis principle described.
- B. Incorrect. Routine LP is not indicated for asymptomatic contacts.
- C. Incorrect. Corticosteroids are not contact prophylaxis.
- D. Incorrect. Close contacts may require chemoprophylaxis and public-health assessment.
- E. Incorrect. Antiseizure medication is not used for contacts without seizures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Close contacts of meningococcal disease require urgent public-health assessment for chemoprophylaxis.
- standard guidance also includes Hib contacts.
- Vaccination is an important preventive measure (Hib, meningococcal and pneumococcal vaccines).
- Follow current public-health guidance for agent, dose, timing and eligibility.

cases.title: A child develops fever, behavioural change and seizures
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child has an insidious onset of fever, headache, vomiting and cough. Over the next two days, the child becomes unusually sleepy, irritable and confused, then develops a focal seizure and right-sided weakness. CT/MRI suggests temporal lobe involvement.

questions.stem: What is the definition of encephalitis?

options.label: C
options.text: Accumulation of CSF within the ventricles

options.label: E
options.text: Degeneration of the peripheral motor nerves

questions.correctAnswerText: Inflammation of the brain parenchyma
questions.initialExplanation: Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma. It may result from direct viral invasion of the brain or from a postinfectious immune-mediated response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Inflammation of the meninges is meningitis.
- B. Correct. This is the definition given.
- C. Incorrect. This describes hydrocephalus.
- D. Incorrect. Neuromuscular junction disease includes myasthenia gravis.
- E. Incorrect. Peripheral nerve inflammation is a neuropathy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Encephalitis = inflammation of brain parenchyma.
- Direct viral invasion (e.g. HSV) is one mechanism.
- Postinfectious immune-mediated encephalopathy may occur several days after an extracranial infection, e.g. varicella.
- Altered behaviour/consciousness, seizures and focal neurological deficits should raise suspicion.

questions.stem: Which group contains the common viral causes of childhood encephalitis listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Enteroviruses, respiratory viruses, arboviruses and herpesviruses

questions.correctAnswerText: Enteroviruses, respiratory viruses, arboviruses and herpesviruses
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include enteroviruses as common viral causes, in addition to respiratory viruses (including influenza), arboviruses and herpesviruses such as HSV, VZV and HHV-6. Some bacterial causes include Mycoplasma, Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella henselae and rickettsial organisms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the viral groups included in the source.
- B. Incorrect. These are not common causes of childhood encephalitis.
- C. Incorrect. These viruses are primarily associated with gastroenteritis, not the main list of encephalitis pathogens.
- D. Incorrect. Fungal encephalitis is uncommon and generally occurs in selected immunocompromised patients.
- E. Incorrect. Hepatitis viruses are not the common encephalitis group listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common viral agents: enteroviruses, respiratory viruses, arboviruses, HSV, VZV and HHV-6.
- Bacterial causes are less common and include Mycoplasma, Lyme disease, cat-scratch disease and rickettsial infections.
- Pathogen distribution depends on geography, season, exposure and immune status.

questions.stem: A child has suspected encephalitis. HSV is uncommon but carries a high risk of severe neurological sequelae if untreated. What is the most appropriate initial specific treatment approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Wait for HSV PCR to become positive before starting treatment

options.label: B
options.text: Treat with antituberculous therapy in each case

options.label: D
options.text: Withhold antiviral treatment unless a vesicular rash is present

options.label: E
options.text: Start high-dose IV acyclovir empirically while investigations for HSV are proceeding

questions.correctAnswerText: Start high-dose IV acyclovir empirically while investigations for HSV are proceeding
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is that all children with encephalitis should initially receive high-dose IV acyclovir until HSV encephalitis has been ruled out, because early treatment is important and delay may lead to devastating outcomes. A rash is not required for HSV encephalitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Waiting for PCR may delay time-critical treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Antituberculous treatment is only indicated when TB is suspected.
- C. Incorrect. Suspected encephalitis requires IV treatment and hospital-level monitoring.
- D. Incorrect. HSV encephalitis can occur without mucocutaneous vesicles.
- E. Correct. Prompt empiric IV acyclovir is recommended when encephalitis is suspected.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HSV encephalitis is uncommon but potentially devastating.
- Start IV acyclovir empirically in suspected encephalitis; do not wait for PCR.
- Clinical guidance notes a high risk of long-term morbidity if HSV encephalitis is untreated.
- Continue or stop treatment according to specialist review and virological results.

questions.stem: Which CSF pattern is most consistent with viral encephalitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Predominantly red cells with no white cells in each case

options.label: B
options.text: No cells, no protein and absent glucose

options.label: C
options.text: Turbid CSF with marked neutrophilia, very high protein and very low glucose in each case

options.label: D
options.text: Clear CSF with lymphocytosis, normal or raised protein and usually normal glucose

questions.correctAnswerText: Clear CSF with lymphocytosis, normal or raised protein and usually normal glucose
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include CSF in encephalitis as often clear, with lymphocytosis, normal or mildly elevated protein and normal glucose. The CBC may be normal and CRP is not necessarily diagnostic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Red cells may occur in HSV encephalitis but are not required and do not define the typical CSF pattern.
- B. Incorrect. This is not an inflammatory CSF profile.
- C. Incorrect. This is more suggestive of bacterial meningitis.
- D. Correct. This is the typical CSF pattern stated in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Eosinophilic CSF suggests selected parasitic/fungal or other uncommon causes, not typical viral encephalitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Encephalitis CSF: usually clear, lymphocytic, normal/mildly high protein, normal glucose.
- HSV PCR and other pathogen-specific PCR/serology are important diagnostic tests.
- EEG may show abnormalities and help detect subclinical seizures.
- A normal early test does not necessarily exclude encephalitis if clinical suspicion remains high.

questions.stem: A child has fever, altered behaviour, seizures and a focal deficit. MRI shows abnormalities in the temporal lobes, and HSV encephalitis is suspected. Which treatment duration is described?

options.label: A
options.text: No antiviral treatment if the CSF glucose is normal

options.label: B
options.text: A single oral dose of acyclovir

options.label: E
options.text: Lifelong acyclovir prophylaxis in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: IV acyclovir for 3 weeks
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include IV acyclovir as the drug of choice for HSV encephalitis and lists a 3-week course. Supportive management includes PICU admission when required, seizure control, fluid management and monitoring.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Normal CSF glucose does not exclude HSV encephalitis.
- B. Incorrect. Oral treatment is inadequate for acute HSV encephalitis.
- C. Correct. This is the duration given.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics alone do not treat HSV encephalitis, and the duration is not 24 hours.
- E. Incorrect. Lifelong prophylaxis is not the routine treatment described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HSV encephalitis: IV acyclovir is the specific treatment listed.
- standard guidance gives a 3-week course; confirm current duration with infectious disease/neurology guidance and virological follow-up.
- Supportive care: PICU if severe, seizure treatment, hydration/fluid restriction when SIADH is present, and monitoring of ICP.
- Long-term follow-up for cognition, behaviour, focal deficits and epilepsy may be needed.

cases.title: A newborn has a lumbosacral swelling with exposed neural tissue
cases.vignette: A newborn is delivered with a lumbosacral sac protruding through a vertebral defect. The sac contains meninges and spinal cord tissue. The infant has weak lower-limb movement, reduced sensation and urinary dribbling. The team evaluates for associated hydrocephalus and Chiari II malformation.

questions.stem: During which period does normal neural tube closure occur?

options.label: C
options.text: During the first year of life

options.label: E
options.text: During the first 28 days after conception

questions.correctAnswerText: During the first 28 days after conception
questions.initialExplanation: Neural tube defects result from failure of normal fusion of the neural plate to form the neural tube during the first 28 days after conception. The cephalic and caudal neuropores close during early embryogenesis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Neural tube closure occurs very early in embryogenesis.
- B. Incorrect. This is well after the normal neural tube closure period.
- C. Incorrect. Neural tube closure is not a postnatal process.
- D. Incorrect. Closure must occur during embryonic development, not after birth.
- E. Correct. Neural tube formation is completed by approximately the fourth week after conception.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neural tube defects result from failure of neural tube closure in the first 28 days after conception.
- The cephalic end forms the brain; the caudal end forms the spinal cord.
- Early folic acid supplementation is important because closure occurs before many pregnancies are recognized.

questions.stem: Which maternal factor is a recognized risk factor for neural tube defects?

options.label: E
options.text: Adequate folic acid intake before conception

questions.correctAnswerText: Folic acid deficiency
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include folic acid deficiency, maternal diabetes, maternal anticonvulsant use, smoking and obesity as risk factors. Genetic and environmental contributions are multifactorial.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron supplementation is not a recognized NTD risk factor.
- B. Incorrect. Normal maternal BMI alone is not the risk factor described.
- C. Correct. Folic acid deficiency is a major preventable risk factor.
- D. Incorrect. Vaccination before pregnancy protects against rubella and is not a neural tube defect risk.
- E. Incorrect. Adequate folic acid reduces risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NTD risks: folate deficiency, maternal diabetes, anticonvulsants, smoking and obesity.
- Recurrence risk increases after a previously affected pregnancy.
- Folic acid should be started before conception and continued through early pregnancy.
- Women taking antiseizure medication should receive preconception counselling and an individualized folate plan.

questions.stem: A fetus is diagnosed antenatally with absence of most of the cranium and brain. The condition is usually lethal, with stillbirth or death shortly after birth. What is the diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Anencephaly
questions.initialExplanation: Anencephaly is failure of development of most of the cranium and brain. It is often detected on antenatal ultrasound and is incompatible with prolonged survival.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Encephalocele is herniation of meninges and/or brain tissue through a skull defect.
- B. Incorrect. Meningocele is protrusion of meninges through a vertebral defect, with the spinal cord usually remaining in place.
- C. Correct. This describes anencephaly.
- D. Incorrect. Myelomeningocele involves protrusion of meninges and spinal cord through a vertebral defect.
- E. Incorrect. Spina bifida occulta is a vertebral arch defect without protrusion of meninges or spinal cord.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Anencephaly: absence of most of the cranium and brain.
- Usually detected by antenatal ultrasound.
- Often results in stillbirth or death shortly after birth.
- Prevention includes preconception folic acid.

questions.stem: A newborn has a midline occipital sac containing herniated brain tissue through a skull defect. Which neural tube defect is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Encephalocele
questions.initialExplanation: Encephalocele is herniation of a sac containing meninges and sometimes brain tissue through a midline skull defect. Most cases are occipital and may be associated with other brain malformations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Meningocele is a spinal defect with protrusion of meninges, not a cranial encephalocele.
- B. Correct. The occipital cranial sac containing brain tissue is characteristic.
- C. Incorrect. Hydrocephalus is ventricular enlargement due to excess CSF.
- D. Incorrect. Spina bifida occulta is a closed vertebral arch defect without neural tissue protrusion.
- E. Incorrect. Anencephaly involves absence of most of the brain and skull.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Encephalocele: cranial midline defect with herniation of meninges ± brain.
- Most are occipital.
- Associated brain malformations are common.
- Assess for hydrocephalus and neurological deficits.

questions.stem: A child has a small midline lumbosacral skin dimple with a tuft of hair. The child is neurologically normal, and an X-ray incidentally shows a defect in the posterior vertebral arch without protrusion of meninges. What is the diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Spina bifida occulta
questions.initialExplanation: Spina bifida occulta is failure of fusion of the vertebral laminae without protrusion of meninges or spinal cord. It is often asymptomatic and may be associated with overlying skin markers such as a tuft of hair, lipoma, nevus, dermal sinus or haemangioma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The vertebral arch defect without neural tissue protrusion is typical.
- B. Incorrect. Meningocele causes a cystic swelling containing meninges protruding through the defect.
- C. Incorrect. Encephalocele is a cranial skull defect, commonly occipital.
- D. Incorrect. Myelomeningocele involves protrusion of meninges and spinal cord.
- E. Incorrect. Anencephaly involves failure of cranial development.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Spina bifida occulta: vertebral arch defect with no meningeal protrusion.
- Usually lumbar/lumbosacral, with no neurological deficit at birth.
- Skin markers include hair tuft, lipoma, nevus, dermal sinus and haemangioma.
- Tethered cord/diastematomyelia may cause later neurological or bladder/bowel problems; MRI is useful when indicated.

questions.stem: A newborn has a cystic lumbosacral swelling containing meninges, but the spinal cord remains in its normal position. Neurological function is largely preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Meningocele
questions.initialExplanation: Meningocele is protrusion of meninges through a defect in the vertebral arch, producing a cystic swelling. The spinal cord is usually normal and the prognosis is generally good after surgical repair.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Anencephaly is absence of most cranial structures.
- B. Correct. A meningeal sac with normal cord is a meningocele.
- C. Incorrect. Encephalocele is a cranial defect.
- D. Incorrect. Myelomeningocele contains both meninges and spinal cord tissue.
- E. Incorrect. Occulta has no protruding meningeal sac.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Meningocele: meninges protrude; spinal cord usually remains normal.
- Myelomeningocele: meninges + spinal cord protrude.
- Meningocele generally has a better neurological prognosis than myelomeningocele.
- Early neurosurgical assessment and repair are important.

questions.stem: A newborn with myelomeningocele has lower-limb weakness, sensory loss, urinary dribbling and a palpable bladder. Which mechanism explains the urinary and bowel symptoms?

options.label: C
options.text: Denervation causing a neuropathic bladder and bowel

options.label: D
options.text: Excessive acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction

questions.correctAnswerText: Denervation causing a neuropathic bladder and bowel
questions.initialExplanation: Myelomeningocele may damage spinal nerve pathways, producing a neuropathic bladder (poor emptying, retention, dribbling, recurrent UTI/VUR/CKD) and neuropathic bowel (incontinence or patulous anus).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Visual pathway damage is unrelated to sacral autonomic dysfunction.
- B. Incorrect. Excess CSF may cause hydrocephalus but does not directly explain neurogenic bladder.
- C. Correct. Spinal cord/nerve dysfunction leads to denervation of bladder and bowel.
- D. Incorrect. Neuromuscular junction excess acetylcholine is not the mechanism.
- E. Incorrect. Primary renal disease does not explain the associated lower-limb weakness and sensory loss.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Myelomeningocele: motor weakness, sensory loss, neuropathic bladder and bowel.
- Bladder denervation → retention/dribbling, palpable bladder, recurrent UTI, VUR and possible CKD.
- Bowel denervation → constipation/incontinence and patulous anus.
- Long-term urology/nephrology follow-up is required.

questions.stem: A newborn with lumbosacral myelomeningocele develops hydrocephalus. Which associated congenital brain malformation is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Arnold-Chiari type II malformation
questions.initialExplanation: Myelomeningocele is strongly associated with Arnold-Chiari type II malformation, in which cerebellar and brainstem structures are displaced downward through the foramen magnum. This may disrupt CSF flow and lead to hydrocephalus; many affected infants require a VP shunt.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Holoprosencephaly is a forebrain cleavage disorder.
- B. Incorrect. Lissencephaly causes abnormal cortical gyration and developmental impairment.
- C. Correct. Chiari II is the classic association with myelomeningocele.
- D. Incorrect. Dandy-Walker is a different posterior fossa malformation associated with hydrocephalus but is not the classic association here.
- E. Incorrect. Joubert syndrome is a distinct cerebellar/brainstem developmental disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Myelomeningocele ↔ Arnold-Chiari II malformation.
- Chiari II can obstruct CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus.
- It is recognized that approximately 80% of affected infants may require a VP shunt.
- Examine lower-limb motor/sensory function and monitor head circumference/fontanelle.

questions.stem: When should the myelomeningocele lesion generally be repaired?

options.label: E
options.text: Soon after birth, with a multidisciplinary team

questions.correctAnswerText: Soon after birth, with a multidisciplinary team
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes repair soon after birth. Care requires a multidisciplinary team including neurosurgery, physiotherapy, urology, nephrology and orthopaedics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Repair of the spinal lesion is required regardless of whether hydrocephalus is present.
- B. Incorrect. Surgical closure is indicated for open myelomeningocele.
- C. Incorrect. Repair is performed in the neonatal period, not deferred until puberty.
- D. Incorrect. Delaying repair until walking increases risks of infection and tissue injury.
- E. Correct. Early surgical assessment and repair are standard management principles.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Protect the lesion and arrange urgent neurosurgical repair soon after birth.
- Multidisciplinary care: neurosurgery, physiotherapy, urology, nephrology and orthopaedics.
- Monitor for hydrocephalus/Chiari II, bladder/bowel dysfunction and lower-limb deformities.
- Long-term rehabilitation and continence/renal care are essential.

questions.stem: What folic acid supplementation is stated for prevention of neural tube defects?

options.label: A
options.text: High-risk females: no folic acid is required

options.label: B
options.text: females: 4 mg once after a positive pregnancy test

options.label: C
options.text: females: 10 mg daily during the third trimester

options.label: D
options.text: females: 0.4 mg daily; high-risk females with a previously affected pregnancy: 4 mg daily, started before conception

options.label: E
options.text: Folic acid is useful after neural tube closure

questions.correctAnswerText: females: 0.4 mg daily; high-risk females with a previously affected pregnancy: 4 mg daily, started before conception
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes 0.4 mg folic acid daily for all females and 4 mg daily for high-risk females with a previously affected child. Supplementation should begin one month before planned conception because neural tube closure occurs very early.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. High-risk women require specific preconception counselling and higher-dose folate under medical guidance.
- B. Incorrect. Starting only after a positive test may be too late because neural tube closure occurs in the first 28 days after conception.
- C. Incorrect. The dose and timing do not match standard guidance.
- D. Correct. This matches the dose and timing stated in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Folic acid must be present before and during early neural tube closure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Start folic acid before conception (standard guidance: at least one month before planned conception).
- standard guidance regimen: 0.4 mg/day for all; 4 mg/day for high-risk women with a previously affected child.
- Neural tube closure is completed during the first 28 days after conception.
- Women using antiseizure medications should have preconception review; do not stop medication abruptly.

cases.title: An infant has progressive head enlargement and a bulging fontanelle
cases.vignette: A 4-month-old infant is brought because the head has increased disproportionately in size. Examination reveals widely separated sutures, a bulging anterior fontanelle and visible scalp veins. The infant has a fixed downward gaze.

questions.stem: What is the definition of hydrocephalus?

options.label: A
options.text: Enlargement of cerebral ventricles due to excessive accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid

options.label: B
options.text: Absence of most of the cerebral hemispheres

options.label: E
options.text: Loss of cerebral white matter due to hypoxia

questions.correctAnswerText: Enlargement of cerebral ventricles due to excessive accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid
questions.initialExplanation: Hydrocephalus is enlargement of the cerebral ventricles caused by excessive CSF accumulation. It may result from increased CSF production, impaired absorption or obstruction within the ventricular system.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the definition.
- B. Incorrect. This describes a severe congenital brain malformation, not hydrocephalus.
- C. Incorrect. This is encephalitis.
- D. Incorrect. This describes craniosynostosis.
- E. Incorrect. This describes a form of acquired brain injury.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hydrocephalus = ventricular enlargement due to excess CSF.
- Mechanisms: increased production, reduced absorption or obstruction.
- In infants, open sutures/fontanelles allow head enlargement.
- In older children, raised ICP symptoms predominate because the skull is less expandable.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the normal CSF pathway from the lateral ventricles to the subarachnoid space?

options.label: A
options.text: Fourth ventricle → aqueduct of Sylvius → lateral ventricles → arachnoid villi

options.label: B
options.text: Subarachnoid space → foramen of Monro → fourth ventricle → cerebral cortex

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral ventricles → central canal → pituitary gland → subarachnoid space

options.label: D
options.text: Cerebellum → foramen magnum → choroid plexus → lateral ventricles

options.label: E
options.text: Foramen of Monro → third ventricle → aqueduct of Sylvius → fourth ventricle → foramina of Magendie and Luschka → subarachnoid space

questions.correctAnswerText: Foramen of Monro → third ventricle → aqueduct of Sylvius → fourth ventricle → foramina of Magendie and Luschka → subarachnoid space
questions.initialExplanation: CSF passes from the lateral ventricles through the foramina of Monro into the third ventricle, then through the aqueduct of Sylvius to the fourth ventricle. It exits through the median foramen of Magendie and lateral foramina of Luschka into the subarachnoid space and is reabsorbed through arachnoid villi.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The direction of flow is reversed and omits the third ventricle.
- B. Incorrect. CSF is produced in the ventricles and flows outward to the subarachnoid space, not in this direction.
- C. Incorrect. The pituitary gland is not part of CSF circulation.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the normal ventricular pathway.
- E. Correct. This is the normal CSF pathway.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → third ventricle → aqueduct of Sylvius → fourth ventricle.
- Exit via foramen of Magendie (median) and foramina of Luschka (lateral).
- CSF circulates in the subarachnoid space and is reabsorbed through arachnoid villi.
- Aqueductal stenosis is a classic cause of non-communicating hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: A child has obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus due to congenital aqueductal stenosis. Which mechanism is responsible?

options.label: A
options.text: Primary loss of spinal motor neurons

options.label: B
options.text: Excessive absorption of CSF through arachnoid villi

options.label: C
options.text: Increased venous return from the heart

options.label: D
options.text: Obstruction to CSF flow within the ventricular system

questions.correctAnswerText: Obstruction to CSF flow within the ventricular system
questions.initialExplanation: Non-communicating hydrocephalus results from obstruction within the ventricular system, preventing normal CSF flow. Congenital causes listed include aqueductal stenosis, Dandy-Walker malformation, atresia of the foramina of Luschka/Magendie and Chiari II malformation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Motor neuron loss causes weakness/hypotonia, not ventricular enlargement.
- B. Incorrect. Increased absorption would reduce CSF accumulation.
- C. Incorrect. Venous return is not the mechanism of obstructive hydrocephalus.
- D. Correct. Aqueductal stenosis obstructs CSF flow between the third and fourth ventricles.
- E. Incorrect. Reduced production does not cause hydrocephalus.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Non-communicating = obstruction inside ventricular system.
- Causes: aqueduct stenosis, Dandy-Walker, atresia of Magendie/Luschka and Chiari II.
- Acquired causes include post-meningitis, post-intraventricular haemorrhage and posterior fossa tumours.
- Congenital infection such as toxoplasmosis may be associated with hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: A premature infant develops progressive ventricular dilatation after an intraventricular haemorrhage. Which mechanism most likely explains this hydrocephalus?

options.label: D
options.text: Excess acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction

questions.correctAnswerText: Impaired CSF absorption following haemorrhage
questions.initialExplanation: Post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus may occur in premature infants after intraventricular haemorrhage. Blood products can impair CSF circulation and absorption, resulting in ventricular enlargement. Meningitis can also impair CSF absorption.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Haemorrhage can interfere with CSF pathways and reabsorption.
- B. Incorrect. Craniosynostosis is a different cranial abnormality.
- C. Incorrect. Reduced production does not cause ventricular enlargement.
- D. Incorrect. This mechanism is unrelated to CSF circulation.
- E. Incorrect. Increased absorption would not cause CSF accumulation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Communicating hydrocephalus often results from impaired CSF reabsorption.
- Causes include subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis and dural sinus thrombosis.
- Post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus is important in preterm infants.
- Follow ventricular size, head circumference and clinical signs.

questions.stem: Which feature is an important early clinical sign of hydrocephalus in an infant?

options.label: A
options.text: Disproportionately large head with widely separated sutures and bulging fontanelle

options.label: E
options.text: Small head circumference with early fontanelle closure

questions.correctAnswerText: Disproportionately large head with widely separated sutures and bulging fontanelle
questions.initialExplanation: In infants, hydrocephalus may present with disproportionate head enlargement, widely open/bulging fontanelles, widely separated sutures and visible dilated scalp veins. A fixed downward gaze ("sunsetting eyes") is an advanced sign.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are typical signs in an infant with an open skull.
- B. Incorrect. Claw hand may occur in lower brachial plexus or peripheral nerve disorders.
- C. Incorrect. This suggests a peripheral facial nerve lesion.
- D. Incorrect. Loss of reflexes suggests a lower motor neuron/peripheral problem.
- E. Incorrect. Microcephaly and early suture closure are not the typical presentation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infant: rapidly increasing OFC, bulging fontanelle, separated sutures, visible veins.
- Advanced sign: fixed downward gaze/sunset eyes.
- Measure OFC serially and plot on a centile chart.
- Examine the spine and lower-limb motor function for associated neural tube defects.

questions.stem: An older child with hydrocephalus develops frontal headache, projectile vomiting and photophobia. Which additional examination finding may support raised intracranial pressure?
questions.correctAnswerText: Papilloedema or Macewen's cracked-pot sign
questions.initialExplanation: In an older child, hydrocephalus may produce symptoms of raised ICP such as frontal headache, projectile vomiting and photophobia. Signs may include an enlarged head, dilated scalp veins, sunset eyes, delayed fontanelle closure, Macewen's sign, craniotabes, an orbital bruit or papilloedema.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Asymmetric Moro suggests focal birth injury or neurological deficit.
- B. Incorrect. Gower sign suggests proximal muscle weakness, classically Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- C. Incorrect. Trousseau sign suggests hypocalcaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Ortolani assesses hip stability.
- E. Correct. Papilloedema and Macewen's sign may support raised ICP.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Older child: headache, projectile vomiting and photophobia.
- Signs: papilloedema, sunset eyes, large head, dilated veins and Macewen's sign.
- Craniotabes may be detected on skull palpation.
- Evaluate for posterior fossa tumour and other causes of raised ICP.

questions.stem: Which investigation is commonly used to assess ventricular dilatation in an infant with an open fontanelle?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cranial ultrasound
questions.initialExplanation: Cranial ultrasound can assess ventricular size in neonates and infants while the fontanelle is open. CT/MRI provide more detailed assessment of ventricular size, brain tissue and the underlying cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. EEG assesses electrical brain activity, not ventricular size.
- B. Incorrect. Hip ultrasound is used for developmental dysplasia of the hip.
- C. Incorrect. Chest radiography does not assess the brain.
- D. Correct. It is a useful non-invasive bedside test in infants.
- E. Incorrect. Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerves.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Antenatal ultrasound can detect congenital hydrocephalus.
- Neonate/infant: cranial ultrasound through the open fontanelle.
- CT or MRI assesses ventricular dilatation, degree of cortical atrophy and cause.
- Monitor OFC serially on a centile chart; consider karyotype/TORCH tests when indicated.

questions.stem: A child with symptomatic progressive hydrocephalus requires definitive treatment. Which procedure is described as the mainstay?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt insertion
questions.initialExplanation: The mainstay of treatment described is surgical diversion of CSF using a VP shunt. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy and external ventricular drainage are other options in selected cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Carotid endarterectomy treats selected carotid artery disease.
- B. Incorrect. Tonsillectomy has no role in hydrocephalus treatment.
- C. Incorrect. Lumbar sympathectomy does not treat hydrocephalus.
- D. Incorrect. Spinal fusion treats selected spinal deformities.
- E. Correct. A VP shunt diverts CSF from the ventricles to the peritoneal cavity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- VP shunt is the main surgical treatment described.
- Alternatives: endoscopic third ventriculostomy or external ventricular drainage in selected patients.
- Treatment aims to reduce ventricular pressure and prevent ongoing brain injury.
- Follow-up must assess head growth, neurological development and shunt function.

questions.stem: A child with a VP shunt develops fever, irritability and worsening vomiting. Which complication must be considered?

options.label: A
options.text: Shunt infection, commonly involving Staphylococcus epidermidis

questions.correctAnswerText: Shunt infection, commonly involving Staphylococcus epidermidis
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include infection, commonly with Staphylococcus epidermidis, as a VP shunt complication. Fever and worsening symptoms of raised ICP may indicate shunt infection or malfunction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Shunt infection is a serious complication and must be investigated promptly.
- B. Incorrect. Spasmus nutans causes nystagmus, head tilt and head nodding.
- C. Incorrect. Migraine does not explain fever in a child with a VP shunt.
- D. Incorrect. DMD causes progressive proximal muscle weakness.
- E. Incorrect. JME causes morning myoclonic jerks in adolescents.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- VP shunt complications: infection (often coagulase-negative staphylococci), obstruction/malfunction and shunt nephritis.
- Symptoms of shunt failure: vomiting, headache, irritability, lethargy, bulging fontanelle or rising OFC.
- Fever and neurological deterioration in a shunted child require urgent assessment.
- Neurosurgical review is required.

questions.stem: A child with long-standing VP shunt infection develops haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension and low complement. Which complication is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Shunt nephritis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include shunt nephritis as an uncommon immune-complex-mediated nephritis following prolonged infection with Staphylococcus epidermidis in a child with a VP shunt. It may present with haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension and low complement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Minimal change disease typically causes nephrotic-range proteinuria and oedema rather than low complement/haematuria as the key association.
- B. Incorrect. Post-streptococcal GN follows streptococcal infection and is not specifically associated with VP shunts.
- C. Incorrect. RTA causes acid-base and electrolyte abnormalities.
- D. Incorrect. Renal vein thrombosis causes renal impairment/haematuria but is not linked to chronic VP shunt infection in this way.
- E. Correct. This is the classic complication described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Shunt nephritis: immune-complex renal disease associated with chronic VP shunt infection.
- Organism listed: Staphylococcus epidermidis.
- Features: haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension and low complement.
- Requires coordinated neurosurgical, infectious disease and nephrology management.

topics.name: Upper and Lower Motor Neuron Lesions

cases.title: A child has increased tone, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child is examined after a previous cerebral insult. The child has increased tone in the lower limbs, brisk deep tendon reflexes, ankle clonus and an extensor plantar response. There is no prominent muscle wasting or fasciculation.

questions.stem: Which finding is most characteristic of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal tone with isolated sensory loss

options.label: B
options.text: Spasticity with hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign

options.label: C
options.text: Fatigable weakness that worsens through the day

options.label: D
options.text: Marked muscle wasting with absent reflexes

options.label: E
options.text: Hypotonia with areflexia and prominent fasciculations

questions.correctAnswerText: Spasticity with hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign
questions.initialExplanation: A UMN lesion occurs above the anterior horn cell or cranial nerve motor nucleus. It typically produces increased tone (spasticity), exaggerated reflexes, clonus and an extensor plantar response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Isolated sensory loss does not define a UMN lesion.
- B. Correct. These are classic UMN signs.
- C. Incorrect. Fatigability suggests neuromuscular junction disease such as myasthenia gravis.
- D. Incorrect. Marked atrophy and reduced reflexes are more typical of LMN lesions.
- E. Incorrect. Hypotonia, areflexia and fasciculations suggest LMN/anterior horn cell disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- UMN lesion: lesion above anterior horn cell/cranial motor nucleus.
- Tone: increased (spasticity or rigidity).
- Deep tendon reflexes: exaggerated; clonus may be present.
- Babinski: positive/extensor plantar response.
- Causes listed: cerebral palsy, stroke/ICH, neurodegenerative disease and brain tumour.

questions.stem: A child has marked hypotonia, reduced deep tendon reflexes, muscle atrophy and fasciculations. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Lower motor neuron lesion
questions.initialExplanation: A LMN lesion involves the anterior horn cell, motor nerve fibre or neuromuscular junction. It produces hypotonia, hyporeflexia/areflexia, muscle wasting and sometimes fasciculations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The combination of hypotonia, atrophy, fasciculations and reduced reflexes indicates LMN involvement.
- B. Incorrect. UMN lesions typically produce increased tone, brisk reflexes and extensor plantar response.
- C. Incorrect. Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia, dysmetria and intention tremor.
- D. Incorrect. Basal ganglia lesions cause extrapyramidal movement abnormalities.
- E. Incorrect. Occipital lesions primarily affect visual pathways.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LMN lesion: anterior horn cell, motor nerve, or neuromuscular junction.
- Tone: reduced/hypotonia.
- Reflexes: reduced or absent.
- Atrophy and fasciculations may occur.
- Causes listed: SMA, GBS, myasthenia gravis and muscular dystrophy/myopathy.

questions.stem: During neurological examination, a child actively moves the limb against gravity but cannot overcome any additional resistance. What is the muscle power grade?
questions.correctAnswerText: Grade 3
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance grades muscle power from 0 to 5. Grade 3 is active movement against gravity but not against added resistance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Grade 4 is movement against gravity and partial resistance.
- B. Incorrect. Grade 1 is visible muscle contraction without limb movement.
- C. Correct. Grade 3 is movement against gravity only.
- D. Incorrect. Grade 2 is active movement with gravity eliminated, but not against gravity.
- E. Incorrect. Grade 5 is normal power against full resistance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 0: no visible contraction.
- 1: visible contraction, no movement.
- 2: movement with gravity eliminated.
- 3: movement against gravity.
- 4: movement against gravity and partial resistance.
- 5: normal power against full resistance.

questions.stem: Which combination best differentiates UMN from LMN lesions on examination?

options.label: A
options.text: Both typically produce identical tone and reflex changes

options.label: B
options.text: UMN: marked early atrophy; LMN: no muscle wasting

options.label: C
options.text: UMN: hypotonia and fasciculations; LMN: spasticity and clonus

options.label: D
options.text: UMN: hypertonia, hyperreflexia and positive Babinski; LMN: hypotonia, hyporeflexia and negative Babinski

options.label: E
options.text: UMN: absent reflexes; LMN: exaggerated reflexes

questions.correctAnswerText: UMN: hypertonia, hyperreflexia and positive Babinski; LMN: hypotonia, hyporeflexia and negative Babinski
questions.initialExplanation: The main examination difference is tone and reflex response: UMN lesions typically cause spasticity and hyperreflexia with an extensor plantar response, whereas LMN lesions cause hypotonia, reduced/absent reflexes and a flexor/negative plantar response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Tone and reflex findings help localize the lesion.
- B. Incorrect. Early prominent atrophy is more typical of LMN injury; disuse atrophy may occur in chronic UMN lesions.
- C. Incorrect. These features are reversed.
- D. Correct. This is the central distinction.
- E. Incorrect. Reflex changes are reversed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- UMN: increased tone, brisk reflexes, Babinski positive, possible clonus.
- LMN: reduced tone, reduced/absent reflexes, Babinski negative, atrophy/fasciculations.
- Localize the lesion using power, tone, reflexes, plantar response and distribution of weakness.
- A child may have mixed signs in complex neurological disease.

cases.title: A toddler has delayed motor milestones and persistent abnormal posture
cases.vignette: A 20-month-old child has delayed sitting and walking, abnormal limb tone, feeding difficulty and an abnormal gait. The child had a significant perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic event. The motor abnormalities have remained non-progressive, although the functional impact changes as the child grows.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines cerebral palsy (CP)?

options.label: A
options.text: A progressive disorder of muscle degeneration due to dystrophin deficiency

options.label: C
options.text: A disorder of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive insult or injury to the developing brain

options.label: D
options.text: A disease caused by ongoing inflammation of peripheral nerves

options.label: E
options.text: A progressive degeneration of anterior horn cells

questions.correctAnswerText: A disorder of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive insult or injury to the developing brain
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe CP as a disorder of movement and posture due to a non-progressive injury or insult to the developing brain. The brain lesion is non-progressive, although musculoskeletal consequences and functional limitations may evolve with growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dystrophin deficiency causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a progressive muscle disease.
- B. Incorrect. Febrile seizures do not define CP.
- C. Correct. This is the definition in the source.
- D. Incorrect. This describes a peripheral neuropathy such as GBS.
- E. Incorrect. This describes an anterior horn cell disorder such as SMA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CP: non-progressive brain insult affecting movement and posture.
- It is the commonest cause of neurodisability in childhood.
- Functional manifestations may change with age, growth and musculoskeletal complications.
- Distinguish CP from progressive neuromuscular/neurodegenerative disorders.

questions.stem: Which feature should prompt evaluation for cerebral palsy in an infant?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal gait in a school-aged child

options.label: B
options.text: Disappearance of primitive reflexes at the expected age

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent primitive Moro/ATNR reflexes beyond 6 months or early hand preference before 12 months

options.label: E
options.text: Normal symmetrical development and age-appropriate milestones

questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent primitive Moro/ATNR reflexes beyond 6 months or early hand preference before 12 months
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include delayed motor milestones, abnormal tone/posture, feeding difficulties, abnormal gait, asymmetric hand function after 12 months, persistence of Moro/ATNR reflexes beyond 6 months and early handedness before 12 months as clinical warning signs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Normal gait in an older child does not suggest CP.
- B. Incorrect. Disappearance of primitive reflexes is expected with maturation.
- C. Incorrect. Normal symmetry and tone are not red flags.
- D. Correct. These findings may indicate early neurological asymmetry or abnormal motor development.
- E. Incorrect. Normal developmental progression is reassuring.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Warning signs: delayed milestones, abnormal tone/posture, feeding problems, abnormal gait.
- Asymmetric hand function after 12 months is concerning.
- Early hand preference before 12 months may indicate unilateral CP.
- Persistence of Moro or ATNR beyond 6 months is a red flag.

questions.stem: Which type of cerebral palsy is the commonest and accounts for approximately 80-90% of cases?
questions.correctAnswerText: Spastic CP
questions.initialExplanation: Spastic cerebral palsy is the most common type, accounting for approximately 80-90%. It is associated with corticospinal/pyramidal tract injury and UMN signs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dyskinetic CP is associated with basal ganglia/extrapyramidal injury.
- B. Incorrect. Atonic CP is less common.
- C. Incorrect. Mixed CP includes features of more than one subtype.
- D. Incorrect. Ataxic CP is uncommon and results from cerebellar injury.
- E. Correct. Spastic CP is the commonest type.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Spastic CP: approximately 80-90%.
- Damage to pyramidal/corticospinal pathways.
- UMN signs: hypertonia, hyperreflexia and positive Babinski.
- Subtypes include hemiplegic, diplegic, quadriplegic and rare monoplegic CP.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child has spasticity predominantly affecting both legs, with the arms relatively spared. The child was born very preterm and has a history of periventricular brain injury. Which CP subtype is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Diplegic CP
questions.initialExplanation: Spastic diplegic CP predominantly affects the lower limbs more than the upper limbs and is commonly associated with prematurity and periventricular white matter injury.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Bilateral lower-limb predominance is typical of diplegia.
- B. Incorrect. Hemiplegic CP affects one side of the body, often with arm involvement and facial sparing.
- C. Incorrect. Ataxic CP is characterized by incoordination, intention tremor and ataxic gait.
- D. Incorrect. Monoplegic CP affects only one limb and is rare.
- E. Incorrect. Quadriplegic CP affects all four limbs, often with trunk involvement and more severe disability.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Spastic diplegia: legs affected more than arms.
- Frequently associated with prematurity and periventricular brain damage.
- Gait may be abnormal, with tiptoe/toe-heel walking and scissoring.
- Assess hips, contractures and mobility over time.

questions.stem: A child with CP has unilateral arm and leg involvement, with the face spared. There is early fisting of the affected hand, a flexed arm and pronated forearm, followed later by toe-walking on the affected side. Which subtype is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Spastic hemiplegic CP
questions.initialExplanation: Spastic hemiplegic CP affects one side of the body, with the face usually spared. Early signs may include fisting and flexion/pronation of the affected arm, asymmetric reaching and later toe-walking on the affected side. Neonatal stroke is one possible cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dyskinetic CP causes involuntary choreoathetoid/dystonic movements rather than a unilateral spastic pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Diplegia affects both legs more than the arms.
- C. Correct. Unilateral arm and leg involvement with typical upper-limb posturing is hemiplegic CP.
- D. Incorrect. Quadriplegia affects all four limbs and often the trunk.
- E. Incorrect. Ataxic CP causes incoordination and balance problems.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hemiplegic CP: unilateral arm and leg involvement, face often spared.
- Early hand fisting/asymmetry and early hand preference are clues.
- Perinatal/neonatal stroke is a possible cause.
- Monitor for seizures, visual-field defects and learning difficulties.

questions.stem: A child with cerebral palsy has involuntary slow writhing movements, dystonia and variable tone. Which anatomical site is most likely affected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Basal ganglia/extrapyramidal pathways
questions.initialExplanation: Dyskinetic (choreoathetoid) CP is associated with injury to extrapyramidal pathways, particularly the basal ganglia. It may cause chorea, athetosis and dystonia, with abnormal tone.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Peripheral sensory nerve injury causes sensory loss/neuropathic symptoms.
- B. Incorrect. Neuromuscular junction disease causes fatigable weakness.
- C. Incorrect. Cerebellar injury causes ataxic CP with incoordination and intention tremor.
- D. Incorrect. Anterior horn cell injury causes LMN weakness, atrophy and areflexia.
- E. Correct. Basal ganglia injury causes dyskinetic/choreoathetoid movements.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dyskinetic CP: extrapyramidal/basal ganglia injury.
- Chorea: irregular involuntary movements.
- Athetosis: slow writhing movements.
- Dystonia: simultaneous agonist/antagonist muscle contraction.
- Intellect may be relatively preserved.

questions.stem: A child with CP has early truncal hypotonia, poor balance, incoordination, intention tremor and an ataxic gait. Which CP subtype is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ataxic CP
questions.initialExplanation: Ataxic CP results from cerebellar injury. Early findings may include truncal and limb hypotonia with poor balance; later, incoordination, intention tremor and an ataxic gait become evident.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Atonic CP is characterized by hypotonia but is not the described cerebellar syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Dyskinetic CP causes chorea, athetosis or dystonia.
- C. Incorrect. Hemiplegic CP is unilateral spastic involvement.
- D. Incorrect. Spastic CP produces hypertonia, hyperreflexia and spastic gait.
- E. Correct. Cerebellar dysfunction produces incoordination, intention tremor and ataxia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ataxic CP: cerebellar injury.
- Early hypotonia, poor trunk control/balance.
- Later intention tremor, incoordination and ataxic gait.
- Assess for other cerebellar causes if the course is progressive.

questions.stem: Which statement helps distinguish cerebral palsy from a progressive neurodegenerative disorder?

options.label: A
options.text: CP typically causes increasing head size

options.label: B
options.text: CP has a non-progressive brain insult, whereas neurodegenerative disease shows a progressive course

options.label: C
options.text: CP is defined by progressive loss of previously acquired motor skills

options.label: D
options.text: CP typically causes hepatosplenomegaly and café-au-lait spots

questions.correctAnswerText: CP has a non-progressive brain insult, whereas neurodegenerative disease shows a progressive course
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance contrasts CP as non-progressive with neurodegenerative disease as progressive. It also notes family history and systemic/skin features may help identify neurodegenerative syndromes, but these are not universal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Head size in CP may be normal or small; progressive macrocephaly is not defining.
- B. Correct. The course of the underlying neurological disorder is the key distinction.
- C. Incorrect. Progressive loss of acquired skills suggests a neurodegenerative/metabolic process rather than the typical non-progressive brain injury of CP.
- D. Incorrect. Hepatosplenomegaly and neurocutaneous signs are not features of CP itself.
- E. Incorrect. Neurodegenerative disorders are progressive by definition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CP: non-progressive brain injury; functional consequences may evolve.
- Neurodegenerative disease: progressive neurological decline.
- Progressive regression should trigger evaluation for metabolic, genetic or neurodegenerative causes.
- CP is mainly a clinical diagnosis; investigations help determine cause and exclude alternatives.

questions.stem: Which complication is reported as a common associated problem in cerebral palsy?

options.label: A
options.text: Epilepsy, intellectual disability, feeding difficulty and aspiration pneumonia

options.label: B
options.text: Progressive peripheral demyelination in typical presentations

options.label: C
options.text: Congenital cataract in children in routine care

options.label: E
options.text: Isolated hyperthyroidism in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Epilepsy, intellectual disability, feeding difficulty and aspiration pneumonia
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include intellectual disability, epilepsy, developmental delay, visual/speech/hearing problems, aspiration and recurrent chest infections, feeding difficulties, GERD, constipation, musculoskeletal pain/spasm, contractures, pressure sores and social problems.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are important associated problems in CP.
- B. Incorrect. Peripheral demyelination is a feature of GBS, not CP.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital cataract is not universal in CP.
- D. Incorrect. Renal stones are not the only or typical major complication.
- E. Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism is not a defining CP complication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CNS: intellectual disability, epilepsy, visual, speech/hearing issues.
- Respiratory: aspiration pneumonia and recurrent chest infections.
- GI: feeding difficulties, GERD and constipation.
- MSK: pain/spasm, hip subluxation, contractures and deformity.
- Skin/social: pressure sores, skin infection and family/social burden.

questions.stem: A child with spastic CP has painful muscle spasticity and joint contractures. Which management approach is described?

options.label: B
options.text: Antiseizure medication in children in routine care regardless of seizure history

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate discontinuation of most physical therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Multidisciplinary care with physiotherapy, baclofen or botulinum toxin for spasticity, and surgery for selected contractures

options.label: E
options.text: No rehabilitation because the brain lesion is non-progressive

questions.correctAnswerText: Multidisciplinary care with physiotherapy, baclofen or botulinum toxin for spasticity, and surgery for selected contractures
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes a multidisciplinary team including paediatrics, physiotherapy, neurology, speech and language therapy, orthopaedics, nutrition, social work and rehabilitation. Spasticity may be treated with baclofen, botulinum toxin or selected neurosurgical approaches; contractures may need surgical correction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotics treat infections but do not manage CP motor dysfunction.
- B. Incorrect. Antiseizure medications are used when epilepsy is present, not routinely in every child.
- C. Incorrect. Physiotherapy is an essential component of treatment.
- D. Correct. This is the multidisciplinary and spasticity-management approach described.
- E. Incorrect. Even though the brain injury is non-progressive, rehabilitation and management of secondary complications are essential.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MDT: paediatrician, neurologist, physiotherapist, speech/language therapist, orthopaedics, nutrition and social support.
- Spasticity: baclofen, botulinum toxin and selected interventions.
- Contractures/deformities may require orthopaedic surgery.
- Feeding, nutrition, communication, mobility and family support are central.
- Explain diagnosis early, while recognizing that prognosis becomes clearer with longitudinal developmental assessment.

cases.title: A young infant is floppy with tongue fasciculations and weak cry
cases.vignette: A 3-month-old infant has severe symmetrical hypotonia, a frog-like posture, marked head lag and absent deep tendon reflexes. The infant has tongue fasciculations, a weak cry, poor sucking and recurrent chest infections. Facial expression and eye movements are preserved, and cognition appears appropriate for age.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Spinal muscular atrophy type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann disease)
questions.initialExplanation: SMA type 1 is a severe anterior horn cell disorder presenting from birth to approximately 6 months with symmetrical hypotonia, weakness, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations and bulbar/respiratory muscle involvement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GBS is an acute postinfectious polyneuropathy with ascending weakness, usually over hours to days/weeks.
- B. Incorrect. Ataxic CP causes incoordination, intention tremor and balance problems, not an anterior horn cell syndrome with tongue fasciculations.
- C. Incorrect. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness, usually ocular/bulbar and fluctuating; fasciculations and absent reflexes are not typical.
- D. Incorrect. DMD usually presents in boys aged 2-3 years with progressive proximal weakness, Gower sign and calf pseudohypertrophy.
- E. Correct. The age, severe symmetric hypotonia, tongue fasciculations, absent reflexes and bulbar weakness are characteristic of SMA type 1.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SMA type 1 = Werdnig-Hoffmann disease.
- Onset: birth to 6 months; severe infantile form.
- LMN signs: severe hypotonia, symmetrical weakness, absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations.
- Facial and extraocular muscles are relatively spared, giving an alert appearance.
- Bulbar and respiratory muscle weakness are major causes of morbidity.

questions.stem: Which genetic abnormality causes the common form of SMA described?

options.label: A
options.text: Mutation of the NF1 gene on chromosome 17

options.label: B
options.text: Mutation of SMN1 on chromosome 5, inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern

options.label: E
options.text: CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene

questions.correctAnswerText: Mutation of SMN1 on chromosome 5, inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern
questions.initialExplanation: SMA is usually an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation/deletion of the survival motor neuron gene SMN1 on chromosome 5. Reduced SMN protein leads to degeneration of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord and motor cranial nerve nuclei.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. NF1 mutation causes neurofibromatosis type 1.
- B. Correct. This is the genetic mechanism described for SMA.
- C. Incorrect. Anti-AChR antibodies cause autoimmune myasthenia gravis.
- D. Incorrect. Dystrophin gene deletion causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- E. Incorrect. CTG repeat expansion is associated with myotonic dystrophy type 1.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SMA: autosomal recessive.
- Gene: SMN1, chromosome 5.
- Pathology: degeneration of anterior horn cells and motor cranial nuclei.
- Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis; prenatal and postnatal testing may be available.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly classifies the four main SMA types?

options.label: A
options.text: Type 1 is the mildest form and Type 4 is the most severe infantile form

options.label: B
options.text: most types begin in the neonatal period

options.label: C
options.text: Type 1: birth-6 months; Type 2: 6-18 months; Type 3: after 18 months; Type 4: adult onset

options.label: D
options.text: Type 2 and 3 are defined by onset after 40 years

options.label: E
options.text: Type 1: adult onset; Type 2: birth-6 months; Type 3: 6-18 months; Type 4: 18 months

questions.correctAnswerText: Type 1: birth-6 months; Type 2: 6-18 months; Type 3: after 18 months; Type 4: adult onset
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance classifies SMA by age of onset and severity: type 1 (acute infantile/Werdnig-Hoffmann) from birth to 6 months, type 2 (intermediate/late infantile) 6-18 months, type 3 (juvenile/Kugelberg-Welander) after 18 months and type 4 in adulthood.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Type 1 is the most severe common infantile form; type 4 is adult onset and milder.
- B. Incorrect. Later-onset forms begin after infancy.
- C. Correct. This matches the classification in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Type 2 and 3 are childhood-onset forms.
- E. Incorrect. The ages are incorrectly assigned.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SMA type 1: birth to 6 months, severe.
- SMA type 2: 6-18 months, intermediate.
- SMA type 3: after 18 months, juvenile and milder.
- SMA type 4: adult onset.
- The source also mentions an extremely severe type 0 in newborns; do not confuse it with the four main clinical types.

questions.stem: Which investigation pattern supports SMA type 1?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal CK with EMG evidence of denervation/fasciculations and confirmatory SMN1 genetic testing

options.label: B
options.text: Markedly elevated CK with a myopathic EMG

options.label: D
options.text: Positive anti-AChR antibodies and decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation

options.label: E
options.text: High ESR, high CK and inflammatory muscle biopsy

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal CK with EMG evidence of denervation/fasciculations and confirmatory SMN1 genetic testing
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that CK is usually normal in SMA. EMG shows denervation and fasciculation activity, and genetic testing confirms the diagnosis. Muscle biopsy was historically used to differentiate neuromuscular disorders but genetic testing is now central.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the expected SMA investigation pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Markedly elevated CK and myopathic changes suggest muscular dystrophy such as DMD.
- C. Incorrect. Albuminocytologic dissociation is characteristic of GBS.
- D. Incorrect. These findings support myasthenia gravis.
- E. Incorrect. Raised inflammatory markers, CK and inflammatory biopsy suggest juvenile dermatomyositis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SMA: CK often normal.
- EMG: denervation and fasciculations.
- SMN1 genetic testing is diagnostic.
- Distinguish anterior horn cell disease from primary muscle disease (e.g. DMD) and NMJ disorders (e.g. MG).

questions.stem: Which statement best describes current treatment options for SMA?

options.label: B
options.text: Pyridostigmine is first-line therapy for most SMA types

options.label: C
options.text: Antibiotics reverse anterior horn cell degeneration

options.label: E
options.text: Supportive care plus disease-modifying treatment such as nusinersen or onasemnogene, where available

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive care plus disease-modifying treatment such as nusinersen or onasemnogene, where available
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include supportive care (respiratory care, aspiration prevention, infection treatment, nutrition via NG/gastrostomy where needed, orthopaedic support and genetic counselling) and specific treatments including nusinersen and onasemnogene abeparvovec (gene therapy), where available.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Respiratory, nutritional and rehabilitation care are essential.
- B. Incorrect. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis, not SMA.
- C. Incorrect. Antibiotics treat infection but do not reverse SMN1-related motor neuron degeneration.
- D. Incorrect. Steroids are used in selected muscular dystrophies, not as curative SMA treatment.
- E. Correct. This includes the supportive and disease-modifying treatment options described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SMA care: airway clearance, respiratory support, aspiration prevention and nutrition.
- Orthopaedic support, physiotherapy and genetic counselling are important.
- Disease-modifying therapies listed: nusinersen and onasemnogene abeparvovec.
- Early diagnosis is important because treatment benefit is greatest before extensive motor neuron loss.

cases.title: A child develops ascending weakness several weeks after gastroenteritis
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child develops progressive weakness beginning in both feet and ascending to the trunk and upper limbs over several days. The child had gastroenteritis approximately 2 weeks earlier. Examination shows symmetrical flaccid weakness and absent tendon reflexes. There is tingling in the toes and intermittent tachycardia.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS)
questions.initialExplanation: GBS is an acute postinfectious autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy. It typically presents with ascending, symmetrical flaccid weakness and areflexia, often 2-3 weeks after a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. DMD is a chronic progressive proximal myopathy in boys, not an acute ascending paralysis.
- B. Incorrect. MG causes fatigable weakness, typically ocular/bulbar/proximal, with preserved sensation and reflexes.
- C. Incorrect. SMA type 1 presents in infancy with chronic severe hypotonia, not an acute postinfectious syndrome in a school-aged child.
- D. Incorrect. CP results from a non-progressive brain injury and does not cause acute ascending weakness.
- E. Correct. The preceding infection, ascending symmetrical weakness and areflexia are classic for GBS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GBS: acute postinfectious autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy.
- Often begins 2-3 weeks after URTI or gastroenteritis.
- Ascending bilateral symmetrical flaccid weakness and areflexia.
- Respiratory and bulbar muscle involvement can cause life-threatening failure.

questions.stem: Which clinical feature is common in GBS and may be an early symptom?

options.label: E
options.text: Distal paraesthesia and tingling in fingers and toes

questions.correctAnswerText: Distal paraesthesia and tingling in fingers and toes
questions.initialExplanation: GBS primarily affects motor nerves but can also involve sensory and autonomic nerves. Distal paraesthesia/tingling in the toes and fingers may be an early symptom. Dysautonomia can cause heart-rate and blood-pressure instability, urinary retention, ileus and altered sweating.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Calf pseudohypertrophy is associated with Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- B. Incorrect. Early hand preference can be an early sign of hemiplegic CP.
- C. Incorrect. Unilateral spasticity suggests UMN injury/hemiplegic CP.
- D. Incorrect. Tongue fasciculations suggest anterior horn cell disease such as SMA.
- E. Correct. Distal tingling/paraesthesia is described as a sensory feature of GBS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sensory: distal tingling/paraesthesia.
- Motor: ascending symmetrical flaccid paralysis and areflexia.
- Autonomic: tachycardia/bradycardia, arrhythmia, hypertension/orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, ileus and altered sweating.
- Bulbar/facial weakness may be missed in young children.

questions.stem: A child with suspected GBS undergoes lumbar puncture during the second week of illness. Which CSF finding is expected?

options.label: B
options.text: High CSF protein with a normal white-cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation)

options.label: C
options.text: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with markedly low glucose

options.label: D
options.text: Very high neutrophil count with low glucose

options.label: E
options.text: Normal protein with many red blood cells

questions.correctAnswerText: High CSF protein with a normal white-cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation)
questions.initialExplanation: GBS causes albuminocytologic dissociation: increased CSF protein with a normal cell count, typically becoming apparent during the second week. EMG/nerve conduction studies show peripheral demyelination and reduced conduction velocity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Eosinophilic CSF is not typical of GBS.
- B. Correct. This is the characteristic CSF finding in GBS.
- C. Incorrect. This suggests TB or another chronic CNS infection.
- D. Incorrect. This is more consistent with bacterial meningitis.
- E. Incorrect. This does not describe albuminocytologic dissociation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GBS LP: high protein, normal cells (albuminocytologic dissociation), often from week 2.
- Nerve conduction velocity is reduced in demyelinating GBS.
- EMG supports peripheral nerve demyelination.
- MRI spine/brain may be used to exclude spinal cord lesions such as tumour, bleed or transverse myelitis.

questions.stem: Which treatment is the drug of choice for acute GBS?
questions.correctAnswerText: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include IVIG as the drug of choice for GBS, with plasma exchange as an alternative. Corticosteroids have no beneficial effect and may delay recovery.
