Supportive care includes respiratory monitoring/support, nutrition, bladder care, physiotherapy and ICU admission when severe.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ethosuximide is used for typical absence epilepsy.
- B. Incorrect. Baclofen reduces spasticity, not autoimmune peripheral demyelination.
- C. Incorrect. Corticosteroids alone do not improve GBS outcomes.
- D. Correct. IVIG is the DOC listed in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GBS treatment: IVIG (DOC) or plasma exchange.
- Steroids do not provide benefit in GBS and may delay recovery.
- Monitor respiratory function, bulbar function, autonomic instability and cardiac rhythm.
- Most children recover, but rehabilitation can take months.

cases.title: A boy has progressive proximal weakness and difficulty rising from the floor
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old boy has frequent falls and difficulty running. When asked to stand from the floor, he uses his hands to climb up his legs. Examination shows a waddling gait and enlarged calves. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD)
questions.initialExplanation: DMD is the commonest muscular dystrophy in boys. It usually presents around 2-3 years with progressive proximal muscle weakness, frequent falls, difficulty running, Gower sign and calf pseudohypertrophy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. MG causes fatigability and ocular/bulbar weakness rather than calf pseudohypertrophy.
- B. Correct. The age and characteristic proximal myopathy signs support DMD.
- C. Incorrect. GBS is an acute postinfectious ascending polyneuropathy.
- D. Incorrect. Becker muscular dystrophy is milder, begins later (often around 11 years) and progresses more slowly.
- E. Incorrect. Juvenile dermatomyositis causes proximal weakness with characteristic skin rash and raised inflammatory markers.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DMD: X-linked recessive dystrophin deficiency.
- Onset around 2-3 years: frequent falls, difficulty running and unstable gait.
- Gower sign and calf pseudohypertrophy are classic.
- Waddling gait becomes apparent as weakness progresses.

questions.stem: Which genetic abnormality causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

options.label: A
options.text: Anti-AChR antibodies at the neuromuscular junction

options.label: B
options.text: CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene

options.label: D
options.text: Mutation/deletion of the dystrophin gene on Xp21

questions.correctAnswerText: Mutation/deletion of the dystrophin gene on Xp21
questions.initialExplanation: DMD is an X-linked recessive disorder due to deletion/mutation of the dystrophin gene on Xp21. Dystrophin links the muscle-fibre cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix; deficiency causes progressive myofibre necrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Anti-AChR antibodies cause autoimmune myasthenia gravis.
- B. Incorrect. CTG repeat expansion causes myotonic dystrophy type 1.
- C. Incorrect. SMN1 mutation causes SMA.
- D. Correct. This is the genetic defect in DMD.
- E. Incorrect. NF2 mutation causes neurofibromatosis type 2.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DMD: X-linked recessive, dystrophin gene at Xp21.
- Female relatives may be carriers; some cases result from de novo mutations.
- Dystrophin deficiency causes progressive muscle-fibre degeneration.
- Genetic testing can confirm diagnosis and allow family counselling.

questions.stem: Which laboratory result is typically found in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal CK with denervation on EMG

questions.correctAnswerText: Markedly elevated serum creatine kinase (CK/CPK)
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include markedly elevated CK/CPK in DMD due to ongoing muscle-fibre breakdown. Genetic testing is diagnostic; EMG shows myopathic changes and muscle biopsy shows muscle-fibre degeneration with connective tissue replacement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Normal CK with denervation is more compatible with SMA.
- B. Incorrect. Low complement and haematuria may occur in immune-complex renal disease, not DMD.
- C. Correct. Markedly raised CK is a hallmark of DMD.
- D. Incorrect. Anti-AChR antibodies support myasthenia gravis.
- E. Incorrect. CSF protein does not diagnose DMD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DMD: CK markedly elevated.
- Genetic testing confirms dystrophin gene abnormality.
- EMG: myopathic pattern.
- Echo/ECG and respiratory evaluation are important because cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure drive morbidity.

questions.stem: Which complication is particularly important to monitor in a child with Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

options.label: A
options.text: Cardiomyopathy and progressive respiratory muscle weakness

questions.correctAnswerText: Cardiomyopathy and progressive respiratory muscle weakness
questions.initialExplanation: DMD affects skeletal and cardiac muscle. Common examples include cardiomyopathy/heart failure, scoliosis, learning/language difficulties in some children and progressive respiratory muscle weakness. Respiratory failure and cardiomyopathy reduce life expectancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are major complications of DMD.
- B. Incorrect. Biliary atresia is a hepatobiliary disorder.
- C. Incorrect. Hydrocephalus is not a universal complication of DMD.
- D. Incorrect. Meningococcal purpura is an acute infectious emergency.
- E. Incorrect. Hearing loss is not the main complication emphasized.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DMD complications: cardiomyopathy, scoliosis, contractures and progressive respiratory muscle weakness.
- Monitor cardiac function with ECG/echocardiography.
- Respiratory support may include nocturnal non-invasive ventilation (e.g. CPAP/BiPAP as clinically indicated).
- Physiotherapy, ankle splinting, steroids and multidisciplinary follow-up are important.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes Becker muscular dystrophy from Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

options.label: A
options.text: Becker is usually milder, progresses more slowly and has a later onset, often around 11 years

options.label: B
options.text: Becker is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder

options.label: C
options.text: Becker is caused by SMN1 mutation

options.label: D
options.text: Becker is typically more severe and starts at birth

options.label: E
options.text: Becker is caused by loss of acetylcholine receptors

questions.correctAnswerText: Becker is usually milder, progresses more slowly and has a later onset, often around 11 years
questions.initialExplanation: Becker muscular dystrophy is similar to DMD but is clinically milder and progresses more slowly because some functional dystrophin remains. Clinical guidance notes onset around 11 years, with later loss of walking and longer survival than DMD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the main clinical difference described.
- B. Incorrect. This describes an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder such as MG.
- C. Incorrect. SMN1 mutation causes SMA.
- D. Incorrect. Becker is generally milder and later onset.
- E. Incorrect. AChR antibodies cause autoimmune myasthenia gravis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DMD: little/no functional dystrophin, early onset and more severe progression.
- Becker: some functional dystrophin, later onset and milder course.
- Both are dystrophinopathies with X-linked inheritance.
- Cardiac involvement can occur in Becker as well.

questions.stem: A child has neonatal hypotonia, weak respiratory effort, feeding problems and later develops delayed relaxation of muscle contraction. There is a family history of adult cataracts and cardiac conduction disease. Which condition is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Myotonic dystrophy type 1
questions.initialExplanation: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is an autosomal dominant CTG repeat expansion disorder. The congenital form may present with reduced fetal movements, oligohydramnios, neonatal hypotonia and respiratory/feeding problems. Later childhood features may include myotonia, facial weakness, cataracts and cardiac conduction abnormalities.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The neonatal hypotonia, later myotonia and family history of cataracts/conduction disease fit DM1.
- B. Incorrect. Juvenile dermatomyositis causes proximal weakness with heliotrope rash and Gottron papules.
- C. Incorrect. SMA causes anterior horn cell degeneration with tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes; myotonia is not typical.
- D. Incorrect. DMD causes progressive proximal weakness in boys, calf pseudohypertrophy and a markedly elevated CK, not myotonia.
- E. Incorrect. GBS is an acute postinfectious neuropathy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Myotonic dystrophy type 1: autosomal dominant CTG repeat expansion.
- Congenital form: neonatal hypotonia, feeding and respiratory complications; reduced fetal movement/oligohydramnios may occur.
- Myotonia = delayed relaxation after contraction.
- Associated features: facial weakness, cataracts, heart block/arrhythmia, endocrine abnormalities and learning difficulties.

cases.title: A teenager develops fluctuating ptosis and fatigable proximal weakness
cases.vignette: A 13-year-old girl has intermittent ptosis and diplopia that worsen late in the day. She becomes tired when chewing and climbing stairs. Sensation and deep tendon reflexes are normal. Strength improves after rest.

questions.stem: What is the underlying mechanism of autoimmune myasthenia gravis?

options.label: A
options.text: Degeneration of anterior horn cells due to SMN1 deficiency

options.label: C
options.text: Antibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction impair neuromuscular transmission

questions.correctAnswerText: Antibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction impair neuromuscular transmission
questions.initialExplanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies against acetylcholine receptors (or, less commonly, MuSK) at the neuromuscular junction impair transmission, producing fatigable skeletal muscle weakness.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. SMN1 deficiency causes spinal muscular atrophy.
- B. Incorrect. Meningeal inflammation is meningitis.
- C. Correct. This is the mechanism described.
- D. Incorrect. Peripheral nerve demyelination is the mechanism in Guillain-Barre syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Dystrophin deficiency causes Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Myasthenia gravis: autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular transmission.
- Antibodies commonly target AChR; some cases involve MuSK.
- Weakness is fatigable and fluctuates.
- Sensation and tendon reflexes are usually preserved.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern is most typical of juvenile myasthenia gravis?

options.label: A
options.text: Tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes from birth

options.label: B
options.text: Ptosis, diplopia, facial/bulbar weakness and proximal fatigability that worsen later in the day

options.label: C
options.text: Progressive calf pseudohypertrophy and Gower sign

options.label: D
options.text: Ascending symmetrical flaccid paralysis with areflexia after diarrhoea

options.label: E
options.text: Spasticity with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar response

questions.correctAnswerText: Ptosis, diplopia, facial/bulbar weakness and proximal fatigability that worsen later in the day
questions.initialExplanation: Juvenile MG usually presents in children older than 10 years with easy fatigability. Ocular muscles commonly cause ptosis and diplopia; facial, chewing, swallowing and proximal limb muscles may also be affected. Symptoms are often worse at the end of the day.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests SMA type 1.
- B. Correct. This is the characteristic fluctuating/fatigable pattern.
- C. Incorrect. This describes DMD.
- D. Incorrect. This describes GBS.
- E. Incorrect. This describes an UMN lesion, such as spastic CP.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Juvenile MG often begins after age 10 years.
- Ocular features: ptosis (sometimes asymmetric) and diplopia.
- Bulbar: dysphagia, chewing difficulty, weak facial expression.
- Proximal muscles are often more affected than distal muscles.
- Diurnal variation: worse toward the end of the day; improves after rest.

questions.stem: Which finding helps distinguish myasthenia gravis from a peripheral neuropathy?

options.label: C
options.text: Distal sensory loss and absent ankle reflexes

options.label: D
options.text: Normal sensation and preserved deep tendon reflexes despite fatigable weakness

options.label: E
options.text: Loss of vibration sense with a positive Romberg sign

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal sensation and preserved deep tendon reflexes despite fatigable weakness
questions.initialExplanation: MG affects neuromuscular transmission rather than sensory nerves or the reflex arc. Therefore sensation and deep tendon reflexes are usually normal despite fatigable weakness.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Atrophy and fasciculations suggest LMN/anterior horn cell disease.
- B. Incorrect. Spasticity and Babinski positivity indicate UMN disease.
- C. Incorrect. Sensory symptoms and areflexia suggest a peripheral neuropathy such as GBS.
- D. Correct. This is the characteristic examination pattern of MG.
- E. Incorrect. Loss of proprioception and a positive Romberg suggest sensory ataxia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MG: fatigable weakness with normal sensation and reflexes.
- Peripheral neuropathy may cause sensory loss and reduced reflexes.
- UMN lesions cause hyperreflexia and Babinski positivity.
- LMN lesions cause wasting, fasciculations and hyporeflexia/areflexia.

questions.stem: Which diagnostic approach is listed to confirm juvenile myasthenia gravis?

options.label: B
options.text: Anti-AChR antibodies (or anti-MuSK in selected cases) and appropriate neuromuscular testing

options.label: D
options.text: Markedly elevated CK and dystrophin gene testing

questions.correctAnswerText: Anti-AChR antibodies (or anti-MuSK in selected cases) and appropriate neuromuscular testing
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include the edrophonium (Tensilon) test, AChR antibodies and, less commonly, anti-MuSK antibodies. Modern evaluation commonly uses antibody testing and electrophysiology (repetitive nerve stimulation/single-fibre EMG) according to specialist availability.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. SMN1 testing diagnoses SMA.
- B. Correct. These tests assess autoimmune neuromuscular transmission failure.
- C. Incorrect. Albuminocytologic dissociation suggests GBS.
- D. Incorrect. These tests are used for muscular dystrophy.
- E. Incorrect. Tuberculin testing assesses TB exposure and is unrelated to MG.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MG diagnosis: clinical fatigability plus AChR antibodies; anti-MuSK in selected antibody-negative cases.
- standard guidance includes edrophonium testing, but current practice uses specialist electrophysiological/serological testing.
- Consider respiratory and bulbar function in any child with suspected MG.
- Normal antibody testing does not completely exclude all juvenile myasthenic syndromes.

questions.stem: A newborn born to a mother with myasthenia gravis develops ptosis, weak sucking and respiratory muscle weakness during the first week. Symptoms resolve over several weeks. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: B
options.text: Transient neonatal myasthenia due to transplacental maternal antibodies

options.label: D
options.text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to an inherited gene mutation

questions.correctAnswerText: Transient neonatal myasthenia due to transplacental maternal antibodies
questions.initialExplanation: Transient neonatal myasthenia occurs when maternal AChR antibodies cross the placenta and affect the newborn. Symptoms include ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, poor feeding/bulbar weakness and respiratory muscle weakness; they typically resolve as maternal antibodies disappear, over approximately 1-10 weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GBS is an acute postinfectious peripheral neuropathy, not a transplacental antibody syndrome.
- B. Correct. The maternal history and transient course support transplacental antibody-mediated neonatal MG.
- C. Incorrect. SMA causes persistent progressive LMN weakness and tongue fasciculations, not transient antibody-mediated weakness.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital myasthenic syndromes are genetic, have no maternal autoantibody mechanism and may not respond to anticholinesterase inhibitors.
- E. Incorrect. DMD presents later in boys with progressive proximal weakness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Transient neonatal MG: maternal AChR antibodies cross placenta.
- Features: ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, poor feeding/bulbar weakness and respiratory muscle weakness.
- Symptoms are temporary as maternal antibodies clear.
- Congenital myasthenic syndrome is genetic and antibody-negative; response to anticholinesterase drugs varies.

questions.stem: Which treatment is listed for juvenile myasthenia gravis?

options.label: D
options.text: IVIG as the lifelong treatment for most patients

options.label: E
options.text: Pyridostigmine; immunosuppression such as prednisolone when indicated, with plasma exchange in crisis

questions.correctAnswerText: Pyridostigmine; immunosuppression such as prednisolone when indicated, with plasma exchange in crisis
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as pyridostigmine or neostigmine, plasma exchange in myasthenic crisis, thymectomy if thymoma is present and prednisolone/immunosuppressive therapy. Respiratory/bulbar deterioration needs urgent hospital management.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Nusinersen is a disease-modifying treatment for SMA.
- B. Incorrect. Baclofen treats spasticity, not NMJ transmission failure.
- C. Incorrect. Ethosuximide treats typical absence epilepsy.
- D. Incorrect. IVIG may be used in selected acute exacerbations, but it is not the only lifelong treatment for all patients.
- E. Correct. These are the management options described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- First-line symptomatic treatment: pyridostigmine.
- Prednisolone/immunosuppression may be required in selected cases.
- Plasma exchange or IVIG may be used in crisis/exacerbation.
- Thymectomy is indicated when thymoma is present.
- Monitor for myasthenic crisis with respiratory or bulbar weakness.

cases.title: A school-aged child develops proximal weakness and a violaceous eyelid rash
cases.vignette: A 8-year-old child develops fever, symmetrical proximal muscle weakness and difficulty climbing stairs. Examination reveals a violaceous rash over the eyelids with periorbital oedema and papules over the metacarpophalangeal joints. There are small subcutaneous calcifications over extensor surfaces.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Juvenile dermatomyositis
questions.initialExplanation: Juvenile dermatomyositis is an inflammatory myopathy usually presenting between 5 and 10 years, with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness and characteristic cutaneous findings including heliotrope rash, Gottron papules and calcinosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GBS is an acute postinfectious ascending neuropathy with areflexia.
- B. Incorrect. DMD causes progressive weakness in boys, Gower sign, pseudohypertrophy and raised CK, not heliotrope rash/Gottron papules.
- C. Incorrect. SMA is an anterior horn cell disorder with hypotonia, areflexia and fasciculations.
- D. Incorrect. MG causes fatigable weakness and ocular/bulbar symptoms without inflammatory skin lesions.
- E. Correct. The proximal weakness and characteristic skin features are typical.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- JDM: age 5-10 years.
- Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness/pain, sometimes dysphagia.
- Heliotrope rash: violaceous eyelid rash with periorbital oedema.
- Gottron papules: over MCP joints.
- Calcinosis cutis may occur over extensor surfaces.

questions.stem: Which laboratory and biopsy findings support juvenile dermatomyositis?

options.label: A
options.text: High CSF protein with normal cells

options.label: B
options.text: Normal CK with EMG denervation and fasciculations

options.label: D
options.text: Reduced nerve conduction velocity with albuminocytologic dissociation

options.label: E
options.text: Raised CK, sometimes elevated ESR/CRP, and muscle biopsy showing inflammatory infiltrates with atrophy

questions.correctAnswerText: Raised CK, sometimes elevated ESR/CRP, and muscle biopsy showing inflammatory infiltrates with atrophy
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include elevated CK, sometimes raised inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) and muscle biopsy showing inflammatory-cell infiltration with atrophy as supportive findings in JDM.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is the CSF pattern associated with GBS.
- B. Incorrect. This pattern suggests SMA/anterior horn cell disease.
- C. Incorrect. Anti-AChR antibodies support MG.
- D. Incorrect. These findings support GBS.
- E. Correct. These are the investigation findings described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- JDM: CK elevated; ESR/CRP may be raised.
- Muscle biopsy: inflammatory cell infiltrate and muscle atrophy.
- Assess swallowing, respiratory function and systemic involvement.
- Treat early to reduce weakness and calcinosis risk.

questions.stem: Which treatment is listed as the drug of choice for juvenile dermatomyositis?

options.label: A
options.text: Corticosteroids, with immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or cyclosporine when indicated

questions.correctAnswerText: Corticosteroids, with immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or cyclosporine when indicated
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include corticosteroids as the drug of choice for JDM, alongside physiotherapy. Methotrexate or cyclosporine may be used as immunosuppressive treatment. The source mentions a prolonged course; exact duration and taper are specialist-directed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the treatment approach given in the source.
- B. Incorrect. IV acyclovir treats HSV encephalitis.
- C. Incorrect. Nusinersen treats SMA.
- D. Incorrect. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.
- E. Incorrect. Carbamazepine treats selected focal seizures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- JDM treatment: corticosteroids plus physiotherapy.
- Methotrexate/cyclosporine are additional immunosuppressive options.
- Monitor muscle strength, CK, skin disease, calcinosis and swallowing.
- Long-term follow-up is required to assess disease activity and treatment adverse effects.

cases.title: Progressive weakness following a gastrointestinal illness
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old boy is brought to hospital because of progressive difficulty walking. Two weeks earlier, he had an episode of gastroenteritis. Weakness began in both feet and has gradually progressed to involve the legs and hands. Examination shows symmetrical flaccid weakness and absent tendon reflexes. He reports tingling in his toes. During observation, his heart rate and blood pressure fluctuate.

questions.stem: Which cerebrospinal fluid result, when obtained during the second week of illness, would best support the suspected diagnosis over poliomyelitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Marked pleocytosis with a predominantly neutrophilic pattern and low glucose

options.label: B
options.text: Normal protein with a markedly reduced CSF white-cell count

options.label: C
options.text: Increased protein with a normal CSF cell count

options.label: D
options.text: Increased white-cell count with normal protein and isolation of poliovirus

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased protein with a normal CSF cell count
questions.initialExplanation: The clinical pattern suggests Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), an acute post-infectious autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy. The characteristic CSF finding is albuminocytological dissociation: raised protein with a normal cell count, typically evident in the second week.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is an inflammatory CSF pattern more suggestive of CNS infection than the characteristic GBS pattern.
- B. Incorrect. A normal protein level does not demonstrate the albuminocytological dissociation described.
- C. Correct. GBS typically produces increased CSF protein with a normal cell count, particularly by the second week.
- D. Incorrect. standard guidance contrasts poliomyelitis with GBS: polio may produce increased CSF cells and virus isolation, and usually causes asymmetric, predominantly motor paralysis.
- E. Incorrect. This is not the characteristic CSF pattern described for GBS.

The preceding gastrointestinal illness, symmetrical ascending weakness, areflexia, sensory tingling and autonomic involvement collectively favour GBS. standard guidance contrasts this with poliomyelitis, which more typically causes asymmetric pure motor paralysis, anterior horn cell destruction and a CSF white-cell increase.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GBS: acute post-infectious autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy.
- Typical pattern: symmetrical ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia.
- Sensory symptoms and autonomic dysfunction may occur.
- CSF: increased protein with normal cells (albuminocytological dissociation), particularly in the second week.
- Poliomyelitis: usually asymmetric, predominantly motor paralysis; CSF cells may be increased and poliovirus may be isolated.

source.raw: CNS lecture, Pages 32–33 — Guillain–Barré syndrome; GBS versus poliomyelitis.

questions.stem: During admission, the child develops a weak cough, difficulty swallowing and episodes of bradycardia alternating with tachycardia. Which management priority is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Admit for close respiratory and cardiovascular monitoring, provide supportive care, and escalate to ICU care if severe

options.label: B
options.text: Discharge with outpatient physiotherapy because most children recover

options.label: C
options.text: Start corticosteroids as the specific treatment because they accelerate recovery in GBS

options.label: D
options.text: Restrict monitoring to limb power because autonomic abnormalities are not associated with GBS

options.label: E
options.text: Delay respiratory assessment until the weakness reaches the upper limbs

questions.correctAnswerText: Admit for close respiratory and cardiovascular monitoring, provide supportive care, and escalate to ICU care if severe
questions.initialExplanation: Bulbar weakness, a weak cough and fluctuating heart rate indicate potentially serious respiratory and autonomic involvement in GBS. An important point is hospital admission, respiratory support and monitoring, with ICU care in severe cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. GBS can progress to bulbar dysfunction, aspiration risk, respiratory muscle paralysis and respiratory failure. Autonomic dysfunction may cause tachycardia, bradycardia, arrhythmias and blood-pressure instability. Close inpatient monitoring and escalation to ICU when severe are therefore essential.
- B. Incorrect. Outpatient management is unsafe when bulbar, respiratory or autonomic complications are developing.
- C. Incorrect. standard guidance specifically states that corticosteroids have no beneficial effect in GBS and may delay recovery. IV immunoglobulin is listed as the drug of choice; plasmapheresis is an alternative.
- D. Incorrect. Autonomic dysfunction is a recognized feature and can be clinically dangerous.
- E. Incorrect. Respiratory involvement can develop during progression and must be assessed early rather than waiting for a particular distribution of limb weakness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GBS may affect motor, sensory and autonomic nerves.
- Bulbar weakness increases aspiration risk.
- Respiratory muscle involvement can cause respiratory failure.
- Dysautonomia may cause tachycardia, bradycardia, arrhythmias and blood-pressure instability.
- Admit, monitor respiratory and cardiovascular status, and use ICU care when severe.
- standard guidance-specific treatment: IVIG is the drug of choice; plasmapheresis is an alternative. Corticosteroids are not beneficial.

source.raw: CNS lecture, Pages 32–33 — GBS clinical picture, autonomic dysfunction, supportive and specific treatment.
source.pages: 32–33 — GBS clinical picture, autonomic dysfunction, supportive and specific treatment

cases.title: A newborn lies in a frog-like posture and has marked head lag
cases.vignette: A 2-month-old infant is noted to lie with abducted, externally rotated limbs in a frog-like posture. On pull-to-sit there is marked head lag. When held vertically, the infant slips through the examiner's hands; on ventral suspension the trunk hangs in a C-shaped curve. The clinician evaluates central versus peripheral causes of hypotonia.

questions.stem: What does the term "floppy infant" describe?

options.label: A
options.text: An infant with spasticity and scissoring

options.label: E
options.text: An infant with recurrent absence seizures

questions.correctAnswerText: An infant with marked hypotonia
questions.initialExplanation: The floppy infant describes an infant with marked hypotonia. Clinical findings include frog-like posture, head lag on traction, a C-shaped rag-doll posture on ventral suspension and slipping through the examiner's hands on vertical suspension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Spasticity and scissoring indicate increased tone, not a floppy infant.
- B. Incorrect. Macrocephaly is a head-size abnormality and does not define hypotonia.
- C. Incorrect. Hyperreflexia is not the defining feature of a floppy infant.
- D. Correct. This is the definition.
- E. Incorrect. Absence seizures are unrelated to infant hypotonia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Floppy infant = marked hypotonia.
- Frog-like posture.
- Marked head lag on pull-to-sit.
- C-shaped/rag-doll trunk on ventral suspension.
- Slips through the hands on vertical suspension.

questions.stem: Which group contains central causes of hypotonia listed?

options.label: A
options.text: GBS, lead neuropathy and peripheral nerve injury

options.label: E
options.text: Brain malformation/injury, metabolic disease, congenital hypothyroidism and chromosomal syndromes

questions.correctAnswerText: Brain malformation/injury, metabolic disease, congenital hypothyroidism and chromosomal syndromes
questions.initialExplanation: Central hypotonia arises from CNS abnormalities including cerebral malformations, hypoxic-ischaemic or haemorrhagic lesions, metabolic disorders, endocrine causes such as congenital hypothyroidism and chromosomal/syndromic conditions such as trisomy 21 and Prader-Willi syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GBS, lead neuropathy and peripheral nerve injury affect the peripheral motor pathway.
- B. Incorrect. DMD/Becker are primary muscle disorders and cause peripheral hypotonia/weakness.
- C. Incorrect. NMJ disorders are peripheral causes.
- D. Incorrect. SMA, congenital myopathy and myasthenia are peripheral causes.
- E. Correct. These are central causes listed in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Central hypotonia: cerebral malformation, HIE/ICH, metabolic disease, hypothyroidism, trisomy 21 and Prader-Willi syndrome.
- Peripheral hypotonia: anterior horn cell, peripheral nerve, NMJ or muscle disease.
- Central causes may be associated with altered consciousness, seizures, developmental delay or dysmorphic features.
- Peripheral causes often have prominent weakness, reduced reflexes and muscle atrophy/fasciculations.

questions.stem: A floppy infant has tongue fasciculations, absent reflexes, weak cry and poor sucking. Which anatomical level of the motor pathway should be considered first?
questions.correctAnswerText: Anterior horn cell (e.g. SMA type 1)
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include SMA type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann syndrome) as a peripheral cause of hypotonia involving the anterior horn cells. Tongue fasciculations, absent reflexes and bulbar weakness are important clues.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia, not an anterior horn cell syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Basal ganglia lesions cause extrapyramidal movement abnormalities.
- C. Incorrect. Occipital lesions affect vision.
- D. Correct. This is the classic anterior horn cell cause of a floppy infant.
- E. Incorrect. Central lesions may cause hypotonia but do not typically produce tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes as the key pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Peripheral floppy infant causes include SMA type 1 (anterior horn cell), neonatal myasthenia (NMJ), congenital myopathies and myotonic dystrophy.
- Tongue fasciculations and areflexia strongly suggest anterior horn cell disease.
- Weak cry/suck and respiratory muscle weakness indicate bulbar/respiratory involvement.
- Genetic testing for SMN1 is central to confirming SMA.

cases.title: An infant has an abnormal skull shape and a palpable ridge over a cranial suture
cases.vignette: A 5-month-old infant has an elongated, asymmetrical skull shape. Examination reveals a palpable ridge along a cranial suture.

questions.stem: Which description best matches scaphocephaly (dolichocephaly)?

options.label: D
options.text: A flat occiput with a broad, short skull

options.label: E
options.text: An asymmetrical flattened head on one side

questions.correctAnswerText: A long, narrow head
questions.initialExplanation: Scaphocephaly (dolichocephaly) is a long, narrow head shape, often related to sagittal suture fusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Scaphocephaly is a long and narrow skull.
- B. Incorrect. A keel-shaped forehead with hypertelorism is trigonocephaly.
- C. Incorrect. An elongated skull upward is turricephaly/oxycephaly.
- D. Incorrect. A flat occiput with a broad short skull is brachycephaly.
- E. Incorrect. Asymmetrical flattening is plagiocephaly.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Brachycephaly: flat occiput/broad short head (e.g. Down syndrome in standard guidance).
- Scaphocephaly/dolichocephaly: long, narrow head.
- Plagiocephaly: asymmetrical/flattened one side, often positional.
- Turricephaly/oxycephaly: vertically elongated head.
- Trigonocephaly: keel-shaped forehead and hypertelorism.

questions.stem: Which statement about plagiocephaly is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is an asymmetrical skull shape with flattening on one side and is often positional

options.label: B
options.text: It is an absent cranial vault

options.label: C
options.text: It is defined by excessive CSF in the ventricles

options.label: D
options.text: It is typically caused by fusion of most cranial sutures

options.label: E
options.text: It is a long, narrow skull

questions.correctAnswerText: It is an asymmetrical skull shape with flattening on one side and is often positional
questions.initialExplanation: Plagiocephaly is an asymmetrical head shape with flattening on one side. Clinical guidance notes that it is usually positional, although craniosynostosis must be considered when there is a fixed abnormal shape or suture ridge.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the description in the source.
- B. Incorrect. Absence of most of the cranial vault is associated with anencephaly.
- C. Incorrect. Excess CSF causing ventricular enlargement is hydrocephalus.
- D. Incorrect. Fusion of multiple sutures causes generalized craniosynostosis.
- E. Incorrect. A long narrow head is scaphocephaly.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Positional plagiocephaly: asymmetrical flattening, often acquired after birth.
- Craniosynostosis should be considered if the deformity is fixed or there is a palpable suture ridge.
- Assess head growth, fontanelles, sutures and neurological development.
- Refer suspected craniosynostosis for craniofacial/neurosurgical evaluation.

questions.stem: What is the definition of craniosynostosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of closure of the neural tube

options.label: B
options.text: Excess accumulation of CSF in the ventricles

options.label: C
options.text: Delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle

options.label: D
options.text: A congenital absence of the cerebellum

options.label: E
options.text: Premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures

questions.correctAnswerText: Premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures
questions.initialExplanation: Craniosynostosis is premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, leading to distortion of the skull shape. It may be localized (one suture) or generalized (multiple sutures).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes a neural tube defect.
- B. Incorrect. This is hydrocephalus.
- C. Incorrect. Delayed fontanelle closure may occur in other conditions and does not define craniosynostosis.
- D. Incorrect. This is a separate congenital brain malformation.
- E. Correct. This is the definition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Craniosynostosis = premature fusion of one or more sutures.
- Localized: single suture; usually causes an abnormal skull shape.
- Generalized: multiple sutures; may cause microcephaly, developmental delay and raised ICP.
- Syndromic associations include Apert and Crouzon syndromes.

questions.stem: A child has generalized craniosynostosis with multiple sutures fused, microcephaly and developmental delay. Which additional association is listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Apert or Crouzon syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that generalized craniosynostosis involves multiple sutures and may be associated with syndromes such as Apert or Crouzon. Crouzon syndrome may also feature exophthalmos.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. DMD is an X-linked muscular dystrophy.
- B. Incorrect. West syndrome is an infantile epilepsy syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. GBS is an acute peripheral neuropathy.
- D. Correct. These are the syndromic associations listed.
- E. Incorrect. MG is a neuromuscular junction disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Generalized craniosynostosis can produce microcephaly and developmental delay.
- Apert and Crouzon syndromes are important associations.
- Crouzon may cause exophthalmos.
- Skull X-ray/CT is used to evaluate suture fusion; surgery is considered in specialist craniofacial centres for raised ICP or deformity.

questions.stem: What is the definition of macrocephaly used?

options.label: A
options.text: Head circumference less than 2 SD below the mean

options.label: B
options.text: OFC above the 97th-98th centile or more than 2 SD above the mean for age and sex

options.label: D
options.text: Any head circumference above 35 cm at birth

questions.correctAnswerText: OFC above the 97th-98th centile or more than 2 SD above the mean for age and sex
questions.initialExplanation: Macrocephaly is defined by an occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) above the 97th/98th centile or more than 2 standard deviations above the mean for age and sex.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes microcephaly.
- B. Correct. This is the definition.
- C. Incorrect. This defines microcephaly.
- D. Incorrect. A single fixed head circumference value is not used to define macrocephaly across ages.
- E. Incorrect. This is within the expected centile range.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Macrocephaly: OFC >97th/98th centile or >2 SD.
- Always interpret head circumference by age and sex.
- Plot serial measurements on a growth chart.
- Causes include familial, hydrocephalus, skeletal/metabolic disorders and raised ICP.

questions.stem: Which group contains causes of macrocephaly listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Familial macrocephaly, hydrocephalus, rickets, thalassaemia, achondroplasia, MPS or Sotos syndrome

questions.correctAnswerText: Familial macrocephaly, hydrocephalus, rickets, thalassaemia, achondroplasia, MPS or Sotos syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include familial macrocephaly, hydrocephalus, rickets, thalassaemia major, achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta, mucopolysaccharidosis, Sotos syndrome and causes of raised ICP such as chronic subdural haematoma, brain tumour and neurofibromatosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are examples in the source.
- B. Incorrect. Dehydration and iron deficiency do not cause the described group of macrocephaly causes.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism may cause developmental delay and macroglossia, but it is not the sole cause listed.
- D. Incorrect. DMD is a muscular dystrophy and is not a cause of macrocephaly.
- E. Incorrect. These are infectious/neurological conditions but not the listed common macrocephaly differential.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Macrocephaly causes: familial, hydrocephalus, skeletal/metabolic disorders (rickets, thalassaemia, achondroplasia, OI, MPS), Sotos syndrome.
- Raised ICP causes: subdural haematoma, brain tumour and neurofibromatosis.
- Rapidly increasing OFC, vomiting, bulging fontanelle or developmental regression requires urgent evaluation.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly defines microcephaly?

options.label: A
options.text: Any head circumference that increases by 1 cm per month

options.label: C
options.text: Head circumference above the mean by 2 SD

options.label: D
options.text: OFC below the 3rd centile or more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex

questions.correctAnswerText: OFC below the 3rd centile or more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe microcephaly as an OFC below the 3rd centile (or below the 2nd centile in some charts) or more than 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A rate of head growth must be interpreted with age and centile charts; this is not the definition.
- B. Incorrect. Abnormal shape is not the same as reduced head circumference.
- C. Incorrect. This is macrocephaly.
- D. Correct. This is the definition in the source.
- E. Incorrect. This defines macrocephaly.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Microcephaly: OFC <3rd centile or <2 SD.
- Primary causes include familial and chromosomal syndromes (trisomy 21, 18 and 13).
- Secondary causes include perinatal asphyxia, meningitis, CP, TORCH, irradiation, PKU, fetal alcohol syndrome and craniosynostosis.
- Assess development, growth, dysmorphic features and exposure/infection history.

cases.title: A child with a persistently small head circumference
cases.vignette: A 14-month-old child is referred because serial measurements show that head circumference is below the third centile for age and sex. The child had significant perinatal asphyxia and a prolonged neonatal admission. The parents ask whether a small head circumference is always inherited.

questions.stem: Which approach best reflects the causes of microcephaly listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Consider hydrocephalus and familial macrocephaly as the relevant explanations

options.label: B
options.text: Assume that typical presentations are due to craniosynostosis and proceed directly to surgery

options.label: C
options.text: Attribute the finding to normal variation without reviewing pregnancy and neonatal history

options.label: D
options.text: Assess genetic/syndromic causes and secondary causes such as perinatal injury, infection, metabolic disease or maternal exposure

options.label: E
options.text: Diagnose a neurocutaneous syndrome whenever head circumference is below the third centile

questions.correctAnswerText: Assess genetic/syndromic causes and secondary causes such as perinatal injury, infection, metabolic disease or maternal exposure
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance divides microcephaly into primary and secondary causes. The history of perinatal asphyxia in this child makes a secondary cause important to consider, but the wider differential must also be reviewed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hydrocephalus and familial macrocephaly are causes of an enlarged head, not the listed explanation for microcephaly.
- B. Incorrect. Craniosynostosis is one possible cause listed, but it is not the only cause and the clinical context does not justify assuming it.
- C. Incorrect. A persistently low head circumference requires assessment of the child's history and possible underlying causes.
- D. Correct. This reflects standard guidance's distinction between primary microcephaly (familial, chromosomal and syndromic causes) and secondary microcephaly (perinatal asphyxia, meningitis, TORCH infection, irradiation, metabolic causes such as PKU and maternal drug exposure).
- E. Incorrect. A small head circumference alone does not establish a neurocutaneous syndrome.

The important reasoning step is to classify the small head circumference and use the antenatal, perinatal, developmental and family history to guide the search for an underlying cause.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Microcephaly: head circumference below the third centile (or more than 2 SD below the mean).
- Primary causes include familial and chromosomal/syndromic causes.
- Secondary causes include perinatal asphyxia, meningitis, TORCH infection, irradiation, metabolic disease and maternal drug exposure.
- Interpret head circumference in the context of serial growth and clinical history.

source.raw: CNS lecture, Page 40 — Abnormal head size; microcephaly.

cases.title: A child develops persistent morning headaches, vomiting and an unsteady gait
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child has several weeks of progressive morning headache and projectile vomiting. Parents report worsening school performance and recent clumsiness. Examination shows papilloedema and truncal ataxia.

questions.stem: Which statement about paediatric brain tumours is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: They are usually primary tumours, are the second most common paediatric cancer after leukaemia and the commonest solid tumour

options.label: C
options.text: They are typically metastatic from lung cancer

options.label: E
options.text: They are less common than most other solid tumours combined and not usually cause raised ICP

questions.correctAnswerText: They are usually primary tumours, are the second most common paediatric cancer after leukaemia and the commonest solid tumour
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that brain tumours in children are almost always primary, are the second most common paediatric tumour after leukaemia and are the most common solid tumour of childhood.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Brain tumours are an important childhood cancer.
- B. Correct. This is the epidemiological summary in the source.
- C. Incorrect. Childhood brain tumours are usually primary, not metastases from adult-type cancers.
- D. Incorrect. They range from low-grade to highly malignant tumours.
- E. Incorrect. Brain tumours commonly cause raised ICP and are the commonest solid tumours.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Paediatric brain tumours are usually primary.
- Second most common paediatric cancer after leukaemia.
- Most common solid tumour in children.
- Approximately 60% are infratentorial and 40% supratentorial.

questions.stem: Which symptom pattern is particularly concerning for raised intracranial pressure due to a brain tumour?

options.label: A
options.text: Brief headache that resolves with hydration and no other symptoms

options.label: B
options.text: A single uncomplicated febrile seizure with full recovery

options.label: C
options.text: Persistent/recurrent headache with morning or projectile vomiting, visual symptoms and progressive gait disturbance

options.label: D
options.text: Isolated pain in one finger after sport

questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent/recurrent headache with morning or projectile vomiting, visual symptoms and progressive gait disturbance
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include persistent or recurrent headache, persistent/morning projectile vomiting, visual symptoms, squint/nystagmus, papilloedema, cranial nerve palsy, seizures, hemiparesis, ataxia and developmental/behavioural deterioration as features of brain tumour/raised ICP.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A brief self-limiting headache without red flags is less concerning.
- B. Incorrect. A single simple febrile seizure does not indicate a brain tumour.
- C. Correct. The combination of progressive headache, vomiting, visual symptoms and ataxia is highly concerning.
- D. Incorrect. A localized finger injury is unrelated.
- E. Incorrect. These are upper respiratory symptoms.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Raised ICP: persistent/recurrent headache, morning/projectile vomiting, papilloedema, diplopia/squint/nystagmus.
- Focal signs: seizures, hemiparesis, cranial nerve palsy and ataxia.
- Behavioural changes, declining school performance, growth/endocrine disturbance may occur.
- Papilloedema is a late sign; its absence does not exclude raised ICP.

questions.stem: Which paediatric brain tumour is most common and can range from low-grade astrocytoma to glioblastoma?
questions.correctAnswerText: Astrocytoma
questions.initialExplanation: Astrocytoma is described as the most common paediatric brain tumour type. It ranges from low-grade to highly malignant forms and may be cystic and slow-growing.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ependymoma commonly arises from the fourth ventricle and is locally invasive.
- B. Incorrect. Brainstem glioma causes cranial nerve and pyramidal tract signs and has a poor prognosis.
- C. Correct. Astrocytoma is the most common tumour type listed.
- D. Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma is a suprasellar tumour arising from Rathke pouch remnants.
- E. Incorrect. Medulloblastoma is a common malignant posterior fossa tumour but not the most common overall.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Astrocytoma: most common type (~40%).
- May be cystic/slow-growing or high-grade malignant.
- Presentation may include raised ICP, seizures, hemiplegia or behavioural changes.
- MRI is the main diagnostic imaging test; treatment depends on grade/location and may include surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A child has progressive headache, vomiting and ataxia. MRI shows a midline posterior fossa tumour. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Medulloblastoma
questions.initialExplanation: Medulloblastoma is typically located in the midline posterior fossa and causes raised ICP and cerebellar signs such as ataxia and abnormal eye movements. Clinical guidance notes a risk of spinal metastases at diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Meningiomas are not the classic midline posterior fossa tumour described.
- B. Incorrect. Pituitary adenomas arise in the sellar region and are uncommon in young children.
- C. Incorrect. Neurofibromas are associated with neurofibromatosis and are not the typical posterior fossa tumour described.
- D. Correct. The posterior fossa midline location with raised ICP and ataxia fits medulloblastoma.
- E. Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma is usually suprasellar and causes visual field defects and pituitary dysfunction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Medulloblastoma: usually midline posterior fossa.
- Features: raised ICP, ataxia and abnormal eye movements.
- Spinal dissemination can occur; evaluate neuraxis according to oncology protocol.
- Treatment commonly includes surgical resection and adjuvant chemotherapy/radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A child with a posterior fossa tumour has ataxia, multiple cranial nerve palsies and pyramidal tract signs. Imaging shows a lesion centred in the brainstem. Which tumour is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Brainstem glioma
questions.initialExplanation: Brainstem glioma may cause ataxia, cranial nerve palsies and pyramidal tract signs. Clinical descriptions include a poor prognosis and treatment that is often mainly palliative, including radiotherapy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Meningocele is a neural tube defect.
- B. Incorrect. Pituitary adenoma causes endocrine/visual changes.
- C. Correct. The brainstem location and combination of cranial nerve and long-tract signs are characteristic.
- D. Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma is suprasellar and causes visual/pituitary problems.
- E. Incorrect. A cerebral hemispheric astrocytoma may cause seizures/focal deficits but does not match the brainstem-centred lesion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Brainstem glioma: ataxia + cranial nerve palsy + pyramidal signs.
- MRI is the key imaging test.
- Prognosis is poor in diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma; management is specialist-led.
- Do not delay urgent neuro-oncology referral.

questions.stem: Which statement about ependymoma is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It occurs in the peripheral nerves

options.label: B
options.text: It is typically located in the suprasellar region

options.label: C
options.text: It commonly arises in the fourth ventricle and may cause raised ICP and cranial nerve palsies

options.label: D
options.text: It is a primary muscle tumour

options.label: E
options.text: It is caused by an SMN1 mutation

questions.correctAnswerText: It commonly arises in the fourth ventricle and may cause raised ICP and cranial nerve palsies
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include ependymoma as a locally invasive tumour, commonly arising from the fourth ventricle. It may cause symptoms of raised ICP and cranial nerve palsy. Treatment usually involves surgery and radiotherapy depending on grade and resection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. It is not a peripheral nerve tumour.
- B. Incorrect. Suprasellar location is typical of craniopharyngioma.
- C. Correct. This is the location and presentation described.
- D. Incorrect. Ependymoma is a CNS tumour, not a muscle tumour.
- E. Incorrect. SMN1 mutation causes SMA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ependymoma: often fourth ventricle, locally invasive.
- Raised ICP and cranial nerve palsy may occur.
- Treatment: surgery and radiotherapy as indicated.
- Prognosis depends on location, grade and completeness of resection.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old has headaches, bitemporal hemianopia, growth failure, weight gain and diabetes insipidus. Imaging shows a calcified cystic suprasellar mass. Which tumour is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Craniopharyngioma
questions.initialExplanation: Craniopharyngioma is a developmental tumour arising from remnants of Rathke pouch. It grows slowly in the suprasellar region, is locally invasive, often has solid/cystic areas and commonly calcifies. It may cause bitemporal hemianopia and pituitary dysfunction, including growth failure and diabetes insipidus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The suprasellar calcified mass with visual field and pituitary dysfunction is characteristic.
- B. Incorrect. Cerebellar astrocytoma causes posterior fossa symptoms but not typical pituitary/endocrine dysfunction.
- C. Incorrect. Medulloblastoma usually arises in the posterior fossa and causes ataxia/raised ICP.
- D. Incorrect. Brainstem glioma causes cranial nerve and pyramidal signs.
- E. Incorrect. Fourth ventricular ependymoma causes posterior fossa/raised ICP signs, not a suprasellar syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Craniopharyngioma: remnant of Rathke pouch, suprasellar.
- Often calcified and cystic.
- Bitemporal hemianopia, growth failure, pituitary hormone deficiency, diabetes insipidus and weight gain.
- Long-term visual and pituitary follow-up is essential after treatment.

cases.title: A school-aged child has recurrent pulsating headaches with vomiting
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child has recurrent episodes of frontal or temporal pulsating headache lasting several hours. The pain may be unilateral or bilateral, is worsened by physical activity and is associated with nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light and sound. The child feels better after sleeping. A parent has a history of migraine.

questions.stem: Which primary headache disorder is most likely?

options.label: E
options.text: Raised intracranial pressure due to tumour

questions.correctAnswerText: Migraine
questions.initialExplanation: Migraine is the most frequent important primary headache in children and adolescents. It may be unilateral or bilateral, pulsating, last 1-72 hours and be associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, photophobia and phonophobia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Tension-type headache is usually symmetrical and described as a band-like pressure or tightness without associated symptoms.
- B. Incorrect. Medication-overuse headache is associated with frequent use of acute analgesics and a chronic headache pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Cluster headache causes repeated attacks of very severe unilateral pain, often with autonomic features.
- D. Correct. The pulsating pain, nausea/vomiting, light/sound sensitivity and relief with sleep are typical.
- E. Incorrect. Raised ICP is suggested by progressive/persistent headache, morning vomiting, papilloedema or focal neurological signs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Migraine is common in school-aged children and adolescents.
- Headache may be unilateral or bilateral and pulsatile.
- Episodes last 1-72 hours.
- Associated symptoms: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, photophobia and phonophobia.
- Pain may worsen with physical activity and improve with sleep.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes tension-type headache from migraine?

options.label: A
options.text: Headache preceded by visual zigzag lines and transient sensory symptoms

options.label: B
options.text: Recurrent unilateral pulsating pain with vomiting and photophobia

options.label: C
options.text: Symmetrical gradual-onset tightness or band-like pressure, usually without other symptoms

options.label: D
options.text: Repeated attacks of very severe one-sided pain

options.label: E
options.text: Headache with papilloedema and progressive neurological deficit

questions.correctAnswerText: Symmetrical gradual-onset tightness or band-like pressure, usually without other symptoms
questions.initialExplanation: Tension-type headache is described as a symmetrical headache of gradual onset, often like a tight band or pressure, without other significant symptoms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes migraine with aura.
- B. Incorrect. This is typical of migraine.
- C. Correct. This is the tension-type description in the source.
- D. Incorrect. This is more consistent with cluster headache.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests a secondary headache with raised ICP.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tension-type: gradual, symmetrical, pressure/band-like, usually no associated symptoms.
- Cluster: repeated attacks of very severe unilateral pain.
- Migraine: pulsatile, may be unilateral/bilateral, with GI and sensory symptoms.
- New or progressive headache with red flags requires investigation for secondary causes.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old reports flashing lights and a zigzag line in one visual field, followed by unilateral pulsating headache. Which type of migraine is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Migraine with aura
questions.initialExplanation: Migraine with aura is less common than migraine without aura. Aura may be visual, sensory, dysphasic or motor and precedes the headache, although aura can occur without a subsequent headache. Positive visual phenomena include flashes and zigzag lines; negative phenomena include scotoma or hemianopia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A transient visual phenomenon preceding the headache is a typical aura.
- B. Incorrect. Migraine without aura has no preceding focal neurological aura.
- C. Incorrect. Cluster headache causes severe unilateral attacks, often with autonomic symptoms, not a typical visual aura.
- D. Incorrect. Tension headache does not usually have focal visual symptoms.
- E. Incorrect. Medication overuse does not explain the stereotyped visual aura.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Migraine with aura is uncommon (~10% ).
- Aura types: visual, sensory, dysphasic or motor.
- Positive visual aura: flashes/zigzag lines.
- Negative visual aura: scotoma or hemianopia.
- Aura may occur without headache.

questions.stem: Which factor is listed as a possible migraine trigger in children and adolescents?

options.label: A
options.text: Dehydration, stress, school demands, exercise, menstruation or certain foods

questions.correctAnswerText: Dehydration, stress, school demands, exercise, menstruation or certain foods
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include exercise, stress, school, menstruation, head trauma, dehydration and certain foods as possible triggers. A positive family history is also common.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These triggers are listed in the source.
- B. Incorrect. VP shunt infection is a separate complication causing symptoms of raised ICP or infection.
- C. Incorrect. Muscular dystrophy does not act as a common migraine trigger.
- D. Incorrect. Folic acid supplementation is not a migraine trigger listed.
- E. Incorrect. Meningitis is a secondary cause of headache, not a routine migraine trigger.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Migraine triggers: stress, school, exercise, menstruation, head trauma, dehydration and some foods.
- Ask about family history, sleep, hydration, missed meals and lifestyle.
- A headache diary can help identify personal triggers and attack frequency.
- Avoid assuming every headache is migraine without checking for red flags.

questions.stem: A child has recurrent migraine attacks with aura and occasionally unilateral weakness. Which rare migraine subtype should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Familial or sporadic hemiplegic migraine
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include familial and sporadic hemiplegic migraine as uncommon forms. Familial hemiplegic migraine may be caused by an inherited calcium-channel defect. Motor aura causes transient weakness and requires careful differentiation from stroke.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Medication overuse causes frequent headache but not stereotyped reversible motor aura.
- B. Correct. Reversible motor weakness with migraine suggests hemiplegic migraine.
- C. Incorrect. Post-LP headache is positional and follows lumbar puncture.
- D. Incorrect. Cluster headache causes severe unilateral pain, not hemiplegic aura.
- E. Incorrect. Tension headache does not produce a motor aura.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hemiplegic migraine is a rare migraine subtype with motor aura.
- Familial form may be autosomal dominant and linked to calcium-channel defects.
- Acute focal weakness must be assessed urgently to exclude stroke or other structural causes.
- Do not label a first episode of weakness as migraine without appropriate assessment.

questions.stem: Which treatment is listed for an acute uncomplicated migraine attack in a child?

options.label: A
options.text: Paracetamol or an NSAID, with an antiemetic when needed

questions.correctAnswerText: Paracetamol or an NSAID, with an antiemetic when needed
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes analgesia such as paracetamol or an NSAID, antiemetics such as prochlorperazine or cyclizine for nausea, and selected triptans (e.g. sumatriptan). Physical measures and psychological support may also help.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the acute treatment options described.
- B. Incorrect. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.
- C. Incorrect. Antibiotics are used for bacterial infection, not primary migraine.
- D. Incorrect. A VP shunt treats selected cases of hydrocephalus.
- E. Incorrect. Nusinersen treats SMA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute migraine: paracetamol or NSAID.
- Antiemetics may help associated nausea/vomiting.
- Triptans (e.g. sumatriptan) are options in selected children under appropriate guidance.
- Sleep, hydration, regular meals, trigger management and psychological support are useful.

questions.stem: A child has frequent, intrusive migraine attacks affecting school attendance. Which prophylactic options are listed?

options.label: D
options.text: Topiramate or valproate, propranolol, or pizotifen in selected cases

questions.correctAnswerText: Topiramate or valproate, propranolol, or pizotifen in selected cases
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include prophylactic options when headaches are frequent and intrusive, including topiramate or valproate, beta-blockers such as propranolol and pizotifen. Pizotifen may cause weight gain and sleepiness; overdose may cause dangerous arrhythmias. Propranolol is contraindicated in asthma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are used for selected infection contact prophylaxis.
- B. Incorrect. These drugs treat suspected infection, not migraine prophylaxis.
- C. Incorrect. Nusinersen treats SMA and baclofen reduces spasticity.
- D. Correct. These are the prophylactic options in the source.
- E. Incorrect. These are acetylcholinesterase inhibitors for myasthenia gravis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider prophylaxis when migraine is frequent or significantly intrusive.
- Options in standard guidance: topiramate, valproate, propranolol and pizotifen.
- Propranolol should be avoided in asthma.
- Pizotifen may cause weight gain/somnolence; overdose can cause arrhythmia.
- Choose prophylaxis according to comorbidities, age and current pediatric guidance.

questions.stem: A child has headache that is worse when lying down or coughing, wakes the child from sleep, and is associated with persistent morning vomiting and declining school performance. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: This is typically migraine without aura

options.label: B
options.text: This is typical uncomplicated tension-type headache

options.label: C
options.text: This is diagnostic of cluster headache

options.label: E
options.text: These are red flags for a secondary headache such as a space-occupying lesion or raised ICP

questions.correctAnswerText: These are red flags for a secondary headache such as a space-occupying lesion or raised ICP
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include positional headache worse lying down/coughing/straining, headache waking the child, persistent or morning vomiting, confusion, personality or school-performance change, growth failure, visual-field defects, papilloedema, torticollis, gait/coordination abnormalities, bradycardia and cranial bruits as red flags.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Migraine may cause morning headache, but persistent vomiting, progression and neurological/behavioural changes need investigation.
- B. Incorrect. Tension headache is usually symmetrical and pressure-like without these red flags.
- C. Incorrect. Cluster headache is a different primary headache disorder with severe unilateral attacks and autonomic symptoms.
- D. Incorrect. These features increase suspicion of raised ICP.
- E. Correct. The combination suggests raised ICP and requires urgent assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Red flags: worsening lying down/cough/strain, headache waking child, persistent/morning vomiting.
- Behaviour/school decline, growth failure and focal neurological/visual signs are concerning.
- Papilloedema is important but may be a late sign.
- Consider tumour, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, infection, vascular causes and other secondary disorders.

topics.name: Bell Palsy and Facial Nerve Palsy

cases.title: A child develops acute unilateral complete facial weakness
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face. The child cannot wrinkle the left forehead, close the left eye tightly or show the left teeth. The angle of the mouth deviates to the right and saliva dribbles from the left side. Taste is reduced over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on the affected side.

questions.stem: Which lesion best explains these findings?

options.label: D
options.text: Right upper motor neuron facial weakness

options.label: E
options.text: Left lower motor neuron facial nerve (VII) palsy

questions.correctAnswerText: Left lower motor neuron facial nerve (VII) palsy
questions.initialExplanation: Bell palsy is an isolated lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve, causing complete ipsilateral facial weakness including the forehead. It may affect eye closure, forehead wrinkling, nasolabial fold, mouth movement and taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The trigeminal nerve supplies facial sensation and mastication, not the facial motor pattern described.
- B. Incorrect. Oculomotor palsy affects eye movements, pupil and eyelid elevation, not the entire side of the face.
- C. Incorrect. Hypoglossal palsy causes tongue weakness/deviation.
- D. Incorrect. UMN facial weakness usually spares the forehead due to bilateral cortical innervation.
- E. Correct. Complete ipsilateral upper and lower facial weakness indicates an LMN VII lesion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bell palsy: isolated LMN VII palsy.
- Complete ipsilateral facial weakness includes forehead and eye closure.
- Mouth deviates to the healthy side.
- May reduce taste on anterior 2/3 of tongue on affected side.
- Differentiate from UMN lesion, in which forehead movement is relatively preserved.

questions.stem: Which feature may suggest an associated cause of Bell palsy rather than idiopathic Bell palsy?

options.label: A
options.text: Ear vesicles suggesting zoster/HSV, or exposure compatible with Lyme disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Ear vesicles suggesting zoster/HSV, or exposure compatible with Lyme disease
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that Bell palsy is often idiopathic but may be associated with herpes simplex virus or Lyme disease. Painful vesicles around the external ear suggest a herpetic cause (e.g. Ramsay Hunt syndrome).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Vesicles near the ear or relevant Lyme exposure suggest a secondary cause.
- B. Incorrect. Calf pseudohypertrophy suggests DMD.
- C. Incorrect. Kernig sign indicates meningeal irritation.
- D. Incorrect. Gower sign indicates proximal muscle weakness.
- E. Incorrect. A bulging fontanelle suggests raised ICP in an infant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bell palsy may be idiopathic.
- Consider HSV/VZV if vesicles or ear pain are present.
- Consider Lyme disease when exposure/clinical context supports it.
- Examine for associated CN VIII involvement, brainstem signs or other focal neurological deficits.

questions.stem: A child with Bell palsy cannot close the affected eye. Which management measure is particularly important to prevent corneal injury?

options.label: A
options.text: Apply topical antibiotic to the tongue

options.label: C
options.text: Frequent lubricating eye drops/ointment and eye protection or patching as needed

questions.correctAnswerText: Frequent lubricating eye drops/ointment and eye protection or patching as needed
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes eye care with lubricating drops or ointment, an eye patch and, in severe cases, tarsorrhaphy to prevent exposure keratitis. Prednisone given within the first week may speed recovery; acyclovir is added when herpes is suspected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotic treatment to the tongue has no role.
- B. Incorrect. Antiseizure drugs do not treat facial nerve palsy.
- C. Correct. Corneal protection is essential when eye closure is impaired.
- D. Incorrect. Lack of lubrication increases the risk of exposure keratitis.
- E. Incorrect. LP is not routine for typical isolated Bell palsy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Protect cornea with lubrication and patch/taping when needed.
- Clinical descriptions include prednisone during the first week to improve recovery.
- Add acyclovir if a herpetic cause is suspected.
- Most children recover completely, although recovery may take several months.
- Consider alternative diagnoses if there is CN VIII involvement, multiple cranial neuropathies or other focal signs.

cases.title: Acute unilateral facial weakness with ear pain
cases.vignette: An 8-year-old child develops sudden weakness of the entire left side of the face. The child cannot wrinkle the left forehead, close the left eye tightly or retain air in the left cheek. There are painful vesicles around the left external ear.

questions.stem: In addition to protecting the exposed eye, which specific treatment should be considered because of the associated finding?

options.label: B
options.text: Acyclovir because the painful external-ear vesicles suggest an associated herpes infection

options.label: C
options.text: IV immunoglobulin for presumed Guillain–Barré syndrome

options.label: D
options.text: Long-term sodium valproate to prevent recurrent facial weakness

options.label: E
options.text: No additional treatment because vesicles are unrelated to facial nerve palsy

questions.correctAnswerText: Acyclovir because the painful external-ear vesicles suggest an associated herpes infection
questions.initialExplanation: The complete ipsilateral facial weakness, including loss of forehead movement and inability to close the eye, indicates a lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy. Clinical guidance notes that painful vesicles around the external ear may indicate an associated herpes infection and advises acyclovir when herpes is suspected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Carbamazepine is listed for focal seizures and does not treat facial nerve palsy.
- B. Correct. The painful external-ear vesicles are a clue to a possible herpes-associated cause; Recommended management includes acyclovir if herpes is suspected.
- C. Incorrect. IVIG is the specific treatment listed for GBS, which presents with an acute polyneuropathy rather than an isolated unilateral facial palsy.
- D. Incorrect. Sodium valproate is an antiseizure medication and has no role in treating this facial palsy.
- E. Incorrect. The vesicles are clinically relevant because Recognized features include herpes simplex virus as a possible associated cause.

Eye protection remains essential because inability to close the eyelid can cause exposure keratitis. standard guidance also lists prednisone when given during the first week to speed recovery, alongside lubricating drops or ointment and eye protection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bell's palsy is an isolated LMN paresis of the seventh cranial nerve.
- LMN facial palsy affects the whole ipsilateral half of the face, including the forehead.
- Painful vesicles around the external ear suggest an associated herpes infection.
- Consider acyclovir if herpes is suspected.
- Protect the eye with lubrication and appropriate covering because incomplete closure can cause exposure keratitis.
- Common examples include prednisone during the first week as a treatment that may speed recovery.
