cases.title: A child becomes unsteady after a viral illness
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child develops an unsteady gait and slurred speech several days after chickenpox. The child has wide-based walking, poor balance and difficulty performing coordinated movements. There is no history of trauma or toxin exposure.

questions.stem: What is the definition of ataxia?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete paralysis of one side of the body

options.label: B
options.text: Loss of sensation in a dermatomal distribution

options.label: E
options.text: Increased muscle tone due to an upper motor neuron lesion

questions.correctAnswerText: Incoordination of voluntary movement
questions.initialExplanation: Ataxia is incoordination of voluntary movement. It may arise from cerebellar dysfunction, loss of proprioceptive input (sensory ataxia) or vestibular dysfunction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes hemiplegia.
- B. Incorrect. This is a sensory deficit, not the definition of ataxia.
- C. Incorrect. Seizure activity is a separate paroxysmal neurological event.
- D. Correct. This is the definition.
- E. Incorrect. This describes spasticity due to UMN injury.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ataxia = incoordination of voluntary movement.
- Types: cerebellar, sensory and vestibular.
- Examine gait, stance, limb coordination, speech, eye movements and proprioception.
- Acute ataxia requires exclusion of infection, intoxication, trauma, tumour and vascular causes.

questions.stem: Which finding is most suggestive of cerebellar ataxia rather than sensory ataxia?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of joint position and vibration sense

options.label: B
options.text: Marked worsening of balance when the eyes are closed with a positive Romberg sign

options.label: C
options.text: Absent distal reflexes with sensory loss

options.label: D
options.text: Intention tremor and dysmetria with a wide-based gait

options.label: E
options.text: Improvement of gait when the eyes are closed

questions.correctAnswerText: Intention tremor and dysmetria with a wide-based gait
questions.initialExplanation: Cerebellar ataxia causes incoordination, intention tremor, dysmetria, poor balance and a wide-based/ataxic gait. Sensory ataxia is due to impaired proprioception and becomes worse when visual compensation is removed (positive Romberg).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Loss of proprioception/vibration supports sensory ataxia.
- B. Incorrect. Worsening with eyes closed suggests sensory ataxia.
- C. Incorrect. Distal areflexia with sensory loss suggests peripheral neuropathy.
- D. Correct. Intention tremor, dysmetria and wide-based gait are cerebellar signs.
- E. Incorrect. Closing the eyes generally worsens sensory ataxia rather than improving it.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cerebellar: dysmetria, intention tremor, poor coordination, wide-based gait.
- Sensory: loss of proprioception/vibration; positive Romberg.
- Vestibular: vertigo, nystagmus and imbalance, often worse with head movement.
- A detailed neurological examination helps localize the cause.

questions.stem: Which group contains recognized causes of acute cerebellar ataxia in children listed?

options.label: B
options.text: Postviral cerebellitis, CNS infection/abscess, toxins, trauma, posterior fossa tumour or vascular haemorrhage

questions.correctAnswerText: Postviral cerebellitis, CNS infection/abscess, toxins, trauma, posterior fossa tumour or vascular haemorrhage
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include multiple causes of cerebellar ataxia including viral cerebellitis (e.g. VZV, Coxsackie and echovirus), bacterial meningitis/abscess, encephalitis, toxins/drugs (lead, phenytoin, alcohol, carbamazepine and lamotrigine), trauma, posterior fossa tumour, vascular haemorrhage, migraine, congenital anomalies, metabolic disease and hereditary syndromes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Eye disease does not explain the listed cerebellar ataxia causes.
- B. Correct. These are the major causes listed in the source.
- C. Incorrect. Muscular dystrophy causes progressive weakness rather than primary cerebellar incoordination.
- D. Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome is not a cause of cerebellar ataxia.
- E. Incorrect. Facial nerve palsy causes facial weakness, not cerebellar coordination loss.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Postviral cerebellitis is often self-limiting.
- Exclude dangerous causes: posterior fossa tumour, abscess, encephalitis, trauma and intracranial haemorrhage.
- Review medications/toxin exposure, especially phenytoin and other neurotoxic agents.
- Persistent or progressive ataxia warrants imaging and specialist evaluation.

questions.stem: A child has progressive cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, recurrent respiratory infections and telangiectasia. Which genetic disorder is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ataxia-telangiectasia
questions.initialExplanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder caused by mutation of the ATM gene. It produces progressive cerebellar ataxia and telangiectasia and may be associated with immune deficiency and recurrent infections.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. DMD causes proximal muscle weakness, Gower sign and pseudohypertrophy.
- B. Correct. Ataxia plus telangiectasia and immune dysfunction are characteristic.
- C. Incorrect. Myotonic dystrophy causes myotonia, facial weakness, cataracts and cardiac conduction problems.
- D. Incorrect. NF2 is associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas and other CNS tumours.
- E. Incorrect. Friedreich ataxia is associated with frataxin deficiency, sensory loss, areflexia, pes cavus, diabetes and cardiomyopathy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ataxia-telangiectasia: autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder (ATM gene).
- Progressive cerebellar ataxia and telangiectasia.
- Immunodeficiency/recurrent infections may occur.
- No effective curative treatment is described; management is supportive and complication-focused.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old has gradually progressive gait ataxia, dysarthria, distal lower-limb wasting, absent reflexes and pes cavus. Examination reveals loss of vibration sense and a positive Romberg sign. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Friedreich ataxia
questions.initialExplanation: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive hereditary ataxia caused by a triplet repeat expansion in the FXN gene, resulting in reduced frataxin. It causes progressive cerebellar and sensory ataxia, dysarthria, distal wasting/areflexia, pes cavus and loss of deep sensation. Diabetes and cardiomyopathy may occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Spasmus nutans is characterized by nystagmus, head tilt and head nodding.
- B. Correct. The progressive ataxia, sensory loss, areflexia and pes cavus are classic.
- C. Incorrect. Ataxia-telangiectasia includes telangiectasia and immune deficiency.
- D. Incorrect. GBS is acute/subacute and typically follows infection rather than slowly progressive inherited ataxia.
- E. Incorrect. Benign paroxysmal vertigo causes episodic vertigo with normal examination between attacks.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Friedreich ataxia: autosomal recessive, FXN gene and frataxin deficiency.
- Progressive gait/sensory ataxia, dysarthria, distal wasting, areflexia and pes cavus.
- Positive Romberg reflects sensory/proprioceptive loss.
- Associated complications include diabetes mellitus and cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: A child has acute ataxia, ophthalmoplegia and areflexia following an infection. Which syndrome should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Miller Fisher syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Miller Fisher syndrome is a variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome. The classic triad is ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lennox-Gastaut is a severe childhood epilepsy syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Sturge-Weber is a neurocutaneous vascular syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. West syndrome presents with infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmia.
- D. Incorrect. Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental regression syndrome, usually in girls.
- E. Correct. This is the classic Miller Fisher triad.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Miller Fisher syndrome: ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia.
- It is a GBS variant and is often postinfectious.
- Assess respiratory/autonomic involvement as in other GBS variants.
- Distinguish from cerebellar ataxia due to posterior fossa disease.

cases.title: A child develops sudden focal weakness
cases.vignette: A 8-year-old child with sickle cell disease suddenly develops right-sided weakness and facial asymmetry. The child has no history of trauma. Urgent brain and vascular imaging is arranged.

questions.stem: Which group contains recognized causes/risk factors for paediatric stroke listed?

options.label: B
options.text: Cardiac disease/endocarditis, sickle cell disease, thrombophilia, inflammation, SLE or vascular disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Cardiac disease/endocarditis, sickle cell disease, thrombophilia, inflammation, SLE or vascular disease
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include cardiac causes (cyanotic CHD, e.g. Tetralogy of Fallot, and endocarditis), blood disorders (sickle cell disease and deficiencies of antithrombotic factors), postinfective causes (e.g. varicella), inflammatory diseases (e.g. SLE), metabolic/genetic causes (homocystinuria/mitochondrial disorders), vascular malformations (AVM/moyamoya) and trauma-related arterial dissection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Physiological jaundice does not cause arterial stroke.
- B. Correct. These are the major categories in the source.
- C. Incorrect. Migraine is a common primary headache, not a general explanation for acute stroke.
- D. Incorrect. Febrile seizures do not cause stroke.
- E. Incorrect. Eye disorders do not explain the described cerebrovascular risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Paediatric stroke can be ischemic/thromboembolic or haemorrhagic.
- Risks: cyanotic CHD/endocarditis, sickle cell, thrombophilia, post-varicella, SLE, homocystinuria/mitochondrial disease, AVM/moyamoya and trauma/dissection.
- Sudden focal neurological deficit is an emergency.
- Do not attribute acute weakness to migraine or postictal state without appropriate assessment.

questions.stem: A child with cyanotic congenital heart disease develops an acute focal neurological deficit. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.label: C
options.text: Thromboembolism related to the cardiac disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Thromboembolism related to the cardiac disease
questions.initialExplanation: Cyanotic congenital heart disease and infective endocarditis are recognized cardiac risk factors for paediatric stroke. Thromboembolic events may result in cerebral arterial occlusion and focal ischemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Anterior horn cell degeneration causes LMN weakness such as SMA.
- B. Incorrect. AChR-related disorders cause neuromuscular weakness, not stroke.
- C. Correct. Cardioembolic stroke is an important mechanism in cyanotic CHD/endocarditis.
- D. Incorrect. Excess CSF absorption does not cause stroke.
- E. Incorrect. Peripheral demyelination causes GBS, not an acute cerebral vascular occlusion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cyanotic CHD and endocarditis increase stroke risk.
- Sickle cell disease is another major paediatric stroke risk.
- Consider cardiac source and thrombophilia/vasculitis in the investigation.
- Urgent imaging is necessary to distinguish ischemic from haemorrhagic stroke.

questions.stem: Which investigation set is most appropriate in the initial assessment of suspected paediatric stroke?

options.label: E
options.text: MRI or CT brain, MR angiography, CBC, coagulation profile, vasculitis screen and metabolic tests

questions.correctAnswerText: MRI or CT brain, MR angiography, CBC, coagulation profile, vasculitis screen and metabolic tests
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes urgent brain imaging (MRI or CT) and vascular imaging (MR angiography), together with CBC, coagulation profile, vasculitis screen and metabolic investigations to identify the cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These investigations do not assess acute cerebrovascular disease.
- B. Incorrect. These studies evaluate orthopaedic disease.
- C. Incorrect. EEG may be useful if seizure is suspected but cannot diagnose or classify stroke alone.
- D. Incorrect. CK and dystrophin testing are used for muscular dystrophy.
- E. Correct. This provides brain imaging and an etiological workup.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Urgent MRI/CT brain to identify infarction or haemorrhage.
- MR angiography to assess cerebral vessels.
- CBC/coagulation, vasculitis and metabolic screens help identify cause.
- Tailor additional cardiac and thrombophilia investigations to clinical context.

questions.stem: Which long-term management principle is emphasized after paediatric arterial ischemic stroke?

options.label: A
options.text: No rehabilitation is needed if the child survives

options.label: B
options.text: Long-term corticosteroids in children in routine care

options.label: C
options.text: Multidisciplinary rehabilitation; low-dose aspirin prophylaxis may be used after arterial ischemic stroke under specialist guidance

options.label: D
options.text: Lifelong broad-spectrum antibiotics for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Multidisciplinary rehabilitation; low-dose aspirin prophylaxis may be used after arterial ischemic stroke under specialist guidance
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is multidisciplinary rehabilitation after stroke and lists low-dose aspirin prophylaxis following arterial ischemic stroke. Antithrombotic treatment should be individualized according to stroke mechanism and paediatric specialist guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Rehabilitation is important for motor, speech, cognitive and developmental recovery.
- B. Incorrect. Steroids are not universal treatment for paediatric stroke.
- C. Correct. This is the management principle described in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not routine long-term stroke prophylaxis.
- E. Incorrect. VP shunt is used for selected hydrocephalus, not routine stroke care.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stroke management: acute specialist stroke care, treatment of cause and rehabilitation.
- MDT may include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, psychology and education support.
- Clinical guidance notes low-dose aspirin after arterial ischemic stroke; individualize and consider haemorrhagic causes/contraindications.
- Address modifiable risk factors and secondary prevention.

cases.title: A preschool child has impaired social interaction and repetitive behaviour
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child has delayed speech, poor eye contact, limited social smiling and little interest in playing with other children. The child rarely points to share interest, repeats phrases heard from others and becomes distressed when daily routines change. The parents also report repetitive hand-flapping and unusual sensitivity to certain sounds.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
questions.initialExplanation: ASD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent impairment in social communication/interaction and restricted or repetitive behaviours, interests or activities. Clinical descriptions include typical recognition during preschool years, often between 2 and 4 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ADHD is characterized by inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, not the core social-communication and restricted behaviour pattern.
- B. Incorrect. GBS is an acute postinfectious peripheral neuropathy.
- C. Incorrect. DMD causes progressive proximal muscle weakness.
- D. Incorrect. Absence seizures cause brief staring episodes and do not explain persistent social-communication differences.
- E. Correct. Impaired eye contact/social interaction, language delay, repetitive behaviours and resistance to routine changes are characteristic.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ASD: social communication/interaction impairment plus restricted/repetitive behaviour.
- Often recognized in preschool years (2-4 years ).
- Boys are more commonly diagnosed than girls (approximately 4:1).
- Early developmental history and observation across settings are important.

questions.stem: Which finding is an example of impaired social interaction in ASD?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of vibration sense and positive Romberg sign

options.label: C
options.text: Lack of social smiling, abnormal eye contact, limited gestures and reduced interest in peers

options.label: D
options.text: Exaggerated deep tendon reflexes with Babinski positivity

questions.correctAnswerText: Lack of social smiling, abnormal eye contact, limited gestures and reduced interest in peers
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include lack of social smiling, difficulty making friends, lack of interest in peers, poor understanding of gestures, impaired imagination, abnormal eye contact and failure to point or imitate as social impairment features.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests sensory ataxia.
- B. Incorrect. This is a feature of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- C. Correct. These are core social interaction features listed.
- D. Incorrect. These findings suggest an upper motor neuron lesion.
- E. Incorrect. Kernig sign indicates meningeal irritation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Social features: poor eye contact, reduced social smile, impaired joint attention/pointing, reduced imitation and limited interest in peers.
- Child may talk at people rather than with them.
- Limited understanding of gestures and non-verbal communication may be present.
- Assess social reciprocity across settings and developmental stages.

questions.stem: A child with ASD repeats the exact phrases spoken by parents and television programmes. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.correctAnswerText: Echolalia
questions.initialExplanation: Echolalia is repetition of words, phrases, intonation or sounds produced by another person. standard guidance also mentions neologisms (invented words/jargon) and delayed speech/language development.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Myotonia is delayed muscle relaxation after contraction.
- B. Incorrect. Dysarthria is impaired articulation due to motor speech dysfunction.
- C. Incorrect. Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing.
- D. Incorrect. Aphasia is an acquired language disorder.
- E. Correct. Repetition of heard speech is echolalia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ASD communication patterns may include delayed speech, echolalia and neologisms.
- Repetitive language may be immediate or delayed.
- Assess functional communication, receptive language and non-verbal communication.
- Speech and language therapy is a key part of management.

questions.stem: Which behaviour is an example of restricted/repetitive patterns in ASD?

options.label: A
options.text: Repetitive hand flapping, insistence on routines and intense preoccupation with particular objects

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing head circumference with bulging fontanelle

questions.correctAnswerText: Repetitive hand flapping, insistence on routines and intense preoccupation with particular objects
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include stereotyped/repetitive movements (e.g. hand flapping), repetitive play, echolalia, insistence on routines, resistance to changes and highly restricted interests.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are classic restricted/repetitive behaviours.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests Bell palsy.
- C. Incorrect. This suggests hydrocephalus.
- D. Incorrect. Morning myoclonic jerks may occur in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
- E. Incorrect. This is a feature of GBS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Repetitive movements: hand flapping, grimacing, tiptoe walking and stereotyped posturing.
- Insistence on routines and marked resistance to change.
- Restricted/fixated interests in particular objects or topics.
- Unusual sensory response: sound sensitivity, apparent indifference to temperature, excessive touching/smelling.

questions.stem: Which statement about associated features of ASD is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: children in routine care with ASD has severe intellectual disability

options.label: B
options.text: ASD is typically associated with hearing loss

options.label: C
options.text: Repetitive behaviours are absent in ASD

options.label: D
options.text: Epilepsy may occur in approximately one-quarter of cases; anxiety, sleep and GI problems, learning difficulties and self-injury may also occur

options.label: E
options.text: Epilepsy not usually occurs in ASD

questions.correctAnswerText: Epilepsy may occur in approximately one-quarter of cases; anxiety, sleep and GI problems, learning difficulties and self-injury may also occur
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include intellectual/learning difficulties, anxiety, sleep disturbance, seizures (approximately 25%), self-injury (10-15%), reduced pain response and gastrointestinal/eating problems as associated features.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Intellectual ability varies; not every child has severe intellectual disability.
- B. Incorrect. Hearing impairment must be considered in the assessment, but it is not universal.
- C. Incorrect. Restricted/repetitive behaviours are part of the diagnostic pattern.
- D. Correct. This summarizes the associated features in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Epilepsy is a recognized comorbidity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Associated features: learning/attention difficulties, anxiety, sleep problems, GI/eating issues.
- Epilepsy is reported in approximately 25%.
- Self-injury may occur in 10-15%.
- Pain response may be reduced or unusual.
- Assess comorbidities rather than attributing every symptom to ASD.

questions.stem: Which approach is appropriate when evaluating a preschool child for ASD?

options.label: A
options.text: Karyotyping as the sole diagnostic criterion

options.label: B
options.text: Take developmental and family history, examine the child, assess hearing, screen (e.g., M-CHAT) and arrange formal assessment

options.label: C
options.text: MRI brain as the diagnostic test in children in routine care

options.label: D
options.text: EEG in children in routine care regardless of seizure history

options.label: E
options.text: Diagnosis based on one episode of delayed speech

questions.correctAnswerText: Take developmental and family history, examine the child, assess hearing, screen (e.g., M-CHAT) and arrange formal assessment
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes detailed developmental/medical history, family history, physical examination (including dysmorphology and OFC), audiological assessment and screening tools such as M-CHAT. EEG is indicated if epilepsy is suspected; karyotyping is considered when a syndrome is suspected; neuroimaging is not routine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Karyotyping may identify a genetic syndrome but is not the sole ASD diagnostic test.
- B. Correct. This is the multidimensional assessment approach described.
- C. Incorrect. MRI is not routinely required to diagnose ASD.
- D. Incorrect. EEG is indicated when seizures or other specific concerns are present.
- E. Incorrect. Speech delay alone is insufficient; broader social-communication and restricted/repetitive features must be assessed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Diagnosis is clinical and developmental.
- Obtain detailed developmental and family history.
- Assess hearing and physical development/OFC.
- M-CHAT is a screening tool, not a stand-alone diagnostic test.
- MRI/EEG/metabolic or genetic testing is targeted to clinical indications, not routine in every child.

questions.stem: Which intervention is considered central to management of ASD?

options.label: C
options.text: Start early multidisciplinary care with family support, education, speech and occupational therapy, and behavioural support

options.label: D
options.text: Complete avoidance of school and social contact

options.label: E
options.text: Antiseizure medication for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Start early multidisciplinary care with family support, education, speech and occupational therapy, and behavioural support
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes multidisciplinary management, early detection/intervention, parental education and support, special education, speech therapy, occupational therapy and behavioural therapy such as applied behaviour analysis (ABA).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. VP shunt treats selected hydrocephalus.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not a treatment for ASD.
- C. Correct. This is the approach described in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Social/educational support and structured learning are important.
- E. Incorrect. Antiseizure medication is used only when epilepsy is present.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early detection and intervention improve functional development.
- MDT: paediatrician, speech/language therapist, occupational therapist, education team and community services.
- Parent education/support and special educational provision are important.
- Behavioural approaches include ABA.
- Treat associated anxiety, sleep problems, epilepsy or GI issues individually.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes Rett syndrome from typical ASD 's differential diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Rett syndrome is caused by dystrophin deficiency

options.label: B
options.text: Rett syndrome is defined by a positive Babinski sign

options.label: C
options.text: Rett syndrome typically presents with an acute ascending paralysis

options.label: D
options.text: Rett syndrome occurs almost exclusively in girls and is associated with regression after initially more typical development

options.label: E
options.text: Rett syndrome is the commonest form of ADHD in boys

questions.correctAnswerText: Rett syndrome occurs almost exclusively in girls and is associated with regression after initially more typical development
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include Rett syndrome as an important ASD differential, occurring almost exclusively in girls and associated with developmental regression. Childhood disintegrative disorder is another differential characterized by deterioration after a period of development. Asperger syndrome (an older diagnostic term) was described as milder with no early language delay.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dystrophin deficiency causes DMD.
- B. Incorrect. Babinski positivity is an UMN sign and does not define Rett syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Ascending paralysis describes GBS.
- D. Correct. This is the key distinction given for Rett syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. ADHD is a separate neurodevelopmental disorder and is more commonly diagnosed in boys.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rett syndrome: almost exclusively girls; developmental regression.
- Childhood disintegrative disorder: significant deterioration after a period of development.
- Asperger syndrome is an older diagnostic term; language development may be relatively preserved.
- Consider hearing impairment and other developmental/neurological conditions in the differential.

topics.name: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and Learning Difficulties

cases.title: A school-aged child is persistently inattentive and hyperactive at home and school
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child repeatedly loses books, fails to finish classroom tasks, interrupts others, leaves the seat frequently and has difficulty waiting for turns. These behaviours have been present for 8 months, occur both at home and school and impair learning and peer relationships. The behaviours are not appropriate for the child's developmental level.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
questions.initialExplanation: ADHD is a neurobehavioural disorder characterized by developmentally inappropriate inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity persisting for more than 6 months and causing functional impairment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GBS is an acute peripheral neuropathy.
- B. Incorrect. ASD is defined by persistent social-communication impairment and restricted/repetitive behaviours.
- C. Correct. Persistent symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity across home and school with impairment support ADHD.
- D. Incorrect. Absence epilepsy causes brief staring episodes, not persistent distractibility and hyperactivity across settings.
- E. Incorrect. CP is a movement/posture disorder due to a non-progressive brain injury.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ADHD is described as the most common neurobehavioural disorder of childhood.
- Symptoms: inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity.
- Symptoms persist >6 months and impair school/social functioning.
- Assessment must consider developmental age, more than one setting and alternative explanations.

questions.stem: Which additional diagnostic requirement is important for ADHD?

options.label: A
options.text: Symptoms occur during one school lesson

options.label: B
options.text: Symptoms begin before 12 years, occur in at least two settings and cause significant functional impairment

options.label: C
options.text: The child must have a structural brain lesion on MRI

options.label: D
options.text: Symptoms begin after 18 years of age

options.label: E
options.text: There must be a positive EEG

questions.correctAnswerText: Symptoms begin before 12 years, occur in at least two settings and cause significant functional impairment
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include symptom onset before 12 years, symptoms noted in at least two settings (e.g. home and school), significant functional impairment, behaviour inconsistent with developmental age and exclusion of other causes as diagnostic requirements.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Symptoms should be present in at least two settings.
- B. Correct. These are key diagnostic requirements.
- C. Incorrect. Structural brain imaging is not routinely required.
- D. Incorrect. ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder with childhood onset.
- E. Incorrect. EEG is not required to diagnose ADHD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Onset before age 12.
- Symptoms in at least two settings.
- Functional impairment in school, social or home life.
- Symptoms must be developmentally inappropriate.
- Exclude other explanations such as learning difficulty, sleep disorders, anxiety, epilepsy or hearing/vision problems.

questions.stem: Which group contains examples of inattentive symptoms of ADHD listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Careless mistakes, difficulty sustaining attention, failure to complete tasks, disorganization, losing necessary items and forgetfulness

options.label: B
options.text: Nystagmus, head tilt and head nodding

options.label: C
options.text: Facial weakness, inability to close an eye and taste loss

options.label: E
options.text: Ascending paralysis, areflexia and sensory tingling

questions.correctAnswerText: Careless mistakes, difficulty sustaining attention, failure to complete tasks, disorganization, losing necessary items and forgetfulness
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include failure to attend to details, difficulty completing schoolwork/following instructions, poor sustained attention, disorganization, avoidance of tasks requiring mental effort, losing necessary items, distractibility and forgetfulness as inattentive symptoms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the inattentive symptoms in the source.
- B. Incorrect. This is the triad of spasmus nutans.
- C. Incorrect. These are features of facial nerve palsy.
- D. Incorrect. These are signs of juvenile dermatomyositis.
- E. Incorrect. These are features of GBS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Inattention: poor attention to detail, careless mistakes, difficulty sustaining attention, failure to finish tasks.
- Disorganization and avoidance of prolonged mental effort.
- Losing items, distractibility and forgetfulness.
- Obtain information from parents and teachers across settings.

questions.stem: Which group contains hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms described?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of vibration sense and positive Romberg sign

options.label: C
options.text: Fidgeting, leaving the seat, excessive talking/running, poor quiet play, interrupting and difficulty waiting

questions.correctAnswerText: Fidgeting, leaving the seat, excessive talking/running, poor quiet play, interrupting and difficulty waiting
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include fidgeting, inability to remain seated, excessive running, difficulty playing quietly, appearing constantly driven, excessive talking, answering before questions are finished, interrupting others and difficulty waiting a turn.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are signs of sensory ataxia.
- B. Incorrect. These are migraine aura features.
- C. Correct. These are examples of hyperactivity and impulsivity.
- D. Incorrect. These suggest SMA.
- E. Incorrect. These suggest infant hydrocephalus.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hyperactivity: fidgeting, leaving seat, excessive running/talking, difficulty playing quietly.
- Impulsivity: answers before question ends, interrupts others and cannot wait turn.
- Symptoms must persist and cause impairment, not simply reflect age-appropriate activity.
- Consider both symptom domains when assessing presentation.

questions.stem: Which is a recognized risk factor for ADHD listed?

options.label: A
options.text: First-degree relative with ADHD, extreme prematurity/VLBW or CNS disorders such as epilepsy and CP

options.label: C
options.text: Normal full-term birth with no family history

questions.correctAnswerText: First-degree relative with ADHD, extreme prematurity/VLBW or CNS disorders such as epilepsy and CP
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include male sex, a first-degree relative with ADHD, CNS disorders (e.g. epilepsy and CP), and extreme prematurity/very low birth weight as risk factors. Genetic and environmental contributions are multifactorial.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the risk factors listed.
- B. Incorrect. A simple febrile seizure alone is not listed as an ADHD risk factor.
- C. Incorrect. This is not a risk factor group.
- D. Incorrect. Folic acid is used to reduce neural tube defect risk.
- E. Incorrect. Refractive error is not an ADHD risk factor.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ADHD is more commonly diagnosed in boys (about 4:1 ).
- Risk factors: family history, extreme prematurity/VLBW and CNS disorders such as epilepsy/CP.
- Etiology is multifactorial, with genetic and environmental contributions.
- Avoid assuming every inattentive child has ADHD; assess learning, sleep, mood, vision/hearing and medical causes.

questions.stem: Which medication is a psychostimulant used in ADHD and described as inhibiting dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake?
questions.correctAnswerText: Methylphenidate
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include methylphenidate as a psychostimulant that inhibits dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake and increases dopaminergic/noradrenergic activity in the prefrontal cortex. Other medication options include dexamphetamine and atomoxetine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ethosuximide treats absence epilepsy.
- B. Incorrect. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.
- C. Correct. Methylphenidate is the psychostimulant described.
- D. Incorrect. Atomoxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, not a psychostimulant.
- E. Incorrect. Baclofen reduces spasticity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ADHD management includes education, behaviour strategies and medication when indicated.
- Psychostimulants: methylphenidate and dexamphetamine.
- Atomoxetine: selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor.
- Coordinate home, school and clinical support.

questions.stem: Which statement about non-pharmacological management of ADHD is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Communication between home, school and clinic, behavioural strategies and educational adaptations are important

options.label: B
options.text: Do not assess learning or mental health comorbidities

options.label: C
options.text: Remove the child from most educational settings

questions.correctAnswerText: Communication between home, school and clinic, behavioural strategies and educational adaptations are important
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is educational measures such as communication between home, school and clinic, one-to-one teaching or reduced distractions when needed, alongside behavioural management techniques. Medication is considered when indicated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the non-pharmacological approach described.
- B. Incorrect. Assess learning, anxiety, mood, sleep and other comorbidities.
- C. Incorrect. Educational inclusion and appropriate support are important.
- D. Incorrect. Parent education and involvement are essential.
- E. Incorrect. Behavioural and educational interventions are important components.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Home-school-clinic communication.
- Behavioural management techniques.
- Educational adaptations and reduced distractions where appropriate.
- Medication is one component of a broader management plan.
- ADHD increases risk of low self-esteem, peer difficulties, anxiety, poor school performance and antisocial behaviour if unsupported.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a specific learning difficulty with its main problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Dyslexia - muscle tone; dyscalculia - seizures; dysgraphia - swallowing

options.label: B
options.text: Dyslexia - speech sound; dyscalculia - gait; dysgraphia - vision

options.label: C
options.text: most three describe the same learning difficulty

options.label: D
options.text: Dyslexia - reading; dyscalculia - numbers; dysgraphia - writing

options.label: E
options.text: Dyslexia - hearing; dyscalculia - vision; dysgraphia - balance

questions.correctAnswerText: Dyslexia - reading; dyscalculia - numbers; dysgraphia - writing
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include dyslexia (difficulty reading), dyscalculia (difficulty learning/comprehending numbers) and dysgraphia (difficulty with writing skills) as specific learning difficulties.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are neurological symptoms, not specific learning disorders.
- B. Incorrect. The pairings do not match the source.
- C. Incorrect. They affect different learning domains.
- D. Correct. These are the correct pairings.
- E. Incorrect. These are not the definitions of the listed learning difficulties.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Learning/intellectual disability is broader and affects understanding, learning new skills and independent functioning.
- Dyslexia: reading difficulty.
- Dyscalculia: number/mathematical learning difficulty.
- Dysgraphia: writing difficulty.
- Assess functional ability and educational needs rather than relying on labels alone.

cases.title: A child has multiple café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child is referred because of multiple café-au-lait macules on the trunk and limbs. Examination reveals axillary freckling and several soft cutaneous neurofibromas. Ocular examination is performed.

questions.stem: Why are neurocutaneous syndromes sometimes called phakomatoses?

options.label: A
options.text: They are caused exclusively by bacterial infection

options.label: B
options.text: The skin and nervous system share a common ectodermal embryological origin

options.label: C
options.text: They are caused by abnormal CSF absorption

options.label: E
options.text: They are most inherited as X-linked recessive disorders

questions.correctAnswerText: The skin and nervous system share a common ectodermal embryological origin
questions.initialExplanation: This is explained that the nervous system and skin have a common ectodermal origin. Embryological disruption can therefore produce syndromes with abnormalities involving both systems.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Neurocutaneous syndromes are genetic/developmental disorders, not a group of bacterial infections.
- B. Correct. This is the embryological basis described in the source.
- C. Incorrect. CSF absorption abnormalities are not the unifying cause of neurocutaneous syndromes.
- D. Incorrect. The CNS and skin are commonly involved, and other organs may also be affected.
- E. Incorrect. Inheritance varies; NF1, NF2 and TSC are autosomal dominant, while ataxia-telangiectasia is autosomal recessive.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neurocutaneous syndromes involve both skin and nervous system.
- Common ectodermal embryological origin explains the combined manifestations.
- Conditions listed include NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber, ataxia-telangiectasia and von Hippel-Lindau disease.
- Other organ systems may be involved depending on the syndrome.

questions.stem: Which combination of findings supports neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)?

options.label: A
options.text: Facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal angioma

options.label: C
options.text: Six or more café-au-lait macules plus axillary freckling or neurofibromas

options.label: E
options.text: Progressive ataxia with telangiectasia and immunodeficiency

questions.correctAnswerText: Six or more café-au-lait macules plus axillary freckling or neurofibromas
questions.initialExplanation: NF1 is an autosomal dominant disorder due to an NF1 gene defect on chromosome 17. It is recognized that two or more diagnostic features are required, including six or more café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, axillary freckling, optic glioma, Lisch nodules, sphenoid dysplasia or a first-degree relative with NF1.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A port-wine stain with leptomeningeal angioma suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Ash-leaf macules and renal angiomyolipomas suggest tuberous sclerosis.
- C. Correct. Multiple café-au-lait macules with axillary freckling/neurofibromas support NF1.
- D. Incorrect. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are characteristic of NF2.
- E. Incorrect. Ataxia with telangiectasia and immune deficiency suggests ataxia-telangiectasia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NF1: autosomal dominant, NF1 gene on chromosome 17.
- standard guidance requires at least two diagnostic features.
- Café-au-lait macules: ≥6, larger than 5 mm before puberty and >15 mm after puberty.
- Other criteria: ≥2 neurofibromas, axillary freckling, optic glioma, Lisch nodules, sphenoid dysplasia or first-degree relative with NF1.

questions.stem: A child with NF1 develops visual impairment. Which associated tumour should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Optic pathway glioma
questions.initialExplanation: Optic glioma is one of the diagnostic features of NF1 and may cause visual impairment. Other complications include benign/malignant tumours, hypertension related to pheochromocytoma or renal artery stenosis, macrocephaly, learning difficulties, epilepsy and scoliosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Medulloblastoma is a posterior fossa tumour, not the classic NF1 visual complication.
- B. Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma is a suprasellar tumour causing visual field and pituitary dysfunction.
- C. Incorrect. Ependymoma is a CNS tumour, more associated with NF2 than the specific NF1 visual feature in this question.
- D. Incorrect. Vestibular schwannomas are characteristic of NF2.
- E. Correct. Optic pathway glioma is a recognized NF1-associated tumour.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NF1: optic glioma may impair vision.
- Lisch nodules are iris hamartomas identified by slit-lamp examination.
- Sphenoid dysplasia may cause eye protrusion.
- Monitor growth, blood pressure, vision, learning, seizures and scoliosis.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes NF2 from NF1?

options.label: A
options.text: NF2 is defined by six or more café-au-lait macules

options.label: B
options.text: NF2 is an autosomal recessive disorder of DNA repair

options.label: C
options.text: NF2 is associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas and may also involve meningiomas and ependymomas

options.label: D
options.text: NF2 is caused by an SMN1 mutation

options.label: E
options.text: NF2 causes cutaneous neurofibromas and no CNS tumours

questions.correctAnswerText: NF2 is associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas and may also involve meningiomas and ependymomas
questions.initialExplanation: NF2 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by an NF2 gene defect on chromosome 22. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the predominant feature, and associated tumours include schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Café-au-lait macules are part of NF1 diagnostic criteria.
- B. Incorrect. Ataxia-telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder.
- C. Correct. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the key NF2 feature.
- D. Incorrect. SMN1 mutation causes SMA.
- E. Incorrect. NF2 is strongly associated with CNS/cranial nerve tumours.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NF2: autosomal dominant, NF2 gene on chromosome 22.
- Bilateral vestibular schwannomas/acoustic neuromas are predominant.
- May also cause schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas.
- Cerebellopontine angle involvement may cause facial nerve palsy and cerebellar ataxia.

cases.title: A child has hypopigmented macules, seizures and facial papules
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old child has several hypopigmented ash-leaf macules on the trunk and a rough plaque over the lumbar region. There are multiple small reddish papules over the nose and cheeks. The child has a history of infantile spasms and developmental difficulties.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Tuberous sclerosis complex
questions.initialExplanation: Tuberous sclerosis is an autosomal dominant disorder, with approximately 70% of cases due to new mutations. It is associated with ash-leaf hypopigmented macules, facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum), shagreen patches, seizures and involvement of multiple organs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Ash-leaf macules, shagreen patch, facial angiofibromas and infantile spasms strongly suggest TSC.
- B. Incorrect. NF2 is associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
- C. Incorrect. Friedreich ataxia causes progressive gait/sensory ataxia, areflexia and pes cavus.
- D. Incorrect. Sturge-Weber causes a facial port-wine capillary malformation with leptomeningeal involvement.
- E. Incorrect. NF1 causes café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, axillary freckling and Lisch nodules.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tuberous sclerosis: autosomal dominant; many cases are new mutations.
- Skin: ash-leaf hypopigmented macules, facial angiofibromas and shagreen patch.
- CNS: seizures/infantile spasms, cortical tubers and subependymal lesions; autism/ADHD and intellectual disability may occur.
- Assess renal, cardiac, retinal and pulmonary involvement.

source.raw: CNS lecture - Page 51; matching PDF image.

questions.stem: Which skin lesion is classically described as an ash-leaf macule in tuberous sclerosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypopigmented, leaf-shaped macule
questions.initialExplanation: Ash-leaf spots are depigmented/hypomelanotic macules and are an important cutaneous clue to tuberous sclerosis. standard guidance's PDF shows the characteristic hypopigmented lesion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Café-au-lait macules are associated with NF1.
- B. Incorrect. Port-wine stain is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital dermal melanocytosis is a blue-grey pigmented patch.
- D. Incorrect. Heliotrope rash is associated with juvenile dermatomyositis.
- E. Correct. Ash-leaf macules are hypopigmented, often leaf-shaped.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TSC: hypomelanotic/ash-leaf macules.
- Other skin features: facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) often appear after age 3; shagreen patch over the lumbar region.
- Skin findings may be easier to identify under Wood lamp examination.
- Look for seizures/developmental concerns and systemic hamartomas.

source.raw: CNS lecture - Page 51; matching PDF image.

questions.stem: Which group contains important systemic manifestations of tuberous sclerosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Cortical tubers/seizures, cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal angiomyolipomas or polycystic kidneys, retinal hamartomas and lung cysts

options.label: C
options.text: Progressive anterior horn cell loss and tongue fasciculations

options.label: D
options.text: Recurrent meningococcal sepsis and adrenal haemorrhage

options.label: E
options.text: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas and café-au-lait macules

questions.correctAnswerText: Cortical tubers/seizures, cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal angiomyolipomas or polycystic kidneys, retinal hamartomas and lung cysts
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include CNS involvement (seizures, infantile spasms, autism/ADHD, intellectual disability, cortical/subependymal lesions), cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal angiomyolipomas/polcystic kidneys, retinal hamartomas and pulmonary cysts.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the multi-organ manifestations described.
- B. Incorrect. These features suggest myotonic dystrophy.
- C. Incorrect. This is characteristic of SMA.
- D. Incorrect. These suggest meningococcal sepsis/Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas suggest NF2; café-au-lait macules are typical of NF1.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TSC is a multisystem disorder.
- CNS: cortical tubers/subependymal nodules, seizures, infantile spasms, autism/ADHD and intellectual disability.
- CVS: cardiac rhabdomyoma.
- Renal: angiomyolipoma and polycystic kidneys.
- Eyes: retinal hamartomas; lungs: cysts.

cases.title: A child has a unilateral facial vascular birthmark and seizures
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child has a congenital red-purple vascular stain involving one side of the face, extending over the forehead and upper eyelid. The child has had focal seizures and is being assessed for visual problems.

questions.stem: Which syndrome is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sturge-Weber syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a neurocutaneous vascular disorder associated with a facial port-wine capillary malformation, leptomeningeal vascular malformations, seizures and ocular complications such as glaucoma. The matching standard guidance PDF contains a clinical photograph of a child with a unilateral facial port-wine lesion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. NF1 is associated with café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, axillary freckling and optic glioma.
- B. Incorrect. NF2 is associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
- C. Incorrect. TSC is associated with ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas and multisystem hamartomas.
- D. Incorrect. Ataxia-telangiectasia causes progressive cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasia and immune deficiency.
- E. Correct. A facial port-wine stain with seizures and possible ocular involvement is characteristic.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sturge-Weber: facial port-wine capillary malformation, often in trigeminal distribution.
- Leptomeningeal angioma can cause seizures, focal neurological deficits/hemiparesis and intracranial calcification.
- Glaucoma is an important ocular complication.
- The diagnosis is clinical and supported by neuroimaging/ophthalmological assessment.

source.raw: CNS lecture - Page 50 (Sturge-Weber is named in the list; hallmark clinical features are supplementary and not expanded in the extracted lecture text).

questions.stem: Which neurological and imaging association is typical of Sturge-Weber syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Anterior horn cell degeneration with tongue fasciculations

options.label: C
options.text: Leptomeningeal angiomatosis with seizures/hemiparesis and tram-track intracranial calcification

options.label: D
options.text: Optic glioma with Lisch nodules and axillary freckling

options.label: E
options.text: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas with acoustic loss

questions.correctAnswerText: Leptomeningeal angiomatosis with seizures/hemiparesis and tram-track intracranial calcification
questions.initialExplanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome involves leptomeningeal vascular malformations that can cause seizures, focal neurological deficits and characteristic intracranial calcifications. Ocular involvement, especially glaucoma, is also important.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is SMA.
- B. Incorrect. This is tuberous sclerosis.
- C. Correct. This is the classic CNS association.
- D. Incorrect. This is NF1.
- E. Incorrect. This is NF2.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sturge-Weber: port-wine stain + leptomeningeal vascular malformation.
- Neurological: focal seizures, hemiparesis and possible developmental problems.
- Imaging may show tram-track cortical calcification.
- Screen for glaucoma and monitor neurological complications.

cases.title: A family has a history of retinal and central nervous system vascular tumours
cases.vignette: A 15-year-old is assessed because a parent has a history of retinal vascular lesions and a central nervous system haemangioblastoma. The child is being screened for an inherited neurocutaneous tumour-predisposition syndrome.

questions.stem: Which syndrome is included 's list of neurocutaneous disorders and is associated with CNS/retinal haemangioblastomas?
questions.correctAnswerText: Von Hippel-Lindau disease
questions.initialExplanation: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is listed among the neurocutaneous syndromes. It is an inherited tumour-predisposition syndrome associated with haemangioblastomas of the retina and CNS, and other visceral tumours/cysts. The OCR text on the final page is incomplete, so this question tests its place in the syndrome group and its core clinical association rather than a detail absent from the readable text.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GBS is an acute autoimmune peripheral neuropathy.
- B. Incorrect. Spina bifida occulta is a neural tube defect.
- C. Incorrect. DMD is an X-linked muscular dystrophy.
- D. Incorrect. West syndrome is an infantile epilepsy syndrome.
- E. Correct. VHL is a neurocutaneous/tumour-predisposition syndrome associated with retinal and CNS haemangioblastomas.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- VHL is included in the neurocutaneous syndrome list on page 50.
- Typical disease associations include retinal/CNS haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and visceral cysts.
- It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
- The printed/OCR text for VHL on the final page is poorly extracted; verify further standard guidance-specific details from the PDF/teacher if needed.
