cases.title: Hypertension in a child with neurofibromatosis type 1
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child is followed for multiple café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling. At a routine review, repeated blood-pressure measurements are elevated. There is no acute illness to explain the finding.

questions.stem: Which associated complications should be considered when investigating the child's hypertension?

options.label: B
options.text: A VP-shunt infection and shunt nephritis

options.label: C
options.text: Optic glioma as the recognized cause of hypertension in NF1

options.label: E
options.text: Pheochromocytoma or renal artery stenosis associated with NF1

questions.correctAnswerText: Pheochromocytoma or renal artery stenosis associated with NF1
questions.initialExplanation: The clinical findings support neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). standard guidance specifically lists hypertension associated with pheochromocytoma or renal artery stenosis as a complication of NF1.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Renal angiomyolipomas are listed under tuberous sclerosis, not as the NF1-associated explanation emphasized here.
- B. Incorrect. Shunt infection and shunt nephritis are complications of ventriculoperitoneal shunts.
- C. Incorrect. Optic glioma is an important NF1 complication, but it does not account for the hypertension association listed.
- D. Incorrect. These are causes or associations of hydrocephalus and do not explain the specific NF1 association.
- E. Correct. Recognized features include pheochromocytoma and renal artery stenosis as complications associated with hypertension in NF1.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NF1 is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, axillary freckling and other diagnostic features.
- Important complications include benign and malignant tumours, optic glioma, learning difficulties, epilepsy, scoliosis and visual or auditory impairment.
- Hypertension in a child with NF1 should prompt consideration of pheochromocytoma and renal artery stenosis.

source.raw: CNS lecture, Page 50 — Neurofibromatosis type 1; clinical features and complications.

cases.title: A symptomatic infant with a congenital shunt
cases.vignette: A 6-week-old infant is brought with poor feeding, sweating during feeds and poor weight gain. Examination shows tachypnoea, tachycardia, a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border and mild hepatomegaly. The infant has signs of pulmonary overcirculation and early heart failure.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ventricular septal defect
questions.initialExplanation: The echocardiogram confirms a defect in the interventricular septum. The clinical picture is also typical of a large VSD causing a left-to-right shunt, pulmonary overcirculation and heart failure during early infancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Ventricular septal defect — Correct. A VSD is a communication between the ventricles. A large defect can cause pulmonary overcirculation, heart failure, recurrent chest infections and failure to thrive.
- B. Coarctation of the aorta — Incorrect. Coarctation produces upper–lower limb blood-pressure and pulse discrepancies; a critically affected neonate may present with circulatory collapse when the ductus closes.
- C. Atrial septal defect — Incorrect. ASD is an interatrial communication. Its characteristic auscultatory finding is a fixed wide split second heart sound, often with an ejection systolic flow murmur at the upper left sternal border.
- D. Patent ductus arteriosus — Incorrect. PDA typically produces a continuous machinery murmur in the left infraclavicular area and may cause bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure when large.
- E. Tetralogy of Fallot — Incorrect. TOF is a cyanotic lesion associated with pulmonary outflow obstruction, a VSD, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- VSD is the most common congenital heart defect in the supplied clinical guidance.
- A large VSD usually produces a left-to-right shunt and increased pulmonary blood flow.
- Feeding difficulty, sweating, tachypnoea, hepatomegaly and poor growth suggest heart failure in an infant.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which haemodynamic change is primarily responsible for the infant's pulmonary congestion?

options.label: A
options.text: Left-to-right shunting with increased pulmonary blood flow

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced blood flow from the left ventricle into the aorta

options.label: C
options.text: Increased systemic vascular resistance from coarctation

options.label: D
options.text: Complete obstruction of pulmonary venous return

options.label: E
options.text: Right-to-left shunting with reduced pulmonary blood flow

questions.correctAnswerText: Left-to-right shunting with increased pulmonary blood flow
questions.initialExplanation: After birth, left ventricular pressure is higher than right ventricular pressure. Blood therefore passes through the VSD from left to right, increasing pulmonary blood flow. A large shunt can cause pulmonary congestion and heart failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Left-to-right shunting — Correct. Oxygenated blood recirculates through the pulmonary circulation, increasing pulmonary blood flow and cardiac workload.
- B. Reduced aortic flow — Incorrect. The central problem in a large uncomplicated VSD is excessive pulmonary flow, not primary obstruction of systemic outflow.
- C. Increased systemic vascular resistance — Incorrect. Coarctation can increase left ventricular afterload, but it does not explain the VSD-related pulmonary overcirculation in this case.
- D. Pulmonary venous obstruction — Incorrect. This is not the mechanism of an isolated VSD.
- E. Right-to-left shunting — Incorrect. This causes systemic desaturation and cyanosis, as may occur in advanced pulmonary vascular disease with Eisenmenger physiology or in cyanotic congenital heart disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Large VSD → left-to-right shunt → increased pulmonary blood flow → pulmonary congestion and heart failure.
- Symptoms often become more apparent after pulmonary vascular resistance falls following birth.
- Persistent large shunts can cause pulmonary vascular disease and eventual shunt reversal.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the fact that the murmur is not particularly loud despite the large defect and significant symptoms?

options.label: A
options.text: Heart failure prevents most turbulent blood flow

options.label: B
options.text: Large defects typically produce low pulmonary blood flow

options.label: C
options.text: The murmur is quiet because the aortic valve is stenosed

options.label: D
options.text: The pressure difference between the ventricles may be smaller across a large non-restrictive defect

options.label: E
options.text: The defect must have closed spontaneously

questions.correctAnswerText: The pressure difference between the ventricles may be smaller across a large non-restrictive defect
questions.initialExplanation: A small restrictive VSD may generate a high-velocity jet and a loud murmur. In a large non-restrictive VSD, ventricular pressures become more similar, reducing the pressure gradient and potentially producing a softer murmur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Heart failure does not abolish turbulence. The more relevant explanation is the smaller pressure gradient across a large defect.
- B. Incorrect. A large VSD commonly increases pulmonary blood flow unless pulmonary vascular resistance becomes markedly elevated.
- C. Incorrect. Aortic stenosis is not the explanation for the murmur intensity described in the VSD section.
- D. Correct. The ventricles communicate freely, so the pressure gradient across the defect may be relatively small. Murmur intensity therefore does not reliably reflect disease severity.
- E. Incorrect. A defect that has closed would not explain the echocardiographic finding or the current haemodynamic symptoms.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Small restrictive VSD: often a loud pansystolic murmur.
- Large non-restrictive VSD: murmur may be softer or occasionally difficult to hear.
- Never judge the severity of a VSD from murmur loudness alone; assess symptoms, growth, examination and echocardiography.

questions.stem: Which investigation is the definitive diagnostic test and can assess the defect's anatomy and pulmonary pressure?
questions.correctAnswerText: Echocardiography
questions.initialExplanation: Echocardiography is the diagnostic investigation for VSD. It defines the anatomy and helps assess the haemodynamic consequences, including pulmonary hypertension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. ECG — Incorrect. It may show ventricular hypertrophy, including biventricular hypertrophy in a significant VSD, but it is not the definitive anatomical test.
- B. Echocardiography — Correct. It demonstrates the defect, its location and haemodynamic effects.
- C. Chest X-ray — Incorrect. It may show cardiomegaly, pulmonary plethora or pulmonary oedema in a large VSD, but it does not define the septal defect.
- D. Pulse oximetry — Incorrect. It assesses oxygen saturation and may be normal in an uncomplicated left-to-right shunt; it does not show the defect.
- E. Full blood count — Incorrect. It may help assess associated problems but cannot establish the structural diagnosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CXR in a significant VSD: cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora; pulmonary oedema may be present.
- ECG may show biventricular hypertrophy.
- Echocardiography is diagnostic and assesses anatomy and pulmonary pressure.

questions.stem: Which combination is most consistent with a haemodynamically significant large VSD?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal growth, normal chest X-ray and no signs of heart failure

options.label: B
options.text: Boot-shaped heart with oligemic lung fields

options.label: C
options.text: Egg-on-side heart with increased pulmonary vascular markings

options.label: D
options.text: Cardiomegaly, pulmonary plethora and evidence of ventricular hypertrophy

options.label: E
options.text: Rib notching with isolated upper-limb hypertension

questions.correctAnswerText: Cardiomegaly, pulmonary plethora and evidence of ventricular hypertrophy
questions.initialExplanation: A large left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary blood flow and cardiac workload. Clinical guidance cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora on chest X-ray, with biventricular hypertrophy on ECG.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is more compatible with a small VSD without significant haemodynamic consequences.
- B. Incorrect. A boot-shaped heart with oligemic lung fields is classically associated with TOF.
- C. Incorrect. An egg-on-side appearance with increased pulmonary vascular markings is associated with TGA.
- D. Correct. Cardiomegaly, pulmonary plethora and ventricular hypertrophy fit a large VSD with pulmonary overcirculation.
- E. Incorrect. Rib notching and upper-limb hypertension suggest coarctation rather than VSD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Large VSD: CXR — cardiomegaly and plethoric lungs.
- ECG — biventricular hypertrophy may occur.
- Small VSD may have a normal CXR and ECG.

questions.stem: What is the appropriate general management approach for this symptomatic infant while definitive correction is being planned?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat heart failure, support nutrition and arrange early defect assessment for closure

options.label: B
options.text: Wait until adulthood even if heart failure persists

options.label: C
options.text: Restrict most feeding to prevent tachypnoea

options.label: E
options.text: Give pulmonary vasodilators as the sole treatment for each VSD

questions.correctAnswerText: Treat heart failure, support nutrition and arrange early defect assessment for closure
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance treatment of heart failure with decongestive therapy, including a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor, alongside nutritional support and early correction of a significant defect to prevent pulmonary hypertension, heart failure and faltering growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Stabilize and treat heart failure, optimize feeding and growth, and assess for early surgical or catheter-based correction as appropriate to the anatomy.
- B. Incorrect. Delaying treatment of a haemodynamically important VSD risks progressive pulmonary vascular disease and other complications.
- C. Incorrect. Feeding support is important. Infants with tachypnoea may need an adapted feeding plan or enteral support, rather than simply having feeds withheld.
- D. Incorrect. Reassurance and observation may be suitable for selected small defects, not a symptomatic infant with heart failure and poor growth.
- E. Incorrect. Pulmonary vasodilators are not the sole routine treatment of an uncomplicated large VSD. The underlying shunt and heart failure must be addressed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat heart failure and optimize nutrition.
- clinical guidance mentions diuretic therapy and captopril for heart failure.
- Early correction of a large VSD is intended to prevent pulmonary hypertension, heart failure and failure to thrive.
- Exact timing and method of closure depend on the defect and the child's clinical state.

questions.stem: A child with a previously large left-to-right VSD later develops cyanosis, clubbing, exertional dyspnoea and a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound. Which complication best explains this change?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute bacterial endocarditis in each case

options.label: C
options.text: Eisenmenger syndrome due to pulmonary vascular disease and shunt reversal

questions.correctAnswerText: Eisenmenger syndrome due to pulmonary vascular disease and shunt reversal
questions.initialExplanation: A large left-to-right shunt can cause progressive pulmonary vascular disease. Increased pulmonary vascular resistance may eventually reverse the shunt to right-to-left, producing cyanosis and other features of Eisenmenger syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Infective endocarditis is a recognized complication of some congenital lesions, but it does not explain this characteristic chronic sequence from a large shunt to pulmonary vascular disease and reversal.
- B. Incorrect. Mitral stenosis does not explain the history of a large VSD followed by shunt reversal.
- C. Correct. Shunt reversal due to elevated pulmonary vascular resistance explains the development of cyanosis and chronic hypoxia. The CVS clinical guidance also describes a loud P2 and right ventricular hypertrophy.
- D. Incorrect. An innocent flow murmur is not associated with cyanosis, clubbing or pulmonary vascular disease.
- E. Incorrect. Spontaneous closure would not explain new cyanosis, clubbing and pulmonary hypertension.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Large unrepaired left-to-right shunt → pulmonary vascular disease → increased pulmonary vascular resistance → right-to-left shunt.
- Eisenmenger features include cyanosis, dyspnoea, chest pain, haemoptysis, clubbing, loud P2 and RVH.
- Prevention depends on timely recognition and correction of significant shunts before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease develops.

questions.stem: Which statement about a small VSD is most consistent with clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: It typically causes Eisenmenger syndrome before school age

options.label: B
options.text: It requires immediate surgical repair in children in routine care

options.label: C
options.text: A normal echocardiogram is expected despite a persistent defect

options.label: D
options.text: It invariably causes severe heart failure during the neonatal period

options.label: E
options.text: It commonly closes spontaneously during the first few years, particularly when muscular

questions.correctAnswerText: It commonly closes spontaneously during the first few years, particularly when muscular
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that small VSDs, especially muscular defects, may close spontaneously during the first two to three years. Clinical and echocardiographic follow-up is required.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Eisenmenger syndrome is associated with significant longstanding shunts and pulmonary vascular disease, not the expected course of every small VSD.
- B. Incorrect. A small uncomplicated VSD is generally followed rather than automatically repaired.
- C. Incorrect. Echocardiography can identify a persistent small defect even when the child is asymptomatic.
- D. Incorrect. Small restrictive VSDs are often asymptomatic and do not usually cause severe heart failure.
- E. Correct. Spontaneous closure during early childhood is described, particularly for muscular VSDs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Small VSD: often asymptomatic, with normal growth and no heart failure.
- Muscular VSDs are particularly likely to close spontaneously.
- Clinical guidance clinical and echocardiographic follow-up.
- Infective endocarditis risk and prophylaxis advice must follow the specific risk category and current local guidance; do not assume every patient needs routine antibiotic prophylaxis.

cases.title: A child with a fixed split second heart sound
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child is referred after a murmur is noticed during a routine examination. The child is active and has no obvious heart failure. Auscultation reveals a fixed wide splitting of the second heart sound and an ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border. Echocardiography demonstrates an interatrial communication with right-sided chamber dilatation.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains the fixed wide splitting of the second heart sound?
questions.correctAnswerText: Atrial septal defect
questions.initialExplanation: A fixed wide split S2 is a classic examination finding in ASD. The right ventricular stroke volume changes relatively little with respiration because of the persistent left-to-right atrial shunt.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. VSD — Incorrect. VSD classically produces a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border.
- B. PDA — Incorrect. PDA is associated with a continuous machinery murmur and, when large, bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure.
- C. Coarctation — Incorrect. The key findings are higher blood pressure in the upper limbs and weak or delayed femoral pulses.
- D. TOF — Incorrect. TOF is associated with cyanosis, a pulmonary ejection systolic murmur and a single S2 when the pulmonary component is absent.
- E. ASD — Correct. Fixed wide splitting of S2 is characteristic of ASD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ASD → left-to-right shunt → right-sided volume loading.
- Fixed wide splitting of S2 is a key clinical clue.
- An ejection systolic murmur may be caused by increased flow across the pulmonary valve; it is not necessarily a murmur directly produced by blood crossing the ASD.

questions.stem: Which type of ASD is the commonest form?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ostium secundum
questions.initialExplanation: Ostium secundum is the commonest ASD type. clinical guidance also describes ostium primum and sinus venosus defects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Ostium primum — Incorrect. It is located in the lower part of the atrial septum near the atrioventricular valves and may be associated with valve abnormalities.
- B. Sinus venosus — Incorrect. It is located near the entry of the SVC and may be associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous return.
- C. Ostium secundum — Correct. This is the commonest type of ASD.
- D. Coronary sinus defect — Incorrect. This is a less common atrial-level communication and is not the commonest type listed.
- E. Complete AVSD — Incorrect. This is a broader endocardial cushion defect involving atrial and ventricular septal components and a common AV valve, not an isolated secundum ASD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Secundum ASD: commonest type.
- Primum ASD: lower septum; may be associated with AV-valve regurgitation.
- Sinus venosus ASD: near SVC; consider associated partial anomalous pulmonary venous return.

questions.stem: Why is an ejection systolic murmur heard at the upper left sternal border in many children with ASD?

options.label: A
options.text: The VSD produces turbulence at the lower left sternal border

options.label: B
options.text: Blood crosses the atrial defect and creates a high-velocity jet through the aortic valve

options.label: C
options.text: The mitral valve is typically severely stenosed

options.label: D
options.text: The ductus arteriosus produces continuous flow

options.label: E
options.text: Increased right-sided flow passes through the pulmonary valve

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased right-sided flow passes through the pulmonary valve
questions.initialExplanation: The left-to-right shunt increases right ventricular output. Increased flow across the pulmonary valve produces an ejection systolic flow murmur at the upper left sternal border.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. VSD produces a pansystolic murmur, typically at the lower left sternal border.
- B. Incorrect. The murmur is not usually a direct jet murmur across the ASD; it is a flow murmur across the pulmonary valve.
- C. Incorrect. Mitral stenosis is not an obligatory feature of ASD. Primum ASD may be associated with AV-valve abnormalities or mitral regurgitation.
- D. Incorrect. PDA produces a continuous machinery murmur in the left infraclavicular region.
- E. Correct. Increased pulmonary blood flow produces increased flow across the pulmonary valve and an ejection systolic murmur.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ASD murmur: ejection systolic at the upper left sternal border due to increased pulmonary flow.
- Fixed wide split S2 is the more characteristic auscultatory clue.
- A primum defect may have an additional apical pansystolic murmur from AV-valve regurgitation.

questions.stem: Which ECG pattern is most consistent with an ostium secundum ASD as described?

options.label: A
options.text: Biventricular hypertrophy as the obligatory finding

options.label: B
options.text: Left ventricular hypertrophy with marked left-axis deviation

options.label: C
options.text: Short PR interval with delta wave

options.label: D
options.text: Complete heart block with no atrial activity

options.label: E
options.text: Right ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviation and right bundle branch block

questions.correctAnswerText: Right ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviation and right bundle branch block
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance associates secundum ASD with a normal ECG or right ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviation and RBBB.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Biventricular hypertrophy is more consistent with a significant VSD.
- B. Incorrect. Clinical guidance superior or left-axis deviation and LBBB with primum ASD, not the usual secundum pattern.
- C. Incorrect. A short PR interval and delta wave suggest Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. This describes a conduction disorder, not the typical ECG pattern of secundum ASD.
- E. Correct. This is the ECG pattern described for secundum ASD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Secundum ASD: ECG may be normal or show RVH, RAD and RBBB.
- Primum ASD: may show RVH, superior/left-axis deviation and LBBB.
- Echocardiography confirms the defect and assesses right-sided dilatation.

questions.stem: Which imaging combination may be seen in a haemodynamically significant ASD?

options.label: B
options.text: Boot-shaped heart with absent pulmonary vascular markings

options.label: D
options.text: Small heart and oligemic lung fields

options.label: E
options.text: Rib notching with isolated pulmonary oligemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora
questions.initialExplanation: A significant ASD can cause right-sided volume loading and increased pulmonary blood flow. Clinical guidance cardiomegaly and plethoric lungs on chest X-ray.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These findings are compatible with a significant left-to-right shunt at atrial level.
- B. Incorrect. A boot-shaped heart is characteristic of TOF.
- C. Incorrect. An egg-on-side appearance is associated with TGA.
- D. Incorrect. A small heart with oligemic lung fields is classically associated with reduced pulmonary blood flow, such as in TOF.
- E. Incorrect. Rib notching suggests collateral circulation in coarctation and is not the expected ASD pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ASD with a significant shunt: cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora may be present.
- ECG supports right-sided volume loading.
- Echocardiography is the diagnostic investigation.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic child has a secundum ASD. Echocardiography shows significant right atrial and right ventricular dilatation. Which closure method is generally described for a suitable large secundum ASD?
questions.correctAnswerText: Transcatheter device closure
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance catheter-based closure with an occlusion device for a large secundum ASD. Closure is considered when the shunt causes right-sided dilatation and the anatomy is suitable.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pulmonary artery banding is used in selected complex congenital conditions, not routine secundum ASD closure.
- B. Incorrect. Small defects may close spontaneously, but a significant shunt with right-sided dilatation requires specialist assessment for closure.
- C. Incorrect. A Blalock–Taussig shunt is a palliative systemic-to-pulmonary shunt used in selected cyanotic lesions.
- D. Incorrect. Balloon atrial septostomy is used to improve mixing in selected conditions such as TGA, not to close an ASD.
- E. Correct. Transcatheter device closure is described for secundum ASD when the anatomy is suitable.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Small ASD: spontaneous closure may occur.
- Large secundum ASD with right-sided dilatation: catheter device closure if suitable.
- Primum ASD: usually requires surgical correction because of associated AV-valve abnormalities.

questions.stem: A child has an ostium primum ASD with associated mitral regurgitation. Which treatment approach best matches clinical guidance?

options.label: C
options.text: Transcatheter occlusion device as the routine method for most primum defects

options.label: E
options.text: No follow-up because primum defects are typically benign

questions.correctAnswerText: Surgical correction
questions.initialExplanation: Ostium primum ASD is associated with the atrioventricular septal region and may involve AV-valve abnormalities. Clinical guidance surgical correction for large primum defects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Indomethacin is used in selected preterm infants to promote ductal closure in PDA, not to close ASD.
- B. Correct. Surgical correction addresses the primum defect and associated AV-valve abnormality.
- C. Incorrect. Device closure is described for suitable secundum ASD, not routinely for primum defects with AV-valve involvement.
- D. Incorrect. Pulmonary valvotomy treats pulmonary valve stenosis.
- E. Incorrect. A primum defect with valve regurgitation requires cardiology follow-up and assessment for repair.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primum ASD: lower atrial septum and possible AV-valve/mitral regurgitation.
- Secundum ASD: device closure may be suitable.
- Primum ASD: surgical repair is described.

questions.stem: Which statement about infective endocarditis risk in ASD is specifically highlighted?

options.label: B
options.text: ASD is typically a high-risk lesion for endocarditis

options.label: C
options.text: each small ASD requires lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis

options.label: D
options.text: Secundum ASD carries the same risk as each other congenital heart defect

options.label: E
options.text: There is no infective endocarditis risk in secundum ASD in the sheet's risk classification

questions.correctAnswerText: There is no infective endocarditis risk in secundum ASD in the sheet's risk classification
questions.initialExplanation: The CVS clinical guidance distinguishes secundum ASD from several other congenital lesions and lists secundum ASD in the negligible-risk category for infective endocarditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the risk framework presented.
- B. Incorrect. The high-risk category includes complex cyanotic congenital heart disease, previous IE and prosthetic valves, among others.
- C. Incorrect. clinical guidance does not recommend lifelong prophylaxis for every small ASD.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance explicitly separates secundum ASD from other congenital defects.
- E. Correct. Secundum ASD is listed as negligible risk in the supplied material.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Secundum ASD is listed in the negligible-risk category.
- Primum ASD and several other structural lesions are treated differently 's risk table.
- Follow current endocarditis-prophylaxis guidance for real clinical decisions; the exam answer here reflects the supplied standard guidance.

cases.title: The infant with bounding pulses
cases.vignette: A 6-week-old infant is reviewed for poor weight gain and recurrent respiratory symptoms. The infant has tachypnoea and feeding difficulty. Examination reveals bounding pulses, a wide pulse pressure and a continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle. Doppler echocardiography demonstrates continuous flow between the descending aorta and pulmonary artery.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Patent ductus arteriosus
questions.initialExplanation: A continuous machinery murmur in the left infraclavicular area, bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure are characteristic of a significant PDA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pulmonary stenosis — Incorrect. It produces an ejection systolic murmur at the pulmonary area and may cause right ventricular hypertrophy.
- B. ASD — Incorrect. ASD is associated with fixed wide splitting of S2 and an ejection systolic flow murmur at the upper left sternal border.
- C. VSD — Incorrect. VSD typically produces a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border.
- D. PDA — Correct. Persistent communication between the aorta and pulmonary artery causes continuous left-to-right flow after birth.
- E. Coarctation — Incorrect. It produces upper–lower limb blood-pressure differences and weak femoral pulses.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PDA → continuous machinery murmur, usually left infraclavicular.
- Large PDA → bounding/collapsing pulses and wide pulse pressure.
- Large shunt may cause pulmonary congestion, heart failure and failure to thrive.

questions.stem: What is the direction of the shunt in a typical postnatal PDA?
questions.correctAnswerText: Left to right
questions.initialExplanation: Aortic pressure is higher than pulmonary arterial pressure after birth, so blood passes from the aorta into the pulmonary artery through the persistent ductus, increasing pulmonary blood flow.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The usual postnatal PDA produces a left-to-right shunt.
- B. Incorrect. Right-to-left ductal flow can occur in selected conditions with high pulmonary vascular pressure, but it is not the usual uncomplicated PDA pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Bidirectional flow is not the defining pattern in an uncomplicated PDA.
- D. Incorrect. The ductus connects the aorta and pulmonary artery, not the pulmonary artery and right atrium.
- E. Incorrect. A patent ductus represents persistent communication and permits blood flow.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typical PDA: aorta → pulmonary artery.
- The shunt increases pulmonary blood flow and can overload the left heart.
- Advanced pulmonary vascular disease can eventually cause shunt reversal.

questions.stem: Which finding is the best explanation for the wide pulse pressure in a large PDA?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete obstruction of the pulmonary valve

options.label: B
options.text: Increased venous return from the lower limbs

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced stroke volume in most cardiac chambers

options.label: D
options.text: Diastolic runoff of blood from the aorta into the pulmonary artery

options.label: E
options.text: Increased diastolic pressure due to reduced runoff

questions.correctAnswerText: Diastolic runoff of blood from the aorta into the pulmonary artery
questions.initialExplanation: Blood continues to leave the aorta through the ductus during diastole. This lowers diastolic pressure, while the increased stroke volume may raise systolic pressure, producing a wide pulse pressure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pulmonary valve obstruction does not explain the characteristic wide pulse pressure of PDA.
- B. Incorrect. Venous return from the lower limbs is not the mechanism of the wide pulse pressure.
- C. Incorrect. A large PDA causes a hyperdynamic circulation rather than uniform reduction in stroke volume.
- D. Correct. Aortic-to-pulmonary runoff during diastole is the key mechanism.
- E. Incorrect. Clinical guidance a fall in diastolic pressure due to diastolic runoff, not an increase.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Large PDA → diastolic runoff → low diastolic BP.
- Increased systolic flow and low diastolic pressure → wide pulse pressure.
- Bounding/collapsing pulse is a clinical correlate.

questions.stem: Which investigation is diagnostic for PDA?
questions.correctAnswerText: Echocardiography
questions.initialExplanation: Echocardiography demonstrates the ductus and assesses its haemodynamic significance. CXR and ECG may show consequences of a large shunt but are not definitive.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Full blood count — Incorrect. It is not a diagnostic test for ductal patency.
- B. Echocardiography — Correct. It confirms the PDA and assesses the shunt and cardiac effects.
- C. Exercise stress test — Incorrect. It is not an appropriate diagnostic investigation in this infant.
- D. CXR — Incorrect. A large PDA may cause cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora, but CXR does not directly establish the ductal anatomy.
- E. ECG — Incorrect. It may show left ventricular hypertrophy and later other chamber effects, but it is not diagnostic.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Echo is diagnostic.
- CXR: cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora in a significant PDA.
- ECG: LVH may occur, with other patterns as haemodynamic effects evolve.

questions.stem: A preterm infant has a haemodynamically significant PDA during the first week of life. Which treatment is specifically described?

options.label: B
options.text: Indomethacin or ibuprofen, with fluid restriction as appropriate

options.label: C
options.text: Prostaglandin E infusion to close the ductus

questions.correctAnswerText: Indomethacin or ibuprofen, with fluid restriction as appropriate
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance anti-prostaglandin therapy with indomethacin or ibuprofen in preterm infants, together with restriction of intravenous fluids when appropriate, to promote ductal closure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Balloon atrial septostomy is used to improve mixing in selected cyanotic heart disease, especially TGA.
- B. Correct. Indomethacin and ibuprofen inhibit prostaglandin synthesis and are used to promote ductal closure in selected preterm infants.
- C. Incorrect. Prostaglandin E maintains ductal patency; it is used in duct-dependent congenital heart disease, not to close a PDA.
- D. Incorrect. Penicillin is not a ductal-closure treatment.
- E. Incorrect. Aortic valve replacement is unrelated to PDA closure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preterm PDA: anti-prostaglandin treatment (indomethacin or ibuprofen) and fluid restriction.
- Prostaglandin E has the opposite purpose: maintaining ductal patency in duct-dependent lesions.
- Management depends on prematurity, haemodynamic significance and neonatal specialist assessment.

questions.stem: , what is a described closure approach for a small PDA in a full-term infant?

options.label: D
options.text: Surgical repair of the mitral valve

options.label: E
options.text: Transcatheter closure using a coil or occluder

questions.correctAnswerText: Transcatheter closure using a coil or occluder
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance transcatheter closure using a coil or duct occluder as the method of choice for a small PDA in a full-term infant, with timing determined by the clinical context.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A child with PDA requires assessment and follow-up; the statement is unsafe and inconsistent with clinical guidance.
- B. Incorrect. Pulmonary artery banding is used in selected complex lesions, not routine PDA closure.
- C. Incorrect. Atrial septostomy creates/enlarges an atrial communication to improve mixing; it does not close the ductus.
- D. Incorrect. Mitral valve surgery does not treat PDA.
- E. Correct. This is the catheter-based approach described in the supplied material.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Small PDA in a full-term infant: catheter closure may be used.
- A large PDA may require surgical ligation according to the supplied clinical guidance.
- Echo guides diagnosis and follow-up.

questions.stem: Which statement about infective endocarditis in PDA is highlighted by standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Small PDA has no risk of infective endocarditis

options.label: B
options.text: PDA is classified identically to secundum ASD in the sheet

options.label: C
options.text: Infective endocarditis is listed as a possible complication even in small PDA

options.label: D
options.text: Endocarditis occurs when pulmonary hypertension is present

options.label: E
options.text: Endocarditis risk is excluded after the first month of life

questions.correctAnswerText: Infective endocarditis is listed as a possible complication even in small PDA
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance specifically notes infective endocarditis as a complication of PDA, including small defects. This distinguishes PDA from secundum ASD in the supplied risk table.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. clinical guidance explicitly notes that IE risk may occur even with a small PDA.
- B. Incorrect. Secundum ASD is placed in the negligible-risk category, whereas PDA is not treated the same way.
- C. Correct. This is the point emphasized.
- D. Incorrect. Pulmonary hypertension is not a prerequisite for infective endocarditis.
- E. Incorrect. clinical guidance does not define an age after which the risk disappears.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PDA complications: heart failure, failure to thrive, recurrent lower respiratory infection, IE, arrhythmia and late Eisenmenger syndrome.
- Do not confuse PDA and secundum ASD 's endocarditis-risk table.
- Current prophylaxis decisions should follow current guidelines and the patient's exact cardiac status.

cases.title: Large shunts and their late consequences

questions.stem: A preterm infant of 28 weeks has a haemodynamically significant PDA and is treated in the first week with indomethacin and restriction of intravenous fluids. On day 7 she develops abdominal distension, bilious aspirates and blood in the stools. Which adverse effect of the therapy is most consistent?
questions.correctAnswerText: Necrotising enterocolitis
questions.initialExplanation: Anti-prostaglandin therapy (indomethacin or ibuprofen) closes the ductus but can cause necrotising enterocolitis, bleeding and renal failure. The picture of abdominal distension, bilious aspirates and bloody stools suggests NEC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Apnoea, jitteriness, flushing and hypotension are adverse effects of prostaglandin E infusion — the *opposite* drug, used to keep the duct open.
- B. Correct. NEC, bleeding and renal failure are the listed adverse effects of indomethacin/ibuprofen.
- C. Incorrect. The infant is not on digoxin.
- D. Incorrect. Hypokalaemia would not cause bloody stools and abdominal distension, and diuretics are not part of this regimen.
- E. Incorrect. Not a recognised complication of this therapy.
- Clinical reasoning: Distinguish the adverse effects of drugs that close the duct (NSAIDs) from drugs that open it (PGE).
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preterm PDA: anti-PG (indomethacin/ibuprofen) + IV fluid restriction in the first week.
- Adverse effects: NEC, bleeding, renal failure.
- PGE adverse effects: apnoea, jitteriness/seizures, flushing, vasodilation, hypotension.
- PDA is not regarded as CHD in preterm infants; it is called persistent if the duct fails to close by 1 month after the expected date of delivery.

source.sheet: PDA — definition and treatment (sheet p. 14–15); Management of the cyanotic newborn (sheet p. 23).

cases.title: A newborn with Down syndrome and a cardiac defect
cases.vignette: A newborn with Down syndrome undergoes cardiac screening. Echocardiography demonstrates an abnormal atrioventricular junction with atrial- and ventricular-level communications and a common atrioventricular valve. The echocardiographic findings are reviewed to define the atrial- and ventricular-level communications and atrioventricular valve anatomy.

questions.stem: Which congenital cardiac lesion is classically associated with Down syndrome?
questions.correctAnswerText: Atrioventricular septal defect
questions.initialExplanation: AVSD, also called an endocardial cushion defect, is a classic cardiac association of trisomy 21.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Ebstein anomaly — Incorrect. clinical guidance mentions its association with maternal lithium exposure.
- B. AVSD — Correct. Down syndrome is strongly associated with AVSD.
- C. Pulmonary stenosis — Incorrect. This is associated with Noonan syndrome and congenital rubella.
- D. Coarctation — Incorrect. clinical guidance highlights its association with Turner syndrome.
- E. Supravalvular aortic stenosis — Incorrect. This is associated with Williams syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Trisomy 21 → AVSD.
- AVSD is also called endocardial cushion defect.
- A newborn with Down syndrome should undergo cardiac assessment, including echocardiography as indicated.

questions.stem: Which combination defines a complete AVSD in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Primum ASD, inlet VSD and a common AV valve

options.label: D
options.text: VSD with pulmonary stenosis and overriding aorta

options.label: E
options.text: Isolated mitral stenosis and aortic stenosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Primum ASD, inlet VSD and a common AV valve
questions.initialExplanation: Complete AVSD includes an ostium primum atrial defect, an inlet ventricular septal defect and a common atrioventricular valve.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the anatomical combination described.
- B. Incorrect. PDA and coarctation are separate lesions and do not form AVSD.
- C. Incorrect. This is an isolated ASD and does not define complete AVSD.
- D. Incorrect. This describes the major components of TOF.
- E. Incorrect. These are obstructive left-sided valvular lesions, not an endocardial cushion defect.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Partial AVSD: primum ASD with abnormal AV valve, often causing mitral regurgitation.
- Complete AVSD: primum ASD + inlet VSD + common AV valve.
- The common AV valve is a key anatomical clue.

questions.stem: Which clinical presentation is described for a complete AVSD?

options.label: A
options.text: Cyanosis at birth or heart failure during early infancy

options.label: D
options.text: Sudden episodic pallor with a normal cardiac examination

questions.correctAnswerText: Cyanosis at birth or heart failure during early infancy
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance complete AVSD as potentially presenting with cyanosis at birth or heart failure in early infancy. Presentation depends on the haemodynamic physiology and associated defects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the presentation described.
- B. Incorrect. Complete AVSD can be clinically significant and may cause early symptoms.
- C. Incorrect. Exertional syncope raises concern for arrhythmia or obstructive cardiac disease rather than being the defining AVSD presentation.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the characteristic AVSD presentation.
- E. Incorrect. Hypertension in adolescence is more relevant to coarctation and other causes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Complete AVSD may present early with cyanosis or heart failure.
- Partial AVSD may resemble primum ASD.
- Clinical findings should be interpreted with echocardiographic anatomy.

questions.stem: A newborn with Down syndrome has no obvious murmur on examination. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Cardiac evaluation is unnecessary if oxygen saturation is normal

options.label: B
options.text: Echocardiographic screening may detect AVSD even when a murmur is not heard

options.label: C
options.text: A chest X-ray alone reliably excludes AVSD

questions.correctAnswerText: Echocardiographic screening may detect AVSD even when a murmur is not heard
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that AVSD can be detected during routine echocardiographic screening in a newborn with Down syndrome and that a murmur may not be heard, particularly in complete lesions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude an acyanotic or partially compensated lesion.
- B. Correct. Echocardiography identifies the anatomy even when clinical auscultation is not diagnostic.
- C. Incorrect. CXR may show secondary findings but cannot reliably exclude AVSD.
- D. Incorrect. Absence of a murmur does not exclude a structural cardiac defect.
- E. Incorrect. ECG may show chamber enlargement or axis changes, but echocardiography defines the lesion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Down syndrome is a strong clue to AVSD.
- No murmur does not exclude significant congenital heart disease.
- Echo is required to define the anatomy.

questions.stem: Which management statement is most consistent with clinical guidance for a significant AVSD?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat heart failure when present and arrange surgical correction in infancy

options.label: B
options.text: Give indomethacin to close the atrial and ventricular components

options.label: D
options.text: Definitive repair is not usually required

options.label: E
options.text: Use a Blalock–Taussig shunt as the routine definitive treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Treat heart failure when present and arrange surgical correction in infancy
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance treatment of heart failure and surgical correction during infancy for AVSD. Timing depends on clinical severity and the detailed anatomy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Treating heart failure and arranging surgical correction in infancy is the approach outlined.
- B. Incorrect. Indomethacin is used in selected PDA cases, not to close septal components of AVSD.
- C. Incorrect. Delaying appropriate repair may expose the child to progressive pulmonary vascular disease and heart failure.
- D. Incorrect. A significant AVSD is a structural defect that may require surgical repair.
- E. Incorrect. A BT shunt is a palliative procedure for selected cyanotic lesions, not routine definitive AVSD repair.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- AVSD with heart failure: stabilize and treat the heart failure.
- Definitive treatment is surgical correction.
- Early specialist assessment is important, especially in infants with Down syndrome.

questions.stem: Which additional structural feature is most likely in a partial AVSD compared with an isolated secundum ASD?

options.label: A
options.text: A patent ductus arteriosus in each patient

options.label: C
options.text: Severe pulmonary valve stenosis in each patient

options.label: E
options.text: Abnormal atrioventricular valve with mitral regurgitation

questions.correctAnswerText: Abnormal atrioventricular valve with mitral regurgitation
questions.initialExplanation: A partial AVSD includes a primum ASD and an abnormal AV valve, often with mitral regurgitation. This distinguishes it from an isolated secundum ASD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. PDA is a separate ductal lesion and is not obligatory in AVSD.
- B. Incorrect. Overriding aorta is one of the components of TOF.
- C. Incorrect. Pulmonary stenosis is not an obligatory feature of partial AVSD.
- D. Incorrect. Interrupted aortic arch is a separate congenital lesion.
- E. Correct. AV-valve abnormality and mitral regurgitation are characteristic associated features of partial AVSD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primum ASD should prompt consideration of AV-valve abnormality.
- Partial AVSD is not simply another name for secundum ASD.
- Echo defines septal and valve anatomy.

cases.title: Complex lesions and staged management

questions.stem: A 6-week-old infant has mild cyanosis, tachypnoea, sweating with feeds and hepatomegaly. The chest X-ray shows plethoric lungs. Echocardiography shows a single arterial trunk arising from the heart and giving rise to both the aorta and the pulmonary arteries. Which management approach is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Prostaglandin E and a Blalock–Taussig shunt

options.label: B
options.text: Treatment of heart failure and urgent surgical correction in infancy

options.label: C
options.text: Rashkind balloon atrial septostomy as definitive therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Supportive care alone as definitive management

questions.correctAnswerText: Treatment of heart failure and urgent surgical correction in infancy
questions.initialExplanation: This is common arterial trunk (truncus arteriosus). It presents with variable-onset cyanosis and features of increased pulmonary blood flow (heart failure, plethora). Urgent surgical correction in infancy is the treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A BT shunt increases pulmonary flow in lesions with *reduced* pulmonary flow; here flow is increased.
- B. Correct. HF care + urgent surgical correction.
- C. Incorrect. Rashkind septostomy improves mixing in TGA, not truncus.
- D. Incorrect. Supportive therapy is the mainstay for single ventricle, not for truncus.
- E. Incorrect. Transplantation is considered in HLHS, not routinely here.
- Clinical reasoning: Truncus is a "plethoric cyanotic" lesion; treat failure then operate early.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Truncus arteriosus: single trunk → aorta and pulmonary artery; cyanosis variable; features of increased pulmonary blood flow.
- DiGeorge syndrome is associated with common arterial trunk.
- Complex CHD: presentation depends on whether cyanosis or HF predominates.

source.sheet: Complex CHD table (sheet p. 29); syndromes (sheet p. 7).

cases.title: The sick neonate with weak femoral pulses
cases.vignette: A 9-day-old neonate presents with poor feeding, lethargy, tachypnoea and signs of circulatory shock. The brachial pulses are palpable, but femoral pulses are weak and difficult to detect. Blood pressure is higher in the upper limbs than in the lower limbs. Echocardiography demonstrates marked narrowing of the aorta near the ductal insertion.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains the upper–lower limb pulse and blood-pressure discrepancy?
questions.correctAnswerText: Coarctation of the aorta
questions.initialExplanation: Coarctation causes narrowing of the aorta, usually near the ductal region. Blood pressure is elevated proximal to the narrowing and reduced distal to it, producing weak femoral pulses and an upper–lower limb pressure difference.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pulmonary stenosis — Incorrect. Pulmonary stenosis causes right ventricular outflow obstruction and a pulmonary area ejection systolic murmur.
- B. Coarctation — Correct. Upper-limb hypertension and weak or delayed femoral pulses are classic signs.
- C. PDA — Incorrect. PDA produces a continuous murmur and, when large, bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure.
- D. TOF — Incorrect. TOF produces cyanosis and reduced pulmonary blood flow rather than the classic four-limb pressure discrepancy.
- E. ASD — Incorrect. ASD is characterized by fixed wide splitting of S2 and right-sided volume loading.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CoA: upper-limb BP higher than lower-limb BP.
- Femoral pulses are weak or delayed.
- Measure BP in all four limbs when CoA is suspected.

questions.stem: Where is the commonest site of coarctation in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: At the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries in most cases

options.label: D
options.text: At the origin of the right coronary artery

options.label: E
options.text: Just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, commonly juxtaductal

questions.correctAnswerText: Just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, commonly juxtaductal
questions.initialExplanation: The supplied clinical guidance describes the common site as just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, commonly in the juxtaductal region.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Coarctation can occur at different levels, but the common site is juxtaductal rather than the iliac bifurcation.
- B. Incorrect. This describes aortic valve or subvalvular disease, not the typical coarctation site.
- C. Incorrect. The pulmonary trunk is not part of the aorta.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the usual site.
- E. Correct. This is the common location specified.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CoA is usually juxtaductal, just distal to the left subclavian artery.
- It is associated with Turner syndrome and may coexist with a bicuspid aortic valve.
- Collateral vessels may develop between proximal and distal aortic segments.

questions.stem: Why may a neonate with severe coarctation deteriorate dramatically when the ductus arteriosus closes?

options.label: A
options.text: Closure of the ductus causes an isolated atrial septal defect

options.label: B
options.text: Distal systemic perfusion may be duct-dependent in severe coarctation

options.label: C
options.text: Closure of the ductus increases pulmonary venous return to the left atrium

options.label: D
options.text: The ductus normally supplies the coronary arteries directly

options.label: E
options.text: The ductus is required to supply blood to the lungs in most neonates

questions.correctAnswerText: Distal systemic perfusion may be duct-dependent in severe coarctation
questions.initialExplanation: In severe neonatal CoA, blood flow to the descending aorta and lower body may depend on a patent ductus arteriosus. Ductal closure can therefore lead to poor distal perfusion, shock, heart failure and metabolic acidosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ductal closure does not create an ASD.
- B. Correct. In severe CoA, the ductus can provide a route for blood to reach the descending aorta beyond the narrowing.
- C. Incorrect. Increased pulmonary venous return is not the mechanism of systemic collapse in CoA.
- D. Incorrect. The ductus connects the pulmonary artery and aorta; it is not the normal direct source of coronary perfusion.
- E. Incorrect. The ductus may support pulmonary or systemic circulation in different duct-dependent congenital lesions; this option is too broad and does not explain CoA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Critical CoA may present after ductal closure with shock and severe metabolic acidosis.
- Weak/absent femoral pulses and poor lower-limb perfusion are important clues.
- Early recognition is essential because deterioration may be rapid.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate immediate management for this shocked neonate with suspected critical CoA?

options.label: A
options.text: Stabilize with ABC resuscitation, start prostaglandin early and arrange urgent cardiac-centre referral

options.label: B
options.text: Observe and repeat examination in one week

options.label: C
options.text: Start long-term oral antihypertensive therapy as the treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Perform routine transcatheter closure of an ASD

options.label: E
options.text: Give indomethacin to close the ductus

questions.correctAnswerText: Stabilize with ABC resuscitation, start prostaglandin early and arrange urgent cardiac-centre referral
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance resuscitation, early prostaglandin to maintain ductal patency, and referral for early surgical intervention in a severely affected infant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. ABC stabilization and prostaglandin maintain ductal flow while urgent specialist management is organized.
- B. Incorrect. Shock in a neonate is an emergency; observation would dangerously delay treatment.
- C. Incorrect. Antihypertensive therapy alone cannot correct a critical anatomical obstruction in a shocked neonate.
- D. Incorrect. ASD closure is unrelated to critical coarctation.
- E. Incorrect. Indomethacin promotes ductal closure and would worsen duct-dependent systemic perfusion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Critical CoA: ABC + prostaglandin + urgent cardiac referral.
- Prostaglandin maintains ductal patency; it is a stabilizing bridge, not definitive repair.
- Definitive treatment is usually surgical repair in severe neonatal disease.

questions.stem: Which chest X-ray finding may appear in an older child with coarctation because of collateral vessel enlargement?
questions.correctAnswerText: Rib notching
questions.initialExplanation: Collateral vessels enlarge to bypass the narrowed aortic segment. In older children, enlarged intercostal collaterals may erode the inferior margins of the ribs, producing rib notching (Rösler sign).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Water-bottle configuration is not the sign described for CoA.
- B. Incorrect. Boot-shaped heart is associated with TOF.
- C. Incorrect. Snowman appearance is associated with supracardiac TAPVR.
- D. Correct. Rib notching is a classic radiographic clue to collateral circulation in older children with CoA.
- E. Incorrect. Egg-on-side appearance is associated with TGA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rib notching is more likely in older children after collateral vessels have developed.
- clinical guidance also describes a figure-of-three sign at the coarctation site.
- Echo Doppler is the preferred diagnostic assessment.

questions.stem: Which investigation is identified as the best echocardiographic assessment for CoA?
questions.correctAnswerText: Echocardiography with Doppler
questions.initialExplanation: Echocardiography establishes the diagnosis and assesses associated congenital lesions. Doppler evaluates flow across the narrowed segment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Abdominal ultrasound alone cannot adequately define the thoracic coarctation.
- B. Incorrect. Exercise ECG is not the diagnostic test for anatomical coarctation.
- C. Correct. Echo with Doppler is identified as the best echo assessment.
- D. Incorrect. EEG evaluates cerebral electrical activity.
- E. Incorrect. Urine microscopy does not assess aortic anatomy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Echo Doppler: key diagnostic assessment.
- CT or MR angiography may further define anatomy.
- Cardiac catheterization may be used preoperatively in selected cases.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with moderate coarctation has persistent upper-limb hypertension and a significant narrowed segment. Which intervention is described for moderate disease in the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Transcatheter balloon dilatation with stenting
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance transcatheter balloon dilatation with stenting for moderate coarctation. Severe coarctation may require surgical repair.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the intervention described for moderate CoA.
- B. Incorrect. Atrial septostomy is used to improve mixing in selected cyanotic lesions such as TGA.
- C. Incorrect. Indomethacin is used in selected PDA cases and is not treatment for aortic narrowing.
- D. Incorrect. Pulmonary valve replacement does not treat CoA.
- E. Incorrect. Hypertension requires management and the anatomical lesion must be assessed; untreated significant CoA carries important risks.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mild CoA: control hypertension/heart failure as appropriate and follow regularly.
- Moderate CoA: balloon dilatation plus stent is described.
- Severe CoA: surgical repair/coarctectomy is described.
- Complications include systemic hypertension, left ventricular failure, infective endocarditis, cerebral aneurysm rupture and sudden death.

questions.stem: Which associated condition should be specifically considered in a child with CoA?

options.label: A
options.text: Williams syndrome and supravalvular aortic stenosis

options.label: C
options.text: Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve

options.label: E
options.text: Maternal lithium exposure and Ebstein anomaly

questions.correctAnswerText: Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve
questions.initialExplanation: Coarctation is a recognized association of Turner syndrome and may coexist with a bicuspid aortic valve.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Williams syndrome is associated with supravalvular aortic stenosis.
- B. Incorrect. Noonan syndrome is associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and pulmonary valve stenosis.
- C. Correct. Both associations are listed in the supplied CVS clinical guidance.
- D. Incorrect. Down syndrome is classically associated with AVSD.
- E. Incorrect. Maternal lithium exposure is associated with Ebstein anomaly.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CoA ↔ Turner syndrome.
- CoA may coexist with bicuspid aortic valve.
- Always examine pulses and measure BP in all four limbs.

cases.title: Pulses, pressures and outflow obstruction

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy has recurrent headaches and epistaxis. Blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg in the right arm. Femoral pulses are delayed compared with the radial pulses. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the upper sternal edge and a continuous murmur between the scapulae. Which finding best explains the interscapular continuous murmur?

options.label: C
options.text: Aortic regurgitation from a bicuspid valve

options.label: D
options.text: Venous hum from the jugular veins

options.label: E
options.text: Blood flowing through enlarged collateral vessels around the narrowed aorta

questions.correctAnswerText: Blood flowing through enlarged collateral vessels around the narrowed aorta
questions.initialExplanation: Older children with milder coarctation are asymptomatic or have hypertension symptoms (headache, epistaxis, dizziness). Collateral vessels between the proximal and distal aorta cause radio-femoral delay and a continuous murmur heard at the back between the scapulae.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A PDA gives a continuous murmur in the left infraclavicular area, not the back.
- B. Incorrect. VSD gives a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge.
- C. Incorrect. Aortic regurgitation causes a diastolic murmur; a bicuspid valve may coexist with CoA but does not explain a continuous murmur between the scapulae.
- D. Incorrect. Venous hum is infraclavicular, innocent, and does not occur with hypertension and delayed femoral pulses.
- E. Correct. Collaterals explain both the radio-femoral delay and the interscapular continuous murmur.
- Clinical reasoning: Hypertension plus delayed femoral pulses should prompt BP measurement in all four limbs, a CXR (rib notching, usually after about 6 years; figure-of-3 sign), echo Doppler, and CT/MR angiography as needed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Adult-type CoA: hypertension symptoms, radio-femoral delay, ESM at the upper sternal edge, collateral murmur at the back.
- CXR: rib notching (>6 years), figure-of-3 sign; ECG: LVH.
- Mild: medical control of hypertension; moderate: balloon dilatation ± stent; severe: surgical repair.
- Complications: hypertension complications, IE, LV failure, cerebral aneurysm rupture, sudden death.
