source.sheet: Coarctation of the aorta — adult type (sheet p. 18–20).

cases.title: The adolescent who faints during exercise
cases.vignette: A 14-year-old boy reports exertional chest pain and two episodes of syncope while playing football. On examination, the peripheral pulse is weak and slow-rising. A systolic ejection murmur is heard in the aortic area and radiates to the carotids. Echocardiography demonstrates significant aortic outflow obstruction.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains the exertional syncope, weak pulse and ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids?
questions.correctAnswerText: Aortic stenosis
questions.initialExplanation: Aortic stenosis obstructs left ventricular outflow. Severe obstruction can reduce cardiac output, particularly during exercise, causing chest pain or syncope. The systolic ejection murmur radiates to the carotids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. ASD — Incorrect. ASD is associated with fixed wide splitting of S2 and a pulmonary flow murmur.
- B. Mitral regurgitation — Incorrect. It produces a pansystolic apical murmur, usually radiating to the axilla.
- C. Aortic stenosis — Correct. It explains the weak slow pulse, exertional symptoms and carotid-radiating ejection systolic murmur.
- D. Pulmonary stenosis — Incorrect. It is a right ventricular outflow lesion and its murmur is heard at the upper left sternal edge, often radiating to the back.
- E. PDA — Incorrect. PDA typically produces a continuous machinery murmur and bounding pulses.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Aortic stenosis → left ventricular outflow obstruction.
- Severe AS may cause exertional chest pain, syncope and sudden death.
- Murmur: ejection systolic in the aortic area, radiating to the carotids.

questions.stem: Which haemodynamic consequence is expected in significant aortic stenosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced systemic vascular resistance due to ductal runoff

options.label: C
options.text: Right ventricular volume overload as the primary effect

options.label: D
options.text: Increased pulmonary blood flow from an atrial left-to-right shunt

options.label: E
options.text: Left ventricular pressure overload and hypertrophy

questions.correctAnswerText: Left ventricular pressure overload and hypertrophy
questions.initialExplanation: Aortic stenosis obstructs left ventricular outflow. The ventricle must generate higher pressure to eject blood, producing pressure overload and left ventricular hypertrophy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ductal runoff is associated with a large PDA.
- B. Incorrect. Isolated right atrial enlargement is not the primary haemodynamic effect of AS.
- C. Incorrect. Right ventricular pressure overload is expected in pulmonary stenosis.
- D. Incorrect. This describes an atrial-level left-to-right shunt such as ASD.
- E. Correct. The obstruction is at the left ventricular outflow tract, so LV pressure rises and hypertrophy develops.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- AS → LV outflow obstruction → LV pressure overload → LVH.
- Severe obstruction reduces cardiac output.
- Exertional syncope and chest pain are important warning symptoms.

questions.stem: Which examination combination is most characteristic of significant aortic stenosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border

options.label: B
options.text: Weak slow pulse, heavy apex beat and systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids

options.label: C
options.text: Bounding pulse, wide pulse pressure and continuous machinery murmur

options.label: D
options.text: Fixed wide split S2 and upper left sternal flow murmur

options.label: E
options.text: Loud P2 and right ventricular heave

questions.correctAnswerText: Weak slow pulse, heavy apex beat and systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance a weak slow pulse, reduced blood pressure, a heavy apex beat, carotid thrill and an ejection systolic murmur in the aortic area radiating to the carotids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A pansystolic lower left sternal murmur is characteristic of VSD.
- B. Correct. These findings reflect left ventricular pressure overload and aortic outflow obstruction.
- C. Incorrect. This is the characteristic large PDA pattern.
- D. Incorrect. This is the classic ASD auscultatory pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Loud P2 and right ventricular heave suggest pulmonary hypertension or right-sided pressure loading.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Aortic stenosis: weak slow pulse and carotid-radiating ESM.
- Ejection click may be heard in valvular AS.
- Echo is diagnostic.

questions.stem: Which investigation is the definitive test for confirming and assessing the severity of aortic stenosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Echocardiography
questions.initialExplanation: Echocardiography establishes the structural diagnosis and evaluates the valve and outflow obstruction. ECG and chest X-ray may show secondary effects such as LVH and cardiomegaly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Abdominal ultrasound does not assess the aortic valve.
- B. Correct. Echo defines the valve and obstruction and is the diagnostic investigation described.
- C. Incorrect. FBC does not diagnose aortic stenosis.
- D. Incorrect. CXR may show cardiomegaly but cannot reliably define the valve lesion.
- E. Incorrect. Urine culture is unrelated to cardiac outflow obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Echo: diagnostic.
- CXR: may show cardiomegaly.
- ECG: may show LVH.

questions.stem: A child with severe symptomatic valvular aortic stenosis is assessed by the cardiac team. Which intervention is described for symptomatic children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Balloon aortic valvotomy
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance balloon valvotomy for symptomatic children with aortic stenosis. A newborn with severe AS may require a different strategy, including aortic valve replacement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Balloon aortic valvotomy is the intervention described for symptomatic children.
- B. Incorrect. Pulmonary artery banding is a palliative procedure for selected shunt lesions.
- C. Incorrect. A BT shunt is used as palliation in selected cyanotic congenital heart disease.
- D. Incorrect. PDA coil closure treats a persistent ductus.
- E. Incorrect. Balloon atrial septostomy improves mixing in selected cyanotic lesions such as TGA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Symptomatic child with AS: balloon valvotomy is described.
- Severe AS in a newborn may require aortic valve replacement.
- Treatment decisions depend on anatomy, severity and specialist assessment.

questions.stem: Which group of complications is most relevant to significant untreated aortic stenosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Nephrotic syndrome, renal stones and enuresis

options.label: B
options.text: Tet spells and paradoxical brain abscess as the defining complications

options.label: C
options.text: Hepatic failure and portal hypertension as the defining complications

options.label: E
options.text: Heart failure, infective endocarditis and sudden death

questions.correctAnswerText: Heart failure, infective endocarditis and sudden death
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance heart failure, infective endocarditis and sudden death among complications of aortic stenosis. Exertional syncope and chest pain should prompt careful evaluation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are renal conditions and are unrelated to the defining complications of AS.
- B. Incorrect. Tet spells and brain abscess are complications associated with cyanotic lesions such as TOF.
- C. Incorrect. Hepatic failure and portal hypertension are not the defining complications listed.
- D. Incorrect. These are chronic respiratory conditions.
- E. Correct. These are the complications listed for AS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- AS complications: heart failure, IE and sudden death.
- Exertional chest pain or syncope is a red flag.
- Follow-up is essential even in children initially described as asymptomatic.

cases.title: The child with a pulmonary area murmur
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child is referred after a systolic murmur is detected. There is no cyanosis or heart failure. Examination reveals a left parasternal heave and an ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge, radiating to the back. Echocardiography demonstrates restricted pulmonary valve opening with increased flow velocity.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains this child's findings?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary stenosis
questions.initialExplanation: Pulmonary stenosis obstructs right ventricular outflow. The characteristic ejection systolic murmur is heard at the upper left sternal edge and may radiate to the back.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Aortic stenosis produces a murmur in the aortic area radiating to the carotids.
- B. Incorrect. CoA causes upper–lower limb BP discrepancy and weak femoral pulses.
- C. Correct. The murmur location and radiation, together with a parasternal heave, fit pulmonary stenosis.
- D. Incorrect. Mitral stenosis produces a mid-diastolic apical murmur.
- E. Incorrect. PDA produces a continuous machinery murmur in the left infraclavicular area.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PS → right ventricular outflow obstruction.
- Murmur: ejection systolic at upper left sternal edge, radiating to the back.
- A left parasternal heave may reflect RV hypertrophy.

questions.stem: Which syndrome association is specifically listed for pulmonary stenosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Noonan syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance associates pulmonary valve stenosis with Noonan syndrome. It also lists congenital rubella as an association.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Down syndrome is classically associated with AVSD.
- B. Incorrect. Turner syndrome is associated with coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve.
- C. Incorrect. Marfan syndrome is associated with aortic disease and mitral valve prolapse rather than the characteristic PS association.
- D. Incorrect. Williams syndrome is associated with supravalvular aortic stenosis.
- E. Correct. Noonan syndrome is associated with pulmonary valve stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Noonan syndrome → pulmonary stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
- Congenital rubella is also associated with pulmonary stenosis in the CVS clinical guidance.
- Williams syndrome → supravalvular aortic stenosis.

questions.stem: What is the primary haemodynamic consequence of significant pulmonary stenosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Right ventricular pressure overload and hypertrophy

options.label: D
options.text: Left atrial volume overload due to mitral regurgitation

questions.correctAnswerText: Right ventricular pressure overload and hypertrophy
questions.initialExplanation: Pulmonary stenosis obstructs right ventricular outflow. The right ventricle must generate higher pressure to eject blood, producing right ventricular hypertrophy and, in severe disease, right-sided heart failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The obstruction is at the right ventricular outflow, so RV pressure rises and RVH develops.
- B. Incorrect. Aortic diastolic runoff occurs in PDA.
- C. Incorrect. Pulmonary venous obstruction is not the mechanism of valvular PS.
- D. Incorrect. This describes left-sided volume loading, not pulmonary stenosis.
- E. Incorrect. Left ventricular pressure overload is seen in aortic stenosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PS → RV outflow obstruction → RVH.
- Severe PS can cause cyanosis and right-sided heart failure early in life.
- Severity determines symptoms and intervention.

questions.stem: Which investigation confirms pulmonary stenosis and defines its anatomy?
questions.correctAnswerText: Echocardiography
questions.initialExplanation: Echocardiography is diagnostic for pulmonary stenosis and evaluates the valve and right ventricular consequences.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. CXR may show cardiomegaly but cannot define the pulmonary valve lesion.
- B. Correct. Echo establishes the diagnosis and assesses anatomy and haemodynamic severity.
- C. Incorrect. Urine protein is unrelated.
- D. Incorrect. Abdominal CT does not assess pulmonary valve anatomy.
- E. Incorrect. EEG is unrelated to structural cardiac disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Echo is diagnostic.
- ECG may show RVH.
- CXR may show cardiomegaly in significant disease.

questions.stem: A child with pulmonary stenosis is symptomatic and has significant valvular obstruction. Which treatment is described as the treatment of choice in most symptomatic children?

options.label: E
options.text: Surgical closure of the interventricular septum

questions.correctAnswerText: Transcatheter balloon dilatation
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance transcatheter balloon dilatation as the treatment of choice in most symptomatic children with pulmonary stenosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. PDA ligation treats a persistent ductus.
- B. Incorrect. Aortic valve replacement treats selected severe aortic valve disease.
- C. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not relieve the anatomical obstruction.
- D. Correct. Balloon dilatation relieves valvular pulmonary outflow obstruction.
- E. Incorrect. VSD closure treats an interventricular communication, not isolated pulmonary stenosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Symptomatic valvular PS: balloon dilatation is described.
- Asymptomatic patients require follow-up and echocardiographic assessment.
- Severe neonatal PS may present with cyanosis and heart failure.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes severe pulmonary stenosis from severe aortic stenosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Both typically produce identical pulse findings

options.label: C
options.text: PS causes LVH; AS causes RVH

options.label: D
options.text: PS causes right ventricular outflow obstruction; AS causes left ventricular outflow obstruction

options.label: E
options.text: PS is associated with a carotid-radiating murmur; AS radiates to the back

questions.correctAnswerText: PS causes right ventricular outflow obstruction; AS causes left ventricular outflow obstruction
questions.initialExplanation: The anatomical side of the obstruction determines which ventricle is pressure-loaded: pulmonary stenosis affects the right ventricle, while aortic stenosis affects the left ventricle.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Severe obstruction of either outflow tract can cause heart failure.
- B. Incorrect. Pulse findings and murmur radiation differ according to lesion location.
- C. Incorrect. The hypertrophy patterns are reversed: PS causes RVH and AS causes LVH.
- D. Correct. This is the central physiological distinction.
- E. Incorrect. AS typically radiates to the carotids; PS radiates to the back.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PS → right ventricle; AS → left ventricle.
- PS murmur radiates to the back; AS murmur radiates to the carotids.
- Echo establishes the anatomy and severity in both lesions.

topics.name: The Cyanotic Newborn — Initial Clinical Approach

cases.title: Central cyanosis in the first hours of life
cases.vignette: A newborn develops central cyanosis shortly after delivery. The tongue and oral mucosa are blue, and pulse oximetry shows low oxygen saturation. The infant is stabilized while A hyperoxia test and arterial blood gas assessment are discussed, and urgent echocardiography is arranged.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly indicates central rather than peripheral cyanosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Cool extremities with normal arterial oxygenation

options.label: B
options.text: Blue hands and feet in a cold newborn with a pink tongue

options.label: C
options.text: Perioral colour change that disappears after warming

questions.correctAnswerText: Bluish tongue and soft palate
questions.initialExplanation: Central cyanosis involves mucous membranes, particularly the tongue and soft palate, and is associated with reduced arterial oxygen saturation. Peripheral cyanosis usually affects the hands and feet and may occur with cold exposure or poor peripheral perfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Cool extremities with normal arterial oxygenation suggest peripheral vasoconstriction or poor peripheral perfusion.
- B. Incorrect. Blue hands and feet with a pink tongue suggest peripheral cyanosis.
- C. Incorrect. Improvement with warming supports peripheral rather than central cyanosis.
- D. Incorrect. Nail-bed colour change alone does not establish central cyanosis.
- E. Correct. Cyanosis of the tongue and soft palate is a key sign of central cyanosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Central cyanosis: tongue and mucous membranes; low arterial oxygen saturation.
- Peripheral cyanosis: hands, feet and sometimes perioral area; may occur with cold or shock.
- Anaemia can make central cyanosis less obvious clinically.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the hyperoxia test in a centrally cyanosed newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: To distinguish cardiac cyanosis from a respiratory cause or persistent pulmonary hypertension

options.label: C
options.text: To diagnose an atrial septal defect specifically

questions.correctAnswerText: To distinguish cardiac cyanosis from a respiratory cause or persistent pulmonary hypertension
questions.initialExplanation: The hyperoxia test assesses the response to 100% oxygen. Persistently low arterial oxygenation despite high inspired oxygen supports cyanotic congenital heart disease, whereas a substantial improvement may support respiratory disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the diagnostic purpose described.
- B. Incorrect. It does not measure renal perfusion.
- C. Incorrect. The test does not identify one particular cardiac defect.
- D. Incorrect. IE requires clinical assessment, blood cultures and echocardiography.
- E. Incorrect. CoA is diagnosed by cardiovascular examination and imaging, particularly echocardiography.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hyperoxia test: 100% oxygen for the period specified, with ABG assessment.
- Persistent low PaO2 despite 100% oxygen supports cyanotic CHD.
- Improvement may suggest respiratory disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension.
- Arterial blood gas is important; pulse oximetry alone is not sufficiently reliable for the PaO2 comparison described.

questions.stem: After a hyperoxia test, the infant's right radial arterial PaO2 remains markedly low despite 100% oxygen. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Cyanotic congenital heart disease becomes more likely

options.label: C
options.text: Cyanotic congenital heart disease is excluded

options.label: D
options.text: The result confirms a PDA without other lesions

options.label: E
options.text: It proves the infant has peripheral cyanosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Cyanotic congenital heart disease becomes more likely
questions.initialExplanation: Failure of arterial oxygenation to improve meaningfully with 100% oxygen supports a cardiac right-to-left shunt physiology, although the result must be interpreted with the clinical assessment and urgent echocardiography.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Persistently low PaO2 despite high inspired oxygen supports cyanotic congenital heart disease 's framework.
- B. Incorrect. The result does not specifically diagnose bronchiolitis.
- C. Incorrect. The test does not exclude cardiac disease; the opposite interpretation is expected.
- D. Incorrect. It does not identify PDA as the only lesion.
- E. Incorrect. Peripheral cyanosis is not diagnosed by a persistently low arterial PaO2.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- A poor PaO2 response to 100% oxygen suggests a cardiac shunt.
- An improved response supports a pulmonary cause or persistent pulmonary hypertension.
- Do not delay ABC stabilization or echocardiography while performing diagnostic tests.

questions.stem: A cyanotic newborn may have a duct-dependent cardiac lesion. Which immediate medication is used to maintain ductal patency while urgent cardiac assessment is arranged?
questions.correctAnswerText: Prostaglandin E infusion
questions.initialExplanation: Prostaglandin E is used to maintain ductal patency in duct-dependent congenital heart disease while the infant is stabilized and definitive assessment or intervention is arranged.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Prostaglandin E — Correct. It maintains ductal patency, which may be essential for systemic or pulmonary blood flow in duct-dependent lesions.
- B. Captopril — Incorrect. It is an ACE inhibitor used in selected heart-failure settings, not for maintaining ductal patency.
- C. Furosemide — Incorrect. It may be used for congestion in selected cases but does not maintain ductal patency and cannot replace emergency stabilization.
- D. Indomethacin — Incorrect. It inhibits prostaglandin synthesis and promotes ductal closure in selected preterm PDA cases.
- E. Ibuprofen — Incorrect. It is also an anti-prostaglandin drug used to promote PDA closure in selected preterm infants.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PGE maintains the ductus.
- Indomethacin/ibuprofen promote ductal closure.
- Potential PGE adverse effects listed include apnoea, flushing, vasodilation and hypotension; monitor in an appropriate setting.
- ABC, urgent echocardiography and cardiac consultation are essential.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the haemoglobin level at which central cyanosis may become clinically visible?

options.label: A
options.text: It is visible when haemoglobin is above 20 g/dL

options.label: B
options.text: It is independent of haemoglobin concentration

options.label: C
options.text: It is typically more obvious in severe anaemia

options.label: D
options.text: It may become clinically apparent when reduced haemoglobin exceeds about 5 g/dL

options.label: E
options.text: It occurs when total haemoglobin is below 5 g/dL

questions.correctAnswerText: It may become clinically apparent when reduced haemoglobin exceeds about 5 g/dL
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that central cyanosis becomes clinically apparent when reduced haemoglobin exceeds approximately 50 g/L (5 g/dL). Severe anaemia may make cyanosis less obvious.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the threshold stated.
- B. Incorrect. The visibility of cyanosis is affected by the absolute amount of reduced haemoglobin.
- C. Incorrect. Anaemia may make cyanosis less pronounced because total haemoglobin is reduced.
- D. Correct. This matches the value.
- E. Incorrect. The relevant value is the concentration of reduced haemoglobin, not total haemoglobin below 5 g/dL.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cyanosis depends on the absolute amount of reduced haemoglobin.
- It may be less obvious in anaemia.
- Always interpret colour with oxygen saturation, perfusion and the full clinical picture.

cases.title: Recurrent cyanotic spells in an infant
cases.vignette: A 5-month-old infant is brought with episodes of sudden worsening cyanosis, rapid breathing and inconsolable crying, often during feeding or crying. During an attack, the infant becomes markedly distressed. The mother reports that the infant sometimes assumes a knee–chest posture after crying. Examination between episodes reveals central cyanosis, clubbing and an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart and oligemic lung fields.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Tetralogy of Fallot
questions.initialExplanation: Cyanotic spells, knee–chest posture, an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a boot-shaped heart with oligemic lungs strongly support TOF.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. TGA — Incorrect. TGA usually presents with severe neonatal cyanosis due to parallel circulations and requires mixing.
- B. TOF — Correct. The combination of pulmonary outflow obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta and RVH produces the characteristic physiology and clinical presentation.
- C. CoA — Incorrect. CoA is characterized by upper–lower limb pressure differences and weak femoral pulses.
- D. ASD — Incorrect. ASD usually produces a left-to-right shunt and fixed wide splitting of S2 rather than tet spells.
- E. PDA — Incorrect. PDA usually causes a continuous machinery murmur and bounding pulses when significant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TOF is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease in children.
- Tet spells and squatting/knee–chest posture are key clinical clues.
- Boot-shaped heart and oligemic lung fields support the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which set correctly lists the four components of TOF?

options.label: A
options.text: VSD, coarctation, PDA and left atrial enlargement

options.label: B
options.text: Aortic stenosis, ASD, LVH and mitral regurgitation

options.label: C
options.text: Pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta and RVH

options.label: D
options.text: Pulmonary atresia, mitral stenosis, ASD and LVH

options.label: E
options.text: ASD, PDA, LVH and pulmonary hypertension

questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta and RVH
questions.initialExplanation: TOF consists of pulmonary outflow obstruction, a large VSD, an overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Coarctation and PDA are not components of TOF.
- B. Incorrect. These are left-sided and atrial lesions, not the TOF tetrad.
- C. Correct. This is the classic tetrad.
- D. Incorrect. This combination does not define TOF.
- E. Incorrect. These are not the four components of TOF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Remember the four components: pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH.
- The degree of pulmonary stenosis largely determines pulmonary blood flow and the timing/severity of cyanosis.
- Infundibular pulmonary stenosis is described as the commonest form.

questions.stem: What is the main haemodynamic explanation for cyanosis in TOF?

options.label: A
options.text: Right-to-left shunting across the VSD because of right ventricular outflow obstruction

options.label: B
options.text: Complete mixing at the atrial level with no ventricular communication

options.label: D
options.text: Increased pulmonary blood flow from a left-to-right shunt

questions.correctAnswerText: Right-to-left shunting across the VSD because of right ventricular outflow obstruction
questions.initialExplanation: Pulmonary stenosis obstructs right ventricular outflow. Blood is therefore directed across the VSD into the overriding aorta, producing systemic desaturation and cyanosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Severe RV outflow obstruction promotes right-to-left flow through the VSD into the aorta.
- B. Incorrect. TOF has a VSD and does not depend on isolated atrial mixing.
- C. Incorrect. Aortic-to-pulmonary runoff describes PDA physiology.
- D. Incorrect. Increased pulmonary flow from a left-to-right shunt is typical of acyanotic lesions such as VSD, ASD and PDA.
- E. Incorrect. Pulmonary venous obstruction is not the mechanism of TOF cyanosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Severity of pulmonary stenosis determines the degree of right-to-left shunting.
- Severe obstruction can cause early neonatal cyanosis and duct dependence.
- Less severe obstruction may cause cyanosis later as infundibular obstruction progresses.

questions.stem: Why may cyanosis in TOF become more apparent at 3–6 months rather than immediately at birth?

options.label: A
options.text: The ductus arteriosus typically remains open until 6 months

options.label: B
options.text: The VSD closes during the first weeks of life

options.label: C
options.text: The aorta gradually moves to the left side

options.label: D
options.text: Infundibular pulmonary stenosis may become more severe with time

questions.correctAnswerText: Infundibular pulmonary stenosis may become more severe with time
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance explains that cyanosis may develop after several months because infundibular hypertrophy and pulmonary outflow obstruction may progress, increasing right-to-left shunting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The ductus does not normally remain open until 6 months.
- B. Incorrect. VSD closure is not the mechanism described and would not explain worsening cyanosis.
- C. Incorrect. Aortic position is part of the congenital anatomy and does not progressively move in this way.
- D. Correct. Increasing infundibular obstruction reduces pulmonary blood flow and increases right-to-left shunting.
- E. Incorrect. Pulmonary venous return does not progressively stop in TOF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TOF cyanosis depends on the degree of RV outflow obstruction.
- Severe obstruction may cause neonatal cyanosis and duct dependence.
- More commonly, cyanosis becomes apparent after infancy begins as obstruction increases.

questions.stem: Which posture may relieve a hypercyanotic spell in an infant with TOF?
questions.correctAnswerText: Knee–chest position
questions.initialExplanation: The knee–chest or squatting position increases systemic vascular resistance, which reduces right-to-left shunting and may improve pulmonary blood flow and oxygenation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the posture described to relieve tet spells.
- B. Incorrect. Neck flexion may compromise the airway and is not the intended manoeuvre.
- C. Incorrect. Trendelenburg is not the recommended posture described.
- D. Incorrect. It does not provide the haemodynamic benefit of the knee–chest posture.
- E. Correct. Knee–chest positioning is an immediate supportive measure during a tet spell.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Knee–chest posture increases systemic vascular resistance.
- Squatting in an older child has a similar physiological purpose.
- A hypercyanotic spell is an emergency; positioning is only one part of treatment.

questions.stem: During a prolonged tet spell, which statement about the murmur is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: It changes into a continuous machinery murmur

options.label: B
options.text: It becomes louder as pulmonary blood flow falls

options.label: C
options.text: It may become softer or disappear because pulmonary blood flow through the stenotic outflow tract falls

options.label: D
options.text: Murmur intensity is unrelated to the severity of the outflow obstruction

options.label: E
options.text: It is replaced by a fixed split S2

questions.correctAnswerText: It may become softer or disappear because pulmonary blood flow through the stenotic outflow tract falls
questions.initialExplanation: During a tet spell, infundibular spasm further reduces pulmonary blood flow. The ejection systolic murmur may become softer or disappear, which is an important clinical clue.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A continuous machinery murmur is associated with PDA.
- B. Incorrect. Reduced flow through the obstructed pulmonary outflow tract may make the murmur softer rather than louder.
- C. Correct. clinical guidance specifically notes that the murmur may decrease or disappear during a tet spell.
- D. Incorrect. The changing murmur intensity during a spell has clinical significance because it reflects reduced pulmonary flow.
- E. Incorrect. Fixed wide splitting of S2 is associated with ASD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tet spell → infundibular spasm → reduced pulmonary blood flow.
- Murmur may become softer/disappear during the spell.
- A quieter murmur during worsening cyanosis is not reassuring.

questions.stem: A prolonged hypercyanotic spell is not settling with positioning and calming. Which combination represents the treatment principles listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Indomethacin, fluid restriction and ductal closure

options.label: B
options.text: Diuretics alone and strict fluid restriction

options.label: C
options.text: Antibiotics alone because most tet spells are infective

options.label: D
options.text: Adenosine followed by immediate elective discharge

options.label: E
options.text: Calm the child, oxygen, morphine, beta-blockade, increase systemic vascular resistance and support intravascular volume as indicated

questions.correctAnswerText: Calm the child, oxygen, morphine, beta-blockade, increase systemic vascular resistance and support intravascular volume as indicated
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance calming, oxygen, morphine, propranolol, a vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine, correction of acidosis when indicated and IV volume support among measures for a prolonged tet spell. Airway and ventilatory support may be required.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is a ductal-closure approach for selected preterm PDA and would not treat a tet spell.
- B. Incorrect. Diuresis and fluid restriction are not the definitive treatment principles for a tet spell and may worsen preload if the child is volume-depleted.
- C. Incorrect. A tet spell is caused by acute worsening of TOF physiology, not necessarily infection.
- D. Incorrect. Adenosine treats selected SVT, not a hypercyanotic spell.
- E. Correct. These measures address agitation, infundibular spasm, systemic vascular resistance, hypovolaemia and acidosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tet spell treatment: calm, knee–chest, oxygen, morphine, beta-blocker, increase SVR, fluid support and correct severe acidosis when present.
- Severe/prolonged spells may require airway and ventilatory support.
- Avoid unnecessary distress and procedures during an acute spell.

source.raw: CVS sheet — Page 25. Drug doses are intentionally omitted because the OCR source requires verification.

questions.stem: Which chest X-ray pattern is classically associated with TOF?

options.label: D
options.text: Boot-shaped heart with oligemic lung fields

questions.correctAnswerText: Boot-shaped heart with oligemic lung fields
questions.initialExplanation: TOF is associated with a boot-shaped cardiac silhouette due to the uplifted apex and a narrow pulmonary artery segment, with reduced pulmonary vascular markings because pulmonary blood flow is decreased.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Snowman appearance is associated with supracardiac TAPVR.
- B. Incorrect. Egg-on-side appearance and pulmonary plethora are associated with TGA.
- C. Incorrect. Rib notching and figure-of-three appearance are associated with CoA.
- D. Correct. Boot-shaped heart and oligemic lungs are the classic TOF pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Cardiomegaly and pulmonary oedema may occur in heart failure but do not define the typical TOF film.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TOF: boot-shaped heart, uplifted apex and oligemic lung fields.
- ECG may show RVH.
- Echo is diagnostic.
- CBC may show polycythaemia due to chronic hypoxia.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the surgical strategy for TOF in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: PDA ligation is the definitive repair

options.label: B
options.text: most patients require lifelong prostaglandin without surgery

options.label: C
options.text: Definitive correction consists of closing the ASD

options.label: D
options.text: Aortic valve replacement is the routine definitive procedure

options.label: E
options.text: A palliative systemic-to-pulmonary shunt may be used early; total correction closes the VSD and relieves RV outflow obstruction

questions.correctAnswerText: A palliative systemic-to-pulmonary shunt may be used early; total correction closes the VSD and relieves RV outflow obstruction
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance a palliative Blalock–Taussig shunt to increase pulmonary blood flow in selected infants, followed by total correction involving VSD closure and repair of the right ventricular outflow obstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. PDA ligation does not correct TOF.
- B. Incorrect. Prostaglandin may be needed in duct-dependent severe disease as a bridge, but it is not the definitive long-term treatment for all patients.
- C. Incorrect. TOF includes a VSD and RV outflow obstruction; closing an ASD alone would not correct the lesion.
- D. Incorrect. Aortic valve replacement is not the routine repair for TOF.
- E. Correct. This describes the palliative and definitive surgical principles.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Palliative BT shunt: increases pulmonary blood flow and supports oxygenation/growth.
- Total correction: VSD closure + relief of RV outflow obstruction.
- clinical guidance gives early infancy as the usual period for definitive repair; actual timing depends on anatomy and specialist assessment.

questions.stem: A child with longstanding TOF develops fever, headache and focal neurological signs. Which serious complication should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Brain abscess
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance highlights brain abscess as an important complication of cyanotic congenital heart disease such as TOF. Right-to-left shunting allows embolic material to bypass pulmonary filtration, and chronic hypoxia may contribute to vulnerability.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Brain abscess is a recognized serious complication in cyanotic CHD and should be considered with fever and focal neurological signs.
- B. Incorrect. Otitis media alone does not adequately explain focal neurological signs; intracranial complications must be considered.
- C. Incorrect. Migraine does not explain fever and focal infective features in this context.
- D. Incorrect. Dehydration does not explain a focal neurological presentation.
- E. Incorrect. A febrile convulsion does not explain focal neurological signs or the cyanotic heart-disease risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TOF complications include tet spells, IE, heart failure, failure to thrive, polycythaemia, thromboembolism, brain abscess and cerebral infarction/thrombosis.
- New fever plus focal neurological signs in a cyanotic child is an emergency.
- Evaluate promptly; do not attribute neurological symptoms to hypoxia without considering intracranial complications.

cases.title: The cyanotic infant

questions.stem: An 11-month-old with unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot and a haemoglobin of 21 g/dL has had 3 days of vomiting with poor oral intake. He suddenly develops right-sided weakness. He is afebrile, with no meningism, and has had no cyanotic spells. CT shows a cerebral infarct. What is the most likely mechanism?

options.label: B
options.text: Infarction secondary to a hypercyanotic spell with convulsions

questions.correctAnswerText: Cerebral thrombosis due to polycythaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic hypoxia increases erythropoietin and RBC mass (polycythaemia), which predisposes to thrombosis, especially with dehydration. In this afebrile child with no spell, cerebral thrombosis is the best explanation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Brain abscess follows paradoxical embolism (no pulmonary filtration) and presents with fever, headache and focal signs.
- B. Incorrect. Infarction after hypercyanotic spells follows convulsions and hypoxia; none occurred.
- C. Correct. Polycythaemia (Hb 21) + dehydration → brain thrombosis.
- D. Incorrect. IE would give persistent fever and other peripheral signs.
- E. Incorrect. Meningitis causes fever and meningism.
- Clinical reasoning: Distinguish the three neurological complications of TOF by the setting: fever + focal signs → abscess; after spell/convulsions → infarction; high Hb/dehydration → thrombosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TOF complications: IE, cyanotic spells, HF (rare), FTT, polycythaemia, thromboembolism, brain abscess, brain infarction, brain thrombosis.
- Polycythaemia results from hypoxia → increased erythropoietin.
- Brain abscess risk comes from the loss of pulmonary filtration with right-to-left shunting.

cases.title: Severe cyanosis in a newborn with little murmur
cases.vignette: A term newborn develops marked central cyanosis on the second day of life. The infant is breathless and poorly oxygenated. Cardiac examination reveals a single loud second heart sound and no obvious murmur. Chest X-ray shows an egg-on-side appearance with increased pulmonary vascular markings. Echocardiography demonstrates that the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle.

questions.stem: What is the defining anatomical abnormality in TGA?

options.label: A
options.text: Both great arteries arise from the right ventricle

options.label: B
options.text: The aortic arch is narrowed just distal to the left subclavian artery

options.label: C
options.text: The aorta arises from the left ventricle and pulmonary artery from the right ventricle

options.label: D
options.text: The aorta arises from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery from the left ventricle

options.label: E
options.text: The pulmonary veins drain into the right atrium

questions.correctAnswerText: The aorta arises from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery from the left ventricle
questions.initialExplanation: In TGA, the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, creating two parallel rather than serial circulations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Both great arteries arising from the right ventricle describes a different conotruncal lesion.
- B. Incorrect. This is the typical region of coarctation.
- C. Incorrect. This is the normal ventriculo-arterial connection.
- D. Correct. This is the defining anatomy of complete TGA.
- E. Incorrect. This describes abnormal pulmonary venous drainage, not TGA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TGA: aorta from RV; pulmonary artery from LV.
- The result is parallel circulation.
- Survival requires a communication that permits mixing.

questions.stem: Why is communication between the two circulations essential for survival in TGA?

options.label: A
options.text: It causes the ductus arteriosus to disappear

options.label: B
options.text: It allows oxygenated and deoxygenated blood to mix so oxygen can reach the systemic circulation

options.label: C
options.text: It reduces the need for pulmonary gas exchange

options.label: D
options.text: It closes the foramen ovale immediately

options.label: E
options.text: It prevents most pulmonary blood flow

questions.correctAnswerText: It allows oxygenated and deoxygenated blood to mix so oxygen can reach the systemic circulation
questions.initialExplanation: The systemic and pulmonary circuits run in parallel in TGA. Mixing through an ASD/PFO, VSD or PDA is essential to deliver oxygenated blood to the body.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The ductus may be essential for mixing and systemic oxygenation.
- B. Correct. Mixing allows oxygenated pulmonary venous blood to enter the systemic circulation.
- C. Incorrect. Pulmonary gas exchange remains necessary.
- D. Incorrect. The communication must remain adequate; closure would worsen mixing.
- E. Incorrect. The purpose of the communication is not to stop pulmonary flow.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TGA is not compatible with life without adequate mixing.
- Mixing may occur through PFO/ASD, VSD or PDA.
- Maintaining ductal patency may be lifesaving while arranging definitive treatment.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern is most characteristic of TGA?

options.label: A
options.text: Bounding pulse and a continuous machinery murmur

options.label: B
options.text: Upper-limb hypertension and absent femoral pulses

options.label: C
options.text: Fixed wide split S2 with no cyanosis

options.label: D
options.text: Cyanosis develops after several years with clubbing and tet spells

options.label: E
options.text: Cyanosis usually becomes evident in the first days of life, with a loud single S2 and often no murmur

questions.correctAnswerText: Cyanosis usually becomes evident in the first days of life, with a loud single S2 and often no murmur
questions.initialExplanation: TGA commonly presents with early severe neonatal cyanosis. Clinical guidance a loud single S2 and that no murmur may be heard because transposition itself does not necessarily create turbulent flow across a valve or septal defect.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is the clinical pattern of a significant PDA.
- B. Incorrect. This is characteristic of coarctation.
- C. Incorrect. Fixed wide splitting of S2 is associated with ASD.
- D. Incorrect. Later cyanosis with tet spells is more characteristic of TOF.
- E. Correct. This matches the described TGA presentation and examination.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TGA: severe early neonatal cyanosis.
- Loud single S2; a murmur may be absent.
- Always assess adequacy of mixing and duct dependence.

questions.stem: Which chest X-ray appearance is associated with TGA?

options.label: D
options.text: Snowman sign with a normal pulmonary vascular pattern

options.label: E
options.text: Egg-on-side heart with increased pulmonary vascular markings

questions.correctAnswerText: Egg-on-side heart with increased pulmonary vascular markings
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance associates TGA with an egg-on-side cardiac silhouette, cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is the classic TOF pattern.
- B. Incorrect. This is associated with CoA.
- C. Incorrect. This does not represent the classic radiographic appearance described.
- D. Incorrect. Snowman appearance is associated with supracardiac TAPVR.
- E. Correct. Egg-on-side appearance with increased pulmonary vascular markings is described for TGA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TGA: egg-on-side appearance, cardiomegaly and plethoric lungs.
- TOF: boot-shaped heart and oligemic lungs.
- Echocardiography is diagnostic.

questions.stem: A severely cyanosed newborn with TGA is deteriorating while awaiting definitive surgery. Which immediate management is appropriate?

options.label: B
options.text: Treat with oral diuretics and discharge

options.label: D
options.text: Prostaglandin E to maintain ductal patency and urgent assessment for balloon atrial septostomy if mixing is inadequate

questions.correctAnswerText: Prostaglandin E to maintain ductal patency and urgent assessment for balloon atrial septostomy if mixing is inadequate
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance prostaglandin infusion for a sick cyanotic neonate with TGA and balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) to improve mixing when needed. Definitive treatment is an early arterial switch operation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stabilization, oxygenation support as needed, urgent echocardiography and cardiac consultation must not be delayed.
- B. Incorrect. A critically cyanosed newborn requires urgent inpatient specialist management, not discharge.
- C. Incorrect. Indomethacin closes the ductus and may worsen systemic oxygenation in duct-dependent TGA.
- D. Correct. Maintaining the ductus and ensuring adequate mixing are immediate priorities.
- E. Incorrect. PDA ligation would remove a potentially essential mixing route.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PGE maintains ductal patency.
- Rashkind balloon atrial septostomy increases atrial mixing.
- Definitive repair: arterial switch operation, performed early.
- Never close a potentially essential ductus before the circulation has been assessed.

questions.stem: Which operation is the definitive surgical correction described for complete TGA?

options.label: B
options.text: Blalock–Taussig shunt as the definitive repair in typical presentations

questions.correctAnswerText: Arterial switch operation
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies early surgical correction by arterial switch operation as the definitive treatment for TGA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Balloon dilatation treats pulmonary valve stenosis.
- B. Incorrect. A BT shunt is a palliative procedure in selected cyanotic lesions and is not the definitive correction for complete TGA.
- C. Correct. The arterial switch restores the great arteries to the appropriate ventriculo-arterial connections.
- D. Incorrect. Mitral valve replacement does not correct transposition.
- E. Incorrect. Coarctectomy treats coarctation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Initial stabilization: PGE and improve mixing if required.
- Definitive repair: early arterial switch operation.
- TGA requires urgent specialist neonatal cardiac care.

cases.title: The cyanotic infant

questions.stem: A term neonate, pink after an uneventful delivery, becomes progressively cyanosed by 36 hours of age. SpO2 is 70% and does not improve with oxygen. There is a loud single second sound, no murmur, and the chest X-ray shows an egg-on-side heart with plethoric lungs. Which event best explains the timing of the deterioration?

options.label: A
options.text: A rise in pulmonary vascular resistance

options.label: C
options.text: A fall in pulmonary vascular resistance causing a massive left-to-right shunt

options.label: D
options.text: Closure of the ductus arteriosus, reducing mixing between the two parallel circulations

questions.correctAnswerText: Closure of the ductus arteriosus, reducing mixing between the two parallel circulations
questions.initialExplanation: In TGA the pulmonary and systemic circulations run in parallel. Survival depends on mixing through a PFO/ASD, VSD or PDA. Functional closure of the duct in the first days of life reduces mixing and unmasks severe cyanosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A rise in PVR is not the mechanism of TGA cyanosis.
- B. Incorrect. The ductus venosus is part of the venous circuit and its closure does not cause cyanosis.
- C. Incorrect. A falling PVR does not cause the deterioration in TGA.
- D. Correct. Duct closure → loss of mixing → severe cyanosis (usually day 2).
- E. Incorrect. Infundibular spasm belongs to TOF tet spells, which present later.
- Clinical reasoning: Treat with prostaglandin to reopen the duct and a Rashkind balloon atrial septostomy to improve mixing, followed by early arterial switch surgery.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TGA = aorta from RV, pulmonary artery from LV; mixing is essential.
- TGA is the commonest cyanotic CHD in neonates (TOF in older children).
- Cyanosis, loud single S2, usually no murmur, egg-on-side heart, plethoric lungs.
- PGE + Rashkind septostomy, then arterial switch operation.

cases.title: A cyanotic neonate with an abnormal pulmonary venous connection
cases.vignette: A neonate presents with cyanosis and respiratory distress. Echocardiography demonstrates that the pulmonary veins do not connect normally to the left atrium. The cardiology team explains that the presentation depends on the degree of obstruction and the associated atrial communication. The differential diagnosis also includes tricuspid atresia, pulmonary atresia, truncus arteriosus, Ebstein anomaly, single-ventricle physiology and hypoplastic left heart syndrome.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is defined by failure of all pulmonary veins to connect normally to the left atrium?
questions.correctAnswerText: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR)
questions.initialExplanation: In TAPVR, pulmonary venous blood drains to the systemic venous circulation rather than directly to the left atrium. Clinical guidance several anatomical drainage patterns and an associated ASD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. CoA is a narrowing of the aorta.
- B. Correct. All pulmonary veins are abnormally connected and do not return directly to the left atrium.
- C. Incorrect. TOF involves pulmonary outflow obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta and RVH.
- D. Incorrect. ASD is an interatrial communication; it may coexist with TAPVR but is not the anomalous venous connection itself.
- E. Incorrect. Aortic stenosis is left ventricular outflow obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TAPVR: pulmonary veins do not connect normally to the LA.
- An atrial communication is important for systemic output.
- Clinical severity depends on venous obstruction and the degree of mixing.

questions.stem: Which radiographic sign is associated with supracardiac TAPVR in the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Snowman appearance
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance associates supracardiac TAPVR with the snowman appearance on chest X-ray.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Snowman appearance is the classic association for supracardiac TAPVR.
- B. Incorrect. Egg-on-side appearance is associated with TGA.
- C. Incorrect. Figure-of-three sign is associated with CoA.
- D. Incorrect. Boot-shaped heart is associated with TOF.
- E. Incorrect. Rib notching is due to collateral vessels in CoA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TAPVR supracardiac type → snowman appearance.
- TOF → boot-shaped heart.
- TGA → egg-on-side heart.
- Ebstein anomaly → box-shaped heart.

questions.stem: Which combination is most characteristic of Ebstein anomaly?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete AV canal with common AV valve

options.label: C
options.text: Pulmonary venous obstruction with snowman appearance

options.label: D
options.text: Juxtaductal aortic narrowing and rib notching

options.label: E
options.text: Downward displacement of the tricuspid valve, enlarged right atrium and small right ventricle

questions.correctAnswerText: Downward displacement of the tricuspid valve, enlarged right atrium and small right ventricle
questions.initialExplanation: Ebstein anomaly involves downward displacement of the tricuspid valve, producing an enlarged right atrium and a small functional right ventricle. Arrhythmias, including SVT, may occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes complete AVSD.
- B. Incorrect. Supravalvular aortic stenosis is associated with Williams syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. This describes TAPVR.
- D. Incorrect. This describes CoA.
- E. Correct. This is the anatomical pattern described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ebstein anomaly: apical displacement of the tricuspid valve.
- Large RA and small functional RV.
- May be associated with cyanosis, tricuspid regurgitation and SVT.
- clinical guidance associates it with a box-shaped cardiac silhouette.

questions.stem: Which ECG feature is highlighted for tricuspid atresia?

options.label: D
options.text: Complete right bundle branch block as the defining finding

questions.correctAnswerText: Left-axis deviation
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance highlights left-axis deviation in tricuspid atresia, reflecting the dominance of the left ventricle when the right ventricle is small or non-functional.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. QT prolongation may occur with electrolyte disturbance or long-QT syndrome.
- B. Correct. Left-axis deviation is specifically listed.
- C. Incorrect. Tall peaked T waves suggest hyperkalaemia.
- D. Incorrect. RBBB may be seen in other congenital lesions but is not the defining ECG feature given here.
- E. Incorrect. A delta wave suggests WPW syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tricuspid atresia: early cyanosis and an obligatory atrial-level communication for systemic venous blood to reach the left side.
- Clinical guidance left-axis deviation.
- Treatment is staged and anatomy-dependent.

questions.stem: A neonate with hypoplastic left heart syndrome becomes critically unwell as the ductus closes. Which mechanism best explains the deterioration?

options.label: A
options.text: A small PDA causes excessive coronary perfusion

options.label: C
options.text: The right ventricle suddenly becomes obstructed by an ASD

options.label: D
options.text: Systemic output becomes duct-dependent because the left ventricle cannot support it

options.label: E
options.text: The ductus closes and directly produces an isolated VSD

questions.correctAnswerText: Systemic output becomes duct-dependent because the left ventricle cannot support it
questions.initialExplanation: In HLHS, the left-sided cardiac structures are severely underdeveloped. Systemic perfusion is duct-dependent; ductal closure can cause profound low cardiac output, acidosis and collapse.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The problem is systemic outflow, not coronary overperfusion.
- B. Incorrect. Pulmonary venous drainage is not the mechanism of systemic collapse.
- C. Incorrect. An ASD does not suddenly obstruct the right ventricle.
- D. Correct. This describes the duct-dependent systemic circulation in HLHS.
- E. Incorrect. Ductal closure does not create a VSD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HLHS: duct-dependent systemic circulation.
- Ductal closure may cause shock, acidosis and death in early infancy.
- Stabilization includes ABC and prostaglandin E to maintain ductal patency, followed by urgent specialist management.

questions.stem: A neonate has severe cyanosis and is suspected to have a duct-dependent complex cardiac lesion. Which broad initial strategy is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Close the ductus immediately in most cyanotic neonates

options.label: B
options.text: Stabilize ABC, maintain ductal patency with prostaglandin when indicated, and obtain urgent echocardiography and cardiac consultation

options.label: C
options.text: Delay assessment until cyanosis persists for several weeks

questions.correctAnswerText: Stabilize ABC, maintain ductal patency with prostaglandin when indicated, and obtain urgent echocardiography and cardiac consultation
questions.initialExplanation: Several complex congenital lesions are duct-dependent. Initial management focuses on stabilization, preserving ductal flow when necessary, and defining anatomy urgently with echocardiography.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ductal closure can be fatal in duct-dependent systemic or pulmonary circulation.
- B. Correct. This is the safe initial approach for suspected duct-dependent congenital heart disease.
- C. Incorrect. Severe neonatal cyanosis requires urgent assessment.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics alone do not correct a duct-dependent cardiac lesion.
- E. Incorrect. Discharging a cyanotic neonate without diagnosis is unsafe.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cyanotic neonate: stabilize and investigate urgently.
- PGE may be lifesaving when ductal patency is required.
- Echocardiography defines the lesion and guides definitive treatment.

cases.title: Murmurs, syndromic screening and the fetal circulation

questions.stem: A cardiology team plans echocardiographic screening for newborns with different syndromic diagnoses. Which syndrome–lesion pairing is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: DiGeorge syndrome — aortic arch anomalies, tetralogy of Fallot and common arterial trunk

options.label: C
options.text: Williams syndrome — valvular pulmonary stenosis as the typical lesion

options.label: E
options.text: Noonan syndrome — coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve

questions.correctAnswerText: DiGeorge syndrome — aortic arch anomalies, tetralogy of Fallot and common arterial trunk
questions.initialExplanation: DiGeorge syndrome is associated with conotruncal and aortic arch anomalies: aortic arch anomalies, TOF and common arterial trunk (about 80%).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Turner syndrome → bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation (~15%). AVSD is the Down syndrome lesion.
- B. Correct. DiGeorge → aortic arch anomalies, TOF, common arterial trunk.
- C. Incorrect. Williams → supravalvular aortic stenosis. Pulmonary stenosis is linked with Alagille and Noonan syndromes.
- D. Incorrect. Down syndrome → AVSD (~30%), not supravalvular AS.
- E. Incorrect. Noonan → hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ASD and pulmonary valve stenosis; coarctation/bicuspid valve belong to Turner syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Down → AVSD; Edwards/Patau → VSD, ASD (complex); Turner → bicuspid AV, CoA.
- Noonan → HCM, ASD, PS; Alagille → PS; Williams → supravalvular AS.
- DiGeorge → arch anomalies, TOF, truncus; fetal alcohol → ASD, VSD, TOF.
- Marfan → aortic dissection, mitral valve prolapse; Kartagener → dextrocardia.
