cases.title: The cyanotic infant

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant has mild-to-moderate central cyanosis, tachypnoea and hepatomegaly. The chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
questions.correctAnswerText: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
questions.initialExplanation: Cyanosis with plethoric lung fields suggests a lesion with increased pulmonary blood flow, such as TAPVR (or TGA). TOF, tricuspid atresia, pulmonary atresia and Ebstein anomaly are all causes of oligaemic lungs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. TOF — oligaemic lungs, boot-shaped heart.
- B. Incorrect. Tricuspid atresia — oligaemic lungs, left-axis deviation.
- C. Incorrect. Pulmonary atresia — oligaemic lungs, duct-dependent, no murmur.
- D. Incorrect. Ebstein anomaly — oligaemic lungs, box-shaped heart.
- E. Correct. TAPVR: all pulmonary veins drain to the systemic venous side; cyanosis variable with HF signs and plethora; supracardiac type shows the snowman sign.
- Clinical reasoning: Classify cyanotic lesions by lung vascularity first.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Oligaemic lungs: pulmonary atresia, tricuspid atresia, PS/pulmonary hypertension, TOF, Eisenmenger, Ebstein.
- Plethoric lungs: VSD, PDA, ASD, AVSD, TAPVR, TGA.
- TAPVR types: supracardiac 50% (into SVC), cardiac 25%, infracardiac 20%, mixed 5%; ASD is associated.

source.raw: Summary — DD of oligaemic vs plethoric lungs (sheet p. 48); TAPVR (sheet p. 29–30).
source.sheet: Summary — DD of oligaemic vs plethoric lungs (sheet p. 48); TAPVR (sheet p. 29–30).

cases.title: Complex lesions and staged management

questions.stem: A neonate has early cyanosis with left-axis deviation on ECG. Echocardiography shows absence of the tricuspid valve, blood passing from the right atrium through an ASD to the left atrium and left ventricle, and a small non-functional right ventricle. Which management plan best fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Maintain pulmonary flow with prostaglandin E; use septostomy if needed, then staged shunt/banding, Glenn and Fontan

options.label: B
options.text: Arterial switch operation in the first week

options.label: D
options.text: Total correction with VSD closure at 6–12 months

options.label: E
options.text: Digoxin and diuretics with routine follow-up

questions.correctAnswerText: Maintain pulmonary flow with prostaglandin E; use septostomy if needed, then staged shunt/banding, Glenn and Fontan
questions.initialExplanation: This is tricuspid atresia, the commonest of the complex lesions. Only the left ventricle functions. Management is medical (PGE, supportive, Rashkind) then surgical palliation: BT shunt, pulmonary artery banding, Glenn or Fontan.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Matches clinical guidance's treatment plan.
- B. Incorrect. Arterial switch is the definitive operation for TGA.
- C. Incorrect. Indomethacin closes the duct and would worsen pulmonary flow.
- D. Incorrect. Total correction at 6–12 months is the strategy for TOF.
- E. Incorrect. Early-onset cyanosis requires urgent specialist management.
- Clinical reasoning: Single-ventricle physiology needs staged palliation instead of biventricular repair.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tricuspid atresia: RA → LA → LV; early cyanosis; left-axis deviation on ECG.
- Medical: PGE + supportive + Rashkind; surgical: BT shunt, PA banding, Glenn, Fontan.
- Oligaemic lung fields are expected (pulmonary blood flow reduced).

cases.title: The infant who sweats during feeds
cases.vignette: A 4-month-old infant is brought because of poor feeding, sweating during feeds, tachypnoea, recurrent chest infections and failure to gain weight. Examination reveals tachycardia, tachypnoea and a tender enlarged liver. There are cool peripheries and basal crackles. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion.

questions.stem: Which combination of findings most strongly supports heart failure in this infant?

options.label: C
options.text: Bradycardia, weight gain and normal respiratory rate

options.label: D
options.text: Fixed wide splitting of S2 without other symptoms

options.label: E
options.text: A single episode of vomiting with normal examination

questions.correctAnswerText: Tachycardia, tachypnoea and tender hepatomegaly
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance emphasizes the “3T + 1C” pattern: tachycardia, tachypnoea, tender enlarged liver and cardiomegaly on chest X-ray. Feeding difficulty, sweating and poor growth are also common infant symptoms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are key clinical features of heart failure in infants.
- B. Incorrect. These findings suggest an acute upper respiratory infection, not the characteristic heart failure pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Bradycardia and normal respiratory rate do not support heart failure.
- D. Incorrect. Fixed wide split S2 suggests ASD but does not by itself establish heart failure.
- E. Incorrect. Isolated vomiting is nonspecific and does not establish heart failure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infant heart failure: tachycardia, tachypnoea, tender hepatomegaly and cardiomegaly.
- Symptoms include sweating with feeds, poor feeding, breathlessness, recurrent chest infections and failure to thrive.
- Infants may show heart failure without the classic ankle oedema or raised JVP seen in adults.

questions.stem: Which symptom is particularly characteristic of heart failure in an infant during feeding?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sweating and interrupted feeds
questions.initialExplanation: Feeding is a significant exertion for an infant. Heart failure may cause breathlessness, sweating and frequent interruption of feeds, leading to poor weight gain.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Morning joint stiffness suggests an inflammatory musculoskeletal disorder.
- B. Incorrect. Polyuria is not the characteristic feeding-related symptom.
- C. Incorrect. Ear pain is unrelated.
- D. Correct. Sweating and interrupted feeds are typical symptoms of infant heart failure.
- E. Incorrect. Haematuria is a renal symptom.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ask about feeding duration, pauses, sweating and breathlessness.
- Poor feeding and recurrent chest infection may be the presenting clues in infants.
- Growth assessment is essential.

questions.stem: Which imaging investigation is described as the diagnostic investigation for heart failure's underlying cardiac cause?
questions.correctAnswerText: Echocardiography
questions.initialExplanation: Echocardiography evaluates cardiac structure and function and is described as diagnostic. CXR supports the diagnosis by showing cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Spirometry may assess lung function in selected patients but is not the diagnostic cardiac investigation.
- B. Correct. Echo identifies structural lesions and assesses cardiac function.
- C. Incorrect. EEG evaluates cerebral electrical activity.
- D. Incorrect. CXR may show cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular redistribution, oedema or pleural effusion, but it does not define cardiac anatomy and function as well as echo.
- E. Incorrect. Abdominal radiography does not diagnose cardiac failure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CXR: cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion; later stages may show interstitial/alveolar oedema and pleural effusion.
- Echo: diagnostic assessment of cardiac anatomy and function.
- ECG monitoring may detect arrhythmias.

questions.stem: Which statement about signs of heart failure in infancy is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Heart failure in infancy cannot cause failure to thrive

options.label: B
options.text: Infants not usually develop pulmonary oedema

options.label: C
options.text: Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea are the most reliable infant signs

options.label: D
options.text: Tender hepatomegaly, tachycardia and tachypnoea are more useful infant findings

options.label: E
options.text: Ankle oedema and raised JVP are typically prominent

questions.correctAnswerText: Tender hepatomegaly, tachycardia and tachypnoea are more useful infant findings
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that ankle oedema, orthopnoea, PND and congested neck veins are not typical signs of heart failure in infancy; they are more commonly seen in older children and adults.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Failure to thrive is a common manifestation of chronic infant heart failure.
- B. Incorrect. Infants can develop pulmonary congestion and oedema.
- C. Incorrect. These are more typical adult/older-child descriptions.
- D. Correct. The 3T findings and hepatomegaly are key infant signs.
- E. Incorrect. These are not reliable or consistently present signs in infants.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infant HF: 3T + 1C.
- Do not rely on adult signs such as ankle oedema, JVP, orthopnoea or PND in infants.
- Poor growth and feeding difficulty are important indicators.

questions.stem: Which CXR finding is most consistent with congestive heart failure in the infant?

options.label: A
options.text: A normal cardiac silhouette is required for the diagnosis

options.label: B
options.text: Egg-on-side heart with a narrow pedicle

options.label: E
options.text: Boot-shaped heart and oligemic lung fields

questions.correctAnswerText: Cardiomegaly with pulmonary vascular congestion
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular redistribution, pulmonary oedema and possible pleural effusion in heart failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A normal cardiac silhouette does not have to be present; cardiomegaly is a common finding.
- B. Incorrect. This is associated with TGA.
- C. Correct. Cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion are typical findings.
- D. Incorrect. Rib notching suggests CoA.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests TOF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HF CXR may show cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular redistribution, Kerley B lines, interstitial/alveolar oedema and pleural effusion.
- Interpret CXR with symptoms, examination and echocardiography.
- CXR findings can progress from vascular congestion to interstitial and then alveolar oedema.

questions.stem: Which treatment plan best matches the general management principles for an infant with acute heart failure?

options.label: A
options.text: Give antibiotics to each patient and avoid cardiac assessment

options.label: B
options.text: Give digitalis to each infant regardless of anatomy or rhythm

options.label: C
options.text: Start an anti-prostaglandin drug to close most congenital shunts

options.label: D
options.text: Call for help, assess ABC, monitor oxygenation, position appropriately, treat congestion and the underlying cause, and support feeding

options.label: E
options.text: Restrict most nutrition until the respiratory rate normalizes

questions.correctAnswerText: Call for help, assess ABC, monitor oxygenation, position appropriately, treat congestion and the underlying cause, and support feeding
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance calling for help, ABC assessment, PICU involvement when needed, semi-sitting position, oxygen and pulse-oximetry monitoring, drugs directed at preload/afterload or contractility as indicated, feeding support and treatment of the underlying cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotics are only indicated when infection is suspected or confirmed; cardiac assessment remains essential.
- B. Incorrect. Digitalis has selected indications and important contraindications and toxicity risks.
- C. Incorrect. Anti-prostaglandins are not routine treatment for all congenital shunts; they may be used in selected preterm PDA cases.
- D. Correct. This captures the main principles of acute management.
- E. Incorrect. Nutrition is important. High-calorie feeding or nasogastric support may be needed when tachypnoea compromises oral feeding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stabilize first: ABC, oxygenation and monitoring.
- Reduce congestion and afterload when appropriate.
- Support nutrition; consider NGT feeding if oral feeding is unsafe or inadequate.
- Always treat the underlying cause.

questions.stem: A child receiving digoxin for heart failure develops vomiting, anorexia and visual disturbance. The serum potassium is low after diuretic therapy. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Digitalis toxicity
questions.initialExplanation: Gastrointestinal symptoms and visual disturbances are recognized manifestations of digitalis toxicity. Hypokalaemia, especially after diuretic treatment, increases the risk.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Rheumatic fever causes inflammatory manifestations and does not explain the digoxin-related pattern.
- B. Correct. The symptom cluster and hypokalaemia strongly suggest digoxin toxicity.
- C. Incorrect. Vomiting, anorexia and visual disturbance are warning features rather than expected therapeutic effects.
- D. Incorrect. PDA closure does not cause this syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. An innocent murmur is unrelated to drug toxicity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Digoxin toxicity: GI symptoms, arrhythmias, CNS/visual disturbance and sometimes other systemic manifestations.
- Hypokalaemia and renal impairment increase risk.
- Management: stop digitalis, correct relevant electrolyte abnormalities, manage arrhythmias and consider digoxin-specific antibody fragments in severe toxicity.
- Check drug levels when indicated; interpretation requires timing and clinical context.

questions.stem: Which medication class reduces preload in a child with congestive heart failure?
questions.correctAnswerText: Loop diuretics such as furosemide
questions.initialExplanation: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that reduces intravascular volume and congestion, thereby reducing preload.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Loop diuretics are preload-reducing drugs listed.
- B. Incorrect. Anticonvulsants do not reduce cardiac preload.
- C. Incorrect. Bronchodilator beta-agonists are not used to reduce cardiac preload.
- D. Incorrect. Anti-prostaglandins promote ductal closure in selected PDA cases; this is not a general preload-reduction strategy.
- E. Incorrect. Antiplatelet drugs affect platelet function, not preload.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preload reduction: loop diuretics such as furosemide; other diuretic options may be used according to the clinical context.
- ACE inhibitors reduce afterload.
- Positive inotropes are reserved for selected low-output states and require specialist monitoring.
- The CVS clinical guidance notes that exact medication doses are not required for memorization.

cases.title: Beyond the basic diagnosis of heart failure

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with severe chronic iron-deficiency anaemia presents with tachycardia, tachypnoea, tender hepatomegaly and cardiomegaly. The pulses are bounding. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal, hyperdynamic heart. Which mechanism of heart failure applies?

options.label: B
options.text: Large left-to-right shunt with high pulmonary blood flow

options.label: D
options.text: Valve damage from rheumatic heart disease

options.label: E
options.text: High-output failure caused by a hyperdynamic circulation

questions.correctAnswerText: High-output failure caused by a hyperdynamic circulation
questions.initialExplanation: Besides pump failure, Clinical guidance high cardiac-output failure (hyperdynamic circulation) from anaemia, an arteriovenous fistula or thyrotoxicosis. A structurally normal heart with bounding pulses and severe anaemia fits.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Obstructed systemic circulation (e.g., critical AS, CoA) is a neonatal cause and the heart is structurally abnormal.
- B. Incorrect. There is no shunt on echo.
- C. Incorrect. Chronic immune-mediated damage describes late myocarditis → dilated cardiomyopathy, with a dilated poorly contracting ventricle.
- D. Incorrect. RHD would show valve lesions and a history of rheumatic fever.
- E. Correct. Anaemia → high output state → failure with the same signs of HF (3T + 1C).
- Clinical reasoning: Treat the cause (anaemia) as well as the failure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HF signs in infancy: tachycardia, tachypnoea, tender enlarged liver, cardiomegaly (3T 1C).
- Causes by group: obstruction (neonates), large L→R shunt (infants), acquired disease (older children).
- High-output HF: anaemia, AV fistula, thyrotoxicosis.

questions.stem: An infant with a large VSD awaiting surgery is receiving furosemide. She becomes weak and lethargic. Serum potassium is 2.9 mmol/L, sodium is low and the bicarbonate is high. Which management statement is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Add hydrochlorothiazide because it conserves potassium

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the furosemide dose because the alkalosis will correct itself

options.label: C
options.text: Add spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist acting on the collecting duct, and monitor for hyperkalaemia

options.label: D
options.text: Add digoxin to correct the hypokalaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Add spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist acting on the collecting duct, and monitor for hyperkalaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Loop diuretics (furosemide) cause hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypovolaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic acting on the collecting duct whose main adverse effect is hyperkalaemia (and gynaecomastia).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Thiazides (distal convoluted tubule) also cause hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.
- B. Incorrect. More furosemide would worsen the hypokalaemia and alkalosis.
- C. Correct. Potassium-sparing action; watch for hyperkalaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Digoxin does not correct potassium, and hypokalaemia increases the risk of digitalis toxicity.
- E. Incorrect. The infant still has a large shunt and needs decongestive therapy until surgery.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Furosemide: hypoK, hypoNa, hypovolaemia, metabolic alkalosis.
- Hydrochlorothiazide: hypoK, metabolic alkalosis.
- Spironolactone: hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia.
- Hypokalaemia predisposes to digitalis toxicity.

cases.title: A child with dilated ventricles and poor systolic function
cases.vignette: An 8-year-old child presents with progressive fatigue, breathlessness and poor exercise tolerance. Examination suggests heart failure. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with a thin wall and reduced systolic function. There is no clear congenital structural lesion.

questions.stem: Which type of cardiomyopathy is described as the most common?
questions.correctAnswerText: Dilated cardiomyopathy
questions.initialExplanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy is described as the most common type in the supplied CVS clinical guidance. It is characterized by ventricular dilatation and impaired contractility.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is described as very rare.
- B. Incorrect. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is important because of reduced compliance and risk of sudden death, but it is not the most common type listed.
- C. Correct. Dilated cardiomyopathy is the most common type highlighted.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital valve disease is not a cardiomyopathy subtype.
- E. Incorrect. This is not the classification emphasized in the supplied standard guidance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dilated cardiomyopathy: most common.
- It produces systolic dysfunction due to reduced contractility.
- Causes listed include idiopathic, post-viral, familial, metabolic, systemic, nutritional and neuromuscular disease such as DMD.

questions.stem: Which echocardiographic pattern supports dilated cardiomyopathy?

options.label: A
options.text: Small ventricular cavity with markedly thickened wall

options.label: B
options.text: Atrial septal defect with fixed split S2

options.label: C
options.text: Dilated ventricle with a thin wall and impaired systolic function

options.label: D
options.text: Normal ventricular size with isolated pulmonary valve stenosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Dilated ventricle with a thin wall and impaired systolic function
questions.initialExplanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy causes chamber enlargement and reduced myocardial contractility. Clinical guidance a dilated ventricle with a thin wall.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A thick wall and small cavity are more consistent with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
- B. Incorrect. This describes ASD.
- C. Correct. This is the pattern described for dilated cardiomyopathy.
- D. Incorrect. This is a valve lesion, not the echo pattern of dilated cardiomyopathy.
- E. Incorrect. This describes coarctation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dilated: enlarged chamber, thin wall, reduced contractility.
- Hypertrophic: thick wall and reduced compliance.
- Restrictive: impaired filling due to reduced compliance, often with normal or small ventricular size.

questions.stem: Which cause of dilated cardiomyopathy is specifically included?

options.label: B
options.text: Simple iron deficiency without cardiac involvement

questions.correctAnswerText: Previous viral myocarditis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance previous viral infection/myocarditis among causes of dilated cardiomyopathy, alongside idiopathic, familial, metabolic, systemic, nutritional and neuromuscular causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Otitis media is not a listed cause.
- B. Incorrect. Nutritional disorders may affect the heart in selected settings, but simple iron deficiency is not the specific cause described in this question.
- C. Correct. Previous viral myocarditis is a listed cause.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital rubella is associated with PDA and pulmonary stenosis in the CHD section; it is not listed as the only cause of DCM.
- E. Incorrect. PDA can cause volume overload and heart failure but is not the defining cause of DCM.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DCM causes listed: idiopathic, post-viral, familial, metabolic, systemic, nutritional and DMD.
- Always look for potentially reversible causes.
- Assess for arrhythmias and thromboembolic risk.

questions.stem: Which type of cardiomyopathy is characterized by a thick ventricular wall and reduced compliance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
questions.initialExplanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is characterized by increased myocardial thickness and impaired ventricular filling due to reduced compliance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. PDA causes a shunt and volume loading, not the defining myocardial phenotype of HCM.
- B. Incorrect. This is not a cardiomyopathy diagnosis.
- C. Incorrect. DCM is characterized by chamber dilatation and reduced contractility.
- D. Correct. Thickened ventricular wall and reduced compliance are characteristic.
- E. Incorrect. Restrictive cardiomyopathy causes impaired filling, but Clinical guidance it as very rare and often with normal or small ventricular size rather than the characteristic thick wall in this option.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HCM → thick wall, reduced compliance and diastolic dysfunction.
- It may cause chest pain, syncope and sudden death.
- Familial inheritance is described.

questions.stem: Which management principle is emphasized for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

options.label: D
options.text: Give digoxin to each patient to increase contractility

options.label: E
options.text: Avoid severe physical activity; beta-blockers may be used, and digitalis is contraindicated in obstructive HCM

questions.correctAnswerText: Avoid severe physical activity; beta-blockers may be used, and digitalis is contraindicated in obstructive HCM
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance advises avoidance of severe physical activity and lists beta-blockers. It also notes that digitalis is contraindicated in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because increasing contractility may worsen outflow obstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Severe physical activity should be avoided.
- B. Incorrect. Indomethacin is not a treatment for HCM.
- C. Incorrect. Ductal closure does not treat HCM.
- D. Incorrect. Digitalis is specifically listed as contraindicated in obstructive HCM.
- E. Correct. This matches the management principles stated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HCM: avoid severe exertion and assess sudden-death risk.
- Beta-blockers are listed.
- Avoid digitalis in obstructive HCM.
- Arrhythmias and sudden death are major concerns.

questions.stem: Which description best fits restrictive cardiomyopathy?

options.label: A
options.text: Marked ventricular dilatation with thin walls and systolic dysfunction

options.label: B
options.text: Pulmonary valve obstruction with RV pressure overload

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced ventricular compliance with diastolic dysfunction and impaired filling

options.label: E
options.text: A left-to-right shunt through the ductus

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced ventricular compliance with diastolic dysfunction and impaired filling
questions.initialExplanation: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is characterized by impaired ventricular filling because the myocardium is stiff and has reduced compliance. Clinical guidance it as very rare.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes dilated cardiomyopathy.
- B. Incorrect. This describes pulmonary stenosis.
- C. Correct. This is the defining pathophysiology.
- D. Incorrect. This describes coarctation.
- E. Incorrect. This describes PDA physiology.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Restrictive cardiomyopathy: rare, reduced compliance, diastolic dysfunction.
- May cause reduced cardiac output, fatigue, dizziness and syncope.
- Clinical guidance systemic/infiltrative causes such as sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, MPS and malignancy.

questions.stem: A child with cardiomyopathy develops syncope and palpitations. What is the most important clinical concern?

options.label: A
options.text: Arrhythmia and risk of sudden cardiac events

options.label: D
options.text: Benign positional vertigo in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Arrhythmia and risk of sudden cardiac events
questions.initialExplanation: Cardiomyopathy may be complicated by arrhythmias. Syncope and palpitations require urgent assessment, particularly in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy where sudden death is a major concern.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Arrhythmia and sudden cardiac events are important risks in cardiomyopathy.
- B. Incorrect. An innocent murmur does not explain syncope in a child with known cardiomyopathy.
- C. Incorrect. Gastroenteritis does not explain this cardiac presentation.
- D. Incorrect. Syncope with palpitations in a child with structural myocardial disease must not be presumed benign.
- E. Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain cardiac syncope.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Palpitations or syncope in cardiomyopathy are red flags.
- Assess rhythm, cardiac function and sudden-death risk.
- Specialist cardiology follow-up is essential.

cases.title: Murmurs, syndromic screening and the fetal circulation

questions.stem: A term infant of a mother with poorly controlled diabetes is tachypnoeic on day 2 with a systolic murmur. Echocardiography shows marked thickening of the ventricular septum and walls with reduced ventricular compliance, and the outflow tract narrows during systole. Which statement correctly describes the condition and an important treatment caution?

options.label: A
options.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy with thin walls; digitalis is the preferred inotrope

options.label: C
options.text: Large VSD with pulmonary plethora; indomethacin is indicated

options.label: D
options.text: Tetralogy of Fallot; prostaglandin E should be started

options.label: E
options.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; digitalis is contraindicated if there is outflow obstruction

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; digitalis is contraindicated if there is outflow obstruction
questions.initialExplanation: Maternal diabetes (infant of a diabetic mother) is a recognised cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, characterised by a thick wall with reduced compliance. Positive inotropes such as digitalis increase contractility and are contraindicated when there is obstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dilated cardiomyopathy has a dilated, thin-walled ventricle with reduced contractility — the opposite of the echo described.
- B. Incorrect. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is very rare, with stiff small/normal ventricles; the question describes marked wall thickening, and beta-blockers are among the drugs used in hypertrophic disease.
- C. Incorrect. A VSD would not explain a thickened septum with systolic outflow narrowing, and indomethacin is used for PDA in preterm infants.
- D. Incorrect. Maternal diabetes is also linked with VSD and TOF, but TOF is a cyanotic lesion with pulmonary stenosis, not diffuse hypertrophy with reduced compliance; PGE is used for duct-dependent lesions.
- E. Correct. HCM = thick wall + reduced compliance (diastolic dysfunction). Management: avoid severe exertion, beta-blockers; digitalis is contraindicated in obstructive lesions such as HOCM.
- Clinical reasoning: The key clue is the maternal diabetes — it links the infant to the cardiomyopathy and the drug caution.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Maternal diabetes → HCM, VSD, TOF.
- Obstructive CHD (e.g., aortic stenosis) and metabolic disease are also causes of HCM.
- HCM complications: chest pain, arrhythmia, syncope, sudden death.
- Digitalis is contraindicated in obstructive lesions (e.g., HOCM).
