cases.title: Beyond the basic diagnosis of heart failure

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with dilated cardiomyopathy has been on oral hydralazine for several months. She develops a facial rash, joint pains and a positive antinuclear antibody test. There has been no sore throat, the echocardiogram is unchanged and blood cultures are negative. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus
questions.initialExplanation: Hydralazine is a direct vasodilator used as an afterload-reducing drug. Its listed adverse effects include tachycardia, nausea and vomiting, and drug-induced SLE.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. No preceding streptococcal infection and no major criteria.
- B. Correct. Rash + arthralgia + positive ANA on hydralazine.
- C. Incorrect. Negative cultures and unchanged echo.
- D. Incorrect. Digitalis toxicity causes GI, CNS and arrhythmic features.
- E. Incorrect. Neutropenia would not cause a lupus-like syndrome, and she is not on captopril.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hydralazine: tachycardia, nausea/vomiting, drug-induced SLE.
- Captopril/enalapril: cough, rash, neutropenia, decreased GFR.
- Preload reducers: diuretics; afterload reducers: vasodilators or ACE inhibitors; contractility: digitalis.

cases.title: Myocardial disease with a specific trigger

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy develops fatigue and breathlessness. He is tachycardic with cardiomegaly. Echocardiography shows a dilated thin-walled left ventricle with a reduced ejection fraction. Which diagnosis and management best fit clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy; treat heart failure, treat arrhythmias and consider cardiac transplantation if refractory

options.label: B
options.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; digoxin and vigorous exercise

options.label: C
options.text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy; avoid most heart failure therapy

options.label: E
options.text: Infective endocarditis; start IV antibiotics for 6 weeks

questions.correctAnswerText: Dilated cardiomyopathy; treat heart failure, treat arrhythmias and consider cardiac transplantation if refractory
questions.initialExplanation: DMD is a listed cause of dilated cardiomyopathy (the commonest type). Echo shows a dilated ventricle with a thin wall and reduced ejection fraction. Treatment: heart-failure therapy, antiarrhythmics and transplantation in refractory cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct.
- B. Incorrect. HCM has a thick wall; severe exercise should be avoided.
- C. Incorrect. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is very rare and has reduced compliance with small/normal ventricular size.
- D. Incorrect. No sore throat or Jones criteria.
- E. Incorrect. No fever or peripheral signs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DCM causes: idiopathic, post-viral, familial, metabolic, systemic, nutritional, DMD.
- Echo: dilated LV, decreased ejection fraction; treat HF, arrhythmias; transplantation.

cases.title: Heart failure after a viral illness
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child had a viral upper respiratory illness about two weeks ago. The child now presents with breathlessness, sweating, poor exercise tolerance and tachycardia. Examination reveals signs of heart failure and an irregular rhythm. Echocardiography shows impaired ventricular function, and cardiac enzymes are elevated.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Myocarditis
questions.initialExplanation: A recent viral illness followed by acute heart failure and arrhythmia strongly suggests myocarditis. Myocardial inflammation can impair contractility and cause heart failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The temporal association with viral illness and acute myocardial dysfunction fits myocarditis.
- B. Incorrect. Pulmonary stenosis causes RV outflow obstruction rather than acute post-viral myocardial dysfunction.
- C. Incorrect. CoA causes systemic outflow obstruction and pulse/BP discrepancies.
- D. Incorrect. An innocent murmur occurs without structural or functional cardiac disease.
- E. Incorrect. ASD usually causes chronic right-sided volume loading rather than acute post-viral ventricular dysfunction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Myocarditis: inflammation of the myocardium, potentially causing necrosis, fibrosis and impaired contractility.
- A recent viral illness 10–14 days earlier is a clue.
- Presentation may include heart failure, arrhythmia or cardiogenic shock.

questions.stem: Which viruses are specifically listed among causes of myocarditis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Coxsackievirus, adenovirus and EBV
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance several infectious causes of myocarditis, particularly viruses such as Coxsackievirus A and B, adenovirus, EBV, measles, varicella and HIV.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are parasitic infections and do not represent the viral causes asked for.
- B. Incorrect. Rhinovirus is not among the specifically listed examples in this section.
- C. Correct. All three are listed viral causes.
- D. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal pathogens and not the listed causes.
- E. Incorrect. Rotavirus is not the viral cause emphasized.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Commonly listed viral causes: Coxsackievirus A/B, adenovirus, EBV, measles, varicella and HIV.
- Other causes include bacterial, fungal, parasitic, toxin-related, autoimmune, metabolic, familial and drug-related conditions.

questions.stem: Which clinical sequence is most characteristic of post-viral myocarditis?

options.label: A
options.text: Viral illness followed by acute heart failure, possible arrhythmia and cardiogenic shock

options.label: C
options.text: Chronic painless haematuria followed by oedema

questions.correctAnswerText: Viral illness followed by acute heart failure, possible arrhythmia and cardiogenic shock
questions.initialExplanation: Post-viral myocarditis may present after a recent viral illness with acute myocardial dysfunction, signs of heart failure, arrhythmia and, in severe cases, cardiogenic shock.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the progression described.
- B. Incorrect. This is an airway emergency such as foreign body aspiration.
- C. Incorrect. This suggests a renal/glomerular disorder.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests asthma.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests rheumatic fever.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Recent viral illness + acute cardiac symptoms → consider myocarditis.
- Muffled heart sounds, arrhythmia and shock may occur.
- Mortality can be high in severe cases.

questions.stem: Which group of investigations is most appropriate when myocarditis is suspected?

options.label: C
options.text: ECG, echocardiography, cardiac enzymes and inflammatory markers

questions.correctAnswerText: ECG, echocardiography, cardiac enzymes and inflammatory markers
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance echocardiography, ECG, CBC, ESR and cardiac enzymes such as CK and LDH, with viral studies where appropriate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are urinary/renal investigations.
- B. Incorrect. These assess allergy and airway function.
- C. Correct. These investigations help assess myocardial injury, cardiac function, rhythm and associated inflammation.
- D. Incorrect. These tests do not assess myocardial inflammation.
- E. Incorrect. Neurological investigations are not the core myocarditis assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Echo: assesses cardiac function and is described as diagnostic.
- ECG: may identify arrhythmias.
- Cardiac enzymes may be elevated.
- Viral studies/serology or PCR may be considered.

questions.stem: What is the principal management approach for a child with acute myocarditis and heart failure?

options.label: B
options.text: Antibiotics alone for each viral myocarditis case

options.label: D
options.text: Supportive and intensive care as needed, treatment of heart failure and management of arrhythmias

options.label: E
options.text: Routine indomethacin to close the ductus

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive and intensive care as needed, treatment of heart failure and management of arrhythmias
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance supportive treatment, ICU care when required, management of heart failure and treatment of arrhythmias. Selected additional therapies require specialist consideration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Exercise may be unsafe during active myocardial inflammation.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not indicated for viral myocarditis unless a bacterial infection is suspected or confirmed.
- C. Incorrect. Myocarditis may progress rapidly and can cause cardiogenic shock or dangerous arrhythmias.
- D. Correct. Stabilization, monitoring and treatment of complications are central.
- E. Incorrect. Indomethacin is used for ductal closure in selected PDA cases, not myocarditis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Myocarditis: supportive/ICU care as needed.
- Treat heart failure and arrhythmias.
- Restrict strenuous activity during active disease under specialist guidance.
- Do not assume a viral prodrome means the condition is benign.

questions.stem: Which relationship between myocarditis and dilated cardiomyopathy is described?

options.label: C
options.text: Myocarditis typically resolves without residual dysfunction

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic immune-mediated myocardial damage may progress to dilated cardiomyopathy

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic immune-mediated myocardial damage may progress to dilated cardiomyopathy
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance direct tissue damage in acute myocarditis and chronic immune-mediated damage that may lead to dilated cardiomyopathy, particularly in older children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. clinical guidance explicitly links chronic myocarditis with DCM.
- B. Incorrect. Myocarditis affects the myocardium and may cause ventricular dysfunction.
- C. Incorrect. Myocarditis may be fulminant, chronic or associated with lasting myocardial dysfunction.
- D. Correct. Persistent myocardial injury can impair contractility and produce ventricular dilatation.
- E. Incorrect. DCM may be a consequence of myocardial injury; it does not prevent myocarditis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute myocarditis → myocardial injury and impaired contractility.
- Chronic immune-mediated injury may lead to DCM.
- Follow cardiac function after acute myocarditis.

cases.title: Myocardial disease with a specific trigger

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child was stung by a scorpion 12 hours ago. He now has tachycardia (170/min), cold extremities, a gallop rhythm, tender hepatomegaly and pulmonary oedema. The chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly, the ECG shows arrhythmia, and CK and LDH are raised. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Toxin-induced myocarditis
questions.initialExplanation: Scorpion venom is a listed toxin cause of myocarditis. Myocardial inflammation and necrosis lead to impaired contractility, heart failure, arrhythmia and cardiogenic shock; CK and LDH are elevated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. No sore throat, Jones criteria or latent period.
- B. Incorrect. No fever, structural heart disease or peripheral stigmata.
- C. Incorrect. Acute pump failure after envenomation is not HCM.
- D. Incorrect. Kawasaki disease is a collagen vascular cause of myocarditis but needs its own clinical picture.
- E. Correct.
- Clinical reasoning: Exposure history identifies the cause; treatment is supportive/ICU care, HF therapy and treatment of arrhythmia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Myocarditis causes: viral (Coxsackie A/B, adenovirus, EBV, measles, varicella, HIV), bacterial (diphtheria, TB), fungal, parasitic, toxins (scorpion venom), collagen vascular (SLE, KD, JIA), drugs, nutritional and endocrine causes.
- Investigations: CXR, echo, CBC/ESR, CK/LDH, ECG, viral studies.
- Treatment: supportive + ICU, HF and arrhythmia management, transplantation in refractory cases.

cases.title: Migratory joint pain after a sore throat
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child presents with fever and painful swelling of the knees and ankles. The pain moves from one large joint to another, and the affected joint becomes normal as the next joint becomes inflamed. The child had a sore throat about three weeks earlier. Examination also reveals a new apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acute rheumatic fever
questions.initialExplanation: Migratory polyarthritis of large joints following a group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal throat infection, together with a new murmur, strongly suggests acute rheumatic fever.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Septic arthritis — Incorrect. Septic arthritis is usually an acute infection of one joint and is not typically migratory.
- B. ARF — Correct. ARF is an autoimmune multisystem inflammatory disease following GAS pharyngitis.
- C. SLE — Incorrect. SLE can cause arthritis and cardiac manifestations, but the preceding GAS infection and Jones-criteria pattern support ARF.
- D. IgA vasculitis — Incorrect. It is associated with palpable purpura, abdominal pain, joint symptoms and possible renal involvement.
- E. JIA — Incorrect. JIA is a chronic inflammatory arthritis; the classic migratory post-streptococcal pattern and carditis suggest ARF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ARF usually affects children aged 5–15 years.
- It follows GAS pharyngitis after a latent period, commonly around 2–3 weeks.
- Large-joint migratory polyarthritis and carditis are major manifestations.

questions.stem: What is the proposed mechanism responsible for acute rheumatic fever?

options.label: A
options.text: A congenital defect in the cardiac conduction system

options.label: B
options.text: Direct bacterial invasion of the myocardium

options.label: D
options.text: Molecular mimicry with cross-reactivity between streptococcal and host tissue antigens

options.label: E
options.text: Deposition of immune complexes due to hepatitis B

questions.correctAnswerText: Molecular mimicry with cross-reactivity between streptococcal and host tissue antigens
questions.initialExplanation: ARF is an autoimmune inflammatory response after GAS infection. Cross-reactivity between streptococcal antigens and host tissues is the mechanism described.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Congenital conduction-system disease is not the mechanism of ARF.
- B. Incorrect. ARF is not simply direct bacterial infection of the myocardium.
- C. Incorrect. This describes the mechanism of myasthenia gravis.
- D. Correct. Molecular mimicry leads to immune cross-reactivity affecting the heart, joints, skin and CNS.
- E. Incorrect. This is not the mechanism described for ARF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GAS pharyngitis → immune cross-reactivity → inflammation of heart, joints, skin and basal ganglia.
- clinical guidance summarizes the clinical pattern as “rheumatic fever licks the joints and bites the heart.”
- Carditis is the most serious major manifestation.

questions.stem: Which combination fulfils the classic Jones-criteria pathway for diagnosing an initial episode of ARF,?

options.label: A
options.text: Fever and arthralgia without evidence of prior GAS infection

options.label: B
options.text: Two major criteria, or one major plus two minor criteria, together with evidence of recent streptococcal infection

options.label: C
options.text: Any cardiac murmur in a child with sore throat

questions.correctAnswerText: Two major criteria, or one major plus two minor criteria, together with evidence of recent streptococcal infection
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance diagnosis using two major criteria or one major plus two minor criteria, with evidence of recent streptococcal infection. Some recognized clinical exceptions are also listed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Evidence of recent streptococcal infection is normally required, subject to the exceptions described.
- B. Correct. This is the diagnostic framework stated in the supplied clinical guidance.
- C. Incorrect. A murmur alone does not satisfy the diagnostic criteria.
- D. Incorrect. One minor criterion alone is insufficient.
- E. Incorrect. A positive ASO supports recent streptococcal infection but does not independently establish ARF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Major: polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules.
- Minor: fever, arthralgia, prolonged PR interval and raised inflammatory markers.
- Evidence of GAS: throat culture, elevated ASO, anti-DNase B or other streptococcal antibodies.
- Common examples include chorea, late-onset carditis and documented recurrent ARF with RHD among diagnostic exceptions.

questions.stem: Which joint pattern is typical of rheumatic polyarthritis?

options.label: C
options.text: Joint deformity with erosions from the beginning

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic painless swelling of the distal interphalangeal joints

options.label: E
options.text: Migratory inflammation of large joints, with each affected joint resolving as another becomes involved

questions.correctAnswerText: Migratory inflammation of large joints, with each affected joint resolving as another becomes involved
questions.initialExplanation: Rheumatic polyarthritis is typically migratory and affects large joints such as knees, ankles, wrists and elbows. It is non-destructive and may respond dramatically to salicylates.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This pattern is more suggestive of other inflammatory arthropathies.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests septic arthritis.
- C. Incorrect. Rheumatic arthritis is described as non-destructive.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the typical ARF pattern.
- E. Correct. This is the classic pattern described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Large joints: knees, ankles, wrists and elbows.
- Migratory, transient and non-destructive.
- Dramatic response to salicylates is described.

questions.stem: The child has a new harsh pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla during acute rheumatic fever. Which lesion does this suggest?

options.label: B
options.text: Mitral stenosis due to chronic fibrosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Acute mitral regurgitation
questions.initialExplanation: Acute rheumatic carditis may cause mitral regurgitation, producing a harsh pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. Chronic rheumatic fibrosis may later lead to mitral stenosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pulmonary stenosis causes a pulmonary-area ejection systolic murmur.
- B. Incorrect. Chronic fibrosis may cause mitral stenosis; Carey–Coombs murmur is a mid-diastolic murmur associated with acute valve oedema.
- C. Incorrect. CoA causes upper–lower limb pressure differences and a systolic murmur at the upper sternal edge.
- D. Correct. Acute MR is the characteristic lesion described in the acute stage.
- E. Incorrect. PDA causes a continuous machinery murmur.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute rheumatic carditis: MR may produce a pansystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla.
- Carey–Coombs murmur: mid-diastolic flow murmur in acute rheumatic carditis.
- Chronic fibrosis may cause mitral stenosis.

questions.stem: Which investigation provides evidence of a recent streptococcal infection?
questions.correctAnswerText: ASO titre
questions.initialExplanation: An elevated antistreptolysin O titre supports recent GAS infection. clinical guidance also lists anti-DNase B, throat culture and other streptococcal antibodies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urine culture detects urinary pathogens, not prior streptococcal pharyngitis.
- B. Incorrect. Troponin may indicate myocardial injury but does not document recent GAS infection.
- C. Incorrect. D-dimer is used in assessment of thrombosis and is not a marker of GAS infection.
- D. Incorrect. Amylase is related to pancreatic disease.
- E. Correct. ASO is an antibody marker of recent streptococcal exposure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Evidence of GAS: throat culture, ASO, anti-DNase B and related antibodies.
- CBC, ESR and CRP assess inflammation but do not by themselves prove GAS infection.
- Cardiac assessment includes ECG, CXR and echocardiography as indicated.

questions.stem: Which measure is most effective for preventing recurrent rheumatic fever?

options.label: A
options.text: Routine diuretics in children in routine care

options.label: B
options.text: Long-term secondary prophylaxis with intramuscular benzathine penicillin

options.label: D
options.text: No treatment after the first episode

questions.correctAnswerText: Long-term secondary prophylaxis with intramuscular benzathine penicillin
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies intramuscular benzathine penicillin as the most effective secondary prevention strategy to prevent recurrent GAS infection and recurrent rheumatic fever.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Diuretics treat congestion in heart failure and do not prevent recurrent ARF.
- B. Correct. Secondary antibiotic prophylaxis reduces recurrence and therefore the risk of cumulative valve damage.
- C. Incorrect. Indomethacin is not secondary prophylaxis for ARF.
- D. Incorrect. Recurrence prevention is a central part of long-term management.
- E. Incorrect. Aspirin treats inflammation in selected acute presentations but does not prevent recurrent GAS infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Eradicate GAS during the acute episode.
- Secondary prophylaxis: intramuscular benzathine penicillin.
- Duration depends on age, time since the last episode and whether carditis/residual valve disease is present.
- Confirm the exact prophylaxis interval and duration against the original clinical guidance and local protocol; the OCR extraction is not fully reliable for every numeric detail.

cases.title: Detailed manifestations and management

questions.stem: An 11-year-old girl has 3 months of clumsiness, dropping objects and emotional lability. She has involuntary jerky movements of the face and limbs that worsen with stress and disappear in sleep, with mild hypotonia. There is no fever, joint pain, rash or murmur. ESR, CRP and ASO are normal and the echocardiogram is normal. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: ARF cannot be diagnosed because two major criteria are required

options.label: B
options.text: Sydenham chorea can be the manifestation of ARF, so normal inflammatory markers and ASO do not exclude it

options.label: C
options.text: Normal ESR, CRP and ASO exclude ARF

options.label: D
options.text: The chorea indicates permanent basal-ganglia damage

options.label: E
options.text: Chorea typically appears within 2 weeks of the sore throat

questions.correctAnswerText: Sydenham chorea can be the manifestation of ARF, so normal inflammatory markers and ASO do not exclude it
questions.initialExplanation: Chorea is a late manifestation (months after the infection), may be the only presentation, involves the basal ganglia and resolves spontaneously without residuals. It is one of the exceptions to the usual Jones-criteria requirements.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Chorea is an exception to the two-major rule.
- B. Correct.
- C. Incorrect. By the time chorea appears the acute-phase markers may have normalised.
- D. Incorrect. Chorea resolves spontaneously without residuals.
- E. Incorrect. The latent period is 2–3 weeks generally, but several months for chorea.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chorea: late onset (months), basal ganglia, hypotonia, emotional lability, increased by stress and decreased in sleep.
- Treatment: psychological, educational and social support, or phenobarbitone/haloperidol.
- Exceptions to the criteria: chorea, late-onset carditis, recurrence in documented RHD.

source.raw: Rheumatic fever — Sydenham chorea, Jones interpretation (sheet p. 39–41).
source.sheet: Rheumatic fever — Sydenham chorea, Jones interpretation (sheet p. 39–41).

questions.stem: A 12-year-old develops migratory painful swelling of the knees and ankles 2 weeks after a sore throat. She also reports wrist aches. Temperature is 38.9°C, ESR is 90 mm/h with raised CRP and white cell count, the ECG shows a prolonged PR interval, and the ASO titre is raised. There is no murmur and the echocardiogram is normal. Which statement about the Jones criteria is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Criteria are not met because two major criteria are typically required

options.label: B
options.text: Criteria are met because fever, arthralgia, ESR and CRP each count separately as minor criteria

options.label: C
options.text: One major plus two minor criteria and evidence of recent streptococcal infection; ESR/CRP count as one, and arthralgia is not counted with arthritis

options.label: D
options.text: Criteria are not met because ASO alone cannot prove recent infection

options.label: E
options.text: Criteria are met if carditis is also present

questions.correctAnswerText: One major plus two minor criteria and evidence of recent streptococcal infection; ESR/CRP count as one, and arthralgia is not counted with arthritis
questions.initialExplanation: Diagnosis requires two major criteria, or one major plus two minor, plus evidence of recent streptococcal infection. Leukocytosis, ESR and CRP together count as one minor criterion, and arthralgia is not counted when arthritis is present.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. One major + two minor is an accepted pathway.
- B. Incorrect. Inflammatory markers count once, and arthralgia is excluded because she has arthritis.
- C. Correct. Major: polyarthritis. Minor: fever ≥ 38.5°C, prolonged PR, raised ESR/CRP/WBC (one). Evidence: raised ASO.
- D. Incorrect. A raised ASO titre is accepted evidence of recent streptococcal infection (others: throat culture, anti-DNase B, anti-streptokinase).
- E. Incorrect. Carditis is not required.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Major: polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
- Minor: fever ≥ 38.5, arthralgia, prolonged PR, raised WBC/CRP/ESR.
- Two majors is a stronger diagnosis than one major + two minor.

source.raw: Rheumatic fever — Jones criteria and interpretation (sheet p. 38–39).
source.sheet: Rheumatic fever — Jones criteria and interpretation (sheet p. 38–39).

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with ARF develops non-itchy pink ring-shaped macules with pale centres over the trunk and proximal thighs. The lesions appear and fade within hours and look more obvious after a hot bath. Which manifestation is this?
questions.correctAnswerText: Erythema marginatum
questions.initialExplanation: Erythema marginatum consists of large erythematous macules with a pale centre and a maple-leaf-like outline, non-pruritic, on the trunk and proximal limbs, recurrent and evanescent, and accentuated by heat.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Subcutaneous nodules are hard, painless nodules over extensor surfaces.
- B. Incorrect. Janeway lesions are painless lesions of infective endocarditis.
- C. Incorrect. Osler nodes are painful nodules of infective endocarditis.
- D. Correct.
- E. Incorrect. Urticaria is itchy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Erythema marginatum: <5%, early, trunk/proximal limbs, evanescent, increased with heat.
- Subcutaneous nodules: <1%.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old with acute rheumatic fever has cardiomegaly, tachycardia and signs of heart failure. She also has firm, painless, round nodules over the extensor surfaces of both elbows and knees. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The nodules are hard and non-tender and are usually associated with severe carditis

options.label: B
options.text: The nodules are tender and indicate infective endocarditis

options.label: C
options.text: The nodules are the commonest major criterion

options.label: D
options.text: The nodules respond dramatically to salicylates

options.label: E
options.text: The nodules are usually found over the flexor surface of the wrist

questions.correctAnswerText: The nodules are hard and non-tender and are usually associated with severe carditis
questions.initialExplanation: Subcutaneous nodules are hard, non-tender, round, located over bony prominences on extensor surfaces, and usually associated with severe carditis. They are uncommon (<1% ).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct.
- B. Incorrect. Painful nodules in IE are Osler nodes, found on the fingers or toes.
- C. Incorrect. Polyarthritis is the commonest manifestation.
- D. Incorrect. The dramatic salicylate response is seen with polyarthritis.
- E. Incorrect. They occur over extensor surfaces.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nodules: elbows, knees, extensor, hard, non-tender, round.
- Nodules and severe carditis often coexist.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl had migratory polyarthritis at age 8 which resolved completely without deformity. She now has exertional dyspnoea and a mid-diastolic apical murmur of mitral stenosis. A student asks why the same disease left the joints normal but scarred the valve. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Joint lesions were destructive and healed with deformity, but valves healed normally

options.label: B
options.text: Arthritis is caused by direct bacterial invasion that antibiotics eradicated, while carditis is autoimmune

options.label: C
options.text: Chronic streptococcal infection remained in the valve

options.label: D
options.text: The arthritis was a separate disease unrelated to the carditis

options.label: E
options.text: Joint, pericardial and basal-ganglia lesions are exudative and heal without fibrosis, whereas endomyocardial lesions are proliferative (Aschoff nodules) and heal with fibrosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Joint, pericardial and basal-ganglia lesions are exudative and heal without fibrosis, whereas endomyocardial lesions are proliferative (Aschoff nodules) and heal with fibrosis
questions.initialExplanation: Rheumatic fever "licks the joints and bites the heart." Exudative lesions (joints, pericardium, basal ganglia) heal without fibrosis; proliferative lesions (Aschoff nodules in endo-myocardium and skin) heal with fibrosis, which causes chronic valve disease such as mitral stenosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Rheumatic arthritis is non-destructive.
- B. Incorrect. ARF is an autoimmune reaction (molecular mimicry), not direct invasion.
- C. Incorrect. The valve damage is immune-mediated.
- D. Incorrect. Both are manifestations of ARF.
- E. Correct.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ARF follows group A β-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis after 2–3 weeks.
- Mechanism: molecular mimicry/cross-reactivity.
- Chronic stage: fibrosis → mitral stenosis.

source.raw: Rheumatic fever — pathogenesis and pathology (sheet p. 38, 40).
source.sheet: Rheumatic fever — pathogenesis and pathology (sheet p. 38, 40).

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with ARF has chest pain worse on inspiration, a pericardial friction rub, muffled heart sounds, tachycardia out of proportion to fever, tender hepatomegaly and a new apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Isolated pericarditis; the murmur is unrelated

options.label: B
options.text: Isolated myocarditis; the apical murmur is functional

options.label: C
options.text: Pancarditis; the murmur reflects endocarditis, with mitral involvement more common than aortic in the acute stage

options.label: D
options.text: Infective endocarditis; start IV antibiotics for 6 weeks

options.label: E
options.text: Pericarditis and myocarditis, because endocarditis not usually occurs in children

questions.correctAnswerText: Pancarditis; the murmur reflects endocarditis, with mitral involvement more common than aortic in the acute stage
questions.initialExplanation: Pancarditis is common in children: pericarditis (pain, rub), myocarditis (muffled sounds, tachycardia, HF) and endocarditis (left-sided, mitral more than aortic, with a harsh pansystolic apical murmur from regurgitation).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A, B. Incorrect. Incomplete; findings span all three layers.
- C. Correct.
- D. Incorrect. IE requires fever, positive cultures and a pre-existing valve lesion; the criteria here fit ARF.
- E. Incorrect. Endocarditis is a key component of rheumatic carditis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Carditis (50–60%) is the most serious manifestation.
- Acute mitral regurgitation: harsh pansystolic murmur propagating to the axilla.
- Pericardial effusion and HF can complicate carditis.

questions.stem: Ten days after the onset of ARF, a child has a new apical pansystolic murmur and a mid-diastolic apical murmur. Echocardiography shows mitral regurgitation. There is no previous history of rheumatic fever. Which statement about the mid-diastolic murmur is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It indicates established fibrotic mitral stenosis requiring balloon dilatation

options.label: B
options.text: It is a Carey–Coombs murmur from oedema of the mitral cusps in the acute stage; fibrotic mitral stenosis develops later

questions.correctAnswerText: It is a Carey–Coombs murmur from oedema of the mitral cusps in the acute stage; fibrotic mitral stenosis develops later
questions.initialExplanation: In acute carditis the mid-diastolic murmur (Carey–Coombs) is caused by oedema of the cusps. Chronic mitral stenosis results from fibrosis and takes years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fibrosis needs time; 10 days is too early.
- B. Correct.
- C. Incorrect. ASD gives fixed splitting of S2 and a pulmonary-area flow murmur.
- D. Incorrect. AR is a left-sternal-edge diastolic murmur.
- E. Incorrect. Diastolic murmurs are never innocent.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute stage: MR (damage of cusps) and Carey–Coombs murmur (oedema).
- Chronic stage: mitral stenosis from fibrosis.
- Innocent murmurs are systolic only.

source.raw: Rheumatic fever — carditis (sheet p. 40); innocent murmur criteria (sheet p. 5).
source.sheet: Rheumatic fever — carditis (sheet p. 40); innocent murmur criteria (sheet p. 5).

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with ARF has migratory arthritis and mild carditis, with no cardiomegaly or heart failure. Which is the most appropriate specific management?

options.label: A
options.text: Salicylates, with penicillin to eradicate group A streptococci, and rest if severe

questions.correctAnswerText: Salicylates, with penicillin to eradicate group A streptococci, and rest if severe
questions.initialExplanation: Arthritis or mild carditis is treated with salicylates; penicillin eradicates GAS; rest is for severe carditis or arthritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct.
- B. Incorrect. Steroids are for severe carditis with cardiomegaly.
- C. Incorrect. Haloperidol is an option for chorea.
- D. Incorrect. Only if heart failure is present.
- E. Incorrect. That is the IE regimen.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Salicylates → dramatic response in arthritis.
- Steroids → severe carditis with cardiomegaly.
- Serial CRP monitors disease activity.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with ARF has pancarditis, marked cardiomegaly, tachypnoea and hepatomegaly. Which plan best matches clinical guidance?

options.label: D
options.text: Prednisolone plus heart-failure treatment, fluid restriction and penicillin; rest for severe disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Prednisolone plus heart-failure treatment, fluid restriction and penicillin; rest for severe disease
questions.initialExplanation: Severe carditis with cardiomegaly is treated with steroids (prednisolone). Heart failure is treated and fluids restricted; penicillin eradicates GAS; rest is advised in severe carditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A, B. Incorrect. Insufficient for severe carditis with HF.
- C. Incorrect. That is IE treatment.
- D. Correct.
- E. Incorrect. Surgery is not the acute treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early complications: HF, arrhythmias; late: RHD, recurrence, IE.
- Monitor disease activity with serial CRP.

source.raw: Rheumatic fever — treatment and complications (sheet p. 41).
source.sheet: Rheumatic fever — treatment and complications (sheet p. 41).

questions.stem: A 15-year-old had ARF with severe carditis and residual mitral valve disease. Which secondary-prevention regimen is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Oral penicillin V for 10 days once a year

options.label: B
options.text: IM benzathine penicillin each 3–4 weeks for 1 year

options.label: D
options.text: Oral penicillin V after each sore throat

options.label: E
options.text: IM benzathine penicillin each 3–4 weeks, continued lifelong because of severe carditis

questions.correctAnswerText: IM benzathine penicillin each 3–4 weeks, continued lifelong because of severe carditis
questions.initialExplanation: Recurrence is prevented by IM benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks. clinical guidance gives the duration as either 10 years after the last episode or until age 21 years (OCR text — confirm against the original page), and lifelong prophylaxis in severe carditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A, B. Incorrect. Too short.
- C. Incorrect. IE prophylaxis is separate.
- D. Incorrect. Oral courses are for treatment of a streptococcal infection, not secondary prophylaxis.
- E. Correct.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IM benzathine penicillin is the most effective secondary prophylaxis.
- Severe carditis: lifelong prophylaxis.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old presents with group A streptococcal pharyngitis. His older sibling had rheumatic fever. Which measure best prevents rheumatic fever in this episode?

options.label: B
options.text: Early diagnosis and a full 10-day course of oral penicillin V

questions.correctAnswerText: Early diagnosis and a full 10-day course of oral penicillin V
questions.initialExplanation: Primary prevention depends on early diagnosis and proper treatment of streptococcal infection with a 10-day course of oral penicillin V.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A, D, E. Incorrect. They treat symptoms or inflammation and do not eradicate GAS.
- B. Correct.
- C. Incorrect. A short course does not eradicate the organism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ARF is more common in 5–15-year-olds, developing countries and low-socioeconomic, crowded conditions.
- Primary prevention: treat streptococcal infection; secondary: benzathine penicillin.

cases.title: Persistent fever in a child with congenital heart disease
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child with a known ventricular septal defect presents with persistent fever, chills, fatigue and weight loss. Examination reveals splenomegaly, splinter haemorrhages and a new murmur. Urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria. Infective endocarditis is suspected.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Infective endocarditis
questions.initialExplanation: Persistent fever in a child with structural heart disease, together with a new murmur and peripheral stigmata such as splinter haemorrhages, strongly suggests IE.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The clinical pattern is characteristic of IE.
- B. Incorrect. An innocent murmur occurs without systemic infection or structural heart complications.
- C. Incorrect. Bronchiolitis causes respiratory symptoms and does not explain a new murmur with embolic or immune features.
- D. Incorrect. A simple viral rhinitis does not explain the systemic and cardiac findings.
- E. Incorrect. Iron deficiency does not explain persistent fever and splinter haemorrhages.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Predisposing cardiac lesion + persistent fever → consider IE.
- New or changing murmur is important.
- Peripheral and immune manifestations may include splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, splenomegaly and haematuria.

questions.stem: Which congenital lesion is specifically excluded from the structural-heart-disease risk group described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Secundum atrial septal defect
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that children with congenital heart disease are at risk of IE, with secundum ASD specifically identified as an exception in its risk discussion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. CoA — Incorrect. CoA is included 's moderate-risk group.
- B. Secundum ASD — Correct. It is specifically listed as negligible risk.
- C. PDA — Incorrect. PDA is included 's risk list.
- D. VSD — Incorrect. VSD is included among lesions associated with IE risk.
- E. TOF — Incorrect. Complex cyanotic congenital heart disease such as TOF is in the high-risk category.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- High risk: complex cyanotic CHD, previous IE and prosthetic valves.
- Secundum ASD: negligible risk.
- VSD, PDA and other lesions are not equivalent to secundum ASD 's table.

questions.stem: Which organism is listed as the commonest causative organism?
questions.correctAnswerText: Viridans streptococci
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies alpha-haemolytic streptococci, particularly viridans streptococci, as the most common causative organisms in its description.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fungal IE may occur in selected patients, such as those with immunodeficiency, but Candida is not the commonest organism.
- B. Incorrect. Mycoplasma is a respiratory pathogen and is not the commonest IE organism listed.
- C. Correct. Viridans streptococci are specifically highlighted as the commonest organism.
- D. Incorrect. Giardia is an intestinal protozoan.
- E. Incorrect. Influenza virus is not a bacterial cause of IE.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viridans streptococci are emphasized.
- Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci are also important.
- Enterococci and HACEK organisms are listed among other causes.

questions.stem: Before starting empirical IV antibiotics in a clinically stable child with suspected IE, which microbiological step is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Give antibiotics first and obtain one culture several days later

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid blood cultures because they are unreliable

options.label: E
options.text: Obtain multiple blood culture sets before antibiotics

questions.correctAnswerText: Obtain multiple blood culture sets before antibiotics
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance emphasizes obtaining multiple blood cultures before starting antibiotics, with at least three samples described. This improves organism identification and allows targeted treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotics may sterilize blood cultures and reduce diagnostic yield.
- B. Incorrect. A throat swab does not establish bloodstream infection or identify the IE pathogen reliably.
- C. Incorrect. Urine culture may identify urinary infection but does not replace blood cultures.
- D. Incorrect. Blood cultures are central to diagnosis and treatment selection.
- E. Correct. Obtain multiple blood cultures before antibiotics when the child's condition allows.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Obtain multiple blood cultures before antibiotics if clinically safe.
- Do not delay life-saving treatment in an unstable child; obtain cultures promptly and start urgent therapy.
- Use echocardiography and clinical criteria alongside microbiology.

questions.stem: Which investigation is used to identify vegetations, valvular lesions or a cardiac abscess?
questions.correctAnswerText: Echocardiography
questions.initialExplanation: Echocardiography is a key investigation in IE and may demonstrate vegetations, valve damage or abscess. A negative study does not always exclude the diagnosis when clinical suspicion remains high.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Spirometry assesses airflow and lung function.
- B. Correct. Echo assesses vegetations and structural complications.
- C. Incorrect. EEG assesses cerebral electrical activity.
- D. Incorrect. Abdominal X-ray does not assess cardiac vegetations.
- E. Incorrect. Skin testing is unrelated to IE diagnosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Echo: vegetation, valve lesion and abscess.
- Absence of visible vegetation on one study does not always exclude IE.
- Assess renal function, electrolytes, inflammatory markers, CBC and urine microscopy.

questions.stem: Which finding is a minor feature in the Duke-criteria summary presented?

options.label: C
options.text: Two positive blood cultures with a typical organism

questions.correctAnswerText: Fever
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance fever among minor criteria, while positive blood cultures with specified patterns and echocardiographic evidence are major criteria in its simplified table.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. New valvular damage is listed as a major echocardiographic finding.
- B. Incorrect. Vegetation is a major echocardiographic finding.
- C. Incorrect. The specified positive blood-culture pattern is a major criterion.
- D. Correct. Fever is listed as a minor criterion.
- E. Incorrect. Abscess is a major imaging finding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Major criteria: characteristic positive blood cultures and positive echocardiographic findings.
- Minor criteria include fever, embolic manifestations, immune-complex disease, predisposing factors and selected microbiological evidence.
- Use the actual diagnostic criteria and specialist interpretation in clinical practice.

questions.stem: Which treatment duration is described for empirical IV antibiotic therapy?

options.label: B
options.text: A prolonged IV course, described as approximately six weeks

options.label: D
options.text: No antibiotics if a murmur is present

questions.correctAnswerText: A prolonged IV course, described as approximately six weeks
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance prolonged empirical IV antibiotic treatment, approximately six weeks, with the exact regimen determined by the suspected organism, cultures, sensitivities and clinical circumstances.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Topical antibiotics are not used for bloodstream/endocardial infection.
- B. Correct. Clinical descriptions include approximately six weeks of IV therapy.
- C. Incorrect. A 24-hour course is inadequate for endocardial infection.
- D. Incorrect. A murmur does not replace the need to treat confirmed IE.
- E. Incorrect. A single oral dose is not sufficient treatment for established IE.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Obtain cultures first when safe, then start appropriate IV antibiotics.
- Treatment is prolonged and guided by microbiology and specialist advice.
- Surgery may be required for abscess, large vegetation or infected prosthetic material.

questions.stem: Which preventive measure is emphasized as the most important for reducing IE risk?

options.label: D
options.text: Restricting physical activity in most children

options.label: E
options.text: Daily prophylactic antibiotics for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Good dental and oral hygiene
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance emphasizes good dental and oral hygiene as the most important preventive measure. Antibiotic prophylaxis is reserved for selected risk groups and procedures according to applicable guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Maintaining oral health reduces recurrent bacteraemia from poor dentition and gingival disease.
- B. Incorrect. Anticoagulation is not routine IE prevention.
- C. Incorrect. Vaccination is not a cause of IE and should not be avoided.
- D. Incorrect. Universal exercise restriction is not the principal preventive strategy.
- E. Incorrect. clinical guidance does not recommend daily antibiotics for every child.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dental/oral hygiene is emphasized as the main preventive measure.
- Antibiotic prophylaxis depends on cardiac risk category and the procedure.
- Do not apply outdated prophylaxis rules indiscriminately; check current guidelines.

cases.title: Fever in a child with structural heart disease

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with an unrepaired VSD has had fever and fatigue for 3 weeks. On examination there are tender nodules on the finger pulps, painless flat red macules on the palms, splinter haemorrhages and splenomegaly. Urine microscopy shows haematuria and the character of the murmur has changed. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Painful nodules are Janeway lesions and painless palm lesions are Osler nodes

options.label: B
options.text: The haematuria indicates an unrelated urinary infection

options.label: C
options.text: Osler nodes are painful and Janeway lesions painless; haematuria suggests immune-complex glomerulonephritis

options.label: E
options.text: A normal echocardiogram would exclude infective endocarditis

questions.correctAnswerText: Osler nodes are painful and Janeway lesions painless; haematuria suggests immune-complex glomerulonephritis
questions.initialExplanation: Osler nodes are painful and Janeway lesions are painless. Splinter haemorrhages, splenomegaly and glomerulonephritis (microscopic haematuria) are recognised features, and a new or changed murmur is the key cardiac sign.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The two are reversed.
- B. Incorrect. In the setting of IE, haematuria reflects glomerulonephritis; low C3/C4 may be found.
- C. Correct.
- D. Incorrect. Splenomegaly is found in about 70%.
- E. Incorrect. Absence of vegetations does not exclude IE.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Signs: high fever, chills, anorexia, weight loss, pallor, clubbing (late), splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, subconjunctival haemorrhage, splenomegaly, GN, hemiplegia.
- Cardiac: new murmur, change in an existing murmur, heart failure.
- Blood cultures (at least 3 before antibiotics), echo, CRP/ESR, urine, C3/C4.

source.raw: Infective endocarditis — clinical picture and diagnosis (sheet p. 43).
source.sheet: Infective endocarditis — clinical picture and diagnosis (sheet p. 43).

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with an unrepaired VSD has a temperature of 39°C. One of three blood-culture bottles grows viridans streptococci. Echocardiography shows a vegetation, and Osler nodes are present. How is this case classified using the Duke criteria?

options.label: A
options.text: Definite IE: one major echocardiographic criterion plus at least three minor criteria

options.label: C
options.text: IE is rejected because one blood culture is positive

options.label: D
options.text: Definite IE if two major criteria are present

options.label: E
options.text: Cannot be classified without a CRP result

questions.correctAnswerText: Definite IE: one major echocardiographic criterion plus at least three minor criteria
questions.initialExplanation: Definite IE requires two major criteria, or one major plus three minor, or five minor criteria. A single positive culture is a minor criterion; positive echo is a major criterion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Major: echo vegetation. Minor: fever, predisposing factor (VSD), single positive culture, immune-complex phenomenon (Osler nodes).
- B. Incorrect. The case meets the definite threshold.
- C. Incorrect. One positive culture counts as a minor criterion; it does not reject the diagnosis.
- D. Incorrect. One major + three minor is also definite.
- E. Incorrect. CRP is not part of the Duke criteria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Major: ≥ 2 positive blood cultures; positive echo (vegetation, new valve damage).
- Minor: fever, embolic phenomenon, immune-complex disease, predisposing factors, single positive culture.
- Definite: 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with congenital heart disease develops fever and a new murmur 3 weeks after a urological instrumentation. Blood cultures grow a Gram-positive coccus. Which organism group is most likely in this setting?
questions.correctAnswerText: Enterococci
questions.initialExplanation: Enterococci are linked to bacteraemia from the gastrointestinal or genitourinary tract. Viridans streptococci are the commonest overall (dental source).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Most common overall, associated with dental procedures.
- B. Incorrect. Associated with IV drug use.
- C. Incorrect. Associated with immune deficiency.
- D. Correct.
- E. Incorrect. HACEK are fastidious Gram-negative organisms.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- α-haemolytic (viridans) streptococci ~50%; Staph aureus/epidermidis ~40%.
- Enterococci: GIT/GU sources; Pseudomonas: IV drug use; fungi: immune deficiency.
- Treatment: IV antibiotics for 6 weeks (high-dose penicillin + gentamicin, or penicillin + ceftriaxone).

source.raw: Infective endocarditis — pathogenesis and organisms (sheet p. 42, 44).
source.sheet: Infective endocarditis — pathogenesis and organisms (sheet p. 42, 44).

questions.stem: Three children are awaiting elective dental extraction: child 1 has unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot, child 2 has an unrepaired VSD and child 3 has a small secundum ASD. 's risk categories, which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: most three need prophylaxis because most have congenital heart disease

options.label: B
options.text: Give pre-procedure amoxicillin to high-/moderate-risk children 1 and 2, not low-risk child 3

options.label: C
options.text: child 1 needs prophylaxis; the VSD is negligible risk

options.label: E
options.text: None need antibiotics because good oral hygiene replaces prophylaxis

questions.correctAnswerText: Give pre-procedure amoxicillin to high-/moderate-risk children 1 and 2, not low-risk child 3
questions.initialExplanation: Prophylaxis is advised for high- and moderate-risk categories before procedures such as dental extraction. Complex cyanotic CHD (TOF, TGA) is high risk; VSD, PDA, primum ASD and CoA are moderate risk; secundum ASD is negligible risk. Good dental hygiene remains the most important factor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Secundum ASD is in the negligible-risk category.
- B. Correct.
- C. Incorrect. VSD is moderate risk.
- D. Incorrect. Reversal of the risk ranking.
- E. Incorrect. Oral hygiene is the most important measure but does not replace prophylaxis in these categories.
- Clinical note: clinical guidance reflects UK practice; apply current local guidelines.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Amoxicillin single dose 30–60 minutes before the procedure (ampicillin IV, ceftriaxone, clindamycin or vancomycin are alternatives).
- Procedures: tooth extraction, adenotonsillectomy.
- All congenital heart disease except secundum ASD predisposes to IE.
