source.sheet: Infective endocarditis — prophylaxis and risk categories (sheet p. 42, 44).

questions.stem: On day 10 of IV penicillin and gentamicin for viridans streptococcal endocarditis in a child with a VSD, fever persists. Echocardiography shows a large mobile vegetation with a perivalvular abscess, and the child has developed new heart failure. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop antibiotics and repeat the cultures

options.label: B
options.text: Switch to oral amoxicillin to complete treatment at home

options.label: D
options.text: Extend the same antibiotics to 12 weeks without further intervention

options.label: E
options.text: Continue IV antibiotics and refer for cardiac surgery

questions.correctAnswerText: Continue IV antibiotics and refer for cardiac surgery
questions.initialExplanation: Surgery is indicated for an abscess, a large vegetation or infected prosthetic material, alongside the prolonged IV antibiotic course.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stopping antibiotics is unsafe.
- B. Incorrect. IE requires about 6 weeks of IV therapy.
- C. Incorrect. Steroids are not part of IE treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics alone will not eradicate an abscess or a large vegetation.
- E. Correct.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Empirical IV antibiotics for 6 weeks.
- Surgery: abscess, large vegetation, infected prosthetic material.
- CRP/ESR are useful for monitoring response.

topics.name: Cardiac Arrhythmias — SVT and Conduction Disorders

cases.title: A very fast regular rhythm in an infant
cases.vignette: A 4-month-old infant is brought with sudden pallor, irritability, vomiting and poor feeding. Heart rate is approximately 260 beats/min and regular. The ECG shows a narrow QRS tachycardia with no clearly visible P waves. The infant is initially alert with acceptable perfusion, but the team is prepared to escalate if instability develops.

questions.stem: What is the most likely rhythm diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Supraventricular tachycardia
questions.initialExplanation: A sudden, very rapid regular narrow-complex tachycardia around 250–300 beats/min in an infant, with absent or difficult-to-see P waves, is characteristic of SVT.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The rate and ECG pattern are typical of SVT.
- B. Incorrect. Ventricular fibrillation is a pulseless life-threatening rhythm, not a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
- C. Incorrect. Complete heart block causes atrioventricular dissociation and often bradycardia.
- D. Incorrect. Sinus bradycardia is the opposite rate pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Sinus arrhythmia is a normal respiratory variation in heart rate in children.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SVT is the most common symptomatic arrhythmia in childhood.
- Rate may be around 250–300/min.
- ECG: very rapid rate, narrow QRS and absent/hidden P waves.
- Normal ECG may be seen between attacks.

questions.stem: Which mechanism is most commonly involved in childhood SVT?

options.label: B
options.text: Complete destruction of the sinoatrial node

options.label: C
options.text: Re-entry involving two pathways, including the AV node and sometimes an accessory pathway

questions.correctAnswerText: Re-entry involving two pathways, including the AV node and sometimes an accessory pathway
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance SVT as a re-entry tachycardia involving two pathways, one involving the AV node and the other potentially an accessory pathway.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pulmonary venous obstruction is a different congenital cardiac problem.
- B. Incorrect. SA-node destruction does not explain the typical re-entry SVT pattern.
- C. Correct. Re-entry is the mechanism described.
- D. Incorrect. PDA is not the re-entry mechanism of SVT.
- E. Incorrect. Aortic stenosis is a structural outflow lesion, not the SVT mechanism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Re-entry is central to common pediatric SVT.
- Structural heart defects may be absent; some associations include Ebstein anomaly and other complex lesions.
- Consider myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, drugs and electrolyte imbalance as potential associated factors.

questions.stem: Which initial treatment is appropriate for a haemodynamically stable child with regular narrow-complex SVT?

options.label: A
options.text: Long-term anticoagulation as the first step

questions.correctAnswerText: Vagal stimulation
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance vagal manoeuvres in stable SVT. In infants, applying ice to the face is described; in older children, a Valsalva manoeuvre may be used.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Anticoagulation is not the first-line acute treatment of typical SVT.
- B. Incorrect. Coarctectomy treats aortic narrowing.
- C. Correct. Vagal stimulation may interrupt AV-node-dependent re-entry.
- D. Incorrect. An unstable patient requires synchronized cardioversion, not routine unsynchronized defibrillation for a perfusing narrow-complex tachycardia.
- E. Incorrect. Indomethacin closes PDA in selected preterm infants.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres first.
- Infant: ice to the face; older child: Valsalva as appropriate.
- Monitor the rhythm and obtain ECG documentation where possible.

questions.stem: If vagal manoeuvres are unsuccessful in a stable child with SVT, which drug is described as the drug of choice?
questions.correctAnswerText: Adenosine
questions.initialExplanation: Adenosine is described as the drug of choice for acute stable SVT. It is given as a rapid IV bolus followed immediately by a saline flush because of its very short half-life.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Digoxin is not the acute first-line drug described for termination of stable SVT and requires careful use.
- B. Incorrect. Indomethacin promotes ductal closure in selected PDA cases.
- C. Incorrect. Furosemide treats congestion and does not terminate SVT.
- D. Incorrect. Prednisolone is not an acute SVT termination drug.
- E. Correct. Adenosine transiently blocks AV nodal conduction and can terminate AV-node-dependent re-entry.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine if needed.
- Adenosine: rapid IV bolus followed by flush.
- Dosing should follow current pediatric resuscitation protocols and monitoring; OCR-derived dose figures are not reproduced here.

questions.stem: The infant with SVT becomes hypotensive and poorly perfused. What is the appropriate next treatment?
questions.correctAnswerText: Synchronized DC cardioversion
questions.initialExplanation: Haemodynamic instability in SVT requires urgent synchronized cardioversion. Clinical guidance DC cardioversion for unstable patients, with escalation if it is not effective.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Oral maintenance therapy is not appropriate as the immediate response to shock.
- B. Incorrect. Hypotension and poor perfusion are signs of instability; observation is unsafe.
- C. Correct. Synchronized cardioversion is indicated for unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse.
- D. Incorrect. Exercise testing has no role in an unstable infant.
- E. Incorrect. Indomethacin treats selected PDA cases.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres and adenosine.
- Unstable SVT: synchronized cardioversion.
- Call for help, ABC and continuous monitoring are essential.
- Exact energy settings must follow current resuscitation protocols.

questions.stem: Which ECG finding suggests Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome?

options.label: C
options.text: Short PR interval with a delta wave

options.label: D
options.text: Long PR interval with absent QRS complexes

questions.correctAnswerText: Short PR interval with a delta wave
questions.initialExplanation: WPW is associated with pre-excitation through an accessory pathway, producing a short PR interval and delta wave on ECG.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fixed wide splitting is an auscultatory finding associated with ASD, not an ECG feature.
- B. Incorrect. Tall peaked T waves suggest hyperkalaemia.
- C. Correct. This is the classic ECG pattern described.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests AV conduction delay or block.
- E. Incorrect. This is not the WPW pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- WPW: short PR + delta wave.
- SVT may be associated with an accessory pathway.
- Clinical guidance ablation of the accessory bundle as a treatment option in WPW.

questions.stem: A fetus of a mother with SLE develops persistent bradycardia. Which mechanism is described for congenital complete heart block?

options.label: B
options.text: Maternal anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies cross the placenta and damage the fetal conduction system

options.label: C
options.text: Fetal hypoglycaemia directly destroys the aortic valve

options.label: E
options.text: Maternal antibodies obstruct pulmonary venous drainage

questions.correctAnswerText: Maternal anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies cross the placenta and damage the fetal conduction system
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance maternal SLE antibodies, especially anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB, crossing the placenta and damaging the developing conduction system, resulting in congenital complete heart block.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Maternal hypertension is not the described mechanism for VSD.
- B. Correct. This is the mechanism described.
- C. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia does not directly destroy the aortic valve.
- D. Incorrect. Ductal closure is not the mechanism of congenital complete heart block.
- E. Incorrect. This does not explain conduction-system fibrosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Maternal SLE/anti-Ro/anti-La → fetal conduction-system injury → congenital complete heart block.
- Severe fetal cases may cause hydrops or fetal death.
- Symptomatic complete heart block may require a permanent pacemaker.

questions.stem: A teenager has exertional syncope and a family history of unexplained sudden death. ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Long-QT syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Long-QT syndrome predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias and may present with syncope, seizures or sudden death, sometimes precipitated by exercise. Family history of unexplained sudden death is an important clue.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. PDA does not produce the defining ECG pattern.
- B. Incorrect. ASD does not explain the prolonged QT pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Sinus arrhythmia is a normal respiratory variation in heart rate.
- D. Correct. The clinical and ECG features support long-QT syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. An innocent murmur does not cause prolonged QT or exertional syncope.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Long-QT syndrome: exertional syncope, palpitations, seizure-like episodes and sudden death.
- Causes may be congenital channelopathy or acquired due to drugs/electrolyte disturbance.
- Clinical guidance beta-blockers and ICD in selected patients.
- Review QT-prolonging drugs and electrolyte abnormalities.

cases.title: Beyond the basic diagnosis of heart failure

questions.stem: A 3-week-old preterm infant with renal impairment is treated with digoxin and furosemide for heart failure. She develops vomiting, poor feeding and a new irregular rhythm. Serum potassium is 2.7 mmol/L and the digoxin level is high. What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the digoxin dose to control the rhythm

options.label: B
options.text: Give calcium to stabilise the rhythm

options.label: C
options.text: Give amiodarone alone and continue digoxin

options.label: D
options.text: Stop digoxin, correct potassium and treat arrhythmia; use digoxin Fab if severe

questions.correctAnswerText: Stop digoxin, correct potassium and treat arrhythmia; use digoxin Fab if severe
questions.initialExplanation: Digitalis toxicity is more likely with hypokalaemia, hypercalcaemia, impaired renal function, preterm age and rheumatic or viral myocarditis. Treatment: stop digitalis, correct electrolytes, treat arrhythmias (phenytoin, lidocaine), and use digoxin antibody fragments (Digibind) when indicated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. More digoxin worsens toxicity.
- B. Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia increases the risk of toxicity; calcium is harmful.
- C. Incorrect. Continuing the offending drug is wrong, and amiodarone is not clinical guidance's treatment of choice here.
- D. Correct. Stop, correct K, treat arrhythmia, antibody fragments.
- E. Incorrect. Digoxin must be stopped, and the hypokalaemia needs correction.
- Clinical reasoning: Recognise the risk factors (hypoK, renal impairment, preterm) before prescribing.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Toxicity: GI (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea), CVS (arrhythmias), CNS (headache, visual disturbance with coloured vision), allergy, gynaecomastia.
- Risk factors: hypoK, hyperCa, renal impairment, rheumatic/viral myocarditis, preterm infant.
- Digitalis is contraindicated in obstructive lesions such as HOCM.

cases.title: Syncope, palpitations and irregular pulses

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with congenital deafness has recurrent exercise-related syncope. The ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. His parents are consanguineous and an older brother died suddenly at the age of 7. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Lange–Nielsen (Jervell and Lange-Nielsen) syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Lange–Nielsen syndrome is the autosomal recessive form of congenital long-QT syndrome associated with deafness. Romano–Ward syndrome is autosomal dominant without deafness.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Autosomal dominant, normal hearing.
- B. Incorrect. WPW shows a short PR interval and delta wave.
- C. Correct.
- D. Incorrect. CHB relates to maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies and bradycardia.
- E. Incorrect. SVT: narrow QRS tachycardia, normal ECG between attacks.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LQTS: syncope (often exercise), seizures (misdiagnosed as epilepsy), sudden death.
- ECG: QT > 0.47 s. Treatment: propranolol, ICD.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old is treated with erythromycin for pneumonia and also has vomiting and diarrhoea. She has two episodes of loss of consciousness with jerking movements that were labelled as seizures. The ECG shows a QT interval of 0.50 s and the serum potassium is low. There is no family history. What is the best management?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat as acquired long-QT syndrome: stop erythromycin, correct potassium (and calcium and magnesium) and monitor the ECG

options.label: E
options.text: Perform ablation of an accessory pathway

questions.correctAnswerText: Treat as acquired long-QT syndrome: stop erythromycin, correct potassium (and calcium and magnesium) and monitor the ECG
questions.initialExplanation: Acquired long-QT syndrome is caused by drugs (erythromycin, ketoconazole) and electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia). Seizure-like episodes may be misdiagnosed as epilepsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct.
- B. Incorrect. The events are arrhythmic syncope, not epilepsy.
- C. Incorrect. An ICD is for selected congenital cases.
- D. Incorrect. Adenosine treats SVT.
- E. Incorrect. No pre-excitation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acquired causes: drugs (erythromycin, ketoconazole), hypoK, hypoCa, hypoMg.
- ECG QT > 0.47 s; congenital forms are treated with propranolol ± ICD.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old had 12 hours of pallor, irritability and vomiting and was found to have a heart rate of 280/min with a narrow QRS and no visible P waves. He converted after vagal stimulation and adenosine, and the ECG in sinus rhythm is normal. The parents ask about the future. Which advice is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Lifelong antiarrhythmic drugs and ablation will be required

options.label: B
options.text: No follow-up is needed because SVT not usually recurs

options.label: D
options.text: Arrange echocardiography; consider propranolol, sotalol or flecainide, usually stopping by age 1 year

options.label: E
options.text: A permanent pacemaker will be required

questions.correctAnswerText: Arrange echocardiography; consider propranolol, sotalol or flecainide, usually stopping by age 1 year
questions.initialExplanation: Echocardiography excludes structural heart disease and assesses function; maintenance therapy prevents recurrence; treatment usually stops around 1 year of age because attacks do not usually continue after infancy. A short PR with delta wave in sinus rhythm would indicate WPW (ablation).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Treatment usually stops by 1 year.
- B. Incorrect. Recurrence is possible, hence maintenance therapy and follow-up.
- C. Incorrect. Echo is required.
- D. Correct.
- E. Incorrect. Pacemakers are for complete heart block.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SVT: most common symptomatic childhood arrhythmia, rate 250–300/min, re-entry via AV node + accessory pathway.
- Infants present with pallor, irritability, vomiting, ± heart failure if prolonged.
- Stable: vagal manoeuvres then adenosine; unstable: DC cardioversion.
- ECG is normal between attacks unless WPW.

questions.stem: A GP notes an irregular pulse in a healthy 8-year-old. The rate increases with inspiration and slows with expiration, by up to 30/min. The ECG shows a P wave before each QRS complex and is otherwise normal. Which statement is correct?

options.label: E
options.text: Normal sinus arrhythmia requiring no treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal sinus arrhythmia requiring no treatment
questions.initialExplanation: Sinus arrhythmia is normal in children and is seen as a change in heart rate with respiration (increase on inspiration, decrease on expiration) of up to 30 beats/min.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. SVT is 250–300/min with no visible P waves.
- B. Incorrect. Complete heart block presents with bradycardia.
- C. Incorrect. WPW has a short PR and delta wave.
- D. Incorrect. LQTS shows a prolonged QT.
- E. Correct.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sinus arrhythmia: normal; heart rate varies with respiration.
- SVT: very rapid, narrow QRS, no P wave.
- WPW: short PR, delta wave; ablation.

cases.title: The adolescent who collapses while running
cases.vignette: A 15-year-old adolescent collapses during exercise. Before the episode, the patient noticed palpitations. There is a family history of sudden unexplained death. The examination reveals a cardiac murmur. The clinician distinguishes benign vasovagal syncope from potentially dangerous cardiac syncope.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of syncope described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Vasovagal (neurologically mediated) syncope
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance vasovagal syncope as the most common cause in adolescents. It is often preceded by a prodrome such as nausea, sweating or headache and may be triggered by prolonged standing, fright or crowded places.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Aortic stenosis can cause cardiac syncope but is not the commonest cause overall.
- B. Incorrect. VT is a potentially dangerous cardiac cause but not the most common cause.
- C. Correct. Vasovagal syncope is the most common cause described.
- D. Incorrect. Complete heart block is a less common cause.
- E. Incorrect. Pulmonary hypertension can cause exertional syncope but is not the commonest cause overall.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vasovagal syncope: common in adolescents, often benign, with prodrome.
- Triggers include prolonged standing, seeing blood, fear and crowded places.
- Cardiac red flags must always be sought.

questions.stem: Which feature most strongly suggests a cardiac cause of syncope?

options.label: A
options.text: A single faint during emotional distress with normal evaluation

options.label: B
options.text: Nausea and sweating after prolonged standing in a crowded room

options.label: C
options.text: Brief faint after seeing blood with a typical prodrome

options.label: D
options.text: Syncope during exercise with palpitations and a family history of sudden unexplained death

options.label: E
options.text: Symptoms that resolve after lying down

questions.correctAnswerText: Syncope during exercise with palpitations and a family history of sudden unexplained death
questions.initialExplanation: Exertional syncope, palpitations and a family history of sudden unexplained death are red flags for cardiac syncope, including arrhythmia or obstructive cardiac disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Emotional distress and a typical prodrome may indicate vasovagal syncope, though assessment is still guided by the full history.
- B. Incorrect. This is a typical vasovagal trigger and prodrome.
- C. Incorrect. This is also typical of vasovagal syncope.
- D. Correct. These features require urgent cardiac evaluation.
- E. Incorrect. Improvement after lying down is compatible with vasovagal syncope.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cardiac red flags: exercise-related syncope, palpitations, abnormal examination and family history of sudden death.
- Consider SVT, heart block, aortic stenosis, HOCM and long-QT syndrome.
- Do not label exertional syncope as vasovagal without proper assessment.

questions.stem: Which initial assessment is recommended for a child presenting with syncope?

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate cardiac catheterization for each patient

options.label: D
options.text: Detailed history, BP, pulse, cardiac examination and 12-lead ECG

options.label: E
options.text: EEG in children in routine care as the test

questions.correctAnswerText: Detailed history, BP, pulse, cardiac examination and 12-lead ECG
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance emphasizes a good history, examination of BP, murmur and pulses, assessment for Marfan features, and a 12-lead ECG.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Renal investigations do not form the core initial syncope assessment.
- B. Incorrect. Cardiac catheterization is not the initial test for every child with syncope.
- C. Incorrect. CXR alone cannot identify the cause of syncope.
- D. Correct. This is the initial assessment described.
- E. Incorrect. EEG is not required for every fainting episode; history and cardiac screening are essential.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- History: circumstances, prodrome, exertion, palpitations, recovery and family history.
- Examination: BP, pulses, murmurs and features of Marfan syndrome.
- 12-lead ECG is an important initial investigation.

questions.stem: Which group of conditions is listed as potential causes of cardiac syncope?

options.label: A
options.text: Otitis media, sinusitis and allergic rhinitis

options.label: B
options.text: UTI, nephrotic syndrome and renal stones

options.label: D
options.text: Iron deficiency, constipation and celiac disease

options.label: E
options.text: Arrhythmia, heart block, aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and long-QT syndrome

questions.correctAnswerText: Arrhythmia, heart block, aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and long-QT syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance cardiac causes such as arrhythmias, heart block, aortic stenosis, HOCM and long-QT syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are ENT/allergic conditions and do not explain cardiac syncope.
- B. Incorrect. Renal disorders do not form the listed cardiac syncope group.
- C. Incorrect. Respiratory disease can cause collapse in severe cases, but this is not the group asked for.
- D. Incorrect. These conditions may cause other symptoms but are not the listed cardiac causes.
- E. Correct. These are the cardiac causes emphasized.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cardiac syncope may signal an arrhythmia or obstructive lesion.
- Exertional symptoms and family history of sudden death are particularly concerning.
- ECG and cardiovascular examination are essential.

questions.stem: Which definition of pulmonary hypertension is given in the supplied CVS clinical guidance?

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced oxygen saturation without pulmonary pressure measurement

options.label: C
options.text: Elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure at rest, with the sheet using a threshold above 25 mmHg

options.label: E
options.text: Any systolic murmur at the pulmonary area

questions.correctAnswerText: Elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure at rest, with the sheet using a threshold above 25 mmHg
questions.initialExplanation: The supplied standard guidance defines pulmonary hypertension using a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 25 mmHg at rest. This is the value in the course clinical guidance and is included here as a source-based examination point.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ejection fraction is a measure of ventricular systolic function.
- B. Incorrect. Oxygen saturation may be abnormal in some patients but does not itself define pulmonary hypertension.
- C. Correct. This matches the definition printed in the supplied clinical guidance.
- D. Incorrect. Systemic hypotension is not the definition.
- E. Incorrect. A murmur alone does not define pulmonary hypertension.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The supplied standard guidance uses mean PAP >25 mmHg at rest.
- This question deliberately reflects the source clinical guidance; contemporary diagnostic definitions have been updated, so use current specialist guidance clinically.
- Causes include idiopathic/familial disease, left-heart disease, post-tricuspid shunts, pulmonary vein disease and chronic lung disease.

questions.stem: A child with a longstanding large VSD develops exertional dyspnoea, loud P2 and right ventricular hypertrophy. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.label: B
options.text: Pulmonary vascular disease caused by longstanding increased pulmonary blood flow

options.label: D
options.text: Acute ductal closure in an otherwise normal heart

options.label: E
options.text: Normal physiological adaptation with no disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary vascular disease caused by longstanding increased pulmonary blood flow
questions.initialExplanation: Longstanding post-tricuspid left-to-right shunts, such as VSD, AVSD and PDA, can cause pulmonary vascular disease and pulmonary hypertension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This does not explain the pulmonary pressure findings.
- B. Correct. Chronic increased pulmonary flow may cause pulmonary vascular remodelling, elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular pressure loading.
- C. Incorrect. Spontaneous closure would not explain loud P2 and RVH.
- D. Incorrect. Ductal closure is relevant to duct-dependent neonatal lesions, not this chronic shunt-related process.
- E. Incorrect. Loud P2 and RVH in this context are pathological clues.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Large longstanding VSD/AVSD/PDA → pulmonary vascular disease.
- Findings may include loud P2 and RVH.
- Early correction of significant shunts helps prevent irreversible pulmonary vascular disease.

questions.stem: Which treatment options for pulmonary hypertension are recommended?

options.label: D
options.text: Balloon atrial septostomy in each patient

options.label: E
options.text: Use pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide, sildenafil or prostacyclin); consider transplant in advanced disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Use pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide, sildenafil or prostacyclin); consider transplant in advanced disease
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance several pulmonary vasodilator options, including inhaled nitric oxide, sildenafil, intravenous prostacyclin and inhaled iloprost, with heart–lung transplantation considered in advanced cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Indomethacin is used to promote PDA closure in selected preterm infants; it is not pulmonary hypertension therapy.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics are used only when infection is a contributing cause and are not the sole treatment.
- C. Incorrect. Aortic valve replacement treats selected severe aortic valve disease.
- D. Incorrect. Balloon atrial septostomy is considered in selected situations, not universally for all pulmonary hypertension.
- E. Correct. These are the therapies listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pulmonary hypertension requires specialist-directed treatment based on the underlying cause and haemodynamics.
- Clinical guidance NO, sildenafil and prostacyclin-based therapy.
- Advanced refractory disease may require transplant assessment.

cases.title: Large shunts and their late consequences

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman with an unrepaired large VSD from childhood has progressive dyspnoea, cyanosis, haemoptysis and finger clubbing. She has a palpable, loud second heart sound and a right ventricular heave. Which set of investigation results is most consistent with her diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Low haemoglobin; plethoric lung fields; LVH; left-to-right flow on Doppler

options.label: B
options.text: Normal haemoglobin; boot-shaped heart; RVH; pulmonary stenosis on echo

options.label: C
options.text: Polycythaemia; cardiomegaly with plethoric lungs; biventricular hypertrophy; left-to-right shunt

options.label: D
options.text: Polycythaemia; egg-on-side heart; normal ECG; parallel circulations

options.label: E
options.text: Polycythaemia; cardiomegaly with oligaemic lung fields; RVH with a tall peaked P wave; right-to-left shunt with high pulmonary pressure on Doppler

questions.correctAnswerText: Polycythaemia; cardiomegaly with oligaemic lung fields; RVH with a tall peaked P wave; right-to-left shunt with high pulmonary pressure on Doppler
questions.initialExplanation: This is Eisenmenger syndrome: irreversible shunt reversal from raised pulmonary vascular resistance. Chronic hypoxia causes polycythaemia; the CXR shows cardiomegaly with oligaemic lung fields; the ECG shows RVH and P pulmonale; Doppler shows the shunt direction and pulmonary pressure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Describes the pattern of an uncomplicated moderate L→R shunt, not a cyanosed adult; anaemia is not expected.
- B. Incorrect. Describes tetralogy of Fallot.
- C. Incorrect. This is the pattern of a large *uncomplicated* VSD in infancy (cardiomegaly, plethora, biventricular hypertrophy).
- D. Incorrect. Describes TGA.
- E. Correct. Polycythaemia (hypoxia), oligaemic fields, RVH + P pulmonale, shunt reversal on Doppler. Cardiac catheterisation measures pressures and the response to vasodilator therapy.
- Clinical reasoning: Onset in the 2nd–3rd decade, with cyanosis, haemoptysis, clubbing and a loud S2, strongly suggests Eisenmenger. Treatment: pulmonary vasodilators (sildenafil, inhaled NO) and heart–lung transplantation in advanced cases; prevention by early surgery.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Eisenmenger can complicate large VSD, ASD or PDA.
- Features: cyanosis, dyspnoea, chest pain, haemoptysis, clubbing, arrhythmias.
- Investigations: CBC (polycythaemia), CXR (cardiomegaly + oligaemic lungs), ECG (RVH + P pulmonale), Doppler, catheterisation.
- Prevention: early surgical treatment of large defects in infancy.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old girl born at 27 weeks was ventilated for several weeks and remains oxygen-dependent. Echocardiography shows no structural lesion but an elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure above 25 mmHg at rest. Which category of pulmonary hypertension does this best represent?

options.label: A
options.text: Pulmonary arterial hypertension due to a post-tricuspid shunt

options.label: B
options.text: Pulmonary venous hypertension due to left-sided heart disease

options.label: C
options.text: Pulmonary hypertension associated with chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia)

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary hypertension associated with chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia)
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance chronic lung disease or bronchopulmonary dysplasia in preterm infants under pulmonary hypertension with respiratory disease. Here a premature infant with long ventilation and oxygen dependence has no structural defect.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Post-tricuspid shunts (VSD, AVSD, PDA) require a structural lesion, which the echo excludes.
- B. Incorrect. Left-sided heart disease, pulmonary vein stenosis or compression would show left-sided or venous abnormalities on echo.
- C. Correct. Preterm infant with bronchopulmonary dysplasia and PH.
- D. Incorrect. PPHN is a neonatal condition in the early newborn period, not a 7-month-old with chronic lung disease.
- E. Incorrect. Idiopathic PAH is sporadic or familial and diagnosed only after excluding known causes — here a clear cause exists.
- Clinical reasoning: Find the cause: lung disease in a former preterm infant is the identifiable trigger. Treatment includes vasodilators (inhaled nitric oxide, sildenafil, prostacyclin analogues) and treating the underlying disease; heart–lung transplantation in advanced cases.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PH definition: mean PAP > 25 mmHg at rest (normal 8–20).
- Groups: pulmonary arterial (idiopathic, post-tricuspid shunts, PPHN), pulmonary venous (left heart disease, pulmonary vein stenosis/compression), with respiratory disease (BPD, interstitial lung disease, OSA).
- Treatment options: inhaled NO, magnesium sulphate, sildenafil, prostacyclin, iloprost, anticoagulants; transplantation in advanced cases.

cases.title: Transition from fetal to neonatal circulation
cases.vignette: A term newborn takes the first breaths after delivery. Pulmonary expansion reduces pulmonary vascular resistance and increases pulmonary blood flow. Left atrial pressure rises relative to right atrial pressure. The ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale begin their functional closure processes.

questions.stem: Which fetal vessel allows oxygenated blood from the placenta to bypass most of the liver?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ductus venosus
questions.initialExplanation: The ductus venosus carries oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein toward the inferior vena cava, bypassing most of the hepatic circulation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The SVC returns systemic venous blood to the right atrium.
- B. Correct. It is the fetal shunt that bypasses the liver.
- C. Incorrect. The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta.
- D. Incorrect. Pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
- E. Incorrect. The foramen ovale allows blood to pass from the right atrium to the left atrium.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ductus venosus: bypasses the liver.
- Foramen ovale: RA → LA.
- Ductus arteriosus: pulmonary artery → aorta in fetal circulation.

questions.stem: What is the main pressure change after the first breath that promotes functional closure of the foramen ovale?

options.label: A
options.text: Pulmonary blood flow increases, raising left atrial pressure above right atrial pressure

options.label: C
options.text: Right atrial pressure rises above left atrial pressure

questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary blood flow increases, raising left atrial pressure above right atrial pressure
questions.initialExplanation: Lung expansion reduces pulmonary vascular resistance. More blood returns to the left atrium from the lungs, increasing left atrial pressure relative to right atrial pressure and promoting functional closure of the foramen ovale.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Increased pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure and presses the septal flap closed.
- B. Incorrect. Systemic venous return continues after birth.
- C. Incorrect. The pressure relationship reverses after birth; left atrial pressure becomes greater.
- D. Incorrect. Pulmonary vascular resistance falls with lung expansion.
- E. Incorrect. The ductus venosus does not open wider as part of the normal postnatal transition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- First breath → lung expansion → reduced PVR → increased pulmonary blood flow.
- Increased pulmonary venous return → LA pressure exceeds RA pressure → functional closure of foramen ovale.
- Oxygen and reduced placental prostaglandin supply contribute to ductal closure.

questions.stem: Which fetal shunt connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ductus arteriosus
questions.initialExplanation: The ductus arteriosus diverts blood away from the fetal lungs by connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The coronary sinus drains venous blood from the myocardium to the right atrium.
- B. Incorrect. Foramen ovale connects the right and left atria.
- C. Incorrect. Ductus venosus bypasses the liver.
- D. Incorrect. The umbilical vein returns placental blood to the fetus.
- E. Correct. It connects pulmonary artery to aorta.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ductus arteriosus: pulmonary artery → aorta.
- Functional closure occurs after birth due to increased oxygen and reduced prostaglandin influence.
- Prostaglandin E can maintain ductal patency in duct-dependent congenital lesions.

questions.stem: Which feature is most consistent with an innocent murmur in a child?

options.label: A
options.text: New murmur with fever and splinter haemorrhages

options.label: B
options.text: Diastolic murmur with cyanosis and poor perfusion

options.label: C
options.text: Soft, short systolic murmur in an otherwise asymptomatic child with normal pulses and no thrill

options.label: D
options.text: Murmur associated with abnormal pulses and cardiomegaly

options.label: E
options.text: Loud murmur with a palpable thrill and heart failure

questions.correctAnswerText: Soft, short systolic murmur in an otherwise asymptomatic child with normal pulses and no thrill
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance innocent murmurs as systolic, soft, short, symptom-free and associated with normal pulses and no thrill. They may vary with posture.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fever and splinter haemorrhages raise concern for infective endocarditis.
- B. Incorrect. A diastolic murmur with cyanosis and poor perfusion is pathological until proven otherwise.
- C. Correct. This matches the criteria for an innocent murmur.
- D. Incorrect. Abnormal pulses and cardiomegaly are red flags for pathological disease.
- E. Incorrect. A thrill and heart failure suggest significant structural disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Innocent murmur: systolic, soft, short, localized, no symptoms, normal pulses and no thrill.
- It may vary with sitting or standing.
- The most common innocent murmur listed is Still's murmur.
- Reassurance is the management when the clinical assessment supports an innocent murmur.

questions.stem: Which statement about innocent murmurs is correct?

options.label: C
options.text: They are associated with structural heart defects in children in routine care

options.label: D
options.text: They typically radiate widely and are associated with a thrill

options.label: E
options.text: They may vary with posture and are commonly heard in otherwise healthy children

questions.correctAnswerText: They may vary with posture and are commonly heard in otherwise healthy children
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance innocent murmurs as common in children, not associated with structural heart defects, and often varying with posture.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Innocent murmurs are systolic, not diastolic, in the criteria listed.
- B. Incorrect. Reassurance is the treatment when the murmur is confidently identified as innocent.
- C. Incorrect. They occur in a structurally normal heart.
- D. Incorrect. Innocent murmurs are localized and have no thrill or significant radiation.
- E. Correct. Positional variation is one of the listed characteristics.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Still's murmur is listed as the commonest innocent murmur.
- A pathological murmur is more likely if diastolic, loud, associated with thrill, symptoms, abnormal pulses or abnormal investigations.
- Do not label a murmur innocent without assessing the child and relevant clinical signs.

questions.stem: A child has a soft systolic murmur that becomes quieter on standing. The child is asymptomatic, has normal pulses, no thrill and normal cardiac investigations. What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.text: Empirical IV antibiotics for six weeks

questions.correctAnswerText: Reassurance
questions.initialExplanation: The findings are consistent with an innocent murmur. clinical guidance identifies reassurance as the treatment once pathological heart disease has been excluded clinically and, when indicated, by investigations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. There are no signs of heart failure.
- B. Correct. Reassurance is appropriate for a confidently diagnosed innocent murmur.
- C. Incorrect. There is no evidence of infective endocarditis.
- D. Incorrect. Prostaglandin is used to maintain ductal patency in selected duct-dependent congenital lesions.
- E. Incorrect. There is no structural defect requiring repair.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Innocent murmur → reassurance.
- Confirm the absence of red flags: symptoms, abnormal pulses, thrill, pathological murmur characteristics or abnormal cardiac testing.
- A diastolic murmur should not be considered innocent based on the criteria.

cases.title: Murmurs, syndromic screening and the fetal circulation

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with a known ventricular septal defect is examined by a trainee. A pansystolic murmur is easily audible at the lower left sternal edge with a palpable thrill. The murmur is still heard when the stethoscope rests lightly on the chest wall, but disappears as soon as the stethoscope is lifted off the chest. Which Levine grade best describes this murmur?
questions.correctAnswerText: Grade V
questions.initialExplanation: A thrill places the murmur at grade IV or above. A murmur that is still heard with the stethoscope only lightly on the chest (but not when lifted off) is grade V. Grade VI is audible even with the stethoscope 1–2 cm off the chest.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Grade II — Incorrect. Audible but soft, equal in intensity to the heart sounds, and never associated with a thrill.
- B. Grade III — Incorrect. Easily audible and louder than S1 and S2, but there is no thrill.
- C. Grade V — Correct. Easily audible, with a thrill, and still heard with the stethoscope only lightly on the chest.
- D. Grade VI — Incorrect. Requires the murmur to remain audible when the stethoscope is held off the chest (1–2 cm).
- E. Grade IV — Incorrect. Easily audible with a thrill, but the "light contact" criterion places it higher, at grade V.
- Clinical reasoning: The thrill and the loudness make this murmur pathological. An innocent murmur is soft (grade 1–2/6), short and has no thrill, so this child cannot be reassured and needs echocardiographic assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Grade I: barely audible; II: soft; III: loud, no thrill; IV: thrill; V: thrill + audible with light contact; VI: thrill + audible off the chest.
- Any thrill excludes an innocent murmur.
- Innocent murmurs are grade 1–2/6, systolic, short, with normal pulses, normal sounds and no symptoms.

source.sheet: Murmur — Levine grading (sheet p. 6) and innocent-murmur criteria (sheet p. 5).

questions.stem: A healthy, thriving 5-year-old is found at a school check to have a soft continuous murmur just below the right clavicle. The murmur is clearly heard when she sits upright but becomes inaudible when she lies flat. Pulses and pulse pressure are normal, there is no thrill, and the chest X-ray and ECG are normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Venous hum (innocent murmur)
questions.initialExplanation: A venous hum is an innocent murmur of children aged about 3–8 years, heard in the infraclavicular region and arising from the jugular veins. It varies with position, and all special tests are normal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Venous hum — Correct. Infraclavicular site, age 3–8 years, jugular venous origin, variation with position, normal pulses and normal ECG/CXR.
- B. Small PDA — Incorrect. The PDA murmur is also continuous, but it is a machinery murmur in the *left* infraclavicular area that does not disappear with posture. Echo is diagnostic, and even a small PDA carries a risk of infective endocarditis and is closed by catheter.
- C. Small VSD — Incorrect. Produces a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, not a continuous murmur.
- D. Secundum ASD — Incorrect. Causes an ejection systolic flow murmur with fixed wide splitting of S2.
- E. Mild pulmonary stenosis — Incorrect. An ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge, not continuous.
- Clinical reasoning: A normal child, normal pulse pressure (no wide pulse pressure as in a large PDA), positional variation and normal investigations point to an innocent origin. The management is reassurance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Still's murmur is the commonest innocent murmur (3–8 years, left lower sternal edge).
- Venous hum: infraclavicular, jugular veins, varies with position.
- Peripheral pulmonary flow murmur: newborns, pulmonary area.
- Structural continuous murmurs (PDA) do not behave like positional innocent murmurs.

source.raw: Murmur — types of innocent murmur (sheet p. 5); PDA clinical picture (sheet p. 14–15).
source.sheet: Murmur — types of innocent murmur (sheet p. 5); PDA clinical picture (sheet p. 14–15).

questions.stem: A student asks why, in fetal life, the coronary and carotid arteries receive blood with a higher oxygen content than the descending aorta. Which description best explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: Umbilical venous blood passes through the liver and then through the expanded lungs, reaching the left heart fully saturated

options.label: B
options.text: Blood from the superior vena cava is directed across the foramen ovale into the left atrium and then supplies the coronary and carotid arteries

options.label: C
options.text: The descending aorta is supplied mainly by the left ventricle, so the lower body receives the best-oxygenated blood in fetal life

options.label: D
options.text: IVC blood crosses the foramen ovale to the left heart; SVC blood passes through the right ventricle and ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta

options.label: E
options.text: The pulmonary veins return large volumes of well-oxygenated blood to the left atrium because the fetal lungs are fully expanded and perfused

questions.correctAnswerText: IVC blood crosses the foramen ovale to the left heart; SVC blood passes through the right ventricle and ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta
questions.initialExplanation: Placental blood is routed by the ductus venosus to the IVC and right atrium, then mostly through the foramen ovale to the left atrium and left ventricle. The coronary and carotid arteries therefore receive relatively well-oxygenated blood, whereas SVC blood goes RV → pulmonary trunk → ductus arteriosus → descending aorta.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The ductus venosus *bypasses* the liver, and the fetal lungs do little work (PVR is high), so blood does not pass through them.
- B. Incorrect. SVC (deoxygenated) blood flows to the RA → RV → pulmonary trunk, not preferentially across the foramen ovale.
- C. Incorrect. The descending aorta receives the ductal blood from the pulmonary trunk, which is poorly oxygenated.
- D. Correct. Describes the streaming of oxygenated blood to the upper body and poorly oxygenated blood to the lower body.
- E. Incorrect. Fetal lungs are not expanded; pulmonary venous return is small until the first breath.
- Clinical reasoning: This pattern explains why ductal closure and the changes at birth matter: the shunts are essential before birth but must close afterwards.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Shunts: ductus venosus (bypasses liver), foramen ovale (RA → LA), ductus arteriosus (pulmonary trunk → aorta).
- Antenatally right-sided pressure exceeds left-sided pressure.
- Blood returns to the placenta via two umbilical arteries.
- Prostaglandin keeps the duct patent; anti-prostaglandins promote closure.

cases.title: A child with an unusual cardiac apex
cases.vignette: A school-age child is referred after a chest examination reveals that the cardiac apex is best felt on the right side. The clinician reviews the position of the heart and abdominal organs to distinguish an isolated abnormal cardiac position from a reversal of the normal arrangement of the viscera.

questions.stem: Which term describes the usual normal arrangement of the thoracic and abdominal organs?
questions.correctAnswerText: Situs solitus
questions.initialExplanation: Situs solitus describes the normal arrangement of the organs. It is distinct from the position of the cardiac apex alone.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ectopia cordis refers to an abnormally located heart outside the normal thoracic position.
- B. Incorrect. Situs inversus describes reversal of the usual arrangement of the organs.
- C. Incorrect. Levocardia describes the heart with its apex directed to the left.
- D. Correct. Situs solitus is the normal visceral arrangement.
- E. Incorrect. Dextrocardia describes a right-sided cardiac apex.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Situs solitus: normal visceral arrangement.
- Situs inversus: reversed arrangement of the organs.
- Do not use the position of the cardiac apex alone to describe the arrangement of all organs.

questions.stem: A child has the abdominal and thoracic organs arranged in the opposite configuration to the usual arrangement. Which term best describes this finding?
questions.correctAnswerText: Situs inversus
questions.initialExplanation: Situs inversus refers to reversal of the usual position of the organs, rather than a right-sided heart in isolation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Coarctation is a narrowing of the aorta.
- B. Incorrect. This is the normal arrangement.
- C. Incorrect. Isolated dextrocardia describes a right-pointing cardiac apex without necessarily reversing all other organs.
- D. Correct. Situs inversus is the reversed arrangement of the organs.
- E. Incorrect. Levocardia describes a left-pointing cardiac apex.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Situs inversus: reversal of the organ arrangement.
- Dextrocardia: right-sided cardiac apex; assess the position of the other organs before describing the overall situs.

questions.stem: The heart is in its usual position, with the cardiac apex directed to the left. Which term is used for this cardiac orientation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Levocardia
questions.initialExplanation: Levocardia describes a heart in the usual left-sided position, with the apex pointing to the left.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dextrocardia means the apex is directed to the right.
- B. Incorrect. Situs inversus refers to reversal of the arrangement of the organs.
- C. Correct. Levocardia is the left-sided cardiac position described.
- D. Incorrect. Pulmonary atresia is a congenital obstruction or absence of the normal pulmonary valve/outflow pathway.
- E. Incorrect. Ebstein anomaly is a congenital abnormality of the tricuspid valve.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Levocardia: cardiac apex points left.
- Dextrocardia: cardiac apex points right.
- Situs describes the arrangement of the organs, not just the direction of the apex.

questions.stem: A child has a right-pointing cardiac apex, but the finding is limited to the heart rather than a reversal of the position of all the organs. Which description is most appropriate?
questions.correctAnswerText: Situs solitus with isolated dextrocardia
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance distinguishes a right-sided cardiac apex from reversal of the positions of all the organs. The position of the abdominal viscera must therefore be considered separately.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A right-pointing apex with otherwise usual visceral arrangement is described as isolated dextrocardia with situs solitus.
- B. Incorrect. Interrupted aortic arch is a duct-dependent congenital vascular lesion.
- C. Incorrect. Situs inversus involves reversal of the organs, not an isolated right-sided heart.
- D. Incorrect. This describes a left-sided heart, not the finding in the vignette.
- E. Incorrect. Levocardia has a left-pointing apex.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dextrocardia is a description of the heart's position.
- Situs inversus is a description of the arrangement of the viscera.
- Record cardiac position and visceral situs separately.

questions.stem: Which radiographic association is correctly matched in the supplied CVS clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Boot-shaped heart — Coarctation of the aorta

options.label: E
options.text: Rib notching — Transposition of the great arteries

questions.correctAnswerText: Box-shaped heart — Ebstein anomaly
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance characteristic cardiac silhouettes, including boot-shaped, egg-on-side, snowman and box-shaped appearances, and rib notching.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Boot-shaped heart is associated with TOF.
- B. Incorrect. Egg-on-side appearance is associated with TGA.
- C. Correct. clinical guidance associates a box-shaped cardiac silhouette with Ebstein anomaly.
- D. Incorrect. Snowman appearance is associated with supracardiac TAPVR, not TOF.
- E. Incorrect. Rib notching is associated with collateral circulation in coarctation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TOF: boot-shaped heart.
- TGA: egg-on-side appearance.
- Supracardiac TAPVR: snowman appearance.
- Coarctation: rib notching.
- Ebstein anomaly: box-shaped cardiac silhouette.

topics.name: Duct-Dependent Left-Heart Obstruction in the Sick Neonate

cases.title: A neonate who collapses as the ductus closes
cases.vignette: A neonate becomes pale, poorly perfused and critically unwell during the early postnatal period. The femoral pulses are difficult to detect.

questions.stem: A sick neonate has circulatory collapse and absent femoral pulses as the ductus arteriosus closes. Which lesion is specifically highlighted?
questions.correctAnswerText: Critical coarctation of the aorta
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance critical coarctation as a duct-dependent left-heart obstructive lesion that may cause circulatory collapse and absent femoral pulses when ductal flow is lost.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. An innocent murmur does not cause neonatal circulatory collapse.
- B. Correct. Critical CoA is specifically associated with collapse and absent femoral pulses.
- C. Incorrect. Mild pulmonary stenosis does not explain absent femoral pulses from systemic outflow obstruction.
- D. Incorrect. A small VSD is not the lesion described by this duct-dependent presentation.
- E. Incorrect. A small secundum ASD does not usually produce duct-dependent systemic circulation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Critical CoA may present when the ductus closes.
- Look for weak or absent femoral pulses and poor systemic perfusion.
- A sick neonate with suspected duct-dependent systemic circulation requires emergency stabilization.

questions.stem: A neonate has circulatory collapse, absent femoral pulses and an absent left brachial pulse. Which lesion is specifically listed with this pulse pattern?
questions.correctAnswerText: Interrupted aortic arch
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance associates interruption of the aortic arch with circulatory collapse and absent femoral and left brachial pulses.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pulmonary stenosis affects right ventricular outflow.
- B. Incorrect. An isolated ASD does not interrupt systemic arterial continuity.
- C. Correct. This pulse pattern is specifically listed for interrupted aortic arch.
- D. Incorrect. Mitral regurgitation does not cause this pattern of absent systemic pulses.
- E. Incorrect. A PDA alone does not explain the described absent pulse pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Interrupted aortic arch is a duct-dependent systemic lesion.
- clinical guidance highlights absent femoral and left brachial pulses.
- Do not delay stabilization while arranging definitive anatomical assessment.

questions.stem: A neonate with hypoplastic left heart syndrome develops profound circulatory collapse as the ductus arteriosus closes. Which finding is listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Isolated upper-limb hypertension with normal perfusion

options.label: B
options.text: Fixed splitting of S2 without poor perfusion

options.label: C
options.text: A continuous machinery murmur as the abnormality

options.label: D
options.text: Bounding femoral pulses with isolated wide pulse pressure

questions.correctAnswerText: peripheral pulses may be absent
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance hypoplastic left heart syndrome as a duct-dependent systemic lesion that may cause circulatory collapse with all peripheral pulses absent.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Upper-limb hypertension with weak lower-limb pulses is more suggestive of coarctation in an older child.
- B. Incorrect. Fixed splitting of S2 is associated with ASD and does not explain shock.
- C. Incorrect. A continuous machinery murmur suggests PDA, not the described HLHS presentation.
- D. Incorrect. Bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure suggest a large PDA.
- E. Correct. This is the pulse finding listed for HLHS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HLHS causes duct-dependent systemic circulation.
- Ductal closure may result in severe low cardiac output and collapse.
- clinical guidance highlights absent peripheral pulses in this presentation.

questions.stem: A neonate is suspected of having a duct-dependent left-heart obstructive lesion and is in circulatory collapse. Which immediate approach best matches the emergency principles listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Give a drug to close the ductus immediately

options.label: B
options.text: Reassure the family and arrange routine outpatient follow-up

options.label: D
options.text: Stabilize ABC and start prostaglandin infusion to maintain ductal patency

options.label: E
options.text: Delay treatment until the child is old enough for elective surgery

questions.correctAnswerText: Stabilize ABC and start prostaglandin infusion to maintain ductal patency
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance ABC stabilization and prostaglandin infusion for critical CoA, interrupted aortic arch and HLHS when systemic circulation is duct-dependent.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Closing the ductus may worsen systemic perfusion in a duct-dependent lesion.
- B. Incorrect. Outpatient reassurance is unsafe in a shocked neonate.
- C. Incorrect. Oral diuretics alone do not restore duct-dependent systemic blood flow.
- D. Correct. Maintaining ductal patency may be lifesaving while urgent specialist assessment and definitive management are arranged.
- E. Incorrect. Neonatal circulatory collapse is an emergency and cannot wait for elective review.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Suspected duct-dependent systemic circulation: ABC stabilization and urgent prostaglandin infusion.
- Critical CoA, interrupted aortic arch and HLHS are highlighted.
- Arrange urgent echocardiography and specialist cardiac management; follow local neonatal emergency protocols.

cases.title: Pulses, pressures and outflow obstruction

questions.stem: A 3-day-old term neonate who was feeding poorly collapses. He is pale, tachypnoeic and has an enlarged liver with severe metabolic acidosis. Oxygen saturation is 98% in the right hand but 83% in the foot. Femoral pulses are weak and arm blood pressure is higher than leg blood pressure. There is no significant murmur. Which diagnosis and immediate action are most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Transposition of the great arteries — start indomethacin to close the duct

options.label: B
options.text: Severe coarctation of the aorta with duct-dependent lower-body flow — ABC resuscitation and prostaglandin infusion

options.label: C
options.text: Tetralogy of Fallot — knee–chest position and propranolol

options.label: D
options.text: Large PDA — indomethacin and fluid restriction

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe coarctation of the aorta with duct-dependent lower-body flow — ABC resuscitation and prostaglandin infusion
questions.initialExplanation: In severe coarctation with a PDA, lower-limb perfusion depends on the duct, so the lower body is bluer than the upper body (differential cyanosis). When the duct closes the neonate collapses with heart failure, weak or absent femoral pulses and severe acidosis. Treatment: ABC, early prostaglandin, urgent referral for surgery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. TGA causes severe cyanosis everywhere with a loud single S2; indomethacin would close the duct needed for mixing.
- B. Correct. Upper-limb BP > lower-limb BP, weak femoral pulses, shock, acidosis, duct dependence.
- C. Incorrect. Tet spells occur later (3–6 months); knee–chest position and propranolol treat a spell.
- D. Incorrect. A large PDA has bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure, not weak femoral pulses; the duct must be kept open here.
- E. Incorrect. A large VSD does not produce an upper–lower limb pressure gradient or shock on day 3.
- Clinical reasoning: Oxygen saturation difference + pulse and BP discrepancy = coarctation with duct-dependent lower body.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Critical CoA: circulatory collapse when the duct closes, absent femoral pulses, severe metabolic acidosis, HF.
- Differential cyanosis: pink upper body, bluish lower body (severe CoA + PDA).
- Treatment: ABC, early prostaglandin, cardiac centre referral.
- Normally leg BP > arm BP; in CoA the arm BP is higher — measure BP in all four limbs.

cases.title: Complex lesions and staged management

questions.stem: A 3-day-old neonate collapses with acidosis, absent peripheral pulses and no murmur. Echocardiography shows hypoplastic left atrium, left ventricle and ascending aorta with mitral and aortic stenosis. Which approach best matches clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: ABC and prostaglandin infusion, followed by definitive surgery (Norwood operation) or cardiac transplantation

options.label: B
options.text: Balloon atrial septostomy followed by arterial switch operation

options.label: D
options.text: Digoxin and discharge with outpatient follow-up

options.label: E
options.text: Blalock–Taussig shunt alone, as in tetralogy of Fallot

questions.correctAnswerText: ABC and prostaglandin infusion, followed by definitive surgery (Norwood operation) or cardiac transplantation
questions.initialExplanation: HLHS is duct-dependent with severely reduced systemic output: collapse, acidosis, absent pulses, usually no murmur. Management: ABC + prostaglandin, then surgical palliation (Norwood) or cardiac transplantation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct.
- B. Incorrect. Arterial switch is for TGA.
- C. Incorrect. Closing the duct is fatal in HLHS.
- D. Incorrect. The infant is critically ill.
- E. Incorrect. A BT shunt adds pulmonary flow and does not restore systemic output.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HLHS: hypoplastic LA, LV, ascending aorta; mitral and aortic stenosis; duct-dependent.
- Presents with differential cyanosis, decreased COP, absent pulsations, acidosis, death in the first month if untreated.
- PGE + supportive; Norwood or transplantation.

topics.name: Additional Cyanotic and Pulmonary Outflow Lesions

cases.title: Reviewing the differential diagnosis of a cyanotic child
cases.vignette: A child with central cyanosis is being assessed for congenital cardiac disease. The clinician reviews additional lesions included in the differential lists on the final CVS teaching page.

questions.stem: Which congenital cardiac lesion is explicitly included in the additional lesion list on the final CVS teaching page?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary atresia
questions.initialExplanation: Pulmonary atresia is explicitly included in the list of additional lesions on page 48, together with tricuspid atresia, pulmonary stenosis or pulmonary hypertension, TOF, Eisenmenger syndrome and Ebstein anomaly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Pulmonary atresia is named in the page 48 list.
- B. Incorrect. An isolated secundum ASD is an acyanotic left-to-right shunt in the usual presentation and is not the lesion asked for.
- C. Incorrect. Mitral valve prolapse is not included in the specified list.
- D. Incorrect. Still's murmur is an innocent murmur.
- E. Incorrect. Isolated mild mitral regurgitation is not included in the specified list.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Additional lesions named on page 48 include pulmonary atresia and tricuspid atresia.
- The same list includes pulmonary stenosis or pulmonary hypertension, TOF, Eisenmenger syndrome and Ebstein anomaly.
- The differential must be interpreted with clinical findings and echocardiography.

cases.title: Pulses, pressures and outflow obstruction

questions.stem: Two neonates are admitted in the first week of life. Neonate 1 is cyanosed with hepatomegaly, a loud ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge radiating to the back, and RVH on ECG. Neonate 2 is in shock with heart failure, weak pulses, left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG and an ejection systolic murmur in the aortic area radiating to the neck. Which pairing of diagnoses is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Neonate 1: critical pulmonary stenosis; Neonate 2: critical aortic stenosis

options.label: B
options.text: Neonate 1: critical aortic stenosis; Neonate 2: critical pulmonary stenosis

options.label: C
options.text: Neonate 1: transposition of the great arteries; Neonate 2: atrial septal defect

options.label: D
options.text: Neonate 1: ventricular septal defect; Neonate 2: patent ductus arteriosus

options.label: E
options.text: Neonate 1: tricuspid atresia; Neonate 2: hypoplastic left heart syndrome

questions.correctAnswerText: Neonate 1: critical pulmonary stenosis; Neonate 2: critical aortic stenosis
questions.initialExplanation: Severe or critical PS presents early with cyanosis and right-sided heart failure (RV outflow obstruction, RVH). Critical AS in the newborn presents with heart failure and shock (LV outflow obstruction, LVH).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. PS: RVH, ESM at the upper left sternal edge radiating to the back, cyanosis + HF; AS: LVH, ESM radiating to the neck, HF and shock.
- B. Incorrect. The sides are reversed.
- C. Incorrect. TGA has a loud single S2 and usually no murmur; ASD is rarely symptomatic in the neonate.
- D. Incorrect. Neither lesion produces cyanosis or shock with these ECG findings.
- E. Incorrect. Tricuspid atresia shows left-axis deviation, not RVH; HLHS lacks a prominent ESM radiating to the neck (usually no murmur).
- Clinical reasoning: The ventricle that is hypertrophied identifies the side of the obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PS → RVH, right-sided HF; AS → LVH, left-sided failure.
- PS murmur radiates to the back, AS murmur radiates to the carotids/neck.
- Newborn critical AS: HF and shock; severe/critical PS: cyanosis + HF early in life.
- Treatment of symptomatic children: balloon dilatation/valvotomy; aortic valve replacement may be needed in newborns.

cases.title: Complex lesions and staged management

questions.stem: A 2-day-old neonate has central cyanosis (SpO2 78%) without respiratory distress or murmur. The hyperoxia test fails to improve oxygenation, and the chest X-ray shows oligaemic lungs. Echocardiography shows no communication between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery and a VSD, with pulmonary blood flow supplied through the ductus arteriosus. What is the most appropriate treatment statement?

options.label: B
options.text: Captopril and furosemide for heart failure

options.label: C
options.text: Prostaglandin E to keep the duct open because the lungs depend on it; later BT shunt or total correction

options.label: D
options.text: Balloon atrial septostomy as the definitive treatment

options.label: E
options.text: Reassurance, as the lesion will improve when pulmonary vascular resistance falls

questions.correctAnswerText: Prostaglandin E to keep the duct open because the lungs depend on it; later BT shunt or total correction
questions.initialExplanation: Pulmonary atresia (with or without VSD) is duct-dependent. Early cyanosis, no murmur ± HF, oligaemic lungs. PGE and supportive care are given first; surgery is palliative (BT shunt) or total correction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Closing the duct would remove the only source of pulmonary blood flow.
- B. Incorrect. There is no heart failure; this is a cyanotic neonate.
- C. Correct. PGE + supportive care, then BT shunt or total correction.
- D. Incorrect. Septostomy is used in TGA/tricuspid atresia and is not definitive here.
- E. Incorrect. Falling PVR does not create pulmonary outflow where none exists.
- Clinical reasoning: Failed hyperoxia test + oligaemic lungs + absent murmur → duct-dependent cyanotic lesion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pulmonary atresia: early cyanosis, no murmur, duct-dependent, blood passes RV → LV → aorta.
- Duct-dependent lesions: TA/PA, Ebstein, TGA, HLHS, critical CoA/AS, interrupted aortic arch.
- PGE adverse effects: apnoea, jitteriness, seizures, flushing, hypotension.

questions.stem: A neonate born to a mother treated with lithium throughout pregnancy has cyanosis, a tricuspid regurgitation murmur and massive cardiomegaly with a box-shaped heart on chest X-ray. Right-to-left shunting occurs across a PFO. Later he has episodes of sudden rapid regular tachycardia. Which anatomical abnormality best explains the findings?

options.label: A
options.text: An overriding aorta above a large VSD with pulmonary stenosis

options.label: B
options.text: Failure of most pulmonary veins to connect to the left atrium

options.label: D
options.text: Downward displacement of the tricuspid valve with a huge right atrium and small functional right ventricle

options.label: E
options.text: Absent tricuspid valve with the left ventricle effective

questions.correctAnswerText: Downward displacement of the tricuspid valve with a huge right atrium and small functional right ventricle
questions.initialExplanation: Maternal lithium is associated with Ebstein anomaly: the tricuspid valve is displaced downwards, producing a huge RA and a small RV, TR, right-to-left shunt at atrial level (PFO) and arrhythmias such as SVT. The CXR shows a box-shaped heart.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Describes TOF (boot-shaped heart, oligaemic lungs).
- B. Incorrect. TAPVR gives plethoric lungs and a snowman sign (supracardiac).
- C. Incorrect. Ventricular inversion is a feature of L-TGA.
- D. Correct. Ebstein anomaly.
- E. Incorrect. Describes tricuspid atresia, with left-axis deviation.
- Clinical reasoning: Drug exposure + CXR shape + arrhythmia identify the lesion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lithium → Ebstein anomaly.
- Ebstein: variable-onset cyanosis, TR murmur, SVT, box-shaped heart, medical treatment with PGE, supportive and antiarrhythmic drugs; surgery rarely needed.
- Ebstein is also listed as a cause of SVT and as a duct-dependent lesion 's summary.

cases.title: Large shunts and their late consequences

questions.stem: A 3-month-old with a large VSD has tachypnoea, sweating on feeds and poor weight gain. Examination shows a soft pansystolic murmur, an ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge and a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, with an enlarged tender liver. Which mechanism best explains the apical mid-diastolic murmur?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased flow across the mitral valve due to the large left-to-right shunt

options.label: C
options.text: Aortic regurgitation caused by the defect

options.label: D
options.text: Tricuspid stenosis from right ventricular hypertrophy

options.label: E
options.text: Carey–Coombs murmur of acute rheumatic carditis

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased flow across the mitral valve due to the large left-to-right shunt
questions.initialExplanation: In a large VSD the increased pulmonary blood flow returns to the left atrium and crosses the mitral valve in larger volume, producing a relative (functional) mitral diastolic murmur. The increased flow across the pulmonary valve produces the ejection systolic murmur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Apical mid-diastolic murmur from increased flow across the mitral valve; the ESM reflects increased flow across the pulmonary valve (functional pulmonary stenosis).
- B. Incorrect. Rheumatic MS needs years of fibrosis and is not expected in a 3-month-old.
- C. Incorrect. Aortic regurgitation causes a diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, not an apical rumble.
- D. Incorrect. Nothing in the history suggests a tricuspid valve lesion.
- E. Incorrect. Carey–Coombs murmur occurs in acute rheumatic carditis (5–15-year-olds), not in this infant.
- Clinical reasoning: In a large VSD the pansystolic murmur may be soft because the defect is large; the extra murmurs signal a large shunt, and the signs of heart failure (tachypnoea, tender hepatomegaly, FTT) confirm it.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Large VSD: soft pansystolic murmur ± functional ESM at the pulmonary area ± apical mid-diastolic murmur.
- Signs of HF: tachypnoea, tachycardia, tender hepatomegaly, under-weight.
- Small VSD: loud pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge with normal growth.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old with an unrepaired large VSD had sweating and tachypnoea at 4 months. Her mother is now pleased because she feeds well and has stopped sweating. On examination the pansystolic murmur is softer than before, the second heart sound is loud and palpable, and there is a right ventricular heave. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: The defect is closing spontaneously and follow-up can be stopped

options.label: B
options.text: Heart failure has resolved because the shunt has reduced

options.label: C
options.text: Left ventricular failure is worsening and diuretics should be increased

options.label: D
options.text: Pulmonary hypertension is probably developing, and urgent echocardiography and early surgical correction are needed

options.label: E
options.text: Established Eisenmenger syndrome; transplantation is the option

questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary hypertension is probably developing, and urgent echocardiography and early surgical correction are needed
questions.initialExplanation: A loud S2 in a child with a large VSD is a bad sign: it indicates pulmonary hypertension. As pulmonary vascular resistance rises, the left-to-right shunt (and the symptoms of congestion) decreases, which can falsely reassure the family. Early correction prevents irreversible disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Spontaneous closure is expected in *small* VSDs (especially muscular), and the signs here (loud S2, RV heave) do not support closure.
- B. Incorrect. Symptoms improved because the shunt is falling as PVR rises, not because the defect is better.
- C. Incorrect. The new findings are right-sided (loud S2, RV heave), not left ventricular failure.
- D. Correct. Loud S2 = pulmonary hypertension → early echo, then surgical or catheter closure (3–6 months in large VSD) to prevent pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Eisenmenger syndrome (shunt reversal) usually appears in the 2nd–3rd decade, and she is not cyanosed.
- Clinical reasoning: Improved symptoms plus softer murmur plus loud S2 = rising PVR, not recovery.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Loud S2 in VSD = pulmonary hypertension (bad sign).
- Large VSD: early surgical or cath correction at 3–6 months.
- Eisenmenger syndrome = irreversible shunt reversal from raised PVR; prevent by early correction.
