cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which pituitary cell type secretes growth hormone?
questions.correctAnswerText: Somatotroph
questions.initialExplanation: Growth hormone is secreted by somatotroph cells in the anterior pituitary.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Thyrotrophs secrete thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).
- B. Correct. Somatotrophs produce growth hormone (GH).
- C. Incorrect. Lactotrophs secrete prolactin.
- D. Incorrect. Corticotrophs secrete adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH).
- E. Incorrect. Gonadotrophs secrete follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH).
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GH is secreted by anterior-pituitary somatotrophs.
- Clinical descriptions include GH as a 191-amino-acid polypeptide.
- The pituitary is controlled by hypothalamic releasing and inhibitory signals.

questions.stem: A random serum GH concentration is measured in the child and is low. Why is a single random GH measurement not sufficient to diagnose GH deficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: GH secretion is pulsatile, so a random sample may be taken between secretory peaks

options.label: B
options.text: GH is secreted by the thyroid gland

options.label: C
options.text: GH is produced during fetal life

options.label: D
options.text: GH is secreted continuously at a constant rate

options.label: E
options.text: GH concentration is completely independent of sleep and exercise

questions.correctAnswerText: GH secretion is pulsatile, so a random sample may be taken between secretory peaks
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is that GH secretion is pulsatile. Therefore, a random GH value has limited diagnostic value; stimulation testing is used when deficiency is suspected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Pulsatile secretion means a random sample may be low even in a child with normal GH reserve.
- B. Incorrect. GH is produced by the anterior pituitary, not the thyroid gland.
- C. Incorrect. GH remains important during childhood and adolescence.
- D. Incorrect. GH is not secreted at a constant rate.
- E. Incorrect. Sleep, stress and exercise influence GH secretion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GH secretion is pulsatile.
- A random GH concentration is not a reliable screening test for deficiency.
- GH stimulation/provocation tests assess the secretory reserve.

questions.stem: Which hypothalamic hormone stimulates GH secretion?
questions.correctAnswerText: Growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH)
questions.initialExplanation: GHRH stimulates somatotrophs to release GH, whereas somatostatin inhibits GH secretion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. GHRH is the principal hypothalamic stimulatory signal for GH secretion.
- B. Incorrect. Somatostatin inhibits GH release.
- C. Incorrect. Dopamine has an important inhibitory effect on prolactin secretion.
- D. Incorrect. CRH stimulates ACTH release.
- E. Incorrect. TRH stimulates TSH and can also influence prolactin.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GHRH stimulates GH.
- Somatostatin inhibits GH.
- GH and IGF-1 participate in negative-feedback regulation of the axis.

questions.stem: Which factor is listed as increasing GH secretion?

options.label: A
options.text: Chronic stimulation of the inhibitory pathway

questions.correctAnswerText: Sleep
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include sleep, stress and exercise among factors that increase GH secretion. Hypoglycaemia and starvation are also listed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stimulation of the inhibitory pathway would reduce, not increase, GH release.
- B. Correct. Sleep is a physiological stimulus for GH secretion.
- C. Incorrect. Hyperglycaemia is listed as reducing GH secretion.
- D. Incorrect. Common examples include GH therapy among factors that decrease endogenous GH secretion through feedback.
- E. Incorrect. Somatostatin inhibits GH release.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Increase GH: sleep, stress, exercise, hypoglycaemia, starvation, arginine and alpha-adrenergic stimulation.
- Decrease GH: hyperglycaemia, beta-adrenergic stimulation and somatostatin ().

questions.stem: A child has normal pituitary GH production but impaired linear growth because the liver produces very little IGF-1. Which statement best explains this relationship?

options.label: A
options.text: IGF-1 is secreted by the adrenal medulla

options.label: C
options.text: GH acts on the thyroid gland

options.label: D
options.text: Many growth-promoting actions of GH are mediated through IGF-1, which is produced largely by the liver

options.label: E
options.text: GH has no role in linear growth

questions.correctAnswerText: Many growth-promoting actions of GH are mediated through IGF-1, which is produced largely by the liver
questions.initialExplanation: This is explained that GH promotes growth partly through insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), formed mainly in the liver.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. IGF-1 is not produced by the adrenal medulla.
- B. Incorrect. IGF-1 promotes, rather than inhibits, growth.
- C. Incorrect. GH has effects on bone, soft tissue, protein synthesis, lipid metabolism and glucose regulation.
- D. Correct. IGF-1 mediates many growth-promoting effects of GH.
- E. Incorrect. GH is an important regulator of linear and soft-tissue growth.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GH is secreted by anterior-pituitary somatotrophs.
- GH stimulates hepatic IGF-1 production.
- GH also has anti-insulin effects and promotes lipolysis and protein synthesis.

cases.title: A toddler with growth failure and recurrent hypoglycaemia
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child is evaluated for poor linear growth, recurrent episodes of hypoglycaemia and prolonged neonatal jaundice. The parents report that the child has a persistently immature facial appearance. Examination also reveals a small phallus.

questions.stem: Which statement about normal birth size in a child with isolated GH deficiency is most consistent with standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Birth length and weight may be normal because GH is not essential for intrauterine growth

options.label: C
options.text: GH deficiency is diagnosed by low birth weight alone

options.label: D
options.text: Severe short length is typically present at birth

options.label: E
options.text: GH deficiency causes congenital limb shortening in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Birth length and weight may be normal because GH is not essential for intrauterine growth
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that children with GH deficiency may have normal length and weight at birth because GH is not essential for fetal growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Normal birth size does not exclude subsequent postnatal GH deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Macrosomia is not the expected feature.
- C. Incorrect. Birth weight alone cannot diagnose GH deficiency.
- D. Incorrect. Severe short length at birth is not a universal feature of isolated GH deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. Congenital limb shortening is not a universal feature of GH deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Birth size may be normal in GH deficiency.
- Growth failure often becomes apparent during infancy or childhood.
- Growth velocity and serial centile tracking are more informative than a single height.

questions.stem: Which neonatal feature is a useful diagnostic clue to congenital hypopituitarism in a male infant?
questions.correctAnswerText: Micropenis
questions.initialExplanation: Micropenis is a recognized clue to congenital gonadotropin deficiency and may occur in congenital hypopituitarism. standard guidance specifically highlights it in the neonatal presentation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Delayed rather than premature dentition may occur in hypothyroidism and other growth disorders.
- B. Incorrect. Exophthalmos is associated with thyroid eye disease, not congenital hypopituitarism.
- C. Correct. Micropenis in a term male infant may indicate deficient pituitary gonadotropin stimulation.
- D. Incorrect. Macroglossia is a classical feature of congenital hypothyroidism.
- E. Incorrect. Large hands and feet are not the characteristic neonatal clue.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal hypopituitarism may present with persistent hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice, apnoea/cyanosis and micropenis in boys.
- Midline facial defects may coexist.
- Evaluate for deficiencies of other pituitary hormones, not GH alone.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with GH deficiency has short stature, increased subcutaneous fat and delayed bone maturation. Which additional finding is most consistent with standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Severe intellectual disability is typically present

options.label: D
options.text: Childish facial appearance with a small nose and mandible

options.label: E
options.text: Marked hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases

questions.correctAnswerText: Childish facial appearance with a small nose and mandible
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include a childish facial appearance, small face/nose/mandible, wide anterior fontanelle in infancy, fine hair and increased subcutaneous fat in children with GH deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. It is recognized that children with GHD generally have normal mentality and normal IQ.
- B. Incorrect. Acromegalic features reflect excess GH, not deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Exophthalmos suggests thyroid eye disease.
- D. Correct. An immature facial appearance with small facial structures is described.
- E. Incorrect. Palmar-crease hyperpigmentation is a clue to primary adrenal insufficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Childhood GHD: reduced growth velocity, short stature and delayed skeletal maturation.
- Increased subcutaneous fat/relative truncal adiposity may occur.
- Mentality and IQ are generally normal in isolated GHD.

questions.stem: A child has growth hormone deficiency together with low TSH and low ACTH. What term is used when all anterior pituitary hormones are deficient?
questions.correctAnswerText: Panhypopituitarism
questions.initialExplanation: Panhypopituitarism refers to deficiency of all anterior pituitary hormones. standard guidance distinguishes isolated GH deficiency from combined pituitary hormone deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GH resistance is a defect in GH action, not a deficiency of all anterior pituitary hormones.
- B. Incorrect. Cushing syndrome results from prolonged glucocorticoid excess.
- C. Correct. Deficiency of multiple anterior pituitary hormones, potentially including GH, TSH and ACTH, is described as panhypopituitarism.
- D. Incorrect. Primary hypothyroidism originates in the thyroid gland and usually produces high TSH.
- E. Incorrect. Graves disease is autoimmune hyperthyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Isolated GHD affects GH alone.
- Panhypopituitarism involves multiple anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies.
- If panhypopituitarism is present, replacement of other deficient hormones is required as well as GH when indicated.

cases.title: A child with low IGF-1 and unexpectedly high GH
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child has severe short stature and poor growth velocity. Laboratory assessment shows low IGF-1 despite high circulating GH.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests Laron syndrome rather than pituitary GH deficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: High IGF-1 with excessive GH action

options.label: D
options.text: High GH with low IGF-1 due to GH receptor resistance

options.label: E
options.text: High TSH with low free T4

questions.correctAnswerText: High GH with low IGF-1 due to GH receptor resistance
questions.initialExplanation: Laron syndrome is caused by defective GH receptors, resulting in GH insensitivity. GH levels may be high while IGF-1 remains low.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests excessive GH effect rather than resistance.
- B. Incorrect. Low GH and low IGF-1 are more consistent with pituitary GH deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. This pattern is consistent with primary adrenal insufficiency.
- D. Correct. High GH with low IGF-1 is the characteristic pattern described for GH receptor resistance.
- E. Incorrect. This is a pattern of primary hypothyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Laron syndrome: GH receptor defect → GH insensitivity.
- GH may be high while IGF-1 is low.
- Clinical guidance notes recombinant IGF-1 therapy as an option in selected GH-resistant patients.

questions.stem: Which investigation is used to assess GH secretory reserve in a child with suspected GH deficiency?
questions.correctAnswerText: GH stimulation/provocation test
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes a GH stimulation test using secretagogues such as insulin, glucagon, clonidine, arginine or exercise to assess GH reserve.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A provocation test evaluates the ability of the pituitary to release GH.
- B. Incorrect. Thyroid ultrasound assesses thyroid anatomy.
- C. Incorrect. Water deprivation testing is used in the evaluation of diabetes insipidus.
- D. Incorrect. Serum calcium does not assess GH secretion.
- E. Incorrect. Urinary cortisol is used in the assessment of Cushing syndrome, not GH reserve.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GH stimulation testing assesses GH secretory reserve.
- IGF-1 and IGF-binding protein may be low in GHD.
- IGF-1 is influenced by liver disease and malnutrition, so results require clinical context.

questions.stem: A child has suspected congenital pituitary hypoplasia and delayed bone age. Which combination of investigations is most appropriate?

options.label: B
options.text: Pituitary MRI and left hand/wrist bone-age radiograph

options.label: C
options.text: Water deprivation test and renal ultrasound

questions.correctAnswerText: Pituitary MRI and left hand/wrist bone-age radiograph
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include pituitary MRI to assess hypoplasia/aplasia and a left hand/wrist X-ray to assess bone age. Bone age is often delayed in GHD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Thyroid ultrasound does not assess pituitary morphology or bone age.
- B. Correct. Both tests address the suspected pituitary structural cause and skeletal maturation.
- C. Incorrect. Water deprivation testing is for suspected DI.
- D. Incorrect. These are unrelated to pituitary assessment.
- E. Incorrect. These investigations assess other respiratory or genetic conditions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bone age: left hand/wrist X-ray.
- GHD commonly causes delayed bone age.
- MRI of the pituitary is appropriate when hypoplasia, aplasia or a structural lesion is suspected.
- Assess other pituitary hormones (e.g. thyroid and cortisol axes) when combined deficiency is possible.

questions.stem: Which statement about recombinant GH treatment is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is given as a single intravenous dose once a year

options.label: B
options.text: It is contraindicated in most children with short stature

options.label: C
options.text: It is given to children with Graves disease

options.label: D
options.text: It is administered by daily subcutaneous injection, usually in the evening, and continued until epiphyseal closure when indicated

options.label: E
options.text: It replaces cortisol and thyroid hormone in panhypopituitarism

questions.correctAnswerText: It is administered by daily subcutaneous injection, usually in the evening, and continued until epiphyseal closure when indicated
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include recombinant GH therapy as daily evening subcutaneous injections, generally continued until epiphyseal closure. Other deficient pituitary hormones must also be replaced in panhypopituitarism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the administration route or schedule described.
- B. Incorrect. Common examples include several indications for GH therapy, but eligibility requires specialist assessment.
- C. Incorrect. GH is not used to treat Graves disease.
- D. Correct. This is the regimen format stated.
- E. Incorrect. GH does not replace cortisol or thyroid hormone.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GH therapy: daily SC recombinant GH.
- Other hormone deficiencies require their own replacement.
- Common examples include Turner syndrome, CKD, Prader–Willi syndrome, selected idiopathic short stature, persistent short stature after IUGR and SHOX deficiency among possible indications.
- Potential adverse effects listed include pseudotumour cerebri, slipped upper femoral epiphysis, insulin resistance and others.

cases.title: Children with growth failure referred for endocrine assessment

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy received cranial irradiation at age 4 years for a brain tumour. For 3 years his height velocity has been low and he has gained truncal fat. Bone age on a left hand–wrist radiograph is 6.5 years. IGF-1 and IGF-binding protein are low, and GH responses to two provocation tests are inadequate. Thyroid function tests and morning cortisol are normal, and pituitary MRI shows no mass lesion. Which test would best determine whether the defect is hypothalamic or pituitary?

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat left hand–wrist radiograph for bone age

questions.correctAnswerText: GHRH stimulation test
questions.initialExplanation: The clinical and biochemical picture already establishes GH deficiency. The remaining question is where the lesion lies. Clinical guidance the GHRH stimulation test specifically to differentiate pituitary from hypothalamic causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Reasoning from the vignette. Cranial irradiation is a listed acquired cause of hypopituitarism. Low IGF-1/IGFBP and failure of two provocation tests confirm GHD. A normal MRI means no structural explanation.
- A. Incorrect. GH is secreted in pulses, so a random sample is of little value and would add nothing after failed provocation tests.
- B. Incorrect. Bone age is already delayed, as expected in GHD. Repeating it does not localise the defect.
- C. Correct. If the pituitary responds to exogenous GHRH, the somatotrophs are intact and the problem is upstream (hypothalamic). No response suggests pituitary damage.
- D. Incorrect. The water deprivation test evaluates diabetes insipidus, not the GH axis.
- E. Incorrect. Karyotype is for children with dysmorphic features or suspected chromosomal short stature. Nothing here suggests it.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acquired causes of hypopituitarism: tumour (e.g. craniopharyngioma), cranial surgery/trauma, meningitis, cranial irradiation, infiltration (e.g. histiocytosis), structural brain malformation or hydrocephalus.
- GHRH stimulation test: separates pituitary from hypothalamic causes of GHD.
- When a brain tumour is suspected, perform a detailed eye and fundus examination.
- Other pituitary axes (TFT, cortisol) must be checked because deficiencies may be combined.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old girl with Turner syndrome (45,X) has received daily subcutaneous GH for 18 months. She now has a limp and pain in the hip and thigh that worsens on walking. Which adverse effect of GH therapy should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis
questions.initialExplanation: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE) is one of the side effects of GH therapy listed. A limp with hip or thigh pain in a child on GH therapy should prompt this diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. The vignette gives a limp and hip/thigh pain during GH treatment, the typical presentation of SUFE.
- A. Incorrect. Pseudotumour cerebri is also a listed GH side effect, but it presents with headache, vomiting and visual symptoms.
- B. Incorrect. Gynaecomastia is listed but is a breast finding, not a hip complaint.
- C. Incorrect. Increased leukaemia risk is listed, but leukaemia would not present as an isolated limp with this time course.
- D. Incorrect. Insulin resistance is listed but is detected biochemically, not by pain.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GH therapy side effects: pseudotumour cerebri, SUFE, gynaecomastia, increased insulin resistance, increased leukaemia risk.
- Turner syndrome is a listed indication for GH.
- GH is given as a daily evening subcutaneous injection until epiphyseal closure.

topics.name: Thyroid Hormone Physiology and Congenital Hypothyroidism

cases.title: A newborn identified by thyroid screening
cases.vignette: A term newborn appears normal at birth. At the routine newborn screening visit, thyroid testing is abnormal. The clinician explains that early diagnosis is essential because thyroid hormone is important for brain maturation and skeletal growth.

questions.stem: Which is an important function of thyroid hormones during early life?

options.label: B
options.text: Maturation of the brain during the first years of life

options.label: C
options.text: Complete inhibition of basal metabolic rate

options.label: D
options.text: Prevention of most pituitary hormone release

questions.correctAnswerText: Maturation of the brain during the first years of life
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is the importance of thyroid hormones in brain maturation during the first years of life, as well as normal skeletal growth and metabolic activity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Thyroid hormones support normal skeletal growth.
- B. Correct. Thyroid hormone is essential for early brain development.
- C. Incorrect. Thyroid hormones increase basal metabolic rate.
- D. Incorrect. They participate in feedback regulation but do not suppress all pituitary hormone release.
- E. Incorrect. Thyroid hormones stimulate gut motility.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Thyroid hormone: brain maturation, skeletal growth, increased BMR, cardiac inotropic/chronotropic effects, gut motility and thermoregulation.
- Untreated congenital hypothyroidism can cause irreversible neurodevelopmental harm.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis?

options.label: B
options.text: Hypothalamic TRH → pituitary TSH → thyroid T4/T3

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypothalamic TRH → pituitary TSH → thyroid T4/T3
questions.initialExplanation: The hypothalamus releases TRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH. TSH stimulates the thyroid gland to produce T4 and T3.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex, not the thyroid.
- B. Correct. This is the sequence shown.
- C. Incorrect. The direction of the axis is reversed.
- D. Incorrect. GH stimulates IGF-1 production, mainly in the liver.
- E. Incorrect. ADH regulates water balance and does not drive the thyroid axis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TRH stimulates TSH.
- TSH stimulates thyroid hormone synthesis and release.
- T3/T4 provide negative feedback to the hypothalamus and pituitary.
- T4 is converted to active T3 in peripheral tissues.

questions.stem: Which enzyme is essential for oxidation and organification of iodide during thyroid hormone synthesis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Thyroid peroxidase
questions.initialExplanation: Thyroid peroxidase catalyses oxidation of iodide and organification of iodine onto tyrosyl residues in thyroglobulin, allowing formation of MIT and DIT and subsequent T3/T4 synthesis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Thyroid peroxidase is central to iodination and coupling reactions in thyroid hormone synthesis.
- B. Incorrect. 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone.
- C. Incorrect. Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens.
- D. Incorrect. 21-hydroxylase is an adrenal steroid synthesis enzyme.
- E. Incorrect. 11-beta hydroxylase is involved in adrenal steroid synthesis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Iodide is oxidized and attached to tyrosine residues in thyroglobulin.
- MIT + DIT forms T3.
- DIT + DIT forms T4.
- Thyroid peroxidase is the key enzyme in the organification/coupling steps.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism?
questions.correctAnswerText: Thyroid dysgenesis
questions.initialExplanation: Thyroid dysgenesis is the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism, accounting for approximately 90% of primary cases. It includes ectopic thyroid, agenesis and hypoplasia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Adrenal insufficiency is a separate endocrine disorder.
- B. Incorrect. TSH excess does not cause the typical congenital hypothyroid pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Hyperparathyroidism affects calcium homeostasis.
- D. Incorrect. Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism.
- E. Correct. Thyroid dysgenesis is the commonest cause described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital hypothyroidism incidence: approximately 1:3,000–4,000 live births.
- Thyroid dysgenesis: most common cause; typically no goitre.
- Dyshormonogenesis is less common and associated with goitre.

questions.stem: A child with congenital hypothyroidism has a goitre and sensorineural hearing loss. Which cause should be suspected?

options.label: A
options.text: Thyroid dyshormonogenesis associated with Pendred syndrome

questions.correctAnswerText: Thyroid dyshormonogenesis associated with Pendred syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include Pendred syndrome as an uncommon inherited disorder associated with goitre, sensorineural hearing loss and an autosomal recessive mutation affecting pendrin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Goitre plus sensorineural hearing loss suggests Pendred syndrome in the context of dyshormonogenesis.
- B. Incorrect. GHD causes reduced linear growth, not this thyroid/hearing combination.
- C. Incorrect. Central DI causes polyuria and polydipsia.
- D. Incorrect. Thyroid dysgenesis usually presents without a goitre.
- E. Incorrect. Graves disease causes autoimmune hyperthyroidism and usually presents with thyrotoxic features.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dyshormonogenesis: approximately 10%, often autosomal recessive and associated with goitre.
- Pendred syndrome: goitre + sensorineural hearing loss.
- Thyroid dysgenesis: ectopic, absent or hypoplastic gland.

questions.stem: Why may a newborn with congenital hypothyroidism appear clinically normal during the first weeks of life?

options.label: B
options.text: TSH crosses the placenta and permanently corrects the defect

options.label: C
options.text: Newborns do not depend on thyroid hormone until puberty

options.label: D
options.text: Maternal transfer of limited thyroid hormone across the placenta can partially protect the newborn before symptoms become apparent

options.label: E
options.text: Thyroid hormone is not required for brain development

questions.correctAnswerText: Maternal transfer of limited thyroid hormone across the placenta can partially protect the newborn before symptoms become apparent
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that most affected infants appear normal at birth and that clinical features become more prominent over weeks to months. Newborn screening is therefore essential.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Most permanent congenital hypothyroidism requires ongoing treatment.
- B. Incorrect. TSH does not cross the placenta.
- C. Incorrect. Thyroid hormone is essential from early life.
- D. Correct. Limited maternal T3/T4 transfer may partially mask early clinical manifestations.
- E. Incorrect. Thyroid hormone is essential for early brain development.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most newborns with congenital hypothyroidism may initially look normal.
- Newborn screening detects cases before symptoms become obvious.
- Delayed diagnosis increases the risk of impaired intellectual development.

questions.stem: Which neonatal presentation is compatible with congenital hypothyroidism?

options.label: E
options.text: Coarse facial features, macroglossia, prolonged jaundice and hypotonia

questions.correctAnswerText: Coarse facial features, macroglossia, prolonged jaundice and hypotonia
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include coarse features, macroglossia, a large anterior fontanelle, hoarse cry, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, umbilical hernia and constipation in congenital hypothyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are clues to primary adrenal insufficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Hypertension with virilization may occur in selected forms of CAH, not congenital hypothyroidism.
- C. Incorrect. These are typical of diabetes insipidus.
- D. Incorrect. These are features of thyrotoxicosis/Graves disease.
- E. Correct. These are characteristic features of congenital hypothyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal congenital hypothyroidism: coarse features, macroglossia, large fontanelle, hoarse cry, jaundice, hypotonia, umbilical hernia and constipation.
- Later: short stature, delayed developmental milestones, delayed teething and bradycardia.
- Clinical diagnosis alone is unreliable in the first month.

questions.stem: A newborn has low free T4 and high TSH. Which level of hypothyroidism is most likely?

options.label: D
options.text: Thyroid hormone resistance with normal TSH

questions.correctAnswerText: Primary hypothyroidism
questions.initialExplanation: In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland fails to produce sufficient hormone, so free T4 is low and pituitary TSH rises in response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism generally produces elevated thyroid hormone with suppressed TSH in primary thyroid hyperfunction.
- B. Correct. Low T4 with high TSH is the typical primary hypothyroid pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Tertiary hypothyroidism is due to hypothalamic dysfunction and also produces low TRH/TSH.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the biochemical pattern described.
- E. Incorrect. Secondary hypothyroidism is due to pituitary dysfunction and has low or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary: low T3/free T4, high TSH.
- Secondary: low T3/free T4, low TSH.
- Tertiary: low TRH leading to low TSH and low thyroid hormone.
- TRH stimulation testing may help distinguish secondary from tertiary disease in selected cases.

questions.stem: A term infant with suspected congenital hypothyroidism has delayed appearance of the distal femoral epiphysis on knee radiograph. What does this finding support?

options.label: A
options.text: Delayed skeletal maturation associated with congenital hypothyroidism

options.label: C
options.text: Advanced bone age due to precocious puberty

questions.correctAnswerText: Delayed skeletal maturation associated with congenital hypothyroidism
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include the absence or delayed appearance of the distal femoral epiphysis on knee radiograph as a supportive finding in congenital hypothyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Delayed epiphyseal appearance reflects delayed skeletal maturation.
- B. Incorrect. Delayed epiphyseal appearance is not the expected normal finding in the described context.
- C. Incorrect. Precocious puberty is associated with advanced bone age.
- D. Incorrect. Vitamin D toxicity is not the explanation for this finding.
- E. Incorrect. Adrenal androgen excess tends to advance skeletal maturation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital hypothyroidism may cause delayed bone maturation.
- Knee radiograph may show absent/delayed distal femoral epiphysis.
- Thyroid ultrasound/scan can help identify ectopic, absent or abnormal thyroid tissue, but treatment should not be delayed while waiting for imaging.

questions.stem: What is the most important principle in treating confirmed congenital hypothyroidism?

options.label: A
options.text: Use growth hormone as the treatment

options.label: B
options.text: Stop follow-up once the infant gains weight

options.label: C
options.text: Start levothyroxine early to reduce the risk of impaired neurodevelopment

options.label: E
options.text: Delay treatment until developmental delay appears

questions.correctAnswerText: Start levothyroxine early to reduce the risk of impaired neurodevelopment
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include levothyroxine as the treatment of choice and emphasizes that starting soon after birth, ideally within the first two weeks, reduces the risk of impaired intellectual development.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GH does not correct thyroid hormone deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Long-term clinical, growth, developmental and TFT follow-up is required.
- C. Correct. Early thyroid hormone replacement is essential.
- D. Incorrect. Antithyroid drugs are used for hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.
- E. Incorrect. Waiting for symptoms risks preventable neurodevelopmental harm.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Levothyroxine is the drug of choice.
- Early diagnosis and treatment are critical.
- Follow growth, development, symptoms and thyroid function tests in endocrine clinic.
- Exact dose should be based on age, weight, TFTs and the current paediatric endocrine protocol.

cases.title: Four children seen in thyroid clinic

questions.stem: A term infant with trisomy 21 is seen at 3 weeks of age because of persistent jaundice, constipation, poor feeding, a hoarse cry and a large anterior fontanelle. The family attributes everything to Down syndrome, and the newborn screening result cannot be found. What is the best next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure, as these features are expected in Down syndrome

options.label: B
options.text: Serum TSH and free T4 now

options.label: E
options.text: Left wrist radiograph for bone age

questions.correctAnswerText: Serum TSH and free T4 now
questions.initialExplanation: Congenital hypothyroidism is more common in Down syndrome, and most affected infants look normal early on. Jaundice, constipation, hoarse cry and a large fontanelle are classic features. Because the screening result is missing, thyroid function must be measured immediately.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Reasoning. The listed features of congenital hypothyroidism are prolonged physiological jaundice, constipation, hoarse cry, large fontanelle, hypotonia and umbilical hernia. Clinical guidance the higher incidence in Down syndrome. Treatment started within the first 2 weeks protects intellectual development, and this infant is already 3 weeks old, so delay is harmful.
- A. Incorrect. Attributing symptoms to Down syndrome risks missing a treatable cause of intellectual impairment.
- B. Correct. TSH and free T4 diagnose primary congenital hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4).
- C. Incorrect. The chromosomal diagnosis is already known.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital heart disease may coexist, but it does not explain these features or replace thyroid testing.
- E. Incorrect. Bone age by hand–wrist film is not the investigation used in neonates. The knee radiograph is used, and imaging should not delay biochemistry.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital hypothyroidism: about 1 in 3,000–4,000 births, more common in Down syndrome.
- It is the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability.
- Clinical diagnosis is unreliable in the first month, so screening is essential.
- Early treatment (first 2 weeks) reduces impaired intellectual development.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Congenital hypothyroidism: epidemiology (Page 10), clinical features (Pages 10–11), treatment (Page 12).

questions.stem: A 5-week-old infant has primary congenital hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4). The thyroid is diffusely enlarged and a technetium scan shows increased uptake. Maternal thyroid function is normal, and the mother took no antithyroid drugs. The parents ask about the risk for a future child. Which diagnosis and counselling are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Thyroid agenesis; the condition is sporadic and the gland takes up no tracer

options.label: B
options.text: Ectopic thyroid; the scan would show a single localised area of uptake and no goitre

options.label: C
options.text: Transient hypothyroidism from maternal TSH-blocking antibodies; it resolves by 6–12 months

options.label: D
options.text: Thyroid dyshormonogenesis, an autosomal recessive disorder; each future pregnancy carries a 1 in 4 risk

options.label: E
options.text: Secondary hypothyroidism from pituitary disease; TSH would be low

questions.correctAnswerText: Thyroid dyshormonogenesis, an autosomal recessive disorder; each future pregnancy carries a 1 in 4 risk
questions.initialExplanation: Dyshormonogenesis (the second most common cause, about 10%) is associated with a goitre and increased uptake, and is autosomal recessive. Dysgenesis (about 90%) gives no goitre and absent or ectopic tissue.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Key clues. Goitre plus increased uptake means the gland is present and trying to work, but hormone synthesis is defective. Normal maternal thyroid status and no drug exposure exclude transient maternal causes.
- A. Incorrect. Agenesis shows decreased/absent uptake and no goitre.
- B. Incorrect. Ectopic tissue localises uptake at an abnormal site, and dysgenesis presents without goitre.
- C. Incorrect. Transient disease requires maternal antibodies or antithyroid drugs, both absent here.
- D. Correct. Autosomal recessive inheritance means 25% recurrence risk for each pregnancy of carrier parents.
- E. Incorrect. Secondary hypothyroidism has low TSH, whereas this infant has high TSH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dysgenesis (about 90%): ectopic, agenesis or hypoplasia; no goitre; scan shows localised uptake (ectopic) or decreased uptake (aplasia).
- Dyshormonogenesis (about 10%): autosomal recessive, goitre, increased uptake. Pendred syndrome adds sensorineural hearing loss.
- TFT pattern: primary = low T4, high TSH; secondary and tertiary = low T4, low TSH.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Congenital hypothyroidism: causes (Pages 9–10), investigations: TFT and thyroid scan (Pages 11–12).

cases.title: An adolescent with slowing growth and a painless goitre
cases.vignette: A 12-year-old girl is brought because of fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, dry skin and weight gain. Her height velocity has slowed. Examination reveals a firm, smooth, non-tender goitre. The family history includes autoimmune thyroid disease.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism in children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hashimoto thyroiditis
questions.initialExplanation: Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune thyroiditis) is identified as the most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism in children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism.
- B. Incorrect. Graves disease is the commonest cause of childhood hyperthyroidism.
- C. Incorrect. Thyroid carcinoma is not the commonest cause.
- D. Incorrect. Pituitary disease causes central hypothyroidism and is uncommon compared with primary autoimmune disease.
- E. Incorrect. Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumour and unrelated to the usual cause of hypothyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acquired hypothyroidism is more common than hyperthyroidism in children,.
- Approximately 99% of acquired cases are primary.
- Hashimoto thyroiditis is the leading cause.

questions.stem: Which antibody profile is most associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies
questions.initialExplanation: Hashimoto thyroiditis is associated with anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies. Clinical guidance notes that a minority of patients may be antibody-negative.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis.
- B. Incorrect. Anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies may be found in autoimmune adrenal insufficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Anti-dsDNA antibodies are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.
- D. Incorrect. TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies are characteristic of Graves disease.
- E. Incorrect. Anti-insulin receptor antibodies are not the standard Hashimoto markers.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hashimoto: anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.
- Associated conditions include type 1 diabetes, Addison disease, vitiligo, alopecia, coeliac disease, Down syndrome and Turner syndrome.
- A negative antibody result does not completely exclude Hashimoto thyroiditis.

questions.stem: Which clinical feature is particularly characteristic of acquired hypothyroidism in a school-aged child?

options.label: A
options.text: Accelerated height velocity with advanced bone age

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced growth velocity with short stature

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced growth velocity with short stature
questions.initialExplanation: Acquired hypothyroidism often presents insidiously with reduced growth velocity and short stature, along with weight gain, constipation, dry skin and cold intolerance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Accelerated growth and advanced bone age suggest excess thyroid hormone or androgen effect.
- B. Correct. Reduced linear growth is an important sign of acquired hypothyroidism in children.
- C. Incorrect. Exophthalmos and lid retraction may occur in Graves disease.
- D. Incorrect. Tachycardia and tremor are typical thyrotoxic features.
- E. Incorrect. Salt-wasting dehydration suggests adrenal insufficiency or salt-wasting CAH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acquired hypothyroidism: fatigue, constipation, dry skin, cold intolerance, weight gain, bradycardia and reduced growth velocity.
- A goitre may be present, particularly in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
- Delayed puberty may occur; rare paradoxical presentations are also mentioned.

questions.stem: A child has low free T4 and markedly elevated TSH. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.correctAnswerText: Primary acquired hypothyroidism
questions.initialExplanation: A low free T4 with high TSH indicates primary thyroid gland failure, as in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Graves disease causes elevated thyroid hormone and usually suppressed TSH.
- B. Correct. Primary thyroid failure produces low thyroid hormone with compensatory elevation of TSH.
- C. Incorrect. Tertiary hypothyroidism is due to hypothalamic dysfunction and low TRH/TSH.
- D. Incorrect. Central DI is an ADH disorder causing polyuria and polydipsia.
- E. Incorrect. Secondary hypothyroidism is due to pituitary dysfunction and typically has low or inappropriately normal TSH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary hypothyroidism: low free T4, high TSH.
- Thyroid ultrasound and isotope scan may help characterize the gland but are not always required for diagnosis.
- Levothyroxine replacement and endocrine follow-up are important.

cases.title: Four children seen in thyroid clinic

questions.stem: An 11-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes has a smooth, firm, non-tender goitre found at a routine visit. He is asymptomatic and growing normally. Free T4 and TSH are normal, and anti-TPO antibodies are strongly positive. What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Start levothyroxine immediately for lifelong replacement

options.label: B
options.text: Diagnose autoimmune thyroiditis, avoid treatment for now and monitor clinically and with periodic thyroid function tests

options.label: C
options.text: Start carbimazole to shrink the goitre

questions.correctAnswerText: Diagnose autoimmune thyroiditis, avoid treatment for now and monitor clinically and with periodic thyroid function tests
questions.initialExplanation: This is Hashimoto thyroiditis in a euthyroid state. Clinical guidance that thyroid function tests may be normal early on, and that levothyroxine is given when thyroid hormone is low. Follow-up in the endocrine clinic is essential.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Diagnosis. A smooth, firm, non-tender goitre with positive anti-TPO in a child with another autoimmune disease (type 1 diabetes) is autoimmune thyroiditis. Normal free T4 and TSH show a euthyroid state.
- A. Incorrect. clinical guidance links levothyroxine to low T3/T4. This boy has normal thyroid hormones.
- B. Correct. Monitor growth, symptoms and TFT; treat when hypothyroidism develops.
- C. Incorrect. Antithyroid drugs treat hyperthyroidism (Graves disease), not this condition.
- D. Incorrect. Surgery is not needed for an asymptomatic autoimmune goitre.
- E. Incorrect. Radioiodine is a second-line option for Graves disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hashimoto thyroiditis: the most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism and of sporadic goitre in childhood and adolescence.
- Antibodies (anti-TPO, anti-Tg) are positive in about 85%, so 10–15% are antibody-negative.
- Associations include type 1 diabetes, Addison disease, vitiligo, alopecia, coeliac disease, Down and Turner syndromes.
- Prognosis is very good and depends partly on whether other autoimmune disease develops.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Acquired hypothyroidism and Hashimoto thyroiditis (Pages 13–14).
source.sheet: Endocrine sheet — Acquired hypothyroidism and Hashimoto thyroiditis (

cases.title: A teenage girl with weight loss, tremor and a vascular goitre
cases.vignette: A 14-year-old girl presents with anxiety, restlessness, sweating, diarrhoea, weight loss and palpitations. Examination reveals tachycardia, a fine tremor, warm peripheries and a diffuse goitre with a bruit. There is lid retraction and lid lag.

questions.stem: What is the most likely cause of childhood hyperthyroidism in this patient?
questions.correctAnswerText: Graves disease
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that approximately 95% of childhood hyperthyroidism is due to Graves disease, an autoimmune condition caused by stimulating antibodies to the TSH receptor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Thyroid dysgenesis is a common cause of congenital hypothyroidism.
- B. Incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism is a deficiency state, not hyperthyroidism.
- C. Incorrect. Panhypopituitarism causes pituitary hormone deficiency.
- D. Incorrect. Hashimoto thyroiditis is the commonest cause of acquired hypothyroidism.
- E. Correct. Graves disease is the commonest cause of childhood hyperthyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Graves disease accounts for most childhood hyperthyroidism.
- It is caused by stimulatory antibodies to TSH receptors.
- It is more common in teenage girls.

questions.stem: Which combination of clinical findings best supports Graves disease?

options.label: B
options.text: Tremor, tachycardia, sweating, weight loss and diffuse goitre

options.label: C
options.text: Bradycardia, cold intolerance and dry skin

options.label: E
options.text: Short stature with delayed bone age and hypoglycaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Tremor, tachycardia, sweating, weight loss and diffuse goitre
questions.initialExplanation: Graves disease produces multisystem thyrotoxicosis. Common examples include anxiety, sweating, diarrhoea, weight loss, tachycardia, tremor, warm vasodilated peripheries and goitre with bruit.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are features of diabetes insipidus.
- B. Correct. This is the typical clinical pattern of thyrotoxicosis.
- C. Incorrect. These are features of hypothyroidism.
- D. Incorrect. These suggest primary adrenal insufficiency.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests pituitary hormone deficiency or another growth disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Graves is multisystemic and autoimmune.
- Eye signs include exophthalmos, ophthalmoplegia, lid retraction and lid lag; these are less common in children than adults.
- Goitre may have a bruit due to increased vascularity.

questions.stem: Which thyroid function test pattern is expected in primary hyperthyroidism due to Graves disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Low free T4 with low TSH

options.label: B
options.text: High TSH with low T3 and low T4

options.label: C
options.text: High free T4 with low TSH

options.label: D
options.text: Normal free T4 with persistently high TSH

options.label: E
options.text: Low free T4 with high TSH

questions.correctAnswerText: High free T4 with low TSH
questions.initialExplanation: Excess thyroid hormone from Graves disease suppresses pituitary TSH through negative feedback, resulting in high free T4 and low TSH.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This pattern suggests central hypothyroidism.
- B. Incorrect. This is a hypothyroid pattern.
- C. Correct. This is the usual biochemical pattern of primary hyperthyroidism.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the expected pattern of untreated Graves disease.
- E. Incorrect. This is the pattern of primary hypothyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Graves: high free T4/T3, suppressed TSH.
- TSH-receptor antibodies support the diagnosis.
- Thyroid ultrasound and radionuclide uptake imaging may support assessment when indicated.

questions.stem: A child with Graves disease is started on carbimazole. Which important adverse effect should the family be taught to recognize urgently?

options.label: C
options.text: Severe hypocalcaemia with carpopedal spasm in each patient

options.label: D
options.text: Neutropenia/agranulocytosis, suggested by sore throat and high fever

questions.correctAnswerText: Neutropenia/agranulocytosis, suggested by sore throat and high fever
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance warns that antithyroid medication can cause neutropenia. Families should seek urgent medical assessment and a blood count if sore throat and high fever occur during treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hearing loss is not the adverse effect described.
- B. Incorrect. Retinal detachment is not the adverse effect described.
- C. Incorrect. Hypocalcaemia is not the characteristic adverse effect highlighted for carbimazole.
- D. Correct. Fever and sore throat may indicate a serious reduction in neutrophils.
- E. Incorrect. DI is unrelated to this drug warning.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Carbimazole is a first-line antithyroid medication.
- Warn families about sore throat and fever and the need for urgent assessment.
- Propranolol may be used initially for symptomatic relief of tachycardia, tremor and anxiety.
- Radioiodine in older children or surgery may be considered as second-line options under specialist care.

questions.stem: A neonate born to a mother with Graves disease develops tachycardia, irritability and poor weight gain. What is the likely mechanism?

options.label: B
options.text: Transplacental passage of maternal TSH, which permanently stimulates the infant's thyroid

options.label: C
options.text: Congenital absence of the pituitary gland

options.label: D
options.text: Maternal anti-TPO antibodies causing permanent thyroid agenesis

options.label: E
options.text: Transplacental passage of maternal TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies

questions.correctAnswerText: Transplacental passage of maternal TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include transient neonatal thyrotoxicosis caused by transplacental passage of maternal TSH-receptor antibodies. It may be serious and requires neonatal treatment, but often resolves as maternal antibodies disappear.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Renal ADH resistance causes nephrogenic DI.
- B. Incorrect. Clinical guidance notes that TSH does not cross the placenta.
- C. Incorrect. Pituitary aplasia causes pituitary hormone deficiency, not transient neonatal Graves.
- D. Incorrect. Anti-TPO antibodies do not cause the described neonatal Graves mechanism.
- E. Correct. Maternal stimulating TSH-receptor antibodies cross the placenta and activate the neonatal thyroid.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal Graves: maternal TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies cross the placenta.
- Transient but potentially life-threatening.
- Maternal antibodies gradually regress; the neonate still requires active clinical assessment and treatment when affected.

cases.title: Four children seen in thyroid clinic

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with Graves disease has completed two separate 2-year courses of carbimazole. Both times she relapsed within months of stopping. She again has palpitations, tremor and weight loss, with high free T4, suppressed TSH and positive TSH-receptor antibodies. Her exophthalmos has not resolved. What is the most appropriate plan?

options.label: A
options.text: A third 2-year course of carbimazole alone, since relapse rates fall with each course

options.label: B
options.text: Propranolol alone, as relapse means the drug has failed

options.label: D
options.text: Stop most treatment and observe, as eye signs persist regardless of treatment

options.label: E
options.text: Definitive therapy with radioiodine or subtotal thyroidectomy, with lifelong follow-up for hypothyroidism

questions.correctAnswerText: Definitive therapy with radioiodine or subtotal thyroidectomy, with lifelong follow-up for hypothyroidism
questions.initialExplanation: Medical treatment (carbimazole or propylthiouracil) is first line and given for about 2 years. Relapse is common. Radioiodine (older child) or subtotal thyroidectomy is second-line definitive therapy. Both usually lead to hypothyroidism, so long-term follow-up and levothyroxine are needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Reasoning. Two failed courses with a positive TSH-receptor antibody indicate persistent disease. At age 16 she is an older child, so radioiodine is suitable.
- A. Incorrect. Repeating the same drug course has already failed twice. Clinical guidance definitive therapy as the second-line step.
- B. Incorrect. Propranolol only relieves symptoms (anxiety, tremor, tachycardia). It does not control hormone excess.
- C. Incorrect. Levothyroxine would add thyroid hormone to a thyrotoxic patient.
- D. Incorrect. Eye signs may persist after control of thyroid hormone excess, but that does not justify leaving thyrotoxicosis untreated.
- E. Correct. This is the second-line pathway, with follow-up for the hypothyroidism that commonly follows.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Graves disease: stimulatory antibodies to the TSH receptor, positive in about 95%.
- Antithyroid drugs carry a risk of neutropenia: urgent blood count if sore throat and high fever.
- Eye signs may not resolve with medical treatment.
- After first- or second-line therapy, thyroxine replacement may be needed, so follow-up is always required.

cases.title: A child with central weight gain and growth failure
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child has gained weight rapidly, especially around the trunk and face, but height velocity has slowed. Examination reveals a rounded face, a dorsocervical fat pad, abdominal striae, acne and easy bruising. The family reports prolonged systemic and inhaled corticosteroid use.

questions.stem: Which hormone is produced mainly by the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cortisol
questions.initialExplanation: The zona fasciculata produces glucocorticoids, especially cortisol. The zona glomerulosa produces mineralocorticoids, and the zona reticularis produces adrenal androgens.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. PTH is produced by the parathyroid glands.
- B. Correct. Cortisol is the main glucocorticoid from the zona fasciculata.
- C. Incorrect. Aldosterone is produced by the zona glomerulosa.
- D. Incorrect. Insulin is produced by pancreatic beta cells.
- E. Incorrect. Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal medulla.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Zona glomerulosa → mineralocorticoids.
- Zona fasciculata → glucocorticoids.
- Zona reticularis → androgens.
- Glucocorticoids and adrenal androgens are controlled by ACTH; aldosterone is mainly regulated by the renin–angiotensin system and potassium.

questions.stem: Which cause of Cushing syndrome is most common in children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Exogenous corticosteroid exposure
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that exogenous corticosteroid administration is the most common cause of Cushing syndrome in children, often iatrogenic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid exposure is the commonest cause described.
- B. Incorrect. Adrenal carcinoma is a rare endogenous cause.
- C. Incorrect. Adrenal hyperplasia is an endogenous cause but is not the most common overall.
- D. Incorrect. Pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma causes Cushing disease but is less common than exogenous steroid exposure.
- E. Incorrect. Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumours are rare in children.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cushing syndrome: prolonged exposure to excessive glucocorticoids.
- Exogenous steroids are the most common cause.
- Endogenous causes may be ACTH-independent (adrenal) or ACTH-dependent (pituitary/ectopic).

questions.stem: Which clinical combination should make Cushing syndrome particularly likely in a child?

options.label: B
options.text: Delayed growth with macroglossia and prolonged jaundice

options.label: C
options.text: Central/truncal obesity with growth failure and reduced growth velocity

options.label: D
options.text: Weight loss, hyperpigmentation and postural hypotension

options.label: E
options.text: Weight gain with increased height velocity

questions.correctAnswerText: Central/truncal obesity with growth failure and reduced growth velocity
questions.initialExplanation: The combination of weight gain and impaired linear growth is a key clue to Cushing syndrome in children. Other features include moon face, buffalo hump, striae, acne, hirsutism, easy bruising and hypertension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests diabetes insipidus or diabetes mellitus.
- B. Incorrect. These features suggest congenital hypothyroidism.
- C. Correct. Weight gain with growth failure is a characteristic paediatric presentation.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests primary adrenal insufficiency.
- E. Incorrect. Increased height velocity is not the typical growth pattern in childhood Cushing syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Childhood Cushing: weight gain/central obesity plus reduced height velocity.
- Moon face, buffalo hump, striae, acne, hirsutism, bruising and hypertension may occur.
- Consider exogenous steroid exposure carefully.

questions.stem: Which test combination is used to investigate suspected Cushing syndrome?

options.label: C
options.text: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, loss of diurnal cortisol variation and dexamethasone suppression testing

options.label: E
options.text: Water deprivation test and urine osmolality

questions.correctAnswerText: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, loss of diurnal cortisol variation and dexamethasone suppression testing
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol, loss of normal diurnal variation and failure to suppress cortisol after dexamethasone as diagnostic investigations. ACTH helps classify the cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GH stimulation and IGF-1 assess the GH axis.
- B. Incorrect. TSH and anti-TPO assess thyroid disease.
- C. Correct. These are the main cortisol-based investigations described.
- D. Incorrect. Calcium and PTH assess parathyroid disorders.
- E. Incorrect. Water deprivation testing is used for suspected DI.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Screen for hypercortisolism with appropriate cortisol tests.
- Loss of normal diurnal variation is important.
- ACTH helps distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent causes.
- Imaging is guided by biochemical classification and specialist evaluation.

questions.stem: A child has Cushing syndrome caused by long-term prescribed glucocorticoids. What is the appropriate general management principle?

options.label: A
options.text: Taper glucocorticoids gradually under supervision and use steroid-sparing treatment when possible

options.label: D
options.text: Start high-dose insulin as definitive treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Taper glucocorticoids gradually under supervision and use steroid-sparing treatment when possible
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include gradual withdrawal of exogenous steroids as the treatment for exogenous Cushing syndrome. Abrupt discontinuation can precipitate adrenal insufficiency because the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis may be suppressed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A supervised gradual taper is the general principle.
- B. Incorrect. Adrenalectomy is not appropriate for exogenous Cushing syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Thyroid hormone does not treat Cushing syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. Insulin does not treat glucocorticoid excess.
- E. Incorrect. Abrupt cessation can cause adrenal crisis in a patient with suppressed adrenal function.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Exogenous glucocorticoids are the commonest cause.
- Reduce/taper steroids safely; do not abruptly discontinue long-term therapy.
- Endogenous disease management depends on its source and may require surgery and/or other specialist treatment.

topics.name: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency and Adrenal Crisis

cases.title: A child with vomiting, hyperpigmentation and circulatory collapse
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child has months of fatigue, weakness, weight loss, nausea and dizziness. The parents have noticed darkening of the palmar creases and oral mucosa. During an intercurrent gastroenteritis, the child develops severe dehydration, hypotension and hypoglycaemia.

questions.stem: Which biochemical pattern is most consistent with primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)?

options.label: E
options.text: Low sodium, low potassium and high cortisol

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency causes cortisol and often aldosterone deficiency, leading to hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypotension and possible hypoglycaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is a hyperthyroid biochemical pattern.
- B. Incorrect. This is the opposite of the expected pattern.
- C. Incorrect. This suggests a calcium/PTH disorder.
- D. Correct. This is the characteristic electrolyte/glucose pattern described.
- E. Incorrect. Primary adrenal insufficiency is associated with low cortisol and commonly high potassium.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary adrenal insufficiency: low cortisol, high ACTH, low aldosterone.
- Electrolytes: low sodium, high potassium.
- Hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis may occur.
- Secondary adrenal insufficiency may lack hyperpigmentation and hyperkalaemia because aldosterone is relatively preserved.

questions.stem: Why does a child with Addison disease develop hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and oral mucosa?

options.label: D
options.text: Increased ACTH and related melanocortin activity

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased ACTH and related melanocortin activity
questions.initialExplanation: In primary adrenal insufficiency, cortisol deficiency removes negative feedback, increasing ACTH. ACTH-related melanocortin activity stimulates pigmentation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ADH regulates water balance and is not the cause of pigmentation.
- B. Incorrect. Aldosterone is reduced in primary adrenal insufficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Insulin does not cause the characteristic hyperpigmentation.
- D. Correct. Increased ACTH is responsible for the characteristic pigmentation.
- E. Incorrect. TSH receptor stimulation is associated with Graves disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hyperpigmentation is a clue to primary, not typical secondary, adrenal insufficiency.
- Look at palmar creases, scars and oral mucosa.
- Primary adrenal insufficiency is often autoimmune and may coexist with other autoimmune diseases.

questions.stem: Which test is described as a confirmatory test for adrenal insufficiency?
questions.correctAnswerText: ACTH stimulation (Synacthen) test
questions.initialExplanation: The Synacthen test evaluates the adrenal cortisol response to exogenous ACTH. Failure of cortisol to rise appropriately supports adrenal insufficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. OGTT is used in selected diabetes diagnostic settings.
- B. Incorrect. Dexamethasone suppression tests for hypercortisolism/Cushing syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Water deprivation testing is used for DI.
- D. Incorrect. GH stimulation assesses GH reserve.
- E. Correct. It directly assesses adrenal responsiveness to ACTH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary adrenal insufficiency: low cortisol, high ACTH.
- ACTH stimulation test: inadequate cortisol response supports adrenal failure.
- In a suspected adrenal crisis, do not delay emergency treatment while waiting for confirmatory testing.

questions.stem: A child with known adrenal insufficiency develops vomiting, diarrhoea, severe dehydration, hypotension and hypoglycaemia during gastroenteritis. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Adrenal crisis
questions.initialExplanation: Intercurrent illness can precipitate adrenal crisis in a child with adrenal insufficiency. An important point is vomiting/diarrhoea, vascular collapse and shock as key features.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. DI causes water loss and hypernatraemia but does not explain known adrenal failure with hypoglycaemia and the typical electrolyte pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Graves disease causes thyrotoxicosis, not adrenal crisis.
- C. Correct. Shock and hypoglycaemia during illness in a child with adrenal insufficiency indicate adrenal crisis.
- D. Incorrect. Functional abdominal pain does not cause shock.
- E. Incorrect. Reflux does not cause this combination of shock and hypoglycaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Adrenal crisis is an emergency.
- Triggers include infection, gastroenteritis, trauma, surgery or failure to increase stress-dose steroid replacement.
- Look for hypotension/shock, dehydration, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia.

questions.stem: What is the immediate management priority in a child with suspected adrenal crisis?

options.label: B
options.text: Wait for the Synacthen test before treatment

options.label: D
options.text: ABC stabilization, isotonic IV fluid, correction of hypoglycaemia and urgent IV hydrocortisone

options.label: E
options.text: Restrict fluids and give oral levothyroxine

questions.correctAnswerText: ABC stabilization, isotonic IV fluid, correction of hypoglycaemia and urgent IV hydrocortisone
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include ABC management, isotonic saline bolus, glucose when hypoglycaemic and IV hydrocortisone. Treatment must not be delayed for diagnostic confirmation in a critically ill child.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antithyroid drugs do not treat adrenal insufficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Delaying treatment in adrenal crisis is dangerous.
- C. Incorrect. Water deprivation testing is not part of emergency management.
- D. Correct. Immediate resuscitation and steroid replacement are essential.
- E. Incorrect. Fluid restriction is inappropriate in shock and levothyroxine does not treat adrenal crisis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Adrenal crisis: ABC, IV isotonic fluids, glucose if needed and parenteral hydrocortisone.
- Monitor blood pressure, glucose, electrolytes, acid–base status and response to treatment.
- Specific fluid/steroid doses should follow the current paediatric emergency protocol.

cases.title: Obesity, atypical genitalia and a collapsing infant

questions.stem: A 17-day-old boy is brought with poor feeding, vomiting, weight loss and lethargy. The heart rate is 190/min, peripheries are cool and blood pressure is low. His genitalia look normal. Sodium is 119 mmol/L, potassium 7.4 mmol/L, glucose 28 mg/dL, and blood gas shows pH 7.10 with bicarbonate 8 mmol/L. An older brother died at 3 weeks of age from "gastroenteritis". Which initial management is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Oral rehydration solution and fludrocortisone, with hydrocortisone after the 17-OHP result

options.label: B
options.text: Fluid restriction and treatment of hyperkalaemia, awaiting karyotype

options.label: C
options.text: Slow hypotonic fluids over 48 hours, as for diabetic ketoacidosis

options.label: D
options.text: ABC, 0.9% saline bolus of 20 mL/kg, 10% dextrose 2–5 mL/kg for hypoglycaemia and IV hydrocortisone, taking a 17-OHP sample without delaying treatment

options.label: E
options.text: Surgical consultation for pyloric stenosis, with correction of alkalosis

questions.correctAnswerText: ABC, 0.9% saline bolus of 20 mL/kg, 10% dextrose 2–5 mL/kg for hypoglycaemia and IV hydrocortisone, taking a 17-OHP sample without delaying treatment
questions.initialExplanation: This is a salt-wasting adrenal crisis from CAH. A 46,XY infant can look normal at birth and present at 1–3 weeks. Treatment is the "3 S": Saline, Sugar, Steroid, after ABC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Reasoning. Shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis at 2–3 weeks, plus a family history of sudden neonatal death, define salt-wasting CAH. Normal-looking genitalia in a male do not exclude it.
- A. Incorrect. Oral treatment is inadequate in shock. Steroids must not wait for confirmatory tests.
- B. Incorrect. Fluid restriction is dangerous in shock, and karyotype does not guide emergency management.
- C. Incorrect. Slow hypotonic fluid correction is an approach for DKA, not for shock with hyponatraemia.
- D. Correct. This follows clinical guidance's adrenal crisis protocol.
- E. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis gives hypochloraemic alkalosis, not hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and acidosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Salt-wasting CAH: the most lethal form of 21-hydroxylase deficiency, adrenal crisis at 2–6 weeks.
- Males may appear normal at birth.
- Adrenal crisis treatment: ABC, saline bolus (20 mL/kg), D10% 2–5 mL/kg, IV hydrocortisone (dose per local protocol).
- Diagnosis: very high 17-OHP, low Na, high K, low glucose, metabolic acidosis.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Adrenal crisis (Page 21); CAH clinical picture (Pages 23–24), diagnosis and management (Page 25).

topics.name: Disorders of Sex Development and Ambiguous Genitalia

cases.title: A newborn with atypical external genitalia
cases.vignette: A term newborn has external genitalia that do not have a typical male or female appearance. There is clitoromegaly and partial labioscrotal fusion. The parents ask the clinician to assign sex immediately. The team recognizes that the situation requires a careful diagnostic and psychosocial approach.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an indication to investigate a newborn for a disorder of sex development?

options.label: B
options.text: Normal testicular descent and normal phallus

options.label: D
options.text: Clitoromegaly with inguinal hernia or markedly atypical genital appearance

options.label: E
options.text: Typical female external genitalia with no other abnormality

questions.correctAnswerText: Clitoromegaly with inguinal hernia or markedly atypical genital appearance
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include clitoromegaly, micropenis, cryptorchidism with severe hypospadias, asymmetry of labioscrotal folds, bifid scrotum and overtly atypical genitalia as reasons to suspect DSD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. An isolated umbilical hernia is not a DSD criterion.
- B. Incorrect. These are reassuring typical findings.
- C. Incorrect. Physiological jaundice alone is not a DSD sign.
- D. Correct. Clitoromegaly and inguinal findings are among the warning signs listed.
- E. Incorrect. Typical normal genital appearance without other concerning features does not by itself indicate DSD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DSD is a medical and psychosocial emergency requiring coordinated care.
- Do not guess or prematurely assign sex based only on external genital appearance.
- Consider CAH, androgen insensitivity, 5-alpha reductase deficiency and antenatal drug exposure.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of a DSD presentation with virilization of a 46,XX newborn?
questions.correctAnswerText: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include congenital adrenal hyperplasia, particularly excess androgen production in a 46,XX infant, as the commonest cause of female virilization among the DSD causes listed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. CAH can cause androgen excess and virilization of a 46,XX infant.
- B. Incorrect. Turner syndrome is 45,X and is associated with gonadal dysgenesis, not 46,XX virilization.
- C. Incorrect. 5-alpha reductase deficiency affects conversion of testosterone to DHT in 46,XY individuals.
- D. Incorrect. Androgen insensitivity occurs in a 46,XY individual with inadequate androgen action.
- E. Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome is typically 47,XXY.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 46,XX virilization: consider CAH first.
- 46,XY undervirilization: consider androgen insensitivity, 5-alpha reductase deficiency and gonadal developmental disorders.
- Rapidly evaluate for salt-wasting CAH because adrenal crisis may be life-threatening.

questions.stem: Which initial approach is appropriate when a newborn is found to have ambiguous genitalia?

options.label: B
options.text: Assign sex immediately based on the external appearance

options.label: D
options.text: History and genital exam, pelvic/gonadal ultrasound, karyotype and multidisciplinary assessment

questions.correctAnswerText: History and genital exam, pelvic/gonadal ultrasound, karyotype and multidisciplinary assessment
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include a careful history and examination, ultrasound of internal structures and gonads, karyotyping, investigations such as 17-hydroxyprogesterone and multidisciplinary management with psychological support.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Early assessment is essential, especially to identify CAH and prevent adrenal crisis.
- B. Incorrect. standard guidance explicitly advises against guessing the infant's sex immediately.
- C. Incorrect. Hormone treatment depends on the diagnosis and is not given empirically to every newborn.
- D. Correct. This summarizes the recommended structured evaluation.
- E. Incorrect. Irreversible procedures should not precede appropriate diagnostic assessment and counselling.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- History: antenatal history, family history (including neonatal deaths/CAH), maternal medication exposure.
- Examination: external genitalia, labioscrotal folds, gonads, phallus/clitoris and associated anomalies.
- Investigations: pelvic/abdominal ultrasound, karyotype, 17-OHP and targeted endocrine/metabolic studies.
- Multidisciplinary team and psychological support are essential.

cases.title: Obesity, atypical genitalia and a collapsing infant

questions.stem: A newborn has perineal hypospadias, a bifid scrotum and a small phallus. Gonads are palpable in the inguinal canals. Karyotype is 46,XY. Sodium, potassium and glucose are normal, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone is normal. Basal testosterone is normal for age, but dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is very low. Which mechanism best explains the findings?

options.label: A
options.text: Impaired conversion of testosterone to DHT (5α-reductase deficiency)

options.label: C
options.text: Androgen receptor unresponsiveness, with normal or high DHT

options.label: D
options.text: Absence of the SRY gene, with ovarian development

options.label: E
options.text: Antenatal exposure to maternal androgenic drugs

questions.correctAnswerText: Impaired conversion of testosterone to DHT (5α-reductase deficiency)
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance explains that SRY drives testis formation, and that testosterone and its metabolite DHT virilise male external genitalia. If testosterone is normal but DHT is low, external virilisation fails while testes are present. This is the 5α-reductase deficiency listed among causes of ambiguous genitalia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Stepwise reasoning. 46,XY with palpable gonads means SRY and testis development occurred. Normal 17-OHP and electrolytes exclude CAH. Normal testosterone with low DHT localises the defect to the conversion step.
- A. Correct. DHT is needed for virilisation of the external genitalia, so low DHT gives undervirilisation despite normal testosterone.
- B. Incorrect. 21-hydroxylase deficiency virilises a 46,XX fetus and raises 17-OHP, which is normal here.
- C. Incorrect. In androgen insensitivity, hormone levels (including DHT) are not low. The problem is inadequate androgen action at the receptor.
- D. Incorrect. Without SRY the gonads become ovaries, but this infant has palpable testes.
- E. Incorrect. Antenatal drugs are a listed cause of virilisation of female fetuses, and do not explain low DHT with normal testosterone in a 46,XY infant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SRY on the Y chromosome → testis; absent SRY → ovary and female genitalia.
- Testosterone and DHT virilise male genitalia.
- Causes of ambiguous genitalia: CAH (46,XX virilisation), androgen insensitivity (46,XY), 5α-reductase deficiency, antenatal drugs.
- Approach: do not guess the sex, history and examination, abdominal ultrasound, karyotype, 17-OHP, multidisciplinary team and psychological support.

cases.title: A 2-week-old infant with vomiting, dehydration and ambiguous genitalia
cases.vignette: A 2-week-old infant is brought with poor feeding, recurrent vomiting, weight loss and dehydration. Blood pressure is low. Laboratory results show hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis. The external genitalia are virilized.

questions.stem: What is the inheritance pattern of congenital adrenal hyperplasia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Autosomal recessive
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include CAH as an autosomal recessive disorder involving an enzyme defect in adrenal steroid biosynthesis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. standard guidance specifies autosomal recessive inheritance.
- B. Incorrect. It is not mitochondrial.
- C. Correct. CAH is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
- D. Incorrect. It is not Y-linked.
- E. Incorrect. It is not an X-linked dominant disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CAH: inherited defect in adrenal steroid biosynthesis.
- Cortisol synthesis is impaired; aldosterone may also be impaired depending on the enzyme defect.
- Increased ACTH drives adrenal hyperplasia and may increase androgen production.

questions.stem: Which enzyme deficiency accounts for most cases of congenital adrenal hyperplasia?
questions.correctAnswerText: 21-hydroxylase deficiency
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include 21-hydroxylase deficiency as the commonest form, accounting for more than 90% of CAH cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Aromatase deficiency is a different disorder of sex-steroid metabolism.
- B. Incorrect. 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency is less common and is associated with hypertension due to DOC.
- C. Correct. 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the commonest CAH enzyme defect.
- D. Incorrect. 3-beta-HSD deficiency is rare.
- E. Incorrect. 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency is much less common and may cause hypertension and undervirilization.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 21-hydroxylase deficiency: >90%.
