- Other enzymes listed: 17-alpha-hydroxylase, 11-beta-hydroxylase and 3-beta-HSD.
- The biochemical phenotype depends on which steroid pathways are blocked.

questions.stem: Which biochemical pattern is most characteristic of salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency?

options.label: D
options.text: Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis
questions.initialExplanation: Severe 21-hydroxylase deficiency reduces cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, causing salt loss, hyperkalaemia, dehydration and possible hypoglycaemia with metabolic acidosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is the opposite electrolyte pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Aldosterone is deficient in salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. CAH causes reduced cortisol, with ACTH generally elevated due to loss of feedback.
- D. Correct. This is the classic salt-wasting crisis pattern.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests a calcium/PTH disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Salt-wasting CAH may present in the first weeks of life.
- Vomiting, dehydration, weight loss, hypotension/shock and electrolyte disturbance are key.
- A 46,XX infant may have ambiguous/virilized external genitalia; a 46,XY infant may have normal-appearing genitalia and still develop salt-wasting crisis.

questions.stem: A child with CAH has early pubic hair, accelerated linear growth and advanced bone age, but reduced mineralocorticoid deficiency is not clinically apparent. Which clinical subtype is most likely?

options.label: E
options.text: Addison disease due to adrenal destruction

questions.correctAnswerText: Simple virilizing CAH
questions.initialExplanation: The simple virilizing form has androgen excess with relatively preserved mineralocorticoid secretion compared with the salt-wasting form. It may present with precocious pubertal signs and accelerated skeletal maturation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Non-classical CAH usually presents later with hirsutism, acne, menstrual disturbance or infertility.
- B. Incorrect. Salt-wasting CAH causes severe mineralocorticoid deficiency and adrenal crisis, often in early infancy.
- C. Correct. This matches simple virilizing CAH.
- D. Incorrect. Panhypopituitarism causes multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies.
- E. Incorrect. Addison disease is adrenal insufficiency due to adrenal destruction and is not characterized by androgen excess.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Classical CAH includes salt-wasting and simple virilizing presentations.
- Androgen excess causes early pubic hair, penile/clitoral enlargement and accelerated growth/bone age.
- Advanced bone age may result in reduced adult height because epiphyseal closure occurs earlier.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with non-classical CAH presents with hirsutism, acne and oligomenorrhoea. Which mechanism best explains these findings?
questions.correctAnswerText: Excess adrenal androgen production
questions.initialExplanation: Non-classical CAH is a milder, later-onset presentation of adrenal steroid enzyme deficiency, often associated with androgen excess and symptoms such as hirsutism, acne and menstrual irregularity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Excess ADH causes water retention, not androgenic symptoms.
- B. Incorrect. Thyrotoxicosis causes weight loss, tremor and tachycardia.
- C. Incorrect. Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus.
- D. Incorrect. PTH resistance causes pseudohypoparathyroidism.
- E. Correct. Adrenal androgen excess explains the symptoms.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Non-classical CAH may present during adolescence or adulthood.
- Females may present with oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, acne and infertility.
- 17-hydroxyprogesterone is an important diagnostic marker.

questions.stem: A child with hypertension and virilization is suspected of having an uncommon form of CAH. Which enzyme deficiency is associated with increased deoxycorticosterone (DOC), a potent sodium-retaining steroid?
questions.correctAnswerText: 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance specifically notes that 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency can cause hypertension because DOC accumulates and has potent mineralocorticoid activity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency also causes hypertension through mineralocorticoid precursors, but the specific DOC note is linked to 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. 21-hydroxylase deficiency typically causes salt wasting, not DOC-mediated hypertension.
- C. Correct. DOC accumulation explains hypertension in 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency.
- D. Incorrect. 5-alpha reductase deficiency affects DHT production and sexual differentiation.
- E. Incorrect. Aromatase deficiency affects androgen-to-oestrogen conversion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency: androgen excess + hypertension due to DOC.
- 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the commonest CAH form and may cause salt wasting.
- CAH phenotype depends on which steroid synthesis step is impaired.

questions.stem: Which laboratory investigation is particularly useful for diagnosing 21-hydroxylase deficiency?
questions.correctAnswerText: Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include a very high serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level as a diagnostic investigation for CAH, particularly 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. TSH assesses thyroid function.
- B. Correct. 17-OHP accumulates when 21-hydroxylase is deficient.
- C. Incorrect. PTH is used to assess parathyroid function.
- D. Incorrect. ADH is involved in water balance and DI.
- E. Incorrect. GH does not diagnose CAH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 17-hydroxyprogesterone is a key marker in 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
- Also assess electrolytes, glucose, acid–base status and karyotype when DSD is present.
- Bone age may be advanced in androgen excess.

cases.title: Four children referred for pubertal or growth concerns

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is tall (above the 99th centile). He has pubic hair stage 3 and penile enlargement. Both testes are small and symmetrical (2 mL), and basal LH and FSH are prepubertal. Bone age is 8.5 years. Blood pressure and electrolytes are normal. What is the best next test?
questions.correctAnswerText: Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone
questions.initialExplanation: Pubic hair and penile enlargement with prepubertal testes and low LH/FSH indicate gonadotropin-independent (peripheral) puberty. In boys, the first sign of true puberty is testicular enlargement to about 4 mL. Adrenal androgen excess from simple virilising CAH explains tall stature, advanced bone age and these signs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Reasoning. Signs that are not concordant (virilisation without testicular growth) point to androgens from outside the pituitary-gonadal axis. Clinical guidance adrenal disorders including CAH, testicular Leydig-cell tumours and exogenous steroids as causes. Symmetrical prepubertal testes make a Leydig-cell tumour unlikely.
- A. Incorrect. MRI is for suspected central precocious puberty, which is unlikely with prepubertal testes and low gonadotropins.
- B. Incorrect. Pelvic ultrasound is used in girls.
- C. Incorrect. GH assessment is irrelevant. Tall stature is explained by androgens.
- D. Incorrect. Nothing suggests thyroid disease.
- E. Correct. Very high 17-OHP confirms 21-hydroxylase deficiency (simple virilising form), which presents with early pubic hair, penile enlargement, accelerated growth and advanced bone age. Adult height will be short without treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Male puberty starts with testicular enlargement (about 4 mL by orchidometer), 9–14 years.
- Precocious puberty in males is rare and usually pathological, so causes must be excluded.
- Central precocious puberty: concordant signs, high LH/FSH. Peripheral: discordant signs, low LH/FSH.
- Simple virilising CAH: early pubic hair, accelerated growth, advanced bone age, short adult height.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Puberty in boys (Page 49); precocious puberty (Pages 51–52); CAH (Page 24).

topics.name: Diabetes Mellitus — Classification, Type 1 Diabetes and Diagnosis

cases.title: A child with polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child has several weeks of increasing thirst, frequent urination, new nocturnal enuresis and weight loss despite a good appetite. Random blood glucose is markedly elevated. Urine testing shows glucose and ketones.

questions.stem: Diabetes mellitus is best defined as:

options.label: A
options.text: Chronic hyperglycaemia due to defects in insulin secretion, insulin action or both

options.label: B
options.text: A disorder caused by excess glucagon

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic hypoglycaemia caused by excess insulin

options.label: E
options.text: Isolated glucosuria with normal blood glucose

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic hyperglycaemia due to defects in insulin secretion, insulin action or both
questions.initialExplanation: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic disorder characterized by hyperglycaemia resulting from impaired insulin secretion, insulin action or both.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the definition given.
- B. Incorrect. Glucagon is involved in glucose regulation, but diabetes is not caused only by excess glucagon.
- C. Incorrect. ADH deficiency/resistance causes diabetes insipidus.
- D. Incorrect. Diabetes is characterized by hyperglycaemia, not chronic hypoglycaemia.
- E. Incorrect. Glucosuria alone does not define diabetes mellitus.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Insulin increases glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue, promotes glycogen/protein synthesis and suppresses hepatic glucose production.
- Diabetes is a disorder of glucose regulation due to insulin secretion/action.
- Type 1 diabetes is the commonest form in children.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes type 1 from type 2 diabetes in children?

options.label: C
options.text: Type 1 is caused mainly by insulin resistance; type 2 by absolute insulin deficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Type 1 involves autoimmune beta-cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency; type 2 usually involves insulin resistance

options.label: E
options.text: Autoantibodies are usually positive in type 2 diabetes

questions.correctAnswerText: Type 1 involves autoimmune beta-cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency; type 2 usually involves insulin resistance
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance contrasts type 1 diabetes, caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, with type 2 diabetes, which is characterized by insulin resistance and is more commonly associated with overweight/obesity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. DKA is less common in type 2 than in type 1.
- B. Incorrect. Type 1 commonly occurs in childhood and is not restricted to obesity.
- C. Incorrect. This reverses the basic pathophysiology.
- D. Correct. This is the key distinction.
- E. Incorrect. Type 2 diabetes is generally autoantibody-negative in the comparison table.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type 1: autoimmune beta-cell destruction, absolute insulin deficiency, often acute onset and autoantibody positivity.
- Type 2: insulin resistance, often gradual onset and associated with obesity/acanthosis nigricans/PCOS/hypertension.
- DKA is common in type 1 and less common in type 2.

questions.stem: Which presentation is most typical of new-onset type 1 diabetes in a child?

options.label: B
options.text: Polyuria with dilute urine and normal blood glucose

options.label: E
options.text: Gradual weight gain with no polyuria

questions.correctAnswerText: Polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss
questions.initialExplanation: The classic early triad in type 1 diabetes is polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss. New nocturnal enuresis and candidal skin infection may also occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These suggest hypothyroidism.
- B. Incorrect. Dilute urine with normal glucose suggests DI or another cause of polyuria.
- C. Correct. This is the classical clinical triad described.
- D. Incorrect. These suggest thyrotoxicosis.
- E. Incorrect. Weight gain without osmotic symptoms is not the classic presentation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type 1 DM: polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss.
- Secondary nocturnal enuresis may be an early clue.
- Around 30% may first present with DKA.

questions.stem: A symptomatic child has polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss. Random plasma glucose is 230 mg/dL. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: B
options.text: urine glucose is required to diagnose diabetes

options.label: C
options.text: This meets the lecture's diagnostic glucose criterion in a symptomatic child

options.label: D
options.text: An OGTT is mandatory in each symptomatic child

options.label: E
options.text: Diabetes is excluded unless fasting glucose is above 300 mg/dL

questions.correctAnswerText: This meets the lecture's diagnostic glucose criterion in a symptomatic child
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include random blood glucose of at least 200 mg/dL in a symptomatic child as a diagnostic criterion for diabetes mellitus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. DI causes polyuria due to impaired water conservation, not hyperglycaemia with classic diabetic symptoms.
- B. Incorrect. Urine glucose may support the diagnosis but does not replace blood glucose testing.
- C. Correct. Random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms is a diagnostic criterion.
- D. Incorrect. OGTT is rarely required for typical symptomatic type 1 diabetes when diagnostic criteria are already met.
- E. Incorrect. The stated threshold is lower than 300 mg/dL.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Symptomatic child: random glucose ≥200 mg/dL is a diagnostic criterion.
- Fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL and 2-hour glucose ≥200 mg/dL are also listed.
- In asymptomatic children, confirm abnormal testing with repeat measurements according to diagnostic guidance.

questions.stem: Which antibody group is associated with autoimmune type 1 diabetes?

options.label: B
options.text: GAD, ZnT8 and islet antigen-2 antibodies

questions.correctAnswerText: GAD, ZnT8 and islet antigen-2 antibodies
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8) and islet antigen-2 (IA-2) autoantibodies among markers of type 1 diabetes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are not the usual diabetes autoantibodies.
- B. Correct. These are pancreatic islet autoantibodies listed.
- C. Incorrect. PTH receptor antibodies are not the type 1 diabetes markers.
- D. Incorrect. These are associated with thyroid autoimmunity/Graves disease.
- E. Incorrect. These do not constitute the principal type 1 diabetes antibody group described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type 1 DM is autoimmune in most children.
- Common examples include GAD, ZnT8 and IA-2 antibodies.
- Type 1 diabetes may coexist with autoimmune thyroid disease, coeliac disease and Addison disease.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old with obesity, acanthosis nigricans, a strong family history of type 2 diabetes and gradual-onset polyuria is suspected of type 2 diabetes. Which additional feature is more typical of type 2 than type 1?

options.label: A
options.text: Absolute insulin deficiency from autoimmune beta-cell destruction

options.label: B
options.text: Frequent DKA as the presenting feature

options.label: C
options.text: Rapid onset with marked weight loss

options.label: E
options.text: Strong family history and evidence of insulin resistance

questions.correctAnswerText: Strong family history and evidence of insulin resistance
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include paediatric type 2 diabetes as commonly associated with obesity, strong family history, acanthosis nigricans, PCOS, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Autoimmune absolute insulin deficiency is the pathophysiology of type 1.
- B. Incorrect. DKA is less common in type 2 than in type 1.
- C. Incorrect. Rapid onset and significant weight loss are more typical of type 1.
- D. Incorrect. Pancreatic autoantibodies are more typical of type 1 diabetes.
- E. Correct. A strong family history and insulin-resistance features support type 2 diabetes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type 2 often occurs after age 10 and in mid-to-late puberty.
- Most affected children are overweight or obese.
- Acanthosis nigricans is a visible marker of insulin resistance.
- Type 2 management includes education, diet, exercise and metformin.

questions.stem: Which condition is an example of monogenic diabetes listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: MODY
questions.initialExplanation: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) is listed as an other specific type of diabetes due to a genetic defect in beta-cell function, often with a strong family history.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is due to resistance to PTH.
- B. Incorrect. Central DI is due to ADH deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Graves disease is autoimmune hyperthyroidism.
- D. Incorrect. Addison disease is primary adrenal insufficiency.
- E. Correct. MODY is a monogenic diabetes syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MODY: genetic beta-cell dysfunction, often strong multigenerational family history.
- Other specific diabetes types listed include neonatal diabetes, cystic fibrosis-related diabetes, syndromic diabetes and drug-induced diabetes.
- Distinguish monogenic diabetes from autoimmune T1DM and insulin-resistant T2DM.

topics.name: Type 1 Diabetes — Insulin Therapy, Education and Long-Term Management

cases.title: A child newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child presents with polyuria and weight loss. The family meets the paediatric diabetes team to learn insulin administration, carbohydrate matching, glucose monitoring, sick-day rules and the prevention of complications.

questions.stem: Which professional group is included in the multidisciplinary paediatric diabetes team?

options.label: E
options.text: Paediatric endocrinologist, diabetes nurse, dietitian, psychologist and social worker

questions.correctAnswerText: Paediatric endocrinologist, diabetes nurse, dietitian, psychologist and social worker
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is a multidisciplinary team including a paediatrician/endocrinologist, specialist diabetes nurse, dietitian, clinical psychologist, social worker and parent/patient support groups.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These specialists are not the core diabetes team.
- B. Incorrect. Ophthalmology may be involved in screening, but this is not the complete core team.
- C. Incorrect. Diabetes care requires multidisciplinary education and follow-up.
- D. Incorrect. Orthopaedic care may be needed for complications but is not the core diabetes team.
- E. Correct. This is the diabetes team described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Paediatric diabetes requires a multidisciplinary team.
- Psychosocial support is important because diabetes is a lifelong condition.
- Family education is central to safe insulin use and complication prevention.

questions.stem: Which is an appropriate goal of treatment in a child with type 1 diabetes?

options.label: A
options.text: Normalize blood glucose at the expense of normal growth

options.label: C
options.text: Support normal growth, emotional well-being, school performance and prevention of complications

options.label: E
options.text: Stop insulin when the child feels well

questions.correctAnswerText: Support normal growth, emotional well-being, school performance and prevention of complications
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include normal growth, emotional well-being, feeling well, normal life and school performance, symptom control and prevention of complications as treatment goals.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Growth and development are central goals, not acceptable trade-offs.
- B. Incorrect. A balanced healthy diet with carbohydrate planning is recommended.
- C. Correct. This reflects the full treatment goals.
- D. Incorrect. Regular exercise is encouraged.
- E. Incorrect. Insulin must continue even when the child feels well.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Goals extend beyond glucose numbers: growth, development, emotional health and daily functioning.
- Family education covers insulin, diet, exercise, monitoring and sick-day management.
- Avoid insulin omission.

questions.stem: Which insulin regimen is described as the preferred flexible approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Basal–bolus multiple daily injections, usually 3–4 injections per day

options.label: B
options.text: Long-acting insulin with no meal coverage

options.label: D
options.text: One dose of insulin once weekly

options.label: E
options.text: Twice-daily premixed insulin is the acceptable regimen

questions.correctAnswerText: Basal–bolus multiple daily injections, usually 3–4 injections per day
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include multiple daily injections with basal long-acting insulin and rapid-acting mealtime insulin as the principal basal–bolus regimen. Insulin pump therapy is another option.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the regimen described.
- B. Incorrect. Basal insulin alone does not adequately cover meals.
- C. Incorrect. Type 1 diabetes requires insulin replacement.
- D. Incorrect. Insulin is not given weekly in type 1 diabetes.
- E. Incorrect. Clinical guidance notes twice-daily regimens but states they are less commonly used than basal–bolus therapy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Basal–bolus: long-acting basal insulin + rapid-acting meal doses.
- Continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (pump) is another approach.
- Regimen selection is individualized and linked to food intake and activity.

questions.stem: Which insulin is most appropriate for rapid mealtime coverage because it has a rapid onset?

options.label: E
options.text: Regular insulin is typically faster than rapid analogues

questions.correctAnswerText: Insulin lispro
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include lispro, aspart and glulisine as rapid-acting analogues with a rapid onset, suitable for mealtime boluses.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Lispro is a rapid-acting insulin analogue.
- B. Incorrect. NPH is intermediate-acting.
- C. Incorrect. Degludec is an ultra-long/long-acting basal insulin.
- D. Incorrect. Glargine is long-acting basal insulin.
- E. Incorrect. Regular insulin has a slower onset than rapid-acting analogues.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rapid analogues: lispro, aspart, glulisine.
- Regular insulin: short-acting.
- NPH: intermediate-acting.
- Glargine, detemir and degludec: long-acting basal analogues.

questions.stem: Which injection site and technique are recommended to reduce lipohypertrophy?

options.label: A
options.text: Rotate injection sites among abdomen, outer arms and thighs using correct technique

options.label: D
options.text: Repeated injections into the same small area

options.label: E
options.text: Inject into the same lipohypertrophic area because absorption is more predictable

questions.correctAnswerText: Rotate injection sites among abdomen, outer arms and thighs using correct technique
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include the abdomen, outer arms and thighs as injection areas and emphasizes site rotation and correct injection technique to prevent lipohypertrophy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Rotation and proper technique reduce lipohypertrophy/lipoatrophy.
- B. Incorrect. Insulin is administered subcutaneously.
- C. Incorrect. Scar tissue should not be used as a routine injection site.
- D. Incorrect. Repeated injection into the same area promotes local tissue changes.
- E. Incorrect. Lipohypertrophic tissue produces unpredictable absorption and should be avoided.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common sites: abdomen, outer arms and thighs.
- Rotate injection sites.
- Inspect injection sites for lipohypertrophy and lipoatrophy.
- Lipohypertrophy may impair predictable insulin absorption.

questions.stem: Which blood glucose value defines hypoglycaemia in a child with diabetes?
questions.correctAnswerText: Below 70 mg/dL
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe hypoglycaemia in a person with diabetes as blood glucose below 70 mg/dL.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the hypoglycaemia definition.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the stated threshold.
- C. Incorrect. This is hyperglycaemia.
- D. Correct. This is the threshold given for diabetes-related hypoglycaemia.
- E. Incorrect. This is marked hyperglycaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Diabetes-related hypoglycaemia: glucose <70 mg/dL.
- Symptoms include hunger, sweating, faintness, dizziness, wobbliness, behavioural change, hallucinations and seizures if severe.
- Young children may present with pallor and altered behaviour.

questions.stem: A conscious child with diabetes has symptomatic hypoglycaemia. What is the immediate management described?

options.label: C
options.text: Give rapidly absorbed oral glucose, such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink

options.label: D
options.text: Wait for the child to become unconscious

questions.correctAnswerText: Give rapidly absorbed oral glucose, such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink
questions.initialExplanation: A conscious child able to swallow should receive rapidly absorbed glucose. Blood glucose should be checked immediately when hypoglycaemia is suspected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Carbohydrate is required to correct low glucose.
- B. Incorrect. Metformin does not treat acute hypoglycaemia.
- C. Correct. Rapid oral glucose is appropriate for a conscious child who can swallow safely.
- D. Incorrect. Treatment should be immediate to prevent progression to seizures or unconsciousness.
- E. Incorrect. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Check blood glucose immediately.
- Conscious and able to swallow: give rapid-acting oral glucose.
- Unconscious or unable to swallow: emergency IV glucose or glucagon according to paediatric protocol.
- Exact rescue doses should follow current local guidance.

questions.stem: Which dietary principle is recommended for children with type 1 diabetes?

options.label: A
options.text: A healthy balanced diet with complex carbohydrates, low saturated fat, adequate protein and fibre

options.label: B
options.text: High saturated fat and no fibre

options.label: C
options.text: High refined sugar intake before each meal

questions.correctAnswerText: A healthy balanced diet with complex carbohydrates, low saturated fat, adequate protein and fibre
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes a healthy balanced diet, favouring complex carbohydrates, limiting refined carbohydrate, keeping fat intake appropriate, and ensuring adequate protein and fibre. Carbohydrate counting helps match insulin to meals.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the dietary approach.
- B. Incorrect. Recommended management includes low fat and high fibre.
- C. Incorrect. High refined sugar intake is not recommended as routine nutrition.
- D. Incorrect. Carbohydrate is not eliminated; it is planned and matched to insulin.
- E. Incorrect. Adequate protein is recommended.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Healthy balanced diet.
- Carbohydrate counting matches insulin to food intake.
- Consider pre-meal glucose and post-meal activity when planning insulin.
- Dietetic education is essential.

questions.stem: A child with type 1 diabetes is planning prolonged vigorous exercise. Which adjustment is described?

options.label: A
options.text: Take no glucose measurements around exercise

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce insulin dose as appropriate and increase carbohydrate intake

options.label: E
options.text: Increase insulin and reduce carbohydrate intake

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduce insulin dose as appropriate and increase carbohydrate intake
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that vigorous or prolonged exercise may require a reduction in insulin dose and increased carbohydrate intake to prevent hypoglycaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Glucose monitoring is important when adapting insulin and carbohydrate intake around exercise.
- B. Incorrect. Insulin must not be stopped in type 1 diabetes.
- C. Correct. This is the adjustment described.
- D. Incorrect. Regular exercise is encouraged.
- E. Incorrect. Increasing insulin while reducing carbohydrates increases hypoglycaemia risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Exercise is encouraged in type 1 diabetes.
- Vigorous prolonged activity may require insulin reduction and additional carbohydrate.
- Individualize the plan using glucose monitoring and the diabetes team.

questions.stem: A child with type 1 diabetes develops fever and vomiting. Blood glucose is high and urine ketones are detectable. Which sick-day principle is most important?

options.label: A
options.text: Give long-acting insulin and avoid contacting the diabetes team

options.label: B
options.text: Stop insulin because the child is not eating

options.label: C
options.text: Continue insulin and follow the sick-day monitoring/adjustment plan

questions.correctAnswerText: Continue insulin and follow the sick-day monitoring/adjustment plan
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is that insulin must always be continued during illness. Additional short-acting insulin and more frequent glucose/ketone monitoring may be required according to the agreed sick-day plan.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Management may require short-acting insulin adjustment and clinical advice; it is not simply long-acting insulin alone.
- B. Incorrect. Stopping insulin in type 1 diabetes during illness can precipitate DKA.
- C. Correct. Insulin should continue, with monitoring and adjustment under the sick-day plan.
- D. Incorrect. Fluid intake should be maintained as clinically appropriate.
- E. Incorrect. Glucose and ketone monitoring become more important during illness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Never stop insulin in type 1 diabetes during illness.
- Increase monitoring of blood glucose and ketones.
- Seek clinical help if vomiting, persistent hyperglycaemia or ketones are present.
- Exact supplemental insulin percentages are not used here as a universal dosing rule.

questions.stem: Which chronic complication is correctly matched with its target organ in type 1 diabetes?
questions.correctAnswerText: Retinopathy — retina
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance divides chronic complications into macrovascular disease, microvascular disease and insulin-therapy-related complications. Retinopathy affects the retina, nephropathy the kidneys and neuropathy the peripheral/autonomic nerves.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Nephropathy affects the kidneys.
- B. Incorrect. Coronary artery disease affects coronary vessels and heart, not the pituitary.
- C. Incorrect. Neuropathy affects nerves.
- D. Incorrect. Lipohypertrophy is a local injection-site complication.
- E. Correct. Diabetic retinopathy is a retinal microvascular complication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute complications: DKA and hypoglycaemia.
- Microvascular complications: retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy.
- Macrovascular complications: hypertension, coronary and cerebrovascular disease.
- Insulin-related complications: lipodystrophy, obesity and insulin resistance.

questions.stem: A child with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes has growth failure, delayed puberty, Cushingoid facies and hepatomegaly. Which syndrome is described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Mauriac syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Mauriac syndrome is associated with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes and is characterized by growth failure/short stature, delayed puberty, Cushingoid facies and hepatomegaly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. McCune–Albright involves precocious puberty, café-au-lait macules and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia.
- B. Incorrect. Kallmann syndrome is associated with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia.
- C. Correct. This is the syndrome described.
- D. Incorrect. DiGeorge syndrome involves thymic, parathyroid and conotruncal cardiac abnormalities.
- E. Incorrect. Pendred syndrome is associated with goitre and sensorineural hearing loss.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mauriac syndrome: poorly controlled type 1 DM.
- Growth failure, short stature, delayed puberty, Cushingoid face and hepatomegaly.
- Good glycaemic control and regular growth/puberty monitoring are important.

cases.title: Children with type 1 diabetes seen in clinic and at school

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with type 1 diabetes (total daily insulin dose 40 units) has fever and tonsillitis and is eating little. His glucose is 342 mg/dL and urine ketones are moderate. He is not vomiting. His mother wants to skip insulin because he is not eating. Which advice is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Omit the basal insulin until he eats normally

options.label: B
options.text: Give an extra 50% of the total daily dose as intermediate-acting insulin

options.label: C
options.text: Continue insulin; add rapid-acting insulin 10–15% of TDD and check glucose and ketones frequently

options.label: D
options.text: Replace insulin with an oral hypoglycaemic agent

options.label: E
options.text: Withhold insulin until the ketones clear and encourage fluids

questions.correctAnswerText: Continue insulin; add rapid-acting insulin 10–15% of TDD and check glucose and ketones frequently
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that insulin must always be continued in sick-day management. Extra short-acting insulin is given when glucose exceeds 300 mg/dL or ketones are present, estimated at 10–15% of the total daily dose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Calculation. 10–15% of 40 units = 4–6 units.
- A. Incorrect. Stopping basal insulin during illness precipitates DKA.
- B. Incorrect. 50% is far above the 10–15% and risks dangerous hypoglycaemia.
- C. Correct. This follows the sick-day rules: continue insulin, add extra short-acting insulin, monitor glucose and ketones.
- D. Incorrect. Oral agents are used in type 2 diabetes, not type 1.
- E. Incorrect. Withholding insulin when ketones are present is the route to DKA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sick-day rules: never stop insulin; extra short-acting insulin if glucose >300 mg/dL or ketones present; 10–15% of total daily dose.
- Monitor glucose and ketones more often during illness.
- Sick-day management is part of family education to prevent DKA.
- Follow the local protocol for exact dosing.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Sick-day management (Page 32); family education (Page 29).

cases.title: A child presenting with vomiting, abdominal pain and deep breathing
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration and increasing drowsiness. The child has deep, laboured breathing and an acetone-like smell to the breath. Blood glucose is elevated, blood/urine ketones are positive and blood gas testing shows metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: Which combination defines diabetic ketoacidosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Glucosuria with normal pH and no ketones

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia/ketonuria and metabolic acidosis
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe DKA by hyperglycaemia (glucose >200 mg/dL), ketones in blood/urine and metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 and bicarbonate ≤15 mmol/L).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hyperglycaemia alone does not establish DKA.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the DKA biochemical pattern.
- C. Incorrect. DKA causes hyperglycaemia and ketoacidosis.
- D. Incorrect. Ketones and acidosis are central to the diagnosis.
- E. Correct. All three components are required for the DKA diagnosis described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DKA diagnostic triad: hyperglycaemia + ketones + metabolic acidosis.
- standard guidance thresholds: glucose >200 mg/dL, pH <7.3 and bicarbonate ≤15 mmol/L.
- Evaluate blood or urine ketones and electrolytes/blood gas.

questions.stem: Which sequence best explains the development of ketonaemia and acidosis in DKA?

options.label: B
options.text: Excess thyroid hormone → reduced lipolysis → ketone accumulation

options.label: E
options.text: Insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormone excess → lipolysis → hepatic ketone production

questions.correctAnswerText: Insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormone excess → lipolysis → hepatic ketone production
questions.initialExplanation: Insulin deficiency increases hyperglycaemia and counter-regulatory hormones. Adipose lipolysis releases free fatty acids, which are converted in the liver to ketone bodies, producing metabolic acidosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ADH deficiency causes DI and does not cause the DKA ketogenesis pathway.
- B. Incorrect. Thyroid hormone excess is not the primary pathway described.
- C. Incorrect. Excess insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis.
- D. Incorrect. PTH regulates calcium and phosphate, not ketone production.
- E. Correct. This is the pathophysiological sequence illustrated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Insulin deficiency → hyperglycaemia and glucosuria → osmotic diuresis and dehydration.
- Counter-regulatory hormones increase lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis.
- Beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate and acetone are ketone bodies; acetone contributes to the characteristic breath smell.

questions.stem: Which is a common precipitating factor for DKA in a child with established type 1 diabetes?
questions.correctAnswerText: Omission of insulin doses
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include insulin omission, infection/stress and insulin pump failure as precipitating factors for DKA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. High-fibre food is not a DKA precipitant.
- B. Correct. Insulin omission can lead to severe insulin deficiency and DKA.
- C. Incorrect. Taking insulin appropriately reduces DKA risk.
- D. Incorrect. Routine vaccination itself is not listed as a precipitating factor.
- E. Incorrect. Water intake alone does not cause DKA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Precipitants: missed insulin, infection/stress and insulin pump failure.
- Ask about insulin delivery, illness, ketones and adherence.
- DKA may be the first presentation of previously undiagnosed type 1 diabetes.

questions.stem: A child with DKA is dehydrated and hypotensive. Which is the most appropriate general sequence of management principles?

options.label: A
options.text: Assess severity and ABC, restore circulation/fluids, then start insulin and manage potassium with close monitoring

options.label: C
options.text: Give insulin bolus before assessing circulation and electrolytes

options.label: E
options.text: Give bicarbonate routinely to most children

questions.correctAnswerText: Assess severity and ABC, restore circulation/fluids, then start insulin and manage potassium with close monitoring
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is severity assessment, ABC stabilization, fluid replacement, insulin infusion after initial fluid therapy, potassium monitoring/replacement and close neurological/electrolyte monitoring. Exact fluid and insulin dosing must follow current paediatric DKA protocols.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This summarizes the staged management principles described.
- B. Incorrect. DKA requires emergency hospital treatment with fluids, insulin and electrolyte management.
- C. Incorrect. Initial assessment and fluid resuscitation are important; an insulin bolus is not the described first step.
- D. Incorrect. Fluid replacement is essential to correct dehydration.
- E. Incorrect. Routine bicarbonate is discouraged because of potential harm, including increased cerebral oedema risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Goals: correct dehydration, reverse ketosis/acidosis, normalize glucose gradually, identify precipitant and avoid treatment complications.
- Insulin infusion is started after initial fluid management according to paediatric protocol.
- Potassium may fall after insulin and rehydration; monitor ECG and serum potassium.
- Avoid routine bicarbonate unless a specialist protocol identifies a specific indication.

questions.stem: During treatment of DKA, a child develops headache, repeated vomiting, declining consciousness and cranial nerve palsy. What complication should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cerebral oedema
questions.initialExplanation: Cerebral oedema is the major life-threatening complication of DKA highlighted. Headache, vomiting, cranial nerve palsy, confusion, seizures, bradycardia and reduced consciousness are warning signs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pseudohypoparathyroidism causes PTH resistance and hypocalcaemia.
- B. Incorrect. DI causes polyuria and polydipsia.
- C. Incorrect. Graves ophthalmopathy causes eye signs, not acute raised intracranial pressure.
- D. Correct. The neurological deterioration is characteristic of cerebral oedema in DKA.
- E. Incorrect. Hypocalcaemia can cause tetany and seizures but does not explain the characteristic DKA neurological deterioration.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cerebral oedema: major life-threatening DKA complication.
- Risk factors listed include younger age, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis, high initial urea, rapid hypotonic fluid administration, early insulin and bicarbonate.
- Warning signs: headache, vomiting, cranial nerve palsy, altered consciousness, seizures, apnoea and bradycardia.
- Requires urgent senior/PICU management.

topics.name: Honeymoon Phase, Somogyi Phenomenon, Dawn Phenomenon and Type 2 Diabetes

cases.title: A child whose insulin requirement falls after diagnosis
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child receiving insulin for hyperglycaemia has improved glucose levels and requires progressively smaller insulin doses after treatment begins. The family asks whether insulin treatment is still required. Another child has recurrent morning hyperglycaemia, and the team compares overnight glucose patterns.

questions.stem: What is the honeymoon phase of type 1 diabetes?

options.label: B
options.text: A period of permanent hyperglycaemia immediately after DKA

options.label: D
options.text: A phase of severe insulin resistance in children in routine care

options.label: E
options.text: Temporary partial remission because surviving beta cells continue to produce some insulin

questions.correctAnswerText: Temporary partial remission because surviving beta cells continue to produce some insulin
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include the honeymoon period as temporary partial remission after diagnosis, when surviving beta cells produce some insulin and glucose control may improve for weeks or months, sometimes longer.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The honeymoon phase is not a cure; autoimmune beta-cell destruction continues.
- B. Incorrect. The phase is characterized by improved glucose control, not persistent worsening.
- C. Incorrect. It is part of the course of type 1 diabetes, not an adrenal disorder.
- D. Incorrect. It is not defined by insulin resistance.
- E. Correct. Residual beta-cell function temporarily reduces insulin requirements.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Honeymoon phase: temporary partial remission in type 1 diabetes.
- Residual beta-cell insulin production reduces exogenous insulin requirements.
- It may last weeks to months, occasionally longer, but it is not a cure.

questions.stem: A child has morning hyperglycaemia after a documented episode of nocturnal hypoglycaemia around 2–3 AM. Which phenomenon is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Somogyi phenomenon
questions.initialExplanation: The Somogyi phenomenon describes morning hyperglycaemia following nocturnal hypoglycaemia, with a counter-regulatory hormonal response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Honeymoon phase is temporary partial remission after new diagnosis.
- B. Correct. The history of overnight hypoglycaemia followed by morning hyperglycaemia supports Somogyi phenomenon.
- C. Incorrect. Reactive hypoglycaemia occurs after meals and does not describe the overnight pattern.
- D. Incorrect. Dawn phenomenon causes morning hyperglycaemia without preceding nocturnal hypoglycaemia.
- E. Incorrect. DI is due to ADH deficiency/resistance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Somogyi: nocturnal hypoglycaemia followed by rebound morning hyperglycaemia.
- Dawn phenomenon: morning hyperglycaemia due to early-morning counter-regulatory hormones without prior nocturnal hypoglycaemia.
- Overnight glucose/CGM data help distinguish the two patterns.

questions.stem: A child has normal glucose overnight but develops morning hyperglycaemia associated with increased early-morning growth hormone and other counter-regulatory hormones. Which phenomenon is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Dawn phenomenon
questions.initialExplanation: Dawn phenomenon is early-morning hyperglycaemia due to increased counter-regulatory hormones, including growth hormone, without preceding nocturnal hypoglycaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Normal overnight glucose followed by an early-morning rise is consistent with dawn phenomenon.
- B. Incorrect. Somogyi follows a nocturnal hypoglycaemic episode.
- C. Incorrect. Honeymoon is partial remission of type 1 diabetes.
- D. Incorrect. Adrenal crisis causes hypotension, hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance.
- E. Incorrect. Ketotic hypoglycaemia is a cause of fasting hypoglycaemia in young children.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dawn phenomenon: early-morning rise in glucose, associated with counter-regulatory hormones.
- Somogyi: rebound after nocturnal hypoglycaemia.
- Measure overnight glucose rather than assuming the cause of every morning high glucose.

questions.stem: Which child most closely fits the typical type 2 diabetes profile described?

options.label: C
options.text: An overweight 13-year-old in mid-to-late puberty with acanthosis nigricans and strong family history

options.label: D
options.text: A newborn with ambiguous genitalia and salt-wasting

options.label: E
options.text: A lean 5-year-old with abrupt onset, weight loss and positive islet antibodies

questions.correctAnswerText: An overweight 13-year-old in mid-to-late puberty with acanthosis nigricans and strong family history
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include type 2 diabetes in adolescents as usually diagnosed after age 10, often in mid-to-late puberty, associated with obesity, strong family history and signs of insulin resistance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is a possible presentation of neonatal diabetes.
- B. Incorrect. DI is a water-balance disorder, not type 2 diabetes.
- C. Correct. This is the characteristic paediatric type 2 profile.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests CAH/DSD.
- E. Incorrect. This is more typical of type 1 diabetes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type 2: older child/adolescent, overweight/obese, gradual symptoms, strong family history.
- Acanthosis nigricans, PCOS, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia suggest insulin resistance.
- DKA is less common than in type 1.
- Common examples include education, diet, exercise and metformin as management components.

cases.title: Children with type 1 diabetes seen in clinic and at school

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes on basal–bolus insulin has had fasting glucose values of 250–300 mg/dL for 10 days. His parents increased the bedtime long-acting dose twice, but morning values rose further and he now wakes with headaches and night sweats. Continuous glucose monitoring shows 48 mg/dL at about 2–3 AM, rising to 280 mg/dL by 7 AM. What is the most appropriate adjustment?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the evening insulin dose by a further 10%

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce the evening insulin dose by about 10% and review overnight glucose

options.label: C
options.text: Add a larger pre-breakfast correction bolus

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduce the evening insulin dose by about 10% and review overnight glucose
questions.initialExplanation: This is the Somogyi phenomenon: excess evening insulin causes nocturnal hypoglycaemia at about 2–3 AM. Counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon and others) then cause morning hyperglycaemia. Treatment is to reduce the evening insulin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Pattern recognition. Documented 2–3 AM hypoglycaemia, symptoms of nocturnal hypoglycaemia (headache, sweats) and worsening fasting glucose after each increase in the evening dose fit Somogyi.
- A. Incorrect. Increasing the dose worsens nocturnal hypoglycaemia and the rebound. This is the error already made twice.
- B. Correct. Decreasing the evening dose (about 10%) removes the hypoglycaemic trigger.
- C. Incorrect. Treating the morning number alone ignores the cause and risks hypoglycaemia later.
- D. Incorrect. Insulin must never be stopped in type 1 diabetes.
- E. Incorrect. Metformin is for type 2 diabetes, not type 1.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Somogyi: normal glucose at bedtime, then nocturnal hypoglycaemia (2–3 AM), counter-regulatory surge, morning hyperglycaemia. Treatment: decrease evening insulin (~10%).
- Dawn phenomenon: normal glucose overnight, early-morning hyperglycaemia from rising GH and other hormones. Treatment: increase evening insulin (~10%).
- Overnight glucose data (e.g. CGM) distinguish the two.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Honeymoon period, Somogyi and dawn phenomenon (Page 38).

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes has morning glucose values of 220–240 mg/dL. Overnight monitoring shows steady values of 100–120 mg/dL from midnight to 4 AM, then a steady rise to 230 mg/dL by 7 AM. No hypoglycaemia is recorded. What is the best adjustment?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduce the evening insulin dose by about 10%

options.label: B
options.text: Add a large bedtime snack of fast-acting carbohydrate

options.label: D
options.text: Admit for treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis

options.label: E
options.text: Increase the evening insulin dose by about 10% and recheck overnight glucose

questions.correctAnswerText: Increase the evening insulin dose by about 10% and recheck overnight glucose
questions.initialExplanation: Normal glucose overnight followed by an early-morning rise, without hypoglycaemia, is the dawn phenomenon. It is driven by early-morning increases in GH and other counter-regulatory hormones. The evening insulin dose is increased slightly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Reducing the dose is the treatment for Somogyi, where nocturnal hypoglycaemia is present. Here it is absent.
- B. Incorrect. Fast-acting carbohydrate at bedtime would raise, not lower, morning glucose.
- C. Incorrect. Omitting insulin in type 1 diabetes risks DKA.
- D. Incorrect. DKA requires ketones and acidosis, and nothing here suggests it.
- E. Correct. A modest increase (about 10%) in the evening insulin addresses the early-morning rise.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dawn: no preceding hypoglycaemia. Somogyi: nocturnal hypoglycaemia first.
- Opposite adjustments: dawn → increase evening insulin; Somogyi → decrease it.
- Always check overnight glucose before adjusting the evening dose.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Somogyi and dawn phenomenon (Page 38).

topics.name: Clinical Examination of a Child with Diabetes

cases.title: A child with type 1 diabetes attending a structured clinical examination
cases.vignette: A 12-year-old child with type 1 diabetes attends an outpatient review. The examiner asks the student to perform a focused general and systemic examination, looking for evidence of acute metabolic decompensation, chronic complications, injection-site problems and associated autoimmune disease.

questions.stem: Which observation during general inspection may suggest acute DKA?

options.label: E
options.text: Kussmaul breathing with dehydration and acetone breath

questions.correctAnswerText: Kussmaul breathing with dehydration and acetone breath
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes assessing the child's breathing pattern, hydration, general state, weight/height and surrounding IV/infusion equipment. Kussmaul breathing and acetone breath suggest DKA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Acne alone does not indicate DKA.
- B. Incorrect. School performance is part of overall assessment but does not indicate acute DKA.
- C. Incorrect. A healed vaccination scar is not a DKA sign.
- D. Incorrect. These are reassuring findings, not signs of DKA.
- E. Correct. Deep Kussmaul breathing and acetone smell are characteristic warning signs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Assess general condition, height, weight, centile, pallor/pink colour, hydration, breathing pattern, oedema and skin lesions.
- Kussmaul breathing and acetone breath suggest DKA.
- Inspect for an IV line/infusion pump and signs of dehydration.

questions.stem: Which site should be inspected for lipohypertrophy in a child receiving repeated insulin injections?
questions.correctAnswerText: Abdomen, thighs and outer arms
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance specifically recommends palpating insulin injection sites in the arms, thighs and abdomen for lipohypertrophy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Palmar creases may be inspected for colour changes but are not injection sites.
- B. Correct. These are the common injection sites listed.
- C. Incorrect. The anterior chest is not among the routine sites listed.
- D. Incorrect. Insulin is not injected into the oral mucosa.
- E. Incorrect. The scalp is not an insulin injection site.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Inspect and palpate insulin injection sites.
- Look for lipohypertrophy or lipoatrophy.
- Site rotation and correct technique reduce local tissue complications.

questions.stem: During examination of a child with diabetes, which finding is particularly relevant to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acanthosis nigricans around the neck
questions.initialExplanation: Acanthosis nigricans is a dark, velvety skin change associated with insulin resistance and is highlighted in the type 2 diabetes section of standard guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Café-au-lait macules may occur in several syndromes and are not the characteristic insulin-resistance sign.
- B. Correct. Acanthosis nigricans is a clinical marker of insulin resistance.
- C. Incorrect. Macroglossia is a feature of congenital hypothyroidism and other syndromes.
- D. Incorrect. Chvostek sign is a sign of latent tetany in hypocalcaemia.
- E. Incorrect. Exophthalmos is associated with Graves disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Examine the neck for goitre and acanthosis nigricans.
- Look for vitiligo and autoimmune associations.
- Acanthosis nigricans supports insulin resistance and may be seen in adolescents with type 2 diabetes.

questions.stem: Which set of systems is included 's periodic examination of children with diabetes?

options.label: A
options.text: Growth/puberty, blood pressure, renal screening, eyes, feet, thyroid and coeliac screening

questions.correctAnswerText: Growth/puberty, blood pressure, renal screening, eyes, feet, thyroid and coeliac screening
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is regular assessment of growth and puberty, blood pressure, microalbuminuria, retinal disease, foot pulses/sensation, injection sites, thyroid and coeliac disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are all part of the periodic assessment described.
- B. Incorrect. Abdominal examination is only one component.
- C. Incorrect. Neurological assessment may be relevant, but Recommended management includes a broader review.
- D. Incorrect. Thyroid screening is included but is not the only assessment.
- E. Incorrect. Respiratory examination alone is insufficient.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Plot growth and BMI and assess pubertal development at clinic visits.
- Monitor blood pressure and microalbuminuria as specified.
- Assess retinal status, feet, pulses, sensation and injection sites.
- Screen for thyroid disease and coeliac disease.
- Encourage influenza vaccination and dental review.

cases.title: A toddler with early-morning episodes of altered behaviour
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child is brought because of recurrent early-morning episodes of lethargy, sweating, confusion and unsteadiness. The child is slim and underweight. During an episode, blood glucose is 42 mg/dL and urine ketones are positive. Insulin is low.

questions.stem: What glucose threshold defines hypoglycaemia in a child without diabetes?
questions.correctAnswerText: Below 2.6 mmol/L (45 mg/dL)
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe childhood hypoglycaemia in children without diabetes as blood glucose below 2.6 mmol/L, approximately 45 mg/dL.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not a hypoglycaemia threshold.
- B. Correct. This is the definition given in the supplied standard guidance.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the hypoglycaemia threshold.
- D. Incorrect. 100 mg/dL is not the stated threshold.
- E. Incorrect. This is hyperglycaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Standard guidance's threshold: <2.6 mmol/L (45 mg/dL) in children without diabetes.
- Always confirm a low bedside glucose with a laboratory sample when feasible, without delaying treatment in an unwell child.
- Symptoms may be autonomic or neuroglycopenic.

questions.stem: Which cause is associated with hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Persistent hyperinsulinism of infancy due to beta-cell dysfunction

options.label: B
options.text: Fatty-acid oxidation defect with suppressed insulin

questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent hyperinsulinism of infancy due to beta-cell dysfunction
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance groups causes of hypoglycaemia into insulin excess and causes without hyperinsulinaemia. Beta-cell disorders, exogenous insulin and sulphonylureas are among the insulin-excess causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Persistent hyperinsulinism of infancy is a beta-cell disorder producing inappropriate insulin secretion.
- B. Incorrect. Fatty-acid oxidation defects are listed among metabolic causes without hyperinsulinaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia is described in the non-hyperinsulinaemic group.
- D. Incorrect. GH deficiency is a hormonal cause without hyperinsulinaemia.
- E. Incorrect. Cortisol deficiency is a hormonal cause without hyperinsulinaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Insulin-excess causes: exogenous insulin, beta-cell disorders/hyperinsulinism, insulinoma, sulphonylureas, autoimmune insulin-receptor antibodies and Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome.
- Non-hyperinsulinaemic causes include metabolic disease, hormonal deficiency, drugs, sepsis and liver disease.
- Insulin and ketone levels during hypoglycaemia help distinguish mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern is typical of idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia of childhood?

options.label: A
options.text: An obese adolescent with acanthosis nigricans and high insulin

options.label: B
options.text: A child with high glucose and absent ketones

options.label: C
options.text: A slim toddler with morning hypoglycaemia, positive urine ketones and low insulin

options.label: D
options.text: A newborn with hyperinsulinaemia and macrosomia in each case

options.label: E
options.text: An adolescent with hypertension and virilization

questions.correctAnswerText: A slim toddler with morning hypoglycaemia, positive urine ketones and low insulin
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia as the commonest cause of hypoglycaemia in children aged 1–5 years, peaking at 18–36 months. Children are often slim, episodes occur in the morning after fasting, and ketones are present with low insulin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests insulin resistance/type 2 diabetes.
- B. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia with absent ketones suggests inappropriate insulin or another metabolic defect.
- C. Correct. This matches the clinical pattern described.
- D. Incorrect. This may suggest hyperinsulinism, such as in an infant of a diabetic mother, rather than idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests a steroid enzyme disorder such as CAH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most common cause of childhood hypoglycaemia (age 1–5 years).
- Peak age: 18–36 months.
- Morning episodes after prolonged fasting; positive ketones and low insulin.
- Usually resolves with age; avoid prolonged fasting and ensure appropriate bedtime/overnight nutrition under clinical advice.

questions.stem: A child with recurrent hypoglycaemia has low insulin and significant ketonaemia. Which group of disorders should be considered among the differential diagnoses?

options.label: B
options.text: Glycogen storage disease and fatty-acid oxidation disorders

options.label: D
options.text: Graves disease and thyroid hormone resistance

questions.correctAnswerText: Glycogen storage disease and fatty-acid oxidation disorders
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include inborn errors of metabolism, including glycogen storage disorders, galactosaemia and fatty-acid oxidation defects, among causes of childhood hypoglycaemia without hyperinsulinaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are adrenal disorders and are not the metabolic group asked about.
- B. Correct. These metabolic disorders are included 's differential.
- C. Incorrect. DI causes water-balance disturbance, not this hypoglycaemia pattern.
- D. Incorrect. Thyroid disorders are not the metabolic group listed here.
- E. Incorrect. Parathyroid disorders do not explain the stated mechanism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hypoglycaemia differential: insulin excess, inborn errors of metabolism, hormonal deficiency, drugs, sepsis and liver disease.
- Ketones and insulin during the episode are critical to mechanism-based diagnosis.
- Consider GH/cortisol deficiency and CAH as endocrine causes.

cases.title: Children with type 1 diabetes seen in clinic and at school

questions.stem: At school sports day, a 9-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes becomes unresponsive and has a brief seizure. He is pale and sweaty, and the meter reads 34 mg/dL. The teacher has an emergency kit but no IV access is available, and the ambulance is 15 minutes away. What is the best immediate treatment?

options.label: B
options.text: A sugary drink poured into his mouth

options.label: D
options.text: Wait for the ambulance in the recovery position

options.label: E
options.text: Glucose tablets placed under the tongue

questions.correctAnswerText: Intramuscular glucagon
questions.initialExplanation: An unconscious child cannot safely take anything by mouth. clinical guidance gives two options for the unconscious child: IV 10% dextrose (2 mL/kg) or intramuscular glucagon. With no IV access, glucagon is the correct choice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Glucagon is given intramuscularly and works without IV access.
- B. Incorrect. Oral fluids to an unconscious or convulsing child risk aspiration. Oral glucose is for conscious children (the "rule of 15" approach).
- C. Incorrect. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia.
- D. Incorrect. The recovery position is right while waiting, but waiting without treating allows brain injury.
- E. Incorrect. Tablets are not appropriate for a patient who cannot swallow safely.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hypoglycaemia in diabetes: glucose below 70 mg/dL. Check glucose immediately.
- Conscious: rapidly absorbed oral glucose (tablets or sugary drink).
- Unconscious: IV dextrose 10% 2 mL/kg or IM glucagon.
- Young children may present with pallor and behavioural change.
