cases.title: A newborn of a diabetic mother with jitteriness
cases.vignette: A 2-hour-old large-for-gestational-age newborn, delivered to a mother with diabetes, becomes jittery and feeds poorly. Bedside glucose is low.

questions.stem: What serum glucose threshold is used for neonatal hypoglycaemia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Less than 45 mg/dL
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe neonatal hypoglycaemia as serum glucose below 45 mg/dL.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the threshold stated in the neonatal section.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the definition used.
- C. Incorrect. This is not a low glucose value.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the stated neonatal threshold.
- E. Incorrect. This is hyperglycaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal hypoglycaemia is common in NICU settings.
- Severe, persistent or recurrent episodes may cause brain injury, learning impairment and epilepsy.
- Interpret glucose values in the context of age after birth, symptoms and the local neonatal protocol.

questions.stem: Which newborn is at increased risk of hypoglycaemia due to hyperinsulinism?

options.label: C
options.text: Infant with normal feeding and normal glucose

options.label: E
options.text: Healthy term infant with no risk factors

questions.correctAnswerText: Infant of a diabetic mother
questions.initialExplanation: Maternal hyperglycaemia can stimulate fetal pancreatic insulin production. After birth, maternal glucose supply stops while neonatal insulin may remain high, producing hypoglycaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Isolated physiological jaundice is not the hyperinsulinism risk asked about.
- B. Correct. Infants of diabetic mothers are a key hyperinsulinism risk group.
- C. Incorrect. Normal feeding and glucose are reassuring.
- D. Incorrect. Reflux is not a cause of neonatal hyperinsulinism.
- E. Incorrect. This does not describe a specific risk factor.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hyperinsulinism risks: infant of diabetic mother, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome, hydrops fetalis, LGA, maternal drugs such as beta blockers and islet-cell hyperplasia.
- Other neonatal risk groups include prematurity, IUGR/SGA, perinatal stress, sepsis and inadequate intake.
- Monitor at-risk infants according to the neonatal protocol.

questions.stem: Which neonatal factor is categorized as reduced glucose stores or production rather than hyperinsulinism?
questions.correctAnswerText: Prematurity
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance places prematurity, IUGR and inadequate calorie intake under decreased production/stores, whereas maternal diabetes and beta-cell hyperplasia are listed under hyperinsulinism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Prematurity is grouped with reduced production/stores.
- B. Incorrect. Islet-cell hyperplasia causes excess insulin.
- C. Incorrect. Maternal beta-blocker exposure is listed with hyperinsulinism-related causes.
- D. Incorrect. Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome is associated with hyperinsulinism.
- E. Incorrect. Maternal diabetes is a hyperinsulinism risk factor.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Reduced stores/production: prematurity, IUGR and inadequate calorie intake.
- Increased utilization: perinatal stress, sepsis, asphyxia, shock, hypothermia and polycythaemia.
- Endocrine causes: CAH and hypopituitarism (including GH deficiency).

questions.stem: A newborn has recurrent severe hypoglycaemia of uncertain cause. Which is the most appropriate diagnostic approach during an episode?

options.label: A
options.text: During hypoglycaemia, sample glucose, insulin/C-peptide, cortisol, GH, ketones and metabolic markers

questions.correctAnswerText: During hypoglycaemia, sample glucose, insulin/C-peptide, cortisol, GH, ketones and metabolic markers
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes an urgent critical sample when the cause is unknown, including glucose, GH, cortisol, insulin, C-peptide, ketones, bicarbonate, lactate, ammonia, amino acids and acylcarnitine profile. First urine after the episode is tested for organic acids; toxicology may be considered.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This captures the critical sample described.
- B. Incorrect. Calcium alone does not establish the cause of hypoglycaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Dexamethasone suppression testing evaluates Cushing syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. TSH alone cannot classify the many possible mechanisms of hypoglycaemia.
- E. Incorrect. Water deprivation testing evaluates DI.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Obtain a critical sample during hypoglycaemia whenever possible, but do not delay treatment.
- Include glucose, insulin/C-peptide, cortisol, GH, ketones, lactate, bicarbonate, ammonia, amino acids and acylcarnitine profile.
- First urine after hypoglycaemia: organic acids.
- Consider toxicology if drug exposure is possible.

questions.stem: A newborn with severe symptomatic hypoglycaemia is lethargic and unable to feed safely. What is the appropriate immediate treatment principle?

options.label: A
options.text: Withhold glucose until a critical sample is completed

options.label: D
options.text: Treat ABCs and give IV glucose according to neonatal protocol

questions.correctAnswerText: Treat ABCs and give IV glucose according to neonatal protocol
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is an ABC-based approach and prompt glucose correction. IV dextrose is used for severe symptomatic hypoglycaemia or when the infant cannot safely take oral feeds. Obtain a critical sample first only when this does not delay emergency treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Do not delay lifesaving glucose treatment to obtain samples.
- B. Incorrect. Oral feeding is unsafe in an obtunded infant and may risk aspiration.
- C. Incorrect. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia.
- D. Correct. Stabilize airway/breathing/circulation and correct glucose urgently with IV glucose.
- E. Incorrect. Fluid restriction does not treat hypoglycaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ABCDE assessment and prompt glucose correction.
- Stable, conscious infant may receive enteral glucose/feed according to neonatal protocol.
- Severe symptomatic or unsafe-to-feed infant requires IV glucose.
- Exact bolus and infusion rates must follow local neonatal guidelines.

cases.title: A child with excessive thirst and large volumes of dilute urine
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child drinks water constantly, passes large volumes of urine and has new nocturnal enuresis. The child is losing weight and becomes dehydrated when water is not readily available. Serum sodium and plasma osmolality are elevated, while urine osmolality is low. The clinician distinguishes central from nephrogenic DI.

questions.stem: What is the primary physiological defect in central diabetes insipidus?

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced ADH secretion from the posterior pituitary

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced ADH secretion from the posterior pituitary
questions.initialExplanation: Central DI is caused by deficient secretion of ADH (arginine vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary, resulting in inability to concentrate urine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Insulin is involved in glucose regulation, not ADH secretion.
- B. Correct. Central DI is due to deficient ADH secretion.
- C. Incorrect. PTH regulates calcium homeostasis.
- D. Incorrect. This describes nephrogenic DI.
- E. Incorrect. Aldosterone regulates sodium/potassium balance and does not cause central DI.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DI: polyuria, polydipsia and dilute urine.
- Central DI: ADH deficiency.
- Nephrogenic DI: renal resistance to ADH.
- Clinical guidance notes urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg in DI.

questions.stem: Which is a recognized cause of central diabetes insipidus?
questions.correctAnswerText: Craniopharyngioma or post-neurosurgical/head trauma injury
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include head trauma, post-surgical injury, brain tumours such as craniopharyngioma, CNS infection, idiopathic and congenital causes of central DI.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These can damage the hypothalamic–posterior pituitary ADH pathway.
- B. Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia can cause nephrogenic DI through renal resistance to ADH.
- C. Incorrect. Hypokalaemia can cause nephrogenic DI.
- D. Incorrect. Lithium is a recognized cause of nephrogenic DI.
- E. Incorrect. Chronic renal/interstitial disease may cause nephrogenic DI.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Central DI: head trauma, surgery, CNS tumour/infection, idiopathic or congenital.
- Nephrogenic DI: renal resistance; causes include congenital forms, lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, chronic kidney disease and interstitial nephritis.
- Consider sickle-cell disease in renal causes.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern supports diabetes insipidus?

options.label: A
options.text: High serum osmolality with low urine osmolality

options.label: C
options.text: High serum calcium with high PTH

options.label: D
options.text: High urine osmolality and low serum sodium

options.label: E
options.text: Low serum osmolality with highly concentrated urine

questions.correctAnswerText: High serum osmolality with low urine osmolality
questions.initialExplanation: DI causes inability to concentrate urine despite increased plasma tonicity. Common examples include serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg, often with hypernatraemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Hyperosmolar plasma with inappropriately dilute urine is characteristic.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests diabetic ketoacidosis or another hypoglycaemic/ketotic state, not DI.
- C. Incorrect. This is a calcium/PTH pattern, not the core DI pattern.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the usual DI pattern.
- E. Incorrect. This pattern suggests appropriate renal concentration.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DI: serum osmolality high, urine osmolality low.
- Hypernatraemia may occur if water intake cannot match urinary losses.
- Clinical signs include polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, constipation, FTT and nocturnal enuresis.

questions.stem: A child has polyuria and dilute urine. A supervised water deprivation test is followed by desmopressin. Which response supports central rather than nephrogenic DI?

options.label: B
options.text: Urine becomes more concentrated after desmopressin

questions.correctAnswerText: Urine becomes more concentrated after desmopressin
questions.initialExplanation: In central DI, the kidneys respond to replacement ADH (desmopressin), so urine osmolality rises and urine output falls. In nephrogenic DI, renal resistance means the response is absent or limited.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Failure to concentrate urine despite desmopressin supports nephrogenic DI.
- B. Correct. A response to desmopressin supports central DI.
- C. Incorrect. Calcium is not the diagnostic response being assessed.
- D. Incorrect. Desmopressin should reduce urine output in central DI.
- E. Incorrect. Glucose does not differentiate central from nephrogenic DI.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Water deprivation/desmopressin testing is used under specialist supervision to distinguish central from nephrogenic DI.
- Central DI: responds to DDAVP.
- Nephrogenic DI: limited/no response to DDAVP.
- MRI brain helps investigate underlying central DI causes.

questions.stem: Which treatment is identified for central diabetes insipidus?
questions.correctAnswerText: Desmopressin (DDAVP)
questions.initialExplanation: Central DI is treated with desmopressin, an ADH analogue. Adequate fluid and calorie intake are also important.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hydrocortisone treats adrenal insufficiency; it is not the specific treatment for central DI.
- B. Incorrect. Metformin is used in type 2 diabetes.
- C. Incorrect. Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism.
- D. Correct. Desmopressin replaces the deficient ADH effect in central DI.
- E. Incorrect. Carbimazole is used in hyperthyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Central DI: desmopressin.
- Nephrogenic DI: thiazide diuretics and other selected approaches; treatment is specialist-led.
- Avoid dehydration and monitor serum sodium and fluid balance.

questions.stem: Which urine output meets standard definition of polyuria in a child?

options.label: B
options.text: Any urine output after drinking water

questions.correctAnswerText: More than 40 mL/kg/24 hours
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe polyuria as urine output greater than 40 mL/kg/24 hours or greater than 2,000 mL/m²/24 hours.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the weight-based threshold.
- B. Incorrect. Urination after drinking is physiological.
- C. Incorrect. This would indicate very low urine output, not polyuria.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the paediatric polyuria threshold.
- E. Incorrect. This is far below the threshold.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Polyuria: >40 mL/kg/24 hours or >2,000 mL/m²/24 hours.
- standard guidance also lists >1 L/day for preschool children and >2 L/day for school-aged children.
- Differential includes DM, DI, primary polydipsia, renal disease, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia and drugs.

cases.title: A child referred for height below the expected centile
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child is referred because the height plotted on the growth chart is below the expected range for age and sex. The family reports that the child has always been small. The clinician repeats the measurement using the correct technique and reviews the growth chart rather than relying on a single recorded value.

questions.stem: Which definition of short stature is given?

options.label: C
options.text: Height below the 2nd/3rd centile or about 2 SD below the mean

options.label: D
options.text: Any child who is shorter than one parent

questions.correctAnswerText: Height below the 2nd/3rd centile or about 2 SD below the mean
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe short stature as height below the second centile (approximately 2 SD below the mean), and also gives height below the third centile for age and sex on WHO charts.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Height above the 97th centile indicates tall stature, not short stature.
- B. Incorrect. standard guidance uses a more extreme threshold (below the 2nd/3rd centile), not simply below the 10th centile.
- C. Correct. This reproduces the definitions.
- D. Incorrect. Familial context is useful, but comparison with a parent alone does not define short stature.
- E. Incorrect. Weight centile alone does not define short stature.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Short stature: height <2nd centile (about 2 SD below mean) or <3rd centile using the WHO chart.
- Interpret height using age- and sex-appropriate growth charts.
- Serial measurements and growth velocity are essential; one measurement alone is insufficient to characterize the growth pattern.

questions.stem: Which technique is appropriate for measuring a 16-month-old child's length?

options.label: C
options.text: Measuring from the top of the head to the knee

questions.correctAnswerText: Supine measurement using an infantometer
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance specifies recumbent length for infants younger than 2 years, measured in the supine position with an infantometer.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A child younger than 2 years should have recumbent length measured with an infantometer.
- B. Incorrect. Standing height is used for children older than 2 years.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the standard measurement method.
- D. Incorrect. Sitting height is not a substitute for total body length.
- E. Incorrect. Parental height helps estimate genetic target height but cannot replace direct measurement.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Length: supine measurement in children <2 years.
- Height: standing measurement in children >2 years.
- Correct positioning and calibrated equipment reduce measurement error.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is being measured in clinic. Which method is appropriate?

options.label: B
options.text: Standing height with a stadiometer, barefoot, heels on the board and knees straight

options.label: C
options.text: Supine length on an infantometer as the standard method for most ages

options.label: D
options.text: Using a tape measure around the head

questions.correctAnswerText: Standing height with a stadiometer, barefoot, heels on the board and knees straight
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes standing height for children older than 2 years, with appropriate positioning against a stadiometer.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Shoes should be removed to avoid measurement error.
- B. Correct. This matches the standing-height technique shown in the PDF.
- C. Incorrect. Supine length is used for infants and young children under 2 years.
- D. Incorrect. Head circumference is a different anthropometric measurement.
- E. Incorrect. Sitting height is used as a component of body-proportion assessment, not as total height.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- >2 years: standing height with a stadiometer.
- Bare feet, straight knees, correct head position and heels against the board.
- Repeat an unexpected measurement before interpreting it clinically.

questions.stem: Which statement about growth velocity is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: It is unrelated to endocrine disease

options.label: B
options.text: It is a sensitive indicator of growth failure

options.label: C
options.text: It is determined by weight gain alone

options.label: D
options.text: It can be assessed after puberty

options.label: E
options.text: It is less useful than a single height measurement

questions.correctAnswerText: It is a sensitive indicator of growth failure
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include growth velocity as a sensitive indicator of growth failure. A child may still be within a centile range but show an abnormal reduction in the rate of linear growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Endocrine disorders are important causes of reduced growth velocity.
- B. Correct. standard guidance specifically emphasizes growth velocity as a sensitive indicator.
- C. Incorrect. Growth velocity refers to linear growth over time, not weight gain alone.
- D. Incorrect. Growth velocity is assessed throughout childhood.
- E. Incorrect. Serial growth velocity adds important information beyond a single height measurement.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Growth velocity = change in height/length over time.
- standard guidance gives approximate rates of 23–27 cm/year in the first year, at least 6 cm/year from 2–5 years, and around 5–6 cm/year after age 5 before puberty.
- Interpret velocity according to age and pubertal stage.

questions.stem: A child has a height below the third centile. Which additional information is most useful for deciding whether the child has true growth failure rather than simply being constitutionally small?

options.label: C
options.text: Serial height measurements plotted over time to calculate growth velocity

questions.correctAnswerText: Serial height measurements plotted over time to calculate growth velocity
questions.initialExplanation: Growth velocity provides a more sensitive assessment of ongoing linear growth than an isolated height value. An important point is serial assessment and plotting on growth charts.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Weight is important but cannot replace serial height assessment.
- B. Incorrect. Head circumference is important in early childhood but does not determine linear growth velocity.
- C. Correct. Serial height measurements reveal whether the child is continuing to grow at an appropriate rate.
- D. Incorrect. Blood glucose may be useful for other clinical questions but does not determine linear growth velocity.
- E. Incorrect. Shoe size is not a validated substitute for height velocity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Plot serial height/length measurements on the appropriate growth chart.
- Calculate growth velocity over a meaningful interval.
- Crossing down centile channels or reduced velocity should prompt assessment for pathological causes.

cases.title: A short child with short parents and normal growth velocity
cases.vignette: An 8-year-old boy is short compared with classmates. Both parents are short. His growth velocity is normal, puberty has begun at an appropriate age and bone age is similar to chronological age. He is otherwise healthy and has no systemic symptoms.

questions.stem: Which formula is used to estimate mid-parental target height for a boy?
questions.correctAnswerText: (Father's height + mother's height) / 2 + 6.5 cm
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives the mid-parental height calculation for boys as the average of the parents' heights plus 6.5 cm.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The formula uses the average of both parental heights, not their difference.
- B. Correct. This is the formula printed.
- C. Incorrect. Father's height alone is not the mid-parental calculation.
- D. Incorrect. Mother's height alone is not the mid-parental calculation.
- E. Incorrect. The minus 6.5 cm adjustment is the formula given for girls.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Boy: (father's height + mother's height)/2 + 6.5 cm.
- Girl: (father's height + mother's height)/2 − 6.5 cm.
- The target height is plotted against the family/growth chart.

questions.stem: Which pattern best supports familial short stature rather than constitutional delay of growth and puberty?

options.label: A
options.text: Shorter birth length, positive family history of short stature, normal puberty, normal growth velocity and bone age similar to chronological age

options.label: B
options.text: Normal birth length, no family history of short stature, delayed puberty and delayed bone age

options.label: C
options.text: Short stature with Cushingoid features and hypertension

options.label: D
options.text: Markedly reduced growth velocity with delayed puberty and chronic diarrhoea

options.label: E
options.text: Disproportionate short limbs and a large head

questions.correctAnswerText: Shorter birth length, positive family history of short stature, normal puberty, normal growth velocity and bone age similar to chronological age
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance compares familial short stature with constitutional growth delay. Familial short stature is associated with a positive family history, normal pubertal timing, normal growth velocity and bone age approximately equal to chronological age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This describes familial short stature 's comparison.
- B. Incorrect. Normal birth size, delayed puberty and delayed bone age are more consistent with constitutional delay.
- C. Incorrect. Cushing syndrome is a pathological endocrine cause of short stature.
- D. Incorrect. Reduced velocity and chronic symptoms raise concern for pathological growth failure.
- E. Incorrect. Disproportionate short limbs suggest skeletal dysplasia, such as achondroplasia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Familial short stature: positive family history, normal growth velocity, normal puberty, bone age ≈ chronological age, shorter predicted adult height.
- Constitutional delay: normal birth size, often boys, family history of delayed puberty, delayed bone age and later pubertal growth spurt.
- Both are normal variants, but the pattern and growth chart differ.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy is short, has not yet entered puberty, and has a family history of late puberty. His growth velocity is preserved and bone age is delayed. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: E
options.text: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

questions.correctAnswerText: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
questions.initialExplanation: Constitutional delay is characterized by delayed skeletal maturation and delayed puberty, often with a family history of late puberty. Growth velocity is usually preserved and adult height is generally expected to be within the normal range.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GH resistance causes impaired growth despite GH and typically low IGF-1.
- B. Incorrect. Familial short stature usually has normal pubertal timing and bone age similar to chronological age.
- C. Incorrect. Achondroplasia causes disproportionate short stature with short limbs.
- D. Incorrect. Cushing syndrome typically causes reduced height velocity with weight gain and characteristic clinical features.
- E. Correct. Delayed puberty, delayed bone age, preserved growth velocity and a family history of late puberty support constitutional delay.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is a common normal variant, especially in boys.
- Bone age is delayed.
- Pubertal growth spurt occurs later, but final height is usually near the expected genetic target.
- Reassess growth and exclude chronic/endocrine disease when the pattern is atypical.

cases.title: A child with disproportionate short stature and possible systemic disease
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child is short and has disproportionately short limbs compared with the trunk. Another child in the clinic has proportionate short stature with reduced growth velocity, fatigue and chronic abdominal symptoms. The clinician distinguishes skeletal dysplasia from endocrine, nutritional and chronic systemic causes.

questions.stem: A child has marked short limbs with a relatively preserved trunk. Which category of short stature does this represent?
questions.correctAnswerText: Disproportionate short stature
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance divides short stature into proportionate and disproportionate forms. Short limbs or a short trunk relative to the rest of the body indicates disproportionate growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Weight faltering alone does not define body-proportion abnormality.
- B. Correct. Short limbs relative to the trunk indicate disproportionate short stature.
- C. Incorrect. Familial short stature is a normal variant and does not automatically produce skeletal disproportion.
- D. Incorrect. Constitutional delay is a normal growth/puberty variant, not a skeletal disproportion diagnosis.
- E. Incorrect. Proportionate short stature involves similar reduction across body segments.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Proportionate: all body segments are reduced in a similar pattern.
- Disproportionate: one body segment is relatively shorter.
- Measure upper and lower segments and calculate the U/L segment ratio where indicated.

questions.stem: Which condition is associated with disproportionate short stature due to short limbs?
questions.correctAnswerText: Achondroplasia
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta and rickets among causes of disproportionate short stature with short limbs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Constitutional delay is usually proportionate.
- B. Incorrect. Coeliac disease may cause proportionate growth failure due to malabsorption.
- C. Incorrect. Familial short stature is usually proportionate.
- D. Incorrect. GH deficiency typically causes proportionate short stature.
- E. Correct. Achondroplasia is a classic skeletal dysplasia causing short-limb disproportion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Short limbs: achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta and rickets.
- Short trunk: kyphoscoliosis and mucopolysaccharidosis.
- Assess dysmorphic/skeletal features as part of the examination.

questions.stem: Which endocrine disorder is listed among pathological causes of short stature?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypothyroidism
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, Cushing syndrome and pseudohypoparathyroidism among endocrine causes of pathological short stature.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Primary polydipsia is not a listed endocrine cause of short stature.
- B. Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism is more often associated with accelerated growth/maturation rather than the classic short-stature endocrine list.
- C. Incorrect. Hyperaldosteronism is not listed as a typical cause of childhood short stature.
- D. Incorrect. Type 2 diabetes is not among the principal short-stature endocrine causes listed.
- E. Correct. Hypothyroidism can impair linear growth and delay skeletal maturation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Endocrine causes: hypothyroidism, GH deficiency/hypopituitarism, Cushing syndrome and pseudohypoparathyroidism.
- Chronic systemic causes include CHD, CF, malabsorption/coeliac disease, IBD, thalassaemia, CKD and JIA.
- Drugs (especially excess glucocorticoids), nutritional and psychosocial deprivation, IUGR/prematurity and genetic syndromes should also be considered.

questions.stem: A short child has delayed bone age on a left hand/wrist radiograph. Which set of conditions is associated with delayed bone age?

options.label: D
options.text: Hyperthyroidism, simple obesity, CAH and precocious puberty

options.label: E
options.text: Hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism, Cushing syndrome, delayed puberty and chronic illness/undernutrition

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism, Cushing syndrome, delayed puberty and chronic illness/undernutrition
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance table lists hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism, cortisol excess/Cushing syndrome, delayed puberty and chronic illness/undernutrition as causes of delayed bone age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Familial short stature usually has bone age similar to chronological age.
- B. Incorrect. Marfan syndrome is associated with tall stature, not the delayed-bone-age pattern in the table.
- C. Incorrect. Achondroplasia causes disproportionate skeletal growth; it is not the specific delayed-bone-age group listed.
- D. Incorrect. These are listed among causes of advanced bone age.
- E. Correct. These are the conditions listed under delayed bone age.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bone age is assessed by left hand/wrist radiograph; standard guidance references the Greulich–Pyle atlas.
- Delayed BA: hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism, Cushing, delayed puberty, chronic illness and undernutrition.
- Advanced BA: hyperthyroidism, simple obesity, CAH, precocious puberty and hyperpituitarism.

questions.stem: A child with short stature has dysmorphic features and suspected chronic disease. Which investigation set is most consistent with the workup described?

options.label: B
options.text: CBC, renal function, coeliac serology, TFT, IGF-1, bone age and karyotype when dysmorphic

options.label: D
options.text: Water deprivation test in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: CBC, renal function, coeliac serology, TFT, IGF-1, bone age and karyotype when dysmorphic
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include a broad, targeted short-stature workup including bone age, CBC, creatinine/urea, TTG, LFT, TFT, IGF-1, karyotype in dysmorphic children and selected special tests such as ESR/CRP, calcium/phosphate/ALP/vitamin D, MRI brain, GH stimulation, echocardiography and immunoglobulins.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stool culture is not a comprehensive short-stature evaluation.
- B. Correct. This matches the investigations listed and adapts them to a child with suspected chronic/systemic or genetic disease.
- C. Incorrect. Glucose alone is insufficient.
- D. Incorrect. Water deprivation testing is used for suspected DI, not routinely in short stature.
- E. Incorrect. ECG alone cannot assess the major endocrine, nutritional, renal or genetic causes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Start with history, examination, accurate growth measurements and bone age.
- Select tests based on the clinical pattern: CBC, renal, coeliac, liver, thyroid and IGF-1 studies as appropriate.
- Karyotype if dysmorphic features suggest chromosomal disease.
- Treatment is primarily directed at the underlying cause; selected children may be candidates for GH therapy.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed as a common normal-variant cause of tall stature?
questions.correctAnswerText: Familial/constitutional tall stature
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include familial/constitutional tall stature as the most common cause of excessive growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Cushing syndrome is associated with reduced height velocity in children.
- B. Incorrect. GH deficiency causes short stature.
- C. Incorrect. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is included among pathological causes of short stature.
- D. Incorrect. Hypothyroidism impairs linear growth.
- E. Correct. Familial tall stature is the commonest cause listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tall stature causes: familial (most common), idiopathic obesity, hyperthyroidism, androgen excess/CAH, GH excess/gigantism and precocious puberty.
- Syndromic causes include Marfan syndrome, homocystinuria, Klinefelter, Beckwith–Wiedemann and Sotos syndrome.
- Sotos syndrome may feature large head, characteristic facial features and learning difficulties.

questions.stem: An adolescent is unusually tall and has long limbs, joint laxity and a family history of aortic disease. Which syndrome from standard guidance should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Marfan syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Marfan syndrome is listed among syndromic causes of tall stature. The combination of tall stature, long limbs and a family history of aortic disease is a clinical prompt to assess for Marfan syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Down syndrome is commonly associated with short stature.
- B. Incorrect. Prader–Willi syndrome is associated with short stature and obesity/hypogonadism.
- C. Incorrect. Turner syndrome is associated with short stature.
- D. Correct. Marfan syndrome is a listed syndromic cause of tall stature and is associated with connective-tissue/aortic manifestations.
- E. Incorrect. Russell–Silver syndrome is associated with IUGR and short stature.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tall stature syndromes: Marfan, homocystinuria, Klinefelter (47,XXY), Beckwith–Wiedemann and Sotos.
- Assess body proportions and associated clinical features rather than assuming tall stature is familial.
- Growth assessment should include height velocity and pubertal status.

cases.title: Children with growth failure referred for endocrine assessment

questions.stem: A healthy 3-year-old girl was born at 36 weeks with intrauterine growth restriction. She has not shown catch-up growth and her height is now below the 3rd centile. Screening for chronic disease (blood count, creatinine, tissue transglutaminase, thyroid function) is normal. Her parents ask about her future height. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: About one third of children with IUGR remain short, and those who fail to catch up are among the recognised candidates for GH therapy

options.label: B
options.text: Children with IUGR typically catch up by 2 years, so no further follow-up is needed

options.label: C
options.text: GH therapy is contraindicated in short children born with IUGR

options.label: D
options.text: IUGR causes disproportionate short stature with short limbs

options.label: E
options.text: Short stature after IUGR indicates GH receptor resistance (Laron syndrome)

questions.correctAnswerText: About one third of children with IUGR remain short, and those who fail to catch up are among the recognised candidates for GH therapy
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that roughly one third of children born after IUGR (or extreme prematurity) remain short. It also lists "IUGR with failure of catch-up growth" as an indication for recombinant GH.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Persistent short stature after IUGR is common (about one third), and failure of catch-up is a listed indication for GH therapy after exclusion of other causes, as done here.
- B. Incorrect. One third of these children do not catch up, so continued growth surveillance is required.
- C. Incorrect. Clinical guidance this exact situation as an indication.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance places IUGR among causes of proportionate short stature. Short limbs suggest skeletal dysplasia such as achondroplasia.
- E. Incorrect. Laron syndrome shows high GH with low IGF-1. Nothing in this case suggests it.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IUGR and extreme prematurity: about one third remain short.
- GH indications: GHD, Turner syndrome, CKD, Prader–Willi syndrome, idiopathic short stature, IUGR without catch-up, SHOX deficiency.
- Exclude chronic disease before attributing short stature to IUGR.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Short stature, causes (Page 47); GH therapy indications (Page 7).

cases.title: An adolescent undergoing assessment of pubertal development
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old girl is brought for assessment of breast development. Her parents are concerned that puberty has started. The clinician explains the normal age range, the first signs of puberty in girls and boys, the pubertal growth spurt and how Tanner staging is used to document sexual maturity.

questions.stem: Which term describes the first appearance of breast tissue in a girl?
questions.correctAnswerText: Thelarche
questions.initialExplanation: Thelarche refers to the appearance of breast tissue and is usually the first clinical sign of puberty in girls.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pubarche is the appearance of pubic hair.
- B. Incorrect. Spermarche is the first ejaculation.
- C. Incorrect. Adrenarche refers to maturation of adrenal androgen production and may lead to pubic/axillary hair, body odour and acne; it is not the same as gonadal puberty.
- D. Incorrect. Menarche is the first menstrual period.
- E. Correct. Thelarche is breast development.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Thelarche: breast development.
- Pubarche: appearance of pubic hair.
- Menarche: first menstrual period.
- Spermarche: first ejaculation.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl has breast development at Tanner breast stage 2. Which statement is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: This is the last stage of female puberty

options.label: C
options.text: This is the usual first clinical sign of female puberty

options.label: E
options.text: It is diagnostic of precocious puberty at across the age range

questions.correctAnswerText: This is the usual first clinical sign of female puberty
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include breast enlargement (thelarche), corresponding to breast stage 2, as the first sign of puberty in girls. Normal onset is usually 8–13 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. At age 12, breast stage 2 is within the normal range.
- B. Incorrect. Breast stage 5 is the mature stage.
- C. Correct. Breast stage 2 is the onset of breast development and the first clinical sign of female puberty.
- D. Incorrect. Menarche is the first menstrual period and occurs later.
- E. Incorrect. Precocious puberty is defined by onset before age 8 in girls, not by Tanner stage alone.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal female puberty onset: 8–13 years.
- First sign: thelarche/Breast Tanner stage 2.
- Menarche is usually the last major pubertal milestone in girls, occurring on average about 2.5 years after puberty begins.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy is assessed for delayed puberty. Which finding represents the first clinical sign of normal male puberty?
questions.correctAnswerText: Testicular enlargement to approximately 4 mL
questions.initialExplanation: The first sign of male puberty is testicular enlargement, reaching approximately 4 mL as measured by an orchidometer.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Axillary hair occurs later in pubertal development.
- B. Correct. Testicular enlargement to approximately 4 mL is the first sign.
- C. Incorrect. Pubic hair generally follows testicular enlargement.
- D. Incorrect. Voice changes occur later.
- E. Incorrect. Spermarche is a late pubertal event.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal male puberty onset: 9–14 years.
- First sign: testicular enlargement to about 4 mL (orchidometer).
- Pubic hair follows, then scrotal skin changes and penile growth.
- The male pubertal growth spurt occurs later than the female growth spurt.

questions.stem: Which description correctly matches Tanner staging of female breast development?

options.label: A
options.text: B3 is the first appearance of pubic hair

options.label: D
options.text: B2 is breast bud with enlargement of the areola; B5 is adult breast with projection of the papilla as the areola recedes

options.label: E
options.text: B1 is adult breast; B5 is prepubertal

questions.correctAnswerText: B2 is breast bud with enlargement of the areola; B5 is adult breast with projection of the papilla as the areola recedes
questions.initialExplanation: The PDF Tanner diagram shows B1 as prepubertal, B2 as breast bud with areolar enlargement, B3 as a juvenile smooth contour, B4 as projection of the areola and papilla above the breast, and B5 as adult breast with projection of the papilla as the areola recedes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Tanner breast staging assesses breast maturation, not pubic hair.
- B. Incorrect. Tanner staging records physical sexual maturation, not chronological age alone.
- C. Incorrect. Testicular development is recorded using male genital stages (G1–G5).
- D. Correct. This matches the B2 and B5 descriptions in the PDF diagram.
- E. Incorrect. The order is reversed; B1 is prepubertal and B5 is adult.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tanner staging is also called Sexual Maturity Rating (SMR).
- Female breast stages: B1–B5.
- Male genital stages: G1–G5.
- Pubic hair stages: PH1–PH5.
- Use the physical examination diagram and describe the observed stage rather than inferring stage from age.

cases.title: Four children referred for pubertal or growth concerns

questions.stem: A 11.5-year-old girl had breast budding at 9.5 years and pubic hair at 10 years. Axillary hair has appeared and she has grown rapidly this year, but she has not had a period. Her mother fears delayed menstruation. What is the best response?

options.label: A
options.text: Karyotype and gonadotropin levels for delayed puberty

options.label: B
options.text: Pelvic ultrasound and a trial of oestradiol

options.label: C
options.text: Normal sequence; menarche usually follows breast onset by about 2.5 years, after the growth spurt

options.label: D
options.text: MRI of the brain to exclude a pituitary lesion

options.label: E
options.text: Treatment with a GnRH analogue to slow progression

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal sequence; menarche usually follows breast onset by about 2.5 years, after the growth spurt
questions.initialExplanation: In girls, puberty starts with breast enlargement, followed by pubic hair, axillary hair and menarche. The growth spurt occurs early, immediately after breast enlargement. Menarche is the last sign, on average 2.5 years after onset.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Delayed puberty means no development by 13 years in girls. She started at 9.5 years.
- B. Incorrect. No investigation or oestrogen is needed for a normal progression.
- C. Correct. Onset at 9.5 years is within the normal 8–13 years range. Menarche at about 12 years is expected.
- D. Incorrect. There are no neurological or atypical features.
- E. Incorrect. Onset after 8 years is not precocious.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Girls: onset 8–13 years; first sign thelarche (Tanner breast stage 2). Boys: onset 9–14 years; first sign testicular volume about 4 mL.
- Girls' growth spurt is early; boys' growth spurt occurs late (about 18 months after testicular enlargement).
- Menarche (girls) and first ejaculation (boys) are the last signs of puberty.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Puberty: features and sequence (Page 49).

topics.name: Precocious Puberty — Central and Peripheral Causes

cases.title: A young girl with early breast development and rapid growth
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old girl develops progressive breast enlargement, pubic hair and a rapid increase in height. Her bone age is advanced. The clinician must decide whether this represents central activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis or peripheral sex-steroid production.

questions.stem: What age cut-off defines precocious puberty?

options.label: C
options.text: Pubic hair at across the age range

options.label: D
options.text: Secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years in girls or before 9 years in boys

options.label: E
options.text: Puberty before 13 years in girls or before 14 years in boys

questions.correctAnswerText: Secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years in girls or before 9 years in boys
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe precocious puberty as development of secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years in girls and before 9 years in boys.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Precocious puberty is defined by the early appearance of secondary sexual characteristics, not menarche alone.
- B. Incorrect. Testicular enlargement after 14 years suggests delayed, not precocious, puberty.
- C. Incorrect. Pubic hair alone may represent premature adrenarche and does not necessarily indicate central puberty.
- D. Correct. These are the age thresholds shown.
- E. Incorrect. These are the thresholds used for delayed puberty.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Precocious puberty: <8 years in girls and <9 years in boys.
- Distinguish true central puberty from peripheral sex-steroid effects and isolated early thelarche/pubarche.
- Progression, growth acceleration and bone age help determine significance.

questions.stem: A girl has progressive breast development, pubic hair, growth acceleration and elevated LH/FSH in a pubertal pattern. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Central (true) precocious puberty
questions.initialExplanation: Central precocious puberty is gonadotropin-dependent and results from premature activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis. Pubertal signs are generally concordant and gonadotropins rise.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Premature adrenarche produces pubic/axillary hair without full gonadal puberty.
- B. Incorrect. Peripheral PP is gonadotropin-independent, with low LH/FSH and often discordant signs.
- C. Incorrect. Delayed puberty is absence of pubertal development beyond the expected age threshold.
- D. Incorrect. Isolated premature thelarche produces breast development without other signs of puberty or growth acceleration.
- E. Correct. Progressive, concordant pubertal changes with a pubertal gonadotropin pattern support central PP.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Central PP: gonadotropin-dependent, high/puberty-range LH and FSH, concordant signs, early activation of the HPG axis.
- Peripheral PP: gonadotropin-independent, low LH/FSH, often discordant signs from sex steroids produced outside the pituitary.
- Bone age is commonly advanced in progressive precocious puberty.

questions.stem: Which is a recognized cause of central precocious puberty listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypothalamic/pituitary activation due to a CNS tumour such as craniopharyngioma

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypothalamic/pituitary activation due to a CNS tumour such as craniopharyngioma
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include idiopathic central PP, congenital CNS abnormalities, acquired CNS injury/infection/surgery/irradiation and CNS tumours such as craniopharyngioma and neurofibromatosis-associated lesions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. CNS lesions can trigger premature activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis.
- B. Incorrect. Leydig-cell tumours produce testosterone independently of pituitary gonadotropins.
- C. Incorrect. Ovarian granulosa-cell tumours are causes of peripheral, gonadotropin-independent PP.
- D. Incorrect. Adrenal tumours and CAH are peripheral androgen sources.
- E. Incorrect. Exogenous sex steroids produce peripheral PP.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Central PP causes: idiopathic (common in girls), congenital CNS anomaly/hydrocephalus, acquired CNS injury/infection/surgery/irradiation and tumours.
- Hypothyroidism is also listed among causes associated with precocious pubertal features.
- CNS evaluation is particularly important in boys and in children with neurological symptoms or atypical features.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has breast development and vaginal bleeding. LH and FSH are suppressed. Ultrasound shows an ovarian mass. What is the most likely mechanism?

options.label: A
options.text: Delayed puberty due to gonadal failure

options.label: D
options.text: Autonomous ovarian sex-steroid production causing peripheral precocious puberty

options.label: E
options.text: Premature activation of the HPG axis

questions.correctAnswerText: Autonomous ovarian sex-steroid production causing peripheral precocious puberty
questions.initialExplanation: An ovarian granulosa-cell tumour may produce oestrogen independently of pituitary gonadotropins, causing peripheral/pseudo precocious puberty with suppressed LH/FSH.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Gonadal failure leads to delayed pubertal development, often with elevated gonadotropins.
- B. Incorrect. ADH deficiency causes diabetes insipidus.
- C. Incorrect. At age 7, progressive puberty is precocious by standard guidance's threshold.
- D. Correct. Autonomous ovarian oestrogen production causes gonadotropin-independent puberty.
- E. Incorrect. Central activation produces a pubertal gonadotropin response.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Peripheral PP: low LH/FSH and sex steroids produced outside the pituitary.
- Causes include adrenal tumour/CAH, ovarian granulosa-cell tumour, testicular Leydig-cell tumour, exogenous sex steroids and McCune–Albright syndrome.
- Clinical signs may be discordant (e.g. isolated oestrogen or androgen effect).

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl has café-au-lait pigmentation, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and progressive precocious puberty. Which syndrome is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: McCune–Albright syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: The PDF page 52 shows the classic McCune–Albright triad: precocious puberty, café-au-lait macules (often described as coast of Maine) and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pendred syndrome is associated with goitre and sensorineural hearing loss.
- B. Incorrect. Turner syndrome causes gonadal dysgenesis and delayed puberty/short stature.
- C. Incorrect. Russell–Silver syndrome is associated with IUGR and short stature.
- D. Correct. This is the classical triad of McCune–Albright syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome may cause hypergonadotropic hypogonadism in boys.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- McCune–Albright: precocious puberty + café-au-lait + polyostotic fibrous dysplasia.
- It may also involve autonomous hyperfunction in other endocrine organs: hyperthyroidism, hyperadrenalism, gigantism/acromegaly and hypophosphataemic rickets.
- More commonly presents in girls.

questions.stem: After examination and pubertal staging, which investigation group is listed for a child with suspected precocious puberty?

options.label: D
options.text: Bone age, pelvic ultrasound in girls, LH/FSH and sex-steroid levels, and MRI of brain/pituitary when indicated

options.label: E
options.text: Water deprivation test and urine culture

questions.correctAnswerText: Bone age, pelvic ultrasound in girls, LH/FSH and sex-steroid levels, and MRI of brain/pituitary when indicated
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes assessment after careful examination and pubertal staging, with bone age, pelvic ultrasound in girls, gonadotropin and sex-steroid levels, and MRI brain/pituitary.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These tests investigate cystic fibrosis and respiratory disease.
- B. Incorrect. These tests assess gastrointestinal inflammation/infection, not puberty.
- C. Incorrect. These tests investigate gastrointestinal conditions, not the pubertal axis.
- D. Correct. These are the investigations listed on the source page.
- E. Incorrect. Water deprivation testing assesses DI.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bone age helps assess skeletal advancement.
- Pelvic ultrasound can assess uterus/ovaries in girls.
- LH/FSH and sex hormones help distinguish central and peripheral PP.
- MRI is selected according to clinical/biochemical assessment, especially when central pathology is suspected.

cases.title: Four children referred for pubertal or growth concerns

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has Tanner breast stage 3, pubic hair stage 2 and one episode of vaginal spotting. She is short (2 SD below the mean), overweight and has constipation, dry skin and a heart rate of 58/min. Bone age is 4.5 years. TSH is markedly elevated with low free T4. Pelvic ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries with cysts. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.text: Levothyroxine for primary hypothyroidism, reassessing puberty once euthyroid

options.label: B
options.text: Long-acting GnRH analogue for central precocious puberty

options.label: C
options.text: Oestrogen-receptor antagonist as for peripheral precocious puberty

options.label: E
options.text: MRI of the brain, then GnRH analogue

questions.correctAnswerText: Levothyroxine for primary hypothyroidism, reassessing puberty once euthyroid
questions.initialExplanation: Precocious puberty can rarely occur in hypothyroidism, and Clinical guidance hypothyroidism among the causes. The pattern here, with growth failure and delayed bone age, is the opposite of true precocious puberty (accelerated growth and advanced bone age). The cause, hypothyroidism, must be treated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Key discriminators. Short stature, bradycardia, constipation, dry skin, delayed bone age and very high TSH point to severe primary hypothyroidism. Progressive true precocious puberty would show tall stature and advanced bone age.
- A. Correct. Treat the underlying cause. The pubertal signs commonly regress with thyroid replacement.
- B. Incorrect. GnRH analogues treat true central precocious puberty. The cause here is thyroid failure.
- C. Incorrect. Receptor antagonists are for peripheral causes of oestrogen excess, which this is not.
- D. Incorrect. The cysts are secondary and need no surgery.
- E. Incorrect. Neuro-imaging and GnRH treatment would not address the cause.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Precocious puberty: signs before 8 years in girls and before 9 years in boys.
- Hypothyroidism: delayed puberty is typical, but precocious puberty may occur (rare).
- Delayed bone age: hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism, Cushing syndrome. Advanced bone age: precocious puberty, CAH, hyperthyroidism, simple obesity.
- Treat the cause; GnRH analogues are for true (central) precocious puberty.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Acquired hypothyroidism (Pages 11, 14); precocious puberty causes and treatment (Pages 51–52); bone age (Page 48).

topics.name: Isolated Premature Thelarche and Premature Adrenarche

cases.title: A toddler with isolated breast enlargement
cases.vignette: A 16-month-old girl is brought because of breast enlargement noticed by her parents. There is no pubic hair, vaginal bleeding, growth acceleration or other sign of sexual maturation. The breast enlargement has not progressed beyond an early stage. The child is otherwise healthy.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely in a 16-month-old girl with isolated breast enlargement and no other pubertal signs?
questions.correctAnswerText: Isolated premature thelarche
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include isolated premature thelarche as breast enlargement, usually between 6 months and 2 years, without other signs of puberty or significant growth acceleration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Delayed puberty is absence of expected pubertal development beyond the age threshold.
- B. Incorrect. Addison disease causes adrenal insufficiency, not isolated breast enlargement.
- C. Correct. This matches the described age and isolated breast development.
- D. Incorrect. Pseudohypoparathyroidism causes PTH resistance, short stature and characteristic skeletal features.
- E. Incorrect. Central PP is usually progressive and accompanied by other concordant pubertal changes and/or growth acceleration.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Isolated premature thelarche: typically 6 months–2 years.
- Breast enlargement may be asymmetric and usually does not progress beyond early stages.
- No other pubertal sign or significant growth acceleration.
- Often benign and self-limiting; reassurance and follow-up are usually sufficient.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has pubic hair but no breast development, no significant growth acceleration and no other evidence of gonadal puberty. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: E
options.text: Ovarian granulosa-cell tumour in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Premature adrenarche
questions.initialExplanation: Premature adrenarche is due to early adrenal androgen production and can cause pubic hair before age 8 in girls or 9 in boys without other signs of sexual development or significant growth acceleration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Central PP usually produces concordant gonadal changes such as breast development in girls.
- B. Incorrect. Delayed puberty is lack of expected pubertal development at older ages.
- C. Correct. Isolated pubic hair without gonadal puberty supports premature adrenarche.
- D. Incorrect. Hypothyroidism may cause growth and pubertal disturbance but does not explain this typical isolated adrenal androgen presentation.
- E. Incorrect. Ovarian tumours are uncommon causes of peripheral PP; isolated adrenarche is usually benign.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Premature adrenarche/pubarche: pubic hair <8 years in girls or <9 years in boys.
- No other sign of puberty or significant growth acceleration.
- Caused by increased adrenal androgen production.
- Usually self-limiting; common in Asian and Afro-Caribbean children.

questions.stem: What is an appropriate approach to a child with premature adrenarche?

options.label: C
options.text: Clinical follow-up, assess bone age/ultrasound as indicated, and exclude central precocious puberty and CAH

options.label: E
options.text: Immediate GnRH analogue treatment in most children

questions.correctAnswerText: Clinical follow-up, assess bone age/ultrasound as indicated, and exclude central precocious puberty and CAH
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance advises follow-up in premature adrenarche, with bone age and ultrasound when needed to exclude central precocious puberty and investigations to exclude CAH. Most cases are benign and self-limiting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Surgery is not indicated for the usual benign condition.
- B. Incorrect. An important point is follow-up; progression or growth acceleration requires reassessment.
- C. Correct. This reflects the evaluation and follow-up guidance shown on pages 52–53.
- D. Incorrect. Levothyroxine is used for hypothyroidism, not routine premature adrenarche.
- E. Incorrect. GnRH analogues are used for selected cases of true central PP, not uncomplicated premature adrenarche.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Reassurance and follow-up are central.
- Bone age and pelvic ultrasound are selected according to progression and clinical concern.
- Exclude CAH and central PP when features are atypical/progressive.
- Isolated premature thelarche also usually requires reassurance/follow-up rather than treatment.

cases.title: An adolescent boy with absent pubertal development
cases.vignette: A 15-year-old boy is referred because he has not developed testicular enlargement or other signs of puberty. He is short compared with classmates and has a family history of late puberty. Bone age is delayed.

questions.stem: How is delayed puberty defined?

options.label: A
options.text: Pubic hair absent at 8 years in girls

options.label: B
options.text: Testicular volume below 4 mL at 8 years

options.label: E
options.text: No pubertal development by 13 years in girls or 14 years in boys

questions.correctAnswerText: No pubertal development by 13 years in girls or 14 years in boys
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe delayed puberty as absence of pubertal development by 13 years in girls and 14 years in boys.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pubic hair is not the defining first sign of puberty and absence at 8 years is not delayed puberty.
- B. Incorrect. Testicular volume below 4 mL at 8 years is prepubertal and not delayed.
- C. Incorrect. Breast development is not expected at 5 years.
- D. Incorrect. Menarche normally occurs later than age 10 and its absence at that age alone does not define delayed puberty.
- E. Correct. These are the age cut-offs stated in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Delayed puberty: no development by 13 years in girls or 14 years in boys.
- It is more common in boys and is often constitutional delay/familial.
- Delayed puberty in girls is less common; pathological causes should be excluded.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy has delayed puberty, delayed bone age, normal growth velocity and a family history of late puberty. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: E
options.text: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

questions.correctAnswerText: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
questions.initialExplanation: Constitutional delay is a common cause of delayed puberty in boys, often associated with a family history of late maturation and delayed bone age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. McCune–Albright is associated with peripheral precocious puberty.
- B. Incorrect. Central PP is early pubertal development.
- C. Incorrect. Graves causes hyperthyroidism and is not the typical diagnosis.
- D. Incorrect. Turner syndrome affects girls and is associated with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
- E. Correct. This is the typical clinical pattern described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Constitutional delay is a common normal variant, particularly in boys.
- Family history of delayed puberty and delayed bone age support the diagnosis.
- Follow growth velocity and pubertal progression; exclude systemic disease if the pattern is atypical.

questions.stem: Which pair of conditions is associated with high gonadotropin secretion in delayed puberty?
questions.correctAnswerText: Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance separates causes of delayed puberty by gonadotropin level. Chromosomal abnormalities such as Turner syndrome (45,XO) and Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) are listed under high gonadotropin secretion due to gonadal failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Systemic disease and anorexia are listed under low gonadotropin secretion.
- B. Correct. Both are chromosomal/gonadal causes with elevated gonadotropins.
- C. Incorrect. Acquired hypothyroidism and systemic illness may cause hypogonadotropic delay.
- D. Incorrect. Intracranial tumour and GnRH deficiency are hypogonadotropic causes.
- E. Incorrect. Kallmann syndrome and panhypopituitarism cause low gonadotropin secretion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Low gonadotropins: hypothalamic/pituitary disorders, GnRH/Kallmann, intracranial tumour, systemic disease and acquired hypothyroidism.
- High gonadotropins: Turner, Klinefelter and gonadal injury after surgery/trauma/radiotherapy/chemotherapy.
- Girls with delayed puberty need careful exclusion of pathological causes.

questions.stem: Which investigation plan is appropriate for an adolescent girl with delayed puberty in whom Turner syndrome or pituitary disease is suspected?

options.label: B
options.text: Karyotype, thyroid and sex-steroid hormone assessment, and MRI if pituitary pathology is suspected

questions.correctAnswerText: Karyotype, thyroid and sex-steroid hormone assessment, and MRI if pituitary pathology is suspected
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes karyotyping when Turner syndrome is suspected, measuring thyroid and sex-steroid hormones and excluding pituitary pathology by MRI.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These tests investigate gastrointestinal inflammation, not pubertal failure.
- B. Correct. This is the investigation approach stated.
- C. Incorrect. Water deprivation testing is for DI.
- D. Incorrect. These investigations do not assess the cause of delayed puberty.
- E. Incorrect. Anti-TPO may help assess autoimmune thyroid disease but is not a sufficient evaluation for delayed puberty.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Investigate according to gonadotropin pattern and clinical context.
- Karyotype for suspected Turner/Klinefelter syndrome.
- Measure thyroid and sex-steroid hormones.
- MRI if a central/pituitary cause is suspected.
- Treat underlying pathology; selected girls may receive specialist-supervised low-dose oestradiol to initiate puberty.

cases.title: Four children referred for pubertal or growth concerns

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy is tall (above the 97th centile) and has no pubertal development. Testicular volume is 3 mL. LH and FSH are raised and testosterone is low. Thyroid function is normal. Which investigation will confirm the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Karyotype
questions.initialExplanation: Delayed puberty with high gonadotropins signals gonadal failure. Of the high-gonadotropin causes (Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome, gonadal injury), only Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) occurs in a boy and is also a listed syndromic cause of tall stature.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Reasoning. Low testosterone with raised LH/FSH shows the pituitary is working and the testes are failing (hypergonadotropic). Tall stature plus male sex leads to Klinefelter syndrome.
- A. Incorrect. A GnRH test would be relevant for hypogonadotropic states.
- B. Incorrect. MRI looks for hypothalamic-pituitary disease, which gives low gonadotropins.
- C. Incorrect. GH assessment does not apply to a tall boy.
- D. Correct. Karyotype shows 47,XXY. clinical guidance advises karyotype for suspected sex chromosome causes of delayed puberty.
- E. Incorrect. 17-OHP assesses CAH, which does not cause this picture.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Delayed puberty (no development by 13 years in girls, 14 in boys): low gonadotropins (hypothalamic-pituitary disorders, GnRH deficiency, Kallmann, systemic disease, hypothyroidism) vs high gonadotropins (Turner, Klinefelter, gonadal damage).
- Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is also a listed cause of tall stature.
- Karyotype, thyroid and sex steroid hormones, and MRI if pituitary pathology is suspected.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Delayed puberty (Page 53); causes of tall stature (Page 48).

cases.title: A child with a low serum calcium concentration
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child is evaluated after a blood test shows low serum calcium. The clinician reviews the difference between total and ionized calcium and the role of parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and calcitonin in maintaining calcium balance.

questions.stem: Which form of circulating calcium is physiologically active?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ionized calcium
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include approximately 50% of circulating calcium as ionized calcium, which is the physiologically active fraction. Protein-bound calcium is not freely diffusible/active.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bone is a major calcium store, but the question asks for the active circulating form.
- B. Correct. Ionized calcium is the active circulating form.
- C. Incorrect. Albumin-bound calcium is part of the non-diffusible fraction.
- D. Incorrect. Globulin-bound calcium is also protein-bound and not the active free fraction.
- E. Incorrect. Calcium complexed with citrate, bicarbonate or phosphate is diffusible but non-ionized.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Approximate calcium fractions: 45% protein-bound, 5% complexed and 50% ionized.
- Ionized calcium is the physiologically active form.
- Interpret total calcium with albumin and consider ionized calcium when protein levels or acid–base status are abnormal.

questions.stem: Which combination best describes the actions of PTH that raise serum calcium?

options.label: A
options.text: Increases phosphate reabsorption and blocks intestinal calcium absorption

options.label: B
options.text: Promotes calcium release from bone, increases renal calcium reabsorption, increases phosphate excretion and stimulates calcitriol production

options.label: C
options.text: Increases renal calcium excretion, reduces calcitriol and suppresses bone resorption

options.label: D
options.text: Suppresses calcium absorption in the small intestine

questions.correctAnswerText: Promotes calcium release from bone, increases renal calcium reabsorption, increases phosphate excretion and stimulates calcitriol production
questions.initialExplanation: PTH acts on bone and kidney, increases renal calcium reabsorption, increases phosphate excretion and promotes renal activation of vitamin D (calcitriol), which increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. PTH promotes phosphate excretion rather than increased renal phosphate reabsorption.
- B. Correct. This integrates the main actions shown in the calcium-homeostasis diagram.
- C. Incorrect. These effects would lower serum calcium and oppose PTH action.
- D. Incorrect. PTH increases calcitriol, which increases intestinal calcium absorption.
- E. Incorrect. PTH acts mainly on bone and kidneys, with indirect intestinal effects through calcitriol.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Calcium homeostasis is controlled mainly by PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin.
- PTH increases serum calcium through bone/kidney actions and increased calcitriol.
- PTH increases renal phosphate excretion, so serum phosphate often falls in primary hyperparathyroidism.
- Calcitriol increases intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.

cases.title: A child with tetany after thyroid surgery
cases.vignette: A 12-year-old child develops perioral tingling, muscle cramps and carpopedal spasm after thyroid surgery. The child is irritable and has a prolonged QT interval. Laboratory tests reveal low serum calcium and high phosphate.

questions.stem: Which is a recognized cause of hypoparathyroidism in a child?

options.label: C
options.text: Accidental or surgical damage/removal of parathyroid tissue during thyroidectomy

options.label: E
options.text: Excess calcitonin secretion as the possible cause

questions.correctAnswerText: Accidental or surgical damage/removal of parathyroid tissue during thyroidectomy
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include iatrogenic hypoparathyroidism after thyroidectomy, congenital causes such as DiGeorge syndrome, autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 and transient neonatal hypoparathyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Excess PTH produces hyperparathyroidism.
- B. Incorrect. Vitamin D increases calcium absorption and does not cause the typical PTH-deficient pattern.
- C. Correct. Thyroid surgery can damage or remove parathyroid glands, reducing PTH secretion.
- D. Incorrect. Graves disease is autoimmune hyperthyroidism, not a direct cause of hypoparathyroidism.
- E. Incorrect. Calcitonin is not listed as the usual cause of childhood hypoparathyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Causes: congenital (especially DiGeorge), post-thyroidectomy, autoimmune (APS1) and transient neonatal.
- Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia due to reduced PTH.
- Consider neonatal transient hypoparathyroidism in preterm, infant-of-diabetic-mother and asphyxiated newborns.

questions.stem: Which clinical manifestation is characteristic of significant hypocalcaemia due to hypoparathyroidism?
questions.correctAnswerText: Carpopedal spasm and tetany
questions.initialExplanation: Hypocalcaemia increases neuromuscular excitability and can cause paresthesia, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, hoarseness, stridor and seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests thyrotoxicosis/Graves disease.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests primary adrenal insufficiency.
- C. Correct. Tetany and carpopedal spasm are classic manifestations of hypocalcaemia.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests diabetes insipidus.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests Cushing syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hypocalcaemia may present with paresthesia, cramps, hyperirritability, carpopedal spasm, hoarseness, stridor and seizures.
- Severe hypocalcaemia is an emergency.
- standard guidance uses serum calcium below approximately 8.5 mg/dL as a clinical threshold; interpret according to albumin, ionized calcium and local laboratory range.

questions.stem: Tapping over the facial nerve causes contraction of the facial muscles in a child with suspected latent tetany. What is this sign called?
questions.correctAnswerText: Chvostek sign
questions.initialExplanation: Chvostek sign is facial muscle contraction after tapping over the facial nerve and may indicate latent tetany due to hypocalcaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Rovsing sign is associated with appendicitis.
- B. Incorrect. Babinski sign is a plantar reflex used in neurological examination.
- C. Incorrect. Trousseau sign is carpal spasm induced by compression of the upper arm, such as with a blood-pressure cuff.
- D. Correct. This is the definition of Chvostek sign.
- E. Incorrect. Murphy sign is associated with gallbladder inflammation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chvostek: tap facial nerve → facial muscle contraction.
- Trousseau: upper-arm cuff compression → carpal spasm.
- These are signs of latent tetany and should be interpreted in clinical context.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern is most consistent with hypoparathyroidism?

options.label: A
options.text: High calcium, high phosphate and low PTH

options.label: B
options.text: Low calcium, low phosphate and high PTH

options.label: C
options.text: High calcium, low phosphate and high PTH

options.label: D
options.text: Low calcium, high phosphate and low PTH

options.label: E
options.text: Normal calcium and phosphate with high PTH

questions.correctAnswerText: Low calcium, high phosphate and low PTH
questions.initialExplanation: In hypoparathyroidism, PTH secretion is low. Reduced renal calcium reabsorption and reduced phosphate excretion produce hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the typical pattern of PTH deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Low calcium with high PTH suggests vitamin D deficiency or another secondary response.
- C. Incorrect. This is the typical pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism.
- D. Correct. This is the biochemical pattern given.
- E. Incorrect. High PTH with normal calcium/phosphate may occur in pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, but the question asks for true hypoparathyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hypoparathyroidism: low PTH, low calcium, high phosphate; ALP is normal or low.
- PTH should rise in response to hypocalcaemia; a low or inappropriately normal result is abnormal.
- Check magnesium, vitamin D, renal function and albumin when evaluating hypocalcaemia.

questions.stem: A newborn with a conotruncal cardiac defect, abnormal facial features, cleft palate, recurrent infections and hypocalcaemic seizures is suspected of having DiGeorge syndrome. Which underlying abnormality explains the combination?

options.label: B
options.text: 22q11 deletion causing thymic and parathyroid developmental abnormalities

questions.correctAnswerText: 22q11 deletion causing thymic and parathyroid developmental abnormalities
questions.initialExplanation: DiGeorge syndrome is associated with a microdeletion on chromosome 22 and abnormal development of the thymus and parathyroid glands, causing T-cell deficiency and hypocalcaemia. Key features include the CATCH-22 mnemonic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes CAH with cortisol/aldosterone deficiency and androgen excess.
- B. Correct. A chromosome 22 microdeletion leads to the characteristic cardiac, facial, thymic, cleft palate and hypocalcaemic features.
- C. Incorrect. Renal ADH resistance causes nephrogenic DI.
- D. Incorrect. GH receptor resistance causes Laron syndrome and short stature.
- E. Incorrect. TSH-receptor antibodies cause Graves disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DiGeorge syndrome: chromosome 22 microdeletion (classically 22q11).
- CATCH-22: Cardiac abnormalities, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia/T-cell defect, Cleft palate, Hypocalcaemia.
- Hypocalcaemia may cause neonatal tetany or seizures.
- Consider immune assessment due to thymic/T-cell abnormality.

topics.name: Pseudohypoparathyroidism and Other Causes of Hypocalcaemia

cases.title: A child with short stature, round face and low calcium despite high PTH
cases.vignette: An 8-year-old child is short, has a round face, stocky habitus and shortened fourth and fifth metacarpals. Laboratory testing shows low calcium and high phosphate, but PTH is elevated.

questions.stem: What is the underlying mechanism of pseudohypoparathyroidism?

options.label: A
options.text: End-organ resistance to PTH due to a defect in intracellular receptor signalling

options.label: B
options.text: Autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicular cells

options.label: D
options.text: Excess PTH production by a parathyroid adenoma

questions.correctAnswerText: End-organ resistance to PTH due to a defect in intracellular receptor signalling
questions.initialExplanation: Pseudohypoparathyroidism is caused by resistance of target organs to PTH action, commonly due to a defect in intracellular signalling. PTH is elevated because the glands respond to low calcium by increasing secretion, but the tissues do not respond appropriately.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the mechanism described.
- B. Incorrect. Autoimmune thyroiditis causes Hashimoto disease.
- C. Incorrect. Absence of PTH secretion causes true hypoparathyroidism, not pseudohypoparathyroidism.
- D. Incorrect. A parathyroid adenoma causes primary hyperparathyroidism.
- E. Incorrect. Calcitonin excess is not the mechanism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pseudohypoparathyroidism: target-organ resistance to PTH.
- Biochemistry: low calcium, high phosphate and high PTH.
- Clinical descriptions include autosomal dominant inheritance in association with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.

questions.stem: Which physical feature is characteristic of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy in pseudohypoparathyroidism?

options.label: A
options.text: Short fourth and fifth metacarpals with a dimple sign

options.label: C
options.text: Café-au-lait macules with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia

options.label: D
options.text: Short limbs with a prominent forehead and trident hands

options.label: E
options.text: Enlarged hands and feet with coarse facial features

questions.correctAnswerText: Short fourth and fifth metacarpals with a dimple sign
