questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include short stature, round face, stocky/obese habitus, short fourth and fifth metacarpals with a dimple sign, intellectual disability and basal ganglia calcification as features of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Short fourth/fifth metacarpals may produce a dimple over the knuckle when making a fist.
- B. Incorrect. Arachnodactyly is associated with Marfan syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. This is the classic pattern of McCune–Albright syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. This describes skeletal features of achondroplasia rather than Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.
- E. Incorrect. Coarse features and enlarged hands/feet suggest other endocrine/metabolic disorders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Albright hereditary osteodystrophy: round face, stocky habitus, short 4th/5th metacarpals, dimple sign, short stature and possible intellectual disability/basal ganglia calcification.
- It is associated with pseudohypoparathyroidism when PTH resistance is present.
- Match the phenotype with calcium/phosphate/PTH results.

questions.stem: A patient has the same physical phenotype as Albright hereditary osteodystrophy, but serum calcium and phosphate are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism
questions.initialExplanation: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism has the Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype but without biochemical evidence of PTH resistance; Clinical guidance notes normal serum calcium and phosphate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. DiGeorge syndrome is associated with congenital hypoparathyroidism, cardiac and thymic abnormalities.
- B. Incorrect. True hypoparathyroidism causes low calcium, high phosphate and low PTH.
- C. Incorrect. Vitamin D deficiency usually causes low/low-normal calcium, low phosphate and secondary elevation of PTH.
- D. Correct. The phenotype is present but calcium/phosphate homeostasis is normal.
- E. Incorrect. Primary hyperparathyroidism usually causes high calcium, low phosphate and high PTH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pseudohypoparathyroidism: AHO phenotype + PTH resistance + low Ca/high phosphate/high PTH.
- Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism: AHO phenotype but normal calcium and phosphate.
- Biochemistry distinguishes the two.

questions.stem: Which is a recognized alternative cause of hypocalcaemia in an infant or child apart from hypoparathyroidism?
questions.correctAnswerText: Vitamin D deficiency
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease, hypomagnesaemia/hyperphosphataemia, malabsorption, low albumin, liver disease, tumour lysis syndrome and massive blood transfusion as other causes of hypocalcaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Familial tall stature is a normal growth variant.
- B. Incorrect. Precocious puberty is unrelated to calcium deficiency.
- C. Correct. Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal calcium absorption and can cause hypocalcaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Cushing syndrome is not listed among the principal hypocalcaemia causes.
- E. Incorrect. Graves disease is not a standard cause of hypocalcaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Other hypocalcaemia causes: vitamin D deficiency, CKD, low magnesium, high phosphate, malabsorption, low albumin, liver disease, tumour lysis and massive transfusion.
- Consider ionized calcium when albumin is low because total calcium may be reduced while active calcium is relatively preserved.
- Correct the underlying cause as well as the calcium deficit.

cases.title: An adolescent with recurrent renal stones and bone pain
cases.vignette: A 15-year-old adolescent presents with recurrent renal stones, constipation, abdominal pain, fatigue and bone pain. Laboratory tests reveal elevated serum calcium, low phosphate and elevated PTH.

questions.stem: Which cause is correctly matched with the type of hyperparathyroidism?

options.label: A
options.text: Primary — vitamin D deficiency; secondary — parathyroid adenoma; tertiary — acute viral illness

options.label: B
options.text: Primary — ADH deficiency; secondary — diabetes mellitus; tertiary — Cushing syndrome

options.label: C
options.text: Primary — hypothyroidism; secondary — Graves disease; tertiary — isolated GH deficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Primary — hypoparathyroidism; secondary — DiGeorge syndrome; tertiary — neonatal hypoglycaemia

options.label: E
options.text: Primary — single parathyroid adenoma; secondary — chronic kidney disease; tertiary — longstanding CKD

questions.correctAnswerText: Primary — single parathyroid adenoma; secondary — chronic kidney disease; tertiary — longstanding CKD
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include primary hyperparathyroidism as commonly due to a single adenoma or familial disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism due to CKD/liver disease, and tertiary hyperparathyroidism after long-standing CKD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vitamin D deficiency can cause secondary PTH elevation, but the remaining pairings are incorrect.
- B. Incorrect. These conditions do not define the three categories of hyperparathyroidism.
- C. Incorrect. Thyroid disease and GH deficiency are not the primary causes listed.
- D. Incorrect. These describe hypoparathyroid or unrelated conditions.
- E. Correct. These are the relationships listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary: parathyroid adenoma/familial.
- Secondary: compensatory PTH elevation in CKD or liver disease as listed.
- Tertiary: autonomous PTH secretion after long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism, commonly longstanding CKD.
- Children are rarely affected compared with adults,.

questions.stem: Which clinical grouping is summarized by the mnemonic “stones, bones, abdominal groans and psychic moans” in hypercalcaemia?

options.label: B
options.text: Tetany, stridor, carpopedal spasm and seizures

options.label: C
options.text: Respiratory failure, skin rash, fever and joint pain

options.label: E
options.text: Renal stones/nephrocalcinosis, bone disease, gastrointestinal symptoms and neuropsychiatric symptoms

questions.correctAnswerText: Renal stones/nephrocalcinosis, bone disease, gastrointestinal symptoms and neuropsychiatric symptoms
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance uses this mnemonic to summarize the manifestations of hypercalcaemia: renal stones/nephrocalcinosis and DI, skeletal complications, abdominal symptoms and psychiatric/neurological features.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are features of thyrotoxicosis.
- B. Incorrect. These are features of hypocalcaemia/tetany.
- C. Incorrect. These are not the classic hypercalcaemia systems.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the mnemonic pattern.
- E. Correct. This is the complete clinical grouping described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stones: renal stones, nephrocalcinosis, polyuria/polydipsia from DI.
- Bones: osteitis fibrosa cystica, bone pain, pathological fractures, osteoporosis/osteomalacia and arthritis.
- Abdominal groans: abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, dehydration and anorexia.
- Psychic moans: depression, memory loss, psychosis, ataxia, confusion and coma.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern is most consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal calcium, normal phosphate and low PTH

options.label: B
options.text: High calcium, high phosphate and suppressed PTH

options.label: C
options.text: Low calcium, low phosphate and high PTH

options.label: D
options.text: Low calcium, high phosphate and low PTH

options.label: E
options.text: High calcium, low phosphate and high PTH

questions.correctAnswerText: High calcium, low phosphate and high PTH
questions.initialExplanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism produces elevated PTH, increasing serum calcium while promoting renal phosphate excretion. standard guidance gives high calcium (above 12 mg/dL), low phosphate (below 3 mg/dL) and high PTH in its described pattern.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This does not support hyperparathyroidism.
- B. Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH suggests a PTH-independent cause.
- C. Incorrect. Low calcium with high PTH may occur in vitamin D deficiency or secondary hyperparathyroidism.
- D. Incorrect. This fits hypoparathyroidism.
- E. Correct. This is the classic biochemical pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium, low phosphate and high PTH.
- Check renal function, vitamin D, urinary calcium and family history when clinically indicated.
- Distinguish PTH-dependent from PTH-independent hypercalcaemia.

questions.stem: An adolescent has severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia due to a parathyroid adenoma. Which treatment principles are described?

options.label: A
options.text: Insulin infusion as the definitive treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Fluid restriction and oral calcium supplementation

options.label: E
options.text: IV hydration, specialist-directed treatment such as bisphosphonate for severe hypercalcaemia, and surgery for a primary adenoma

questions.correctAnswerText: IV hydration, specialist-directed treatment such as bisphosphonate for severe hypercalcaemia, and surgery for a primary adenoma
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include hydration, IV bisphosphonate (e.g. pamidronate) for severe hypercalcaemia and surgery for primary hyperparathyroidism due to an adenoma. It also lists steroids for selected calcitriol-mediated causes such as sarcoidosis or vitamin D intoxication.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Insulin does not treat primary hyperparathyroidism or hypercalcaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Desmopressin treats central DI.
- C. Incorrect. Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism.
- D. Incorrect. Fluid restriction and calcium supplementation would worsen or fail to treat hypercalcaemia.
- E. Correct. This combines emergency management of severe hypercalcaemia with definitive treatment of a primary adenoma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia requires urgent specialist management and IV hydration.
- Common examples include IV bisphosphonate (pamidronate) for severe cases.
- Steroids are useful in selected vitamin D/calcitriol-mediated causes, including sarcoidosis and vitamin D intoxication,.
- Primary hyperparathyroidism due to an adenoma is treated surgically.
- Common examples include furosemide after hydration; loop diuretics are not routine in every hypercalcaemic patient and should be used only when clinically indicated under specialist guidance.

cases.title: A newborn with cardiac defects and hypocalcaemic seizures
cases.vignette: A newborn has a conotruncal cardiac defect, abnormal facial features, cleft palate and recurrent hypocalcaemic seizures. Further assessment shows evidence of T-cell deficiency.

questions.stem: Which syndrome best explains the combination of cardiac abnormality, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate and hypocalcaemia?
questions.correctAnswerText: DiGeorge syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: DiGeorge syndrome is associated with a chromosome 22 microdeletion and may cause cardiac abnormalities, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia/T-cell deficiency, cleft palate and hypocalcaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Turner syndrome is associated with short stature, gonadal dysgenesis and delayed puberty.
- B. Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome is associated with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism in boys.
- C. Incorrect. McCune–Albright causes precocious puberty, café-au-lait spots and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia.
- D. Incorrect. Pendred syndrome is associated with goitre and sensorineural hearing loss.
- E. Correct. The combination is characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DiGeorge: microdeletion of chromosome 22 (22q11).
- CATCH-22 mnemonic: cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic abnormality/T-cell deficiency, cleft palate and hypocalcaemia.
- Hypocalcaemia results from parathyroid hypoplasia or dysfunction.
- Assess immune function because of thymic/T-cell abnormalities.

cases.title: A toddler with vomiting, constipation and polyuria

questions.stem: A 2.5-year-old boy has had anorexia, vomiting, constipation, irritability, polyuria and polydipsia for 2 weeks. For 4 months his parents have given a vitamin D supplement far above the recommended amount "to strengthen bones". Serum calcium is 13.8 mg/dL and PTH is suppressed. What is the best management?

options.label: B
options.text: Stop vitamin D and calcium supplements and give IV hydration; steroids are effective in vitamin D intoxication

options.label: E
options.text: Fluid restriction to treat the polyuria

questions.correctAnswerText: Stop vitamin D and calcium supplements and give IV hydration; steroids are effective in vitamin D intoxication
questions.initialExplanation: High calcium with a suppressed PTH means PTH-independent hypercalcaemia. Vitamin D toxicity is a listed cause. Treatment is to stop the cause, give IV fluids, and use steroids, which Clinical guidance are effective in vitamin D intoxication.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Symptoms. Vomiting, constipation and anorexia are the "abdominal groans"; irritability fits "psychic moans"; polyuria and polydipsia reflect hypercalcaemia-related concentrating defect.
- A. Incorrect. Surgery is for primary hyperparathyroidism due to an adenoma, where PTH is high.
- B. Correct. Remove the source, hydrate, and use steroids for vitamin D intoxication. For severe hypercalcaemia, IV fluids with furosemide and IV bisphosphonate (e.g. pamidronate) are also described.
- C. Incorrect. Giving calcium would worsen hypercalcaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Desmopressin treats central DI. This polyuria is caused by hypercalcaemia.
- E. Incorrect. Fluid restriction would worsen dehydration and hypercalcaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium, low phosphate, high PTH (single adenoma or familial), treated surgically.
- Other causes of hypercalcaemia: vitamin D toxicity, excess calcium intake, drugs (thiazides, hypervitaminosis A), Williams syndrome, ectopic causes (TB, sarcoidosis, Addison disease), prolonged immobilisation.
- Steroids help in hypercalcaemia of sarcoidosis, vitamin D intoxication, malignancy and subcutaneous fat necrosis.
- Mnemonic: stones, bones, abdominal groans and psychic moans.

topics.name: Foundational Endocrine Control and Adrenal Steroid Physiology — Additional Clinical Integration

cases.title: A child with abnormalities affecting more than one endocrine axis
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child is investigated for growth failure and abnormal thyroid and adrenal function tests. The clinician reviews the main endocrine glands, the hormones controlled by the anterior and posterior pituitary and the mechanisms that regulate hormone secretion.

questions.stem: Which group contains endocrine glands listed in the introductory page of standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, parathyroid, pancreas, ovaries/testes and thymus

options.label: D
options.text: Liver, spleen, gallbladder, appendix and colon

questions.correctAnswerText: Pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, parathyroid, pancreas, ovaries/testes and thymus
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance's introductory diagram identifies the pituitary, thyroid, adrenal and parathyroid glands, gonads, pancreas and thymus as major endocrine organs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the endocrine glands and organs illustrated on the introductory page.
- B. Incorrect. These are musculoskeletal tissues, not the listed endocrine glands.
- C. Incorrect. These are respiratory structures.
- D. Incorrect. These organs have other functions and are not the list shown.
- E. Incorrect. The kidney has important endocrine functions, but this option is not the introductory list shown.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Major endocrine organs: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreas, gonads and thymus.
- The hypothalamus regulates pituitary function.
- Endocrine disorders may involve one gland or multiple hormonal axes.

questions.stem: A child has low cortisol due to pituitary ACTH deficiency. Which anterior pituitary hormone normally stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce cortisol?
questions.correctAnswerText: ACTH
questions.initialExplanation: ACTH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the adrenal cortex, especially the zona fasciculata, to produce glucocorticoids such as cortisol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. FSH acts on the gonads.
- B. Incorrect. TSH stimulates the thyroid gland.
- C. Correct. ACTH stimulates adrenal glucocorticoid production.
- D. Incorrect. GH promotes growth and stimulates IGF-1 production.
- E. Incorrect. Prolactin acts mainly on the mammary glands.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Anterior pituitary: TSH, ACTH, GH, FSH, LH and prolactin.
- Posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin.
- ACTH controls cortisol and adrenal androgen production through the HPA axis.

questions.stem: A child has low aldosterone despite normal ACTH. Which regulatory system most directly controls aldosterone secretion?
questions.correctAnswerText: Renin–angiotensin system and salt/water balance
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance distinguishes aldosterone regulation from cortisol/androgen regulation. Aldosterone is influenced mainly by salt and water balance through the renin–angiotensin system, whereas cortisol and adrenal androgen production are under ACTH control.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Prolactin regulation is unrelated to aldosterone.
- B. Incorrect. This pathway regulates growth.
- C. Incorrect. This controls gonadal development and sex-steroid production.
- D. Incorrect. This axis controls thyroid hormone production.
- E. Correct. Renin–angiotensin signalling and potassium/sodium balance are major regulators of aldosterone.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Zona glomerulosa → mineralocorticoids/aldosterone.
- Zona fasciculata → glucocorticoids/cortisol.
- Zona reticularis → adrenal androgens.
- Aldosterone: renin–angiotensin and potassium/salt balance.
- Cortisol and adrenal androgens: ACTH/HPA axis.

topics.name: Cushing Syndrome — ACTH Classification and Biochemical Features

cases.title: A child with Cushingoid features and abnormal electrolytes
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child has central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple abdominal striae, hirsutism, easy bruising and hypertension. Height velocity is reduced. The clinician evaluates the source of cortisol excess and distinguishes exogenous steroid exposure from endogenous adrenal or pituitary disease.

questions.stem: A child has Cushing syndrome after prolonged corticosteroid treatment for asthma. Which category does this represent?
questions.correctAnswerText: Exogenous (iatrogenic) Cushing syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include exogenous glucocorticoid administration as the commonest cause of Cushing syndrome in children, including treatment for conditions such as nephrotic syndrome and bronchial asthma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Prolonged prescribed corticosteroid exposure causes exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Primary adrenal insufficiency is cortisol deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. DI is a disorder of ADH secretion/action.
- D. Incorrect. An adrenal adenoma is an endogenous ACTH-independent cause.
- E. Incorrect. Ectopic ACTH secretion is an endogenous ACTH-dependent cause.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Exogenous corticosteroids are the most common cause of Cushing syndrome in children.
- Ask specifically about oral, inhaled, topical and injected steroid exposure.
- Long-term steroids must be tapered safely; abrupt discontinuation may precipitate adrenal insufficiency.

questions.stem: A child has confirmed endogenous Cushing syndrome. Plasma ACTH is suppressed and imaging reveals an adrenal tumour. How should the condition be classified?
questions.correctAnswerText: ACTH-independent (primary adrenal) Cushing syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: An adrenal cortisol-producing tumour acts independently of pituitary ACTH, so excess cortisol suppresses ACTH by negative feedback.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Secondary adrenal insufficiency is due to inadequate ACTH and low cortisol, not cortisol excess.
- B. Incorrect. Exogenous disease is due to administered glucocorticoids.
- C. Incorrect. Addison disease is primary adrenal insufficiency.
- D. Correct. An adrenal tumour with suppressed ACTH is ACTH-independent.
- E. Incorrect. ACTH-dependent disease is driven by pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) or ectopic ACTH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ACTH-independent: adrenal adenoma, carcinoma or hyperplasia.
- ACTH-dependent: pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) or ectopic ACTH-secreting tumour.
- Measure ACTH after confirming hypercortisolism to guide localization.

questions.stem: Which biochemical abnormalities may accompany endogenous Cushing syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Hypernatraemia with low serum osmolality and dilute urine

options.label: D
options.text: Low glucose with ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include raised random blood glucose, low potassium and metabolic alkalosis among the investigations associated with Cushing syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests a calcium/PTH disorder.
- B. Incorrect. This describes a possible DI-related water-balance pattern, not Cushing syndrome.
- C. Correct. These are the biochemical abnormalities noted.
- D. Incorrect. This is the biochemical pattern of DKA.
- E. Incorrect. This pattern suggests adrenal insufficiency or salt-wasting CAH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cushing syndrome: cortisol excess, hyperglycaemia, possible hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.
- Confirm cortisol excess with urinary free cortisol, loss of diurnal variation and dexamethasone suppression testing.
- ACTH and imaging are used to determine the source.

questions.stem: A child has confirmed endogenous Cushing syndrome due to a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma. Which management approach is most consistent with standard guidance?

options.label: D
options.text: Treat the underlying source, usually with surgical resection and/or radiotherapy as appropriate

questions.correctAnswerText: Treat the underlying source, usually with surgical resection and/or radiotherapy as appropriate
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that endogenous Cushing syndrome is managed according to its source and is usually treated with surgical resection and/or radiotherapy. Exogenous disease is managed by gradual steroid withdrawal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Abrupt steroid withdrawal applies neither to endogenous pituitary tumour treatment nor safely to long-term prescribed steroid therapy.
- B. Incorrect. Desmopressin treats central DI.
- C. Incorrect. Fludrocortisone replaces mineralocorticoid and does not treat cortisol excess.
- D. Correct. Management is directed at the tumour/source of endogenous cortisol excess.
- E. Incorrect. Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Exogenous Cushing: gradual supervised withdrawal of glucocorticoid.
- Endogenous Cushing: treatment depends on source; often surgery and/or radiotherapy.
- Monitor growth, blood pressure, glucose, bone health and recovery of the HPA axis.

cases.title: Obesity, atypical genitalia and a collapsing infant

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl with marked obesity is brought because her mother fears "Cushing disease". She is taller than 90% of children her age, her growth velocity is normal, and her bone age is 2 years advanced. Blood pressure and fasting glucose are normal. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Cushing disease; MRI of the pituitary should be arranged urgently

options.label: B
options.text: Exogenous Cushing syndrome from hidden steroid exposure

options.label: C
options.text: Simple obesity, as growth acceleration with advanced bone age argues against cortisol excess

options.label: D
options.text: GH deficiency, which gives truncal obesity with accelerated growth

options.label: E
options.text: Hypothyroidism, which gives obesity with advanced bone age

questions.correctAnswerText: Simple obesity, as growth acceleration with advanced bone age argues against cortisol excess
questions.initialExplanation: In children, Cushing syndrome produces weight gain with growth failure (reduced height velocity) and delayed bone age. Simple obesity is associated with tall stature and advanced bone age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Cushing disease would cause reduced growth velocity with delayed bone age. Imaging is premature without biochemical evidence.
- B. Incorrect. Exogenous steroids also suppress growth, so the same logic excludes it.
- C. Correct. Tall stature and advanced bone age point to simple obesity. Idiopathic obesity is a listed cause of tall stature and advanced bone age.
- D. Incorrect. GH deficiency causes short stature with delayed bone age.
- E. Incorrect. Hypothyroidism causes growth failure with delayed bone age.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cushing syndrome in children: obesity plus growth failure, delayed puberty and delayed bone age.
- Simple obesity: tall stature, advanced bone age.
- The diagnosis of Cushing syndrome is questioned mainly in obese children who are also short.
- Delayed bone age: hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism, Cushing syndrome, delayed puberty, chronic illness. Advanced bone age: hyperthyroidism, simple obesity, CAH, precocious puberty.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Cushing syndrome (Pages 18–19); causes of delayed and advanced bone age, and tall stature (Page 48).

topics.name: Adrenal Insufficiency — Primary, Secondary and Congenital Causes

cases.title: A child with recurrent adrenal symptoms and possible secondary adrenal failure
cases.vignette: An 11-year-old child presents with fatigue, weakness, weight loss and recurrent dizziness. The clinician reviews adrenal insufficiency causes and determines whether the defect is at the adrenal gland or due to pituitary/hypothalamic dysfunction. The history includes either previous pituitary surgery or a long course of glucocorticoid therapy.

questions.stem: Which condition is a cause of secondary adrenal insufficiency?

options.label: E
options.text: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex

questions.correctAnswerText: Panhypopituitarism causing ACTH deficiency
questions.initialExplanation: Secondary adrenal insufficiency results from pituitary failure and reduced ACTH stimulation. Common examples include panhypopituitarism, pituitary surgery/trauma/tumour and long-term glucocorticoid therapy among causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bilateral adrenalectomy causes primary adrenal insufficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Tuberculosis may destroy the adrenal glands and cause primary adrenal insufficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Adrenal haemorrhage/infarction is a primary adrenal cause.
- D. Correct. Reduced pituitary ACTH causes reduced adrenal cortisol production.
- E. Incorrect. Autoimmune adrenal destruction causes primary Addison disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary: adrenal gland failure (Addison, haemorrhage/infarction, TB, surgery, CAH, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy).
- Secondary: pituitary ACTH deficiency (panhypopituitarism, pituitary tumour/surgery/trauma or chronic steroid suppression).
- Secondary adrenal insufficiency generally preserves aldosterone better than primary disease, so hyperkalaemia is less characteristic.

questions.stem: A previously healthy boy develops progressive neurological deterioration and adrenal insufficiency. Which congenital adrenal disorder is listed as an X-linked cause?
questions.correctAnswerText: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy as a rare neurodegenerative metabolic disorder that can cause primary adrenal insufficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy can affect the adrenal cortex and nervous system.
- B. Incorrect. Pendred syndrome causes goitre and sensorineural hearing loss.
- C. Incorrect. McCune–Albright is associated with peripheral precocious puberty and fibrous dysplasia.
- D. Incorrect. Kallmann syndrome causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia.
- E. Incorrect. Laron syndrome is GH receptor resistance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is a congenital cause of primary adrenal insufficiency.
- Consider adrenal insufficiency in boys with progressive neurological disease.
- Primary adrenal insufficiency may have hyperpigmentation, low sodium and high potassium.

questions.stem: A child with meningococcal septicaemia develops sudden shock, hypoglycaemia and acute adrenal failure. Which named cause should be considered?

options.label: C
options.text: Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome due to adrenal haemorrhage

questions.correctAnswerText: Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome due to adrenal haemorrhage
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include adrenal haemorrhage/infarction (Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome), including neonatal or meningococcal septicaemia, as a cause of primary adrenal insufficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pendred syndrome is a thyroid/hearing disorder.
- B. Incorrect. Sheehan syndrome is postpartum pituitary necrosis.
- C. Correct. Severe sepsis, classically meningococcal, may cause bilateral adrenal haemorrhage and acute adrenal failure.
- D. Incorrect. McCune–Albright syndrome causes endocrine hyperfunction and fibrous dysplasia.
- E. Incorrect. Mauriac syndrome is a complication of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Waterhouse–Friderichsen: adrenal haemorrhage/infarction associated with severe sepsis.
- Presents with shock and acute primary adrenal insufficiency.
- Treat as an emergency with resuscitation and parenteral glucocorticoid replacement.

questions.stem: What is the usual long-term replacement treatment for confirmed primary Addison disease?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes lifelong hormonal replacement with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone for primary adrenal insufficiency. Hydrocortisone replaces cortisol, while fludrocortisone replaces mineralocorticoid activity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin treats central DI.
- B. Incorrect. These are diabetes treatments.
- C. Incorrect. These drugs treat hyperthyroidism.
- D. Correct. Both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement are required in primary adrenal failure.
- E. Incorrect. Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary Addison disease: lifelong hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone.
- Teach stress dosing during febrile illness, gastroenteritis, major trauma and surgery.
- Clinical descriptions include doubling or tripling hydrocortisone during significant stress; follow the child's individualized adrenal sick-day plan.

topics.name: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia — Clinical Phenotypes and Long-Term Management

cases.title: A newborn with virilization and a later salt-wasting crisis
cases.vignette: A 46,XX newborn has atypical external genitalia with clitoromegaly and labioscrotal fusion. At 2–3 weeks of age, the infant develops vomiting, dehydration, hypotension and poor weight gain. Electrolytes reveal low sodium and high potassium.

questions.stem: At what age does salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency commonly present with adrenal crisis?

options.label: D
options.text: In the first hour after birth in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: 2–6 weeks of life
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include salt-wasting CAH as the most lethal form of 21-hydroxylase deficiency, often presenting with adrenal crisis at approximately 2–6 weeks of life.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the usual paediatric presentation.
- B. Incorrect. Salt-wasting CAH commonly presents in early infancy, not only at puberty.
- C. Incorrect. This is much later than the usual neonatal presentation.
- D. Incorrect. Some infants may appear well at birth and deteriorate over the first weeks.
- E. Correct. This is the age range highlighted.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most lethal classical form.
- Crisis often develops at 2–6 weeks.
- Vomiting, dehydration, weight loss, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis are warning signs.

questions.stem: A 46,XX infant with classical CAH has ambiguous external genitalia at birth. What is the mechanism?

options.label: C
options.text: Excess adrenal androgen exposure in utero causing virilization

questions.correctAnswerText: Excess adrenal androgen exposure in utero causing virilization
questions.initialExplanation: In 21-hydroxylase deficiency, impaired cortisol synthesis leads to increased ACTH and adrenal androgen production. In a 46,XX fetus, excess androgen exposure can virilize the external genitalia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ADH deficiency causes central DI.
- B. Incorrect. GH receptor resistance causes Laron syndrome and short stature.
- C. Correct. Excess adrenal androgens in utero produce clitoromegaly and labioscrotal fusion in a 46,XX infant.
- D. Incorrect. PTH excess causes hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcaemia.
- E. Incorrect. Maternal TSH does not cross the placenta; TSH itself is not responsible for virilization.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 46,XX classical CAH: virilized/ambiguous external genitalia may be present at birth.
- 46,XY infants may have normal-appearing genitalia at birth and still develop a life-threatening salt-wasting crisis.
- Karyotype is essential in the evaluation of ambiguous genitalia.

questions.stem: A boy with simple virilizing 21-hydroxylase deficiency develops early pubic hair and penile enlargement. He is initially tall for age, but his predicted adult height is reduced. Which mechanism explains the reduced adult height?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced androgen production delays bone age

options.label: B
options.text: Androgen excess permanently prevents growth hormone secretion

options.label: C
options.text: Excess aldosterone causes premature epiphyseal closure

options.label: D
options.text: Androgen excess accelerates growth and bone maturation, causing early epiphyseal closure

options.label: E
options.text: ADH deficiency causes shortening of long bones

questions.correctAnswerText: Androgen excess accelerates growth and bone maturation, causing early epiphyseal closure
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that simple virilizing CAH causes accelerated linear growth and advanced bone age in childhood, but adult height may be short because skeletal maturation and epiphyseal closure occur early.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Androgen excess advances rather than delays bone age.
- B. Incorrect. GH secretion is not the primary mechanism.
- C. Incorrect. Aldosterone excess is not the mechanism described.
- D. Correct. Early androgen exposure accelerates bone age and can reduce final adult height.
- E. Incorrect. DI does not cause shortening of long bones.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Simple virilizing CAH: early pubic hair, penile/clitoral enlargement and accelerated growth.
- Bone age is advanced.
- Childhood height may be increased, but adult height can be reduced due to early epiphyseal closure.
- Monitor growth and skeletal maturity during treatment.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl has hirsutism, acne, oligomenorrhoea and infertility. Her history suggests non-classical CAH. Which clinical pattern best matches standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Late-onset androgen excess with hirsutism, acne, oligomenorrhoea and possible infertility

options.label: B
options.text: Congenital ambiguous genitalia as the feature

options.label: C
options.text: Hypoglycaemia with low insulin and ketones as the defining feature

options.label: D
options.text: Neonatal salt-wasting crisis at 2 weeks in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Late-onset androgen excess with hirsutism, acne, oligomenorrhoea and possible infertility
questions.initialExplanation: Non-classical CAH is a late-onset form of enzyme deficiency. Common examples include oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, acne and infertility as possible adolescent/adult manifestations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the clinical picture described for non-classical CAH.
- B. Incorrect. Ambiguous genitalia may occur in classical 46,XX CAH but is not the defining presentation of non-classical CAH.
- C. Incorrect. This describes a ketotic hypoglycaemia pattern, not CAH.
- D. Incorrect. Salt-wasting crisis is a feature of severe classical CAH.
- E. Incorrect. This is a hypoparathyroid/pseudohypoparathyroid biochemical pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Non-classical CAH: late onset, often presenting in adolescence or adulthood.
- Symptoms: hirsutism, acne, oligomenorrhoea and infertility.
- 17-hydroxyprogesterone is a key diagnostic marker.

questions.stem: A child with known CAH is scheduled for surgery and later develops a febrile illness. Which management principle is important to prevent adrenal crisis?

options.label: C
options.text: Stop hydrocortisone whenever the child has fever

options.label: D
options.text: Restrict fluids and sodium in typical presentations

options.label: E
options.text: Increase hydrocortisone to a stress dose during illness, trauma or surgery according to the individualized plan

questions.correctAnswerText: Increase hydrocortisone to a stress dose during illness, trauma or surgery according to the individualized plan
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is stress dosing during infection, illness and surgery. It also describes lifelong hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement for classical CAH, with monitoring of growth, bone age, plasma androgens and 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mineralocorticoid replacement may be required in salt-wasting disease.
- B. Incorrect. Antithyroid medication does not treat CAH.
- C. Incorrect. Steroids must not be stopped during illness; interruption can precipitate adrenal crisis.
- D. Incorrect. Fluid and electrolyte management depends on the clinical state; restriction is not routine.
- E. Correct. Stress-dose hydrocortisone helps meet the increased cortisol requirement during physiological stress.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Classical CAH requires long-term/lifelong hormone replacement.
- Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone are used as indicated by the form of CAH.
- During infection/illness/surgery, increase glucocorticoid according to the child's sick-day plan.
- Monitor growth, bone age, plasma androgens and 17-OHP in endocrine clinic.
- Exact doses must follow the specialist's individualized protocol.

topics.name: Type 1 Diabetes — Epidemiology, Aetiology and Follow-up

cases.title: A child with a strong family history and evidence of autoimmune diabetes
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child presents with marked hyperglycaemia and begins insulin treatment. A parent asks about possible causes and whether siblings are at risk. The family receives information about age distribution, genetic susceptibility, environmental associations and screening for related autoimmune conditions.

questions.stem: Which age pattern is described for type 1 diabetes in children?

options.label: C
options.text: in the first 4 weeks of life

options.label: E
options.text: Bimodal peaks around 4–7 years and 10–14 years

questions.correctAnswerText: Bimodal peaks around 4–7 years and 10–14 years
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include type 1 diabetes as having bimodal peaks in childhood, approximately 4–7 years and 10–14 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Type 1 diabetes commonly presents during childhood.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the age distribution of childhood type 1 diabetes.
- C. Incorrect. Neonatal diabetes is a distinct specific type.
- D. Incorrect. This is the peak age for idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia.
- E. Correct. These are the two age peaks listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type 1 diabetes accounts for most childhood diabetes (approximately 95%).
- Bimodal peaks: 4–7 years and 10–14 years.
- Presentation may be acute over days to weeks.

questions.stem: Which genetic association is listed as increasing susceptibility to type 1 diabetes?
questions.correctAnswerText: HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 as genetic susceptibility associations for autoimmune type 1 diabetes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. 22q11 deletion is associated with DiGeorge syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Down syndrome is associated with increased risk of several autoimmune conditions but is not the HLA susceptibility answer.
- C. Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome is a sex-chromosome disorder associated with hypogonadism and tall stature.
- D. Correct. These HLA types are listed.
- E. Incorrect. HLA-B27 is associated with spondyloarthropathies, not the main type 1 diabetes association.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type 1 diabetes is multifactorial with genetic, environmental and autoimmune contributions.
- HLA-DR3/DR4 are listed.
- Monozygotic twins have increased concordance; family risk is higher when a parent or both parents are affected.

questions.stem: Which environmental association is listed as potentially increasing the risk of type 1 diabetes?

options.label: D
options.text: Viral infection, particularly with seasonal/geographical variation

questions.correctAnswerText: Viral infection, particularly with seasonal/geographical variation
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include viral infection as an environmental risk association and notes geographical and seasonal variation. Breastfeeding is described as being associated with a lower risk.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vaccination is not listed as a risk factor.
- B. Incorrect. High fibre intake is not listed as a risk factor.
- C. Incorrect. Breastfeeding is described as associated with lower risk, not higher risk.
- D. Correct. Viral infection is included among environmental associations.
- E. Incorrect. Exercise is beneficial for general metabolic health and is not listed as a type 1 diabetes risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Genetic susceptibility: HLA-DR3/DR4.
- Environmental associations listed: viral infection, geographical/seasonal variation, vitamin D deficiency and infant feeding factors.
- Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune, not caused by a single environmental exposure.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic child has an abnormal fasting glucose result on one occasion. Which approach is described before diagnosing diabetes in an asymptomatic child?

options.label: B
options.text: Require at least two abnormal blood glucose readings on separate days; OGTT may be used in selected cases

options.label: C
options.text: Diagnose diabetes from one random capillary glucose after exercise

options.label: E
options.text: Diagnose diabetes from one trace of urine glucose

questions.correctAnswerText: Require at least two abnormal blood glucose readings on separate days; OGTT may be used in selected cases
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that an asymptomatic child should have at least two abnormal blood glucose readings on two days. An OGTT is rarely required to diagnose typical type 1 diabetes but may be used in selected diagnostic situations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Calcium and PTH assess parathyroid disease.
- B. Correct. This matches the confirmation principle.
- C. Incorrect. A single capillary reading after exercise is not an appropriate diagnostic basis.
- D. Incorrect. Waiting for DKA is unsafe and unnecessary.
- E. Incorrect. Urine glucose alone is not sufficient to diagnose diabetes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Symptomatic child: diagnostic blood glucose criteria apply with classic symptoms.
- Asymptomatic child: repeat/confirm abnormal glucose testing.
- HbA1c is used to assess longer-term glycaemic control; Clinical guidance notes it may be unreliable in haemoglobinopathies.
- Screen thyroid function and coeliac disease at diagnosis and continue thyroid screening annually.

cases.title: Children with type 1 diabetes seen in clinic and at school

questions.stem: An 11-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes since age 7 attends her routine review. Her parents ask which complication screening begins now. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Annual retinal photography, microalbuminuria and blood pressure checks must start immediately because the duration exceeds 2 years

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing is needed except HbA1c until puberty

options.label: C
options.text: cataract screening is needed, as retinopathy not usually occurs in children

options.label: D
options.text: Height, weight, BMI and annual thyroid screening continue now; annual blood pressure, microalbuminuria and retinal screening begin from age 12

options.label: E
options.text: Annual blood pressure, microalbuminuria and retinal examination are needed after 18 years

questions.correctAnswerText: Height, weight, BMI and annual thyroid screening continue now; annual blood pressure, microalbuminuria and retinal screening begin from age 12
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance sets annual blood pressure, microalbuminuria (early sign of nephropathy) and eye screening from 12 years of age. Growth, pubertal development and BMI are assessed at every visit, and thyroid screening is annual.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. clinical guidance's starting age for these three screens is 12 years, not duration-based.
- B. Incorrect. HbA1c alone misses growth, thyroid and other planned assessments.
- C. Incorrect. Retinopathy and cataract are rare in children, but monitoring is still advised from 12 years.
- D. Correct. This matches clinical guidance's schedule.
- E. Incorrect. Screening begins in adolescence, long before adulthood.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Each visit: height, weight and BMI plotted on the growth chart, pubertal staging, injection sites.
- Annual from age 12: blood pressure, microalbuminuria, retinal photography.
- Check foot pulses and sensation; promote foot care.
- Screen thyroid function annually; coeliac screening at diagnosis and again if symptomatic.
- Annual influenza vaccination and dental review.

topics.name: Short Stature — Numerical Growth Assessment and Body Proportions

cases.title: A child whose height and body proportions are being measured
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child is assessed for short stature. The clinician records standing height, compares it with age-related expected values and examines upper-to-lower segment proportions to decide whether the short stature is proportionate or disproportionate.

questions.stem: Which approximate length values are given for a healthy child?

options.label: A
options.text: 30 cm at birth, 50 cm at 1 year and 70 cm at 4 years

options.label: B
options.text: The lecture gives no expected length values

options.label: C
options.text: 75 cm at birth, 100 cm at 1 year and 120 cm at 4 years

options.label: D
options.text: 100 cm at birth, 120 cm at 1 year and 150 cm at 4 years

options.label: E
options.text: 50 cm at birth, 75 cm at 1 year and 100 cm at 4 years

questions.correctAnswerText: 50 cm at birth, 75 cm at 1 year and 100 cm at 4 years
questions.initialExplanation: The source page lists approximate normal length values of 50 cm at birth, 75 cm at 1 year and 100 cm at 4 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These values are substantially below standard guidance's expected values.
- B. Incorrect. standard guidance explicitly provides these values.
- C. Incorrect. Birth length of 75 cm is not physiologically plausible.
- D. Incorrect. These values are far above the expected measurements.
- E. Correct. These are the approximate values.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Approximate length: 50 cm at birth, 75 cm at 1 year, 100 cm at 4 years.
- These are teaching estimates, not substitutes for plotting accurate measurements on a growth chart.
- Measure length supine under 2 years and standing height after 2 years as described.

questions.stem: Which formula can be used to estimate height in a child older than 2 years?
questions.correctAnswerText: Age in years × 5 + 80 cm
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives the approximate height formula for children older than 2 years as age in years multiplied by 5, plus 80 cm.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Weight is not used in the formula.
- B. Incorrect. The formula uses age in years, not months.
- C. Incorrect. Mid-parental target height is calculated from the parents' heights, not by subtracting 20 cm.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the formula.
- E. Correct. This is the formula shown on the source page.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Approximate height formula for >2 years: age (years) × 5 + 80 cm.
- Use it as a rough estimate only; actual assessment should use measured height and growth charts.
- Growth velocity remains more sensitive than a single estimated height.

questions.stem: A child has a short trunk relative to the legs. Which measurement is used to assess this body-proportion difference?
questions.correctAnswerText: Upper segment/lower segment ratio
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include the upper-to-lower segment ratio as a method of assessing body proportions. Lower segment is measured from the anterior superior iliac spine to the floor, and upper segment is sitting height (height minus lower segment).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Head circumference does not assess trunk-to-leg proportion.
- B. Incorrect. Arm span may be useful in selected skeletal/connective-tissue disorders but is not the specified U/L ratio.
- C. Correct. U/L segment ratio evaluates relative trunk and leg proportions.
- D. Incorrect. BMI assesses weight relative to height, not body segment proportions.
- E. Incorrect. Waist-to-hip ratio is not the measure described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lower segment: ASIS to floor.
- Upper segment: sitting height (height − lower segment).
- Approximate U/L ratios: 1.7:1 at birth, 1.3:1 at 3 years, 1:1 at 7–10 years and 0.9:1 at puberty.
- Interpret ratios against age and the clinical examination.

cases.title: A child with persistent polyuria despite desmopressin
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child has persistent polyuria and polydipsia. Urine remains dilute after a supervised desmopressin assessment.

questions.stem: Which treatment approach is listed for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

options.label: A
options.text: Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone as routine treatment

options.label: B
options.text: Thiazide diuretic-based management with selected additional agents such as indomethacin under specialist supervision

options.label: E
options.text: Desmopressin as the effective treatment in typical presentations

questions.correctAnswerText: Thiazide diuretic-based management with selected additional agents such as indomethacin under specialist supervision
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance differentiates central DI, treated with desmopressin, from nephrogenic DI, in which the kidney is resistant to ADH. It lists thiazide diuretics and other selected agents for nephrogenic DI. Treatment is specialist-led and also includes adequate fluid intake and management of the cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hydrocortisone/fludrocortisone replace adrenal hormones and are not routine treatment for nephrogenic DI.
- B. Correct. Thiazide-based treatment and selected adjuncts such as indomethacin are listed for nephrogenic DI.
- C. Incorrect. Carbimazole treats hyperthyroidism.
- D. Incorrect. Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism.
- E. Incorrect. Nephrogenic DI is characterized by renal resistance, so desmopressin usually has limited or no effect.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Central DI: ADH deficiency → responds to DDAVP.
- Nephrogenic DI: renal ADH resistance → thiazide-based regimen and cause-specific management.
- Maintain adequate fluid access and monitor hydration, sodium and growth.
- Exact medication choices and monitoring should be individualized by paediatric endocrinology/nephrology.

topics.name: Other Specific Types of Diabetes and Type 2 Diabetes Management

cases.title: A child with diabetes that does not fit the usual type 1 or type 2 pattern
cases.vignette: A 4-month-old infant develops persistent hyperglycaemia and requires insulin. Another child with cystic fibrosis develops diabetes during follow-up, while a third child develops hyperglycaemia after prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is an example of neonatal diabetes listed?

options.label: D
options.text: Transient or permanent diabetes due to defective pancreatic beta-cell function

options.label: E
options.text: Diabetes insipidus due to ADH deficiency

questions.correctAnswerText: Transient or permanent diabetes due to defective pancreatic beta-cell function
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include neonatal diabetes as a specific type of diabetes that may be transient or permanent and is related to defective beta-cell function.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Graves disease is autoimmune hyperthyroidism.
- B. Incorrect. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is PTH resistance.
- C. Incorrect. Hyperinsulinism causes hypoglycaemia, not neonatal diabetes.
- D. Correct. Neonatal diabetes can result from genetic defects affecting pancreatic beta-cell function and may be transient or permanent.
- E. Incorrect. DI is a water-balance disorder caused by ADH deficiency or resistance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Other specific diabetes types include MODY, neonatal diabetes, cystic-fibrosis-associated diabetes, syndromic/chromosomal diabetes, endocrine-associated diabetes (e.g. Cushing) and drug-induced diabetes.
- Neonatal diabetes may be transient or permanent.
- Consider genetic testing and specialist review in diabetes presenting in the first months of life.

questions.stem: A child with cystic fibrosis develops diabetes due to progressive pancreatic insufficiency. Which diabetes category is this?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cystic-fibrosis-associated diabetes (other specific type)
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include cystic-fibrosis-associated diabetes as a specific type related to pancreatic insufficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Gestational diabetes occurs during pregnancy.
- B. Correct. Pancreatic damage/insufficiency in cystic fibrosis can impair insulin secretion.
- C. Incorrect. DI is caused by ADH deficiency or resistance.
- D. Incorrect. It is not automatically autoimmune type 1 diabetes.
- E. Incorrect. It is not defined by insulin resistance/obesity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CF-related diabetes is an “other specific type”.
- Other listed causes include genetic/chromosomal syndromes, Cushing syndrome and drug-induced diabetes.
- Classification should reflect the underlying mechanism rather than assigning all childhood diabetes to type 1 or type 2.

questions.stem: An overweight 13-year-old has type 2 diabetes with acanthosis nigricans. Which initial management components are listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Education, diet, exercise and metformin
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include education, exercise, dietary management and oral hypoglycaemic medication (metformin) as management components for type 2 diabetes in children and adolescents.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These replace adrenal hormones in primary adrenal insufficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Desmopressin treats central DI; water restriction is not the general treatment.
- C. Correct. These are the treatment components given in the source.
- D. Incorrect. These are used for hyperthyroidism and symptom control.
- E. Incorrect. These treat hypocalcaemia, not type 2 diabetes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type 2 diabetes: education, lifestyle intervention and metformin.
- Assess obesity, blood pressure, lipid profile, PCOS and acanthosis nigricans.
- Individualize escalation and monitoring with the paediatric diabetes team.

topics.name: Diabetes Monitoring and DKA Severity/Management Details

cases.title: A child with diabetes requires glycaemic follow-up and emergency assessment
cases.vignette: A child with type 1 diabetes attends clinic for follow-up. The clinician reviews HbA1c, screening for associated autoimmune disease and the emergency blood gas results of another child admitted with DKA. The team must grade acidosis and monitor potassium during treatment.

questions.stem: What is the role of HbA1c 's diabetes follow-up?

options.label: A
options.text: It directly measures pancreatic insulin secretion

options.label: B
options.text: It replaces most blood glucose monitoring

options.label: C
options.text: It measures the blood glucose in the previous 10 minutes

options.label: D
options.text: It is used to diagnose diabetes insipidus

options.label: E
options.text: It estimates glycaemic control over approximately the previous 2–3 months

questions.correctAnswerText: It estimates glycaemic control over approximately the previous 2–3 months
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include HbA1c as a marker of average blood glucose over approximately 2–3 months and uses it for monitoring long-term glycaemic control. It also notes that HbA1c may be unreliable in haemoglobinopathies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. HbA1c does not directly measure insulin secretion.
- B. Incorrect. HbA1c complements but does not replace regular glucose/CGM monitoring.
- C. Incorrect. A single recent glucose value is measured by a blood glucose test, not HbA1c.
- D. Incorrect. DI is assessed by plasma/urine osmolality and water-balance studies.
- E. Correct. HbA1c reflects glycaemic exposure over the preceding weeks to months.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HbA1c: longer-term glycaemic monitoring (approximately 2–3 months ).
- Common examples include a target HbA1c below 7.0%.
- HbA1c may be unreliable in haemoglobinopathies.
- Continue self-monitoring/CGM and ketone monitoring as indicated.

questions.stem: A child with DKA has a pH of 7.12 and bicarbonate of 4 mmol/L. How is the DKA classified 's severity table?
questions.correctAnswerText: Severe DKA
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance's severity table classifies severe DKA with pH below approximately 7.15 and bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The child has marked metabolic acidosis consistent with severe DKA.
- B. Correct. pH 7.12 and bicarbonate 4 mmol/L meet the severe thresholds table.
- C. Incorrect. Mild DKA has less severe acidosis.
- D. Incorrect. Moderate DKA has an intermediate degree of acidosis.
- E. Incorrect. DKA is a metabolic acidosis, not respiratory alkalosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Standard guidance grades DKA by clinical status and degree of acidosis.
- Severe DKA: pH <7.15 and bicarbonate <5 mmol/L in the table.
- Assess circulation, dehydration, neurological status and electrolyte disturbance; manage in an appropriate paediatric setting.

questions.stem: A child with DKA initially has a high serum potassium. After fluids and insulin are started, the potassium falls. What is the most appropriate explanation and monitoring approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Potassium has no role in DKA management

options.label: B
options.text: Total-body potassium is typically increased, so monitoring is unnecessary

options.label: C
options.text: Potassium replacement should be given without checking renal function or urine output

options.label: D
options.text: Insulin causes potassium to leave cells and raise serum potassium

options.label: E
options.text: Total-body potassium is depleted despite possible initial serum elevation; monitor ECG/serum potassium and replace when appropriate after urine output is established

questions.correctAnswerText: Total-body potassium is depleted despite possible initial serum elevation; monitor ECG/serum potassium and replace when appropriate after urine output is established
questions.initialExplanation: In DKA, potassium shifts out of cells due to insulin deficiency and acidosis, so the serum level may initially be high or normal despite total-body potassium depletion. Insulin and rehydration drive potassium back into cells, potentially causing hypokalaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Potassium monitoring and replacement are essential parts of DKA management.
- B. Incorrect. Total-body potassium is commonly depleted due to urinary losses.
- C. Incorrect. Potassium replacement requires monitoring and assessment of renal function/urine output.
- D. Incorrect. Insulin shifts potassium into cells, lowering serum potassium.
- E. Correct. This is the key potassium principle in DKA described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Initial serum K may be high while total-body K is depleted.
- Insulin and rehydration lower serum K.
- Monitor serum potassium and ECG.
- Begin potassium replacement according to protocol and only when renal output/clinical conditions are appropriate.

questions.stem: Why is intravenous sodium bicarbonate generally avoided in paediatric DKA?

options.label: A
options.text: It prevents potassium from entering cells

options.label: B
options.text: It permanently damages the thyroid gland

options.label: C
options.text: It may increase the risk of cerebral oedema and is reserved for exceptional severe acidosis under specialist protocol

options.label: D
options.text: It is the first-line treatment for children in routine care with DKA

questions.correctAnswerText: It may increase the risk of cerebral oedema and is reserved for exceptional severe acidosis under specialist protocol
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance advises avoiding bicarbonate except in very severe profound acidosis (pH below 7.1 and bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L), because IV bicarbonate may increase the risk of cerebral oedema.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bicarbonate is not used to control potassium shifts.
- B. Incorrect. Thyroid damage is not the relevant mechanism.
- C. Correct. This reflects the caution and limited indication.
- D. Incorrect. Routine bicarbonate is specifically discouraged.
- E. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia is not the primary reason to avoid bicarbonate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Avoid routine bicarbonate in DKA.
- standard guidance gives a narrow threshold for profound acidosis; decisions require senior specialist input.
- Correct dehydration, insulin deficiency and electrolyte disturbance while monitoring neurological status.

cases.title: A child on treatment for severe DKA

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl (30 kg) with DKA (pH 7.05, glucose 620 mg/dL) received a 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 20 minutes for shock, then maintenance plus deficit fluid with 0.9% saline. IV regular insulin 0.1 U/kg/h was started 1 hour after rehydration began. Six hours later glucose is 236 mg/dL, pH 7.24, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L and ketones remain positive. What is the next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop the insulin infusion because glucose is below 250 mg/dL

options.label: B
options.text: Give IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis faster

options.label: C
options.text: Double the insulin infusion rate to clear ketones faster

options.label: D
options.text: Continue the same fluid and insulin without change

options.label: E
options.text: Continue insulin and change the fluid to 5% dextrose in 0.9% saline (or half dextrose-saline) to avoid hypoglycaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Continue insulin and change the fluid to 5% dextrose in 0.9% saline (or half dextrose-saline) to avoid hypoglycaemia
questions.initialExplanation: When glucose falls to 250 mg/dL or below, fluids are changed to dextrose-containing saline to avoid hypoglycaemia. Insulin is continued because ketosis and acidosis are not yet corrected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stopping insulin lets ketogenesis continue. Insulin is needed to reverse ketosis and acidosis, so dextrose is added instead.
- B. Incorrect. Bicarbonate is avoided unless pH <7.1 with bicarbonate <5, because it increases cerebral oedema risk. This child's pH is 7.24.
- C. Incorrect. A faster glucose fall is harmful. clinical guidance advises against dropping glucose by more than 100 mg/dL per hour.
- D. Incorrect. Unchanged saline with continuing insulin risks hypoglycaemia.
- E. Correct. This matches clinical guidance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Shock: 10–20 mL/kg 0.9% saline over 20 minutes; then correct dehydration gradually over 48–72 hours to avoid cerebral oedema.
- Insulin: regular insulin 0.05–0.1 U/kg/h by pump, started after 1 hour of rehydration.
- Glucose ≤250 mg/dL: change to dextrose-containing saline. Do not lower glucose faster than 100 mg/dL/h.
- Potassium replacement starts once urine is passed (20–40 mEq per 500 mL of fluid) with ECG and serum monitoring.

questions.stem: A child with DKA has glucose 860 mg/dL, sodium 125 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L and pH 7.04. A junior doctor wants to give hypertonic saline for the low sodium. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Hyperglycaemia draws water out of cells, lowering measured sodium; interpret sodium with glucose and trends

options.label: B
options.text: True sodium depletion that needs 3% saline

options.label: E
options.text: Hyponatraemia caused by excess hypotonic fluids already given

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyperglycaemia draws water out of cells, lowering measured sodium; interpret sodium with glucose and trends
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that very high glucose draws water out of cells by osmosis, which makes the measured serum sodium appear low. Sodium should be interpreted with the glucose level and followed over time.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The osmotic effect of glucose explains the low value. Monitoring sodium (and potassium) is part of DKA care.
- B. Incorrect. Hypertonic saline is not indicated for an apparent fall caused by hyperglycaemia.
- C. Incorrect. SIADH is not suggested, and fluid restriction would be harmful in DKA.
- D. Incorrect. Diabetes insipidus would produce high, not low, sodium.
- E. Incorrect. Fluids have not yet been given in this scenario.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Monitor electrolytes (especially K and Na), ABG and glucose regularly, plus fluid balance and neurological state.
- Initial potassium is often high but falls with insulin and rehydration.
- Do not give bicarbonate except for very severe acidosis (pH <7.1 and bicarbonate <5).

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with new-onset type 1 diabetes is treated for severe DKA. Six hours into treatment he develops a severe headache, repeated vomiting and drowsiness. His heart rate falls from 120 to 52/min, blood pressure rises to 140/85 mmHg, breathing is irregular and pupils are sluggish. Glucose is 290 mg/dL. What is the best immediate management?

options.label: C
options.text: Elevate the head and give IV mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg or 3% saline; transfer to PICU

questions.correctAnswerText: Elevate the head and give IV mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg or 3% saline; transfer to PICU
questions.initialExplanation: Headache, vomiting, falling heart rate, rising blood pressure and irregular breathing (Cushing triad) in a child on DKA treatment mean cerebral oedema. Treatment reduces intracranial pressure: semi-sitting position, mannitol or hypertonic saline, and PICU care with intubation and ventilation if required.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Risk factors present. Young age and new-onset diabetes, with severe acidosis, are listed risk factors.
- A. Incorrect. More fluid would raise intracranial pressure further.
- B. Incorrect. Bicarbonate is itself a risk factor for cerebral oedema.
- C. Correct. This is clinical guidance's treatment of cerebral oedema.
- D. Incorrect. A faster fall in glucose worsens risk. Insulin is not the treatment.
- E. Incorrect. Lumbar puncture is dangerous with raised intracranial pressure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cerebral oedema: the major life-threatening DKA complication (about 1%), with high mortality and neurological morbidity.
- Risk factors: age <5 years, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis, high initial urea, rapid hypotonic fluids, IV insulin bolus or early infusion, bicarbonate.
- Signs: headache, vomiting, cranial nerve palsy, convulsion, apnoea, bradycardia (Cushing triad), confusion, coma.
- Other DKA complications: arrhythmia and electrolyte imbalance, acute tubular necrosis, intracranial thrombosis, pancreatitis, aspiration pneumonia, DIC and multiorgan failure.

questions.stem: A child treated for DKA has improved: pH 7.34, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, alert and tolerating oral intake. The IV insulin infusion is still running and subcutaneous insulin is prescribed. Which sequence is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop the IV infusion immediately, then give subcutaneous insulin

options.label: B
options.text: Give the first subcutaneous dose, continue the IV infusion for about another hour, then stop it

options.label: C
options.text: Stop IV insulin and wait 6 hours before the first subcutaneous dose

options.label: D
options.text: Continue the IV infusion until HbA1c normalises

options.label: E
options.text: Give subcutaneous insulin after discharge the next day

questions.correctAnswerText: Give the first subcutaneous dose, continue the IV infusion for about another hour, then stop it
questions.initialExplanation: Subcutaneous insulin takes time to be absorbed. The IV infusion is therefore stopped about 1 hour after the subcutaneous dose, so insulin cover is not interrupted.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stopping IV insulin first leaves a gap in cover and risks recurrent ketosis.
- B. Correct. This is clinical guidance's overlap rule.
- C. Incorrect. A 6-hour gap would allow ketoacidosis to recur.
- D. Incorrect. HbA1c reflects 2–3 months and is not a stopping criterion.
- E. Incorrect. Delaying subcutaneous insulin leaves the child without basal cover.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Once improved clinically and on ABG, stop IV fluids and restart oral diet.
- Start subcutaneous insulin, then stop the IV infusion 1 hour later.
- Antibiotics are not routinely prescribed in DKA. Identify and treat the precipitating cause (infection, missed insulin, pump failure).

cases.title: A child with acquired hypothyroidism and an adolescent with Graves disease
cases.vignette: A 12-year-old girl with Hashimoto thyroiditis has low free T4 and high TSH with reduced growth velocity. A second adolescent has Graves disease with tachycardia, tremor and a diffuse goitre. The clinician selects treatment appropriate to each thyroid disorder.

questions.stem: What is the standard treatment for acquired primary hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto thyroiditis?

options.label: E
options.text: Levothyroxine replacement with clinical and TFT follow-up

questions.correctAnswerText: Levothyroxine replacement with clinical and TFT follow-up
questions.initialExplanation: Acquired primary hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine replacement. The child requires monitoring of thyroid function, symptoms, growth and development.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin treats central DI.
- B. Incorrect. GH does not correct thyroid hormone deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Carbimazole suppresses thyroid hormone synthesis and is used for hyperthyroidism.
- D. Incorrect. These replace adrenal hormones.
- E. Correct. Levothyroxine replaces the deficient thyroid hormone.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism in children.
- Treat with levothyroxine.
- Monitor TFTs, symptoms and growth.
- Consider associated autoimmune disease, including type 1 DM and coeliac disease.

questions.stem: A teenager with Graves disease remains symptomatic with tachycardia and tremor while definitive thyroid control is being established. Which treatment approach is listed?

options.label: D
options.text: Carbimazole first-line, propranolol for symptoms; consider radioiodine or surgery in selected older children

questions.correctAnswerText: Carbimazole first-line, propranolol for symptoms; consider radioiodine or surgery in selected older children
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include carbimazole as first-line medical treatment for Graves disease and beta-blockers such as propranolol for initial symptom relief. Radioiodine or surgery may be considered in selected older children as second-line options.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These replace adrenal hormones.
- B. Incorrect. Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism and desmopressin treats central DI.
- C. Incorrect. These treat diabetes, not thyrotoxicosis.
- D. Correct. This matches the treatment sequence described.
- E. Incorrect. These treat hypocalcaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Carbimazole: first-line antithyroid medication.
- Warn about sore throat/high fever and urgent blood count because of potential neutropenia/agranulocytosis.
- Propranolol may relieve tachycardia, tremor and anxiety.
- Radioiodine or surgery is reserved for selected cases under specialist care.

topics.name: Precocious Puberty — Treatment According to Mechanism

cases.title: A child with progressive central precocious puberty
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old girl has progressive breast development, pubic hair, advanced bone age and a pubertal LH response. The endocrine team explains that treatment depends on whether puberty is driven by premature activation of the central HPG axis or by peripheral sex-steroid production.

questions.stem: Which treatment is described for true central precocious puberty?
questions.correctAnswerText: Long-acting GnRH analogue therapy
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that true central precocious puberty is treated with GnRH analogues to suppress premature activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis. Peripheral precocious puberty requires treatment directed at the sex-steroid source or action.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin treats central DI.
- B. Incorrect. Calcium gluconate treats severe hypocalcaemia.
- C. Incorrect. These replace adrenal hormones.
- D. Correct. GnRH analogues suppress gonadotropin secretion in central PP.
- E. Incorrect. Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- True/central PP: GnRH analogues.
- Pseudo/peripheral PP: treat underlying source; sex-steroid/androgen action blockers may be used in selected cases.
- Treatment aims to slow pubertal progression and preserve adult height and psychosocial well-being.

cases.title: A child with severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child with known hypoparathyroidism develops stridor, carpopedal spasm and a generalized seizure. Serum calcium is markedly low. The clinician must correct the acute calcium deficit and arrange long-term replacement.

questions.stem: What is the appropriate treatment for severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia due to hypoparathyroidism?

options.label: D
options.text: Slow intravenous calcium gluconate, followed by oral calcium and vitamin D replacement

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow intravenous calcium gluconate, followed by oral calcium and vitamin D replacement
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes slow IV calcium gluconate for severe hypocalcaemia, followed by oral calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Monitor cardiac rhythm and serum calcium during treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fluid restriction does not correct a severe calcium deficit.
- B. Incorrect. Carbimazole treats hyperthyroidism.
- C. Incorrect. Insulin is used for diabetes and may lower serum potassium; it does not treat hypocalcaemia.
- D. Correct. This is the acute and subsequent management described.
- E. Incorrect. Desmopressin treats central DI.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia: slow IV calcium gluconate under monitoring.
- Follow with oral calcium and vitamin D.
- Treat the underlying cause (e.g. post-surgical, autoimmune or DiGeorge-related hypoparathyroidism).
- Watch for arrhythmia and recurrent symptoms.

topics.name: Polyuria and Polydipsia — Differential Diagnosis Beyond DI

cases.title: A child with polyuria and polydipsia but no hyperglycaemia
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child has excessive thirst and large urine volumes. Blood glucose is normal.

questions.stem: Which group contains causes of polyuria in children listed apart from diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus?

options.label: D
options.text: Graves disease, cleft palate and Meckel diverticulum

options.label: E
options.text: Polydipsia, CKD, RTA, Fanconi/Bartter, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia and diuretics/lithium

questions.correctAnswerText: Polydipsia, CKD, RTA, Fanconi/Bartter, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia and diuretics/lithium
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include primary polydipsia, renal causes including CKD, RTA, Fanconi and Bartter syndromes, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia and drugs (diuretics, vitamin D, lithium and amphotericin B) among the differential diagnoses of polyuria/polydipsia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are not the listed causes of polyuria.
- B. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal disorders and do not represent the key polyuria differential.
- C. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal obstructive conditions.
- D. Incorrect. These conditions do not form the listed polyuria differential.
- E. Correct. This is the differential list from the source page.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Polyuria differential: DM, DI, primary polydipsia and renal/electrolyte/drug causes.
- Hypercalcaemia and hypokalaemia may impair renal concentrating ability.
- Review medication exposure and measure serum/urine osmolality and electrolytes.

cases.title: A child with polydipsia and large volumes of dilute urine

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl drinks about 3 L daily and passes about 2.8 L of urine, with nocturnal enuresis. Plasma glucose is normal. Serum sodium is 134 mmol/L, calcium 9.6 mg/dL and potassium 4.0 mmol/L. Plasma osmolality is 278 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.correctAnswerText: Primary polydipsia
questions.initialExplanation: Polyuria is confirmed (above 40 mL/kg/24 h), but the plasma is not concentrated. In diabetes insipidus clinical guidance gives serum osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg (with high sodium) and urine osmolality below 300. Here plasma osmolality and sodium are low-normal and the dilute urine is an appropriate response to water excess.
questions.detailedExplanation:
