- A and B. Incorrect. Both central and nephrogenic DI produce hypernatraemia and serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg because water is lost. This girl's plasma is dilute.
- C. Incorrect. Normal glucose excludes diabetes mellitus.
- D. Correct. Excess water intake dilutes the plasma, and the kidneys appropriately excrete dilute urine.
- E. Incorrect. Calcium is normal, so hypercalcaemia does not explain the polyuria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DI: serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality <300, high sodium. Water deprivation and DDAVP response separate central from nephrogenic DI.
- Causes of polyuria and polydipsia: diabetes mellitus, DI, primary polydipsia, renal causes (CKD, RTA, Fanconi, Bartter), hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, drugs.
- Polyuria: >40 mL/kg/24 h or >2000 mL/m²/24 h.

source.raw: Endocrine sheet — Diabetes insipidus, diagnosis (Page 43); causes of polyuria and polydipsia (Page 43).

topics.name: Puberty — Male Tanner Staging and Delayed Puberty Treatment

cases.title: An adolescent boy undergoing Tanner staging
cases.vignette: A 13-year-old boy is examined because of delayed pubertal progression. Testicular volume is recorded and genital stage is assessed. The clinician explains how penile growth and pubic hair distribution change through puberty and when treatment may be considered for delayed puberty.

questions.stem: Which change corresponds to Tanner genital stage G3 in a boy?

options.label: A
options.text: Initial enlargement of the scrotum and testes

options.label: C
options.text: Further testicular growth with increase in penile length

options.label: E
options.text: Increased breadth of the penis with development of the glans

questions.correctAnswerText: Further testicular growth with increase in penile length
questions.initialExplanation: The PDF Tanner diagram shows G1 as prepubertal, G2 as enlargement of testes/scrotum, G3 as further testicular growth and penile lengthening, G4 as increased penile breadth and glans development, and G5 as adult genitalia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes G2.
- B. Incorrect. This describes G5.
- C. Correct. This is the G3 description shown in the diagram.
- D. Incorrect. This describes G1.
- E. Incorrect. This describes G4.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- G1: prepubertal.
- G2: testes/scrotum enlarge, scrotal skin reddens/thins.
- G3: penis length increases with further testicular growth.
- G4: increased penile breadth and glans development.
- G5: adult genitalia.
- Pubic hair staging (PH1–PH5) is recorded separately from genital stage.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl has delayed puberty after evaluation has excluded an underlying structural or endocrine disorder. Which treatment option is described to initiate puberty when needed?

options.label: C
options.text: Specialist-supervised low-dose oestradiol for several months

questions.correctAnswerText: Specialist-supervised low-dose oestradiol for several months
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that treatment should address any underlying pathology and that low-dose oestradiol may be used for several months to induce puberty in girls when necessary.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Carbimazole treats hyperthyroidism.
- B. Incorrect. Fludrocortisone replaces mineralocorticoid in primary adrenal insufficiency.
- C. Correct. This is the treatment described for selected girls with delayed puberty.
- D. Incorrect. Desmopressin treats central DI.
- E. Incorrect. Calcium gluconate treats hypocalcaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Delayed puberty: identify/treat the underlying cause first.
- Selected girls may receive low-dose oestradiol for a limited period under specialist supervision.
- Boys with constitutional delay may require individualized assessment and management; do not assume all cases need hormone treatment.

cases.title: A child with short stature and a delayed hand radiograph
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child with short stature undergoes a left hand and wrist radiograph to assess skeletal maturation. The endocrinologist compares the image with a standard atlas to estimate bone age and interpret whether skeletal maturation is delayed or advanced.

questions.stem: Which method is identified as a widely used system for assessing bone age?
questions.correctAnswerText: Greulich–Pyle atlas
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include the Greulich–Pyle atlas, based on a left hand and wrist radiograph, as the most widely used bone-age assessment method.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Apgar assesses the newborn's immediate condition.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the bone-age method described.
- C. Incorrect. Glasgow Coma Scale assesses consciousness.
- D. Correct. This is the method named.
- E. Incorrect. Denver screening evaluates child development, not skeletal maturation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bone age: left hand/wrist radiograph.
- Greulich–Pyle atlas is the widely used system described.
- Delayed or advanced bone age helps narrow the differential diagnosis of short stature and pubertal disorders.

cases.title: A child with pituitary disease and low cortisol
cases.vignette: A 12-year-old child with a known pituitary lesion develops fatigue, nausea and recurrent hypoglycaemia. Serum cortisol is low, but there is no hyperpigmentation or hyperkalaemia. The clinician distinguishes secondary adrenal insufficiency from primary Addison disease.

questions.stem: Which biochemical pattern is more consistent with secondary adrenal insufficiency due to pituitary ACTH deficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Low cortisol with low or inappropriately normal ACTH; aldosterone is often relatively preserved

options.label: D
options.text: High free T4 with suppressed TSH

options.label: E
options.text: Low cortisol with markedly high ACTH, hyperkalaemia and hyperpigmentation in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Low cortisol with low or inappropriately normal ACTH; aldosterone is often relatively preserved
questions.initialExplanation: Secondary adrenal insufficiency is caused by inadequate ACTH from pituitary disease or suppression after long-term glucocorticoid therapy. ACTH is low or inappropriately normal, and aldosterone is usually preserved because it is mainly regulated by the renin–angiotensin system and potassium.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the biochemical pattern of secondary adrenal insufficiency.
- B. Incorrect. High cortisol with low ACTH suggests an ACTH-independent cortisol excess state.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the pattern of secondary adrenal failure.
- D. Incorrect. This is a hyperthyroid biochemical pattern.
- E. Incorrect. This describes primary Addison disease with high ACTH, often hyperpigmentation and mineralocorticoid deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary adrenal insufficiency: low cortisol, high ACTH, often low aldosterone, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia.
- Secondary: low cortisol with low/inappropriately normal ACTH; potassium is often normal because aldosterone is relatively preserved.
- History of pituitary disease or prolonged glucocorticoid therapy supports a secondary cause.

topics.name: Growth Hormone — Physiological Actions and Interpretation of IGF-1

cases.title: A child with poor growth and a low IGF-1 result
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child has reduced height velocity and delayed bone age. IGF-1 is low, but the child is also undernourished and has abnormal liver function tests. The endocrinologist reviews the physiological actions of GH and explains why IGF-1 must be interpreted with clinical context.

questions.stem: Which metabolic effect of growth hormone is described?

options.label: B
options.text: Suppression of linear and soft-tissue growth

options.label: C
options.text: Anti-insulin effect with increased gluconeogenesis/hyperglycaemia and lipolysis

options.label: D
options.text: Direct inhibition of IGF-1 production in the liver

options.label: E
options.text: Strong insulin-like reduction in blood glucose in most tissues

questions.correctAnswerText: Anti-insulin effect with increased gluconeogenesis/hyperglycaemia and lipolysis
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that GH increases linear and soft-tissue growth, stimulates protein synthesis and has an anti-insulin effect, contributing to increased glucose and lipolysis. Many growth actions are mediated through IGF-1.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. GH stimulates protein synthesis.
- B. Incorrect. GH promotes linear and soft-tissue growth.
- C. Correct. GH has anti-insulin effects and promotes lipolysis, while supporting growth and protein synthesis.
- D. Incorrect. GH stimulates hepatic IGF-1 production.
- E. Incorrect. GH is not a glucose-lowering hormone like insulin.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GH: linear growth, bone/soft tissue growth and protein synthesis.
- GH has anti-insulin effects and promotes lipolysis.
- IGF-1 mediates many growth-promoting effects and is produced largely in the liver.

questions.stem: A child with suspected GH deficiency has a low IGF-1 concentration but also significant malnutrition and chronic liver disease. How should the IGF-1 result be interpreted?

options.label: B
options.text: A random GH level is typically more reliable than clinical assessment

options.label: C
options.text: Low IGF-1 typically proves pituitary GH deficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Malnutrition and liver disease can lower IGF-1, so the result is not specific for GHD

options.label: E
options.text: IGF-1 is unaffected by nutritional or hepatic status

questions.correctAnswerText: Malnutrition and liver disease can lower IGF-1, so the result is not specific for GHD
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance specifically notes that IGF-1 is affected by liver disease and malnutrition. A low result must therefore be interpreted with growth pattern, clinical status and other investigations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Liver disease may reduce IGF-1 production.
- B. Incorrect. GH secretion is pulsatile, so random GH measurement has limited value.
- C. Incorrect. Low IGF-1 is not diagnostic by itself.
- D. Correct. Both liver dysfunction and undernutrition can reduce IGF-1 independently of pituitary GH deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. standard guidance explicitly lists liver disease and malnutrition as confounders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IGF-1 may be low in GHD, but also in malnutrition and liver disease.
- Interpret IGF-1 alongside growth velocity, bone age and clinical findings.
- GH stimulation testing assesses secretory reserve when indicated.

topics.name: Congenital Hypothyroidism — Maternal Causes and Newborn Screening

cases.title: A newborn identified by screening despite an unremarkable examination
cases.vignette: A newborn appears clinically normal in the first days of life. The mother has a history of thyroid disease and used antithyroid medication during pregnancy. Newborn screening later detects an abnormal TSH result.

questions.stem: Why is newborn screening important for congenital hypothyroidism?

options.label: A
options.text: Most affected infants may appear normal in the first weeks, while early treatment prevents avoidable neurodevelopmental harm

options.label: B
options.text: Congenital hypothyroidism cannot be detected by laboratory screening

options.label: C
options.text: most affected infants have obvious severe symptoms at birth

options.label: E
options.text: Treatment should wait until developmental delay appears

questions.correctAnswerText: Most affected infants may appear normal in the first weeks, while early treatment prevents avoidable neurodevelopmental harm
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that most infants are asymptomatic at birth and are difficult to distinguish clinically from normal newborns during the first month. Newborn screening detects cases before symptoms become obvious.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Screening permits early diagnosis and treatment before irreversible neurodevelopmental injury.
- B. Incorrect. Newborn screening uses thyroid function testing, particularly TSH.
- C. Incorrect. Many infants initially appear normal.
- D. Incorrect. Screening is performed in the newborn period.
- E. Incorrect. Delaying treatment increases the risk of impaired intellectual development.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most congenital hypothyroid infants initially appear normal.
- Newborn screening (standard guidance references the Guthrie test/screening programme) detects cases early.
- Start levothyroxine promptly; An important point is treatment within the first 2 weeks.

questions.stem: A newborn has transient hypothyroidism after maternal thyroid disease and antithyroid medication exposure during pregnancy. Which mechanism is listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Transplacental passage of maternal TSH-blocking antibodies or antithyroid drugs

options.label: B
options.text: Maternal ACTH stimulating the fetal thyroid

options.label: C
options.text: ADH crossing the placenta and suppressing TSH

questions.correctAnswerText: Transplacental passage of maternal TSH-blocking antibodies or antithyroid drugs
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include transient neonatal hypothyroidism due to transplacental passage of maternal TSH-blocking antibodies or antithyroid medications. It may resolve within approximately 6 months to 1 year.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These maternal factors may transiently impair neonatal thyroid hormone synthesis or stimulation.
- B. Incorrect. ACTH controls adrenal cortisol production, not thyroid hormone synthesis.
- C. Incorrect. ADH is not the mechanism.
- D. Incorrect. PTH regulates calcium, not thyroid gland development.
- E. Incorrect. Insulin does not cause this thyroid disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Transient congenital hypothyroidism may follow maternal TSH-blocking antibodies or antithyroid drugs.
- Clinical guidance notes resolution within approximately 6 months–1 year in these transient cases.
- Maternal iodine deficiency is also a worldwide cause of congenital hypothyroidism and can be prevented through adequate iodine intake/iodized salt.

topics.name: Graves Disease — Antibody and Imaging Confirmation

cases.title: A teenager with suspected autoimmune thyrotoxicosis
cases.vignette: A 15-year-old girl has weight loss, tremor, tachycardia and a diffuse goitre with a bruit. Thyroid tests show high free T4 and suppressed TSH.

questions.stem: Which antibody is positive in approximately 95% of Graves disease cases?
questions.correctAnswerText: TSH-receptor antibody
questions.initialExplanation: Graves disease is caused by stimulating antibodies to the TSH receptor. Clinical guidance notes TSH-receptor antibodies are positive in approximately 95% of cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies are associated with autoimmune adrenal insufficiency.
- B. Correct. TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies are the characteristic marker.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the defining Graves antibody.
- D. Incorrect. Anti-ADH antibody is not a standard Graves marker.
- E. Incorrect. Anti-CCP antibodies are associated with rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Graves: stimulatory TSH-receptor antibodies.
- TSH-receptor Ab is positive in approximately 95%.
- Anti-TPO may also be present but is not as specific as TSH-receptor Ab.

questions.stem: A child with Graves disease has diffuse high thyroid uptake on radionuclide imaging. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Uptake imaging measures pituitary GH secretion

options.label: B
options.text: Increased uptake supports active hormone synthesis by the thyroid gland

options.label: C
options.text: No uptake is expected in most untreated Graves disease

options.label: D
options.text: High uptake is diagnostic of congenital hypothyroidism

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased uptake supports active hormone synthesis by the thyroid gland
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include thyroid ultrasound and radionuclide scanning with high uptake as supportive imaging in Graves disease, which is caused by stimulation of the thyroid gland.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Thyroid uptake imaging assesses thyroid function, not GH secretion.
- B. Correct. Diffuse increased uptake supports active thyroid hormone synthesis, as in Graves disease.
- C. Incorrect. Untreated Graves usually shows increased uptake.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism due to thyroid agenesis or dysgenesis may show absent or altered uptake, not the Graves pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Low uptake is not the typical pattern of untreated Graves disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Graves: high free T4/T3, suppressed TSH, TSH-receptor antibodies and increased radionuclide uptake.
- Thyroid imaging is supportive and selected according to the clinical situation.
- Persistent follow-up is required after medical or definitive therapy because hypothyroidism may develop and require levothyroxine.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which embryological event is responsible for an isolated cleft palate?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of fusion of the palatine processes

options.label: B
options.text: Failure of separation of the foregut from the respiratory tract

options.label: C
options.text: Failure of fusion of the frontonasal and maxillary processes

options.label: E
options.text: Failure of descent of the thyroid gland

questions.correctAnswerText: Failure of fusion of the palatine processes
questions.initialExplanation: Cleft palate results from failure of fusion of the palatine processes. Cleft lip is associated with failure of fusion of the frontonasal and maxillary processes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Failure of fusion of the palatine processes produces cleft palate.
- B. Incorrect. Foregut separation abnormalities are related to tracheoesophageal malformations.
- C. Incorrect. standard guidance associates failure of fusion of the frontonasal and maxillary processes with cleft lip.
- D. Incorrect. Neural tube closure defects cause neural tube abnormalities.
- E. Incorrect. This is related to thyroid developmental abnormalities, not cleft palate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cleft lip: failure of fusion of frontonasal and maxillary processes.
- Cleft palate: failure of fusion of the palatine processes.
- Clinical descriptions include cleft lip/palate as multifactorial, involving genetic and environmental factors.

questions.stem: A newborn with cleft palate has recurrent coughing during feeds and poor weight gain. Which additional complication is particularly associated with this congenital defect?
questions.correctAnswerText: Recurrent aspiration pneumonia
questions.initialExplanation: Poor coordination of feeding and swallowing can lead to aspiration. Common examples include aspiration pneumonia, failure to thrive, speech problems, dentition problems and recurrent otitis media among the complications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis occurs in children with aganglionosis.
- B. Incorrect. Meckel diverticulum may cause painless gastrointestinal bleeding.
- C. Correct. Aspiration pneumonia is a recognized complication of cleft palate because feeding and swallowing may be impaired.
- D. Incorrect. Intussusception is telescoping of one bowel segment into another.
- E. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes gastric outlet obstruction and projectile non-bilious vomiting.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cleft lip/palate complications: feeding difficulty, FTT, aspiration pneumonia, speech and dental problems, recurrent otitis media and conductive hearing impairment.
- Follow-up requires a multidisciplinary team.

questions.stem: A newborn has micrognathia, glossoptosis and a U-shaped cleft palate. Which diagnosis best describes this combination?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pierre Robin sequence
questions.initialExplanation: Pierre Robin sequence is characterized by micrognathia, glossoptosis and cleft palate. The small mandible contributes to posterior displacement of the tongue.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Patau syndrome is a chromosomal disorder that may include cleft lip/palate, but it is not the named sequence described by this triad.
- B. Incorrect. VACTERL is an association of vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies.
- C. Correct. The combination of mandibular hypoplasia, glossoptosis and cleft palate is characteristic.
- D. Incorrect. Down syndrome may be associated with congenital anomalies, but this specific triad defines Pierre Robin sequence.
- E. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis presents with progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pierre Robin sequence: micrognathia + glossoptosis + cleft palate.
- Cleft lip/palate may occur in isolation or with other congenital anomalies or syndromes.

questions.stem: Which timing is paired correctly with surgical correction of cleft lip and cleft palate?

options.label: A
options.text: Cleft lip in the first 3 months; cleft palate at 6–12 months

options.label: B
options.text: Timing is identical for both defects and is typically after eruption of permanent teeth

options.label: C
options.text: Both are routinely repaired in the first 2 weeks

options.label: D
options.text: Cleft lip at 6–12 months; cleft palate in the first 3 months

options.label: E
options.text: Cleft lip after 2 years; cleft palate after 5 years

questions.correctAnswerText: Cleft lip in the first 3 months; cleft palate at 6–12 months
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives the first 3 months for cleft lip repair and 6–12 months for cleft palate repair.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the pairing recorded in the original standard guidance.
- B. Incorrect. standard guidance provides different timing for lip and palate repair.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the timing given.
- D. Incorrect. It reverses the timing stated.
- E. Incorrect. These ages are not standard guidance's stated timing.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cleft lip repair: first 3 months,.
- Cleft palate repair: 6–12 months,.
- Individual surgical timing may vary with the multidisciplinary team's assessment and local practice.

questions.stem: Which treatment is most consistent with standard guidance's recommended management?

options.label: C
options.text: A course of systemic antibacterial therapy

options.label: D
options.text: A topical antifungal such as nystatin or miconazole

questions.correctAnswerText: A topical antifungal such as nystatin or miconazole
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes topical antifungal treatment for oral thrush, specifically nystatin or miconazole.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The adherent white oral plaques support oral candidiasis rather than a reflux-related or bacterial condition. Once the clinical diagnosis is established, the treatment stated is a topical antifungal.

- A. Incorrect. Metoclopramide is discussed in the GERD section, not as treatment for oral candidiasis; standard guidance also cautions against its use as a pediatric antiemetic because of extrapyramidal adverse effects.
- B. Incorrect. Proton pump inhibitors are listed in the GERD treatment section and do not treat Candida infection of the oral mucosa.
- C. Incorrect. Recognized features include Candida albicans as the cause and recommends an antifungal, not antibacterial treatment.
- D. Correct. Nystatin or miconazole are the topical antifungal agents specifically named.
- E. Incorrect. Fundoplication is an operation described for selected severe or refractory GERD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Oral thrush is an oropharyngeal Candida infection, commonly due to *Candida albicans*.
- The plaques are typically difficult to remove with a tongue depressor.
- standard guidance names topical nystatin or miconazole as treatment.
- Persistent, severe or recurrent thrush in an older child, especially with FTT, should raise concern for possible immunodeficiency.

cases.title: An infant with persistent white oral plaques
cases.vignette: A 2-month-old infant is brought because of white plaques over the oral mucosa. The plaques do not wipe away easily with a tongue depressor. The infant is otherwise well.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Oral candidiasis
questions.initialExplanation: Oral thrush is caused by Candida, commonly Candida albicans. It typically appears as white plaques on the oral mucosa that are difficult to remove.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Adherent white oral plaques in an infant are characteristic of oral candidiasis.
- B. Incorrect. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease causes oral lesions with an associated rash on the hands and feet.
- C. Incorrect. Herpangina causes acute painful vesicular or ulcerative lesions, typically involving the posterior oropharynx.
- D. Incorrect. Aphthous ulcers are painful recurrent mucosal ulcers, not adherent white plaques.
- E. Incorrect. Leukoplakia is a different oral mucosal lesion and is not the typical infant presentation described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Oral thrush = oropharyngeal candidiasis.
- Candida albicans is the organism highlighted.
- The plaques are difficult to remove with a tongue depressor.

questions.stem: An older child has severe, persistent and recurrent oral candidiasis with poor weight gain. Which underlying problem should be particularly considered?

options.label: A
options.text: Isolated iron deficiency without other features

questions.correctAnswerText: Immunodeficiency
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that thrush can occur in healthy neonates and infants, but persistent, severe or recurrent candidiasis in an older child should prompt consideration of immunodeficiency, particularly when associated with failure to thrive.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron deficiency alone does not explain the described recurrent candidiasis.
- B. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting in early infancy.
- C. Incorrect. Functional constipation does not account for recurrent oral candidiasis.
- D. Correct. Persistent or recurrent severe oral candidiasis in an older child is a warning feature for possible immunodeficiency.
- E. Incorrect. Teething is a physiological process and does not explain persistent candidal plaques.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Thrush is common in healthy neonates and infants.
- Persistent, severe or recurrent thrush in an older child is a red flag.
- Associated FTT strengthens the need to assess for an underlying immune problem.

cases.title: A child with painful oral lesions
cases.vignette: A preschool child presents with fever, irritability and painful oral lesions. The clinician distinguishes between recurrent aphthous ulcers, viral ulcerative illnesses and primary herpetic gingivostomatitis. The family asks about the likely cause and supportive treatment.

questions.stem: A school-aged child has recurrent aphthous ulcers. Which group of conditions is included 's differential diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Hirschsprung disease, anal atresia and encopresis

options.label: C
options.text: Coeliac disease, SLE and inflammatory bowel disease

options.label: D
options.text: Pyloric stenosis, duodenal atresia and malrotation

questions.correctAnswerText: Coeliac disease, SLE and inflammatory bowel disease
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include coeliac disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, inflammatory bowel disease, Behçet disease and cyclic neutropenia among the differential diagnoses of recurrent aphthous ulcers.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are oesophageal disorders, not the listed differential for recurrent aphthous ulcers.
- B. Incorrect. These are anorectal or bowel-motility disorders.
- C. Correct. All three are explicitly included 's differential diagnosis.
- D. Incorrect. These are congenital or obstructive gastrointestinal disorders and are not the listed aphthous-ulcer associations.
- E. Incorrect. These are causes of intestinal bleeding or obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Recurrent aphthous ulcers are common but may be associated with systemic disease.
- standard guidance differentials: coeliac disease, SLE, IBD, Behçet disease and cyclic neutropenia.
- Treat symptomatically and address an underlying cause when identified.

questions.stem: A child has fever and painful posterior oral ulcers due to coxsackievirus infection. The illness is self-limiting. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Herpangina
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance associates herpangina with coxsackievirus and describes it as self-limiting, with hydration and supportive care.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Oral candidiasis produces adherent white plaques.
- B. Incorrect. Dental caries is tooth decay associated with oral bacteria and dietary sugars.
- C. Incorrect. Herpetic gingivostomatitis is caused by HSV-1 and commonly presents with fever, painful ulcers and irritability.
- D. Incorrect. Aphthous ulcers are recurrent ulcers of uncertain etiology and are not the specific viral syndrome described.
- E. Correct. Herpangina is a coxsackievirus-associated, self-limiting illness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Herpangina: coxsackievirus; supportive care and adequate hydration.
- Hand-foot-and-mouth disease: coxsackievirus A.
- Herpetic gingivostomatitis: HSV-1; painful oral ulcers, fever and irritability.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child develops fever, irritability and painful widespread oral ulcers. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.correctAnswerText: HSV-1
questions.initialExplanation: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is caused by herpes simplex virus type 1. Clinical descriptions include fever, pain, irritability and oral ulcers in preschool children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Giardia causes intestinal infection with diarrhoea and malabsorption symptoms.
- B. Correct. HSV-1 is the cause of primary herpetic gingivostomatitis.
- C. Incorrect. Candida causes oral thrush with adherent white plaques.
- D. Incorrect. Rotavirus is a major cause of acute gastroenteritis.
- E. Incorrect. H. pylori is associated with gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Herpetic gingivostomatitis: HSV-1.
- Management is supportive: analgesia, increased fluid intake and cold fluids.
- Maintain hydration because oral pain may reduce intake.

cases.title: Delayed eruption of teeth
cases.vignette: A 14-month-old child has no erupted primary teeth. The parents are concerned about delayed teething. There are no acute symptoms, and the clinician reviews normal eruption timing and possible causes of delayed eruption.

questions.stem: Which primary tooth normally erupts first, at approximately 6 months of age?
questions.correctAnswerText: Lower central incisor
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include the lower central incisors as the first primary teeth to erupt, at about 6 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Lower central incisors are usually the first primary teeth to erupt.
- B. Incorrect. Upper central incisors generally erupt later than the lower central incisors.
- C. Incorrect. Canines erupt later than the central incisors.
- D. Incorrect. First primary molars erupt later in infancy.
- E. Incorrect. Second primary molars are among the last primary teeth to erupt.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- First primary teeth: lower central incisors, around 6 months.
- Common examples include delayed teething as no eruption beyond 13 months.
- The first permanent tooth to erupt is usually the first molar at approximately 6 years.

questions.stem: A 15-month-old child has not developed any erupted teeth. Which condition is included 's differential diagnosis of delayed teething?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypothyroidism
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include hypothyroidism among the causes to consider in delayed teething, alongside rickets, Down syndrome, achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta, hypopituitarism and idiopathic delay.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Appendicitis is an acute abdominal condition.
- B. Correct. Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of delayed tooth eruption.
- C. Incorrect. Intussusception causes intestinal obstruction and episodic abdominal pain.
- D. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious projectile vomiting in early infancy.
- E. Incorrect. Meckel diverticulum may cause gastrointestinal bleeding or obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Delayed teething: no eruption beyond 13 months.
- Differentials include rickets, Down syndrome, hypothyroidism, achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta and hypopituitarism.
- Natal teeth are present at birth and may be extracted if there is a risk of aspiration.

cases.title: A thriving infant with frequent regurgitation
cases.vignette: A 3-month-old infant frequently brings up small amounts of milk after feeds. The episodes are effortless and non-projectile. The infant is comfortable, feeds well and follows the expected growth trajectory. There is no choking, respiratory complication or evidence of oesophagitis.

questions.stem: Which term best describes the effortless return of small amounts of milk into the mouth in an otherwise thriving infant?
questions.correctAnswerText: Regurgitation or posseting
questions.initialExplanation: Regurgitation is the non-forceful return of gastric contents into the oesophagus or mouth. Posseting refers to small amounts of milk returning, often with swallowed air.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing.
- B. Incorrect. Bilious vomiting suggests bile-stained contents and may indicate intestinal obstruction.
- C. Incorrect. Haematemesis is vomiting blood.
- D. Incorrect. Projectile vomiting is forceful and is classically associated with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
- E. Correct. The history describes non-forceful regurgitation/posseting.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vomiting: forceful ejection of gastric contents.
- Regurgitation: non-forceful return of gastric contents.
- Posseting: small-volume, non-forceful milk return, common in infancy.

questions.stem: The infant is growing normally and has no troublesome symptoms or complications. How should the condition be classified?
questions.correctAnswerText: Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux (GER)
questions.initialExplanation: Physiological GER is common in infancy and occurs without troublesome symptoms or complications. A thriving infant without failure to thrive is generally managed with reassurance and feeding advice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Severe oesophagitis would be associated with complications such as pain, feeding refusal or bleeding.
- B. Incorrect. Oesophageal atresia typically presents in the newborn with excessive secretions and choking during the first feed.
- C. Incorrect. GERD implies troublesome symptoms or complications, such as poor weight gain, oesophagitis or respiratory manifestations.
- D. Incorrect. Gastric outlet obstruction causes persistent vomiting and other obstructive features.
- E. Correct. Normal growth and absence of complications support physiological GER.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GER: reflux without troublesome symptoms or complications.
- GERD: reflux associated with troublesome symptoms or complications.
- Most infant reflux resolves spontaneously by 12–24 months,.

questions.stem: Which mechanism contributes to physiological reflux in early infancy?

options.label: A
options.text: Immaturity of lower oesophageal sphincter tone

options.label: B
options.text: Complete absence of gastric acid secretion

options.label: C
options.text: Failure of intestinal ganglion cell migration

options.label: D
options.text: Obstruction of the distal ileum by meconium

questions.correctAnswerText: Immaturity of lower oesophageal sphincter tone
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include immature lower oesophageal sphincter tone as a principal contributor to reflux in early life.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Immature lower oesophageal sphincter tone permits reflux of gastric contents.
- B. Incorrect. Absence of gastric acid secretion is not the mechanism given for infant reflux.
- C. Incorrect. This mechanism causes Hirschsprung disease.
- D. Incorrect. Meconium ileus causes distal intestinal obstruction and is associated with cystic fibrosis.
- E. Incorrect. Congenital absence of the pylorus is not the described cause.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Factors contributing to infant GER: immature LES tone, increased intra-abdominal pressure, predominantly liquid diet, horizontal posture and delayed gastric emptying.
- Prematurity and neurodevelopmental disorders are among the risk factors for severe disease or complications.

questions.stem: An infant with recurrent reflux has poor weight gain, choking during feeds and repeated aspiration pneumonia. What is the most appropriate classification?
questions.correctAnswerText: GERD
questions.initialExplanation: The presence of troublesome symptoms and complications, including failure to thrive, choking and aspiration pneumonia, indicates pathological gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lactose intolerance causes osmotic diarrhoea, bloating and acidic stools.
- B. Incorrect. Functional abdominal pain is a chronic pain disorder and does not explain infant aspiration.
- C. Correct. Poor weight gain and respiratory complications indicate GERD.
- D. Incorrect. Physiological GER occurs without troublesome symptoms or complications and is associated with normal growth.
- E. Incorrect. Posseting is small-volume, non-forceful milk return and does not explain aspiration complications and FTT.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GERD features in infants may include feeding refusal, poor weight gain, choking, recurrent wheeze, aspiration pneumonia and apnoea.
- In older children, heartburn and recurrent regurgitation may be prominent.
- Sandifer syndrome is dystonic neck posturing associated with reflux.

questions.stem: An infant repeatedly arches the back and extends the neck after feeding in association with reflux. What is this posture called?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sandifer syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Sandifer syndrome describes dystonic posturing of the neck and back associated with gastro-oesophageal reflux.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Sandifer syndrome is the characteristic dystonic neck posturing described.
- B. Incorrect. Murphy sign is associated with gallbladder inflammation.
- C. Incorrect. Opisthotonus is severe extensor posturing and is not the named reflux-associated posture.
- D. Incorrect. Rovsing sign is associated with appendicitis.
- E. Incorrect. Kernig sign is a meningeal irritation sign.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sandifer syndrome: dystonic neck posturing associated with GERD.
- Reflux symptoms in infants can include feeding-related choking, arching and head/neck extension.

questions.stem: Which investigation is described as the best quantitative and sensitive test when objective assessment of acid reflux is required?
questions.correctAnswerText: 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring as the best quantitative and sensitive investigation for documenting acid reflux.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stool culture is used in selected cases of suspected infectious diarrhoea.
- B. Incorrect. A barium swallow has poor sensitivity and specificity for GERD. It may help identify anatomical abnormalities but does not diagnose or grade reflux reliably.
- C. Incorrect. A plain abdominal radiograph does not quantify oesophageal acid reflux.
- D. Incorrect. Abdominal ultrasound is used for selected abdominal conditions, such as pyloric stenosis, not for quantifying reflux.
- E. Correct. It measures oesophageal pH over 24 hours and quantifies acid reflux episodes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 24-hour pH monitoring: quantitative assessment of acid reflux.
- Impedance monitoring can detect weakly acidic and non-acid reflux where available.
- Barium swallow is not recommended as a diagnostic test for GERD.

questions.stem: A child with suspected GERD has persistent symptoms and possible oesophagitis. Which investigation is most useful for identifying oesophagitis and related mucosal complications?
questions.correctAnswerText: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include endoscopy as useful for diagnosing oesophagitis and complications and for excluding other causes of vomiting. Biopsy may be taken.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sweat chloride testing is used in the evaluation of cystic fibrosis.
- B. Incorrect. A plain abdominal film does not assess oesophageal mucosal inflammation.
- C. Incorrect. Stool microscopy is used for selected infectious or parasitic causes of diarrhoea.
- D. Correct. Endoscopy directly assesses the oesophageal mucosa and allows biopsy.
- E. Incorrect. A Meckel scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa in suspected Meckel diverticulum.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- GERD is usually diagnosed clinically.
- Investigations are considered for atypical history, complications or failure to respond to treatment.
- Endoscopy: oesophagitis/complications and exclusion of alternative causes.
- Scintigraphy is described as assessing gastric emptying and documenting aspiration.

questions.stem: What is an appropriate initial conservative measure for an otherwise well infant with uncomplicated reflux?

options.label: E
options.text: Reassure the caregivers and optimize feeding technique

questions.correctAnswerText: Reassure the caregivers and optimize feeding technique
questions.initialExplanation: Uncomplicated infant reflux has an excellent prognosis. An important point is parental reassurance, appropriate feeding volumes, small frequent feeds and feeding-position advice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Reflux is not a bacterial infection requiring routine antibiotics.
- B. Incorrect. Stopping all feeds is inappropriate and may compromise nutrition.
- C. Incorrect. Surgery is reserved for selected severe or refractory cases with complications.
- D. Incorrect. Antidiarrhoeal medication does not treat GERD.
- E. Correct. Reassurance and appropriate feeding measures are the initial conservative approach.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Small, frequent feeds and avoidance of overfeeding are conservative measures.
- standard guidance also mentions thickened feeds and upright/semi-sitting positioning after feeding.
- Feeding-position advice must not replace safe-sleep recommendations: infants should still be placed supine for sleep.

questions.stem: An infant has severe reflux with persistent complications despite appropriate medical treatment. Which operation is described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Nissen fundoplication
questions.initialExplanation: Nissen fundoplication wraps the gastric fundus around the intra-abdominal oesophagus. Common examples include refractory oesophagitis, strictures, chronic pulmonary disease and persistent vomiting with FTT among indications for surgery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ramstedt pyloromyotomy is the definitive operation for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
- B. Incorrect. Duodenoduodenostomy is a repair used for duodenal atresia.
- C. Incorrect. The Ladd procedure is used to treat intestinal malrotation with volvulus or obstructive bands.
- D. Incorrect. A pull-through operation is used in the surgical management of Hirschsprung disease.
- E. Correct. Nissen fundoplication is the anti-reflux procedure described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nissen fundoplication: gastric fundus wrapped around the lower oesophagus.
- Considered in selected severe or refractory GERD.
- GERD complications include oesophagitis, bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia, stricture, Barrett oesophagus and respiratory complications.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which pharmacological group is described as the most potent and first-line option?

options.label: B
options.text: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole

options.label: D
options.text: Metoclopramide as a routine pediatric antiemetic

questions.correctAnswerText: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include proton pump inhibitors, including omeprazole and esomeprazole, as the most potent pharmacological treatment and identifies them as first-line in its treatment outline.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has troublesome symptoms and poor weight gain rather than uncomplicated physiological reflux. The question asks specifically about the pharmacological hierarchy stated in the supplied standard guidance. That clinical guidance lists antacids and H2 antagonists, then describes proton pump inhibitors as the most potent and first-line treatment.

- A. Incorrect. Ranitidine and cimetidine are listed as H2 antagonists, but Recognized features include PPIs as the most potent and first-line option.
- B. Correct. Omeprazole and esomeprazole are the PPIs named.
- C. Incorrect. Clinical guidance notes significant adverse effects with domperidone and says its use should be discouraged.
- D. Incorrect. Clinical guidance that metoclopramide is contraindicated as a pediatric antiemetic because central action may cause extrapyramidal effects.
- E. Incorrect. Antacids are listed, but they are not the pharmacological group identified by standard guidance as most potent and first-line.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PPIs named: omeprazole and esomeprazole.
- H2 antagonists named: ranitidine and cimetidine.
- standard guidance discourages domperidone because of significant adverse effects.
- standard guidance cautions against metoclopramide as a pediatric antiemetic because of extrapyramidal side effects.
- This item reflects the treatment hierarchy written in the supplied GIT clinical guidance.

cases.title: A newborn who chokes during the first feed
cases.vignette: A newborn develops excessive frothy oral secretions shortly after birth. During the first feeding attempt, the infant coughs, chokes and becomes cyanosed. The antenatal history includes polyhydramnios. A nasogastric tube cannot be advanced into the stomach.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Oesophageal atresia with or without tracheoesophageal fistula

questions.correctAnswerText: Oesophageal atresia with or without tracheoesophageal fistula
questions.initialExplanation: Excessive frothy secretions and choking/cyanosis during the first feed are classic features of oesophageal atresia, often associated with a tracheoesophageal fistula.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The combination of frothy salivation, choking and cyanosis on feeding strongly suggests EA/TEF.
- B. Incorrect. Duodenal atresia usually presents with early bilious vomiting and a double-bubble radiograph.
- C. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis presents several weeks later with progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting.
- D. Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium passage and bowel obstruction.
- E. Incorrect. GER may cause regurgitation, but it does not typically cause inability to pass an NGT and the characteristic neonatal presentation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EA/TEF: persistent frothy salivation, coughing, choking and cyanosis during feeding.
- Polyhydramnios may be present antenatally.
- The newborn may initially appear normal before the first feed.

questions.stem: Which anatomical subtype is the most common form of EA/TEF?

options.label: C
options.text: Double fistula with proximal and distal communications

options.label: D
options.text: Oesophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula

questions.correctAnswerText: Oesophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include oesophageal atresia with a distal TEF as the commonest subtype, accounting for approximately 85% of cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. EA with proximal fistula is uncommon.
- B. Incorrect. H-type fistula occurs without oesophageal atresia and is less common.
- C. Incorrect. A double fistula is rare.
- D. Correct. EA with distal fistula is the commonest pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Isolated EA is listed as a less common subtype.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The most common configuration: proximal oesophageal blind pouch + distal TEF.
- An H-type fistula may present later with feeding problems and recurrent aspiration pneumonia.
- The exact percentages are approximate and should be checked against the source PDF if required.

questions.stem: A newborn with suspected EA/TEF undergoes insertion of an NGT followed by chest and abdominal radiography. Which finding supports oesophageal atresia?

options.label: A
options.text: Target sign in the right upper abdomen

options.label: B
options.text: NGT is coiled in the upper oesophageal pouch

options.label: C
options.text: NGT passes freely into the stomach

questions.correctAnswerText: NGT is coiled in the upper oesophageal pouch
questions.initialExplanation: In oesophageal atresia, the NGT cannot reach the stomach and coils in the upper oesophageal pouch on radiography.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A target/doughnut sign is associated with intussusception on ultrasound.
- B. Correct. A coiled tube in the upper chest is the characteristic radiographic clue.
- C. Incorrect. Free passage into the stomach argues against oesophageal atresia.
- D. Incorrect. Free intraperitoneal air suggests perforation.
- E. Incorrect. A double-bubble sign suggests duodenal atresia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NGT coiled in the upper pouch supports EA.
- Gas in the abdomen suggests an associated distal TEF.
- H-type fistula may require contrast oesophagram or endoscopic evaluation.

questions.stem: A neonate with EA/TEF is being assessed for associated congenital abnormalities. Which group of anomalies is represented by VACTERL association?

options.label: A
options.text: Vertebral, auditory, cardiac, tracheal, endocrine and lung

options.label: B
options.text: Vascular, airway, cranial, thyroid, endocrine and liver

options.label: C
options.text: Vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb

options.label: D
options.text: Ventricular, aortic, coronary, tracheal, oesophageal and limb

options.label: E
options.text: Visceral, anal, cerebral, thoracic, renal and lymphatic

questions.correctAnswerText: Vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb
questions.initialExplanation: VACTERL is an association of vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies. Clinical guidance notes that associated congenital malformations occur in a substantial proportion of EA/TEF cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Auditory and endocrine abnormalities are not the listed components.
- B. Incorrect. These are not the components of VACTERL.
- C. Correct. This is the expansion of VACTERL.
- D. Incorrect. It includes cardiovascular terms but does not reproduce the VACTERL association.
- E. Incorrect. This is not the accepted expansion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- V — Vertebral anomalies.
- A — Anal/anorectal malformations.
- C — Cardiac defects.
- TE — Tracheoesophageal fistula and/or oesophageal atresia.
- R — Renal anomalies.
- L — Limb anomalies.

questions.stem: What is the appropriate initial stabilization of a newborn with suspected EA/TEF before definitive surgical repair?

options.label: B
options.text: Delay assessment until the infant develops aspiration pneumonia

options.label: C
options.text: Keep NPO, provide upper-pouch drainage/NGT management and intravenous fluids

options.label: D
options.text: Start oral feeds in small amounts

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep NPO, provide upper-pouch drainage/NGT management and intravenous fluids
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes keeping the infant nil by mouth, providing NGT management and intravenous fluids, and giving respiratory support when required before urgent surgical correction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pyloromyotomy is used for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
- B. Incorrect. Stabilization and early surgical assessment are required; waiting for aspiration is unsafe.
- C. Correct. NPO status, secretion management, IV fluids and respiratory support when needed are the initial measures.
- D. Incorrect. Oral feeding risks aspiration.
- E. Incorrect. Laxatives do not treat EA/TEF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Suspected EA/TEF: stop oral feeds, prevent aspiration, provide IV fluids and respiratory support if needed.
- Definitive repair involves ligation of the fistula and oesophageal repair/anastomosis when feasible.
- Follow-up may be complicated by GERD, stricture, dysphagia, FTT and chronic cough.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which investigation is specifically described for confirming this suspected lesion?

options.label: B
options.text: Abdominal ultrasound measuring pyloric muscle thickness

options.label: C
options.text: Plain abdominal radiography looking for a double-bubble sign

options.label: D
options.text: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites

options.label: E
options.text: Contrast oesophagram or fibre-optic endoscopy using methylene blue

questions.correctAnswerText: Contrast oesophagram or fibre-optic endoscopy using methylene blue
questions.initialExplanation: An isolated H-type fistula may be diagnosed later because there is no oesophageal atresia. Recommended management includes a contrast oesophagram or fibre-optic endoscopy with methylene blue for its evaluation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The delayed feeding-related respiratory symptoms and recurrent aspiration are compatible with the H-type form described. In contrast to oesophageal atresia, the oesophageal lumen remains continuous, so an NGT may reach the stomach. Recognized features include two diagnostic approaches for the isolated fistula: an oesophagram with contrast (Gastrografin or barium) or fibre-optic endoscopy with methylene blue.

- A. Incorrect. pH monitoring is used for objective assessment of acid reflux, not to demonstrate an H-type fistula.
- B. Incorrect. Pyloric ultrasound is used in suspected hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
- C. Incorrect. A double-bubble sign is associated with duodenal atresia.
- D. Incorrect. Stool microscopy is not the investigation described for a tracheoesophageal communication.
- E. Correct. Both contrast oesophagram and fibre-optic endoscopy with methylene blue are listed for isolated H-type TEF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- H-type TEF occurs without oesophageal atresia and may therefore present later.
- Feeding difficulty and recurrent aspiration pneumonia are important clinical clues.
- Common examples include contrast oesophagram or fibre-optic endoscopy with methylene blue for diagnosis.
- A coiled NGT in the upper oesophageal pouch is a clue to oesophageal atresia, not the isolated H-type pattern.

cases.title: A young infant with progressive projectile vomiting
cases.vignette: A 4-week-old boy is brought because of progressively worsening vomiting after feeds. The vomit is projectile and non-bilious. He remains hungry after vomiting but has started losing weight. Examination may reveal dehydration, visible gastric peristalsis and an olive-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
questions.initialExplanation: Progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting in a young infant, often followed by persistent hunger, is characteristic of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Intussusception commonly causes episodic colicky pain and later vomiting in infants.
- B. Correct. The age and projectile non-bilious vomiting pattern are typical of pyloric stenosis.
- C. Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium passage and constipation/obstruction.
- D. Incorrect. Duodenal atresia classically causes bilious vomiting from the first day of life.
- E. Incorrect. Gastroenteritis typically includes diarrhoea and may include fever or infectious contacts.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typical onset: 2–8 weeks, with a peak around 2–3 weeks.
- Vomiting is projectile and non-bilious.
- The infant may remain hungry immediately after vomiting.

questions.stem: Which examination finding is classically associated with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Empty rectum with explosive stool on withdrawal

options.label: D
options.text: Fixed right iliac fossa mass with guarding

options.label: E
options.text: Olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant

questions.correctAnswerText: Olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include an olive-shaped pyloric mass in the right upper quadrant and visible left-to-right gastric peristaltic waves.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the classical pyloric finding.
- B. Incorrect. An empty rectum with explosive stool after examination is associated with Hirschsprung disease.
- C. Incorrect. A sausage-shaped mass may be found in intussusception.
- D. Incorrect. Right iliac fossa tenderness/guarding suggests appendicitis.
- E. Correct. The palpable olive-shaped mass is a classical sign of pyloric stenosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pyloric stenosis: olive-shaped mass in RUQ.
- Visible gastric peristalsis may move from left to right.
- A test feed may demonstrate the peristaltic waves.

questions.stem: A dehydrated infant with prolonged pyloric stenosis has low chloride, low potassium and elevated bicarbonate. Which acid–base disturbance is expected?

options.label: D
options.text: High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis due to ketoacidosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
questions.initialExplanation: Repeated loss of gastric hydrochloric acid through vomiting produces hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Potassium depletion and dehydration may also occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis is not the expected pattern after prolonged gastric acid loss.
- B. Incorrect. The primary disturbance is metabolic, not respiratory.
- C. Incorrect. Primary respiratory alkalosis is not caused by gastric hydrochloric acid loss.
- D. Incorrect. DKA causes high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and is not the typical pyloric stenosis pattern.
- E. Correct. This is the characteristic biochemical pattern of prolonged vomiting in pyloric stenosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pyloric stenosis: hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
- Dehydration may cause raised urea.
- Paradoxical aciduria may occur despite systemic metabolic alkalosis.
- Correct fluid, electrolyte and acid–base abnormalities before surgery.

questions.stem: Which investigation is described as the most sensitive and diagnostic test for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Abdominal ultrasound
questions.initialExplanation: Abdominal ultrasound is the key diagnostic investigation. It assesses pyloric muscle thickness and channel length.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Ultrasound is the most sensitive and diagnostic investigation described.
- B. Incorrect. pH monitoring assesses acid reflux.
- C. Incorrect. A Meckel scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa.
- D. Incorrect. Stool culture investigates selected infectious diarrhoeal illnesses.
- E. Incorrect. Colonoscopy does not diagnose pyloric stenosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ultrasound is the principal diagnostic test for pyloric stenosis.
- Common examples include pyloric muscle thickness greater than 4 mm and length greater than 14 mm as supportive measurements; verify thresholds with the original reference and local radiology practice.

questions.stem: After diagnosis of pyloric stenosis, what should be done before definitive pyloromyotomy?

options.label: B
options.text: Start oral feeds and observe for one week

options.label: C
options.text: Correct fluid, electrolyte and acid–base disturbances

options.label: E
options.text: Proceed directly to surgery without correcting dehydration

questions.correctAnswerText: Correct fluid, electrolyte and acid–base disturbances
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is correction of dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities and metabolic alkalosis before definitive surgery. The operation is Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Appendectomy treats appendicitis, not pyloric stenosis.
- B. Incorrect. Persistent gastric outlet obstruction requires definitive treatment after stabilization.
- C. Correct. Stabilization is required before pyloromyotomy.
- D. Incorrect. Antidiarrhoeal medication has no role in pyloric obstruction.
- E. Incorrect. Uncorrected dehydration and electrolyte/acid–base abnormalities increase perioperative risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Initial step: resuscitation and correction of biochemical abnormalities.
- Definitive treatment: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.
- Prognosis after appropriate treatment is excellent.

cases.title: A newborn with bilious vomiting on the first day of life
cases.vignette: A newborn develops bilious vomiting within the first 24 hours. The abdomen is not markedly distended. Plain abdominal radiography demonstrates two prominent gas-filled bubbles in the upper abdomen and no distal bowel gas.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Duodenal atresia
questions.initialExplanation: Duodenal atresia typically presents in the neonatal period with bilious vomiting. A double-bubble sign without distal bowel gas is characteristic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious projectile vomiting later in infancy.
- B. Incorrect. Functional constipation does not present with neonatal bilious vomiting and a double-bubble sign.
- C. Correct. The timing, bilious vomiting and radiographic pattern support duodenal atresia.
- D. Incorrect. GERD causes regurgitation or vomiting but not the characteristic radiographic obstruction.
- E. Incorrect. Colic causes crying episodes in an otherwise healthy infant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Duodenal atresia: bilious vomiting from the first day of life.
- Abdominal distension may be limited.
- Double-bubble sign with absent distal bowel gas.

questions.stem: Which congenital condition is particularly associated with duodenal atresia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Down syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Key features include a strong association between duodenal atresia and Down syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Turner syndrome is not the association emphasized for duodenal atresia.
- B. Correct. Down syndrome is the characteristic association noted.
- C. Incorrect. Marfan syndrome is a connective-tissue disorder.
- D. Incorrect. Achondroplasia is a skeletal dysplasia.
- E. Incorrect. Neurofibromatosis type 1 is not the relevant association.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Duodenal atresia is associated with Down syndrome.
- Polyhydramnios may occur antenatally.
- Other congenital anomalies may coexist.

questions.stem: What is the appropriate initial management of a newborn with suspected duodenal atresia?

options.label: A
options.text: NPO, nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids

questions.correctAnswerText: NPO, nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes decompression with an NGT, withholding oral feeds and providing IV fluids before urgent surgical repair.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. NPO, NGT decompression and IV fluids are the initial steps.
- B. Incorrect. A gluten-free diet is treatment for coeliac disease.
- C. Incorrect. Feeding is unsafe in an obstructed neonate.
- D. Incorrect. Antidiarrhoeal medication has no role in congenital intestinal obstruction.
- E. Incorrect. Laxatives and enemas do not treat duodenal atresia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stabilize the neonate with NPO, gastric decompression and IV fluids.
- Definitive treatment is surgical resection/anastomosis as appropriate.
- Bilious vomiting in a neonate must be treated as possible intestinal obstruction until assessed.

cases.title: A neonate with intestinal obstruction and thick meconium
cases.vignette: A newborn develops abdominal distension and failure to pass normal meconium. Imaging and clinical assessment suggest distal small-bowel obstruction.

questions.stem: A neonate has distal ileal obstruction caused by thick, inspissated meconium. Which underlying disorder should be strongly suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cystic fibrosis
questions.initialExplanation: Meconium ileus is caused by thick, inspissated meconium obstructing the distal ileum. Clinical guidance notes that almost all affected neonates have cystic fibrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Meconium ileus is strongly associated with cystic fibrosis.
- B. Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease can cause neonatal obstruction, but meconium ileus specifically raises concern for cystic fibrosis.
- C. Incorrect. Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease and does not cause this neonatal obstruction.
- D. Incorrect. Coeliac disease is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy and does not cause neonatal meconium ileus.
- E. Incorrect. Achalasia is an oesophageal motility disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Meconium ileus: thick, inspissated meconium obstructing the distal ileum.
- Strong association with cystic fibrosis.
- Other causes of neonatal intestinal obstruction include jejunal/ileal atresia and malrotation with volvulus.

questions.stem: Why is intestinal malrotation with volvulus a surgical emergency?

options.label: A
options.text: It can compromise blood supply and cause midgut infarction

options.label: B
options.text: It causes isolated reflux without intestinal injury

options.label: C
options.text: It produces chronic constipation without obstruction

questions.correctAnswerText: It can compromise blood supply and cause midgut infarction
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is that malrotation with volvulus is dangerous because twisting of the bowel can compromise mesenteric blood flow and lead to infarction of the midgut.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Vascular compromise can rapidly cause bowel ischaemia and infarction.
- B. Incorrect. Volvulus is an obstructive and potentially ischaemic emergency, not isolated reflux.
- C. Incorrect. Volvulus causes acute intestinal obstruction, not merely chronic constipation.
- D. Incorrect. Lactose malabsorption is a brush-border enzyme problem and does not explain volvulus.
- E. Incorrect. Oral ulceration is unrelated to intestinal malrotation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Malrotation with volvulus can cause midgut ischaemia and infarction.
- Bilious vomiting in a neonate or young infant is a major warning sign of obstruction.
- Prompt surgical assessment is essential when volvulus is suspected.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which historical detail is specifically identified as a risk factor for this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Macrolide exposure during the first 6 weeks of life

options.label: B
options.text: A history of recurrent oral candidiasis

options.label: E
options.text: A previous episode of lactose intolerance

questions.correctAnswerText: Macrolide exposure during the first 6 weeks of life
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include macrolide intake during the first 6 weeks of life among the risk factors associated with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The vomiting pattern and age are already suggestive of pyloric stenosis. The additional medication history is relevant because clinical guidance specifically records early macrolide exposure as an associated risk factor.

- A. Correct. Macrolide intake in the first 6 weeks is explicitly listed.
- B. Incorrect. Persistent or recurrent thrush in an older child may suggest immunodeficiency; it is not listed as a pyloric stenosis risk factor.
- C. Incorrect. Gluten exposure is discussed in the coeliac disease section, not as a risk factor for pyloric stenosis.
- D. Incorrect. Rotavirus vaccination is discussed as prevention of rotavirus gastroenteritis, not as a pyloric stenosis risk factor.
- E. Incorrect. Lactose intolerance is discussed as a cause of diarrhoea and is not listed as a pyloric stenosis risk factor.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis commonly presents at 2–8 weeks, with a peak around 2–3 weeks.
- Common examples include male sex, first-born status, positive family history (especially maternal side) and macrolide exposure in the first 6 weeks as associated factors.
- The typical vomiting is projectile and non-bilious; the infant may remain hungry after vomiting.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is matched to the three-bubble pattern?
questions.correctAnswerText: Jejunal atresia
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance's radiographic summary associates the triple-bubble sign with jejunal atresia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The source clinical guidance presents a comparison of the bubble patterns in congenital gastrointestinal obstruction. It links a single-bubble pattern with pyloric stenosis/annular pancreas, a double-bubble pattern with duodenal atresia, and a triple-bubble pattern with jejunal atresia. The three-bubble finding therefore points to jejunal rather than duodenal obstruction.

- A. Incorrect. standard guidance associates pyloric stenosis with the single-bubble pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Duodenal atresia is associated with the double-bubble sign.
- C. Correct. clinical guidance explicitly matches the triple-bubble sign with jejunal atresia.
- D. Incorrect. GER is not a congenital small-bowel atresia and does not produce this radiographic pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease is associated with distal aganglionosis and a transition zone on contrast enema, not the triple-bubble pattern described here.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Single bubble: pyloric stenosis / annular pancreas 's diagram.
- Double bubble: duodenal atresia.
- Triple bubble: jejunal atresia.
- clinical guidance also notes that jejunal or ileal atresia/stenosis may involve multiple atretic segments.

cases.title: A child with acute watery diarrhoea
cases.vignette: A 10-month-old infant is brought with two days of frequent watery stools, vomiting and low-grade fever. The illness began with vomiting after a brief upper respiratory prodrome. The infant has no blood in the stool. Several children at the nursery have similar symptoms.

questions.stem: How is acute diarrhoea defined by duration?
questions.correctAnswerText: Less than 14 days
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe acute diarrhoea as diarrhoea lasting less than 14 days. Persistent diarrhoea begins acutely and continues for 14 days or longer.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Acute diarrhoea is less than 14 days in the supplied clinical guidance.
- B. Incorrect. Four weeks is not the definition used in this standard guidance.
- C. Incorrect. standard guidance does not define acute diarrhoea using a 7-day cut-off.
- D. Incorrect. Three days is not standard guidance's duration threshold.
- E. Incorrect. standard guidance classifies diarrhoea lasting at least 14 days as chronic/persistent according to the context.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute diarrhoea: less than 14 days.
- Chronic diarrhoea: described as lasting more than 2 weeks.
- Persistent diarrhoea: begins acutely and lasts 14 days or longer.
- The source uses overlapping duration wording around the 14-day boundary; use the exact local course definition in examinations.

questions.stem: A breastfed infant passes 8 loose stools each day but is feeding well, active and gaining weight normally. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: E
options.text: Normal stool pattern in a thriving breastfed infant

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal stool pattern in a thriving breastfed infant
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that a thriving breastfed infant may normally pass approximately 7–10 stools per day. Stool frequency must be interpreted in relation to the child's usual pattern and growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Obstruction would usually present with other symptoms such as vomiting and distension.
- B. Incorrect. Coeliac disease requires an appropriate clinical and diagnostic assessment; frequent stools alone are insufficient.
- C. Incorrect. Stool frequency alone does not establish secretory diarrhoea.
- D. Incorrect. IBD is not diagnosed from stool frequency alone.
- E. Correct. Normal feeding, activity and growth support a physiological pattern in a breastfed infant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Assess stool pattern relative to baseline, feeding and growth.
- Clinical guidance notes that 7–10 stools daily may be normal in a thriving breastfed infant.
- Avoid diagnosing diarrhoeal disease from frequency alone.

questions.stem: A child has watery diarrhoea that continues even during fasting. Stool volume is high and stool pH is not acidic. Which mechanism is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Secretory diarrhoea
questions.initialExplanation: Secretory diarrhoea results from increased intestinal secretion and/or reduced absorption. It continues during fasting, unlike typical osmotic diarrhoea, which improves when the causative non-absorbable substance is removed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Increased motility may contribute to diarrhoea, but it does not explain the characteristic fasting response described.
- B. Incorrect. Overflow soiling is associated with faecal impaction.
- C. Incorrect. Osmotic diarrhoea is caused by non-absorbable substances and generally improves with fasting; stool is often acidic in carbohydrate malabsorption.
- D. Incorrect. Functional constipation causes hard, infrequent stools.
- E. Correct. Persistence during fasting and high stool volume support a secretory mechanism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Osmotic diarrhoea: non-absorbable solutes; improves with fasting; may have acidic stool and positive reducing substances.
- Secretory diarrhoea: active electrolyte and water secretion; persists during fasting.
- standard guidance gives cholera and ETEC as examples of secretory diarrhoea.

questions.stem: Which stool profile best supports osmotic diarrhoea due to lactose malabsorption?

options.label: B
options.text: Stool pH above 7 with negative reducing substances

options.label: C
options.text: Persistent watery stool during fasting with no osmotic gap

options.label: D
options.text: Bloody stool with mucus and normal pH

options.label: E
options.text: Acidic stool with positive reducing substances

questions.correctAnswerText: Acidic stool with positive reducing substances
questions.initialExplanation: Unabsorbed lactose is fermented by intestinal bacteria, producing organic acids and gas. This results in acidic stool and positive reducing substances.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes constipation with overflow.
- B. Incorrect. This does not fit carbohydrate malabsorption.
- C. Incorrect. Persistence during fasting suggests a secretory mechanism.
- D. Incorrect. Blood and mucus suggest inflammatory or invasive infectious causes rather than uncomplicated lactose malabsorption.
- E. Correct. Acidic stool and reducing substances support carbohydrate malabsorption.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lactose malabsorption: osmotic diarrhoea.
- Stool may be acidic with reducing substances.
- Gas production can cause abdominal distension and cramps.

questions.stem: Which organism is identified as the commonest cause of viral gastroenteritis in children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Rotavirus
questions.initialExplanation: Rotavirus is identified as the commonest viral cause of childhood gastroenteritis and is described as highly contagious.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Shigella is bacterial and may cause dysentery.
- B. Incorrect. Salmonella is bacterial.
- C. Correct. Rotavirus is the main viral pathogen highlighted.
- D. Incorrect. Giardia is a protozoal parasite associated with chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption.
- E. Incorrect. Campylobacter is bacterial.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rotavirus: double-stranded RNA virus in the Reoviridae family.
- Transmission is faeco-oral, including contaminated hands and objects.
- Vaccination is an important preventive measure.

questions.stem: A child develops vomiting followed by watery diarrhoea and low-grade fever during winter. The illness is self-limiting. Which pattern is most consistent with viral gastroenteritis?

options.label: B
options.text: Chronic greasy stool and weight loss over months

options.label: C
options.text: Painless massive rectal bleeding without diarrhoea

options.label: D
options.text: Bloody diarrhoea with persistent high fever as the usual pattern

options.label: E
options.text: Vomiting followed by watery diarrhoea, often with a low-grade fever

questions.correctAnswerText: Vomiting followed by watery diarrhoea, often with a low-grade fever
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include viral gastroenteritis as commonly occurring in winter, sometimes following an upper respiratory prodrome, with vomiting followed by watery diarrhoea and low-grade fever.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is more characteristic of pyloric stenosis.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests chronic malabsorption rather than acute viral gastroenteritis.
- C. Incorrect. Painless gastrointestinal bleeding suggests causes such as Meckel diverticulum.
- D. Incorrect. Bloody diarrhoea and marked systemic features suggest invasive bacterial disease or another inflammatory cause.
- E. Correct. This is the clinical pattern described for viral gastroenteritis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral gastroenteritis: vomiting may precede watery diarrhoea.
- Low-grade fever and winter predominance are described.
- Dehydration is the major complication to assess.

questions.stem: A child develops bloody diarrhoea and then acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia and haemolytic anaemia. Which E. coli pathotype is classically associated with this complication?
questions.correctAnswerText: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli
questions.initialExplanation: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli, particularly the Shiga toxin-producing strain highlighted, is associated with haemorrhagic colitis and haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. EAEC is associated with watery diarrhoea.
- B. Incorrect. ETEC is associated with watery diarrhoea, including travellers' diarrhoea.
