- C. Incorrect. EIEC invades the intestinal mucosa and may produce dysentery-like illness.
- D. Correct. EHEC produces Shiga toxin and is associated with HUS.
- E. Incorrect. EPEC is associated with outbreaks in nurseries and day-care settings.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EHEC, including O157:H7: Shiga toxin, haemorrhagic colitis and HUS.
- HUS: haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury.
- Avoid treating suspected Shiga toxin-producing infection casually with antimotility drugs; management requires careful clinical assessment.

questions.stem: A child develops fever, abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhoea after exposure to contaminated food. Rectal prolapse and HUS are listed complications of the suspected infection. Which organism is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Shigella
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include Shigella as highly contagious, transmitted by the faeco-oral route and associated with bloody diarrhoea, dysentery, fever and possible rectal prolapse or HUS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The clinical pattern and complications match Shigella infection.
- B. Incorrect. Candida causes oral or other mucocutaneous candidiasis.
- C. Incorrect. Rotavirus usually causes watery diarrhoea rather than dysentery.
- D. Incorrect. H. pylori is associated with gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.
- E. Incorrect. Giardia causes foul-smelling watery diarrhoea, bloating and malabsorption.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Shigella: faeco-oral transmission and high contagiousness.
- Dysentery with fever and abdominal pain.
- Complications include seizures, arthritis and HUS.

questions.stem: Which feature is a recognized complication of Salmonella infection highlighted?
questions.correctAnswerText: Osteomyelitis
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include localized extraintestinal Salmonella infections, including osteomyelitis, meningitis and pneumonia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pierre Robin sequence is a congenital craniofacial condition.
- B. Incorrect. Dental enamel defects may be associated with coeliac disease.
- C. Incorrect. Barrett oesophagus is a complication of chronic GERD.
- D. Correct. Osteomyelitis is among the extraintestinal infections listed.
- E. Incorrect. Achalasia is an oesophageal motility disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Salmonella is transmitted through contaminated food, including eggs, and by the faeco-oral route.
- Fever and diarrhoea may occur, sometimes with blood.
- Immunocompromised children are at greater risk of severe complications.

questions.stem: What is the major complication responsible for much of the morbidity and mortality associated with childhood acute gastroenteritis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Dehydration
questions.initialExplanation: Dehydration is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in acute gastroenteritis and is the central target of assessment and treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dental caries is unrelated to the acute systemic complications of gastroenteritis.
- B. Correct. Fluid and electrolyte losses can lead to hypovolaemia, shock and death.
- C. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis is a separate obstructive condition.
- D. Incorrect. Barrett oesophagus is associated with chronic reflux.
- E. Incorrect. Oesophageal stricture is a complication of oesophageal injury or chronic inflammation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Assess hydration in every child with significant diarrhoea and/or vomiting.
- Other complications include hypovolaemic shock, metabolic acidosis, AKI, malnutrition and HUS.
- Rehydration is the mainstay of treatment.

questions.stem: In which child with acute gastroenteritis does standard guidance recommend stool examination and culture?

options.label: A
options.text: children in routine care with functional constipation

options.label: B
options.text: A child with isolated uncomplicated regurgitation

options.label: D
options.text: children in routine care with mild, short-lived watery diarrhoea

options.label: E
options.text: A child with blood or mucus in the stool

questions.correctAnswerText: A child with blood or mucus in the stool
questions.initialExplanation: Stool investigation is not routinely required in uncomplicated gastroenteritis. Common examples include blood or mucus in stool, suspected sepsis, immunocompromise, recent travel, failure to improve by day 7 and diagnostic uncertainty as indications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Functional constipation is not an indication for infectious stool testing.
- B. Incorrect. Regurgitation is not an indication for stool culture.
- C. Incorrect. A thriving breastfed infant may have frequent normal stools and does not automatically require stool culture.
- D. Incorrect. Routine stool culture is not recommended for every uncomplicated case.
- E. Correct. Blood or mucus in stool is one of standard guidance's indications.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stool tests are selective, not routine.
- Consider them for sepsis, bloody/mucoid stool, immunocompromise, travel, persistent illness or uncertain diagnosis.
- Electrolytes/urea are important when clinically significant dehydration is suspected.

questions.stem: Why are antimotility drugs such as loperamide generally discouraged in children with acute gastroenteritis?

options.label: B
options.text: They correct electrolyte abnormalities too rapidly

options.label: C
options.text: They are ineffective or potentially harmful and may distract from rehydration

options.label: E
options.text: They typically cause immediate renal failure

questions.correctAnswerText: They are ineffective or potentially harmful and may distract from rehydration
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance discourages antidiarrhoeal and routine antiemetic use because they may be ineffective, cause adverse effects and distract from the essential intervention: rehydration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These drugs do not eradicate viral infection.
- B. Incorrect. Antimotility drugs do not correct electrolyte abnormalities.
- C. Correct. clinical guidance highlights lack of efficacy, adverse effects, possible prolonged bacterial excretion and diversion of attention from ORS.
- D. Incorrect. They do not prevent transmission.
- E. Incorrect. This is not the reason stated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rehydration is the priority in childhood AGE.
- Antidiarrhoeal drugs are generally discouraged.
- Antibiotics are not routine treatment for uncomplicated gastroenteritis.

questions.stem: Which situation is listed as an indication for considering antibiotics in a child with gastroenteritis?

options.label: A
options.text: Mild diarrhoea in a thriving child with no dehydration

options.label: B
options.text: Sepsis or extraintestinal spread of bacterial infection

options.label: D
options.text: each episode of uncomplicated viral watery diarrhoea

questions.correctAnswerText: Sepsis or extraintestinal spread of bacterial infection
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that antibiotics are not routine in gastroenteritis. It lists selected indications, including sepsis, extraintestinal bacterial spread, selected high-risk children and specific treatable pathogens.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mild uncomplicated diarrhoea is managed supportively.
- B. Correct. Sepsis and extraintestinal spread are explicit indications.
- C. Incorrect. Posseting is not an indication for antibiotics.
- D. Incorrect. Viral gastroenteritis does not require routine antibiotics.
- E. Incorrect. Functional constipation is not an indication for antibiotics.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most AGE is self-limiting and does not require antibiotics.
- Common examples include sepsis, extraintestinal bacterial infection, selected young infants with Salmonella/Shigella, immunocompromise/malnutrition and protozoal infection among circumstances where specific therapy may be indicated.
- Choose antimicrobial therapy according to organism, severity and current local guidance.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which *E. coli* pathotype best fits this outbreak pattern?
questions.correctAnswerText: Enteropathogenic *E. coli* (EPEC)
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance associates EPEC with outbreaks in nurseries involving neonates and in day-care centres, with an incubation period of approximately 1–2 days.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The childcare cluster and short incubation period are the discriminating clues. The question is not asking for the most common cause of diarrhoea overall; it asks which of the listed *E. coli* pathotypes matches the setting and timing described.

- A. Correct. EPEC is linked to epidemics in nurseries for neonates and day-care centres; its listed incubation period is 1–2 days.
- B. Incorrect. EHEC, particularly O157:H7, is associated with haemorrhagic colitis and haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. EIEC is associated with sudden-onset diarrhoea containing blood, pus and mucus, often with fever and abdominal pain.
- D. Incorrect. ETEC is associated with travellers' diarrhoea and an incubation period of 1–3 days.
- E. Incorrect. EAEC is associated with watery diarrhoea, but the nursery/day-care outbreak association is assigned to EPEC.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EPEC: nursery/day-care outbreaks; incubation 1–2 days.
- ETEC: travellers' diarrhoea; incubation 1–3 days.
- EIEC: blood, pus and mucus with fever and abdominal pain; incubation 18–24 hours.
- EHEC O157:H7: haemorrhagic colitis and HUS.
- EAEC: watery diarrhoea.

topics.name: Dehydration and Rehydration in Acute Gastroenteritis

cases.title: An infant with diarrhoea and reduced urine output
cases.vignette: An 8-month-old infant is brought with frequent watery stools and repeated vomiting. The parents report reduced fluid intake and fewer wet nappies. On examination, the infant is irritable, has sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. The clinician must grade dehydration, recognize shock, classify the sodium disturbance and select an appropriate rehydration plan.

questions.stem: Why are infants particularly vulnerable to dehydration compared with older children?

options.label: A
options.text: They have a lower body-water content and lower metabolic rate

options.label: B
options.text: They can independently increase their fluid intake when thirsty

options.label: C
options.text: They have a fully mature renal tubular system

options.label: D
options.text: They have a higher body-water content, higher metabolic rate and immature renal concentrating/reabsorptive function

options.label: E
options.text: They have a smaller surface-area-to-weight ratio

questions.correctAnswerText: They have a higher body-water content, higher metabolic rate and immature renal concentrating/reabsorptive function
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include high total body-water content, high metabolic rate, a relatively large surface-area-to-weight ratio, immature renal tubular reabsorption and inability to communicate thirst as reasons infants are at increased risk.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Clinical descriptions include higher, not lower, total body-water content and metabolic rate.
- B. Incorrect. Infants cannot reliably request fluids or independently replace losses.
- C. Incorrect. Renal tubular function is immature in infants.
- D. Correct. These physiological features increase water turnover and reduce the infant's ability to compensate.
- E. Incorrect. A larger surface-area-to-weight ratio contributes to greater insensible water loss.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infants have greater fluid requirements relative to body size.
- Greater insensible losses and immature renal conservation increase dehydration risk.
- Infants depend on caregivers to provide additional fluids.

questions.stem: 's clinical classification, which percentage of body-weight loss usually corresponds to moderate dehydration?
questions.correctAnswerText: Usually 5–10%
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance classifies mild/no clinical dehydration as usually less than 5% weight loss, moderate clinical dehydration as approximately 5–10%, and severe dehydration/shock as greater than 10%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Moderate dehydration is usually associated with 5–10% body-weight loss.
- B. Incorrect. This exceeds standard guidance's severe dehydration threshold.
- C. Incorrect. Less than 5% is the mild/no clinical dehydration range.
- D. Incorrect. This does not represent standard guidance's moderate category.
- E. Incorrect. This is not a clinically appropriate classification threshold.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mild: usually <5%.
- Moderate: usually 5–10%.
- Severe: usually >10%.
- Clinical assessment is based on the overall pattern of signs, not a single finding.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly indicates decompensated hypovolaemic shock rather than uncomplicated clinical dehydration?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal blood pressure, warm extremities and normal pulses

options.label: C
options.text: Mild thirst with normal peripheral perfusion

options.label: D
options.text: Hypotension with prolonged capillary refill and weak pulses

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypotension with prolonged capillary refill and weak pulses
questions.initialExplanation: Hypotension is a late sign indicating decompensated shock. Prolonged capillary refill, cold extremities and weak peripheral pulses also indicate impaired perfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are reassuring perfusion findings.
- B. Incorrect. A single loose stool does not establish dehydration or shock.
- C. Incorrect. Mild thirst without perfusion abnormality does not indicate shock.
- D. Correct. Hypotension with prolonged CRT and weak pulses indicates decompensated hypovolaemic shock.
- E. Incorrect. Isolated dry lips are insufficient to diagnose shock.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early shock signs include tachycardia, tachypnoea and delayed CRT.
- Late/decompensated signs include hypotension, weak pulses, cold/mottled extremities and reduced consciousness.
- Do not wait for hypotension before recognizing possible shock.

questions.stem: A child with gastroenteritis has a serum sodium concentration of 158 mmol/L. How is the dehydration classified by sodium level?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypernatraemic
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance classifies dehydration with serum sodium above 150 mmol/L as hypernatraemic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia refers to low blood glucose, not sodium classification.
- B. Incorrect. Isotonic dehydration has sodium 's normal range.
- C. Incorrect. The child has a sodium-defined dehydration pattern and clinical fluid loss.
- D. Correct. A sodium of 158 mmol/L is above the stated 150 mmol/L threshold.
- E. Incorrect. Hyponatraemic dehydration is associated with low sodium.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Standard guidance's sodium categories: isotonic 130–150 mmol/L, hypotonic <130 mmol/L and hypertonic >150 mmol/L.
- Reference ranges may differ between textbooks and laboratories; use the local laboratory range.
- Hypernatraemic dehydration requires careful correction.

questions.stem: Why can hypernatraemic dehydration be less obvious on clinical examination, particularly in an obese infant?

options.label: A
options.text: There is no reduction in total body water

options.label: C
options.text: Hypernatraemia typically causes early hypotension before other signs

options.label: D
options.text: Sodium causes immediate generalized oedema in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Water shifts from extracellular to intracellular spaces, making the degree of dehydration less apparent

questions.correctAnswerText: Water shifts from extracellular to intracellular spaces, making the degree of dehydration less apparent
questions.initialExplanation: In hypernatraemic dehydration, water loss exceeds sodium loss. The resulting hypertonicity shifts water out of cells and clinical dehydration may be less obvious than expected, particularly in an obese infant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Total body-water loss is central to dehydration.
- B. Incorrect. Hypernatraemia commonly results from water loss exceeding sodium loss.
- C. Incorrect. Hypotension is a late sign of shock and is not invariably the first feature.
- D. Incorrect. Generalized oedema is not the defining finding.
- E. Correct. Clinical guidance notes that hypertonic dehydration can be difficult to recognize clinically, particularly in obese infants.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hypernatraemic dehydration: water loss exceeds sodium loss.
- Clinical signs may be less obvious than in other types.
- Neurological manifestations can include irritability, altered consciousness, hyperreflexia and seizures.

questions.stem: A child with hypernatraemic dehydration is being rehydrated. Why should the serum sodium be corrected gradually over approximately 48–72 hours?

options.label: A
options.text: To prevent rapid movement of water into brain cells and cerebral oedema

options.label: B
options.text: To prevent a rise in stool frequency

options.label: C
options.text: To prevent hypoglycaemia caused by ORS

options.label: D
options.text: To ensure complete eradication of intestinal pathogens

options.label: E
options.text: To induce a controlled increase in intracranial pressure

questions.correctAnswerText: To prevent rapid movement of water into brain cells and cerebral oedema
questions.initialExplanation: Rapid reduction in serum sodium can cause water to move into brain cells, producing cerebral oedema. standard guidance therefore emphasizes slow correction with serial sodium monitoring.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Slow correction reduces the risk of cerebral oedema and neurological deterioration.
- B. Incorrect. The purpose is neurological safety, not reducing stool frequency.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the mechanism described.
- D. Incorrect. Sodium correction does not eradicate the pathogen.
- E. Incorrect. Increasing intracranial pressure is dangerous, not a treatment goal.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hypernatraemic dehydration: correct slowly, generally over 48–72 hours.
- standard guidance gives a target sodium reduction of less than 0.5 mmol/L/hour and less than 12 mmol/L/day.
- Monitor plasma sodium regularly and follow a supervised paediatric fluid protocol.

questions.stem: Which is the preferred basic approach for a child with gastroenteritis who has no clinical dehydration?

options.label: C
options.text: Continue breastfeeding and other usual feeds, encourage fluids and replace ongoing losses

options.label: E
options.text: Give IV fluids to children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Continue breastfeeding and other usual feeds, encourage fluids and replace ongoing losses
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes preventing dehydration by continuing breastfeeding and milk feeds, encouraging appropriate fluids and replacing ongoing gastrointestinal losses.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Restricting fluids worsens the risk of dehydration.
- B. Incorrect. Breastfeeding should continue.
- C. Correct. This is the preventive approach for a child without clinical dehydration.
- D. Incorrect. Routine antidiarrhoeal medication is discouraged.
- E. Incorrect. IV fluids are not required for every child.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- No clinical dehydration: continue normal feeding and breastfeeding.
- Encourage appropriate fluid intake and ORS when needed to replace losses.
- Avoid high-sugar drinks such as fruit juices and carbonated drinks as rehydration substitutes.

questions.stem: Which statement about oral rehydration solution (ORS) is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It should be diluted with the specified amount of water and used within 24 hours

options.label: B
options.text: It should be mixed with juice to improve absorption

options.label: C
options.text: It is contraindicated in children in routine care with diarrhoea

options.label: D
options.text: It should be prepared as a concentrated solution to reduce stool output

options.label: E
options.text: It is a probiotic that kills intestinal pathogens

questions.correctAnswerText: It should be diluted with the specified amount of water and used within 24 hours
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that ORS powder should be diluted only in water, prepared according to instructions and used within 24 hours. It is not bacteriostatic or a probiotic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Correct dilution and timely use are essential.
- B. Incorrect. Juice changes the composition and osmolarity and is not the recommended diluent.
- C. Incorrect. ORS is useful in many children with dehydration who can tolerate enteral rehydration.
- D. Incorrect. Concentrating ORS can create dangerous electrolyte and osmolarity disturbances.
- E. Incorrect. ORS works through intestinal sodium-glucose co-transport; it is not a probiotic or antimicrobial.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prepare ORS exactly as directed, using water only.
- Use prepared solution within 24 hours,.
- ORS supports sodium and water absorption through preserved intestinal glucose-sodium co-transport.

questions.stem: Which child is not an appropriate candidate for oral rehydration alone?

options.label: A
options.text: A child who tolerates small frequent amounts of ORS

options.label: B
options.text: A child with mild dehydration who is drinking

options.label: C
options.text: An alert child with no clinical dehydration

options.label: E
options.text: A child who continues breastfeeding and has no red flags

questions.correctAnswerText: A child in hypovolaemic shock
questions.initialExplanation: Shock requires urgent resuscitation with intravenous isotonic fluid. Common examples include shock, severe dehydration and persistent vomiting among situations in which ORS alone is inappropriate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes a child who can receive oral rehydration.
- B. Incorrect. Mild dehydration is generally suitable for ORS if the child can drink.
- C. Incorrect. A child without dehydration can be managed with oral fluids and continued feeds.
- D. Correct. Hypovolaemic shock requires urgent IV or intraosseous access and resuscitation.
- E. Incorrect. Breastfeeding and oral intake should continue when clinically appropriate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IV fluid indications include shock, moderate-to-severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, hypertonic dehydration and inability to take oral fluids.
- Consider nasogastric ORS in selected children who cannot drink enough but do not require immediate IV resuscitation.
- Reassess clinical response frequently.

questions.stem: Using the Holliday–Segar method, what is the daily maintenance fluid requirement for a child weighing 15 kg?
questions.correctAnswerText: 1,250 mL/day
questions.initialExplanation: For the first 10 kg, use 100 mL/kg/day; for the next 5 kg, use 50 mL/kg/day. The total is 1,000 + 250 = 1,250 mL/day.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This underestimates the maintenance requirement.
- B. Incorrect. This includes only the first 10 kg.
- C. Incorrect. This overestimates the calculation for 15 kg using the stated method.
- D. Incorrect. This is above the calculated maintenance requirement.
- E. Correct. First 10 kg = 1,000 mL; next 5 kg = 250 mL; total = 1,250 mL/day.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Holliday–Segar: first 10 kg × 100 mL/kg/day.
- Second 10 kg × 50 mL/kg/day.
- Each subsequent kg × 20 mL/kg/day.
- For 15 kg: 1,250 mL/day using standard guidance's example.

questions.stem: A child weighs 8 kg and is estimated to have 5% dehydration. Using standard guidance's deficit formula (weight × percentage dehydration × 10), what is the estimated fluid deficit?
questions.correctAnswerText: 400 mL
questions.initialExplanation: Fluid deficit = 8 × 5 × 10 = 400 mL.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is four times the calculated amount.
- B. Incorrect. This doubles the calculated amount.
- C. Incorrect. This does not apply the 5% dehydration factor.
- D. Correct. standard guidance's formula gives 400 mL.
- E. Incorrect. This underestimates the deficit.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Deficit formula: weight (kg) × percentage dehydration × 10 = mL.
- Always distinguish deficit replacement from maintenance and ongoing losses.
- Clinical fluid prescriptions require reassessment and monitoring.

questions.stem: A 4-kg infant has 10 episodes of ongoing stool/vomit loss after initial rehydration. Using standard guidance's estimate of 10 mL/kg per episode, what is the replacement volume?
questions.correctAnswerText: 400 mL
questions.initialExplanation: Ongoing loss = weight × number of episodes × 10 mL. Therefore, 4 × 10 × 10 = 400 mL.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is only 10 mL/kg for one episode in this infant.
- B. Correct. Four kilograms multiplied by ten episodes and 10 mL gives 400 mL.
- C. Incorrect. This is half the calculated total.
- D. Incorrect. This does not account for all ten episodes.
- E. Incorrect. This doubles the calculated replacement.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ongoing loss formula: weight × number of episodes × 10 mL.
- Ongoing losses are added to the fluid plan after initial rehydration.
- Monitor intake, output, weight and electrolyte status.

questions.stem: A child presents with hypovolaemic shock due to gastroenteritis. Which initial fluid is used for bolus resuscitation?
questions.correctAnswerText: 0.9% sodium chloride
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes an isotonic crystalloid bolus, such as 0.9% sodium chloride, for hypovolaemic shock, with reassessment and repeat bolus if indicated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dextrose alone is not an appropriate initial resuscitation fluid for hypovolaemic shock.
- B. Correct. Normal saline is the isotonic crystalloid specified.
- C. Incorrect. Oral juice is not a resuscitation fluid.
- D. Incorrect. ORS powder must be correctly diluted and is not a substitute for IV resuscitation in shock.
- E. Incorrect. Hypotonic maintenance fluid is not used for shock bolus resuscitation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Shock: ABC assessment, urgent access and isotonic crystalloid resuscitation.
- standard guidance mentions normal saline and Ringer lactate as crystalloid options.
- Reassess after each bolus and escalate care if shock persists.
- Exact bolus volumes and repetition should follow current local paediatric resuscitation guidance.

cases.title: A child with chronic foul-smelling diarrhoea after drinking untreated water
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old child has several weeks of foul-smelling watery stools, abdominal distension, flatulence, anorexia and poor weight gain. The family recently stayed in an area with untreated water.

questions.stem: Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.correctAnswerText: Giardia lamblia
questions.initialExplanation: Giardiasis is caused by Giardia lamblia, a flagellated protozoan transmitted by ingestion of cysts in contaminated water or food. It may cause foul-smelling diarrhoea, bloating and failure to thrive.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The exposure and chronic malabsorptive symptoms fit giardiasis.
- B. Incorrect. Candida causes mucocutaneous candidiasis and is not the typical cause of this diarrhoeal syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. H. pylori is associated with gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.
- D. Incorrect. Rotavirus usually causes an acute episode of watery gastroenteritis.
- E. Incorrect. Shigella typically causes acute dysentery with fever and blood in the stool.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Giardia lamblia is a flagellated protozoan.
- Transmission: ingestion of cysts in contaminated water or food.
- Symptoms may include foul-smelling watery diarrhoea, flatulence, abdominal distension and FTT.
- Many infected people may be asymptomatic.

questions.stem: What is the usual route of transmission of giardiasis?

options.label: A
options.text: Faeco-oral ingestion of cysts from contaminated food or water

questions.correctAnswerText: Faeco-oral ingestion of cysts from contaminated food or water
questions.initialExplanation: Giardia cysts are ingested through contaminated water or food, producing faeco-oral transmission.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the route described.
- B. Incorrect. The infective cyst is ingested rather than penetrating intact skin.
- C. Incorrect. Giardia is not transmitted by respiratory droplets.
- D. Incorrect. Mosquitoes do not transmit Giardia.
- E. Incorrect. Transplacental transmission is not the usual route.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Incubation period: approximately 1–2 weeks.
- Cysts are the infective form acquired from contaminated food or water.
- Hand hygiene and safe sanitation reduce transmission.

questions.stem: A single stool microscopy sample is negative in a child with a strong clinical suspicion of giardiasis. What is the best next approach?

options.label: C
options.text: Diagnose coeliac disease without further testing

options.label: D
options.text: Examine three stool samples or use stool Giardia antigen testing

questions.correctAnswerText: Examine three stool samples or use stool Giardia antigen testing
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that one stool sample has limited sensitivity, whereas three samples increase sensitivity. Stool ELISA for Giardia antigen is also highly sensitive.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A Meckel scan investigates ectopic gastric mucosa in suspected Meckel diverticulum.
- B. Incorrect. A single negative sample does not exclude giardiasis because cyst shedding may be intermittent.
- C. Incorrect. Coeliac disease is a differential diagnosis, but it should not be diagnosed from a negative stool sample alone.
- D. Correct. Repeated stool samples or stool antigen testing improve diagnostic yield.
- E. Incorrect. Plain radiography does not diagnose Giardia infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- One stool sample: approximately 50–70% sensitivity.
- Three stool samples: greater than 95% sensitivity.
- Stool Giardia antigen ELISA is also described as highly sensitive.
- Duodenal aspirate/string test or biopsy may be considered in selected cases.

questions.stem: Which medication is identified as the drug of choice for giardiasis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Metronidazole
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include metronidazole as the drug of choice for giardiasis and also mentions tinidazole as a single-dose option.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Loperamide is an antimotility drug and is not an antiparasitic treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Mesalazine is used in inflammatory bowel disease.
- C. Incorrect. Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor used for acid suppression.
- D. Incorrect. Prednisolone is a corticosteroid and is not used to eradicate Giardia.
- E. Correct. Metronidazole is the drug of choice stated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Giardia: metronidazole (DOC ).
- Tinidazole is also mentioned as a single-dose option.
- Most patients have an excellent prognosis; hygiene and sanitation help prevent reinfection.

cases.title: A toddler with chronic diarrhoea and abdominal distension
cases.vignette: A 20-month-old child develops chronic bulky, pale, offensive stools after gluten-containing foods are introduced. The child has abdominal distension, irritability and poor weight gain. A second older child in the same clinic has unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia and short stature but few gastrointestinal symptoms.

questions.stem: Coeliac disease is best described as:

options.label: A
options.text: An acute bacterial infection of the colon

options.label: B
options.text: An immune-mediated enteropathy caused by permanent sensitivity to gluten in genetically predisposed individuals

options.label: C
options.text: An IgE-mediated immediate reaction to most dietary proteins

options.label: D
options.text: A congenital obstruction of the pylorus

options.label: E
options.text: A congenital absence of intestinal ganglion cells

questions.correctAnswerText: An immune-mediated enteropathy caused by permanent sensitivity to gluten in genetically predisposed individuals
questions.initialExplanation: Coeliac disease is a chronic immune-mediated small-intestinal disorder triggered by gluten in genetically predisposed individuals.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Coeliac disease is not an acute bacterial infection.
- B. Correct. This is the definition given.
- C. Incorrect. Coeliac disease is not an immediate IgE-mediated food allergy.
- D. Incorrect. Pyloric obstruction is a separate congenital or acquired gastric outlet disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Absence of enteric ganglion cells causes Hirschsprung disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Gluten-containing cereals highlighted: wheat, barley and rye.
- Coeliac disease is immune-mediated and occurs in genetically predisposed individuals.
- It causes proximal small-intestinal mucosal injury and malabsorption.

questions.stem: Which pathological sequence best explains the malabsorption in coeliac disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Villous hypertrophy followed by increased absorptive surface

options.label: B
options.text: Complete absence of gastric parietal cells

options.label: C
options.text: Hypertrophy of the pyloric circular muscle

options.label: D
options.text: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes

options.label: E
options.text: Transmural granulomatous inflammation of the entire gastrointestinal tract

questions.correctAnswerText: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes
questions.initialExplanation: Gluten exposure, particularly gliadin, triggers immune-mediated mucosal injury. Clinical descriptions include villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and lymphocyte infiltration, reducing the absorptive surface.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Villous hypertrophy would not explain the reduced absorptive surface.
- B. Incorrect. Parietal-cell loss is not the pathogenesis of coeliac disease.
- C. Incorrect. Pyloric muscle hypertrophy causes pyloric stenosis.
- D. Correct. This is the characteristic histological pattern described.
- E. Incorrect. Transmural granulomatous inflammation is more characteristic of Crohn disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Gliadin exposure triggers mucosal immune injury.
- Histology: villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + lymphocyte infiltration.
- Proximal small intestine is particularly affected, leading to malabsorption.

questions.stem: A toddler has chronic bulky, pale, offensive stools, abdominal distension, poor weight gain and irritability after gluten introduction. Which clinical pattern is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Typical (classical) coeliac disease
questions.initialExplanation: Classical coeliac disease commonly presents in young children with gastrointestinal symptoms and malabsorption, including chronic diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, abdominal distension and failure to thrive.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The presentation is a typical classical gastrointestinal pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Potential coeliac disease refers to positive antibodies with currently negative biopsy.
- C. Incorrect. Latent coeliac disease describes currently normal histology despite evidence of gluten-dependent enteropathy at another time.
- D. Incorrect. Functional abdominal pain does not explain steatorrhoea and faltering growth.
- E. Incorrect. Silent coeliac disease has positive serology and mucosal lesions without clinical symptoms.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Classical coeliac disease: usually prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, often in children under 2 years.
- Features: chronic diarrhoea/steatorrhoea, abdominal distension, anorexia, vomiting, FTT and irritability.
- Growth delay and muscle wasting may occur.

questions.stem: An older child has unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia resistant to treatment, short stature and recurrent aphthous ulcers, with minimal gastrointestinal symptoms. Which diagnosis should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Atypical coeliac disease
questions.initialExplanation: Atypical coeliac disease may present with extraintestinal manifestations and few or no gastrointestinal symptoms. standard guidance includes refractory iron-deficiency anaemia, short stature, delayed puberty and recurrent aphthous ulcers.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Acute viral gastroenteritis is a short-duration illness.
- B. Correct. The extraintestinal presentation is characteristic of atypical coeliac disease.
- C. Incorrect. Meconium ileus presents with neonatal intestinal obstruction.
- D. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting in early infancy.
- E. Incorrect. Infantile colic causes crying episodes in an otherwise thriving young infant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Atypical coeliac disease may be predominantly extraintestinal.
- Look for refractory iron-deficiency anaemia, short stature, delayed puberty, oral ulcers, bone disease and neurological/skin manifestations.
- Consider coeliac disease even when gastrointestinal symptoms are limited.

questions.stem: A child is being screened for coeliac disease. Why should total serum IgA be measured when interpreting IgA-based coeliac serology?

options.label: A
options.text: IgA deficiency may cause false-negative IgA-based coeliac antibody tests

options.label: B
options.text: IgA is the immunoglobulin produced in the intestine

options.label: C
options.text: Serum IgA confirms the presence of villous atrophy

options.label: D
options.text: IgA deficiency typically causes a false-positive anti-tTG IgA result

options.label: E
options.text: IgA measurement replaces most other diagnostic tests

questions.correctAnswerText: IgA deficiency may cause false-negative IgA-based coeliac antibody tests
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is measuring total serum IgA because selective IgA deficiency can cause false-negative IgA-based anti-tTG and anti-endomysial tests.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. IgA deficiency can make IgA-based serology falsely reassuring.
- B. Incorrect. Other immunoglobulin classes are also present and important.
- C. Incorrect. Serum IgA does not establish histological villous atrophy.
- D. Incorrect. The concern is false-negative, not false-positive, IgA-based serology.
- E. Incorrect. Total IgA does not replace coeliac-specific antibodies or histological assessment when indicated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Initial serology commonly includes anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) IgA with total serum IgA.
- If IgA deficiency is present, an appropriate IgG-based test is needed.
- A negative IgA-based test in an IgA-deficient child does not reliably exclude coeliac disease.

questions.stem: Which investigation is described as the definitive diagnostic test (gold standard) for coeliac disease?

options.label: C
options.text: Duodenal/jejunal biopsy obtained at upper GI endoscopy

questions.correctAnswerText: Duodenal/jejunal biopsy obtained at upper GI endoscopy
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include small-intestinal biopsy obtained during upper GI endoscopy as the definitive diagnostic test, with at least four biopsy samples described.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ultrasound does not confirm coeliac enteropathy.
- B. Incorrect. Plain radiography does not diagnose coeliac mucosal disease.
- C. Correct. Histology assesses villous injury and is the gold-standard approach described in this standard guidance.
- D. Incorrect. Stool culture investigates selected infectious causes of diarrhoea.
- E. Incorrect. Sweat chloride is used in cystic fibrosis assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Coeliac diagnosis: history, examination, serology and biopsy as indicated.
- Clinical descriptions include duodenal/jejunal biopsy as the definitive test.
- The child should be consuming gluten during diagnostic assessment unless a specialist advises otherwise.

questions.stem: What is the cornerstone of long-term treatment for confirmed coeliac disease?

options.label: E
options.text: Lifelong lactose-free diet in each patient

questions.correctAnswerText: Lifelong gluten-free diet
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet, with nutritional supplementation and follow-up as needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Colectomy is not the routine treatment for coeliac disease.
- B. Incorrect. Coeliac disease is not treated with long-term antibiotics.
- C. Correct. Strict lifelong exclusion of gluten is the cornerstone of treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Gluten exposure perpetuates the immune-mediated enteropathy.
- E. Incorrect. Lactose restriction may be needed temporarily in selected patients with secondary lactose intolerance, but it is not universal treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lifelong gluten-free diet.
- Replace deficiencies such as iron and vitamin D when present.
- Ongoing follow-up assesses symptoms, growth, nutritional status and adherence.

questions.stem: A child with long-standing untreated coeliac disease is at increased risk of which gastrointestinal malignancy highlighted?
questions.correctAnswerText: Small-intestinal lymphoma
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include small-bowel lymphoma as the most common gastrointestinal malignancy highlighted as a long-term complication of neglected or untreated coeliac disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Wilms tumour is a renal embryonal tumour.
- B. Incorrect. Hepatoblastoma is a primary liver tumour of childhood.
- C. Incorrect. Neuroblastoma is a tumour of neural crest-derived tissue.
- D. Incorrect. Retinoblastoma is a retinal malignancy.
- E. Correct. Small-bowel lymphoma is the complication emphasized.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Complications of poorly controlled coeliac disease include growth delay, anaemia, micronutrient deficiency and reduced bone mineralization.
- Small-bowel lymphoma is a serious long-term complication described.
- Good dietary adherence and specialist follow-up are important.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which category best describes this presentation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Silent coeliac disease
questions.initialExplanation: Silent coeliac disease is defined by the absence of clinical symptoms despite positive antibodies and a positive biopsy. It may be identified by screening children in risk groups.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The key is the relationship between symptoms, serology and histology. This child has no clinical picture, but both antibody testing and biopsy are positive. That combination matches standard definition of silent coeliac disease.

- A. Incorrect. Typical symptomatic coeliac disease includes clinical features as well as positive antibodies and biopsy.
- B. Incorrect. Latent coeliac disease is described as having normal histology at the present time, despite gluten-dependent enteropathy being demonstrated at another time.
- C. Incorrect. Potential coeliac disease has positive antibodies with a negative biopsy, with or without symptoms.
- D. Correct. No clinical picture + positive antibodies + positive biopsy is the definition of silent coeliac disease.
- E. Incorrect. Lactose intolerance does not explain the positive coeliac serology and biopsy pattern described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Symptomatic coeliac disease: clinical picture + positive antibodies + positive biopsy.
- Silent coeliac disease: no clinical picture + positive antibodies + positive biopsy.
- Latent coeliac disease: currently normal histology, but gluten-dependent enteropathy has been shown at another time.
- Potential coeliac disease: positive antibodies with negative biopsy, with or without symptoms.
- Screening of children in risk groups may identify silent disease.

cases.title: A thriving toddler with frequent loose stools
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child passes 5–7 loose stools daily, mostly during the daytime. The stools contain visible undigested vegetable matter. Appetite, activity and growth are normal. The child drinks large quantities of fruit juice. There is no blood in the stool, fever or evidence of malabsorption.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Toddler diarrhoea (chronic nonspecific diarrhoea)
questions.initialExplanation: Toddler diarrhoea typically occurs in otherwise healthy children with frequent loose stools, often containing undigested food, while appetite, activity and growth remain normal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Coeliac disease commonly causes evidence of malabsorption or growth impairment, though presentations vary.
- B. Incorrect. Cystic fibrosis may cause malabsorption, steatorrhoea and poor growth.
- C. Incorrect. IBD may cause blood in stool, systemic symptoms, growth failure and inflammatory features.
- D. Correct. Normal growth and activity with daytime loose stools containing undigested vegetables are characteristic.
- E. Incorrect. Giardia may cause foul-smelling diarrhoea, bloating and FTT, often after contaminated water exposure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Toddler diarrhoea: common in roughly 6 months to 3 years.
- Frequent loose stools may contain undigested vegetables and occur mainly during the day.
- Growth and general health remain normal.
- Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion of red flags/organic disease.

questions.stem: Which dietary advice is most appropriate for this child?

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce excessive juice intake, normalize fibre intake and increase dietary fat appropriately

options.label: D
options.text: Begin a lifelong gluten-free diet without investigation

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduce excessive juice intake, normalize fibre intake and increase dietary fat appropriately
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes reassurance, reducing fluids especially fruit juice, increasing dietary fat and normalizing fibre intake.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Restricting all fluids is unsafe and unnecessary.
- B. Correct. This matches the dietary approach described.
- C. Incorrect. Excess fruit juice, particularly apple juice, may contribute to toddler diarrhoea.
- D. Incorrect. Gluten restriction is not indicated without evidence of coeliac disease.
- E. Incorrect. standard guidance suggests increasing fat rather than eliminating it.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Reassure parents; symptoms usually improve with age.
- Reduce excessive fruit juice, especially apple juice.
- Normalize fibre and provide an appropriate balanced diet.
- Clinical guidance notes spontaneous improvement commonly by around 4–5 years.

cases.title: An infant with diarrhoea, dermatitis and alopecia
cases.vignette: A 6-week-old infant develops chronic diarrhoea, irritability, poor growth and a rash around the mouth and anus. The hair is brittle and there is patchy alopecia. Serum zinc is low.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acrodermatitis enteropathica
questions.initialExplanation: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an inherited disorder of zinc absorption characterized by diarrhoea, periorificial/acral dermatitis and alopecia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Atopic dermatitis does not explain the full triad with chronic diarrhoea and zinc deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Cow's milk protein allergy may cause diarrhoea and eczema but does not produce the typical zinc-deficiency syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Coeliac disease can cause diarrhoea and malabsorption but does not classically produce this characteristic triad.
- D. Correct. The combination of diarrhoea, periorificial rash and alopecia is characteristic.
- E. Incorrect. HSV causes acute painful oral ulceration, not this chronic syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acrodermatitis enteropathica: inherited zinc deficiency syndrome.
- Classically presents with diarrhoea, periorificial/acral dermatitis and alopecia.
- It may present in the first weeks after birth.

questions.stem: Which inheritance pattern is associated with acrodermatitis enteropathica?
questions.correctAnswerText: Autosomal recessive
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include acrodermatitis enteropathica as an inherited autosomal recessive disorder.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mitochondrial inheritance is not the pattern stated.
- B. Incorrect. It is not described as X-linked dominant.
- C. Incorrect. standard guidance does not describe an autosomal dominant pattern.
- D. Incorrect. standard guidance specifies an inherited autosomal recessive condition.
- E. Correct. The described inheritance is autosomal recessive.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Inherited zinc deficiency.
- Autosomal recessive.
- Consider the diagnosis in an infant with chronic diarrhoea and characteristic rash/alopecia.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern supports the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: High serum zinc and high alkaline phosphatase

options.label: C
options.text: High serum calcium and low phosphate

options.label: D
options.text: Low serum zinc and low alkaline phosphatase

options.label: E
options.text: High serum sodium and high potassium

questions.correctAnswerText: Low serum zinc and low alkaline phosphatase
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include low serum zinc and low alkaline phosphatase as supportive laboratory findings.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Clinical descriptions include low rather than high zinc and alkaline phosphatase.
- B. Incorrect. Bilirubin and transaminases do not establish acrodermatitis enteropathica.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the characteristic biochemical pattern.
- D. Correct. Low serum zinc with low alkaline phosphatase supports zinc deficiency in this syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Sodium and potassium are not the diagnostic laboratory pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Investigations: low serum zinc and low alkaline phosphatase.
- Skin biopsy may be supportive but is not diagnostic.
- Clinical descriptions include oral zinc replacement as lifelong treatment; confirm exact elemental zinc dosing against the original clinical guidance and current specialist guidance.

topics.name: Food Allergy and Cow's Milk Protein Allergy

cases.title: An infant with recurrent symptoms after cow's milk formula
cases.vignette: A 3-month-old infant develops recurrent diarrhoea, vomiting, irritability and eczema after cow's milk formula is introduced. Some episodes begin within minutes with urticaria and facial swelling, while other symptoms develop more gradually. The infant is growing poorly.

questions.stem: A child develops urticaria and facial swelling within 15 minutes of eating a specific food. Which mechanism is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: IgE-mediated food allergy
questions.initialExplanation: The rapid onset of urticaria and angioedema within minutes is characteristic of an IgE-mediated food allergy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Coeliac disease is a gluten-triggered immune-mediated enteropathy, not an immediate food reaction.
- B. Incorrect. Osmotic diarrhoea is a mechanism of diarrhoea, not an immediate allergic mechanism.
- C. Incorrect. Non-IgE-mediated reactions are typically delayed by hours and often involve the gastrointestinal tract.
- D. Correct. IgE-mediated reactions typically occur within minutes and may cause urticaria, angioedema or anaphylaxis.
- E. Incorrect. Lactase deficiency causes carbohydrate malabsorption and osmotic diarrhoea.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IgE-mediated food allergy: usually minutes to up to 2 hours after exposure.
- Manifestations: urticaria, angioedema and anaphylaxis.
- Non-IgE-mediated food allergy tends to be delayed and commonly gastrointestinal.

questions.stem: Which food allergy is identified as the commonest food allergy in infants?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cow's milk protein allergy
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include cow's milk protein allergy as the commonest food allergy in infants. Egg and nuts are also listed among common infant food allergens.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fish is listed among allergens in older children.
- B. Incorrect. Peanut is an important allergen but is not identified as the commonest infant allergy.
- C. Correct. CMPA is the commonest infant food allergy highlighted by standard guidance.
- D. Incorrect. Sesame is also listed among allergens in older children.
- E. Incorrect. Shellfish is listed among food allergens more relevant to older children.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common infant food allergens: cow's milk, egg and nuts.
- Older children may react to peanut, tree nuts, fish, shellfish and sesame.
- CMPA may be IgE-mediated, non-IgE-mediated or mixed.

questions.stem: A breastfed infant develops gastrointestinal symptoms consistent with cow's milk protein intolerance. Which dietary approach is described?

options.label: C
options.text: Add more cow's milk formula to the infant's diet

options.label: D
options.text: Eliminate cow's milk and its products from the mother's diet

options.label: E
options.text: Replace breast milk with fruit juice

questions.correctAnswerText: Eliminate cow's milk and its products from the mother's diet
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that a breastfed infant may develop cow's milk protein intolerance through maternal dietary exposure. The approach described is maternal elimination of cow's milk and dairy products.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Breastfeeding need not automatically be stopped.
- B. Incorrect. Continued cow's milk protein exposure may perpetuate symptoms.
- C. Incorrect. Adding cow's milk formula would increase exposure.
- D. Correct. Maternal dairy elimination is the approach described for a breastfed infant with suspected CMPA.
- E. Incorrect. Fruit juice is not an appropriate replacement for breast milk or infant formula.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CMPA may occur in exclusively breastfed infants.
- Maternal cow's milk elimination may be required in selected cases.
- Ensure maternal and infant nutritional adequacy during an elimination diet.

questions.stem: An infant is suspected of having non-IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy. Which approach is described as diagnostic?

options.label: A
options.text: Give unrestricted cow's milk and observe for several months

options.label: B
options.text: Eliminate cow's milk protein for a period, assess symptom improvement, then perform a supervised challenge

options.label: C
options.text: Diagnose solely from a raised total IgE level

questions.correctAnswerText: Eliminate cow's milk protein for a period, assess symptom improvement, then perform a supervised challenge
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include an elimination period followed by a medically supervised re-challenge as the diagnostic approach. Symptoms should improve with elimination and recur after reintroduction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Unsupervised continued exposure is not a diagnostic protocol.
- B. Correct. Elimination followed by supervised challenge is the diagnostic strategy described.
- C. Incorrect. Total IgE alone does not diagnose non-IgE-mediated CMPA.
- D. Incorrect. Ultrasound does not establish cow's milk protein allergy.
- E. Incorrect. A Meckel scan is used for suspected Meckel diverticulum.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- History is central to food allergy assessment.
- Clinical descriptions include an elimination period of 2–8 weeks followed by challenge.
- Challenge should be medically supervised in the described protocol.
- A previous history of anaphylaxis is a contraindication to an unsupervised challenge.

questions.stem: A child has a history of anaphylaxis after cow's milk ingestion. What is the safest interpretation of standard guidance's milk challenge protocol?

options.label: A
options.text: The child should undergo an unsupervised home challenge

options.label: B
options.text: Challenge should begin with a full glass of milk

options.label: C
options.text: Allergy is excluded because symptoms occurred previously

options.label: D
options.text: A milk challenge is contraindicated in the described protocol because of the anaphylaxis history

options.label: E
options.text: Challenge is unnecessary but cow's milk should be given daily

questions.correctAnswerText: A milk challenge is contraindicated in the described protocol because of the anaphylaxis history
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance specifically notes a history of anaphylaxis as a contraindication to the described challenge procedure. Any reintroduction in high-risk allergy requires specialist assessment and a safe setting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. An unsupervised challenge is unsafe in a child with previous anaphylaxis.
- B. Incorrect. Starting with a large amount is unsafe.
- C. Incorrect. Previous anaphylaxis supports a serious immediate allergy history.
- D. Correct. This is the contraindication highlighted.
- E. Incorrect. Ongoing exposure is not an appropriate substitute for a supervised management plan.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Challenge testing can provoke severe reactions.
- Previous anaphylaxis is a major safety warning.
- High-risk cases require allergy specialist input.

questions.stem: Which formula is an appropriate first-line formula option described for an infant requiring treatment for cow's milk protein allergy?

options.label: A
options.text: Unmodified soy formula for each infant

options.label: C
options.text: Ordinary goat's milk as a guaranteed safe substitute

questions.correctAnswerText: Extensively hydrolysed formula
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes extensively hydrolysed formula as a treatment option, with amino-acid-based formula for selected cases. It warns that soy protein intolerance may coexist.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Clinical guidance notes that soy intolerance can coexist and advises against soy-based formula as a routine treatment choice.
- B. Correct. Extensively hydrolysed formula is the principal formula option described.
- C. Incorrect. Goat's milk proteins may cross-react and are not a guaranteed safe substitute.
- D. Incorrect. Standard formula contains intact cow's milk proteins.
- E. Incorrect. Rice water is nutritionally inadequate as an infant formula.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- First option: extensively hydrolysed formula.
- Amino-acid-based formula may be used in selected severe or persistent cases.
- Do not assume soy formula is suitable for all infants with CMPA.
- Ensure adequate nutrition and growth monitoring.

cases.title: An infant with persistent acidic diarrhoea after gastroenteritis
cases.vignette: A 7-month-old infant develops fever, vomiting and diarrhoea due to an acute viral gastroenteritis. Fever and vomiting resolve, but watery diarrhoea continues. The stools are acidic and contain reducing substances. The infant develops abdominal distension, excessive gas and perianal excoriation.

questions.stem: Which enzyme normally hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose at the small-intestinal brush border?
questions.correctAnswerText: Lactase
questions.initialExplanation: Lactase is the brush-border enzyme that hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Amylase digests starch.
- B. Correct. Lactase digests lactose into glucose and galactose.
- C. Incorrect. Lipase digests dietary fats.
- D. Incorrect. Sucrase hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose.
- E. Incorrect. Pepsin is a gastric protease involved in protein digestion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lactose = glucose + galactose.
- Lactase is located on the small-intestinal brush border.
- Lactase deficiency leads to lactose malabsorption and osmotic diarrhoea.

questions.stem: The infant's diarrhoea persists after the acute viral illness has resolved. What is the most likely mechanism?

options.label: C
options.text: Secondary lactase deficiency due to brush-border injury

questions.correctAnswerText: Secondary lactase deficiency due to brush-border injury
questions.initialExplanation: Viral gastroenteritis can damage the intestinal villous brush border, reducing lactase activity and causing secondary lactose intolerance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bile production is not the mechanism described.
- B. Incorrect. Ganglion cell number is unrelated to lactase activity.
- C. Correct. Post-gastroenteritis mucosal injury can temporarily reduce lactase activity.
- D. Incorrect. Insulin secretion does not cause this pattern of carbohydrate malabsorption.
- E. Incorrect. Pyloric abnormality does not explain post-infectious acidic diarrhoea.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Secondary lactose intolerance may follow gastroenteritis or giardiasis.
- Other causes listed include chemotherapy and congenital lactase deficiency (rare).
- Symptoms may persist after the initial infectious symptoms have resolved.

questions.stem: Which combination of stool findings supports lactose malabsorption?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal stool pH with no reducing substances and high faecal calprotectin

options.label: B
options.text: Acidic stool with positive reducing substances

options.label: C
options.text: Alkaline stool with negative reducing substances

options.label: D
options.text: Blood and pus with a positive bacterial culture in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Greasy stool with low faecal elastase

questions.correctAnswerText: Acidic stool with positive reducing substances
questions.initialExplanation: Unabsorbed lactose undergoes bacterial fermentation, generating acids and reducing substances. This produces acidic stool and a positive reducing-substance test.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This does not support lactose malabsorption.
- B. Correct. Acidic pH and positive reducing substances support lactose malabsorption.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the expected pattern of carbohydrate malabsorption.
- D. Incorrect. Blood and pus suggest an inflammatory or invasive infectious cause.
- E. Incorrect. Greasy stool and low faecal elastase suggest pancreatic insufficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stool pH: acidic (approximately <5.5).
- Reducing substances may be positive.
- Hydrogen breath testing and elimination/challenge are other diagnostic approaches described.

questions.stem: What is the dietary treatment described for an infant with symptomatic lactose intolerance?

options.label: C
options.text: Unmodified cow's milk in larger volumes

questions.correctAnswerText: Lactose-free formula
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include lactose-free formula as the dietary treatment for symptomatic infant lactose intolerance, especially during a secondary post-infectious episode.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Increasing lactose worsens the osmotic load.
- B. Incorrect. Nutrition must continue; dietary modification should preserve adequate calorie and nutrient intake.
- C. Incorrect. Unmodified cow's milk contains lactose and is not the described treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Gluten is unrelated to lactose digestion.
- E. Correct. Lactose-free formula reduces exposure to the poorly digested carbohydrate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lactose-free formula is described as treatment.
- Assess whether intolerance is secondary and potentially temporary.
- Reintroduction may be considered after recovery under appropriate clinical advice.

cases.title: An infant with steatorrhoea and later neurological symptoms
cases.vignette: An infant has chronic greasy stools, abdominal distension and failure to thrive. Later in childhood, the patient develops ataxia, weakness and nystagmus. Blood film shows acanthocytes and cholesterol is low.

questions.stem: Which underlying defect is responsible for abetalipoproteinaemia?

options.label: B
options.text: Absence of apolipoprotein B, impairing chylomicron formation

questions.correctAnswerText: Absence of apolipoprotein B, impairing chylomicron formation
questions.initialExplanation: Abetalipoproteinaemia is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by absence of apolipoprotein B, leading to defective chylomicron formation and fat malabsorption.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Excess bile salts are not the described mechanism.
- B. Correct. standard guidance links apo-B absence to failure of chylomicron formation and fat retention in enterocytes.
- C. Incorrect. Lactase deficiency causes lactose malabsorption, not defective lipoprotein assembly.
- D. Incorrect. Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus.
- E. Incorrect. Ganglion-cell absence causes Hirschsprung disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Abetalipoproteinaemia: autosomal recessive.
- Apo-B deficiency → impaired chylomicron formation → fat malabsorption.
- Fat-soluble vitamin absorption is reduced.

questions.stem: Which peripheral blood film finding is associated with abetalipoproteinaemia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acanthocytes
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include acanthocytes as a characteristic blood-film finding in abetalipoproteinaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sickle cells are associated with sickle cell disease.
- B. Incorrect. Target cells occur in several haematological and hepatic disorders but are not the characteristic finding given.
- C. Incorrect. Schistocytes suggest mechanical or microangiopathic haemolysis.
- D. Incorrect. Spherocytes may occur in hereditary spherocytosis or immune haemolysis.
- E. Correct. Acanthocytes are the characteristic spiculated red cells described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Blood film: acanthocytes.
- Cholesterol and fat-soluble vitamins may be low.
- Neurological/retinal manifestations may develop from vitamin E and other fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies.

questions.stem: A child with abetalipoproteinaemia develops ataxia and nystagmus. Deficiency of which nutrient is particularly implicated in the neurological manifestations described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Vitamin E
questions.initialExplanation: Vitamin E deficiency can cause neurological manifestations including ataxia and nystagmus. Abetalipoproteinaemia impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vitamin K deficiency causes impaired coagulation.
- B. Incorrect. Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia.
- C. Correct. Vitamin E deficiency is the key association with ataxia and nystagmus in this condition.
- D. Incorrect. B12 deficiency can cause neurological disease but is not the specific fat-soluble vitamin deficiency highlighted.
- E. Incorrect. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not the described neurological syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E and K.
- Vitamin E deficiency: neurological dysfunction, including ataxia and nystagmus.
- Management includes reduced long-chain fatty acid intake, medium-chain fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation.

cases.title: An adolescent with chronic bloody diarrhoea and weight loss
cases.vignette: A 13-year-old child presents with months of abdominal pain, diarrhoea containing blood and mucus, fatigue and weight loss. Examination reveals pallor and reduced growth velocity. Another adolescent has chronic abdominal pain, weight loss and recurrent perianal fistulae. The clinician must distinguish ulcerative colitis from Crohn disease and select appropriate investigations.

questions.stem: Which description best distinguishes ulcerative colitis from Crohn disease?

options.label: A
options.text: UC is transmural and discontinuous; Crohn disease is superficial and continuous

options.label: B
options.text: Both diseases are limited to the stomach

options.label: C
options.text: UC typically causes granulomas throughout the bowel wall

options.label: D
options.text: UC usually affects the colon continuously with mucosal inflammation; Crohn disease is transmural and may affect any part of the GI tract

options.label: E
options.text: Crohn disease typically affects the rectum

questions.correctAnswerText: UC usually affects the colon continuously with mucosal inflammation; Crohn disease is transmural and may affect any part of the GI tract
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance contrasts UC, which is classically continuous and superficial, with Crohn disease, which is discontinuous and transmural and can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This reverses the characteristic patterns.
- B. Incorrect. Neither condition is limited to the stomach.
- C. Incorrect. Non-caseating granulomas are associated with Crohn disease, not the typical UC pattern.
- D. Correct. This accurately summarizes the distinction described.
- E. Incorrect. Crohn disease can affect any site from mouth to anus, classically including the terminal ileum.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- UC: continuous colonic inflammation, mucosa/submucosa, bloody diarrhoea and mucus.
- Crohn disease: skip lesions, transmural inflammation, any GI site, fistulae/strictures and perianal disease.
- Both can cause growth failure and extraintestinal manifestations.

questions.stem: A child has chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhoea and recurrent perianal fistulae. Which diagnosis is more strongly suggested?
questions.correctAnswerText: Crohn disease
questions.initialExplanation: Perianal fistulae and abscesses are characteristic clues to Crohn disease because of its transmural inflammatory pattern.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Functional constipation does not explain chronic inflammatory symptoms and perianal fistulae.
- B. Incorrect. Toddler diarrhoea occurs in otherwise healthy, thriving young children.
- C. Correct. Perianal disease, fistulae and weight loss strongly support Crohn disease.
- D. Incorrect. Acute viral gastroenteritis is short-lived and does not cause chronic perianal fistulae.
- E. Incorrect. UC is typically characterized by continuous colonic mucosal inflammation and bloody diarrhoea.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Crohn disease: transmural inflammation, fistulae, strictures, fissures and perianal disease.
- Growth failure and nutritional deficiencies are important paediatric presentations.
- Extraintestinal manifestations are more common in Crohn disease.

questions.stem: Which investigation is described as a sensitive marker of gastrointestinal inflammation in children with suspected IBD?
questions.correctAnswerText: Faecal calprotectin
questions.initialExplanation: Faecal calprotectin is described as a sensitive marker of gastrointestinal inflammation and can support the evaluation of suspected IBD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urine ketones may be relevant in diabetic ketoacidosis or metabolic assessment.
- B. Correct. Faecal calprotectin is a useful marker of intestinal inflammation.
- C. Incorrect. Sweat chloride is used in cystic fibrosis assessment.
- D. Incorrect. Bilirubin reflects hepatic/biliary processes rather than intestinal inflammation.
- E. Incorrect. Amylase may be used in the assessment of pancreatitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Faecal calprotectin: sensitive marker of intestinal inflammation.
- CBC may show anaemia, leukocytosis and thrombocytosis.
- ESR and CRP may be elevated; albumin and micronutrients may be reduced.

questions.stem: Which investigation provides diagnostic confirmation of ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease?
questions.correctAnswerText: Colonoscopy/endoscopy with biopsy
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include endoscopy with biopsy as diagnostic for IBD. Imaging and inflammatory markers can support assessment but do not replace tissue evaluation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Endoscopic examination with biopsy is the diagnostic approach emphasized.
- B. Incorrect. Urinalysis is not diagnostic for IBD.
- C. Incorrect. Hydrogen breath testing evaluates selected carbohydrate malabsorption disorders.
- D. Incorrect. ECG does not assess intestinal mucosal disease.
- E. Incorrect. Plain radiography may identify complications such as colonic dilatation but does not confirm IBD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IBD diagnosis is based on clinical assessment, laboratory tests, endoscopy and histology.
- Faecal calprotectin is a sensitive inflammatory marker, not the definitive diagnostic test.
- Colonoscopy and biopsy help distinguish UC from Crohn disease.

questions.stem: A child with severe ulcerative colitis develops fever, systemic toxicity and marked colonic dilatation on abdominal imaging. Which serious complication should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Toxic megacolon
questions.initialExplanation: Toxic megacolon is a dangerous complication of severe colitis characterized by colonic dilatation and systemic toxicity, with a risk of perforation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The clinical picture of severe colitis, systemic illness and colonic dilatation is consistent with toxic megacolon.
- B. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis is gastric outlet obstruction in early infancy.
- C. Incorrect. Barrett oesophagus is a complication of chronic reflux.
- D. Incorrect. Meconium ileus is neonatal distal small-bowel obstruction associated with cystic fibrosis.
- E. Incorrect. Achalasia is an oesophageal motility disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Toxic megacolon is a serious complication of severe UC.
- Perforation and systemic deterioration are major concerns.
- Severe colitis requires urgent specialist and surgical assessment.

questions.stem: Which statement about surgery in ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Surgery permanently prevents recurrence of Crohn disease at each site

options.label: B
options.text: Colectomy cures typical presentations of Crohn disease

options.label: C
options.text: Colectomy is curative for ulcerative colitis, whereas surgery is not generally curative for Crohn disease

options.label: D
options.text: each patient with UC requires immediate colectomy

options.label: E
options.text: Surgery is not usually indicated in either condition

questions.correctAnswerText: Colectomy is curative for ulcerative colitis, whereas surgery is not generally curative for Crohn disease
questions.initialExplanation: This is explained that total colectomy is curative for ulcerative colitis, while Crohn disease may recur and surgery is reserved for selected complications or refractory localized disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Surgery does not eliminate the possibility of Crohn recurrence.
- B. Incorrect. Crohn disease may recur after surgery.
- C. Correct. This is the key surgical distinction described.
- D. Incorrect. Most patients are initially managed medically; colectomy is reserved for selected circumstances.
- E. Incorrect. Surgery is indicated for selected complications, including perforation, obstruction, bleeding and refractory disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- UC: total colectomy is curative for the colonic disease.
- Crohn disease: surgery is for selected complications or refractory disease; recurrence can occur.
- Perianal abscess requires drainage.

questions.stem: Which pair of extraintestinal associations is correctly matched?

options.label: A
options.text: UC — Meckel diverticulum; Crohn disease — pyloric stenosis

options.label: B
options.text: UC — cystic fibrosis; Crohn disease — coeliac disease

options.label: C
options.text: UC — primary sclerosing cholangitis; Crohn disease — perianal fistulae

options.label: D
options.text: UC — achalasia; Crohn disease — Hirschsprung disease

options.label: E
options.text: UC — intussusception; Crohn disease — duodenal atresia

questions.correctAnswerText: UC — primary sclerosing cholangitis; Crohn disease — perianal fistulae
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance associates primary sclerosing cholangitis with UC and emphasizes perianal disease as a feature of Crohn disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Meckel diverticulum and pyloric stenosis are not the relevant extraintestinal associations.
- B. Incorrect. These are not the matched IBD associations described.
- C. Correct. Both associations are listed.
- D. Incorrect. Achalasia and Hirschsprung disease are separate gastrointestinal disorders.
- E. Incorrect. Intussusception and duodenal atresia are obstructive conditions, not IBD extraintestinal manifestations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Extraintestinal manifestations may involve eyes, skin, joints, liver and blood.
- Common examples include uveitis with both conditions.
- PSC is associated with UC in the supplied comparison; Crohn disease is linked with perianal disease and fistulae.

questions.stem: A child with IBD has erythema nodosum and painful red nodules over the shins. Which association is given?
questions.correctAnswerText: Erythema nodosum — Crohn disease
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include erythema nodosum in association with Crohn disease and pyoderma gangrenosum in association with UC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lactose intolerance causes gastrointestinal symptoms rather than this IBD-associated skin manifestation.
- B. Incorrect. Oesophageal atresia is a congenital anomaly.
- C. Incorrect. Meckel diverticulum causes bleeding, obstruction or diverticulitis.
- D. Correct. This matches standard guidance's extraintestinal comparison.
- E. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis is unrelated to erythema nodosum.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Crohn disease: erythema nodosum is listed.
- UC: pyoderma gangrenosum and PSC are listed.
- IBD can cause arthritis, uveitis, clubbing, growth failure and delayed puberty.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which medication is specifically listed as an immunomodulator for steroid-dependent or steroid-resistant disease?
questions.correctAnswerText: Azathioprine (or 6-mercaptopurine)
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine as immunomodulators used in steroid-resistant or steroid-dependent inflammatory bowel disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical issue is dependence on corticosteroids: symptoms recur as the steroid dose is reduced. clinical guidance identifies immunomodulators as part of the medical treatment plan for these cases and names azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine.

- A. Incorrect. 5-ASA agents such as mesalamine are included in the treatment section, but standard guidance separately names azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine as the immunomodulators for steroid-resistant or dependent cases.
- B. Incorrect. Steroids are used to induce remission, with tapering described; repeating them does not answer the question about the listed immunomodulator.
- C. Incorrect. Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor discussed in the GERD section.
- D. Incorrect. Lactulose is not the immunomodulator described for IBD.
- E. Correct. Azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine is the pair specifically identified in the source clinical guidance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
