- 5-ASA agents named include sulfasalazine and mesalamine.
- Clinical guidance oral steroids at 1–2 mg/kg/day for 3–4 weeks followed by tapering; IV steroids may be used in severe cases.
- Azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine is listed for steroid-resistant or steroid-dependent disease.
- Infliximab is also listed in the IBD treatment section.

cases.title: A newborn who has not passed meconium
cases.vignette: A term newborn has abdominal distension, bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium in the first 24 hours. Rectal examination reveals a narrow, empty rectum; after withdrawal of the finger, there is an explosive passage of stool and flatus.

questions.stem: What is the underlying pathological abnormality in Hirschsprung disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Excessive ganglion cells in the distal colon

options.label: C
options.text: Absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of part of the bowel

questions.correctAnswerText: Absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of part of the bowel
questions.initialExplanation: Hirschsprung disease is congenital aganglionic megacolon caused by failure of neural crest-derived ganglion cells to populate a segment of the bowel.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The disease is characterized by absence, not excess, of ganglion cells.
- B. Incorrect. Villous injury is associated with enteropathies such as coeliac disease.
- C. Correct. Aganglionosis affects the myenteric and submucosal plexuses, producing a contracted, non-relaxing segment.
- D. Incorrect. Lactase activity does not cause Hirschsprung disease.
- E. Incorrect. Pyloric muscle hypertrophy causes pyloric stenosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hirschsprung disease = congenital aganglionic megacolon.
- Usually involves the rectosigmoid region.
- The aganglionic segment fails to relax and causes functional obstruction.

questions.stem: Which neonatal history is particularly suggestive of Hirschsprung disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Recurrent painless rectal bleeding at 5 years

options.label: B
options.text: Passage of meconium within 2 hours with normal feeding

options.label: C
options.text: Episodic colicky pain with red currant jelly stool

options.label: D
options.text: Failure to pass meconium during the first 24 hours

options.label: E
options.text: Projectile non-bilious vomiting beginning at 6 weeks

questions.correctAnswerText: Failure to pass meconium during the first 24 hours
questions.initialExplanation: Failure to pass meconium in the first 24 hours is a key neonatal clue to Hirschsprung disease, particularly with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Painless rectal bleeding may suggest Meckel diverticulum.
- B. Incorrect. Early passage of meconium is reassuring, although it does not absolutely exclude all disease.
- C. Incorrect. Episodic colic with red currant jelly stool suggests intussusception.
- D. Correct. Delayed meconium passage is a classic neonatal presentation.
- E. Incorrect. Projectile non-bilious vomiting at several weeks suggests pyloric stenosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal Hirschsprung: delayed meconium, distension, bilious vomiting and feeding reluctance.
- Later presentation may include chronic constipation, FTT or enterocolitis.
- Down syndrome is an associated condition noted.

questions.stem: What is the classical rectal examination finding in Hirschsprung disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Large amount of hard stool filling the rectum

options.label: B
options.text: A tender mass in the right iliac fossa

options.label: C
options.text: A palpable sausage-shaped upper abdominal mass

options.label: D
options.text: A normal rectum with a positive stool occult blood test

options.label: E
options.text: Narrow, empty rectum followed by explosive stool and flatus after withdrawal

questions.correctAnswerText: Narrow, empty rectum followed by explosive stool and flatus after withdrawal
questions.initialExplanation: The contracted aganglionic distal segment leaves the rectum narrow and empty. Withdrawal may be followed by explosive passage of stool and gas.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stool in the rectum is more typical of functional constipation.
- B. Incorrect. Right iliac fossa tenderness is associated with appendicitis.
- C. Incorrect. A sausage-shaped mass may occur in intussusception.
- D. Incorrect. Occult blood alone is not the classical diagnostic finding.
- E. Correct. This is the classical rectal examination finding described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Empty, narrow rectum in Hirschsprung disease.
- Explosive stool and flatus after withdrawal of the examining finger.
- Functional constipation more commonly has palpable stool in the rectum.

questions.stem: Which investigation provides the definitive histological diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Suction rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells

questions.correctAnswerText: Suction rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells
questions.initialExplanation: Rectal biopsy demonstrates aganglionosis and increased acetylcholinesterase staining in nerve trunks, providing the histological diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Rectal biopsy is the definitive diagnostic investigation described.
- B. Incorrect. Ultrasound does not establish the histological absence of ganglion cells.
- C. Incorrect. Hydrogen breath testing evaluates carbohydrate malabsorption.
- D. Incorrect. Stool culture detects selected enteric pathogens.
- E. Incorrect. Oesophageal pH monitoring assesses acid reflux.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rectal biopsy: definitive histological diagnosis.
- Clinical guidance notes absence of ganglion cells and increased acetylcholinesterase staining.
- Anorectal manometry may show high anal tone.
- Contrast enema can help identify the transition zone and estimate the affected segment.

questions.stem: Which contrast enema finding supports Hirschsprung disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Narrow distal segment with a dilated proximal colon and transition zone

options.label: E
options.text: Bird-beak sign at the lower oesophageal sphincter

questions.correctAnswerText: Narrow distal segment with a dilated proximal colon and transition zone
questions.initialExplanation: The contrast enema may show a narrowed aganglionic distal segment with proximal bowel dilatation and a transition zone.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the characteristic transition pattern described for Hirschsprung disease.
- B. Incorrect. Target sign is associated with intussusception on ultrasound.
- C. Incorrect. Double-bubble sign suggests duodenal atresia.
- D. Incorrect. Free air suggests perforation.
- E. Incorrect. Bird-beak sign is associated with achalasia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Contrast enema can suggest the location/length of aganglionosis.
- Rectal biopsy remains the definitive diagnostic test.
- Treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with pull-through/anastomosis, sometimes staged.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child has constipation since birth, abdominal distension, poor growth and recurrent episodes of fever with foul diarrhoea. Which complication of Hirschsprung disease is particularly concerning?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis
questions.initialExplanation: Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis is a potentially life-threatening complication that can present with fever, abdominal distension and profuse diarrhoea, sometimes bloody.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lactose intolerance causes osmotic diarrhoea and bloating but not this dangerous systemic presentation.
- B. Incorrect. Barrett oesophagus is a complication of chronic reflux.
- C. Incorrect. Coeliac crisis is associated with severe coeliac disease.
- D. Correct. The symptoms are concerning for enterocolitis in a child with Hirschsprung disease.
- E. Incorrect. Infantile colic is a benign crying syndrome in young infants.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis is serious and may be life-threatening.
- Red flags include fever, distension, lethargy and profuse or bloody diarrhoea.
- Requires urgent assessment and treatment.

cases.title: A school-aged child with painful hard stools and withholding behaviour
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child has infrequent passage of large hard stools, painful defecation and withholding behaviour. The child has normal growth and no neonatal history of delayed meconium. Examination reveals a palpable faecal mass. There are no red flags for organic disease.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Functional constipation
questions.initialExplanation: Functional constipation is the commonest cause of constipation in children. Normal growth, onset after infancy, withholding behaviour and palpable stool support the diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease often begins from birth and may cause delayed meconium, distension and FTT.
- B. Correct. The child's age, withholding and faecal loading without red flags are typical.
- C. Incorrect. Intussusception causes episodic colicky pain and obstruction.
- D. Incorrect. Duodenal atresia presents in the neonatal period with bilious vomiting.
- E. Incorrect. Meckel diverticulum may cause painless bleeding or obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Functional constipation is the most common cause in children.
- Withholding behaviour can perpetuate a cycle of hard stools, pain and further withholding.
- Normal growth and absence of red flags support a functional diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which finding is more typical of functional constipation than Hirschsprung disease?

options.label: D
options.text: Empty narrow rectum with explosive stool after examination

questions.correctAnswerText: Stool palpable in the rectum
questions.initialExplanation: Functional constipation commonly involves faecal retention and stool in the rectum. Hirschsprung disease is associated with a narrow, empty rectum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Constipation from birth suggests an organic cause such as Hirschsprung disease.
- B. Correct. Rectal stool is typical of functional constipation.
- C. Incorrect. Delayed meconium is a red flag for Hirschsprung disease.
- D. Incorrect. This is the classical Hirschsprung rectal examination finding.
- E. Incorrect. Enterocolitis is a complication of Hirschsprung disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Functional constipation usually develops after infancy, commonly after toilet training or painful stool passage.
- Hirschsprung: onset from birth, delayed meconium, distension, empty rectum, increased anal tone, transition zone and absent ganglion cells.
- Use red flags to decide when further investigation/referral is needed.

questions.stem: A child with functional constipation has faecal impaction. What is the appropriate sequence of treatment described?

options.label: D
options.text: Disimpaction followed by maintenance laxative therapy

questions.correctAnswerText: Disimpaction followed by maintenance laxative therapy
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes relieving faecal impaction first, then continuing maintenance therapy for months to maintain soft regular stools and prevent recurrence.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Significant impaction should be relieved before or as part of a structured maintenance plan.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics and bowel rest are not the routine approach.
- C. Incorrect. Surgery is not standard treatment for functional constipation.
- D. Correct. Disimpaction followed by maintenance therapy is the sequence described.
- E. Incorrect. Adequate fluid and fibre intake are part of supportive management.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat faecal impaction first.
- Continue maintenance laxatives for months; titrate to achieve soft stools.
- Explain the plan to caregivers and use positive reinforcement.
- Polyethylene glycol is listed among laxative options.

questions.stem: Which behavioural measure is recommended as part of bowel training?

options.label: A
options.text: Delay defecation whenever the urge occurs

options.label: D
options.text: Sit on the toilet for 5–10 minutes after meals in a good position

options.label: E
options.text: Avoid sitting on the toilet after meals

questions.correctAnswerText: Sit on the toilet for 5–10 minutes after meals in a good position
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes regular toilet sitting for 5–10 minutes after meals as part of bowel training, with parental education and positive reinforcement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Withholding aggravates constipation.
- B. Incorrect. Punishment is inappropriate and can worsen withholding.
- C. Incorrect. Children should have appropriate access to the toilet.
- D. Correct. This is the bowel-training measure described.
- E. Incorrect. Post-meal toilet sitting is specifically recommended.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Toilet sitting after meals uses the gastrocolic response.
- Encourage a supportive posture and positive reinforcement.
- Adequate fluids and fibre support treatment.

questions.stem: , encopresis is defined as involuntary passage of faeces into inappropriate places after approximately what age?
questions.correctAnswerText: 4 years
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe encopresis/faecal soiling as involuntary passage of faeces into inappropriate places after the expected age of bowel control, approximately 4 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Two years is below the age specified.
- B. Correct. standard guidance uses approximately 4 years.
- C. Incorrect. This is far earlier than the expected age of bowel control.
- D. Incorrect. One year is too early.
- E. Incorrect. This is later than the age used in the definition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Encopresis: involuntary passage of stool after expected bowel control.
- It may be primary or secondary.
- Most cases are retentive and associated with constipation/overflow.

questions.stem: A child with constipation has failure to pass meconium within 24 hours, abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: B
options.text: These are expected after normal toilet training

options.label: C
options.text: This is uncomplicated functional constipation and requires reassurance

options.label: D
options.text: These are red flags for Hirschsprung disease or intestinal obstruction and warrant urgent referral

options.label: E
options.text: These are typical of lactose intolerance

questions.correctAnswerText: These are red flags for Hirschsprung disease or intestinal obstruction and warrant urgent referral
questions.initialExplanation: Delayed meconium, abdominal distension and vomiting are red flags in a constipated child. They raise concern for Hirschsprung disease or intestinal obstruction and require urgent assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Toddler diarrhoea presents with loose stools in an otherwise thriving toddler.
- B. Incorrect. These are not normal features of toilet training.
- C. Incorrect. These findings are not compatible with a routine functional diagnosis without further assessment.
- D. Correct. The clinical features are explicit red flags.
- E. Incorrect. Lactose intolerance causes diarrhoea and bloating, not delayed meconium and neonatal obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Red flags include delayed meconium, onset from birth, distension with vomiting, ribbon stools, neurological/spinal abnormalities and abnormal anal anatomy.
- Faltering growth or symptoms triggered by cow's milk also need further assessment.
- Do not label a child as having functional constipation when red flags are present.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which sequence matches the operative plan?

options.label: B
options.text: Resection of the affected segment with colostomy, followed later by anastomosis

options.label: E
options.text: Nissen fundoplication followed by rectal dilation

questions.correctAnswerText: Resection of the affected segment with colostomy, followed later by anastomosis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include Hirschsprung disease as requiring two-step surgery: resection with colostomy, followed by anastomosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The diagnostic evidence establishes aganglionosis, so the question is about the surgical sequence described in the supplied clinical guidance. Its treatment summary explicitly lists two stages: first resection with colostomy, then anastomosis.

- A. Incorrect. Ramstedt pyloromyotomy is the operation for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; fundoplication is described for selected GERD cases.
- B. Correct. This is the two-step surgical sequence written in the Hirschsprung section.
- C. Incorrect. Appendectomy is used for appendicitis, not congenital aganglionosis.
- D. Incorrect. Duodenal surgery is relevant to duodenal atresia, not Hirschsprung disease.
- E. Incorrect. Fundoplication treats selected reflux disease and rectal dilation is not the staged operation described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Definitive diagnosis: rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells and increased acetylcholinesterase staining in nerve trunks.
- Contrast enema may show a narrowed distal aganglionic segment, dilated proximal colon and a transition zone.
- The supplied clinical guidance describes two-step surgery: resection + colostomy, then anastomosis.

cases.title: A school-aged child with migrating abdominal pain
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child develops abdominal pain that initially begins around the umbilicus and later localizes to the right iliac fossa. The pain worsens with walking and coughing. The child has anorexia, vomiting and fever. Examination reveals localized tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acute appendicitis
questions.initialExplanation: Pain that starts periumbilically and migrates to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia, vomiting and fever, is a classical presentation of acute appendicitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Infantile colic is a crying syndrome in young infants.
- B. Incorrect. GERD causes regurgitation or heartburn rather than migrating right iliac fossa pain.
- C. Correct. The migration and localized right iliac fossa signs are characteristic.
- D. Incorrect. Toddler diarrhoea causes loose stools in a thriving young child.
- E. Incorrect. Functional abdominal pain is recurrent/chronic and usually lacks acute focal peritoneal signs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Appendicitis is a common cause of acute abdominal pain requiring surgery in children.
- Pain classically migrates from periumbilical region to the right iliac fossa.
- Movement, coughing or jumping may aggravate pain.
- Anorexia, vomiting and fever may occur.

questions.stem: Palpation of the left iliac fossa produces pain in the right iliac fossa in a child with suspected appendicitis. What is this sign called?
questions.correctAnswerText: Rovsing sign
questions.initialExplanation: Rovsing sign is right iliac fossa pain elicited by palpation of the left iliac fossa.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. McBurney's point is the site of maximal tenderness classically assessed in appendicitis.
- B. Incorrect. Murphy sign is associated with gallbladder inflammation.
- C. Correct. This is the definition of Rovsing sign.
- D. Incorrect. Cullen sign is periumbilical bruising associated with intra-abdominal bleeding.
- E. Incorrect. Psoas sign is pain elicited by movement/stretching of the psoas muscle in some appendicitis cases.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- McBurney's point: localized right iliac fossa tenderness.
- Rovsing sign: left iliac fossa palpation causes right iliac fossa pain.
- Rebound tenderness and guarding suggest peritoneal irritation.

questions.stem: A child has a history and examination strongly suggestive of appendicitis, but the white cell count is normal. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: The child must have viral gastroenteritis

options.label: B
options.text: A normal CBC does not exclude appendicitis

options.label: C
options.text: Appendicitis can be diagnosed if CRP is elevated

options.label: D
options.text: The child has functional abdominal pain

questions.correctAnswerText: A normal CBC does not exclude appendicitis
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is that appendicitis is mainly a clinical diagnosis and a normal CBC does not rule it out.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A normal CBC does not establish viral gastroenteritis.
- B. Correct. Clinical judgement remains central.
- C. Incorrect. No single laboratory marker consistently confirms or excludes appendicitis.
- D. Incorrect. Acute migratory focal pain and guarding are not typical of functional pain.
- E. Incorrect. A normal white cell count cannot reliably exclude appendicitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Diagnosis is mainly clinical.
- CBC may show leukocytosis, but a normal count does not exclude the diagnosis.
- Urinalysis helps assess urinary causes; ultrasound may support the diagnosis.
- No laboratory or imaging test is consistently diagnostic in every child.

questions.stem: Why is appendicitis particularly dangerous and difficult to diagnose in preschool children?

options.label: A
options.text: The diagnosis is more difficult and perforation may occur rapidly because the omentum is less developed

options.label: C
options.text: Preschool children not usually develop fever

options.label: D
options.text: The appendix is absent in this age group

options.label: E
options.text: The omentum completely prevents perforation in young children

questions.correctAnswerText: The diagnosis is more difficult and perforation may occur rapidly because the omentum is less developed
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that diagnosis is difficult in very young children and perforation may occur rapidly because the omentum is less developed and may not effectively wall off the inflamed appendix.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Both the diagnostic difficulty and rapid perforation risk are emphasized.
- B. Incorrect. Preschool children may have significant symptoms, although they may be less specific.
- C. Incorrect. Fever may occur.
- D. Incorrect. The appendix is present in preschool children.
- E. Incorrect. This is explained that the less developed omentum is less able to contain the process.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Appendicitis is less common but potentially serious in preschool children.
- Early diagnosis can be difficult.
- Perforation may occur early; do not underestimate subtle symptoms.

questions.stem: A child with appendicular mass is clinically stable. Which initial management approach is described?

options.label: E
options.text: IV fluids and IV antibiotics followed by planned elective appendectomy after more than 6 weeks

questions.correctAnswerText: IV fluids and IV antibiotics followed by planned elective appendectomy after more than 6 weeks
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include conservative initial management of appendicular mass with IV fluids and antibiotics, followed by elective appendectomy after an interval.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Colonoscopy is not the described treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Appendicular mass requires appropriate treatment and monitoring.
- C. Incorrect. Antidiarrhoeal medication does not treat appendicular mass.
- D. Incorrect. Gluten-free diet treats coeliac disease.
- E. Correct. This is the staged management described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Uncomplicated appendicitis: appendectomy.
- Perforation may require surgery and peritoneal lavage.
- Appendicular abscess may require drainage and antibiotics.
- Appendicular mass: initial conservative management and interval surgery; local surgical practice may vary.

cases.title: A child with painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old child is brought with a sudden episode of significant painless rectal bleeding. There is no fever, diarrhoea or abdominal tenderness. The child is haemodynamically stable after assessment.

questions.stem: What is the underlying embryological abnormality in Meckel diverticulum?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of the duodenal lumen to recanalize

options.label: B
options.text: Failure of neural crest cell migration into the colon

options.label: E
options.text: Incomplete separation of trachea and oesophagus

questions.correctAnswerText: Persistence of the vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct
questions.initialExplanation: Meckel diverticulum results from persistence of the embryonic vitellointestinal duct, which normally involutes during fetal development.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Duodenal atresia has a different developmental mechanism.
- B. Incorrect. This mechanism causes Hirschsprung disease.
- C. Incorrect. This causes cleft palate.
- D. Correct. This is the embryological basis described.
- E. Incorrect. This is related to tracheoesophageal malformations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Meckel diverticulum: remnant of the vitellointestinal duct.
- Clinical descriptions include the rule of twos: about 2% prevalence, approximately 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches in length and two common types of ectopic tissue.
- Ectopic gastric and pancreatic tissue may be present.

questions.stem: Which investigation is used to detect ectopic gastric mucosa in suspected Meckel diverticulum?
questions.correctAnswerText: Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan
questions.initialExplanation: The Meckel scan uses technetium-labelled pertechnetate to detect ectopic gastric mucosa within the diverticulum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the investigation described for suspected Meckel diverticulum.
- B. Incorrect. Sweat chloride helps diagnose cystic fibrosis.
- C. Incorrect. pH monitoring evaluates acid reflux.
- D. Incorrect. Anorectal manometry may support assessment of Hirschsprung disease.
- E. Incorrect. Hydrogen breath testing assesses selected carbohydrate malabsorption disorders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Painless significant GI bleeding in a child: consider Meckel diverticulum.
- Meckel scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa.
- Complications also include obstruction, intussusception, volvulus and diverticulitis.
- Definitive treatment is surgical resection.

cases.title: An infant with episodic screaming and pallor
cases.vignette: A 9-month-old infant develops sudden recurrent episodes of severe colicky abdominal pain. During each episode, the child screams, becomes pale and draws the legs up. Between episodes, the child becomes quiet and increasingly lethargic. Later, bilious vomiting and blood-stained mucus in the stool develop.

questions.stem: What is intussusception?

options.label: A
options.text: Twisting of the bowel around its mesentery

options.label: B
options.text: Invagination of a proximal segment of bowel into a distal segment

options.label: C
options.text: Failure of the duodenum to recanalize

questions.correctAnswerText: Invagination of a proximal segment of bowel into a distal segment
questions.initialExplanation: Intussusception occurs when a proximal segment of bowel telescopes into a distal segment, leading to intestinal obstruction and possible vascular compromise.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Twisting of bowel around its mesentery describes volvulus.
- B. Correct. This is the definition given.
- C. Incorrect. This is a developmental mechanism associated with duodenal atresia.
- D. Incorrect. This describes Hirschsprung disease.
- E. Incorrect. This describes appendicitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Intussusception: telescoping of proximal bowel into distal bowel.
- It is a common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants after the neonatal period.
- Venous obstruction may precede arterial compromise, ischaemia, mucosal bleeding and perforation.

questions.stem: Which age group is most typical for intussusception?
questions.correctAnswerText: 3 months to 2 years
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives a peak age of 3 months to 2 years, with approximately half of cases occurring below one year.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the peak age described.
- B. Incorrect. Adolescence is not the typical age range.
- C. Incorrect. This age is more relevant to congenital neonatal obstruction.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the paediatric epidemiology described.
- E. Incorrect. Intussusception can occur in older children, but this is not the peak age.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Peak age: 3 months to 2 years.
- The commonest type is ileocolic/ileocaecal.
- Lymphoid hyperplasia after viral infection is a common proposed lead point in young children.

questions.stem: Which stool description is classically associated with intussusception, although it is often a late finding?

options.label: A
options.text: Black tarry stool in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Red currant jelly stool
questions.initialExplanation: Red currant jelly stool results from blood and mucus passing from the injured intestinal mucosa. An important point is that this is a characteristic but late finding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Melena is digested blood and is not the characteristic stool description of intussusception.
- B. Incorrect. Greasy pale stool suggests fat malabsorption.
- C. Incorrect. Rice-water stool is classically associated with cholera.
- D. Incorrect. Clay-coloured stool suggests reduced bile pigment in the intestine.
- E. Correct. Blood and mucus produce the red currant jelly appearance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The classic triad may include colicky pain, vomiting and red currant jelly stool, but all features may not be present.
- Red currant jelly stool is often late; do not wait for it before suspecting intussusception.
- A sausage-shaped abdominal mass may be palpable.

questions.stem: Which abdominal ultrasound finding supports intussusception?

options.label: A
options.text: Coiled nasogastric tube in the chest

options.label: B
options.text: Transition zone with a narrow rectum

questions.correctAnswerText: Target or doughnut sign
questions.initialExplanation: On ultrasound, intussusception classically produces a target or doughnut sign in cross-section.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A coiled NGT supports oesophageal atresia.
- B. Incorrect. A transition zone with narrow distal bowel supports Hirschsprung disease.
- C. Incorrect. Bird-beak sign is associated with achalasia on contrast swallow.
- D. Incorrect. Double-bubble sign suggests duodenal atresia.
- E. Correct. Target/doughnut sign is characteristic of intussusception.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Abdominal ultrasound: target/doughnut sign.
- Plain abdominal radiograph may show dilated small bowel and paucity of distal colonic/rectal gas.
- Ultrasound can also help assess response after enema reduction.

questions.stem: A haemodynamically stable infant with confirmed intussusception has no evidence of perforation or peritonitis. Which intervention may be both diagnostic and therapeutic?
questions.correctAnswerText: Air or contrast enema reduction
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include air or contrast enema as both diagnostic and therapeutic, with a high success rate in suitable patients.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fundoplication is an anti-reflux operation.
- B. Correct. Enema reduction can confirm and reduce intussusception in an appropriate stable child.
- C. Incorrect. Laxatives do not treat the telescoped bowel.
- D. Incorrect. Surgery is reserved for failed reduction or complications such as perforation, peritonitis or gangrene.
- E. Incorrect. Oesophageal dilation treats selected oesophageal strictures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stabilize first if dehydrated or shocked.
- NPO and NGT decompression may be used.
- Air/contrast enema is diagnostic and therapeutic in suitable patients.
- Surgery is required if enema reduction fails or perforation, peritonitis or gangrene is suspected.

topics.name: Chronic Abdominal Pain and Functional Abdominal Pain Disorders

cases.title: A school-aged child with recurrent periumbilical pain
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child has recurrent episodes of central abdominal pain, mainly during the day. The episodes interrupt some school activities but the child has normal growth, a normal examination and no fever, weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding or persistent vomiting. The family reports recent school stress.

questions.stem: Which definition of chronic abdominal pain is used?

options.label: A
options.text: Abdominal pain accompanied by fever for 48 hours

options.label: B
options.text: Pain occurring once a year for three years

options.label: D
options.text: Episodes at least four times per month, sufficient to interrupt normal activities, for at least two months

options.label: E
options.text: Any abdominal pain lasting more than 24 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Episodes at least four times per month, sufficient to interrupt normal activities, for at least two months
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives an updated definition of chronic abdominal pain as episodes occurring at least four times per month, interrupting normal activities and lasting for at least two months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fever and a 48-hour duration suggest an acute illness rather than chronic abdominal pain.
- B. Incorrect. The frequency and duration do not meet the specified definition.
- C. Incorrect. Meal association alone does not define chronic abdominal pain.
- D. Correct. This reproduces the updated definition.
- E. Incorrect. One day of pain is acute, not chronic by standard definition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chronic abdominal pain: at least four episodes per month for at least two months, interrupting activities.
- Functional causes are more common than organic causes in the school-aged group described.
- Clinical guidance notes a prevalence around 10% in school-aged children.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern most strongly supports functional abdominal pain in this child?

options.label: A
options.text: Persistent right upper quadrant pain with weight loss

options.label: B
options.text: Severe nocturnal epigastric pain with haematemesis

options.label: D
options.text: Progressive abdominal distension with bilious vomiting

options.label: E
options.text: Periumbilical pain, mainly diurnal, normal growth and no alarm features

questions.correctAnswerText: Periumbilical pain, mainly diurnal, normal growth and no alarm features
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include functional pain as commonly periumbilical, occurring mainly during the day in a healthy-appearing child with normal growth and no alarm features.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Persistent localized pain and weight loss are red flags for organic disease.
- B. Incorrect. Nocturnal epigastric pain with haematemesis raises concern for peptic ulcer disease or upper GI bleeding.
- C. Incorrect. Bloody diarrhoea and poor growth suggest an inflammatory or malabsorptive condition.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests intestinal obstruction.
- E. Correct. This fits the typical functional pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Functional abdominal pain: commonly central/periumbilical and diurnal.
- Normal growth and normal examination are reassuring.
- Pain is real even when there is no demonstrable structural disease.

questions.stem: Which feature is a red flag suggesting an organic cause of chronic abdominal pain?

options.label: A
options.text: Pain that improves when the child returns to normal activities

options.label: B
options.text: Weight loss, blood in stool and growth faltering

options.label: D
options.text: Normal growth with periumbilical daytime pain

options.label: E
options.text: Pain associated with school stress and no other symptoms

questions.correctAnswerText: Weight loss, blood in stool and growth faltering
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include constitutional symptoms, weight loss, growth faltering, blood in stool, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, night waking and perianal disease among red flags.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Return to normal activities is generally encouraged in functional pain management.
- B. Correct. Weight loss, bloody diarrhoea and growth failure raise concern for IBD or other organic disease.
- C. Incorrect. Normal growth and examination are reassuring, though follow-up remains important.
- D. Incorrect. This is a common functional pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Psychosocial stress can contribute to functional disorders, especially without alarm features.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Red flags: localized pain away from the umbilicus, fever, weight loss, arthritis, family history of IBD/coeliac/peptic ulcer, night waking, bleeding, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, urinary symptoms, perianal disease and delayed puberty.
- Investigate according to the red flags rather than ordering broad tests in every child.

questions.stem: Which management principle is emphasized for functional abdominal pain?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell the child the pain is imaginary

options.label: B
options.text: Start long-term antibiotics for most patients

options.label: C
options.text: Perform surgery to remove the appendix in children in routine care

options.label: D
options.text: Explain that the pain is real, reassure the family and encourage return to usual activities and school

options.label: E
options.text: Recommend prolonged school absence until most pain disappears

questions.correctAnswerText: Explain that the pain is real, reassure the family and encourage return to usual activities and school
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes validating the child's pain, explaining the absence of evidence for a serious underlying disease when appropriate, reassuring the family and encouraging normal activities. Behavioural approaches may help.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The child's pain is real and should not be dismissed.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics have no routine role in functional abdominal pain.
- C. Incorrect. Functional abdominal pain is not an indication for appendectomy.
- D. Correct. This follows the management principles.
- E. Incorrect. Prolonged avoidance of normal activities may reinforce disability.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Validate the pain and explain the diagnosis clearly.
- Encourage school attendance and regular activity.
- Behavioural therapy, relaxation and biofeedback may be useful.
- standard guidance cautions that complete disappearance of pain is not always a realistic immediate goal.

cases.title: A thriving young infant with prolonged crying episodes
cases.vignette: A 6-week-old infant cries for prolonged periods, especially in the evening. During episodes, the infant stiffens, draws up the legs and passes flatus. The infant feeds well, grows normally and has a normal physical examination. There is no fever, bilious vomiting or blood in the stool.

questions.stem: Which definition of infantile colic is described?

options.label: A
options.text: Persistent crying after 1 year of age

options.label: C
options.text: Crying for more than 1 hour once per month

options.label: D
options.text: Crying for more than 3 hours per day, on more than 3 days per week, for more than 3 weeks in an otherwise healthy infant

options.label: E
options.text: Crying associated with fever and poor growth

questions.correctAnswerText: Crying for more than 3 hours per day, on more than 3 days per week, for more than 3 weeks in an otherwise healthy infant
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance uses the rule of threes: more than 3 hours/day, more than 3 days/week and more than 3 weeks, in an otherwise healthy infant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Colic commonly occurs in the first months of life.
- B. Incorrect. Crying after feeding alone does not establish colic.
- C. Incorrect. This does not meet the rule of threes.
- D. Correct. It matches the definition.
- E. Incorrect. Fever and poor growth require assessment for an underlying illness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rule of threes: >3 hours/day, >3 days/week, >3 weeks.
- Usually occurs in the first 4 months; peak around 6 weeks.
- The infant should otherwise be healthy and thriving.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate approach to investigation and management in an otherwise thriving infant with typical colic and a normal examination?

options.label: E
options.text: Diagnosis by exclusion, usually no investigations, and parental reassurance

questions.correctAnswerText: Diagnosis by exclusion, usually no investigations, and parental reassurance
questions.initialExplanation: Colic is a clinical diagnosis after considering other causes. Investigations are usually unnecessary when the infant is thriving and has no red flags. Reassurance is the main management.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Colic is not a bacterial infection.
- B. Incorrect. Endoscopy is not routine in typical colic.
- C. Incorrect. Surgery is not indicated without evidence of an acute surgical condition.
- D. Incorrect. CT is not indicated in a typical uncomplicated presentation.
- E. Correct. This is the approach described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Check for red flags such as fever, poor feeding, poor growth, bilious vomiting or blood in stool.
- Reassure caregivers and explain the self-limiting course.
- Clinical guidance notes that colic commonly resolves by around 4–5 months.

topics.name: Anterior Abdominal Wall Defects and Anal Atresia

cases.title: A newborn with exposed abdominal contents
cases.vignette: A newborn is found to have protruding abdominal contents at birth. The clinician must distinguish an omphalocele from gastroschisis by the presence of a covering sac, the location of the defect and associated congenital abnormalities.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes omphalocele from gastroschisis?

options.label: A
options.text: Omphalocele is covered by a sac; gastroschisis is not covered by a sac

options.label: B
options.text: Omphalocele not usually involves the umbilical region

options.label: C
options.text: Omphalocele is typically right-sided and uncovered

options.label: D
options.text: Gastroschisis is typically covered by an intact sac

options.label: E
options.text: The two conditions are identical in anatomy

questions.correctAnswerText: Omphalocele is covered by a sac; gastroschisis is not covered by a sac
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance distinguishes omphalocele by its covering sac (amnion) and central umbilical location, while gastroschisis has exposed bowel without a covering sac.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The presence or absence of a sac is a key distinguishing feature.
- B. Incorrect. Omphalocele is typically central and umbilical.
- C. Incorrect. Omphalocele is central at the umbilicus and is covered by a sac.
- D. Incorrect. Gastroschisis is not covered by a sac.
- E. Incorrect. They are distinct congenital abdominal wall defects.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Omphalocele: central, at umbilicus, covered by a sac.
- Gastroschisis: usually to the right of the umbilicus, not covered by a sac.
- Protect exposed bowel and arrange urgent neonatal/surgical care.

questions.stem: Which congenital association is particularly relevant to omphalocele?
questions.correctAnswerText: Trisomy 13 or 18 and Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that omphalocele is more commonly associated with other congenital and chromosomal anomalies, including trisomy 13, trisomy 18 and Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Achalasia is an oesophageal motility disorder.
- B. Incorrect. Functional constipation is unrelated.
- C. Correct. These associations are specifically listed for omphalocele.
- D. Incorrect. Infantile colic is a benign crying syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Lactose intolerance is not a congenital abdominal wall association.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Omphalocele: assess carefully for associated congenital anomalies.
- Gastroschisis is described as less commonly associated with other anomalies.
- Management involves covering/protecting the defect, surgical closure and nutritional support.

cases.title: A newborn with no visible anal opening
cases.vignette: A term newborn has no normal anal opening. The abdomen becomes distended, and the infant fails to pass meconium during the first 24 hours. Bilious vomiting develops.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Imperforate anus (anal atresia)
questions.initialExplanation: Absence of a normal anal opening with failure to pass meconium, abdominal distension and bilious vomiting is consistent with anal atresia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Coeliac disease presents after gluten exposure and does not cause an absent anus.
- B. Incorrect. GER causes regurgitation and does not explain an absent anal opening.
- C. Correct. This is a congenital anorectal malformation.
- D. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious projectile vomiting later in infancy.
- E. Incorrect. Colic occurs in an otherwise healthy young infant with normal anatomy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Imperforate anus: congenital anorectal malformation with absent normal anal opening.
- Failure to pass meconium, distension and bile-stained vomiting may occur.
- Surgical management is required; Clinical descriptions include colostomy and subsequent reconstruction.

cases.title: A young child with early childhood tooth decay
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child from a low-resource household has multiple decayed primary teeth. The family reports frequent sugary drinks and prolonged bottle use. The clinician discusses the major organisms involved and preventive oral hygiene.

questions.stem: Which organism is predominantly associated with early childhood dental caries?
questions.correctAnswerText: Streptococcus mutans
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include Streptococcus mutans, alongside Streptococcus sobrinus, as an important bacterium involved in dental caries in the presence of dietary sugars.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Shigella causes bacillary dysentery.
- B. Incorrect. Candida is a yeast associated with mucocutaneous infection, not the principal caries organism described.
- C. Correct. S. mutans is the predominant organism highlighted.
- D. Incorrect. Giardia is an intestinal protozoan.
- E. Incorrect. H. pylori is associated with gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dental caries involves oral bacteria and frequent sugar exposure.
- Recognized features include S. mutans and S. sobrinus.
- Prevention includes supervised brushing with fluoride toothpaste and reducing sugar exposure.

questions.stem: Which advice is appropriate for prevention of dental caries in a young child?

options.label: C
options.text: Rinse the mouth vigorously with water after each brushing to remove fluoride

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid parental supervision of toothbrushing before age 7

options.label: E
options.text: Brush twice daily with fluoridated toothpaste once teeth erupt

questions.correctAnswerText: Brush twice daily with fluoridated toothpaste once teeth erupt
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes brushing twice daily with fluoridated toothpaste as soon as teeth erupt, with a smear for young children and a pea-sized amount from age 3 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bottle feeding should be discouraged from around age 1 year.
- B. Incorrect. Added sugar increases caries risk.
- C. Incorrect. standard guidance advises spitting out toothpaste rather than rinsing after brushing from age 3 years.
- D. Incorrect. Parents/carers should brush or supervise brushing until around age 7 years.
- E. Correct. This is the preventive approach described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Start brushing as soon as teeth erupt.
- Use fluoride toothpaste twice daily.
- Up to 3 years: flat smear; thereafter, pea-sized amount.
- Supervise brushing until around 7 years.
- Avoid added sugar in weaning foods and drinks.

cases.title: A child who accidentally ingests a household cleaning product
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after accidentally drinking a household drain-cleaning product. The child has severe oral and retrosternal burning pain, drooling, vomiting and dysphagia. The family asks whether vomiting should be induced to remove the substance.

questions.stem: Which mechanism of tissue injury is classically associated with ingestion of a strong alkali?
questions.correctAnswerText: Liquefaction necrosis
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that alkalis cause liquefaction necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration and potentially more extensive injury. Acids classically cause coagulation necrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Coagulation necrosis is associated with acids.
- B. Correct. Alkalis cause liquefaction necrosis.
- C. Incorrect. Caseating granulomas are not the pattern of corrosive injury.
- D. Incorrect. Fat necrosis is not the mechanism described.
- E. Incorrect. Caustic ingestion causes direct destructive tissue injury.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Alkalis: liquefaction necrosis and deeper penetration.
- Acids: coagulation necrosis with eschar formation.
- Symptoms include burning pain, drooling, vomiting, dysphagia and respiratory compromise.

questions.stem: A child with suspected corrosive ingestion is stable after initial airway, breathing and circulation assessment. Which investigation is recommended to assess oesophageal injury?
questions.correctAnswerText: Endoscopy within 24 hours
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes endoscopic assessment within 24 hours to evaluate the extent of oesophageal injury after corrosive ingestion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Meckel scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa.
- B. Incorrect. Hydrogen breath testing evaluates carbohydrate malabsorption.
- C. Incorrect. Barium enema is unrelated to corrosive oesophageal injury.
- D. Incorrect. Colonoscopy does not assess the acute oesophageal injury.
- E. Correct. This is the timing stated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stabilize ABC first.
- Admit, keep NPO and provide IV fluids/supportive care as indicated.
- Recommended management includes endoscopy within 24 hours.
- Airway symptoms such as stridor or respiratory distress require urgent management.

questions.stem: Which intervention is contraindicated after a child ingests a corrosive substance?

options.label: A
options.text: Inducing vomiting or attempting chemical neutralization

options.label: B
options.text: Assessment and stabilization of airway and circulation

options.label: D
options.text: Keeping the child nil by mouth pending assessment

questions.correctAnswerText: Inducing vomiting or attempting chemical neutralization
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include emesis, gastric lavage, neutralization and activated charcoal among contraindicated interventions after corrosive ingestion. Re-exposure during vomiting or chemical reactions may worsen injury.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Inducing vomiting or neutralizing the corrosive agent is contraindicated.
- B. Incorrect. ABC stabilization is essential.
- C. Incorrect. Monitoring for airway injury is essential.
- D. Incorrect. NPO status is part of the initial supportive approach described.
- E. Incorrect. Specialist assessment and appropriately timed endoscopy are part of care.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Do not induce vomiting.
- Do not attempt neutralization.
- Do not perform gastric lavage or give activated charcoal for corrosive injury.
- Avoid blind interventions that may worsen oesophageal damage.

topics.name: Eosinophilic Oesophagitis and Oesophageal Foreign Bodies

cases.title: An atopic child with food sticking in the chest
cases.vignette: An 11-year-old child with a history of atopy presents with recurrent dysphagia, vomiting and episodes in which solid food feels stuck behind the sternum. Endoscopy reveals linear furrows and a ringed or trachealized appearance of the oesophagus.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Eosinophilic oesophagitis
questions.initialExplanation: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is an inflammatory disorder characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the oesophageal mucosa. It is more common in children with atopy and may cause dysphagia and food sticking.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Meckel diverticulum causes bleeding or obstruction.
- B. Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease causes constipation and distal intestinal obstruction.
- C. Incorrect. Oesophageal atresia presents in the neonatal period with frothy secretions and choking on feeds.
- D. Correct. Atopy, dysphagia and food sticking with characteristic endoscopic changes suggest eosinophilic oesophagitis.
- E. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes projectile non-bilious vomiting in early infancy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Eosinophilic oesophagitis is associated with atopy.
- Symptoms include dysphagia, vomiting, regurgitation and food sticking.
- Endoscopy may show linear furrows and trachealization.

questions.stem: Which investigation confirms eosinophilic oesophagitis?

options.label: C
options.text: Endoscopy with oesophageal biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration

questions.correctAnswerText: Endoscopy with oesophageal biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration
questions.initialExplanation: Endoscopy can show characteristic furrows and rings, while biopsy demonstrates eosinophilic infiltration and confirms the diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Abdominal radiography does not assess oesophageal mucosal histology.
- B. Incorrect. Meckel scan is used for suspected ectopic gastric mucosa.
- C. Correct. Endoscopic biopsy is required to demonstrate oesophageal eosinophilic inflammation.
- D. Incorrect. Stool culture evaluates selected enteric infection.
- E. Incorrect. Anorectal manometry is used in selected constipation/Hirschsprung evaluations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Diagnosis requires oesophageal biopsies.
- Endoscopy may reveal linear furrows and trachealization.
- Treatment includes swallowed topical steroids and dietary restriction in selected young children.

cases.title: A toddler who suddenly develops choking and dysphagia
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child suddenly starts coughing and choking while playing with small objects. The coughing improves, but the child later develops dysphagia and repeated vomiting. A plain radiograph shows a radiopaque object in the oesophagus. The clinician must decide whether removal is urgent.

questions.stem: Which objects are common sites of oesophageal foreign-body impaction described?

options.label: C
options.text: Upper oesophageal sphincter, level of the aortic arch and lower oesophageal sphincter

questions.correctAnswerText: Upper oesophageal sphincter, level of the aortic arch and lower oesophageal sphincter
questions.initialExplanation: Key features include anatomical narrowings of the oesophagus, including the upper oesophageal sphincter, the aortic arch level and the lower oesophageal sphincter, as common sites of foreign-body impaction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal sites but not the oesophageal narrowings described.
- B. Incorrect. These are not the characteristic oesophageal narrowing points.
- C. Correct. These are the sites listed.
- D. Incorrect. These are not oesophageal impaction sites.
- E. Incorrect. These are biliary structures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Coins are the commonest oesophageal foreign bodies.
- Symptoms may include choking, cough, dysphagia and vomiting.
- Consider aspiration and airway compromise as well as oesophageal obstruction.

questions.stem: Which foreign body requires urgent removal rather than observation?

options.label: A
options.text: A disk battery lodged in the oesophagus

options.label: B
options.text: A blunt object in an asymptomatic child with no obstruction

options.label: C
options.text: A soft food bolus that has passed spontaneously

options.label: D
options.text: A small blunt object that has passed into the stomach and the child is well

options.label: E
options.text: An incidental radiographic finding of no foreign body

questions.correctAnswerText: A disk battery lodged in the oesophagus
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that sharp objects, disk batteries and foreign bodies associated with respiratory symptoms should be removed. A blunt object may be observed for a limited period in selected circumstances.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. An oesophageal disk battery can cause rapid tissue injury and requires urgent removal.
- B. Incorrect. Selected blunt objects may be observed depending on location and clinical context.
- C. Incorrect. A spontaneously passed bolus does not require oesophageal removal.
- D. Incorrect. A blunt object that has reached the stomach may be managed according to object size, symptoms and local guidance.
- E. Incorrect. No foreign body is present.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Disk batteries in the oesophagus: urgent removal.
- Sharp objects and foreign bodies with respiratory symptoms: urgent removal.
- Do not apply an observation rule without considering object type, location, symptoms and age.

cases.title: A child with progressive dysphagia to liquids and solids
cases.vignette: A 12-year-old child has progressive dysphagia, initially more noticeable with liquids, regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis. The child has recurrent chest infections. A contrast swallow shows a tapering bird-beak appearance of the distal oesophagus.

questions.stem: Which underlying abnormality characterizes achalasia?

options.label: A
options.text: Villous atrophy in the small bowel

options.label: C
options.text: Absence of intestinal ganglion cells in the rectum

options.label: D
options.text: Failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation with loss of oesophageal peristalsis

options.label: E
options.text: Excessive lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and hyperperistalsis

questions.correctAnswerText: Failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation with loss of oesophageal peristalsis
questions.initialExplanation: Achalasia is an oesophageal motility disorder characterized by failure of LES relaxation and loss of normal oesophageal peristalsis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Villous atrophy is associated with enteropathies such as coeliac disease.
- B. Incorrect. Pyloric muscle hypertrophy causes gastric outlet obstruction.
- C. Incorrect. This describes Hirschsprung disease.
- D. Correct. This is the defining motor abnormality.
- E. Incorrect. Achalasia involves impaired relaxation, not excessive relaxation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Achalasia: failure of LES relaxation and loss of oesophageal peristalsis.
- Symptoms include dysphagia, regurgitation, halitosis and recurrent chest infections.
- Clinical guidance notes that dysphagia may be more prominent with liquids.

questions.stem: Which investigation is described as more sensitive for confirming achalasia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Oesophageal manometry
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include manometry as more sensitive for confirming achalasia. Barium swallow may show a bird-beak or rat-tail appearance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Faecal calprotectin is a marker of intestinal inflammation.
- B. Correct. Manometry assesses oesophageal motor function and LES relaxation.
- C. Incorrect. Plain abdominal radiography does not assess oesophageal motility.
- D. Incorrect. Sweat chloride is used in cystic fibrosis assessment.
- E. Incorrect. Stool microscopy investigates selected infectious/parasitic causes of diarrhoea.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Manometry: more sensitive investigation.
- Barium swallow: bird-beak/rat-tail sign.
- Endoscopy may help exclude structural lesions or other causes.

questions.stem: Which treatment option is described as a definitive mechanical approach for achalasia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pneumatic dilatation or surgical myotomy
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include pneumatic dilatation and surgical myotomy as treatment options, with botulinum toxin injection and calcium-channel blockers as other approaches.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Gluten-free diet is used for coeliac disease.
- B. Incorrect. Pyloromyotomy treats hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
- C. Incorrect. Achalasia is not a bacterial infection.
- D. Correct. These interventions aim to relieve the functional obstruction at the LES.
- E. Incorrect. Colectomy may be curative for UC, not achalasia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Achalasia treatments: pneumatic dilatation, surgical myotomy and endoscopic botulinum toxin.
- Nifedipine may have a temporary effect.
- Management is specialist-led and depends on patient factors.

topics.name: Gastritis, Peptic Ulcer Disease and Helicobacter pylori

cases.title: An adolescent with nocturnal epigastric pain
cases.vignette: A 14-year-old has recurrent dull epigastric pain, sometimes waking the child at night. There is intermittent nausea and vomiting. A first-degree relative has a history of peptic ulcer disease.

questions.stem: Which symptom pattern in a child should raise suspicion of duodenal ulcer disease?

options.label: B
options.text: Colicky pain with drawing up of the legs

options.label: C
options.text: Epigastric pain that wakes the child at night, especially with a relevant family history

options.label: D
options.text: Painless daytime loose stools with normal growth

options.label: E
options.text: Projectile non-bilious vomiting at 4 weeks of age

questions.correctAnswerText: Epigastric pain that wakes the child at night, especially with a relevant family history
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that duodenal ulcers are uncommon in children but should be considered with nocturnal epigastric pain, pain radiating to the back or a first-degree family history of peptic ulcer disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Oral thrush is unrelated to peptic ulcer disease.
- B. Incorrect. Episodic colic with drawing up of the legs suggests intussusception.
- C. Correct. These are the specific warning features listed.
- D. Incorrect. This pattern may fit toddler diarrhoea.
- E. Incorrect. Projectile non-bilious vomiting in early infancy suggests pyloric stenosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Duodenal ulcer is uncommon in children but important to consider with nocturnal epigastric pain.
- Other clues: pain radiating to the back and a first-degree family history.
- Bleeding or perforation may present with more acute features.

questions.stem: Which statement about Helicobacter pylori is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a helical Gram-negative, urease-producing bacterium

options.label: C
options.text: It is a yeast causing oral candidiasis

options.label: D
options.text: It is a flagellated protozoan parasite

options.label: E
options.text: It is a Gram-positive spore-forming organism

questions.correctAnswerText: It is a helical Gram-negative, urease-producing bacterium
questions.initialExplanation: H. pylori is described as a helical, Gram-negative, urease-producing bacterium associated with chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the organism description given.
- B. Incorrect. H. pylori is a bacterium, not a virus.
- C. Incorrect. Candida is a yeast.
- D. Incorrect. This describes Giardia.
- E. Incorrect. Clinical descriptions include H. pylori as Gram-negative and helical, not Gram-positive and spore-forming.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- H. pylori: helical, Gram-negative and urease-producing.
- Many infected individuals may be asymptomatic.
- Associated conditions include chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease; long-term associations include gastric malignancy.

questions.stem: Which diagnostic approach is described as the best test for H. pylori infection in children?

options.label: B
options.text: Hydrogen breath test for lactose malabsorption

questions.correctAnswerText: Endoscopy with biopsy
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include upper GI endoscopy with biopsy as the best diagnostic approach for H. pylori in children. It also lists urease breath testing and stool antigen testing in selected contexts.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urine dipstick does not detect H. pylori.
- B. Incorrect. Hydrogen breath testing is used for selected carbohydrate malabsorption conditions.
- C. Incorrect. Meckel scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa.
- D. Incorrect. Plain abdominal radiography does not diagnose H. pylori infection.
- E. Correct. Endoscopy with biopsy is the best diagnostic approach specified in the supplied paediatric standard guidance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- H. pylori diagnosis: endoscopy and biopsy.
- Urea breath testing is also mentioned.
- Stool antigen testing is used to confirm successful eradication.
- Follow current paediatric guidance when deciding whom to test and treat.

questions.stem: Which combination is listed as an H. pylori eradication regimen?
questions.correctAnswerText: Amoxicillin + clarithromycin + proton pump inhibitor
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include a combination of amoxicillin, clarithromycin and a proton pump inhibitor, and an alternative combination using metronidazole with amoxicillin and a PPI.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are laxative agents.
- B. Correct. This is one of the combinations shown.
- C. Incorrect. These are antifungal agents used in mucocutaneous candidiasis.
- D. Incorrect. These drugs do not eradicate H. pylori.
- E. Incorrect. These are used in inflammatory bowel disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common examples include PPI-based combination therapy with two antibiotics.
- Treatment choice should reflect local antimicrobial resistance and current paediatric guidance.
- Stool antigen testing is listed for confirming eradication.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which complication should be suspected from this change in presentation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Peptic ulcer perforation
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include acute abdominal pain as a presentation of peptic ulcer perforation. A sudden change from recurrent ulcer symptoms to acute abdominal pain should therefore raise concern for perforation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The source describes peptic ulcer disease as potentially causing epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia. It separately identifies acute abdominal pain as a presentation of perforation. The clinical change in this vignette is therefore the key warning feature.

- A. Incorrect. Physiological GER is common in infancy and does not explain an acute complication in a child with known ulcer disease.
- B. Incorrect. Functional constipation does not account for acute abdominal pain in the context of known peptic ulcer disease.
- C. Correct. Perforation is the ulcer complication linked to acute abdominal pain.
- D. Incorrect. Toddler diarrhoea is a chronic loose-stool pattern in a thriving young child.
- E. Incorrect. Oral candidiasis causes adherent oral plaques and does not explain acute abdominal pain.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common examples include nocturnal dull epigastric pain, nausea/vomiting, bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia among peptic ulcer presentations.
- Acute abdominal pain is specifically associated with perforation in the source clinical guidance.
- Bleeding and perforation are important acute complications to keep in mind.

topics.name: Vomiting in Children — Age-Based Differential and Red Flags

cases.title: A vomiting infant with a possible surgical emergency
cases.vignette: A 6-week-old infant is brought with repeated vomiting. The clinician must determine whether the vomit is bilious or non-bilious, projectile or effortless, and whether there are associated signs of obstruction, bleeding, dehydration, raised intracranial pressure or systemic disease.

questions.stem: What does bilious vomiting in a neonate most importantly suggest?

options.label: C
options.text: Possible intestinal obstruction requiring urgent assessment

questions.correctAnswerText: Possible intestinal obstruction requiring urgent assessment
questions.initialExplanation: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a major red flag for intestinal obstruction, including congenital atresia or malrotation with volvulus, and requires urgent assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Functional abdominal pain is not the diagnosis in a neonate with bilious vomiting.
- B. Incorrect. Posseting is small-volume, non-forceful milk regurgitation and is not bile-stained.
- C. Correct. Bilious vomiting may indicate a surgical obstruction and must not be dismissed.
- D. Incorrect. Bilious vomiting is not normal feeding behaviour.
- E. Incorrect. Teething does not cause bilious vomiting.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bilious vomiting in a neonate: treat as possible intestinal obstruction until assessed.
- Non-bilious projectile vomiting in the first weeks suggests pyloric stenosis.
- Look for abdominal distension, tenderness, blood in stool and systemic compromise.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old infant has progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting and remains hungry after vomiting. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pyloric stenosis
questions.initialExplanation: Projectile non-bilious vomiting in the first weeks of life, often with persistent hunger after vomiting, is characteristic of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Intussusception commonly presents with episodic colicky pain and vomiting in infants.
- B. Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease typically presents with delayed meconium and constipation/obstruction.
- C. Correct. Age and non-bilious projectile vomiting are typical.
- D. Incorrect. Duodenal atresia typically causes bilious vomiting from the first day of life.
- E. Incorrect. Volvulus typically causes bilious vomiting and may rapidly compromise bowel blood supply.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Projectile non-bilious vomiting in young infants: think pyloric stenosis.
- Bilious vomiting: think intestinal obstruction.
- Clinical context and age are central to the differential.

questions.stem: A child presents with vomiting, abdominal distension, severe abdominal tenderness and blood in the stool. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: B
options.text: These are red flags for a possible surgical abdomen or serious intestinal pathology

options.label: C
options.text: These are reassuring features of uncomplicated reflux

options.label: D
options.text: These are typical of uncomplicated teething

questions.correctAnswerText: These are red flags for a possible surgical abdomen or serious intestinal pathology
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include abdominal tenderness, distension, blood in the stool and pain on movement among features that should raise concern for a surgical abdomen or serious intestinal disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Colic occurs in an otherwise healthy infant with a normal examination.
- B. Correct. The findings warrant urgent assessment for obstruction, intussusception, appendicitis, inflammatory disease or other serious causes.
- C. Incorrect. Reflux does not explain this combination of abdominal red flags.
- D. Incorrect. Teething does not explain these abdominal signs.
- E. Incorrect. The features increase concern for obstruction rather than excluding it.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vomiting red flags: bile, haematemesis, abdominal tenderness/pain on movement, distension, hepatosplenomegaly, blood in stool, shock, seizures/bulging fontanelle and faltering growth.
- Assess hydration, perfusion and the possibility of a surgical abdomen.
- Do not attribute persistent or severe vomiting to reflux without assessing for alternative causes.

questions.stem: A vomiting infant has a bulging fontanelle and seizures. Which underlying problem should be considered?

options.label: B
options.text: Raised intracranial pressure or central nervous system disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Raised intracranial pressure or central nervous system disease
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include a bulging fontanelle or seizures as red flags for raised intracranial pressure or central nervous system pathology, including infection or intracranial haemorrhage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Constipation does not explain signs of raised intracranial pressure.
- B. Correct. These neurological red flags require urgent evaluation for CNS pathology.
- C. Incorrect. Lactose intolerance causes gastrointestinal symptoms but does not explain bulging fontanelle or seizures.
- D. Incorrect. Toddler diarrhoea does not cause these neurological findings.
- E. Incorrect. Dental caries does not cause these neurological features.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vomiting with bulging fontanelle or seizures is a neurological red flag.
- Consider CNS infection, intracranial haemorrhage or raised intracranial pressure.
- Urgent assessment is required.

questions.stem: A child has chronic vomiting, poor weight gain and faltering growth. Which broad interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Poor growth confirms normal infant posseting

options.label: C
options.text: Growth failure is a red flag requiring investigation for chronic gastrointestinal or systemic disease

options.label: E
options.text: Growth failure is unrelated to chronic vomiting

questions.correctAnswerText: Growth failure is a red flag requiring investigation for chronic gastrointestinal or systemic disease
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance includes faltering growth among red flags in a vomiting child. Chronic conditions such as GERD with complications, coeliac disease and other gastrointestinal disorders should be considered.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Normal posseting is associated with normal growth.
- B. Incorrect. Physiological reflux should occur without growth compromise or complications.
- C. Correct. Faltering growth alongside chronic vomiting requires assessment for underlying disease.
- D. Incorrect. Reassurance alone is not sufficient when red flags are present.
- E. Incorrect. Poor growth may be a consequence or clue to chronic disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Faltering growth is a red flag.
- Consider chronic GERD with complications, coeliac disease and other malabsorptive, inflammatory or systemic causes.
- Investigations should be guided by the history and examination.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which explanation is specifically listed as a cause of blood in the vomit of a healthy neonate?

options.label: A
options.text: Swallowed maternal blood from the birth canal

questions.correctAnswerText: Swallowed maternal blood from the birth canal
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include swallowed maternal blood from the birth canal as one cause of blood in the vomit of an otherwise healthy neonate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Clinical guidance separates neonatal vomiting into healthy and sick neonates. Under healthy neonates, it lists blood due to either neonatal haemorrhagic disease (vitamin K deficiency) or swallowed maternal blood from the birth canal. The immediate post-delivery context in this case supports the maternal source described in the question.

- A. Correct. Swallowed maternal blood from the birth canal is explicitly listed under causes in healthy neonates.
- B. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes projectile, non-bilious vomiting and is described as presenting in the following weeks of life.
- C. Incorrect. Duodenal atresia is a congenital obstruction associated with bilious vomiting, not the maternal blood explanation.
- D. Incorrect. Rotavirus is a cause of acute gastroenteritis and is not the neonatal blood source listed.
- E. Incorrect. Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis is not the explanation given for blood-stained vomit immediately after delivery.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- In a healthy neonate, Common examples include swallowed maternal blood from the birth canal as a cause of blood in vomit.
- The other neonatal blood-related cause listed is neonatal haemorrhagic disease due to vitamin K deficiency.
- Blood-stained vomiting should be interpreted in the context of the infant's clinical condition and timing.

topics.name: Intravenous Fluid Solutions — Composition and Classification

cases.title: Selecting and identifying intravenous fluid solutions
cases.vignette: A child admitted with gastrointestinal illness requires intravenous fluid therapy. The team reviews the intravenous solutions listed and distinguishes crystalloid solutions from colloids. The purpose of this case is to recognize the composition and classification of the listed fluids, not to prescribe a fluid regimen without considering the child's clinical state.

questions.stem: Which substance is listed as an example of a colloid intravenous fluid in the supplied GIT clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Human albumin
questions.initialExplanation: The intravenous fluid page lists crystalloids such as normal saline and Ringer lactate, and colloids such as human albumin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is also a saline–dextrose solution, not the colloid example.
- B. Correct. Human albumin is the colloid listed.
- C. Incorrect. Ringer lactate is a crystalloid.
- D. Incorrect. This is a saline–dextrose solution, not the colloid example.
- E. Incorrect. Normal saline is a crystalloid.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Colloid listed: human albumin.
- Crystalloids listed: normal saline and Ringer lactate.
- Fluid selection depends on the indication and the child's clinical and biochemical status.

questions.stem: Which pair contains the crystalloid solutions specifically named in the intravenous fluid section?

options.label: D
options.text: Human albumin and packed red blood cells

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal saline and Ringer lactate
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies normal saline and Ringer lactate as examples of crystalloid intravenous fluids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are blood components rather than the crystalloid examples requested.
- B. Incorrect. These are blood products, not the named crystalloid solutions.
- C. Incorrect. Albumin is a colloid, and immunoglobulin is not one of the named crystalloid solutions.
