- D. Incorrect. Albumin is the colloid example; packed red cells are a blood component.
- E. Correct. Both are crystalloid solutions listed on the page.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Crystalloids: normal saline and Ringer lactate.
- Colloid example: human albumin.
- Do not confuse intravenous fluids with blood components.

questions.stem: What is the sodium chloride concentration of normal saline?
questions.correctAnswerText: 0.9% NaCl
questions.initialExplanation: The page labels normal saline as 0.9% sodium chloride.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the normal saline concentration listed.
- B. Incorrect. 0.45% sodium chloride is listed in a saline–dextrose combination.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the normal saline concentration listed.
- D. Incorrect. 0.18% sodium chloride is listed as a dilute saline–dextrose solution.
- E. Correct. Normal saline is 0.9% NaCl.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal saline = 0.9% NaCl.
- The same page lists Ringer lactate as another crystalloid.
- Do not confuse normal saline with the lower-concentration saline–dextrose mixtures.

questions.stem: Which solution is correctly described as 0.45% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose?

options.label: C
options.text: A saline–dextrose intravenous solution listed on page 31

questions.correctAnswerText: A saline–dextrose intravenous solution listed on page 31
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include 0.45% NaCl with 5% dextrose as one of the intravenous solutions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is normal saline, which contains 0.9% NaCl and no dextrose in the formulation named.
- B. Incorrect. Packed red blood cells are a blood component, not a saline–dextrose solution.
- C. Correct. This is the exact saline–dextrose combination listed.
- D. Incorrect. Ringer lactate is a crystalloid with a different electrolyte composition.
- E. Incorrect. Human albumin is a colloid.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance 0.45% NaCl + 5% dextrose.
- It is distinct from 0.9% normal saline.
- Recognize the composition; actual fluid selection must follow current pediatric fluid guidance.

questions.stem: Which concentration is paired with 5% dextrose as the dilute saline solution also described as 1/5 normal saline?
questions.correctAnswerText: 0.18% NaCl
questions.initialExplanation: The page lists 0.18% NaCl with 5% dextrose and also describes 5% dextrose in one-fifth normal saline.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. 10% NaCl is not the saline concentration listed for this combination.
- B. Incorrect. 5% NaCl is not the saline concentration listed for this combination.
- C. Incorrect. 0.45% NaCl is the other saline concentration listed with 5% dextrose.
- D. Incorrect. 0.9% NaCl is normal saline.
- E. Correct. 0.18% NaCl is the concentration listed for the one-fifth normal saline mixture.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 0.18% NaCl + 5% dextrose is listed as 5% dextrose in one-fifth normal saline.
- 0.45% NaCl + 5% dextrose is a separate listed solution.
- These are standard guidance-listed formulations, not automatic choices for routine pediatric maintenance or resuscitation.

questions.stem: Which dextrose concentrations are explicitly listed on the intravenous fluid page?
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance dextrose 5% or 10% among the intravenous fluid preparations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are not the dextrose concentrations specified on the page.
- B. Correct. Both 5% and 10% dextrose are listed.
- C. Incorrect. These are not the concentrations listed in this table.
- D. Incorrect. These are sodium chloride concentrations, not dextrose concentrations.
- E. Incorrect. These are not the concentrations listed in this table.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The page lists dextrose 5% and 10%.
- It separately lists saline–dextrose combinations.
- Always distinguish the concentration of dextrose from the concentration of sodium chloride.

topics.name: Approach to a child with anaemia

cases.title: Pallor in a school-aged child
cases.vignette: An 8-year-old child is brought because of progressive pallor and reduced exercise tolerance. A full blood count shows a haemoglobin concentration below the expected range for age. Red-cell indices and the reticulocyte count are reviewed before further tests are selected.

questions.stem: According to the course clinical guidance, which haemoglobin value defines anaemia in a child aged 1-12 years?
questions.correctAnswerText: Haemoglobin below 11 g/dL
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe anaemia in children aged 1-12 years as haemoglobin below 11 g/dL.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. clinical guidance gives this threshold for neonates, not school-aged children.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the stated paediatric threshold.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the threshold provided for this age group.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance gives this threshold for infants aged 1-12 months.
- E. Correct. This is the age-related threshold stated in the course clinical guidance for children aged 1-12 years.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Interpret haemoglobin using the child's age.
- Common examples include Hb <14 g/dL in neonates, <10 g/dL at 1-12 months and <11 g/dL at 1-12 years.
- Do not apply one haemoglobin cut-off to every paediatric age group.

questions.stem: The child's mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is 66 fL. How should the red cells be classified using the course-clinical guidance cut-off?
questions.correctAnswerText: Microcytic
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance classifies red cells as microcytic when MCV is below 70 fL and macrocytic when it is above 100 fL.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Macrocytosis is associated with an MCV above 100 fL.
- B. Incorrect. Chromicity is assessed using haemoglobin content/concentration, not MCV alone.
- C. Incorrect. Reticulocytopenia describes a low reticulocyte count, not red-cell size.
- D. Correct. An MCV of 66 fL is below the course-clinical guidance threshold of 70 fL.
- E. Incorrect. The result is below the stated microcytic cut-off.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MCV <70 fL: microcytic.
- MCV >100 fL: macrocytic.
- MCV describes average red-cell size; MCH/MCHC relate to haemoglobin content/concentration.

questions.stem: The same child has an elevated reticulocyte count, increased indirect bilirubin and raised LDH. Which process is most strongly suggested?

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced haemoglobin synthesis without red-cell destruction

options.label: D
options.text: Increased red-cell destruction with a marrow response

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased red-cell destruction with a marrow response
questions.initialExplanation: Reticulocytosis with raised indirect bilirubin and LDH is the haemolysis pattern listed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Neurological dysfunction from B12 deficiency does not by itself establish haemolysis.
- B. Incorrect. Reduced haemoglobin synthesis alone does not produce this characteristic combination of haemolysis markers.
- C. Incorrect. A platelet-production problem does not explain the haemolysis markers.
- D. Correct. Reticulocytosis reflects marrow compensation, while indirect bilirubin and LDH rise with red-cell destruction.
- E. Incorrect. Neutrophil destruction does not explain raised indirect bilirubin and reticulocytosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Reticulocyte count is a practical marker of marrow response.
- Haemolysis: reticulocytes and LDH increase, indirect bilirubin increases and haptoglobin decreases.
- Interpret the reticulocyte count together with the blood film and clinical context.

questions.stem: Which site is the main location of haematopoiesis throughout postnatal life?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bone marrow
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include the bone marrow as the main site of haematopoiesis throughout postnatal life.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The yolk sac is an early embryonic site of haematopoiesis.
- B. Incorrect. The thymus supports T-cell maturation, not general blood-cell production.
- C. Incorrect. The liver is an important fetal haematopoietic site, not the main postnatal site.
- D. Incorrect. The spleen contributes during fetal development and may become a site of extramedullary haematopoiesis in disease.
- E. Correct. Bone marrow is the principal postnatal site of blood-cell production.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early embryonic haematopoiesis begins in the yolk sac.
- The fetal liver and spleen contribute during fetal life.
- Bone marrow is the main postnatal site.

cases.title: Macrocytosis with another possible underlying cause
cases.vignette: A child has macrocytosis on the full blood count.

questions.stem: Which of the following is specifically listed as another differential diagnosis of macrocytic anaemia?

options.label: B
options.text: Iron deficiency due to poor dietary intake

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic liver disease
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include chronic liver diseases among the differential diagnoses of macrocytic anaemia, in addition to megaloblastic anaemia and aplastic anaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Chronic liver disease is explicitly listed on page 12.
- B. Incorrect. Iron deficiency is typically microcytic and hypochromic.
- C. Incorrect. Sickle cell trait is usually asymptomatic and is not listed as a macrocytic cause.
- D. Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease is an inherited bleeding disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Acute blood loss is not listed in this macrocytic differential.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Standard guidance's macrocytic differential includes B12/folate deficiency, aplastic anaemia, chronic liver disease, bone-marrow infiltration such as MDS, hypothyroidism, Down syndrome and Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
- Macrocytosis should not automatically be equated with B12 deficiency.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Differential diagnosis of macrocytic anaemia, Page 12.
source.sheet: Haematology sheet – Differential diagnosis of macrocytic anaemia,

cases.title: A toddler with pallor and a restricted diet
cases.vignette: A 15-month-old child is brought with pallor, poor appetite and reduced activity. The child drinks large amounts of unmodified cow's milk and eats little iron-rich food. The family reports that the child sometimes eats soil from plant pots.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Iron deficiency anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Iron deficiency is the most common anaemia in childhood, peaks between 6 and 24 months, and is associated with low-iron diets and excessive cow's-milk intake.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia rather than an isolated nutritional microcytic picture.
- B. Correct. The age, restricted iron intake, excessive cow's milk, pallor and pica strongly support iron deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis typically causes haemolysis, jaundice and splenomegaly.
- D. Incorrect. B12 deficiency is associated with macrocytosis and may cause neurological manifestations.
- E. Incorrect. Sickle cell disease is a chronic haemolytic disorder with characteristic crises.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Iron deficiency is the commonest paediatric anaemia.
- Peak age: 6-24 months.
- Excessive cow's milk and poor complementary feeding are important dietary risks.
- Pica may be a clinical clue.

questions.stem: Which dietary factor in this history contributes to iron deficiency?
questions.correctAnswerText: Excessive unmodified cow's-milk intake
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance lists cow's-milk feeding and a diet deficient in iron as causes of reduced iron intake; it also identifies cow's milk as a food to avoid in excess in toddlers.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pulses and beans are listed as iron-containing foods.
- B. Incorrect. Dark-green vegetables are listed among useful dietary sources of iron.
- C. Incorrect. Fortified cereals are listed among useful dietary iron sources.
- D. Incorrect. Red meat is listed as a food high in iron.
- E. Correct. Excessive cow's milk can displace iron-rich foods and is listed as a dietary risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Excess cow's milk can replace iron-rich solid foods.
- Iron-rich foods include red meat, liver, pulses, fortified cereals and green vegetables.
- Tea can inhibit iron absorption because of tannins.

questions.stem: What is the term for the child's repeated eating of soil?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pica
questions.initialExplanation: Pica is the inappropriate eating of non-food materials such as soil, chalk or gravel and is specifically listed among the symptoms of iron deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Koilonychia describes spoon-shaped nails.
- B. Incorrect. Glossitis refers to inflammation or smoothness of the tongue.
- C. Incorrect. Ecchymosis is a larger area of bleeding into the skin.
- D. Correct. Eating soil is a classic example of pica.
- E. Incorrect. Dactylitis is painful swelling of the hands or feet, classically in sickle cell disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pica may accompany iron deficiency.
- Other features include pallor, fatigue, poor feeding and reduced concentration.
- Koilonychia, angular stomatitis and glossitis are possible physical signs.

questions.stem: Which iron-study pattern best supports iron deficiency anaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Low serum iron, low ferritin and high TIBC

options.label: B
options.text: Low serum iron, high ferritin and low TIBC

options.label: C
options.text: Normal serum iron, high ferritin and normal TIBC

options.label: D
options.text: High serum iron, low ferritin and high TIBC

options.label: E
options.text: High serum iron, high ferritin and low TIBC

questions.correctAnswerText: Low serum iron, low ferritin and high TIBC
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include low serum iron and ferritin with increased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) in iron deficiency anaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Depleted iron stores lower ferritin and serum iron, while TIBC rises.
- B. Incorrect. High ferritin and low TIBC do not fit standard guidance's iron-deficiency pattern.
- C. Incorrect. This does not show depleted iron stores.
- D. Incorrect. High serum iron is inconsistent with uncomplicated iron deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. This is the opposite of the typical iron-deficiency pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IDA: serum iron low, ferritin low, TIBC high.
- Ferritin reflects iron stores.
- Investigate the underlying cause when clinically indicated.

cases.title: Comparing iron bioavailability in milk
cases.vignette: An 8-month-old infant is receiving different milk feeds. The parents ask why the type of milk matters when considering the amount of iron the infant actually absorbs. The clinician reviews the numerical comparison in the course clinical guidance.

questions.stem: According to the numerical table on page 6, which statement about iron absorption is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Breast milk and cow's milk both have approximately 50% iron absorption.

options.label: B
options.text: Formula has approximately 50% absorption, while breast milk has approximately 10%.

options.label: C
options.text: Breast milk has approximately 50% absorption, while formula and cow's milk each have approximately 10%.

options.label: D
options.text: Cow's-milk iron is absorbed at approximately 50%, while formula and breast milk are absorbed at approximately 10%.

options.label: E
options.text: most three milk sources have the same iron-absorption proportion.

questions.correctAnswerText: Breast milk has approximately 50% absorption, while formula and cow's milk each have approximately 10%.
questions.initialExplanation: The page 6 table lists breast milk at about 1.5 mg/L with 50% absorption, infant formula at 5–9 mg/L with 10% absorption, and cow's milk at 0.5 mg/L with 10% absorption.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The numerical table gives breast milk 50% absorption but formula and cow's milk 10%.
- B. Incorrect. The table gives formula 10%, not 50%.
- C. Correct. This is the absorption pattern in the numerical table on page 6.
- D. Incorrect. Cow's-milk iron is listed with 10% absorption, not 50%.
- E. Incorrect. The table gives a higher absorbed proportion for breast milk than for formula or cow's milk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Iron absorption occurs mainly in the proximal small intestine, especially the duodenum.
- The page 6 table lists breast milk: 1.5 mg/L, 50% absorption; formula: 5–9 mg/L, 10%; cow's milk: 0.5 mg/L, 10%.
- Source inconsistency: page 7 prose says cow's milk has a higher iron content than breast milk, whereas the page 6 numerical table lists a lower concentration for cow's milk. This question tests the absorption percentages in the table and does not rely on the conflicting statement about iron concentration.

topics.name: Confirming and treating iron deficiency anaemia

cases.title: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia
cases.vignette: A 20-month-old child has pallor, tachycardia and a soft flow murmur. The full blood count shows low haemoglobin, low MCV, low MCH and low MCHC. The blood film shows microcytes with anisocytosis and poikilocytosis.

questions.stem: Which red-cell pattern is expected in this child?

options.label: E
options.text: Pancytopenia with a normal red-cell size

questions.correctAnswerText: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Iron deficiency classically produces microcytic hypochromic anaemia with reduced MCV, MCH and MCHC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The indices described are the typical pattern of iron deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. The child has anaemia with abnormal red-cell indices, not isolated reticulocytosis.
- C. Incorrect. Macrocytosis suggests a different group of disorders, including megaloblastic anaemia.
- D. Incorrect. The MCV is reduced, so the anaemia is not normocytic.
- E. Incorrect. The case describes an isolated microcytic pattern, not pancytopenia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IDA: low MCV, low MCH and low MCHC.
- A reactive thrombocytosis may also occur.
- Blood film may show microcytes, anisocytosis and poikilocytosis.

questions.stem: Which additional blood-film feature may be seen in iron deficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Predominant schistocytes as the defining finding

options.label: D
options.text: Blast cells replacing normal blood cells

questions.correctAnswerText: Anisocytosis and poikilocytosis
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance describes microcytes, anisocytosis and poikilocytosis in the blood film of a child with iron deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Schistocytes suggest fragmentation haemolysis, not uncomplicated iron deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Sickle-shaped cells suggest sickle cell disease.
- C. Correct. Variation in red-cell size and shape is described.
- D. Incorrect. Blast cells raise concern for acute leukaemia.
- E. Incorrect. Spherocytes are important in hereditary spherocytosis and may also occur in immune haemolysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Examine the blood film alongside the indices and iron studies.
- Sickle cells and spherocytes point toward haemolytic disorders.
- Blasts require urgent assessment for marrow malignancy.

questions.stem: Which initial treatment is recommended for an otherwise stable child with nutritional iron deficiency?

options.label: C
options.text: Oral iron therapy with dietary advice

questions.correctAnswerText: Oral iron therapy with dietary advice
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance dietary advice and oral iron as first-line treatment. Transfusion is reserved for very severe anaemia with instability.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. B12 replacement is for vitamin B12 deficiency, not iron deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Transfusion is not routine in a stable child with IDA.
- C. Correct. Oral iron and correction of dietary factors are the usual treatment described.
- D. Incorrect. Splenectomy has no role in routine nutritional iron deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. Platelet transfusion does not correct iron deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat with oral iron and dietary modification.
- standard guidance gives an elemental iron dose range of 3-6 mg/kg/day; verify the prescribed dose against the original clinical guidance and local protocol.
- Continue treatment long enough to replenish iron stores.

questions.stem: After starting oral iron, which early laboratory response is expected at approximately 48-72 hours?

options.label: E
options.text: A fall in reticulocyte count to zero

questions.correctAnswerText: Reticulocytosis
questions.initialExplanation: The response table places reticulocytosis at approximately 48-72 hours after iron therapy begins.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Reticulocytosis is an early sign that the marrow is responding to iron replacement.
- B. Incorrect. Haemoglobin rises over subsequent days to weeks rather than normalizing immediately.
- C. Incorrect. Thrombocytopenia is not the expected response to iron replacement.
- D. Incorrect. Blast cells are not an expected consequence of iron therapy.
- E. Incorrect. A marrow response should increase reticulocytes, not abolish them.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance marrow response and reticulocytosis within the first few days.
- Haemoglobin rises over the following weeks.
- Iron stores take longer to replenish than symptoms or haemoglobin begin to improve.

cases.title: Completing treatment for iron deficiency
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child with nutritional iron deficiency starts oral iron and dietary modification. The child's appetite and activity improve, and the haemoglobin begins to rise. The parents ask whether they can stop treatment as soon as the child looks well.

questions.stem: Which treatment duration is recommended in the course clinical guidance to replenish iron stores?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue oral iron for approximately 3–6 months.

options.label: B
options.text: Stop as soon as appetite improves.

options.label: C
options.text: Give one dose after reticulocytosis appears.

options.label: D
options.text: Continue until the first rise in haemoglobin.

options.label: E
options.text: Replace oral iron routinely with a single packed red-cell transfusion.

questions.correctAnswerText: Continue oral iron for approximately 3–6 months.
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives a treatment duration of 3–6 months and states that iron should continue for at least 3 months to replenish iron stores.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The stated duration is 3–6 months, with at least 3 months recommended to replenish stores.
- B. Incorrect. Clinical improvement does not prove that iron stores have been replenished.
- C. Incorrect. Reticulocytosis is an early marrow response, not a signal that treatment is complete.
- D. Incorrect. Haemoglobin begins to improve before iron stores are fully replenished.
- E. Incorrect. Packed red-cell transfusion is reserved for very severe anaemia with instability, not routine completion of iron therapy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Oral iron dose: 3–6 mg/kg/day.
- Expected early response includes reticulocytosis at about 48–72 hours.
- Continue treatment long enough to replenish stores; It is recognized 3–6 months and at least 3 months.

source.sheet: Haematology sheet – Iron deficiency treatment and response,

cases.title: Expected haemoglobin response to oral iron
cases.vignette: A child with iron deficiency anaemia starts oral iron with good adherence. At follow-up, the family asks what haemoglobin response is expected over the following weeks if treatment is effective.

questions.stem: What approximate rate of haemoglobin rise is stated in the course clinical guidance with good compliance?

options.label: B
options.text: No haemoglobin increase until iron stores are fully replenished

questions.correctAnswerText: About 1 g/dL per week
questions.initialExplanation: The iron-response table states that, with good compliance, haemoglobin rises by about 1 g/dL per week.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. standard guidance does not describe a rise of several grams per day.
- B. Incorrect. Haemoglobin begins to increase before iron stores are fully replenished.
- C. Incorrect. This is far slower than the response stated.
- D. Incorrect. Haemoglobin does not normalize immediately after the first dose.
- E. Correct. clinical guidance gives approximately 1 g/dL per week with good compliance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Reticulocytosis: approximately 48–72 hours.
- Haemoglobin rises over the following days to weeks.
- With good compliance, standard guidance gives an approximate Hb rise of 1 g/dL per week.
- Iron-store replenishment takes longer than the initial clinical response.
