topics.name: Persistent iron deficiency and the microcytic differential

cases.title: Failure to improve as expected
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child has microcytic anaemia and is prescribed oral iron. At follow-up, the haemoglobin has not improved as expected. The family reports good adherence, and

questions.stem: Which underlying condition listed in the course clinical guidance can cause iron malabsorption?
questions.correctAnswerText: Coeliac disease
questions.initialExplanation: Coeliac disease is listed as a cause of reduced iron absorption and may be investigated with tissue-transglutaminase antibodies and endoscopy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sickle cell trait is usually asymptomatic and does not explain iron malabsorption.
- B. Incorrect. ITP is an immune platelet disorder.
- C. Correct. Coeliac disease can impair proximal small-intestinal absorption, including iron absorption.
- D. Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease can cause bleeding and iron loss, but it is not a malabsorption disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolysis rather than intestinal iron malabsorption.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider malabsorption when IDA does not respond despite adequate therapy.
- Coeliac disease and cow's-milk protein intolerance are listed.
- Investigations mentioned include TTG testing and endoscopy.

questions.stem: Which condition in the course clinical guidance is a potential source of chronic gastrointestinal blood loss in a child?
questions.correctAnswerText: Meckel's diverticulum
questions.initialExplanation: Meckel's diverticulum is listed among the gastrointestinal causes of blood loss that may contribute to iron deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fanconi anaemia is an inherited bone-marrow-failure syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-triggered haemolysis.
- C. Correct. Meckel's diverticulum is specifically listed as a possible source of gastrointestinal blood loss.
- D. Incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis causes red-cell destruction.
- E. Incorrect. Diamond-Blackfan anaemia causes pure red-cell aplasia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Persistent IDA warrants assessment of adherence, intake, absorption and blood loss.
- Clinical guidance Meckel's diverticulum among possible sources of blood loss.
- Heavy menstrual bleeding and hookworm are also listed in relevant age groups/exposures.

questions.stem: In which situation does standard guidance indicate that parenteral iron may be considered?

options.label: A
options.text: An asymptomatic child with iron-replete stores

options.label: B
options.text: Malabsorption or intolerance to oral iron

options.label: C
options.text: As a substitute for treating an ongoing bleeding source

options.label: D
options.text: children in routine care with newly diagnosed mild IDA

options.label: E
options.text: A child with normal iron studies

questions.correctAnswerText: Malabsorption or intolerance to oral iron
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance malabsorption, intolerance to oral iron and non-compliance as indications to consider parenteral iron.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron should not be given without an indication.
- B. Correct. These are the indications stated.
- C. Incorrect. Iron replacement does not remove the need to identify and manage ongoing blood loss.
- D. Incorrect. Oral iron is the standard initial treatment for most stable children.
- E. Incorrect. Normal iron studies do not establish iron deficiency requiring replacement.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Oral iron is first-line for most children.
- Parenteral iron is considered when oral treatment cannot be used effectively.
- Clinical guidance that parenteral iron is not inherently faster or more effective.

questions.stem: A child with IDA is severely symptomatic, haemodynamically unstable and has very severe anaemia. Which intervention may be required?
questions.correctAnswerText: Packed red-cell transfusion
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance reserves packed red-cell transfusion for very severe iron deficiency anaemia when the patient is unstable.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not a treatment for nutritional IDA.
- B. Correct. Severe symptomatic anaemia with instability may require carefully managed red-cell transfusion.
- C. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected bleeding disorders, not iron deficiency.
- D. Incorrect. Platelets do not correct low haemoglobin from iron deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion is not routine IDA treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat the underlying iron deficiency.
- Transfusion is not routine in stable IDA.
- Reserve transfusion for very severe disease with clinical instability, with appropriate monitoring.

cases.title: A child with persistent microcytosis
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child is found to have mild microcytic hypochromic anaemia during a routine assessment. The child is otherwise well. Iron studies do not show depleted stores, and the red-cell count is relatively preserved.

questions.stem: Which Mentzer index result favours thalassaemia rather than iron deficiency?

options.label: E
options.text: It cannot be calculated from MCV and red-cell count

questions.correctAnswerText: Less than 13
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that a Mentzer index below 13 favours thalassaemia, while a value above 13 favours iron deficiency anaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A Mentzer index below 13 is the course-clinical guidance clue for thalassaemia.
- B. Incorrect. standard guidance does not use this as a universal cut-off.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the stated threshold.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance associates a value above 13 with iron deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. The index is calculated from MCV divided by the red-cell count.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mentzer index = MCV ÷ RBC count.
- <13 favours thalassaemia.
- >13 favours iron deficiency; use iron studies and haemoglobin analysis as appropriate.

questions.stem: Which iron-study pattern is more consistent with thalassaemia than uncomplicated iron deficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Low ferritin as the defining abnormality

options.label: B
options.text: Low serum iron with absent marrow iron stores

options.label: C
options.text: Normal or increased serum iron with normal or increased ferritin

options.label: E
options.text: Low serum iron with low ferritin and high TIBC

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal or increased serum iron with normal or increased ferritin
questions.initialExplanation: The comparison table distinguishes thalassaemia from IDA by showing normal or increased serum iron and ferritin in thalassaemia, rather than the depleted iron pattern of IDA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Low ferritin indicates depleted iron stores rather than uncomplicated thalassaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Absent marrow iron stores support iron deficiency.
- C. Correct. This is the pattern shown for thalassaemia in the course-clinical guidance comparison.
- D. Incorrect. Low ferritin and high TIBC are characteristic of IDA.
- E. Incorrect. This is typical of iron deficiency anaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Do not prescribe iron solely because an anaemia is microcytic.
- Review ferritin, serum iron and TIBC.
- Thalassaemia and IDA can coexist, so interpret the whole clinical picture.

questions.stem: A child with microcytosis has basophilic stippling on the blood film and a history of exposure to old paint. Which additional test is most appropriate?
questions.correctAnswerText: Blood lead level
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic lead poisoning is included in the microcytic anaemia differential, and clinical guidance identifies basophilic stippling with an increased blood lead level.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A direct Coombs test investigates immune-mediated red-cell destruction.
- B. Correct. A blood lead level directly evaluates the suspected exposure-related cause.
- C. Incorrect. B12 deficiency usually causes macrocytosis rather than the described microcytic pattern.
- D. Incorrect. Cold agglutinin testing is relevant to cold-antibody haemolysis.
- E. Incorrect. Platelet-function analysis evaluates platelet dysfunction, not lead-related microcytosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chronic lead poisoning is a differential diagnosis of microcytic anaemia.
- Basophilic stippling is an important blood-film clue.
- A targeted exposure history is essential.

questions.stem: Which index is used to describe variation in red-cell size?
questions.correctAnswerText: Red-cell distribution width (RDW)
questions.initialExplanation: RDW measures variation in red-cell size, described as anisocytosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. PT assesses the extrinsic/common coagulation pathway.
- B. Incorrect. Reticulocyte count reflects marrow response rather than size variation among red cells.
- C. Incorrect. MPV describes average platelet size.
- D. Correct. RDW quantifies variation in red-cell size.
- E. Incorrect. aPTT assesses the intrinsic/common coagulation pathway.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- RDW reflects anisocytosis.
- MCV reflects average red-cell size.
- Use CBC indices with morphology and iron studies rather than in isolation.

cases.title: Microcytosis in chronic kidney disease
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child with chronic kidney disease is found to have pallor and reduced exercise tolerance. The full blood count shows microcytic anaemia. Iron studies show low serum iron, normal-to-high ferritin and low total iron-binding capacity (TIBC).

questions.stem: Which interpretation best fits the iron-study pattern described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Anaemia of chronic disease
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance's comparison table describes anaemia of chronic disease as low serum iron with normal or increased ferritin and low TIBC. Chronic kidney disease is also listed among causes of anaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron deficiency is associated with low serum iron, low ferritin and high TIBC.
- B. Incorrect. standard guidance's thalassaemia pattern has normal or increased serum iron and ferritin.
- C. Incorrect. Sideroblastic anaemia is associated with normal-to-high serum iron and ferritin and normal TIBC in the table.
- D. Incorrect. Lead poisoning is listed as a microcytic differential and is associated with basophilic stippling and a high blood lead level; it does not match the iron-study pattern given.
- E. Correct. Low serum iron, preserved or increased ferritin and low TIBC match anaemia of chronic disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IDA: low serum iron, low ferritin, high TIBC.
- Anaemia of chronic disease: low serum iron, normal/high ferritin, low TIBC.
- Thalassaemia and sideroblastic anaemia have different patterns 's comparison table.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Causes of anaemia and microcytic differential, Pages 5 and 10.
source.sheet: Haematology sheet – Causes of anaemia and microcytic differential,

cases.title: A microcytic pattern with increased iron stores
cases.vignette: A child is investigated for microcytic hypochromic anaemia. Serum iron and ferritin are normal-to-high, TIBC is normal, and marrow iron stores are present. The clinician compares the results with the course-clinical guidance table of microcytic anaemia.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best matches this laboratory pattern?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sideroblastic anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance's table describes sideroblastic anaemia as having high or normal serum iron, high or normal ferritin, normal TIBC and present marrow iron stores.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. IDA has low serum iron, low ferritin, high TIBC and absent marrow iron stores.
- B. Incorrect. Anaemia of chronic disease has low serum iron and low TIBC, with normal or high ferritin.
- C. Incorrect. The table gives thalassaemia a normal-to-high iron/ferritin pattern but a normal or low TIBC and increased iron in nucleated red cells; the complete pattern in this case is assigned to sideroblastic anaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Lead poisoning is listed separately and is associated with basophilic stippling and increased blood lead.
- E. Correct. This matches the sideroblastic column of standard guidance's comparison table.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Do not assume every microcytic anaemia is iron deficiency.
- Sideroblastic pattern: serum iron high/normal, ferritin high/normal, TIBC normal and marrow iron present.
- The table also includes IDA, anaemia of chronic disease and beta-thalassaemia.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Differential diagnosis of microcytic hypochromic anaemia, Page 10.
source.sheet: Haematology sheet – Differential diagnosis of microcytic hypochromic anaemia,

cases.title: Macrocytosis in a child with poor nutrition
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child presents with fatigue and pallor. The full blood count shows macrocytic anaemia. The blood film shows large red cells and hypersegmented neutrophils. Dietary history reveals a very restricted diet.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains the blood picture?
questions.correctAnswerText: Megaloblastic anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Megaloblastic anaemia is associated with folate or vitamin B12 deficiency and produces macrocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sickle cell disease causes chronic haemolytic anaemia with sickled cells.
- B. Incorrect. Iron deficiency usually causes microcytic hypochromic anaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Acute blood loss does not produce the characteristic megaloblastic morphology.
- D. Incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolysis and spherocytes.
- E. Correct. Macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils is the classic megaloblastic blood-film pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Megaloblastic anaemia results from folate or B12 deficiency.
- Blood film: macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.
- Evaluate folate and B12 rather than assuming the cause from MCV alone.

questions.stem: Which medication listed may cause folate deficiency through antifolate activity?
questions.correctAnswerText: Methotrexate
questions.initialExplanation: Methotrexate is included among antifolate drugs that can cause folate deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected bleeding disorders.
- B. Incorrect. Ferrous sulfate is an iron preparation.
- C. Incorrect. Hydroxycobalamin is a form of vitamin B12 replacement.
- D. Incorrect. Penicillin V is an antibiotic and is not listed as an antifolate.
- E. Correct. Methotrexate interferes with folate metabolism and is listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Folate deficiency may result from poor intake, malabsorption or increased utilization.
- Clinical guidance methotrexate, phenytoin and trimethoprim among antifolate drugs.
- Review medication history in macrocytic anaemia.

questions.stem: Which additional clinical feature is more suggestive of vitamin B12 deficiency than isolated folate deficiency?

options.label: B
options.text: A prolonged PT with a normal platelet count

options.label: D
options.text: Petechiae with an isolated low platelet count

options.label: E
options.text: Subacute combined degeneration with posterior-column and pyramidal-tract involvement

questions.correctAnswerText: Subacute combined degeneration with posterior-column and pyramidal-tract involvement
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is neurological manifestations in B12 deficiency, including peripheral neuropathy, posterior-column degeneration and pyramidal-tract involvement. These are not expected in isolated folate deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Koilonychia and microcytosis support iron deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. A prolonged PT indicates a coagulation-pathway abnormality, not B12-related neurological disease.
- C. Incorrect. Spoon-shaped nails are associated with iron deficiency.
- D. Incorrect. This pattern suggests a platelet disorder such as ITP.
- E. Correct. Subacute combined degeneration is a characteristic neurological complication of B12 deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- B12 is required for normal myelin-related function.
- Neurological signs strongly support B12 deficiency.
- Isolated folate deficiency does not produce the characteristic B12 neurological syndrome.

questions.stem: A child with macrocytic anaemia has a low B12 level. Why should folate be assessed and B12 deficiency excluded before giving folate alone?

options.label: A
options.text: Folate alone may improve the blood picture while B12-related neurological injury continues

options.label: D
options.text: Folate prevents B12 absorption in each patient

questions.correctAnswerText: Folate alone may improve the blood picture while B12-related neurological injury continues
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance warns that folate treatment alone can worsen or fail to prevent the neurological consequences of unrecognized B12 deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Correcting folate without treating B12 deficiency can leave the neurological process untreated.
- B. Incorrect. Intravascular haemolysis is not the expected effect of folate replacement.
- C. Incorrect. Folate does not cause factor VIII or IX deficiency.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the mechanism described.
- E. Incorrect. Folate is not a platelet-destroying treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Check B12 when evaluating megaloblastic anaemia.
- Treat the specific deficiency; do not use folate alone when B12 deficiency is present.
- B12 deficiency may cause irreversible neurological complications if missed.

cases.title: Comparing body stores of folate and vitamin B12
cases.vignette: An adolescent with a restricted diet is being assessed for megaloblastic anaemia. The clinician compares the body's reserve of folate with that of vitamin B12, as described in the course clinical guidance.

questions.stem: Which statement about body stores is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Folate stores usually last 2–3 years, while B12 stores last 2–4 months.

options.label: B
options.text: Both folate and B12 stores normally last a few days.

options.label: C
options.text: Folate and B12 are stored for identical periods.

options.label: D
options.text: Folate stores last about 2–4 months, whereas B12 stores last about 2–3 years.

options.label: E
options.text: B12 is not stored in the body.

questions.correctAnswerText: Folate stores last about 2–4 months, whereas B12 stores last about 2–3 years.
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include body stores of folate as approximately 2–4 months and body stores of vitamin B12 as approximately 2–3 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The two time periods are reversed.
- B. Incorrect. Clinical guidance substantially longer reserves for both vitamins.
- C. Incorrect. Folate and B12 stores differ markedly.
- D. Correct. This is the comparison given on page 11.
- E. Incorrect. It is recognized that B12 body stores last approximately 2–3 years.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Folate: body stores about 2–4 months.
- Vitamin B12: body stores about 2–3 years.
- Folate is absorbed in the small intestine; the B12–intrinsic factor complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Folate and cyanocobalamin, Page 11.

cases.title: Macrocytosis with neurological symptoms
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child from a strictly vegan household presents with fatigue, tingling in the feet and unsteady walking. The blood count shows macrocytosis. There is no history of animal-source food intake.

questions.stem: Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Vitamin B12 deficiency
questions.initialExplanation: Vitamin B12 is found in animal-source foods, and a vegan diet is listed as a cause of low intake. Neurological manifestations support B12 deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vitamin C deficiency may cause vascular fragility and gum problems, not this megaloblastic-neurological syndrome.
- B. Correct. Restricted animal-food intake with macrocytosis and neurological symptoms strongly supports B12 deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Vitamin K deficiency causes a coagulation abnormality.
- D. Incorrect. Iron deficiency generally causes microcytosis and does not explain this neurological pattern.
- E. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-triggered haemolysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- B12 is obtained from animal-source foods.
- Body stores last longer than folate stores.
- Neurological findings are a key discriminator from isolated folate deficiency.

questions.stem: Where is the vitamin B12-intrinsic factor complex normally absorbed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Terminal ileum
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include intrinsic factor binding to B12 in the stomach, followed by absorption of the complex in the terminal ileum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The jejunum is not the site specified for the intrinsic factor-B12 complex.
- B. Incorrect. The duodenum is the principal site of iron absorption.
- C. Incorrect. Intrinsic factor is produced in the stomach and binds B12 there, but absorption occurs distally.
- D. Correct. The terminal ileum is the stated site of B12 absorption.
- E. Incorrect. The colon is not the normal absorption site for this complex.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Intrinsic factor is required for normal B12 absorption.
- The complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
- Ileal disease or resection can cause deficiency.

questions.stem: Which neurological pathway involvement is described in B12 deficiency?
questions.correctAnswerText: Posterior columns and pyramidal tracts
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance identifies posterior-column degeneration and pyramidal-tract lesions as features of subacute combined degeneration in B12 deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Cerebellar dysfunction may contribute to ataxia, but it is not the defining tract pattern given.
- B. Correct. These are the tracts specifically described.
- C. Incorrect. standard guidance does not describe isolated neuromuscular-junction involvement.
- D. Incorrect. Neuromuscular-junction disease does not explain the megaloblastic picture.
- E. Incorrect. Isolated optic-chiasm disease is not the typical B12 neurological pattern described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- B12 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy and sensory ataxia.
- Posterior-column and pyramidal-tract involvement is described as subacute combined degeneration.
- Neurological symptoms may be more diagnostically important than the degree of anaemia.

questions.stem: A child has permanent B12 malabsorption due to an underlying absorption disorder. Which treatment principle is appropriate?

options.label: B
options.text: Give folate alone and stop once the MCV falls

options.label: C
options.text: No replacement is required after neurological symptoms develop

options.label: D
options.text: Replace vitamin B12 and continue long-term treatment when the cause persists

questions.correctAnswerText: Replace vitamin B12 and continue long-term treatment when the cause persists
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance B12 replacement and treatment of the underlying cause; long-term replacement is needed when the underlying deficiency mechanism persists.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron does not replace vitamin B12.
- B. Incorrect. Folate alone does not treat B12 deficiency and may mask the haematological abnormality while neurological injury continues.
- C. Incorrect. B12 deficiency should still be treated; delayed treatment may limit neurological recovery.
- D. Correct. Replacement corrects the deficiency, and persistent malabsorption may require ongoing therapy.
- E. Incorrect. Platelet transfusions do not correct B12 deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat B12 deficiency and the underlying cause.
- Terminal-ileal disease/resection and intrinsic-factor problems are important causes.
- Do not substitute folate for B12 when B12 deficiency is present.

cases.title: Dark urine after fava beans
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old boy develops pallor, jaundice, abdominal discomfort and dark urine two days after eating fava beans. His mother recalls a similar episode after an infection. The blood count shows acute anaemia with biochemical evidence of haemolysis.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains the episodic haemolysis?
questions.correctAnswerText: G6PD deficiency
questions.initialExplanation: G6PD deficiency is an X-linked red-cell enzyme disorder in which oxidant exposure, including fava beans and infection, can precipitate acute haemolysis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding, not oxidant haemolysis.
- B. Correct. The trigger, delayed onset, dark urine, jaundice and acute haemolysis strongly suggest G6PD deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia and reticulocytopenia.
- D. Incorrect. ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia and bleeding manifestations.
- E. Incorrect. Iron deficiency causes chronic impaired haemoglobin synthesis rather than an acute oxidant-triggered haemolytic episode.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- G6PD deficiency is an X-linked red-cell enzyme disorder.
- Fava beans, infections, naphthalene and selected drugs are listed triggers.
- Acute haemolysis may begin 24-72 hours after oxidant exposure.

questions.stem: What is the key biochemical consequence of reduced G6PD activity in red cells?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced NADPH production and impaired protection against oxidative stress

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced NADPH production and impaired protection against oxidative stress
questions.initialExplanation: G6PD is part of the pentose phosphate pathway. Reduced NADPH limits regeneration of reduced glutathione, leaving red cells vulnerable to oxidative injury.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Reduced NADPH and impaired reduced-glutathione protection lead to haemoglobin oxidation and red-cell damage.
- B. Incorrect. Factor VIII is a coagulation protein and is not synthesized through the G6PD pathway.
- C. Incorrect. Intrinsic factor is involved in B12 absorption and is unrelated to G6PD.
- D. Incorrect. Vitamin K-dependent coagulation is unrelated to the red-cell oxidative pathway.
- E. Incorrect. Platelet adhesion is a haemostatic process, not the G6PD pathway.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- G6PD generates NADPH through the pentose phosphate pathway.
- NADPH supports reduced glutathione.
- Oxidative stress causes haemoglobin denaturation and red-cell destruction.

questions.stem: Which blood-film findings are characteristic of oxidant injury in G6PD deficiency?
questions.correctAnswerText: Heinz bodies and bite cells
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include Heinz bodies, bite cells and blister cells in G6PD-related oxidative haemolysis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sickle and target cells are associated with haemoglobin disorders.
- B. Incorrect. Blasts and Auer rods suggest acute myeloid leukaemia.
- C. Correct. Heinz bodies represent denatured haemoglobin, and splenic removal produces bite cells.
- D. Incorrect. Spherocytes are more characteristic of hereditary spherocytosis or immune haemolysis.
- E. Incorrect. These are megaloblastic blood-film findings.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Heinz bodies: precipitated denatured haemoglobin.
- Bite/blister cells: red-cell changes after splenic removal of damaged portions.
- Interpret the film with the history of oxidant exposure and haemolysis.

questions.stem: Which inheritance pattern is associated with G6PD deficiency?
questions.correctAnswerText: X-linked recessive
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance identifies G6PD deficiency as an X-linked recessive disorder.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mitochondrial inheritance is not the pattern for G6PD deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Several other disorders, including sickle cell disease and thalassaemia, are autosomal recessive.
- C. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency is not Y-linked.
- D. Correct. This is the inheritance pattern stated.
- E. Incorrect. Autosomal dominant inheritance is described for many cases of hereditary spherocytosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- G6PD deficiency is X-linked recessive.
- Boys are commonly clinically affected.
- Female heterozygotes may have variable expression due to X-inactivation.

cases.title: A recent haemolytic episode
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old boy is admitted with jaundice and dark urine after taking a potentially oxidant medication. Haemolysis is confirmed. A quantitative G6PD assay obtained during the acute episode is reported as normal, but clinical suspicion remains high.

questions.stem: Why can a G6PD enzyme assay be falsely reassuring during or soon after an acute haemolytic episode?

options.label: A
options.text: Older, more enzyme-deficient red cells may have been destroyed, leaving younger reticulocytes with higher enzyme activity

options.label: B
options.text: The spleen produces new normal G6PD genes

options.label: C
options.text: Platelets release G6PD and falsely increase the result

options.label: D
options.text: Bilirubin directly converts G6PD into a normal enzyme

options.label: E
options.text: Haemolysis typically increases the number of mature deficient red cells

questions.correctAnswerText: Older, more enzyme-deficient red cells may have been destroyed, leaving younger reticulocytes with higher enzyme activity
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance warns that the enzyme assay may be falsely negative during an acute attack because reticulocytes have relatively higher G6PD activity. It recommends repeating the test after recovery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Preferential destruction of older deficient cells leaves a younger circulating population that can make measured activity appear normal.
- B. Incorrect. The spleen does not replace the patient's inherited genetic defect.
- C. Incorrect. Platelet G6PD release is not the explanation given.
- D. Incorrect. Bilirubin does not normalize the enzyme assay.
- E. Incorrect. Acute haemolysis removes vulnerable red cells rather than increasing them.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- A normal assay during an acute attack does not always exclude G6PD deficiency.
- Reticulocytes have higher G6PD activity than older red cells.
- clinical guidance advises repeating the assay about 2-3 months after the acute episode.

questions.stem: What is the first management step when oxidant-induced haemolysis is suspected?

options.label: B
options.text: Start lifelong iron without checking iron status

questions.correctAnswerText: Stop the suspected oxidant trigger
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes stopping oxidant agents. Supportive care and packed red-cell transfusion are considered if anaemia is severe.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not acute management of G6PD-related haemolysis.
- B. Incorrect. Iron is not a treatment for acute haemolysis unless deficiency is separately demonstrated.
- C. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected bleeding disorders.
- D. Incorrect. Platelet transfusion does not treat red-cell haemolysis.
- E. Correct. Removing the oxidant trigger is the immediate key step.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stop the oxidant agent.
- Assess severity and provide supportive care.
- Packed red-cell transfusion may be needed in severe anaemia.

questions.stem: A newborn develops severe indirect hyperbilirubinaemia in the first day of life. G6PD deficiency is suspected. Which complication is the major concern in severe untreated neonatal jaundice?
questions.correctAnswerText: Kernicterus
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance neonatal jaundice in G6PD deficiency and warns that severe indirect hyperbilirubinaemia may lead to kernicterus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Renal papillary necrosis may occur in sickle cell disease.
- B. Correct. Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia can cause bilirubin encephalopathy/kernicterus.
- C. Incorrect. Tumour lysis syndrome is a complication of rapid tumour-cell breakdown, often around leukaemia treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Splenic sequestration is a sickle-cell crisis.
- E. Incorrect. Haemarthrosis is associated with coagulation-factor deficiency such as haemophilia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- G6PD deficiency may present with neonatal jaundice.
- Severe indirect hyperbilirubinaemia can cause kernicterus.
- Early recognition and appropriate bilirubin management are essential.

questions.stem: Which advice is most important for the family after confirming G6PD deficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Give aspirin routinely during febrile illnesses

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid known oxidant foods, chemicals and medications and seek care for jaundice, pallor or dark urine

options.label: E
options.text: Encourage fava-bean intake to build red-cell resistance

questions.correctAnswerText: Avoid known oxidant foods, chemicals and medications and seek care for jaundice, pallor or dark urine
questions.initialExplanation: The prevention section stresses avoidance of oxidant triggers and educating parents about warning signs such as jaundice, pallor and dark urine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Aspirin is listed among potential oxidant drugs at high doses and should not be used routinely in this context.
- B. Correct. Trigger avoidance and recognition of early haemolysis symptoms are central preventive measures.
- C. Incorrect. Routine dietary iron restriction is not recommended for G6PD deficiency.
- D. Incorrect. standard guidance does not recommend avoiding all vaccinations.
- E. Incorrect. Fava beans are a recognized trigger and should be avoided.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Provide a written list of drugs and chemicals to avoid.
- Fava beans and naphthalene are important exposures.
- Parents should recognize pallor, jaundice and dark urine promptly.

cases.title: Jaundice and splenomegaly in a child
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child is assessed for intermittent jaundice, pallor and a palpable spleen. The father had a splenectomy in childhood for a similar disorder. The full blood count shows anaemia with an increased MCHC and reticulocytosis.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hereditary spherocytosis
questions.initialExplanation: Hereditary spherocytosis causes chronic haemolysis, jaundice and splenomegaly, often with a family history and increased MCHC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The family history, chronic haemolytic features, splenomegaly and raised MCHC strongly support hereditary spherocytosis.
- B. Incorrect. IDA is typically microcytic and hypochromic and does not cause this inherited haemolytic pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding rather than chronic haemolysis.
- D. Incorrect. ALL may cause pallor and organomegaly, but the raised MCHC and inherited haemolytic history point elsewhere.
- E. Incorrect. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia with a low reticulocyte count.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hereditary spherocytosis is commonly autosomal dominant, although cases without a family history occur.
- Chronic haemolysis causes anaemia, jaundice and splenomegaly.
- Gallstones and aplastic crisis are recognized complications.

questions.stem: Which combination of test results best supports hereditary spherocytosis over autoimmune haemolytic anaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Low MCHC with a positive direct Coombs test

options.label: B
options.text: Low platelet count with prolonged bleeding time

options.label: E
options.text: Raised MCHC with a negative direct Coombs test

questions.correctAnswerText: Raised MCHC with a negative direct Coombs test
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include increased MCHC, reticulocytosis, spherocytes and a negative Coombs test in hereditary spherocytosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A positive direct Coombs test supports immune-mediated haemolysis.
- B. Incorrect. Thrombocytopenia with prolonged bleeding time suggests a platelet disorder.
- C. Incorrect. Pancytopenia and reticulocytopenia suggest marrow failure.
- D. Incorrect. Prolonged PT and aPTT suggest a coagulation problem.
- E. Correct. Raised MCHC and a negative direct Coombs test support a non-immune membrane disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HS: spherocytes, reticulocytosis, raised MCHC and negative Coombs test.
- Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia often has a positive direct antiglobulin test.
- Osmotic fragility and EMA binding are diagnostic investigations described.

questions.stem: Which investigation is described as demonstrating increased red-cell fragility in hereditary spherocytosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Osmotic fragility test
questions.initialExplanation: In hereditary spherocytosis, red cells lyse at higher saline concentrations than normal because they are more osmotically fragile.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ristocetin cofactor activity evaluates von Willebrand factor function.
- B. Incorrect. Cold agglutination testing evaluates cold-antibody haemolysis.
- C. Incorrect. Haemoglobin electrophoresis evaluates haemoglobin variants and thalassaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Chromosome-breakage testing is used in Fanconi anaemia.
- E. Correct. The osmotic fragility test demonstrates increased susceptibility to lysis in hypotonic saline.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Osmotic fragility is described as a diagnostic test for HS.
- EMA binding by flow cytometry is another investigation.
- Blood film shows spherocytes.

questions.stem: A child with severe hereditary spherocytosis is being considered for splenectomy. Which preventive plan is appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Use platelet transfusions as the infection-prevention measure

options.label: B
options.text: Perform it in infancy in each affected child without vaccination

options.label: C
options.text: Give lifelong iron chelation to children in routine care after splenectomy

options.label: E
options.text: Perform it after age 6 when indicated, vaccinate against encapsulated organisms beforehand and give penicillin afterwards

questions.correctAnswerText: Perform it after age 6 when indicated, vaccinate against encapsulated organisms beforehand and give penicillin afterwards
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes delaying splenectomy until after age 6 when possible, giving Hib, meningococcal and pneumococcal vaccines before surgery, and oral penicillin afterwards.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Platelet transfusions do not prevent postsplenectomy infection.
- B. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not routine for every child and early surgery increases infection risk.
- C. Incorrect. Iron chelation is used for iron overload, not as routine post-splenectomy prophylaxis.
- D. Incorrect. Pneumococcal vaccination is specifically recommended before splenectomy.
- E. Correct. This matches the preventive strategy described in the course clinical guidance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Splenectomy is reserved for selected children with severe disease or troublesome symptoms.
- Vaccinate against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Hib before surgery.
- Penicillin prophylaxis is recommended after splenectomy.

cases.title: Aplastic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child has hereditary spherocytosis with a history of intermittent jaundice and splenomegaly. The child develops fever and marked pallor over a short period. The haemoglobin has fallen substantially, and the reticulocyte count is unexpectedly low rather than increased.

questions.stem: Which event best explains this sudden deterioration?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased splenic destruction with an appropriate reticulocyte response

options.label: B
options.text: Transient aplastic crisis associated with parvovirus B19

options.label: C
options.text: A new episode of iron deficiency caused by excess cow's-milk intake

options.label: D
options.text: A vaso-occlusive crisis caused by HbS polymerisation

questions.correctAnswerText: Transient aplastic crisis associated with parvovirus B19
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include parvovirus B19 as a cause of an uncommon, transient aplastic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis. A sudden haemoglobin fall with a low reticulocyte count indicates reduced red-cell production rather than the usual compensatory response to haemolysis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Increased red-cell destruction would usually provoke a marrow response and reticulocytosis.
- B. Correct. Parvovirus B19 may temporarily suppress red-cell production in a child with chronic haemolysis.
- C. Incorrect. Iron deficiency is not the best explanation for this sudden fall in haemoglobin with reticulocytopenia.
- D. Incorrect. The case does not describe sickle cell disease or a vaso-occlusive presentation.
- E. Incorrect. Isolated platelet destruction does not explain the acute anaemia and low reticulocyte count.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hereditary spherocytosis causes chronic haemolysis.
- Parvovirus B19 may precipitate a transient aplastic crisis.
- A sudden fall in haemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count is different from the usual haemolytic pattern.
- Clinical guidance notes that one or two transfusions may be required during the 3–4-week period when red cells are not being produced.

cases.title: Chronic haemolysis from an enzyme defect
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child has a history of neonatal jaundice followed by persistent pallor and intermittent jaundice. The spleen is enlarged and there is evidence of chronic haemolysis. The family is told that the disorder affects red-cell energy production.

questions.stem: Which enzyme deficiency is the most likely cause?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pyruvate kinase deficiency
questions.initialExplanation: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is an autosomal recessive red-cell glycolytic enzyme defect that reduces ATP production and shortens red-cell survival.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency is triggered by oxidative stress and is not a glycolytic ATP-production defect.
- B. Incorrect. Intrinsic-factor deficiency impairs B12 absorption and causes megaloblastic anaemia.
- C. Correct. The chronic haemolysis and neonatal jaundice fit pyruvate kinase deficiency.
- D. Incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency causes haemophilia A and deep-tissue bleeding.
- E. Incorrect. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency is not the red-cell enzyme disorder described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pyruvate kinase deficiency is autosomal recessive.
- It is a red-cell glycolysis defect.
- Reduced ATP leads to shortened RBC survival and chronic haemolysis.

questions.stem: What is the direct consequence of pyruvate kinase deficiency in red cells?
questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced ATP production
questions.initialExplanation: Pyruvate kinase is required for ATP generation in glycolysis; deficiency reduces red-cell ATP and compromises red-cell survival.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The course clinical guidance links reduced pyruvate kinase activity to reduced ATP production.
- B. Incorrect. Platelet adhesion is not the mechanism of this red-cell enzyme disorder.
- C. Incorrect. Intrinsic factor is involved in B12 absorption.
- D. Incorrect. NADPH production is related to the pentose phosphate pathway and G6PD.
- E. Incorrect. Factor IX is a coagulation protein.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- G6PD deficiency affects oxidative defence.
- Pyruvate kinase deficiency affects glycolytic ATP generation.
- Both can cause haemolytic anaemia but have different triggers and mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern is described for pyruvate kinase deficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Neonatal jaundice followed by chronic haemolysis and splenomegaly

options.label: D
options.text: Isolated petechiae with a normal haemoglobin

questions.correctAnswerText: Neonatal jaundice followed by chronic haemolysis and splenomegaly
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include neonatal jaundice and later chronic haemolysis with splenomegaly in pyruvate kinase deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the described clinical course.
- B. Incorrect. Macrocytosis with sensory ataxia suggests B12 deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow suggests aplastic anaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Isolated petechiae suggest a platelet disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Recurrent haemarthrosis suggests haemophilia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Think of chronic non-immune haemolysis in a child with neonatal jaundice and splenomegaly.
- Distinguish enzyme defects by their biochemical pathways and triggers.
- Reticulocytosis and indirect hyperbilirubinaemia support haemolysis.

questions.stem: Which treatment options are listed in the course clinical guidance for pyruvate kinase deficiency?

options.label: B
options.text: Oral iron alone in each patient

options.label: C
options.text: Red-cell transfusion and splenectomy in selected cases

questions.correctAnswerText: Red-cell transfusion and splenectomy in selected cases
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance lists packed red-cell transfusion and splenectomy as treatment options for pyruvate kinase deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These treatments are used for selected coagulation disorders.
- B. Incorrect. Iron is not a treatment for haemolysis unless iron deficiency is also present.
- C. Correct. These are the options stated for clinically significant disease.
- D. Incorrect. These are components of leukaemia treatment, not enzyme-deficiency treatment.
- E. Incorrect. IVIG and platelet-directed management are relevant to selected immune thrombocytopenia cases.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Management depends on severity and transfusion requirement.
- Common examples include transfusion and splenectomy.
- Avoid treating every haemolytic anaemia as iron deficiency.

cases.title: Microcytosis with a variable alpha-globin gene defect
cases.vignette: A newborn is evaluated because the family has a history of thalassaemia. The clinician explains that the severity of alpha-thalassaemia depends on how many of the four alpha-globin genes are functional.

questions.stem: On which chromosome are the alpha-globin genes located according to the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Chromosome 16
questions.initialExplanation: The alpha-globin genes are located on chromosome 16, with four alpha-globin genes in total.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Alpha-thalassaemia is not an X-linked disorder.
- B. Incorrect. The beta-globin genes are located on chromosome 11.
- C. Correct. Chromosome 16 is stated.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the chromosome location stated.
- E. Incorrect. This is not the chromosome location given for alpha-globin genes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Alpha-globin genes: chromosome 16.
- Four alpha-globin genes are present.
- Clinical severity relates to the number of affected genes.

questions.stem: A child has a two-gene alpha-globin deletion and mild microcytic hypochromic anaemia. Which alpha-thalassaemia category best fits?
questions.correctAnswerText: Alpha-thalassaemia trait
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include alpha-thalassaemia trait with two affected alpha-globin genes and mild microcytic hypochromic anaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Haemoglobin H disease involves three affected alpha genes and causes more significant microcytic anaemia with haemolysis.
- B. Correct. Two affected alpha genes produce the trait phenotype described.
- C. Incorrect. A silent carrier has one affected gene and usually a normal CBC.
- D. Incorrect. Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis involves loss of all four alpha genes.
- E. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia major is a different beta-globin disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- One affected gene: silent carrier, usually normal CBC.
- Two affected genes: alpha-thalassaemia trait.
- Three affected genes: HbH disease.
- Four affected genes: Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis.

questions.stem: A fetus has deletion or inactivation of all four alpha-globin genes. Which outcome is most likely?

options.label: B
options.text: Silent carrier state with a normal CBC

options.label: D
options.text: Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis with severe fetal anaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis with severe fetal anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Loss of all four alpha-globin genes produces Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis, associated with profound anaemia and fetal or early neonatal death.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron deficiency does not cause this inherited fetal globin-chain disorder.
- B. Incorrect. A silent carrier has only one affected alpha gene.
- C. Incorrect. Alpha-thalassaemia trait involves two affected genes and is much milder.
- D. Correct. No functional alpha chains leads to severe fetal disease with hydrops.
- E. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia trait is unrelated to loss of all alpha genes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Four-gene alpha deletion: Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis.
- Three-gene involvement: HbH disease.
- Two-gene involvement: alpha-thalassaemia trait.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes haemoglobin H disease?

options.label: A
options.text: most four alpha-globin genes are normal

options.label: B
options.text: One alpha-globin gene is affected with a completely normal CBC in each patient

options.label: C
options.text: It is a form of vitamin B12 deficiency

options.label: D
options.text: It is caused by factor VIII deficiency

options.label: E
options.text: Three alpha-globin genes are affected, producing microcytic anaemia with mild haemolysis

questions.correctAnswerText: Three alpha-globin genes are affected, producing microcytic anaemia with mild haemolysis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include HbH disease as the three-gene alpha-thalassaemia state, producing microcytic anaemia and mild haemolysis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Normal alpha genes do not produce HbH disease.
- B. Incorrect. A one-gene silent carrier usually has a normal CBC.
- C. Incorrect. B12 deficiency is a nutritional megaloblastic disorder.
- D. Incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency causes haemophilia A.
- E. Correct. This is the phenotype stated for HbH disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HbH disease: three alpha genes affected.
- Expect microcytosis and some haemolysis.
- Severity increases as the number of functional alpha genes falls.

cases.title: Severe anaemia beginning in infancy
cases.vignette: A 9-month-old infant is referred for severe pallor, poor growth, jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly. The infant was well at birth but became progressively anaemic over the past several months. The family originates from a region where thalassaemia is common.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Beta-thalassaemia major
questions.initialExplanation: Beta-thalassaemia major causes severe transfusion-dependent haemolytic anaemia that becomes apparent at approximately 3-6 months as fetal haemoglobin declines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron deficiency can cause microcytosis and pallor but does not explain the characteristic severe inherited haemolytic syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia.
- C. Correct. Severe anaemia, growth failure, jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly in infancy fit beta-thalassaemia major.
- D. Incorrect. Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic rather than this chronic severe haemolytic picture.
- E. Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Beta-thalassaemia major commonly becomes clinically apparent after the first few months of life.
- Chronic haemolysis leads to pallor, jaundice and splenomegaly.
- Marrow expansion can cause characteristic skeletal changes.

questions.stem: Which mechanism causes the anaemia in beta-thalassaemia major?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced beta-chain synthesis with excess unpaired alpha chains causing ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced intrinsic factor with impaired B12 absorption

options.label: D
options.text: Oxidant injury due to reduced NADPH production

options.label: E
options.text: Failure of platelet adhesion due to absent von Willebrand factor

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced beta-chain synthesis with excess unpaired alpha chains causing ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis
questions.initialExplanation: Reduced beta-chain synthesis leaves excess alpha chains, which precipitate in erythroid cells and cause ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the central pathophysiology described for beta-thalassaemia major.
- B. Incorrect. This causes B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anaemia.
- C. Incorrect. This is the mechanism of immune thrombocytopenia.
- D. Incorrect. This describes the oxidative mechanism of G6PD deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. This describes a von Willebrand factor-related haemostatic problem.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Beta-thalassaemia is a quantitative beta-globin synthesis defect.
- Excess alpha chains damage erythroid precursors and mature red cells.
- The consequences include ineffective erythropoiesis, haemolysis and marrow expansion.

questions.stem: Which haemoglobin-electrophoresis pattern is expected in beta-thalassaemia major?

options.label: A
options.text: Predominant HbA with a small HbS fraction

options.label: B
options.text: Isolated increased HbA with no other change

options.label: C
options.text: Normal HbA with absent HbF and absent HbA2

options.label: E
options.text: Markedly increased HbF, increased HbA2 and very low or absent HbA

questions.correctAnswerText: Markedly increased HbF, increased HbA2 and very low or absent HbA
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include haemoglobin electrophoresis as diagnostic, with very high HbF, increased HbA2 and low or absent HbA in beta-thalassaemia major.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This pattern is more consistent with sickle trait.
- B. Incorrect. A normal HbA-predominant pattern does not support beta-thalassaemia major.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the expected abnormal pattern.
- D. Incorrect. HbS predominance suggests sickle cell disease.
- E. Correct. This is the characteristic pattern described for beta-thalassaemia major.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hb electrophoresis is diagnostic for beta-thalassaemia.
- HbF is markedly increased in major disease.
- HbA is markedly reduced or absent in beta-thalassaemia major.

questions.stem: Why are regular transfusions used in transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia major?

options.label: B
options.text: To maintain haemoglobin, support normal growth and suppress excessive ineffective marrow expansion

questions.correctAnswerText: To maintain haemoglobin, support normal growth and suppress excessive ineffective marrow expansion
questions.initialExplanation: This is explained that regular transfusion maintains haemoglobin, supports growth and reduces medullary and extramedullary haematopoiesis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Repeated transfusion contributes to iron loading; it is not intended to increase iron absorption.
- B. Correct. Maintaining an adequate haemoglobin suppresses excessive marrow drive and its skeletal and organ consequences.
- C. Incorrect. Transfusion does not destroy the spleen.
- D. Incorrect. Immune platelet destruction is a separate disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Transfusion does not prevent B12 deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Regular transfusion is used to maintain haemoglobin and suppress ineffective erythropoiesis.
- Marrow expansion contributes to skeletal changes and extramedullary haematopoiesis.
- Repeated transfusions create a risk of iron overload.

topics.name: Complications and long-term care in beta-thalassaemia

cases.title: A transfusion-dependent child with new complications
cases.vignette: A 12-year-old child with beta-thalassaemia major has received repeated blood transfusions since infancy. The child now has delayed puberty, poor growth, skin hyperpigmentation and reduced cardiac function. Serum ferritin is markedly increased.

questions.stem: Which complication most likely explains the multisystem findings?
questions.correctAnswerText: Transfusional iron overload
questions.initialExplanation: Repeated transfusions cause iron accumulation in organs including the heart, liver, pancreas and pituitary gland.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Cardiac dysfunction, endocrine abnormalities, skin pigmentation and high ferritin fit iron overload.
- B. Incorrect. Iron deficiency does not explain a high iron burden after repeated transfusions.
- C. Incorrect. Vitamin K deficiency causes impaired coagulation.
- D. Incorrect. ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia.
- E. Incorrect. Folate deficiency does not cause iron deposition in multiple organs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Iron overload is a major complication of chronic transfusion.
- Cardiac deposition can cause cardiomyopathy.
- Liver, pancreas, pituitary and skin may also be affected.

questions.stem: Which treatment is used to reduce iron overload in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Iron chelation therapy
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes iron chelation to manage transfusional iron overload and lists deferoxamine and deferasirox.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Platelet transfusion does not reduce tissue iron.
- B. Incorrect. Additional iron would worsen iron overload.
- C. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected bleeding disorders.
- D. Correct. Chelation removes excess iron and reduces organ deposition.
- E. Incorrect. Vitamin K does not chelate iron.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Iron chelation is essential in chronically transfused patients.
- Clinical guidance deferoxamine and deferasirox.
- Monitor for iron-related cardiac, hepatic and endocrine complications.

questions.stem: Which intervention is identified as potentially curative for beta-thalassaemia major?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bone-marrow or haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include bone-marrow transplantation as a curative treatment option for beta-thalassaemia major in selected patients.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin does not treat thalassaemia.
- B. Correct. Haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation can provide a curative option in appropriately selected patients.
- C. Incorrect. Platelet transfusions do not correct the underlying beta-globin defect.
- D. Incorrect. Iron is not the primary problem and would worsen iron loading.
- E. Incorrect. Splenectomy may be considered for selected complications but is not curative.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chronic transfusion and iron chelation are core long-term measures.
- Stem-cell transplantation is the curative option described.
- Genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis are also emphasized.

questions.stem: Which endocrine consequence may result from iron deposition in the pituitary gland?

options.label: D
options.text: Diabetes insipidus as the defining feature

options.label: E
options.text: Impaired growth and delayed sexual maturation

questions.correctAnswerText: Impaired growth and delayed sexual maturation
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance links pituitary iron deposition with impaired growth and sexual maturation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a separate inherited endocrine disorder.
- B. Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism is not the characteristic pituitary iron-overload consequence given.
- C. Incorrect. Clinical guidance impaired growth and delayed maturation, not universal precocious puberty.
- D. Incorrect. Diabetes insipidus is not identified as the defining complication.
- E. Correct. This is the endocrine effect specifically listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Iron deposition affects multiple endocrine organs.
- Pituitary injury can cause poor growth and delayed puberty.
- Pancreatic iron deposition may cause diabetes.

cases.title: When to start iron chelation in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia major has received repeated red-cell transfusions. The serum ferritin is reported above the threshold stated in the course clinical guidance. The team discusses treatment to reduce iron deposition in organs.

questions.stem: Which approach matches the iron-chelation plan described?

options.label: A
options.text: Start oral iron because repeated transfusions deplete iron stores.

options.label: C
options.text: Use platelet transfusions to remove excess iron.

options.label: D
options.text: Consider chelation when ferritin exceeds the stated threshold; the sheet lists subcutaneous deferoxamine and oral deferasirox.

options.label: E
options.text: Use desmopressin to increase urinary iron excretion.

questions.correctAnswerText: Consider chelation when ferritin exceeds the stated threshold; the sheet lists subcutaneous deferoxamine and oral deferasirox.
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance indicates iron chelation when serum ferritin is above 1000 and says it is started from approximately 2–3 years of age. It lists deferoxamine by subcutaneous injection and deferasirox orally.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Repeated transfusions cause iron overload; additional iron would not address it.
- B. Incorrect. Clinical descriptions include starting chelation from about 2–3 years when the stated ferritin criterion is met.
- C. Incorrect. Platelet transfusion is not an iron-chelation treatment.
- D. Correct. This matches the threshold, age and two agents/routes listed.
- E. Incorrect. Desmopressin is described in the bleeding-disorder section, not as treatment for iron overload.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Transfusional iron overload can affect the heart, liver, pancreas, pituitary gland and skin.
- Clinical guidance ferritin above 1000 as the indication and says chelation starts from about 2–3 years of age.
- Deferoxamine: subcutaneous injection; deferasirox: oral.
- OCR caution: the ferritin unit in the extracted clinical guidance appears as “ng/dl”. Verify the unit against the original standard guidance PDF before using it clinically; the question tests the threshold as transcribed, not an independently corrected unit.
