topics.name: Sickle cell disease: painful vaso-occlusive crisis

cases.title: Severe limb pain after dehydration
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child with known sickle cell disease presents with severe pain in both legs after several hours of outdoor activity with poor fluid intake. The child is febrile and has no clear evidence of trauma. The family reports previous similar episodes.

questions.stem: Which process is responsible for the painful crisis?

options.label: A
options.text: HbS polymerization causing sickling, increased viscosity and vaso-occlusion

questions.correctAnswerText: HbS polymerization causing sickling, increased viscosity and vaso-occlusion
questions.initialExplanation: Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes, deforming red cells into rigid sickle shapes that obstruct small vessels and cause ischaemia and pain.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. HbS polymerization leads to sickling, vascular occlusion and tissue ischaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Iron deficiency does not cause vaso-occlusion.
- C. Incorrect. Platelet autoantibodies cause ITP, not a sickle-cell pain crisis.
- D. Incorrect. Intrinsic-factor deficiency causes B12 malabsorption.
- E. Incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency causes haemophilia A.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HbS results from substitution of valine for glutamic acid in the beta chain.
- Hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration, fever and infection promote sickling.
- Vaso-occlusion causes tissue ischaemia and pain.

questions.stem: Which factor in this history most likely precipitated the crisis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Dehydration
questions.initialExplanation: Dehydration is a recognized precipitating factor for sickling and vaso-occlusive crises.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Dehydration promotes sickling and is listed as a trigger.
- B. Incorrect. Rest is not a precipitating factor.
- C. Incorrect. Hypoxia, rather than normal oxygenation, is a trigger.
- D. Incorrect. Avoiding cold exposure is part of crisis prevention.
- E. Incorrect. Adequate hydration helps reduce the risk of sickling.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Triggers include hypoxia, fever, acidosis, infection, dehydration, excessive exercise, stress and cold.
- Ask about recent illness, fluid intake and environmental exposure.
- Prevention focuses on avoiding recognized triggers.

questions.stem: A 20-month-old child with sickle cell disease develops painful swelling of the hands and feet. What is this manifestation called?
questions.correctAnswerText: Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome)
questions.initialExplanation: Dactylitis is a common vaso-occlusive manifestation in young children with sickle cell disease, presenting as painful swelling of the hands and feet.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the classic hand-foot syndrome of sickle cell disease.
- B. Incorrect. Spherocytosis describes spherical red cells and is not the clinical syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Ecchymosis is a skin bruise from bleeding.
- D. Incorrect. Hemarthrosis is bleeding into a joint, commonly associated with haemophilia.
- E. Incorrect. Koilonychia is spoon-shaped nail change associated with iron deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dactylitis is common in children younger than 2 years, although it may occur in young children more broadly.
- It results from vaso-occlusion in the small bones of the hands and feet.
- Consider osteomyelitis in the differential diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which treatment approach is appropriate for an uncomplicated painful vaso-occlusive crisis?

options.label: A
options.text: Routine exchange transfusion for each painful episode

options.label: C
options.text: Analgesia, correction of dehydration and treatment of any identified infection

questions.correctAnswerText: Analgesia, correction of dehydration and treatment of any identified infection
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance describes analgesia, hydration, oxygen when hypoxic or in respiratory distress, and antibiotics when infection is suspected. Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe complications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion is used in selected severe situations such as acute chest syndrome or stroke, not every pain crisis.
- B. Incorrect. Platelet transfusion does not treat sickle-cell pain.
- C. Correct. This is the core approach to an uncomplicated painful crisis.
- D. Incorrect. Iron does not correct sickling and may be harmful if iron overload is present.
- E. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not treatment for an uncomplicated vaso-occlusive crisis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat pain promptly.
- Correct dehydration and treat infection when present.
- Give oxygen when there is hypoxia or respiratory distress.
- Transfusion is reserved for specific severe indications.

topics.name: Sickle cell disease: acute chest syndrome and neurological complications

cases.title: A child with sickle cell disease develops respiratory distress
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child with sickle cell disease is admitted with chest pain. Several hours later, the child develops fever, cough, tachypnoea and hypoxia. Chest radiography shows new pulmonary infiltrates.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acute chest syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Acute chest syndrome is a serious sickle-cell complication characterized by respiratory symptoms, fever, hypoxia and new chest radiographic infiltrates.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron deficiency does not cause this acute pulmonary syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Sickle trait is usually asymptomatic and does not explain this presentation.
- C. Correct. The combination of fever, cough, respiratory distress, hypoxia and new infiltrates is typical.
- D. Incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis causes chronic haemolysis, not acute chest syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. ITP causes thrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute chest syndrome is one of the most serious sickle-cell complications.
- Look for fever, cough, respiratory distress, hypoxia and new infiltrates.
- Severe cases may require respiratory support and urgent transfusion.

questions.stem: Why is acute chest syndrome considered an emergency?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a harmless manifestation of sickle trait

options.label: C
options.text: It is defined by a low platelet count alone

options.label: E
options.text: It can progress to severe hypoxia and require mechanical ventilation or emergency transfusion

questions.correctAnswerText: It can progress to severe hypoxia and require mechanical ventilation or emergency transfusion
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance warns that acute chest syndrome can cause severe hypoxia and may require mechanical ventilation and emergency transfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. It is associated with sickle cell disease, not a benign trait presentation.
- B. Incorrect. clinical guidance identifies it as a potentially life-threatening complication.
- C. Incorrect. A low platelet count alone does not define acute chest syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. It is a pulmonary vaso-occlusive/inflammatory complication, not isolated iron deficiency.
- E. Correct. Rapid respiratory deterioration is the reason urgent recognition and escalation are essential.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Assess oxygen saturation and respiratory status.
- Escalate early if hypoxia or respiratory compromise develops.
- Exchange transfusion is considered in severe acute chest syndrome.

questions.stem: A child with sickle cell disease suddenly develops hemiplegia and a seizure. Which complication should be suspected?

options.label: B
options.text: Cerebrovascular accident due to sickle-related vaso-occlusion

questions.correctAnswerText: Cerebrovascular accident due to sickle-related vaso-occlusion
questions.initialExplanation: Sickle cell disease can cause CNS vaso-occlusion, stroke, seizures and focal motor deficits.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hereditary elliptocytosis is a red-cell membrane disorder and does not explain this presentation.
- B. Correct. Acute focal neurological deficits in a child with sickle cell disease require urgent evaluation for stroke.
- C. Incorrect. Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia rather than acute hemiplegia.
- D. Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding, not vaso-occlusive stroke.
- E. Incorrect. Iron deficiency does not cause this acute focal neurological syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stroke is a serious complication of sickle cell disease.
- Seizures, hemiplegia and other focal deficits are warning signs.
- Severe cases may require exchange transfusion.

questions.stem: Which intervention is specifically listed for severe sickle-cell complications such as stroke or acute chest syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Splenectomy as the acute first step

questions.correctAnswerText: Exchange transfusion
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance lists exchange transfusion for severe complications including acute chest syndrome and stroke.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron does not correct the underlying sickling process.
- B. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not the emergency treatment for stroke or acute chest syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Platelet transfusion does not treat sickle-related vaso-occlusion.
- D. Correct. Exchange transfusion reduces the proportion of circulating HbS in selected severe complications.
- E. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected bleeding disorders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Exchange transfusion is used for selected severe sickle complications.
- Do not apply transfusion indiscriminately to every pain crisis.
- The clinical indication and severity guide the transfusion strategy.

cases.title: Sudden pallor and splenic enlargement
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child with sickle cell disease becomes acutely pale and lethargic. The abdomen is distended, and the spleen is now markedly enlarged compared with a previous examination. The child is tachycardic and hypotensive.

questions.stem: Which crisis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Splenic sequestration crisis
questions.initialExplanation: Splenic sequestration results from pooling of a large volume of blood in the spleen, producing acute anaemia, splenomegaly and possible hypovolaemic shock.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Aplastic crisis causes reduced marrow production and reticulocytopenia, typically without acute massive splenic pooling.
- B. Incorrect. A pain crisis causes ischaemic pain rather than acute splenic pooling and shock.
- C. Correct. The sudden splenic enlargement, pallor and shock are characteristic of sequestration.
- D. Incorrect. Iron deficiency is usually gradual and does not cause this acute presentation.
- E. Incorrect. Megaloblastic crisis is associated with folate deficiency and does not explain sudden splenic enlargement.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Splenic sequestration causes acute pooling of blood, acute anaemia and splenomegaly.
- Hypovolaemic shock may occur.
- It is particularly relevant in young children who still have splenic tissue.

questions.stem: Which infectious agent is classically associated with aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease?
questions.correctAnswerText: Parvovirus B19
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include parvovirus B19 as the usual cause of aplastic crisis, which produces transient bone-marrow suppression.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hepatitis A is not the classic trigger described.
- B. Correct. Parvovirus B19 suppresses erythropoiesis and can precipitate aplastic crisis.
- C. Incorrect. Pertussis does not cause the characteristic aplastic crisis.
- D. Incorrect. EBV is mentioned in other haematological contexts but is not the usual cause listed for aplastic crisis.
- E. Incorrect. Rotavirus is a gastrointestinal pathogen and is not the cause stated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Parvovirus B19 can cause transient aplastic crisis.
- Expect a sudden fall in haemoglobin with reduced reticulocyte production.
- This is particularly important in patients with chronic haemolytic anaemia.

questions.stem: A child with sickle cell disease develops sudden severe anaemia, jaundice and a marked rise in haemolysis markers without new splenic enlargement. Which crisis is most consistent?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hyperhaemolytic crisis
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance describes a hyperhaemolytic crisis as increased red-cell destruction causing severe anaemia and jaundice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sequestration is characterized by acute blood pooling and splenic enlargement.
- B. Correct. Increased haemolysis with worsening jaundice supports a hyperhaemolytic crisis.
- C. Incorrect. Aplastic crisis is caused by reduced marrow production, usually with a low reticulocyte count.
- D. Incorrect. Megaloblastic crisis results from folate deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. Acute chest syndrome is a respiratory complication with new pulmonary infiltrates.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Differentiate crises by the mechanism and clinical findings.
- Sequestration: acute splenic enlargement and shock.
- Aplastic: marrow suppression and reticulocytopenia.
- Hyperhaemolytic: increased haemolysis and jaundice.

questions.stem: Why are children with sickle cell disease at increased risk of infection with encapsulated organisms as they grow older?

options.label: A
options.text: They lose their thymus during infancy

options.label: B
options.text: Repeated splenic vaso-occlusion can lead to functional asplenia or autosplenectomy

options.label: C
options.text: They develop an inherited absence of most immunoglobulins

options.label: D
options.text: Their bone marrow stops producing most white cells

options.label: E
options.text: Their platelet count is typically severely reduced

questions.correctAnswerText: Repeated splenic vaso-occlusion can lead to functional asplenia or autosplenectomy
questions.initialExplanation: Repeated splenic infarction can cause autosplenectomy and impaired splenic function, increasing susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Thymic loss is not the reason for the characteristic infection risk.
- B. Correct. Functional asplenia reduces clearance of encapsulated organisms.
- C. Incorrect. The infection risk is related to splenic dysfunction, not universal absence of immunoglobulins.
- D. Incorrect. Sickle cell disease does not cause universal cessation of white-cell production.
- E. Incorrect. A persistently severe platelet reduction is not the mechanism described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Functional asplenia may develop after recurrent splenic infarction.
- Risk rises for infection with encapsulated organisms.
- Prevention includes appropriate vaccination and prophylactic penicillin as described.

topics.name: Sickle cell disease: prevention and sickle trait

cases.title: Preventive review of a child with HbSS
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old child with HbSS is reviewed while clinically well. The family asks how to reduce future painful crises and prevent serious infection. The child has no acute pain or respiratory symptoms today.

questions.stem: Which medication is used to increase fetal haemoglobin and reduce vaso-occlusive events?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide)
questions.initialExplanation: Hydroxyurea increases HbF production, making red cells less prone to sickling and reducing crises.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Prednisolone is not routine sickle-cell disease prevention.
- B. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected bleeding disorders.
- C. Correct. Hydroxyurea raises HbF and reduces the propensity to sickle.
- D. Incorrect. Ferrous sulfate treats iron deficiency, not sickle-cell polymerization.
- E. Incorrect. Deferasirox is an iron chelator used for iron overload.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hydroxyurea increases HbF.
- HbF reduces HbS polymerization and sickling.
- Continue trigger avoidance and regular preventive care.

questions.stem: Which preventive antibiotic is described for children with sickle cell disease because of functional asplenia?

options.label: B
options.text: Ciprofloxacin for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Penicillin
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes prophylactic oral penicillin during childhood, or lifelong in selected circumstances, because functional asplenia increases infection risk.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Metronidazole is not the preventive antibiotic listed.
- B. Incorrect. Routine ciprofloxacin prophylaxis is not recommended.
- C. Incorrect. Isoniazid is used for tuberculosis prevention or treatment, not this indication.
- D. Correct. Penicillin prophylaxis is listed.
- E. Incorrect. Acyclovir is an antiviral drug.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Functional asplenia increases risk from encapsulated bacteria.
- Clinical guidance prophylactic penicillin.
- Vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Hib is important.

questions.stem: Which vaccines are specifically emphasized for a child with sickle-cell disease and functional asplenia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hib, pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance specifically lists Hib, pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination to reduce infection risk in children with functional asplenia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hepatitis B is not a substitute for the vaccines emphasized for asplenia.
- B. Incorrect. Polio vaccination alone does not address the encapsulated-bacteria risk.
- C. Correct. These are the vaccines highlighted.
- D. Incorrect. Influenza vaccine may be part of routine care but does not replace the listed vaccines.
- E. Incorrect. Additional preventive vaccination is specifically recommended.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prioritize vaccines that protect against encapsulated organisms.
- Penicillin prophylaxis is also emphasized.
- Counsel families to seek prompt assessment for fever.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic adolescent has HbAS on electrophoresis. Which statement best describes sickle cell trait in the course clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: It is usually asymptomatic, with HbA predominating and HbS forming a smaller fraction

options.label: B
options.text: It is identical to HbSS disease with frequent painful crises

options.label: D
options.text: It typically causes severe chronic haemolytic anaemia

options.label: E
options.text: It is caused by a beta-thalassaemia mutation alone

questions.correctAnswerText: It is usually asymptomatic, with HbA predominating and HbS forming a smaller fraction
questions.initialExplanation: Sickle cell trait is the heterozygous HbAS state and is usually asymptomatic. Clinical guidance HbA as the larger fraction and HbS as a smaller fraction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. HbAS is the carrier state, usually asymptomatic, with HbA predominating.
- B. Incorrect. HbSS is sickle cell anaemia and causes recurrent clinical complications.
- C. Incorrect. HbA is present and predominates in HbAS.
- D. Incorrect. Severe chronic haemolysis is not expected in uncomplicated sickle trait.
- E. Incorrect. Sickle trait is caused by inheritance of one HbS allele, not beta-thalassaemia alone.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HbSS: sickle cell disease.
- HbAS: sickle cell trait, usually asymptomatic.
- Clinical guidance that sickling in trait occurs only under severe hypoxaemia.

cases.title: Nocturnal hypoxaemia in sickle cell disease
cases.vignette: A child with sickle cell disease has adenotonsillar hypertrophy and symptoms during sleep. The family asks whether this could affect the child's sickle-cell complications.

questions.stem: Which sequence of consequences is described in the course clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy causes iron deficiency, which directly produces haemarthrosis.

options.label: B
options.text: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy may cause sleep apnoea and nocturnal hypoxaemia, increasing the risk of vaso-occlusive crises and/or stroke.

options.label: C
options.text: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy prevents sickling by increasing HbF.

options.label: D
options.text: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy causes isolated thrombocytopenia and prolonged PT.

options.label: E
options.text: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy prevents renal complications in sickle cell disease.

questions.correctAnswerText: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy may cause sleep apnoea and nocturnal hypoxaemia, increasing the risk of vaso-occlusive crises and/or stroke.
questions.initialExplanation: The sickle-cell complications section links adenotonsillar hypertrophy to sleep apnoea, nocturnal hypoxaemia and an increased risk of vaso-occlusive crises and/or stroke.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This sequence is not described in the sickle-cell section.
- B. Correct. This is the chain of complications stated.
- C. Incorrect. Hydroxyurea is the treatment listed as increasing HbF; adenotonsillar hypertrophy does not do this.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the complication pathway described.
- E. Incorrect. Recognized features include this as a risk pathway, not a protective effect.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sickle cell disease can cause sleep-related complications.
- standard guidance links adenotonsillar hypertrophy → sleep apnoea → nocturnal hypoxaemia → vaso-occlusive crises and/or stroke.

cases.title: Renal complications in sickle cell disease
cases.vignette: A child with established sickle cell disease develops recurrent enuresis and is found to have evidence of chronic renal dysfunction. There is no new painful crisis at the time of review.

questions.stem: Which chronic complication is specifically listed in the course clinical guidance?

options.label: C
options.text: Renal dysfunction, including chronic kidney disease and enuresis

questions.correctAnswerText: Renal dysfunction, including chronic kidney disease and enuresis
questions.initialExplanation: The complications list for sickle cell disease explicitly includes renal dysfunction, chronic kidney disease and enuresis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency causes haemophilia A.
- B. Incorrect. Immune platelet destruction is the mechanism of ITP.
- C. Correct. Renal dysfunction, CKD and enuresis are listed complications of sickle cell disease.
- D. Incorrect. Pure red-cell aplasia is described in the Diamond-Blackfan section.
- E. Incorrect. Vitamin K deficiency is listed among acquired coagulation disorders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sickle cell disease can affect the kidneys as well as the bones, spleen, lungs, CNS, eyes and liver.
- standard guidance specifically lists renal dysfunction, CKD and enuresis.

cases.title: Sickle cell trait and malaria
cases.vignette: A child is found to have HbAS on haemoglobin electrophoresis and is otherwise asymptomatic. The family lives in a region where malaria is endemic and asks about an association mentioned in the course clinical guidance.

questions.stem: Which statement about sickle cell trait is listed?

options.label: A
options.text: It causes the same recurrent vaso-occlusive crises as HbSS.

options.label: B
options.text: It is associated with absent HbA and 90–95% HbS.

options.label: C
options.text: It is described as providing protection against malaria.

options.label: E
options.text: It causes severe neonatal hydrops fetalis.

questions.correctAnswerText: It is described as providing protection against malaria.
questions.initialExplanation: The sickle cell trait section describes HbAS as usually asymptomatic and lists protection against malaria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Clinical descriptions include sickle cell trait as usually asymptomatic; HbSS is the sickle cell anaemia form.
- B. Incorrect. clinical guidance gives HbA about 60–80% and HbS about 20–40% in trait.
- C. Correct. Protection against malaria is specifically listed in the trait section.
- D. Incorrect. Transfusion dependence is associated with severe beta-thalassaemia major, not ordinary HbAS trait.
- E. Incorrect. Hydrops fetalis is associated with loss of all four alpha-globin genes (Hb Bart's), not sickle trait.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HbAS is usually asymptomatic.
- Clinical guidance HbS about 20–40% and HbA about 60–80%.
- Protection against malaria is listed as an association of sickle cell trait.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Sickle cell trait, Page 24.

cases.title: Acute jaundice and pallor after an illness
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child develops acute pallor, jaundice and dark urine. The blood count shows normocytic normochromic anaemia with reticulocytosis. The blood film shows spherocytes, and the direct antiglobulin test is positive.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Warm AIHA commonly involves IgG autoantibodies, extravascular haemolysis, a positive direct antiglobulin test and spherocytes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease causes mucosal bleeding, not immune haemolysis.
- B. Incorrect. IDA is microcytic and does not cause a positive Coombs test.
- C. Correct. The acute haemolytic presentation and positive direct antiglobulin test strongly support AIHA.
- D. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia trait is usually mild and microcytic.
- E. Incorrect. Aplastic anaemia causes reticulocytopenia and pancytopenia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- AIHA causes premature red-cell destruction by autoantibodies.
- Warm AIHA commonly involves IgG.
- Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is an important investigation.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is most commonly associated with warm AIHA in the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: IgG
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include warm autoantibodies as IgG and active around normal body temperature.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Warm AIHA is associated with IgG autoantibodies.
- B. Incorrect. IgM is the typical antibody class in cold agglutinin disease.
- C. Incorrect. IgE is associated with allergic and parasitic responses.
- D. Incorrect. IgA is not the characteristic class given.
- E. Incorrect. IgD is not the characteristic antibody in warm AIHA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Warm AIHA: usually IgG.
- Cold agglutinin disease: commonly IgM.
- Warm antibodies act near 35-40°C.

questions.stem: Which site and mechanism are most typical of warm AIHA?

options.label: A
options.text: Red-cell destruction in the kidney tubules

options.label: B
options.text: Failure of red-cell production in a hypocellular marrow

questions.correctAnswerText: Extravascular haemolysis in the spleen
questions.initialExplanation: Warm IgG-coated red cells are removed mainly by splenic macrophages, producing predominantly extravascular haemolysis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Intravascular haemolysis may produce haemoglobinuria, but it is not the typical warm-AIHA mechanism described.
- B. Incorrect. Hypocellular marrow suggests aplastic anaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Platelet destruction is the mechanism of ITP.
- D. Correct. Splenic Fc-receptor-mediated clearance is the mechanism described for warm AIHA.
- E. Incorrect. Coagulation-factor consumption is relevant to DIC.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Warm AIHA is mainly extravascular.
- Spherocytes may appear on the blood film.
- Direct Coombs testing detects antibody or complement coating of red cells.

questions.stem: Which treatment is listed as the drug of choice for warm AIHA in the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Corticosteroids
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include corticosteroids, such as prednisolone or IV methylprednisolone, as first-line treatment for warm AIHA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected bleeding disorders.
- B. Incorrect. Iron treats iron deficiency, not antibody-mediated haemolysis.
- C. Incorrect. Hydroxyurea is used in sickle cell disease to increase HbF.
- D. Correct. Steroids are the drug of choice in the course clinical guidance.
- E. Incorrect. Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic used for selected bleeding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat the underlying cause when identified.
- Steroids are first-line for warm AIHA.
- Refractory cases may require additional immunosuppression or rituximab.

cases.title: Haemoglobinuria after cold exposure
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child develops pallor, jaundice and dark urine after playing outside in cold weather. Blood tests show haemolysis. The direct antiglobulin test is positive, and cold agglutination testing is strongly positive.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cold-antibody autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Cold-antibody AIHA may cause haemolysis and haemoglobinuria after cold exposure, with a positive cold agglutination test.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Cold-triggered haemolysis and a strongly positive cold agglutination test fit the presentation.
- B. Incorrect. HS causes chronic haemolysis, often with a family history and increased MCHC, but cold agglutination is not typical.
- C. Incorrect. IDA does not cause episodic cold-induced haemoglobinuria.
- D. Incorrect. Aplastic anaemia causes marrow failure and reticulocytopenia, not haemolysis.
- E. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia trait is usually mild and microcytic.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cold AIHA may follow infections such as Mycoplasma or EBV.
- Haemolysis may follow cold exposure.
- Cold agglutination testing is a characteristic investigation.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is most commonly associated with cold agglutinin disease?
questions.correctAnswerText: IgM
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance describes cold-antibody AIHA as usually involving IgM, which can activate complement and cause agglutination.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. IgG is the typical antibody in warm AIHA.
- B. Incorrect. IgE is not the characteristic antibody in cold agglutinin disease.
- C. Correct. IgM is the typical cold agglutinin antibody described.
- D. Incorrect. IgD is not the antibody described.
- E. Incorrect. IgA is not the typical cold agglutinin antibody.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Warm AIHA: IgG.
- Cold agglutinin disease: IgM.
- Cold antibodies may cause agglutination and complement-mediated haemolysis.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best distinguishes cold-antibody haemolysis from warm AIHA?

options.label: A
options.text: Complement activation with predominantly intravascular haemolysis

questions.correctAnswerText: Complement activation with predominantly intravascular haemolysis
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance links cold antibodies with complement activation and intravascular haemolysis, in contrast to the predominantly splenic extravascular haemolysis of warm AIHA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Complement activation is the distinguishing mechanism emphasized for cold-antibody AIHA.
- B. Incorrect. Reduced alpha-globin synthesis causes alpha-thalassaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Stem-cell failure causes aplastic anaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Reduced red-cell ATP is the mechanism of pyruvate kinase deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. This describes warm IgG-mediated extravascular haemolysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cold antibodies require complement for their haemolytic effect.
- Cold haemolysis may be intravascular.
- Avoid cold exposure and treat any underlying trigger.

questions.stem: Which management measure is specifically emphasized for cold-antibody AIHA?

options.label: B
options.text: Deliberately expose the child to cold to induce tolerance

options.label: C
options.text: Give oral iron as the treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Perform routine splenectomy in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Avoid cold exposure
questions.initialExplanation: The cold-AIHA management section emphasizes treatment of the cause and avoidance of cold exposure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Avoidance of cold is a central supportive measure.
- B. Incorrect. Cold exposure can precipitate haemolysis and should be avoided.
- C. Incorrect. Iron does not treat immune haemolysis unless deficiency coexists.
- D. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not routine treatment for cold AIHA in children.
- E. Incorrect. Factor IX concentrate treats haemophilia B.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat any underlying infection or associated condition.
- Avoid cold exposure.
- Selected severe or refractory cases may require specialist-directed therapies.

cases.title: Cold-reactive haemolysis with an IgG antibody
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child develops pallor and dark urine after prolonged exposure to cold weather. Investigations support acute intravascular haemolysis. Immunological assessment identifies a cold-reactive IgG antibody rather than the IgM antibody described in the common cold-agglutinin pattern.

questions.stem: Which condition is most consistent with this combination?

options.label: B
options.text: Isoimmune haemolytic disease of the newborn

questions.correctAnswerText: Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria separately and associates it with cold IgG, not IgM. This distinguishes it from the common cold-agglutinin pattern described in the same section.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Warm AIHA is associated with IgG active at approximately 35–40°C and usually causes extravascular haemolysis in the spleen.
- B. Incorrect. Isoimmune haemolysis is due to passively acquired antibodies, as in haemolytic disease of the newborn.
- C. Incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis is an intrinsic red-cell membrane disorder, not a cold-antibody condition.
- D. Correct. The cold-reactive IgG finding matches the paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria entry.
- E. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency is associated with oxidant-triggered haemolysis and Heinz bodies, bite cells and blister cells.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Warm AIHA: IgG, active around 35–40°C, usually extravascular haemolysis.
- Cold-agglutinin pattern: IgM, complement-associated activity and agglutination.
- Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria: cold IgG, not IgM.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Extracorpuscular haemolytic anaemia, Page 25.

cases.title: Pancytopenia without organomegaly
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child presents with fatigue, recurrent infections and easy bruising. The full blood count shows low haemoglobin, low white-cell count and thrombocytopenia. There is no significant lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Aplastic anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Aplastic anaemia is bone-marrow failure producing peripheral pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow. The absence of organomegaly or lymphadenopathy supports the pattern described.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron deficiency usually causes microcytic anaemia, not pancytopenia.
- B. Incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolytic anaemia rather than marrow failure.
- C. Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease causes a bleeding tendency but does not cause pancytopenia.
- D. Incorrect. Sickle trait is usually asymptomatic and does not cause pancytopenia.
- E. Correct. Pancytopenia with no significant organomegaly is characteristic of aplastic anaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Aplastic anaemia: pancytopenia due to hypocellular marrow.
- Anaemia causes pallor; neutropenia predisposes to infection; thrombocytopenia causes bleeding.
- Significant lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses.

questions.stem: Which bone-marrow finding confirms the suspected marrow-failure pattern?

options.label: B
options.text: Increased iron stores with normal cellularity

options.label: C
options.text: Hypocellular marrow with increased fat spaces

options.label: E
options.text: Hypercellular marrow completely replaced by blasts

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypocellular marrow with increased fat spaces
questions.initialExplanation: Aplastic anaemia is associated with a hypoplastic or hypocellular bone marrow with increased fat and no evidence of malignancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Increased megakaryocytes may be seen in ITP.
- B. Incorrect. Iron stores do not define aplastic marrow failure.
- C. Correct. This is the marrow appearance described.
- D. Incorrect. Plasma-cell excess is not the described finding.
- E. Incorrect. A marrow replaced by blasts suggests acute leukaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bone-marrow aspiration/biopsy is central to confirming aplastic anaemia.
- Expect hypocellularity and increased fat.
- Exclude malignant marrow infiltration.

questions.stem: Which group of exposures is listed among acquired causes of aplastic anaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Excess cow's milk and low dietary iron

options.label: D
options.text: Certain drugs, benzene, irradiation and infections

questions.correctAnswerText: Certain drugs, benzene, irradiation and infections
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance lists infections, chemicals such as benzene, selected drugs and irradiation among acquired causes of aplastic anaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This pattern contributes to nutritional iron deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Intrinsic-factor deficiency causes B12 malabsorption.
- C. Incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency causes haemophilia A.
- D. Correct. These are all recognized acquired associations listed.
- E. Incorrect. These are triggers for oxidant haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Aplastic anaemia may be inherited, acquired or idiopathic.
- Acquired causes include infections, drugs, chemicals and irradiation.
- Review medication and exposure history.

questions.stem: Which treatment strategy is included for severe aplastic anaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Splenectomy as definitive treatment in children in routine care

options.label: B
options.text: Supportive blood-component transfusion and infection control, with stem-cell transplantation considered

options.label: D
options.text: Oral iron and dietary advice alone

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive blood-component transfusion and infection control, with stem-cell transplantation considered
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include supportive packed red-cell and platelet transfusions, infection control and bone-marrow or stem-cell transplantation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not definitive treatment for aplastic anaemia.
- B. Correct. These are the core supportive and definitive strategies described.
- C. Incorrect. Desmopressin does not treat marrow failure.
- D. Incorrect. Nutritional iron replacement does not correct pancytopenia from marrow failure.
- E. Incorrect. Iron chelation does not restore marrow cellularity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Support red-cell and platelet deficits as clinically indicated.
- Control infection, especially in neutropenia.
- Stem-cell transplantation is an important definitive option.

cases.title: Congenital anomalies with progressive cytopenias
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child is referred for short stature, microcephaly, abnormal thumbs and café-au-lait skin pigmentation. The full blood count shows pancytopenia with an increased MCV. Bone-marrow examination is hypocellular.

questions.stem: Which inherited disorder best explains the combination?
questions.correctAnswerText: Fanconi anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Fanconi anaemia is an inherited bone-marrow-failure syndrome associated with pancytopenia, macrocytosis and congenital abnormalities including short stature, skin pigmentation and thumb/radial defects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding.
- B. Incorrect. IDA causes microcytosis and does not explain the congenital anomalies.
- C. Incorrect. ITP usually produces isolated thrombocytopenia.
- D. Incorrect. Warm AIHA causes immune haemolysis, not congenital marrow failure.
- E. Correct. The congenital anomalies and progressive marrow failure strongly support Fanconi anaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fanconi anaemia is the most common inherited form of aplastic anaemia.
- It is autosomal recessive.
- Look for short stature, microcephaly, café-au-lait pigmentation and thumb/radial abnormalities.

questions.stem: Which genetic inheritance pattern is described for Fanconi anaemia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Autosomal recessive
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance describes Fanconi anaemia as an autosomal recessive disorder involving mutations in FANC genes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fanconi anaemia is not Y-linked.
- B. Incorrect. Autosomal dominant inheritance is described for many cases of hereditary spherocytosis, not Fanconi anaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Mitochondrial inheritance is not the pattern given.
- D. Correct. This is the inheritance pattern stated.
- E. Incorrect. Fanconi anaemia is not described as X-linked dominant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fanconi anaemia: autosomal recessive.
- Multiple FANC genes may be involved.
- Bone-marrow failure often becomes apparent during early childhood.

questions.stem: Which test is specifically used to identify the chromosome-instability phenotype of Fanconi anaemia?

options.label: C
options.text: Chromosome-breakage test on peripheral blood lymphocytes

questions.correctAnswerText: Chromosome-breakage test on peripheral blood lymphocytes
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include chromosome-breakage testing of peripheral blood lymphocytes as a test used to identify affected individuals and for family or prenatal assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Cold agglutination testing evaluates cold-antibody haemolysis.
- B. Incorrect. Osmotic fragility testing evaluates hereditary spherocytosis.
- C. Correct. Chromosome instability with increased breakage is the diagnostic principle described.
- D. Incorrect. Ristocetin cofactor activity evaluates von Willebrand factor function.
- E. Incorrect. Direct Coombs testing evaluates immune-mediated red-cell destruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fanconi anaemia is associated with chromosome instability.
- Clinical guidance chromosome-breakage testing and genetic studies.
- Bone marrow is typically hypocellular.

questions.stem: Which additional long-term risk is emphasized in the Fanconi anaemia section?

options.label: B
options.text: Increased risk of leukaemia and solid tumours

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased risk of leukaemia and solid tumours
questions.initialExplanation: Key features include an increased risk of leukaemia and solid tumours in Fanconi anaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron deficiency is not the key long-term risk described.
- B. Correct. Malignancy risk is an important long-term complication.
- C. Incorrect. Fanconi anaemia increases rather than eliminates malignancy risk.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance explicitly identifies increased malignancy risk.
- E. Incorrect. Haemarthrosis is associated with coagulation-factor deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fanconi anaemia combines congenital abnormalities and marrow failure.
- Monitor for haematological and solid malignancies.
- Genetic counselling is important.

topics.name: Other inherited marrow-failure syndromes and TEC

cases.title: An infant with anaemia and congenital abnormalities
cases.vignette: A 3-month-old infant presents with pallor and poor feeding. The haemoglobin is low and the MCV is increased, while the white-cell and platelet counts are preserved. Examination reveals a congenital thumb abnormality.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia is a pure red-cell aplasia that often presents in infancy with macrocytic anaemia and may be associated with congenital anomalies, including a triphalangeal thumb.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia rather than isolated red-cell failure.
- B. Correct. Early infancy, isolated red-cell anaemia, macrocytosis and a congenital anomaly fit DBA.
- C. Incorrect. DIC causes consumptive coagulopathy in a critically ill child.
- D. Incorrect. TEC usually occurs later in childhood after a viral illness, without congenital anomalies.
- E. Incorrect. ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DBA is a pure red-cell aplasia.
- It often presents in infancy with macrocytic anaemia.
- Congenital abnormalities may include skeletal, craniofacial and renal anomalies.

questions.stem: Which feature would favour Shwachman-Diamond syndrome over Diamond-Blackfan anaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute intravascular haemolysis after fava-bean exposure

options.label: B
options.text: Isolated thrombocytopenia after a viral infection

options.label: C
options.text: Isolated pure red-cell aplasia in infancy

options.label: D
options.text: Severe mucosal bleeding with normal platelet count

options.label: E
options.text: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency with chronic diarrhoea and neutropenia

questions.correctAnswerText: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency with chronic diarrhoea and neutropenia
questions.initialExplanation: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is described with pancreatic exocrine failure, chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive and neutropenia or pancytopenia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is characteristic of G6PD-related oxidative haemolysis.
- B. Incorrect. This is more typical of acute ITP.
- C. Incorrect. Isolated pure red-cell aplasia is more characteristic of DBA.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests a platelet-function or von Willebrand disorder.
- E. Correct. Pancreatic insufficiency and neutropenia are key clues to Shwachman-Diamond syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Shwachman-Diamond syndrome: pancreatic exocrine failure plus marrow dysfunction.
- Chronic diarrhoea and failure to thrive may be present.
- Clinical guidance notes an increased risk of leukaemia.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 2-year-old develops isolated anaemia several weeks after a viral illness. The MCV is normal, white cells and platelets are normal, and the child begins to recover spontaneously. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood
questions.initialExplanation: TEC usually affects children aged 6 months to 5 years, may follow a viral infection and causes an isolated red-cell defect with spontaneous recovery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. DIC is a consumptive coagulopathy in a critically ill patient.
- B. Correct. The age, preceding viral illness, isolated anaemia and spontaneous recovery fit TEC.
- C. Incorrect. Leukaemia often causes broader marrow abnormalities and may produce blasts or organ infiltration.
- D. Incorrect. DBA presents in infancy and is often associated with congenital anomalies and macrocytosis.
- E. Incorrect. Fanconi anaemia causes inherited marrow failure with congenital anomalies and often macrocytosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TEC: age 6 months-5 years.
- Often follows a viral illness.
- Isolated red-cell defect, usually normocytic, with spontaneous recovery over weeks.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly distinguishes aplastic anaemia from DBA and TEC?

options.label: A
options.text: Spontaneous recovery after a viral illness

questions.correctAnswerText: Pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow
questions.initialExplanation: Aplastic anaemia affects all three major blood-cell lineages and is associated with a hypocellular marrow. DBA and TEC predominantly affect red-cell production.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Spontaneous recovery after a viral illness is characteristic of TEC.
- B. Correct. Pancytopenia with hypocellular marrow is the defining pattern of aplastic anaemia.
- C. Incorrect. A normal white-cell count does not establish aplastic anaemia.
- D. Incorrect. A normal platelet count may be seen in isolated red-cell disorders.
- E. Incorrect. Isolated anaemia may occur in DBA or TEC.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Aplastic anaemia affects RBCs, WBCs and platelets.
- DBA is predominantly pure red-cell aplasia.
- TEC is a transient isolated red-cell disorder in young children.

cases.title: A child with recurrent bleeding
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child is referred for a history of recurrent bleeding. The clinician needs to determine whether the bleeding pattern points to a platelet disorder or a coagulation-factor deficiency before ordering targeted tests.

questions.stem: Which bleeding pattern most strongly suggests a platelet disorder?

options.label: A
options.text: Recurrent deep muscle haematomas and haemarthrosis

options.label: B
options.text: Spontaneous intracranial bleeding as the presentation

options.label: C
options.text: Delayed bleeding into joints after trauma

options.label: D
options.text: Deep retroperitoneal bleeding with normal platelet function

options.label: E
options.text: Petechiae, purpura and mucosal bleeding such as epistaxis or gum bleeding

questions.correctAnswerText: Petechiae, purpura and mucosal bleeding such as epistaxis or gum bleeding
questions.initialExplanation: Platelet disorders typically cause mucocutaneous bleeding and superficial skin findings such as petechiae, purpura and bruising.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Deep muscle bleeding and haemarthrosis suggest a coagulation-factor disorder such as haemophilia.
- B. Incorrect. Intracranial bleeding can occur in severe disorders but is not the distinguishing routine pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Delayed deep bleeding is more consistent with coagulation-factor deficiency.
- D. Incorrect. Deep-tissue bleeding suggests coagulation problems rather than a primary platelet disorder.
- E. Correct. This is the typical platelet-disorder pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Platelet disorders: mucosal bleeding, petechiae and immediate bleeding.
- Coagulation disorders: deep tissue bleeding, muscle haematoma and haemarthrosis.
- The history of bleeding after trauma is diagnostically useful.

questions.stem: Which bleeding pattern is most characteristic of haemophilia?

options.label: A
options.text: Recurrent gum bleeding with a low platelet count

options.label: B
options.text: Isolated conjunctival petechiae after a viral illness

options.label: E
options.text: Purpura with normal coagulation and platelet tests in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Deep muscle bleeding and haemarthrosis
questions.initialExplanation: Coagulation-factor deficiencies typically cause deep-tissue bleeding, including muscle haematomas and haemarthrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mucosal bleeding with thrombocytopenia points toward a platelet disorder.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the typical deep-bleeding pattern of haemophilia.
- C. Incorrect. Petechiae are more typical of platelet-number or function disorders.
- D. Correct. Recurrent joint and deep-muscle bleeding is characteristic of haemophilia.
- E. Incorrect. The clinical and laboratory findings depend on the specific disorder; this is not a defining haemophilia pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Haemophilia: deep bleeding and haemarthrosis.
- Platelet disorders: mucosal and superficial bleeding.
- Delayed oozing after trauma suggests a coagulation abnormality.

questions.stem: Which screening test evaluates the extrinsic coagulation pathway?
questions.correctAnswerText: Prothrombin time (PT)
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include PT as the test of the extrinsic pathway and lists factors II, V, VII and X in its measured pathway.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. aPTT evaluates the intrinsic and common pathways.
- B. Incorrect. Platelet count measures platelet number, not the extrinsic pathway.
- C. Correct. PT evaluates the extrinsic and common pathways.
- D. Incorrect. Ristocetin cofactor activity evaluates von Willebrand factor function.
- E. Incorrect. Bleeding time historically assessed platelet-related haemostasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PT: extrinsic/common pathway.
- aPTT: intrinsic/common pathway.
- Thrombin time evaluates conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin.

questions.stem: A child has suspected coagulation-factor deficiency. Which test is most directly used to assess the intrinsic pathway?
questions.correctAnswerText: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include aPTT as the screening test for the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. PT primarily assesses the extrinsic and common pathways.
- B. Incorrect. Platelet count evaluates platelet number.
- C. Incorrect. Ferritin assesses iron stores.
- D. Incorrect. A blood film may identify morphological abnormalities but does not directly measure the intrinsic pathway.
- E. Correct. aPTT assesses factors in the intrinsic pathway and common pathway.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- APTT is commonly prolonged in haemophilia A and B.
- PT is usually normal in isolated haemophilia A or B.
- Always interpret screening tests alongside the bleeding history and specific factor assays.

cases.title: Recurrent joint swelling in a young boy
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old boy develops a painful swollen knee after minor trauma. He has had prolonged bleeding after circumcision and recurrent deep bruising. His platelet count and PT are normal, but aPTT is prolonged.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Haemophilia
questions.initialExplanation: Haemophilia causes deep-tissue bleeding and haemarthrosis with a prolonged aPTT and usually normal PT and platelet count.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ITP causes thrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding, not isolated prolonged aPTT.
- B. Incorrect. HS causes haemolytic anaemia.
- C. Correct. The deep bleeding pattern and prolonged aPTT strongly suggest haemophilia.
- D. Incorrect. DIC usually causes systemic illness with multiple abnormal coagulation tests and low platelets.
- E. Incorrect. IDA does not cause haemarthrosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Haemophilia is usually X-linked recessive.
- Haemarthrosis and muscle haematomas are hallmark features.
- PT and platelet count are generally normal; aPTT is prolonged.

questions.stem: Which factor is deficient in haemophilia A?
questions.correctAnswerText: Factor VIII
questions.initialExplanation: Haemophilia A is caused by factor VIII deficiency, whereas haemophilia B is caused by factor IX deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Factor VIII deficiency defines haemophilia A.
- B. Incorrect. von Willebrand factor deficiency causes von Willebrand disease.
- C. Incorrect. Factor VII belongs to the extrinsic pathway and is not the cause of haemophilia A.
- D. Incorrect. Factor IX deficiency causes haemophilia B.
- E. Incorrect. Factor XI deficiency is haemophilia C.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Haemophilia A: factor VIII deficiency.
- Haemophilia B: factor IX deficiency.
- Haemophilia C: factor XI deficiency.

questions.stem: Which test confirms the specific type of haemophilia?

options.label: E
options.text: Specific factor assay showing reduced factor VIII or IX activity

questions.correctAnswerText: Specific factor assay showing reduced factor VIII or IX activity
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes measuring factor VIII or IX levels to establish the specific haemophilia diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ferritin measures iron stores.
- B. Incorrect. Direct Coombs testing investigates immune red-cell destruction.
- C. Incorrect. Osmotic fragility is used in hereditary spherocytosis.
- D. Incorrect. Cold agglutination testing evaluates cold-antibody haemolysis.
- E. Correct. Specific factor assays identify the deficient coagulation factor.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- APTT is a screening clue.
- Factor assay confirms haemophilia type and severity.
- Severity relates to the residual factor activity.

questions.stem: Which treatment may be used for selected patients with mild haemophilia A?

options.label: E
options.text: Desmopressin to release endogenous von Willebrand factor and factor VIII

questions.correctAnswerText: Desmopressin to release endogenous von Willebrand factor and factor VIII
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that desmopressin may be used in mild haemophilia A because it increases endogenous release of von Willebrand factor and factor VIII.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Deferasirox is an iron chelator.
- B. Incorrect. Iron does not correct factor VIII deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Platelet transfusion is not routine prophylaxis for haemophilia.
- D. Incorrect. Hydroxyurea is used in sickle cell disease to increase HbF.
- E. Correct. Desmopressin can raise endogenous factor VIII and von Willebrand factor in responsive mild haemophilia A.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Recombinant factor VIII is used for haemophilia A.
- Desmopressin may help selected patients with mild haemophilia A.
- Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs and unnecessary intramuscular injections as advised.

cases.title: Preventing recurrent joint bleeding in severe haemophilia A
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old boy has severe haemophilia A and has already experienced repeated joint bleeds. The team wants to reduce further spontaneous joint bleeding and prevent progressive joint damage.

questions.stem: Which long-term strategy most closely follows the prophylaxis plan in the course clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Regular intravenous factor VIII prophylaxis two to three times weekly, aiming to maintain factor VIII activity above 2%

options.label: B
options.text: Desmopressin as the sole long-term treatment for each severe case

options.label: C
options.text: Routine platelet transfusions after each minor injury

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid most activity and give factor replacement after permanent joint deformity develops

options.label: E
options.text: Lifelong oral iron to prevent factor VIII deficiency

questions.correctAnswerText: Regular intravenous factor VIII prophylaxis two to three times weekly, aiming to maintain factor VIII activity above 2%
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes prophylactic factor VIII in severe haemophilia to prevent spontaneous joint bleeding. It gives an intravenous schedule of two to three times weekly to maintain factor VIII above 2%; primary prophylaxis usually begins at 2–3 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the schedule, target and preventive purpose stated in the course clinical guidance.
- B. Incorrect. Desmopressin is described for selected mild haemophilia A, not as sole prophylaxis for every severe case.
- C. Incorrect. Haemophilia is a coagulation-factor deficiency; platelet transfusions are not routine prophylaxis.
- D. Incorrect. Clinical descriptions include active prophylaxis to prevent spontaneous joint bleeding, not waiting for established deformity.
- E. Incorrect. Iron does not replace factor VIII or prevent haemarthrosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Haemophilia A is due to factor VIII deficiency.
- Severe disease is associated with spontaneous joint and muscle bleeding.
- clinical guidance gives factor VIII prophylaxis two to three times weekly, maintaining a level above 2%.
- Primary prophylaxis usually begins at 2–3 years of age.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Haemophilia prophylaxis and long-term complications, Pages 35–36.
source.sheet: Haematology sheet – Haemophilia prophylaxis and long-term complications,

cases.title: Grading the severity of haemophilia A
cases.vignette: A boy with recurrent joint bleeding is found to have factor VIII activity of 0.5% of normal. The clinical team uses the factor-level table in the course clinical guidance to grade disease severity.

questions.stem: How is this level classified?
questions.correctAnswerText: Severe haemophilia
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe severe haemophilia as factor VIII activity below 1%, with a tendency to spontaneous joint and muscle bleeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mild disease is listed as factor VIII above 5% up to 40%.
- B. Incorrect. A factor VIII activity of 0.5% is markedly reduced.
- C. Incorrect. Moderate disease is listed as 1–5%.
- D. Incorrect. The case gives a factor VIII activity level used to grade haemophilia; it does not describe vWF testing.
- E. Correct. 0.5% is below the less-than-1% threshold for severe haemophilia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Severe: factor VIII below 1%; spontaneous joint/muscle bleeds.
- Moderate: 1–5%; bleeding after minor trauma.
- Mild: above 5–40%; bleeding after surgery.

cases.title: Factor XI deficiency
cases.vignette: A child has a mild inherited bleeding tendency. Specific coagulation testing identifies reduced factor XI activity, while the history does not suggest the severe recurrent joint bleeding classically associated with severe haemophilia A or B.

questions.stem: Which condition is associated with factor XI deficiency in the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Haemophilia C
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include haemophilia C as factor XI deficiency. It is described as very rare, autosomal recessive and usually milder, with some patients having no bleeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Haemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Haemophilia B is factor IX deficiency.
- C. Correct. Haemophilia C is the factor XI deficiency described.
- D. Incorrect. Type I von Willebrand disease is a partial vWF deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. DIC is an acquired consumptive coagulopathy, not an inherited factor XI deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Haemophilia A: factor VIII deficiency.
- Haemophilia B: factor IX deficiency.
- Haemophilia C: factor XI deficiency; very rare and described as autosomal recessive and generally milder.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Inherited coagulation disorders, Page 33.

cases.title: Inhibitors complicating haemophilia treatment
cases.vignette: A child with haemophilia has a reduced response to replacement treatment.

questions.stem: Which complication can reduce or completely inhibit the effect of factor VIII or factor IX replacement?

options.label: D
options.text: Development of inhibitors (antibodies to factor VIII or IX)

questions.correctAnswerText: Development of inhibitors (antibodies to factor VIII or IX)
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include inhibitors as antibodies to factor VIII or IX that may reduce or completely inhibit treatment effect. It gives an occurrence of approximately 5–20%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron overload is a complication of repeated transfusion, especially in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Functional hyposplenism is associated with sickle cell disease and infection risk.
- C. Incorrect. Platelet sequestration is not the factor-replacement complication described.
- D. Correct. Inhibitors are antibodies to factor VIII or IX and can reduce or block replacement treatment.
- E. Incorrect. B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and may cause neurological manifestations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance gives inhibitor development in approximately 5–20%.
- Inhibitors may reduce or completely inhibit factor treatment.
- standard guidance mentions very high factor doses or bypassing agents such as factor VIIa for bleeding, and possible immune-tolerance induction.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Complications of haemophilia treatment, Page 36.
source.sheet: Haematology sheet – Complications of haemophilia treatment,

cases.title: Recurrent epistaxis and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction
cases.vignette: A 12-year-old girl has recurrent epistaxis, easy bruising, heavy menstrual bleeding and prolonged oozing after dental extraction. Her platelet count is normal. The family reports similar bleeding in several relatives.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Von Willebrand disease
questions.initialExplanation: Von Willebrand disease is a common inherited bleeding disorder and typically causes mucocutaneous bleeding, including epistaxis, menorrhagia and prolonged bleeding after procedures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia rather than an isolated inherited bleeding tendency.
- B. Incorrect. Haemophilia B more typically causes deep tissue bleeding and haemarthrosis.
- C. Incorrect. HS causes chronic haemolysis.
- D. Correct. The mucosal bleeding pattern and family history support von Willebrand disease.
- E. Incorrect. Sickle cell disease causes haemolysis and vaso-occlusive complications.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder.
- Mucosal bleeding, epistaxis, menorrhagia and post-procedure bleeding are typical.
- Family history is common but may be absent.

questions.stem: What is the primary role of von Willebrand factor in haemostasis?

options.label: A
options.text: It facilitates platelet adhesion to damaged endothelium and protects factor VIII from clearance

options.label: D
options.text: It activates vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum

questions.correctAnswerText: It facilitates platelet adhesion to damaged endothelium and protects factor VIII from clearance
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include two major functions of vWF: platelet adhesion to damaged endothelium and protection of factor VIII from inactivation and clearance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Both functions are explicitly described in the course clinical guidance.
- B. Incorrect. Plasminogen activation is part of fibrinolysis and is not the primary vWF role.
- C. Incorrect. Haemoglobin is produced during erythropoiesis.
- D. Incorrect. B12 absorption involves intrinsic factor and the terminal ileum.
- E. Incorrect. vWF does not destroy platelets.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- VWF supports platelet adhesion.
- vWF carries and stabilizes factor VIII.
- Deficiency can cause mucocutaneous bleeding and a reduced factor VIII level.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern is most consistent with von Willebrand disease in the course clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Low platelet count with prolonged PT and low fibrinogen

options.label: B
options.text: Shortened PT and shortened aPTT with high fibrinogen

options.label: C
options.text: Prolonged PT with normal aPTT and severe thrombocytopenia

options.label: D
options.text: Normal PT, normal aPTT and absent factor IX

options.label: E
options.text: Normal PT with prolonged bleeding time and prolonged aPTT in many cases

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal PT with prolonged bleeding time and prolonged aPTT in many cases
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance normal PT, prolonged bleeding time and reduced vWF antigen/activity; aPTT may be prolonged because vWF stabilizes factor VIII.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This pattern suggests a consumptive coagulopathy such as DIC.
- B. Incorrect. This is not a recognized pattern for vWD.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the characteristic vWD profile.
- D. Incorrect. Isolated factor IX deficiency is haemophilia B.
- E. Correct. This reflects the pattern described for vWD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PT is usually normal in vWD.
- vWF antigen and functional activity are reduced.
- aPTT can be prolonged due to reduced factor VIII stabilization.

questions.stem: Which treatment may be used for mild von Willebrand disease and selected mucosal bleeding?

options.label: A
options.text: Desmopressin and/or tranexamic acid, depending on the bleeding site and clinical context

options.label: C
options.text: Routine factor IX replacement for each patient

questions.correctAnswerText: Desmopressin and/or tranexamic acid, depending on the bleeding site and clinical context
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include desmopressin as a way to release endogenous vWF and factor VIII, and tranexamic acid as an option for mucosal bleeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These treatments are listed for selected vWD presentations.
- B. Incorrect. Hydroxyurea is used for sickle cell disease.
- C. Incorrect. Factor IX replacement is for haemophilia B, not vWD.
- D. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not standard treatment for vWD.
- E. Incorrect. Iron chelation treats iron overload.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treatment depends on vWD type and bleeding severity.
- Desmopressin can increase endogenous vWF and factor VIII in responsive patients.
- Tranexamic acid is useful for selected mucosal bleeding.

cases.title: Type I von Willebrand disease
cases.vignette: An adolescent girl presents with mild mucosal bleeding and a history of prolonged mucosal or post-procedure bleeding. The clinician explains that von Willebrand disease can be classified according to whether von Willebrand factor is partially reduced, functionally abnormal or completely absent.

questions.stem: Which type is described in the course clinical guidance as a partial deficiency and the commonest form?
questions.correctAnswerText: Type I
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include type I von Willebrand disease as a partial deficiency of vWF and the commonest type, accounting for approximately 60–80%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Type III is described as complete absence of vWF.
- B. Incorrect. Type II is described as a qualitative defect in vWF.
- C. Incorrect. Haemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency.
- D. Correct. Type I is the partial vWF deficiency and is listed as the commonest type.
- E. Incorrect. Haemophilia B is factor IX deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type I: partial vWF deficiency; commonest (about 60–80%).
- Type II: qualitative vWF defect.
- Type III: complete absence of vWF.
- Clinical descriptions include type I as generally mild and sometimes diagnosed around late puberty.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Von Willebrand disease, Page 33.

cases.title: A blood product no longer recommended for von Willebrand disease
cases.vignette: A child with von Willebrand disease requires treatment for a bleeding episode. The clinician reviews the products and measures discussed in the course clinical guidance and avoids an older product that standard guidance says is no longer used for this condition.

questions.stem: Which product does standard guidance state is no longer used to treat von Willebrand disease because it has not undergone viral inactivation?

options.label: C
options.text: Recombinant factor VIII in selected severe cases

questions.correctAnswerText: Cryoprecipitate
questions.initialExplanation: The von Willebrand disease section states that cryoprecipitate is no longer used because it has not undergone viral inactivation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin is listed as a treatment option for suitable cases because it releases endogenous vWF and factor VIII.
- B. Incorrect. Tranexamic acid is listed for mucosal bleeding.
- C. Incorrect. Recombinant factor VIII is listed for severe types of vWD.
- D. Incorrect. These are general preventive measures, not a blood product.
- E. Correct. This is the product specifically identified as no longer used for vWD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Desmopressin may increase endogenous vWF and factor VIII in responsive patients.
- Tranexamic acid is listed for mucosal bleeding.
- It is recognized that cryoprecipitate is no longer used for vWD because it has not undergone viral inactivation.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Von Willebrand disease management, Pages 34–35.
source.sheet: Haematology sheet – Von Willebrand disease management,

cases.title: Petechiae after a viral illness
cases.vignette: A previously well 4-year-old child develops widespread petechiae and bruising approximately two weeks after an upper respiratory tract infection. There is no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Haemoglobin and white-cell count are normal, but the platelet count is markedly reduced.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)
questions.initialExplanation: ITP is the commonest cause of thrombocytopenia in childhood and often follows a viral infection, presenting with petechiae, purpura and bruising.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The isolated low platelet count, recent viral illness and otherwise well child strongly support ITP.
- B. Incorrect. Haemophilia causes deep bleeding with a prolonged aPTT, not isolated thrombocytopenia.
- C. Incorrect. IDA causes microcytic anaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia major causes severe chronic haemolytic anaemia.
- E. Incorrect. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ITP is the commonest childhood cause of thrombocytopenia.
- Often follows an upper respiratory infection by 1-3 weeks.
- Typical examination: petechiae, purpura and bruising without organomegaly.

questions.stem: Which mechanism causes ITP?

options.label: D
options.text: IgG autoantibodies coat platelets, leading to splenic destruction

questions.correctAnswerText: IgG autoantibodies coat platelets, leading to splenic destruction
questions.initialExplanation: In ITP, antiplatelet IgG autoantibodies coat platelets, which are then recognized and destroyed in splenic sinusoids through Fc receptors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Reduced beta-globin synthesis causes beta-thalassaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Alpha-globin deficiency causes alpha-thalassaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Oxidative haemoglobin damage occurs in G6PD deficiency.
- D. Correct. This is the immune mechanism described.
- E. Incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency causes haemophilia A.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ITP is an immune-mediated platelet-destruction disorder.
- Antibody-coated platelets are cleared in the spleen.
- The remainder of the CBC is often normal in typical acute ITP.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern is most consistent with typical ITP?

options.label: A
options.text: Low haemoglobin with high reticulocytes and positive Coombs test

options.label: B
options.text: Low factor VIII with normal platelet count

options.label: C
options.text: High platelet count with prolonged PT

options.label: D
options.text: Low platelet count with normal haemoglobin and white-cell count, and normal PT/aPTT

options.label: E
options.text: Pancytopenia with prolonged PT and aPTT

questions.correctAnswerText: Low platelet count with normal haemoglobin and white-cell count, and normal PT/aPTT
questions.initialExplanation: Typical ITP is an isolated thrombocytopenia. PT and aPTT are usually normal, and the other cell lines are generally preserved.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This pattern suggests immune haemolytic anaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Reduced factor VIII indicates haemophilia A rather than ITP.
- C. Incorrect. This does not fit isolated immune platelet destruction.
- D. Correct. This is the characteristic laboratory profile described.
- E. Incorrect. Pancytopenia suggests marrow failure; prolonged coagulation tests may occur in DIC.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typical ITP: isolated thrombocytopenia.
- PT and aPTT are normal.
- Blood film usually shows reduced platelet number with otherwise preserved morphology.

questions.stem: A child thought to have ITP also has bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly and blasts on the blood film. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Give desmopressin and ignore the blood film

options.label: C
options.text: Diagnose uncomplicated ITP without further evaluation

options.label: D
options.text: Reconsider the diagnosis and perform bone-marrow evaluation to exclude leukaemia or marrow failure

questions.correctAnswerText: Reconsider the diagnosis and perform bone-marrow evaluation to exclude leukaemia or marrow failure
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance warns that atypical features such as bone pain, organomegaly, anaemia, neutropenia or blasts require further investigation to exclude acute leukaemia or aplastic anaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin does not treat ITP and cannot replace diagnostic assessment.
- B. Incorrect. Iron therapy does not address possible marrow malignancy.
- C. Incorrect. Organomegaly, bone pain and blasts are atypical and potentially serious.
- D. Correct. These are red flags against typical isolated ITP and require diagnostic reassessment.
- E. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not immediate treatment for a newly suspected ITP presentation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion.
- Bone pain, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, additional cytopenias or blasts are red flags.
- Bone-marrow examination is not routine in typical ITP but is considered when features are atypical.

cases.title: Bleeding in a critically ill child
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child is admitted to intensive care with severe sepsis and shock. The child develops petechiae, bruising, persistent oozing from venepuncture sites and areas of skin necrosis. Laboratory tests show thrombocytopenia and prolonged coagulation times.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains the simultaneous bleeding and thrombotic manifestations?
questions.correctAnswerText: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
questions.initialExplanation: DIC involves widespread activation of coagulation with consumption of platelets and clotting factors, producing both bleeding and thrombosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Haemophilia causes factor-specific deep bleeding, not widespread clotting activation.
- B. Correct. The critically ill septic child with bleeding and skin necrosis has a typical DIC presentation.
- C. Incorrect. vWD causes mucocutaneous bleeding, not systemic consumptive coagulopathy.
- D. Incorrect. IDA does not cause a consumptive coagulation syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. ITP causes isolated platelet destruction and does not explain consumption of coagulation factors with thrombosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DIC is a systemic consumptive coagulopathy.
- Bleeding and thrombosis may occur together.
- Sepsis and shock are important triggers in children.

questions.stem: Which laboratory combination is most consistent with DIC?

options.label: A
options.text: Low platelets, prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen and increased D-dimer

options.label: B
options.text: Normal platelets, normal PT/aPTT and normal fibrinogen

options.label: D
options.text: Isolated prolonged aPTT with normal fibrinogen and normal D-dimer

options.label: E
options.text: High platelets, shortened PT and shortened aPTT

questions.correctAnswerText: Low platelets, prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen and increased D-dimer
