questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include thrombocytopenia, prolonged coagulation tests, reduced fibrinogen and raised D-dimer/FDP in DIC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the characteristic consumptive pattern described.
- B. Incorrect. Normal results do not support DIC.
- C. Incorrect. This is an iron-deficiency pattern, not a coagulation profile.
- D. Incorrect. Isolated prolonged aPTT suggests a factor deficiency or inhibitor rather than DIC.
- E. Incorrect. DIC consumes platelets and coagulation factors rather than producing this pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DIC: platelets low, PT/aPTT prolonged, fibrinogen low, D-dimer high.
- D-dimer reflects fibrin breakdown.
- Interpret results in the context of critical illness and the underlying cause.

questions.stem: What is the most important principle in the management of DIC?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat the underlying cause while providing appropriate supportive care

options.label: B
options.text: Give iron as the sole treatment

options.label: C
options.text: Give routine desmopressin to each patient

options.label: E
options.text: Ignore sepsis and treat the platelet count

questions.correctAnswerText: Treat the underlying cause while providing appropriate supportive care
questions.initialExplanation: DIC management is challenging and centres on treating the cause, managing shock and providing blood components when indicated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Treating sepsis, shock or another trigger is fundamental; supportive products are given according to clinical need.
- B. Incorrect. Iron does not correct coagulation-factor and platelet consumption.
- C. Incorrect. Desmopressin is not routine DIC therapy.
- D. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not a treatment for DIC.
- E. Incorrect. Treating the underlying cause is essential; focusing only on platelets is inadequate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stabilize the patient and treat the trigger, especially sepsis or shock.
- Blood components may be required for significant bleeding or procedures.
- Heparin use is controversial and depends on specialist assessment and the clinical context.

questions.stem: Which cause is emphasized with multiple asterisks in the course-clinical guidance DIC section?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sepsis
questions.initialExplanation: Sepsis is highlighted as a major cause of DIC in the course clinical guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia.
- B. Correct. Sepsis is specifically emphasized in the list of DIC causes.
- C. Incorrect. Iron deficiency is not a typical trigger of DIC.
- D. Incorrect. Coeliac disease may cause malabsorption and iron deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. Sickle trait is not listed as a DIC cause.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sepsis is a major paediatric DIC trigger.
- Other listed causes include tissue injury, shock, malignancy, venom/toxin and neonatal conditions.
- Recognize DIC early in a critically ill child with bleeding or thrombosis.

cases.title: Supportive treatment of bleeding DIC
cases.vignette: A critically ill child with sepsis and shock develops bleeding from venepuncture sites. The platelet count and fibrinogen are low, coagulation times are prolonged and D-dimer is raised. The clinical picture is consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

questions.stem: Which management package is listed in the course clinical guidance for this situation?

options.label: B
options.text: ICU care, treatment of shock and the underlying cause, with fresh frozen plasma and platelet transfusion as indicated

options.label: C
options.text: Routine splenectomy followed by lifelong penicillin

options.label: E
options.text: Stop most treatment until the platelet count normalizes spontaneously

questions.correctAnswerText: ICU care, treatment of shock and the underlying cause, with fresh frozen plasma and platelet transfusion as indicated
questions.initialExplanation: The DIC section describes ICU care, treatment of shock and the underlying cause, and use of FFP and platelet transfusion as part of management.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron does not correct consumptive coagulopathy or shock.
- B. Correct. This matches the treatment elements listed.
- C. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not a treatment for DIC.
- D. Incorrect. Desmopressin is not listed as sole treatment for DIC.
- E. Incorrect. clinical guidance emphasizes urgent supportive management and treatment of the cause.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DIC may cause both bleeding and thrombosis.
- Treat the underlying cause, manage shock and provide supportive blood components when indicated.
- Clinical guidance notes that heparin use is controversial.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Disseminated intravascular coagulation, Page 40.

cases.title: A child with pallor, fever, bruising and bone pain
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old child presents with fatigue, pallor, recurrent fever, bruising and leg pain. Examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly and generalized lymphadenopathy. The full blood count shows anaemia and thrombocytopenia, and the blood film contains blasts.

questions.stem: Which malignancy is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.text: Acute leukaemia, most likely acute lymphoblastic leukaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Acute leukaemia, most likely acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is the commonest childhood leukaemia and commonly presents in early childhood with marrow failure and organ infiltration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ITP usually causes isolated thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well child.
- B. Incorrect. HS causes chronic haemolysis and does not explain blasts.
- C. Incorrect. IDA does not cause blasts, generalized lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
- D. Incorrect. vWD causes mucocutaneous bleeding but not blasts or marrow infiltration.
- E. Correct. The age, pallor, fever, bruising, bone pain, organomegaly and blasts strongly support acute leukaemia, most commonly ALL.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ALL is the commonest childhood leukaemia.
- Peak age: 2-5 years.
- Marrow failure causes pallor, infection and bleeding; infiltration causes bone pain and organomegaly.

questions.stem: Which investigation is diagnostic for acute leukaemia in the course clinical guidance?

options.label: B
options.text: Bone-marrow aspiration showing a substantial blast-cell population

questions.correctAnswerText: Bone-marrow aspiration showing a substantial blast-cell population
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include bone-marrow aspiration with blast-cell assessment as the diagnostic investigation for acute leukaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ferritin assesses iron stores.
- B. Correct. Bone-marrow examination establishes the marrow blast population and supports classification.
- C. Incorrect. Platelet-function analysis evaluates platelet function.
- D. Incorrect. Osmotic fragility testing evaluates hereditary spherocytosis.
- E. Incorrect. Direct Coombs testing investigates immune haemolysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Peripheral blood may show blasts, but marrow examination is central to diagnosis.
- Flow-cytometric immunophenotyping classifies the leukaemia.
- Cytogenetic testing contributes to risk assessment.

questions.stem: Which finding is associated with a poorer prognosis in childhood ALL?

options.label: A
options.text: Low disease burden with no detectable minimal residual disease

options.label: B
options.text: Age 2-5 years with a low initial WBC count and favourable cytogenetics

options.label: C
options.text: Absence of CNS disease and a rapid response to induction

options.label: E
options.text: Age below 1 year or at least 10 years, high initial WBC count or adverse cytogenetics

questions.correctAnswerText: Age below 1 year or at least 10 years, high initial WBC count or adverse cytogenetics
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance lists age extremes, high initial WBC, CNS involvement, adverse cytogenetics and slow response or persistent minimal residual disease as high-risk features.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Undetectable minimal residual disease after induction is generally a favourable response.
- B. Incorrect. This describes a more favourable pattern than the risk factors listed.
- C. Incorrect. Absence of CNS involvement and rapid treatment response are not the high-risk findings.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance identifies hyperdiploidy as favourable, while hypodiploidy is adverse.
- E. Correct. These are recognized poor-prognostic features listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- High-risk features include age <1 year or ≥10 years and initial WBC >50,000/mm³.
- CNS involvement and adverse cytogenetics worsen risk.
- Slow response or persistent measurable residual disease is concerning.

questions.stem: A child with ALL develops hyperkalaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia shortly after chemotherapy. What is the most likely complication?
questions.correctAnswerText: Tumour lysis syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Rapid destruction of tumour cells releases intracellular contents, causing hyperkalaemia, hyperuricaemia and hyperphosphataemia with secondary hypocalcaemia and possible acute kidney injury.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The electrolyte pattern after chemotherapy is characteristic of tumour lysis syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Warm AIHA causes immune red-cell destruction and haemolysis.
- C. Incorrect. Aplastic crisis is due to transient marrow suppression, commonly from parvovirus B19.
- D. Incorrect. Iron overload develops after repeated transfusion and does not cause this acute biochemical pattern.
- E. Incorrect. vWD causes mucocutaneous bleeding, not tumour-cell lysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tumour lysis can occur before or after chemotherapy.
- Expect high potassium, uric acid and phosphate with low calcium.
- Acute kidney injury is an important consequence; hydration and urate-lowering prophylaxis are emphasized.

cases.title: Persistent painless lymphadenopathy and an abdominal mass
cases.vignette: A 15-year-old adolescent has persistent painless cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats and weight loss. A separate younger child presents with a rapidly enlarging abdominal mass and features of intestinal obstruction. Both require assessment for lymphoma.

questions.stem: Which histological feature is the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma?
questions.correctAnswerText: Reed-Sternberg cells
questions.initialExplanation: Reed-Sternberg cells are the characteristic pathological hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Reed-Sternberg cells define the classic histological hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma.
- B. Incorrect. Hypersegmented neutrophils are seen in megaloblastic anaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Spherocytes occur in hereditary spherocytosis and immune haemolysis.
- D. Incorrect. Auer rods are associated with myeloid blasts.
- E. Incorrect. Heinz bodies occur in oxidative haemoglobin injury, such as G6PD deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hodgkin lymphoma: Reed-Sternberg cells.
- It often presents with painless lymphadenopathy and B symptoms.
- Adolescents are an important age group.

questions.stem: Which presentation is more characteristic of non-Hodgkin lymphoma in children?

options.label: A
options.text: Disease confined almost exclusively to cervical lymph nodes in children in routine care

options.label: B
options.text: Isolated petechiae after a viral infection

options.label: C
options.text: Chronic microcytic anaemia without a mass

options.label: D
options.text: Extranodal disease, including an abdominal mass causing obstruction

questions.correctAnswerText: Extranodal disease, including an abdominal mass causing obstruction
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance contrasts Hodgkin lymphoma, which is essentially nodal, with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which more often involves extranodal sites, including the abdomen.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the typical extranodal pattern of NHL.
- B. Incorrect. This is more consistent with ITP.
- C. Incorrect. This does not suggest lymphoma.
- D. Correct. Abdominal extranodal disease and bowel obstruction are described for childhood NHL.
- E. Incorrect. Haemarthrosis suggests a coagulation-factor deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hodgkin lymphoma: predominantly nodal disease.
- NHL: extranodal sites are more common in children.
- Abdominal mass and intestinal obstruction are important NHL presentations.

questions.stem: A child from a malaria-endemic region presents with a rapidly growing jaw mass. Which lymphoma subtype is most consistent with the endemic form described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Burkitt lymphoma
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include endemic Burkitt lymphoma as associated with EBV and malaria-endemic regions, with characteristic jaw or facial-bone involvement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. CLL is a chronic leukaemia and is not the described childhood jaw tumour.
- B. Correct. Endemic Burkitt lymphoma classically involves the jaw or other facial bones.
- C. Incorrect. Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is a myeloid leukaemia, not a jaw lymphoma.
- D. Incorrect. Nodular sclerosing is a Hodgkin lymphoma subtype and is not the classic jaw mass described.
- E. Incorrect. Lymphocyte-depleted Hodgkin lymphoma is a Hodgkin subtype, not Burkitt lymphoma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Burkitt lymphoma is a B-cell NHL.
- Endemic Burkitt is associated with EBV and malaria-endemic regions.
- Jaw/facial-bone involvement is a characteristic presentation.

questions.stem: Which investigation is essential to establish the diagnosis of a suspected lymphoma and guide further staging?

options.label: E
options.text: Lymph-node biopsy followed by appropriate imaging for staging

questions.correctAnswerText: Lymph-node biopsy followed by appropriate imaging for staging
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include lymph-node biopsy as a key diagnostic investigation and CT or MRI imaging for staging, with PET used to monitor response in the described setting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Reticulocyte count assesses marrow response, not lymphoma diagnosis.
- B. Incorrect. Bleeding time is not a lymphoma diagnostic test.
- C. Incorrect. Direct Coombs testing evaluates immune haemolysis.
- D. Incorrect. Ferritin does not establish lymphoma histology.
- E. Correct. Tissue diagnosis is essential, and imaging defines disease extent.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Obtain tissue diagnosis with lymph-node biopsy when appropriate.
- Stage disease with imaging.
- Burkitt lymphoma is treated with multi-agent chemotherapy in the course clinical guidance.

cases.title: Mild microcytosis in a family with thalassaemia
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child is found to have mild microcytic anaemia during a family screening programme. The child is active and has no jaundice, splenomegaly or growth impairment. One parent is known to carry beta-thalassaemia.

questions.stem: Which beta-thalassaemia category best fits a well child with mild anaemia and no significant symptoms?
questions.correctAnswerText: Beta-thalassaemia trait (minor)
questions.initialExplanation: Beta-thalassaemia trait is usually asymptomatic or associated with mild anaemia and generally does not require treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sickle cell disease is a separate haemoglobin structural disorder.
- B. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia major causes severe transfusion-dependent anaemia.
- C. Correct. The mild microcytosis and absence of significant symptoms fit beta-thalassaemia trait.
- D. Incorrect. Hb Bart's is a severe alpha-thalassaemia syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Intermedia produces a more significant haemolytic anaemia than the trait state.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Beta-thalassaemia trait: mild or no symptoms.
- It generally does not require treatment.
- Avoid unnecessary iron unless iron deficiency is independently demonstrated.

questions.stem: Which description best fits beta-thalassaemia intermedia?

options.label: B
options.text: Complete absence of most alpha-globin chains

options.label: C
options.text: Moderate haemolysis and significant anaemia, with some beta-chain production retained

options.label: D
options.text: typically asymptomatic with a completely normal CBC

options.label: E
options.text: Severe transfusion dependence from early infancy in each patient

questions.correctAnswerText: Moderate haemolysis and significant anaemia, with some beta-chain production retained
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include beta-thalassaemia intermedia as having moderate haemolysis and severe anaemia, with mutations that permit some HbA and/or increased HbF production.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Platelet destruction is the mechanism of ITP.
- B. Incorrect. Complete absence of alpha chains causes Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis.
- C. Correct. This is the phenotype described for intermedia.
- D. Incorrect. This is more consistent with a silent carrier or mild trait state.
- E. Incorrect. Transfusion dependence from infancy is characteristic of major disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Beta-thalassaemia has trait, intermedia and major forms.
- Intermedia has an intermediate clinical severity.
- Residual beta-chain production and HbF influence the phenotype.

questions.stem: Which investigation is most useful to distinguish beta-thalassaemia from iron deficiency when a child has persistent microcytosis?

options.label: E
options.text: Haemoglobin electrophoresis interpreted with iron studies and red-cell indices

questions.correctAnswerText: Haemoglobin electrophoresis interpreted with iron studies and red-cell indices
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance identifies haemoglobin electrophoresis as diagnostic for thalassaemia and also provides Mentzer index and iron-study patterns to distinguish it from IDA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Coombs testing evaluates immune haemolysis.
- B. Incorrect. Platelet-function analysis evaluates platelet dysfunction.
- C. Incorrect. Cold agglutinins are relevant to cold-antibody haemolysis.
- D. Incorrect. PT and aPTT assess coagulation, not globin-chain synthesis.
- E. Correct. Electrophoresis identifies abnormal haemoglobin fractions, while iron studies and indices help separate thalassaemia from iron deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Use the Mentzer index as a screening clue, not a stand-alone diagnosis.
- Check iron stores before prescribing iron.
- Haemoglobin electrophoresis helps classify beta-thalassaemia.

questions.stem: Which approach is described for prenatal diagnosis of beta-thalassaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: DNA analysis of a chorionic-villus sample

questions.correctAnswerText: DNA analysis of a chorionic-villus sample
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that prenatal diagnosis of beta-thalassaemia can be performed using DNA analysis of a chorionic-villus sample and emphasizes genetic counselling.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the prenatal diagnostic method described.
- B. Incorrect. Platelet-function testing does not identify fetal beta-globin mutations.
- C. Incorrect. Osmotic fragility is used in the assessment of hereditary spherocytosis.
- D. Incorrect. Cold agglutinin testing is unrelated to prenatal globin-gene diagnosis.
- E. Incorrect. A maternal Coombs test evaluates red-cell antibodies, not fetal thalassaemia genotype.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Genetic counselling is important in thalassaemia.
- Prenatal diagnosis is possible by fetal DNA analysis.
- Discuss carrier status and reproductive risk with affected families.

topics.name: Sickle-cell genotypes and related haemoglobin disorders

cases.title: Interpreting haemoglobin electrophoresis
cases.vignette: Three children are reviewed after haemoglobin screening. One has severe chronic haemolysis, another is asymptomatic, and a third has moderate anaemia with persistent splenomegaly. Their haemoglobin electrophoresis patterns differ.

questions.stem: Which electrophoresis pattern is expected in HbSS sickle cell anaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: HbA and HbS are present in equal proportions in each patient

options.label: B
options.text: HbS predominates, HbF is present in a variable proportion and HbA is absent

options.label: C
options.text: HbF is absent and HbS is absent

questions.correctAnswerText: HbS predominates, HbF is present in a variable proportion and HbA is absent
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include HbSS disease as having predominantly HbS, some HbF and no HbA because both beta-globin genes carry the sickle mutation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Equal HbA and HbS is not the described HbSS pattern.
- B. Correct. HbSS produces HbS predominance with no normal HbA.
- C. Incorrect. HbS is the defining haemoglobin in HbSS disease.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the pattern of sickle cell disease.
- E. Incorrect. HbA predominance is more consistent with the carrier state.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HbSS: no HbA.
- HbS is the dominant fraction.
- HbF varies and can be increased by hydroxyurea.

questions.stem: A child with HbAS is well and has no history of painful crises. Which electrophoresis pattern supports sickle cell trait?
questions.correctAnswerText: HbA approximately 60-80% and HbS approximately 20-40%
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance describes sickle trait as a heterozygous state with HbA predominating and HbS forming a smaller fraction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. HbSS disease has no HbA.
- B. Incorrect. Very high HbF is associated with beta-thalassaemia major.
- C. Incorrect. HbA2 alone is not the sickle-trait pattern.
- D. Incorrect. This does not represent sickle trait.
- E. Correct. These are the approximate proportions listed for HbAS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HbAS is usually asymptomatic.
- HbA predominates over HbS.
- Sickling in trait is described as occurring only under severe hypoxaemia.

questions.stem: A child has moderate chronic anaemia, a sickle-cell genotype and splenomegaly persisting beyond early childhood. Which compound haemoglobin disorder is listed in the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sickle cell-beta-thalassaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include sickle cell-beta-thalassaemia as inheritance of an HbS gene from one parent and a beta-thalassaemia gene from the other, with moderate anaemia and possible splenomegaly beyond age 5.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the compound heterozygous disorder described.
- B. Incorrect. Hb Bart's is a severe alpha-thalassaemia syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia trait alone does not include an HbS allele.
- D. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency is an enzyme defect and does not produce this compound haemoglobin genotype.
- E. Incorrect. HS is a red-cell membrane disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sickle-beta-thalassaemia combines HbS and beta-thalassaemia alleles.
- The phenotype may be intermediate in severity.
- Persistent splenomegaly may be seen beyond early childhood.

questions.stem: Which complication is highlighted for HbSC disease during adolescence?

options.label: A
options.text: Pure red-cell aplasia with a congenital thumb anomaly

options.label: C
options.text: Universal transfusion dependence from 3 months of age

options.label: D
options.text: Proliferative retinopathy and osteonecrosis of the hips or shoulders

options.label: E
options.text: Absent alpha-globin chains causing hydrops fetalis

questions.correctAnswerText: Proliferative retinopathy and osteonecrosis of the hips or shoulders
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that HbSC disease may have fewer painful crises than HbSS but is associated with proliferative retinopathy and osteonecrosis, particularly in adolescence.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A congenital thumb anomaly with pure red-cell aplasia suggests Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency causes haemophilia A.
- C. Incorrect. Transfusion dependence from infancy is more typical of beta-thalassaemia major.
- D. Correct. These are complications specifically listed for HbSC disease.
- E. Incorrect. This describes Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HbSC is another sickle-cell disease genotype.
- Painful crises may be fewer than in HbSS, but important complications remain.
- Retinopathy and osteonecrosis deserve clinical attention.

cases.title: A child with simultaneous anaemia and thrombocytopenia
cases.vignette: An 8-year-old child presents with pallor, jaundice, bruising and petechiae. The full blood count shows anaemia and thrombocytopenia. The direct Coombs test is positive, and haemolysis markers are increased.

questions.stem: Which combined immune disorder is suggested by autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia in the same patient?
questions.correctAnswerText: Evans syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Evans syndrome is the association of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia with immune thrombocytopenia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fanconi anaemia causes inherited marrow failure.
- B. Correct. The combination of immune red-cell destruction and immune platelet destruction defines Evans syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. DIC is a systemic consumptive coagulopathy and does not define this autoimmune combination.
- D. Incorrect. vWD is an inherited platelet-adhesion disorder and does not cause AIHA.
- E. Incorrect. Sickle trait is usually asymptomatic.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Evans syndrome = AIHA + immune thrombocytopenia.
- Look for evidence of haemolysis and an isolated platelet abnormality.
- Assess for underlying autoimmune or lymphoproliferative conditions when indicated.

questions.stem: Which test is most important for demonstrating red-cell-bound autoantibodies in AIHA?
questions.correctAnswerText: Direct antiglobulin (direct Coombs) test
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include the direct antiglobulin test as the most important investigation for detecting autoantibodies attached to red cells.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Chromosome-breakage testing is used for Fanconi anaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Electrophoresis evaluates haemoglobin variants.
- C. Incorrect. Osmotic fragility tests red-cell membrane stability in HS.
- D. Incorrect. Ristocetin cofactor activity evaluates vWF function.
- E. Correct. The direct Coombs test detects antibody and/or complement coating of red cells.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- AIHA: direct Coombs test is central to diagnosis.
- Warm AIHA usually involves IgG.
- Cold-antibody AIHA may involve complement and positive cold agglutination tests.

questions.stem: A child with warm AIHA has severe ongoing haemolysis despite first-line corticosteroids. Which additional treatment is listed for refractory disease?
questions.correctAnswerText: Rituximab
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, among options for refractory AIHA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected bleeding disorders.
- B. Incorrect. Iron does not suppress autoantibody-mediated haemolysis.
- C. Incorrect. Hydroxyurea increases HbF in sickle cell disease; it is not first-line immune therapy for AIHA.
- D. Correct. Rituximab targets B cells and is listed for refractory AIHA.
- E. Incorrect. Factor IX concentrate treats haemophilia B.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Warm AIHA: corticosteroids are first-line.
- Refractory cases may require rituximab or other specialist therapies.
- Treat any associated underlying disease.

questions.stem: Which clinical association is listed among secondary causes of warm AIHA?

options.label: D
options.text: Iron deficiency from cow's milk alone

questions.correctAnswerText: Systemic lupus erythematosus
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include autoimmune/collagen-vascular diseases, lymphoproliferative malignancy and infections among possible secondary causes of warm AIHA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. vWD is a separate inherited bleeding disorder.
- B. Incorrect. Alpha-thalassaemia is an inherited globin-synthesis disorder.
- C. Correct. SLE is listed as a secondary association of warm AIHA.
- D. Incorrect. Dietary iron deficiency is not a cause of warm autoantibody formation.
- E. Incorrect. Sickle trait is not a listed cause of warm AIHA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Warm AIHA may be idiopathic or secondary.
- Consider autoimmune disease, malignancy, infection and drug exposure.
- Evaluate the cause as well as treating haemolysis.

cases.title: A child with newly diagnosed immune thrombocytopenia
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child has widespread petechiae after a viral illness. The child is active, haemodynamically stable and has no significant mucosal bleeding. The platelet count is low, while the other blood-cell lines are normal.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate initial approach for a well child with typical ITP and no significant bleeding?
questions.correctAnswerText: Observation, safety advice and follow-up
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance describes most childhood ITP as acute, benign and self-limiting, with many children recovering spontaneously. Observation is appropriate in many well children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Chemotherapy is not treatment for typical ITP.
- B. Incorrect. Splenectomy is not initial treatment for acute childhood ITP.
- C. Correct. A stable child with minor skin findings can often be observed with advice to avoid trauma and return for bleeding.
- D. Incorrect. Platelet transfusion is generally avoided in ITP except in severe life-threatening bleeding.
- E. Incorrect. Iron chelation treats iron overload and has no role here.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Many childhood ITP cases resolve spontaneously.
- Observe well children with minor bleeding manifestations.
- Avoid trauma and unnecessary intramuscular injections.

questions.stem: A child with ITP develops severe persistent mucosal bleeding. Which treatment is listed as the drug of choice?
questions.correctAnswerText: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance IVIG as the drug of choice for severe or persistent bleeding in acute ITP; it reduces platelet destruction by blocking Fc receptors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hydroxyurea is used in sickle cell disease.
- B. Incorrect. Factor IX replacement is for haemophilia B.
- C. Incorrect. Iron does not treat immune platelet destruction.
- D. Incorrect. Desmopressin is not definitive treatment for ITP.
- E. Correct. IVIG is listed for significant bleeding or severe thrombocytopenia with clinical concern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IVIG is used for severe or persistent bleeding in the course clinical guidance.
- Corticosteroids are another listed option.
- Treatment decisions depend on bleeding severity, not platelet count alone.

questions.stem: Why are platelet transfusion and splenectomy generally avoided in acute childhood ITP?

options.label: A
options.text: They are contraindicated because ITP typically causes thrombosis

options.label: B
options.text: They are not routine treatments; platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding and splenectomy is avoided in acute disease

options.label: C
options.text: They are required in children in routine care with petechiae

options.label: E
options.text: They cure the underlying autoantibody immediately

questions.correctAnswerText: They are not routine treatments; platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding and splenectomy is avoided in acute disease
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that platelet transfusion and splenectomy should be avoided in acute ITP except for severe life-threatening bleeding situations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ITP is primarily a bleeding disorder from platelet destruction; universal thrombosis is not the reason.
- B. Correct. This reflects the management caution in the course clinical guidance.
- C. Incorrect. Most children with mild skin-only manifestations can be observed.
- D. Incorrect. Iron deficiency is not the reason these treatments are avoided.
- E. Incorrect. Platelet transfusion does not remove the autoantibody, and splenectomy is not routine acute therapy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Do not transfuse platelets routinely for skin-only ITP.
- Reserve platelet transfusion for life-threatening bleeding in specialist-led care.
- Splenectomy is not routine in acute paediatric ITP.

questions.stem: A child's ITP persists for more than 6 months. Which treatment class is listed as first-line for chronic ITP in the course clinical guidance?

options.label: C
options.text: Thrombopoietin-receptor agonists such as eltrombopag or romiplostim

questions.correctAnswerText: Thrombopoietin-receptor agonists such as eltrombopag or romiplostim
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe chronic ITP as lasting at least 6 months and lists thrombopoietin-receptor agonists as first-line treatment options in chronic disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hydroxyurea is used in sickle cell disease, not as standard chronic ITP therapy.
- B. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion is used for selected severe sickle-cell complications.
- C. Correct. Eltrombopag and romiplostim are the agents listed.
- D. Incorrect. Factor VIII replacement treats haemophilia A.
- E. Incorrect. Iron treats iron deficiency, not chronic immune platelet destruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Newly diagnosed ITP: up to 3 months.
- Persistent ITP: 3-6 months.
- Chronic ITP: at least 6 months.
- Clinical guidance TPO-receptor agonists, rituximab and selected use of splenectomy for chronic/refractory disease.

cases.title: Screening in chronic immune thrombocytopenia
cases.vignette: A 13-year-old girl has immune thrombocytopenia that has persisted for more than 6 months. During follow-up, the clinician reviews associated causes that should be considered in chronic disease.

questions.stem: Which condition does standard guidance specifically recommend screening for in a child with chronic ITP?
questions.correctAnswerText: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
questions.initialExplanation: The chronic ITP section states that SLE screening should be performed because SLE is an important cause of a low platelet count.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. standard guidance specifically recommends SLE screening in chronic ITP.
- B. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia major is a chronic haemolytic anaemia, not the associated condition singled out for chronic ITP screening.
- C. Incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis is a red-cell membrane disorder.
- D. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency is an enzyme-related haemolytic disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Sickle cell trait is usually asymptomatic and is not the screening association listed for chronic ITP.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chronic ITP is defined as duration of at least 6 months.
- standard guidance specifically recommends SLE screening in chronic ITP.

cases.title: A child with newly diagnosed acute leukaemia
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child undergoes bone-marrow examination and flow-cytometric immunophenotyping. The family asks how the subtype is determined and how treatment is organized. The child is also assessed for early complications of therapy.

questions.stem: Which acute leukaemia subtype accounts for the majority of childhood acute leukaemia in the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL)
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include ALL as approximately 75-80% of childhood acute leukaemia, with AML accounting for a smaller proportion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia is uncommon.
- B. Incorrect. AML represents a smaller proportion, around 20-25%.
- C. Correct. ALL is the commonest acute childhood leukaemia.
- D. Incorrect. CLL is rare in children.
- E. Incorrect. CML is a chronic myeloid disorder and much less common in children.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ALL is the commonest childhood leukaemia.
- B-cell lineage is the largest group.
- Flow cytometry and cytogenetics help classify disease and assess risk.

questions.stem: Which treatment sequence is described for ALL?
questions.correctAnswerText: Induction, consolidation and maintenance
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include induction of remission, consolidation to maintain remission and prevent resistance, and long-term maintenance for approximately 2-3 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These treatments relate to selected immune-haematological disorders.
- B. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion and hydroxyurea are not the standard ALL phases described.
- C. Correct. These are the three treatment phases listed.
- D. Incorrect. This is not a leukaemia chemotherapy sequence.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics are important supportive therapy but do not treat the malignant clone.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Induction aims to achieve remission.
- Consolidation reduces residual disease and resistance.
- Maintenance is prolonged; clinical guidance gives a duration of about 2-3 years.
- CNS prophylaxis is essential.

questions.stem: Why is intrathecal methotrexate used during ALL treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: To prevent sickling by increasing HbF

options.label: C
options.text: To provide CNS prophylaxis and reduce the risk of CNS relapse

questions.correctAnswerText: To provide CNS prophylaxis and reduce the risk of CNS relapse
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance describes intrathecal chemotherapy, including methotrexate, as CNS prophylaxis because the CNS is a potential sanctuary site for leukaemia relapse.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hydroxyurea, not methotrexate, is used to increase HbF in sickle cell disease.
- B. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency is managed by avoiding oxidants and treating haemolysis.
- C. Correct. Intrathecal therapy is used to prevent or treat CNS involvement.
- D. Incorrect. Iron replacement is used for iron deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. Methotrexate is not a platelet-production stimulant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ALL treatment includes CNS prophylaxis.
- Intrathecal methotrexate is listed.
- CNS disease is also a poor prognostic feature.

questions.stem: A child with acute leukaemia develops fever with severe neutropenia during chemotherapy. What is the appropriate immediate management principle?

options.label: C
options.text: Delay antibiotics until culture results return

options.label: E
options.text: Urgent assessment and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics

questions.correctAnswerText: Urgent assessment and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
questions.initialExplanation: Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency. Recommended management includes broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fever with severe neutropenia requires urgent hospital assessment and treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected bleeding disorders.
- C. Incorrect. Treatment should not be delayed while waiting for culture results.
- D. Incorrect. Iron does not treat neutropenic infection.
- E. Correct. Prompt empiric IV antibiotics are needed because neutropenic patients can deteriorate rapidly.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Febrile neutropenia is an emergency.
- Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly after appropriate cultures are obtained, without delaying treatment.
- Supportive care also includes infection control, management of bleeding and anaemia, and tumour-lysis prevention.

cases.title: Thrombocytopenia with systemic features
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child presents with pallor, bruising and reduced urine output after a gastrointestinal illness. The full blood count shows thrombocytopenia and anaemia. The blood film demonstrates red-cell fragmentation.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis should be considered when thrombocytopenia is accompanied by microangiopathic haemolysis and renal involvement?
questions.correctAnswerText: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)
questions.initialExplanation: HUS is listed among non-immune causes of platelet destruction and can present with thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, often with renal involvement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The combination of thrombocytopenia, fragmentation haemolysis and renal dysfunction is characteristic of HUS.
- B. Incorrect. Iron deficiency does not produce thrombocytopenia with fragmented red cells as the defining pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis, not acute microangiopathic haemolysis.
- D. Incorrect. vWD causes mucocutaneous bleeding but does not cause platelet consumption with MAHA.
- E. Incorrect. Typical ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia without haemolytic anaemia or renal injury.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HUS and TTP are listed among non-immune causes of platelet destruction.
- Look for thrombocytopenia together with evidence of MAHA.
- Renal or neurological involvement helps guide the differential.

questions.stem: Which process can cause thrombocytopenia through reduced platelet production?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bone-marrow infiltration by leukaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include bone-marrow infiltration by leukaemia among acquired causes of reduced platelet production.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Isolated nutritional iron deficiency is not the listed mechanism for thrombocytopenia.
- B. Correct. Leukaemic infiltration disrupts normal marrow haematopoiesis and can reduce platelet production.
- C. Incorrect. vWF deficiency impairs platelet adhesion rather than platelet production.
- D. Incorrect. Cold-antibody haemolysis affects red cells.
- E. Incorrect. This is a mechanism of increased platelet destruction, as in ITP.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Thrombocytopenia may result from reduced production or increased destruction.
- Marrow infiltration, aplastic anaemia and drug effects reduce production.
- Consider marrow examination when additional cytopenias or atypical features are present.

questions.stem: A newborn has thrombocytopenia and bilateral absent radii. Which congenital syndrome is listed in the thrombocytopenia differential?
questions.correctAnswerText: TAR syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: TAR stands for thrombocytopenia-absent radius syndrome and is specifically listed among congenital causes of thrombocytopenia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is associated with pancreatic insufficiency and marrow dysfunction.
- B. Correct. Thrombocytopenia with absent radii is the defining association.
- C. Incorrect. DBA is a pure red-cell aplasia.
- D. Incorrect. HS is a red-cell membrane disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Fanconi anaemia can cause radial/thumb abnormalities but is characterized by inherited marrow failure and pancytopenia; the named thrombocytopenia syndrome here is TAR.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TAR syndrome: thrombocytopenia with absent radii.
- Fanconi anaemia may also have radial/thumb abnormalities but causes pancytopenia.
- Distinguish syndromes using the complete phenotype and blood counts.

questions.stem: Which congenital disorder is listed as a cause of thrombocytopenia with abnormal platelet production or function?
questions.correctAnswerText: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is specifically included in the congenital causes of thrombocytopenia in the course clinical guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sickle trait is usually asymptomatic.
- B. Incorrect. An alpha-thalassaemia silent carrier usually has a normal CBC.
- C. Incorrect. B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and may cause pancytopenia, but it is not the congenital platelet syndrome listed.
- D. Correct. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is listed among inherited causes of thrombocytopenia.
- E. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency causes oxidative haemolysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital thrombocytopenia causes include Wiskott-Aldrich and TAR syndrome.
- Acquired causes include aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, drugs and sepsis.
- Classify the mechanism before narrowing the diagnosis.

cases.title: Thrombocytopenia with a giant haemangioma
cases.vignette: An infant has a large giant haemangioma and develops a markedly reduced platelet count. The clinician reviews the non-immune causes of increased platelet destruction or consumption listed in the thrombocytopenia section.

questions.stem: Which syndrome is named in the course clinical guidance in association with a giant haemangioma?
questions.correctAnswerText: Kasabach–Merritt syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include giant haemangioma with Kasabach–Merritt syndrome among non-immune causes of thrombocytopenia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the association explicitly named in the course clinical guidance.
- B. Incorrect. Evans syndrome is described as autoimmune haemolytic anaemia plus immune thrombocytopenia.
- C. Incorrect. Wiskott–Aldrich is listed among congenital causes of thrombocytopenia.
- D. Incorrect. TAR syndrome is associated with thrombocytopenia and absent radii.
- E. Incorrect. Bernard–Soulier syndrome is listed among congenital platelet disorders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The thrombocytopenia differential includes immune and non-immune causes.
- Clinical guidance giant haemangioma with Kasabach–Merritt syndrome.
- Do not confuse it with Evans syndrome, TAR syndrome or Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome.

source.raw: Haematology sheet – Causes of thrombocytopenia, Page 37.

cases.title: Grading thrombocytopenia by platelet count
cases.vignette: A child is reviewed after a full blood count shows a platelet count of 18 × 10⁹/L. The clinician uses the severity categories in the course clinical guidance to estimate bleeding risk.

questions.stem: How is this platelet count classified?
questions.correctAnswerText: Severe thrombocytopenia
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe severe thrombocytopenia as a platelet count below 20 × 10⁹/L and associates it with a risk of spontaneous bleeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mild thrombocytopenia is listed as 50–150 × 10⁹/L.
- B. Correct. A count of 18 × 10⁹/L is below the severe threshold of 20 × 10⁹/L.
- C. Incorrect. Moderate thrombocytopenia is listed as 20–50 × 10⁹/L.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance gives the normal platelet range as 150–450 × 10⁹/L.
- E. Incorrect. Thrombocytosis means an increased, not reduced, platelet count.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal platelet count: 150–450 × 10⁹/L.
- Mild thrombocytopenia: 50–150 × 10⁹/L.
- Moderate thrombocytopenia: 20–50 × 10⁹/L.
- Severe thrombocytopenia: below 20 × 10⁹/L, with risk of spontaneous bleeding.

cases.title: Purpura despite a normal platelet count
cases.vignette: An 8-year-old child presents with purpura and bruising. The platelet count is normal.

questions.stem: Which condition is an example of a vascular cause of purpura with a normal platelet count?
questions.correctAnswerText: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis)
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include HSP among acquired vascular causes of purpura in which the platelet count may be normal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Leukaemia may reduce platelet production and cause thrombocytopenia.
- B. Incorrect. DIC consumes platelets and coagulation factors.
- C. Correct. HSP is listed as a vascular cause of purpura with a normal platelet count.
- D. Incorrect. ITP causes thrombocytopenic purpura.
- E. Incorrect. Aplastic anaemia commonly causes thrombocytopenia as part of pancytopenia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Purpura is not always caused by thrombocytopenia.
- Vascular causes may occur with a normal platelet count.
- Clinical guidance HSP, meningococcal disease and scurvy among acquired vascular causes.

questions.stem: A child with chronic kidney disease develops mucosal bleeding despite a normal platelet count. Which acquired platelet dysfunction is listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Uraemia-related platelet dysfunction
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include uraemia as an acquired cause of qualitative platelet dysfunction, which can occur despite a normal platelet count.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia major causes chronic haemolytic anaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency is a coagulation-factor disorder.
- C. Incorrect. Cold agglutinin disease causes immune haemolysis.
- D. Correct. Uraemia can impair platelet function and cause a bleeding tendency.
- E. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency causes haemolysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- A normal platelet count does not guarantee normal platelet function.
- Uraemia and cardiopulmonary bypass are listed acquired causes.
- Consider functional platelet disorders when mucosal bleeding occurs with a normal count.

questions.stem: Which congenital platelet-function disorder is specifically named in the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Glanzmann thrombasthenia
questions.initialExplanation: Glanzmann syndrome is listed among rare congenital platelet-function disorders.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia intermedia is a globin-chain synthesis disorder.
- B. Incorrect. HS is a red-cell membrane disorder.
- C. Incorrect. Fanconi anaemia is an inherited marrow-failure syndrome.
- D. Correct. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a qualitative platelet disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Haemophilia B is factor IX deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Qualitative platelet disorders can cause mucocutaneous bleeding with a normal platelet count.
- Glanzmann thrombasthenia is listed as a congenital example.
- Bernard-Soulier syndrome is also listed in the thrombocytopenia differential.

questions.stem: A child has petechiae and purpura but a normal platelet count. Which broad category should be considered?

options.label: D
options.text: Non-thrombocytopenic purpura due to vascular disease or platelet dysfunction

questions.correctAnswerText: Non-thrombocytopenic purpura due to vascular disease or platelet dysfunction
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance classifies purpura into thrombocytopenic and non-thrombocytopenic forms. The latter may result from vascular abnormalities or platelet dysfunction despite a normal platelet count.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Thrombocytopenic purpura requires a reduced platelet count.
- B. Incorrect. Haemophilia causes deep bleeding rather than the typical petechial pattern.
- C. Incorrect. IDA does not explain purpura with normal platelets.
- D. Correct. This is the appropriate category when platelet number is normal.
- E. Incorrect. Leukaemia is an important differential but is not the only cause.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Check the platelet count before labelling purpura as thrombocytopenic.
- Normal platelet count: consider vascular causes and qualitative platelet defects.
- Clinical pattern and systemic features guide further investigation.

topics.name: Acquired coagulation disorders and special coagulation tests

cases.title: Prolonged coagulation tests in a sick child
cases.vignette: A 2-week-old infant presents with bleeding from the umbilical stump. Another child with advanced liver disease develops easy bruising. Both cases require interpretation of coagulation tests and recognition of acquired factor deficiencies.

questions.stem: Which acquired condition is listed as a cause of coagulation-factor deficiency?
questions.correctAnswerText: Vitamin K deficiency
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance lists vitamin K deficiency, advanced liver disease, DIC, anticoagulants and acquired coagulation inhibitors as causes of acquired coagulation disorders.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. HS causes red-cell haemolysis.
- B. Incorrect. Iron deficiency affects haemoglobin synthesis rather than coagulation-factor activity.
- C. Incorrect. G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-related haemolysis.
- D. Correct. Vitamin K deficiency is specifically listed as an acquired cause.
- E. Incorrect. Sickle trait does not cause coagulation-factor deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acquired coagulation disorders include vitamin K deficiency and advanced liver disease.
- DIC and anticoagulants can also alter coagulation tests.
- Consider acquired inhibitors in patients previously treated with factor VIII or IX.

questions.stem: Which test evaluates fibrinogen deficiency or dysfunction most directly among the routine tests listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Thrombin time
questions.initialExplanation: The course clinical guidance identifies thrombin time as a test for deficiency or dysfunction of fibrinogen.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ferritin reflects iron stores.
- B. Correct. Thrombin time assesses the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin.
- C. Incorrect. MCV measures average red-cell size.
- D. Incorrect. Reticulocyte count reflects marrow response.
- E. Incorrect. Platelet count measures platelet number.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PT assesses the extrinsic/common pathway.
- aPTT assesses the intrinsic/common pathway.
- Thrombin time evaluates fibrinogen function.
- D-dimer reflects fibrin breakdown.

questions.stem: What does an increased D-dimer indicate in the context of a suspected consumptive coagulopathy?
questions.correctAnswerText: Increased fibrin formation and breakdown
questions.initialExplanation: D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product. It increases when cross-linked fibrin is formed and subsequently broken down, as occurs in DIC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Iron depletion is assessed with iron studies.
- B. Incorrect. D-dimer is not a direct marker of platelet production.
- C. Incorrect. Red-cell size is assessed using MCV.
- D. Correct. D-dimer reflects breakdown of cross-linked fibrin.
- E. Incorrect. D-dimer does not measure B12 stores.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- D-dimer is a fibrin degradation marker.
- It is typically increased in DIC.
- Interpret it with clinical context, PT/aPTT, fibrinogen and platelet count.

questions.stem: Which statement about neonatal coagulation-factor levels is given?

options.label: A
options.text: Most clotting factors are lower in neonates, except factor VIII and fibrinogen

options.label: B
options.text: Neonates have no intrinsic pathway activity

options.label: C
options.text: PT and aPTT are not usually prolonged in neonates

options.label: D
options.text: Factor VIII and fibrinogen are absent at birth

options.label: E
options.text: most coagulation factors are higher than adult levels

questions.correctAnswerText: Most clotting factors are lower in neonates, except factor VIII and fibrinogen
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that most clotting-factor levels are lower in neonates, with factor VIII and fibrinogen as exceptions; preterm infants have even lower levels.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the neonatal haemostasis note stated in the course clinical guidance.
- B. Incorrect. Neonates have coagulation activity, although factor levels differ from older children.
- C. Incorrect. Coagulation tests must be interpreted using age-appropriate reference ranges.
- D. Incorrect. Factor VIII and fibrinogen are exceptions and are not described as absent.
- E. Incorrect. Clinical guidance that most factor levels are lower.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal coagulation differs physiologically from that of older children.
- Most factor levels are lower, with factor VIII and fibrinogen noted as exceptions.
- Preterm infants have even lower levels; use age-specific interpretation.

cases.title: Distinguishing lymphoid and myeloid leukaemia
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child has acute leukaemia confirmed on bone-marrow testing. Flow cytometry and morphology are used to distinguish lymphoid from myeloid disease. The clinician also reviews genetic and clinical risk factors.

questions.stem: Which immunophenotypic group accounts for the largest proportion of ALL in the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: B-cell lineage
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include B-cell ALL as the majority, approximately 75%, while T-cell ALL accounts for a smaller proportion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Megakaryocytic disease is not the largest ALL group.
- B. Incorrect. Plasma-cell lineage is not the dominant childhood ALL group.
- C. Incorrect. Erythroid lineage is not the classification stated for the majority of ALL.
- D. Correct. B-cell lineage is the largest group listed.
- E. Incorrect. T-cell ALL is a smaller group and is associated with poorer prognosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- B-cell ALL is the commonest immunophenotypic group.
- T-cell ALL is less common and is listed as having a poorer prognosis.
- Flow cytometry is used for immunophenotyping.

questions.stem: Which clinical feature is particularly associated with acute myeloid leukaemia in the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Gum hyperplasia and chloroma
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes gum hyperplasia, chloroma and a large spleen as features that may be seen in AML.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These findings are associated with iron deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Dactylitis is a vaso-occlusive manifestation of sickle cell disease.
- C. Correct. These are the AML-associated features specifically listed.
- D. Incorrect. Spoon-shaped nails are associated with iron deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. Haemarthrosis suggests a coagulation-factor deficiency such as haemophilia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- AML accounts for a smaller proportion of childhood acute leukaemia than ALL.
- Gum hyperplasia and chloroma are useful clinical clues.
- Marrow examination and immunophenotyping establish classification.

questions.stem: Which chromosomal finding is described as favourable in childhood ALL?

options.label: B
options.text: Persistent minimal residual disease after induction

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyperdiploidy
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include hyperdiploidy as a favourable cytogenetic feature, while hypodiploidy and certain translocations are associated with poorer prognosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) is listed as adverse.
- B. Incorrect. Persistent minimal residual disease after induction indicates an inadequate response and higher risk.
- C. Correct. Hyperdiploidy is described as favourable.
- D. Incorrect. t(4;11) is also listed as a poor prognostic feature.
- E. Incorrect. Hypodiploidy is listed as a poor prognostic feature.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hyperdiploidy: favourable.
- Hypodiploidy and selected translocations: unfavourable.
- Response to induction and minimal residual disease are important prognostic markers.

questions.stem: Which factor is listed as a genetic predisposition or associated condition for childhood leukaemia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Down syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include Down syndrome among chromosomal conditions associated with increased risk of childhood leukaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Nutritional iron deficiency is not a genetic predisposition to leukaemia.
- B. Incorrect. vWD is an inherited bleeding disorder.
- C. Incorrect. Sickle trait is not listed as a leukaemia predisposition.
- D. Incorrect. HS is a red-cell membrane disorder and is not listed as a leukaemia risk factor.
- E. Correct. Down syndrome is specifically included among genetic/chromosomal risk associations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Childhood leukaemia is multifactorial.
- Genetic predisposition and environmental factors may contribute.
- Clinical guidance Down syndrome, Bloom syndrome and several inherited marrow/immunodeficiency disorders.

cases.title: Comparing lymph-node and extranodal malignancy
cases.vignette: A 14-year-old adolescent has painless cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with fever, night sweats and weight loss. A younger child from a malaria-endemic region presents with a rapidly growing facial mass.

questions.stem: Which clinical features are classically termed B symptoms in Hodgkin lymphoma?

options.label: B
options.text: Fever, night sweats and weight loss

questions.correctAnswerText: Fever, night sweats and weight loss
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include fever, night sweats and weight loss as B symptoms of Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are not lymphoma B symptoms.
- B. Correct. These are the classic B symptoms listed.
- C. Incorrect. These are features of a respiratory viral prodrome.
- D. Incorrect. These suggest platelet-related bleeding.
- E. Incorrect. These are features of haemolysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hodgkin lymphoma often presents with painless lymphadenopathy.
- B symptoms include fever, night sweats and weight loss.
- Mediastinal disease may cause cough, dyspnoea or SVC obstruction.

questions.stem: Which Hodgkin lymphoma subtype is described as the commonest in the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Nodular sclerosing
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include nodular sclerosing as the most frequent Hodgkin lymphoma subtype, followed by mixed cellularity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Large-cell lymphoma is included among non-Hodgkin types.
- B. Incorrect. Lymphocyte-predominant disease is a separate subtype and not the most frequent.
- C. Incorrect. Lymphocyte-depleted disease is described as rare.
- D. Correct. Nodular sclerosing is listed as the commonest type.
- E. Incorrect. Burkitt lymphoma is a non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nodular sclerosing is the commonest Hodgkin subtype.
- Mixed cellularity is another frequent subtype.
- Reed-Sternberg cells are the diagnostic hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.stem: Which lymphoma is classified as a B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma and is associated with EBV in the course clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Burkitt lymphoma
questions.initialExplanation: Burkitt lymphoma is described as a B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma and is associated with EBV, particularly in the endemic form.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lymphoblastic lymphoma is listed among T-cell NHL types.
- B. Incorrect. Nodular sclerosing is a Hodgkin lymphoma subtype.
- C. Incorrect. CLL is a chronic leukaemia, not Burkitt lymphoma.
- D. Incorrect. Lymphocyte-depleted is also a Hodgkin subtype.
- E. Correct. Burkitt is a B-cell NHL and EBV is an important association.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Burkitt lymphoma is a B-cell NHL.
- The endemic form is associated with EBV and malaria-endemic regions.
- Sporadic and immunodeficiency-associated variants are also described.

questions.stem: Which approach is most appropriate to establish and stage suspected childhood lymphoma?

options.label: A
options.text: Use serum ferritin alone to establish subtype

options.label: C
options.text: Use a direct Coombs test as the definitive lymphoma test

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain tissue diagnosis by lymph-node biopsy and use appropriate imaging for staging

options.label: E
options.text: Begin long-term iron therapy before any diagnostic assessment

questions.correctAnswerText: Obtain tissue diagnosis by lymph-node biopsy and use appropriate imaging for staging
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include lymph-node biopsy as a key diagnostic investigation and CT/MRI or other appropriate imaging for staging and response assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ferritin is not a definitive lymphoma diagnostic test.
- B. Incorrect. Platelet count may be part of the CBC but cannot establish lymphoma histology.
- C. Incorrect. Direct Coombs testing evaluates immune haemolysis.
- D. Correct. Histology establishes the diagnosis, and imaging determines disease extent.
- E. Incorrect. Empirical iron therapy must not replace investigation of a suspected malignancy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lymph-node biopsy provides tissue diagnosis.
- Imaging is used for staging and response assessment.
- Treatment may include multi-agent chemotherapy with or without radiotherapy according to subtype and stage.

cases.title: The normal haemoglobin pattern at birth
cases.vignette: A term newborn has a haemoglobin electrophoresis performed as part of an assessment. The clinician explains that the proportions of haemoglobin types in a newborn differ from those in an older child or adult.

questions.stem: Which pattern is listed as normal at birth in the course clinical guidance?

options.label: B
options.text: HbF approximately 74%, HbA approximately 25% and HbA2 approximately 1%

options.label: E
options.text: HbA is absent and HbA2 is the predominant normal haemoglobin

questions.correctAnswerText: HbF approximately 74%, HbA approximately 25% and HbA2 approximately 1%
questions.initialExplanation: The page 3 chart lists the newborn pattern as HbA about 25%, HbA2 about 1% and HbF about 74%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This resembles the adult pattern shown rather than the newborn pattern.
- B. Correct. HbF is the predominant haemoglobin at birth in the course-clinical guidance chart.
- C. Incorrect. HbS predominance is not the normal newborn pattern.
- D. Incorrect. These proportions are not listed as normal.
- E. Incorrect. Common examples include HbA at about 25% at birth.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HbF consists of two alpha and two gamma chains.
- HbA consists of two alpha and two beta chains.
- HbA2 consists of two alpha and two delta chains.
- Newborn chart: HbF about 74%, HbA about 25%, HbA2 about 1%.

cases.title: The changing sites of fetal haematopoiesis
cases.vignette: A student reviews the developmental sequence of blood-cell production before and after birth. The course clinical guidance describes an early embryonic site, followed by fetal organs, and then the postnatal site.

questions.stem: Which sequence best matches the timeline?

options.label: A
options.text: Bone marrow from conception, followed by the yolk sac after birth

options.label: B
options.text: Spleen throughout fetal life, followed by the liver after birth

options.label: C
options.text: Yolk sac in the first 8 weeks, liver and spleen from about 8 weeks to 6 months, then bone marrow as the main postnatal site

options.label: D
options.text: Thymus in the first 8 weeks, then kidney and spleen throughout childhood

options.label: E
options.text: Liver during the first 8 weeks, followed by the yolk sac until adulthood

questions.correctAnswerText: Yolk sac in the first 8 weeks, liver and spleen from about 8 weeks to 6 months, then bone marrow as the main postnatal site
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives the yolk sac as the site during the first 8 weeks, the spleen and liver from about 8 weeks to 6 months, and bone marrow as the main site throughout postnatal life.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bone marrow is the main postnatal site, not the initial site from conception.
- B. Incorrect. standard guidance places liver and spleen in the fetal period and bone marrow after birth.
- C. Correct. This is the developmental sequence and timing shown.
- D. Incorrect. The thymus and kidney are not given as the main sequence.
- E. Incorrect. The sequence reverses the stated early and later fetal sites.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Yolk sac: first 8 weeks.
- Liver and spleen: approximately 8 weeks to 6 months.
- Bone marrow: main site throughout postnatal life.

cases.title: A child develops fever, cough, coryza and a spreading rash
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old unvaccinated child is brought with high fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis. Small white lesions are visible on the buccal mucosa. A maculopapular rash begins behind the ears and on the face, then spreads to the trunk and limbs over the following day.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Measles
questions.initialExplanation: Measles classically causes a febrile prodrome with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, followed by Koplik spots and a spreading maculopapular rash.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. The three Cs, Koplik spots and cephalocaudal rash progression are characteristic of measles.
- C. Incorrect. Rubella is usually milder and is strongly associated with postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy.
- A. Incorrect. Roseola typically causes several days of high fever followed by rash as the fever resolves.
- E. Incorrect. Parvovirus B19 causes a slapped-cheek appearance and a lacy/reticular rash.
- D. Incorrect. Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper-like rash with streptococcal pharyngitis and strawberry tongue.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Measles: fever + cough + coryza + conjunctivitis.
- Koplik spots are a characteristic early oral finding.
- Rash usually begins behind the ears/face and spreads downwards.
- Lack of vaccination increases the likelihood.

questions.stem: Which oral finding is most characteristic of measles?

options.label: E
options.text: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa

questions.correctAnswerText: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
questions.initialExplanation: Koplik spots are small whitish lesions on the buccal mucosa and are described as a pathognomonic clue to measles.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. Koplik spots strongly support measles in a child with the typical prodrome.
- D. Incorrect. Strawberry tongue is associated with scarlet fever.
- A. Incorrect. Vesicles and ulcers on the palate may occur with HSV or enterovirus infections.
- B. Incorrect. Aphthous ulcers are not the classic measles enanthem.
- C. Incorrect. An adherent gray membrane suggests diphtheria, not measles.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Koplik spots: buccal mucosa, early measles clue.
- They may be easier to identify before the exanthem is fully developed.
- Strawberry tongue is a different clinical sign.

questions.stem: Which description best matches the typical measles rash progression in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Begins in the flexural creases with prominent Pastia lines

options.label: B
options.text: Appears after the fever has completely resolved

options.label: C
options.text: Begins on the palms and soles and remains limited to those sites

options.label: D
options.text: Begins behind the ears/face and spreads to involve the body within about 24 hours

options.label: E
options.text: Starts as a single painless ulcer at the tick bite site

questions.correctAnswerText: Begins behind the ears/face and spreads to involve the body within about 24 hours
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance a maculopapular rash starting behind the ears, face and head, then spreading over the body within about 24 hours.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. This is the classic sequence described for measles.
- C. Incorrect. A rash involving palms and soles may occur in other infections, but it is not the typical measles progression.
- B. Incorrect. Rash after fever resolution is typical of roseola.
- E. Incorrect. A painless expanding lesion at a tick-bite site suggests erythema migrans in Lyme disease.
- A. Incorrect. Flexural Pastia lines are associated with scarlet fever.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Measles rash is maculopapular and spreads from the head/face downwards.
- Clinical guidance widespread involvement within about 24 hours.
- A rash appearing as high fever settles suggests roseola instead.

questions.stem: Which statement about measles complications and management is supported by clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Penicillin V is the specific antiviral treatment

options.label: B
options.text: Supportive care is usual; vitamin A is given for 2 days, and complications include pneumonia and encephalitis

options.label: C
options.text: Acyclovir is routinely required in most uncomplicated cases

options.label: D
options.text: No complications occur after the rash appears

options.label: E
options.text: A single dose of antibiotics prevents SSPE

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive care is usual; vitamin A is given for 2 days, and complications include pneumonia and encephalitis
questions.initialExplanation: The measles table describes supportive treatment, vitamin A for 2 days, isolation and MMR vaccination as prevention. Complications include otitis media, pneumonia and encephalitis; late SSPE is also listed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. This reflects the supportive approach and the complications listed in the source.
- A. Incorrect. Penicillin treats susceptible bacterial infections, not measles virus.
- C. Incorrect. Acyclovir is an antiviral used for herpes-family infections, not routine uncomplicated measles.
- D. Incorrect. Measles can cause serious respiratory and neurological complications.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not prevent SSPE.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treatment: supportive care + vitamin A for 2 days.
- Isolate to reduce transmission.
- Complications: otitis media, pneumonia and encephalitis; SSPE is a rare late complication.
- Prevention: MMR vaccine.

cases.title: A mildly febrile child has postauricular lymphadenopathy and rash
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child develops a low-grade fever and a fine maculopapular rash. Examination reveals enlarged postauricular and occipital lymph nodes. The child is otherwise relatively well. The family asks about the risks if the same infection occurs during pregnancy.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Rubella
questions.initialExplanation: Rubella is usually a mild illness characterized by low-grade fever, maculopapular rash and postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. Mild systemic illness with postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy is characteristic.
- B. Incorrect. Measles usually has a more prominent febrile prodrome with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots.
- C. Incorrect. Mumps is characterized by painful parotid swelling.
- A. Incorrect. Scarlet fever is associated with streptococcal sore throat, strawberry tongue and a sandpaper rash.
- E. Incorrect. Varicella causes crops of pruritic vesicles at different stages.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rubella is often milder than measles.
- Postauricular and occipital lymphadenopathy is a useful clue.
- Congenital infection is the major concern in pregnancy.

questions.stem: Which feature best helps distinguish rubella from measles in this child?

options.label: A
options.text: Koplik spots with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis

options.label: B
options.text: Severe parotid pain aggravated by chewing

options.label: C
options.text: Crops of pruritic vesicles in different stages

options.label: D
options.text: Postauricular and occipital lymphadenopathy with a relatively mild illness

options.label: E
options.text: A sandpaper rash with Pastia lines

questions.correctAnswerText: Postauricular and occipital lymphadenopathy with a relatively mild illness
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance emphasizes postauricular and occipital lymphadenopathy in rubella, often with a mild illness and maculopapular rash.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. This is the key distinguishing pattern.
- A. Incorrect. These are characteristic of measles.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests mumps.
- C. Incorrect. This suggests varicella.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests scarlet fever.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rubella: mild fever + postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy + maculopapular rash.
- Measles: three Cs and Koplik spots.
- Mumps: parotitis.

questions.stem: A woman infected with rubella during pregnancy delivers an infant with sensorineural hearing loss, cataract and patent ductus arteriosus. Which diagnosis best explains this combination?
questions.correctAnswerText: Congenital rubella syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists congenital rubella syndrome with sensorineural hearing loss, cataract/glaucoma and congenital heart disease, particularly PDA and pulmonary stenosis. It also includes IUGR, thrombocytopenia and a blueberry-muffin rash.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. Cataract, sensorineural hearing loss and PDA form a classic congenital rubella pattern.
- A. Incorrect. Congenital varicella is associated with characteristic limb, skin, eye and neurological abnormalities, not this classic triad.
- C. Incorrect. Neonatal HSV commonly causes skin/eye/mouth disease, encephalitis or disseminated infection.
- D. Incorrect. CMV classically causes periventricular calcifications, microcephaly and hearing loss, but cataract/PDA is not the classic combination.
- E. Incorrect. Congenital toxoplasmosis is classically associated with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital rubella: SNHL + cataract + CHD (PDA/pulmonary stenosis).
- Other findings: IUGR, thrombocytopenia, blueberry-muffin rash.
- Maternal infection during pregnancy is the key risk context.

questions.stem: Which preventive measure is listed for rubella in the source?
questions.correctAnswerText: MMR vaccination
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance MMR vaccination at 12-18 months as prevention for rubella, measles and mumps.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. MMR protects against measles, mumps and rubella.
- D. Incorrect. Acyclovir is used for selected herpes infections.
- B. Incorrect. Penicillin is not rubella prophylaxis.
- A. Incorrect. BCG protects against severe tuberculosis.
- C. Incorrect. Rotavirus vaccine prevents rotavirus gastroenteritis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rubella prevention: MMR.
- The source lists the MMR schedule at 12-18 months.
- Susceptible pregnant women require particular attention because of fetal risk.

cases.title: A child develops painful parotid enlargement
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old boy develops fever, headache and malaise followed by painful swelling near the angle of the jaw. The swelling begins on one side and becomes bilateral. He reports pain when chewing and when eating sour foods.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Mumps
questions.initialExplanation: Mumps classically causes painful parotid swelling, often beginning unilaterally and then becoming bilateral, with pain aggravated by chewing or sour foods.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. Parotitis with pain on chewing is characteristic of mumps.
- E. Incorrect. Rubella causes mild fever, rash and postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy.
- D. Incorrect. Measles causes the three Cs, Koplik spots and a spreading rash.
- C. Incorrect. Roseola causes high fever followed by rash as fever resolves.
