- A. Incorrect. EBV causes tonsillopharyngitis, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly rather than typical painful parotitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mumps: fever/headache/malaise followed by parotid swelling.
- Swelling may start unilateral and become bilateral.
- Pain increases with chewing and sour foods.

questions.stem: Which description of the parotid swelling is most typical of mumps in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Vesicular lesions over the parotid duct

options.label: B
options.text: Tender submandibular swelling with honey-coloured crusts

options.label: C
options.text: A fluctuant orbital swelling with proptosis

options.label: D
options.text: Painless, steadily enlarging cervical node without parotid involvement

options.label: E
options.text: Painful swelling that may begin unilaterally and then become bilateral

questions.correctAnswerText: Painful swelling that may begin unilaterally and then become bilateral
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes parotid swelling in mumps as initially unilateral and then bilateral, painful/tender and worse with chewing or sour foods.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. This matches the clinical description.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the typical mumps presentation.
- A. Incorrect. Vesicular lesions suggest HSV or another vesicular viral infection.
- B. Incorrect. Honey-coloured crusts suggest impetigo.
- C. Incorrect. Proptosis suggests orbital cellulitis or another orbital process.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mumps swelling is parotid, painful and often bilateral.
- Pain on chewing/sour foods is a useful clue.
- It is not the same as cervical lymphadenopathy in rubella.

questions.stem: A postpubertal boy with mumps develops testicular pain and swelling. Which complication is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Orchitis
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists orchitis in boys, especially postpubertal males, as a complication of mumps. Oophoritis may occur in girls.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. Orchitis is a recognized complication of mumps in boys.
- E. Incorrect. Oophoritis refers to ovarian involvement and may occur in girls.
- B. Incorrect. Hydrops fetalis is associated with fetal parvovirus B19 infection.
- D. Incorrect. Erythema nodosum is not the listed mumps complication.
- A. Incorrect. Aplastic crisis is associated with parvovirus B19, particularly in chronic hemolytic disorders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mumps complications include orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis and CNS involvement.
- Orchitis is particularly important in postpubertal boys.
- Aseptic meningitis/encephalitis may also occur.

questions.stem: Which statement about uncomplicated mumps management and prevention is correct?

options.label: D
options.text: Supportive treatment is used; prevention is by MMR vaccine

options.label: E
options.text: Penicillin V for 10 days is the specific treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive treatment is used; prevention is by MMR vaccine
questions.initialExplanation: The viral disease comparison in the source lists supportive treatment for mumps and MMR vaccination for prevention.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. The source lists supportive treatment and MMR prevention.
- C. Incorrect. Acyclovir is used for selected herpes infections, not uncomplicated mumps.
- E. Incorrect. Penicillin V is used for streptococcal infection such as scarlet fever.
- B. Incorrect. Antituberculous treatment is unrelated to mumps.
- A. Incorrect. MMR vaccine is listed for prevention.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Uncomplicated mumps: supportive care.
- Prevent with MMR vaccination.
- Assess for orchitis, pancreatitis and neurological complications when clinically indicated.

cases.title: An infant develops a rash as a high fever settles
cases.vignette: A 10-month-old infant has had high fever for three days but remains relatively well between fever spikes. On the fourth day, the temperature settles and a pink maculopapular rash appears, mainly over the trunk. The infant has no preceding prominent respiratory prodrome.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best fits the sequence of fever followed by rash as the fever resolves?
questions.correctAnswerText: Roseola infantum
questions.initialExplanation: Roseola (sixth disease/exanthem subitum) is associated with HHV-6/7. The child develops several days of high fever, then a maculopapular rash appears as the fever resolves.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. Fever resolution followed by a trunk-predominant rash is characteristic.
- E. Incorrect. Measles rash appears after a prodrome with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis.
- D. Incorrect. Scarlet fever is associated with sore throat, strawberry tongue and a sandpaper rash.
- B. Incorrect. Rubella often has postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy with mild fever.
- A. Incorrect. Varicella causes pruritic vesicles in crops at different stages.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Roseola: HHV-6/7, sixth disease.
- High fever for several days, then rash as fever settles.
- Rash is often trunk-predominant and fades relatively quickly.

questions.stem: Which complication is specifically associated with roseola?
questions.correctAnswerText: Febrile convulsions
questions.initialExplanation: The roseola section notes that high fever may be associated with febrile convulsions. Most cases are self-limiting and have an excellent prognosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. Febrile convulsions are listed as an associated complication.
- B. Incorrect. Orchitis is a complication of mumps.
- A. Incorrect. Congenital cataract is a feature of congenital rubella syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Splenic rupture is a complication of infectious mononucleosis.
- D. Incorrect. TB meningitis is an extrapulmonary manifestation of tuberculosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Roseola is usually self-limiting.
- High fever may precipitate febrile convulsions.
- Treatment is supportive with hydration and antipyretics.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes roseola from measles in a febrile infant?

options.label: A
options.text: Roseola causes a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue

options.label: B
options.text: Measles rash appears after fever resolves, whereas roseola rash begins before fever

options.label: C
options.text: In roseola the rash appears as fever resolves; measles has a preceding three-C prodrome and Koplik spots

options.label: D
options.text: Measles is caused by HHV-6 and roseola by a paramyxovirus

options.label: E
options.text: Both diseases are defined by painful parotitis

questions.correctAnswerText: In roseola the rash appears as fever resolves; measles has a preceding three-C prodrome and Koplik spots
questions.initialExplanation: The key temporal clue is that roseola rash follows the defervescence of a high fever, whereas measles typically has cough, coryza and conjunctivitis before the rash, with Koplik spots.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. This captures the principal clinical distinction.
- E. Incorrect. Painful parotitis is typical of mumps.
- B. Incorrect. The timing is reversed.
- A. Incorrect. Sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue suggest scarlet fever.
- D. Incorrect. The etiologies are reversed: roseola is HHV-6/7 and measles is a paramyxovirus.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Roseola: HHV-6/7; fever first, rash after defervescence.
- Measles: paramyxovirus; three Cs, Koplik spots, then rash.
- A careful timeline is often more useful than rash morphology alone.

questions.stem: What is the usual management of uncomplicated roseola described in the source?

options.label: C
options.text: Routine acyclovir for children in routine care

options.label: E
options.text: Supportive care with hydration and antipyretics

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive care with hydration and antipyretics
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes supportive treatment, good hydration and antipyretics for roseola. Most children recover well.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. This matches the management listed.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated viral roseola.
- A. Incorrect. Tuberculosis requires a separate antimicrobial regimen.
- C. Incorrect. Acyclovir is not routine treatment for HHV-6/7 roseola.
- B. Incorrect. Lymph node drainage is unrelated to uncomplicated roseola.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Roseola is usually self-limiting.
- Treat symptoms and maintain hydration.
- Assess and manage febrile seizures if they occur.

cases.title: A schoolchild develops a slapped-cheek rash
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child develops a mild febrile illness followed by striking erythema over both cheeks. A few days later, a lacy reticular rash appears over the arms and legs. The child is otherwise well.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: B
options.text: Erythema infectiosum due to Parvovirus B19

questions.correctAnswerText: Erythema infectiosum due to Parvovirus B19
questions.initialExplanation: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease/slapped-cheek syndrome) is caused by Parvovirus B19 and classically causes bright cheek erythema followed by a lacy or reticular rash.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. The age and slapped-cheek followed by lacy rash are characteristic.
- D. Incorrect. Roseola usually affects infants and produces rash as high fever resolves.
- C. Incorrect. Measles has cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots.
- A. Incorrect. Rubella has mild fever, rash and postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy.
- E. Incorrect. Scarlet fever has a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Parvovirus B19 = fifth disease / slapped-cheek syndrome.
- Classically affects school-age children.
- Lacy/reticular rash may follow the cheek erythema.

questions.stem: Which rash description is most characteristic of Parvovirus B19 infection in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Koplik spots followed by a descending maculopapular rash

options.label: B
options.text: Erythematous macule expanding centrifugally from a tick bite

options.label: C
options.text: Slapped cheeks followed by a lacy or reticulated rash on the extremities

options.label: E
options.text: Pruritic vesicles in crops at different stages

questions.correctAnswerText: Slapped cheeks followed by a lacy or reticulated rash on the extremities
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance erythema infectiosum as a slapped-cheek syndrome followed by a lacy/reticulated rash, particularly on the extremities.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. This is the classic clinical pattern.
- E. Incorrect. This describes varicella.
- A. Incorrect. This describes measles.
- D. Incorrect. This describes scarlet fever.
- B. Incorrect. This describes erythema migrans in Lyme disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Slapped cheek + lacy rash = Parvovirus B19.
- Usually a mild self-limiting illness in otherwise healthy children.
- Maternal infection and chronic hemolytic disease are important special situations.

questions.stem: A child with sickle cell disease develops sudden pallor and worsening anemia after contact with a child who had a slapped-cheek rash. Which complication should be suspected?

options.label: D
options.text: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia due to EBV

questions.correctAnswerText: Transient aplastic crisis
questions.initialExplanation: Parvovirus B19 can suppress erythropoiesis and cause a transient aplastic crisis, particularly in children with chronic hemolytic anemia such as sickle cell disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Parvovirus B19 is associated with transient aplastic crisis in chronic hemolytic disorders.
- D. Incorrect. EBV may be associated with autoimmune hemolytic anemia, but the exposure and rash point to parvovirus.
- C. Incorrect. Splenic rupture is associated with infectious mononucleosis and splenomegaly.
- B. Incorrect. Hemorrhagic cystitis is not the typical complication of Parvovirus B19.
- E. Incorrect. Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Parvovirus B19 can cause transient aplastic crisis in chronic hemolytic anemia.
- Consider it with an abrupt hemoglobin fall and reticulocytopenia after exposure.
- Monitor clinically significant anemia carefully.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman is exposed to a child with Parvovirus B19. Which fetal complication is highlighted?

options.label: A
options.text: Hydrops fetalis due to severe fetal anemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Hydrops fetalis due to severe fetal anemia
questions.initialExplanation: The source states that Parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy may cause hydrops fetalis and fetal death due to severe anemia, although many infected fetuses recover.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Severe fetal anemia may lead to hydrops fetalis.
- B. Incorrect. Congenital rubella syndrome is due to rubella virus.
- D. Incorrect. Neural tube defects are developmental malformations, not the fetal complication listed here.
- C. Incorrect. This is associated with congenital varicella, not Parvovirus B19.
- E. Incorrect. Neonatal HSV causes skin/eye/mouth, CNS or disseminated infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy can cause fetal anemia and hydrops fetalis.
- Fetal loss is possible but not inevitable.
- This complication is distinct from congenital rubella syndrome.

cases.title: An adolescent has fever, tonsillopharyngitis and generalized lymphadenopathy
cases.vignette: A 15-year-old adolescent presents with prolonged fever, marked sore throat, enlarged tonsils with exudate, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and palpable splenomegaly. The blood film shows atypical lymphocytes. The family reports that symptoms have persisted for more than a week.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: D
options.text: Infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein-Barr virus

options.label: E
options.text: Scarlet fever due to group A streptococcus

questions.correctAnswerText: Infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein-Barr virus
questions.initialExplanation: The combination of fever, tonsillopharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes is typical of EBV infectious mononucleosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. The clinical pattern and atypical lymphocytosis support EBV infectious mononucleosis.
- E. Incorrect. Scarlet fever causes sore throat and sandpaper rash with strawberry tongue, but does not typically cause this generalized lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Measles has cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a spreading rash.
- B. Incorrect. Mumps is characterized by parotitis.
- A. Incorrect. Hepatitis A causes a gastrointestinal prodrome and jaundice/hepatomegaly rather than exudative tonsillopharyngitis with atypical lymphocytes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EBV infectious mononucleosis: fever + tonsillopharyngitis + lymphadenopathy + splenomegaly.
- Atypical lymphocytes are a useful hematological clue.
- Adolescents commonly present with more recognizable disease.

questions.stem: Which investigation finding supports infectious mononucleosis in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Thick and thin Giemsa blood films showing Plasmodium

options.label: C
options.text: Atypical lymphocytes with EBV serology; heterophile testing may be negative in young children

options.label: E
options.text: Nasopharyngeal PCR positive for Bordetella pertussis

questions.correctAnswerText: Atypical lymphocytes with EBV serology; heterophile testing may be negative in young children
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes atypical lymphocytes in EBV infection and notes that the Monospot/heterophile antibody test may be negative in young children. EBV-specific serology can support diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. Atypical lymphocytes and EBV serology support the diagnosis; a negative heterophile test in a young child does not exclude EBV.
- A. Incorrect. Blood films are used to diagnose malaria.
- B. Incorrect. Stool microscopy is used in amoebiasis and other intestinal parasitic infections.
- D. Incorrect. Mantoux testing evaluates TB infection.
- E. Incorrect. Nasopharyngeal PCR is used for pertussis diagnosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EBV: atypical lymphocytes.
- Monospot may be negative in young children.
- EBV-specific serology is useful when clinical suspicion remains.

questions.stem: A child with suspected EBV mononucleosis is prescribed amoxicillin for tonsillitis and develops a widespread rash. Which explanation best fits the source?

options.label: A
options.text: It is diagnostic of Lyme disease

options.label: B
options.text: This is the typical reaction to BCG

options.label: D
options.text: The rash proves the child has measles

options.label: E
options.text: An aminopenicillin-associated rash can occur in EBV infectious mononucleosis

questions.correctAnswerText: An aminopenicillin-associated rash can occur in EBV infectious mononucleosis
questions.initialExplanation: The source advises avoiding ampicillin/amoxicillin in infectious mononucleosis because a prominent rash may occur during EBV infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. Aminopenicillin-associated rash is a well-known clue in EBV mononucleosis.
- D. Incorrect. Measles has a characteristic prodrome and Koplik spots; an antibiotic-associated rash alone does not diagnose measles.
- B. Incorrect. BCG causes a localized papule/ulcer and scar at the inoculation site, not this generalized drug-associated rash.
- C. Incorrect. Vaccine-associated paralytic polio is a neurological complication of OPV, not a rash.
- A. Incorrect. Lyme disease is associated with erythema migrans after tick exposure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Avoid ampicillin/amoxicillin in suspected EBV mononucleosis when possible.
- A widespread rash may follow aminopenicillin exposure.
- Do not mistake this for proof of measles or a primary drug allergy without clinical assessment.

questions.stem: An adolescent with EBV mononucleosis develops sudden severe left upper abdominal pain, dizziness and hypotension. Which complication must be urgently considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Splenic rupture
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists splenic rupture among complications of infectious mononucleosis. Splenomegaly makes the spleen vulnerable, so acute abdominal pain and circulatory compromise require emergency assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. Sudden abdominal pain and shock in a patient with splenomegaly should raise concern for splenic rupture.
- D. Incorrect. Orchitis is a complication of mumps.
- B. Incorrect. Aplastic crisis is associated with Parvovirus B19, especially in chronic hemolytic anemia.
- C. Incorrect. Pott disease is skeletal tuberculosis of the spine.
- A. Incorrect. Intussusception is an intestinal disorder with episodic colicky pain, vomiting and possible bloody stool.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EBV complications include splenic rupture, airway obstruction, CNS disease, hepatitis, myocarditis and autoimmune hemolysis.
- Severe abdominal pain in a patient with splenomegaly is an emergency.
- Steroids are reserved for selected severe complications such as significant upper-airway obstruction, not routine uncomplicated disease.

cases.title: A child develops an itchy vesicular eruption in successive crops
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old unvaccinated child develops fever and an intensely itchy eruption. New vesicles continue to appear over several days. Examination shows macules, papules, vesicles and crusted lesions at the same time, with the greatest concentration on the trunk and scalp.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Varicella (chickenpox)
questions.initialExplanation: Varicella due to varicella-zoster virus causes a fever-associated, pruritic vesicular eruption in crops, with lesions at different stages of evolution.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Pruritic vesicles appearing in successive crops with lesions at different stages are characteristic of varicella.
- D. Incorrect. Impetigo produces superficial vesicles/pustules that rupture and form honey-coloured crusts.
- C. Incorrect. HFMD causes oral lesions and lesions on hands and feet.
- E. Incorrect. Herpes zoster is a localized dermatomal eruption due to reactivation of latent VZV.
- B. Incorrect. Erythema infectiosum causes slapped cheeks and a lacy rash, not crops of vesicles.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Varicella: VZV, pruritic vesicles in crops.
- Lesions may be present at different stages simultaneously.
- Trunk and scalp are commonly involved before widespread peripheral distribution.

questions.stem: Which transmission routes are listed for varicella in the source?

options.label: D
options.text: Respiratory droplets, direct contact with vesicular fluid and transplacental transmission

questions.correctAnswerText: Respiratory droplets, direct contact with vesicular fluid and transplacental transmission
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists droplet spread, direct contact with vesicular fluid and transplacental transmission as routes of VZV transmission.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. These are the routes listed for varicella.
- C. Incorrect. Tick transmission is associated with Lyme disease and rickettsial infections.
- E. Incorrect. Fecal-oral transmission occurs in infections such as hepatitis A and amoebiasis.
- A. Incorrect. Contaminated food and water are associated with enteric infections such as typhoid.
- B. Incorrect. Blood transmission is possible for selected infections but is not the routine route described for varicella.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- VZV spreads by respiratory droplets and direct contact with lesions.
- Transplacental spread is also listed.
- The incubation period in the source is 14-21 days.

questions.stem: A child receiving immunosuppressive therapy develops widespread varicella with progressive systemic illness. Which antiviral is recognized for indicated severe/high-risk cases?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acyclovir
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists acyclovir for selected indications, particularly immunodeficiency/immunocompromised patients, while uncomplicated varicella is generally managed supportively.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. Acyclovir is the antiviral listed for indicated high-risk/severe cases.
- E. Incorrect. Penicillin V treats susceptible streptococcal infections such as scarlet fever.
- B. Incorrect. Metronidazole is used for selected protozoal/anaerobic infections, including symptomatic amoebiasis in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Isoniazid is used in TB treatment/prevention.
- A. Incorrect. Albendazole is used for helminth infections such as enterobiasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Uncomplicated varicella: supportive treatment.
- Acyclovir is reserved for source-listed indications, including immunodeficiency/high-risk cases.
- Avoid aspirin as an antipyretic in varicella because of the risk of Reye syndrome noted.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old who had chickenpox in infancy develops grouped vesicles and pain confined to one thoracic dermatome. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Herpes zoster due to reactivation of latent VZV

questions.correctAnswerText: Herpes zoster due to reactivation of latent VZV
questions.initialExplanation: Herpes zoster (shingles) is caused by reactivation of latent VZV in sensory ganglia, producing a vesicular eruption in a dermatomal distribution. The source notes that thoracic dermatomes are common and neuralgic pain is often less prominent in children than in adults.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption after previous varicella indicates zoster.
- C. Incorrect. Primary varicella causes a widespread eruption in crops over multiple body regions.
- B. Incorrect. HFMD causes oral lesions and lesions on hands and feet.
- E. Incorrect. Disseminated HSV has different patterns and is especially concerning in neonatal/immunocompromised patients.
- D. Incorrect. Erythema migrans is an expanding erythematous lesion after tick bite in Lyme disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Zoster = reactivation of latent VZV.
- Vesicular eruption follows a sensory dermatome.
- Recurrent or multidermatomal zoster should raise concern for underlying immunocompromise, e.g. HIV.
- Childhood zoster is more common after primary varicella in the first year of life.

cases.title: A child deteriorates after an initially uncomplicated varicella eruption
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child develops fever and a generalized, intensely itchy vesicular eruption in successive crops. After several days, the child appears to be improving. On the following day, the fever rises again, and several lesions become increasingly tender with expanding surrounding erythema and purulent discharge. The child is now markedly unwell.

questions.stem: Which complication described in the varicella section of standard guidance clinical guidance best explains this change in the clinical course?

options.label: B
options.text: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus as herpes zoster

options.label: C
options.text: Secondary bacterial infection of the skin lesions by staphylococci or streptococci

questions.correctAnswerText: Secondary bacterial infection of the skin lesions by staphylococci or streptococci
questions.initialExplanation: A renewed fever accompanied by increasing local tenderness, erythema and purulent discharge suggests bacterial superinfection of varicella lesions. standard guidance clinical guidance specifically lists secondary skin infection by staphylococci or streptococci as a complication.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. The source identifies secondary bacterial skin infections by *Staphylococcus* or *Streptococcus* among the complications associated with chickenpox. The new fever and deterioration in the appearance of previously vesicular lesions support this complication rather than an uncomplicated viral course. The source also links severe secondary infection with necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shock syndrome.
- A. Incorrect. Cerebellitis/ataxia is included in the source's enterovirus complication material; it would cause neurological features such as gait incoordination, not purulent and increasingly tender skin lesions.
- B. Incorrect. Herpes zoster is caused by reactivation of latent VZV and produces a dermatomal vesicular eruption. It does not explain the described purulent change in existing chickenpox lesions.
- D. Incorrect. Glomerulonephritis is a renal complication listed in the viral disease comparison, but it does not account for the local skin findings and renewed fever.
- E. Incorrect. Myocarditis/pericarditis are cardiovascular complications listed in the viral-complication material; they do not explain the evolving infected skin lesions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Varicella lesions may develop secondary bacterial infection.
- standard guidance clinical guidance names staphylococci and streptococci as causes.
- Severe secondary infection may be associated with necrotizing fasciitis or toxic shock syndrome.
- A new fever or marked deterioration after initial improvement should prompt reassessment for a complication.

source.raw: Infectious Diseases lecture sheet — Page 9, *Chickenpox: complications*.

topics.name: Hand-Foot-and-Mouth Disease and Other Enterovirus Presentations

cases.title: A preschool child has painful oral ulcers and lesions on the hands and feet
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child develops low-grade fever, poor oral intake and painful oral vesicles/ulcers. Small vesicular lesions are also present on the palms and soles. Several children at nursery have had similar symptoms.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
questions.initialExplanation: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is a common enterovirus illness in preschool children, frequently associated with Coxsackie virus, and causes oral lesions with lesions on the hands and feet.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. The combination of painful oral lesions and vesicles on palms/soles is characteristic.
- D. Incorrect. Measles causes a systemic prodrome, Koplik spots and a widespread maculopapular rash.
- E. Incorrect. Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash and pharyngitis.
- C. Incorrect. Rubella is characterized by mild fever, rash and postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy.
- A. Incorrect. EBV causes tonsillopharyngitis, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HFMD: enterovirus/Coxsackie, often in preschool children.
- Oral vesicles/ulcers + hand and foot lesions are the key pattern.
- Painful oral disease can lead to dehydration.

questions.stem: Which complication is most important to assess in a young child with painful oral lesions from HFMD?

options.label: C
options.text: Dehydration due to poor oral intake

questions.correctAnswerText: Dehydration due to poor oral intake
questions.initialExplanation: Painful oral vesicles and ulcers may reduce fluid intake in young children. The source lists supportive management and attention to hydration for enteroviral illnesses.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. Reduced intake from painful oral lesions can cause dehydration.
- B. Incorrect. Splenic rupture is a complication of EBV infectious mononucleosis.
- E. Incorrect. Hydrops fetalis is associated with fetal Parvovirus B19 infection.
- A. Incorrect. Intestinal perforation may complicate typhoid fever, not uncomplicated HFMD.
- D. Incorrect. Disseminated BCG infection occurs in immunocompromised individuals after BCG.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HFMD is usually self-limiting.
- Monitor hydration and ability to drink.
- Supportive management is the mainstay.

questions.stem: The infectious disease comparison in Clinical guidance several systemic complications that may occur with enteroviruses. Which combination is included?

options.label: A
options.text: Pott disease, TB lymphadenitis and miliary spread

options.label: E
options.text: Congenital cataract, PDA and sensorineural deafness

questions.correctAnswerText: Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis/pericarditis and pleurodynia
questions.initialExplanation: The source's viral complication table lists enterovirus-associated CNS disease (meningitis/meningoencephalitis/cerebellitis/ataxia), respiratory and gastrointestinal disease, myocarditis/pericarditis and pleurodynia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. These are all included among enteroviral complications in the source.
- E. Incorrect. These are features of congenital rubella syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. These are complications of mumps.
- A. Incorrect. These are extrapulmonary forms of tuberculosis.
- D. Incorrect. These are complications of Parvovirus B19.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Enteroviruses are not limited to hand-foot-and-mouth disease.
- CNS complications include meningitis/meningoencephalitis and cerebellitis/ataxia.
- Myocarditis, pericarditis and pleurodynia are also listed.

questions.stem: What is the usual treatment for uncomplicated hand-foot-and-mouth disease?

options.label: C
options.text: Supportive care with hydration and antipyretics

options.label: D
options.text: Metronidazole for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive care with hydration and antipyretics
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists supportive treatment for enteroviral disease, with hydration and antipyretics. Antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated viral HFMD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. This is the recommended supportive approach.
- B. Incorrect. Acyclovir is used for selected HSV/VZV infections, not routine HFMD.
- A. Incorrect. Penicillin V is used for streptococcal infection such as scarlet fever.
- E. Incorrect. Antituberculous treatment is for TB, not HFMD.
- D. Incorrect. Metronidazole is used for selected protozoal/anaerobic infections, not uncomplicated HFMD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Uncomplicated HFMD: supportive care.
- Maintain hydration and give antipyretics as needed.
- Consider assessment if poor intake, dehydration or neurological/cardiac symptoms develop.

cases.title: A young child has painful gingivostomatitis and refuses to drink
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child develops fever, irritability and painful vesicles and ulcers involving the lips, gingiva, tongue and hard palate. The child refuses fluids and has reduced urine output.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Primary HSV gingivostomatitis
questions.initialExplanation: Primary HSV infection in young children can present as painful gingivostomatitis, with vesicles and ulcers involving the lips, gingiva, tongue and hard palate. Poor oral intake may lead to dehydration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The widespread painful oral vesicles/ulcers with fever in a young child are typical of primary HSV gingivostomatitis.
- C. Incorrect. Herpangina usually causes vesicles/ulcers predominantly in the posterior oropharynx.
- B. Incorrect. Scarlet fever produces pharyngitis, strawberry tongue and a sandpaper rash.
- E. Incorrect. Rubella causes a mild febrile rash illness and lymphadenopathy.
- D. Incorrect. Impetigo causes superficial skin lesions that rupture and form honey-coloured crusts.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary HSV gingivostomatitis is common in preschool children.
- Painful oral vesicles/ulcers can cause dehydration.
- HSV may also cause skin, eye, CNS or disseminated disease.

questions.stem: Which extra-oral HSV presentation is correctly matched with its site?

options.label: B
options.text: Herpetic whitlow - finger infection with painful grouped vesicles

options.label: D
options.text: Neonatal disseminated HSV - a localized honey-crusted skin rash

options.label: E
options.text: Eczema herpeticum - isolated painless ulcer at a tick bite

questions.correctAnswerText: Herpetic whitlow - finger infection with painful grouped vesicles
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists HSV-associated conditions including eczema herpeticum, herpetic whitlow, keratoconjunctivitis and CNS infection/encephalitis, as well as neonatal disseminated disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. Herpetic whitlow is HSV infection of a finger, producing painful grouped vesicles.
- E. Incorrect. Eczema herpeticum is widespread HSV vesicular infection over eczematous skin, not erythema migrans.
- C. Incorrect. Keratoconjunctivitis affects the eye, not the kidney.
- A. Incorrect. HSV encephalitis affects the CNS; parotitis suggests mumps.
- D. Incorrect. Neonatal disseminated HSV can involve multiple organs and may present with sepsis-like illness, pneumonitis and DIC, not only localized skin disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HSV manifestations include gingivostomatitis, eczema herpeticum, herpetic whitlow and keratoconjunctivitis.
- CNS disease includes meningitis/encephalitis.
- Neonatal infection may be localized, CNS or disseminated.

questions.stem: A 12-day-old neonate develops poor feeding, fever, lethargy, respiratory distress and coagulopathy. The mother had active genital vesicles around delivery. Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?
questions.correctAnswerText: Disseminated neonatal HSV infection
questions.initialExplanation: The source identifies neonatal HSV transmission around delivery and describes disseminated infection with sepsis, pneumonitis and DIC, which carries high mortality.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The timing, maternal exposure and multisystem neonatal illness are concerning for disseminated HSV.
- E. Incorrect. Roseola is a self-limited febrile rash illness in infants/young children.
- B. Incorrect. Congenital rubella is associated with congenital anomalies such as cataract, hearing loss and heart disease.
- D. Incorrect. HFMD is usually a childhood oral/acral vesicular illness, not neonatal sepsis with DIC.
- C. Incorrect. Enterobiasis causes nocturnal perianal itching, not neonatal systemic disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal HSV may be acquired prenatally/perinatally, particularly around delivery.
- Disseminated disease can resemble neonatal sepsis.
- The source lists pneumonitis, DIC and high mortality.
- This is a time-critical neonatal infection.

questions.stem: A neonate with suspected HSV encephalitis has seizures and altered consciousness. Which management principle is most appropriate from the source?

options.label: B
options.text: Urgent antiviral treatment with acyclovir for indicated severe/CNS HSV disease

options.label: C
options.text: Observe without treatment because neonatal HSV is typically benign

options.label: D
options.text: Withhold antivirals until a skin rash appears

options.label: E
options.text: Give penicillin V as the specific antiviral

questions.correctAnswerText: Urgent antiviral treatment with acyclovir for indicated severe/CNS HSV disease
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists acyclovir for selected HSV indications and emphasizes that early treatment of HSV encephalitis improves prognosis. Neonatal disseminated infection is severe and requires urgent management.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. Suspected neonatal/CNS HSV is severe and requires urgent antiviral therapy as described.
- D. Incorrect. CNS or disseminated disease may occur without a typical skin eruption; treatment should not wait for skin lesions.
- E. Incorrect. Penicillin V is an antibacterial drug, not an HSV antiviral.
- A. Incorrect. Albendazole treats helminth infections.
- C. Incorrect. Neonatal HSV may have high mortality, particularly disseminated infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acyclovir is listed for indicated HSV disease.
- Early treatment of HSV encephalitis is associated with a better prognosis in the source.
- Neonatal disseminated HSV is a medical emergency.
- Do not rely on the presence of skin vesicles to exclude CNS/disseminated HSV.

cases.title: Selecting a lesion-based test in suspected neonatal HSV
cases.vignette: A 12-day-old neonate is admitted with fever, poor feeding and lethargy. Several grouped vesicles are noted on the skin. The mother had active genital vesicles around the time of delivery. The team obtains a sample from one of the infant's vesicular lesions for virological investigation.

questions.stem: Which molecular investigation specifically listed clinical guidance should be performed on the vesicular-fluid sample?

options.label: B
options.text: Thick and thin Giemsa-stained blood films

options.label: C
options.text: Mantoux testing with measurement of induration

options.label: E
options.text: PCR of vesicular fluid for HSV

questions.correctAnswerText: PCR of vesicular fluid for HSV
questions.initialExplanation: The HSV section lists PCR of vesicular fluid as a diagnostic investigation. The maternal history and neonatal vesicles make HSV an important diagnosis to investigate urgently.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. PCR of vesicular fluid is specifically listed in the HSV diagnostic section and directly uses material from the lesion described in the case.
- A. Incorrect. Anti-HAV IgM is used to identify recent hepatitis A infection; it is unrelated to a neonatal vesicular eruption.
- B. Incorrect. Thick and thin Giemsa-stained blood films are the key parasitological investigation listed for malaria.
- C. Incorrect. Mantoux testing assesses immune reactivity to TB antigens and is not a diagnostic test for HSV lesions.
- D. Incorrect. Stool microscopy for cysts is part of the amoebiasis work-up, not the investigation of vesicular skin lesions.

standard guidance clinical guidance also lists a Tzanck (written as “Zank” in the OCR text) smear. The question asks specifically for the molecular test performed on vesicular fluid, for which PCR is the matching answer.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HSV diagnosis clinical guidance includes clinical assessment, PCR of vesicular fluid and Tzanck smear.
- Neonatal HSV may present as localized disease, CNS disease or disseminated infection.
- A neonatal sepsis-like presentation with maternal/perinatal HSV exposure requires urgent evaluation.

source.raw: Infectious Diseases lecture sheet — Page 9, *HSV infection: diagnosis and complications*.

cases.title: A child develops a gastrointestinal prodrome followed by jaundice
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child develops fever, malaise, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. Several days later, the family notices yellow discoloration of the eyes and dark urine. Examination reveals hepatomegaly. The child has no chronic liver disease.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acute hepatitis A
questions.initialExplanation: Hepatitis A is an acute viral hepatitis transmitted by the fecal-oral route. It may cause a prodrome of fever, malaise, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain followed by jaundice and hepatomegaly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. The gastrointestinal prodrome followed by jaundice and hepatomegaly fits acute hepatitis A.
- A. Incorrect. EBV typically causes tonsillopharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes.
- D. Incorrect. Typhoid causes prolonged fever, abdominal symptoms and sometimes rose spots, but the classic sequence is not acute icteric hepatitis.
- E. Incorrect. Visceral leishmaniasis causes prolonged fever, marked hepatosplenomegaly, cachexia and pancytopenia.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital rubella is a fetal infection causing congenital abnormalities.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HAV is an RNA picornavirus.
- Transmission: fecal-oral.
- Clinical course: preicteric symptoms → icteric phase → convalescence.
- Most children recover with supportive care.

questions.stem: Which serological result indicates recent or acute hepatitis A infection?
questions.correctAnswerText: Anti-HAV IgM
questions.initialExplanation: The source states that HAV-specific IgM indicates recent infection, whereas IgG indicates previous infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. Anti-HAV IgM is the marker of recent/acute infection.
- A. Incorrect. Anti-HAV IgG indicates previous infection or immunity.
- B. Incorrect. Mantoux testing evaluates TB infection.
- C. Incorrect. Anti-HBs is a marker of hepatitis B immunity.
- D. Incorrect. EBNA antibodies relate to EBV infection, not HAV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HAV IgM: recent/acute infection.
- HAV IgG: previous infection/immunity.
- Interpret serology in the clinical context.

questions.stem: A child with hepatitis A has persistent vomiting, dehydration and a prolonged prothrombin time. Which management decision is supported by the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat with metronidazole as a specific antiviral

options.label: B
options.text: Give routine acyclovir to most HAV cases

options.label: D
options.text: Admit for supportive care and monitoring

options.label: E
options.text: Discharge without assessment because HAV not usually causes severe disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Admit for supportive care and monitoring
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists admission for severe vomiting, dehydration or prolonged PT. Treatment is mainly supportive with adequate hydration and nutrition. Fulminant hepatic failure is rare in children but can occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. Severe vomiting, dehydration and prolonged PT are admission indications in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Although prognosis is usually good, severe disease and rare fulminant hepatic failure can occur.
- C. Incorrect. Antituberculous therapy treats TB, not HAV.
- B. Incorrect. Acyclovir treats selected herpes virus infections, not hepatitis A.
- A. Incorrect. Metronidazole is not an antiviral treatment for HAV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HAV treatment is mainly supportive.
- Admit for severe vomiting, dehydration or prolonged PT.
- Fulminant hepatic failure is rare in children (<1% in the source) but is important to recognize.

questions.stem: Which preventive measure is specifically listed for close contacts of hepatitis A?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hepatitis A vaccine
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists hygienic measures, food sanitation and hepatitis A vaccine for close contacts as prevention.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. HAV vaccine is listed for close contacts.
- D. Incorrect. BCG prevents severe forms of tuberculosis.
- A. Incorrect. OPV protects against poliomyelitis.
- C. Incorrect. MMR prevents measles, mumps and rubella.
- B. Incorrect. Isoniazid is used for TB chemoprophylaxis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HAV prevention: hand hygiene and food sanitation.
- HAV vaccine is listed for close contacts.
- Most cases resolve with supportive treatment.

cases.title: An infant has recurrent infections, oral thrush and poor growth
cases.vignette: A 9-month-old infant is assessed for poor weight gain, recurrent bacterial infections, persistent oral candidiasis, chronic diarrhea and generalized lymphadenopathy. The mother has known HIV infection. An initial HIV antibody test is positive.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Paediatric HIV infection
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes paediatric HIV with nonspecific symptoms such as weight loss, fever, diarrhea, failure to thrive, recurrent infections and oral thrush. Vertical transmission is an important route.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. The maternal history and pattern of recurrent infections, thrush and poor growth support HIV infection.
- A. Incorrect. HAV usually causes an acute self-limited illness with a gastrointestinal prodrome and jaundice.
- C. Incorrect. Roseola causes fever followed by rash, not chronic recurrent infections.
- B. Incorrect. Enterobiasis causes nocturnal perianal itching and sleep disturbance.
- E. Incorrect. Scarlet fever is an acute streptococcal illness with sore throat and sandpaper rash.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Paediatric HIV may present with FTT, recurrent infections, chronic diarrhea and oral thrush.
- Vertical transmission is an important route in children.
- Consider HIV in an infant with recurrent/severe or unusual infections and maternal risk.

questions.stem: Why is an HIV antibody test alone not reliable for diagnosing HIV infection in an infant younger than 18 months?

options.label: A
options.text: The antibody test detects bacterial infection

options.label: B
options.text: Maternal antibodies typically protect the infant from HIV

options.label: C
options.text: HIV not usually produces antibodies in children

options.label: D
options.text: Maternal HIV antibodies may cross the placenta and cause a false-positive antibody result

options.label: E
options.text: Infants cannot have HIV RNA in blood

questions.correctAnswerText: Maternal HIV antibodies may cross the placenta and cause a false-positive antibody result
questions.initialExplanation: The source states that HIV serology is not diagnostic early in infants under 18 months because maternal antibodies may persist and cause a false-positive antibody test. It identifies DNA PCR as the best diagnostic test in this age group.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. Transplacentally acquired maternal antibodies can remain detectable in the infant.
- C. Incorrect. Infected children can produce their own HIV antibodies, but maternal antibodies confound early serology.
- A. Incorrect. HIV antibody assays detect antibodies, not bacterial infection.
- E. Incorrect. Viral nucleic acid can be detected by PCR.
- B. Incorrect. Maternal antibodies do not reliably protect the infant from infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Under 18 months: maternal antibodies may cause false-positive HIV serology.
- The source identifies HIV DNA PCR as the best diagnostic test.
- Two negative HIV DNA PCR tests within the first 3 months of life are described as indicating that the infant is not infected.

questions.stem: Which clinical category in the source includes opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, severe growth faltering and encephalopathy?
questions.correctAnswerText: Category C - severely symptomatic
questions.initialExplanation: The source classifies paediatric HIV as N (asymptomatic), A (mildly symptomatic), B (moderately symptomatic) and C (severely symptomatic). Category C includes opportunistic infections, severe growth faltering, encephalopathy and malignancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. These severe manifestations are listed under category C.
- E. Incorrect. Category N is asymptomatic.
- A. Incorrect. Category A is mildly symptomatic and may include lymphadenopathy or parotid enlargement.
- B. Incorrect. Category B includes recurrent bacterial infections, candidiasis, chronic diarrhea and lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis.
- D. Incorrect. The source does not classify HIV infection using a latent HIV category in this way.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- N: asymptomatic.
- A: mild symptoms, e.g. lymphadenopathy/parotid enlargement.
- B: moderate symptoms, e.g. recurrent bacterial infections/candidiasis/chronic diarrhea.
- C: severe disease with opportunistic infections, severe FTT, encephalopathy and malignancy.

questions.stem: Which management strategy is included in the source for an infant diagnosed with HIV?

options.label: A
options.text: Give isoniazid as the treatment for HIV

options.label: E
options.text: Start antiretroviral therapy shortly after diagnosis, with nutritional and multidisciplinary support

questions.correctAnswerText: Start antiretroviral therapy shortly after diagnosis, with nutritional and multidisciplinary support
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists antiretroviral therapy, PCP prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole, aggressive treatment of infections, nutritional support, a multidisciplinary team and regular follow-up. It emphasizes that infants should start ART shortly after diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. This includes the infant ART recommendation and the supportive components listed.
- D. Incorrect. The source specifically states that infants should start ART shortly after diagnosis.
- A. Incorrect. Isoniazid is used for TB treatment/prevention, not as HIV treatment.
- C. Incorrect. Vaccination should be reviewed according to clinical status and the source's schedule; clinical guidance does not recommend stopping all vaccines permanently.
- B. Incorrect. Supportive care alone is not adequate HIV management.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ART is central to HIV management.
- The source names zidovudine, lamivudine and protease inhibitor therapy as examples.
- Cotrimoxazole is listed for PCP prophylaxis.
- Nutritional support and multidisciplinary follow-up are important.
- Infants should start ART soon after diagnosis as stated.

questions.stem: Which combination is recognized to reduce vertical transmission of HIV?

options.label: A
options.text: Maternal ART, Caesarean delivery when indicated, infant zidovudine for 6 weeks and avoidance of breastfeeding where advised

options.label: B
options.text: Maternal penicillin, infant BCG and no maternal follow-up

options.label: E
options.text: Maternal acyclovir and infant MMR at birth

questions.correctAnswerText: Maternal ART, Caesarean delivery when indicated, infant zidovudine for 6 weeks and avoidance of breastfeeding where advised
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists maternal ART, elective Caesarean section, avoidance of prolonged rupture of membranes/unnecessary instrumentation, zidovudine for the infant for 6 weeks and contraindication of breastfeeding as measures to reduce vertical transmission. This question reflects the source's teaching content.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These measures are listed in the source to reduce vertical transmission.
- B. Incorrect. Penicillin and BCG do not prevent vertical HIV transmission.
- E. Incorrect. Acyclovir and MMR do not constitute the HIV prevention plan described.
- C. Incorrect. Isoniazid and OPV are not the listed vertical HIV prevention regimen.
- D. Incorrect. Metronidazole and HBIG are not the listed interventions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Maternal ART is a key measure to reduce vertical transmission.
- The source lists infant zidovudine for 6 weeks.
- It also lists delivery planning and avoidance of prolonged rupture of membranes/unnecessary instrumentation.
- Breastfeeding advice here is recorded as stated in the 2024 course clinical guidance; follow the source's curriculum context.

cases.title: A child has sore throat, strawberry tongue and a sandpaper rash
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat and headache. The tongue is initially coated white and later becomes red and prominent. A diffuse fine erythematous rash began on the neck and spread to the trunk and extremities. The skin feels rough like sandpaper, and redness is accentuated in flexural creases.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Scarlet fever
questions.initialExplanation: Scarlet fever is caused by group A beta-hemolytic streptococci producing pyrogenic exotoxin. It causes fever, sore throat, strawberry tongue and a characteristic sandpaper-like rash.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. The sore throat, strawberry tongue and sandpaper rash support scarlet fever.
- B. Incorrect. Measles has the three Cs, Koplik spots and a spreading maculopapular rash.
- C. Incorrect. Rubella usually causes a milder illness with postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy.
- A. Incorrect. Varicella causes crops of itchy vesicles at different stages.
- D. Incorrect. Parvovirus B19 causes slapped cheeks and a lacy rash.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cause: group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus.
- Pyrogenic exotoxin causes the rash.
- Features: fever, sore throat, strawberry tongue and sandpaper rash.

questions.stem: Which finding is particularly supportive of scarlet fever on skin examination?

options.label: A
options.text: Grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution

options.label: B
options.text: Lacy reticular rash after slapped-cheek erythema

options.label: C
options.text: Sandpaper-like rash with Pastia lines in flexural creases

options.label: D
options.text: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa

options.label: E
options.text: Erythema migrans at a tick-bite site

questions.correctAnswerText: Sandpaper-like rash with Pastia lines in flexural creases
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes a diffuse maculopapular rash with a sandpaper texture and prominent flexural involvement, including Pastia lines in the cubital fossa.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. Sandpaper rash and Pastia lines are classic scarlet fever findings.
- B. Incorrect. This describes Parvovirus B19 infection.
- A. Incorrect. This describes herpes zoster.
- D. Incorrect. This is a measles enanthem.
- E. Incorrect. This is Lyme erythema migrans.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Scarlet fever rash: diffuse, fine, rough/sandpaper.
- Pastia lines are accentuated in flexural skin creases.
- Desquamation may follow after several days.

questions.stem: Which treatment is listed for scarlet fever in the source?
questions.correctAnswerText: Penicillin V for 10 days
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists penicillin V for 10 days for scarlet fever caused by group A beta-hemolytic streptococci.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. This is the antibiotic regimen named in the source.
- C. Incorrect. Acyclovir is used for selected HSV/VZV infections.
- E. Incorrect. Isoniazid and rifampicin are part of TB treatment regimens.
- A. Incorrect. Metronidazole is used for selected protozoal/anaerobic infections.
- B. Incorrect. Albendazole is used for helminth infections such as enterobiasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Scarlet fever is a GAS toxin-mediated illness.
- The source recommends Penicillin V for 10 days.
- Complications include rheumatic fever, PSGN and reactive arthritis.

questions.stem: Which complication group is associated with scarlet fever in the source?

options.label: C
options.text: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever and reactive arthritis

options.label: E
options.text: Hydrops fetalis and transient aplastic crisis

questions.correctAnswerText: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever and reactive arthritis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance PSGN, rheumatic fever and reactive arthritis among complications associated with group A streptococcal infection/scarlet fever.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. These are post-streptococcal immune complications.
- E. Incorrect. These are complications of Parvovirus B19.
- A. Incorrect. These may occur with EBV infectious mononucleosis.
- B. Incorrect. These are features of severe falciparum malaria.
- D. Incorrect. These are forms of extrapulmonary TB.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Scarlet fever is caused by GAS.
- Complications include PSGN, rheumatic fever and reactive arthritis.
- Treat appropriately with the antibiotic course.

cases.title: Choosing a throat investigation in suspected scarlet fever
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child presents with fever and sore throat. The tongue is initially coated and later becomes red and prominent, while a rough, diffuse rash has appeared over the trunk and is accentuated in the flexural creases. The clinician wants to investigate the suspected group A streptococcal throat infection using a specimen-based test named clinical guidance.

questions.stem: Which investigation best matches that request?

options.label: A
options.text: Thick and thin blood films stained with Giemsa

options.label: D
options.text: Throat swab for culture and sensitivity

questions.correctAnswerText: Throat swab for culture and sensitivity
questions.initialExplanation: The scarlet fever section lists throat swab culture and sensitivity as part of the diagnostic work-up. It also lists serology, including ASO titre and anti-DNase antibodies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. A throat swab for culture and sensitivity is the specimen-based pharyngeal investigation explicitly listed in the scarlet fever section.
- A. Incorrect. Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films are used in the malaria investigation pathway.
- B. Incorrect. Stool microscopy using multiple samples is listed for intestinal amoebiasis, not streptococcal pharyngitis.
- C. Incorrect. Mantoux and IGRA are tests used in the assessment of TB infection.
- E. Incorrect. Nasopharyngeal sampling for PCR/other testing is included in the pertussis section, not the scarlet fever investigation list.

The source also lists ASO titre and anti-DNase antibodies under serological investigations. They are not the specimen-based throat test asked for in this case.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Scarlet fever is associated with group A beta-haemolytic streptococci and pyrogenic exotoxin.
- standard guidance clinical guidance lists clinical assessment, ASO titre/anti-DNase antibodies and throat swab culture and sensitivity.
- The typical clinical pattern includes sore throat, strawberry tongue, sandpaper-like rash and Pastia lines.

source.raw: Infectious Diseases lecture sheet — Pages 13–14, *Scarlet fever: diagnosis and clinical features*.

cases.title: An infant has paroxysmal coughing spells and post-tussive vomiting
cases.vignette: A 3-month-old infant has had coryzal symptoms and a mild fever for about 10 days. The child now develops repeated bouts of spasmodic coughing followed by vomiting. During some attacks, the infant becomes cyanosed and briefly stops breathing. No clear inspiratory whoop is heard.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pertussis (whooping cough)
questions.initialExplanation: Pertussis is caused by Bordetella pertussis and classically progresses from a catarrhal stage to a paroxysmal stage with spasmodic coughing, inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting. Young infants may present with apnea and may not have a typical whoop.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The catarrhal prodrome followed by paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting is typical.
- D. Incorrect. Scarlet fever causes pharyngitis and a sandpaper rash.
- E. Incorrect. Measles causes fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and a maculopapular rash.
- C. Incorrect. Typhoid causes prolonged fever and gastrointestinal symptoms.
- B. Incorrect. Primary HSV in young children typically causes painful gingivostomatitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pertussis: Bordetella pertussis, droplet transmission.
- Catarrhal phase precedes paroxysmal cough.
- Infants may present with apnea/cyanosis and may lack the classic whoop.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes the stages of pertussis in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Catarrhal stage → paroxysmal stage → convalescent stage

options.label: B
options.text: Latent stage → miliary stage → fibrotic stage

options.label: C
options.text: Prodrome → Koplik stage → descending rash stage

options.label: D
options.text: Vesicular stage → crusting stage → dermatomal stage

questions.correctAnswerText: Catarrhal stage → paroxysmal stage → convalescent stage
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes catarrhal symptoms for about 1-2 weeks, a paroxysmal cough phase lasting several weeks, and a convalescent phase with gradual reduction in cough episodes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the sequence of pertussis stages.
- E. Incorrect. This describes the phases of hepatitis A.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the staged course of pertussis.
- B. Incorrect. These are TB-related concepts, not pertussis stages.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the pertussis clinical sequence.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Catarrhal stage: coryza and low-grade fever.
- Paroxysmal stage: spasmodic cough, whoop, post-tussive vomiting.
- Convalescent stage: gradual improvement, but cough may persist for weeks.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern is described as typical of pertussis in the source?

options.label: E
options.text: Isolated raised bilirubin and prolonged PT

questions.correctAnswerText: Marked leukocytosis with absolute lymphocytosis
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists a high white blood cell count with absolute lymphocytosis as a supportive finding in pertussis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. Leukocytosis with lymphocytosis is the characteristic laboratory pattern described.
- A. Incorrect. This is not the typical pertussis pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Pancytopenia and massive splenomegaly may occur in visceral leishmaniasis.
- C. Incorrect. This does not describe the source's pertussis laboratory pattern.
- E. Incorrect. This is more consistent with hepatic synthetic dysfunction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pertussis CBC: leukocytosis with absolute lymphocytosis.
- Diagnosis includes nasopharyngeal swab PCR/ELISA.
- Clinical suspicion is particularly important in young infants with apnea.

questions.stem: A young infant with suspected pertussis has apnea and oxygen desaturation. Which management approach is supported by the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Admit, provide oxygen/supportive care and feeding support, and treat with a macrolide

options.label: B
options.text: Start aspirin and observe at home

options.label: C
options.text: Discharge with no monitoring because the infant has no whoop

questions.correctAnswerText: Admit, provide oxygen/supportive care and feeding support, and treat with a macrolide
questions.initialExplanation: The source recommends admission for severe disease, apnea or very young infants, with oxygen if saturation is low, NG feeding or IV fluids as needed, and macrolides as the drug of choice. Isolation and contact management are also important.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This reflects the admission, respiratory support, feeding support and antibiotic approach.
- C. Incorrect. Young infants may have apnea without a classic whoop and require monitoring.
- E. Incorrect. Metronidazole is not pertussis treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Antituberculous treatment is for TB.
- B. Incorrect. Aspirin is not appropriate pertussis management and observation at home is unsafe in an infant with apnea.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Admit if very young, severe, or apnea present.
- Oxygen for low saturation; NG feeding/IV fluids if needed.
- Macrolide is DOC in the source.
- Isolation is recommended; macrolides are listed for contacts.
- DPT vaccination is the preventive measure.

questions.stem: Which preventive measure is listed for pertussis in the source?
questions.correctAnswerText: DPT vaccination
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists DPT vaccination for prevention. It also notes isolation and macrolide treatment for contacts in the pertussis section.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. DPT vaccination protects against diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus.
- A. Incorrect. BCG prevents severe TB.
- B. Incorrect. Hepatitis A vaccine prevents HAV.
- C. Incorrect. MMR prevents measles, mumps and rubella.
- E. Incorrect. OPV prevents poliomyelitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pertussis prevention: DPT-containing vaccine.
- Isolation is recommended.
- The source lists macrolides for contacts.

cases.title: A child develops fever and a rash after a tick exposure
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child returns from a rural area with high fever, severe headache and malaise. The child has a history of tick exposure around dogs. A maculopapular rash appears and becomes petechial, involving the palms and soles. Laboratory tests show thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases and hyponatraemia.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

options.label: B
options.text: Rocky Mountain spotted fever due to Rickettsia rickettsii

questions.correctAnswerText: Rocky Mountain spotted fever due to Rickettsia rickettsii
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance Rocky Mountain spotted fever as a tick-borne infection caused by R. rickettsii. High fever, headache, malaise and a maculopapular-to-petechial rash involving the palms and soles are characteristic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. Tick exposure plus fever and a petechial rash involving palms and soles strongly supports RMSF.
- A. Incorrect. Typhoid is transmitted fecal-orally and may produce rose spots on the trunk, abdominal symptoms and relative bradycardia.
- C. Incorrect. Lyme disease is transmitted by ticks but classically causes erythema migrans at the bite site.
- E. Incorrect. Measles causes cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a descending maculopapular rash.
- D. Incorrect. Leishmaniasis is transmitted by sandflies; the visceral form causes prolonged fever and marked hepatosplenomegaly.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Agent: Rickettsia rickettsii, an obligate intracellular Gram-negative organism.
- Vector: tick; clinical guidance identifies dogs as a reservoir.
- Incubation: 2-14 days (approximately 10 days in the table).
- Rash may be maculopapular, petechial or purpuric and may involve palms and soles.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern is described as supportive of Rocky Mountain spotted fever?

options.label: A
options.text: Pancytopenia with massive splenomegaly as the defining early pattern

options.label: B
options.text: High serum amylase with normal liver enzymes

options.label: C
options.text: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal platelets

questions.correctAnswerText: Thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia and elevated ALT/AST
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists anaemia/thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia and elevated liver transaminases, with serology and PCR as diagnostic investigations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. These findings are specifically listed in the Rickettsia column.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the laboratory pattern described.
- C. Incorrect. Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is not the expected pattern.
- A. Incorrect. Pancytopenia with marked hepatosplenomegaly is more suggestive of visceral leishmaniasis.
- B. Incorrect. Raised amylase is not a typical diagnostic clue for RMSF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider RMSF in a febrile child after tick exposure, especially with rash.
- CBC may show thrombocytopenia.
- Hyponatraemia and elevated transaminases may support the diagnosis.
- Serology and PCR are listed in the source.

questions.stem: Which statement about the management and prevention of Rocky Mountain spotted fever matches the course clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Antibiotics are contraindicated because the disease is viral

options.label: B
options.text: Isoniazid is the drug of choice

options.label: C
options.text: Treatment is limited to metronidazole and oral rehydration

options.label: D
options.text: Severe cases require admission and supportive care with prompt antibiotic treatment; the sheet lists doxycycline, tetracyclines and macrolides

options.label: E
options.text: There is a routine childhood vaccine and no need for antibiotics

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe cases require admission and supportive care with prompt antibiotic treatment; the sheet lists doxycycline, tetracyclines and macrolides
questions.initialExplanation: The PDF's treatment column lists admission for severe cases, IV fluids and antipyretics, and antibiotics including doxycycline, tetracyclines and macrolides/azithromycin. The source states that no vaccine is available.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. This reflects the treatment and prevention column on page 16.
- E. Incorrect. The source explicitly states that no vaccine is available.
- C. Incorrect. Metronidazole is not the listed treatment for rickettsiosis.
- B. Incorrect. Isoniazid is an antituberculous drug.
- A. Incorrect. Rickettsiae are bacteria-like obligate intracellular organisms, not viruses.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Severe disease: admission and supportive care.
- The course clinical guidance lists doxycycline/tetracycline-class drugs and macrolides.
- No vaccine is listed.
- The age-specific drug wording in the 2024 clinical guidance should be treated as a course-note statement, not a substitute for current local treatment guidance.

cases.title: A child has prolonged spiking fever and abdominal symptoms after unsafe food exposure
cases.vignette: An 11-year-old child develops progressively increasing, high spiking fever after eating street food during travel. The child complains of headache, myalgia, cough, abdominal pain and anorexia. During the second week, bowel habit changes from diarrhoea to constipation. Examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly and faint rose-coloured spots over the trunk. The pulse is relatively slow for the degree of fever.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: E
options.text: Typhoid fever due to Salmonella Typhi

questions.correctAnswerText: Typhoid fever due to Salmonella Typhi
questions.initialExplanation: Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi and is transmitted by the fecal-oral route through contaminated food or water. The source describes high spiking fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal symptoms, rose spots and hepatosplenomegaly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. The exposure, prolonged fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots and abdominal symptoms fit enteric fever.
- D. Incorrect. RMSF follows tick exposure and commonly causes a rash involving palms and soles.
- A. Incorrect. Lyme disease follows tick exposure and classically causes erythema migrans.
- B. Incorrect. HAV causes a gastrointestinal prodrome followed by jaundice.
- C. Incorrect. Visceral leishmaniasis causes prolonged fever, marked splenomegaly, cachexia and pancytopenia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Agent: Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi.
- Transmission: fecal-oral, often contaminated food or water.
- Incubation: 3-30 days (usually 1-2 weeks).
- Relative bradycardia, rose spots, abdominal symptoms and hepatosplenomegaly are useful clues.

questions.stem: Which description of the rose spots in typhoid fever is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A painless expanding macule at a tick bite site

options.label: B
options.text: A lacy reticular rash over the limbs after slapped cheeks

options.label: C
options.text: Petechiae restricted to the palms and soles

options.label: D
options.text: Vesicles in crops at different stages

options.label: E
options.text: Faint rose-coloured spots over the trunk

questions.correctAnswerText: Faint rose-coloured spots over the trunk
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes rose spots on the trunk as a feature of typhoid fever.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. Rose spots over the trunk are the rash described for typhoid.
- C. Incorrect. A petechial/purpuric rash involving palms and soles is a clue to RMSF.
- D. Incorrect. This is typical of varicella.
- B. Incorrect. This is erythema infectiosum due to Parvovirus B19.
- A. Incorrect. This describes erythema migrans in Lyme disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typhoid: rose spots on the trunk.
- RMSF: maculopapular-to-petechial rash, possibly involving palms and soles.
- Lyme: erythema migrans at the tick-bite site.

questions.stem: Which specimen is most likely to yield a positive culture during the first week of typhoid fever?
questions.correctAnswerText: Blood
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists blood culture as the important early test, with positivity reported in the first week. Stool and urine cultures become useful from the second week; bone marrow culture is also mentioned.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. Blood culture is the preferred culture specimen in the first week.
- A. Incorrect. Stool culture is listed from the second week.
- E. Incorrect. Urine culture is also listed from the second week.
- D. Incorrect. Typhoid is not diagnosed by a skin swab.
- B. Incorrect. A nasopharyngeal specimen is not the culture sample listed for typhoid.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- First week: blood culture.
- From the second week: stool and urine cultures may become positive.
- Bone marrow culture and PCR detection of typhi antigen are also listed.
- A single test result should be interpreted in relation to illness timing and prior antibiotics.

questions.stem: Which serious complication of typhoid fever is specifically recognized?
questions.correctAnswerText: Intestinal haemorrhage or perforation
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists intestinal haemorrhage and perforation as important gastrointestinal complications of typhoid fever. It also lists osteomyelitis, glomerulonephritis, myocarditis, hepatitis and neurological complications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. Intestinal bleeding and perforation are serious complications listed for typhoid.
- C. Incorrect. Hydrops fetalis is associated with Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy.
- A. Incorrect. Splenic rupture is a complication of infectious mononucleosis.
- B. Incorrect. Disseminated BCG infection occurs after BCG in an immunocompromised child.
- E. Incorrect. Congenital cataract is associated with congenital rubella syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typhoid complications include intestinal haemorrhage/perforation.
- Other listed complications: osteomyelitis, GN, myocarditis, hepatitis and neurological manifestations.
- Severe disease may be complicated by shock, DIC, renal failure and multiorgan failure.

questions.stem: A child with severe typhoid fever requires hospital treatment. Which approach is described in the course clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: IV fluids and antipyretics with IV antibiotics, including a third-generation cephalosporin or azithromycin

options.label: B
options.text: No antibiotics because typhoid is viral

questions.correctAnswerText: IV fluids and antipyretics with IV antibiotics, including a third-generation cephalosporin or azithromycin
questions.initialExplanation: The source recommends admission for severe cases, IV fluids and antipyretics, and a course of IV antibiotics for approximately 2 weeks. The listed effective agents include a third-generation cephalosporin and azithromycin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the typhoid treatment column on page 16.
- E. Incorrect. Acyclovir treats selected herpesvirus infections.
- C. Incorrect. These are anthelmintics, not typhoid treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Isoniazid is an antituberculous drug and is not typhoid monotherapy.
- B. Incorrect. Typhoid is caused by Salmonella, a bacterium.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Severe typhoid: admit and give supportive care.
- Clinical guidance IV antibiotic treatment for about 2 weeks.
- Third-generation cephalosporins and azithromycin are listed.
- Drug selection in practice must account for local resistance patterns.

cases.title: A child develops an expanding painless rash after a tick bite
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child from a rural area presents in summer with an enlarging, painless erythematous lesion at the site of a tick bite. The child also has fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia and tender lymphadenopathy. Several weeks later, the child develops facial weakness and palpitations.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: D
options.text: Lyme disease due to Borrelia burgdorferi

questions.correctAnswerText: Lyme disease due to Borrelia burgdorferi
questions.initialExplanation: Lyme disease is caused by the spirochaete Borrelia burgdorferi and is transmitted by tick bite. Erythema migrans is the characteristic expanding, usually painless lesion at the bite site.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. The tick exposure and expanding painless erythematous lesion are typical of Lyme disease.
- A. Incorrect. RMSF causes fever and a maculopapular/petechial rash, often including palms and soles.
- E. Incorrect. Typhoid is transmitted fecal-orally and causes prolonged fever and rose spots.
- B. Incorrect. Leishmaniasis is transmitted by sandflies and causes cutaneous ulcers or visceral disease.
- C. Incorrect. Varicella causes itchy vesicles in successive crops.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Agent: Borrelia burgdorferi (spirochaete).
- Vector: tick; more common in summer and rural areas in the source.
- Incubation: 4-30 days.
- Erythema migrans is the classical early skin manifestation.

questions.stem: Which clinical feature may appear in late Lyme disease, weeks to months after infection?

options.label: B
options.text: Koplik spots and a descending maculopapular rash

options.label: C
options.text: Generalized exfoliation with a positive Nikolsky sign

options.label: E
options.text: Facial nerve palsy, meningitis, myocarditis/carditis or recurrent large-joint arthritis

questions.correctAnswerText: Facial nerve palsy, meningitis, myocarditis/carditis or recurrent large-joint arthritis
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes late manifestations involving the CNS (meningoencephalitis, facial nerve palsy and peripheral neuropathy), CVS (myocarditis/heart block) and joints (recurrent large-joint arthritis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. These are the neurological, cardiac and joint manifestations described.
- B. Incorrect. This is measles.
- A. Incorrect. These are typhoid manifestations/complications.
