- C. Incorrect. This describes staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. This is enterobiasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early: erythema migrans and systemic symptoms.
- Late: facial nerve palsy, meningitis/meningoencephalitis, peripheral neuropathy, myocarditis/heart block and arthritis.
- Joint involvement commonly affects large joints in the source.

questions.stem: Which diagnostic approach is described for Lyme disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Thick and thin Giemsa blood films are diagnostic

options.label: B
options.text: Diagnosis is mainly clinical; serology may become positive later, usually after more than 4 weeks

options.label: C
options.text: Diagnosis is made by stool microscopy

options.label: D
options.text: A single early negative serology excludes the disease

options.label: E
options.text: Mantoux testing is the confirmatory test

questions.correctAnswerText: Diagnosis is mainly clinical; serology may become positive later, usually after more than 4 weeks
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that Lyme disease is diagnosed mainly clinically and that serology may become positive late in disease, particularly after 4 weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. This is the diagnostic approach in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Early serology may be negative; it does not exclude early Lyme disease.
- C. Incorrect. Stool microscopy is used for selected intestinal parasites.
- A. Incorrect. Thick and thin blood films are used for malaria.
- E. Incorrect. Mantoux testing is used in the assessment of TB infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Erythema migrans with appropriate exposure is primarily a clinical diagnosis.
- Serology may be negative early and more likely positive after 4 weeks.
- Do not use an early negative serology result alone to exclude the disease.

questions.stem: Which treatment pairing is stated for Lyme disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Albendazole for older children and mebendazole for younger children

options.label: B
options.text: Isoniazid for uncomplicated cases and rifampicin for severe cases

options.label: C
options.text: Doxycycline for older children and amoxicillin for younger children; IV third-generation cephalosporin for severe neurological or cardiac disease

options.label: D
options.text: Penicillin V for most manifestations, including severe carditis

options.label: E
options.text: Metronidazole for most ages; no IV treatment is used

questions.correctAnswerText: Doxycycline for older children and amoxicillin for younger children; IV third-generation cephalosporin for severe neurological or cardiac disease
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists doxycycline as the drug of choice for children older than 8 years, amoxicillin for younger children, and an IV third-generation cephalosporin for severe carditis or neurological disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. This is the age-stratified and severe-disease approach described in the course clinical guidance.
- E. Incorrect. Metronidazole is not Lyme disease treatment.
- A. Incorrect. These drugs are used for helminth infections.
- B. Incorrect. These are antituberculous drugs.
- D. Incorrect. Penicillin V is used for group A streptococcal pharyngitis/scarlet fever, not all Lyme manifestations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance: doxycycline for children older than 8 years; amoxicillin for younger children.
- Severe carditis or neurological disease: IV third-generation cephalosporin.
- In clinical practice, use current pediatric Lyme protocols and local guidance.

cases.title: Several children develop abrupt vomiting after a shared meal
cases.vignette: Several children from the same school develop sudden nausea, repeated vomiting and watery diarrhoea a few hours after eating food prepared by the same food handler. They have no fever and most recover within a day.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: D
options.text: Staphylococcal food poisoning due to preformed enterotoxin

questions.correctAnswerText: Staphylococcal food poisoning due to preformed enterotoxin
questions.initialExplanation: Staphylococcal food poisoning is caused by ingestion of preformed Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin in contaminated food. The source describes abrupt vomiting and watery diarrhoea, usually without fever, beginning 2-7 hours after ingestion and lasting 12-24 hours.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. Multiple people with rapid-onset vomiting and diarrhoea after a shared meal strongly suggest preformed staphylococcal enterotoxin.
- B. Incorrect. Typhoid has a longer incubation and a prolonged febrile illness.
- C. Incorrect. Amoebic dysentery usually has a more gradual onset, colicky pain, frequent stools and tenesmus.
- A. Incorrect. HAV has a longer incubation and may progress to jaundice.
- E. Incorrect. Visceral leishmaniasis causes a prolonged systemic illness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Source: contaminated food and food handlers.
- Incubation: 2-7 hours (confirmed visually from PDF page 17).
- Symptoms: vomiting and watery diarrhoea, usually no fever.
- Duration: commonly 12-24 hours.

questions.stem: Which approach to diagnosis and prevention is stated in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Diagnose by EBV serology and avoid amoxicillin

options.label: B
options.text: Diagnose by Mantoux test and isolate most household contacts for months

options.label: C
options.text: Use thick and thin blood films and mosquito control

options.label: D
options.text: Perform stool tape testing and treat the whole household with albendazole

options.label: E
options.text: Test the suspected food for enterotoxin and exclude infected food handlers; refrigerate food or eat it promptly

questions.correctAnswerText: Test the suspected food for enterotoxin and exclude infected food handlers; refrigerate food or eat it promptly
questions.initialExplanation: The source recommends culture and testing for enterotoxin in the suspected food. Prevention includes excluding infected food handlers and eating food immediately or refrigerating it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. These are the diagnostic and preventive measures described.
- B. Incorrect. Mantoux testing is for TB infection.
- C. Incorrect. Blood films and mosquito control are used in malaria.
- D. Incorrect. Tape testing and albendazole are used for enterobiasis.
- A. Incorrect. EBV serology and avoidance of aminopenicillins relate to infectious mononucleosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The disease is toxin-mediated; symptoms may begin rapidly after ingestion.
- Confirm by testing suspected food for enterotoxin as described.
- Food-handler hygiene and appropriate food storage are key preventive measures.

cases.title: A child develops fever, hypotension, diffuse erythroderma and multisystem abnormalities
cases.vignette: A 12-year-old child presents with acute high fever, vomiting and diarrhoea. The child is hypotensive and has diffuse sunburn-like erythroderma involving the palms and soles. Examination shows conjunctival and oral mucosal hyperaemia. Blood tests reveal thrombocytopenia and raised renal and liver markers. Blood cultures are negative.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Toxic shock syndrome is caused by toxin-mediated systemic disease, classically involving TSST-1 from Staphylococcus aureus. The source lists fever above 39°C, hypotension and diffuse erythroderma with desquamation as major criteria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. Acute fever, shock, diffuse erythroderma and multisystem involvement fit TSS.
- E. Incorrect. SSSS causes superficial epidermal cleavage, fragile skin and a positive Nikolsky sign, usually without the systemic shock criteria described.
- B. Incorrect. Impetigo is a localized superficial skin infection with honey-coloured crusts.
- A. Incorrect. Scarlet fever causes pharyngitis, strawberry tongue and a sandpaper rash, not the full shock/multiorgan pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Lyme disease causes erythema migrans and may cause later neurological, cardiac or joint disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cause: TSST-1, classically associated with S. aureus; group A streptococci can also cause toxic shock.
- Major features: fever >39°C, hypotension and diffuse erythroderma/desquamation.
- Blood culture may be negative in toxin-mediated staphylococcal TSS.

questions.stem: According to the clinical criteria in the source, what is required in addition to all major criteria for a probable case of TSS?

options.label: A
options.text: At least three minor criteria and no alternative explanation, with negative blood cultures

options.label: B
options.text: Positive Mantoux test and an abnormal chest X-ray

options.label: C
options.text: One minor criterion and a positive blood culture for S. aureus

options.label: D
options.text: At least three skin lesions with honey-coloured crusts

options.label: E
options.text: A positive stool culture for Salmonella Typhi

questions.correctAnswerText: At least three minor criteria and no alternative explanation, with negative blood cultures
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists major criteria that are all required, at least three minor criteria, and exclusion of another explanation with negative blood cultures. Minor criteria include mucosal inflammation, GI symptoms, liver and renal abnormalities, muscle involvement/raised CPK, CNS changes and thrombocytopenia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the criteria structure in the source.
- C. Incorrect. The source requires negative blood culture as an exclusion feature and at least three minor criteria.
- B. Incorrect. These are TB investigations, not TSS criteria.
- D. Incorrect. Honey-coloured crusts are typical of impetigo.
- E. Incorrect. Stool culture for Salmonella is unrelated to TSS diagnostic criteria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Major: fever >39°C, hypotension, diffuse erythroderma/desquamation.
- At least three minor criteria: mucous membrane involvement, GI, liver, renal, muscle, CNS abnormalities or thrombocytopenia.
- Exclude another explanation; the source specifies negative blood cultures.

questions.stem: Which treatment combination is described for toxic shock syndrome?

options.label: D
options.text: Fluids/inotropes, IV cephalosporin plus clindamycin, source drainage and IVIG in severe cases

questions.correctAnswerText: Fluids/inotropes, IV cephalosporin plus clindamycin, source drainage and IVIG in severe cases
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists supportive management with fluids and inotropes, third-generation cephalosporin plus clindamycin, surgical drainage of infected sites and IVIG in severe cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. This includes the management elements listed in the TSS column.
- E. Incorrect. Albendazole treats helminth infections.
- A. Incorrect. Acyclovir treats selected herpesvirus infections and is not TSS treatment.
- C. Incorrect. These are antituberculous drugs.
- B. Incorrect. Topical mupirocin may be used for mild localized impetigo, not systemic shock.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TSS is an emergency requiring hemodynamic support.
- Treat the toxin-producing infection and drain the source when present.
- Clinical guidance clindamycin with a third-generation cephalosporin.
- IVIG is listed for severe cases.

cases.title: A neonate develops diffuse tender erythema and superficial skin peeling
cases.vignette: A 9-day-old neonate develops irritability, fever and widespread erythema. The skin becomes tender and begins to peel in superficial sheets, especially around the face and neck. Gentle pressure causes epidermal separation. The affected areas heal without scarring.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS)
questions.initialExplanation: SSSS (Ritter disease) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B from S. aureus. In neonates it may cause generalized exfoliation with superficial epidermal cleavage and a positive Nikolsky sign.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. Neonatal diffuse tender erythema and superficial exfoliation with epidermal separation are typical of SSSS.
- B. Incorrect. TSS is defined by fever, hypotension, erythroderma and multisystem abnormalities.
- D. Incorrect. Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune blistering disorder and is not the toxin-mediated syndrome described.
- C. Incorrect. Varicella causes itchy vesicles in crops at different stages.
- A. Incorrect. Impetigo is localized superficial infection with honey-coloured crusting; it does not usually cause generalized skin exfoliation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cause: S. aureus exfoliative toxins A and B.
- Neonates may develop generalized exfoliation (Ritter disease).
- Superficial epidermal cleavage; Nikolsky sign positive.
- Healing is usually without scarring.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes SSSS from toxic shock syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: SSSS is caused by Salmonella Typhi, whereas TSS is caused by Borrelia

options.label: B
options.text: SSSS causes superficial epidermal cleavage/Nikolsky sign; TSS causes systemic shock and organ dysfunction

options.label: C
options.text: TSS is typically localized to a small area of skin

options.label: D
options.text: SSSS causes deep dermal ulcers that heal with permanent scarring

options.label: E
options.text: Both are diagnosed by rose spots on the trunk

questions.correctAnswerText: SSSS causes superficial epidermal cleavage/Nikolsky sign; TSS causes systemic shock and organ dysfunction
questions.initialExplanation: The source separates TSS and SSSS into adjacent but distinct columns: TSS is toxin-mediated systemic shock, whereas SSSS results from exfoliative toxins causing superficial epidermal separation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. This captures the key clinical distinction.
- E. Incorrect. Rose spots are associated with typhoid fever.
- A. Incorrect. SSSS is associated with S. aureus exfoliative toxins; TSS is associated with TSST-1 and can also be caused by group A streptococci.
- C. Incorrect. TSS is a systemic disease, not a localized skin infection.
- D. Incorrect. The source describes superficial cleavage with healing without scarring.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SSSS: exfoliative toxins A/B, superficial cleavage, Nikolsky positive, heals without scarring.
- TSS: fever, hypotension, diffuse erythroderma/desquamation and multiorgan involvement.
- Do not confuse the two adjacent columns in the original table.

questions.stem: Which treatment is described for a child with SSSS?

options.label: A
options.text: IV antistaphylococcal antibiotic such as flucloxacillin, with analgesia and careful fluid monitoring

options.label: E
options.text: Penicillin V alone for 10 days in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: IV antistaphylococcal antibiotic such as flucloxacillin, with analgesia and careful fluid monitoring
questions.initialExplanation: The SSSS column recommends intravenous antistaphylococcal antibiotics such as flucloxacillin, analgesia and monitoring hydration/fluid balance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the specific treatment stated in the SSSS column.
- E. Incorrect. Penicillin V is used for scarlet fever in the source, not as the stated SSSS regimen.
- C. Incorrect. Tinidazole is an anti-protozoal drug, not SSSS treatment.
- D. Incorrect. These are antimalarial drugs.
- B. Incorrect. Isoniazid is used for TB prophylaxis/treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SSSS requires systemic antistaphylococcal antibiotics.
- Monitor fluid balance because extensive skin loss increases dehydration risk.
- Complications include dehydration and secondary infection.
- Localized bullous impetigo may occur in older children.

cases.title: A toddler develops honey-coloured crusted lesions around the mouth
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child with atopic eczema develops erythematous macules on the face and hands. These become small vesicles and pustules, rupture and form confluent honey-coloured crusts. New lesions appear after scratching and touching adjacent skin.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Impetigo
questions.initialExplanation: Impetigo is a localized, highly contagious superficial skin infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. The classic lesion is a honey-coloured crust following rupture of vesicles or pustules.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. The honey-coloured crusts, superficial lesions and autoinoculation fit impetigo.
- E. Incorrect. SSSS causes widespread superficial epidermal cleavage and generalized exfoliation.
- B. Incorrect. TSS is a systemic illness with shock and multiorgan involvement.
- A. Incorrect. Lyme disease causes erythema migrans after tick exposure.
- D. Incorrect. Parvovirus B19 causes slapped-cheek erythema and a lacy rash.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Organisms: S. aureus or S. pyogenes.
- Common in infants/young children, especially with pre-existing skin disease such as eczema.
- Sites: face, neck and hands.
- Honey-coloured crusting is characteristic.

questions.stem: Which management option is stated for impetigo?

options.label: C
options.text: No treatment is needed and school attendance is unrestricted while lesions are wet

options.label: E
options.text: Topical mupirocin may be used for mild cases; systemic flucloxacillin is generally needed for more severe infections

questions.correctAnswerText: Topical mupirocin may be used for mild cases; systemic flucloxacillin is generally needed for more severe infections
questions.initialExplanation: The source states that topical antibiotics such as mupirocin may be effective for mild cases, while narrow-spectrum systemic antibiotics such as flucloxacillin are generally needed for more severe infections. Children should not attend nursery or school until lesions are dry.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. This is the treatment approach described in the impetigo section.
- D. Incorrect. Acyclovir is used for selected herpesvirus infections.
- A. Incorrect. Antituberculous therapy is not used for impetigo.
- B. Incorrect. Chloroquine is an antimalarial drug.
- C. Incorrect. Clinical guidance exclusion from school/nursery until lesions are dry.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mild impetigo: topical mupirocin may be effective.
- More severe infection: systemic narrow-spectrum antistaphylococcal antibiotic such as flucloxacillin.
- Highly contagious; spread occurs by autoinoculation from infected exudate.
- Exclude from nursery/school until lesions are dry.

questions.stem: A child has unilateral eyelid erythema, tenderness and oedema, but no proptosis or painful restriction of eye movement. Which diagnosis is most consistent with the source definition?
questions.correctAnswerText: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis
questions.initialExplanation: Preseptal cellulitis involves the eyelid and adjacent skin anterior to the orbital septum. The source describes fever, erythema, tenderness and oedema, usually unilateral.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. Eyelid inflammation without orbital signs is consistent with preseptal cellulitis.
- E. Incorrect. Orbital cellulitis is suggested by proptosis, painful or restricted eye movement and sometimes reduced visual acuity.
- D. Incorrect. Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a serious complication, not the initial diagnosis from this isolated presentation.
- B. Incorrect. HSV keratoconjunctivitis primarily affects the ocular surface and conjunctiva/cornea.
- A. Incorrect. Acute glaucoma presents with raised intraocular pressure and a different ocular picture.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preseptal/periorbital cellulitis is anterior to the orbital septum.
- Usually unilateral.
- Fever, eyelid erythema, tenderness and oedema are typical.
- Assess carefully for orbital signs.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests progression to orbital cellulitis and requires urgent imaging/specialist assessment?

options.label: B
options.text: A lacy rash over the limbs

options.label: C
options.text: Proptosis with painful or restricted ocular movement, with or without reduced visual acuity

options.label: D
options.text: A positive Nikolsky sign without orbital symptoms

questions.correctAnswerText: Proptosis with painful or restricted ocular movement, with or without reduced visual acuity
questions.initialExplanation: The source contrasts preseptal cellulitis with orbital cellulitis. Proptosis and painful or limited ocular movement, with or without reduced visual acuity, suggest orbital involvement. CT or MRI should assess posterior spread and management should involve an ophthalmologist.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. These are the orbital signs described in the source.
- A. Incorrect. This is impetigo.
- D. Incorrect. Nikolsky sign is associated with SSSS, not orbital cellulitis.
- B. Incorrect. This is erythema infectiosum.
- E. Incorrect. This is enterobiasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Orbital cellulitis: proptosis, painful/restricted eye movements and possible visual impairment.
- Perform CT or MRI when orbital cellulitis is suspected.
- Manage with an ophthalmologist.
- Complications include abscess, meningitis and cavernous sinus thrombosis.

cases.title: A schoolchild has nocturnal perianal itching and disturbed sleep
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child is brought because of intense perianal itching, particularly at night. The child is restless, sleeps poorly and has recently developed nocturnal enuresis. A sibling has similar symptoms.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Enterobiasis due to Enterobius vermicularis
questions.initialExplanation: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) is a small white threadlike nematode that commonly affects preschool and school-age children. Nocturnal perianal itching, sleep disturbance, restlessness and enuresis are characteristic symptoms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. Nocturnal perianal itching with sleep disturbance is typical of enterobiasis.
- B. Incorrect. Amoebiasis causes intestinal colitis/dysentery or, less commonly, liver abscess.
- A. Incorrect. Giardia is not described in the teaching text of this clinical guidance; it should not be assumed from this characteristic pinworm presentation.
- D. Incorrect. Visceral leishmaniasis causes prolonged fever, marked splenomegaly, hepatomegaly and cachexia.
- C. Incorrect. Malaria causes febrile paroxysms, chills, anaemia and splenomegaly.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Agent: Enterobius vermicularis, a small white threadlike nematode.
- More common in preschool and school-age children.
- Symptoms: nocturnal perianal itching, sleep disturbance, restlessness and enuresis.
- Person-to-person fecal-oral transmission; autoinfection may occur.

questions.stem: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm enterobiasis?

options.label: A
options.text: Thick and thin Giemsa-stained blood films

options.label: B
options.text: Cellophane tape test applied to the perianal area at night and examined the following morning

options.label: D
options.text: Three stool cultures for Salmonella Typhi

options.label: E
options.text: Blood culture during the first week of fever

questions.correctAnswerText: Cellophane tape test applied to the perianal area at night and examined the following morning
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance a transparent adhesive cellophane tape test pressed against the perineum at night and examined in the morning for eggs or adult worms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. The tape test is the specific diagnostic method described.
- D. Incorrect. Blood culture is the key early culture in typhoid fever; stool culture is not the pinworm test.
- A. Incorrect. Thick and thin blood films diagnose malaria.
- C. Incorrect. Mantoux testing assesses TB infection.
- E. Incorrect. Blood culture is used in suspected enteric fever, not enterobiasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Diagnostic test: perianal transparent tape test.
- Apply at night and examine the tape the next morning.
- Eggs/adult worms may be seen microscopically.
- A routine stool sample is less suitable than the perianal tape test for this infection.

questions.stem: A child is diagnosed with enterobiasis. Which management and prevention strategy is recommended?

options.label: A
options.text: Use topical mupirocin and exclude the child until skin lesions dry

options.label: B
options.text: Give chloroquine prophylaxis to most family members

options.label: C
options.text: Give IV ceftriaxone and isolate for 6 months

options.label: D
options.text: Treat the child and household members, repeat the anthelmintic dose after 2 weeks and emphasize hand hygiene

options.label: E
options.text: Treat the symptomatic child once and ignore household contacts

questions.correctAnswerText: Treat the child and household members, repeat the anthelmintic dose after 2 weeks and emphasize hand hygiene
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance albendazole or mebendazole with a repeat dose after 2 weeks. It also states that infected individuals and family members should be treated together and that hand hygiene is the most effective preventive measure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. This combines the treatment and household prevention measures in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Household members should be treated at the same time.
- C. Incorrect. Ceftriaxone is an antibiotic and is not the treatment for pinworm.
- B. Incorrect. Chloroquine is used for malaria prophylaxis in selected settings.
- A. Incorrect. Mupirocin and exclusion until lesions dry relate to impetigo.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Albendazole or mebendazole is listed.
- Repeat the dose after 2 weeks.
- Treat household contacts at the same time.
- Hand hygiene is the most effective prevention measure.

cases.title: A preschool child develops gradual-onset dysentery and tenesmus
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old child develops gradually increasing colicky abdominal pain and frequent bowel motions after drinking water from an unsafe source. The child passes six to eight stools per day, has tenesmus and a heme-positive stool. The child has no significant fever or systemic toxicity.

questions.stem: Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.correctAnswerText: Entamoeba histolytica
questions.initialExplanation: Amoebiasis is caused by Entamoeba histolytica and is transmitted by ingestion of cysts in food or water contaminated by feces. Trophozoites colonize the large intestine and may invade the mucosa.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. Fecal-oral exposure followed by colicky abdominal pain, frequent heme-positive stools and tenesmus is typical of amoebic dysentery.
- A. Incorrect. Enterobius causes nocturnal perianal itching and sleep disturbance.
- C. Incorrect. P. falciparum causes severe malaria with fever, haemolysis and possible cerebral disease.
- E. Incorrect. L. donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis with fever and hepatosplenomegaly.
- D. Incorrect. B. burgdorferi causes Lyme disease after tick exposure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Agent: Entamoeba histolytica.
- Transmission: fecal-oral ingestion of cysts in contaminated food or drink.
- Amebic dysentery is reported in approximately 5-10% of infections.
- Trophozoites colonize the large intestine and may invade the mucosal lining.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern is most characteristic of amoebic dysentery in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Fever with chills, sweats, haemolytic anaemia and splenomegaly

options.label: B
options.text: Sudden painless watery diarrhoea with vomiting 2-7 hours after a meal and no fever

options.label: C
options.text: Gradual colicky abdominal pain, frequent diarrhoea, tenesmus and heme-positive stool, often without prominent fever

options.label: E
options.text: High spiking fever with relative bradycardia and rose spots

questions.correctAnswerText: Gradual colicky abdominal pain, frequent diarrhoea, tenesmus and heme-positive stool, often without prominent fever
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes gradual-onset colicky abdominal pain, six to eight bowel motions per day, tenesmus and heme-positive stool. Generalized constitutional symptoms are usually absent; fever occurs in only a minority of patients.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. This is the clinical pattern of amoebic dysentery.
- B. Incorrect. This describes staphylococcal food poisoning.
- E. Incorrect. This describes typhoid fever.
- D. Incorrect. This describes enterobiasis.
- A. Incorrect. This describes malaria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Amebic dysentery often has gradual onset.
- Colicky pain, frequent stools and tenesmus are typical.
- Fever and systemic toxicity may be absent.
- Distinguish it from abrupt toxin-mediated food poisoning.

questions.stem: A child with previous dysentery develops fever, right upper abdominal pain, tender hepatomegaly and a right-sided pleural effusion several months later. Which complication should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Amoebic liver abscess
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes amoebic liver abscess as an uncommon complication, usually occurring months to years after exposure. It may occur without a clear history of intestinal disease and presents with fever, abdominal pain/distension, tender hepatomegaly and right-sided atelectasis or effusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. The delayed fever, right upper abdominal pain, hepatomegaly and right-sided thoracic finding fit amoebic liver abscess.
- C. Incorrect. Splenic rupture is associated with splenomegaly, classically in EBV mononucleosis.
- A. Incorrect. TB peritonitis may cause chronic abdominal symptoms and ascites, not this characteristic amoebic abscess pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Osteomyelitis causes focal bone pain and inflammation.
- D. Incorrect. Cerebral malaria presents with altered consciousness, seizures or coma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Amoebic liver abscess is uncommon in children (approximately 1% in the source).
- May occur months to years after exposure.
- May occur without a preceding recognized intestinal illness.
- A single abscess, often in the right hepatic lobe, is described.

questions.stem: Which diagnostic approach is described for intestinal amoebiasis?

options.label: B
options.text: Stool microscopy from three samples, with stool antigen testing or PCR

questions.correctAnswerText: Stool microscopy from three samples, with stool antigen testing or PCR
questions.initialExplanation: The source recommends stool microscopic examination for cysts using three samples, with stated sensitivity of approximately 80-90%, and stool testing for E. histolytica antigen or PCR.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. These are the tests described for amoebiasis.
- C. Incorrect. The tape test is used for enterobiasis.
- E. Incorrect. Mantoux and chest imaging are used in TB assessment.
- D. Incorrect. Giemsa-stained blood films are used for malaria.
- A. Incorrect. Nasopharyngeal PCR is used in respiratory infections such as pertussis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Three stool samples improve microscopic detection.
- Stool antigen or PCR can identify E. histolytica.
- For liver abscess, the source lists raised WBC/ESR/liver enzymes and ultrasound, CT or MRI.

questions.stem: Which treatment distinction is stated for symptomatic and asymptomatic amoebiasis?

options.label: A
options.text: Symptomatic disease: albendazole; asymptomatic carriers: acyclovir

options.label: B
options.text: Both symptomatic and asymptomatic disease: chloroquine

options.label: C
options.text: Symptomatic disease: metronidazole or tinidazole; asymptomatic carriers: a luminal agent such as paromomycin or iodoquinol

options.label: D
options.text: Symptomatic disease: INH; asymptomatic carriers: rifampicin

options.label: E
options.text: Both symptomatic and asymptomatic disease: flucloxacillin

questions.correctAnswerText: Symptomatic disease: metronidazole or tinidazole; asymptomatic carriers: a luminal agent such as paromomycin or iodoquinol
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists metronidazole or tinidazole as the drug of choice for symptomatic amoebiasis and paromomycin or iodoquinol to eradicate infection in asymptomatic carriers.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. This is the symptomatic-versus-asymptomatic distinction.
- A. Incorrect. Albendazole is used for helminths; acyclovir treats selected herpesvirus infections.
- D. Incorrect. These are antituberculous drugs.
- B. Incorrect. Chloroquine is an antimalarial.
- E. Incorrect. Flucloxacillin is an antistaphylococcal antibiotic.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Symptomatic amoebiasis: metronidazole or tinidazole in the source.
- Asymptomatic carriage: paromomycin or iodoquinol to eradicate luminal infection.
- Prevention: sanitation and interruption of fecal-oral transmission.

cases.title: A child develops a painless ulcer on an exposed area after sandfly exposure
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child from an area with sandflies develops a papule on the forearm. It slowly enlarges into a nodule and then a painless ulcer. The lesion eventually heals, leaving a scar. The child has no fever or organomegaly.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cutaneous leishmaniasis
questions.initialExplanation: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is transmitted by the sandfly. Clinical guidance a lesion on an exposed area progressing from papule to nodule to painless ulcer, eventually healing with a scar.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. The sandfly exposure and painless ulcerative lesion with scarring are characteristic.
- C. Incorrect. Impetigo causes superficial vesicles/pustules that rupture and form honey-coloured crusts.
- D. Incorrect. Erythema migrans is an expanding macule after tick bite in Lyme disease.
- A. Incorrect. Varicella causes itchy vesicles in crops.
- B. Incorrect. Enterobiasis causes nocturnal perianal itching.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vector: sandfly.
- Cutaneous species listed: L. major, L. tropica and L. mexicana.
- Lesion: papule → nodule → painless ulcer → scar.
- Lesions occur on exposed areas.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child has prolonged intermittent fever, marked splenomegaly, hepatomegaly and severe wasting after living in a sandfly-endemic area. Which form of leishmaniasis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar)
questions.initialExplanation: Visceral leishmaniasis commonly affects young children and involves reticuloendothelial organs including the liver, spleen, bone marrow and lymph nodes. The classic clinical picture is high fever, marked splenomegaly, hepatomegaly and severe cachexia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The prolonged fever, massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly and wasting are typical of kala-azar.
- C. Incorrect. Cutaneous disease causes a localized papule/nodule/ulcer on exposed skin.
- E. Incorrect. Lyme disease follows tick exposure and produces erythema migrans or late neurocardiac/joint findings.
- D. Incorrect. Amoebiasis causes intestinal dysentery or hepatic abscess.
- B. Incorrect. Enterobiasis causes nocturnal itching and sleep disturbance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Visceral leishmaniasis: kala-azar.
- Species listed: L. chagasi, L. infantum and L. donovani.
- Usually affects children under 5 years.
- Reticuloendothelial involvement: liver, spleen, bone marrow and lymph nodes.

questions.stem: Which haematological complication is particularly associated with advanced visceral leishmaniasis?

options.label: A
options.text: Profound pancytopenia, with severe anaemia and bleeding tendency

options.label: E
options.text: Marked lymphocytosis with normal haemoglobin and platelets

questions.correctAnswerText: Profound pancytopenia, with severe anaemia and bleeding tendency
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes massive hepatosplenomegaly and profound pancytopenia in terminal kala-azar. Anaemia may be severe enough to precipitate heart failure, and bleeding episodes such as epistaxis are frequent. Secondary bacterial infections are an important cause of death.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Bone marrow/reticuloendothelial involvement can produce pancytopenia and severe anaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Eosinophilia is not the defining blood picture described.
- B. Incorrect. Polycythaemia and thrombocytosis are not expected in advanced visceral leishmaniasis.
- E. Incorrect. The source emphasizes pancytopenia, not isolated lymphocytosis.
- C. Incorrect. Severe disease is associated with pancytopenia, not isolated neutrophilia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Advanced kala-azar: massive hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia.
- Severe anaemia can precipitate heart failure.
- Epistaxis/bleeding and secondary bacterial infection are important complications.
- Untreated disease has very high mortality in the source.

questions.stem: Which medications are named in the source for treatment of leishmaniasis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam) and amphotericin B
questions.initialExplanation: The leishmaniasis section names sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam) and amphotericin B as treatments.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Both are listed in the source.
- D. Incorrect. These are antivirals used for herpesvirus infections.
- E. Incorrect. These are anthelmintics used for helminth infections.
- C. Incorrect. These are antituberculous drugs.
- B. Incorrect. These are antimalarial drugs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance names sodium stibogluconate and amphotericin B.
- Visceral disease has significant morbidity and mortality if untreated.
- The source lists cutaneous and visceral forms separately.

cases.title: A febrile child has returned from a malaria-endemic area
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child returns from a malaria-endemic region and develops intermittent high fever with chills and sweating. Examination shows pallor and splenomegaly. The child also has jaundice, headache and vomiting.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?
questions.correctAnswerText: Malaria
questions.initialExplanation: The source emphasizes that malaria should be considered in any febrile child who has returned from a malaria-endemic area within the previous year. Typical features include paroxysms of fever, chills, sweating, haemolytic anaemia and splenomegaly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. Travel to an endemic area with intermittent fever, chills, anaemia and splenomegaly is highly suggestive.
- D. Incorrect. Typhoid causes prolonged high fever and gastrointestinal symptoms, but the malaria travel/vector risk and paroxysms are key here.
- A. Incorrect. Lyme disease follows tick exposure and causes erythema migrans and possible late cardioneurological features.
- B. Incorrect. Enterobiasis causes nocturnal perianal itching.
- E. Incorrect. Scarlet fever causes sore throat and a sandpaper rash.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider malaria in a febrile child returning from an endemic region within the previous year.
- Vector: infected female Anopheles mosquito.
- Infective stage: sporozoite.
- Common clinical pattern: paroxysmal fever, chills, sweats, anaemia and splenomegaly.

questions.stem: Which Plasmodium species is described as acute and potentially fatal?
questions.correctAnswerText: Plasmodium falciparum
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists P. falciparum as acute and fatal, P. vivax as the commonest, P. ovale, and P. malariae as mild but chronic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. P. falciparum is the species emphasized as acute and potentially fatal.
- C. Incorrect. P. vivax is listed as the commonest species.
- B. Incorrect. P. ovale is listed but not described as the acute fatal species in this table.
- E. Incorrect. P. malariae is described as mild but chronic.
- D. Incorrect. P. falciparum is clearly identified in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- P. falciparum: acute, severe and potentially fatal.
- P. vivax: commonest.
- P. malariae: described as mild but chronic.
- Incubation period listed: 9-40 days.

questions.stem: Which blood test approach is recommended when the first smear is negative but malaria remains clinically suspected?

options.label: A
options.text: Exclude malaria permanently after one negative smear

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat thick and thin Giemsa-stained blood films several times a day for up to 3 days

options.label: E
options.text: Use stool microscopy as the confirmatory test

questions.correctAnswerText: Repeat thick and thin Giemsa-stained blood films several times a day for up to 3 days
questions.initialExplanation: The source identifies thick and thin Giemsa-stained blood films as diagnostic and explicitly states that a single negative smear does not exclude malaria. Smears should be obtained several times a day for 3 days when suspicion remains.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. This is the recommendation written in the malaria investigation section.
- A. Incorrect. One negative smear does not exclude malaria.
- C. Incorrect. The tape test diagnoses enterobiasis.
- D. Incorrect. Mantoux testing assesses TB infection and is not repeated in this way for malaria.
- E. Incorrect. Stool microscopy is not the diagnostic test for malaria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Thick and thin blood films with Giemsa stain are the key tests.
- One negative smear does not rule out malaria.
- Repeat smears several times daily for 3 days if suspicion persists.
- CBC and LFT may provide supportive information but do not replace parasitological diagnosis.

questions.stem: A child with P. falciparum infection develops drowsiness, convulsions and coma. Which additional metabolic abnormalities are specifically noted in cerebral malaria?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists drowsiness, convulsions and coma as manifestations of cerebral malaria, with hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis as associated metabolic abnormalities.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Both are specifically listed in the cerebral malaria section.
- B. Incorrect. This is the opposite glucose and acid-base pattern.
- D. Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia and respiratory alkalosis are not the stated complications.
- C. Incorrect. Hypernatraemia and metabolic alkalosis are not the stated pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Isolated hypokalaemia/respiratory alkalosis does not match the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cerebral malaria: drowsiness → convulsions → coma.
- Hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis are important associated abnormalities.
- Other severe complications listed include microthrombosis, hemiplegia, GI bleeding, renal failure and pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: Which route of malaria transmission is listed in addition to the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito?

options.label: A
options.text: Tick bite and direct skin contact

options.label: D
options.text: Blood transfusion, contaminated needles and transplacental transmission

questions.correctAnswerText: Blood transfusion, contaminated needles and transplacental transmission
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists mosquito transmission as the main route, but also identifies blood transfusion, contaminated needles and transplacental transmission.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. These are the additional routes listed.
- A. Incorrect. Tick bites transmit infections such as Lyme disease and rickettsiosis.
- C. Incorrect. Fecal-oral transmission is associated with infections such as typhoid and amoebiasis.
- E. Incorrect. Respiratory droplets transmit infections such as TB and pertussis.
- B. Incorrect. Sandfly bites transmit leishmaniasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Main vector: infected female Anopheles mosquito.
- Infective stage: sporozoite.
- Other routes: transfusion, contaminated needles and transplacental spread.
- Humans are the host/reservoir; parasites involve liver and red blood cells.

questions.stem: A neonate born in a malaria-endemic region develops fever, restlessness, poor feeding, pallor, jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly at 3 weeks of age. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Congenital malaria
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes congenital malaria as acquired prenatally or perinatally. It may manifest between 10 and 30 days of age with fever, restlessness, drowsiness, cyanosis, poor feeding, pallor, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, vomiting and diarrhoea.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The timing and neonatal systemic features match congenital malaria.
- B. Incorrect. Neonatal HSV may cause sepsis-like illness, pneumonitis, DIC, skin/eye/mouth disease or encephalitis, often in the context of maternal HSV exposure.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital rubella causes congenital anomalies such as cataract, SNHL and PDA.
- C. Incorrect. Enterobiasis is a childhood intestinal nematode infection causing nocturnal perianal itching.
- E. Incorrect. Congenital TB has a different presentation and epidemiological context.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital malaria may be acquired prenatally or perinatally.
- Timing in the source: typically 10-30 days of age, but the range is wider.
- Features: fever, poor feeding, pallor, jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly.
- It may be associated with adverse pregnancy and neonatal outcomes.

questions.stem: Which preventive measure is listed for malaria in the course clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Insect repellents, covering exposed skin, mosquito nets and vector-control measures

options.label: C
options.text: Excluding infected food handlers and refrigerating meals

options.label: D
options.text: BCG vaccination and chemoprophylaxis with isoniazid

options.label: E
options.text: Hand hygiene and treatment of household members with albendazole

questions.correctAnswerText: Insect repellents, covering exposed skin, mosquito nets and vector-control measures
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists preventing mosquito bites by covering exposed skin, using insect repellents and mosquito nets, and controlling mosquito breeding places with larvicidal measures. It states that no efficient vaccine is available in the course clinical guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the malaria prevention measures listed.
- E. Incorrect. These measures relate to enterobiasis.
- B. Incorrect. MMR prevents measles, mumps and rubella.
- D. Incorrect. BCG and INH prophylaxis relate to TB.
- C. Incorrect. These are food-safety measures for staphylococcal food poisoning.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Personal prevention: cover exposed skin, use insect repellent and sleep under mosquito nets.
- Vector control: eliminate breeding places and use larvicidal measures as listed.
- The source states no efficient malaria vaccine was available in the course material.
- Travel chemoprophylaxis should be guided by destination-specific current recommendations.

cases.title: A child with severe falciparum malaria develops metabolic and neurological complications
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child with confirmed *Plasmodium falciparum* infection becomes drowsy and then develops convulsions. Bedside testing also identifies hypoglycaemia. The child is anaemic and hypotensive. Alongside appropriate antimalarial therapy, the team plans supportive management based on the measures listed clinical guidance.

questions.stem: Which supportive-management bundle most closely matches the malaria section of standard guidance clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat the fever and avoid correcting metabolic abnormalities until the blood film becomes negative

options.label: B
options.text: Provide rehydration and antipyretics, treat convulsions and hypoglycaemia, and address anaemia and hypotension

options.label: C
options.text: Give albendazole and repeat it after two weeks, without other supportive measures

options.label: D
options.text: Use topical antibiotics and observe the child without monitoring circulation

options.label: E
options.text: Give INH chemoprophylaxis as the sole treatment for the acute episode

questions.correctAnswerText: Provide rehydration and antipyretics, treat convulsions and hypoglycaemia, and address anaemia and hypotension
questions.initialExplanation: The malaria treatment section lists supportive measures that include antipyretics, rehydration, treatment of convulsions, correction of hypoglycaemia, treatment of anaemia and management of hypotension. The vignette contains several of these complications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. This option brings together the supportive measures explicitly listed in the malaria section. The neurological and metabolic findings in the case make seizure and hypoglycaemia management particularly important, while anaemia and hypotension also require attention.
- A. Incorrect. The source does not recommend limiting treatment to fever control or delaying correction of hypoglycaemia and convulsions.
- C. Incorrect. Albendazole is an anthelmintic used for helminth infections such as enterobiasis; it is not malaria treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Topical antibiotics are not part of the listed malaria management, and the child has systemic and neurological complications requiring supportive care.
- E. Incorrect. Isoniazid is listed for TB chemoprophylaxis, not as treatment for acute malaria.

The medication list in the course clinical guidance names chloroquine phosphate, quinine sulfate and primaquine (for prevention of relapse). It does not provide a species-specific treatment protocol or doses in the material used for this question; these should not be inferred from this question.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cerebral malaria includes drowsiness, convulsions and coma.
- Hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis are specifically noted in cerebral malaria.
- Supportive management listed: antipyretics, rehydration, treatment of convulsions, correction of hypoglycaemia, treatment of anaemia and management of hypotension.
- The source names chloroquine phosphate, quinine sulfate and primaquine; it does not set out a complete species-specific regimen in these pages.

source.raw: Infectious Diseases lecture sheet — Pages 23–24, *Malaria: cerebral malaria, diagnosis and treatment*.

cases.title: Planning prophylaxis before travel to a malaria-endemic area
cases.vignette: The parents of a 10-year-old child are preparing for a prolonged family visit to a malaria-endemic area. During a pre-travel review, they ask when the chloroquine prophylaxis schedule in their paediatric standard guidance notes is supposed to begin and when it should end after the family returns.

questions.stem: According to the schedule written in the 2024 course clinical guidance, which timing is given for chloroquine prophylaxis?

options.label: A
options.text: Start on the day of departure and stop on the day of return

options.label: B
options.text: Start 8 weeks before departure and stop 2 weeks after return

options.label: C
options.text: Start 3 days before departure and continue for 3 days after return

options.label: D
options.text: Start 2 weeks before travel and continue for 8 weeks after return

options.label: E
options.text: Start after fever develops and continue until the blood film is negative

questions.correctAnswerText: Start 2 weeks before travel and continue for 8 weeks after return
questions.initialExplanation: The malaria prophylaxis section of the 2024 course clinical guidance states that chloroquine is started 2 weeks before travel to an endemic area and continued for 8 weeks after return.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. This is the exact timing stated clinical guidance's malaria prophylaxis section.
- A. Incorrect. The source specifies that prophylaxis begins before travel and continues after return; it is not limited to the travel dates.
- B. Incorrect. The pre-travel and post-travel durations are reversed relative to the course clinical guidance.
- C. Incorrect. These durations are not the schedule stated in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Prophylaxis is described for travel to an endemic area, not as a treatment started after symptoms develop.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The 2024 standard guidance clinical guidance lists chloroquine prophylaxis for travel to an endemic area.
- Timing in that clinical guidance: begin 2 weeks before travel and continue for 8 weeks after return.
- clinical guidance separately lists personal/vector prevention: covering exposed skin, insect repellents, mosquito nets and vector-control measures.
- This item records the course-clinical guidance schedule for examination coverage; it is not a substitute for current destination-specific travel-medicine advice or local resistance guidance.

source.raw: Infectious Diseases lecture sheet — Page 24, *Malaria: prophylaxis and prevention*.

topics.name: Tuberculosis in Children - Risk Factors, Latent Infection and Primary TB

cases.title: A young child has close household contact with an adult with pulmonary TB
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child is brought for assessment after a parent is found to have infectious pulmonary tuberculosis. The child is currently active and has no cough or fever. The family lives in an overcrowded home, and the child is undernourished. Assessment distinguishes latent infection from active disease and appropriate screening is arranged.

questions.stem: Which organism causes tuberculosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
questions.initialExplanation: Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an aerobic, acid-fast, intracellular bacillus. It is identified by Ziehl-Neelsen staining and can be cultured on Lowenstein-Jensen medium.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. M. tuberculosis is the acid-fast bacillus responsible for TB.
- E. Incorrect. Salmonella Typhi causes enteric fever.
- B. Incorrect. Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease.
- C. Incorrect. R. rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
- D. Incorrect. E. histolytica causes amoebiasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TB agent: M. tuberculosis.
- Aerobic, acid-fast, intracellular bacillus.
- Ziehl-Neelsen stain demonstrates acid-fast bacilli.
- Lowenstein-Jensen medium is used for culture.

questions.stem: Which group contains risk factors for paediatric TB recognized?

options.label: A
options.text: Breastfeeding, prematurity and a family history of eczema

options.label: B
options.text: Poverty/malnutrition, close contact with an infected adult, HIV/immunodeficiency, MDR-TB exposure and travel to an endemic area

options.label: C
options.text: Tick exposure, summer season and rural residence

options.label: D
options.text: Eating undercooked food and drinking contaminated water

options.label: E
options.text: Atopic eczema and a previous mild local vaccine reaction

questions.correctAnswerText: Poverty/malnutrition, close contact with an infected adult, HIV/immunodeficiency, MDR-TB exposure and travel to an endemic area
questions.initialExplanation: The TB section lists poor socioeconomic conditions, poverty and malnutrition, contact with an infected adult, MDR-TB strains, immunodeficiency including HIV and travel to an endemic area as risk factors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. All listed factors are identified in the TB risk section.
- A. Incorrect. These are listed in the vaccination clinical guidance as conditions that are not contraindications to routine vaccination.
- C. Incorrect. These are epidemiological clues for tick-borne infections such as Lyme disease.
- D. Incorrect. These are risk factors for fecal-oral infections such as typhoid and amoebiasis.
- E. Incorrect. These are not the major TB risk factors listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Close household contact with infectious TB is a major paediatric risk factor.
- Poverty, overcrowding and malnutrition increase risk.
- HIV/immunodeficiency and MDR-TB exposure are important.
- Infants and young children can progress from infection to disease more readily than adults.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes latent TB infection from active TB disease in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Latent TB is diagnosed by a positive blood film; active TB by stool microscopy

options.label: B
options.text: Latent TB is typically symptomatic and contagious; active TB has no symptoms

options.label: C
options.text: Latent TB: no symptoms, not contagious and usually normal chest X-ray; active TB: symptomatic, may be contagious and has an abnormal chest X-ray

options.label: D
options.text: Active TB cannot cause death if untreated

options.label: E
options.text: Both latent and active TB typically have negative TST and IGRA

questions.correctAnswerText: Latent TB: no symptoms, not contagious and usually normal chest X-ray; active TB: symptomatic, may be contagious and has an abnormal chest X-ray
questions.initialExplanation: The source contrasts latent TB (organisms present but inactive, asymptomatic and not transmissible) with active disease (organisms active, symptoms present and potential transmission). Both may have positive TST/IGRA; chest X-ray is usually normal in latent infection and abnormal in active disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. This is the distinction shown in the source table.
- B. Incorrect. The features are reversed.
- E. Incorrect. Both latent and active infection can have positive TST/IGRA.
- A. Incorrect. Blood film is used for malaria; stool microscopy is used for selected intestinal infections.
- D. Incorrect. The source warns that untreated active TB can lead to death.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Latent TB: asymptomatic, not contagious, positive TST/IGRA, normal CXR.
- Active TB: symptoms, possible infectiousness, positive TST/IGRA and often abnormal CXR.
- Latent TB can progress to active disease, especially in infants, children under 4 years, HIV and immunocompromised patients.
- A positive TST/IGRA indicates infection, not by itself the distinction between latent and active disease.

questions.stem: Which structures form the primary TB complex in the lung as described?

options.label: B
options.text: Ghon focus, TB lymphangitis and hilar TB lymphadenitis

options.label: C
options.text: Pleural plaque, pulmonary embolus and bronchiectasis

options.label: E
options.text: A solitary renal granuloma with no lymphatic involvement

questions.correctAnswerText: Ghon focus, TB lymphangitis and hilar TB lymphadenitis
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes the primary complex as a Ghon focus with TB lymphangitis and TB lymphadenitis involving hilar lymph nodes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. These are the three components listed in the primary complex.
- C. Incorrect. These are not the components of the primary TB complex.
- A. Incorrect. Cavitation and pleural disease may occur in progressive TB but do not define the primary complex.
- E. Incorrect. Renal TB is an extrapulmonary manifestation.
- D. Incorrect. Miliary TB is a disseminated form caused by haematogenous spread.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary complex = Ghon focus + lymphangitis + hilar lymphadenitis.
- Good immunity may lead to healing, fibrosis and calcification.
- Poor immunity can permit progressive primary disease and spread.

cases.title: A child has chronic cough, weight loss and night sweats
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child has lived with an adult who has untreated pulmonary TB. Over several weeks, the child develops chronic cough, weight loss, anorexia, night sweats and intermittent fever. The cough is sometimes productive. Chest imaging shows hilar lymphadenopathy and pulmonary parenchymal changes.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern is most consistent with pulmonary TB?

options.label: A
options.text: Chronic cough with or without sputum, night fever/sweats, anorexia and weight loss

options.label: C
options.text: Acute itchy vesicles in crops with crusting

options.label: D
options.text: Sudden vomiting and watery diarrhoea within 2-7 hours of a meal

options.label: E
options.text: Expanding painless erythema at a tick-bite site

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic cough with or without sputum, night fever/sweats, anorexia and weight loss
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes pulmonary TB with contact history, general TB toxemia (night fever, night sweats, anorexia and weight loss) and chronic cough, with or without expectoration. Sputum may be mucoid, purulent or blood-stained.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the pulmonary TB symptoms listed.
- D. Incorrect. This is typical of staphylococcal food poisoning.
- B. Incorrect. This is enterobiasis.
- C. Incorrect. This is varicella.
- E. Incorrect. This is erythema migrans in Lyme disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pulmonary TB: chronic cough is a key symptom.
- General features: night fever, night sweats, anorexia and weight loss.
- Other symptoms may include chest pain, dyspnoea and wheeze.
- Pneumonia and pleural effusion may occur.

questions.stem: A child has chronic cervical lymph node enlargement. The nodes are firm, discrete, mobile and non-tender. Which form of TB is described?
questions.correctAnswerText: TB lymphadenitis
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes TB lymphadenitis as cervical lymph node enlargement with firm, discrete, mobile and non-tender nodes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the clinical description of TB lymphadenitis.
- B. Incorrect. TB meningitis presents with neurological signs and abnormal CSF.
- D. Incorrect. Urogenital TB involves the urinary tract, often through haematogenous spread to the kidneys.
- C. Incorrect. Pott disease is skeletal TB of the spine.
- E. Incorrect. TB pericarditis affects the pericardium.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TB lymphadenitis commonly involves cervical nodes.
- Nodes are described as firm, discrete, mobile and non-tender.
- Lymph node enlargement can also cause pressure manifestations depending on location.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with TB exposure develops irritability, vomiting, convulsions and signs of raised intracranial pressure. CSF shows high protein, lymphocyte-predominant cells and low glucose. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Tuberculous meningitis
questions.initialExplanation: The source notes that CNS TB is particularly important in children under 5 years and has high morbidity and mortality. TB meningitis may cause raised ICP, irritability and convulsions; CSF typically has high protein, high cells (mainly lymphocytes) and low glucose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. The age, TB exposure, raised ICP and CSF pattern strongly support TB meningitis.
- D. Incorrect. Viral meningitis often has a different CSF pattern, usually without the markedly low glucose described.
- B. Incorrect. Lyme arthritis causes recurrent large-joint inflammation, not this meningitic CSF profile.
- C. Incorrect. Cerebral malaria causes altered consciousness, seizures or coma in a febrile child with malaria; the described CSF pattern and TB contact suggest TB meningitis.
- A. Incorrect. HSV gingivostomatitis causes painful oral vesicles/ulcers.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CNS TB is especially important in children under 5 years.
- TB meningitis: raised ICP, irritability and convulsions.
- CSF: raised protein, lymphocyte-predominant pleocytosis and low glucose.
- High morbidity and mortality; prompt treatment is essential.

questions.stem: Which statement about skeletal TB (Pott disease) is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It occurs in the small bones of the hands

options.label: B
options.text: It commonly affects the lower thoracic spine, with lumbar and cervical involvement also described

options.label: C
options.text: It is defined by a positive Nikolsky sign

options.label: D
options.text: It is a form of cutaneous leishmaniasis

questions.correctAnswerText: It commonly affects the lower thoracic spine, with lumbar and cervical involvement also described
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists Pott disease as skeletal TB of the spine, with the lower thoracic region being the commonest site, followed by lumbar and cervical regions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. This is the site distribution listed.
- A. Incorrect. The source does not describe Pott disease as a hand-bone infection.
- D. Incorrect. Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a separate sandfly-borne parasitic disease.
- E. Incorrect. TB arthritis can affect the hip, ankle, knee and elbow, but Pott disease refers to spinal TB.
- C. Incorrect. Nikolsky sign is associated with SSSS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pott disease = spinal tuberculosis.
- Lower thoracic spine is the commonest site in the source.
- Lumbar and cervical involvement may also occur.
- TB arthritis may involve hip, ankle, knee and elbow, causing pain, swelling and restricted movement.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly matches extrapulmonary TB forms with their clinical features?

options.label: A
options.text: TB arthritis: painless skin ulcer; abdominal TB: nocturnal perianal itching

options.label: B
options.text: Urogenital TB: erythema migrans; miliary TB: rose spots

options.label: C
options.text: TB pericarditis: honey-coloured crusts; skeletal TB: Koplik spots

options.label: D
options.text: Abdominal TB: chronic diarrhoea, tenesmus, bleeding or ascites; miliary TB: haematogenous dissemination with hepatosplenomegaly

options.label: E
options.text: TB lymphadenitis: vesicles in crops; miliary TB: isolated parotid swelling

questions.correctAnswerText: Abdominal TB: chronic diarrhoea, tenesmus, bleeding or ascites; miliary TB: haematogenous dissemination with hepatosplenomegaly
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes abdominal TB as TB enteritis with chronic diarrhoea, tenesmus and bleeding, or TB peritonitis with ascites. Miliary TB results from widespread haematogenous dissemination to multiple organs and may cause hepatosplenomegaly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. Both extrapulmonary patterns are correctly matched.
- B. Incorrect. Erythema migrans is Lyme disease; rose spots occur in typhoid.
- A. Incorrect. Painless skin ulcers may occur in cutaneous leishmaniasis; nocturnal itching suggests enterobiasis.
- C. Incorrect. Honey-coloured crusts are impetigo; Koplik spots are measles.
- E. Incorrect. These are not the described manifestations of TB lymphadenitis or miliary TB.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Abdominal TB: enteritis or peritonitis with ascites.
- TB arthritis: pain, swelling and limited movement; X-ray may show bone rarefaction/destruction.
- Other sites listed: urogenital, pericardial and skin (lupus vulgaris).
- Miliary TB: widespread haematogenous dissemination with hepatosplenomegaly.

cases.title: A child with TB contact has a positive tuberculin skin test
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child who has had close contact with an adult with infectious TB undergoes investigation. A purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test is administered intradermally. The child returns for reading two days later.

questions.stem: Which set of investigations is included in the TB work-up described in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Serum amylase, stool tape test and abdominal ultrasound

options.label: B
options.text: CBC/ESR/CRP, chest imaging, sputum or gastric aspirate for acid-fast bacilli, culture and GeneXpert/PCR

options.label: C
options.text: EBV serology and heterophile antibody test

options.label: E
options.text: Giemsa blood films and stool microscopy

questions.correctAnswerText: CBC/ESR/CRP, chest imaging, sputum or gastric aspirate for acid-fast bacilli, culture and GeneXpert/PCR
questions.initialExplanation: The TB investigation section lists CBC with lymphocytosis, raised ESR and positive CRP; CXR or CT chest; sputum, stomach wash or gastric aspirate for direct smear using Ziehl-Neelsen stain; Lowenstein-Jensen culture; and newer molecular methods such as GeneXpert, PCR and whole-genome sequencing.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. This covers the major investigation categories listed in the source.
- A. Incorrect. These tests do not form the TB diagnostic work-up.
- E. Incorrect. Giemsa blood films diagnose malaria; stool microscopy evaluates selected intestinal parasites.
- C. Incorrect. These tests support EBV mononucleosis diagnosis.
- D. Incorrect. Nasopharyngeal PCR is used for pertussis, not TB.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CXR/CT may show hilar lymphadenopathy, collapse, consolidation, effusion or miliary changes.
- Samples: sputum, stomach wash or gastric aspirate, particularly in younger children.
- Ziehl-Neelsen stain demonstrates acid-fast bacilli.
- Lowenstein-Jensen culture may take 3-6 weeks.
- GeneXpert/PCR can provide information about drug-resistance mutations.

questions.stem: What is the immunological principle underlying the Mantoux test?

options.label: B
options.text: Type IV delayed hypersensitivity to TB antigens

options.label: C
options.text: Direct detection of viable mycobacteria in blood

questions.correctAnswerText: Type IV delayed hypersensitivity to TB antigens
questions.initialExplanation: The source explains that the Mantoux test is based on a delayed hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction to TB bacilli after intradermal administration of purified protein derivative (PPD).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. This is the principle stated in the source.
- A. Incorrect. Type I hypersensitivity is immediate and IgE-mediated.
- C. Incorrect. Mantoux is an immune response test, not a direct microbiological test.
- D. Incorrect. PPD is used to provoke a delayed T-cell response.
- E. Incorrect. Complement fixation is not the principle of the Mantoux test.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mantoux = Type IV delayed hypersensitivity.
- It measures cell-mediated immune reactivity to PPD.
- A positive test indicates TB infection/exposure, not necessarily active disease.

questions.stem: Which procedure and reading method are correct for the Mantoux test as described in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Subcutaneous PPD; measure vesicle diameter after 7 days

options.label: B
options.text: Intramuscular 1 mL PPD; measure redness after 30 minutes

options.label: C
options.text: Intradermal 0.1 mL containing 5 TU PPD; measure induration, not erythema, at 48-72 hours

options.label: D
options.text: Oral PPD; measure fever after 24 hours

options.label: E
options.text: Intravenous PPD; read the result after 2 weeks

questions.correctAnswerText: Intradermal 0.1 mL containing 5 TU PPD; measure induration, not erythema, at 48-72 hours
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance specifies 0.1 mL containing 5 units of PPD injected intradermally into the flexor surface of the forearm. The induration—not the surrounding erythema—is measured after 48-72 hours.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. This is the technique described on page 27.
- B. Incorrect. The test is intradermal, not intramuscular, and is not read after 30 minutes.
- D. Incorrect. PPD is not administered orally.
- A. Incorrect. The source specifies an intradermal injection and measurement of induration, not vesicle size.
- E. Incorrect. Mantoux is read at 48-72 hours, not after 2 weeks.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dose/volume in the source: 0.1 mL containing 5 TU PPD.
- Route/site: intradermal, flexor surface of forearm.
- Read at 48-72 hours.
- Measure induration in millimetres, not erythema.

questions.stem: Which interpretation of the Mantoux thresholds matches the table?

options.label: A
options.text: ≥10 mm is typically negative in children in routine care

options.label: B
options.text: ≥5 mm in children without risk factors; ≥15 mm for close contacts

options.label: C
options.text: The test is interpreted by erythema rather than induration

options.label: D
options.text: Any induration is diagnostic of active pulmonary TB

options.label: E
options.text: Use ≥5 mm for close contacts or immunosuppressed children, ≥10 mm for other risk groups and ≥15 mm without risk factors

questions.correctAnswerText: Use ≥5 mm for close contacts or immunosuppressed children, ≥10 mm for other risk groups and ≥15 mm without risk factors
questions.initialExplanation: The table on page 27 uses different cut-offs according to risk: 5 mm for close contacts and children with clinical/radiological evidence or immunosuppression (including HIV); 10 mm for children with increased risk of disseminated disease or increased exposure; and 15 mm for children without risk factors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. This matches the risk-stratified thresholds shown in the source.
- B. Incorrect. The 5 mm threshold applies to the highest-risk groups, not children without risk factors.
- A. Incorrect. A 10 mm induration can be positive in children with increased risk.
- C. Incorrect. Induration, not erythema, is measured.
- D. Incorrect. TST indicates TB infection; it does not by itself distinguish latent from active disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ≥5 mm: close contact, clinical/radiological evidence or immunosuppression including HIV.
- ≥10 mm: increased risk of disseminated disease (e.g. young age, diabetes, CKD, lymphoma) or increased exposure.
- ≥15 mm: children with no risk factors.
- Interpret according to risk, not as one universal threshold.

questions.stem: Which statement about false Mantoux results and IGRA is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: BCG vaccination makes each IGRA positive

options.label: C
options.text: HIV is a common cause of false-positive TST and IGRA typically excludes TB if negative

options.label: D
options.text: BCG may cause a false-positive TST; IGRA uses antigens not expressed by BCG, but a negative IGRA does not reliably exclude TB infection

options.label: E
options.text: IGRA is a skin test that measures erythema

questions.correctAnswerText: BCG may cause a false-positive TST; IGRA uses antigens not expressed by BCG, but a negative IGRA does not reliably exclude TB infection
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists BCG and non-TB mycobacteria as causes of false-positive TST results. False negatives may occur with malnutrition, very young age, HIV, reading error, improper injection, disseminated TB and recent viral infection/MMR. IGRA is a blood-based test using TB antigens absent from BCG; a positive result indicates TB infection rather than BCG vaccination, but a negative result does not reliably rule out infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. This accurately summarizes the TST limitations and IGRA principle.
- C. Incorrect. HIV is listed as a cause of false-negative TST due to immune deficiency, not false-positive TST.
- B. Incorrect. Malnutrition is listed as a cause of false-negative results.
- E. Incorrect. IGRA is a blood-based assay, not a skin test.
- A. Incorrect. The antigens used in IGRA are not expressed by BCG, so BCG vaccination does not cause the same false-positive effect.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- False-positive TST: BCG and immune reactivity to non-TB mycobacteria.
- False-negative TST: malnutrition, very young age, HIV, reading/injection errors, disseminated TB and recent viral infection/MMR.
- IGRA is a blood test using antigens absent from BCG.
- Positive IGRA suggests TB infection rather than BCG effect; negative IGRA does not reliably exclude infection.

cases.title: A child is diagnosed with pulmonary TB and the family asks about the treatment course
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child has chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats and radiological changes consistent with pulmonary TB. Molecular testing supports M. tuberculosis infection. There is no evidence of meningitis, bone involvement or miliary spread.

questions.stem: Which treatment duration and sequence are listed for uncomplicated pulmonary TB in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Two months of isoniazid alone, followed by ten months of ethambutol alone

options.label: B
options.text: Twelve months of metronidazole and tinidazole

options.label: C
options.text: Six weeks of acyclovir followed by penicillin

options.label: D
options.text: Two months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by four months of isoniazid and rifampicin

options.label: E
options.text: Three days of azithromycin followed by no further treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Two months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by four months of isoniazid and rifampicin
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes a six-month pulmonary TB regimen: an initial two-month phase with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by four months of isoniazid and rifampicin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. This is the pulmonary TB regimen shown on page 28.
- A. Incorrect. It omits key drugs and does not match the two-phase regimen.
- C. Incorrect. These drugs are not the TB regimen.
- E. Incorrect. A short macrolide course is not TB treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Metronidazole and tinidazole are used for selected protozoal infections.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pulmonary TB: 6 months total.
- Intensive phase: 2 months HRZE.
- Continuation phase: 4 months HR.
- Use current national TB protocols and susceptibility information in clinical care.

questions.stem: Which regimen duration is listed for miliary TB, bone/joint TB and TB meningitis?

options.label: B
options.text: No treatment if the child is younger than 5 years

options.label: D
options.text: Three months of isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide followed by nine months of isoniazid and rifampicin

questions.correctAnswerText: Three months of isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide followed by nine months of isoniazid and rifampicin
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists a prolonged 12-month regimen for miliary TB, bone/joint TB and TB meningitis: three months of isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide, then nine months of isoniazid and rifampicin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- D. Correct. This is the prolonged regimen described on page 28.
- C. Incorrect. Ceftriaxone alone is not the listed TB regimen.
- A. Incorrect. Amoxicillin is not TB treatment.
- E. Incorrect. Isoniazid monotherapy is not the active multidrug regimen described.
- B. Incorrect. Young age increases the risk of severe TB; it is not a reason to withhold treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Miliary, bone/joint and CNS TB: 12 months.
- Initial phase: 3 months HRZ.
- Continuation phase: 9 months HR.
- Regimens must be individualized by TB specialists according to national guidance and drug susceptibility.

questions.stem: What adjunctive treatment is specifically recommended initially for tuberculous meningitis in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Dexamethasone to reduce the risk of long-term sequelae

questions.correctAnswerText: Dexamethasone to reduce the risk of long-term sequelae
questions.initialExplanation: The source states that dexamethasone is given initially in tuberculous meningitis to decrease the risk of long-term sequelae.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the adjunctive treatment specified.
