- E. Incorrect. Acyclovir treats herpesvirus infections, not TB.
- B. Incorrect. Aspirin is not the adjunctive treatment described.
- D. Incorrect. Albendazole is an anthelmintic.
- C. Incorrect. Dexamethasone is explicitly mentioned.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TB meningitis is a severe extrapulmonary form.
- Clinical guidance initial dexamethasone.
- It is given with appropriate multidrug antituberculous treatment.

questions.stem: Which statement about BCG vaccine is correct according to the TB prevention section?

options.label: A
options.text: It is contraindicated in immunocompetent newborns

options.label: B
options.text: It is a recombinant vaccine given intravenously

options.label: C
options.text: It is an inactivated oral vaccine used to prevent typhoid

options.label: D
options.text: It prevents each case of pulmonary TB with 100% effectiveness

options.label: E
options.text: It is a live attenuated vaccine given intradermally in the left deltoid region and helps prevent TB meningitis and disseminated TB

questions.correctAnswerText: It is a live attenuated vaccine given intradermally in the left deltoid region and helps prevent TB meningitis and disseminated TB
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes BCG as live attenuated and administered intradermally in the left deltoid region, starting at birth. It notes partial protection against pulmonary TB and greater effectiveness in preventing TB meningitis and disseminated disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. This matches the vaccine type, route, site and main protective benefit described.
- C. Incorrect. BCG is not an inactivated oral typhoid vaccine.
- B. Incorrect. It is not recombinant or intravenous.
- A. Incorrect. BCG is given from birth in the source; the contraindication is immunodeficiency/immunosuppressive treatment.
- D. Incorrect. The source explicitly describes partial rather than complete protection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- BCG: live attenuated.
- Route/site: intradermal, left deltoid.
- Begins at birth in the schedule.
- Protects against severe childhood TB, particularly meningitis and disseminated disease.
- Contraindicated in immunodeficiency and immunosuppressive therapy as stated.

questions.stem: Which local reaction timeline is described after BCG vaccination?

options.label: B
options.text: Erythema/papule followed by ulceration at 3-6 weeks and scar formation within 2-6 months

options.label: D
options.text: Dermatomal vesicles several months later in each recipient

questions.correctAnswerText: Erythema/papule followed by ulceration at 3-6 weeks and scar formation within 2-6 months
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes the local BCG reaction as erythema and papule formation, followed by ulceration in 3-6 weeks and scar formation within 2-6 months. Regional lymphadenitis may occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. This is the expected local reaction timeline in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Generalized desquamation suggests a different disorder such as SSSS, not the expected BCG response.
- A. Incorrect. Koplik spots are associated with measles.
- C. Incorrect. This timing and vomiting/diarrhoea pattern relate to staphylococcal food poisoning, not BCG.
- D. Incorrect. Dermatomal vesicles suggest herpes zoster, not a routine BCG reaction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- BCG local reaction: erythema → papule → ulceration → scar.
- Ulceration: around 3-6 weeks.
- Scar: around 2-6 months.
- Regional lymphadenitis may occur.
- Disseminated BCG infection is a concern in immunocompromised individuals.

questions.stem: Which preventive medication is listed for high-risk close contacts of a person with TB?
questions.correctAnswerText: Isoniazid (INH) chemoprophylaxis
questions.initialExplanation: The TB prevention section lists chemoprophylaxis for high-risk close contacts, using isoniazid (INH).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. INH is the medication named for TB chemoprophylaxis in the source.
- A. Incorrect. Metronidazole is used for selected protozoal/anaerobic infections.
- B. Incorrect. Acyclovir treats selected herpesvirus infections.
- E. Incorrect. Chloroquine is an antimalarial.
- D. Incorrect. Flucloxacillin is an antistaphylococcal antibiotic.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Screen close contacts of infectious TB cases.
- The source lists INH chemoprophylaxis for high-risk close contacts.
- BCG vaccination and contact chemoprophylaxis are different preventive approaches.
- In practice, exclude active disease and follow the local TB contact-management protocol before preventive therapy.

topics.name: Integrated Differential Diagnosis of Fever and Rash

cases.title: A child presents with fever and a rash of uncertain morphology
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child is brought with fever and a new generalized rash. The rash is classified as maculopapular, vesicular/bullous or petechial/purpuric. The child is assessed for toxicity, mucosal involvement, bleeding, neurological features and signs of shock.

questions.stem: Which group contains causes of a maculopapular rash recognized?

options.label: C
options.text: Roseola (HHV-6/7), enterovirus, Parvovirus B19, measles/rubella, scarlet fever, typhoid and Lyme disease

options.label: E
options.text: TSS, orbital cellulitis and TB meningitis

questions.correctAnswerText: Roseola (HHV-6/7), enterovirus, Parvovirus B19, measles/rubella, scarlet fever, typhoid and Lyme disease
questions.initialExplanation: The source's fever-and-rash table lists HHV-6/7 (roseola), enterovirus, Parvovirus B19, measles/rubella, scarlet fever, rheumatic fever (erythema marginatum), typhoid (rose spots) and Lyme disease (erythema migrans) among maculopapular-rash causes. Kawasaki disease and systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis are also included under other causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- C. Correct. These infections are all listed in the maculopapular-rash column.
- A. Incorrect. These are infections discussed elsewhere in the course, but they are not the listed maculopapular-rash group in the table.
- B. Incorrect. These are mainly vesicular, bullous or pustular causes.
- D. Incorrect. These belong to the petechial/purpuric differential and other causes.
- E. Incorrect. These are not the listed maculopapular-rash group.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Maculopapular differential: roseola, enterovirus, Parvovirus B19, measles/rubella, scarlet fever, rheumatic fever, typhoid and Lyme disease.
- Other causes listed: Kawasaki disease and systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
- Use age, vaccination status, exposure history, rash distribution and fever timeline to narrow the differential.

questions.stem: A febrile child has a petechial or purpuric rash. Which infectious causes are recognized and should be considered?

options.label: A
options.text: Bacterial sepsis/endocarditis; viral enterovirus or adenovirus infection

questions.correctAnswerText: Bacterial sepsis/endocarditis; viral enterovirus or adenovirus infection
questions.initialExplanation: The petechial/purpuric-rash column lists meningococcal and other bacterial sepsis, infective endocarditis, and viral infections including enteroviruses and adenoviruses.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the infectious causes in the petechial/purpuric column.
- E. Incorrect. Roseola and Parvovirus B19 are listed under maculopapular rash.
- B. Incorrect. Varicella and impetigo are listed under vesicular/bullous/pustular eruptions.
- D. Incorrect. Lyme and typhoid are listed in the maculopapular-rash differential.
- C. Incorrect. These parasitic infections do not form the listed petechial/purpuric group.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fever plus petechiae/purpura requires urgent consideration of meningococcal/other bacterial sepsis.
- Infective endocarditis is also listed.
- Viral causes in the table include enteroviruses and adenoviruses.
- Assess for shock, toxicity and bleeding urgently.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly represents causes of vesicular, bullous or pustular eruptions in the source?

options.label: A
options.text: Meningococcal sepsis, infective endocarditis and ITP

options.label: B
options.text: Roseola, rubella, typhoid and Lyme disease

options.label: C
options.text: TB lymphadenitis, Pott disease and TB meningitis

options.label: E
options.text: Varicella-zoster virus, HSV, Coxsackie virus, impetigo, boils, staphylococcal bullous impetigo and SSSS

questions.correctAnswerText: Varicella-zoster virus, HSV, Coxsackie virus, impetigo, boils, staphylococcal bullous impetigo and SSSS
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists VZV, HSV and Coxsackie virus among viral vesicular causes. Bacterial causes include impetigo, boils, staphylococcal bullous impetigo and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are also listed under other causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- E. Correct. These are the viral and bacterial causes in the vesicular/bullous/pustular column.
- B. Incorrect. These are maculopapular-rash causes.
- A. Incorrect. These are causes listed under petechial/purpuric rash.
- D. Incorrect. These are other causes of maculopapular rash.
- C. Incorrect. These are extrapulmonary TB manifestations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral vesicular causes: VZV, HSV and Coxsackie.
- Bacterial causes: impetigo, boils, staphylococcal bullous impetigo and SSSS.
- Other causes: erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

questions.stem: Which non-infectious conditions are listed among the differential diagnoses of petechial/purpuric rash?

options.label: B
options.text: Henoch-Schönlein purpura, immune thrombocytopenic purpura and vasculitis

options.label: E
options.text: Kawasaki disease and systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis

questions.correctAnswerText: Henoch-Schönlein purpura, immune thrombocytopenic purpura and vasculitis
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists Henoch-Schönlein purpura, thrombocytopenia such as ITP and vasculitis under other causes of petechial/purpuric rash. Malaria is also included in that column.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- B. Correct. All three are listed under other causes of petechial/purpuric rash.
- E. Incorrect. Kawasaki disease and systemic-onset JIA are listed among other causes of maculopapular rash.
- C. Incorrect. Erythema multiforme, SJS and TEN are listed under vesicular/bullous/pustular eruptions.
- D. Incorrect. Rheumatic fever and Lyme disease are listed in the maculopapular-rash differential.
- A. Incorrect. Roseola and enterovirus are listed under maculopapular rash.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Petechial/purpuric differential includes infection, haematological disease and vasculitis.
- Other causes listed: HSP, ITP, vasculitis and malaria.
- Do not assume every purpuric rash is infectious.

topics.name: Bone and Joint Infections (Septic Arthritis and Osteomyelitis)

cases.title: A febrile child with simultaneous joint and bone involvement
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child is brought with fever and a rapidly painful, swollen knee. The child refuses to bear weight. Examination suggests an acute suppurative joint infection, and the clinical team is also concerned about adjacent osteomyelitis. The treating physician reviews the organisms specifically associated with these two conditions clinical guidance.

questions.stem: Which organism is explicitly linked clinical guidance to both suppurative arthritis and osteomyelitis?
questions.correctAnswerText: *Staphylococcus aureus*
questions.initialExplanation: The bacterial-infection section specifically lists *Staphylococcus aureus* as a cause of suppurative arthritis and osteomyelitis. The paired joint and bone infections therefore point to the organism named in that list.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. standard guidance clinical guidance's *Staphylococcus aureus* disease list includes sepsis, suppurative arthritis and osteomyelitis. Both suspected sites of infection in this vignette are therefore linked to the same organism in the source.
- B. Incorrect. *Bordetella pertussis* is the cause of whooping cough in the course material; it is not the organism listed for these suppurative bone and joint infections.
- C. Incorrect. *Salmonella Typhi* causes enteric fever and is associated with intestinal and systemic complications, not this paired list of staphylococcal infections.
- D. Incorrect. *Borrelia burgdorferi* causes Lyme disease, which is associated with erythema migrans and later neurological, cardiac and joint manifestations. It is not the organism named for suppurative arthritis plus osteomyelitis in the staphylococcal section.
- E. Incorrect. *Enterobius vermicularis* causes enterobiasis, classically associated with nocturnal perianal itching.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Standard guidance clinical guidance lists *S. aureus* as a cause of sepsis, suppurative arthritis and osteomyelitis.
- The same section also lists impetigo, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, parotitis, membranous tracheitis complicating viral croup and pneumonia.
- This question completes the invasive bone/joint-infection portion of the *Staphylococcus aureus* list, which was not directly assessed in the existing bank.

source.raw: Infectious Diseases lecture sheet — Page 17, *Staphylococcus & streptococcal disease: diseases caused by Staphylococcus aureus*.
source.pages: 17, *Staphylococcus & streptococcal disease: diseases caused by Staphylococcus aureus*

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: The neonatal period is defined as which time interval?
questions.correctAnswerText: The first 28 days of life
questions.initialExplanation: The neonatal period covers the first 28 days after birth. standard guidance divides it into early neonatal life (birth to day 7) and late neonatal life (day 7 to day 28).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Six weeks extends beyond the neonatal period.
- B. Correct. The neonatal period is the first 28 days of life.
- C. Incorrect. Two weeks is not the definition used.
- D. Incorrect. The first 7 days are the early neonatal period, not the entire neonatal period.
- E. Incorrect. Three months is well beyond the neonatal period.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal period: birth to 28 completed days.
- Early neonatal period: birth to the end of day 7.
- Late neonatal period: day 7 to day 28.
- The term *neonate* refers to an infant aged 28 days or younger.

questions.stem: A baby is born before completing 37 weeks of gestation. How should the baby be classified?
questions.correctAnswerText: Preterm
questions.initialExplanation: A preterm baby is born before completing 37 weeks of gestation. A term baby is delivered from 37 completed weeks through 41 weeks, while post-term is 42 weeks or more.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. SGA is defined by birth weight below the 10th centile for gestational age, not by gestational age alone.
- B. Correct. Birth before 37 completed weeks is preterm.
- C. Incorrect. Post-maturity is a clinical description associated with prolonged gestation, not birth before 37 weeks.
- D. Incorrect. Post-term refers to delivery at or beyond 42 weeks.
- E. Incorrect. Term begins at 37 completed weeks.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preterm: <37 completed weeks.
- Term: 37-41 weeks 's classification.
- Post-term: ≥42 weeks.
- Gestational age is calculated from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP), not from the date of conception.

questions.stem: Which birth-weight threshold defines very low birth weight (VLBW)?
questions.correctAnswerText: Less than 1,500 g
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe low birth weight (LBW) as below 2,500 g, very low birth weight (VLBW) as below 1,500 g and extremely low birth weight (ELBW) as below 1,000 g.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the VLBW threshold.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the standard threshold used in the source.
- C. Correct. VLBW is birth weight below 1,500 g.
- D. Incorrect. This is the threshold for LBW.
- E. Incorrect. This is the threshold for ELBW.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LBW: <2,500 g.
- VLBW: <1,500 g.
- ELBW: <1,000 g.
- Birth weight is the weight recorded during the first hour of life.

questions.stem: A newborn's weight is at the 7th centile for gestational age. Which classification is correct?
questions.correctAnswerText: Small for gestational age (SGA)
questions.initialExplanation: SGA is defined as a birth weight below the 10th centile for gestational age. AGA lies between the 10th and 90th centiles, while LGA is above the 90th centile.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Post-term status is based on gestational age, not birth-weight centile.
- B. Correct. The 7th centile is below the 10th centile.
- C. Incorrect. Macrosomia is an absolute birth-weight concept and is not defined solely by being below the 10th centile.
- D. Incorrect. AGA is between the 10th and 90th centiles.
- E. Incorrect. LGA is above the 90th centile.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SGA: birth weight <10th centile for gestational age.
- AGA: 10th-90th centile.
- LGA: >90th centile.
- SGA and IUGR are related but not synonymous: SGA is a birth-weight classification, whereas IUGR describes failure to achieve genetic growth potential.

questions.stem: A newborn is above the 90th birth-weight centile for gestational age but weighs 4.1 kg. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The baby is AGA because the absolute weight is normal

options.label: B
options.text: The baby is SGA because the weight is below 4.5 kg

options.label: C
options.text: LGA and macrosomia are interchangeable terms

options.label: D
options.text: The baby is LGA because of the centile, even though the weight is below the lecture's 4.5-kg macrosomia threshold

options.label: E
options.text: The baby is post-term because the weight is high

questions.correctAnswerText: The baby is LGA because of the centile, even though the weight is below the lecture's 4.5-kg macrosomia threshold
questions.initialExplanation: LGA is defined relative to gestational age (>90th centile), while macrosomia is an absolute birth-weight threshold (>4.5 kg). They are not interchangeable.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. AGA is based on centiles, not the absolute weight alone.
- B. Incorrect. SGA is below the 10th centile, not below a fixed weight.
- C. Incorrect. LGA is centile-based; macrosomia is absolute-weight based.
- D. Correct. A baby can be LGA without exceeding 4.5 kg.
- E. Incorrect. Post-term classification depends on gestational age.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Interpret birth weight using gestational-age centiles.
- LGA: >90th centile.
- standard guidance separately describes macrosomia as birth weight >4.5 kg.
- Do not confuse LGA, macrosomia, SGA and IUGR.

cases.title: A regional unit reviews its monthly mortality data and a mother worries about her baby's weight

questions.stem: A regional hospital reviews one month of data: (1) a fetus delivered at 26 weeks' gestation with no signs of life; (2) a live-born term infant who died on day 5; (3) a live-born preterm infant who died on day 20; (4) a fetal loss at 20 weeks' gestation with no signs of life. Which statement correctly assigns these events to the mortality rates?

options.label: A
options.text: Events 1, 2 and 3 are most included in the perinatal mortality rate

options.label: B
options.text: Event 4 is a stillbirth because the fetus showed no signs of life

options.label: C
options.text: Event 1 is a neonatal death because the baby not usually breathed

options.label: D
options.text: Perinatal mortality includes events 1 and 2; neonatal mortality includes events 2 and 3

options.label: E
options.text: Perinatal mortality includes events 2 and 3; neonatal mortality includes events 1 and 2

questions.correctAnswerText: Perinatal mortality includes events 1 and 2; neonatal mortality includes events 2 and 3
questions.initialExplanation: The perinatal mortality rate counts stillbirths plus deaths in the first week of life. The neonatal mortality rate counts deaths of live-born infants within the first 4 weeks. Stillbirth is defined as an infant born with no signs of life at 24 weeks or more.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Event 3 died on day 20, after the first week, so it is not a perinatal death.
- B. Incorrect. A stillbirth requires gestation of 24 weeks or more; a loss at 20 weeks does not qualify.
- C. Incorrect. A neonatal death requires a live-born infant. Event 1 is a stillbirth.
- D. Correct. Event 1 is a stillbirth, so it counts only in perinatal mortality. Event 2 died within the first week of a live birth, so it counts in both rates. Event 3 is a late neonatal death, so it counts only in neonatal mortality. Event 4 counts in neither.
- E. Incorrect. This reverses the logic: the stillbirth cannot be a neonatal death, and a day-20 death is not perinatal.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stillbirth: no signs of life at ≥24 weeks.
- Perinatal mortality = stillbirths + deaths in the first 7 days, per 1,000 live births and stillbirths.
- Neonatal mortality = deaths of live-born infants within 28 days, per 1,000 live births.
- Early neonatal period: birth to day 7. Late neonatal period: day 7 to day 28.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 4 (Introduction: mortality definitions, stillbirth).

topics.name: Routine Newborn Examination and Normal Findings

cases.title: A term newborn undergoes the first head-to-toe examination
cases.vignette: A healthy term newborn is examined shortly after delivery. The clinician measures the occipitofrontal circumference, assesses the fontanelles and sutures, checks the eyes and mouth, and distinguishes normal birth-related findings from abnormalities needing referral.

questions.stem: What is the approximate normal occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) of a term newborn?
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives a normal newborn OFC of approximately 35 ± 2 cm. Head circumference should be measured and plotted using an age- and sex-appropriate chart.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is above the approximate normal range.
- B. Incorrect. This is markedly above the expected term-newborn OFC.
- C. Incorrect. This is far below the expected term-newborn range.
- D. Incorrect. This is smaller than the approximate value given.
- E. Correct. Common examples include 35 ± 2 cm.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Term newborn OFC: about 35 ± 2 cm.
- Measure accurately and interpret with gestational age and growth charts.
- Abnormal head size or trajectory may suggest microcephaly, macrocephaly or a neurological condition.

questions.stem: Which statement about the fontanelles is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The anterior fontanel normally closes at birth

options.label: B
options.text: The posterior fontanel closes after the anterior fontanel

options.label: C
options.text: The anterior fontanel usually closes between 9 and 18 months, while the posterior fontanel closes by approximately 2 months

options.label: D
options.text: Both fontanelles normally close at 6 months

options.label: E
options.text: The posterior fontanel normally remains open until 18 months

questions.correctAnswerText: The anterior fontanel usually closes between 9 and 18 months, while the posterior fontanel closes by approximately 2 months
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that the anterior fontanel closes at approximately 9-18 months and the posterior fontanel from birth to 2 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The anterior fontanel is normally open at birth.
- B. Incorrect. The posterior fontanel closes before the anterior fontanel.
- C. Correct. This matches the timings.
- D. Incorrect. The two fontanelles do not normally close at the same time.
- E. Incorrect. The posterior fontanel usually closes much earlier.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Anterior fontanel: closes around 9-18 months.
- Posterior fontanel: closes by about 2 months.
- Assess fontanelle size and tension in the context of hydration, intracranial pressure and growth.
- Cranial sutures may overlap at birth due to moulding.

questions.stem: A newborn has a diffuse, soft scalp swelling over the presenting part immediately after delivery. It crosses suture lines and is already visible at birth. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Caput succedaneum
questions.initialExplanation: Caput succedaneum is a diffuse subcutaneous fluid swelling over the presenting part. It is present immediately after birth and can cross suture lines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Immediate onset, soft consistency and crossing sutures are typical of caput succedaneum.
- B. Incorrect. Cephalohaematoma is a subperiosteal blood collection that does not cross suture lines and often appears hours after birth.
- C. Incorrect. Subgaleal haemorrhage is a deeper, diffuse blood collection that may cause severe blood loss and shock.
- D. Incorrect. Hydrocephalus causes abnormal ventricular enlargement and progressive head enlargement, not a localized scalp swelling.
- E. Incorrect. Craniosynostosis is premature fusion of cranial sutures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Caput succedaneum: subcutaneous oedema, immediate, crosses sutures, usually resolves in days.
- Cephalohaematoma: subperiosteal blood, appears after hours, does not cross sutures, resolves over weeks.
- Subgaleal haemorrhage can cause major blood loss and requires urgent assessment.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 4; birth injury comparison - Page 40.

questions.stem: Which screening examination should be performed in every newborn to detect conditions such as congenital cataract?

options.label: C
options.text: Fundoscopy after pupil dilation in each newborn

questions.correctAnswerText: Red reflex examination
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes checking the red reflex in all newborns. An absent or abnormal red reflex requires ophthalmology assessment because it may indicate congenital cataract or another significant ocular abnormality.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A newborn cannot perform a conventional visual acuity chart.
- B. Incorrect. A cover test does not replace red reflex screening.
- C. Incorrect. Routine dilated fundoscopy in every newborn is not the specific screening test named.
- D. Correct. Red reflex screening can identify media opacity and congenital cataract.
- E. Incorrect. Tonometry measures intraocular pressure and is not the routine screening described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Perform red reflex screening in all newborns.
- Absent/asymmetric/abnormal red reflex → urgent ophthalmology review.
- standard guidance also notes that pupillary light reflex is present at birth and that newborns do not usually produce tears at birth.

cases.title: A baby becomes cyanosed during feeding but improves when crying
cases.vignette: A term newborn develops respiratory distress and cyanosis during feeding and when calm. The infant improves when crying. A nasogastric tube cannot be passed through either nostril.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bilateral choanal atresia
questions.initialExplanation: Newborns are obligate nasal breathers. Bilateral choanal atresia can cause immediate respiratory distress and cyanosis during quiet breathing or feeding, with improvement when the baby cries and breathes through the mouth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Unilateral choanal atresia often presents later and may be less symptomatic.
- B. Incorrect. Laryngomalacia causes inspiratory stridor, typically worse with feeding or supine positioning, but does not prevent passage of an NGT through the nose.
- C. Incorrect. Tracheoesophageal fistula may cause choking/cyanosis with feeds but does not produce bilateral nasal obstruction.
- D. Correct. Bilateral obstruction produces the classic cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying.
- E. Incorrect. CDH causes severe respiratory distress with a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the chest.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bilateral choanal atresia: respiratory distress/cyanosis when calm or feeding, improves with crying.
- Inability to pass a nasal catheter/NGT is an important clue.
- Confirm with CT and arrange urgent ENT/surgical management.
- Clinical guidance notes an association with CHARGE syndrome.

questions.stem: Which congenital association is particularly linked to choanal atresia?
questions.correctAnswerText: CHARGE association
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that approximately 60% of choanal atresia cases are associated with other congenital malformations, particularly CHARGE.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. CHARGE includes coloboma, heart defect, choanal atresia, growth/developmental delay, genital abnormalities and ear deformity.
- B. Incorrect. VACTERL describes vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal and limb anomalies.
- C. Incorrect. CATCH-22 is associated with DiGeorge syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. Pierre Robin sequence includes micrognathia, glossoptosis and airway obstruction, but is not the named association.
- E. Incorrect. TORCH refers to congenital infections.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CHARGE: Coloboma, Heart defect, choanal Atresia, Retarded growth/development, Genital abnormalities, Ear deformity.
- Bilateral choanal atresia is an airway emergency.
- Unilateral disease may be detected later.

cases.title: A healthy newborn has several skin and hormonal-withdrawal findings
cases.vignette: A term newborn has small white papules on the nose, a transient pustular rash on an erythematous base, blue-gray macules over the lumbosacral region and mild breast enlargement. The infant is otherwise well and feeding normally.

questions.stem: White papules over the nose and cheeks caused by obstruction of sebaceous glands are called:
questions.correctAnswerText: Milia
questions.initialExplanation: Milia are small white papules caused by retention cysts from obstructed sebaceous glands. They commonly occur on the nose and cheeks and resolve spontaneously.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Milia are white sebaceous retention cysts.
- B. Incorrect. Transient neonatal pustular melanosis heals with brown pigmented macules.
- C. Incorrect. Miliaria is due to sweat-gland obstruction, often following thermal stress or over-wrapping.
- D. Incorrect. Erythema toxicum is a pustular rash on an erythematous base.
- E. Incorrect. Cutis marmorata is a reticular vascular pattern that appears when the baby is cooled.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Milia: white papules, blocked sebaceous glands, spontaneous resolution.
- Miliaria: blocked sweat ducts, associated with heat/over-wrapping.
- Most benign neonatal skin lesions do not require treatment.

questions.stem: A well term newborn develops pustules on an erythematous base over the trunk and face at 2-3 days of age. The fluid contains eosinophils. What is the diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Erythema toxicum neonatorum
questions.initialExplanation: Erythema toxicum is common in term newborns. It usually appears at 2-3 days with pustules on an erythematous base; pustular fluid contains eosinophils and the rash resolves spontaneously.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The timing, appearance and eosinophils identify erythema toxicum.
- B. Incorrect. Congenital syphilis may cause a systemic illness and characteristic rash, not this typical benign eruption.
- C. Incorrect. Neonatal HSV may produce vesicular lesions and systemic disease; it is not a benign eosinophilic pustular eruption.
- D. Incorrect. Miliaria consists of sweat-related papules/vesicles, often after heat exposure.
- E. Incorrect. Transient neonatal pustular melanosis is characterized by pustules that heal with residual brown macules; smears typically show neutrophils.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Erythema toxicum: common in term infants, onset day 2-3, pustules on erythematous base, eosinophils, self-limited.
- Transient neonatal pustular melanosis: neutrophils and residual hyperpigmented macules.
- A well-appearing infant with classic erythema toxicum needs reassurance, not antibiotics.

questions.stem: Blue-gray, ill-defined macules over the lumbosacral area and buttocks are most consistent with:
questions.correctAnswerText: Congenital dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots)
questions.initialExplanation: Congenital dermal melanocytosis presents as blue-gray macular discoloration, most commonly over the lumbosacral region and buttocks. It is more common in darker-skinned infants and usually fades over months to years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Infantile haemangiomas are vascular tumours that commonly appear during the first month and later regress.
- B. Correct. This is the typical site and appearance of congenital dermal melanocytosis.
- C. Incorrect. Cutis marmorata is a reticular mottled vascular pattern provoked by cooling.
- D. Incorrect. Port-wine stains are vascular malformations present from birth and usually persist/grow with the child.
- E. Incorrect. Salmon patches are pink vascular macules, often on the eyelids, glabella or nape.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mongolian spots = congenital dermal melanocytosis.
- Document location and appearance to distinguish from bruising or inflicted injury.
- Most fade over the first months to years.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a port-wine stain from an infantile haemangioma?

options.label: A
options.text: Both are typically absent at birth and regress completely

options.label: B
options.text: Infantile haemangioma not usually grows after birth

options.label: C
options.text: Port-wine stain is caused by sebaceous obstruction; haemangioma is caused by sweat-duct obstruction

options.label: D
options.text: Port-wine stain typically disappears by the end of the first year

options.label: E
options.text: Port-wine stain is a vascular malformation present at birth; infantile haemangioma often appears during the first month and later regresses

questions.correctAnswerText: Port-wine stain is a vascular malformation present at birth; infantile haemangioma often appears during the first month and later regresses
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance differentiates a port-wine stain (naevus flammeus), present from birth and growing with the child, from an infantile haemangioma, which often appears during the first month, proliferates and later involutes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Port-wine stains are present at birth and usually persist.
- B. Incorrect. Infantile haemangiomas typically proliferate during infancy before regression.
- C. Incorrect. Those mechanisms describe milia and miliaria, not vascular lesions.
- D. Incorrect. Port-wine stains generally do not disappear spontaneously.
- E. Correct. This is the defining distinction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Port-wine stain: congenital vascular malformation; may be associated with Sturge-Weber or Klippel-Trenaunay syndromes.
- Infantile haemangioma: often appears in the first month, grows then regresses; treatment is considered when large or function-threatening (e.g. airway/vision).
- Common examples include oral propranolol for selected problematic infantile haemangiomas.

questions.stem: A newborn has breast enlargement and a small amount of milk discharge during the first week. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.label: C
options.text: Arrange urgent surgical drainage in typical presentations

options.label: D
options.text: Reassure the parents and avoid squeezing because this may lead to mastitis or abscess

options.label: E
options.text: Squeeze the breast to empty the milk

questions.correctAnswerText: Reassure the parents and avoid squeezing because this may lead to mastitis or abscess
questions.initialExplanation: Neonatal breast enlargement and occasional “witch's milk” occur due to withdrawal of maternal hormones. It usually resolves spontaneously within weeks; squeezing should be avoided.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not indicated in uncomplicated physiological neonatal breast enlargement.
- B. Incorrect. Hormonal therapy is not indicated.
- C. Incorrect. Surgery is not required in a normal hormonal-withdrawal response.
- D. Correct. Reassurance and avoidance of manipulation are recommended.
- E. Incorrect. Squeezing may cause mastitis or breast abscess.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal gynaecomastia can occur in both sexes.
- “Witch's milk” may occur due to maternal hormone withdrawal.
- Do not squeeze the breast.
- Vaginal mucoid discharge, small vaginal bleeding and neonatal acne may also occur as transient hormonal-withdrawal effects.

cases.title: A newborn has an abnormal umbilical cord finding and routine examination
cases.vignette: A term newborn is examined in the nursery. The umbilical stump is dry, the liver edge is palpable just below the costal margin, and the clinician examines the cord vessels, abdominal wall, genitalia and passage of meconium. The parents ask about normal heart and respiratory rates.

questions.stem: How many vessels are normally present in the umbilical cord?
questions.correctAnswerText: Two arteries and one vein
questions.initialExplanation: A normal umbilical cord contains two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein. A single umbilical artery may be associated with congenital renal anomalies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. There is normally one vein, not two.
- B. Incorrect. This reverses the usual number of veins and arteries.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the normal vessel arrangement.
- D. Correct. The normal cord has two arteries and one vein.
- E. Incorrect. Three arteries are not normal.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal cord: 2 arteries + 1 vein.
- Single umbilical artery should prompt assessment for associated anomalies, especially renal abnormalities.
- Inspect the cord and stump during the newborn examination.

questions.stem: A dry umbilical stump separates spontaneously on day 8 of life. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The stump should typically be surgically removed on day 2

options.label: B
options.text: This is within the expected period described in the lecture

options.label: C
options.text: This is evidence of congenital immunodeficiency

options.label: D
options.text: The umbilical stump normally separates after 6 weeks

questions.correctAnswerText: This is within the expected period described in the lecture
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that the umbilical stump usually dries and separates between 7 and 10 days of age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Routine surgical removal is not required.
- B. Correct. Day 8 is within the expected 7-10-day period.
- C. Incorrect. Normal separation does not indicate immunodeficiency.
- D. Incorrect. Clinical descriptions include separation within the first 1-2 weeks, not after 6 weeks.
- E. Incorrect. Omphalitis is suggested by erythema, swelling, purulent discharge or systemic illness, not normal separation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Umbilical stump normally separates around 7-10 days.
- Umbilical hernia is common and usually resolves spontaneously within the first 2-3 years.
- A large or abnormal umbilical lesion with infection signs requires assessment.

questions.stem: A newborn has a liver edge palpable 1.5 cm below the right costal margin. In an otherwise healthy newborn, this finding is:

options.label: A
options.text: A normal finding described in the lecture

questions.correctAnswerText: A normal finding described in the lecture
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that the liver may normally be palpable approximately 1-2 cm below the costal margin in a newborn.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the normal range described.
- B. Incorrect. Heart failure may cause hepatomegaly but cannot be diagnosed from this isolated finding.
- C. Incorrect. Mild palpable liver edge can be normal in a newborn.
- D. Incorrect. Biliary atresia is associated with persistent jaundice, pale stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly, not an isolated normal liver edge.
- E. Incorrect. Sepsis requires clinical and laboratory assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- A newborn liver edge may be palpable 1-2 cm below the costal margin.
- Interpret hepatomegaly with jaundice, feeding, perfusion, respiratory status and other findings.
- The abdominal examination should include umbilicus, liver, spleen, bladder and genitalia.

questions.stem: What is the normal respiratory rate of a term newborn?
questions.correctAnswerText: 40-60 breaths/min
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives the normal respiratory rate as 40-60 breaths per minute. A rate above 60 breaths/min is tachypnoea in the respiratory distress section.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is below the usual range given.
- B. Incorrect. This is markedly below the expected neonatal range.
- C. Incorrect. This is lower than the stated normal range.
- D. Incorrect. Persistent rates above 60 breaths/min are tachypnoea and require assessment.
- E. Correct. Normal newborn RR is 40-60 breaths/min.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal neonatal RR: 40-60/min.
- Normal neonatal HR: 120-160/min.
- Newborn breathing is mainly abdominal and newborns are obligate nasal breathers.
- Periodic breathing may occur; persistent apnoea, grunting, recession or cyanosis is not normal.

questions.stem: A term newborn has a heart rate of 145/min, blood pressure of 70/50 mmHg and an apex beat in the fourth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: The apex beat is normally in the sixth intercostal space

options.label: B
options.text: The heart rate indicates severe bradycardia

options.label: C
options.text: The blood pressure indicates severe hypertension

options.label: D
options.text: These findings establish congenital heart disease

options.label: E
options.text: the three findings are within the normal values given in the lecture

questions.correctAnswerText: the three findings are within the normal values given in the lecture
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include a normal newborn heart rate of 120-160/min, a term newborn BP of approximately 70/50 mmHg and the apex beat at the fourth intercostal space, midclavicular line.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. standard guidance places the apex in the fourth intercostal space.
- B. Incorrect. A heart rate of 145/min is within the expected range.
- C. Incorrect. 70/50 mmHg is the normal term newborn value listed.
- D. Incorrect. These normal findings do not establish congenital heart disease.
- E. Correct. The stated values are consistent with the source's normal newborn findings.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Term newborn HR: 120-160/min.
- BP: approximately 70/50 mmHg.
- Apex beat: fourth intercostal space, midclavicular line.
- Normal term blood volume: about 85-90 mL/kg.

cases.title: A newborn undergoes a complete screening examination before discharge
cases.vignette: A well newborn is examined before discharge. The clinician checks the red reflex, nasal patency, palate, femoral pulses, pre- and post-ductal oxygen saturation, hip stability, anus, spine and hearing. The purpose is to identify clinically silent but potentially important congenital abnormalities.

questions.stem: Which bedside test is used in routine newborn screening to detect critical congenital heart disease?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pulse oximetry
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance includes pulse oximetry screening as part of the cardiovascular newborn examination to identify critical congenital heart disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Blood glucose screens for hypoglycaemia in at-risk infants.
- B. Correct. Pulse oximetry assesses oxygen saturation and helps screen for critical CHD.
- C. Incorrect. The New Ballard score estimates gestational age.
- D. Incorrect. Bilirubin testing assesses jaundice.
- E. Incorrect. Urine ketones are not the routine CHD screen.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Routine newborn checks include pulse oximetry screening for critical CHD.
- Palpate femoral pulses to help detect coarctation of the aorta.
- Examine for murmurs, perfusion, cyanosis and signs of heart failure.

questions.stem: Weak or absent femoral pulses in a newborn should raise suspicion of:
questions.correctAnswerText: Coarctation of the aorta
questions.initialExplanation: Femoral pulse palpation is part of routine newborn screening for coarctation of the aorta. Weak femoral pulses may indicate impaired blood flow to the lower body.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Coarctation can reduce or delay femoral pulses.
- B. Incorrect. TOF causes cyanosis but is not specifically detected by weak femoral pulses.
- C. Incorrect. PDA may cause bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure, not weak femoral pulses as the key screening sign.
- D. Incorrect. Jaundice does not cause absent femoral pulses.
- E. Incorrect. TTN is a respiratory condition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Palpate brachial and femoral pulses during newborn examination.
- Weak/delayed femoral pulses suggest coarctation.
- Pulse oximetry and careful cardiovascular examination are complementary screening methods.

questions.stem: A newborn has an imperforate anus, abnormal spinal midline findings and weak femoral pulses. Which statement best describes the purpose of the routine newborn examination?

options.label: B
options.text: It is unnecessary if the Apgar score is normal

options.label: C
options.text: Screen for silent congenital abnormalities, including anorectal, neural tube, cardiac and hip defects

options.label: D
options.text: It is performed when the infant becomes symptomatic

options.label: E
options.text: It is limited to recording weight and temperature

questions.correctAnswerText: Screen for silent congenital abnormalities, including anorectal, neural tube, cardiac and hip defects
questions.initialExplanation: The routine newborn examination is designed to detect structural abnormalities and signs of disease before symptoms become apparent. Common examples include examination of the anus, back/spine, femoral pulses and hips among the screening components.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Newborn examination complements, rather than replaces, antenatal screening.
- B. Incorrect. A normal Apgar score does not exclude congenital malformations.
- C. Correct. It aims to detect important congenital abnormalities, including imperforate anus, neural tube defects, coarctation and DDH.
- D. Incorrect. Routine examination is performed even in apparently healthy newborns.
- E. Incorrect. The examination is much broader than basic observations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Routine screening includes eyes/red reflex, nose/NGT if choanal atresia suspected, mouth/palate, hearing, pulse oximetry, umbilical cord, genitalia, femoral pulses, hips, anus and spine.
- A normal Apgar score does not exclude structural abnormalities.
- Document any abnormal finding and arrange targeted investigations.

cases.title: A newborn attends the routine blood-spot screening programme
cases.vignette: A well 5-day-old newborn has established feeding. A heel-prick blood sample is taken for the newborn blood-spot screening programme. The parents ask why the test is performed when the baby looks healthy.

questions.stem: When is the heel-prick blood-spot screening sample usually collected?

options.label: B
options.text: Around day 5, once feeding is established

questions.correctAnswerText: Around day 5, once feeding is established
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include taking a heel-prick sample around day 5, after feeding has been established; the screening window is given as approximately day 2-8.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Six weeks is too late for the newborn blood-spot programme.
- B. Correct. Day 5 is the standard timing stated.
- C. Incorrect. The source describes sampling after feeding is established, not immediately at birth.
- D. Incorrect. Six months is too late.
- E. Incorrect. Day 1 is earlier than the usual timing described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Newborn blood-spot screening (historically Guthrie test): heel-prick sample.
- standard guidance places routine collection around day 5, within a day 2-8 window.
- Screening aims to identify conditions for which early treatment improves outcomes.

questions.stem: Which disorder is included in the newborn blood-spot screening list?
questions.correctAnswerText: Phenylketonuria
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include congenital hypothyroidism, sickle cell/thalassaemia, cystic fibrosis, phenylketonuria, MCAD deficiency, maple syrup urine disease, isovaleric acidaemia, glutaric aciduria and homocystinuria among screening conditions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. CDH is generally detected antenatally or on postnatal examination/imaging.
- B. Incorrect. Appendicitis is not a neonatal screening disorder.
- C. Correct. Phenylketonuria is included in the blood-spot screening panel.
- D. Incorrect. PDA is assessed clinically and by echocardiography, not newborn blood-spot screening.
- E. Incorrect. DDH is screened by physical examination and ultrasound when indicated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Blood-spot screening includes metabolic and endocrine disorders.
- Conditions listed include PKU, MCAD, MSUD, isovaleric acidaemia, glutaric aciduria and homocystinuria.
- Other newborn screens include hearing, pulse oximetry and clinical examination.

cases.title: A regional unit reviews its monthly mortality data and a mother worries about her baby's weight

questions.stem: A term boy weighs 3.4 kg at birth and 3.1 kg on day 4. He breastfeeds well, passes urine and stool normally and looks well. His mother is worried. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A 9% loss exceeds the physiological limit, so supplementation and admission are needed

options.label: B
options.text: The loss is physiological; he should regain birth weight by about 10 days and then gain roughly 25-30 g/day

options.label: C
options.text: Birth weight should already have been regained by day 3, so this is abnormal

options.label: D
options.text: After regaining birth weight, the expected gain is about 10 g/day

options.label: E
options.text: Any weight loss in a term baby means dehydration and needs IV fluids

questions.correctAnswerText: The loss is physiological; he should regain birth weight by about 10 days and then gain roughly 25-30 g/day
questions.initialExplanation: The loss is 300 g out of 3,400 g, about 8.8%. Clinical descriptions include physiological weight loss of up to about 10% of birth weight in the first 3-5 days, with recovery by about 10 days of age, then a gain of 25-30 g/day.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. 8.8% is within the physiological limit, and a well-feeding baby needs no admission.
- B. Correct. The loss is within the expected range, and the recovery time and later gain match standard guidance.
- C. Incorrect. Recovery is expected by about day 10, not day 3.
- D. Incorrect. 25-30 g/day is the expected gain; 10 g/day would be poor.
- E. Incorrect. A well baby with normal urine output and feeding is not dehydrated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Physiological weight loss: up to ~10% in the first 3-5 days; birth weight regained by ~10 days.
- Normal weight gain afterwards: 25-30 g/day.
- Weight loss with poor feeding, reduced urine output or jaundice needs assessment.
- Normal term birth length is about 50 cm.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 7 (normal term newborn: weight and growth).

cases.title: Eye, mouth and neck findings during the first examination

questions.stem: Baby 1 was born after a precipitate delivery and has a flat bright-red patch on the white of one eye, with no discharge. Baby 2 is 36 hours old and has red eyes with a purulent discharge. Which management is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both are normal transient findings and need reassurance

options.label: B
options.text: Baby 1 needs urgent ophthalmology review for cataract; Baby 2 needs reassurance

options.label: C
options.text: Baby 1 needs antibiotics; Baby 2 will resolve spontaneously within weeks

options.label: D
options.text: Both need urgent treatment because both represent gonococcal infection

options.label: E
options.text: Baby 1 needs reassurance because it is harmless and resolves in weeks; Baby 2 needs immediate treatment because gonococcal infection is possible

questions.correctAnswerText: Baby 1 needs reassurance because it is harmless and resolves in weeks; Baby 2 needs immediate treatment because gonococcal infection is possible
questions.initialExplanation: Subconjunctival haemorrhage can follow precipitate delivery and is harmless, resolving within weeks. Red eyes with discharge in the first 48 hours (ophthalmia neonatorum) may be gonococcal and need immediate treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The first finding is benign, but the second is not normal and must not be reassured.
- B. Incorrect. A red scleral patch is not a red reflex problem. The absent red reflex is the cataract screening sign.
- C. Incorrect. This reverses the two babies' needs.
- D. Incorrect. A haemorrhage without discharge is not infection.
- E. Correct. Differentiating the benign bleed from a purulent conjunctivitis within 48 hours is the point of the case.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Subconjunctival haemorrhage: due to precipitate delivery, harmless, resolves within weeks.
- Ophthalmia neonatorum (red eyes + discharge) in the first 48 hours: may be gonococcal; immediate treatment.
- Absent red reflex: ophthalmology consultation (congenital cataract).
- Newborns have a pupillary light reflex but no tears at birth.

questions.stem: A term newborn has small white cysts on the palate and gum margins and a bluish translucent swelling in the floor of the mouth. The baby feeds well. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: These are benign self-resolving lesions, but the palate should still be palpated to screen for cleft palate

options.label: B
options.text: The white cysts are early teeth and must be removed to prevent aspiration

options.label: C
options.text: The floor-of-mouth swelling needs urgent ENT surgery because it causes airway obstruction

options.label: D
options.text: White oral lesions are candidiasis and need antifungal treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: These are benign self-resolving lesions, but the palate should still be palpated to screen for cleft palate
questions.initialExplanation: Epstein's pearls (palate/gum cysts), Bohn's nodules (mucous gland cysts) and ranula (mucous retention cyst in the floor of the mouth) are self-resolving. Every newborn still needs palpation of the palate to screen for cleft palate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Describes the lesions correctly and keeps the cleft palate screening step.
- B. Incorrect. Natal teeth are teeth, usually lower incisors; loose ones are removed. Epstein's pearls are cysts.
- C. Incorrect. A ranula is a self-resolving mucous retention cyst, not an emergency in a well-feeding baby.
- D. Incorrect. Candidiasis is not part of the described findings; cysts are not plaques.
- E. Incorrect. Bohn's nodules are mucous gland cysts with no thyroid link.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Epstein's pearls: palate/gum cysts. Bohn's nodules: mucous gland cysts. Ranula: floor-of-mouth mucous retention cyst. All self-resolve.
- Tongue-tie is also described in the examination.
- Screen all newborns for cleft palate by palpation.
- Natal teeth (front lower incisors): remove if loose, to avoid aspiration.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 5 (Examination: Mouth); Page 9 (natal teeth).

questions.stem: A newborn girl has a short neck with skin webbing. Another baby has a swelling in the anterior midline of the neck, and a third has a lateral neck swelling. Which classification matches standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Webbing occurs in Down and Edwards syndromes; the midline swelling is a sternomastoid tumour

options.label: B
options.text: Webbing occurs in Turner and Noonan syndromes; the midline swelling is a cystic hygroma and the lateral swelling is a thyroglossal cyst

options.label: C
options.text: Webbing occurs in Turner and Noonan syndromes; the midline swelling is a thyroid/thyroglossal cyst; lateral swellings include sternomastoid tumour, cystic hygroma and lymph nodes

options.label: D
options.text: Webbing indicates CHARGE association; most neck swellings are lymph nodes

options.label: E
options.text: A short neck is abnormal in newborns and typically needs imaging

questions.correctAnswerText: Webbing occurs in Turner and Noonan syndromes; the midline swelling is a thyroid/thyroglossal cyst; lateral swellings include sternomastoid tumour, cystic hygroma and lymph nodes
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance links neck webbing to Turner and Noonan syndromes. Central neck swellings are thyroid or thyroglossal in origin, while peripheral (lateral) swellings include sternomastoid tumour, cystic hygroma and lymph nodes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. standard guidance names Turner and Noonan, and a midline swelling is not a sternomastoid tumour.
- B. Incorrect. The locations of thyroglossal cyst and cystic hygroma are reversed.
- C. Correct. Matches webbing and the central versus peripheral division.
- D. Incorrect. CHARGE is linked to choanal atresia, not neck webbing.
- E. Incorrect. A short neck is the normal newborn neck.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal newborn neck is short.
- Webbed neck: Turner and Noonan syndromes.
- Central neck swelling: thyroid/thyroglossal cyst.
- Peripheral swelling: sternomastoid tumour, cystic hygroma, lymph node.

cases.title: Elimination, skin and midline findings in the nursery

questions.stem: A term boy has not passed urine for 30 hours. A distended, palpable bladder is felt above the pubis. Which diagnosis and next step are most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Renal agenesis; reassure and repeat examination in 24 hours

options.label: C
options.text: Normal variation; 95% pass urine within 24 hours so wait another day

options.label: D
options.text: Congenital hypothyroidism; send thyroid function tests

options.label: E
options.text: Renal outlet obstruction such as posterior urethral valves; prompt ultrasound of the renal tract

questions.correctAnswerText: Renal outlet obstruction such as posterior urethral valves; prompt ultrasound of the renal tract
questions.initialExplanation: A palpable, large bladder with absent urine suggests urinary outflow obstruction, particularly posterior urethral valves in boys. standard guidance advises prompt evaluation with ultrasound.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. In renal agenesis there is no urine to fill the bladder, so a large palpable bladder is not expected.
- B. Incorrect. Shock is on the differential of absent urine, but a distended bladder points to obstruction, and shock would show circulatory signs.
- C. Incorrect. Passage within 24 hours is expected; failure with a palpable bladder needs action, not waiting.
- D. Incorrect. Hypothyroidism is not the explanation for a distended bladder.
- E. Correct. Matches the palpable bladder, the male sex and standard guidance's recommended step.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ~95% of healthy term babies pass urine in the first 24 hours.
- DD of delayed urine: renal agenesis, renal outlet obstruction, shocked neonate.
- Palpable large bladder in a boy: think posterior urethral valves; urgent ultrasound.
- Posterior urethral valves are often diagnosed antenatally.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 7 (DD of delayed passage of urine); Page 9 (palpable large bladder).

questions.stem: A well term baby, examined in a cool room, has a lacy reddish-purple pattern over the trunk and limbs that fades once the baby is wrapped. There are also flat pink patches on the upper eyelids and nape that fade when the baby cries. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Mottled skin in a cooled baby typically indicates sepsis and needs cultures and antibiotics

options.label: B
options.text: The eyelid and nape patches are port-wine stains that grow with the child and need laser

options.label: C
options.text: The reticular pattern indicates Sturge-Weber syndrome

options.label: D
options.text: Cutis marmorata is cold-related mottling that improves during the first month; persistence is abnormal. Salmon patches are benign and fade in infancy

options.label: E
options.text: Both findings are variants of erythema toxicum and need an eosinophil smear

questions.correctAnswerText: Cutis marmorata is cold-related mottling that improves during the first month; persistence is abnormal. Salmon patches are benign and fade in infancy
questions.initialExplanation: Cutis marmorata is a reticular vascular pattern when the baby is cooled; it improves over the first month and is abnormal only if it persists. Salmon patches (nevus simplex) on the eyelids, glabella and nape fade over the first year.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mottling is non-specific. In a well baby it responds to warming, and sepsis is only one cause in the differential.
- B. Incorrect. Port-wine stains are fixed vascular malformations that grow with the child; salmon patches fade.
- C. Incorrect. Sturge-Weber is linked to a port-wine stain, not to cutis marmorata.
- D. Correct. Describes both lesions and their natural course.
- E. Incorrect. Erythema toxicum is a pustular rash on an erythematous base.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cutis marmorata: reticular pattern on cooling; improves in the first month; abnormal if persistent.
- Salmon patch (angel's kiss on the forehead/eyelids, stork bite on the nape): blanches, fades in the first year.
- Harlequin colour change and acrocyanosis in the first 24 hours are normal findings.
- Mottled skin in a sick baby has many causes (sepsis, cold stress, shock, Down syndrome, hypothyroidism).

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 8 (cutis marmorata, salmon patch); Page 9 (Harlequin colour change).

questions.stem: During the routine examination of a term newborn you find: milia on the nose, a loose tooth in the lower gum present since birth, a skin tag anterior to the ear, and a tuft of hair over the lumbosacral spine. What is the correct plan?

options.label: A
options.text: Evaluate the hair tuft for an underlying spinal abnormality, remove the loose tooth to avoid aspiration, and refer the skin tag to a plastic surgeon

options.label: B
options.text: Reassure about most four findings; the tooth will fall out on its own

options.label: C
options.text: Remove the milia surgically and ignore the hair tuft

options.label: D
options.text: The hair tuft needs no investigation, but the tooth must be preserved

options.label: E
options.text: Request MRI of the brain because of the skin tag

questions.correctAnswerText: Evaluate the hair tuft for an underlying spinal abnormality, remove the loose tooth to avoid aspiration, and refer the skin tag to a plastic surgeon
questions.initialExplanation: A midline tuft of hair, swelling or naevus over the spine or skull may indicate an underlying vertebral, spinal cord or brain abnormality and needs evaluation. Loose natal teeth are removed to avoid aspiration, and ear skin tags are removed by a plastic surgeon.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Matches standard guidance for all three significant findings; milia need nothing.
- B. Incorrect. A loose natal tooth is an aspiration risk, and the hair tuft needs evaluation.
- C. Incorrect. Milia self-resolve, and a hair tuft is the one that needs attention.
- D. Incorrect. Loose teeth should be removed.
- E. Incorrect. A preauricular tag is a cosmetic finding for plastic surgery, not an indication for brain MRI.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Midline abnormality over spine/skull (hair tuft, swelling, naevus): further evaluation.
- Natal teeth: remove if loose (aspiration risk).
- Extra digits, skin tags anterior to the ear, accessory auricles: plastic surgeon.
- Heart murmurs in the first days are often transient, but some reflect congenital heart disease.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 9 (significant abnormalities on routine examination).

cases.title: Routine care after a good Apgar score, temperature control and resuscitation drugs

questions.stem: A term baby is born vaginally, cries immediately, is pink, has a heart rate of 140/min and flexes actively. The Apgar scores are 9 at 1 minute and 10 at 5 minutes. Which plan is appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Begin the Newborn Life Support sequence because it applies to each delivery

options.label: B
options.text: Admit to the NICU for observation because the 1-minute score is below 10

options.label: C
options.text: Keep warm, breastfeed, give vitamin K/eye prophylaxis and arrange hearing and blood-spot screening

options.label: D
options.text: Delay vitamin K until there is bleeding

options.label: E
options.text: Give oral glucose and withhold feeding for 6 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep warm, breastfeed, give vitamin K/eye prophylaxis and arrange hearing and blood-spot screening
questions.initialExplanation: An Apgar of 8-10 indicates good general condition. standard guidance's plan is to keep the baby warm and start breastfeeding, with routine newborn care: vitamin K IM, prophylactic eye erythromycin, umbilical cord care, hearing test and newborn screening.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The resuscitation sequence is used when Apgar is below 7 or breathing/heart rate are inadequate.
- B. Incorrect. A score of 9 is within the good range; admission is not needed.
- C. Correct. Matches standard guidance's action plan for a score of 8-10.
- D. Incorrect. Vitamin K is given prophylactically at birth to prevent haemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
- E. Incorrect. Early breastfeeding is encouraged.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Apgar 8-10: good condition; keep warm and start breastfeeding.
- Routine newborn care: vitamin K IM, eye prophylaxis (erythromycin), cord care, hearing test, newborn screening.
- Apgar <7: follow the Newborn Life Support sequence.
- 1-minute score guides resuscitation need; 5-minute score shows response.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 11 (Apgar action plan and newborn care).

cases.title: A newborn is apnoeic immediately after delivery
cases.vignette: A term infant is delivered after an uncomplicated labour. After birth, the baby is floppy and gasping. The team places the baby under a radiant warmer, dries the infant and assesses breathing and heart rate. The neonatal team follows the Newborn Life Support sequence rather than waiting for the Apgar score.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the 1-minute Apgar score?

options.label: A
options.text: To determine whether the infant has congenital heart disease

options.label: B
options.text: To assess the newborn's immediate condition and indicate the need or method of resuscitation

options.label: C
options.text: To diagnose the cause of neonatal encephalopathy

options.label: D
options.text: To predict long-term neurological outcome with certainty

questions.correctAnswerText: To assess the newborn's immediate condition and indicate the need or method of resuscitation
questions.initialExplanation: The 1-minute Apgar score gives an indication of the baby's immediate condition and the need or method of resuscitation. The 5-minute score helps assess the response to resuscitation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Congenital heart disease requires clinical assessment and investigations such as pulse oximetry and echocardiography.
- B. Correct. This is the purpose described.
- C. Incorrect. Apgar does not identify the underlying cause of encephalopathy.
- D. Incorrect. Apgar alone cannot reliably predict an individual infant's long-term neurological outcome.
- E. Incorrect. Gestational age is assessed using menstrual/ultrasound dating or a maturity score such as New Ballard.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Apgar is recorded at 1 and 5 minutes; repeat every 5 minutes while resuscitation continues when indicated.
- 1-minute score: immediate status/resuscitation need.
- 5-minute score: response to resuscitation.
- Do not delay resuscitation to calculate Apgar.

questions.stem: Which five components are assessed in the Apgar score?

options.label: A
options.text: Heart rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, temperature and weight

options.label: B
options.text: Airway, blood pressure, glucose, activity and reflexes

options.label: C
options.text: Colour, temperature, feeding, urine and stool

options.label: D
options.text: Appearance, pulse, grimace, activity and respiration

options.label: E
options.text: Tone, gestational age, head circumference, length and weight

questions.correctAnswerText: Appearance, pulse, grimace, activity and respiration
questions.initialExplanation: The Apgar score assesses Appearance (colour), Pulse (heart rate), Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (muscle tone) and Respiration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Oxygen saturation and blood pressure are not Apgar components.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the Apgar mnemonic.
- C. Incorrect. Feeding, urine and stool are part of newborn assessment, not Apgar.
- D. Correct. These are the five Apgar components.
- E. Incorrect. These are anthropometric and maturity measures, not Apgar items.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- APGAR = Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration.
- Each component is scored 0, 1 or 2.
- Apgar assesses condition; it does not replace clinical assessment of breathing and heart rate during resuscitation.

questions.stem: Which newborn requires a skilled resuscitation team to be present at delivery 's high-risk list?

options.label: B
options.text: An uncomplicated term infant after a normal vaginal delivery

options.label: C
options.text: A term infant with normal fetal activity and clear liquor

options.label: D
options.text: A well term infant with normal antenatal scans and no maternal risk factors

options.label: E
options.text: A term infant delivered after an uncomplicated labour with no risk factors

questions.correctAnswerText: A 30-week preterm infant
questions.initialExplanation: Prematurity is a major indication for a skilled neonatal team at delivery. Other high-risk situations listed include caesarean delivery, meconium-stained liquor, maternal diabetes, reduced fetal movements, known congenital malformation and multiple pregnancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A 30-week infant is very preterm and requires an appropriately skilled neonatal team.
- B. Incorrect. This describes a low-risk delivery if no other concerns exist.
- C. Incorrect. These are reassuring features.
- D. Incorrect. No high-risk feature is described.
- E. Incorrect. There is no stated risk factor in this scenario.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Anticipate resuscitation in preterm births and other high-risk deliveries.
- Review antenatal history, prepare equipment and brief the team before birth.
- Risk factors also include meconium, maternal diabetes, fetal compromise, multiple gestation and congenital anomalies.

questions.stem: A newborn is gasping and has ineffective breathing immediately after birth. What is the next key step after warming, drying and opening the airway?

options.label: A
options.text: Obtain a chest radiograph before ventilation

options.label: C
options.text: Give five inflation breaths and assess for chest movement and heart-rate response

options.label: E
options.text: Start chest compressions immediately in each apnoeic baby

questions.correctAnswerText: Give five inflation breaths and assess for chest movement and heart-rate response
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance's Newborn Life Support algorithm emphasizes effective lung inflation. If the baby is gasping or not breathing, open the airway and give five inflation breaths, then assess chest movement and heart-rate response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Imaging must not delay ventilation.
- B. Incorrect. Resuscitation must not be delayed for an Apgar score.
- C. Correct. Effective lung inflation is the key initial intervention for an apnoeic or gasping newborn.
- D. Incorrect. Oral glucose does not treat apnoea at birth.
- E. Incorrect. Chest compressions are considered only if the heart rate remains below 60/min after effective ventilation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Initial steps: dry, maintain temperature, position airway, assess breathing and heart rate.
- If apnoeic/gasping: open airway and give five inflation breaths.
- Reassess chest movement and heart rate.
- Effective ventilation is the central priority in neonatal resuscitation.

questions.stem: A newborn does not show chest movement during mask inflation breaths. Which action should be taken first?

options.label: E
options.text: Recheck head position and airway patency, then optimize mask seal and ventilation technique

questions.correctAnswerText: Recheck head position and airway patency, then optimize mask seal and ventilation technique
questions.initialExplanation: The PDF algorithm emphasizes correcting airway position and ventilation technique when chest movement is absent. Options include neutral head position, two-person airway control, jaw thrust, checking mask size/seal and considering suction or an alternative airway if needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not correct airway obstruction or ineffective ventilation.
- B. Incorrect. Ventilation is essential; the technique should be corrected rather than stopped.
- C. Incorrect. Feeding is unsafe during active resuscitation.
- D. Incorrect. Phototherapy has no role in immediate respiratory resuscitation.
- E. Correct. Airway positioning and an effective mask seal should be corrected first.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Correct head position is neutral; flexion or overextension can obstruct the airway.
- Chin lift or jaw thrust may improve airway patency.
- Mask should cover the mouth, nose and chin, but not the eyes.
- Consider two-person airway control, suction if obstructed, laryngeal mask or endotracheal tube if mask ventilation remains ineffective.

questions.stem: Which oxygen saturation targets are shown 's preductal SpO₂ chart during the first 10 minutes after birth?
questions.initialExplanation: The PDF resuscitation flowchart shows the preductal saturation targets rising gradually after birth: approximately 60% at 2 minutes, 70% at 3 minutes, 80% at 4 minutes, 85% at 5 minutes and 90% at 10 minutes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Immediate 100% saturation is not the normal transition target.
- B. Correct. These are the values displayed 's flowchart.
- C. Incorrect. These values are too low for the target progression shown.
- D. Incorrect. Saturation normally rises progressively after birth; 90-100% is not expected within the first 2 minutes.
- E. Incorrect. This sequence rises too rapidly and does not match the source table.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Use a right-hand/right-wrist preductal pulse oximeter where available.
- Normal transition involves a gradual increase in oxygen saturation over the first 10 minutes.
- Oxygen concentration should be adjusted according to saturation and the applicable neonatal resuscitation guideline.

questions.stem: During neonatal resuscitation, when should chest compressions be started 's algorithm?

options.label: A
options.text: If the heart rate remains below 60/min after effective ventilation

options.label: B
options.text: If the baby has a weak cry but normal heart rate

options.label: D
options.text: If oxygen saturation is below 90% at 2 minutes

options.label: E
options.text: If the 1-minute Apgar score is below 7

questions.correctAnswerText: If the heart rate remains below 60/min after effective ventilation
questions.initialExplanation: Chest compressions are indicated when the heart rate remains below 60/min despite effective ventilation. Ventilation must be optimized before compressions are started.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Persistent HR below 60/min after effective ventilation is the trigger.
- B. Incorrect. A weak cry with normal heart rate does not meet the criterion.
- C. Incorrect. Apnoea requires ventilation, not automatic compressions.
- D. Incorrect. Saturation targets rise gradually; low saturation at 2 minutes alone is not the indication for compressions.
- E. Incorrect. Apgar score alone does not determine the need for compressions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ventilate effectively first.
- If HR remains <60/min, begin coordinated chest compressions and ventilation.
- Reassess heart rate regularly and follow the current neonatal resuscitation algorithm.

questions.stem: What is the compression-to-ventilation ratio used during neonatal resuscitation when chest compressions are required?
questions.initialExplanation: Neonatal resuscitation uses three chest compressions followed by one ventilation, synchronized at a 3:1 ratio.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This ratio is used in some other resuscitation contexts, not neonatal resuscitation.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the standard neonatal ratio described.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the ratio.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the neonatal resuscitation ratio.
- E. Correct. The neonatal ratio is 3 compressions to 1 ventilation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal compression-to-ventilation ratio: 3:1.
- This provides approximately 90 compressions and 30 ventilations per minute.
- Increase oxygen as indicated while compressions are delivered, and reassess HR every 30 seconds.

questions.stem: Which technique and anatomical landmark are correct for neonatal chest compressions?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the two-thumb encircling technique over the lower third of the sternum, just below the nipple line

options.label: C
options.text: Press over the upper sternum using two fingers

options.label: D
options.text: Compress over the left lower ribs

options.label: E
options.text: Press over the abdomen to reduce venous return

questions.correctAnswerText: Use the two-thumb encircling technique over the lower third of the sternum, just below the nipple line
questions.initialExplanation: The PDF shows compression over the lower third of the sternum, just below the nipple line, depressing the chest by approximately one-third of its anteroposterior diameter. The two-thumb encircling technique is preferred when possible.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the illustrated landmark and preferred technique.
- B. Incorrect. Pressure over the xiphoid risks injury to the liver and other abdominal organs.
- C. Incorrect. The upper sternum is not the correct compression site.
- D. Incorrect. Compression is not delivered over the ribs.
- E. Incorrect. Abdominal pressure is not a resuscitation technique.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Landmark: lower third of sternum just below the nipple line.
- Depth: about one-third of the anteroposterior chest diameter (standard guidance gives around 1-1.5 cm).
