- Two-thumb encircling chest technique is preferred; two-finger technique may be used when alone.
- Avoid pressure over the xiphoid or abdomen.

cases.title: A high-risk delivery requires preparation and stabilization
cases.vignette: A 29-week pregnancy is complicated by severe pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction. The neonatal team prepares the warmer, oxygen/air blender, T-piece device, appropriately sized masks, suction, laryngoscope, endotracheal tubes, vascular access equipment and medications before delivery.

questions.stem: Which item is essential for effective neonatal mask ventilation and is illustrated in the PDF?

options.label: B
options.text: A face mask that covers the mouth, nose and chin without covering the eyes

options.label: C
options.text: A mask that covers the mouth

options.label: D
options.text: A mask that covers the eyes and forehead

options.label: E
options.text: A mask that leaves the nose uncovered

questions.correctAnswerText: A face mask that covers the mouth, nose and chin without covering the eyes
questions.initialExplanation: The PDF illustrates the correct mask size as one that covers the mouth, nose and chin, but not the eyes. An appropriately sized mask and seal are essential for effective ventilation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Adult equipment is not appropriate for a newborn.
- B. Correct. This is the correct mask fit shown in the PDF.
- C. Incorrect. The nose must also be covered for effective ventilation.
- D. Incorrect. A mask that covers the eyes is too large and may obstruct positioning.
- E. Incorrect. The nose must be included within the mask.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Choose a neonatal mask of appropriate size.
- Correct mask fit: mouth, nose and chin covered; eyes not covered.
- If ventilation is ineffective, reassess mask seal, head position and airway patency.

questions.stem: A newborn remains profoundly bradycardic despite effective ventilation and synchronized chest compressions. Which medication is listed for this situation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Epinephrine (adrenaline)
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include epinephrine for persistent heart rate below 60/min despite adequate ventilation and external cardiac compressions. Vascular access and the current neonatal resuscitation protocol determine the appropriate route and dose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vitamin K prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
- B. Incorrect. Phototherapy treats selected unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Phenobarbital is an anticonvulsant used for neonatal seizures.
- D. Correct. Epinephrine is used when severe bradycardia persists despite effective ventilation and compressions.
- E. Incorrect. Surfactant treats respiratory distress syndrome due to surfactant deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Optimize ventilation and chest compressions before medication.
- Persistent HR <60/min despite effective ventilation and compressions: consider epinephrine.
- Exact routes and doses should follow the current neonatal resuscitation guideline; do not use an OCR-derived dose without verification.

questions.stem: A newborn has a history of major blood loss during delivery and remains poorly perfused despite appropriate ventilation and resuscitation. Which intervention is listed for suspected hypovolaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: An isotonic crystalloid or blood as a volume expander

options.label: B
options.text: Intramuscular vitamin K as the intervention

questions.correctAnswerText: An isotonic crystalloid or blood as a volume expander
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include an isotonic crystalloid or blood as a volume expander when blood loss is suspected. Volume replacement is not routine for every bradycardic newborn; it is considered when there is evidence of hypovolaemia or blood loss.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A volume expander is appropriate when poor perfusion is due to suspected blood loss/hypovolaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Vitamin K prevents bleeding but does not restore circulating volume.
- C. Incorrect. Oral feeding is unsafe during active resuscitation.
- D. Incorrect. Phototherapy treats unconjugated jaundice.
- E. Incorrect. Surfactant treats RDS and does not correct hypovolaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider volume expansion when there is a history/sign of significant blood loss and persistent poor perfusion.
- Common examples include isotonic crystalloid or blood.
- Assess for haemorrhage, shock and ongoing blood loss; follow local neonatal resuscitation protocols.

cases.title: Routine care after a good Apgar score, temperature control and resuscitation drugs

questions.stem: After a placental abruption, a pale newborn has a heart rate of 40/min despite effective ventilation and synchronized chest compressions. The blood gas shows severe lactic acidosis and the glucose is very low. Which pairing of problem and listed resuscitation drug is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypoglycaemia: sodium bicarbonate; lactic acidosis: dextrose

options.label: B
options.text: Heart rate <60 despite ventilation and compressions: epinephrine; severe lactic acidosis: sodium bicarbonate; hypoglycaemia: 10% dextrose; blood loss: volume expander

options.label: C
options.text: Heart rate <60 before ventilation is established: epinephrine as the first intervention

options.label: D
options.text: Blood loss: sodium bicarbonate; lactic acidosis: volume expander

questions.correctAnswerText: Heart rate <60 despite ventilation and compressions: epinephrine; severe lactic acidosis: sodium bicarbonate; hypoglycaemia: 10% dextrose; blood loss: volume expander
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance's drug table lists epinephrine for a heart rate below 60/min despite adequate ventilation and external compressions, sodium bicarbonate for severe lactic acidosis, 10% dextrose for hypoglycaemia, and isotonic crystalloid or blood for blood loss.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The two drugs are swapped.
- B. Correct. Each problem is matched to its listed drug.
- C. Incorrect. Ventilation comes first; epinephrine is for a heart rate that remains low despite effective ventilation and compressions.
- D. Incorrect. Blood loss is treated with volume, and bicarbonate is for severe acidosis.
- E. Incorrect. Epinephrine does not correct hypoglycaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Drugs come after effective ventilation and compressions.
- Epinephrine: HR <60 despite ventilation + compressions. Bicarbonate: severe lactic acidosis. Dextrose: hypoglycaemia. Volume: blood loss.
- Doses in the scanned table must be checked against current local neonatal guidelines.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 13 (Drugs used in neonatal resuscitation).

topics.name: Prematurity - Classification, Clinical Features and Initial Care

cases.title: A baby is delivered at 29 weeks' gestation
cases.vignette: A male infant is delivered at 29 weeks because of severe maternal pre-eclampsia and fetal compromise. The infant weighs 1,150 g, has thin shiny skin, prominent eyes, soft poorly formed ear cartilage, few sole creases and undescended testes. He is admitted to the NICU for thermal, respiratory and nutritional support.

questions.stem: Which gestational age category applies to this infant?
questions.correctAnswerText: Very preterm
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance classifies infants born before 37 weeks as preterm and identifies very preterm infants as those born before 32 weeks. A 29-week infant is therefore very preterm.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Post-term is 42 weeks or more.
- B. Incorrect. Term begins at 37 completed weeks.
- C. Incorrect. Post-maturity is associated with prolonged gestation, not 29 weeks.
- D. Correct. Birth at 29 weeks is before 32 weeks and is very preterm.
- E. Incorrect. Late preterm refers to 34 to 36 completed weeks.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preterm: <37 completed weeks.
- Very preterm: <32 weeks.
- Extremely preterm: <28 weeks.
- The earlier the gestational age, the greater the risk of respiratory, neurological, gastrointestinal and thermal complications.

questions.stem: Which physical finding is most characteristic of prematurity?

options.label: A
options.text: Dry peeling skin, long nails and abundant scalp hair

options.label: B
options.text: Strong suck-swallow coordination and vigorous cry in each infant

options.label: C
options.text: Thin shiny skin, little subcutaneous fat, soft ear cartilage and few plantar creases

options.label: D
options.text: Thick subcutaneous fat, firm ear cartilage and deep plantar creases

options.label: E
options.text: Large breast nodule and fully descended testes

questions.correctAnswerText: Thin shiny skin, little subcutaneous fat, soft ear cartilage and few plantar creases
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include premature newborns as having thin shiny skin, little subcutaneous fat, soft ear cartilage with poor recoil, small breast tissue and fewer plantar creases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dry peeling skin, long nails and abundant hair are associated with post-maturity.
- B. Incorrect. Preterm infants often have weak suck and poor coordination of sucking and swallowing.
- C. Correct. This is the typical physical appearance of prematurity.
- D. Incorrect. These findings suggest greater maturity.
- E. Incorrect. A large breast nodule and descended testes are signs of greater maturity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prematurity: thin shiny skin, little SC fat, lanugo, soft ear cartilage, small breast nodule, smooth scrotum/undescended testes and sparse sole creases.
- Immature suck-swallow coordination may necessitate tube feeding.
- Physical findings must be interpreted with gestational age and clinical history.

questions.stem: A premature male infant has an underdeveloped scrotum with few rugae and both testes are undescended. What does this finding suggest?

options.label: E
options.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Prematurity and immature genital development
questions.initialExplanation: In premature boys, the scrotum is often smooth with few rugae and the testes may be undescended. These are physical maturity findings used in gestational-age assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Post-term infants show signs of prolonged maturation.
- B. Incorrect. A mature term male usually has more developed scrotal rugae and descended testes.
- C. Correct. The described genital features are typical of prematurity.
- D. Incorrect. Biliary atresia causes neonatal cholestasis.
- E. Incorrect. CAH may cause genital ambiguity/virilization in a 46,XX infant, but smooth scrotum and undescended testes in a preterm male are maturity signs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Male preterm genitalia: smooth scrotum, fewer rugae, testes may be undescended.
- Female preterm genitalia: labia minora/clitoris may be more prominent due less labia majora fat.
- Genital features contribute to New Ballard physical maturity assessment.

questions.stem: Which score is used to estimate gestational age after birth using physical and neuromuscular maturity?
questions.correctAnswerText: New Ballard score
questions.initialExplanation: The New Ballard score estimates gestational age using physical maturity and neuromuscular maturity signs. Clinical guidance notes an approximate accuracy of plus or minus 2 weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. New Ballard combines physical and neuromuscular maturity findings.
- B. Incorrect. Downes score is another respiratory distress assessment, not a gestational-age score.
- C. Incorrect. Glasgow Coma Scale assesses consciousness.
- D. Incorrect. Silverman-Andersen assesses severity of respiratory distress.
- E. Incorrect. Apgar assesses immediate newborn condition and response to resuscitation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- New Ballard score: physical + neuromuscular maturity.
- It estimates gestational age when dates are uncertain.
- Approximate precision described: ±2 weeks.
- It does not replace reliable antenatal dating where available.

questions.stem: Which group contains only physical maturity components of the New Ballard score?

options.label: A
options.text: Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure and oxygen saturation

options.label: B
options.text: Moro, rooting, sucking and stepping reflexes

options.label: C
options.text: Posture, square window, arm recoil, scarf sign and popliteal angle

options.label: D
options.text: Apgar, blood glucose, bilirubin and haemoglobin

options.label: E
options.text: Skin, lanugo, ear cartilage, breast tissue, genitalia and plantar creases

questions.correctAnswerText: Skin, lanugo, ear cartilage, breast tissue, genitalia and plantar creases
questions.initialExplanation: The physical maturity section of the New Ballard score includes skin, lanugo, ear cartilage/recoil, eye opening, breast size, male/female genitalia and sole creases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are physiological observations, not Ballard scoring items.
- B. Incorrect. Primitive reflexes are assessed in the neurological examination but are not the physical maturity list.
- C. Incorrect. These are neuromuscular maturity components.
- D. Incorrect. These are clinical measurements and laboratory tests.
- E. Correct. These are physical maturity components.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Physical Ballard: skin, lanugo, ear recoil/cartilage, eyes, breast, genitalia and sole creases.
- Neuromuscular Ballard: posture, square window, arm recoil, scarf sign, popliteal angle and heel-to-ear.
- The two domains are combined to estimate gestational age.

questions.stem: Which set contains only neuromuscular components of the New Ballard score?

options.label: A
options.text: Posture, square window, arm recoil, scarf sign, popliteal angle and heel-to-ear

options.label: B
options.text: Ear recoil, breast size and genital development

options.label: D
options.text: Heart rate, tone and suck reflex

questions.correctAnswerText: Posture, square window, arm recoil, scarf sign, popliteal angle and heel-to-ear
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include six neuromuscular findings: posture, square window, arm recoil, scarf sign, popliteal angle and heel-to-ear.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the neuromuscular components.
- B. Incorrect. These are also physical maturity findings.
- C. Incorrect. These are physical maturity findings.
- D. Incorrect. Tone and sucking are clinically assessed but this is not the full New Ballard neuromuscular list.
- E. Incorrect. Apgar and pulse oximetry do not estimate gestational age.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neuromuscular Ballard: posture, square window, arm recoil, scarf sign, popliteal angle, heel-to-ear.
- Increasing maturity is associated with more flexed posture and greater resistance to extension.
- Interpret with the physical maturity score.

questions.stem: Why are premature infants particularly vulnerable to hypothermia?

options.label: A
options.text: They have more subcutaneous fat and better heat regulation

options.label: B
options.text: They have a fully mature hypothalamus

options.label: C
options.text: They have little subcutaneous fat, thin skin, a relatively large surface area and immature temperature regulation

options.label: D
options.text: They have a lower surface area relative to body weight

options.label: E
options.text: They produce excessive brown fat and sweat

questions.correctAnswerText: They have little subcutaneous fat, thin skin, a relatively large surface area and immature temperature regulation
questions.initialExplanation: This is explained that premature infants lose heat easily because they have low subcutaneous fat, thin skin, a high surface-area-to-weight ratio and immature temperature control.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Preterm infants have less subcutaneous fat, not more.
- B. Incorrect. Temperature regulation is immature.
- C. Correct. These factors increase heat loss and impair thermoregulation.
- D. Incorrect. Their surface area relative to body weight is high, not low.
- E. Incorrect. Preterm infants have limited thermogenic reserves and do not sweat excessively as a protective mechanism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preterm infants are at high risk of hypothermia.
- Maintain a neutral thermal environment and monitor temperature closely.
- Hypothermia increases oxygen and glucose consumption and worsens morbidity.

questions.stem: A preterm infant becomes cold after being placed near a cold external wall without direct contact. Which mechanism of heat loss is occurring?
questions.correctAnswerText: Radiation
questions.initialExplanation: Radiation is heat transfer from the infant to a colder nearby surface without direct contact. Recognized features include it as one of the four main mechanisms of neonatal heat loss.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Conduction occurs through direct contact with a colder surface.
- B. Incorrect. Metabolic heat production is not a heat-loss mechanism.
- C. Correct. Radiation occurs without direct contact, such as heat loss to a cold wall/window.
- D. Incorrect. Convection occurs when moving air or fluid carries heat away.
- E. Incorrect. Evaporation is heat loss as water changes from liquid to vapour, e.g. wet skin after birth.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Four mechanisms: evaporation, conduction, convection and radiation.
- Dry the newborn promptly to reduce evaporative loss.
- Use a warm environment/incubator and avoid cold surfaces, draughts and nearby cold walls.

questions.stem: A premature infant is too immature to coordinate sucking and swallowing safely. Which feeding route is preferred initially?

options.label: A
options.text: No enteral feeds until term-equivalent age in each infant

questions.correctAnswerText: Nasogastric or orogastric tube feeding
questions.initialExplanation: Premature infants, particularly those below approximately 34 weeks, may not coordinate suck-swallow-breathe safely. Recommended management includes NG/OG tube feeding when oral feeding is not safe or possible.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Enteral feeding is generally introduced when clinically appropriate; it is not withheld until term-equivalent age in every infant.
- B. Incorrect. Large oral bolus feeds increase aspiration risk when coordination is immature.
- C. Incorrect. Nutrition is not delivered intramuscularly.
- D. Correct. NG/OG feeding safely delivers expressed breast milk or preterm formula.
- E. Incorrect. Forceful oral feeding is unsafe.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Breast milk/colostrum is preferred for preterm infants.
- NG/OG feeding is used when the infant cannot suck and swallow safely.
- Very small trophic feeds may be started early in stable infants; exact volume depends on the neonatal protocol.
- TPN may be needed in extremely premature or critically ill infants.

questions.stem: A very preterm infant receives small-volume enteral feeds while parenteral nutrition continues. What is the purpose of trophic feeding?

options.label: A
options.text: To replace most breast milk permanently

options.label: B
options.text: To stimulate intestinal maturation and tolerance while providing small amounts of enteral nutrition

options.label: D
options.text: To provide the full daily caloric requirement immediately

options.label: E
options.text: To prevent the need for monitoring

questions.correctAnswerText: To stimulate intestinal maturation and tolerance while providing small amounts of enteral nutrition
questions.initialExplanation: Trophic feeding provides small volumes of milk to stimulate gut function and maturation in very preterm infants. It is not intended to meet the full nutritional requirement initially.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Breast milk remains the preferred enteral feed when available.
- B. Correct. The aim is to stimulate intestinal adaptation and improve feed tolerance.
- C. Incorrect. Trophic feeding does not treat jaundice.
- D. Incorrect. Trophic feeds are small-volume feeds, not full nutritional replacement.
- E. Incorrect. Feeding intolerance and NEC signs must still be monitored.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Trophic feeds: small-volume enteral milk in very preterm infants.
- They support gut maturation and feed tolerance.
- Monitor abdominal distension, vomiting, stool, perfusion and systemic status.
- Breast milk is preferred when available.

cases.title: Routine care after a good Apgar score, temperature control and resuscitation drugs

questions.stem: A 28-week infant is admitted to the NICU with a temperature of 35.2 °C. A colleague says that mild cooling is harmless once the baby is warmed. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Slight hypothermia (35-36 °C) is protective because it lowers oxygen consumption

options.label: B
options.text: Admission temperature has no relationship to outcome once the baby is rewarmed

options.label: C
options.text: Overheating to about 38 °C is preferred in extremely preterm infants

options.label: D
options.text: Hypothermia is a concern in term infants after cold stress

options.label: E
options.text: Maintain 36.5–37.5 °C; hypothermia increases morbidity and mortality, especially in very preterm infants

questions.correctAnswerText: Maintain 36.5–37.5 °C; hypothermia increases morbidity and mortality, especially in very preterm infants
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that normal body temperature (36.5-37.5 °C) must be maintained during resuscitation and in the NICU, and that each degree below this on admission in very preterm infants increases mortality by 28%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hypothermia increases energy consumption, hypoxia and hypoglycaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Admission temperature is associated with mortality.
- C. Incorrect. Overheating is also harmful; the target is normothermia.
- D. Incorrect. Preterm infants are the most vulnerable because of thin skin, little fat and a large surface area.
- E. Correct. States the target and the mortality relationship.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Maintain 36.5-37.5 °C during resuscitation and NICU care.
- Each 1 °C below this on admission (very preterm): mortality +28%.
- Heat loss: convection, radiation, evaporation, conduction.
- Hypothermia (<35 °C ) causes hypoxia, hypoglycaemia and poor weight gain.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 14 (temperature during resuscitation); Pages 19-20 (hypothermia).

cases.title: Preterm infants beyond respiratory disease: oxygen, fluids, organ immaturity and outcomes

questions.stem: A 29-week infant, 1 day old, needs intravenous fluids. Which statement agrees with standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Use 10% dextrose on day 1 and add electrolytes from day 2; preterm infants need more fluid than term infants (day 1 about 90 versus 60-75 mL/kg/day)

options.label: B
options.text: Use normal saline on day 1 and start dextrose on day 3

options.label: C
options.text: Preterm and term infants have the same fluid requirement

options.label: D
options.text: Preterm infants need less fluid because of their size and should be restricted to about 40 mL/kg/day

options.label: E
options.text: Use 5% dextrose without electrolytes for the whole first week

questions.correctAnswerText: Use 10% dextrose on day 1 and add electrolytes from day 2; preterm infants need more fluid than term infants (day 1 about 90 versus 60-75 mL/kg/day)
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that preterm infants need more fluid than term babies. The fluid on day 1 is 10% dextrose, and on day 2 it is 10% dextrose with electrolytes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Matches the fluid type on days 1 and 2 and the preterm-versus-term difference.
- B. Incorrect. Dextrose is the day-1 fluid, and preterm infants are prone to hypoglycaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Preterm infants have higher requirements.
- D. Incorrect. Restriction to 40 mL/kg/day is not.
- E. Incorrect. standard guidance specifies 10% dextrose, with electrolytes added from day 2.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preterm infants need more fluid per kg than term infants.
- Day 1 fluid: 10% dextrose. Day 2: 10% dextrose + electrolytes.
- Very immature or sick infants (typically <1 kg) often need total parenteral nutrition.
- The fluid table was scanned with OCR; check the exact volumes against the original page.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 21 (IVF in preterm versus term infants).

cases.title: A threatened preterm delivery at 32 weeks

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks with threatened preterm labour has amniocentesis. The lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio is 1.2. Which interpretation and plan are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The ratio is above 2.5 (mature lung); no steroids are needed

options.label: B
options.text: The ratio is in the transitional range (1.5-2); no action is needed

options.label: C
options.text: The ratio is immature, so give the mother surfactant by injection

options.label: D
options.text: L/S 1.2 indicates immature lungs; give antenatal steroids and plan delivery with neonatal intensive care

options.label: E
options.text: A ratio below 1.5 indicates a mature lung, so neonatal surfactant will be unnecessary

questions.correctAnswerText: L/S 1.2 indicates immature lungs; give antenatal steroids and plan delivery with neonatal intensive care
questions.initialExplanation: A lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio above 2.5 indicates a mature lung, 1.5-2 transitional, and below 1.5 immature. For an immature lung, antenatal steroids (24-34 weeks, two doses 12 hours apart, about 48 hours before delivery) reduce RDS and mortality.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. 1.2 is not above 2.5.
- B. Incorrect. 1.2 is below the transitional range.
- C. Incorrect. Surfactant is given to the baby through the endotracheal tube, not to the mother.
- D. Correct. Interprets the ratio correctly and applies standard guidance's prevention.
- E. Incorrect. A low ratio means immature lungs, so surfactant is more likely to be needed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- L/S ratio: >2.5 mature; 1.5-2 transitional; <1.5 immature.
- Antenatal steroids at 24-34 weeks: two doses 12 hours apart, about 48 hours before delivery.
- Steroids reduce RDS incidence and mortality (about 40% ).
- Surfactant (lecithin) mature around 35-36 weeks.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 32 (antenatal fetal lung maturity test; prevention of RDS).

cases.title: A 29-week infant develops progressive respiratory distress shortly after birth
cases.vignette: A male infant born at 29 weeks develops tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring and subcostal recession within the first hour after delivery. Air entry is reduced bilaterally and chest radiography shows diffuse granular ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

questions.correctAnswerText: Respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease)
questions.initialExplanation: RDS is the commonest respiratory disorder in premature infants. It is caused by surfactant deficiency and usually presents at delivery or within the first few hours with progressive respiratory distress.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. CDH presents with severe distress, scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the chest.
- B. Incorrect. PPHN may cause severe hypoxaemia and differential cyanosis, but the described radiographic pattern and prematurity suggest RDS.
- C. Correct. Prematurity, early progressive distress and a ground-glass X-ray with air bronchograms strongly support RDS.
- D. Incorrect. TTN is usually a self-limited disorder of term/near-term infants due to delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid.
- E. Incorrect. MAS is associated with meconium-stained liquor, fetal stress and patchy hyperinflation/consolidation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- RDS = hyaline membrane disease due to surfactant deficiency.
- Occurs almost exclusively in preterm infants.
- Symptoms begin at delivery or within about 4 hours and may progress.
- Chest X-ray: diffuse granular/ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms; severe cases become bilaterally opaque.

questions.stem: Which cells synthesize pulmonary surfactant?
questions.correctAnswerText: Type II pneumocytes
questions.initialExplanation: Pulmonary surfactant is synthesized by type II pneumocytes. Clinical guidance notes that production starts around 20 weeks and becomes mature at approximately 35-36 weeks of gestation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Endothelial cells line pulmonary blood vessels.
- B. Incorrect. Alveolar macrophages provide immune defence and phagocytosis.
- C. Incorrect. Type I pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface.
- D. Incorrect. Ciliated airway cells help clear mucus and particles.
- E. Correct. Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type II pneumocytes → surfactant.
- Surfactant production begins around 20 weeks and matures around 35-36 weeks.
- Premature birth before adequate surfactant maturation increases RDS risk.

questions.stem: What is the main physiological function of surfactant?

options.label: A
options.text: Stimulate mucus production in the bronchi

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce alveolar surface tension and prevent collapse at end-expiration

options.label: D
options.text: Prevent oxygen diffusion across the alveolar membrane

options.label: E
options.text: Increase alveolar surface tension and promote collapse

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduce alveolar surface tension and prevent collapse at end-expiration
questions.initialExplanation: Surfactant reduces surface tension inside the alveoli, prevents alveolar collapse at the end of expiration, improves lung compliance and reduces the work of breathing.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bronchial mucus production is not its main action.
- B. Incorrect. Surfactant does not increase pulmonary vascular resistance.
- C. Correct. This is its principal function.
- D. Incorrect. Surfactant supports lung expansion and efficient gas exchange.
- E. Incorrect. Surfactant lowers surface tension rather than increasing it.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension.
- Prevents atelectasis at end-expiration.
- Improves lung compliance and reduces work of breathing.
- Deficiency causes atelectasis, V/Q mismatch, hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis.

questions.stem: Which components make up the majority of pulmonary surfactant?

options.label: D
options.text: Lipids (about 90%), mainly phosphatidylcholine/lecithin, with surfactant proteins around 10%

questions.correctAnswerText: Lipids (about 90%), mainly phosphatidylcholine/lecithin, with surfactant proteins around 10%
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that surfactant is approximately 90% lipid and 10% surfactant proteins (A, B, C and D). Phosphatidylcholine/lecithin is the major lipid fraction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The proportions are reversed and glucose is not the main constituent.
- B. Incorrect. Surfactant is not mostly water and albumin.
- C. Incorrect. Phosphatidylserine is not the only component.
- D. Correct. This matches the composition table in the source.
- E. Incorrect. It contains several phospholipids and proteins, not cholesterol alone.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Surfactant: ~90% lipid and ~10% protein.
- Major lipid: phosphatidylcholine (lecithin).
- Phosphatidylglycerol is another important phospholipid.
- Surfactant proteins: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: Which maternal or neonatal factor is listed as increasing the risk of RDS?
questions.correctAnswerText: Male sex
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include male sex, prematurity, maternal smoking/narcotic addiction, caesarean delivery, family history, perinatal asphyxia, sepsis, hypothermia and acidosis among factors increasing RDS risk. Female sex, antenatal steroids and IUGR are listed as factors associated with reduced risk in the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Male sex is listed as a risk factor.
- B. Incorrect. PROM is listed in the decreased-risk column, but it may be associated with other obstetric risks.
- C. Incorrect. Female sex is listed as a factor decreasing risk.
- D. Incorrect. IUGR is listed as a factor decreasing risk 's table, although IUGR infants have other important risks.
- E. Incorrect. Antenatal corticosteroids stimulate surfactant production and reduce RDS risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Major risk factor: prematurity; incidence is inversely related to gestational age.
- Male sex is a risk factor.
- Antenatal corticosteroids reduce RDS incidence and severity.
- Some listed factors are standard guidance-specific and should not be interpreted as eliminating overall neonatal risk.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman at 28 weeks is at high risk of preterm delivery. Which intervention reduces the incidence and severity of neonatal RDS?

options.label: C
options.text: Antenatal corticosteroids such as betamethasone or dexamethasone

questions.correctAnswerText: Antenatal corticosteroids such as betamethasone or dexamethasone
questions.initialExplanation: Antenatal corticosteroids stimulate fetal lung maturation and surfactant production. Clinical descriptions include their use between 24 and 34 weeks when preterm delivery is likely.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vitamin K prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics are used for specific maternal infection/PROM indications, not as the universal RDS-prevention treatment.
- C. Correct. Antenatal corticosteroids reduce RDS incidence and neonatal mortality.
- D. Incorrect. Phototherapy treats neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia after birth.
- E. Incorrect. Diuretics do not stimulate fetal surfactant production.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Antenatal betamethasone/dexamethasone promotes surfactant production and lung maturation.
- standard guidance places treatment in the 24-34-week gestational window.
- The source gives two doses 12 hours apart; exact regimen should follow the current obstetric protocol.
- Antenatal steroids reduce RDS and neonatal mortality.

questions.stem: A premature infant with severe RDS requires surfactant replacement. Which route is described?

options.label: E
options.text: Intratracheal administration through an endotracheal tube

questions.correctAnswerText: Intratracheal administration through an endotracheal tube
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include natural surfactant replacement (e.g. Survanta or Curosurf) administered through an endotracheal tube. Respiratory support may include supplemental oxygen, CPAP/HFNC or mechanical ventilation as needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Surfactant must reach the alveoli and is not given orally.
- B. Incorrect. Intramuscular injection does not deliver surfactant to the airways.
- C. Incorrect. Rectal administration has no role.
- D. Incorrect. Subcutaneous administration is not appropriate.
- E. Correct. Intratracheal administration through an ETT is the route described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Surfactant replacement is delivered intratracheally, usually through an ETT.
- Natural preparations listed include beractant (Survanta) and poractant alfa (Curosurf).
- Monitor for bradycardia, apnoea, ETT blockage, pulmonary haemorrhage and pneumothorax.
- Exact dose and repeat interval must follow the current NICU protocol.

questions.stem: Which respiratory support method may be used in a premature infant with RDS who is breathing spontaneously?

options.label: D
options.text: CPAP or high-flow nasal cannula as appropriate

questions.correctAnswerText: CPAP or high-flow nasal cannula as appropriate
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance includes supplemental oxygen and non-invasive respiratory support such as CPAP or high-flow nasal cannula, with mechanical ventilation for infants who require it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. An oral airway does not treat surfactant deficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Water deprivation is unrelated to neonatal respiratory support.
- C. Incorrect. Chest compressions are used during resuscitation for profound bradycardia, not routine RDS.
- D. Correct. CPAP/HFNC are non-invasive forms of respiratory support.
- E. Incorrect. Phototherapy treats jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NICU and incubator care are required for significant RDS.
- Respiratory support may include oxygen, CPAP, HFNC or mechanical ventilation.
- Surfactant is considered for appropriate infants with surfactant-deficient RDS.
- Monitor blood gases, oxygenation, respiratory effort and complications.

questions.stem: Which complication is associated with severe RDS and its treatment in premature infants?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include bronchopulmonary dysplasia, pneumothorax, PDA, intraventricular haemorrhage, pulmonary haemorrhage and complications of ETT/mechanical ventilation among complications associated with RDS and its treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Congenital syphilis is a TORCH/other congenital infection.
- B. Incorrect. Congenital cataract is an ocular abnormality, not an RDS complication.
- C. Incorrect. DDH is a congenital orthopaedic disorder.
- D. Correct. BPD is a chronic lung disease associated with prematurity and respiratory support.
- E. Incorrect. Biliary atresia is a cause of neonatal cholestasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- RDS complications include BPD, pneumothorax, PDA, IVH and pulmonary haemorrhage.
- Mortality increases as gestational age decreases.
- Antenatal steroids, surfactant and NICU care improve outcomes.
- BPD is assessed in relation to ongoing respiratory/oxygen needs at later postmenstrual age.

cases.title: A very preterm infant has recurrent pauses in breathing
cases.vignette: A 27-week infant in the NICU has repeated episodes of cessation of breathing associated with oxygen desaturation and bradycardia. The team evaluates whether these episodes represent apnoea of prematurity or are secondary to infection, anaemia, hypoglycaemia or another neonatal complication.

questions.stem: Which definition of neonatal apnoea is given?

options.label: A
options.text: Cessation of breathing for more than 5 seconds in each infant

options.label: C
options.text: Cessation of breathing for more than 20 seconds, or a shorter pause associated with bradycardia or cyanosis

options.label: D
options.text: Any episode of periodic breathing without desaturation

questions.correctAnswerText: Cessation of breathing for more than 20 seconds, or a shorter pause associated with bradycardia or cyanosis
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe neonatal apnoea as cessation of breathing for more than 20 seconds, or a shorter pause if associated with bradycardia, cyanosis or pallor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A pause of 5 seconds alone is not the definition in the source.
- B. Incorrect. Respiratory rate below 60/min is not apnoea.
- C. Correct. This is the definition stated.
- D. Incorrect. Periodic breathing without clinically significant bradycardia, cyanosis or desaturation is not automatically apnoea.
- E. Incorrect. Sneezing is not apnoea.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Apnoea: >20 seconds, or shorter with bradycardia/cyanosis/pallor.
- Preterm infants are at increased risk due to immature respiratory control.
- Distinguish apnoea from normal periodic breathing.

questions.stem: Which pattern of apnoea is most common in premature infants?
questions.correctAnswerText: Central 40%, obstructive 10%, mixed 50%
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives approximate proportions of central apnoea 40%, obstructive 10% and mixed apnoea 50% in premature infants.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This incorrectly makes obstructive apnoea the dominant type.
- B. Incorrect. These proportions do not match the source.
- C. Incorrect. This reverses the relative proportions.
- D. Incorrect. Apnoea is not exclusively obstructive.
- E. Correct. Mixed apnoea is the largest group 's distribution.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Central: absent respiratory effort.
- Obstructive: respiratory effort persists but airflow is blocked.
- Mixed: central and obstructive components.
- Mixed apnoea is the most common pattern listed.

questions.stem: A 30-week infant who previously had no apnoea develops new recurrent apnoeic episodes, temperature instability and poor feeding. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop monitoring because apnoea is self-limiting

options.label: B
options.text: Consider a secondary cause such as sepsis, IVH, NEC, hypoglycaemia, anaemia or respiratory disease

options.label: C
options.text: Apnoea of prematurity should be assumed without further evaluation

options.label: D
options.text: This is typically normal periodic breathing

options.label: E
options.text: Give caffeine and do not investigate

questions.correctAnswerText: Consider a secondary cause such as sepsis, IVH, NEC, hypoglycaemia, anaemia or respiratory disease
questions.initialExplanation: Apnoea in a premature infant may be due to immature respiratory control, but new or worsening episodes require assessment for secondary causes. Common examples include infection, IVH/seizures, NEC, GERD, respiratory disease, anaemia/polycythaemia, PDA/heart failure, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and electrolyte abnormalities.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Continuous monitoring and clinical assessment remain important.
- B. Correct. The accompanying systemic signs require investigation for an underlying cause.
- C. Incorrect. A new deterioration should not automatically be attributed to prematurity.
- D. Incorrect. Periodic breathing does not explain new temperature instability and poor feeding.
- E. Incorrect. Caffeine may be appropriate, but secondary causes must be considered.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Apnoea of prematurity is a diagnosis made after considering other causes.
- Secondary causes: sepsis, IVH/seizures, NEC, GERD, RDS, anaemia/polycythaemia, PDA/HF, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance.
- New apnoea plus poor feeding or temperature instability should raise concern for infection.

questions.stem: Which medication is used for recurrent apnoea of prematurity?
questions.correctAnswerText: Caffeine citrate
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include caffeine citrate (and theophylline) as pharmacological treatment for apnoea of prematurity. Management also includes airway positioning, stimulation and respiratory support when needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ursodeoxycholic acid is used in selected cholestatic disorders.
- B. Incorrect. Furosemide is a diuretic and is not the treatment listed for apnoea.
- C. Incorrect. Phenobarbital is an anticonvulsant.
- D. Correct. Caffeine is a respiratory stimulant used for apnoea of prematurity.
- E. Incorrect. Indomethacin may be used for PDA closure and is not an apnoea treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Initial steps: assess airway, position, stimulation and oxygenation.
- Caffeine citrate is commonly used for recurrent apnoea of prematurity.
- Severe events may require bag-mask ventilation, CPAP or mechanical ventilation.
- Investigate and treat secondary causes.

cases.title: A ventilated preterm infant suddenly deteriorates
cases.vignette: A 29-week infant with severe RDS is receiving positive-pressure ventilation. The infant suddenly develops worsening cyanosis, bradycardia and desaturation. Breath sounds are markedly reduced on the right side, and the right hemithorax appears more expanded. Transillumination is positive on the affected side.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pneumothorax
questions.initialExplanation: Pneumothorax is a recognized complication of severe RDS and positive-pressure ventilation. It may present with sudden respiratory deterioration, cyanosis, desaturation and unilateral reduced breath sounds.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Physiological jaundice does not cause acute respiratory collapse.
- B. Incorrect. IVH may cause neurological deterioration, seizures or apnoea but not unilateral chest findings.
- C. Correct. Sudden deterioration with unilateral reduced air entry and positive transillumination supports pneumothorax.
- D. Incorrect. PDA usually causes a murmur, bounding pulses and signs of heart failure rather than sudden unilateral loss of breath sounds.
- E. Incorrect. NEC presents with feeding intolerance, abdominal distension and bloody stool.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pneumothorax risk is increased in ventilated infants and severe RDS.
- Signs: sudden deterioration, cyanosis, desaturation, bradycardia and unilateral reduced breath sounds.
- Positive transillumination supports the diagnosis; chest X-ray confirms when the infant is stable enough.

questions.stem: A ventilated preterm infant develops a tension pneumothorax with severe compromise. What is the immediate management principle?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate needle decompression, followed by chest drain when indicated

options.label: C
options.text: Wait for a routine chest X-ray before intervention

questions.correctAnswerText: Immediate needle decompression, followed by chest drain when indicated
questions.initialExplanation: A tension pneumothorax is an emergency. Clinical descriptions include immediate needle decompression followed by chest drainage. Imaging should not delay life-saving decompression in a critically unstable infant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Immediate decompression relieves intrathoracic pressure; a chest drain provides ongoing evacuation.
- B. Incorrect. Phototherapy treats jaundice.
- C. Incorrect. Waiting for imaging can be fatal in tension pneumothorax.
- D. Incorrect. Increasing ventilator pressure may worsen the air leak.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not decompress the pleural space.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tension pneumothorax: clinical emergency.
- Immediate needle decompression if severe compromise, followed by chest drain.
- Reassess ventilation and underlying lung disease.
- Avoid escalating positive pressure without correcting the air leak.

questions.stem: Which bedside investigation can rapidly support the diagnosis of pneumothorax in a critically ill newborn?
questions.correctAnswerText: Transillumination of the chest
questions.initialExplanation: Transillumination can rapidly demonstrate increased light transmission through a hemithorax containing air. Chest X-ray is used to confirm the diagnosis when the infant is stable.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Abdominal palpation does not diagnose pneumothorax.
- B. Correct. This is the bedside test described.
- C. Incorrect. Ortolani assesses hip stability.
- D. Incorrect. Heel-prick blood spot screens for metabolic/endocrine disorders.
- E. Incorrect. Red reflex screens for ocular media opacity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Transillumination: rapid bedside aid.
- Chest X-ray confirms and shows the air collection/lung collapse.
- In a very unstable infant with suspected tension pneumothorax, do not delay decompression for imaging.

cases.title: A very preterm infant remains oxygen-dependent at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age
cases.vignette: A 25-week infant has required prolonged respiratory support and supplemental oxygen. At 36 weeks' postmenstrual age, the infant still needs oxygen. The chest radiograph shows coarse bilateral opacities with cystic changes. The team discusses chronic lung disease of prematurity.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include BPD as chronic lung disease in premature infants, associated with immature lungs, oxygen exposure, mechanical ventilation and infection. standard guidance uses ongoing oxygen requirement at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age as a diagnostic marker.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Persistent oxygen need at 36 weeks PMA in a very preterm infant supports BPD.
- B. Incorrect. MAS occurs around birth in infants exposed to meconium and is an acute condition.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital lobar emphysema is a focal congenital lung lesion.
- D. Incorrect. Choanal atresia causes upper-airway obstruction, not chronic parenchymal lung disease.
- E. Incorrect. TTN resolves within approximately 24-48 hours and does not cause chronic oxygen dependence.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- BPD: chronic lung disease of prematurity.
- Risk factors: extreme prematurity, mechanical ventilation/pressure-volume trauma, oxygen toxicity and infection.
- standard guidance uses oxygen requirement at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age.
- CXR may show coarse opacities and cystic changes.

questions.stem: Which is a recognized long-term complication of bronchopulmonary dysplasia?

options.label: B
options.text: Pulmonary hypertension and recurrent respiratory infections

questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary hypertension and recurrent respiratory infections
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include recurrent chest infections/wheeze, severe RSV/pertussis infection, pulmonary hypertension and developmental delay as possible consequences of BPD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Congenital cataract is unrelated to BPD.
- B. Correct. These are recognized late complications.
- C. Incorrect. Cleft palate is a congenital malformation, not a BPD complication.
- D. Incorrect. Biliary atresia is a congenital cholestatic disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Neonatal tetanus is an infectious disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- BPD may lead to recurrent respiratory infections, wheezing and pulmonary hypertension.
- Some children have growth and developmental difficulties.
- Prevent respiratory infections and provide long-term respiratory/developmental follow-up.

cases.title: A preterm infant has a continuous murmur and bounding pulses
cases.vignette: A 27-week infant has difficulty being weaned from respiratory support. The infant develops recurrent apnoea and signs of heart failure. Examination reveals bounding peripheral pulses, a wide pulse pressure and a continuous murmur.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Patent ductus arteriosus
questions.initialExplanation: PDA is common in very premature infants. A haemodynamically significant PDA may cause a continuous murmur, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, apnoea, heart failure and difficulty weaning respiratory support.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. TOF causes cyanosis and a systolic ejection murmur, not the typical PDA pulse pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Pulmonary atresia causes cyanotic congenital heart disease.
- C. Incorrect. Aortic stenosis causes an ejection systolic murmur and does not produce the classic PDA findings.
- D. Incorrect. Coarctation is associated with weak/delayed femoral pulses and upper-lower limb BP difference.
- E. Correct. The examination and clinical course are characteristic of PDA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PDA is common in very preterm infants.
- Signs: continuous murmur, bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure.
- May cause apnoea/bradycardia, heart failure and difficulty weaning ventilation.
- Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis and assesses haemodynamic significance.

questions.stem: A preterm infant has a haemodynamically significant PDA. Which treatment options are listed?

options.label: C
options.text: Ibuprofen or paracetamol; surgical/device closure if medical treatment fails

questions.correctAnswerText: Ibuprofen or paracetamol; surgical/device closure if medical treatment fails
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include ibuprofen or paracetamol for medical PDA closure. If medical treatment fails or is unsuitable, device/surgical closure may be considered.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vitamin K/FFP treat bleeding due to deficiency/coagulopathy.
- B. Incorrect. Desmopressin treats central diabetes insipidus.
- C. Correct. These are the treatment options described in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Surfactant treats RDS, not ductal patency.
- E. Incorrect. These treat severe jaundice/haemolysis, not PDA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PDA: confirm by echocardiography.
- Medical options: ibuprofen or paracetamol.
- If closure is unsuccessful or contraindicated, consider specialist surgical/device closure.
- Treatment choice depends on haemodynamic significance and the infant's condition.

cases.title: A very preterm infant deteriorates during the first 72 hours
cases.vignette: A 26-week infant who initially appeared stable develops pallor, apnoeic episodes and a tense, bulging anterior fontanelle on the second day of life. The neonatal team is concerned about bleeding from the fragile germinal matrix.

questions.stem: When does intraventricular haemorrhage most commonly occur in premature infants?

options.label: A
options.text: Within the first 72 hours of life

questions.correctAnswerText: Within the first 72 hours of life
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that IVH usually occurs within the first 72 hours in premature infants because of the fragility of the germinal matrix vasculature.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the time window emphasized.
- B. Incorrect. It may occur after birth during the first days, not only during delivery.
- C. Incorrect. This is not a disease of adolescence.
- D. Incorrect. IVH of prematurity is an early neonatal complication.
- E. Incorrect. The usual onset is much earlier.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IVH is particularly associated with very preterm infants.
- Most cases occur within the first 72 hours.
- Fragile germinal matrix vessels are prone to rupture.
- Risk factors include severe RDS, hypoxia/asphyxia and pneumothorax.

questions.stem: Which clinical finding may occur in a premature infant with significant IVH?

options.label: A
options.text: A continuous murmur with bounding pulses

options.label: B
options.text: Bilateral choanal obstruction relieved by crying

options.label: E
options.text: Tense/bulging anterior fontanelle with apnoea or seizures

questions.correctAnswerText: Tense/bulging anterior fontanelle with apnoea or seizures
questions.initialExplanation: IVH may be asymptomatic or present with pallor, jaundice, seizures, a tense/pulsatile fontanelle, apnoea and deterioration. Severe haemorrhage may cause shock or death.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is more suggestive of PDA.
- B. Incorrect. This is the classic presentation of bilateral choanal atresia.
- C. Incorrect. Pale stools and dark urine suggest conjugated jaundice/cholestasis.
- D. Incorrect. Erythema toxicum is a benign neonatal skin eruption.
- E. Correct. These findings are described for IVH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IVH presentation ranges from asymptomatic to seizures, pallor, jaundice, apnoea, tense AF and cardiovascular collapse.
- Cranial ultrasound is the usual bedside screening/diagnostic test in preterm infants.
- Severe IVH may lead to post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus and neurodevelopmental disability.

questions.stem: Which investigation is most useful for bedside detection of IVH in a very preterm infant?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cranial ultrasound
questions.initialExplanation: Cranial ultrasound is used to detect IVH in premature infants. CT or MRI may be used when additional detail or assessment of complications is needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Chest X-ray assesses lung/chest pathology.
- B. Incorrect. Echocardiography evaluates cardiac structure and PDA.
- C. Incorrect. Abdominal ultrasound assesses abdominal organs.
- D. Correct. Cranial ultrasound is accessible and can be performed at the bedside.
- E. Incorrect. Red reflex examines the ocular media.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cranial ultrasound is the key bedside test for IVH screening/diagnosis.
- Monitor for ventricular dilatation/hydrocephalus.
- Management is supportive and directed at complications; transfusion or neurosurgical intervention may be required in selected cases.

cases.title: A premature infant develops delayed motor abnormalities
cases.vignette: A 28-week infant has an episode of cerebral hypoxia-ischaemia during the neonatal period. The initial examination is not dramatic, but later follow-up reveals abnormal lower-limb tone and delayed motor milestones. MRI shows white-matter injury around the ventricles.

questions.stem: What is the underlying lesion in periventricular leukomalacia (PVL)?

options.label: A
options.text: Obstruction of the extrahepatic bile ducts

options.label: E
options.text: Necrosis and cystic injury of periventricular white matter

questions.correctAnswerText: Necrosis and cystic injury of periventricular white matter
questions.initialExplanation: PVL is injury to the periventricular white matter, commonly related to hypoxia-ischaemia in premature infants. It may lead to cystic changes and later motor/cognitive difficulties.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes biliary atresia.
- B. Incorrect. Surfactant deficiency causes RDS.
- C. Incorrect. Retinal neovascularization is part of ROP.
- D. Incorrect. Hepatic haemorrhage is unrelated to PVL.
- E. Correct. This is the pathological lesion described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PVL: periventricular white-matter injury/necrosis, often with cyst formation.
- Associated with prematurity and hypoxic-ischaemic insults.
- Clinical effects may become more apparent weeks later.

questions.stem: Which long-term neurological outcome is strongly associated with PVL?
questions.correctAnswerText: Spastic diplegic cerebral palsy
questions.initialExplanation: PVL affects periventricular white matter and corticospinal pathways to the lower limbs, and standard guidance links it strongly with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy. Cognitive and behavioural difficulties may also occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Spastic diplegia is a classic long-term consequence of PVL.
- B. Incorrect. Congenital cataract is an ocular abnormality.
- C. Incorrect. Hearing loss may occur in other neonatal conditions, but it is not the defining PVL outcome.
- D. Incorrect. Facial nerve palsy is a birth injury involving the facial nerve.
- E. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia is an acute metabolic disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PVL → periventricular white matter injury.
- Important late outcome: spastic diplegic CP.
- Developmental, cognitive and behavioural follow-up is required.
- MRI is useful for detecting white-matter injury.

cases.title: An extremely preterm infant requires prolonged oxygen therapy
cases.vignette: A 25-week infant with a birth weight of 850 g has required oxygen and respiratory support. During follow-up, the ophthalmology team arranges retinal screening because immature retinal vessels are vulnerable to abnormal proliferation.

questions.stem: What is the principal mechanism underlying retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia

options.label: B
options.text: Retinal infection by congenital toxoplasmosis in each case

options.label: C
options.text: Immature retinal vascularization with abnormal vessel proliferation

options.label: D
options.text: Congenital absence of the optic nerve

questions.correctAnswerText: Immature retinal vascularization with abnormal vessel proliferation
questions.initialExplanation: ROP occurs in premature infants because retinal vascularization is incomplete. Oxygen exposure and changes in oxygenation may contribute to abnormal retinal vascular proliferation, fibrosis and retinal detachment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bilirubin deposition in basal ganglia causes kernicterus.
- B. Incorrect. Toxoplasmosis can cause chorioretinitis but is not the mechanism of ROP.
- C. Correct. Immature retinal vessels may undergo abnormal proliferation and cause retinal damage.
- D. Incorrect. Optic nerve absence is a different congenital abnormality.
- E. Incorrect. Nasolacrimal obstruction causes watery eye/discharge.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ROP primarily affects very premature/low-birth-weight infants.
- Immature retinal vasculature is vulnerable to abnormal proliferation.
- Severe disease can lead to fibrosis, retinal detachment and blindness.
- Oxygen should be titrated carefully to avoid both hypoxia and hyperoxia.

questions.stem: Which infants should undergo ROP screening?

options.label: B
options.text: Birth weight below 1,500 g or gestational age below 32 weeks

questions.correctAnswerText: Birth weight below 1,500 g or gestational age below 32 weeks
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include infants weighing below 1,500 g or born before 32 weeks as candidates for ROP screening.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ROP is associated with prematurity.
- B. Correct. This is the screening threshold described.
- C. Incorrect. LGA/macrosomia is not the screening criterion.
- D. Incorrect. Mode of delivery is not the screening criterion.
- E. Incorrect. Jaundice does not determine ROP screening.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Screen very preterm and very low birth-weight infants.
- standard guidance thresholds: <1,500 g and/or <32 weeks.
- Ophthalmology follow-up timing is based on gestational age and postnatal age under the ROP screening protocol.

questions.stem: An infant has treatment-requiring ROP. Which treatment options are listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF therapy
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include laser treatment and anti-VEGF therapy for severe/treatment-requiring ROP. Early screening and follow-up are essential to prevent retinal detachment and visual loss.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ursodeoxycholic acid may be used in selected cholestatic disease.
- B. Incorrect. Surfactant treats RDS.
- C. Correct. These are the treatment modalities described.
- D. Incorrect. Vitamin K prevents haemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
- E. Incorrect. These treat neonatal jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ROP prevention: careful oxygen titration.
- Screening is essential in eligible preterm/VLBW infants.
- Severe disease: laser or intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy; selected cases may need surgery.
- Untreated severe ROP can cause retinal detachment and blindness.

cases.title: Preterm infants beyond respiratory disease: oxygen, fluids, organ immaturity and outcomes

questions.stem: A 27-week infant was resuscitated with 100% oxygen and later kept at oxygen saturations of 97-100% for weeks. At screening, the retina shows abnormal vessel proliferation. Which oxygen strategy would be consistent with standard guidance for the next preterm infant?

options.label: A
options.text: Start with 100% oxygen and aim for 97-100% to prevent NEC

options.label: B
options.text: Start with 21-30% oxygen and avoid saturations below 80%

options.label: C
options.text: Avoid supplemental oxygen entirely because it causes ROP

options.label: D
options.text: Start with 21-30% oxygen; avoid saturations below 91% (more NEC and death) and above 95% (more retinopathy of prematurity)

options.label: E
options.text: Start with 21-30% oxygen and avoid saturations above 98%, since hypoxaemia is harmless

questions.correctAnswerText: Start with 21-30% oxygen; avoid saturations below 91% (more NEC and death) and above 95% (more retinopathy of prematurity)
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes starting resuscitation of preterm infants with 21-30% oxygen, correcting hypoxaemia, and avoiding both low saturations (<91%, higher NEC and mortality) and high saturations (>95%, higher ROP).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. High oxygen and high saturations increase the risk of ROP.
- B. Incorrect. Saturations below 91% are already linked with NEC and death.
- C. Incorrect. Oxygen is needed to correct hypoxaemia; the aim is to use the least possible for the shortest time.
- D. Correct. Matches the starting concentration and both saturation limits.
- E. Incorrect. Hypoxaemia is harmful; both extremes must be avoided.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preterm resuscitation: start with 21-30% oxygen.
- SpO₂ <91%: more NEC and death. SpO₂ >95%: more ROP.
- ROP prevention: least oxygen for the least duration.
- Screen ROP in infants ≤1,500 g or <32 weeks.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 17 (oxygen therapy in preterm infants; ROP).

cases.title: A very low birth-weight infant develops feeding intolerance and abdominal distension
cases.vignette: A 29-week, 1,050-g infant has been receiving enteral feeds for 10 days. The infant develops increasing abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, bloody stool, temperature instability and apnoeic episodes. Abdominal radiography shows pneumatosis intestinalis.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC)
questions.initialExplanation: NEC is an acute inflammatory necrotizing disease of the intestine, mainly affecting premature and very low birth-weight infants. It presents with feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, vomiting and bloody stool.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Intussusception usually occurs in older infants and children and does not explain the classic preterm NICU presentation.
- B. Incorrect. Physiological reflux does not cause bloody stool, systemic instability or pneumatosis.
- C. Incorrect. Biliary atresia causes conjugated jaundice, pale stool and dark urine.
- D. Correct. The infant's risk profile, clinical presentation and pneumatosis strongly support NEC.
- E. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting, usually in older infants.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NEC predominantly affects preterm/VLBW infants.
- Symptoms: feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, bloody stool and systemic instability.
- Pneumatosis intestinalis is a characteristic radiographic sign.

questions.stem: Which radiological finding is characteristic of NEC?

options.label: A
options.text: Double-bubble sign in the upper abdomen

options.label: B
options.text: Diffuse perihilar streaking and fluid in fissures

options.label: C
options.text: Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall)

questions.correctAnswerText: Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall)
questions.initialExplanation: Pneumatosis intestinalis, representing gas within the intestinal wall, is a characteristic radiological sign of NEC. Portal venous gas and pneumoperitoneum may also be seen.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A double-bubble sign suggests duodenal obstruction/atresia.
- B. Incorrect. This is a radiographic feature of TTN.
- C. Correct. This is the characteristic radiological finding of NEC.
- D. Incorrect. This is typical of RDS.
- E. Incorrect. Bowel loops in the chest suggest congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NEC X-ray findings: pneumatosis intestinalis, dilated loops, portal venous gas and free air if perforation.
- Pneumoperitoneum suggests intestinal perforation and may require surgery.
- Interpret X-ray with clinical signs and serial examinations.

questions.stem: Which factor increases the risk of NEC in a premature infant?

options.label: D
options.text: Normal intestinal barrier and mature immunity

options.label: E
options.text: Term gestation with normal birth weight

questions.correctAnswerText: Prematurity and formula/aggressive enteral feeding
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include prematurity, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, abnormal bacterial colonization, formula feeding, PDA, polycythaemia, umbilical catheters, ibuprofen and aggressive/hyperosmolar feeds among NEC risk factors. Breast milk is protective.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Breast milk is protective rather than a risk factor.
- B. Correct. Prematurity and formula/aggressive enteral feeding increase NEC risk.
- C. Incorrect. Skin-to-skin contact is beneficial and not a risk factor.
- D. Incorrect. Intestinal immaturity and immature immunity are central to NEC susceptibility.
- E. Incorrect. NEC is much more common in premature/VLBW infants.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NEC risk factors: prematurity, hypoxia/ischaemia, abnormal bacterial colonization, formula/hyperosmolar feeds, PDA, polycythaemia, UVC and some medications.
- Human breast milk is protective.
- Risk rises as gestational age and birth weight decrease.

questions.stem: A premature infant has suspected NEC with abdominal distension, bloody stool and systemic instability. Which initial management is most appropriate?

options.label: B
options.text: Stop enteral feeds, decompress the stomach with an NG tube, provide IV fluids/antibiotics and supportive NICU care

questions.correctAnswerText: Stop enteral feeds, decompress the stomach with an NG tube, provide IV fluids/antibiotics and supportive NICU care
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include immediate cessation of enteral feeds (NPO), NG decompression, IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and supportive care in the NICU. Surgery is considered for perforation or clinical deterioration/failure of medical management.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Phototherapy treats neonatal jaundice.
- B. Correct. This is the initial management approach described.
- C. Incorrect. NEC is a potentially life-threatening neonatal emergency requiring hospital care.
- D. Incorrect. Continuing feeds can worsen intestinal injury.
- E. Incorrect. Laxatives are inappropriate in suspected NEC.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NEC: NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and close monitoring.
- Monitor abdominal findings, perfusion, platelets, inflammatory markers, electrolytes and acid-base status.
- Surgery is required for perforation or selected severe/progressive disease.
- Preventive care includes breast milk, cautious feeding advancement and infection prevention.

cases.title: A preterm infant with several risk factors develops a surgical abdomen

questions.stem: A 29-week, 1,100 g infant at day 12 has an umbilical venous catheter, was treated with ibuprofen for a PDA, is polycythaemic and had rapid feed advancement. He develops bilious vomiting, bloody stool, abdominal wall erythema and shock. The abdominal X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis, gas in the portal venous system and gas under the diaphragm. What is the best next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue feeds with a hyperosmolar formula to maintain gut function

options.label: B
options.text: Stop feeds, decompress with NG tube, give IV fluids/antibiotics, support breathing/circulation and obtain surgical review

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the abdominal X-ray in 48 hours before changing management

options.label: D
options.text: Give extra ibuprofen to treat the PDA and relieve gut hypoperfusion

options.label: E
options.text: Insert a chest drain for the free air

questions.correctAnswerText: Stop feeds, decompress with NG tube, give IV fluids/antibiotics, support breathing/circulation and obtain surgical review
questions.initialExplanation: This is NEC with perforation (free gas under the diaphragm). standard guidance's treatment is NICU care, nil by mouth, IV fluids, NG tube on free drainage, IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole), systemic respiratory and circulatory support, and surgical consultation for GI perforation or failure of medical treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Aggressive and hyperosmolar feeds are risk factors for NEC.
- B. Correct. Combines medical management with surgical consultation for perforation.
- C. Incorrect. Free air means perforation, so waiting delays treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Ibuprofen is itself listed as a risk factor for NEC.
- E. Incorrect. The free air is intraperitoneal; a chest drain is for pleural air.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- NEC risk factors: prematurity, asphyxia, polycythaemia, PDA, aggressive/bottle/hyperosmolar feeds, UVC, drugs such as ibuprofen.
- X-ray: pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, dilated loops, free air (football sign) with perforation.
- Surgery: perforation or failure of medical therapy.
- Prevention: avoid aggressive feeding, breastfeeding, antenatal steroids, early treatment of sepsis.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Pages 18-19 (Necrotizing enterocolitis: risk factors, X-ray, treatment).

topics.name: Other Complications of Prematurity and Feeding Support

cases.title: A very preterm infant develops several systemic complications
cases.vignette: A 27-week infant weighing 920 g remains in the NICU. In addition to respiratory disease, the infant has difficulty maintaining temperature, recurrent low glucose, anaemia and poor feed tolerance. The team reviews the multisystem effects of immaturity and the principles of nutritional support.

questions.stem: Which mechanism contributes most directly to hypothermia in a very premature infant?

options.label: B
options.text: Thin skin, little subcutaneous fat, large surface area relative to weight and immature thermoregulation

options.label: D
options.text: Increased ability to produce shivering heat

options.label: E
options.text: Thick subcutaneous fat and mature temperature regulation

questions.correctAnswerText: Thin skin, little subcutaneous fat, large surface area relative to weight and immature thermoregulation
questions.initialExplanation: Premature infants lose heat easily because of thin skin, low subcutaneous fat, a high surface-area-to-weight ratio and immature hypothalamic temperature regulation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Preterm infants have less muscle mass and limited heat reserves.
- B. Correct. These factors increase heat loss and vulnerability to hypothermia.
- C. Incorrect. Excessive sweating is not the reason for neonatal hypothermia.
- D. Incorrect. Shivering thermogenesis is limited in newborns.
- E. Incorrect. Preterm infants have little subcutaneous fat and immature temperature control.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prematurity predisposes to hypothermia because of skin immaturity, low SC fat and high surface area.
- Hypothermia increases oxygen/glucose consumption and worsens metabolic instability.
- Maintain neutral thermal environment, dry/wrap promptly and monitor temperature.

questions.stem: Why are premature infants more prone to anaemia during NICU admission?

options.label: B
options.text: Increased intestinal iron absorption in most preterm infants

options.label: C
options.text: Longer red-cell lifespan and increased erythropoietin

options.label: E
options.text: Shorter red-cell lifespan, low iron stores, frequent blood sampling and low erythropoietin response

questions.correctAnswerText: Shorter red-cell lifespan, low iron stores, frequent blood sampling and low erythropoietin response
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include anaemia of prematurity as multifactorial: shortened red-cell survival, low iron stores, frequent phlebotomy and relatively low erythropoietin production.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vitamin K is involved in coagulation, not red-cell production.
- B. Incorrect. Premature infants often have limited nutrient stores and immature absorption.
- C. Incorrect. Premature infants have a shorter red-cell lifespan and relatively low erythropoietin response.
- D. Incorrect. Red-cell production is not excessively increased.
- E. Correct. These mechanisms contribute to anaemia of prematurity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Anaemia of prematurity: short RBC lifespan, low EPO, low iron stores, phlebotomy and rapid growth.
- Iron supplementation is used during follow-up as indicated.
- PRBC transfusion is reserved for selected severe/symptomatic cases under NICU policy.

questions.stem: A very preterm infant develops dehydration, electrolyte disturbances and rising creatinine. Which explanation best accounts for this susceptibility?

options.label: A
options.text: Immature renal function with limited fluid/electrolyte regulation and vulnerability to hypotension

options.label: E
options.text: Fully mature tubular handling of sodium and water

questions.correctAnswerText: Immature renal function with limited fluid/electrolyte regulation and vulnerability to hypotension
questions.initialExplanation: Key features include renal immaturity in premature infants, leading to difficulty regulating fluid and electrolytes and increased risk of hypotension, dehydration and acute renal failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Immature tubular and renal function explains fluid/electrolyte instability.
- B. Incorrect. Renal concentrating ability is immature.
- C. Incorrect. Premature infants do not have excessive renal filtration reserve.
- D. Incorrect. Renal reserve is limited, not increased.
- E. Incorrect. Tubular handling of sodium and water is immature.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preterm kidneys have immature concentrating and electrolyte-handling functions.
- Monitor fluid balance, urine output, electrolytes, blood pressure and renal function.
- Hypotension and dehydration can precipitate acute kidney injury.

questions.stem: Which is an appropriate nutritional approach for a very preterm infant who cannot yet suck and swallow safely?

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid breast milk because it increases NEC risk

options.label: D
options.text: Withhold most enteral nutrition until discharge

options.label: E
options.text: Use expressed breast milk through an NG/OG tube when appropriate, with parenteral nutrition if enteral intake is insufficient

questions.correctAnswerText: Use expressed breast milk through an NG/OG tube when appropriate, with parenteral nutrition if enteral intake is insufficient
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes breast milk/colostrum as the preferred nutrition. NG/OG feeding is used when the infant cannot coordinate sucking and swallowing, while TPN may be necessary in extremely premature or critically ill infants.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Cow's milk is not an appropriate substitute for neonatal breast milk/formula.
- B. Incorrect. Breast milk is protective against NEC.
- C. Incorrect. Large oral feeds risk aspiration and feeding intolerance.
- D. Incorrect. Enteral feeding is introduced when clinically appropriate; it is not withheld until discharge.
- E. Correct. Tube feeding with breast milk is appropriate when oral coordination is immature.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Breast milk/colostrum is the preferred nutrition for preterm infants.
- NG/OG feeding is used when oral feeding is unsafe.
- Trophic feeds may be started in selected stable infants.
- TPN is considered when enteral nutrition is insufficient or contraindicated.

cases.title: Preterm infants beyond respiratory disease: oxygen, fluids, organ immaturity and outcomes

questions.stem: A 28-week infant has hypoglycaemia, mainly indirect jaundice and a low albumin on day 2. At 3 weeks the infant is dehydrated with electrolyte imbalance and hypotension.
