At 7 weeks the bones are poorly mineralized with low calcium, phosphate and vitamin D. Which pairing of organ and problem is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Liver: poor bone mineralization; kidney: hypoglycaemia; bone: jaundice

options.label: B
options.text: Kidney: hypoglycaemia and jaundice; liver: electrolyte imbalance; bone: hypotension

options.label: C
options.text: Liver: acute renal failure; kidney: hypoalbuminaemia; bone: dehydration

options.label: D
options.text: most three problems are caused by immature lungs

options.label: E
options.text: Liver: hypoglycaemia/jaundice/hypoalbuminaemia; kidney: fluid/electrolyte problems; bone: osteopenia

questions.correctAnswerText: Liver: hypoglycaemia/jaundice/hypoalbuminaemia; kidney: fluid/electrolyte problems; bone: osteopenia
questions.initialExplanation: An immature liver with low stores and immature enzymes leads to hypoglycaemia, indirect jaundice and hypoalbuminaemia. Immature kidneys cause electrolyte imbalance, hypotension, dehydration and acute renal failure. Low calcium, phosphate and vitamin D cause osteopenia of prematurity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Organs and problems are mismatched.
- B. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia and jaundice come from the liver, not the kidney.
- C. Incorrect. Renal failure is a kidney problem, and albumin is made by the liver.
- D. Incorrect. Lung immaturity causes RDS, not these metabolic problems.
- E. Correct. Each problem is attributed to the right organ.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Liver immaturity: hypoglycaemia, indirect jaundice, hypoalbuminaemia.
- Renal immaturity: electrolyte imbalance, hypotension, dehydration, ARF.
- Bone: osteopenia of prematurity (low calcium, phosphate, vitamin D).
- Hypoalbuminaemia raises the kernicterus risk.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Pages 20-21 (Metabolic complications of prematurity: liver, kidneys, bone).
source.pages: 20-21 (Metabolic complications of prematurity: liver, kidneys, bone)

questions.stem: The parents of a 27-week, 900 g infant who is about to be discharged ask about long-term outcomes. Which statement agrees with standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Cerebral palsy affects more than half of very-low-birth-weight infants, and learning difficulties are rare

options.label: B
options.text: Hearing loss occurs in 20-30% and nearly most need amplification

options.label: C
options.text: Learning difficulties are commonest; CP occurs in 5–10%; visual and respiratory problems are also common

options.label: D
options.text: Visual problems occur in infants who had ROP, and refractive errors are uncommon

options.label: E
options.text: Late problems occur after IVH, and respiratory infection risk equals that of term infants

questions.correctAnswerText: Learning difficulties are commonest; CP occurs in 5–10%; visual and respiratory problems are also common
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include late outcomes: about 5-10% of very-low-birth-weight infants develop cerebral palsy, but the commonest impairment is learning difficulty. Hearing impairment affects 1-2% and needs amplification; about 1% are blind in both eyes, and refractive errors and squints are common. There is also a higher risk of respiratory failure from bronchiolitis and lower respiratory tract infection, especially with BPD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Cerebral palsy is 5-10%, and learning difficulty is the commonest problem.
- B. Incorrect. Hearing impairment is 1-2%.
- C. Correct. Matches clinical guidance's outcome figures and the respiratory risk.
- D. Incorrect. Refractive errors and squints are common.
- E. Incorrect. Late problems are not limited to IVH, and respiratory risk is increased.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- VLBW late outcomes: cerebral palsy 5-10%; commonest impairment is learning difficulty.
- Hearing impairment 1-2% need amplification; blindness in both eyes about 1%.
- Refractive errors and squints are common.
- Increased risk of respiratory failure from bronchiolitis/LRTI, especially with BPD.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 21 (late-onset complications after discharge).

cases.title: A newborn is delivered at 42 weeks and has dry peeling skin
cases.vignette: A baby is born at 42 weeks and 3 days. The infant is alert with abundant scalp hair, long nails and dry, wrinkled, peeling skin stained by meconium. The baby appears relatively thin despite prolonged gestation. The neonatal team monitors for complications related to placental insufficiency and intrapartum stress.

questions.stem: How is post-term pregnancy defined?

options.label: C
options.text: Delivery at or beyond 42 completed weeks

questions.correctAnswerText: Delivery at or beyond 42 completed weeks
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe post-term delivery as birth at 42 weeks or more.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The threshold is 42 weeks, not 44 weeks.
- B. Incorrect. Birth after 35 weeks may still be preterm or late preterm.
- C. Correct. Post-term begins at 42 completed weeks.
- D. Incorrect. This defines preterm birth.
- E. Incorrect. This is within the term range.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Post-term: ≥42 completed weeks.
- Many post-term pregnancies have no identifiable cause.
- Previous post-term pregnancy is a risk factor; anencephaly is listed as a fetal association.

questions.stem: Which physical appearance is most characteristic of a post-mature infant?

options.label: A
options.text: Small breast nodule and underdeveloped genitalia

options.label: C
options.text: Thin shiny skin, lanugo and few sole creases

options.label: D
options.text: Soft ear cartilage and smooth scrotum

options.label: E
options.text: Dry wrinkled peeling skin, long nails, abundant hair and possible meconium staining

questions.correctAnswerText: Dry wrinkled peeling skin, long nails, abundant hair and possible meconium staining
questions.initialExplanation: Post-mature infants may appear alert with abundant hair, long nails and dry, wrinkled, peeling skin, sometimes stained by meconium.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are more consistent with prematurity.
- B. Incorrect. Generalized oedema suggests hydrops or another pathological process.
- C. Incorrect. These are signs of prematurity.
- D. Incorrect. These are immature physical features.
- E. Correct. These are the characteristic post-maturity findings listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Post-mature appearance: alert, abundant hair, long nails, dry/wrinkled/peeling skin and meconium staining.
- Birth weight may be average or reduced due to placental insufficiency.
- Do not confuse post-maturity with LGA.

questions.stem: Which complication is particularly important to anticipate in a post-term infant with meconium staining and a history of fetal distress?
questions.correctAnswerText: Meconium aspiration syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Post-term infants are at increased risk of intrapartum stress and meconium passage, which can lead to meconium aspiration syndrome. Other complications listed include asphyxia, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, polycythaemia and PPHN.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism is not a specific post-term complication.
- B. Incorrect. Biliary atresia is a cause of conjugated jaundice.
- C. Incorrect. ROP is associated with prematurity, not post-term birth.
- D. Incorrect. DDH is a developmental orthopaedic condition.
- E. Correct. Meconium-stained liquor and fetal distress raise concern for MAS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Post-term complications: intrapartum asphyxia, MAS, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, polycythaemia and PPHN.
- Assess respiratory status, perfusion and glucose after birth.
- Prepare for appropriate resuscitation if fetal compromise/meconium is present.

topics.name: Large for Gestational Age and Macrosomia

cases.title: A large newborn is delivered to a mother with poorly controlled diabetes
cases.vignette: A term infant is born weighing 4.6 kg. The baby has a plethoric, rounded appearance and is large for gestational age. The mother had poorly controlled gestational diabetes. The neonatal team plans to monitor for hypoglycaemia, polycythaemia and birth injury.

questions.stem: How is an infant classified as large for gestational age (LGA)?

options.label: A
options.text: Birth weight between the 10th and 90th centiles

options.label: B
options.text: Any infant weighing more than 3 kg

options.label: C
options.text: Birth weight above the 90th centile for gestational age

questions.correctAnswerText: Birth weight above the 90th centile for gestational age
questions.initialExplanation: LGA is defined as birth weight above the 90th centile for gestational age. It is a centile-based classification and is not identical to macrosomia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The 10th-90th centile range defines AGA.
- B. Incorrect. LGA is defined by centile for gestational age, not a fixed 3-kg threshold.
- C. Correct. This is the definition of LGA.
- D. Incorrect. Below the 10th centile defines SGA.
- E. Incorrect. Below 2,500 g defines low birth weight.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LGA: >90th centile for gestational age.
- AGA: 10th-90th centile.
- SGA: <10th centile.
- Macrosomia is an absolute weight concept; standard guidance uses >4.5 kg.

questions.stem: Which is the most common cause of LGA listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Familial/constitutional large size
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include familial/constitutional size as the most common cause of LGA, followed by maternal diabetes, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and hydrops fetalis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Maternal undernutrition is associated with reduced fetal growth.
- B. Incorrect. Maternal smoking is associated with impaired fetal growth.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism is not a typical cause of LGA.
- D. Correct. Familial/constitutional large size is listed as the commonest cause.
- E. Incorrect. Placental insufficiency causes IUGR/SGA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LGA causes: familial/constitutional, infant of diabetic mother, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and hydrops.
- LGA may occur in both term and preterm infants.
- Maternal diabetes is an important acquired risk factor.

questions.stem: Which complication should be anticipated in an LGA infant born to a diabetic mother?

options.label: C
options.text: Hypoglycaemia due to absent fetal insulin

options.label: D
options.text: Neonatal hypoglycaemia due to persistent fetal hyperinsulinaemia

options.label: E
options.text: Severe surfactant deficiency in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Neonatal hypoglycaemia due to persistent fetal hyperinsulinaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta and causes fetal hyperglycaemia, stimulating fetal insulin production. After delivery, maternal glucose supply stops but the infant's insulin remains high, causing hypoglycaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Biliary atresia is unrelated.
- B. Incorrect. ROP is associated with prematurity and retinal vascular immaturity.
- C. Incorrect. The problem is persistent insulin excess, not absent insulin.
- D. Correct. This is the key mechanism in infants of diabetic mothers.
- E. Incorrect. RDS risk may be increased in infants of diabetic mothers, but it is not inevitable.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infant of diabetic mother: maternal glucose crosses placenta → fetal hyperglycaemia → fetal hyperinsulinism → neonatal hypoglycaemia after cord separation.
- Feed early and monitor glucose in at-risk infants.
- Other risks: polycythaemia, jaundice, birth injury and congenital anomalies.

questions.stem: A large infant develops shoulder dystocia during delivery. Which additional complication is particularly associated with macrosomia/LGA?

options.label: B
options.text: Birth trauma, including brachial plexus injury and clavicle fracture

options.label: D
options.text: Intraventricular haemorrhage due to prematurity in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Birth trauma, including brachial plexus injury and clavicle fracture
questions.initialExplanation: Macrosomia increases the risk of difficult delivery, shoulder dystocia and birth injuries such as brachial plexus palsy and clavicle fracture.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Biliary atresia is a cholestatic disorder.
- B. Correct. These are classic birth injuries associated with LGA/macrosomia.
- C. Incorrect. ROP is associated with prematurity and retinal immaturity.
- D. Incorrect. IVH is mainly associated with very preterm infants.
- E. Incorrect. CMV is a congenital infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LGA/macrosomia increases shoulder dystocia and birth trauma risk.
- Injuries include brachial plexus palsy, clavicle fracture and other skeletal injuries.
- Preventive planning includes maternal diabetes control, delivery planning and preparedness for neonatal resuscitation.

cases.title: Twins are delivered preterm after a complicated monochorionic pregnancy
cases.vignette: A monochorionic twin pregnancy is complicated by discordant growth and fetal fluid imbalance. The twins are delivered preterm.

questions.stem: Which complication is particularly associated with monochorionic twin pregnancies?

options.label: B
options.text: Coarctation of the aorta in each twin pair

options.label: C
options.text: Congenital cataract in each twin pair

questions.correctAnswerText: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) occurs in monochorionic twins because of placental vascular anastomoses that allow unbalanced blood flow from donor to recipient. standard guidance estimates an incidence of approximately 10-15% in monochorionic pregnancies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. TTTS is specifically associated with monochorionic placentation.
- B. Incorrect. Coarctation is not a universal twin complication.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital cataract is not a universal twin complication.
- D. Incorrect. Biliary atresia is not a complication specific to twin pregnancy.
- E. Incorrect. Neonatal tetanus is an infection unrelated to chorionicity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TTTS occurs in monochorionic twins due to placental vascular anastomoses.
- standard guidance gives an approximate incidence of 10-15%.
- Monitor for discordant growth, fluid imbalance and cardiovascular compromise.

questions.stem: Which group contains complications of multiple pregnancy listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Preterm delivery, IUGR, congenital anomalies, TTTS and delivery trauma

questions.correctAnswerText: Preterm delivery, IUGR, congenital anomalies, TTTS and delivery trauma
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include preterm labour, IUGR, congenital anomalies, TTTS in monochorionic twins, complicated delivery and birth trauma, and conjoined twins among multiple pregnancy complications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This includes the main complications listed.
- B. Incorrect. Jaundice is not the only or defining multiple pregnancy complication.
- C. Incorrect. Neonatal seizures may occur but do not represent the full list.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism is not the only complication.
- E. Incorrect. These are not the principal complications of multiple pregnancy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Multiple pregnancy increases the risk of prematurity and IUGR.
- Monochorionic twins are at risk of TTTS.
- Congenital anomalies and difficult delivery/birth trauma may occur.
- Conjoined twins are a rare complication.

cases.title: Counselling about a monochorionic twin pregnancy

questions.stem: Ultrasound shows a twin pregnancy with a single placenta. The couple asks about risks. Which statement agrees with standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Twin-to-twin transfusion occurs in 10-15% of dichorionic pregnancies, and anomaly rates are equal in both types

options.label: B
options.text: Dichorionic twins have an 8% risk of congenital abnormality and monochorionic twins 4%

options.label: C
options.text: Monochorionic twins have the higher risk of congenital abnormality (about 8% versus 4% in dichorionic) and twin-to-twin transfusion in about 10-15%

options.label: D
options.text: Twins are at no increased risk of preterm labour; conjoined twins carry risk

options.label: E
options.text: Twin pregnancy does not increase the risk of growth restriction

questions.correctAnswerText: Monochorionic twins have the higher risk of congenital abnormality (about 8% versus 4% in dichorionic) and twin-to-twin transfusion in about 10-15%
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance gives a 4% risk of congenital abnormality in dichorionic and 8% in monochorionic twins, and twin-to-twin transfusion in about 10-15% of monochorionic pregnancies. Preterm labour and IUGR are also increased.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Twin-to-twin transfusion is a monochorionic complication.
- B. Incorrect. The percentages are reversed.
- C. Correct. Matches both figures.
- D. Incorrect. Preterm labour is a major complication of multiple births.
- E. Incorrect. IUGR is also increased.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Newborn complications: preterm labour, IUGR, congenital abnormalities, TTTS, birth trauma, conjoined twins.
- Congenital anomalies: 4% (dichorionic) versus 8% (monochorionic).
- TTTS in 10-15% of monochorionic pregnancies.

cases.title: A newborn has a low birth weight and asymmetric body proportions
cases.vignette: A term infant is born with a birth weight below the 10th centile. The head circumference is relatively preserved, but weight and abdominal growth are reduced. The mother had severe pre-eclampsia and smoked during pregnancy. The neonatal team distinguishes fetal growth restriction from being simply small for gestational age.

questions.stem: What is the best definition of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)?

options.label: A
options.text: Birth weight below 2,500 g regardless of gestational age

options.label: B
options.text: Failure of the fetus to achieve its genetically determined growth potential

options.label: D
options.text: Any newborn with a head circumference below 35 cm

questions.correctAnswerText: Failure of the fetus to achieve its genetically determined growth potential
questions.initialExplanation: IUGR describes failure of the fetus to achieve its genetic growth potential. SGA is a statistical birth-weight category, usually below the 10th centile for gestational age, and the two terms are related but not synonymous.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. LBW is an absolute birth-weight threshold, not the definition of IUGR.
- B. Correct. This is the definition described.
- C. Incorrect. This defines preterm birth.
- D. Incorrect. Head circumference alone does not define IUGR.
- E. Incorrect. This defines LGA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IUGR: failure to reach genetic growth potential.
- SGA: birth weight <10th centile for gestational age.
- SGA and IUGR are not interchangeable; a constitutionally small infant may be SGA without pathological growth restriction.
- Assess weight, length, head circumference and maternal/placental history.

questions.stem: A newborn has reduced weight, length and head circumference. The pregnancy was complicated by a congenital infection during the first trimester. Which pattern of IUGR is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Symmetrical IUGR
questions.initialExplanation: Symmetrical IUGR affects weight, length and head circumference. It usually results from an early fetal insult, often in the first trimester, including chromosomal abnormalities, congenital malformations and TORCH infections.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. LGA is birth weight above the 90th centile.
- B. Incorrect. Asymmetrical IUGR predominantly affects weight, while head growth is relatively spared; it usually results from later placental/maternal compromise.
- C. Correct. All growth parameters are reduced and the insult occurred early.
- D. Incorrect. Macrosomia is an excessive absolute birth weight.
- E. Incorrect. Post-maturity relates to prolonged gestation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Symmetrical IUGR: weight, length and OFC all reduced.
- Typically an early first-trimester insult.
- Causes: chromosomal abnormalities, congenital malformation and TORCH infection.
- Prognosis may be poorer because cell number and overall organ growth are affected early.

questions.stem: A newborn has a low weight and reduced abdominal circumference, but head circumference is relatively preserved. The mother had severe pre-eclampsia in the third trimester. Which pattern is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Asymmetrical IUGR due to late placental insufficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Symmetrical IUGR due to early fetal infection

questions.correctAnswerText: Asymmetrical IUGR due to late placental insufficiency
questions.initialExplanation: Asymmetrical IUGR predominantly affects weight, while head growth is relatively spared (brain-sparing). It commonly follows a third-trimester maternal/placental insult such as pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The preserved head circumference and maternal pre-eclampsia support asymmetrical IUGR.
- B. Incorrect. Post-term infants are born at ≥42 weeks and may have dry peeling skin and other dysmaturity features.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism is a separate endocrine disorder.
- D. Incorrect. Symmetrical IUGR usually follows an early insult and affects weight, length and head circumference.
- E. Incorrect. LGA describes a birth weight above the 90th centile.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Asymmetrical IUGR: weight is most affected; head circumference is relatively spared.
- Typically a later third-trimester insult.
- Maternal/placental causes: pre-eclampsia, undernutrition, diabetes/vascular disease, smoking/alcohol, placental insufficiency and multiple gestation.
- Prognosis is generally better than symmetrical IUGR if the insult is late and head growth is spared.

questions.stem: Which complication is particularly likely in an IUGR newborn because of reduced glycogen and fat stores?

options.label: B
options.text: Retinopathy of prematurity in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia
questions.initialExplanation: IUGR infants have reduced glycogen reserves and limited subcutaneous fat, increasing the risk of hypoglycaemia and hypothermia. Chronic fetal hypoxia also predisposes to polycythaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Biliary atresia is a cholestatic disorder.
- B. Incorrect. ROP is associated with prematurity and retinal immaturity; it is not inevitable in IUGR.
- C. Correct. Low glycogen predisposes to hypoglycaemia, while low fat stores increase heat loss.
- D. Incorrect. These are not the typical metabolic risks.
- E. Incorrect. Cataract is not a characteristic consequence of IUGR.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IUGR complications: birth asphyxia, MAS, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, polycythaemia, PPHN and congenital anomalies.
- Reduced glycogen → hypoglycaemia.
- Reduced SC fat → hypothermia.
- Chronic intrauterine hypoxia → increased EPO and polycythaemia.

questions.stem: A newborn with IUGR is plethoric and has respiratory distress. Which mechanism explains the increased risk of polycythaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Maternal iron deficiency suppresses fetal erythropoiesis

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic intrauterine hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin production

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic intrauterine hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin production
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic fetal hypoxia increases erythropoietin production, stimulating fetal erythropoiesis and increasing haematocrit. Polycythaemia increases blood viscosity and may impair perfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Maternal iron deficiency may contribute to anaemia, not polycythaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Platelet transfer does not explain increased red-cell mass.
- C. Incorrect. Insulin is not the mechanism responsible for hypoxia-induced polycythaemia.
- D. Correct. This is the mechanism of hypoxia-related fetal polycythaemia.
- E. Incorrect. Reduced bilirubin conjugation causes unconjugated jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chronic fetal hypoxia → ↑EPO → polycythaemia.
- Hyperviscosity may contribute to respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia, thrombosis and neurological symptoms.
- Evaluate haematocrit and treat according to symptoms/viscosity and local neonatal protocol.

cases.title: Four SGA term infants and discharge planning

questions.stem: Four term infants with intrauterine growth restriction are ready for review. Which one can be discharged?

options.label: A
options.text: 2,300 g, sucks well, gaining weight, keeps temperature at room temperature, and the mother can care for the baby

options.label: B
options.text: 2,300 g, feeds poorly and becomes cold in the cot

options.label: C
options.text: 1,700 g, feeds well and has a stable temperature

options.label: D
options.text: 2,200 g, gaining weight, but the mother is unable to care for the infant

questions.correctAnswerText: 2,300 g, sucks well, gaining weight, keeps temperature at room temperature, and the mother can care for the baby
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance advises NICU admission for birth weight below 1,800 g, and discharge when the baby sucks well, gains weight, maintains temperature at room temperature and the mother can care for the infant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Meets all four discharge criteria.
- B. Incorrect. Poor feeding and hypothermia fail the criteria.
- C. Incorrect. Below 1,800 g, so NICU admission applies.
- D. Incorrect. Maternal ability to care is one of the criteria.
- E. Incorrect. Weight loss means the weight-gain criterion is not met.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Admit to NICU if birth weight <1,800 g.
- Discharge criteria: sucking well, weight gain, temperature maintained at room temperature, mother capable.
- IUGR complications: asphyxia/MAS, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, polycythaemia, PPHN, thrombocytopenia.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Pages 23-24 (IUGR complications and management).

topics.name: Neonatal Sepsis - Early-Onset and Late-Onset Infection

cases.title: A 2-day-old newborn develops respiratory distress and poor feeding
cases.vignette: A 34-week infant is admitted at 48 hours of life with tachypnoea, apnoeic episodes, poor feeding, lethargy and temperature instability. The mother had prolonged rupture of membranes for 22 hours and suspected chorioamnionitis.

questions.stem: How is early-onset neonatal sepsis (EOS) usually defined?

options.label: B
options.text: Infection acquired after 28 days of life

options.label: C
options.text: Infection acquired after prolonged NICU admission

options.label: E
options.text: Infection acquired shortly before or during delivery, usually presenting in the first week and commonly within 72 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Infection acquired shortly before or during delivery, usually presenting in the first week and commonly within 72 hours
questions.initialExplanation: EOS is usually acquired shortly before or during delivery, often through the birth canal. Clinical guidance notes that most cases present in the first week, with many occurring within the first 72 hours.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. EOS occurs in the early neonatal period, not exclusively after 3 months.
- B. Incorrect. This is well beyond the neonatal period and does not describe EOS.
- C. Incorrect. Hospital-acquired infection after delivery is more typical of LOS.
- D. Incorrect. Clinical descriptions include neonatal sepsis mainly as a serious systemic bacterial infection.
- E. Correct. This matches the timing and route described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EOS: acquired before/during delivery, usually in the first week (often ≤72 hours).
- LOS: acquired after delivery, after the first 72 hours/first week depending on the classification used.
- EOS commonly presents with respiratory distress.
- Timing helps guide likely organisms and empirical therapy.

questions.stem: Which maternal history is a significant risk factor for EOS?

options.label: E
options.text: Rupture of membranes for more than 18 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Rupture of membranes for more than 18 hours
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include prolonged rupture of membranes (PROM >18 hours), chorioamnionitis/UTI, maternal bacteraemia, maternal GBS carriage, prematurity and a previous infant with GBS infection among EOS risk factors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. An uncomplicated prior term delivery is not a specific risk factor.
- B. Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis is not an EOS risk factor.
- C. Incorrect. Myopia does not increase neonatal sepsis risk.
- D. Incorrect. Iron supplementation is not an EOS risk factor.
- E. Correct. PROM over 18 hours increases exposure to ascending infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EOS risks: prematurity, PROM >18 h, chorioamnionitis, maternal UTI/bacteraemia, GBS carriage and a previous GBS-infected infant.
- Ask about maternal fever, intrapartum antibiotics, GBS status and duration of membrane rupture.
- A newborn may be infected even when maternal symptoms are mild.

questions.stem: Which organism is a major cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Group B beta-haemolytic Streptococcus
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include GBS, E. coli, Klebsiella, Haemophilus influenzae, Listeria monocytogenes and Pseudomonas among organisms that may cause EOS, with GBS particularly important.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Rotavirus causes gastroenteritis, not typical bacterial EOS.
- B. Incorrect. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is not a major neonatal EOS organism.
- C. Incorrect. Coagulase-negative staphylococci are more often associated with late-onset/NICU-acquired infection.
- D. Correct. GBS is a major early-onset pathogen and is associated with maternal genital tract carriage.
- E. Incorrect. Candida can cause neonatal infection, especially in high-risk NICU infants, but is not the major organism emphasized for EOS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EOS organisms: GBS and Gram-negative organisms such as E. coli and Klebsiella; also Listeria and others listed.
- LOS organisms: CONS, Staph aureus, GBS, Pseudomonas and Klebsiella.
- Organism distribution depends on maternal risk and local NICU epidemiology.

questions.stem: A newborn with suspected EOS is lethargic, poorly feeding and has temperature instability. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The absence of fever excludes neonatal sepsis

options.label: B
options.text: Early neonatal sepsis often has non-specific manifestations

options.label: C
options.text: Poor feeding is not usually associated with sepsis

options.label: D
options.text: Neonatal sepsis typically presents with a specific localizing sign

questions.correctAnswerText: Early neonatal sepsis often has non-specific manifestations
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is that early manifestations of neonatal sepsis are often non-specific. They may include respiratory distress/apnoea, temperature instability, lethargy or irritability, poor perfusion/mottling, poor feeding, vomiting, abdominal distension, diarrhoea and weak Moro/suck reflexes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Preterm infants may develop hypothermia rather than fever.
- B. Correct. Non-specific systemic features are common in newborns.
- C. Incorrect. Poor feeding is a recognized early manifestation.
- D. Incorrect. Neonatal sepsis often presents without a clear focus initially.
- E. Incorrect. Apnoea may be a presenting sign of neonatal sepsis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early sepsis signs: respiratory distress/apnoea, temperature instability, lethargy/irritability, poor perfusion, poor feeding and weak primitive reflexes.
- A preterm infant may be hypothermic rather than febrile.
- Sepsis can progress rapidly; assess the whole infant and do not rely on one sign.

questions.stem: A newborn with suspected sepsis has mottled skin. Which differential diagnosis is listed?

options.label: C
options.text: Cold stress, shock, Down syndrome and congenital hypothyroidism

questions.correctAnswerText: Cold stress, shock, Down syndrome and congenital hypothyroidism
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance specifically warns that mottled skin is not specific to sepsis and lists cold stress, shock, Down syndrome and congenital hypothyroidism as differentials.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are respiratory disorders and do not form the listed differential for mottling.
- B. Incorrect. Neonatal breast enlargement is a hormonal-withdrawal finding and does not explain mottling.
- C. Correct. These are the differentials named in the source.
- D. Incorrect. These are causes of cholestasis.
- E. Incorrect. These are orthopaedic conditions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mottling may reflect impaired perfusion but is not specific for sepsis.
- Consider hypothermia/cold stress, shock, chromosomal conditions and hypothyroidism.
- Interpret skin colour with temperature, capillary refill, pulses, blood pressure and clinical status.

questions.stem: Which investigation provides microbiological confirmation of neonatal sepsis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Blood culture and sensitivity
questions.initialExplanation: Blood culture and sensitivity is the key microbiological investigation. CBC, CRP/procalcitonin, urine culture, chest X-ray, CSF culture and swabs from relevant sites help assess the infant and identify a source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pulse oximetry assesses oxygenation.
- B. Incorrect. CBC may show leucocytosis/leucopenia or thrombocytopenia but does not identify the pathogen.
- C. Correct. Blood culture can identify the organism and guide antibiotic selection.
- D. Incorrect. Chest X-ray can support pneumonia diagnosis but cannot confirm bloodstream infection.
- E. Incorrect. CRP is a marker of inflammation and is not specific or microbiological confirmation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sepsis workup: CBC/differential/platelets, CRP or procalcitonin, blood culture and sensitivity, urine C&S, chest X-ray, CSF C&S when indicated and swabs from relevant sites.
- Obtain cultures before antibiotics when this can be done without delaying urgent treatment.
- A normal early CBC/CRP does not reliably exclude sepsis.

questions.stem: A 2-day-old infant has suspected EOS. Which empirical antibiotic combination is described?

options.label: A
options.text: Ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside such as gentamicin

questions.correctAnswerText: Ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside such as gentamicin
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include IV ampicillin plus gentamicin as an empirical EOS regimen. Ampicillin provides coverage for organisms such as GBS and Listeria, while gentamicin provides Gram-negative coverage including E. coli.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the empirical regimen given for EOS.
- B. Incorrect. Metronidazole alone does not cover the main EOS organisms.
- C. Incorrect. Vancomycin may be considered in selected LOS cases or resistant Gram-positive infection but is not the routine initial EOS combination in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Flucloxacillin plus gentamicin is listed for LOS.
- E. Incorrect. Oral therapy is inappropriate for suspected systemic neonatal sepsis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EOS empirical therapy: IV ampicillin + gentamicin.
- Alternative listed: ampicillin + a third-generation cephalosporin in selected circumstances.
- Empirical antibiotics should be reviewed against culture results and local neonatal antimicrobial guidance; exact drug choice/duration is protocol-dependent.

questions.stem: Which empirical antibiotic combination is listed for late-onset neonatal sepsis (LOS)?

options.label: D
options.text: Ampicillin plus gentamicin in each NICU setting

questions.correctAnswerText: Flucloxacillin plus gentamicin
questions.initialExplanation: For LOS, Common examples include IV flucloxacillin plus gentamicin, with vancomycin or meropenem considered if there is no clinical improvement or resistant organisms are suspected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These drugs treat toxoplasmosis.
- B. Correct. This is the combination stated for LOS.
- C. Incorrect. Acyclovir treats suspected neonatal HSV, not routine bacterial LOS.
- D. Incorrect. Ampicillin plus gentamicin is listed as an EOS regimen; LOS treatment depends on NICU pathogens and local resistance.
- E. Incorrect. Oral penicillin V is not appropriate empirical treatment for systemic neonatal sepsis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LOS is often associated with hospitalization, invasive devices (ETT/UVC) and NICU-acquired organisms.
- standard guidance's empirical regimen: flucloxacillin + gentamicin.
- If not improving, consider escalation (e.g. vancomycin/meropenem) according to cultures, local resistance and specialist advice.
- Antibiotic duration depends on organism, site, cultures and clinical response; do not apply a single duration to every infant.

cases.title: A newborn develops sepsis after NICU admission
cases.vignette: A 31-week infant has been hospitalized since birth and has an endotracheal tube and umbilical venous catheter. On day 11, the infant develops apnoea, temperature instability and poor perfusion. Blood cultures are taken.

questions.stem: Which feature most strongly supports late-onset rather than early-onset sepsis?

options.label: B
options.text: Presentation during the first hour of life

options.label: E
options.text: Infection associated with postnatal hospitalization and invasive devices after the first 72 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Infection associated with postnatal hospitalization and invasive devices after the first 72 hours
questions.initialExplanation: LOS is acquired after delivery, often in the NICU or community, and is associated with hospitalization and invasive procedures such as ETT and UVC. It typically occurs after the first 72 hours/first week.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Chorioamnionitis is an intrapartum/perinatal EOS risk factor.
- B. Incorrect. Infection presenting in the first hours is more consistent with EOS.
- C. Incorrect. PROM is a risk factor for EOS.
- D. Incorrect. Maternal GBS carriage is a classic EOS risk factor.
- E. Correct. This is the typical LOS setting.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LOS: postnatal acquisition, often NICU/community.
- Risk factors: prematurity, prolonged hospitalization, ETT/UVC and other invasive procedures.
- LOS organisms include CONS, Staph aureus, GBS, Pseudomonas and Klebsiella.

questions.stem: Which organism is particularly associated with NICU-acquired late-onset sepsis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CONS)
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include CONS as an important LOS/NICU pathogen, along with Staphylococcus aureus, GBS, Pseudomonas and Klebsiella.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Rubella is a congenital viral infection.
- B. Incorrect. Rotavirus causes gastroenteritis.
- C. Incorrect. Toxoplasma is a congenital infection, not a typical NICU-acquired bacterial sepsis organism.
- D. Correct. CONS is a common NICU-associated bloodstream pathogen, particularly in infants with intravascular lines.
- E. Incorrect. Parvovirus B19 is a congenital infection associated with fetal anaemia/hydrops.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LOS pathogens: CONS, Staph aureus, GBS, Pseudomonas and Klebsiella.
- Invasive lines and prolonged NICU admission increase risk.
- Culture and sensitivity should guide narrowing or changing antibiotics.

cases.title: A pregnant woman develops a flu-like illness after eating contaminated food
cases.vignette: A pregnant woman develops a mild influenza-like illness after eating unpasteurized soft cheese. Her premature newborn is delivered with meconium-stained amniotic fluid, a widespread rash and respiratory distress. The infant later develops meningitis.

questions.stem: Which organism should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Listeria monocytogenes
questions.initialExplanation: Listeria is foodborne and may cause maternal bacteraemia with mild flu-like symptoms. It can cross the placenta and cause miscarriage, preterm birth, fetal infection and severe neonatal sepsis, pneumonia or meningitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. CMV is associated with periventricular calcifications, microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss.
- B. Incorrect. Rubella is associated with cataracts, PDA and deafness, not the described foodborne maternal illness.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital varicella causes skin scarring, limb/digital abnormalities and neurological/ocular damage.
- D. Correct. The food exposure, maternal flu-like illness and neonatal sepsis/meningitis fit congenital/perinatal listeriosis.
- E. Incorrect. Toxoplasmosis is associated with hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and intracranial calcifications.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Listeria is transmitted through contaminated food and may cause maternal flu-like bacteraemia.
- Transplacental spread may cause miscarriage, preterm delivery or neonatal sepsis.
- Neonatal features can include unusual meconium staining in a preterm infant, widespread rash, septicaemia, pneumonia and meningitis.
- It has a high mortality in severe neonatal infection.

cases.title: A preterm infant with a central line becomes ill after the first week

questions.stem: A 16-day-old preterm infant with an umbilical venous catheter has apnoea, poor feeding, seizures and a tense, bulging anterior fontanelle. The white count is high with a low platelet count, and CRP is raised. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: This is early-onset sepsis, which usually presents with meningitis and needs a 5-day course

options.label: B
options.text: This is late-onset sepsis; antibiotics should wait until the culture results return

options.label: C
options.text: This is late-onset sepsis presenting as pyelonephritis because of oliguria

options.label: D
options.text: This is hepatitis with direct jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly

options.label: E
options.text: This is late-onset sepsis with meningitis; obtain blood and CSF cultures, start IV antibiotics immediately, and treat for longer (14-21 days) if meningitis is confirmed

questions.correctAnswerText: This is late-onset sepsis with meningitis; obtain blood and CSF cultures, start IV antibiotics immediately, and treat for longer (14-21 days) if meningitis is confirmed
questions.initialExplanation: Late-onset sepsis occurs after the first 72 hours/first week, often in hospitalized infants with invasive devices, and commonly presents with meningitis. Sepsis work-up includes blood and CSF culture, and empirical IV antibiotics are started immediately. standard guidance gives 10-14 days, extended to 14-21 days for meningitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. EOS usually presents with respiratory distress, and the timing here is late.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics are started empirically without waiting.
- C. Incorrect. Oliguria suggests pyelonephritis; seizures and bulging fontanelle suggest meningitis.
- D. Incorrect. Hepatitis presents with direct jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly.
- E. Correct. Matches the timing, device risk, focal sign and plan.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LOS: after the first week/72 hours; NICU or community acquired; main presentation is meningitis.
- Focal infections: pneumonia, meningitis, pyelonephritis (oliguria), hepatitis (direct jaundice, HSM), arthritis/osteomyelitis.
- Empirical LOS regimen: flucloxacillin + gentamicin; escalate if not improving.
- Duration 10-14 days; 14-21 days for meningitis.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Pages 25-26 (late-onset sepsis: presentation, focal infections, treatment).

questions.stem: A septic neonate has mottled skin, petechiae, bleeding from puncture sites and generalized oedema with sclerema. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Mottled skin proves sepsis and carries a bad prognosis

options.label: B
options.text: Sclerema is a late sign of severe sepsis with poor prognosis; mottling alone is non-specific and may occur with cold stress or shock

options.label: C
options.text: Petechiae and bleeding from puncture sites are benign findings

options.label: D
options.text: Sclerema is the typical sign of congenital hypothyroidism

options.label: E
options.text: Poor Moro and suckling reflexes indicate recovery

questions.correctAnswerText: Sclerema is a late sign of severe sepsis with poor prognosis; mottling alone is non-specific and may occur with cold stress or shock
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include petechiae, bruising, puncture-site bleeding, oedema and sclerema among skin findings in sepsis, with sclerema marking a bad prognosis. Mottled skin has several other causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mottling can be due to cold stress, shock, Down syndrome or hypothyroidism.
- B. Correct. Separates the prognostic sign from the non-specific one.
- C. Incorrect. Bleeding signs in a septic baby suggest serious illness.
- D. Incorrect. Sclerema is linked with severe sepsis.
- E. Incorrect. Poor Moro and suckling are early non-specific signs of sepsis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Skin signs in sepsis: petechiae, bruising, bleeding, oedema, sclerema (bad prognosis).
- DD of mottled skin: sepsis, cold stress, shock, Down syndrome, congenital hypothyroidism.
- Early signs are non-specific: poor feeding, lethargy, temperature instability, poor Moro and suckling.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Pages 25-26 (clinical picture and DD of mottled skin).
source.pages: 25-26 (clinical picture and DD of mottled skin)

cases.title: A newborn has growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly and petechiae
cases.vignette: A term infant is born small for gestational age. Examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, petechiae and thrombocytopenia. The mother recalls a febrile illness with a rash during pregnancy.

questions.stem: What does the TORCH acronym represent?

options.label: A
options.text: Tetanus, Osteomyelitis, Rheumatic fever, CMV and HIV

options.label: B
options.text: Toxoplasmosis, Orthopaedic disease, Rotavirus, Cholestasis and Hypoglycaemia

options.label: C
options.text: Tuberculosis, Otitis, Respiratory infection, Cholera and Hepatitis

options.label: D
options.text: Thyroid disease, Obesity, Renal disease, Cardiac disease and Haemolysis

options.label: E
options.text: Toxoplasmosis, Other infections, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus and Herpes simplex virus

questions.correctAnswerText: Toxoplasmosis, Other infections, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus and Herpes simplex virus
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe TORCH as Toxoplasmosis, Other infections (including syphilis, parvovirus B19, HIV, HBV and herpes zoster), Rubella, CMV and HSV.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the TORCH acronym.
- B. Incorrect. These terms do not match TORCH.
- C. Incorrect. These are unrelated conditions.
- D. Incorrect. These are not congenital infections in this acronym.
- E. Correct. This is the TORCH group listed in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TORCH: Toxoplasma, Other (syphilis/parvovirus/HIV/HBV/varicella-zoster), Rubella, CMV, HSV.
- Infections may be acquired in utero or during the birth process.
- Maternal history of fever/rash, previous abortion or relevant exposure is important.

questions.stem: Which combination of findings should raise suspicion of a congenital TORCH infection?

options.label: A
options.text: IUGR/LBW, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, petechiae/thrombocytopenia and direct jaundice

options.label: B
options.text: Birth weight above the 90th centile with no other findings

questions.correctAnswerText: IUGR/LBW, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, petechiae/thrombocytopenia and direct jaundice
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include common congenital infection findings as IUGR/prematurity, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anaemia, thrombocytopenia/neutropenia, petechiae, hepatitis/direct jaundice, seizures, microcephaly and chorioretinitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are characteristic systemic features of congenital infection.
- B. Incorrect. LGA without systemic abnormalities does not suggest congenital infection.
- C. Incorrect. Isolated nasal congestion is not a typical TORCH pattern.
- D. Incorrect. Caput succedaneum is a benign birth-related scalp swelling.
- E. Incorrect. Milia and neonatal breast enlargement are benign neonatal findings.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Suspect TORCH with IUGR/LBW, HSM, lymphadenopathy, petechiae, cytopenias and conjugated jaundice.
- Neurological/ocular signs: seizures, microcephaly and chorioretinitis.
- Congenital infection may be asymptomatic at birth but have later manifestations, especially sensorineural hearing loss.

cases.title: A newborn has hydrocephalus and chorioretinitis
cases.vignette: A newborn has hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and intracranial calcifications. The mother reports frequent contact with cat litter and eating undercooked meat during pregnancy.

questions.stem: Which congenital infection is classically associated with the triad of hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and intracranial calcifications?
questions.correctAnswerText: Toxoplasmosis
questions.initialExplanation: Congenital toxoplasmosis is classically associated with hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and intracranial calcifications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Congenital rubella is associated with cataracts, PDA/pulmonary stenosis and sensorineural deafness.
- B. Incorrect. Neonatal HSV causes skin/eye/mouth disease, encephalitis or disseminated infection.
- C. Correct. This is the classic toxoplasmosis triad.
- D. Incorrect. CMV is associated with microcephaly, periventricular calcifications and sensorineural hearing loss.
- E. Incorrect. Congenital syphilis is associated with characteristic rash and bone/teeth lesions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Toxoplasmosis: hydrocephalus + chorioretinitis + intracranial calcifications.
- Transmission increases with gestational age, but earlier infection tends to cause more severe fetal disease.
- Prevent maternal infection by avoiding cat faeces/contaminated soil and undercooked meat.

questions.stem: Which imaging finding is more characteristic of congenital toxoplasmosis than congenital CMV?
questions.correctAnswerText: Diffuse intracranial calcifications
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance's comparison table describes diffuse cerebral calcifications in toxoplasmosis and periventricular calcifications in CMV.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sensorineural hearing loss is particularly associated with congenital CMV.
- B. Correct. Diffuse calcifications are the pattern listed for toxoplasmosis.
- C. Incorrect. PDA and cataracts are classic congenital rubella findings.
- D. Incorrect. Periventricular calcifications are characteristic of congenital CMV.
- E. Incorrect. A blueberry muffin rash may occur in congenital infections such as rubella/CMV and is not specific for toxoplasmosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Toxoplasmosis: diffuse intracranial calcification.
- CMV: periventricular calcification, microcephaly and SNHL.
- Rubella: cataract, PDA/pulmonary stenosis and deafness.
- Match the clinical pattern with appropriate serology/PCR and imaging.

questions.stem: Which diagnostic approach is listed for congenital toxoplasmosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Toxoplasma-specific IgM with persistently raised IgG, plus PCR from appropriate samples and imaging

questions.correctAnswerText: Toxoplasma-specific IgM with persistently raised IgG, plus PCR from appropriate samples and imaging
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include toxoplasma serology (specific IgM and persistently raised IgG), PCR from blood/CSF and imaging for cerebral calcifications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the diagnostic approach given.
- B. Incorrect. These tests investigate thyroid disease.
- C. Incorrect. Direct Coombs testing assesses immune-mediated haemolysis.
- D. Incorrect. These tests assess glucose regulation.
- E. Incorrect. Red reflex screens for ocular media opacity but cannot diagnose systemic toxoplasmosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital toxoplasmosis: maternal/fetal history, IgM/IgG interpretation, PCR and imaging.
- Treatment: pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine (with specialist monitoring/folinic acid according to protocol).
- Prevention: avoid contact with cat litter/faeces and undercooked meat during pregnancy.

cases.title: A newborn has cataracts, deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus
cases.vignette: A newborn has bilateral cataracts, sensorineural hearing loss and a continuous murmur. The mother had fever and rash during early pregnancy.

questions.stem: Which combination is the classic congenital rubella triad?

options.label: A
options.text: Hutchinson teeth, osteitis and rash of palms/soles

options.label: B
options.text: Cataract, congenital heart disease (especially PDA/pulmonary stenosis) and sensorineural deafness

options.label: E
options.text: Vesicular rash, encephalitis and disseminated disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Cataract, congenital heart disease (especially PDA/pulmonary stenosis) and sensorineural deafness
questions.initialExplanation: Congenital rubella is classically associated with cataracts, congenital heart disease (PDA and pulmonary stenosis) and sensorineural deafness.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are features of congenital syphilis.
- B. Correct. This is the classic rubella triad.
- C. Incorrect. This is the classic toxoplasmosis triad.
- D. Incorrect. This is a typical congenital CMV pattern.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests neonatal HSV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rubella: cataracts/microphthalmia/glaucoma, PDA/pulmonary stenosis and SNHL.
- Other features: IUGR, blueberry muffin rash, hepatosplenomegaly and CNS involvement.
- Prevention: rubella vaccination before pregnancy (live vaccine is not given during pregnancy).

questions.stem: Which statement about transmission of congenital rubella is listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Transmission decreases with advancing gestation and is more severe with early first-trimester infection

options.label: B
options.text: Rubella is transmitted through contaminated food

options.label: D
options.text: Maternal infection not usually affects the fetus

options.label: E
options.text: Transmission increases steadily with gestation and is most severe in the third trimester

questions.correctAnswerText: Transmission decreases with advancing gestation and is more severe with early first-trimester infection
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance's comparison table notes that rubella transmission decreases with gestational age and that infection in early pregnancy, especially the first trimester, is associated with severe fetal effects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the pattern in the source table.
- B. Incorrect. Rubella is not primarily foodborne.
- C. Incorrect. Rubella is acquired transplacentally.
- D. Incorrect. Maternal rubella can cause significant congenital abnormalities.
- E. Incorrect. This trend is closer to toxoplasma transmission, though severity does not necessarily increase with later infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- First-trimester rubella poses the greatest risk of congenital rubella syndrome.
- Transmission falls with gestational age table.
- Prevention through vaccination before pregnancy is essential.

questions.stem: Which test is listed for diagnosis of congenital rubella?

options.label: B
options.text: Direct Coombs test and reticulocyte count

options.label: E
options.text: Rubella-specific IgM serology and PCR from appropriate secretions

questions.correctAnswerText: Rubella-specific IgM serology and PCR from appropriate secretions
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include rubella-specific IgM serology and isolation/PCR from secretions, along with relevant clinical and imaging findings.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Calcium/PTH assess parathyroid function.
- B. Incorrect. These tests investigate haemolysis.
- C. Incorrect. Urine glucose is not diagnostic of congenital rubella.
- D. Incorrect. Sweat chloride evaluates cystic fibrosis.
- E. Correct. This matches the investigations listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital rubella: specific IgM and PCR/viral isolation from appropriate samples.
- Assess cardiac, ophthalmic, hearing and neurological complications.
- No specific antiviral treatment is described; management is supportive and complication-directed.

cases.title: A newborn has microcephaly, petechiae and sensorineural hearing loss
cases.vignette: A newborn is small for gestational age with microcephaly, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia. Cranial imaging shows periventricular calcifications. At follow-up, the infant has sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.stem: Which congenital infection is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
questions.initialExplanation: Congenital CMV may cause microcephaly, periventricular calcification, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia and sensorineural hearing loss. Most affected infants may be asymptomatic at birth, with later hearing and developmental effects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Toxoplasmosis is associated with hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and diffuse calcification.
- B. Incorrect. Rubella is more classically associated with cataracts, PDA/pulmonary stenosis and deafness.
- C. Incorrect. HSV causes skin/eye/mouth disease, encephalitis or disseminated infection.
- D. Incorrect. Syphilis causes characteristic rash and bone/teeth manifestations.
- E. Correct. The combination is characteristic of congenital CMV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CMV: often asymptomatic at birth, but a minority have petechiae, HSM, microcephaly and CNS/eye/hearing disease.
- Periventricular calcification and SNHL are high-yield clues.
- Hearing loss may become apparent later even when the newborn initially appears well.

questions.stem: Which statement about congenital CMV is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is transmitted through the birth canal

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately 90% are asymptomatic at birth, but later sensorineural hearing loss may occur

options.label: C
options.text: It causes the classic cataract-PDA-deafness triad

options.label: D
options.text: most infants have severe disease at birth

options.label: E
options.text: There is a routine CMV vaccine for pregnant women

questions.correctAnswerText: Approximately 90% are asymptomatic at birth, but later sensorineural hearing loss may occur
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that about 90% of congenital CMV infections are asymptomatic at birth. A minority develop symptomatic disease, and later hearing impairment is an important long-term complication.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. CMV can be transmitted transplacentally; transmission is not restricted to labour.
- B. Correct. This is the key epidemiological point given in the source.
- C. Incorrect. Cataract-PDA-deafness is the classic rubella triad.
- D. Incorrect. Most are asymptomatic at birth.
- E. Incorrect. It is recognized there is no CMV vaccine.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most congenital CMV infants are asymptomatic at birth.
- Symptomatic cases: HSM, petechiae, microcephaly, thrombocytopenia, CNS abnormalities and SNHL.
- Later hearing loss is a major reason for follow-up.
- No vaccine is available.

questions.stem: Which diagnostic tests are listed for congenital CMV?

options.label: D
options.text: CMV-specific IgM and PCR from urine, blood or CSF

questions.correctAnswerText: CMV-specific IgM and PCR from urine, blood or CSF
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include CMV-specific IgM serology and isolation/PCR from urine, blood and CSF, with imaging for periventricular calcification.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Direct Coombs assesses immune haemolysis.
- B. Incorrect. Glucose/ketone testing does not diagnose CMV.
- C. Incorrect. Toxoplasma IgG alone does not diagnose congenital CMV.
- D. Correct. This is the investigation group described in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Rubella IgM diagnoses rubella, not CMV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CMV diagnosis: IgM and PCR from appropriate specimens; urine PCR is useful in the neonatal period.
- Cranial imaging may show periventricular calcifications.
- Symptomatic congenital CMV may be treated with valganciclovir for 1 year; management requires specialist monitoring.

cases.title: A newborn develops vesicles and seizures during the second week of life
cases.vignette: A 12-day-old infant is brought with poor feeding, fever and clusters of vesicles around the eye and mouth. The infant later develops seizures and altered consciousness. The mother reports a history of genital herpes.

questions.stem: Which route of transmission is most common for neonatal HSV?

options.label: B
options.text: Transplacental infection in the first trimester in typical presentations

questions.correctAnswerText: Intrapartum exposure during delivery
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that neonatal HSV is predominantly acquired during labour/delivery from exposure to maternal genital secretions. Congenital infection in utero is less common.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. HSV is not foodborne.
- B. Incorrect. Intrauterine HSV is possible but is not the predominant route.
- C. Correct. Intrapartum exposure is the main route described.
- D. Incorrect. HSV is not transmitted by mosquitoes.
- E. Incorrect. Breast milk is not the main route described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal HSV is commonly acquired intrapartum.
- Transmission risk is higher with maternal primary infection and active genital lesions at delivery.
- Cesarean delivery is considered when maternal active genital lesions are present,.

questions.stem: Which clinical spectrum of neonatal HSV is described?

options.label: E
options.text: Skin/eye/mouth localized disease, encephalitis/CNS disease, or disseminated disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Skin/eye/mouth localized disease, encephalitis/CNS disease, or disseminated disease
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include HSV disease presenting as localized skin, eye or mouth vesicles, encephalitis, or disseminated systemic infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia may occur in sick neonates but is not the clinical classification of HSV.
- B. Incorrect. These findings are associated with congenital syphilis.
- C. Incorrect. This is the classic toxoplasmosis pattern.
- D. Incorrect. This pattern is associated with congenital rubella.
- E. Correct. These are the main forms of neonatal HSV disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HSV: skin/eye/mouth, CNS encephalitis, or disseminated disease.
- Vesicles may be absent in CNS/disseminated infection; do not exclude HSV when a neonate is septic or encephalopathic.
- Diagnosis: PCR from vesicle swab, blood and CSF as appropriate.
- Treatment: IV acyclovir promptly when neonatal HSV is suspected.

questions.stem: Which diagnostic test is listed for suspected neonatal HSV?

options.label: B
options.text: PCR from vesicle swabs and blood/CSF as appropriate

questions.correctAnswerText: PCR from vesicle swabs and blood/CSF as appropriate
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include a swab from vesicles and PCR testing. Blood and CSF PCR are also important in evaluating systemic or CNS disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urine glucose does not diagnose HSV.
- B. Correct. PCR identifies HSV DNA in appropriate specimens.
- C. Incorrect. Red reflex screens for congenital cataract.
- D. Incorrect. Direct Coombs assesses immune haemolysis.
- E. Incorrect. Thyroid function tests assess hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Suspected neonatal HSV: obtain lesion swab PCR and evaluate blood/CSF according to presentation.
- Start IV acyclovir promptly; do not wait for results in a strongly suspected case.
- Maternal active genital HSV at labour may prompt cesarean delivery.

topics.name: Congenital Syphilis, Varicella and Parvovirus B19

cases.title: A newborn has a rash on the palms and soles and abnormal long bones
cases.vignette: A 6-week-old infant has persistent nasal discharge, a generalized rash involving the palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly and abnormal long-bone radiographs. The mother had untreated syphilis during pregnancy.

questions.stem: Which additional finding is characteristic of congenital syphilis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hutchinson teeth and osteitis/osteochondritis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include congenital syphilis with a characteristic rash on the palms and soles, bone lesions (osteitis/osteochondritis) and later dental abnormalities such as Hutchinson (notched/peg-shaped) teeth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are characteristic findings of congenital syphilis.
- B. Incorrect. This is the congenital toxoplasmosis triad.
- C. Incorrect. Microcephaly and periventricular calcifications are more typical of congenital CMV.
- D. Incorrect. Vesicles and encephalitis suggest HSV.
- E. Incorrect. This is the congenital rubella triad.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital syphilis: rash including palms/soles, bone lesions and Hutchinson teeth.
- Treatment: penicillin, with regimen determined by age, stage and maternal/newborn evaluation.
- Maternal screening and adequate treatment during pregnancy prevent congenital syphilis.

questions.stem: A mother contracts varicella at 14 weeks of pregnancy. Which fetal findings are listed as possible congenital varicella syndrome manifestations?

options.label: C
options.text: Severe skin scarring, ocular/neurological damage and digital dysplasia

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe skin scarring, ocular/neurological damage and digital dysplasia
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes an approximately 2% risk of congenital varicella syndrome when maternal infection occurs before 20 weeks, with severe skin scarring, ocular and neurological damage and digital dysplasia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is congenital CMV.
- B. Incorrect. This is congenital rubella.
- C. Correct. These are the characteristic manifestations listed.
- D. Incorrect. This is congenital toxoplasmosis.
- E. Incorrect. These are congenital syphilis features.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital varicella syndrome risk is low but significant with maternal infection before 20 weeks.
- Features: dermatomal skin scarring, limb/digital abnormalities and ocular/neurological injury.
- Management and maternal post-exposure prophylaxis depend on gestational age and local obstetric guidance.

questions.stem: A fetus develops severe anaemia, hydrops and ascites after maternal infection. Which congenital infection is a recognized cause?
questions.correctAnswerText: Parvovirus B19
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that congenital parvovirus B19 may cause severe fetal anaemia due to suppression of erythropoiesis, leading to hydrops fetalis and possible intrauterine death.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Rubella is associated with cataracts, PDA/pulmonary stenosis and deafness.
- B. Correct. Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursors and may cause aplastic anaemia and hydrops.
- C. Incorrect. HSV causes neonatal skin/eye/mouth, CNS or disseminated infection.
- D. Incorrect. Toxoplasmosis causes hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and intracranial calcification.
- E. Incorrect. CMV causes microcephaly, periventricular calcification and hearing loss.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Parvovirus B19 → fetal red-cell aplasia/severe anaemia.
- Severe fetal anaemia may cause hydrops (oedema/ascites from cardiac failure) and intrauterine death.
- Maternal exposure/infection warrants fetal assessment for anaemia/hydrops.

topics.name: Neonatal Respiratory Distress - Recognition and Differential Diagnosis

cases.title: A newborn develops tachypnoea, grunting and chest recession
cases.vignette: A 2-hour-old newborn develops a respiratory rate of 76/min, nasal flaring, subcostal and intercostal recession, expiratory grunting and central cyanosis. Assessment includes respiratory, cardiovascular, neurological and metabolic systems.

questions.stem: Which respiratory rate is considered tachypnoea in a newborn?
questions.correctAnswerText: More than 60 breaths/min
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe neonatal tachypnoea as a respiratory rate greater than 60 breaths per minute.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A rate of 40-60/min may be normal in a newborn.
- B. Incorrect. This is markedly elevated, but the diagnostic threshold is already above 60/min.
- C. Correct. More than 60 breaths/min is tachypnoea.
- D. Incorrect. This is well below the neonatal tachypnoea threshold.
- E. Incorrect. A rate of 50/min is within the usual neonatal range.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal newborn RR: approximately 40-60/min.
- Tachypnoea: RR >60/min.
- Count respirations for a full minute because newborn breathing can be irregular.
- Assess recession, grunting, nasal flaring, cyanosis and oxygen saturation in addition to the respiratory rate.

questions.stem: Which group contains the cardinal clinical signs of neonatal respiratory distress listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Weak femoral pulses, wide pulse pressure and continuous murmur

options.label: B
options.text: Tachypnoea, nasal flaring, chest recession, grunting and cyanosis

options.label: C
options.text: Jaundice, pale stool, dark urine and hepatomegaly

options.label: D
options.text: Abdominal distension, bloody stool and bilious vomiting

questions.correctAnswerText: Tachypnoea, nasal flaring, chest recession, grunting and cyanosis
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include tachypnoea, acting alae nasi (nasal flaring), subcostal/intercostal/suprasternal recession, grunting and cyanosis as signs of neonatal respiratory distress.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These findings suggest a haemodynamically significant PDA.
- B. Correct. These are the respiratory distress signs in the source.
- C. Incorrect. These findings suggest cholestatic jaundice.
- D. Incorrect. These findings suggest NEC or intestinal obstruction.
- E. Incorrect. These are features that may occur in congenital infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Look for increased work of breathing: nasal flaring, recession and grunting.
- Cyanosis indicates impaired oxygenation but may be absent despite significant distress.
- A newborn with respiratory distress requires prompt ABC assessment and oxygenation monitoring.

questions.stem: A newborn has respiratory distress, but the chest examination and radiograph do not fully explain the severity. Which non-respiratory categories should also be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cardiovascular, CNS and metabolic/haematological causes
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance divides causes of neonatal respiratory distress into respiratory and non-respiratory causes. Non-respiratory causes include CHD/heart failure/PPHN, perinatal asphyxia or intracranial haemorrhage, neuromuscular disorders, metabolic acidosis, severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and polycythaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Gastrointestinal disease can cause respiratory compromise in selected conditions, but this is not the main non-respiratory classification.
- B. Correct. These systems contain important non-pulmonary causes of respiratory distress.
- C. Incorrect. Physiological jaundice does not explain respiratory distress.
- D. Incorrect. Orthopaedic abnormalities are not the key categories.
- E. Incorrect. Skin lesions do not account for the broad differential.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Respiratory causes: RDS, TTN, MAS, pneumonia, aspiration, chronic lung disease, pulmonary haemorrhage, lung hypoplasia, CDH, airway obstruction and pleural disease.
- Non-respiratory causes: cardiac, CNS, neuromuscular, metabolic and haematological disorders.
- Always consider sepsis, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and anaemia in a sick neonate.

cases.title: A term infant born by elective caesarean section has mild respiratory distress
cases.vignette: A term baby is delivered by elective caesarean section without labour. Within two hours, the infant develops mild tachypnoea but remains relatively well perfused. Chest radiography shows prominent perihilar vascular markings and fluid in the interlobar fissures. The symptoms improve over the next 36 hours.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN)
questions.initialExplanation: TTN is a self-limited respiratory disorder caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid. It commonly occurs in term or near-term infants, particularly after elective caesarean delivery without labour, and usually resolves within 24-48 hours.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. MAS is associated with meconium-stained liquor and patchy consolidation/hyperinflation.
- B. Incorrect. RDS is primarily associated with prematurity and surfactant deficiency, with a granular ground-glass appearance and air bronchograms.
- C. Incorrect. CDH causes severe distress, scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the chest.
- D. Incorrect. PPHN causes significant hypoxaemia and pulmonary hypertension, not the typical self-limited TTN course.
- E. Correct. Caesarean delivery without labour, mild early distress, fissural fluid and rapid resolution are typical of TTN.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TTN = delayed fetal lung-fluid clearance.
- Risk factors include elective caesarean delivery, maternal diabetes, maternal asthma and excess maternal analgesia.
- Symptoms are usually mild and begin within hours after birth.
- Resolution usually occurs within 24-48 hours.

questions.stem: Which chest X-ray pattern is most consistent with TTN?

options.label: A
options.text: Prominent perihilar vascular markings with fluid in the interlobar fissures

options.label: B
options.text: Patchy consolidation with areas of hyperinflation after meconium exposure

options.label: C
options.text: Multiple bowel loops in the left hemithorax

options.label: D
options.text: Diffuse granular ground-glass shadowing with air bronchograms

options.label: E
options.text: A completely opaque hemithorax with mediastinal shift due to pleural air

questions.correctAnswerText: Prominent perihilar vascular markings with fluid in the interlobar fissures
questions.initialExplanation: TTN produces a “wet lung” appearance with prominent perihilar vascular markings and fluid in the fissures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the typical TTN radiographic pattern.
- B. Incorrect. This is typical of MAS.
- C. Incorrect. Bowel loops in the thorax suggest CDH.
- D. Incorrect. This is the classic RDS pattern.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests a large pneumothorax.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TTN: perihilar streaking/prominent vascular markings and fissural fluid.
- RDS: ground-glass/granular lungs with air bronchograms.
- MAS: hyperinflation with patchy consolidation and atelectasis.
- Radiology must be interpreted with gestational age and clinical course.

questions.stem: A term infant with TTN is mildly tachypnoeic but maintains oxygenation. Which management approach is most appropriate?

options.label: D
options.text: Supportive care, monitoring and oxygen if required

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive care, monitoring and oxygen if required
questions.initialExplanation: TTN is usually self-limited. Management is supportive, with oxygen if required, monitoring of respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, and IV fluids if oral feeding is unsafe due to tachypnoea.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion is used for severe hyperbilirubinaemia or selected haematological conditions, not TTN.
- B. Incorrect. Surgery is required for selected structural abnormalities such as CDH, not TTN.
- C. Incorrect. Chest drainage is used for pneumothorax, not TTN.
- D. Correct. Supportive management is appropriate for most infants with TTN.
- E. Incorrect. Surfactant is used for selected cases of surfactant-deficient RDS, not routine TTN.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TTN: supportive treatment and observation.
- Give oxygen only as needed and monitor saturation.
- Avoid oral feeding if significant tachypnoea makes feeding unsafe.
- Most cases resolve within 24-48 hours.

cases.title: A post-term infant is born through thick meconium-stained liquor
cases.vignette: A 41-week-and-6-day infant is delivered after fetal distress. Thick meconium is present in the amniotic fluid and stains the skin, nails and umbilical cord. Shortly after birth, the infant develops severe respiratory distress, grunting and cyanosis. Chest radiography shows hyperinflation with patchy areas of consolidation and collapse.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS)
questions.initialExplanation: MAS causes severe respiratory distress in term or post-term infants exposed to meconium-stained liquor, usually in the setting of intrauterine asphyxia. Aspirated meconium causes airway obstruction, air trapping, atelectasis and chemical pneumonitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. BPD is chronic lung disease of prematurity, not an acute presentation after delivery.
- B. Incorrect. TTN is typically mild and self-limited, with perihilar streaking and fissural fluid.
- C. Incorrect. CMV causes congenital systemic/neurological findings rather than acute meconium-related airway disease.
- D. Correct. Meconium exposure, fetal distress, severe distress and patchy hyperinflation/consolidation strongly support MAS.
- E. Incorrect. RDS is primarily a disease of prematurity due to surfactant deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MAS is usually seen in term/post-term infants with meconium-stained liquor and fetal asphyxia.
- Meconium may cause complete obstruction (atelectasis), partial obstruction (air trapping), chemical pneumonitis and secondary infection.
- It may be complicated by pneumothorax and PPHN.

questions.stem: Which mechanism explains the hyperinflation seen in MAS?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete airway obstruction causing total lung collapse

options.label: B
options.text: Extra-alveolar air caused by congenital diaphragmatic hernia

options.label: C
options.text: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid

options.label: D
options.text: Lack of surfactant in most alveoli

options.label: E
options.text: Partial airway obstruction producing a ball-valve effect with air trapping

questions.correctAnswerText: Partial airway obstruction producing a ball-valve effect with air trapping
