questions.initialExplanation: Meconium may partially obstruct small airways, allowing air to enter during inspiration but limiting expiration. This ball-valve effect causes air trapping and hyperinflation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Complete obstruction causes distal atelectasis/collapse rather than hyperinflation.
- B. Incorrect. CDH is a structural diaphragmatic defect.
- C. Incorrect. Delayed lung-fluid clearance causes TTN.
- D. Incorrect. Surfactant deficiency is the mechanism of RDS.
- E. Correct. Partial obstruction leads to air trapping.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MAS mechanisms: complete obstruction → collapse; partial obstruction → air trapping; chemical pneumonitis and possible secondary infection.
- X-ray: hyperinflation and patchy consolidation/collapse.
- Air leak (pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum) is an important complication.

questions.stem: A non-vigorous newborn is delivered through meconium-stained liquor and is apnoeic. What is the appropriate immediate approach according to current neonatal resuscitation guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Give prophylactic antibiotics before assessing breathing

options.label: B
options.text: Routine endotracheal intubation and tracheal suction before any ventilation in each case

options.label: D
options.text: Delay ventilation until chest radiography is performed

options.label: E
options.text: Begin standard initial steps and positive-pressure ventilation promptly; suction if airway obstruction is suspected and interferes with ventilation

questions.correctAnswerText: Begin standard initial steps and positive-pressure ventilation promptly; suction if airway obstruction is suspected and interferes with ventilation
questions.initialExplanation: Current 2025 AHA/AAP neonatal resuscitation guidance does not recommend routine oral, nasal or endotracheal suctioning solely because the liquor is meconium-stained, even in non-vigorous infants. Prompt ventilation takes priority. Suction is considered when visible or suspected airway obstruction prevents effective ventilation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not correct immediate apnoea or airway obstruction.
- B. Incorrect. Routine direct laryngoscopy and tracheal suction are not recommended for every non-vigorous meconium-exposed newborn.
- C. Incorrect. Ventilation is prioritized; compressions are added only when heart rate remains below 60/min despite effective ventilation.
- D. Incorrect. Imaging must not delay resuscitation.
- E. Correct. Start standard resuscitation and effective ventilation; clear the airway only when obstruction is suspected and ventilation is ineffective.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Meconium-stained liquor alone is not an indication for routine tracheal suction.
- Prioritize effective ventilation in an apnoeic/gasping newborn.
- Consider mouth/nose suction if visible material obstructs the airway; consider tracheal suction if obstruction persists during ventilation.
- The original standard guidance includes an older direct-suction description; follow the current local resuscitation algorithm.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 33; 2025 AHA/AAP Neonatal Resuscitation Guidelines.

questions.stem: Which serious complications may develop in an infant with MAS?

options.label: A
options.text: PPHN and air-leak syndromes such as pneumothorax

questions.correctAnswerText: PPHN and air-leak syndromes such as pneumothorax
questions.initialExplanation: MAS can cause severe ventilation-perfusion mismatch, pulmonary vasoconstriction and persistent pulmonary hypertension. Hyperinflation and air trapping may lead to pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. PPHN and air leaks are important MAS complications.
- B. Incorrect. Breast enlargement is a benign hormonal-withdrawal finding.
- C. Incorrect. These are orthopaedic conditions.
- D. Incorrect. These are unrelated congenital conditions.
- E. Incorrect. Hypothyroidism is not a specific MAS complication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MAS may cause hypoxaemic respiratory failure, PPHN and secondary infection.
- Air trapping predisposes to pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum.
- Severe cases require NICU respiratory and cardiovascular support.

cases.title: A newborn has severe respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen
cases.vignette: A newborn develops severe respiratory distress immediately after birth. The abdomen appears scaphoid, air entry is reduced on the left, and bowel sounds are heard in the left hemithorax. Heart sounds are displaced to the right. Chest radiography reveals gas-filled bowel loops in the left chest with mediastinal shift.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH)
questions.initialExplanation: CDH is a congenital defect in the diaphragm that allows abdominal contents to herniate into the thoracic cavity, compressing the developing lung and causing pulmonary hypoplasia and respiratory distress.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. TTN causes mild early respiratory distress and wet-lung radiographic changes.
- B. Incorrect. Pneumonia can cause respiratory distress but does not explain bowel sounds in the chest.
- C. Correct. Scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in the chest and mediastinal shift are classic for CDH.
- D. Incorrect. RDS is caused by surfactant deficiency and usually affects premature infants.
- E. Incorrect. Choanal atresia causes upper-airway obstruction and cyanosis relieved by crying.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CDH: abdominal viscera herniate through a diaphragmatic defect into the thorax.
- Postnatal signs: severe distress, scaphoid abdomen, poor air entry on affected side, bowel sounds in chest and displaced heart sounds.
- Pulmonary hypoplasia and PPHN are major determinants of severity.

questions.stem: Which type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia is the commonest and usually posterolateral?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bochdalek hernia
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that Bochdalek hernia is the commonest type (approximately 85-90%), usually posterolateral and more often on the left side. Morgagni hernia is retrosternal/anterior and more often right-sided.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Bochdalek is the common posterolateral type and usually left-sided.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the common type described.
- C. Incorrect. Morgagni hernia is anterior/retrosternal and less common.
- D. Incorrect. Hiatal hernia is a different diaphragmatic defect involving the oesophageal hiatus.
- E. Incorrect. Diaphragmatic eventration is abnormal elevation of the diaphragm rather than herniation through a posterolateral defect.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bochdalek: posterolateral, usually left-sided, about 85-90%.
- Morgagni: anterior/retrosternal, more commonly right-sided.
- CDH occurs in approximately 1 in 4,000 births.
- Up to half of cases may have associated anomalies.

questions.stem: A newborn with suspected CDH requires resuscitation. Which airway/ventilation strategy is preferred?

options.label: A
options.text: Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation, avoiding bag-mask ventilation

options.label: B
options.text: Oral feeding to expand the stomach

options.label: D
options.text: CPAP by mask as the treatment in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation, avoiding bag-mask ventilation
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance advises endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Bag-mask ventilation should be avoided because it inflates the stomach and bowel within the thorax, worsening lung compression and respiratory compromise. Insert an NG tube for gastric decompression.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Intubation and controlled ventilation are preferred in a newborn with significant CDH.
- B. Incorrect. Oral feeding is unsafe and worsens gastric distension.
- C. Incorrect. Bag-mask ventilation may inflate herniated abdominal viscera and worsen thoracic compression.
- D. Incorrect. Severe CDH requires controlled airway management and specialist NICU care.
- E. Incorrect. Compressions are not the first intervention unless the infant meets resuscitation criteria after ventilation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CDH: intubate and ventilate; avoid bag-mask ventilation when CDH is suspected.
- Insert NG/OG tube for continuous gastric decompression.
- NPO, IV fluids and NICU stabilization.
- Definitive surgical repair is performed after stabilization, not as the first resuscitation step.

questions.stem: Which associated pathophysiological problem contributes significantly to mortality in CDH?

options.label: A
options.text: Pulmonary hypoplasia with persistent pulmonary hypertension

questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary hypoplasia with persistent pulmonary hypertension
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include pulmonary hypoplasia as a major determinant of mortality in CDH and also lists PPHN and gastro-oesophageal reflux as complications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Underdeveloped lungs and pulmonary hypertension impair oxygenation and circulation.
- B. Incorrect. Neonatal acne is benign and unrelated to CDH prognosis.
- C. Incorrect. Physiological jaundice is not the main cause of mortality in CDH.
- D. Incorrect. Hormonal breast enlargement is unrelated.
- E. Incorrect. Caput succedaneum is a benign scalp swelling.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CDH mortality is strongly related to pulmonary hypoplasia and PPHN.
- Stabilize ventilation and circulation before surgical repair.
- Long-term follow-up may be needed for respiratory and gastrointestinal complications.

cases.title: A newborn has a blue tongue and low oxygen saturation
cases.vignette: A newborn has bluish discoloration of the tongue and oral mucosa with low oxygen saturation. The infant is assessed for pulmonary disease, cyanotic congenital heart disease and other causes. A second newborn in the nursery has blue hands and feet but a pink tongue and normal central oxygenation.

questions.stem: Which finding indicates central rather than peripheral cyanosis?

options.label: C
options.text: Cool extremities with normal tongue colour

questions.correctAnswerText: Blue tongue and soft palate
questions.initialExplanation: Central cyanosis is seen in mucous membranes, especially the tongue and soft palate, and is usually associated with reduced arterial oxygen saturation. Peripheral cyanosis mainly affects hands, feet, lips/around the mouth, nose tip or ear lobules and may occur with hypothermia or poor perfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ear lobules can show peripheral cyanosis.
- B. Incorrect. The tip of the nose can be affected in peripheral cyanosis.
- C. Incorrect. Cool extremities with pink mucosa suggest peripheral vasoconstriction rather than central cyanosis.
- D. Incorrect. Blue hands and feet suggest peripheral cyanosis.
- E. Correct. Tongue and soft-palate discoloration indicates central cyanosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Central cyanosis: tongue and mucous membranes; assess arterial oxygenation urgently.
- Peripheral cyanosis: hands/feet and acral areas; consider cold stress, shock or low cardiac output.
- Do not diagnose central cyanosis from perioral colour alone without checking the tongue/mucosa.

questions.stem: Which group contains important causes of central cyanosis in a newborn listed?

options.label: C
options.text: Severe respiratory disease, cyanotic congenital heart disease, polycythaemia and methaemoglobinaemia

options.label: D
options.text: Physiological breast enlargement and vaginal withdrawal bleeding

options.label: E
options.text: Milia, neonatal acne and erythema toxicum

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe respiratory disease, cyanotic congenital heart disease, polycythaemia and methaemoglobinaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include pulmonary disorders such as severe RDS, MAS, TTN, pneumonia, pneumothorax, choanal atresia, CDH and PPHN; cyanotic CHD such as TOF, TGA, truncus arteriosus, pulmonary atresia and TAPVR; and other causes including polycythaemia and methaemoglobinaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are orthopaedic/birth injuries.
- B. Incorrect. These are scalp birth injuries and do not account for central cyanosis.
- C. Correct. These are the major cause groups.
- D. Incorrect. These are normal hormonal-withdrawal changes.
- E. Incorrect. These are benign skin findings and do not cause central cyanosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Central cyanosis: pulmonary, cardiac or abnormal haemoglobin causes.
- Cyanotic CHD differential: TOF, TGA, truncus arteriosus, pulmonary atresia and TAPVR.
- Severe respiratory causes include RDS, MAS, pneumonia, pneumothorax, CDH and PPHN.
- Assess airway, breathing, circulation, saturation and perfusion immediately.

questions.stem: A newborn has central cyanosis and severe hypoxaemia despite supplemental oxygen. Which test is described to help distinguish a cyanotic congenital heart lesion from pulmonary disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Hyperoxia test using 100% oxygen with assessment of arterial PaO₂ response

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyperoxia test using 100% oxygen with assessment of arterial PaO₂ response
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include the hyperoxia (nitrogen washout) test: exposure to 100% oxygen for approximately 10 minutes followed by assessment of arterial PaO₂ or oxygen saturation. Limited rise in PaO₂ may suggest cyanotic congenital heart disease, whereas improvement may suggest pulmonary disease or PPHN. This is a traditional teaching test; echocardiography and modern clinical assessment are essential.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the test described.
- B. Incorrect. Ortolani assesses hip stability.
- C. Incorrect. Guthrie screening detects selected metabolic/endocrine conditions.
- D. Incorrect. Sweat chloride is used in cystic fibrosis diagnosis.
- E. Incorrect. Direct Coombs tests immune-mediated haemolysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hyperoxia test: described in the source as 100% oxygen for about 10 minutes with arterial PaO₂ assessment.
- Failure of PaO₂ to rise substantially may suggest cyanotic CHD.
- Improvement may suggest pulmonary disease/PPHN.
- In current practice, stabilize the infant and obtain urgent echocardiography/cardiology input; do not delay treatment for a hyperoxia test.
- standard guidance contains a specific PaO₂ threshold; interpret it cautiously and follow current neonatal/cardiology protocols.

cases.title: A comfortable-looking blue newborn

questions.stem: A term newborn has central cyanosis with SpO₂ 82% but little respiratory distress, and the chest radiograph shows clear lungs. After 10 minutes in 100% oxygen, the saturation and right radial PaO₂ stay low. What is the best next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the hyperoxia test after 30 minutes

options.label: B
options.text: Give surfactant through an endotracheal tube

options.label: D
options.text: Start a prostaglandin E infusion while stabilizing ABC, and arrange urgent cardiac consultation and echocardiography

options.label: E
options.text: Treat as sepsis and wait for cultures

questions.correctAnswerText: Start a prostaglandin E infusion while stabilizing ABC, and arrange urgent cardiac consultation and echocardiography
questions.initialExplanation: Failure of oxygenation to improve in 100% oxygen points to cyanotic congenital heart disease. standard guidance's immediate management is to stabilize airway, breathing and circulation, start a prostaglandin E infusion (5 ng/kg/min), and obtain urgent cardiac consultation and echocardiography.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Repeating the test delays treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Surfactant treats RDS; the lungs are clear.
- C. Incorrect. There is no air leak to drain.
- D. Correct. Matches standard guidance's management of suspected cyanotic heart disease.
- E. Incorrect. Sepsis may coexist, but it does not explain the hyperoxia result.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hyperoxia test: PaO₂ or saturation stays low in 100% oxygen: cyanotic CHD; it improves: respiratory disease or PPHN.
- Immediate steps: ABC, prostaglandin E infusion, urgent cardiology and echocardiography.
- Cyanotic CHD: TOF, TGA, truncus arteriosus, pulmonary atresia, TAPVR.
- Do not delay treatment for the test; the PaO₂ threshold in the scan should be checked against current protocols.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 36 (management of the cyanosed newborn).

cases.title: A macrosomic newborn develops jitteriness a few hours after birth
cases.vignette: A 4.5-kg infant is born to a mother with poorly controlled pre-existing diabetes. The baby is plethoric and has a large body size. At 3 hours of life, the infant develops jitteriness and poor feeding. The neonatal team checks the blood glucose and screens for other complications of maternal diabetes.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains early neonatal hypoglycaemia in an infant of a diabetic mother?

options.label: A
options.text: The newborn develops absolute insulin deficiency

options.label: B
options.text: Maternal glucose causes fetal hyperinsulinaemia; after birth glucose stops but insulin remains high

options.label: C
options.text: The newborn has no hepatic glycogen stores in each case

options.label: D
options.text: Placental transfer of glucagon causes persistent hyperglycaemia

options.label: E
options.text: Maternal insulin freely crosses the placenta and suppresses fetal insulin

questions.correctAnswerText: Maternal glucose causes fetal hyperinsulinaemia; after birth glucose stops but insulin remains high
questions.initialExplanation: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta and stimulates fetal pancreatic beta cells to produce more insulin. After delivery, the maternal glucose supply is interrupted while fetal hyperinsulinaemia persists, resulting in neonatal hypoglycaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The problem is relative excess of fetal insulin, not insulin deficiency.
- B. Correct. This is the classic pathophysiology of neonatal hypoglycaemia in infants of diabetic mothers.
- C. Incorrect. Reduced glycogen stores can contribute to hypoglycaemia in other infants, but fetal hyperinsulinaemia is the main mechanism in IDM.
- D. Incorrect. Glucagon transfer is not the mechanism described.
- E. Incorrect. Maternal insulin does not freely cross the placenta in clinically significant amounts.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Maternal hyperglycaemia → fetal hyperglycaemia → fetal hyperinsulinaemia.
- After cord clamping, maternal glucose supply stops but neonatal insulin remains high.
- Hypoglycaemia is common during the first day of life.
- Risk is related to the degree of maternal glycaemic control.

questions.stem: Which clinical feature may indicate symptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia in an infant of a diabetic mother?

options.label: A
options.text: Jitteriness, poor feeding, apnoea, lethargy or seizures

questions.correctAnswerText: Jitteriness, poor feeding, apnoea, lethargy or seizures
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that infants with hypoglycaemia may be asymptomatic or present with jitteriness, poor feeding, apnoea, convulsions, lethargy or pallor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are recognized manifestations of neonatal hypoglycaemia.
- B. Incorrect. Caput succedaneum is a birth-related scalp swelling.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital dermal melanocytosis is a benign skin pigmentation.
- D. Incorrect. Vaginal discharge may occur due to maternal hormone withdrawal.
- E. Incorrect. Milia is a benign skin finding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal hypoglycaemia may be asymptomatic.
- Symptoms include jitteriness, poor feeding, apnoea, lethargy, pallor and seizures.
- At-risk infants require early feeding and glucose monitoring.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic infant of a diabetic mother is found to have a low blood glucose level. What is the initial approach described?

options.label: A
options.text: Give an IV dextrose bolus to each asymptomatic infant regardless of the glucose level

options.label: D
options.text: Encourage immediate feeding and use oral dextrose as indicated

questions.correctAnswerText: Encourage immediate feeding and use oral dextrose as indicated
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance distinguishes management by symptoms: an asymptomatic infant should be fed immediately, with oral dextrose as described. A symptomatic infant requires IV glucose and close monitoring. Exact thresholds and treatment regimens should follow the current neonatal hypoglycaemia protocol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. IV treatment is not automatically required for every asymptomatic low reading; management depends on severity, repeat measurements and protocol.
- B. Incorrect. Feeding should be encouraged when safe.
- C. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion is not a treatment for neonatal hypoglycaemia.
- D. Correct. Early feeding is the first approach for an asymptomatic at-risk infant.
- E. Incorrect. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prevent hypoglycaemia with early feeding/breastfeeding.
- Management depends on symptoms, severity and the local neonatal threshold.
- Symptomatic or severe hypoglycaemia requires urgent IV glucose.
- Do not memorize isolated glucose treatment doses without checking the current neonatal protocol.

questions.stem: A newborn of a diabetic mother develops jitteriness and seizures on the second day of life despite normal blood glucose. Which electrolyte abnormality should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypocalcaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include transient hypoparathyroidism in IDM as a cause of hypocalcaemia, which commonly presents around the second day of life with jitteriness or seizures. Hypomagnesaemia may also occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hyperkalaemia can cause cardiac and neuromuscular problems but is not the key association in IDM here.
- B. Correct. Hypocalcaemia is a recognized metabolic complication in IDM and may cause jitteriness or seizures.
- C. Incorrect. Hypernatraemia may cause neurological symptoms but is not the specific complication emphasized here.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the characteristic abnormality described.
- E. Incorrect. Common examples include hypomagnesaemia, not hypermagnesaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IDM may develop hypocalcaemia due to transient hypoparathyroidism.
- Typical onset: second day of life.
- Symptoms: jitteriness and seizures.
- Check magnesium if seizures persist despite normal glucose and calcium.

questions.stem: An infant of a diabetic mother has seizures. Blood glucose and calcium are normal. Which additional biochemical test is specifically recommended?
questions.correctAnswerText: Serum magnesium
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes checking serum magnesium in an infant with convulsions when glucose and calcium are normal, because hypomagnesaemia can cause neuromuscular irritability and seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Amylase is not part of the metabolic seizure screen described.
- B. Correct. Serum magnesium should be checked in this setting.
- C. Incorrect. Uric acid does not assess the relevant electrolyte cause.
- D. Incorrect. Sweat chloride investigates cystic fibrosis.
- E. Incorrect. Troponin evaluates myocardial injury.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- In IDM with seizures: check glucose and calcium first; if both are normal, assess magnesium.
- Hypomagnesaemia may coexist with hypocalcaemia.
- Treat clinically significant electrolyte abnormalities under neonatal monitoring.

questions.stem: Which mechanism contributes to polycythaemia in an infant of a diabetic mother?

options.label: B
options.text: Maternal vitamin K deficiency increases fetal haematocrit

options.label: C
options.text: Maternal insulin directly destroys fetal red cells

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic fetal hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin production

options.label: E
options.text: Reduced bilirubin conjugation stimulates red-cell production

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic fetal hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin production
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance links polycythaemia in IDM to increased erythropoietin production associated with fetal hypoxia. Increased red-cell mass may lead to hyperviscosity and thrombosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia does not cause increased platelet production.
- B. Incorrect. Vitamin K deficiency affects coagulation rather than red-cell mass.
- C. Incorrect. Insulin does not directly destroy fetal red cells.
- D. Correct. Chronic intrauterine hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin and erythropoiesis.
- E. Incorrect. Bilirubin metabolism does not cause polycythaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IDM may develop polycythaemia (central venous haematocrit >65%).
- Hyperviscosity may cause poor perfusion and renal vein thrombosis.
- Plethora may be an initial clue.
- Partial exchange transfusion is considered in selected symptomatic cases under specialist guidance.

questions.stem: A newborn of a diabetic mother has respiratory distress, a murmur and echocardiographic evidence of interventricular septal hypertrophy. Which condition is most likely?

options.label: D
options.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of the infant of a diabetic mother

options.label: E
options.text: Endocardial cushion defect in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of the infant of a diabetic mother
questions.initialExplanation: Maternal hyperglycaemia and fetal hyperinsulinaemia may cause myocardial hypertrophy, particularly of the interventricular septum. Many infants are asymptomatic and the echocardiographic changes usually resolve over weeks to months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. PDA produces a ductal shunt and may cause a continuous murmur, but it does not explain septal hypertrophy.
- B. Incorrect. TOF is a cyanotic congenital heart defect with a characteristic structural combination.
- C. Incorrect. Coarctation causes impaired lower-body perfusion and weak femoral pulses.
- D. Correct. Septal hypertrophy in an IDM is typical of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy associated with maternal diabetes.
- E. Incorrect. Endocardial cushion defect is a congenital structural lesion and is not the specific diabetic-mother association.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IDM → fetal hyperinsulinaemia → myocardial hypertrophy, especially the interventricular septum.
- Most infants are asymptomatic; a minority develop respiratory distress or heart failure.
- Echocardiographic findings often resolve over weeks to months.
- Perform echocardiography when there is a murmur or evidence of heart failure.

questions.stem: Which congenital anomaly is particularly associated with maternal diabetes and described as the most specific skeletal anomaly?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sacral agenesis
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include congenital anomalies in IDM, including cardiac defects, neural tube defects, renal agenesis, small left colon syndrome and sacral agenesis. Sacral agenesis is described as the most specific association.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Craniosynostosis is not the diabetic-mother association highlighted.
- B. Incorrect. Congenital scoliosis is not the specific anomaly in the source.
- C. Correct. Sacral agenesis is the specific skeletal association emphasized.
- D. Incorrect. Clubfoot is a congenital orthopaedic deformity but is not the specific diabetic embryopathy association listed.
- E. Incorrect. Polydactyly is not the specific anomaly described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Maternal diabetes increases the risk of congenital malformations, especially with poor periconceptional glycaemic control.
- Cardiac anomalies are common (e.g. TGA, VSD, ASD).
- Neural tube defects and renal anomalies may occur.
- Sacral agenesis is a particularly characteristic association.

cases.title: Unexpected presentations in infants of diabetic mothers

questions.stem: A mother with long-standing diabetes complicated by retinopathy and nephropathy delivers at 37 weeks a baby weighing 2.0 kg (below the 10th centile). Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Impossible: each infant of a diabetic mother is macrosomic, so the dates must be wrong

options.label: B
options.text: Being SGA removes the risk of hypoglycaemia

options.label: C
options.text: Maternal diabetic microvascular disease can restrict growth; monitor glucose and calcium even when the infant is small

options.label: D
options.text: Growth restriction in diabetes occurs with gestational diabetes

options.label: E
options.text: Small size is caused by hypoglycaemia in utero

questions.correctAnswerText: Maternal diabetic microvascular disease can restrict growth; monitor glucose and calcium even when the infant is small
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes a three-fold increase in growth restriction in mothers with long-standing diabetic microvascular disease. Macrosomia is the classic finding in IDM, but not the only one.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. IDM are often macrosomic, not always.
- B. Incorrect. The metabolic risks of IDM are related to glycaemic control.
- C. Correct. Matches standard guidance's note and still applies IDM monitoring.
- D. Incorrect. standard guidance ties growth restriction to long-standing microvascular disease.
- E. Incorrect. Fetal hyperglycaemia and hyperinsulinaemia are the typical mechanism, not hypoglycaemia in utero.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Classic IDM: macrosomia, plethoric face; risk relates to maternal glycaemic control.
- Long-standing microvascular disease: three-fold increase in IUGR.
- IDM risks: hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, polycythaemia, jaundice, birth asphyxia, cardiomyopathy, anomalies.

cases.title: A newborn has a scalp swelling after a difficult delivery
cases.vignette: A term infant is delivered after prolonged labour and vacuum-assisted delivery. A soft scalp swelling is visible immediately over the presenting part and crosses the cranial suture lines. The clinician must distinguish benign caput succedaneum from cephalohaematoma and potentially dangerous subgaleal haemorrhage.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes caput succedaneum from cephalohaematoma?

options.label: A
options.text: Caput usually appears several days after birth

options.label: B
options.text: Caput is subcutaneous oedema that appears immediately and crosses suture lines

options.label: C
options.text: Caput typically causes severe hypovolaemic shock

options.label: D
options.text: Caput is restricted to the parietal bone

options.label: E
options.text: Caput is subperiosteal blood that not usually crosses sutures

questions.correctAnswerText: Caput is subcutaneous oedema that appears immediately and crosses suture lines
questions.initialExplanation: Caput succedaneum is a subcutaneous fluid collection that is present immediately after delivery, diffuse and crosses suture lines. Cephalohaematoma is a subperiosteal blood collection that appears after several hours and does not cross suture lines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Caput is usually present at birth.
- B. Correct. Immediate onset and crossing sutures are classic caput features.
- C. Incorrect. Severe hypovolaemic shock is associated with subgaleal haemorrhage, not uncomplicated caput.
- D. Incorrect. Caput occurs over the presenting part and is diffuse rather than limited to one bone.
- E. Incorrect. This describes cephalohaematoma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Caput succedaneum: subcutaneous fluid, immediate, diffuse, crosses sutures, resolves in a few days.
- Cephalohaematoma: subperiosteal blood, appears after hours, localized, does not cross sutures, resolves over weeks.
- Large cephalohaematoma may contribute to anaemia and jaundice.

questions.stem: A newborn develops a localized swelling over the parietal bone several hours after birth. The swelling does not cross suture lines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cephalohaematoma
questions.initialExplanation: Cephalohaematoma is a subperiosteal haemorrhage, usually over a parietal bone. It appears hours after birth and does not cross suture lines because the periosteum is attached at the sutures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Subgaleal haemorrhage is diffuse, boggy and may extend widely across the scalp.
- B. Incorrect. Craniosynostosis is premature fusion of cranial sutures.
- C. Correct. Delayed appearance, localized swelling and sutural restriction are classic.
- D. Incorrect. Hydrocephalus causes progressive ventricular/head enlargement, not a localized scalp swelling.
- E. Incorrect. Caput is present immediately, diffuse and crosses sutures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cephalohaematoma: subperiosteal blood; cannot cross sutures.
- It may be associated with linear skull fracture, anaemia or jaundice when large.
- Usually resolves over weeks; avoid aspiration because of infection risk.

questions.stem: A baby develops a rapidly enlarging, diffuse, boggy scalp swelling after vacuum delivery. The swelling extends from the orbital ridges to the occiput. The infant becomes pale, tachycardic and hypotensive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Subgaleal haemorrhage
questions.initialExplanation: Subgaleal haemorrhage is bleeding into the subaponeurotic space. It can spread widely across the scalp, hold a large volume of blood and cause severe hypovolaemic shock and coagulopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Congenital dermal melanocytosis is a benign pigmented skin lesion.
- B. Incorrect. Cephalohaematoma is confined to one bone and does not cross sutures.
- C. Correct. Diffuse boggy swelling after vacuum delivery with circulatory compromise is classic for subgaleal haemorrhage.
- D. Incorrect. Meningocele is a congenital neural tube defect.
- E. Incorrect. Caput is oedema, not a large blood collection causing shock.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Subgaleal haemorrhage is uncommon but life-threatening.
- Diffuse, fluctuant/boggy swelling can extend across the scalp.
- Large blood loss may lead to hypovolaemic shock and coagulopathy.
- Monitor head circumference, haemoglobin, perfusion, blood pressure and coagulation urgently.

questions.stem: A baby has an adducted, internally rotated arm, an extended elbow and a pronated forearm in a “waiter's tip” posture after shoulder dystocia. Which injury is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Erb-Duchenne palsy
questions.initialExplanation: Erb-Duchenne palsy is an upper brachial plexus injury involving C5-C6 roots. It produces the classic waiter's tip posture: the arm is adducted and internally rotated, the elbow is extended and the forearm is pronated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. C5-C6 injury causes the waiter's tip posture.
- B. Incorrect. Klumpke palsy involves lower roots (C8-T1) and may cause claw hand with impaired grasp.
- C. Incorrect. Facial nerve palsy causes unilateral facial weakness.
- D. Incorrect. Phrenic nerve palsy causes diaphragmatic weakness and respiratory compromise.
- E. Incorrect. Radial nerve palsy causes wrist/finger extension weakness and does not produce the classic posture.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Erb palsy: upper roots C5-C6.
- Waiter's tip: adduction + internal rotation + elbow extension + forearm pronation.
- Moro reflex may be absent on the affected side, while grasp is preserved.
- Phrenic nerve injury (C3-C5) may coexist.

questions.stem: A newborn has a claw-hand posture and absent grasp reflex after a difficult delivery. Which brachial plexus injury is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Klumpke palsy
questions.initialExplanation: Klumpke palsy is a lower brachial plexus injury involving C8-T1. It may produce a claw hand and absent grasp reflex, while the Moro reflex is relatively preserved.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Erb palsy involves C5-C6, causes waiter's tip posture and often an absent Moro reflex with preserved grasp.
- B. Incorrect. Facial nerve palsy affects facial muscles.
- C. Correct. C8-T1 injury affects hand function and grasp, producing a claw-hand posture.
- D. Incorrect. Phrenic nerve palsy affects diaphragmatic movement.
- E. Incorrect. Long thoracic nerve injury causes scapular winging and is not the classic neonatal plexus pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Klumpke: lower roots C8-T1.
- Claw hand; absent grasp reflex, preserved Moro reflex.
- Horner syndrome may occur with T1 involvement.
- Both Erb and Klumpke injuries require early physiotherapy and follow-up; refer if recovery is incomplete.

questions.stem: A newborn develops unilateral facial asymmetry when crying after forceps delivery. The nasolabial fold is absent on one side and the infant cannot close that eye firmly. Which injury is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Facial nerve palsy
questions.initialExplanation: Neonatal facial nerve palsy may occur after instrumental delivery, usually due to compression/injury near the parotid region. It causes ipsilateral weakness of the whole face, an absent nasolabial fold, mouth deviation to the healthy side and impaired eye closure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Erb palsy affects the upper limb, not facial muscles.
- B. Incorrect. Clavicle fracture may cause pseudoparalysis and asymmetric Moro reflex.
- C. Incorrect. Klumpke palsy affects hand and lower brachial plexus function.
- D. Incorrect. HIE causes generalized neurological dysfunction rather than an isolated peripheral facial palsy.
- E. Correct. Unilateral whole-face weakness after instrumental delivery is typical.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Facial nerve palsy: often associated with instrumental delivery.
- Ipsilateral whole-face weakness, asymmetrical cry and inability to close the eye.
- Protect the cornea with lubricating drops/artificial tears.
- Most cases recover; assess feeding and eye closure.

questions.stem: A newborn has pseudoparalysis of one arm, crepitus over the clavicle and an asymmetric Moro reflex after shoulder dystocia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Clavicle fracture
questions.initialExplanation: Clavicle fracture is the commonest neonatal fracture and is often associated with shoulder dystocia. It may cause pseudoparalysis of the affected arm, asymmetric Moro reflex, crepitus and later callus formation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Septic arthritis may cause painful restricted limb movement but does not fit the delivery-related crepitus.
- B. Incorrect. Torticollis causes head tilt and limited neck rotation.
- C. Correct. The history and examination are characteristic of clavicle fracture.
- D. Incorrect. Klumpke palsy causes lower plexus weakness and claw hand.
- E. Incorrect. Erb palsy causes a characteristic waiter's tip posture but does not cause clavicular crepitus.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clavicle fracture is the commonest neonatal fracture.
- Risk factor: shoulder dystocia/macrosomia.
- Clinical signs: pseudoparalysis, asymmetric Moro, crepitus and callus.
- X-ray confirms the diagnosis.

questions.stem: What is the usual management of an uncomplicated neonatal clavicle fracture?

options.label: D
options.text: Immediate open reduction and internal fixation in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Immobilization of the arm/shoulder and supportive care

questions.correctAnswerText: Immobilization of the arm/shoulder and supportive care
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include immobilization of the arm and shoulder (e.g. a figure-of-eight bandage) and notes that prognosis is excellent; most uncomplicated fractures heal without specific surgery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Routine surgical repair is not necessary.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not treat a closed birth-related fracture.
- C. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion treats selected severe hyperbilirubinaemia/haemolysis.
- D. Incorrect. Surgery is rarely needed for an uncomplicated neonatal clavicle fracture.
- E. Correct. Conservative support and gentle handling are usually sufficient.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most neonatal clavicle fractures heal spontaneously.
- Provide comfort, gentle handling and temporary immobilization as directed.
- Prognosis is excellent.
- Reassess limb movement and neurovascular status.

cases.title: An infant with Erb palsy who is not recovering

questions.stem: A 10-week-old infant had shoulder dystocia at birth and a waiter's-tip posture with an absent Moro reflex. Physiotherapy has been given, but the arm is still weak. Which management is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop physiotherapy because lack of recovery means a permanent lesion

options.label: B
options.text: Reassure and wait; recovery usually occurs by 2 years, so referral is not needed

options.label: D
options.text: Immobilize the arm in a cast for 6 months

options.label: E
options.text: Continue physiotherapy and refer to an orthopaedic or plastic surgeon because recovery has not occurred by 2-3 months

questions.correctAnswerText: Continue physiotherapy and refer to an orthopaedic or plastic surgeon because recovery has not occurred by 2-3 months
questions.initialExplanation: Full recovery of brachial plexus injury occurs in more than 90% of cases within 3 months, but infants not recovered by 2-3 months should be referred to an orthopaedic or plastic surgeon. Most recover by 2 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Physiotherapy is the treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Referral is advised if no recovery by 2-3 months.
- C. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion is for severe jaundice.
- D. Incorrect. Treatment is physiotherapy, not prolonged casting.
- E. Correct. Matches clinical guidance's prognosis and referral advice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Erb palsy (C5-C6): waiter's tip; absent Moro, grasp preserved; may coexist with phrenic nerve palsy (C4-C5).
- Klumpke palsy (C7-C8, T1): claw hand; absent grasp, Moro preserved; Horner syndrome (T1).
- Treatment: physiotherapy; >90% recover in 3 months.
- Refer if not resolved by 2-3 months.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 41 (brachial plexus injury: associations, treatment, prognosis).

topics.name: Neonatal Jaundice - Bilirubin Physiology and Classification

cases.title: A newborn develops yellow discoloration of the skin and sclera
cases.vignette: A 3-day-old newborn is noted to have yellow discoloration of the skin and sclera. Total serum bilirubin is elevated. The clinician explains the difference between unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin and why free unconjugated bilirubin can be neurotoxic.

questions.stem: At approximately what serum bilirubin level does jaundice usually become clinically visible in a newborn?
questions.correctAnswerText: 5 mg/dL
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that jaundice usually becomes clinically apparent in a newborn when the serum bilirubin is above approximately 5 mg/dL. Visual assessment is not sufficiently accurate to determine severity; measure serum or transcutaneous bilirubin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Jaundice may be visible well before this level.
- B. Incorrect. This is a much higher bilirubin level and is not the usual visibility threshold.
- C. Incorrect. standard guidance gives a normal bilirubin level below about 2 mg/dL.
- D. Incorrect. This is below the clinical visibility threshold described.
- E. Correct. Clinical jaundice usually becomes visible at approximately 5 mg/dL.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal bilirubin: <2 mg/dL.
- Clinical jaundice often becomes visible at >5 mg/dL.
- Visual inspection cannot accurately quantify bilirubin.
- Interpret bilirubin by age in hours, gestational age, risk factors and the relevant treatment chart.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes unconjugated bilirubin from conjugated bilirubin?

options.label: A
options.text: Conjugated bilirubin is the main cause of kernicterus

options.label: B
options.text: Both forms are lipid-soluble and cannot cross membranes

options.label: C
options.text: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and albumin-bound; conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and excreted in bile

options.label: D
options.text: Unconjugated bilirubin is excreted directly as pale stool

options.label: E
options.text: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and excreted directly in urine

questions.correctAnswerText: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and albumin-bound; conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and excreted in bile
questions.initialExplanation: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and travels bound to albumin. Hepatocytes conjugate it using glucuronyl transferase, producing water-soluble conjugated bilirubin, which is excreted into bile and the intestine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Free unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and cause kernicterus; conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus.
- B. Incorrect. The two forms differ in solubility and metabolism.
- C. Correct. This is the key biochemical distinction.
- D. Incorrect. Conjugated bilirubin enters bile and contributes to stool pigment after intestinal metabolism.
- E. Incorrect. Unconjugated bilirubin is not water-soluble and is not directly excreted in urine.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Heme breakdown → biliverdin → unconjugated bilirubin.
- Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and albumin-bound.
- Hepatic glucuronyl transferase conjugates bilirubin.
- Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and excreted in bile.
- Free unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and cause kernicterus.

questions.stem: Which statement about neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It typically causes pale stools and dark urine

options.label: B
options.text: It is typically due to biliary obstruction

options.label: C
options.text: It carries no risk of neurological injury

options.label: D
options.text: It may cause kernicterus when free unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier

options.label: E
options.text: It not usually occurs in haemolytic disease

questions.correctAnswerText: It may cause kernicterus when free unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier
questions.initialExplanation: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble. If albumin-binding capacity is exceeded, free unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and deposit in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei, causing bilirubin encephalopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pale stools and dark urine suggest conjugated/obstructive jaundice.
- B. Incorrect. Unconjugated jaundice has many causes, including haemolysis, prematurity and impaired conjugation.
- C. Incorrect. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia can cause kernicterus.
- D. Correct. This is the mechanism of bilirubin neurotoxicity.
- E. Incorrect. Rh and ABO incompatibility are important causes of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Unconjugated jaundice: usually yellowish skin; normal urine colour and pigmented stool.
- Conjugated/obstructive jaundice: may produce greenish-yellow colour, dark urine and pale stool.
- Kernicterus risk is associated with free unconjugated bilirubin, not conjugated bilirubin.
- Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is always pathological and requires evaluation.

cases.title: A newborn develops jaundice on the second day and remains otherwise well
cases.vignette: A term newborn develops mild jaundice at 48 hours. The infant is feeding well, has no pallor or organomegaly, and the bilirubin is predominantly unconjugated. The level rises gradually and begins to fall during the first week.

questions.stem: Which pattern is most consistent with physiological neonatal jaundice?

options.label: A
options.text: Jaundice with severe pallor and hepatosplenomegaly from birth

options.label: B
options.text: Onset after the first day, predominantly unconjugated bilirubin, well-appearing infant and spontaneous decline during the first week

options.label: D
options.text: Direct hyperbilirubinaemia with pale stool and dark urine

options.label: E
options.text: Onset during the first 24 hours with rapid bilirubin rise

questions.correctAnswerText: Onset after the first day, predominantly unconjugated bilirubin, well-appearing infant and spontaneous decline during the first week
questions.initialExplanation: Physiological jaundice commonly starts on the second day of life, is unconjugated and occurs in an otherwise well infant. In term infants it typically peaks around day 4 and decreases by the end of the first week.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pallor and hepatosplenomegaly suggest haemolysis, infection or another pathological cause.
- B. Correct. This matches the timing and clinical course described.
- C. Incorrect. Prolonged jaundice requires evaluation and is not physiological by definition.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests conjugated/obstructive jaundice and is pathological.
- E. Incorrect. Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Physiological jaundice: onset after 24 hours, unconjugated and infant otherwise well.
- Term: peak around day 4 and falls by the end of week 1.
- Preterm: peak around days 6-8 and may take longer to resolve.
- First-day jaundice or a rapidly rising bilirubin requires urgent assessment for pathology.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests pathological rather than physiological jaundice?

options.label: A
options.text: Declining bilirubin by the end of the first week

options.label: B
options.text: Mild unconjugated jaundice peaking on day 4

options.label: C
options.text: Onset at 48 hours in a well term infant

options.label: D
options.text: Jaundice in the first 24 hours or bilirubin rising faster than 5 mg/dL/day

options.label: E
options.text: No pallor, organomegaly or feeding problem

questions.correctAnswerText: Jaundice in the first 24 hours or bilirubin rising faster than 5 mg/dL/day
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include jaundice during the first 24 hours, a rapid bilirubin rise (>5 mg/dL/day), illness, organomegaly, conjugated bilirubin and prolonged jaundice as features of pathological jaundice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A falling bilirubin during the first week is compatible with physiological resolution.
- B. Incorrect. This is the typical physiological peak in a term infant.
- C. Incorrect. This is compatible with physiological jaundice if other findings are reassuring.
- D. Correct. First-day jaundice and rapid rise are pathological red flags.
- E. Incorrect. A well infant without red flags is more consistent with physiological jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Jaundice within first 24 hours: always investigate.
- Rate of rise >5 mg/dL/day is a pathological red flag.
- Ill appearance, pallor, organomegaly, direct bilirubin elevation or prolonged course requires workup.
- Treatment thresholds should be based on age in hours, gestational age and current bilirubin guidelines, not a single fixed value.

questions.stem: Which group contains causes of increased bilirubin production in unconjugated neonatal jaundice?

options.label: B
options.text: Galactosaemia and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis

options.label: C
options.text: Biliary atresia, choledochal cyst and Alagille syndrome

options.label: D
options.text: Rh/ABO haemolysis, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, cephalohaematoma, bruising and polycythaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Rh/ABO haemolysis, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, cephalohaematoma, bruising and polycythaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Increased bilirubin production results from haemolysis or breakdown of extravasated blood. Common examples include immune haemolysis (Rh/ABO), non-immune haemolysis (G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia and pyruvate kinase deficiency), cephalohaematoma, intracranial haemorrhage, bruising and polycythaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These syndromes impair bilirubin uptake/conjugation rather than increase production.
- B. Incorrect. These are metabolic/intrahepatic causes of conjugated jaundice.
- C. Incorrect. These are causes of cholestasis/conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
- D. Correct. These conditions increase bilirubin production.
- E. Incorrect. Hypothyroidism may reduce bilirubin conjugation but is not the main increased-production group.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Increased production: immune/non-immune haemolysis, bruising, cephalohaematoma, intracranial haemorrhage and polycythaemia.
- Decreased conjugation: prematurity, Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar and hypothyroidism.
- Increased enterohepatic circulation: poor intake/breastfeeding jaundice and bowel obstruction.
- Always consider sepsis in a sick jaundiced newborn.

questions.stem: A newborn has persistent unconjugated jaundice due to absent glucuronyl transferase activity. The condition is autosomal recessive, severe and unresponsive to phenobarbitone. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I
questions.initialExplanation: Crigler-Najjar type I is an autosomal recessive disorder with absent glucuronyl transferase activity. It causes severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and is unresponsive to phenobarbitone. Type II has partial enzyme deficiency and may respond to phenobarbitone.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Gilbert syndrome causes mild intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, often triggered by fasting or stress.
- B. Correct. Absent enzyme activity with severe disease and no phenobarbitone response indicates type I.
- C. Incorrect. Breast milk jaundice is a benign prolonged unconjugated jaundice in an otherwise healthy breastfed infant.
- D. Incorrect. Type II has partial enzyme deficiency and is generally less severe.
- E. Incorrect. Biliary atresia causes conjugated cholestasis with pale stools and dark urine.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Crigler-Najjar I: AR, absent glucuronyl transferase, severe, kernicterus risk, no phenobarbitone response.
- Crigler-Najjar II: partial enzyme deficiency, milder, may respond to phenobarbitone.
- Gilbert: AD, mild unconjugated bilirubin rise, often with fasting/stress/exercise.
- Type I may require intensive bilirubin-lowering treatment and specialist assessment for liver transplantation.

cases.title: A newborn of an Rh-negative mother develops severe early jaundice
cases.vignette: A mother is Rh-negative and has not received documented anti-D prophylaxis in a previous pregnancy. Her current newborn is Rh-positive and develops marked jaundice with pallor and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory testing shows anaemia, raised reticulocytes and a positive direct Coombs test.

questions.stem: What is the underlying mechanism of Rh haemolytic disease of the newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: Maternal IgM crosses the placenta and destroys fetal platelets

options.label: B
options.text: Maternal anti-D IgG crosses the placenta and destroys fetal Rh-positive red blood cells

options.label: D
options.text: Fetal antibodies attack maternal red cells

questions.correctAnswerText: Maternal anti-D IgG crosses the placenta and destroys fetal Rh-positive red blood cells
questions.initialExplanation: Rh haemolytic disease occurs when an Rh-negative mother becomes sensitized to Rh-positive fetal red cells. Maternal anti-D IgG crosses the placenta in a subsequent Rh-positive pregnancy and causes fetal/neonatal haemolysis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. IgM does not cross the placenta in the way required to cause this disease.
- B. Correct. Anti-D IgG crosses the placenta and causes immune destruction of fetal Rh-positive red cells.
- C. Incorrect. Maternal diabetes is associated with neonatal metabolic and cardiac complications, not anti-D haemolysis.
- D. Incorrect. The maternal immune response targets fetal Rh-positive red cells.
- E. Incorrect. Bilirubin is a product of haemoglobin breakdown; it does not cause the haemolysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rh disease: Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive fetus + maternal sensitization.
- Maternal anti-D IgG crosses placenta and causes fetal haemolysis.
- The first Rh-positive pregnancy is often less affected, unless the mother was previously sensitized.
- Severe disease may cause hydrops fetalis, anaemia and heart failure.

questions.stem: Which event may sensitize an Rh-negative mother before a later Rh-positive pregnancy?

options.label: A
options.text: Fetomaternal exposure during abortion, ectopic pregnancy, amniocentesis or incompatible transfusion

questions.correctAnswerText: Fetomaternal exposure during abortion, ectopic pregnancy, amniocentesis or incompatible transfusion
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that the first pregnancy may be affected if the mother was already sensitized through previous exposure, such as abortion, ectopic pregnancy, amniocentesis or an incompatible blood transfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These events can expose an Rh-negative mother to Rh-positive red cells and trigger anti-D antibody formation.
- B. Incorrect. Phototherapy is a neonatal jaundice treatment.
- C. Incorrect. Breastfeeding does not cause Rh sensitization.
- D. Incorrect. Iron supplementation does not expose the mother to fetal Rh-positive red cells.
- E. Incorrect. Vitamin K does not cause Rh sensitization.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sensitization may occur after delivery, miscarriage/abortion, ectopic pregnancy, invasive procedures or transfusion.
- Maternal anti-D can persist and affect subsequent Rh-positive fetuses.
- Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis prevents sensitization when administered to eligible Rh-negative mothers.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern is most consistent with Rh haemolytic disease of the newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: Raised direct bilirubin with pale stool and dark urine

options.label: B
options.text: Low platelets with normal bilirubin and no anaemia

options.label: C
options.text: Low haemoglobin, raised total/indirect bilirubin, raised reticulocytes and positive direct Coombs test

options.label: D
options.text: Normal haemoglobin and absent reticulocyte response in each case

options.label: E
options.text: High haemoglobin, low reticulocytes and negative Coombs test

questions.correctAnswerText: Low haemoglobin, raised total/indirect bilirubin, raised reticulocytes and positive direct Coombs test
questions.initialExplanation: Immune haemolysis causes anaemia, increased red-cell turnover and elevated unconjugated bilirubin. The direct Coombs test detects antibody/complement coating of neonatal red blood cells.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is a cholestatic pattern, not the classic Rh haemolysis pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Thrombocytopenia alone does not establish Rh haemolytic disease.
- C. Correct. This is the typical haemolytic pattern.
- D. Incorrect. The typical response includes increased reticulocytes as the marrow compensates.
- E. Incorrect. Haemolysis generally causes anaemia and reticulocytosis, not high Hb with low reticulocytes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Investigations: maternal/infant blood group and Rh, CBC/Hb, total and indirect bilirubin, reticulocyte count and direct Coombs test.
- Severe haemolysis may cause hydrops fetalis, hepatosplenomegaly, heart failure and severe jaundice.
- Monitor bilirubin and haemoglobin closely.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of administering anti-D immunoglobulin to an eligible Rh-negative mother?

options.label: D
options.text: Prevent maternal sensitization to Rh-positive fetal red cells

questions.correctAnswerText: Prevent maternal sensitization to Rh-positive fetal red cells
questions.initialExplanation: Anti-D immunoglobulin binds fetal Rh-positive red cells that enter the maternal circulation, preventing the maternal immune system from becoming sensitized. Key features include administration within 72 hours after delivery of an Rh-positive infant, alongside antenatal prophylaxis according to the obstetric protocol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. It does not increase fetal haemoglobin.
- B. Incorrect. Anti-D does not treat neonatal jaundice.
- C. Incorrect. Anti-D does not prevent CMV.
- D. Correct. Anti-D prevents maternal anti-D antibody formation.
- E. Incorrect. It has no role in fetal insulin regulation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Anti-D prophylaxis is for unsensitized Rh-negative mothers at risk of carrying an Rh-positive fetus.
- Clinical guidance notes administration within 72 hours after delivery of an Rh-positive infant.
- Antenatal prophylaxis and additional doses after sensitizing events follow obstetric guidelines.
- Anti-D is preventive, not treatment for an already sensitized mother.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes ABO incompatibility from Rh haemolytic disease?

options.label: A
options.text: ABO disease occurs when the mother is Rh-negative

options.label: B
options.text: ABO disease is usually milder, often in group O mothers with IgG anti-A/anti-B antibodies

options.label: C
options.text: ABO antibodies are typically IgM and readily cross the placenta

options.label: D
options.text: ABO disease is typically more severe and causes hydrops in most infants

options.label: E
options.text: ABO disease not usually causes neonatal jaundice

questions.correctAnswerText: ABO disease is usually milder, often in group O mothers with IgG anti-A/anti-B antibodies
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that ABO incompatibility is more common but usually less severe than Rh disease. Some group O mothers have IgG anti-A/anti-B antibodies that cross the placenta and haemolyse fetal A or B red cells. Infant haemoglobin is often normal or only slightly reduced, and hepatosplenomegaly is generally absent.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ABO incompatibility depends on ABO blood groups, not maternal Rh status.
- B. Correct. This summarizes the typical pattern described.
- C. Incorrect. Many ABO antibodies are IgM, which do not cross the placenta; the clinically relevant antibodies are IgG.
- D. Incorrect. ABO disease is usually less severe than Rh disease.
- E. Incorrect. ABO haemolysis can cause neonatal unconjugated jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ABO incompatibility: commonly group O mother with A or B infant.
- Some maternal IgG anti-A/anti-B cross the placenta.
- Usually milder than Rh disease; Hb often normal/slightly reduced and HSM usually absent.
- Direct Coombs may be positive; management is monitoring and bilirubin treatment if indicated.

cases.title: A breastfed newborn has prolonged unconjugated jaundice
cases.vignette: A 4-day-old term infant is exclusively breastfed and has poor milk transfer, infrequent feeds and reduced urine output. The infant is mildly dehydrated and has unconjugated jaundice. A separate 3-week-old infant is thriving, well hydrated and remains mildly jaundiced despite effective breastfeeding.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes breastfeeding jaundice from breast milk jaundice?

options.label: B
options.text: Breastfeeding jaundice follows low intake early; breast-milk jaundice occurs later in thriving infants

options.label: D
options.text: Breast milk jaundice requires permanent cessation of breastfeeding

options.label: E
options.text: Breast milk jaundice typically causes pale stool and dark urine

questions.correctAnswerText: Breastfeeding jaundice follows low intake early; breast-milk jaundice occurs later in thriving infants
questions.initialExplanation: Breastfeeding jaundice is associated with inadequate milk intake during the first week, causing dehydration, reduced caloric intake and increased enterohepatic circulation. Breast milk jaundice typically occurs during the second week or later in a healthy, well-hydrated breastfed infant and may persist for several weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Breastfeeding jaundice is usually unconjugated.
- B. Correct. Timing and hydration/feeding status distinguish the two entities.
- C. Incorrect. Both occur in the neonatal period.
- D. Incorrect. Breast milk jaundice is benign in most cases and breastfeeding should generally continue after appropriate evaluation.
- E. Incorrect. Both are typically unconjugated; pale stools and dark urine suggest conjugated cholestasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Breastfeeding jaundice: first week, inadequate intake, dehydration and increased enterohepatic circulation.
- Breast milk jaundice: second week onward, healthy and well-hydrated infant, may persist up to 12 weeks.
- Both are predominantly unconjugated.
- Evaluate prolonged jaundice and exclude pathological causes before labeling it breast milk jaundice.

questions.stem: A thriving, well-hydrated exclusively breastfed infant has unconjugated jaundice at 3 weeks of age. No haemolysis, infection, hypothyroidism or cholestasis is identified. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Start exchange transfusion in each case

options.label: C
options.text: Continue breastfeeding, provide reassurance and follow bilirubin appropriately

options.label: E
options.text: Start antibiotics without evidence of infection

questions.correctAnswerText: Continue breastfeeding, provide reassurance and follow bilirubin appropriately
questions.initialExplanation: Breast milk jaundice is a benign unconjugated jaundice in an otherwise healthy, breastfed infant. standard guidance advises continuing breastfeeding; jaundice may persist for up to 12 weeks. Other causes of prolonged jaundice must first be excluded.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion is reserved for dangerous bilirubin levels or specific indications, not uncomplicated breast milk jaundice.
- B. Incorrect. Ursodeoxycholic acid is not a treatment for unconjugated breast milk jaundice.
- C. Correct. Continue breastfeeding and ensure appropriate follow-up after excluding pathological causes.
- D. Incorrect. Routine cessation of breastfeeding is not recommended.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics are indicated only when infection is suspected/confirmed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Breast milk jaundice: healthy, thriving infant; unconjugated; later onset; may persist up to 12 weeks.
- Continue breastfeeding.
- Breastfeeding jaundice instead requires improved milk transfer, more frequent feeding and hydration.
- Always assess direct bilirubin in prolonged jaundice.

cases.title: Unexpected presentations in infants of diabetic mothers

questions.stem: An infant of a diabetic mother is plethoric with a haematocrit of 68% on day 3. He has indirect hyperbilirubinaemia. Which explanation best fits the jaundice?

options.label: A
options.text: Polycythaemia and a shortened red-cell lifespan (and prematurity) increase the bilirubin load

options.label: B
options.text: Excess maternal insulin crossing the placenta inhibits glucuronyl transferase

options.label: C
options.text: Rh sensitization caused by maternal diabetes

options.label: D
options.text: Breast milk inhibits conjugation in most infants of diabetic mothers

questions.correctAnswerText: Polycythaemia and a shortened red-cell lifespan (and prematurity) increase the bilirubin load
questions.initialExplanation: This is explained IDM hyperbilirubinaemia by polycythaemia, reduced red-cell lifespan and prematurity. Polycythaemia results from erythropoietin stimulation by fetal hypoxia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Matches standard guidance's causes.
- B. Incorrect. Insulin does not inhibit glucuronyl transferase.
- C. Incorrect. Rh sensitization is unrelated to maternal diabetes.
- D. Incorrect. Breast milk jaundice is not a feature specific to IDM.
- E. Incorrect. Hypocalcaemia causes jitteriness and seizures, not unconjugated jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IDM jaundice: polycythaemia, reduced RBC lifespan, prematurity.
- Polycythaemia: Hct >65%, from erythropoietin and fetal hypoxia; can cause hyperviscosity and renal vein thrombosis; partial exchange transfusion.
- Observe IDM for jaundice.

cases.title: A series of jaundiced newborns needing assessment and treatment decisions

questions.stem: A term infant is jaundiced at 20 hours of age with pallor, low haemoglobin and a high reticulocyte count. Mother and baby have compatible blood groups, and the direct Coombs test is negative. Which investigations are most appropriate next?

options.label: B
options.text: Liver scan and abdominal ultrasound for biliary atresia

options.label: C
options.text: TORCH screen and metabolic screen for conjugated jaundice

options.label: D
options.text: Peripheral blood film, red-cell enzyme assay (e.g., G6PD) and osmotic fragility test, with a septic screen

options.label: E
options.text: Repeat anti-D testing in the mother

questions.correctAnswerText: Peripheral blood film, red-cell enzyme assay (e.g., G6PD) and osmotic fragility test, with a septic screen
questions.initialExplanation: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is always pathological. With haemolysis and a negative Coombs test, standard guidance's unconjugated algorithm points to blood film, enzyme assay and osmotic fragility test, alongside a septic screen.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These investigate conjugated jaundice and biliary atresia.
- B. Incorrect. Imaging of the biliary tree is for conjugated jaundice.
- C. Incorrect. These belong to the conjugated pathway.
- D. Correct. Matches the Coombs-negative haemolysis pathway.
- E. Incorrect. The mother's anti-D status does not apply to compatible blood groups.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Day-1 jaundice: always pathological.
- Haemolysis causes: Rh and ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, pyruvate kinase deficiency.
- Coombs positive: check blood groups; Coombs negative: film, enzyme assay, osmotic fragility, septic screen.
- Also consider thyroid function tests.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 48 (investigation of hyperbilirubinaemia in the newborn).

questions.stem: A 12-day-old exclusively breastfed infant is thriving and well hydrated, with unconjugated jaundice. Haemolysis, infection, hypothyroidism and cholestasis are excluded. Which mechanism best explains the jaundice and distinguishes it from breastfeeding jaundice?

options.label: A
options.text: Dehydration from poor milk intake increasing enterohepatic circulation

options.label: C
options.text: Breast-milk pregnanediol and free fatty acids, with increased beta-glucuronidase, reduce conjugation and increase enterohepatic circulation

questions.correctAnswerText: Breast-milk pregnanediol and free fatty acids, with increased beta-glucuronidase, reduce conjugation and increase enterohepatic circulation
questions.initialExplanation: Breast milk jaundice is multifactorial: milk pregnanediol decreases conjugation, high free fatty acids decrease uptake and conjugation, and increased glucuronidase activity increases enterohepatic circulation. Breastfeeding jaundice is due to low milk intake, dehydration and increased enterohepatic circulation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes breastfeeding jaundice, in a dehydrated baby.
- B. Incorrect. Absent enzyme describes Crigler-Najjar type I.
- C. Correct. Matches standard guidance's mechanism for breast milk jaundice.
- D. Incorrect. Haemolysis has been excluded.
- E. Incorrect. Cholestasis has been excluded and the bilirubin is unconjugated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Breast milk jaundice: week 2, well-hydrated, may reach 30 mg/dL, no kernicterus risk, may last up to 12 weeks; continue breastfeeding.
- Breastfeeding jaundice: first week, low intake, dehydration; improve feeding and hydration.
- Both are diagnoses of exclusion.
- The table was scanned with OCR; check details against the original page.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 48 (breast milk versus breastfeeding jaundice).

cases.title: A term infant remains jaundiced at 3 weeks
cases.vignette: A 3-week-old term infant is still jaundiced. The parents notice dark urine and pale stools. Examination reveals hepatomegaly. Laboratory testing shows an elevated direct bilirubin fraction.

questions.stem: What definition of prolonged neonatal jaundice is used?

options.label: A
options.text: Jaundice lasting more than 7 days in each newborn

options.label: B
options.text: Jaundice lasting more than 2 weeks in a term infant or more than 3 weeks in a preterm infant

options.label: D
options.text: Any jaundice in the first week

options.label: E
options.text: Jaundice persisting for more than 6 months

questions.correctAnswerText: Jaundice lasting more than 2 weeks in a term infant or more than 3 weeks in a preterm infant
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe prolonged jaundice as jaundice lasting more than 2 weeks in term infants or more than 3 weeks in preterm infants. It requires assessment for unconjugated and conjugated causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This reflects an older definition noted, not the current definition used in the main text.
- B. Correct. This is the definition specified.
- C. Incorrect. Onset after 24 hours can be physiological and does not define prolonged jaundice.
- D. Incorrect. Jaundice in the first week is common and is not automatically prolonged.
- E. Incorrect. Evaluation should begin much earlier.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prolonged jaundice: >2 weeks in term infants and >3 weeks in preterm infants.
- Always measure total and direct/conjugated bilirubin.
- Evaluate for infection (especially UTI), hypothyroidism, haemolysis, breast milk jaundice and cholestatic disease.
- Pale stool and dark urine require urgent assessment for biliary obstruction.

questions.stem: Which combination strongly suggests conjugated cholestatic jaundice rather than unconjugated jaundice?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal urine and normally pigmented stool

options.label: D
options.text: Pale/clay stool, dark urine and hepatomegaly

options.label: E
options.text: Yellow skin with no other findings at 48 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Pale/clay stool, dark urine and hepatomegaly
questions.initialExplanation: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is associated with hepatobiliary dysfunction. In obstructive cholestasis, reduced bile pigment reaches the intestine, producing pale stool, while conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and appears in dark urine. Hepatomegaly and poor growth may coexist.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Normal urine and pigmented stool are more consistent with unconjugated jaundice.
- B. Incorrect. Cephalohaematoma increases bilirubin production through breakdown of extravasated blood, usually causing unconjugated jaundice.
- C. Incorrect. These are non-specific neonatal illness/hypoglycaemia signs.
- D. Correct. This is the classic obstructive cholestasis pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Mild jaundice at 48 hours may be physiological if other findings are reassuring.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Conjugated jaundice: dark urine, pale stool, hepatomegaly and possible failure to thrive.
- Conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus.
- Direct hyperbilirubinaemia is always pathological and requires investigation.
- Inspect stool colour; parents' report/photos may help identify pale stools.

questions.stem: Which group contains important causes of conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia listed?

options.label: B
options.text: Biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, congenital infection, Alagille syndrome, cystic fibrosis, galactosaemia and tyrosinaemia

options.label: C
options.text: G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis and Rh incompatibility

options.label: D
options.text: Breastfeeding jaundice and breast milk jaundice

questions.correctAnswerText: Biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, congenital infection, Alagille syndrome, cystic fibrosis, galactosaemia and tyrosinaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance groups causes of conjugated jaundice into obstructive, infective, genetic, metabolic and idiopathic neonatal hepatitis. Examples include biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, TORCH, Alagille syndrome, cystic fibrosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, tyrosinaemia, galactosaemia, Rotor syndrome and Dubin-Johnson syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These conditions cause predominantly unconjugated jaundice.
- B. Correct. These represent the main differential categories in the source.
- C. Incorrect. These are haemolytic causes of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
- D. Incorrect. These are usually unconjugated breastfeeding-related causes.
- E. Incorrect. These are disorders of bilirubin conjugation and cause unconjugated jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Conjugated jaundice differential: obstruction, infection, genetic/metabolic disease and neonatal hepatitis.
- Always consider biliary atresia in an infant with pale stools and dark urine.
- Investigations include fractionated bilirubin, LFTs, abdominal ultrasound, infection/metabolic tests and specialist hepatology input.

cases.title: An infant has persistent jaundice, pale stools and dark urine
cases.vignette: A 5-week-old infant has persistent jaundice that began during the first two weeks of life. The parents report progressively pale stools and dark urine. Examination shows hepatomegaly. The infant is not thriving. The direct bilirubin is elevated and liver enzymes show a cholestatic pattern.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Biliary atresia
questions.initialExplanation: Biliary atresia is progressive fibrosis and obliteration of the extrahepatic and intrahepatic biliary tree, causing obstruction of bile flow. It typically presents with neonatal cholestasis, persistent jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and hepatomegaly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Physiological jaundice is unconjugated, begins after 24 hours and resolves during the first weeks.
- B. Incorrect. Crigler-Najjar causes severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without pale stools/dark urine.
- C. Incorrect. ABO incompatibility causes haemolytic unconjugated jaundice, usually earlier.
- D. Incorrect. Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and occurs in an otherwise thriving, well-hydrated infant with pigmented stool.
- E. Correct. The persistent cholestatic pattern with pale stool and dark urine is typical of biliary atresia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Biliary atresia: progressive fibrosis/obliteration of bile ducts → obstructive cholestasis.
- Early features: jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and hepatomegaly.
- Late disease: biliary cirrhosis, ascites, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, fat malabsorption and failure to thrive.
- Untreated disease progresses to liver failure.

questions.stem: Which investigation pattern supports the diagnosis of biliary atresia?

options.label: A
options.text: Low direct bilirubin, normal GGT and normal bile excretion

options.label: B
options.text: Positive direct Coombs test with reticulocytosis

options.label: D
