options.text: Direct hyperbilirubinaemia, raised GGT/ALP, small gallbladder on US and absent bowel excretion on HIDA

questions.correctAnswerText: Direct hyperbilirubinaemia, raised GGT/ALP, small gallbladder on US and absent bowel excretion on HIDA
questions.initialExplanation: Biliary atresia causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with a cholestatic liver enzyme pattern. Ultrasound may show a contracted or absent gallbladder. HIDA scintigraphy may show good hepatic uptake but failure of tracer excretion into the intestine. Cholangiography and liver biopsy may be needed for confirmation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Normal direct bilirubin and bile excretion argue against obstruction.
- B. Incorrect. This is a haemolysis pattern.
- C. Incorrect. This suggests a metabolic problem such as hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia.
- D. Correct. This is the characteristic investigative pattern described.
- E. Incorrect. Periventricular calcification suggests congenital CMV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Biliary atresia workup: fractionated bilirubin, LFTs/GGT, abdominal ultrasound, HIDA scan, cholangiography and liver biopsy.
- HIDA: good liver uptake but absent excretion into gut may support biliary obstruction.
- A normal ultrasound does not completely exclude biliary atresia.
- Early referral to paediatric hepatobiliary surgery is essential.

questions.stem: What is the definitive initial surgical procedure for biliary atresia, and when is it most successful?

options.label: A
options.text: Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy, ideally before 60 days of age

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate liver transplantation in each newborn

questions.correctAnswerText: Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy, ideally before 60 days of age
questions.initialExplanation: Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy restores bile drainage by connecting the porta hepatis to the intestine. Clinical guidance notes that success is highest when the procedure is performed before 60 days of age. Some infants later require liver transplantation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Kasai is the initial surgical approach and early surgery improves the chance of bile drainage.
- B. Incorrect. Pyloromyotomy treats hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
- C. Incorrect. Liver transplantation may be required if Kasai fails or liver disease progresses, but it is not the initial procedure in every newborn.
- D. Incorrect. Cholecystectomy does not correct the obliterated biliary tree.
- E. Incorrect. Splenectomy has no role in the initial management of biliary atresia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy should be performed as early as possible, ideally before 60 days.
- Provide nutritional support and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
- Complications include cholangitis, failure to thrive, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, ascites and hepatic failure.
- Liver transplantation is considered when Kasai is unsuccessful or progressive liver failure develops.

cases.title: A newborn's unconjugated bilirubin is above the treatment line
cases.vignette: A 3-day-old term infant has unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. The total serum bilirubin is plotted against the infant's age in hours and gestational-age/risk category. The value lies above the phototherapy threshold but below the exchange transfusion threshold.

questions.stem: What is the principle behind phototherapy for neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Phototherapy converts conjugated bilirubin into unconjugated bilirubin

options.label: C
options.text: Blue-green light converts bilirubin into more water-soluble photoisomers that can be excreted without hepatic conjugation

questions.correctAnswerText: Blue-green light converts bilirubin into more water-soluble photoisomers that can be excreted without hepatic conjugation
questions.initialExplanation: Phototherapy uses blue-green light (standard guidance gives a wavelength around 450 nm) to convert unconjugated bilirubin into photoisomers that are more water-soluble and can be excreted in bile and urine without requiring normal hepatic conjugation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Phototherapy is used for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not to convert direct bilirubin into indirect bilirubin.
- B. Incorrect. Albumin breakdown is not the mechanism.
- C. Correct. Photochemical isomerization/photo-oxidation reduces the need for hepatic conjugation.
- D. Incorrect. Its primary mechanism is photochemical conversion, not direct enzyme stimulation.
- E. Incorrect. Phototherapy does not treat jaundice by haemolysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Phototherapy: blue-green light, approximately 450 nm.
- Converts unconjugated bilirubin into more water-soluble photoisomers.
- Treatment threshold depends on bilirubin plotted against age in hours, gestational age and neurotoxicity risk factors.
- Maintain feeding, hydration and temperature monitoring during therapy.

questions.stem: Which statement about phototherapy is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is indicated when the total bilirubin is above the appropriate phototherapy threshold line

options.label: B
options.text: It eliminates the need for bilirubin monitoring

options.label: E
options.text: It is routinely used for each case of conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: It is indicated when the total bilirubin is above the appropriate phototherapy threshold line
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that the need for phototherapy is determined by plotting total bilirubin against age in hours on an appropriate treatment chart. Phototherapy is started when bilirubin crosses the phototherapy threshold. It may also be used while preparing for exchange transfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The decision is chart-based, not determined by one fixed bilirubin number.
- B. Incorrect. Bilirubin monitoring must continue during treatment.
- C. Incorrect. Eye protection is required according to the device/protocol.
- D. Incorrect. Feeding should be maintained and supported; increased feeding may improve bilirubin elimination.
- E. Incorrect. Phototherapy is not used for direct hyperbilirubinaemia; it may cause bronze baby syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Plot total serum bilirubin by age in hours and relevant risk factors.
- Start phototherapy when the appropriate threshold is reached.
- It can be used during preparation for exchange transfusion.
- Direct/conjugated jaundice requires investigation of the underlying hepatobiliary cause, not routine phototherapy.

questions.stem: Which group contains important nursing and monitoring measures during phototherapy?

options.label: A
options.text: Give no fluids and restrict breastfeeding

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the infant fully clothed and stop most feeds

options.label: C
options.text: Expose the skin appropriately, protect the eyes, maintain feeding/hydration and monitor temperature and bilirubin

options.label: D
options.text: Cover the entire skin and expose the face

questions.correctAnswerText: Expose the skin appropriately, protect the eyes, maintain feeding/hydration and monitor temperature and bilirubin
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes exposing the infant's skin while protecting the eyes, positioning the lamp at the prescribed distance, turning the infant, increasing feeding/IV fluids as appropriate, and monitoring temperature, hydration and bilirubin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Adequate hydration and feeding are important.
- B. Incorrect. Clothing reduces exposed skin and stopping feeds is inappropriate.
- C. Correct. These measures maximize treatment while reducing complications.
- D. Incorrect. Most skin surface should be exposed safely, with eyes protected.
- E. Incorrect. Temperature must be monitored.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Protect eyes and expose as much skin as safely possible.
- Maintain breastfeeding/feeds and hydration.
- Monitor temperature, fluid balance, urine/stool output and bilirubin response.
- Follow device-specific lamp distance and irradiance instructions; do not rely on a universal distance.

questions.stem: Which complication is associated with phototherapy?

options.label: C
options.text: Dehydration, temperature instability, loose stools, rash and bronze-baby syndrome with cholestasis

questions.correctAnswerText: Dehydration, temperature instability, loose stools, rash and bronze-baby syndrome with cholestasis
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include dehydration, hyperthermia, watery diarrhoea, dermatitis/erythema, retinal injury if eyes are unprotected, bronze baby syndrome in direct jaundice and possible hypocalcaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Neural tube defects are congenital malformations.
- B. Incorrect. Phototherapy does not cause biliary atresia.
- C. Correct. These are the listed phototherapy complications.
- D. Incorrect. Subgaleal haemorrhage is a birth injury.
- E. Incorrect. Congenital heart disease is not a phototherapy complication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Phototherapy complications: dehydration, temperature instability, loose stools, rash and possible hypocalcaemia.
- Eye protection reduces retinal exposure.
- Bronze baby syndrome is associated with phototherapy in infants with conjugated jaundice.
- Monitor hydration and temperature.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes exchange transfusion in severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: It removes unconjugated bilirubin and maternal antibodies while correcting anaemia

options.label: B
options.text: It treats conjugated jaundice by restoring bile flow

options.label: C
options.text: It replaces phototherapy in most mild jaundice

options.label: D
options.text: It is used for neonatal hypoglycaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: It removes unconjugated bilirubin and maternal antibodies while correcting anaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Exchange transfusion removes bilirubin and circulating antibodies, and can correct anaemia in haemolytic disease. It is used when bilirubin reaches the exchange threshold or when severe neurotoxicity risk requires urgent treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the three major aims described.
- B. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion does not correct biliary obstruction.
- C. Incorrect. It is reserved for selected severe cases, not routine mild jaundice.
- D. Incorrect. It is not a treatment for hypoglycaemia.
- E. Incorrect. It reduces circulating bilirubin rather than increasing production.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Exchange transfusion removes unconjugated bilirubin, antibodies and sensitized red cells, and corrects anaemia.
- Indication is based on age-specific exchange threshold, rate of rise, haemolysis and neurotoxicity risk.
- Intensive phototherapy is continued while preparing for exchange when indicated.
- This is an NICU procedure with significant risks.

questions.stem: Which complication may occur during or after exchange transfusion?

options.label: B
options.text: Hypocalcaemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia, heart failure or transfusion-transmitted infection

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypocalcaemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia, heart failure or transfusion-transmitted infection
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include metabolic complications (hypocalcaemia, acidosis, hyperkalaemia), heart failure, transfusion-transmitted infection and complications of umbilical venous catheterization such as sepsis, thrombosis and NEC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is a normal hormonal-withdrawal finding.
- B. Correct. These are the complications described in the source.
- C. Incorrect. DDH is an orthopaedic developmental condition.
- D. Incorrect. Cataract is a congenital ocular condition.
- E. Incorrect. Choanal atresia is a congenital airway obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Exchange transfusion complications: hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, thrombocytopenia, haemodynamic instability and transfusion-related infection.
- UVC-related risks include sepsis, thrombosis and NEC.
- Requires continuous monitoring and experienced neonatal staff.

questions.stem: When may IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) be considered in Rh or ABO haemolytic disease?

options.label: A
options.text: In each infant with physiological jaundice

options.label: B
options.text: As the first treatment for conjugated jaundice

options.label: E
options.text: Consider IVIG if bilirubin rises despite intensive phototherapy, to reduce exchange-transfusion need

questions.correctAnswerText: Consider IVIG if bilirubin rises despite intensive phototherapy, to reduce exchange-transfusion need
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include IVIG as an option in Rh or ABO isoimmune haemolysis when bilirubin continues to rise despite continuous intensive phototherapy. It may reduce the need for exchange transfusion in selected infants.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. IVIG is not used for routine physiological jaundice.
- B. Incorrect. IVIG does not treat cholestasis or biliary obstruction.
- C. Incorrect. IVIG has no role in correcting neonatal hypoglycaemia.
- D. Incorrect. IVIG does not prevent retinopathy of prematurity.
- E. Correct. This is the indication described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IVIG is an adjunct in selected isoimmune haemolytic disease with rising bilirubin despite intensive phototherapy.
- It may reduce the need for exchange transfusion.
- It is not a routine treatment for all neonatal jaundice.
- Follow current neonatal guidance and individualize with specialist input.

cases.title: A series of jaundiced newborns needing assessment and treatment decisions

questions.stem: An infant with severe Rh disease is being prepared for exchange transfusion. Which description of the technique is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Double-volume exchange with O-negative blood via umbilical venous catheter; give calcium as required

options.label: B
options.text: Exchange one blood volume with stored AB blood in 100 mL aliquots

options.label: C
options.text: Remove blood first without replacement, then give blood afterwards

options.label: D
options.text: Use any blood group, change 50 mL at a time, and give calcium if seizures occur

options.label: E
options.text: Perform the exchange through a peripheral cannula using plasma

questions.correctAnswerText: Double-volume exchange with O-negative blood via umbilical venous catheter; give calcium as required
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include a double-volume exchange (2 × 85-90 mL/kg) with fresh O-negative blood, small aliquots (10-20 mL) replaced through the UVC, and 10% dextrose and calcium gluconate given at 100 mL intervals.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Matches the volume, blood type, aliquot size, access and supportive measures.
- B. Incorrect. The exchange is double volume, with small aliquots.
- C. Incorrect. Blood is removed and replaced in equal small amounts.
- D. Incorrect. Calcium and dextrose are given at set intervals, not only for seizures.
- E. Incorrect. Whole blood is used, through the UVC.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Exchange transfusion removes bilirubin and antibodies and corrects anaemia.
- Indications: bilirubin above the exchange line (Rh/ABO incompatibility).
- Complications: hypocalcaemia, acidosis, hyperkalaemia, heart failure, infections, UVC sepsis/thrombosis/NEC.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 50 (exchange transfusion: procedure and complications).

cases.title: A jaundiced newborn becomes lethargic and develops a high-pitched cry
cases.vignette: A preterm infant with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia becomes lethargic and hypotonic, feeds poorly and develops a high-pitched cry. Later, the infant becomes hypertonic with arching of the back and seizures.

questions.stem: What is the pathological basis of kernicterus?

options.label: A
options.text: Deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei

options.label: B
options.text: Infection of the meninges by Group B Streptococcus

options.label: C
options.text: Deposition of conjugated bilirubin in the cerebellum

questions.correctAnswerText: Deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei
questions.initialExplanation: Kernicterus is chronic bilirubin encephalopathy due to deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in vulnerable brain regions, particularly the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the definition given.
- B. Incorrect. This describes bacterial meningitis.
- C. Incorrect. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and does not cause kernicterus in the usual mechanism.
- D. Incorrect. Germinal matrix haemorrhage is a complication of prematurity.
- E. Incorrect. Retinal vascular proliferation is part of ROP.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Kernicterus = bilirubin encephalopathy due to unconjugated bilirubin deposition.
- Main sites: basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei.
- Risk relates to free unconjugated bilirubin, exposure duration and blood-brain barrier vulnerability.
- Prevent by recognizing severe jaundice early and treating according to age-specific thresholds.

questions.stem: Which clinical findings are early manifestations of acute bilirubin encephalopathy?

options.label: B
options.text: Jitteriness with stimulus and no other abnormality

options.label: E
options.text: Hypotonia, lethargy, poor feeding, high-pitched cry and reduced Moro reflex

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypotonia, lethargy, poor feeding, high-pitched cry and reduced Moro reflex
questions.initialExplanation: The early phase of acute bilirubin encephalopathy may present with hypotonia, lethargy, poor feeding, high-pitched cry and loss/reduction of primitive reflexes such as Moro.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are features of conjugated obstructive jaundice.
- B. Incorrect. Benign jitteriness can be stimulus-provoked and suppressible; it is not the characteristic ABE picture.
- C. Incorrect. Unilateral facial weakness suggests facial nerve palsy.
- D. Incorrect. Hypertonia, opisthotonus, seizures and coma are later/severe features.
- E. Correct. These are the early signs listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early acute bilirubin encephalopathy: hypotonia, lethargy, poor feeding, high-pitched cry and reduced Moro.
- Progression may lead to hypertonia, opisthotonus, seizures and coma.
- Severe bilirubin encephalopathy is a neonatal emergency.

questions.stem: Which long-term neurological outcome is associated with chronic bilirubin encephalopathy in survivors?

options.label: E
options.text: Choreoathetoid cerebral palsy with possible sensorineural deafness and learning difficulties

questions.correctAnswerText: Choreoathetoid cerebral palsy with possible sensorineural deafness and learning difficulties
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that survivors of chronic bilirubin encephalopathy may develop choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, learning difficulties, sensorineural deafness, intellectual impairment and seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Klumpke palsy is a lower brachial plexus injury.
- B. Incorrect. Spastic diplegia is more strongly associated with periventricular leukomalacia.
- C. Incorrect. Peripheral facial palsy is a birth injury.
- D. Incorrect. Hydrocephalus/chorioretinitis suggests congenital toxoplasmosis.
- E. Correct. These are characteristic long-term sequelae of kernicterus.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chronic kernicterus: choreoathetoid CP, SNHL, learning difficulties, intellectual disability and seizures.
- Established neurological injury is not reversed by later bilirubin reduction.
- Prevention depends on prompt recognition and treatment of severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

cases.title: A series of jaundiced newborns needing assessment and treatment decisions

questions.stem: A 33-week infant on day 3 has sepsis, acidosis and hypoxia. The albumin is low and the infant is receiving a drug that competes with bilirubin for albumin binding. Why is this infant at risk of kernicterus at a total bilirubin that would be safe in a healthy term baby?

options.label: A
options.text: Conjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier in sick infants

options.label: B
options.text: Prematurity, sepsis, acidosis/hypoxia and low albumin increase free bilirubin and CNS penetration

options.label: C
options.text: Kernicterus depends on the total bilirubin level

options.label: D
options.text: Preterm infants are at lower risk because their blood-brain barrier is immature

options.label: E
options.text: Hypothermia and hypoglycaemia lower the risk

questions.correctAnswerText: Prematurity, sepsis, acidosis/hypoxia and low albumin increase free bilirubin and CNS penetration
questions.initialExplanation: Kernicterus risk depends on bilirubin level, factors that increase blood-brain barrier permeability (preterm, acidosis, sepsis, hypoxia), factors that increase free unconjugated bilirubin (hypoalbuminaemia, drugs such as aspirin or sulphonamide) and duration of exposure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and does not cause kernicterus.
- B. Correct. Combines both mechanisms present in this infant.
- C. Incorrect. Free bilirubin, barrier permeability and duration all matter.
- D. Incorrect. Immaturity increases barrier permeability and raises the risk.
- E. Incorrect. Hypothermia and hypoglycaemia are listed among the risk factors.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Kernicterus: unconjugated bilirubin deposits in basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei.
- Risk: level of bilirubin, free bilirubin, barrier permeability, duration.
- Chronic form: choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, deafness, learning difficulty.
- Treat and prevent risk factors.

cases.title: A term newborn has severe metabolic acidosis and neurological depression after delivery
cases.vignette: A term infant is delivered after placental abruption and prolonged fetal bradycardia. Umbilical arterial blood gas shows profound metabolic acidosis. The 5-minute Apgar score remains very low, and the infant is hypotonic with poor spontaneous movement and seizures.

questions.stem: Which set of findings is used as essential characteristics of perinatal asphyxia?

options.label: C
options.text: Severe metabolic/mixed acidosis, Apgar 0–3 for over 5 minutes, neurological signs and multiorgan dysfunction

options.label: D
options.text: Respiratory rate above 60/min without other abnormalities

options.label: E
options.text: Apgar 7 at 1 minute and isolated jaundice

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe metabolic/mixed acidosis, Apgar 0–3 for over 5 minutes, neurological signs and multiorgan dysfunction
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include four essential characteristics: profound metabolic/mixed acidosis in umbilical arterial blood, persistently very low Apgar score, neurological manifestations and evidence of multi-organ dysfunction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Low birth weight alone does not diagnose asphyxia.
- B. Incorrect. Caput succedaneum is a birth-related scalp swelling.
- C. Correct. This contains the four criteria listed.
- D. Incorrect. Tachypnoea alone is not sufficient.
- E. Incorrect. A normal or mildly reduced Apgar and isolated jaundice do not establish perinatal asphyxia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Perinatal asphyxia involves impaired gas exchange causing hypoxaemia, hypercarbia and acidosis.
- An important point is cord arterial pH <7, Apgar 0-3 beyond 5 minutes, neurological manifestations and multisystem dysfunction.
- A low Apgar score alone is not sufficient to diagnose HIE.
- Assess the full perinatal history, blood gases, neurological examination and organ function.

questions.stem: Which obstetric event is a recognized cause of an acute intrapartum hypoxic-ischaemic insult?

options.label: B
options.text: Normal vaginal delivery without fetal compromise

options.label: E
options.text: Placental abruption or umbilical cord prolapse

questions.correctAnswerText: Placental abruption or umbilical cord prolapse
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include placental abruption, ruptured uterus, cord compression/prolapse, maternal hypotension/hypoxia, obstructed labour, fetal IUGR and anaemia among causes of impaired fetal oxygen delivery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Neonatal acne is unrelated to intrapartum oxygen delivery.
- B. Incorrect. An uncomplicated delivery without fetal compromise is not an asphyxial event.
- C. Incorrect. Breast enlargement is a hormonal-withdrawal finding.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital dermal melanocytosis is a benign skin lesion.
- E. Correct. These events can acutely interrupt placental or umbilical blood flow.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Intrauterine causes: placental abruption/rupture and impaired placental supply.
- Intrapartum causes: cord compression/prolapse, obstructed labour and maternal shock/hypoxia.
- Postnatal causes are uncommon and include severe failure to breathe, severe cardiac disease or haemorrhage.
- HIE usually follows a significant hypoxic event immediately before or during labour/delivery.

questions.stem: A term infant is irritable, excessively responsive to stimulation, has hyperventilation and staring episodes but no seizures. Which HIE stage is most consistent with these findings?
questions.correctAnswerText: Stage 1 (mild)
questions.initialExplanation: Mild HIE (Stage 1) is characterized by hyperalertness, irritability, excessive responses to stimulation and sometimes staring or hyperventilation. The infant may have a good prognosis with recovery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stage 3 includes stupor/coma, flaccidity, absent responses and prolonged/refractory seizures.
- B. Incorrect. Stage 2 includes lethargy, hypotonia, poor feeding and commonly seizures.
- C. Incorrect. Kernicterus is bilirubin encephalopathy, a different condition.
- D. Incorrect. The findings are compatible with mild HIE.
- E. Correct. Hyperalertness and irritability are typical of Stage 1.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stage 1 (mild): hyperalert, irritable, hyperreflexia, usually no seizures, duration <24 hours.
- Stage 2 (moderate): lethargy, hypotonia, weak suck/Moro, seizures may occur.
- Stage 3 (severe): stupor/coma, flaccidity, absent reflexes, prolonged/refractory seizures and multi-organ failure.
- Severity is assessed using a structured neurological examination and appropriate monitoring.

questions.stem: A term infant after perinatal asphyxia is lethargic, hypotonic, unable to suck effectively and has brief apnoeic episodes with seizures. Which HIE stage is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Stage 2 (moderate)
questions.initialExplanation: Moderate HIE (Stage 2) is characterized by lethargy, hypotonia, abnormal movements, poor suck/feeding, apnoea and seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mild HIE usually presents with irritability/hyperalertness and no seizures.
- B. Incorrect. Severe HIE features stupor/coma, flaccidity, absent responses and often prolonged refractory seizures.
- C. Incorrect. These neurological abnormalities after an asphyxial event indicate encephalopathy.
- D. Incorrect. Physiological sleep does not explain persistent hypotonia, poor suck and seizures.
- E. Correct. The combination of lethargy, hypotonia, feeding difficulty and seizures is typical of Stage 2.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Moderate HIE: lethargy, hypotonia, weak suck, weak Moro, apnoea and seizures.
- Seizures are common in Stage 2.
- Neurological signs may begin immediately or develop within 48 hours.
- Monitor for multi-organ dysfunction.

questions.stem: A newborn has no normal spontaneous movement, is stuporous/comatose, has flaccid limbs, absent reflexes and prolonged refractory seizures. Which HIE stage is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Stage 3
questions.initialExplanation: Severe HIE (Stage 3) is characterized by stupor or coma, no normal spontaneous movement, flaccidity, absent reflexes, prolonged/refractory seizures and multi-organ failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia can cause seizures, but the overall post-asphyxial neurological picture indicates severe HIE.
- B. Incorrect. Stage 1 is hyperalert/irritable with relatively preserved tone and reflexes.
- C. Incorrect. These are severe neurological abnormalities, not normal transition.
- D. Correct. These findings are characteristic of severe HIE.
- E. Incorrect. Stage 2 has lethargy and hypotonia but not typically profound coma/flaccidity with absent reflexes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Severe HIE: coma/stupor, flaccidity, absent reflexes, refractory seizures and multi-organ failure.
- Prognosis is poor; mortality and severe neurodevelopmental disability are high.
- EEG may show burst suppression or an isoelectric pattern in severe disease.
- Provide intensive supportive care and evaluate eligibility for therapeutic hypothermia early.

questions.stem: Which organs may be affected in addition to the brain in severe HIE?

options.label: B
options.text: Heart, kidneys, lungs, liver, gastrointestinal tract and haematological system

questions.correctAnswerText: Heart, kidneys, lungs, liver, gastrointestinal tract and haematological system
questions.initialExplanation: HIE may cause multi-organ dysfunction due to systemic hypoxia and poor perfusion. Common examples include respiratory failure, hypotension/arrhythmias, renal failure/oliguria, feeding intolerance/NEC, thrombocytopenia, bleeding and liver dysfunction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bone and joint injury is not the main multi-organ pattern.
- B. Correct. HIE can affect multiple organ systems.
- C. Incorrect. Thyroid dysfunction is not the only relevant organ complication.
- D. Incorrect. The injury is systemic, not restricted to the skin.
- E. Incorrect. The eyes are not the only organ system affected.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CNS: encephalopathy and seizures.
- Respiratory/cardiovascular: respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, hypotension and arrhythmias.
- Renal: oliguria and acute kidney injury.
- Gastrointestinal/haematological: feed intolerance, NEC, thrombocytopenia, DIC and bleeding.
- Metabolic: hypo/hyperglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyponatraemia and hypomagnesaemia.

questions.stem: A term infant has moderate HIE and is assessed at 3 hours of life. Which statement about therapeutic hypothermia is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Cooling to approximately 33-34°C for 72 hours should be initiated within the first 6 hours in eligible infants of at least 36 weeks' gestation with moderate/severe HIE

options.label: B
options.text: Cooling should begin after 48 hours in each infant with mild HIE

options.label: C
options.text: Cooling is contraindicated in most infants with seizures

options.label: D
options.text: Therapeutic hypothermia is indicated in each preterm infant regardless of gestational age

questions.correctAnswerText: Cooling to approximately 33-34°C for 72 hours should be initiated within the first 6 hours in eligible infants of at least 36 weeks' gestation with moderate/severe HIE
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include therapeutic hypothermia for eligible infants at or above 36 weeks' gestation with moderate or severe HIE. Cooling is to a core/rectal temperature of approximately 33-34°C for 72 hours and should begin within the first 6 hours of life.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This summarizes the eligibility and timing stated.
- B. Incorrect. Cooling is time-critical and should not be delayed to 48 hours; mild HIE is not routinely included in the classic criteria.
- C. Incorrect. Seizures are common in moderate/severe HIE and do not automatically contraindicate cooling.
- D. Incorrect. Evidence-based eligibility is gestational-age and severity dependent; not every preterm infant qualifies.
- E. Incorrect. Cooling is time-limited, generally 72 hours, followed by controlled rewarming.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Therapeutic hypothermia: eligible infants ≥36 weeks with moderate/severe HIE.
- Start within 6 hours of birth.
- Target core temperature about 33-34°C for 72 hours.
- Avoid hyperthermia; each degree above normal can worsen brain injury.
- Use a specialist neonatal cooling protocol with continuous temperature and cardiovascular monitoring.

cases.title: Term infants after perinatal asphyxia

questions.stem: A term infant with moderate HIE has oliguria, rising creatinine and hyponatraemia on day 1. Seizures are controlled. Which fluid strategy agrees with standard guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Aggressive fluid loading to force a urine output

options.label: B
options.text: Give diuretics and stop most glucose

options.label: C
options.text: Free water in large volumes to correct the sodium

options.label: E
options.text: Restrict fluids because of transient renal impairment and SIADH, with careful monitoring of glucose, calcium and electrolytes

questions.correctAnswerText: Restrict fluids because of transient renal impairment and SIADH, with careful monitoring of glucose, calcium and electrolytes
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes fluid restriction in HIE because of transient renal impairment and the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion, with monitoring and treatment of hypoglycaemia and electrolyte imbalance, especially hypocalcaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fluid loading worsens fluid overload in SIADH.
- B. Incorrect. Glucose must be monitored and maintained.
- C. Incorrect. Free water would worsen dilutional hyponatraemia.
- D. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia must be prevented.
- E. Correct. Matches standard guidance's management.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HIE management: respiratory support, anticonvulsants, fluid restriction, treat hypotension (volume and inotropes), correct acidosis, monitor glucose and electrolytes, nutrition and family support.
- Therapeutic hypothermia (33-34 °C for 72 hours, start within 6 hours, ≥36 weeks).
- Avoid overheating.

questions.stem: Two term infants have had HIE. Infant A was hyperalert with hyperactive reflexes and no seizures for less than 24 hours. Infant B was lethargic and hypotonic with seizures, and abnormal signs persisted beyond 2 weeks of age. Which prognosis is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Infant A: poor outcome; Infant B: full recovery expected

options.label: B
options.text: Infant A: complete recovery usually expected; Infant B: full recovery unlikely because abnormalities persist beyond 2 weeks

options.label: C
options.text: Both have an equally good prognosis

options.label: D
options.text: Infant A: severe disability; Infant B: no deficits

options.label: E
options.text: Prognosis cannot be related to the clinical stage

questions.correctAnswerText: Infant A: complete recovery usually expected; Infant B: full recovery unlikely because abnormalities persist beyond 2 weeks
questions.initialExplanation: Stage 1 (mild) HIE lasts less than 24 hours and usually recovers completely. In stage 2, infants who recover clinically by 2 weeks have a good prognosis, but persistent abnormalities beyond that time make full recovery unlikely.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Reverses the prognoses.
- B. Correct. Matches stage 1 and the 2-week rule for stage 2.
- C. Incorrect. Severity and duration affect prognosis.
- D. Incorrect. Mild HIE rarely causes disability.
- E. Incorrect. The staging system is used for prognosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stage 1 (<24 hours): good, complete recovery.
- Stage 2 (2-14 days): good if clinically normal by 2 weeks.
- Stage 3 (severe): mortality 30-40%; most survivors without cooling have disability, including cerebral palsy.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 57 (clinical staging and prognosis of HIE).

cases.title: A newborn has repetitive eye deviation, lip smacking and apnoea
cases.vignette: A 2-day-old newborn has repetitive episodes of eye rolling, sustained eye deviation, lip smacking, sucking movements and occasional apnoea with oxygen desaturation. There is no obvious generalized convulsion.

questions.stem: Which type of neonatal seizure is described as the commonest?
questions.correctAnswerText: Subtle seizures
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include subtle seizures as the most common neonatal seizure type. They may consist of ocular/orofacial movements, limb movements or autonomic changes such as apnoea and desaturation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are not the predominant neonatal seizure pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Myoclonic jerks are one seizure type but are not the most common.
- C. Incorrect. Atonic seizures are not the commonest neonatal seizure type described.
- D. Correct. Subtle seizures are the commonest type listed.
- E. Incorrect. Status epilepticus is a severe seizure emergency, not the commonest seizure type.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Subtle seizures are the commonest neonatal seizure type.
- They may be difficult to recognize clinically.
- EEG/aEEG is important because clinical movements alone may not confirm an epileptic seizure.

questions.stem: Which finding is an example of an oculo-orofacial subtle neonatal seizure?

options.label: A
options.text: Symmetrical Moro reflex after a sudden noise

options.label: B
options.text: Normal rooting when the cheek is stroked

options.label: C
options.text: Brief tremor that stops when the limb is held

options.label: D
options.text: Eye deviation with chewing, sucking or lip-smacking movements

questions.correctAnswerText: Eye deviation with chewing, sucking or lip-smacking movements
questions.initialExplanation: Oculo-orofacial subtle seizures may present with eye rolling, deviation, staring, nystagmus, chewing, sucking, lip smacking or blinking.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is a normal primitive Moro reflex.
- B. Incorrect. Rooting is a normal primitive reflex.
- C. Incorrect. A tremor that stops with gentle restraint is more suggestive of jitteriness.
- D. Correct. These are the oculo-orofacial features listed.
- E. Incorrect. Sneezing is a normal newborn response.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Subtle oculo-orofacial signs: eye rolling/deviation, staring, nystagmus, chewing, sucking, lip smacking and blinking.
- Limb signs may include bicycling/pedalling movements.
- Autonomic signs may include apnoea, desaturation and heart-rate changes.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes neonatal jitteriness from an epileptic convulsion?

options.label: A
options.text: Jitteriness is typically associated with abnormal EEG

options.label: C
options.text: Convulsions not usually cause autonomic changes

options.label: E
options.text: Jitteriness is stimulus-provoked and stops when held; epileptic movements are not suppressed by restraint

questions.correctAnswerText: Jitteriness is stimulus-provoked and stops when held; epileptic movements are not suppressed by restraint
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance distinguishes jitteriness from convulsions by stimulus sensitivity and suppressibility. Jitteriness may be triggered by stimulation and stops when the limb is held, whereas seizure movements are not suppressed by restraint and may be accompanied by ocular or autonomic phenomena.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Jitteriness generally has a normal EEG.
- B. Incorrect. Ocular phenomena are more suggestive of seizures, not simple jitteriness.
- C. Incorrect. Seizures may cause autonomic changes such as apnoea, desaturation and heart-rate alteration.
- D. Incorrect. Convulsions are not usually stimulus-provoked.
- E. Correct. This is the most useful bedside distinction described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Jitteriness: stimulus-provoked, suppressible by holding the limb, no ocular/autonomic changes, usually normal EEG.
- Convulsion: not suppressed by restraint, may have ocular phenomena and autonomic changes, EEG abnormality may be present.
- Consider hypoglycaemia and hypocalcaemia in a jittery newborn.

questions.stem: A newborn has suspected seizures. Which investigation set is most appropriate initially?

options.label: B
options.text: Check glucose, calcium, magnesium, CBC, blood gas/electrolytes; add CSF, EEG or imaging as indicated

questions.correctAnswerText: Check glucose, calcium, magnesium, CBC, blood gas/electrolytes; add CSF, EEG or imaging as indicated
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes blood investigations for reversible metabolic causes, CBC and acid-base/electrolyte assessment, CSF if meningitis is suspected, EEG or continuous EEG, neuroimaging (cranial ultrasound, CT/MRI) and metabolic screening when appropriate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hip ultrasound assesses DDH, not seizures.
- B. Correct. This addresses common reversible causes and identifies neurological/infective pathology.
- C. Incorrect. Red reflex screens for ocular media opacity.
- D. Incorrect. Urine testing alone is insufficient.
- E. Incorrect. Bilirubin alone does not investigate the broad differential of neonatal seizures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Check glucose, calcium, magnesium, electrolytes, CBC and blood gas.
- Consider CSF when meningitis/encephalitis is suspected and it is safe to perform.
- EEG/cEEG confirms and monitors electrographic seizures.
- Cranial ultrasound may detect IVH; MRI is useful for ischaemic lesions and malformations.
- Consider metabolic screening when indicated by history/examination.

questions.stem: Which cause is listed as the commonest underlying cause of neonatal seizures?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include HIE as the commonest cause of neonatal seizures. Other causes include infection, intracranial haemorrhage/stroke, metabolic abnormalities, kernicterus, brain malformations, drug withdrawal and pyridoxine deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. HIE is identified as the commonest cause in the source.
- B. Incorrect. Caput succedaneum is a birth-related scalp swelling.
- C. Incorrect. DDH is an orthopaedic condition.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital cataract does not typically cause neonatal seizures.
- E. Incorrect. Uncomplicated physiological jaundice does not cause seizures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Commonest cause: HIE.
- Other causes: meningitis/encephalitis/sepsis, IVH/stroke, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, sodium disorders, inborn errors, kernicterus, malformations and pyridoxine deficiency.
- Identify the cause rather than treating every seizure as primary epilepsy.

questions.stem: A newborn has seizures associated with severe hypoglycaemia. What is the management priority?

options.label: B
options.text: Give a long-term anticonvulsant without checking glucose

options.label: D
options.text: Delay treatment until MRI is completed

options.label: E
options.text: Stabilize airway, breathing and circulation, correct hypoglycaemia promptly and assess for other reversible causes

questions.correctAnswerText: Stabilize airway, breathing and circulation, correct hypoglycaemia promptly and assess for other reversible causes
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes initial ABC stabilization, oxygenation as needed, IV access and urgent identification/correction of reversible causes such as hypoglycaemia and hypocalcaemia before escalating anticonvulsant treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fluid management is individualized; blanket fluid restriction is not the response to hypoglycaemic seizures.
- B. Incorrect. Anticonvulsants alone do not correct hypoglycaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Treatment must not be delayed for imaging.
- E. Correct. Treating the underlying metabolic disturbance is essential and time-critical.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stabilize ABC first.
- Check bedside glucose immediately.
- Correct hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbances promptly.
- Investigate infection, intracranial haemorrhage and HIE as indicated.
- Do not delay emergency correction of reversible causes for imaging.

questions.stem: Which anticonvulsant is listed as first-line therapy for neonatal seizures?
questions.correctAnswerText: Phenobarbital
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include phenobarbital as first-line treatment. If seizures persist, phenytoin is listed as second-line, benzodiazepines such as diazepam or midazolam as subsequent options, and pyridoxine may be considered in refractory cases. Treatment should be guided by neonatal seizure protocols and EEG.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Phenytoin is listed as second-line.
- B. Incorrect. Diazepam is listed among later-line options.
- C. Incorrect. Carbamazepine is not listed as first-line acute treatment for neonatal seizures in this standard guidance.
- D. Correct. Phenobarbital is the first-line drug listed in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Midazolam is also listed among later-line options.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- First-line: phenobarbital.
- If persistent: consider phenytoin, then benzodiazepines under specialist guidance.
- Refractory seizures may require pyridoxine trial and/or anaesthetic therapy in a specialist NICU.
- Exact loading/maintenance doses are protocol-specific; verify current neonatal guidance rather than relying on potentially misread OCR values.

cases.title: Several newborns with abnormal movements

questions.stem: Three newborns have these movements: (1) rhythmic jerking of the right arm and face that continues when the limb is gently held; (2) stiffening posture of the trunk and limbs; (3) brief shock-like jerks of the fingers and toes. Which pairing is correct, and what is the first check?

options.label: D
options.text: (1) focal clonic; (2) tonic; (3) myoclonic; check blood glucose and calcium first

questions.correctAnswerText: (1) focal clonic; (2) tonic; (3) myoclonic; check blood glucose and calcium first
questions.initialExplanation: Clonic seizures are rhythmic twitching of a muscle group (focal, multifocal or generalized), tonic seizures are rigid posturing, and myoclonic jerks are brief focal or generalized jerks, mainly of distal muscles. Movements that do not stop on holding are not jitteriness.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The types are mismatched.
- B. Incorrect. The types are mismatched.
- C. Incorrect. Movement continuing when held is not jitteriness.
- D. Correct. Matches each type and the first reversible causes.
- E. Incorrect. Subtle seizures are eye, orofacial, limb-cycling or autonomic phenomena.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Subtle seizures are commonest; clonic, tonic and myoclonic are other types.
- Jitteriness stops on holding the limb and is stimulus-provoked.
- Stabilize ABC, treat hypoglycaemia (dextrose) and hypocalcaemia (calcium gluconate).
- First-line drug: phenobarbital.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Pages 58-59 (clinical features of seizures; management).

questions.stem: A well term baby has brief focal clonic seizures on day 4. Glucose, calcium, magnesium and sodium are normal; CSF and imaging are normal. Several maternal relatives had seizures as newborns that resolved in infancy, and there is no maternal drug use. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Benign familial neonatal seizures
questions.initialExplanation: Benign familial neonatal seizures are a listed cause of neonatal seizures. Normal metabolic and structural work-up with a family pattern and a well infant fits this diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A family pattern and a normal work-up in a well infant are typical.
- B. Incorrect. HIE, the commonest cause, requires a perinatal hypoxic event and encephalopathy.
- C. Incorrect. Abstinence syndrome requires maternal substance use.
- D. Incorrect. Pyridoxine deficiency is considered when seizures are refractory; standard guidance gives pyridoxine as a late step.
- E. Incorrect. Kernicterus needs severe jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Commonest cause: HIE. Other causes: infection, haemorrhage/stroke, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, sodium disorders, inborn errors, kernicterus, malformations, maternal substance abuse, benign familial seizures, pyridoxine deficiency.
- Drug ladder: phenobarbital, phenytoin, benzodiazepines, pyridoxine, general anaesthesia.
- Prognosis depends on the cause.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 58 (causes of neonatal seizures); Page 59 (management).

cases.title: A newborn is plethoric and develops hypoglycaemia and respiratory distress
cases.vignette: A term infant born after a pregnancy complicated by IUGR and maternal smoking is noted to have a plethoric face. The infant develops respiratory distress, lethargy and hypoglycaemia. A central venous haematocrit is 68%.

questions.stem: What is the definition of neonatal polycythaemia used?
questions.correctAnswerText: Central venous haematocrit above 65%
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe neonatal polycythaemia as a central venous haematocrit (Hct/PCV) greater than 65%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is markedly elevated but not the diagnostic threshold.
- B. Incorrect. This is below the diagnostic threshold.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the threshold in the source.
- D. Incorrect. standard guidance uses a value above 65%.
- E. Correct. Central venous Hct >65% defines neonatal polycythaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal polycythaemia: central venous Hct >65%.
- A capillary heel-prick haematocrit may overestimate the value; confirm with a venous sample.
- Increased red-cell mass increases blood viscosity and may impair perfusion.
- Plethora may be the only finding in an asymptomatic infant.

questions.stem: Which group contains recognized causes of neonatal polycythaemia?

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic intrauterine hypoxia (IUGR, maternal diabetes, smoking), twin-to-twin transfusion and delayed cord clamping

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic intrauterine hypoxia (IUGR, maternal diabetes, smoking), twin-to-twin transfusion and delayed cord clamping
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include increased fetal erythropoiesis due to intrauterine hypoxia (IUGR, IDM and maternal smoking), increased blood volume from twin-to-twin transfusion or delayed cord clamping, and fetal abnormalities such as trisomy 21 and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vitamin K prevents bleeding and does not cause polycythaemia.
- B. Incorrect. These do not increase neonatal red-cell mass.
- C. Incorrect. Maternal iron deficiency is associated with anaemia, not neonatal polycythaemia.
- D. Correct. These are the main cause groups described.
- E. Incorrect. These congenital abnormalities are not the principal causes listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Increased erythropoiesis: fetal hypoxia from IUGR, IDM and maternal smoking.
- Increased blood volume: twin-to-twin transfusion and delayed cord clamping.
- Associated fetal conditions include Down syndrome and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
- Consider the cause when assessing a plethoric newborn.

questions.stem: Which clinical manifestation may occur in symptomatic neonatal polycythaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Respiratory distress, jaundice, lethargy, hypotonia, irritability, seizures or hypoglycaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Respiratory distress, jaundice, lethargy, hypotonia, irritability, seizures or hypoglycaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Polycythaemia may be asymptomatic or cause symptoms related to hyperviscosity and impaired perfusion. Common examples include respiratory distress, jaundice, lethargy, hypotonia, irritability, convulsions and hypoglycaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the clinical features described.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests severe bilirubin encephalopathy.
- C. Incorrect. A continuous murmur with bounding pulses suggests PDA.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests facial nerve palsy.
- E. Incorrect. Pale stool and dark urine suggest cholestatic jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Polycythaemia may be asymptomatic with only a plethoric face.
- Hyperviscosity may cause respiratory, neurological, metabolic and gastrointestinal complications.
- Common examples include NEC, stroke, heart failure and learning difficulties among possible complications.
- Check glucose, bilirubin, hydration and perfusion.

questions.stem: A symptomatic newborn has confirmed polycythaemia with a central venous haematocrit of 67%. Which treatment is described for symptomatic hyperviscosity?

options.label: A
options.text: Exchange transfusion with donor blood to increase haematocrit

options.label: D
options.text: Partial exchange transfusion with careful hydration and NICU monitoring

questions.correctAnswerText: Partial exchange transfusion with careful hydration and NICU monitoring
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include good hydration for at-risk infants and partial exchange transfusion for selected polycythaemic infants, particularly when symptomatic. Exact thresholds and technique should follow current neonatal protocols and specialist assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Increasing haematocrit would worsen hyperviscosity.
- B. Incorrect. Iron does not acutely reduce red-cell concentration or viscosity.
- C. Incorrect. Splenectomy has no role in neonatal polycythaemia management.
- D. Correct. Partial exchange transfusion reduces haematocrit and viscosity; hydration and monitoring are important.
- E. Incorrect. Phototherapy treats unconjugated jaundice, not hyperviscosity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat the infant, not the laboratory value alone.
- Assess symptoms, venous Hct, hydration and perfusion.
- Partial exchange transfusion may be considered in symptomatic or severe cases under NICU guidance.
- Thresholds (>70% asymptomatic and >60% symptomatic) should be checked against current local policy.

cases.title: A healthy term infant has a gradual decline in haemoglobin during the first months
cases.vignette: A term infant is clinically well but has a gradual fall in haemoglobin during the first 8-12 weeks of life. There is no evidence of bleeding or haemolysis. The clinician explains the physiological anaemia of infancy.

questions.stem: What is the expected haemoglobin pattern in a term infant described?

options.label: A
options.text: Haemoglobin rises continuously during the first week

options.label: B
options.text: Haemoglobin remains at birth level throughout infancy

options.label: C
options.text: Haemoglobin falls to 4 g/dL by 2 weeks in each infant

options.label: D
options.text: Haemoglobin falls from approximately 14-24 g/dL at birth to around 10-11 g/dL by 8-12 weeks

options.label: E
options.text: Haemoglobin is normally below 8 g/dL at birth

questions.correctAnswerText: Haemoglobin falls from approximately 14-24 g/dL at birth to around 10-11 g/dL by 8-12 weeks
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include a physiological fall in haemoglobin after birth, reaching approximately 10-11 g/dL by 8-12 weeks in term infants. This reflects the transition from fetal to postnatal oxygenation, reduced erythropoietin stimulation and the relatively short lifespan of neonatal red cells.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Haemoglobin does not continuously rise during the first week as the normal pattern described.
- B. Incorrect. A physiological decline occurs after birth.
- C. Incorrect. A fall to 4 g/dL is not physiological.
- D. Correct. This matches the pattern stated in the source.
- E. Incorrect. The normal Hb at birth is much higher.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Physiological anaemia of infancy: Hb falls after birth as erythropoietin stimulation decreases.
- Term infant Hb may reach approximately 10-11 g/dL at 8-12 weeks.
- Preterm infants experience a more pronounced fall due to shorter RBC survival, lower iron stores and rapid growth.
- Term infants generally require no treatment; preterm infants may need iron supplementation.

topics.name: Haemorrhagic Disease of the Newborn - Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding

cases.title: A newborn develops gastrointestinal bleeding during the first week
cases.vignette: A 5-day-old infant who did not receive vitamin K prophylaxis develops bruising, bleeding from the umbilical stump and melaena. Platelet count is normal, but PT and aPTT are prolonged.

questions.stem: Which coagulation factors are vitamin K-dependent?

options.label: A
options.text: Factors VIII, IX, XI and XII

options.label: B
options.text: Factors I, V, VIII and XIII

options.label: C
options.text: Factors I, II, V and VIII

options.label: D
options.text: Factors II, VII, IX and X

options.label: E
options.text: Factors V, VIII, XI and XII

questions.correctAnswerText: Factors II, VII, IX and X
questions.initialExplanation: Vitamin K is required for synthesis of coagulation factors II, VII, IX and X. Deficiency causes impaired coagulation and bleeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Factors VIII, XI and XII are not vitamin K-dependent.
- B. Incorrect. These are not the vitamin K-dependent factors.
- C. Incorrect. Factors I, V and VIII are not vitamin K-dependent.
- D. Correct. Factors II, VII, IX and X require vitamin K.
- E. Incorrect. Factors V, VIII, XI and XII are not vitamin K-dependent.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vitamin K-dependent factors: II, VII, IX and X.
- Vitamin K is fat-soluble and is obtained from diet and intestinal bacterial synthesis.
- Newborns have low stores and a relatively sterile gut, so prophylaxis is important.
- All newborns should receive vitamin K at birth according to local protocol.

questions.stem: Which factor predisposes a newborn to vitamin K deficiency bleeding?

options.label: C
options.text: Low vitamin K stores, immature liver, low intake, absent intestinal flora, malabsorption and maternal anticonvulsant use

options.label: E
options.text: Excessive vitamin K stores and mature intestinal flora

questions.correctAnswerText: Low vitamin K stores, immature liver, low intake, absent intestinal flora, malabsorption and maternal anticonvulsant use
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include low neonatal stores, hepatic immaturity, low intake (breast milk contains relatively little vitamin K), lack of intestinal bacterial synthesis at birth, liver disease/malabsorption and maternal drugs such as anticonvulsants or warfarin as risk factors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Platelet count does not determine vitamin K availability.
- B. Incorrect. Albumin concentration is not the underlying mechanism.
- C. Correct. These factors reduce vitamin K availability or function.
- D. Incorrect. Iron supplementation is not a risk factor for VKDB.
- E. Incorrect. Newborns have low stores and immature gut flora.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prematurity and liver immaturity increase risk.
- Breast milk has relatively low vitamin K content.
- No established intestinal flora at birth means limited endogenous vitamin K synthesis.
- Maternal anticonvulsants (e.g. phenobarbital/phenytoin) and warfarin can predispose.

questions.stem: Which timing correctly matches the classical and late forms of vitamin K deficiency bleeding?
questions.correctAnswerText: Classical: day 2-7; late: 2-8 weeks
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe classical VKDB as occurring in the second to seventh day of life, often when prophylaxis was not given. Late VKDB occurs from 2 to 8 weeks and is associated with liver disease or malabsorption; intracranial haemorrhage is more common.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Classical and late VKDB occur after birth at the specified times.
- B. Incorrect. These ages are outside the neonatal VKDB classification.
- C. Correct. These are the time ranges described.
- D. Incorrect. The timing is reversed.
- E. Incorrect. The first 24 hours is the early form and is rare.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early VKDB: within 24 hours; rare, associated with maternal drugs affecting vitamin K.
- Classical VKDB: day 2-7.
- Late VKDB: 2-8 weeks, often associated with liver disease/malabsorption and more intracranial bleeding.
- Prevention with vitamin K prophylaxis is essential.

questions.stem: A newborn has suspected vitamin K deficiency bleeding. Which laboratory pattern is expected?

options.label: B
options.text: Normal PT/aPTT with markedly prolonged bleeding time

options.label: C
options.text: Low platelet count, shortened PT and shortened aPTT

options.label: D
options.text: Normal platelet count, prolonged PT and aPTT, and normal bleeding time

options.label: E
options.text: High platelets and normal coagulation tests

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal platelet count, prolonged PT and aPTT, and normal bleeding time
questions.initialExplanation: Vitamin K deficiency affects coagulation-factor synthesis, not platelet number or primary platelet function. Clinical descriptions include a normal platelet count, prolonged PT and aPTT, and normal bleeding time.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Direct Coombs detects antibody-mediated red-cell coating and is unrelated to VKDB.
- B. Incorrect. A prolonged bleeding time suggests a platelet/vessel problem rather than isolated vitamin K deficiency.
- C. Incorrect. Thrombocytopenia is not the primary abnormality in VKDB.
- D. Correct. This is the expected pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Coagulation tests are usually prolonged.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CBC: platelets usually normal; Hb falls if bleeding is severe.
- PT and aPTT: prolonged.
- Bleeding time: normal.
- Treatment includes vitamin K; serious bleeding may require fresh frozen plasma and/or blood transfusion according to clinical severity.

questions.stem: What is the most effective routine prevention of vitamin K deficiency bleeding in the newborn?

options.label: E
options.text: Delaying the first feed for 24 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Vitamin K prophylaxis at birth
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is that all newborns should receive vitamin K at birth to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding. The route and dose should follow the local neonatal prophylaxis protocol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Vitamin K prophylaxis prevents deficiency of factors II, VII, IX and X.
- B. Incorrect. Exchange transfusion is not routine prophylaxis.
- C. Incorrect. Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Iron does not prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
- E. Incorrect. Delaying feeding does not prevent VKDB.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Give vitamin K prophylaxis to all newborns according to the local protocol.
- Vitamin K deficiency can cause umbilical, gastrointestinal, skin/injection-site or intracranial bleeding.
- Babies with cholestasis/malabsorption or maternal exposure to enzyme-inducing drugs need particular attention.
- Treat serious active bleeding with vitamin K and appropriate blood products under neonatal specialist care.

cases.title: A newborn has limited hip abduction and asymmetric thigh creases
cases.vignette: A 6-week-old girl, born breech and with a positive family history, is found to have asymmetric thigh and gluteal creases with limited abduction of the left hip. The examiner performs the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres and arranges hip imaging.

questions.stem: Which is a recognized risk factor for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)?

options.label: B
options.text: Male sex, cephalic presentation and multiparity

options.label: C
options.text: Female sex, breech presentation, first-born child or positive family history

questions.correctAnswerText: Female sex, breech presentation, first-born child or positive family history
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include female sex (female:male ratio about 6:1), first-born status, positive family history, breech presentation and neuromuscular disorders/neural tube defects among DDH risk factors. It is more common on the left.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Caesarean section alone is not the risk factor; breech presentation is important regardless of delivery mode.
- B. Incorrect. Female sex and breech presentation increase risk.
- C. Correct. These are major DDH risk factors described.
- D. Incorrect. Neonatal jaundice is not a DDH risk factor.
- E. Incorrect. Maternal iron deficiency is not a recognized DDH risk factor.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DDH risks: female, breech, first-born, family history, neuromuscular disorders/NTD.
- More common on the left side.
- Routine newborn hip examination includes Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres.
- Screen high-risk infants with hip ultrasound.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the Ortolani manoeuvre?

options.label: D
options.text: To dislocate a stable hip intentionally

options.label: E
options.text: To detect a dislocated hip that can be reduced back into the acetabulum

questions.correctAnswerText: To detect a dislocated hip that can be reduced back into the acetabulum
questions.initialExplanation: The Ortolani manoeuvre detects a dislocated femoral head that can be reduced into the acetabulum. A palpable “clunk” during abduction and gentle anterior lifting suggests a positive test.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The manoeuvre assesses hip stability, not knee ligaments.
- B. Incorrect. Clavicle fracture is assessed by palpation and radiography.
- C. Incorrect. Femoral nerve function is not assessed by Ortolani.
- D. Incorrect. Barlow is the manoeuvre that tests whether a located hip is dislocatable.
- E. Correct. Ortolani reduces a dislocated hip and detects reducibility.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ortolani: reduce a dislocated hip into the acetabulum.
- Barlow: provoke posterior dislocation of an unstable but located hip.
- Both are part of newborn hip screening.
- Avoid forceful manoeuvres; examine gently.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the Barlow manoeuvre?

options.label: A
options.text: It measures the angle of knee flexion

options.label: B
options.text: It reduces a dislocated hip into the acetabulum

options.label: D
options.text: It detects an absent femoral pulse

options.label: E
options.text: It tests whether a located but unstable hip can be dislocated posteriorly

questions.correctAnswerText: It tests whether a located but unstable hip can be dislocated posteriorly
questions.initialExplanation: The Barlow manoeuvre tests whether the femoral head can be displaced posteriorly out of the acetabulum, indicating an unstable/dislocatable hip.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Knee angle is not the purpose of Barlow.
- B. Incorrect. This describes Ortolani.
- C. Incorrect. Moro is a primitive reflex.
- D. Incorrect. Femoral pulses are assessed separately for coarctation.
- E. Correct. Barlow assesses whether a located hip is dislocatable.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Barlow: dislocatable hip.
- Ortolani: reduction of a dislocated hip.
- Positive findings warrant imaging and paediatric orthopaedic follow-up.
- A negative newborn examination does not exclude later-presenting DDH.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant has a positive Galeazzi sign. What does this indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: One knee sits lower with hips/knees flexed, suggesting unilateral hip dislocation or shortening

options.label: C
options.text: Both feet are fixed in equinovarus

options.label: D
options.text: One arm has an absent Moro reflex

options.label: E
options.text: There is a positive red reflex

questions.correctAnswerText: One knee sits lower with hips/knees flexed, suggesting unilateral hip dislocation or shortening
questions.initialExplanation: A positive Galeazzi sign is a difference in apparent knee height when both hips and knees are flexed, suggesting unilateral femoral shortening or hip dislocation. Other DDH signs include asymmetric skin creases and limited hip abduction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the Galeazzi sign described.
- B. Incorrect. This is a vascular finding and not Galeazzi.
- C. Incorrect. This describes clubfoot.
- D. Incorrect. An asymmetric Moro reflex suggests a birth injury such as brachial plexus injury or clavicle fracture.
- E. Incorrect. Red reflex is an ocular screening test.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DDH signs: asymmetric thigh/gluteal creases, limited abduction, Galeazzi sign and later waddling gait/limp.
- Bilateral DDH may be harder to detect from asymmetry alone.
- Examine both hips and compare abduction and knee height.

questions.stem: Which imaging approach is appropriate for suspected DDH?

options.label: D
options.text: Hip ultrasound in early infancy; AP pelvic X-ray after approximately 4-6 months

questions.correctAnswerText: Hip ultrasound in early infancy; AP pelvic X-ray after approximately 4-6 months
questions.initialExplanation: Ultrasound is used to assess the cartilaginous infant hip early in life, particularly in high-risk babies. Recommended management includes an AP pelvic X-ray after about 4-6 months, when the femoral head ossification centre becomes more useful radiographically.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Imaging is indicated for positive examination findings or high-risk infants.
- B. Incorrect. Chest X-ray does not assess hip development.
- C. Incorrect. CT brain does not diagnose DDH.
- D. Correct. This is the imaging approach in the source.
- E. Incorrect. MRI spine is not the routine DDH study.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early DDH imaging: ultrasound.
- Later infancy: AP pelvis X-ray becomes useful after around 4-6 months.
- Ultrasound screening is recommended for high-risk infants, such as breech presentation, family history or associated talipes.
- Refer positive examination findings promptly.

questions.stem: What is the usual initial treatment for DDH in a young infant?

options.label: D
options.text: Pavlik harness; hip spica or surgery may be required depending on age and response

questions.correctAnswerText: Pavlik harness; hip spica or surgery may be required depending on age and response
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include a Pavlik harness or hip spica as conservative treatment, with surgery considered if conservative treatment fails or the child presents later.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotics treat infection, not hip dysplasia.
- B. Incorrect. Vitamin K prevents bleeding.
- C. Incorrect. Phototherapy treats unconjugated jaundice.
- D. Correct. This matches the treatment options in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Amputation has no role in DDH.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early treatment improves hip development and reduces later deformity.
- Pavlik harness is commonly used in young infants.
- Hip spica casting or operative reduction may be required if harness treatment fails or for later presentation.
- Orthopaedic follow-up and imaging are essential.

cases.title: A newborn has a fixed inward-turned foot
cases.vignette: A newborn is noted to have a foot held in equinus and varus. The foot cannot be fully corrected by gentle passive manipulation. The clinician distinguishes true congenital talipes equinovarus from positional talipes due to intrauterine compression.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes true congenital talipes equinovarus from positional talipes?

options.label: A
options.text: Positional talipes is caused by fetal hypoxia

options.label: B
options.text: True clubfoot is fixed and cannot be fully corrected passively; positional talipes can be corrected to neutral with gentle manipulation

options.label: C
options.text: Both conditions are identical and require no assessment

options.label: D
options.text: Positional talipes is typically fixed and bilateral

options.label: E
options.text: True clubfoot typically resolves spontaneously in a few days

questions.correctAnswerText: True clubfoot is fixed and cannot be fully corrected passively; positional talipes can be corrected to neutral with gentle manipulation
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance distinguishes true talipes equinovarus, which is fixed and often bilateral, from positional talipes due to intrauterine compression, which can be corrected to the neutral position by passive manipulation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Positional talipes is related to intrauterine positioning/compression, not fetal hypoxia.
- B. Correct. Fixed deformity versus passive correctability is the key distinction.
- C. Incorrect. True clubfoot requires orthopaedic assessment and treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Positional talipes is usually flexible and correctable.
- E. Incorrect. True clubfoot does not reliably resolve spontaneously.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- True talipes equinovarus: fixed deformity, may be bilateral, may be associated with familial/idiopathic causes, oligohydramnios or neuromuscular disorders such as spina bifida.
- Positional talipes: flexible and correctable with passive movement.
- Clubfoot is associated with DDH; assess the hips as well.
- Refer for orthopaedic assessment and Ponseti casting/bracing when indicated.

topics.name: Primitive Reflexes and Neurological Examination of the Newborn

cases.title: A newborn undergoes a structured neurological examination
cases.vignette: A term newborn is assessed for tone, posture and primitive reflexes. Rooting, sucking, Moro, palmar and plantar grasp, stepping, placing, asymmetrical tonic neck and Galant reflexes are checked. Reflexes are compared bilaterally and with age- and maturity-appropriate findings.

questions.stem: What is the origin of primitive reflexes in the newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: They are voluntary movements controlled by the mature frontal cortex

options.label: B
options.text: They are pathological movements in each newborn

options.label: C
options.text: They are caused by maternal hormones

options.label: D
options.text: They are mediated mainly at subcortical levels because the cerebral cortex is still functionally immature

options.label: E
options.text: They are produced by the spinal cord after 1 year of age

questions.correctAnswerText: They are mediated mainly at subcortical levels because the cerebral cortex is still functionally immature
questions.initialExplanation: Primitive reflexes are automatic responses mediated at subcortical levels in the immature newborn nervous system. They gradually become inhibited as cortical control develops.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Primitive reflexes are involuntary rather than learned voluntary actions.
- B. Incorrect. Primitive reflexes are normal findings in newborns.
- C. Incorrect. They are neurological responses, not hormone-mediated behaviours.
- D. Correct. This is the definition.
- E. Incorrect. They are present in early infancy and are not restricted to later spinal control.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primitive reflexes are subcortically mediated.
- They are expected in normal newborns and gradually disappear with cortical maturation.
- standard guidance gives approximately 4-6 months for disappearance of many primitive reflexes.
- Interpret reflexes according to gestational age and the specific reflex.

questions.stem: What is the significance of an asymmetrical primitive reflex response?

options.label: A
options.text: It proves that the infant has hypoglycaemia

options.label: B
options.text: It may indicate a focal neurological deficit or birth injury

options.label: D
options.text: It is diagnostic of congenital hypothyroidism

questions.correctAnswerText: It may indicate a focal neurological deficit or birth injury
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that normal neonatal reflexes indicate normal neurological function, an asymmetrical response suggests a focal neurological deficit, and persistence beyond the expected age may indicate cortical damage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia may affect neurological function but is not diagnosed from asymmetry alone.
- B. Correct. Asymmetry may indicate unilateral neurological or musculoskeletal pathology.
- C. Incorrect. A reflex should generally be symmetrical.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism is not diagnosed by an asymmetric reflex.
- E. Incorrect. Asymmetry should prompt careful reassessment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal reflexes should be present and generally symmetrical.
- Asymmetry may indicate focal neurological deficit, brachial plexus injury, clavicle fracture or other focal pathology.
- Persistence of primitive reflexes beyond the expected age may suggest cortical dysfunction.
- Moro is highlighted as particularly reliable and easy to elicit.

questions.stem: How is the Moro reflex elicited, and what is the normal response?

options.label: A
options.text: A brief controlled lowering of the supported infant elicits arm extension/abduction and hand opening, followed by flexion/adduction

options.label: B
options.text: Stroking the cheek causes the infant to turn toward the stimulus

options.label: C
options.text: Touching the sole causes the toes to curl downward

options.label: D
options.text: Holding the infant upright causes alternate stepping movements

options.label: E
options.text: Touching the palm causes the fingers to clasp the examiner's thumb

questions.correctAnswerText: A brief controlled lowering of the supported infant elicits arm extension/abduction and hand opening, followed by flexion/adduction
questions.initialExplanation: The Moro reflex is elicited by a brief, safe change in head/body support. The normal response is extension and abduction of the arms with opening/fanning of the hands, followed by flexion and adduction. The infant may also flex the hips and knees.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the normal biphasic Moro response.
- B. Incorrect. This describes the rooting reflex.
- C. Incorrect. This describes the plantar grasp reflex.
- D. Incorrect. This describes the stepping reflex.
- E. Incorrect. This describes the palmar grasp reflex.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Moro: arms extend/abduct, hands open/fan, then arms flex/adduct.
- It is an important and relatively easy primitive reflex to elicit.
- An absent or asymmetric Moro may suggest neurological injury, brachial plexus palsy or clavicle fracture.
- Perform the manoeuvre safely with the head and body supported.

questions.stem: Stroking a newborn's cheek causes the head to turn toward the stimulus and the mouth to open. Which reflex is being elicited?
questions.correctAnswerText: Rooting reflex
questions.initialExplanation: The rooting reflex is elicited by stroking the cheek. The infant turns toward the stimulus and opens the mouth, helping locate the nipple during feeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Palmar grasp occurs when the palm is touched.
- B. Correct. This is the rooting response.
- C. Incorrect. Parachute is a protective extension response that appears later in infancy.
- D. Incorrect. Moro is elicited by a sudden change in support/startle.
- E. Incorrect. Galant is elicited by stroking alongside the spine.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rooting: stroke cheek → head turns toward stimulus and mouth opens.
- Helps the infant find the nipple.
