- Sucking reflex: stimulation of the lips/mouth initiates sucking.

questions.stem: Which response describes the stepping reflex?

options.label: A
options.text: Turning the head causes extension of the ipsilateral limbs and flexion of the contralateral limbs

options.label: B
options.text: Stroking the spine produces trunk curvature

options.label: C
options.text: Stroking the cheek causes head turning

options.label: D
options.text: Touching the palm causes finger flexion

options.label: E
options.text: Holding the infant upright with the soles touching a surface produces alternate flexion and extension of the legs

questions.correctAnswerText: Holding the infant upright with the soles touching a surface produces alternate flexion and extension of the legs
questions.initialExplanation: The stepping reflex is elicited by supporting the infant upright so the soles touch a flat surface. The infant makes stepping-like alternating movements.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes the asymmetrical tonic neck reflex.
- B. Incorrect. This describes the Galant reflex.
- C. Incorrect. This describes rooting.
- D. Incorrect. This describes palmar grasp.
- E. Correct. This is the stepping response.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stepping: hold upright with feet touching surface → alternating leg movements.
- Placing: touch the dorsum of the foot against a table edge → flexion of hip/knee and lifting of the foot.
- These are primitive motor responses and are not evidence of independent walking.

questions.stem: When the head of a supine newborn is turned to one side, the arm and leg on that side extend while the opposite limbs flex. Which reflex is this?
questions.correctAnswerText: Asymmetrical tonic neck reflex (ATNR)
questions.initialExplanation: The asymmetrical tonic neck reflex is elicited by turning the infant's head to one side. The limbs on the face side extend, while the opposite limbs flex, producing the “fencing” posture.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Moro causes bilateral extension/abduction followed by flexion.
- B. Incorrect. Galant produces trunk/hip curvature toward a stimulus alongside the spine.
- C. Incorrect. Rooting is a head-turning response after cheek stimulation, not the fencing posture.
- D. Incorrect. Plantar grasp causes toe flexion.
- E. Correct. This is the ATNR response.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ATNR: head turns → ipsilateral limbs extend, contralateral limbs flex.
- Also called the fencing posture.
- Persistent primitive reflexes beyond the expected developmental period may indicate cortical dysfunction.

questions.stem: Stroking the skin alongside the newborn's spine causes the trunk and hips to curve toward the stimulated side. Which reflex is this?
questions.correctAnswerText: Galant (truncal incurvation) reflex
questions.initialExplanation: The Galant reflex is elicited by stroking the skin alongside the spine from the shoulder region toward the coccyx while the infant is supported prone. The trunk and hips curve toward the stimulated side.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Rooting follows cheek stimulation.
- B. Incorrect. Moro is a startle response.
- C. Correct. This describes the Galant response.
- D. Incorrect. Sucking follows stimulation of the lips or mouth.
- E. Incorrect. Parachute is a protective extension response.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Galant: stroke beside spine → trunk/hip curve toward stimulus.
- Palmar grasp: touch palm → fingers clasp.
- Plantar grasp: touch base of toes → toes flex/curl downward.
- Compare responses on both sides.

questions.stem: Which statement about the forward parachute reflex is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It indicates a focal neurological deficit in each infant

options.label: B
options.text: It is elicited by stroking the cheek

options.label: C
options.text: It is present at birth and disappears by 4 weeks

options.label: D
options.text: It is characterized by a strong palmar grasp

options.label: E
options.text: It is a protective extension response that appears after approximately 7 months and persists

questions.correctAnswerText: It is a protective extension response that appears after approximately 7 months and persists
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include the parachute reflex as an extension of the arms/hands when the infant is held and moved forward as if falling. It appears after approximately 7 months and persists as a protective response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The parachute reflex is a normal protective response.
- B. Incorrect. Stroking the cheek elicits rooting.
- C. Incorrect. This describes neither its onset nor its expected persistence.
- D. Incorrect. Palmar grasp is a separate primitive reflex.
- E. Correct. The parachute response appears later and normally persists.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Parachute: protective extension of the arms when moved forward.
- Appears after about 7 months and persists.
- Do not confuse it with primitive neonatal reflexes that normally disappear as cortical control matures.
- Assess reflexes in relation to age and developmental stage.

cases.title: Elimination, skin and midline findings in the nursery

questions.stem: A term boy has not passed meconium by day 3. The abdomen is distended and the anus is visibly patent. His older sister has cystic fibrosis. Which is the most likely cause?

options.label: E
options.text: Normal variation in a term newborn

questions.correctAnswerText: Meconium ileus
questions.initialExplanation: About 95% of healthy term babies pass meconium in the first 24-48 hours. Delayed passage has a differential of anal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus (cystic fibrosis) and organic obstruction. A patent anus excludes anal atresia, and the family history of cystic fibrosis points to meconium ileus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A visibly patent anus argues against anal atresia.
- B. Correct. Meconium ileus is the cystic fibrosis-related cause on standard guidance's list.
- C. Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease is on the list, but nothing here points to it, whereas the cystic fibrosis history strongly favours meconium ileus.
- D. Incorrect. Renal agenesis belongs to the differential of delayed passage of urine, not meconium.
- E. Incorrect. Passage beyond 48 hours with distension is not a normal variant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ~95% of term babies pass meconium within 24-48 hours.
- DD of delayed meconium: anal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus (cystic fibrosis), organic obstruction.
- Always inspect the anus for imperforate anus.
- Cystic fibrosis is also in the blood-spot screening programme.

source.raw: Neonatology sheet - Page 7 (DD of delayed passage of meconium).

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which urine description is most suggestive of glomerular haematuria?

options.label: B
options.text: Tea- or cola-coloured urine with dysmorphic red cells

options.label: D
options.text: Bright-red urine with isomorphic red cells and clots

options.label: E
options.text: Black urine due to homogentisic acid

questions.correctAnswerText: Tea- or cola-coloured urine with dysmorphic red cells
questions.initialExplanation: Glomerular bleeding typically produces tea- or cola-coloured urine because blood mixes with urine during passage through the nephron. Red cells become dysmorphic after crossing the glomerular filtration barrier.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Orange urine after rifampicin — Incorrect. Rifampicin can discolor urine but does not indicate haematuria.
- B. Tea/cola urine with dysmorphic cells — Correct. This is the characteristic glomerular pattern described.
- C. Cloudy offensive urine — Incorrect. This suggests UTI but does not establish glomerular bleeding.
- D. Bright-red urine with isomorphic cells and clots — Incorrect. This pattern suggests an extraglomerular source, such as lower urinary tract bleeding.
- E. Black urine — Incorrect. Clinical guidance homogentisic acid in alkaptonuria as one possible cause of dark urine.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Glomerular haematuria: tea/cola colour, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts and often proteinuria.
- Extraglomerular haematuria: bright red, isomorphic RBCs and possible clots.
- Always distinguish true haematuria from pigmenturia and drug/food-related urine discoloration.

questions.stem: Which urine microscopy finding most strongly supports a glomerular source of bleeding?
questions.correctAnswerText: Red-cell casts
questions.initialExplanation: Red-cell casts form within renal tubules and strongly support bleeding originating within the nephron, particularly glomerular inflammation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Isomorphic RBCs — Incorrect. These are more consistent with an extraglomerular source.
- B. Squamous epithelial cells — Incorrect. They may indicate contamination of the sample.
- C. Crystals — Incorrect. They may occur with stones or metabolic abnormalities but do not establish glomerular bleeding.
- D. Bacteria and nitrites — Incorrect. These support bacterial UTI rather than glomerular haematuria.
- E. Red-cell casts — Correct. They indicate that red cells have entered the tubular lumen and formed casts, supporting glomerular disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- RBC casts usually indicate glomerular disease.
- WBC casts suggest pyelonephritis.
- Hyaline casts may be seen in normal urine, fever, nephrotic syndrome or heart failure.
- Granular casts may be seen in renal parenchymal disease.

questions.stem: A urine sample is needed urgently from a severely ill young infant. Which collection method provides a relatively uncontaminated specimen directly from the bladder?

options.label: D
options.text: A sample taken from the nappy

questions.correctAnswerText: Suprapubic aspiration
questions.initialExplanation: Suprapubic aspiration obtains urine directly from the bladder using a needle. Clinical guidance it as an option in infants or newborns when urgent diagnosis is required, although it is invasive.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Suprapubic aspiration — Correct. It provides a direct bladder sample and may be used in a severely ill infant requiring urgent diagnosis.
- B. Unclean midstream sample — Incorrect. Proper cleansing and collection technique are important to reduce contamination.
- C. Adhesive bag — Incorrect. It is non-invasive but has a higher contamination risk from skin or faeces.
- D. Nappy sample — Incorrect. It is unsuitable for reliable urine culture because of contamination.
- E. Clean catch — Incorrect. It is the recommended non-invasive collection method when feasible, but the question asks for the direct bladder method.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clean catch: recommended non-invasive method when feasible.
- Midstream urine: preferable in school-age children.
- SPA: direct and relatively uncontaminated, but invasive.
- Bag specimens have contamination limitations and must be interpreted cautiously.

questions.stem: Which urine finding is most suggestive of proteinuria on simple visual inspection?
questions.correctAnswerText: Frothy urine
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance associates frothy urine with proteinuria. Visual appearance is only a clue; urine dipstick and quantitative protein measurement are required.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Orange urine — Incorrect. Some medications and foods can discolor urine.
- B. Black urine — Incorrect. Clinical guidance alkaptonuria among causes of black urine.
- C. Dark concentrated urine — Incorrect. This may occur with dehydration and does not itself prove proteinuria.
- D. Frothy urine — Correct. Protein in urine may cause persistent frothing.
- E. Offensive smell — Incorrect. It may occur in UTI or selected metabolic conditions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Frothy urine: consider proteinuria.
- Cloudy/turbid urine: consider UTI.
- Dark urine has a broad differential, including haematuria, haemoglobinuria, drugs, diet and metabolites.

questions.stem: Urine microscopy shows more than 5 white blood cells per high-power field, but urine culture is negative. What is this called?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sterile pyuria
questions.initialExplanation: Pyuria with a negative urine culture is termed sterile pyuria. Clinical guidance causes including renal stones, tuberculosis, febrile illness, dehydration, appendicitis, Kawasaki disease and SLE.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Haemoglobinuria — Incorrect. This refers to free haemoglobin in urine, often due to haemolysis.
- B. Nephrotic-range proteinuria — Incorrect. This refers to heavy urinary protein loss.
- C. Gross haematuria — Incorrect. This means visible blood in urine.
- D. Glycosuria — Incorrect. This is glucose in the urine.
- E. Sterile pyuria — Correct. White cells are present, but routine culture is negative.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pyuria: more than 5 WBC/HPF.
- Pyuria with positive culture supports UTI.
- Sterile pyuria requires a differential beyond routine bacterial UTI, including TB, stones, systemic inflammation and adjacent abdominal disease.

questions.stem: A child with fever has white-cell casts in the urine. Which diagnosis is most strongly suggested?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pyelonephritis
questions.initialExplanation: WBC casts indicate inflammation within the kidney and are associated with pyelonephritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Alport syndrome — Incorrect. It causes hereditary nephritis with haematuria, hearing and ocular features.
- B. Pyelonephritis — Correct. WBC casts support upper urinary tract infection involving renal tissue.
- C. Orthostatic proteinuria — Incorrect. It is posture-dependent protein excretion without inflammatory casts.
- D. Stones without infection — Incorrect. Stones may cause haematuria but do not typically explain WBC casts.
- E. Minimal change nephropathy — Incorrect. It causes nephrotic-range proteinuria rather than WBC casts as the defining finding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- WBC casts: think pyelonephritis.
- RBC casts: think glomerular disease.
- Hyaline casts may be nonspecific.
- Interpret microscopy with symptoms, dipstick, culture and renal function.

questions.stem: A child has bright-red urine with clots and is found to have isomorphic red cells. Which source is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Extraglomerular urinary tract
questions.initialExplanation: Bright-red urine, isomorphic red cells and clots point toward bleeding outside the glomerulus, such as the ureter, bladder or urethra.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Extraglomerular urinary tract — Correct. This matches the colour, RBC morphology and presence of clots.
- B. Type IV collagen defect — Incorrect. This is associated with Alport syndrome and glomerular haematuria.
- C. Immune-complex GN — Incorrect. It causes glomerular haematuria, often with dysmorphic cells and casts.
- D. Glomerular capillaries — Incorrect. Glomerular bleeding more typically produces tea/cola-coloured urine and dysmorphic cells.
- E. Minimal change nephropathy — Incorrect. It presents with heavy proteinuria and oedema, not this bleeding pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Glomerular: cola/tea urine, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, proteinuria.
- Extraglomerular: bright red, isomorphic RBCs, clots.
- The history should establish whether haematuria is initial, terminal or throughout the stream.

cases.title: Recurrent febrile UTIs and renal scarring
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old girl has had three episodes of febrile UTI. Renal ultrasound shows urinary tract dilatation. Micturating cystourethrography demonstrates retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into both ureters and the renal pelvis. The clinician explains that recurrent infection and raised voiding pressure may damage the renal parenchyma.

questions.stem: What is the defining feature of vesicoureteric reflux?

options.label: A
options.text: Protein leakage through the glomerular filtration barrier

options.label: C
options.text: Forward flow of urine from the kidney into the bladder

options.label: E
options.text: Retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureter and renal pelvis

questions.correctAnswerText: Retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureter and renal pelvis
questions.initialExplanation: VUR is the abnormal retrograde passage of urine from the bladder into the upper urinary tract.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes proteinuria due to filtration-barrier dysfunction.
- B. Incorrect. This describes impaired kidney filtration, not reflux.
- C. Incorrect. This is the normal direction of urine flow.
- D. Incorrect. Renal artery obstruction causes vascular impairment and may contribute to hypertension.
- E. Correct. This is the definition of VUR.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- VUR: bladder → ureter/renal pelvis.
- Primary VUR is related to an abnormal vesicoureteric junction.
- Secondary VUR may occur with recurrent UTI, urinary obstruction or neuropathic bladder.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cause of secondary VUR?

options.label: B
options.text: Congenital abnormality of the vesicoureteric junction

questions.correctAnswerText: Recurrent cystitis or urinary obstruction
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance distinguishes primary VUR, caused by an abnormal vesicoureteric junction, from secondary reflux due to conditions such as recurrent UTI, posterior urethral valves or neuropathic bladder.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Alport syndrome — Incorrect. It is a type IV collagen disorder causing hereditary nephritis.
- B. Congenital junction abnormality — Incorrect. This is the mechanism of primary VUR.
- C. Minimal change nephropathy — Incorrect. It is a glomerular protein-losing disease.
- D. Recurrent cystitis or obstruction — Correct. These are listed causes of secondary VUR.
- E. Renal agenesis — Incorrect. It is a congenital renal developmental anomaly, not the usual mechanism of secondary reflux.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary VUR: abnormal vesicoureteric junction; often familial.
- Secondary VUR: recurrent UTI, obstruction (e.g. PUV), neuropathic bladder or previous procedures.
- Ask about recurrent febrile UTI and voiding dysfunction.

questions.stem: How can longstanding severe VUR damage the kidney?

options.label: A
options.text: Reflux transmits voiding pressure to the renal pelvis and promotes infection, scarring and hydronephrosis

options.label: C
options.text: It increases glomerular basement membrane thickness

options.label: D
options.text: It reduces bladder pressure during voiding

options.label: E
options.text: It causes immediate complete renal agenesis

questions.correctAnswerText: Reflux transmits voiding pressure to the renal pelvis and promotes infection, scarring and hydronephrosis
questions.initialExplanation: VUR can cause urinary stasis and recurrent infection. Pressure transmitted during voiding may dilate the upper urinary tract and damage renal tissue, leading to reflux nephropathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This explains the pathway to pyelonephritis, renal scarring, hypertension and CKD.
- B. Incorrect. VUR may contribute to incomplete emptying and urinary stasis.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the mechanism of reflux nephropathy.
- D. Incorrect. Reflux does not protect the renal pelvis from pressure.
- E. Incorrect. Renal agenesis is a congenital failure of development and cannot be caused by VUR.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- VUR → stasis/recurrent infection + transmitted pressure → renal scarring.
- Severe bilateral reflux nephropathy may lead to hypertension and CKD.
- Recurrent pyelonephritis is a major pathway to renal damage.

questions.stem: Which investigation is used to diagnose and grade VUR?
questions.correctAnswerText: MCUG (micturating cystourethrogram)
questions.initialExplanation: MCUG involves introducing contrast into the bladder and imaging during filling and voiding. It demonstrates reflux and helps grade its severity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Renal biopsy — Incorrect. It is invasive and used for selected renal parenchymal diagnoses.
- B. Serum creatinine — Incorrect. It assesses renal function but cannot demonstrate reflux.
- C. MCUG — Correct. It is the investigation used for VUR diagnosis and grading.
- D. KUB — Incorrect. It may identify some stones or spinal abnormalities but does not diagnose reflux.
- E. DMSA — Incorrect. It is a static renal scan used to identify cortical defects and scars.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ultrasound: anatomy and urinary tract dilatation.
- MCUG: VUR and urethral obstruction.
- DMSA: renal cortical scars.
- MAG3/DTPA renogram: dynamic drainage and obstruction assessment.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Grade I VUR?

options.label: A
options.text: Reflux with gross dilatation and tortuosity of the ureter

options.label: C
options.text: Reflux into a severely dilated collecting system with loss of papillary impressions

questions.correctAnswerText: Reflux into a non-dilated ureter
questions.initialExplanation: Grade I is the mildest VUR grade and involves reflux into a non-dilated ureter.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Marked dilatation and tortuosity correspond to severe reflux.
- B. Incorrect. This does not define Grade I reflux.
- C. Incorrect. This describes the severe end of the VUR grading scale.
- D. Correct. This is the Grade I description.
- E. Incorrect. No reflux would mean no VUR.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Grade I: reflux into a non-dilated ureter.
- Grade II: reflux reaches the upper collecting system without dilatation.
- Grades IV–V: increasing dilatation; Grade V includes marked ureteral dilatation/tortuosity and loss of papillary impressions.
- Grade is determined by MCUG.

questions.stem: What is the general approach described for low-grade VUR (Grades I–III)?

options.label: D
options.text: Mandatory ureteric reimplantation in children in routine care

options.label: E
options.text: Observation and selected low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis, because reflux may resolve spontaneously

questions.correctAnswerText: Observation and selected low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis, because reflux may resolve spontaneously
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that Grades I–III may disappear spontaneously and may be managed with follow-up and prophylactic antibiotics in selected patients.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Steroids do not correct the abnormal vesicoureteric junction.
- B. Incorrect. Dialysis is not indicated for reflux itself.
- C. Incorrect. Nephrectomy is not a treatment for uncomplicated low-grade VUR.
- D. Incorrect. Surgery is reserved for selected severe or persistent cases, not every low-grade reflux.
- E. Correct. This is the conservative approach described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Grades I–III may resolve spontaneously.
- clinical guidance mentions low-dose trimethoprim as a commonly used prophylactic option, with alternatives.
- Management must be individualized to recurrence, renal scarring and the child's clinical course.

questions.stem: A child has Grade V VUR with marked ureteric dilatation and recurrent febrile UTIs despite appropriate conservative management. Which intervention is described for severe VUR?

options.label: A
options.text: Ureteric reimplantation or endoscopic injection at the ureteric junction

questions.correctAnswerText: Ureteric reimplantation or endoscopic injection at the ureteric junction
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance surgical reimplantation of the ureter or endoscopic injection of synthetic material at the ureteric junction for Grades IV–V.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the interventions listed for severe reflux.
- B. Incorrect. Renal artery angioplasty is used in selected renovascular disease, not VUR.
- C. Incorrect. Circumcision is not definitive treatment for severe VUR.
- D. Incorrect. Severe reflux with recurrent febrile UTI and renal-risk features requires active specialist follow-up.
- E. Incorrect. Coarctectomy treats aortic narrowing.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Severe VUR (Grades IV–V): may require ureteric reimplantation or endoscopic injection.
- Assess for recurrent pyelonephritis and renal scars.
- DMSA is used to assess renal cortical scarring.

cases.title: Fever in an infant with no clear source
cases.vignette: A 7-month-old infant presents with fever, vomiting, poor feeding and irritability. There is no obvious respiratory focus. Urine analysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria, and urine culture grows Escherichia coli. The clinician must distinguish upper from lower UTI, determine whether the infection is atypical, and choose the appropriate investigations and follow-up.

questions.stem: What is the most common causative organism of childhood UTI?
questions.correctAnswerText: Escherichia coli
questions.initialExplanation: E. coli, usually originating from intestinal flora and ascending through the urethra, is listed as the most common cause of childhood UTI.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pseudomonas — Incorrect. It is particularly associated with urinary tract abnormalities, long-standing catheterization or neurogenic bladder.
- B. Staphylococcus aureus — Incorrect. It is among other possible organisms, not the most common.
- C. Klebsiella — Incorrect. It is noted particularly in newborns but is not the commonest overall.
- D. Proteus — Incorrect. It is an important cause and is noted as more common in boys, but it is not the commonest organism.
- E. E. coli — Correct. Clinical guidance it as the most common organism, approximately 80%.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- E. coli is the commonest organism in childhood UTI.
- Proteus is associated with alkaline urine because it splits urea to ammonia.
- Ascending infection is the commonest route; blood-borne spread is important in the neonatal period.

questions.stem: Which presentation is more typical of UTI in neonates and young infants than in older children?

options.label: C
options.text: Non-specific symptoms such as poor feeding, irritability and vomiting

questions.correctAnswerText: Non-specific symptoms such as poor feeding, irritability and vomiting
questions.initialExplanation: Neonates and infants often present with non-specific features, including fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, lethargy, irritability, poor feeding or faltering growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Loin pain — Incorrect. This is a more localizing symptom of pyelonephritis in older children.
- B. Suprapubic pain — Incorrect. It is a more specific symptom of lower UTI in older children.
- C. Non-specific infant symptoms — Correct. These are listed for neonates and infants.
- D. Urgency and frequency — Incorrect. These are more typical of older children who can describe urinary symptoms.
- E. Dysuria and frequency — Incorrect. These are more specific urinary symptoms in older children.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infants: often non-specific symptoms and may have poor feeding or faltering growth.
- Older children: dysuria, urgency, frequency, loin pain or suprapubic pain.
- UTI should remain in the differential of unexplained fever in an infant.

questions.stem: Which feature most strongly suggests upper UTI (pyelonephritis) rather than isolated cystitis in an older child?

options.label: C
options.text: High fever with loin pain and tenderness

options.label: D
options.text: Secondary enuresis without fever or pain

options.label: E
options.text: Dysuria and frequency without systemic symptoms

questions.correctAnswerText: High fever with loin pain and tenderness
questions.initialExplanation: High fever, rigors and loin pain/tenderness suggest renal parenchymal involvement (pyelonephritis), whereas cystitis more commonly causes dysuria, frequency, urgency and suprapubic pain.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urgency alone is more typical of lower urinary tract symptoms.
- B. Incorrect. Suprapubic discomfort is typical of cystitis.
- C. Correct. Fever with loin pain and tenderness supports upper UTI.
- D. Incorrect. Secondary enuresis can occur with lower UTI but does not by itself indicate pyelonephritis.
- E. Incorrect. These symptoms are typical of lower UTI/cystitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pyelonephritis: fever, rigors, loin pain/tenderness, vomiting and systemic illness.
- Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain and sometimes haematuria.
- Infants may have nonspecific presentations of upper UTI.

questions.stem: Which result is diagnostic for UTI in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: E
options.text: Urine dipstick nitrite alone in each circumstance

questions.correctAnswerText: Urine culture and sensitivity
questions.initialExplanation: Urine culture and sensitivity is the diagnostic test for UTI. Dipstick and microscopy support the diagnosis, but culture identifies the organism and antibiotic susceptibility.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Ultrasound — Incorrect. It assesses anatomy and dilatation, not the microbiological diagnosis.
- B. Serum creatinine — Incorrect. It assesses renal function rather than proving UTI.
- C. DMSA — Incorrect. It is used to assess renal cortical defects/scarring.
- D. Urine culture and sensitivity — Correct. This is the diagnostic test identified.
- E. Nitrite alone — Incorrect. A positive nitrite supports UTI, but a negative result does not exclude it and culture is required.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Urinalysis: WBCs, nitrites, leukocyte esterase and bacteria.
- Nitrite positive supports UTI; a negative nitrite does not exclude infection.
- Culture confirms the organism and guides antibiotic sensitivity.

questions.stem: Which finding makes a UTI atypical and supports more extensive investigation?

options.label: A
options.text: Infection caused by E. coli in a well child

options.label: B
options.text: Poor urine flow or failure to respond to suitable antibiotics within 48 hours

options.label: C
options.text: First uncomplicated cystitis in an otherwise well older child

options.label: E
options.text: Normal renal function and normal ultrasound

questions.correctAnswerText: Poor urine flow or failure to respond to suitable antibiotics within 48 hours
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance serious illness, septicaemia, poor urine flow, abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, non-E. coli organisms, poor response within 48 hours and a family history of renal anomalies as reasons for extensive investigation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. E. coli in a well child — Incorrect. E. coli is the commonest usual organism.
- B. Poor flow or poor response — Correct. Both are listed as atypical features.
- C. First uncomplicated cystitis — Incorrect. It does not by itself represent an atypical infection.
- D. Rapid response — Incorrect. This is reassuring rather than an atypical feature.
- E. Normal tests — Incorrect. Normal findings do not create an indication for extensive investigation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Atypical UTI: serious illness/septicaemia, poor flow, mass, raised creatinine, non-E. coli organism or failure to respond within 48 hours.
- Recurrent UTI also prompts further assessment.
- Consider structural abnormalities such as VUR or obstruction.

questions.stem: Which imaging test is used to detect renal scars after UTI,?
questions.correctAnswerText: DMSA scan
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies DMSA as the scan used to demonstrate renal scarring, including after UTI.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. MCUG — Incorrect. It assesses VUR and urinary tract anatomy during bladder filling and voiding.
- B. DMSA — Correct. It detects renal cortical defects/scarring.
- C. Echocardiogram — Incorrect. It assesses the heart.
- D. KUB — Incorrect. It may detect some stones or spinal abnormalities but is not the renal scar study.
- E. Renal artery Doppler — Incorrect. It evaluates renal vascular flow, not cortical scars as the principal purpose.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ultrasound: anatomical assessment and urinary tract dilatation.
- MCUG: VUR and urethral anatomy.
- DMSA: renal scars.
- MAG3/DTPA renogram: dynamic drainage/obstruction assessment.

questions.stem: A child with suspected acute pyelonephritis is systemically unwell and unable to tolerate oral fluids. Which management approach is most appropriate?

options.label: C
options.text: Fluid restriction in children in routine care

options.label: D
options.text: Admission when indicated, hydration, antipyretics and IV antibiotics

questions.correctAnswerText: Admission when indicated, hydration, antipyretics and IV antibiotics
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance management of pyelonephritis with admission, IV fluids, antipyretics and IV antibiotics in the relevant age/severity groups, adjusted to culture sensitivity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Nephrectomy — Incorrect. It is not routine UTI treatment.
- B. Steroids — Incorrect. They are not routine first-line treatment for bacterial pyelonephritis.
- C. Fluid restriction — Incorrect. Clinical guidance hydration, not universal fluid restriction, for pyelonephritis.
- D. Hydration and antibiotics — Correct. These measures are listed, with route and duration determined by age and clinical state.
- E. No treatment — Incorrect. Pyelonephritis is an upper UTI that requires treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pyelonephritis is an upper UTI and may damage the kidney.
- Treatment includes hydration, antipyretics and antibiotics selected according to culture sensitivity.
- Follow-up includes BP, renal growth and renal function.

questions.stem: Which measure is included for prevention of recurrent childhood UTI?
questions.correctAnswerText: Treating and preventing constipation
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance includes constipation prevention, adequate fluid intake, regular voiding and good perineal hygiene as preventive measures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Restricting fluids — Incorrect. Adequate fluid intake is recommended.
- B. Delaying urination — Incorrect. Infrequent voiding can contribute to urinary stasis.
- C. Constipation management — Correct. It is specifically listed as a preventive measure.
- D. Nephrectomy — Incorrect. It is not a preventive measure for routine UTI.
- E. Avoiding voiding — Incorrect. Regular voiding is encouraged.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Encourage adequate fluid intake and regular voiding.
- Treat constipation.
- Maintain good perineal hygiene.
- Follow individualized advice for children with VUR or recurrent infection.

cases.title: A child with generalized oedema and frothy urine
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old child is brought with progressive periorbital puffiness, abdominal distension and swelling of the legs. The urine is frothy. Urine testing shows heavy proteinuria. Serum albumin is low and serum lipids are elevated. Blood pressure and renal function are initially normal.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Nephrotic syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia are the classic features of nephrotic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. PSGN — Incorrect. It typically presents with a nephritic pattern: haematuria, hypertension, oedema and oliguria.
- B. RTA — Incorrect. It causes normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and tubular manifestations.
- C. Pyelonephritis — Incorrect. It causes fever and urinary symptoms/systemic illness, not this characteristic protein-losing pattern.
- D. Nephrotic syndrome — Correct. The clinical and biochemical findings match the defining features.
- E. HUS — Incorrect. It is defined by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and AKI.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia.
- Nephritic syndrome: haematuria, hypertension, oedema and oliguria.
- Frothy urine may be a clinical clue to proteinuria.

questions.stem: What is the most common primary cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome?
questions.correctAnswerText: Minimal change nephropathy
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance minimal change nephropathy as the commonest primary cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome, accounting for approximately 85%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. PSGN — Incorrect. It is classically a nephritic syndrome.
- B. Membranous nephropathy — Incorrect. It is a less common cause and is discussed among other glomerular diseases.
- C. Alport syndrome — Incorrect. It is a hereditary nephritis rather than the commonest idiopathic nephrotic cause.
- D. Amyloidosis — Incorrect. It is not the commonest childhood cause in the supplied clinical guidance.
- E. Minimal change nephropathy — Correct. It is the commonest primary cause and usually responds to steroids.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Minimal change nephropathy is the commonest primary childhood nephrotic syndrome.
- Typical age given: approximately 2–6 years.
- Most cases respond well to corticosteroids.

questions.stem: What is the main mechanism contributing to generalized oedema in nephrotic syndrome as explained?

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced plasma albumin causing reduced oncotic pressure and fluid shift into the interstitium

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced plasma albumin causing reduced oncotic pressure and fluid shift into the interstitium
questions.initialExplanation: Heavy urinary albumin loss lowers plasma oncotic pressure. Fluid shifts from the intravascular space into the interstitium, producing generalized oedema.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Increased oncotic pressure — Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome causes hypoalbuminaemia and reduced oncotic pressure.
- B. Increased red cell mass — Incorrect. It does not explain the oedema of nephrotic syndrome.
- C. Reduced albumin and oncotic pressure — Correct. This is the mechanism described.
- D. Increased GFR — Incorrect. Clinical guidance altered filtration-barrier permeability and protein loss, not increased GFR as the oedema mechanism.
- E. Urinary sodium concentration alone — Incorrect. Sodium and water retention can contribute, but the mechanism emphasized is reduced albumin and oncotic pressure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Heavy proteinuria → hypoalbuminaemia → reduced plasma oncotic pressure → fluid shift into tissues → oedema.
- Oedema may be periorbital, dependent, genital, ascitic or generalized.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern supports typical steroid-sensitive minimal change nephrotic syndrome rather than an atypical presentation?

options.label: A
options.text: Low complement and impaired renal function

options.label: D
options.text: Age 2–6 years, normal BP and normal complement

questions.correctAnswerText: Age 2–6 years, normal BP and normal complement
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance typical minimal change nephropathy as occurring commonly at 2–6 years, with normal BP, normal complement, preserved renal function, selective proteinuria and good steroid response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Low complement and impaired renal function are warning features.
- B. Incorrect. Systemic features and non-selective proteinuria are atypical.
- C. Incorrect. Persistent renal impairment is not typical of uncomplicated steroid-sensitive minimal change disease.
- D. Correct. These features support typical minimal change disease.
- E. Incorrect. Persistent hypertension and gross haematuria are atypical and suggest another glomerular disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typical MCNS: age 2–6 years, normal BP, normal complement and renal function, selective proteinuria and good steroid response.
- Atypical features require reconsideration of diagnosis and may indicate renal biopsy.

questions.stem: According to the definitions, when is a nephrotic syndrome relapse recorded?

options.label: C
options.text: Proteinuria of +++ or more for 3 consecutive days

questions.correctAnswerText: Proteinuria of +++ or more for 3 consecutive days
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance defines relapse as +++ or more proteinuria for 3 consecutive days. Remission is no or trace proteinuria for 3 consecutive days.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Normal urine protein — Incorrect. This supports remission, not relapse.
- B. Trace proteinuria — Incorrect. No or trace proteinuria for 3 days is clinical guidance's definition of remission.
- C. +++ or more for 3 days — Correct. This is the stated relapse definition.
- D. Oedema alone — Incorrect. Oedema may accompany relapse but is not the stated urine-based definition.
- E. One positive dipstick — Incorrect. clinical guidance requires persistence for 3 consecutive days.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Remission: no/trace proteinuria for 3 consecutive days.
- Relapse: +++ or more for 3 consecutive days.
- clinical guidance defines steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome by remission within 4 weeks of steroid therapy.

questions.stem: Why are children with nephrotic syndrome at increased risk of infection?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased complement production in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Urinary loss of immunoglobulins and impaired immune function

questions.correctAnswerText: Urinary loss of immunoglobulins and impaired immune function
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance urinary loss of immunoglobulins and impaired T-cell function as contributors to infection risk in nephrotic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Increased complement in every case — Incorrect. This is not the mechanism described.
- B. Increased neutrophil function — Incorrect. It is not the mechanism described.
- C. Excessive immunoglobulin production — Incorrect. clinical guidance emphasizes urinary loss, not excessive production.
- D. High albumin — Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by low serum albumin.
- E. Urinary immunoglobulin loss — Correct. Loss of protective proteins contributes to susceptibility to infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nephrotic syndrome complications include infection, thrombosis, hypovolaemia, relapse, treatment adverse effects and dyslipidaemia.
- clinical guidance highlights pneumococcal and seasonal influenza vaccination and penicillin prophylaxis during relapse; apply local clinical guidance.

questions.stem: Which adverse effect is associated with prolonged corticosteroid therapy for nephrotic syndrome?

options.label: D
options.text: Reduced blood pressure in most patients

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyperglycaemia, obesity and growth retardation
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance metabolic, musculoskeletal, dermatological, infectious, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric adverse effects of steroids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hypoglycaemia and weight loss — Incorrect. Steroids may cause hyperglycaemia and weight gain.
- B. Hyperglycaemia, obesity and growth retardation — Correct. All are listed steroid adverse effects.
- C. Protection from infection — Incorrect. Steroids increase susceptibility to infection.
- D. Reduced BP — Incorrect. Steroids may cause hypertension, not universal BP reduction.
- E. Hypocalcaemia only — Incorrect. This is not the characteristic steroid adverse-effect profile.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Steroid adverse effects: hyperglycaemia, weight gain/Cushingoid appearance, myopathy, osteoporosis, poor wound healing/striae, infection, growth retardation, hypertension, gastric irritation/ulcer, cataract and mood changes.
- Monitor growth, BP, weight and infection risk during prolonged treatment.

questions.stem: Which complication should be considered when a child with nephrotic syndrome develops sudden unilateral limb swelling and pain?
questions.correctAnswerText: Venous thrombosis
questions.initialExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome is associated with a hypercoagulable state and increased risk of thromboembolism. Sudden painful limb swelling requires urgent assessment for venous thrombosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hydrocele — Incorrect. It causes scrotal swelling, not limb swelling.
- B. Renal agenesis — Incorrect. It is a congenital anomaly.
- C. Orthostatic proteinuria — Incorrect. It does not cause acute limb swelling.
- D. Venous thrombosis — Correct. Thromboembolism is a recognized complication of nephrotic syndrome.
- E. Cystitis — Incorrect. It causes lower urinary symptoms, not unilateral limb swelling.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nephrotic syndrome can cause hypercoagulability and thrombosis.
- New focal swelling, pain, chest pain or breathlessness requires urgent evaluation.
- Infection, hypovolaemia and thrombosis are important potentially serious complications.

cases.title: Severe oedema at first presentation
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old girl develops progressive eyelid swelling followed by abdominal distension and lower-limb oedema. Her mother notices persistent froth in the urine and rapid weight gain. Urine dipstick is ++++, the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 3.4, serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL and cholesterol is 285 mg/dL. Blood pressure and renal function are initially normal, and there is no macroscopic haematuria. During observation she becomes dizzy, has abdominal discomfort and passes very little urine.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best integrates the urine and blood results?

options.label: A
options.text: The child has isolated microscopic haematuria

options.label: B
options.text: The findings are most consistent with nephrotic syndrome

options.label: D
options.text: The results establish haemolytic uraemic syndrome

options.label: E
options.text: The findings are diagnostic of renal tubular acidosis

questions.correctAnswerText: The findings are most consistent with nephrotic syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Heavy proteinuria, marked hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia form the characteristic nephrotic pattern.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Microscopic haematuria does not explain the marked protein loss and low serum albumin.
- B. Correct. The combination is characteristic of nephrotic syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Cystitis does not cause this degree of protein loss and hypoalbuminaemia.
- D. Incorrect. HUS requires the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury.
- E. Incorrect. RTA causes a tubular acid–base disturbance, not this nephrotic biochemical pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance serum albumin below 2.5 g/dL and cholesterol above 250 mg/dL among the supportive findings.
- Heavy proteinuria is the central urinary abnormality.

questions.stem: Which additional pattern would make minimal-change nephropathy the most likely underlying diagnosis in this child?

options.label: A
options.text: Persistent hypertension, low C3 and impaired renal function

options.label: B
options.text: Gross haematuria, systemic manifestations and non-selective proteinuria

options.label: C
options.text: Normal blood pressure, normal complement and preserved renal function

options.label: D
options.text: A renal mass with bilateral hydronephrosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal blood pressure, normal complement and preserved renal function
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance typical steroid-sensitive minimal-change nephrotic syndrome as commonly occurring in young children with normal blood pressure, normal complement and normal renal function.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are atypical features and should prompt consideration of another glomerular disease.
- B. Incorrect. Gross haematuria and non-selective proteinuria are warning features.
- C. Correct. This is the typical pattern described for minimal-change disease.
- D. Incorrect. A mass and hydronephrosis suggest a structural or obstructive problem.
- E. Incorrect. Thrombocytopenia and schistocytes point toward HUS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typical minimal-change pattern: young age, normal BP, normal complement, normal renal function, selective proteinuria and good steroid response.
- Renal biopsy is not routinely indicated in a typical presentation.

questions.stem: The child becomes dizzy, has abdominal discomfort, oliguria and a low blood pressure despite having generalized oedema. Which complication should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Intravascular volume depletion (hypovolaemia)
questions.initialExplanation: A child with nephrotic oedema can still have reduced effective circulating volume. Dizziness, abdominal pain, low blood pressure and poor urine output are warning features of hypovolaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The clinical pattern suggests inadequate intravascular volume despite fluid accumulation in the tissues.
- B. Incorrect. Generalized oedema alone does not prove adequate circulating volume; the low BP and dizziness argue against this.
- C. Incorrect. Hyperlipidaemia does not explain the circulatory symptoms.
- D. Incorrect. Orthostatic proteinuria is an isolated urine finding and does not cause this acute presentation.
- E. Incorrect. A renal tumour would not explain the characteristic nephrotic biochemical pattern and acute volume-depletion signs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance associates low urinary sodium (below 10 mmol/L) and raised haemoglobin/haematocrit with hypovolaemia.
- This requires urgent assessment and treatment rather than simply escalating diuretics.

questions.stem: A child with nephrotic syndrome has severe generalized oedema requiring inpatient treatment. Which sequence is specifically described for severe oedema?

options.label: A
options.text: Start oral antibiotics, then restrict most protein

options.label: C
options.text: Give repeated furosemide before assessing circulating volume

options.label: D
options.text: Give 20% IV albumin first, followed by IV furosemide when indicated

questions.correctAnswerText: Give 20% IV albumin first, followed by IV furosemide when indicated
questions.initialExplanation: For severe generalized oedema, Clinical guidance intravenous 20% human albumin infusion followed by intravenous furosemide.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not routine oedema treatment, and protein restriction is not the described intervention.
- B. Incorrect. Severe oedema may require admission and close monitoring.
- C. Incorrect. Diuretic use without assessing intravascular volume can worsen hypovolaemia.
- D. Correct. This is the sequence described for severe oedema.
- E. Incorrect. Nephrectomy is not a treatment for ordinary childhood nephrotic syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Severe generalized oedema or complications may require admission.
- Monitor blood pressure, weight, input, output and clinical response.
- clinical guidance also emphasizes salt and fluid restriction as appropriate to the child's clinical state.

questions.stem: Once the child is assessed and the clinician decides to start standard initial steroid treatment for typical idiopathic nephrotic syndrome, which starting regimen is written in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: E
options.text: No corticosteroid treatment is used in minimal-change disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Prednisolone 60 mg/m²/day or 2 mg/kg/day
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance oral prednisolone 60 mg/m²/day or 2 mg/kg/day as the initial daily regimen.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the daily induction regimen listed.
- B. Correct. It matches the dose stated.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the regimen described.
- D. Incorrect. A single hydrocortisone dose is not the listed nephrotic-syndrome regimen.
- E. Incorrect. Clinical guidance a good steroid response in most children with minimal-change disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The source clinical guidance describes daily prednisolone followed by a remission-guided continuation/tapering schedule.
- Verify the exact duration and taper from the original teaching PDF and current local protocol before prescribing.

questions.stem: Which monitoring plan best matches the important clinical response measures during treatment of a child with severe nephrotic oedema?

options.label: A
options.text: Monitor the urine colour once a week

options.label: B
options.text: Measure height and ignore fluid balance

options.label: C
options.text: Monitor blood pressure, weight, fluid input and urine output

options.label: E
options.text: Stop monitoring once the oedema begins to improve

questions.correctAnswerText: Monitor blood pressure, weight, fluid input and urine output
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance specifically lists blood pressure, weight, input/output and clinical improvement as monitoring targets during oedema treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urine colour alone cannot assess volume status or treatment response.
- B. Incorrect. Fluid balance and cardiovascular status are essential in a child with major oedema.
- C. Correct. These are the core monitoring parameters listed.
- D. Incorrect. Routine daily brain imaging is not part of nephrotic oedema monitoring.
- E. Incorrect. Monitoring must continue while the child remains at risk of fluid shifts and treatment complications.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Observe BP, weight, input/output and clinical response.
- Reassess for hypovolaemia, infection, thrombosis and treatment adverse effects.

cases.title: Repeated relapses and an atypical response
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old boy was treated for nephrotic syndrome. His urine initially became negative for protein, but he has since had repeated relapses. On the current assessment he has persistent hypertension, microscopic haematuria and reduced renal function. Complement is low. Despite a full course of daily prednisolone, he has not achieved remission after several weeks.

questions.stem: A different child in the clinic achieves complete remission within four weeks of starting corticosteroids. How is this response classified?
questions.correctAnswerText: Steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance defines steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome as remission within four weeks of steroid therapy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Steroid dependence is characterized by relapse soon after steroids are stopped.
- B. Incorrect. Steroid resistance means failure to achieve remission after the specified full-dose treatment period.
- C. Correct. Remission within four weeks meets clinical guidance's definition.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital nephrotic syndrome is defined by very early onset, not treatment response.
- E. Incorrect. This is a blood-pressure diagnosis, not a nephrotic response category.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Remission: no or trace proteinuria for three consecutive days.
- Steroid-sensitive: remission within four weeks of steroid treatment.

questions.stem: A child remains protein-positive despite receiving full-dose prednisolone for the treatment period described. Which classification is most appropriate?
questions.correctAnswerText: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance classifies a child who does not achieve remission after approximately 4–6 weeks of full-dose steroid therapy as having steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Failure to remit after the stated full-dose period is the defining feature.
- B. Incorrect. Infrequent relapse describes a child who responds initially but relapses occasionally.
- C. Incorrect. Steroid dependence involves relapse within 14 days of stopping steroid treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Orthostatic proteinuria is posture-dependent and is not a steroid-response category.
- E. Incorrect. Persistent proteinuria is the opposite of remission.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Steroid-resistant NS: no remission after 4–6 weeks of full-dose treatment.
- Reassess the diagnosis and consider renal biopsy when resistance or atypical features are present.

questions.stem: A child repeatedly becomes protein-positive within two weeks of stopping prednisolone. Which pattern does this describe?
questions.correctAnswerText: Steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance defines steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome by relapse within 14 days of stopping corticosteroid therapy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Steroid sensitivity describes achieving remission within four weeks, not the timing of relapse after withdrawal.
- B. Correct. Relapse within 14 days of stopping treatment meets the stated definition.
- C. Incorrect. Steroid resistance is failure to achieve remission during full-dose treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Transient proteinuria is short-lived and associated with triggers such as fever or exercise.
- E. Incorrect. Orthostatic proteinuria depends on posture, not steroid withdrawal.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Steroid-dependent NS: relapse within 14 days after steroid cessation.
- Confirm relapse using the urine definition: +++ or more for three consecutive days.

questions.stem: A child has three relapses during the last five months. Which category best matches the relapse frequency thresholds?
questions.correctAnswerText: Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance defines frequent relapses as two or more relapses within six months, or four or more within twelve months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Resistance is failure to achieve remission with full-dose steroids.
- B. Incorrect. Congenital NS presents in the first three months of life.
- C. Incorrect. Transient proteinuria resolves and does not produce this relapse pattern.
- D. Correct. Three relapses within five months exceed the two-relapse threshold within six months.
- E. Incorrect. Orthostatic proteinuria is posture-dependent, not a relapse-frequency classification.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Frequent relapse: at least 2 relapses in 6 months or at least 4 in 12 months.
- These categories help identify children who may require an alternative treatment strategy.

questions.stem: Which combination in the current child most strongly supports renal biopsy rather than assuming typical minimal-change disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Age 3 years, normal BP and normal renal function

options.label: C
options.text: Good steroid response and no macroscopic haematuria

options.label: D
options.text: Normal renal function and no systemic features

options.label: E
options.text: Persistent hypertension, haematuria, low complement and impaired renal function

questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent hypertension, haematuria, low complement and impaired renal function
questions.initialExplanation: Persistent hypertension, haematuria, low complement and abnormal renal function are atypical features and are listed as indications for renal biopsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is a typical presentation in which biopsy is not routinely indicated.
- B. Incorrect. Selective proteinuria and normal complement support typical minimal-change disease.
- C. Incorrect. A good steroid response and absence of macroscopic haematuria are reassuring features.
- D. Incorrect. These findings do not suggest an atypical glomerular process.
- E. Correct. Multiple atypical features make histological assessment important.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Other biopsy warning features include age below 1 year or above 10 years, systemic/extrarenal manifestations, non-selective proteinuria, frequent relapse, steroid dependence, steroid resistance and congenital NS.

questions.stem: Biopsy in a child with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome shows segmental areas of glomerular sclerosis, with IgM and C3 deposits described on immunofluorescence. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) by segmental sclerosis and notes IgM and C3 deposits on immunofluorescence. It is an important cause of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Minimal-change disease has essentially normal light microscopy and immunofluorescence, with foot-process effacement on electron microscopy.
- B. Correct. Segmental sclerosis is the defining histological clue.
- C. Incorrect. PSGN is an acute nephritic disease associated with low C3 and evidence of preceding streptococcal infection.
- D. Incorrect. Alport syndrome is a hereditary type IV collagen disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Pyelonephritis is an infection and does not produce this biopsy pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- FSGS is listed as the most common cause of steroid-resistant NS.
- Clinical guidance progression to advanced CKD in a proportion of patients and recurrence after transplantation.

questions.stem: A child has frequent relapses and significant adverse effects from repeated high-dose corticosteroids. Which approach is supported by the alternative-treatment list?

options.label: B
options.text: Use antibiotics as the long-term treatment

options.label: C
options.text: Consider a steroid-sparing agent such as levamisole, a calcineurin inhibitor or another listed alternative

options.label: E
options.text: Treat with an antihypertensive drug alone regardless of proteinuria

questions.correctAnswerText: Consider a steroid-sparing agent such as levamisole, a calcineurin inhibitor or another listed alternative
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance alternative therapy for steroid resistance, frequent relapse, severe steroid adverse effects and relapse while on a high prednisolone dose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ongoing follow-up is essential in nephrotic syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not replace immunosuppressive treatment for the underlying nephrotic disease.
- C. Correct. The listed options include cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, levamisole, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and rituximab.
- D. Incorrect. Nephrectomy is not routine management of relapsing idiopathic NS.
- E. Incorrect. Blood-pressure treatment alone does not address the underlying nephrotic syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Select alternative therapy according to the response pattern, adverse effects and specialist assessment.
- Calcineurin inhibitors include cyclosporine and tacrolimus.

questions.stem: A child receiving cyclophosphamide for nephrotic syndrome is being monitored. Which adverse-effect combination is particularly important to screen for?

options.label: E
options.text: Leukopenia, haemorrhagic cystitis and possible infertility

questions.correctAnswerText: Leukopenia, haemorrhagic cystitis and possible infertility
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance leukopenia, bone-marrow suppression, haemorrhagic cystitis, alopecia and infertility among cyclophosphamide adverse effects. It recommends regular CBC monitoring.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hirsutism and gum hyperplasia are associated with cyclosporine.
- B. Incorrect. Hypotension is not the key toxicity profile described for cyclophosphamide.
- C. Incorrect. These are not the characteristic cyclophosphamide toxicities listed.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the adverse-effect pattern described.
- E. Correct. These are important toxicities requiring monitoring and specialist supervision.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance weekly CBC monitoring and stopping cyclophosphamide if WBC falls below 5,000, as stated in that teaching material.
- Cyclosporine adverse effects listed separately include nephrotoxicity, hypertension, hirsutism and gingival hyperplasia.

cases.title: Cola-coloured urine after a sore throat
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old boy presents with cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema, reduced urine output and hypertension. His mother reports a sore throat about two weeks earlier. Blood tests show raised urea and creatinine, and complement C3 is low.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
questions.initialExplanation: PSGN classically follows streptococcal throat infection after a latent period of about 1–3 weeks and presents with gross haematuria, oedema and hypertension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Fanconi syndrome — Incorrect. It causes proximal tubular losses, polyuria and metabolic disturbances.
- B. Orthostatic proteinuria — Incorrect. It causes isolated posture-dependent proteinuria without this nephritic picture.
- C. Enuresis — Incorrect. It is involuntary urination during sleep, not an acute nephritic illness.
- D. PSGN — Correct. The preceding sore throat, cola-coloured urine and hypertension fit clinical guidance's description.
- E. Minimal change nephrotic syndrome — Incorrect. It typically presents with oedema and heavy proteinuria rather than the classic post-infectious nephritic picture.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PSGN after throat infection: latent period about 1–3 weeks.
- After skin infection: clinical guidance gives approximately 3–6 weeks.
- Typical presentation: cola-coloured urine, oedema, hypertension and reduced urine output.

questions.stem: Which complement pattern is highlighted as typical of PSGN?

options.label: A
options.text: High C4 with normal C3 as the defining pattern

questions.correctAnswerText: Low C3
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies low C3 as a key investigation finding in PSGN and notes that C3 usually normalizes over approximately 6–8 weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. High C4 — Incorrect. clinical guidance emphasizes low C3; high C4 is not the stated finding.
- B. Low C3 — Correct. Low C3 is a classic clue 's PSGN section.
- C. Complement never affected — Incorrect. clinical guidance specifically lists low C3.
- D. Low IgE — Incorrect. IgE is not the complement marker used for PSGN.
- E. High C3 — Incorrect. This is not the pattern described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PSGN: low C3.
- clinical guidance gives C3 normalization at about 6–8 weeks.
- Persistent low C3 beyond the expected period warrants reassessment.

questions.stem: Which investigation provides evidence of recent streptococcal infection?
questions.correctAnswerText: ASO titre
questions.initialExplanation: An elevated antistreptolysin O titre supports recent GAS infection. clinical guidance also lists anti-DNase B, throat culture and other streptococcal antibodies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urine culture detects urinary pathogens, not prior streptococcal pharyngitis.
- B. Incorrect. Troponin may indicate myocardial injury but does not document recent GAS infection.
- C. Incorrect. Amylase is related to pancreatic disease.
- D. Incorrect. D-dimer is used in assessment of thrombosis and is not a marker of GAS infection.
- E. Correct. ASO is an antibody marker of recent streptococcal exposure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Evidence of GAS: throat culture, ASO, anti-DNase B and related antibodies.
- CBC, ESR and CRP assess inflammation but do not by themselves prove GAS infection.
- Cardiac assessment is not the primary confirmation of PSGN; renal function and complement are important.

questions.stem: Which complication of acute nephritic syndrome is particularly associated with severe hypertension?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypertensive encephalopathy
questions.initialExplanation: Severe hypertension in PSGN may cause neurological symptoms and hypertensive encephalopathy. Other listed complications include heart failure and pulmonary oedema.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Sensorineural deafness — Incorrect. It is associated with Alport syndrome.
- B. Orthostatic proteinuria — Incorrect. It is a benign posture-related condition.
- C. Renal stones — Incorrect. They are a separate urinary tract problem.
- D. Hypertensive encephalopathy — Correct. It is listed as a complication of severe hypertension.
- E. Hydrocele — Incorrect. It is fluid accumulation in the tunica vaginalis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Important PSGN complications: hypertensive encephalopathy, heart failure, pulmonary oedema, hyperkalaemia and AKI.
- Monitor BP, urine output, renal function and electrolytes.

questions.stem: A child with PSGN develops breathlessness, basal crackles and severe hypertension. Which complication is most likely?

options.label: B
options.text: Pulmonary oedema due to fluid overload

questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary oedema due to fluid overload
questions.initialExplanation: Acute nephritic syndrome can reduce renal excretion of salt and water, causing fluid overload, hypertension and pulmonary oedema.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Cystitis does not explain breathlessness and crackles from pulmonary congestion.
- B. Correct. This is a recognized serious complication of acute nephritic syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Hydrocele is unrelated.
- D. Incorrect. Orthostatic proteinuria is benign and does not cause fluid overload.
- E. Incorrect. Alport syndrome is a hereditary nephritis and does not explain this acute fluid-overload episode.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PSGN may cause salt/water retention and reduced urine output.
- Monitor fluid status, BP, lung findings, urine output and electrolytes.
- Pulmonary oedema and hypertensive encephalopathy are emergencies.

questions.stem: Which pattern best distinguishes nephritic from nephrotic syndrome?

options.label: C
options.text: Nephritic: haematuria, hypertension, oedema and oliguria

questions.correctAnswerText: Nephritic: haematuria, hypertension, oedema and oliguria
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance nephritic syndrome by haematuria, hypertension, oedema and oliguria. Nephrotic syndrome is dominated by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This pattern is more consistent with salt-wasting tubulopathies.
- B. Incorrect. Enuresis is a separate voiding disorder.
- C. Correct. These are the classic nephritic features.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests proximal tubular dysfunction such as Fanconi syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. This describes the nephrotic pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nephritic: haematuria + hypertension + oedema + oliguria.
- Nephrotic: heavy proteinuria + hypoalbuminaemia + oedema + hyperlipidaemia.
- A child can have overlapping features; interpret the full clinical picture and investigations.

questions.stem: Which approach is most appropriate for uncomplicated PSGN with oedema and hypertension?

options.label: C
options.text: Routine high-dose steroids for children in routine care

options.label: D
options.text: Supportive management with monitoring of BP, fluid balance, urine output and renal function

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive management with monitoring of BP, fluid balance, urine output and renal function
questions.initialExplanation: Management of typical PSGN is mainly supportive. The immediate priorities are control of fluid overload and hypertension, monitoring renal function and treating any ongoing streptococcal infection as indicated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Nephrectomy is not indicated for typical PSGN.
- B. Incorrect. Transplantation is not indicated for an acute, usually self-limiting episode.
- C. Incorrect. Steroids are not routine treatment for uncomplicated PSGN.
- D. Correct. Supportive care and close monitoring are central in the typical case.
- E. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected enuresis or water-balance conditions, not PSGN.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Monitor fluid overload, BP, urine output, electrolytes and renal function.
- Manage hypertension and pulmonary oedema when present.
- Follow complement recovery and clinical resolution.
- Reassess if renal impairment or low complement persists beyond the expected course.

topics.name: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), Hyperkalaemia and Dialysis

cases.title: Oliguria after severe dehydration
cases.vignette: A 5-year-old child has had several days of vomiting and diarrhoea with poor oral intake. The child is lethargic, has dry mucous membranes and reduced urine output. Blood tests show rising urea and creatinine. Urine is concentrated, with low urinary sodium. During admission, the child develops hyperkalaemia with ECG changes.

questions.stem: Which category of AKI is most likely at presentation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pre-renal AKI
questions.initialExplanation: Severe dehydration and reduced circulating volume decrease renal perfusion, causing pre-renal AKI.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Post-renal AKI — Incorrect. It results from urinary tract obstruction.
- B. Renal agenesis — Incorrect. It is a congenital developmental anomaly.
- C. Nephrotic syndrome — Incorrect. It causes heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema.
- D. CKD — Incorrect. CKD requires persistent kidney damage or reduced GFR for more than 3 months.
- E. Pre-renal AKI — Correct. Hypovolaemia from vomiting and diarrhoea is a classic cause.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pre-renal AKI: reduced renal perfusion due to dehydration, hypovolaemia, shock or reduced effective circulation.
- Intrinsic AKI: renal parenchymal damage.
- Post-renal AKI: urinary tract obstruction.
- Pre-renal AKI is the most common category in the supplied clinical guidance.

questions.stem: Which urine profile favours pre-renal rather than intrinsic renal AKI in the comparison table?

options.label: A
options.text: Urine sodium <20 mmol/L and urine osmolality >500

options.label: B
options.text: FE sodium >3% with low urine concentration

options.label: C
options.text: Urine sodium >40 mmol/L and urine osmolality <300

options.label: E
options.text: Urine sodium >40 mmol/L and FE sodium >3%

questions.correctAnswerText: Urine sodium <20 mmol/L and urine osmolality >500
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance's comparison table describes pre-renal AKI as having low urine sodium and concentrated urine, whereas intrinsic renal AKI has higher urine sodium and less concentrated urine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Low sodium and high osmolality — Correct. This is the pre-renal pattern stated.
- B. High FE sodium — Incorrect. clinical guidance gives FE sodium <1% for pre-renal AKI and >3% for renal AKI.
- C. High sodium and low osmolality — Incorrect. This pattern favours intrinsic renal AKI 's table.
- D. Low osmolality and low specific gravity — Incorrect. These are associated with impaired tubular concentrating ability.
- E. High sodium and FE sodium — Incorrect. These findings favour intrinsic renal injury.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pre-renal pattern: urine osmolality >500, urine Na <20, FE Na <1%, specific gravity >1.020.
- Renal AKI pattern: urine osmolality <300, urine Na >40, FE Na >3%, specific gravity <1.010.
- Interpret urine indices in context, particularly after diuretics or fluid therapy.

questions.stem: A child with AKI develops hyperkalaemia and ECG changes. Which treatment is used to stabilize the myocardial cell membrane?
questions.correctAnswerText: IV calcium gluconate
questions.initialExplanation: IV calcium gluconate is used to stabilize the myocardial cell membrane and reduce the immediate risk of hyperkalaemia-related arrhythmia. It does not remove potassium from the body.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Oral phosphate — Incorrect. It does not treat hyperkalaemia and may worsen electrolyte disturbance.
- B. Desmopressin — Incorrect. It is used in selected water-balance disorders and enuresis, not hyperkalaemia.
- C. Prednisolone — Incorrect. It is not an emergency membrane-stabilizing treatment.
- D. Oral iron — Incorrect. It treats iron deficiency and has no role in acute hyperkalaemia.
- E. IV calcium gluconate — Correct. clinical guidance identifies it as membrane-stabilizing treatment under ECG monitoring.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Calcium gluconate stabilizes the myocardium; it does not lower serum potassium.
- Insulin with glucose and salbutamol shift potassium into cells.
- Other measures, including potassium removal and dialysis, are considered according to severity and response.
- Hyperkalaemia is an emergency requiring ECG and clinical monitoring.

questions.stem: Which ECG change is listed as a feature of hyperkalaemia?

options.label: B
options.text: U waves as the defining finding

questions.correctAnswerText: Tall peaked T waves
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance tall peaked T waves, prolonged PR interval, widening of the QRS complex, ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest among ECG changes or consequences of severe hyperkalaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Delta waves — Incorrect. They are associated with pre-excitation, not hyperkalaemia.
- B. U waves — Incorrect. U waves are more classically associated with hypokalaemia.
- C. Tall peaked T waves — Correct. This is a classic ECG feature listed.
- D. Short QT — Incorrect. This is not the hyperkalaemia pattern presented.
- E. ST elevation — Incorrect. It is not the defining ECG change listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hyperkalaemia can cause peaked T waves, PR prolongation and QRS widening.
- Severe cases may progress to ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest.
- Treat immediately when severe hyperkalaemia or ECG changes are present.

questions.stem: Which is an indication for dialysis in AKI ?

options.label: D
options.text: Severe hyperkalaemia not responding to conservative treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe hyperkalaemia not responding to conservative treatment
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance refractory severe hyperkalaemia, fluid overload with pulmonary oedema or severe hypertension, severe refractory metabolic acidosis and uraemic complications as indications for dialysis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Normal renal function — Incorrect. Dialysis is not indicated with normal renal function in the absence of another compelling indication.
- B. Enuresis — Incorrect. It is unrelated to renal replacement therapy.
- C. Orthostatic proteinuria — Incorrect. It is generally benign and does not require dialysis.
- D. Refractory severe hyperkalaemia — Correct. It is explicitly listed.
- E. Mild proteinuria — Incorrect. It is not an indication for acute dialysis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dialysis indications: refractory fluid overload, hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, uraemic encephalopathy/convulsions/coma and selected severe electrolyte or multisystem complications.
- Clinical status and response to treatment matter; a single creatinine threshold should not be used in isolation.

questions.stem: Which statement about peritoneal dialysis in infants and small children is given?

options.label: A
options.text: It requires a permanent arteriovenous fistula

options.label: B
options.text: It is the most common dialysis modality in infants and small children

options.label: D
options.text: It is not usually used in infants

questions.correctAnswerText: It is the most common dialysis modality in infants and small children
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance peritoneal dialysis as the most common modality in infants and small children. Dialysate is infused into the peritoneal cavity, allowed to dwell, then drained.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. AV fistula — Incorrect. Vascular access is relevant to haemodialysis, not peritoneal dialysis.
- B. Common modality — Correct. This is the statement in the supplied clinical guidance.
