- C. Pleural membrane — Incorrect. Peritoneal dialysis uses the peritoneal membrane.
- D. Never used — Incorrect. clinical guidance identifies it as commonly used in small children.
- E. Cannot correct fluid overload — Incorrect. Peritoneal dialysis can remove fluid and solutes, although haemodialysis is described as more efficient.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PD uses the peritoneal membrane and dialysate exchanges.
- HD is described as more efficient, with vascular access and shorter sessions.
- Modality choice depends on patient factors and clinical setting.

questions.stem: A child has persistent severe hyperkalaemia, pulmonary oedema and worsening uraemic symptoms despite medical management. What is the best next step?

options.label: B
options.text: Urgent renal replacement therapy assessment and dialysis

questions.correctAnswerText: Urgent renal replacement therapy assessment and dialysis
questions.initialExplanation: Refractory hyperkalaemia, pulmonary oedema and uraemic complications are major dialysis indications in AKI. The child needs urgent nephrology and critical-care involvement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin does not treat AKI-related hyperkalaemia or pulmonary oedema.
- B. Correct. The clinical picture meets several indications for urgent renal replacement therapy.
- C. Incorrect. Antibiotics are only relevant if infection is present and do not treat the renal emergencies described.
- D. Incorrect. Persistent life-threatening complications despite medical treatment require escalation.
- E. Incorrect. These are emergencies, not routine follow-up problems.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Refractory hyperkalaemia, pulmonary oedema/fluid overload, severe acidosis and uraemic encephalopathy are dialysis indications.
- Stabilize the patient while arranging renal replacement therapy.
- The dialysis modality depends on age, haemodynamic status and local expertise.

cases.title: Pallor and oliguria after bloody diarrhoea
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child develops bloody diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Several days later, the child becomes pale and lethargic, with reduced urine output and bruising. Blood tests show anaemia, thrombocytopenia and rising creatinine. The blood film demonstrates schistocytes.

questions.stem: Which triad defines haemolytic uraemic syndrome?

options.label: C
options.text: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and AKI

questions.correctAnswerText: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and AKI
questions.initialExplanation: HUS is classically defined by the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The platelet count is typically low in HUS.
- B. Incorrect. It omits the defining thrombocytopenia and AKI combination.
- C. Correct. This is the classic triad presented.
- D. Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is not part of the diagnostic triad.
- E. Incorrect. HUS causes haemolytic anaemia, not polycythaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HUS triad: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI.
- Typical HUS often follows bloody diarrhoea.
- Peripheral blood film may show schistocytes/helmet cells.

questions.stem: Typical diarrhoea-associated HUS is commonly linked to which organism?
questions.correctAnswerText: Verotoxin-producing E. coli
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance typical HUS as commonly following bloody diarrhoea caused by verotoxin-producing E. coli, particularly the O157:H7 strain.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Tuberculosis is not the usual diarrhoea-associated HUS cause.
- B. Incorrect. Plasmodium is not the typical organism listed for diarrhoea-associated HUS.
- C. Incorrect. Mycoplasma is not the typical cause described.
- D. Correct. This is the common infectious association given.
- E. Incorrect. Candida is not the organism identified.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typical/D+ HUS: often follows bloody diarrhoea.
- Verotoxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 is highlighted.
- Atypical HUS is described as complement-mediated and may be familial or associated with other disease/drug triggers.

questions.stem: Which blood film finding supports microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia in HUS?
questions.correctAnswerText: Schistocytes or helmet cells
questions.initialExplanation: Mechanical fragmentation of red cells in the microvasculature produces schistocytes, also called helmet cells, on the blood film.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Target cells — Incorrect. They are associated with other conditions and are not the key HUS finding.
- B. Spherocytes — Incorrect. They may be seen in other haemolytic conditions but are not the characteristic film finding highlighted for HUS.
- C. Schistocytes — Correct. They support microangiopathic haemolysis.
- D. Howell–Jolly bodies — Incorrect. They are associated with absent or impaired splenic function.
- E. Hypersegmented neutrophils — Incorrect. They suggest megaloblastic change, not MAHA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HUS investigations: anaemia, thrombocytopenia, reticulocytosis, raised urea/creatinine and schistocytes.
- Clinical guidance a negative Coombs test and normal PT/PTT in the typical laboratory pattern.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern best supports HUS rather than immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia?

options.label: C
options.text: High platelet count with normal renal function

options.label: E
options.text: Negative Coombs test with schistocytes and thrombocytopenia

questions.correctAnswerText: Negative Coombs test with schistocytes and thrombocytopenia
questions.initialExplanation: HUS causes non-immune microangiopathic haemolysis. Clinical guidance a negative Coombs test, schistocytes, thrombocytopenia and renal impairment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Neutrophilia alone does not establish HUS.
- B. Incorrect. Eosinophilia is not a defining feature.
- C. Incorrect. HUS is characterized by thrombocytopenia, not thrombocytosis.
- D. Incorrect. A positive Coombs test supports immune-mediated haemolysis, not the typical HUS pattern.
- E. Correct. This matches microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia and AKI.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HUS = non-immune MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI.
- Blood film: schistocytes.
- Coombs test: typically negative in the pattern described.
- PT/PTT are usually normal in typical HUS.

questions.stem: What is the main initial management principle for typical HUS?

options.label: A
options.text: Supportive management, careful fluid/electrolyte control and renal support as needed

options.label: D
options.text: Immediate renal transplantation in children in routine care

options.label: E
options.text: High-dose steroids as the treatment for typical presentations

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive management, careful fluid/electrolyte control and renal support as needed
questions.initialExplanation: The immediate priorities are supportive care, monitoring of renal function, fluid balance, electrolytes and blood pressure, with dialysis if severe renal complications develop.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the core approach for typical diarrhoea-associated HUS.
- B. Incorrect. Nephrectomy does not treat the systemic microangiopathic process.
- C. Incorrect. Desmopressin is not HUS treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Transplantation is not the immediate treatment of an acute episode.
- E. Incorrect. Steroids are not the universal sole treatment for typical HUS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Monitor haemoglobin, platelets, renal function, urine output, electrolytes and BP.
- Treat complications and provide renal replacement therapy when indicated.
- Distinguish typical diarrhoea-associated HUS from atypical complement-mediated disease.

questions.stem: A child with HUS develops refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload and uraemic symptoms. Which intervention may be required?
questions.correctAnswerText: Dialysis
questions.initialExplanation: Severe AKI complications, including refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload and uraemia, may require dialysis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin is not treatment for HUS-related renal failure.
- B. Correct. These are recognized indications for renal replacement therapy.
- C. Incorrect. Circumcision does not treat AKI.
- D. Incorrect. An enuresis alarm treats nocturnal enuresis.
- E. Incorrect. Ureteric reimplantation treats selected severe VUR.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HUS may cause severe AKI.
- Dialysis is considered for refractory fluid overload, hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis or uraemic complications.
- Early pediatric nephrology involvement is important.

cases.title: Poor growth, pallor and bone pain
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child has a history of recurrent urinary tract problems and now presents with poor growth, fatigue, pallor and bone pain. Blood tests show elevated urea and creatinine, normocytic normochromic anaemia, hyperphosphataemia and metabolic acidosis. The abnormalities have persisted for more than three months.

questions.stem: Which definition of CKD is consistent with the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Any isolated rise in creatinine lasting one day

options.label: D
options.text: Renal injury markers and/or GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² persisting for more than 3 months

questions.correctAnswerText: Renal injury markers and/or GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² persisting for more than 3 months
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance defines CKD as chronic renal impairment with kidney damage markers and/or reduced GFR persisting for more than 3 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A one-day creatinine rise suggests an acute change and does not meet the chronic duration criterion.
- B. Incorrect. An isolated UTI does not establish CKD.
- C. Incorrect. Oliguria for hours is an acute urine-output feature, not a CKD definition.
- D. Correct. This matches the definition given.
- E. Incorrect. One febrile day of proteinuria may be transient and does not establish chronic kidney disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CKD requires persistence for more than 3 months.
- Evidence may include structural/urinary markers of kidney damage and/or reduced GFR.
- Distinguish CKD from AKI using time course and evidence of chronicity.

questions.stem: Which GFR range corresponds to stage 5 CKD in the staging table?
questions.correctAnswerText: Below 15 mL/min/1.73 m²
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance classifies stage 5 CKD as GFR below 15 mL/min/1.73 m² and describes it as end-stage renal failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 30–59 — Incorrect. This is stage 3.
- B. >90 — Incorrect. This is the stage 1 GFR range, if there is evidence of kidney damage.
- C. 60–89 — Incorrect. This is stage 2.
- D. 15–29 — Incorrect. This is stage 4.
- E. <15 — Correct. This is stage 5 in the supplied classification table.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stage 1: GFR >90 with evidence of kidney damage.
- Stage 2: 60–89.
- Stage 3: 30–59.
- Stage 4: 15–29.
- Stage 5: <15 mL/min/1.73 m².

questions.stem: What is the main cause of normocytic normochromic anaemia in CKD highlighted?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced erythropoietin production by the diseased kidney

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced erythropoietin production by the diseased kidney
questions.initialExplanation: A diseased kidney produces less erythropoietin, reducing stimulation of red blood cell production and contributing to normocytic normochromic anaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Reduced erythropoietin — Correct. This is the main mechanism emphasized.
- B. Increased B12 absorption — Incorrect. It does not explain CKD-associated anaemia.
- C. Excess erythropoietin — Incorrect. CKD is associated with reduced, not increased, erythropoietin production.
- D. Platelet production — Incorrect. Platelets do not explain the anaemia mechanism.
- E. Increased red cell lifespan — Incorrect. Clinical guidance reduced red cell survival among contributing factors.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CKD anaemia is commonly normocytic and normochromic.
- Reduced erythropoietin is a major mechanism.
- clinical guidance also lists reduced iron/B12 intake, uraemic marrow suppression and reduced red cell survival as contributors.

questions.stem: Which biochemical pattern is associated with CKD-related renal osteodystrophy?

options.label: A
options.text: Low/normal calcium, high phosphate and secondary hyperparathyroidism

options.label: B
options.text: High calcium, low phosphate and low PTH

options.label: D
options.text: High calcium, high vitamin D and suppressed PTH in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Normal mineral metabolism in advanced CKD

questions.correctAnswerText: Low/normal calcium, high phosphate and secondary hyperparathyroidism
questions.initialExplanation: Reduced phosphate excretion and impaired activation of vitamin D contribute to hyperphosphataemia, reduced calcium availability and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the characteristic pattern emphasized.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the pattern described in the CKD section.
- C. Incorrect. clinical guidance highlights raised phosphate due to reduced renal excretion.
- D. Incorrect. It does not represent the usual secondary hyperparathyroid pattern described.
- E. Incorrect. Mineral and bone complications are important features of CKD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CKD → reduced phosphate excretion and reduced vitamin D activation.
- Hyperphosphataemia and reduced calcium absorption stimulate secondary hyperparathyroidism.
- Renal osteodystrophy may cause bone pain, deformity and fractures.

questions.stem: Which acid–base disturbance is commonly associated with CKD in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: C
options.text: Respiratory alkalosis as the primary renal abnormality

questions.correctAnswerText: Metabolic acidosis
questions.initialExplanation: Reduced renal bicarbonate handling and reduced acid excretion contribute to metabolic acidosis in CKD.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Metabolic alkalosis — Incorrect. clinical guidance identifies metabolic acidosis as the characteristic abnormality.
- B. No change — Incorrect. Metabolic acidosis is a recognized complication of CKD.
- C. Respiratory alkalosis — Incorrect. It is not the primary renal acid–base disturbance described.
- D. Respiratory acidosis — Incorrect. It is not the typical CKD-related disturbance.
- E. Metabolic acidosis — Correct. This is due to impaired renal acid handling.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CKD can cause metabolic acidosis due to reduced H+ excretion and impaired HCO3− handling.
- clinical guidance includes bicarbonate therapy among conservative management measures.

questions.stem: Which treatment is used to manage CKD-related anaemia when indicated?

options.label: C
options.text: Recombinant erythropoietin with iron/folate supplementation as needed

options.label: E
options.text: High-dose loop diuretic as sole therapy

questions.correctAnswerText: Recombinant erythropoietin with iron/folate supplementation as needed
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance subcutaneous recombinant erythropoietin, together with iron and folate supplementation, as treatment for CKD-associated anaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Insulin — Incorrect. It is used for glucose control, not anaemia treatment.
- B. Cyclophosphamide — Incorrect. It is an immunosuppressive drug and is not routine CKD anaemia therapy.
- C. Erythropoietin and supplements — Correct. This is the management approach described.
- D. Desmopressin — Incorrect. It is listed for selected cases of nocturnal enuresis, not CKD anaemia.
- E. Loop diuretic alone — Incorrect. Diuretics do not correct the erythropoietin deficiency causing CKD anaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CKD anaemia: consider erythropoietin and iron/folate when indicated.
- CKD bone disease: phosphate restriction/binders, calcium and active vitamin D are discussed.
- Growth failure management includes correcting acidosis and anaemia, adequate calories and selected growth-hormone therapy.

questions.stem: A child with advanced CKD develops poor linear growth. Which combination of factors may contribute?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased renal clearance of most hormones

options.label: B
options.text: Increased appetite with normal growth hormone physiology

options.label: D
options.text: Acidosis, anaemia, inadequate nutrition and renal bone disease

options.label: E
options.text: Excess erythropoietin and excess vitamin D

questions.correctAnswerText: Acidosis, anaemia, inadequate nutrition and renal bone disease
questions.initialExplanation: CKD affects growth through multiple mechanisms, including metabolic acidosis, anaemia, inadequate nutrition, bone/mineral disorders and disturbances of growth regulation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This does not explain the growth failure pattern.
- B. Incorrect. This does not represent the mechanisms described.
- C. Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not cause CKD-related growth failure.
- D. Correct. These are relevant mechanisms in chronic renal disease.
- E. Incorrect. CKD more commonly causes reduced erythropoietin production and impaired vitamin D activation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Assess height, weight and growth velocity in children with CKD.
- Correct nutrition, acidosis, anaemia and mineral-bone disturbances.
- Selected children may require specialist growth-hormone assessment.

questions.stem: A child with end-stage CKD has refractory fluid overload and uraemic symptoms. Which definitive renal replacement options should be discussed?

options.label: E
options.text: No renal replacement options are available in childhood

questions.correctAnswerText: Dialysis and renal transplantation
questions.initialExplanation: Advanced CKD may require renal replacement therapy. clinical guidance discusses dialysis and renal transplantation as options in severe chronic renal failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Dialysis and transplantation are renal replacement options for end-stage disease.
- B. Incorrect. Ureteric reimplantation treats selected VUR, not end-stage CKD.
- C. Incorrect. These do not replace renal function.
- D. Incorrect. These treat nocturnal enuresis.
- E. Incorrect. Children can receive dialysis and renal transplantation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stage 5 CKD may require renal replacement therapy.
- Peritoneal dialysis is commonly used in infants and small children.
- Transplantation is considered according to patient status and specialist assessment.

cases.title: Recurrent haematuria during respiratory infections
cases.vignette: An 11-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of visible haematuria. Each episode begins during, or within a day or two of, an upper respiratory tract infection. Between episodes he feels well. Urine testing may show microscopic haematuria and proteinuria.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: IgA nephropathy
questions.initialExplanation: IgA nephropathy commonly causes recurrent gross or microscopic haematuria occurring concurrently with, or very soon after, an upper respiratory tract infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. PSGN — Incorrect. It classically follows infection after a latent period, rather than occurring concurrently or within 1–2 days.
- B. IgA nephropathy — Correct. The timing of haematuria with the URTI is characteristic.
- C. RTA — Incorrect. It causes chronic normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and tubular symptoms.
- D. Minimal change nephropathy — Incorrect. It usually presents with nephrotic syndrome and heavy proteinuria.
- E. Wilms tumour — Incorrect. It more commonly presents with an abdominal mass.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IgA nephropathy: recurrent haematuria concurrent with or shortly after URTI.
- PSGN: haematuria occurs after a latent period of weeks.
- Clinical guidance renal biopsy showing mesangial IgA deposition.

questions.stem: Which histological finding is expected in IgA nephropathy?

options.label: A
options.text: Minimal change on light microscopy as the defining finding

options.label: B
options.text: Amyloid deposition in the collecting duct

options.label: D
options.text: Type IV collagen absence in most glomeruli

questions.correctAnswerText: Mesangial IgA deposition
questions.initialExplanation: IgA nephropathy is characterized by mesangial deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Minimal change disease is a separate cause of nephrotic syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Amyloid deposition is not the defining lesion of IgA nephropathy.
- C. Incorrect. Linear anti-GBM deposition is associated with anti-GBM disease.
- D. Incorrect. Type IV collagen gene abnormalities are associated with Alport syndrome.
- E. Correct. Mesangial IgA deposition is the defining biopsy finding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IgA nephropathy is a mesangial IgA-mediated glomerular disease.
- Biopsy is considered when the clinical situation warrants confirmation or risk assessment.
- Monitor BP, proteinuria and renal function.

questions.stem: Which timing best distinguishes IgA nephropathy from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

options.label: A
options.text: IgA nephropathy occurs after skin infection

options.label: B
options.text: IgA nephropathy occurs during or very soon after URTI; PSGN follows after a latent period

options.label: C
options.text: Both typically occur six months after infection

options.label: D
options.text: PSGN occurs during the sore throat; IgA nephropathy occurs years later

options.label: E
options.text: Timing is not usually clinically useful

questions.correctAnswerText: IgA nephropathy occurs during or very soon after URTI; PSGN follows after a latent period
questions.initialExplanation: IgA nephropathy causes synpharyngitic haematuria, while PSGN typically occurs after an immune latent period following streptococcal infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. IgA nephropathy is classically associated with URTI, not exclusively skin infection.
- B. Correct. This is the key clinical distinction.
- C. Incorrect. The two conditions do not share a fixed six-month latency.
- D. Incorrect. This reverses the typical timing.
- E. Incorrect. Timing is a useful clinical clue in the differential diagnosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- “Synpharyngitic” haematuria suggests IgA nephropathy.
- Delayed haematuria after GAS infection suggests PSGN.
- Use complement, renal function, urine findings and clinical course to refine the differential.

questions.stem: Which clinical parameter should be followed to identify progression or increasing renal risk in a child with IgA nephropathy?

options.label: B
options.text: Blood pressure, proteinuria and renal function

questions.correctAnswerText: Blood pressure, proteinuria and renal function
questions.initialExplanation: Persistent proteinuria, hypertension and deterioration in renal function are important markers of progressive glomerular disease and should be monitored.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Allergy testing is unrelated to renal progression.
- B. Correct. These parameters reflect renal involvement and risk of progression.
- C. Incorrect. Visual acuity is not the main renal monitoring parameter in IgA nephropathy.
- D. Incorrect. Stool frequency does not assess glomerular progression.
- E. Incorrect. Hair colour is unrelated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Monitor urine protein, BP and renal function.
- Persistent or increasing proteinuria raises concern for progressive disease.
- Management is individualized according to renal risk and specialist review.

questions.stem: Which presentation is less typical of IgA nephropathy and should prompt consideration of another glomerular disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Episodes of haematuria occurring very soon after sore throat

options.label: C
options.text: Heavy proteinuria, marked hypoalbuminaemia and generalized oedema as the dominant presentation

questions.correctAnswerText: Heavy proteinuria, marked hypoalbuminaemia and generalized oedema as the dominant presentation
questions.initialExplanation: IgA nephropathy commonly presents with haematuria. A dominant nephrotic picture may indicate another glomerular disease or more advanced/atypical involvement and requires assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Very early haematuria after URTI is characteristic.
- B. Incorrect. Mesangial IgA deposition is the defining biopsy feature.
- C. Correct. This is more characteristic of nephrotic syndrome than the classic IgA presentation.
- D. Incorrect. This is a typical IgA nephropathy clue.
- E. Incorrect. Microscopic haematuria may occur in IgA nephropathy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Classic IgA nephropathy: recurrent haematuria around URTI.
- Heavy proteinuria, low albumin and generalized oedema should prompt a broader glomerular differential.
- Renal biopsy and follow-up are guided by severity.

cases.title: Haematuria with hearing difficulty
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old boy has persistent microscopic haematuria and intermittent proteinuria. His parents report progressive difficulty hearing conversations. Ophthalmological examination identifies anterior lenticonus. There is a family history of renal disease in male relatives.

questions.stem: Alport syndrome is caused by a genetic defect affecting which structural protein?
questions.correctAnswerText: Type IV collagen
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance Alport syndrome as a hereditary nephritis caused by mutations in genes coding for type IV collagen.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Elastin — Incorrect. It is not the protein implicated.
- B. Type IV collagen — Correct. Mutations affecting type IV collagen produce the renal, auditory and ocular manifestations.
- C. Fibrillin — Incorrect. It is associated with other connective-tissue disorders, not Alport syndrome as described here.
- D. Type I collagen — Incorrect. It is not the collagen type identified in Alport syndrome.
- E. Type II collagen — Incorrect. It is not the relevant basement-membrane collagen described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Alport syndrome: hereditary nephritis due to type IV collagen gene mutations.
- Clinical guidance X-linked inheritance in approximately 85% of cases, with other inheritance patterns possible.

questions.stem: Which combination is characteristic of Alport syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Oedema, severe hyperlipidaemia and low complement in each case

options.label: B
options.text: Nephritis, sensorineural deafness and ocular abnormalities

questions.correctAnswerText: Nephritis, sensorineural deafness and ocular abnormalities
questions.initialExplanation: Alport syndrome affects the kidneys, ears and eyes. clinical guidance highlights haematuria/proteinuria, sensorineural deafness and ocular findings such as anterior lenticonus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Nephrotic picture with low complement — Incorrect. This does not describe the characteristic inherited collagen disorder.
- B. Renal, auditory and ocular features — Correct. This is the classic triad described.
- C. Renal stones — Incorrect. They are not the characteristic triad.
- D. UTI and hydrocele — Incorrect. These are unrelated conditions.
- E. Hyperthyroidism — Incorrect. It is not a defining manifestation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Alport: nephritis + sensorineural deafness + eye abnormalities.
- Anterior lenticonus is highlighted as a characteristic ocular sign.
- Follow renal function, hearing and ophthalmological status.

questions.stem: Which inheritance pattern accounts for most cases in the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: X-linked inheritance
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that approximately 85% of cases are X-linked, with autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant forms also possible.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. X-linked disease is the predominant pattern given.
- B. Incorrect. Mitochondrial inheritance is not the main pattern described.
- C. Incorrect. Alport syndrome is genetic, not an acquired infection.
- D. Incorrect. AD is possible but not the predominant pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Y-linked inheritance is not described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- X-linked in approximately 85% of cases.
- Boys are generally more severely affected in X-linked disease.
- Family history is useful; assess relatives when appropriate.

questions.stem: Which ocular finding is specifically highlighted as characteristic of Alport syndrome?
questions.correctAnswerText: Anterior lenticonus
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies anterior lenticonus as a characteristic ocular finding in Alport syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Papilloedema indicates raised intracranial pressure and is not the characteristic ocular sign.
- B. Incorrect. A cherry-red spot occurs in selected metabolic/retinal disorders.
- C. Incorrect. Kayser–Fleischer rings are associated with Wilson disease.
- D. Correct. Anterior lenticonus is specifically described.
- E. Incorrect. Bitot spots are associated with vitamin A deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Anterior lenticonus is a characteristic Alport eye feature.
- Corneal erosions and macular flecks are also listed.
- Audiometry and ophthalmological assessment complement renal evaluation.

questions.stem: Which investigation combination is appropriate when Alport syndrome is suspected?

options.label: D
options.text: Urinalysis/RFT, audiometry, ophthalmological examination and genetic testing

questions.correctAnswerText: Urinalysis/RFT, audiometry, ophthalmological examination and genetic testing
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance renal assessment, hearing evaluation, ophthalmological examination, renal biopsy in selected cases and genetic testing.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lumbar puncture is unrelated.
- B. Incorrect. Allergy and pulmonary tests do not diagnose Alport syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. These tests do not evaluate the syndrome.
- D. Correct. It assesses the renal, auditory and ocular systems and can confirm the genetic cause.
- E. Incorrect. They may assess cardiac/thoracic disease but not the defining Alport triad.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Renal: urinalysis and renal function.
- Ear: audiometry.
- Eye: ophthalmological examination.
- Genetic testing may confirm the collagen gene abnormality.
- Renal biopsy may show mesangial proliferative changes and glomerular sclerosis.

questions.stem: Which long-term outcome may occur in boys with severe X-linked Alport syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Permanent spontaneous closure of the ureter

options.label: C
options.text: Progression to end-stage renal disease in early adulthood

options.label: D
options.text: Isolated liver failure without renal disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Progression to end-stage renal disease in early adulthood
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance progressive renal disease in Alport syndrome, with severe cases progressing to end-stage renal disease in adolescence or young adulthood.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Persistent or recurrent haematuria is a common early manifestation.
- B. Incorrect. Ureteral closure is unrelated.
- C. Correct. Progressive nephritis may lead to ESRD, particularly in affected boys with X-linked disease.
- D. Incorrect. Liver failure is not the defining course.
- E. Incorrect. Progressive renal impairment is a central concern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Alport syndrome may progress to CKD and ESRD.
- Control hypertension and proteinuria and monitor renal function.
- Dialysis and transplantation may be required in advanced disease.

cases.title: A school-age child with bedwetting
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child is brought because of persistent bedwetting. The child has never been dry at night for a sustained period. There is no dysuria, fever or daytime incontinence. The parents are concerned and have been punishing the child. The clinician reviews fluid intake, constipation, sleep symptoms and possible underlying disease.

questions.stem: What is the definition of nocturnal enuresis?

options.label: B
options.text: Involuntary urination during sleep after the expected age of night-time bladder control

options.label: D
options.text: Dysuria with a positive urine culture

questions.correctAnswerText: Involuntary urination during sleep after the expected age of night-time bladder control
questions.initialExplanation: Nocturnal enuresis is involuntary voiding during sleep after the age at which night-time bladder control is expected. clinical guidance gives night-time dryness as usually achieved between 3 and 5 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Daytime frequency is a different urinary symptom.
- B. Correct. This matches the definition.
- C. Incorrect. Polyuria with exercise does not define enuresis.
- D. Incorrect. Dysuria with bacteriuria suggests UTI.
- E. Incorrect. Continuous leakage from birth suggests a different congenital or anatomical problem.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance gives daytime dryness at about 2 years and night-time dryness at about 3–5 years.
- Assess fluid intake, urinary symptoms, constipation, sleep and possible underlying disease.

questions.stem: A child previously achieved bladder control for more than 6 months but has started wetting the bed again. This is classified as:
questions.correctAnswerText: Secondary enuresis
questions.initialExplanation: Secondary enuresis occurs when a child who previously achieved bladder control for 6 months or longer begins wetting again.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Primary enuresis — Incorrect. clinical guidance defines this as never having achieved bladder control.
- B. Orthostatic proteinuria — Incorrect. It is posture-dependent urinary protein loss.
- C. Daytime frequency — Incorrect. It does not describe recurrent bedwetting after prior dryness.
- D. Secondary enuresis — Correct. The child had a sustained dry period and then relapsed.
- E. Sterile pyuria — Incorrect. It refers to urinary white cells with a negative culture.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Primary: bladder control was never achieved.
- Secondary: bladder control was achieved for at least 6 months, then lost.
- Consider emotional upset, constipation, UTI, polyuria, sleep disorders and neurological causes.

questions.stem: Which condition should be considered when a child with enuresis has excessive thirst and large-volume urine output?
questions.correctAnswerText: Diabetes mellitus or diabetes insipidus
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, CKD and other causes of polyuria among the conditions that may contribute to bedwetting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Both DM and DI can cause polyuria and compensatory polydipsia.
- B. Incorrect. VUR is relevant to recurrent UTI and renal scarring, but it does not explain polyuria as the primary clue here.
- C. Incorrect. Hypospadias is a urethral meatus abnormality and does not typically cause polyuria.
- D. Incorrect. Torsion causes acute scrotal pain and is unrelated to bedwetting.
- E. Incorrect. Hydrocele causes scrotal swelling, not polyuria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ask about fluid intake, polyuria, polydipsia, dysuria, frequency and daytime symptoms.
- Consider DM, DI, CKD, UTI, constipation and sleep disorders.
- Examine abdomen for a distended bladder and assess neurological/spinal findings when indicated.

questions.stem: Which investigation is recommended as the basic initial urine test in a child with enuresis?

options.label: A
options.text: MCUG in children in routine care

options.label: B
options.text: CT scan in children in routine care

options.label: E
options.text: DMSA scan in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Urinalysis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance urine analysis to look for UTI, glucosuria and urine specific gravity. Blood tests and imaging are selected according to the clinical picture rather than performed routinely in every child.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. MCUG is used when there is a specific indication such as suspected VUR or obstruction.
- B. Incorrect. CT is not a routine initial test for bedwetting.
- C. Correct. Urinalysis is the basic initial test.
- D. Incorrect. Renal biopsy is invasive and not routine in enuresis.
- E. Incorrect. DMSA is used for renal cortical scars, not routine primary enuresis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Initial urinalysis: UTI, glucosuria, specific gravity.
- Further blood tests/imaging depend on history and examination.
- Do not over-investigate uncomplicated primary monosymptomatic enuresis.

questions.stem: What is the appropriate general approach for a child under 5 years with uncomplicated nocturnal enuresis,?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate long-term desmopressin for children in routine care

options.label: E
options.text: No active treatment is generally required

questions.correctAnswerText: No active treatment is generally required
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that children younger than 5 years generally do not require treatment. Reassurance and supportive advice are important.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin is considered in selected older children, not routinely in all children under 5.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics are indicated only when bacterial infection is present.
- C. Incorrect. Transplantation is not relevant to uncomplicated enuresis.
- D. Incorrect. Ureteric reimplantation treats selected severe VUR.
- E. Correct. This is the age-based approach described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Under 5 years: generally no treatment.
- School-age children: motivational counselling, reward charts, alarms and selected medication.
- Avoid punishment; reassure parents and child.

questions.stem: Which important adverse effect is associated with desmopressin used for nocturnal enuresis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hyponatraemia and seizures
questions.initialExplanation: Desmopressin is an ADH analogue that reduces overnight urine production. clinical guidance highlights hyponatraemia and seizures as important adverse effects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hypernatraemia — Incorrect. clinical guidance specifically warns about hyponatraemia.
- B. Hypercalcaemia — Incorrect. It is not the adverse effect highlighted for desmopressin.
- C. Hyponatraemia and seizures — Correct. This is the adverse-effect warning in the supplied material.
- D. Hyperphosphataemia — Incorrect. It is not the stated adverse effect.
- E. Renal scarring — Incorrect. It is not an adverse effect of desmopressin.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Desmopressin reduces nocturnal urine production.
- clinical guidance highlights hyponatraemia and seizures; fluid advice and careful prescribing are important.
- Enuresis alarms are another treatment option described.

questions.stem: Which measure is recommended as part of behavioural management of nocturnal enuresis?

options.label: A
options.text: Restricting fluid intake for the entire day

options.label: B
options.text: Waking the child repeatedly throughout the night as the strategy

options.label: C
options.text: Punishing the child after wet nights

options.label: D
options.text: Motivational counselling, a star chart and appropriate evening fluid advice

questions.correctAnswerText: Motivational counselling, a star chart and appropriate evening fluid advice
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance reassurance, avoiding punishment, managing evening fluid intake, emptying the bladder before bed and using a star chart for dry nights.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fluid intake should be managed appropriately; all-day fluid restriction is not recommended.
- B. Incorrect. Repeated waking is not the sole recommended strategy and may disrupt sleep.
- C. Incorrect. Punishment may harm the child's psychological development and self-esteem.
- D. Correct. These are behavioural measures described.
- E. Incorrect. Emptying the bladder before bedtime is encouraged.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Reassure; do not punish.
- Encourage regular voiding and emptying the bladder before sleep.
- Consider evening fluid timing and reward charts.
- Enuresis alarms are effective but may take weeks and require persistence.

topics.name: IgA Vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein Purpura) and Renal Involvement

cases.title: Purpura, abdominal pain and haematuria
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old boy develops palpable purpuric lesions over the lower limbs and buttocks after an upper respiratory infection. He complains of ankle pain and severe colicky abdominal pain. Urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria and mild proteinuria.

questions.stem: Which group of features forms the characteristic clinical picture of IgA vasculitis?

options.label: E
options.text: Purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain and renal involvement

questions.correctAnswerText: Purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain and renal involvement
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance IgA vasculitis as a small-vessel vasculitis characterized by palpable purpura, joint symptoms, abdominal pain and renal involvement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Respiratory signs do not represent the typical clinical picture.
- B. Incorrect. Deafness and lenticonus are associated with Alport syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Polyuria and glycosuria suggest metabolic or tubular disorders.
- D. Incorrect. Hepatic manifestations are not the characteristic tetrad.
- E. Correct. This is the clinical combination described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IgA vasculitis: palpable purpura, joint involvement, abdominal pain and nephritis.
- Clinical guidance it as the commonest systemic vasculitis in childhood.
- Commonly follows an upper respiratory infection.

questions.stem: Which age group is most typical for IgA vasculitis in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: D
options.text: 3–12 years, with a peak around 4–7 years

options.label: E
options.text: across the age range but exclusively newborns

questions.correctAnswerText: 3–12 years, with a peak around 4–7 years
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance gives the typical age as 3–12 years, with a peak around 4–7 years, and notes a male predominance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Neonates are not the typical age group.
- B. Incorrect. It is not an adult-only vasculitis.
- C. Incorrect. The condition is common in childhood, not limited to late adolescence.
- D. Correct. This matches the age distribution.
- E. Incorrect. It is not exclusive to newborns.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Typical age: 3–12 years.
- Peak: 4–7 years.
- More common in boys.
- A preceding URTI is reported in about half of cases.

questions.stem: Which skin finding is the cornerstone of the diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Palpable purpura, particularly over dependent lower-limb and buttock areas

options.label: E
options.text: Petechiae with severe thrombocytopenia in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Palpable purpura, particularly over dependent lower-limb and buttock areas
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance symmetrical palpable purpura, especially on the lower limbs and buttocks, as the hallmark and often the first clinical feature.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urticaria may occur initially, but palpable purpura is the key diagnostic feature.
- B. Correct. This is the characteristic cutaneous manifestation described.
- C. Incorrect. Vesicles are not the typical rash pattern.
- D. Incorrect. Hypopigmented macules are not the characteristic rash.
- E. Incorrect. Platelets are usually normal or slightly raised in IgA vasculitis; thrombocytopenia suggests another diagnosis such as ITP.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Palpable purpura, often symmetrical and dependent.
- Lower limbs and buttocks are common sites.
- Platelets are usually normal or slightly increased, unlike ITP.

questions.stem: Which gastrointestinal complication is specifically highlighted as important in IgA vasculitis?

options.label: E
options.text: Volvulus due to malrotation in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Intussusception
questions.initialExplanation: Severe colicky abdominal pain and GI bleeding may occur in IgA vasculitis. clinical guidance identifies intussusception as an important complication.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease causes constipation and bowel obstruction.
- B. Correct. Intussusception is specifically highlighted.
- C. Incorrect. Biliary atresia causes conjugated jaundice and pale stools.
- D. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes projectile non-bilious vomiting in young infants.
- E. Incorrect. Malrotation/volvulus is a separate congenital surgical emergency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IgA vasculitis may cause colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and GI bleeding.
- Intussusception is an important complication.
- Severe abdominal pain or bleeding requires urgent assessment.

questions.stem: Which renal finding in a child with IgA vasculitis requires follow-up because it may indicate nephritis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent haematuria or proteinuria
questions.initialExplanation: Renal involvement may appear during the acute illness or weeks later. clinical guidance emphasizes follow-up to detect persistent haematuria or proteinuria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Transillumination supports hydrocele, not IgA nephritis.
- B. Incorrect. A normal result is reassuring at that time but does not remove the need for follow-up if clinically indicated.
- C. Correct. These are the renal manifestations requiring monitoring.
- D. Incorrect. Rhinorrhoea is not a marker of renal involvement.
- E. Incorrect. Cough is not the renal follow-up marker specified.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IgA vasculitis nephritis may appear after the rash or during the acute illness.
- Follow BP and urinalysis.
- Persistent renal involvement requires longer-term follow-up.

questions.stem: What is the main treatment approach for uncomplicated IgA vasculitis?

options.label: E
options.text: Supportive care, hydration, bed rest and NSAIDs for joint pain when appropriate

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive care, hydration, bed rest and NSAIDs for joint pain when appropriate
questions.initialExplanation: Most cases are self-limiting. Clinical guidance supportive treatment, including bed rest, adequate hydration and NSAIDs for joint pain; corticosteroids are reserved for severe manifestations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Nephrectomy is not indicated for uncomplicated IgA vasculitis.
- B. Incorrect. Dialysis is required only in selected severe renal complications, not every patient.
- C. Incorrect. Chemotherapy has no routine role in uncomplicated IgA vasculitis.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not routine treatment for immune-mediated vasculitis.
- E. Correct. This is the supportive approach described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most cases are self-limiting.
- Supportive care and symptom control are central.
- Steroids may be used for severe nephritis, severe abdominal pain/bleeding, significant scrotal oedema or CNS/pulmonary involvement.

questions.stem: Which follow-up plan is emphasized after IgA vasculitis?

options.label: A
options.text: No follow-up is needed if the rash disappears

options.label: D
options.text: Urinalysis and BP monitoring, with longer follow-up if renal involvement persists

options.label: E
options.text: Routine chest CT for most children

questions.correctAnswerText: Urinalysis and BP monitoring, with longer follow-up if renal involvement persists
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance urine analysis and BP measurement after diagnosis, with at least a period of follow-up to detect persistent renal involvement. Children with persistent nephritis require longer-term follow-up.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Renal manifestations may appear later, even after the rash improves.
- B. Incorrect. Daily echocardiography is unrelated to the recommended renal monitoring.
- C. Incorrect. Hearing tests are relevant to Alport syndrome, not routine IgA vasculitis follow-up.
- D. Correct. This monitors haematuria, proteinuria and hypertension.
- E. Incorrect. Routine chest CT is not indicated for all children.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Monitor urine and BP after diagnosis.
- Persistent haematuria/proteinuria warrants longer nephrology follow-up.
- Severe renal disease and hypertension are risk factors for progressive CKD.

cases.title: Purpura followed by urinary abnormalities
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old boy develops palpable purpura over the lower legs and buttocks. He also has ankle pain and episodes of colicky abdominal pain. Two weeks later, urine testing shows microscopic haematuria and proteinuria. Blood pressure is currently normal.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains the combination of dependent palpable purpura, joint symptoms, abdominal pain and renal findings?
questions.correctAnswerText: IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura)
questions.initialExplanation: IgA vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis characterized by palpable purpura, arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain and possible nephritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ITP is associated with thrombocytopenia; Clinical guidance platelet counts are usually normal or slightly high in HSP.
- B. Incorrect. Cystitis does not explain the purpura, arthritis and colicky abdominal pain.
- C. Incorrect. Wilms tumour typically presents with an abdominal mass.
- D. Correct. The four-system pattern is characteristic of IgA vasculitis.
- E. Incorrect. Minimal-change disease causes nephrotic syndrome but not the classic purpura–joint–gut pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HSP is also called IgA vasculitis.
- Clinical guidance it as the commonest systemic vasculitis in childhood.
- The classic systems involved are skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract and kidneys.

questions.stem: The child initially has only the skin and joint findings. Which later development should be actively sought because renal involvement may appear after the rash?
questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent haematuria or proteinuria
questions.initialExplanation: Renal involvement may occur during the acute illness or weeks later. Urinalysis and blood-pressure monitoring are therefore important even when the initial presentation is mainly cutaneous and articular.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Haematuria and proteinuria are the main renal findings to monitor.
- B. Incorrect. Hypospadias is a congenital genital anomaly.
- C. Incorrect. Jaundice is not the delayed renal feature of HSP.
- D. Incorrect. Hydrocele is not a marker of HSP nephritis.
- E. Incorrect. Cataract is not the expected renal complication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance estimates renal involvement in approximately 40–50% of cases.
- Renal signs may begin during the acute phase or weeks later.

questions.stem: Which child with HSP has the greatest risk of progressive chronic kidney disease?

options.label: A
options.text: A child with a brief rash and normal urine

options.label: B
options.text: A child with mild ankle pain

options.label: C
options.text: A child with isolated transient abdominal discomfort

options.label: D
options.text: A child whose purpura resolves without renal findings

options.label: E
options.text: A child with heavy proteinuria, oedema, hypertension and deteriorating renal function

questions.correctAnswerText: A child with heavy proteinuria, oedema, hypertension and deteriorating renal function
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance heavy proteinuria, oedema, hypertension and worsening renal function as risk factors for progressive CKD in HSP nephritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Normal urine and absence of renal involvement are reassuring.
- B. Incorrect. Joint symptoms alone do not indicate progressive renal disease.
- C. Incorrect. Abdominal pain alone is not a marker of renal progression.
- D. Incorrect. Resolution without renal findings is reassuring.
- E. Correct. These are the renal warning features listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most children recover, but significant renal involvement needs closer and longer follow-up.
- Persistent renal involvement or need for treatment warrants long-term nephrology follow-up.

questions.stem: Which follow-up strategy is specifically emphasized for children with HSP?

options.label: A
options.text: No follow-up once the rash disappears

options.label: B
options.text: Monitor urine and blood pressure for one year to detect persistent renal abnormalities

options.label: C
options.text: Daily renal biopsy for one month

options.label: E
options.text: Stop urine testing if abdominal pain resolves

questions.correctAnswerText: Monitor urine and blood pressure for one year to detect persistent renal abnormalities
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance follow-up for a year to detect persistent haematuria or proteinuria. It also lists urinalysis and blood-pressure measurement during follow-up.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Renal involvement may appear after the rash and can persist after skin symptoms resolve.
- B. Correct. Urinalysis and BP monitoring detect ongoing renal disease.
- C. Incorrect. Routine repeated biopsy is not recommended.
- D. Incorrect. Nephrectomy has no routine role in HSP.
- E. Incorrect. Resolution of abdominal pain does not exclude renal involvement.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance says all children should be followed for one year.
- Children with persistent renal involvement or who need treatment for nephritis require longer follow-up.

questions.stem: A child with HSP develops severe abdominal pain with gastrointestinal bleeding and significant nephritis. Which treatment approach is described for severe disease?

options.label: C
options.text: Corticosteroids may be used in severe nephritis or severe abdominal/GI manifestations

questions.correctAnswerText: Corticosteroids may be used in severe nephritis or severe abdominal/GI manifestations
questions.initialExplanation: Most HSP is self-limiting and treated supportively. clinical guidance reserves corticosteroids for severe renal, gastrointestinal, scrotal, CNS or pulmonary manifestations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Supportive treatment is common, but severe disease may require corticosteroids or specialist-directed immunosuppression.
- B. Incorrect. Circumcision is unrelated to vasculitis.
- C. Correct. This matches the severe-disease indications.
- D. Incorrect. Chemotherapy is not routine HSP therapy.
- E. Incorrect. Transplantation is not an acute treatment for HSP.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most cases are self-limiting; supportive care includes hydration and symptom control.
- Severe nephritis, abdominal pain/bleeding, scrotal oedema, CNS involvement or pulmonary haemorrhage may require corticosteroids.
- Immunosuppressive agents may be used by specialists for significant kidney disease.

cases.title: Poor growth, polyuria and rickets
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child is brought because of poor weight gain, excessive thirst and frequent urination. The child has episodes of dehydration and bowed legs. Blood tests show hypokalaemic, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with low phosphate. Urine testing reveals glucose and phosphate despite normal blood glucose.

questions.stem: Fanconi syndrome is caused by generalized dysfunction of which part of the nephron?
questions.correctAnswerText: Proximal renal tubule
questions.initialExplanation: Fanconi syndrome is a generalized proximal tubular defect causing urinary loss of glucose, phosphate, amino acids, bicarbonate, uric acid, sodium and water.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Glomerulus — Incorrect. Glomerular disorders primarily alter filtration-barrier function.
- B. Thin descending limb — Incorrect. It is not the site identified for Fanconi syndrome.
- C. Renal pelvis — Incorrect. It is part of the urine drainage system, not a tubular reabsorption site.
- D. Proximal tubule — Correct. This is the site of the generalized defect described.
- E. Distal collecting duct — Incorrect. Distal tubular/collecting duct defects cause other disorders, not the generalized proximal losses described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fanconi syndrome = generalized proximal tubular dysfunction.
- Urinary losses include glucose, phosphate, amino acids, bicarbonate and other solutes.
- Clinical features include polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, failure to thrive and hypophosphataemic rickets.

questions.stem: Which urine findings are expected in Fanconi syndrome?

options.label: C
options.text: Massive albuminuria with normal tubular function

questions.correctAnswerText: Glycosuria, phosphaturia and aminoaciduria
questions.initialExplanation: Because the proximal tubule normally reabsorbs several filtered solutes, generalized proximal tubular dysfunction causes urinary losses such as glucose, phosphate and amino acids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Nitrite-positive bacteriuria — Incorrect. This suggests bacterial UTI.
- B. Glycosuria, phosphaturia and aminoaciduria — Correct. These are classic proximal tubular losses listed.
- C. Albuminuria alone — Incorrect. Fanconi syndrome is a tubular reabsorption defect rather than isolated glomerular albumin leakage.
- D. Haematuria and casts — Incorrect. These suggest glomerular disease.
- E. Ketonuria — Incorrect. It is not the defining Fanconi pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Think proximal tubule when glucose, phosphate and amino acids are lost together.
- clinical guidance links Fanconi syndrome with metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemic rickets.

questions.stem: Which acid–base and electrolyte pattern is expected in Fanconi syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypokalaemic, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis
questions.initialExplanation: Proximal tubular loss of bicarbonate contributes to normal-anion-gap, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. Potassium may also be lost in the urine, causing hypokalaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the pattern described.
- B. Incorrect. Clinical guidance a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Hypochloraemic alkalosis is not the expected acid–base disturbance.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the typical Fanconi pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Respiratory alkalosis is not the primary tubular defect.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fanconi syndrome: proximal bicarbonate loss → metabolic acidosis.
- Potassium wasting may cause hypokalaemia.
- Phosphate loss can cause rickets and poor growth.

questions.stem: Which bone complication is associated with phosphate loss in Fanconi syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis as the defining complication

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypophosphataemic rickets
questions.initialExplanation: Renal phosphate wasting reduces phosphate available for bone mineralization and can cause hypophosphataemic rickets.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. It is the bone complication specifically listed.
- B. Incorrect. It is not the characteristic complication described.
- C. Incorrect. Osteogenesis imperfecta is a collagen disorder.
- D. Incorrect. Osteopetrosis is a separate bone disorder involving impaired bone resorption.
- E. Incorrect. Achondroplasia is a genetic skeletal dysplasia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fanconi → phosphaturia → hypophosphataemia → rickets/poor growth.
- Look for polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration and biochemical tubular losses.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a congenital cause of Fanconi syndrome listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cystinosis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance cystinosis, Lowe syndrome, tyrosinaemia, galactosaemia, glycogen storage disease and Wilson disease among congenital or inherited conditions associated with Fanconi syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Appendicitis — Incorrect. It is not a congenital renal tubular cause.
- B. Cystinosis — Correct. It is a listed inherited cause.
- C. Hydrocele — Incorrect. It is fluid in the tunica vaginalis.
- D. Rheumatic fever — Incorrect. It is a post-streptococcal inflammatory disease.
- E. Asthma — Incorrect. It is a respiratory disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital associations include cystinosis, Lowe syndrome, tyrosinaemia, galactosaemia, GSD and Wilson disease.
- Acquired causes include selected drugs/toxins and amyloidosis.

questions.stem: Which management plan best addresses the main abnormalities in Fanconi syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Hydration, correction of acidosis, and replacement of potassium and phosphate as needed

options.label: D
options.text: Fluid restriction and potassium restriction in each patient

questions.correctAnswerText: Hydration, correction of acidosis, and replacement of potassium and phosphate as needed
questions.initialExplanation: Management replaces ongoing losses, corrects dehydration and acidosis, and addresses bone disease with phosphate and active vitamin D when indicated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotics are only indicated if infection is present.
- B. Correct. This approach addresses volume, electrolyte and acid–base abnormalities.
- C. Incorrect. Nephrectomy does not correct generalized proximal tubular dysfunction.
- D. Incorrect. These children may have salt and water losses, and potassium depletion; universal restriction would be inappropriate.
- E. Incorrect. Desmopressin is not treatment for Fanconi syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hydration and correction of acidosis.
- Replace potassium, phosphate and alkali as clinically required.
- Bone disease may need phosphate and active vitamin D.
- Monitor growth, electrolytes and renal function.

cases.title: Poor growth with multiple urinary losses
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child has faltering growth, excessive thirst, polyuria and recurrent dehydration. Examination reveals features of rickets. Blood testing shows hypokalaemic, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. Urine testing demonstrates glucose and phosphate loss despite no evidence of diabetes mellitus. Another child in the clinic has recurrent dehydration, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and hypercalciuria, while an older child has hypomagnesaemia and low urinary calcium.

questions.stem: Which renal defect best explains the first child's simultaneous urinary loss of glucose, phosphate, amino acids and bicarbonate?
questions.correctAnswerText: Generalized proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome)
questions.initialExplanation: Fanconi syndrome is a generalized proximal tubular defect causing urinary loss of several normally reabsorbed substances, including glucose, phosphate, amino acids, bicarbonate, uric acid, sodium and water.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Glomerular disease causes protein or blood leakage, not this generalized proximal tubular wasting pattern.
- B. Correct. Multiple proximal tubular solutes are lost together.
- C. Incorrect. Urethral obstruction causes impaired urine flow, not selective solute wasting.
- D. Incorrect. Hypertension does not explain glycosuria and phosphaturia.
- E. Incorrect. Minimal-change disease causes heavy proteinuria rather than multiple tubular losses.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fanconi syndrome: generalized proximal tubule defect.
- Look for glycosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, bicarbonate loss, polyuria and dehydration.

questions.stem: Which combination of clinical and biochemical findings best fits Fanconi syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Hypertension, low urinary glucose and respiratory alkalosis

options.label: C
options.text: Polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, failure to thrive and hypophosphataemic rickets

options.label: D
options.text: Gross haematuria, low C3 and hypertension

questions.correctAnswerText: Polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, failure to thrive and hypophosphataemic rickets
questions.initialExplanation: Loss of water and solutes through the proximal tubule causes polyuria, dehydration, poor growth and phosphate-deficiency bone disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Clinical guidance hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis rather than hyperkalaemic alkalosis.
- B. Incorrect. Glycosuria and phosphate wasting are expected.
- C. Correct. This is the clinical pattern described for Fanconi syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. This is a nephritic pattern such as PSGN.
- E. Incorrect. These findings suggest HUS.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fanconi syndrome can produce hypokalaemia and hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.
- Rickets results from phosphate loss.

questions.stem: A child develops Fanconi syndrome after exposure to a nephrotoxic medication. Which cause is included?
questions.correctAnswerText: Aminoglycoside exposure
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance aminoglycosides and toxins among acquired causes of Fanconi syndrome. It also lists inherited and metabolic conditions such as cystinosis and Lowe syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Aminoglycosides are listed as a possible acquired cause.
- B. Incorrect. Salbutamol is not listed as a cause of generalized proximal tubular dysfunction.
- C. Incorrect. Topical emollients do not explain Fanconi syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. Routine iron treatment is not a listed cause.
- E. Incorrect. Hydrocele is a scrotal fluid collection, not a tubular disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Causes include cystinosis, Lowe syndrome, tyrosinaemia, galactosaemia, glycogen storage disease, Wilson disease, aminoglycosides and toxins.

questions.stem: Which management combination best addresses the major losses in Fanconi syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Fluid restriction and loop diuretic alone

options.label: B
options.text: Steroids and penicillin for children in routine care

options.label: D
options.text: Adequate hydration, bicarbonate/alkali, potassium and phosphate replacement, with active vitamin D for bone disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Adequate hydration, bicarbonate/alkali, potassium and phosphate replacement, with active vitamin D for bone disease
questions.initialExplanation: Treatment replaces fluid and the substances lost through the proximal tubule. Clinical guidance hydration, sodium bicarbonate/alkali, potassium, phosphate and active vitamin D for bone disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fluid restriction may worsen dehydration and does not replace lost solutes.
- B. Incorrect. Steroids and penicillin do not correct proximal tubular wasting.
- C. Incorrect. These are not treatments for Fanconi syndrome.
- D. Correct. This approach addresses hydration, acidosis, potassium and phosphate depletion.
- E. Incorrect. Restricting replacement without correcting losses is inappropriate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat dehydration and metabolic acidosis.
- Replace potassium and phosphate as needed.
- Treat rickets with phosphate and active vitamin D under specialist care.

cases.title: A child with salt wasting and hypokalaemic alkalosis
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child has poor growth, polyuria, polydipsia, recurrent dehydration, vomiting and constipation. Blood tests show hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Blood pressure is normal or low. Urine studies show renal salt wasting. Further testing is needed to distinguish a loop-of-Henle defect from a distal convoluted tubule defect.

questions.stem: Bartter syndrome is associated with a defect in which nephron segment?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ascending loop of Henle
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance Bartter syndrome as an autosomal recessive defect involving the Na-K-2Cl transporter in the ascending loop of Henle.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Glomerular basement membrane — Incorrect. It is affected in glomerular diseases such as Alport-related pathology, not Bartter syndrome.
- B. Ascending loop of Henle — Correct. clinical guidance identifies the Na-K-2Cl transporter at this site.
- C. Proximal tubule — Incorrect. This is the site affected in Fanconi syndrome.
- D. Collecting duct — Incorrect. It is not the described primary defect in Bartter syndrome.
- E. Distal convoluted tubule — Incorrect. This is the site associated with Gitelman syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bartter: ascending loop of Henle; Na-K-2Cl transporter.
- Gitelman: distal convoluted tubule; Na-Cl cotransporter.
- Both may cause hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: Which feature helps distinguish Gitelman syndrome from Bartter syndrome in the supplied comparison?

options.label: B
options.text: Gitelman syndrome is caused by a glomerular basement membrane defect

options.label: E
options.text: Gitelman syndrome is associated with low serum magnesium

questions.correctAnswerText: Gitelman syndrome is associated with low serum magnesium
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance low serum magnesium with increased urinary magnesium loss as a feature of Gitelman syndrome. Bartter syndrome typically has normal serum magnesium in the comparison.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. BP is usually normal or low 's comparison.
- B. Incorrect. Gitelman is a tubular transporter disorder.
- C. Incorrect. Both syndromes are associated with hypokalaemia.
- D. Incorrect. Both are associated with metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis.
- E. Correct. Hypomagnesaemia is a useful distinguishing feature.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Gitelman: low serum magnesium and low urinary calcium.
- Bartter: high urinary calcium/hypercalciuria and possible nephrocalcinosis.
- Both can present with polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration and poor growth.

questions.stem: Which urinary calcium pattern is more characteristic of Bartter syndrome?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypercalciuria
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance associates Bartter syndrome with increased urinary calcium and possible nephrocalcinosis. Gitelman syndrome is associated with low urinary calcium.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Complete absence of urinary calcium is not the pattern described.
- B. Correct. Hypercalciuria is the key urinary calcium pattern for Bartter in the comparison.
- C. Incorrect. Hypocalciuria is more characteristic of Gitelman syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. Calcium-containing casts are not the defining feature.
- E. Incorrect. Glycosuria suggests proximal tubular dysfunction, such as Fanconi syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bartter: hypercalciuria and risk of nephrocalcinosis.
- Gitelman: hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia.
- Check BP, potassium, bicarbonate, magnesium and urinary calcium.

questions.stem: Which transporter is affected in Gitelman syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule

options.label: B
options.text: Glucose transporter in the proximal tubule

options.label: C
options.text: Na-K-2Cl transporter in the ascending loop

options.label: D
options.text: Type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane

questions.correctAnswerText: Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance Gitelman syndrome as a defect in the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the Gitelman defect described.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the transporter affected in Gitelman syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. This is the transporter/site associated with Bartter syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. Type IV collagen defects are associated with Alport syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Aquaporin-2 defects are associated with other water-balance disorders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Gitelman: DCT Na-Cl cotransporter.
- Bartter: ascending loop Na-K-2Cl transporter.
- Both are salt-wasting tubulopathies with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: Which age pattern is described for Bartter compared with Gitelman syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Gitelman typically presents in the neonatal period; Bartter in old age

options.label: C
options.text: Age at presentation is identical in most patients

options.label: D
options.text: Bartter usually presents earlier and may be severe in neonates/infants; Gitelman often presents later

options.label: E
options.text: Both are restricted to the first week of life

questions.correctAnswerText: Bartter usually presents earlier and may be severe in neonates/infants; Gitelman often presents later
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance Bartter syndrome as potentially presenting in the neonatal period or infancy, whereas Gitelman syndrome is generally less severe and tends to present later in childhood or adulthood.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Both can present in childhood.
- B. Incorrect. The patterns are reversed.
- C. Incorrect. Age of onset is a useful distinguishing clue.
- D. Correct. This matches the age pattern in the comparison.
- E. Incorrect. Gitelman commonly presents later.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bartter: earlier, often more severe; neonatal/infant presentations occur.
- Gitelman: often later childhood/adult and less severe.
- Both can cause failure to thrive, vomiting, dehydration, constipation and hypotonia.

questions.stem: Which treatment combination is listed for Bartter syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Restrict fluids and give potassium-binding resin

options.label: D
options.text: Desmopressin and thiazide as the treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Fluids, potassium replacement and indomethacin
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance fluid and potassium replacement with indomethacin for Bartter syndrome. Gitelman treatment focuses on potassium and magnesium supplementation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The disorder involves renal salt wasting and hypokalaemia; routine fluid restriction is inappropriate.
- B. Correct. These measures are listed for Bartter syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Ureteric reimplantation treats selected VUR.
- D. Incorrect. Desmopressin is not the core treatment described.
- E. Incorrect. Steroids do not correct the transporter defect.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bartter: fluids + potassium + indomethacin.
- Gitelman: potassium and magnesium supplementation.
- Treatment is tailored to electrolyte losses and clinical status.

questions.stem: A child has hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Gitelman syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Hypokalaemic alkalosis with hypomagnesaemia and low urinary calcium is the characteristic pattern of Gitelman syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Gitelman — Correct. The electrolyte and urine-calcium pattern fits Gitelman syndrome.
- B. Nephrotic syndrome — Incorrect. It causes heavy proteinuria and oedema.
- C. Bartter — Incorrect. Bartter is associated with hypercalciuria and usually normal serum magnesium in the comparison.
- D. Fanconi — Incorrect. It causes proximal tubular losses with metabolic acidosis, glycosuria and phosphaturia.
- E. Distal RTA — Incorrect. It causes normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Gitelman: hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis + hypomagnesaemia + hypocalciuria.
- Bartter: hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis + hypercalciuria.
- The pattern helps localize the tubular defect.

cases.title: Poor growth with multiple urinary losses
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child has faltering growth, excessive thirst, polyuria and recurrent dehydration. Examination reveals features of rickets. Blood testing shows hypokalaemic, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. Urine testing demonstrates glucose and phosphate loss despite no evidence of diabetes mellitus. Another child in the clinic has recurrent dehydration, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and hypercalciuria, while an older child has hypomagnesaemia and low urinary calcium.

questions.stem: A neonate has severe polyuria, dehydration, failure to thrive, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and high urinary calcium. Which disorder is most consistent with clinical guidance's comparison?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bartter syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Bartter syndrome is caused by a defect in the sodium–potassium–chloride transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. It is often more severe and may present in the neonatal period or infancy, with hypercalciuria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Gitelman syndrome usually presents later, is less severe and is associated with low urinary calcium and low serum magnesium.
- B. Correct. Early severe presentation and hypercalciuria point toward Bartter syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Fanconi syndrome causes proximal tubular solute wasting and metabolic acidosis.
- D. Incorrect. Distal RTA causes metabolic acidosis, not metabolic alkalosis.
- E. Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome causes protein loss and oedema.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bartter: loop of Henle transporter defect, early/severe presentation, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, hypercalciuria and possible nephrocalcinosis.
- Clinical guidance fluids, potassium and indomethacin as treatment.

questions.stem: An older child has milder salt-wasting symptoms, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, low serum magnesium and low urinary calcium. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.correctAnswerText: Gitelman syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Gitelman syndrome is due to a defect in the distal convoluted tubule sodium–chloride cotransporter. It is usually less severe, presents later and is associated with hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bartter syndrome is more often earlier and more severe, with hypercalciuria.
- B. Incorrect. Fanconi syndrome produces generalized proximal tubular losses and metabolic acidosis.
- C. Correct. The later, milder pattern with low magnesium and low urinary calcium is characteristic.
- D. Incorrect. Type IV RTA causes hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis.
- E. Incorrect. Glomerulonephritis produces haematuria and often hypertension.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Gitelman: distal convoluted tubule defect, later presentation, hypokalaemic alkalosis, low serum magnesium and low urinary calcium.
- Clinical guidance potassium and magnesium supplementation.

topics.name: Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) and Acid–Base Concepts

cases.title: Failure to thrive with persistent metabolic acidosis
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child presents with poor growth, vomiting, polyuria, polydipsia, constipation and episodes of dehydration. Blood tests show a persistent normal-anion-gap, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with hypokalaemia. Urine pH remains inappropriately high despite systemic acidosis. Renal ultrasound shows nephrocalcinosis.

questions.stem: What is the defining acid–base disturbance in renal tubular acidosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent normal-anion-gap, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis
questions.initialExplanation: RTA is a chronic state of normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis caused by a renal tubular defect in acid excretion or bicarbonate handling.
