questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. High-anion-gap acidosis is seen in conditions such as lactic acidosis, DKA, uraemia and selected poisonings.
- B. Incorrect. RTA is a metabolic, not primary respiratory, disorder.
- C. Correct. This is the definition presented.
- D. Incorrect. Metabolic alkalosis is associated with salt-wasting conditions such as Bartter and Gitelman.
- E. Incorrect. Respiratory alkalosis is not the defining renal tubular disturbance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- RTA: normal-anion-gap, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.
- The cause is a renal tubular acidification or bicarbonate reabsorption defect.
- Assess serum potassium and urine pH to help classify the type.

questions.stem: What is the primary defect in distal (Type I) RTA?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced aldosterone production causing hyperkalaemia in each case

options.label: B
options.text: Failure of bicarbonate reabsorption by the proximal tubule

options.label: E
options.text: Failure of hydrogen ion excretion by the distal tubule

questions.correctAnswerText: Failure of hydrogen ion excretion by the distal tubule
questions.initialExplanation: Distal RTA (Type I) results from impaired hydrogen ion secretion in the distal nephron, preventing appropriate urinary acidification.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Reduced aldosterone activity is associated with Type IV RTA.
- B. Incorrect. This is the primary defect in proximal (Type II) RTA.
- C. Incorrect. Glucose handling is not the defining defect.
- D. Incorrect. The glomerular filtration barrier is not the site of the tubular acidification defect.
- E. Correct. This is the Type I defect described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type I distal RTA: impaired H+ secretion by the distal tubule.
- Urine pH remains inappropriately high during systemic acidosis.
- Nephrocalcinosis and renal stones may occur.

questions.stem: What is the primary defect in proximal (Type II) RTA?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of hydrogen secretion in the collecting duct

options.label: B
options.text: Increased distal potassium secretion as the defect

options.label: D
options.text: Failure of bicarbonate reabsorption by the proximal tubule

questions.correctAnswerText: Failure of bicarbonate reabsorption by the proximal tubule
questions.initialExplanation: Proximal RTA occurs when the proximal tubule cannot adequately reabsorb filtered bicarbonate, leading to urinary bicarbonate loss and metabolic acidosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes distal RTA.
- B. Incorrect. Potassium handling may be affected, but this is not the defining proximal defect.
- C. Incorrect. Aldosterone-related abnormalities are associated with Type IV RTA.
- D. Correct. This is the primary Type II defect.
- E. Incorrect. RTA is due to a tubular function defect, not primary glomerular filtration failure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Proximal RTA: impaired HCO3− reabsorption in PCT.
- May be associated with Fanconi syndrome.
- Urine pH may fall below 5.5 once serum bicarbonate has fallen below the reabsorptive threshold.

questions.stem: Which urine pH pattern helps distinguish distal from proximal RTA?

options.label: A
options.text: Both types typically have urine pH above 9

options.label: B
options.text: Urine pH is not usually useful

options.label: C
options.text: Distal RTA typically has acidic urine; proximal RTA typically alkaline urine

options.label: D
options.text: Distal RTA urine pH can not usually fall below about 5.5; proximal RTA urine pH may fall below 5.5

options.label: E
options.text: Both types typically have urine pH below 4

questions.correctAnswerText: Distal RTA urine pH can not usually fall below about 5.5; proximal RTA urine pH may fall below 5.5
questions.initialExplanation: Distal RTA has an inability to acidify urine appropriately, so urine pH remains above approximately 5.5 during systemic acidosis. In proximal RTA, urine pH may fall once plasma bicarbonate has decreased sufficiently.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Such extreme alkalinity is not the defining pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Urine pH is an important part of the comparison.
- C. Incorrect. The pattern is reversed.
- D. Correct. This is the differentiating pattern described.
- E. Incorrect. The urine pH does not remain extremely acidic in both types.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Distal RTA: inappropriately high urine pH during acidosis.
- Proximal RTA: urine pH can fall below 5.5 after bicarbonate depletion.
- Interpret urine pH alongside serum acid–base status.

questions.stem: Which clinical finding is particularly associated with distal RTA?
questions.correctAnswerText: Nephrocalcinosis or renal stones
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance distal RTA as being associated with renal stones/nephrocalcinosis, rickets due to chronic acidosis and hypokalaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia is not a defining feature.
- B. Incorrect. Jaundice is unrelated.
- C. Incorrect. Distal RTA is associated with metabolic acidosis, often hypokalaemia.
- D. Correct. Nephrocalcinosis and renal stones are important features of distal RTA.
- E. Incorrect. Fixed wide split S2 is an ASD finding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Distal RTA: normal-gap acidosis, hypokalaemia, high urine pH and nephrocalcinosis/stones.
- Chronic acidosis can cause bone buffering and rickets.
- Polyuria, polydipsia, constipation, hypotonia and poor growth may occur.

questions.stem: Which electrolyte abnormality is a major safety concern when correcting acidosis in a child with RTA?
questions.correctAnswerText: Life-threatening hypokalaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance warns that potassium should be addressed before or alongside correction of acidosis because bicarbonate treatment can worsen hypokalaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hypermagnesaemia is not the issue described.
- B. Incorrect. Thrombocytopenia is unrelated.
- C. Incorrect. Hypernatraemia is not the main warning highlighted.
- D. Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is not the acute correction risk emphasized.
- E. Correct. Severe hypokalaemia can be dangerous and may worsen during correction of acidosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Correct potassium and acidosis carefully.
- clinical guidance specifically warns against correcting acidosis before considering potassium because of potentially life-threatening hypokalaemia.
- Treatment aims to support normal growth and prevent nephrocalcinosis.

questions.stem: A child with suspected Type IV RTA has hyperkalaemia and normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced aldosterone production or renal unresponsiveness to aldosterone

options.label: C
options.text: Failure of glomerular basement membrane filtration

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced aldosterone production or renal unresponsiveness to aldosterone
questions.initialExplanation: Type IV RTA is associated with reduced aldosterone production or impaired response to aldosterone, resulting in reduced potassium and acid excretion and hyperkalaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the mechanism described.
- B. Incorrect. Increased bicarbonate reabsorption would not explain the acidosis.
- C. Incorrect. The glomerular filtration barrier is not the mechanism.
- D. Incorrect. Excess acid secretion would not cause the described pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Insulin affects potassium distribution but is not the defining cause of Type IV RTA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type IV RTA: reduced aldosterone production or resistance.
- Hyperkalaemia + normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
- Sodium loss and volume depletion may also occur.

questions.stem: Which formula is used to calculate the serum anion gap in the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Na − (Cl + HCO3)
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance gives the anion gap as sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the formula.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the standard formula.
- C. Incorrect. The anion gap is not the sum of these electrolytes.
- D. Correct. This is the formula provided.
- E. Incorrect. This reverses and combines the wrong terms.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3).
- clinical guidance gives less than 12 as normal/absence of raised gap.
- RTA and diarrhoea are listed causes of normal-gap acidosis.

questions.stem: Which condition is associated with a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Diabetic ketoacidosis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance DKA among causes of high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, whereas diarrhoea and RTA are examples of normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Diarrhoea — Incorrect. It is listed as a normal-gap acidosis cause.
- B. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor — Incorrect. It is listed among normal-gap acidosis causes.
- C. RTA — Incorrect. RTA is a classic normal-gap acidosis.
- D. Ureterosigmoidostomy — Incorrect. It is also listed among normal-gap acidosis causes.
- E. DKA — Correct. Ketoacid accumulation increases the anion gap.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal gap: diarrhoea, RTA, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, ureterosigmoidostomy.
- High gap: lactic acidosis, DKA, inborn errors of metabolism, uraemia/AKI/CKD and selected poisonings.
- Classify the acidosis before selecting the differential.

cases.title: Poor growth with persistent hyperchloraemic acidosis
cases.vignette: An infant has poor weight gain, recurrent vomiting, muscle weakness and polyuria. Blood tests repeatedly show low bicarbonate, low potassium and high chloride with a normal anion gap. Urine remains inappropriately alkaline despite systemic acidosis. Imaging later shows nephrocalcinosis.

questions.stem: Which acid–base pattern is most consistent with renal tubular acidosis in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: E
options.text: High anion gap metabolic alkalosis with hyperkalaemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Normal-anion-gap, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis
questions.initialExplanation: RTA is described as a chronic normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, typically with hyperchloraemia. Potassium is often low in types I and II.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. RTA produces acidosis, not alkalosis.
- B. Incorrect. Respiratory acidosis is caused by inadequate carbon dioxide elimination.
- C. Incorrect. Respiratory alkalosis is not the primary acid–base disorder described.
- D. Correct. This is the characteristic pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Type IV RTA can involve hyperkalaemia, but the defining acid–base disturbance remains metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- RTA: normal anion gap, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.
- Types I and II are commonly associated with hypokalaemia; type IV is associated with hyperkalaemia.

questions.stem: The child's urine pH remains above 5.5 despite systemic acidosis, and nephrocalcinosis is present. Which tubular defect is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of distal hydrogen-ion secretion (type I distal RTA)

questions.correctAnswerText: Failure of distal hydrogen-ion secretion (type I distal RTA)
questions.initialExplanation: Distal RTA results from impaired hydrogen-ion secretion in the distal tubule. The urine cannot be appropriately acidified and may remain above pH 5.5–6.0.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Failure to excrete hydrogen ions explains the inappropriately high urine pH during systemic acidosis.
- B. Incorrect. Reduced filtration alone does not define distal RTA.
- C. Incorrect. Proximal bicarbonate handling is the main defect in type II RTA.
- D. Incorrect. Increased aldosterone effect does not explain distal acidification failure.
- E. Incorrect. UTI may alter urine pH but does not explain the persistent tubular acidification defect and clinical pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type I distal RTA: failure of H⁺ excretion by the distal tubule.
- Urine pH may remain above 5.5–6.0.
- clinical guidance links distal RTA with renal stones/nephrocalcinosis.

questions.stem: Another child has proximal bicarbonate wasting. As systemic acidosis becomes established, which urine pH behaviour is possible in type II RTA?

options.label: A
options.text: Urine pH must remain above 8 in each sample

options.label: D
options.text: Urine is typically protein-free and glucose-free

options.label: E
options.text: Urine pH is diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome

questions.correctAnswerText: Urine pH can fall below 5.5
questions.initialExplanation: In proximal RTA, bicarbonate reabsorption is impaired in the proximal tubule. Once serum bicarbonate has fallen sufficiently, the distal nephron may still acidify the urine, allowing urine pH to fall below 5.5.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Persistently high urine pH despite systemic acidosis is more characteristic of distal RTA.
- B. Correct. Clinical guidance that urine pH can fall below 5.5 in proximal RTA.
- C. Incorrect. Urine pH varies with the acid–base state and tubular response.
- D. Incorrect. This is not a defining feature of proximal RTA.
- E. Incorrect. Urine pH does not diagnose nephrotic syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type II proximal RTA: failure of bicarbonate reabsorption by the proximal tubule.
- Urine pH can fall below 5.5 after serum bicarbonate has fallen.

questions.stem: A child has hyperkalaemia, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis and evidence of reduced aldosterone production or response. Which type of RTA should be considered?

options.label: E
options.text: No renal tubular disorder is possible

questions.correctAnswerText: Type IV RTA
questions.initialExplanation: Type IV RTA is associated with reduced aldosterone production or reduced responsiveness to aldosterone and causes hyperkalaemia with metabolic acidosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Type I distal RTA is usually associated with hypokalaemia and impaired distal H⁺ secretion.
- B. Incorrect. Type II proximal RTA is associated with bicarbonate wasting and commonly hypokalaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Clinical guidance type III as a mixed type I and II pattern, not the characteristic aldosterone-related hyperkalaemic pattern.
- D. Correct. This is the described mechanism of type IV RTA.
- E. Incorrect. This combination is specifically described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Type IV RTA: reduced aldosterone production or end-organ response.
- It may cause sodium loss, potassium retention, hyperchloraemia and metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A child with distal RTA has both hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis. Which safety point is emphasized when planning replacement?

options.label: A
options.text: Give bicarbonate first and ignore potassium

options.label: C
options.text: Correct potassium before/with alkali because bicarbonate can worsen hypokalaemia

options.label: D
options.text: Use fluid restriction as the treatment

options.label: E
options.text: Give loop diuretics to increase potassium loss

questions.correctAnswerText: Correct potassium before/with alkali because bicarbonate can worsen hypokalaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance warns that correcting acidosis before potassium supplementation may precipitate life-threatening hypokalaemia. Potassium replacement must therefore be considered carefully before or during alkali correction under clinical supervision.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This ignores the warning.
- B. Incorrect. Potassium may need replacement when low.
- C. Correct. It reflects the safety point emphasized in the teaching material.
- D. Incorrect. Fluid restriction alone does not correct the tubular acid–base defect.
- E. Incorrect. Additional potassium loss could worsen hypokalaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treatment aims to correct acidosis, support normal growth and prevent nephrocalcinosis.
- Potassium and bicarbonate/alkali replacement are used according to the type and laboratory findings.
- Correct potassium safely; monitor electrolytes and acid–base status.

topics.name: Renal Agenesis and Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney (MCDK)

cases.title: Antenatal oligohydramnios and abnormal kidneys
cases.vignette: A fetus is noted to have severe oligohydramnios on antenatal ultrasound. After delivery, the newborn has respiratory distress and characteristic facial and limb abnormalities. Imaging suggests bilateral renal agenesis. In a separate child, ultrasound identifies a unilateral enlarged kidney containing multiple non-communicating cysts with little or no functioning renal tissue.

questions.stem: What is the major consequence of bilateral renal agenesis?

options.label: D
options.text: Polyhydramnios due to excessive fetal urine

questions.correctAnswerText: Oligohydramnios with pulmonary hypoplasia
questions.initialExplanation: Bilateral renal agenesis prevents normal fetal urine production. Severe oligohydramnios causes pulmonary hypoplasia and the Potter sequence, which is usually fatal because of respiratory failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is not the central mechanism.
- B. Incorrect. Congenital nephrotic syndrome is a protein-losing glomerular disorder, not renal agenesis.
- C. Correct. This is the sequence described: bilateral renal agenesis → reduced fetal urine → oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia and fetal compression.
- D. Incorrect. Reduced fetal urine causes oligohydramnios, not polyhydramnios.
- E. Incorrect. Jaundice is not the defining consequence.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bilateral renal agenesis → severe oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia → Potter sequence.
- Unilateral renal agenesis may be discovered incidentally or during assessment for associated anomalies.
- Bilateral disease is generally incompatible with sustained survival because of pulmonary hypoplasia.

questions.stem: Which finding is part of the Potter sequence described?

options.label: E
options.text: Low-set ears, beaked nose and pulmonary hypoplasia

questions.correctAnswerText: Low-set ears, beaked nose and pulmonary hypoplasia
questions.initialExplanation: Potter sequence results from severe oligohydramnios and fetal compression. Clinical guidance low-set ears, beaked nose, prominent epicanthic folds/downward slanting eyes, limb deformities and pulmonary hypoplasia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Raccoon eyes and opsoclonus are associated with neuroblastoma.
- B. Incorrect. Blue sclera and hearing abnormalities suggest connective-tissue or other inherited disorders, not Potter sequence.
- C. Incorrect. Fixed wide splitting of S2 is associated with ASD.
- D. Incorrect. These are features associated with other congenital syndromes, including Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome.
- E. Correct. These are features listed in the Potter sequence section.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Potter sequence is caused by severe oligohydramnios.
- Pulmonary hypoplasia is the life-limiting feature.
- Recognize the combination of renal absence, low fluid, characteristic facies and limb deformities.

questions.stem: What is the developmental mechanism described for multicystic dysplastic kidney?

options.label: B
options.text: Failure of union between the ureteric bud and nephrogenic mesenchyme

options.label: C
options.text: Obstruction of the renal artery after birth

options.label: D
options.text: Failure of the glomerular basement membrane to form type IV collagen

questions.correctAnswerText: Failure of union between the ureteric bud and nephrogenic mesenchyme
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance MCDK as resulting from failure of union between the ureteric bud and nephrogenic mesenchyme, producing a non-functioning structure with multiple fluid-filled cysts.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Aldosterone excess does not cause MCDK.
- B. Correct. This is the embryological mechanism stated.
- C. Incorrect. Renal artery obstruction is not the developmental mechanism described.
- D. Incorrect. Type IV collagen defects are associated with Alport syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. PDA is a congenital cardiac lesion and unrelated to renal cyst development.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MCDK is a developmental abnormality.
- The affected kidney contains large fluid-filled cysts with little or no functional renal tissue.
- The cystic structure does not communicate normally with the bladder.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the natural history of unilateral MCDK?

options.label: A
options.text: About half may involute by 2 years, and nephrectomy is reserved for selected large or hypertensive cases

options.label: C
options.text: It typically progresses rapidly to bilateral renal failure

options.label: D
options.text: It produces urine normally through the cysts

questions.correctAnswerText: About half may involute by 2 years, and nephrectomy is reserved for selected large or hypertensive cases
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that about half of MCDKs involute by 2 years. Nephrectomy is considered only when the affected kidney remains very large or causes hypertension, which is rare.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the natural history and intervention threshold described.
- B. Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome is not the expected consequence.
- C. Incorrect. Unilateral MCDK does not inevitably cause bilateral renal failure.
- D. Incorrect. The MCDK is described as non-functioning and does not produce urine.
- E. Incorrect. Routine immediate nephrectomy is not recommended.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Unilateral MCDK: often monitored; spontaneous involution may occur.
- Nephrectomy is reserved for selected persistent very large lesions or hypertension.
- Bilateral MCDK may lead to Potter sequence because both kidneys fail to produce urine.

questions.stem: A newborn has bilateral multicystic dysplastic kidneys and severe oligohydramnios. Which mechanism explains the associated respiratory failure?

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced fetal urine production causes oligohydramnios and impaired lung development

options.label: D
options.text: Increased fetal glomerular filtration causes bronchospasm

options.label: E
options.text: Excess renal erythropoietin causes pulmonary oedema

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced fetal urine production causes oligohydramnios and impaired lung development
questions.initialExplanation: Bilateral non-functioning kidneys markedly reduce fetal urine output. Severe oligohydramnios impairs lung development, causing pulmonary hypoplasia and respiratory failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. VUR does not cause neonatal asthma or Potter sequence.
- B. Correct. This is the mechanism described for bilateral renal agenesis or bilateral MCDK in the Potter sequence.
- C. Incorrect. Hypercalciuria is associated with renal stones/nephrocalcinosis, not this fetal lung-development mechanism.
- D. Incorrect. Increased GFR is not the mechanism; fetal urine production is reduced.
- E. Incorrect. Erythropoietin does not cause the pulmonary hypoplasia described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bilateral non-functioning renal tissue → low fetal urine → oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia.
- The pulmonary consequence, rather than the cysts themselves, explains the life-threatening respiratory presentation.

cases.title: An antenatal renal abnormality
cases.vignette: A newborn is delivered after a pregnancy complicated by severe oligohydramnios. The baby has respiratory distress and characteristic Potter-like facial features. Antenatal imaging had suggested absent renal structures bilaterally. In a separate child seen in clinic, ultrasound shows a unilateral cluster of large non-communicating renal cysts with little recognizable renal tissue.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains the respiratory problem in the newborn described in the first vignette?

options.label: A
options.text: Severe oligohydramnios leading to pulmonary hypoplasia

options.label: B
options.text: Excess fetal urine production causing pulmonary overgrowth

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe oligohydramnios leading to pulmonary hypoplasia
questions.initialExplanation: Bilateral renal agenesis markedly reduces fetal urine production. The resulting oligohydramnios is associated with pulmonary hypoplasia and Potter sequence.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Reduced fetal urine leads to severe oligohydramnios, impaired lung development and respiratory failure.
- B. Incorrect. The problem is reduced fetal urine, not excess urine.
- C. Incorrect. Urethral inflammation does not explain the antenatal sequence.
- D. Incorrect. Increased surfactant production is not the mechanism described.
- E. Incorrect. Congenital NS causes heavy protein loss and oedema, not this classic Potter sequence.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bilateral renal agenesis: severe oligohydramnios, Potter facies and pulmonary hypoplasia.
- Clinical guidance bilateral renal agenesis with Potter sequence as usually fatal because of pulmonary hypoplasia.

questions.stem: The second child's ultrasound shows large fluid-filled cysts, absent normal renal parenchyma and no connection with the bladder. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.correctAnswerText: Multicystic dysplastic kidney
questions.initialExplanation: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is described as a non-functioning cystic structure with large fluid-filled cysts, little or no normal renal tissue and no communication with the bladder.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pyelonephritis is an infection and does not produce this congenital cystic architecture.
- B. Incorrect. VUR is retrograde urine flow from the bladder to the ureter/renal pelvis.
- C. Correct. The ultrasound description matches MCDK.
- D. Incorrect. Minimal-change disease is a glomerular disorder causing proteinuria.
- E. Incorrect. RTA is a tubular acid–base disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Many unilateral MCDKs involute during early childhood.
- Nephrectomy is generally reserved for a kidney that remains very large or causes hypertension; this is uncommon.

questions.stem: A newborn has unilateral absence of a kidney on imaging but is otherwise clinically well. Which statement best reflects the description?

options.label: A
options.text: each case immediately causes fatal pulmonary hypoplasia

options.label: B
options.text: The finding may be discovered incidentally or during evaluation for another anomaly

options.label: C
options.text: It is diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome

options.label: E
options.text: It is the same lesion as bilateral multicystic dysplastic kidneys

questions.correctAnswerText: The finding may be discovered incidentally or during evaluation for another anomaly
questions.initialExplanation: Unilateral renal agenesis may be asymptomatic and discovered incidentally or during evaluation for associated anomalies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The severe Potter sequence described is associated with bilateral renal agenesis.
- B. Correct. This is the stated presentation of unilateral agenesis.
- C. Incorrect. Agenesis is a structural congenital anomaly, not a protein-losing glomerular syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. A well child with a solitary functioning kidney does not automatically require dialysis.
- E. Incorrect. MCDK is a cystic dysplastic structure, whereas agenesis is absence of the kidney.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Distinguish unilateral from bilateral renal agenesis.
- Bilateral disease has a much more severe fetal and neonatal consequence.

topics.name: Polycystic Kidney Disease: ARPKD and ADPKD

cases.title: Bilateral renal enlargement in childhood
cases.vignette: A newborn has a history of antenatal oligohydramnios. Examination reveals bilateral enlarged kidneys, respiratory distress and hypertension. Later in childhood, the family is counselled about associated liver disease and possible chronic renal impairment. Another adolescent has hypertension and a family history of renal cysts; imaging demonstrates bilateral cystic kidneys.

questions.stem: Which inheritance pattern is associated with infantile polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD)?
questions.correctAnswerText: Autosomal recessive
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance distinguishes infantile ARPKD, which is autosomal recessive, from adult-type ADPKD, which is autosomal dominant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Y-linked inheritance is not described.
- B. Incorrect. Mitochondrial inheritance is not described.
- C. Incorrect. Autosomal dominant inheritance is associated with ADPKD.
- D. Correct. ARPKD is autosomal recessive.
- E. Incorrect. X-linked inheritance is not the pattern described for ARPKD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ARPKD = autosomal recessive, typically presents in infancy.
- ADPKD = autosomal dominant, often presents later but may be detected in childhood.
- Family history and imaging help distinguish inherited cystic kidney disorders.

questions.stem: Which combination is most characteristic of infantile ARPKD?

options.label: A
options.text: Bilateral enlarged kidneys, hypertension and respiratory distress

options.label: C
options.text: Small kidneys, hypokalaemic alkalosis and hypercalciuria

options.label: D
options.text: Unilateral renal cyst with normal BP

options.label: E
options.text: Recurrent haematuria during URTI and hearing loss

questions.correctAnswerText: Bilateral enlarged kidneys, hypertension and respiratory distress
questions.initialExplanation: ARPKD causes diffuse bilateral renal enlargement. Antenatal oligohydramnios may contribute to pulmonary hypoplasia and respiratory distress; hypertension and renal dysfunction may also occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the typical presentation listed.
- B. Incorrect. These are congenital genitourinary conditions, not ARPKD.
- C. Incorrect. This suggests a salt-wasting tubulopathy such as Bartter syndrome.
- D. Incorrect. Unilateral isolated cystic disease is more consistent with another renal anomaly such as MCDK.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests Alport syndrome or IgA nephropathy depending on the hearing and timing features.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ARPKD: bilateral enlarged kidneys, hypertension, respiratory distress and possible CRF.
- Respiratory problems may relate to pulmonary hypoplasia after oligohydramnios.
- Congenital hepatic periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension may appear later.

questions.stem: Which extra-renal association is particularly important in ARPKD?

options.label: A
options.text: Congenital hepatic periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension

questions.correctAnswerText: Congenital hepatic periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that ARPKD is commonly associated with congenital hepatic periportal fibrosis, which may lead to liver cirrhosis or portal hypertension later in childhood.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the extra-renal association highlighted.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests ASD.
- C. Incorrect. TOF is a congenital cardiac lesion and is not the characteristic ARPKD association.
- D. Incorrect. These are associated with Alport syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. These are features of neuroblastoma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ARPKD affects kidneys and liver.
- Consider portal hypertension and hepatic involvement during long-term follow-up.
- Management may require renal and liver support depending on severity.

questions.stem: Which statement about ADPKD in childhood is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: It not usually progresses to CKD

options.label: C
options.text: It is autosomal dominant and may present with childhood hypertension

options.label: D
options.text: It is autosomal recessive and typically causes fatal neonatal pulmonary hypoplasia

questions.correctAnswerText: It is autosomal dominant and may present with childhood hypertension
questions.initialExplanation: ADPKD is autosomal dominant. Clinical guidance that childhood presentations may include hypertension, while progressive CKD more commonly becomes important later in life.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ADPKD is typically bilateral.
- B. Incorrect. ADPKD may progress to CKD, often later in adulthood.
- C. Correct. This matches the inheritance and childhood presentation.
- D. Incorrect. This describes a severe fetal/neonatal pattern more consistent with ARPKD, not ADPKD.
- E. Incorrect. Clinical guidance liver and pancreatic cysts, cerebral aneurysms/haemorrhage and mitral valve prolapse.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ADPKD = autosomal dominant, bilateral cystic kidneys.
- Childhood clue: hypertension.
- Extra-renal associations: liver/pancreatic cysts, cerebral aneurysms/haemorrhage and mitral valve prolapse.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes ARPKD from ADPKD based on age and associated findings?

options.label: A
options.text: ARPKD is usually infantile with enlarged kidneys/liver fibrosis; ADPKD presents later and may cause aneurysms

options.label: B
options.text: ARPKD is typically unilateral; ADPKD is typically neonatal and fatal

options.label: D
options.text: Both are caused by type IV collagen defects

questions.correctAnswerText: ARPKD is usually infantile with enlarged kidneys/liver fibrosis; ADPKD presents later and may cause aneurysms
questions.initialExplanation: ARPKD presents earlier and has important liver associations. ADPKD may be detected in childhood with hypertension but is often progressive later and has extra-renal cystic and vascular associations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This captures the major distinctions in the supplied clinical guidance.
- B. Incorrect. Both are generally bilateral; the age pattern is reversed.
- C. Incorrect. ARPKD is not limited to VUR.
- D. Incorrect. Type IV collagen defects cause Alport syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. Hypertension is a key possible childhood manifestation of ADPKD.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ARPKD: infancy, bilateral enlarged kidneys, pulmonary hypoplasia risk, hepatic fibrosis/portal hypertension.
- ADPKD: AD inheritance, childhood hypertension possible, liver/pancreatic cysts and cerebral aneurysm associations.
- Monitor BP and renal function.

questions.stem: Which management options are specifically mentioned for severe ARPKD?

options.label: C
options.text: Control hypertension, dialysis or renal transplantation, and liver support

questions.correctAnswerText: Control hypertension, dialysis or renal transplantation, and liver support
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance management focused on BP control, renal replacement therapy when needed and support for hepatic disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ureteric reimplantation treats selected VUR, not polycystic kidney disease.
- B. Incorrect. These are treatments for selected nocturnal enuresis cases.
- C. Correct. These are the options listed in the ARPKD section.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not treat the underlying inherited cystic renal disease.
- E. Incorrect. Routine nephrectomy is not the treatment described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ARPKD treatment is supportive and organ-directed.
- Control hypertension and monitor renal function.
- Dialysis/transplantation and liver support may be required in severe disease.

cases.title: An antenatal renal abnormality
cases.vignette: A newborn is delivered after a pregnancy complicated by severe oligohydramnios. The baby has respiratory distress and characteristic Potter-like facial features. Antenatal imaging had suggested absent renal structures bilaterally. In a separate child seen in clinic, ultrasound shows a unilateral cluster of large non-communicating renal cysts with little recognizable renal tissue.

questions.stem: A newborn has bilaterally enlarged kidneys, hypertension and respiratory distress. Later follow-up identifies hepatic periportal fibrosis with portal hypertension. Which condition is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Adult-type autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease
questions.initialExplanation: The infantile autosomal recessive form is associated with bilateral enlarged kidneys and congenital hepatic periportal fibrosis. Severe disease may cause respiratory distress due to pulmonary hypoplasia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ADPKD more commonly presents later and is associated with liver/pancreatic cysts and other adult-type extrarenal features.
- B. Correct. The neonatal presentation and hepatic association are characteristic of ARPKD.
- C. Incorrect. Unilateral agenesis does not cause bilateral renal enlargement.
- D. Incorrect. Orthostatic proteinuria does not cause enlarged kidneys or portal hypertension.
- E. Incorrect. PUV causes bladder outlet obstruction in boys and may produce bilateral hydronephrosis, but does not explain the hepatic association.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ARPKD: antenatal oligohydramnios may be present; postnatal findings include bilateral renal enlargement, hypertension and respiratory distress.
- Congenital hepatic periportal fibrosis may lead to cirrhosis and portal hypertension.

questions.stem: A teenager with a family history of cystic kidney disease is found to have renal cysts. The clinician also asks about hepatic and pancreatic cysts and intracranial aneurysm risk. Which disorder is being considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance ADPKD as associated with cysts in the liver and pancreas, cerebral aneurysms and mitral valve prolapse.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. MCDK is a usually unilateral, non-functioning cystic renal structure.
- B. Incorrect. ARPKD is the infantile form emphasized with congenital hepatic periportal fibrosis and early bilateral renal enlargement.
- C. Incorrect. Renal agenesis means absence of renal tissue, not multiple cysts.
- D. Correct. The extrarenal features listed point toward ADPKD.
- E. Incorrect. Fanconi syndrome is a proximal tubular disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ADPKD is usually recognized later than the severe infantile ARPKD pattern.
- Family history and extrarenal cystic/vascular associations are useful clues.

questions.stem: Which feature most strongly separates the infantile ARPKD pattern from the ADPKD pattern described?

options.label: A
options.text: Both conditions are defined by a single non-functioning unilateral cystic kidney

options.label: B
options.text: ADPKD is typically associated with Potter sequence at birth

options.label: C
options.text: ARPKD is associated with congenital hepatic periportal fibrosis and early bilateral renal enlargement

options.label: D
options.text: ARPKD is caused by glomerular immune-complex deposition

options.label: E
options.text: ADPKD causes posterior urethral obstruction in male infants

questions.correctAnswerText: ARPKD is associated with congenital hepatic periportal fibrosis and early bilateral renal enlargement
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance emphasizes the infantile presentation of ARPKD, with bilateral enlarged kidneys and congenital hepatic periportal fibrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A single non-functioning cystic kidney describes MCDK more closely.
- B. Incorrect. Potter sequence is associated with severe fetal oligohydramnios, not a defining feature of ADPKD.
- C. Correct. This is the key distinction emphasized.
- D. Incorrect. Immune-complex deposition is a glomerular mechanism, not the cause of ARPKD.
- E. Incorrect. ADPKD does not cause congenital urethral valve obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ARPKD: infantile, bilateral renal enlargement, congenital hepatic fibrosis.
- ADPKD: later presentation and extrarenal cysts/vascular associations.

cases.title: An abnormal urethral opening in a newborn boy
cases.vignette: A newborn boy is examined before circumcision. The external urethral meatus is located on the ventral surface of the penis rather than at the tip of the glans. The clinician explains the possible anatomical types and why foreskin should be preserved before urological assessment.

questions.stem: What is the definition of hypospadias?

options.label: A
options.text: Fluid accumulation in the tunica vaginalis

options.label: B
options.text: Congenital obstruction of the posterior urethra

options.label: D
options.text: Urethral meatus on the dorsal surface of the penis

options.label: E
options.text: Urethral meatus abnormally placed on the ventral surface of the penis

questions.correctAnswerText: Urethral meatus abnormally placed on the ventral surface of the penis
questions.initialExplanation: Hypospadias is a congenital abnormality in which the external urethral opening is located on the ventral side of the penis rather than at the normal position at the tip of the glans.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes hydrocele.
- B. Incorrect. This describes posterior urethral valves.
- C. Incorrect. This describes undescended testis.
- D. Incorrect. A dorsal meatal position is not the definition of hypospadias.
- E. Correct. This is the definition given.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hypospadias = ventral ectopic urethral meatus.
- Examine the position of the meatus before circumcision.
- Consider associated inguinal hernia and undescended testis.

questions.stem: Which type of hypospadias is described as the most common?
questions.correctAnswerText: Glandular
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance the glandular type, with the meatus on the glans, as the most common form. Perineal hypospadias is described as rare but severe.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urethral agenesis is not a hypospadias type.
- B. Incorrect. Penoscrotal is a more proximal form and is not the commonest.
- C. Correct. Glandular hypospadias is listed as the commonest type.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance identifies glandular as the most common.
- E. Incorrect. Perineal is rare and severe.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Glandular = most common.
- Perineal = rare but severe.
- Types are classified by the location of the ectopic meatus.

questions.stem: Why should an infant with hypospadias not undergo circumcision before urological assessment?

options.label: E
options.text: Foreskin may be required for surgical reconstruction

questions.correctAnswerText: Foreskin may be required for surgical reconstruction
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance specifically warns against circumcision in infants with hypospadias because preputial tissue may be required for later urethral reconstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Circumcision does not cause VUR.
- B. Incorrect. Circumcision does not cause renal agenesis.
- C. Incorrect. It does not affect renal urine production.
- D. Incorrect. It has no role in testicular descent.
- E. Correct. Preserving tissue may assist later urethral reconstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Do not circumcise before urological assessment.
- The foreskin may be required for repair.
- clinical guidance gives surgical correction at approximately 1–2 years.

questions.stem: Which associated findings are mentioned with hypospadias?
questions.correctAnswerText: Inguinal hernia and undescended testes
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance inguinal hernia and undescended testes as rare associations of hypospadias.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are features in the differential of pediatric hypertension.
- B. Incorrect. These are associated with ADPKD.
- C. Incorrect. These are associated with Alport syndrome.
- D. Correct. Both are specifically mentioned.
- E. Incorrect. These are features associated with neuroblastoma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Look for associated undescended testes and inguinal hernia.
- Avoid circumcision until surgical planning is complete.
- Refer for urological assessment.

questions.stem: At what approximate age does the supplied clinical guidance recommend surgical correction of hypospadias?

options.label: D
options.text: No surgical correction is ever required

options.label: E
options.text: Immediately at birth in typical presentations

questions.correctAnswerText: 1–2 years
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance gives an approximate surgical correction age of 1–2 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Repair is not routinely delayed until puberty.
- B. Correct. This is the timing stated in the supplied standard guidance.
- C. Incorrect. This is later than the age specified.
- D. Incorrect. Surgical correction is the treatment described.
- E. Incorrect. clinical guidance does not recommend routine immediate neonatal repair.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Refer early and preserve foreskin.
- clinical guidance gives repair at 1–2 years.
- Exact timing and technique depend on anatomical severity and specialist assessment.

cases.title: Findings during a newborn examination
cases.vignette: During a newborn examination, a boy is found to have a urethral opening on the ventral surface of the penis. The parents request circumcision. The same examination identifies a painless, transilluminating scrotal swelling in another infant, while a third child has an empty hemiscrotum with a palpable inguinal testis.

questions.stem: Why should circumcision be deferred in the newborn with the ventrally displaced urethral opening?

options.label: B
options.text: The foreskin may be needed for later surgical reconstruction

options.label: C
options.text: The condition typically resolves after circumcision

options.label: E
options.text: Circumcision is the definitive treatment for hypospadias

questions.correctAnswerText: The foreskin may be needed for later surgical reconstruction
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance specifically advises that infants with hypospadias should not be circumcised because preputial tissue may be required for reconstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Circumcision does not cause PUV.
- B. Correct. Preserving foreskin tissue may assist later repair.
- C. Incorrect. Circumcision does not correct the abnormal meatal position.
- D. Incorrect. There is no causal relationship with renal agenesis.
- E. Incorrect. Surgical correction of the urethral position is the treatment; circumcision is not the repair.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hypospadias: urethral meatus opens on the ventral side of the penis.
- Clinical guidance surgical correction around 1–2 years of age.

cases.title: A painless translucent scrotal swelling
cases.vignette: A 4-month-old boy is found to have a unilateral painless scrotal swelling during routine examination. The swelling transilluminates. There are no signs of acute pain or systemic illness. The parents ask whether surgery is immediately required.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hydrocele
questions.initialExplanation: Hydrocele is fluid accumulation in the tunica vaginalis and commonly produces a painless scrotal swelling with positive transillumination.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Testicular tumour — Incorrect. A solid mass does not typically transilluminate like fluid.
- B. Hydrocele — Correct. The clinical picture and positive transillumination support fluid within the tunica vaginalis.
- C. Incarcerated hernia — Incorrect. It may be painful or irreducible and is not identified by simple transillumination.
- D. Epididymitis — Incorrect. It usually causes pain and inflammatory features.
- E. Testicular torsion — Incorrect. Torsion typically causes acute pain and requires urgent assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hydrocele: fluid in the tunica vaginalis.
- Often painless; transillumination may be positive.
- Many cases resolve spontaneously during infancy.

questions.stem: Which finding supports hydrocele rather than a solid testicular mass?

options.label: B
options.text: Severe acute pain and a high-riding testis

questions.correctAnswerText: Positive transillumination
questions.initialExplanation: Fluid in the tunica vaginalis allows light to pass through the swelling, producing positive transillumination.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A solid mass generally does not transilluminate like a hydrocele.
- B. Incorrect. These findings raise concern for testicular torsion.
- C. Correct. A positive transillumination test supports a fluid-filled swelling.
- D. Incorrect. An empty scrotum suggests undescended testis or other causes.
- E. Incorrect. Fever and tenderness suggest an inflammatory or infective process.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hydrocele: painless, fluid-filled, often transilluminates.
- Acute painful scrotum is not typical of a simple hydrocele and requires urgent evaluation for torsion or infection.
- Examine the groin and testis as part of the assessment.

questions.stem: What is the expected natural history of most infant hydroceles?

options.label: D
options.text: most require surgery in the neonatal period

questions.correctAnswerText: Most resolve by 12 months
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that most hydroceles resolve spontaneously by 12 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hydrocele is not a precursor to testicular tumour.
- B. Correct. This is the natural history described.
- C. Incorrect. Many resolve spontaneously.
- D. Incorrect. Immediate surgery is not required in every infant.
- E. Incorrect. Hydrocele does not cause renal failure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Observe most uncomplicated infant hydroceles.
- Persistent hydrocele beyond 18–24 months may require repair.
- Reassess sooner if pain, irreducibility or other concerning features develop.

questions.stem: An otherwise well child still has a hydrocele at 20 months. Which management is most consistent with clinical guidance?

options.label: B
options.text: Consider surgical repair because persistence beyond 18–24 months may require intervention

questions.correctAnswerText: Consider surgical repair because persistence beyond 18–24 months may require intervention
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that most hydroceles resolve by 12 months and persistent cases beyond 18–24 months may need repair.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Persistent swelling requires reassessment and possible surgical treatment.
- B. Correct. This is the threshold described in the supplied material.
- C. Incorrect. Steroids do not correct a persistent hydrocele.
- D. Incorrect. Dialysis is unrelated.
- E. Incorrect. Nephrectomy treats selected renal conditions, not hydrocele.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most infant hydroceles resolve by 12 months.
- Persistence beyond 18–24 months may require repair.
- Always distinguish uncomplicated hydrocele from hernia, torsion, infection and tumour.

cases.title: Findings during a newborn examination
cases.vignette: During a newborn examination, a boy is found to have a urethral opening on the ventral surface of the penis. The parents request circumcision. The same examination identifies a painless, transilluminating scrotal swelling in another infant, while a third child has an empty hemiscrotum with a palpable inguinal testis.

questions.stem: A painless scrotal swelling transilluminates and is thought to be a hydrocele. Which plan best matches the natural history described?

options.label: C
options.text: Observation initially, with repair considered if it persists beyond 18–24 months

options.label: D
options.text: Antibiotics for six months in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Observation initially, with repair considered if it persists beyond 18–24 months
questions.initialExplanation: Most infant hydroceles resolve spontaneously by 12 months. clinical guidance suggests repair if a hydrocele persists beyond approximately 18–24 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Orchiectomy is not the treatment for a simple hydrocele.
- B. Incorrect. Chemotherapy has no role in uncomplicated hydrocele.
- C. Correct. This matches the observation and persistence thresholds.
- D. Incorrect. A simple hydrocele is fluid in the tunica vaginalis, not a bacterial infection.
- E. Incorrect. Examination is needed to distinguish hydrocele from hernia and other scrotal causes.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hydrocele: fluid in the tunica vaginalis, often painless and transilluminating.
- Most resolve by 12 months; persistent cases may need repair after 18–24 months.

cases.title: An empty hemiscrotum in a newborn
cases.vignette: A term male newborn is examined and the right testis cannot be felt in the scrotum. The examiner can feel a testis in the inguinal canal and attempts to bring it down into the scrotum. The family asks whether the condition can be observed and what complications may occur if it is not corrected.

questions.stem: Which statement about undescended testis is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It occurs in approximately 5% of term newborns and is more common in preterm infants

options.label: B
options.text: It is a cause of nephrotic syndrome

options.label: C
options.text: It is more common in term than preterm infants

questions.correctAnswerText: It occurs in approximately 5% of term newborns and is more common in preterm infants
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance gives an approximate prevalence of 5% in term newborns and notes that undescended testes are more common in preterm infants.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the epidemiology given.
- B. Incorrect. Undescended testis is a genital developmental condition, not a glomerular disease.
- C. Incorrect. clinical guidance specifically states that it is more common in preterm infants.
- D. Incorrect. It may be unilateral or bilateral.
- E. Incorrect. Diagnosis should ideally be made during newborn and infant examination.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Examine testicular position during newborn and infant assessments.
- More common in preterm infants.
- Early recognition allows timely orchidopexy and assessment for associated conditions.

questions.stem: Which examination manoeuvre is used to help distinguish a retractile testis from a truly undescended testis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Milking test
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance refers to a milking test to help distinguish a retractile testis from an undescended testis during examination.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Valsalva may be relevant to other examinations but is not the manoeuvre specified.
- B. Incorrect. Transillumination is used in assessment of hydrocele.
- C. Incorrect. Renal punch tenderness assesses renal angle tenderness, not testicular position.
- D. Incorrect. Ballottement is a renal examination manoeuvre, not the testicular descent test described.
- E. Correct. This is the examination method named in the supplied material.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Examine the groin and scrotum carefully.
- Distinguish an undescended testis from a retractile testis.
- A retractile testis generally does not require surgery.

questions.stem: A testis is undescended but palpable in the inguinal canal. Which treatment is described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Orchidopexy
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that a palpable undescended testis requires orchidopexy to bring and fix the testis in the scrotum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Orchidopexy is the procedure described.
- B. Incorrect. Removal is not the routine management of an undescended testis.
- C. Incorrect. Nephrectomy removes a kidney and is unrelated.
- D. Incorrect. Ureteric reimplantation is used for selected severe VUR.
- E. Incorrect. Hydrocelectomy treats a persistent hydrocele.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Palpable undescended testis → orchidopexy.
- clinical guidance gives an approximate age of 1 year.
- Early correction is intended to reduce later complications and facilitate examination.

questions.stem: What is the next step when an undescended testis is impalpable?

options.label: B
options.text: Assume the testis is normal and discharge

options.label: C
options.text: Consider laparoscopy to identify whether a testis is present

questions.correctAnswerText: Consider laparoscopy to identify whether a testis is present
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that an impalpable undescended testis may require laparoscopy to determine whether the testis is present and locate it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Indomethacin is used in selected PDA cases, not cryptorchidism.
- B. Incorrect. An impalpable testis requires further evaluation.
- C. Correct. Laparoscopy may identify an intra-abdominal testis or confirm absence.
- D. Incorrect. Dialysis is unrelated.
- E. Incorrect. Transillumination is used for fluid-filled scrotal swellings, not to locate an impalpable testis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Palpable → orchidopexy.
- Impalpable → consider laparoscopy.
- Bilateral impalpable testes require urgent assessment, including karyotype as described.

questions.stem: A newborn has bilateral impalpable testes. Which investigation is specifically emphasized as urgent?
questions.correctAnswerText: Karyotype
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that bilateral impalpable testes require urgent karyotype assessment. This is important because disorders of sex development may need to be excluded.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the specific urgent investigation mentioned.
- B. Incorrect. Renal biopsy is not the initial test for bilateral impalpable testes.
- C. Incorrect. MCUG assesses VUR and urethral anatomy.
- D. Incorrect. DMSA assesses renal cortical scarring.
- E. Incorrect. VMA/HVA are used in neuroblastoma assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bilateral impalpable testes → urgent karyotype.
- Assess genital anatomy and associated findings carefully.
- Early specialist referral is essential.

questions.stem: Which group of complications is associated with undescended testes?
questions.correctAnswerText: Torsion, infertility and malignancy
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies increased risks of testicular torsion, infertility and malignancy in undescended testes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are renal conditions and are not complications of cryptorchidism.
- B. Incorrect. These are electrolyte/acid-base complications, not testicular complications.
- C. Incorrect. These may occur in acute nephritic illness.
- D. Correct. These are the three complications listed.
- E. Incorrect. These are associated with severe fetal renal abnormalities and oligohydramnios.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Undescended testis increases risk of torsion, infertility and malignancy.
- Orchidopexy is recommended around 1 year in the supplied clinical guidance.
- Retractile testes usually do not require surgery.

questions.stem: A child has an empty scrotum. The testis can be felt below the external inguinal ring but outside the scrotum. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ectopic testis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance defines ectopic testis as a testis that is palpated below the external inguinal ring but outside the scrotum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the definition.
- B. Incorrect. Hydrocele is fluid around the testis and often transilluminates.
- C. Incorrect. Torsion typically presents with acute pain and swelling.
- D. Incorrect. A tumour is a mass lesion, not a displaced testis.
- E. Incorrect. A retractile testis can be brought into the scrotum and usually remains there temporarily.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Empty scrotum differential: undescended, ectopic or retractile testis, agenesis and previous orchiectomy.
- Examine both groins and scrotal contents.
- Distinguishing retractile from true undescended testis guides management.

cases.title: Findings during a newborn examination
cases.vignette: During a newborn examination, a boy is found to have a urethral opening on the ventral surface of the penis. The parents request circumcision. The same examination identifies a painless, transilluminating scrotal swelling in another infant, while a third child has an empty hemiscrotum with a palpable inguinal testis.

questions.stem: A 1-year-old boy still has an undescended palpable testis. Which intervention is described, and what additional step is urgent if both testes are impalpable?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassurance; no further assessment is ever required

options.label: B
options.text: Hydrocele repair; no genetic assessment is needed

options.label: D
options.text: Orchidopexy; urgent karyotype if both testes are impalpable

questions.correctAnswerText: Orchidopexy; urgent karyotype if both testes are impalpable
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance orchidopexy for an undescended testis, ideally around one year. Bilateral impalpable testes require urgent karyotyping.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Persistent undescended testes need assessment and treatment because of later risks.
- B. Incorrect. Hydrocele repair does not correct an undescended testis.
- C. Incorrect. Circumcision is unrelated to testicular position.
- D. Correct. Both the treatment and the urgent investigation are stated.
- E. Incorrect. Nephrectomy and renal biopsy do not address this genital finding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Complications of undescended testes include torsion, infertility and malignancy.
- If impalpable, laparoscopy may be required to identify whether a testis is present.

topics.name: Posterior Urethral Valves (PUV) and Prune-Belly Syndrome

cases.title: A male infant with poor urinary stream and bilateral hydronephrosis
cases.vignette: A 2-month-old boy has a poor urinary stream, dribbling and recurrent urinary tract infection. Antenatal ultrasound had shown a distended bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis. Current imaging suggests congenital obstruction of the posterior urethra. The clinician is concerned about reflux, pyelonephritis and progressive renal damage.

questions.stem: In which patients does posterior urethral valve obstruction occur?
questions.correctAnswerText: Male patients
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that posterior urethral valves are a congenital obstructive lesion occurring only in males.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. PUV is a congenital urethral obstruction in boys.
- B. Incorrect. It is not equally distributed between sexes.
- C. Incorrect. It is not a lesion of premature girls.
- D. Incorrect. Many cases are identified antenatally or in infancy.
- E. Incorrect. PUV does not occur in females according to the supplied clinical guidance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PUV: congenital obstructing mucosal fold/membrane in the posterior urethra.
- Occurs in boys.
- Antenatal ultrasound can detect bladder and upper urinary tract abnormalities.

questions.stem: Which clinical presentation is most suggestive of PUV in an infant?

options.label: C
options.text: Poor urinary stream, dribbling and recurrent UTI

options.label: D
options.text: Cola-coloured urine two weeks after sore throat

questions.correctAnswerText: Poor urinary stream, dribbling and recurrent UTI
questions.initialExplanation: PUV obstructs bladder outflow and may cause poor stream, dribbling, urinary infection and bilateral hydronephrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests hydrocele.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests IgA nephropathy.
- C. Correct. These symptoms are directly listed in the PUV section.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests PSGN.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests nephrotic syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Poor urinary stream and dribbling in a boy should raise concern for obstruction.
- PUV may be detected antenatally.
- Recurrent UTI and bilateral hydronephrosis are important clues.

questions.stem: If PUV is not treated early, which sequence of complications is described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bilateral VUR → hydronephrosis/pyelonephritis → CKD
questions.initialExplanation: Persistent bladder outlet obstruction can increase pressure, promote reflux and cause upper tract dilatation, infection and progressive renal damage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the progression described.
- B. Incorrect. These are cardiac and renal complications unrelated to PUV.
- C. Incorrect. These conditions are unrelated to the obstructive mechanism.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the pathophysiological sequence of PUV.
- E. Incorrect. Alport syndrome is an inherited collagen disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Untreated PUV can cause bilateral reflux, hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis and CKD.
- Early diagnosis and decompression are important to preserve renal function.
- Monitor renal function and urinary tract anatomy after treatment.

questions.stem: Which treatment is described for PUV?

options.label: C
options.text: Endoscopic valve ablation, with urinary diversion when needed

questions.correctAnswerText: Endoscopic valve ablation, with urinary diversion when needed
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance endoscopic valve ablation as the main treatment, with urinary diversion considered in selected cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Routine nephrectomy is not the treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Indomethacin promotes PDA closure and does not treat urethral obstruction.
- C. Correct. This is the management described.
- D. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected enuresis or water-balance problems.
- E. Incorrect. Circumcision does not relieve posterior urethral obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PUV requires urological intervention to relieve the obstruction.
- Endoscopic valve ablation is described.
- Urinary diversion may be required in selected cases.
- Long-term follow-up is needed because renal damage may persist.

questions.stem: Prune-belly syndrome is also known as:
questions.correctAnswerText: Absent musculature syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance calls prune-belly syndrome “absent musculature syndrome” because of deficient abdominal wall musculature, giving the abdomen a wrinkled appearance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Potter sequence results from severe oligohydramnios.
- B. Correct. This is the alternate name stated.
- C. Incorrect. Minimal change syndrome is a glomerular disease.
- D. Incorrect. Fanconi syndrome is generalized proximal tubular dysfunction.
- E. Incorrect. Alport syndrome is hereditary nephritis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prune-belly = absent musculature syndrome.
- The abdominal wall appears wrinkled.
- It is associated with urinary tract dilatation and cryptorchidism.

questions.stem: Which combination is associated with prune-belly syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Bilateral renal cysts and hepatic periportal fibrosis

options.label: C
options.text: Wrinkled abdominal wall, large bladder, dilated ureters and cryptorchidism

options.label: D
options.text: Small bladder, short ureters and hydrocele

questions.correctAnswerText: Wrinkled abdominal wall, large bladder, dilated ureters and cryptorchidism
questions.initialExplanation: Prune-belly syndrome is characterized by deficient abdominal wall musculature, a large bladder, dilated ureters and undescended testes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests ARPKD.
- B. Incorrect. These are features of Alport syndrome.
- C. Correct. This is the combination listed.
- D. Incorrect. Clinical guidance a large bladder and dilated ureters.
- E. Incorrect. This is the clinical tetrad of IgA vasculitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prune-belly: absent abdominal musculature, large bladder, dilated ureters and cryptorchidism.
- Consider associated urinary tract obstruction and infection.
- Assess renal function and testicular position.

questions.stem: A male infant has PUV, recurrent UTI and bilateral hydronephrosis. Which long-term issue must be monitored even after valve ablation?

options.label: A
options.text: Chronic kidney disease and renal function

options.label: C
options.text: Hearing loss from type IV collagen disease in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Development of a patent ductus arteriosus

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic kidney disease and renal function
questions.initialExplanation: Even after relief of the obstruction, renal dysplasia or established damage may persist. clinical guidance warns that untreated or late-treated PUV may progress to CKD, so renal function requires follow-up.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Renal function and CKD risk are important long-term concerns.
- B. Incorrect. VSD is not caused by PUV.
- C. Incorrect. Hearing loss is associated with Alport syndrome, not an inevitable PUV consequence.
- D. Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism is not a PUV complication.
- E. Incorrect. PDA is a congenital cardiac lesion unrelated to PUV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Relieve obstruction early.
- Continue monitoring renal function, BP, infection and upper tract dilatation.
- Established renal dysplasia or scarring may persist after surgery.

cases.title: A male infant with a weak urinary stream
cases.vignette: A 2-month-old boy has a persistently poor urinary stream, dribbling and recurrent urinary infection. Ultrasound demonstrates a large bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis. The antenatal scan had also suggested urinary tract dilatation.

questions.stem: Which congenital lesion best explains the combination of sex, weak urinary stream and bilateral upper-tract dilatation?

options.label: A
options.text: Vesicoureteric reflux in a female infant

questions.correctAnswerText: Posterior urethral valves
questions.initialExplanation: Posterior urethral valves are a congenital obstructive lesion occurring only in boys. They obstruct urine flow from the bladder and may cause bilateral hydronephrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. VUR may cause recurrent UTI and renal damage but does not explain the characteristic congenital urethral obstruction in a male infant.
- B. Incorrect. Hypospadias is an abnormally placed urethral meatus on the ventral penis.
- C. Incorrect. Unilateral agenesis does not produce bilateral hydronephrosis from bladder outlet obstruction.
- D. Correct. The age, sex, weak stream and bilateral dilatation are classic clues.
- E. Incorrect. Minimal-change nephropathy causes heavy proteinuria and oedema.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PUV occurs only in male infants.
- It can lead to VUR, hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis and chronic kidney disease if not treated early.

questions.stem: After initial stabilization and assessment, which treatment is described as the definitive intervention for posterior urethral valves?
questions.correctAnswerText: Endoscopic valve ablation
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance endoscopic valve ablation as the treatment for PUV; urinary diversion may be needed in selected cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Endoscopic ablation relieves the congenital urethral obstruction.
- B. Incorrect. Steroids do not correct a mechanical outlet obstruction.
- C. Incorrect. Nephrectomy is not the routine definitive treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Circumcision does not remove the obstructing posterior urethral membrane.
- E. Incorrect. This is not a treatment for a structural urinary obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early recognition and relief of obstruction help limit renal damage.
- Monitor for hydronephrosis, VUR, infection and CKD.

cases.title: An abdominal mass in a young child
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child is brought after a caregiver notices an abdominal swelling while bathing. The child is otherwise relatively well, but blood pressure is elevated and urine microscopy shows painless haematuria. Imaging identifies a unilateral renal mass. The differential diagnosis includes Wilms tumour and neuroblastoma. A second child has an irregular abdominal mass that crosses the midline, weight loss, periorbital bruising and elevated urinary catecholamine metabolites.

questions.stem: Wilms tumour arises from which tissue?
questions.correctAnswerText: Embryonal renal tissue
questions.initialExplanation: Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma) arises from embryonal renal tissue. Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest cells, commonly in the adrenal region or sympathetic chain.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urothelial tumours arise from the urinary tract lining, not embryonal renal tissue.
- B. Incorrect. Neuroblastoma may arise in the adrenal medulla, but Wilms tumour is renal embryonal tissue.
- C. Correct. This is the origin of Wilms tumour stated.
- D. Incorrect. Wilms tumour is not defined as a tumour of collecting duct cells.
- E. Incorrect. Neural crest origin is characteristic of neuroblastoma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Wilms tumour = nephroblastoma, embryonal renal tissue.
- Neuroblastoma = neural crest origin, often adrenal/neck/pelvic sympathetic sites.
- Wilms tumour is the most common renal tumour in childhood.

questions.stem: Which age group is most typical for Wilms tumour in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: E
options.text: Peak at 1–5 years, with most cases under 5 years

questions.correctAnswerText: Peak at 1–5 years, with most cases under 5 years
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance gives a peak age of 1–5 years and notes that more than 80% of cases occur before 5 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. It is not exclusively neonatal.
- B. Incorrect. This is much older than the typical age.
- C. Incorrect. Wilms tumour is primarily a tumour of young children.
- D. Incorrect. Wilms tumour is a pediatric renal tumour.
- E. Correct. This matches the age distribution.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Wilms tumour: usually 1–5 years.
- Neuroblastoma can occur from birth through early childhood.
- Age helps but does not replace imaging and diagnostic assessment.

questions.stem: Which abdominal mass feature favours Wilms tumour over neuroblastoma?

options.label: A
options.text: A mass that commonly crosses the midline

options.label: B
options.text: A unilateral renal mass that usually does not cross the midline

options.label: C
options.text: A mass associated with raccoon eyes and bone metastases

options.label: E
options.text: A mass arising from adrenal/neck/pelvic neural crest tissue

questions.correctAnswerText: A unilateral renal mass that usually does not cross the midline
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance Wilms tumour as usually unilateral and as an abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. Neuroblastoma commonly crosses the midline and may arise outside the kidney.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Crossing the midline is more characteristic of neuroblastoma.
- B. Correct. This is the characteristic Wilms pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Raccoon eyes and bone metastases are neuroblastoma clues.
- D. Incorrect. Opsoclonus-myoclonus is a paraneoplastic association of neuroblastoma.
- E. Incorrect. Neural crest/adrenal or sympathetic chain origin favours neuroblastoma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Wilms: usually unilateral, renal, usually does not cross midline.
- Neuroblastoma: often crosses the midline and may arise from adrenal, neck or pelvic sympathetic tissue.
- Avoid forceful palpation of a suspected renal tumour.

questions.stem: Which syndromic association is classically linked with Wilms tumour?
questions.correctAnswerText: WAGR syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance aniridia, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome, WAGR and Denys–Drash syndrome among Wilms tumour associations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. WAGR stands for Wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies and intellectual/developmental impairment.
- B. Incorrect. Marfan syndrome is associated with connective-tissue and aortic disease.
- C. Incorrect. Ataxia-telangiectasia is associated with progressive ataxia, telangiectasia and immunodeficiency.
- D. Incorrect. Noonan syndrome is associated with pulmonary stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
- E. Incorrect. Kartagener syndrome is associated with primary ciliary dyskinesia and situs abnormalities.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Wilms associations: aniridia, Beckwith–Wiedemann, WAGR and Denys–Drash.
- Consider genetic/syndromic assessment when relevant features are present.
- Clinical guidance familial Wilms tumour as uncommon.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly supports neuroblastoma rather than Wilms tumour?

options.label: D
options.text: An isolated unilateral renal mass without metastasis

questions.correctAnswerText: Elevated urinary VMA/HVA
questions.initialExplanation: Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest cells and may produce catecholamine metabolites. Clinical guidance elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA) as useful investigations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Painless haematuria is a clinical feature listed for Wilms tumour.
- B. Incorrect. Embryonal renal tissue is the origin of Wilms tumour.
- C. Incorrect. WAGR is associated with Wilms tumour.
- D. Incorrect. This pattern is more consistent with Wilms tumour.
- E. Correct. Elevated VMA/HVA supports neuroblastoma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neuroblastoma: neural crest origin; urine VMA/HVA may be elevated.
- Imaging may show calcification; Clinical guidance calcification in approximately 10%.
- Wilms tumour is renal in origin and may present with painless haematuria and hypertension.

questions.stem: A child with an abdominal mass has periorbital ecchymoses, proptosis, bone pain and pancytopenia. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Neuroblastoma with metastatic spread
questions.initialExplanation: Neuroblastoma may metastasize to bone and bone marrow, causing bone pain and pancytopenia. Periorbital ecchymoses ("raccoon eyes") and proptosis are important metastatic clues.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are characteristic features of metastatic neuroblastoma.
- B. Incorrect. PUV causes urinary obstruction and hydronephrosis.
- C. Incorrect. Hydrocele causes a painless scrotal swelling, not bone or orbital metastases.
- D. Incorrect. Wilms tumour more commonly presents as a unilateral renal mass; lung metastases are listed as an important metastatic site.
- E. Incorrect. Minimal change nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome, not a metastatic mass.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neuroblastoma: bone/bone marrow metastases, bone pain, pancytopenia, raccoon eyes, proptosis and skin nodules.
- Opsoclonus-myoclonus ("dancing eyes") is a recognized paraneoplastic association.
- Wilms tumour may metastasize to lungs.

questions.stem: Which investigation is used to assess urinary catecholamine metabolites in suspected neuroblastoma?
questions.correctAnswerText: Urinary VMA and HVA
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance urinary VMA and HVA as investigations for neuroblastoma, reflecting catecholamine metabolism by the tumour.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. C3 is used in the assessment of selected glomerular diseases such as PSGN.
- B. Incorrect. ASO is evidence of recent streptococcal infection.
- C. Incorrect. These support UTI diagnosis.
- D. Correct. These are the metabolites specifically listed.
- E. Incorrect. This quantifies proteinuria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
