- Neuroblastoma: urinary VMA/HVA may be elevated.
- Imaging includes abdominal ultrasound and CT/MRI for localization/staging.
- CBC, bone marrow assessment, LFTs, electrolytes and LDH may be part of evaluation.

questions.stem: Which statement best matches the treatment approach described for localized Wilms tumour?

options.label: A
options.text: No treatment because spontaneous regression is expected

options.label: E
options.text: Surgical nephrectomy as part of multidisciplinary management

questions.correctAnswerText: Surgical nephrectomy as part of multidisciplinary management
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance nephrectomy and biopsy for Wilms tumour, with chemotherapy and radiotherapy used according to stage and risk. Treatment is multidisciplinary.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Wilms tumour requires oncological treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Desmopressin is used in selected enuresis cases.
- C. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not treat a renal malignancy.
- D. Incorrect. Ureteric reimplantation treats selected VUR.
- E. Correct. Surgery is central for localized Wilms tumour in the supplied clinical guidance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Wilms tumour: multidisciplinary treatment; surgery, chemotherapy and selected radiotherapy according to stage.
- Neuroblastoma treatment depends on age, stage and biological characteristics; localized disease may be treated surgically, while advanced disease requires multimodal therapy.
- clinical guidance gives a good prognosis for Wilms tumour, with an approximate 80% cure rate.

questions.stem: Which statement about neuroblastoma prognosis is most accurate?

options.label: B
options.text: each case has the same excellent prognosis

options.label: C
options.text: Metastatic disease typically has a better prognosis than localized disease

options.label: D
options.text: It depends on age, stage and biological characteristics; advanced disease has a poorer prognosis

options.label: E
options.text: Prognosis is determined by urine VMA level

questions.correctAnswerText: It depends on age, stage and biological characteristics; advanced disease has a poorer prognosis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that neuroblastoma prognosis depends on age, stage and biological character, with advanced disease associated with a poorer prognosis. Relapse is also noted as common.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Clinical guidance that relapse is common.
- B. Incorrect. Outcomes vary substantially by risk group and stage.
- C. Incorrect. Advanced metastatic disease is associated with poorer prognosis.
- D. Correct. These are the prognostic factors identified.
- E. Incorrect. VMA/HVA are diagnostic markers, not the sole determinant of prognosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neuroblastoma prognosis: age + stage + biological characteristics.
- Advanced disease: poorer prognosis.
- Relapse is common.
- Opsoclonus-myoclonus is described as a favourable prognostic association.

cases.title: An abdominal mass in a young child
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old child is brought because the parents noticed an abdominal mass while bathing him. The child is otherwise relatively well but has occasional haematuria and elevated blood pressure. Imaging shows a unilateral renal mass. A second child of a similar age has an abdominal mass that crosses the midline, weight loss, pallor and periorbital bruising.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best fits the first child's painless renal mass with haematuria and hypertension?
questions.correctAnswerText: Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma)
questions.initialExplanation: Wilms tumour arises from embryonal renal tissue and commonly presents in young children with an abdominal mass. Haematuria and hypertension may occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest tissue and may originate in the adrenal gland or sympathetic chain.
- B. Correct. The renal origin, young age and clinical findings support Wilms tumour.
- C. Incorrect. MCDK is a congenital cystic renal anomaly.
- D. Incorrect. RTA does not cause an abdominal mass.
- E. Incorrect. Glomerulonephritis may cause haematuria and hypertension but not a solid renal mass.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Wilms tumour is the most common renal tumour in childhood.
- It usually presents between 1 and 5 years of age.

questions.stem: Which examination finding would support Wilms tumour rather than neuroblastoma in a child with an abdominal mass?

options.label: A
options.text: A mass that typically crosses the midline

options.label: D
options.text: A mass that usually does not cross the midline

options.label: E
options.text: Bone marrow metastases as the defining initial feature

questions.correctAnswerText: A mass that usually does not cross the midline
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance Wilms tumour as usually unilateral, with a renal mass that typically does not cross the midline. Neuroblastoma more often crosses the midline.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Crossing the midline is more characteristic of neuroblastoma in the comparison table.
- B. Incorrect. Opsoclonus–myoclonus is a recognized neuroblastoma association.
- C. Incorrect. Raccoon eyes may occur with metastatic neuroblastoma.
- D. Correct. This is the distinguishing feature given for Wilms tumour.
- E. Incorrect. Bone marrow involvement is a metastatic feature of neuroblastoma, not the defining presentation of Wilms tumour.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Wilms: usually unilateral and does not cross the midline.
- Neuroblastoma: may cross the midline and has characteristic metastatic/paraneoplastic features.

questions.stem: The second child has an abdominal mass crossing the midline, periorbital bruising and possible opsoclonus. Which investigation is particularly useful in the diagnostic work-up described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Urine VMA and HVA
questions.initialExplanation: Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest cells and may produce catecholamine metabolites. Clinical guidance urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA) in its investigation section.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. C3 is used in selected glomerular disease assessments.
- B. Correct. Urinary VMA/HVA are listed for neuroblastoma.
- C. Incorrect. This evaluates proteinuria, not a neural-crest tumour.
- D. Incorrect. ASO helps assess recent streptococcal infection.
- E. Incorrect. Sweat chloride is used in cystic fibrosis evaluation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neuroblastoma: neural crest origin; may arise in adrenal, neck or pelvic sites.
- clinical guidance also lists imaging, CBC, bone marrow assessment and urinary metabolites.

questions.stem: A child with a renal mass is found to have aniridia and a genitourinary anomaly. Which tumour association should raise concern?
questions.correctAnswerText: WAGR syndrome and Wilms tumour
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance aniridia, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome, WAGR and Denys–Drash syndrome among associations of Wilms tumour.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. WAGR includes Wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies and developmental impairment.
- B. Incorrect. Gitelman syndrome is a renal tubular salt-wasting disorder.
- C. Incorrect. Fanconi syndrome is a proximal tubular disorder.
- D. Incorrect. IgA vasculitis is a systemic small-vessel vasculitis.
- E. Incorrect. Bartter syndrome is a loop-of-Henle salt-wasting disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Wilms tumour associations: aniridia, Beckwith–Wiedemann, WAGR and Denys–Drash.
- Recognizing syndromic features is important when assessing a child with a renal mass.

questions.stem: Which treatment combination is described for Wilms tumour in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: C
options.text: Nephrectomy, chemotherapy and radiotherapy in selected/advanced cases

questions.correctAnswerText: Nephrectomy, chemotherapy and radiotherapy in selected/advanced cases
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance multidisciplinary management that includes nephrectomy and chemotherapy, with radiotherapy used in selected or advanced cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These measures do not treat a renal malignancy.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not eradicate Wilms tumour.
- C. Correct. This matches the treatment approach listed.
- D. Incorrect. Dialysis is renal replacement therapy, not definitive tumour treatment.
- E. Incorrect. This is treatment for posterior urethral valves.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Management is multidisciplinary.
- Clinical guidance a generally good prognosis for Wilms tumour, with a cure rate around 80% in its summary.

questions.stem: Which additional finding most strongly supports neuroblastoma over Wilms tumour in a child with an abdominal mass?

options.label: B
options.text: A mass confined to one kidney without systemic features

options.label: D
options.text: Raccoon eyes with bone pain or marrow involvement

questions.correctAnswerText: Raccoon eyes with bone pain or marrow involvement
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance neuroblastoma with possible bone and bone-marrow metastases, bone pain, proptosis/raccoon eyes and skin nodules.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This does not suggest a tumour.
- B. Incorrect. A unilateral renal mass is more characteristic of Wilms tumour.
- C. Incorrect. Orthostatic proteinuria is a benign urinary protein pattern.
- D. Correct. These are metastatic features listed for neuroblastoma.
- E. Incorrect. Hydrocele is a benign scrotal fluid collection and does not suggest an abdominal malignancy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neuroblastoma: neural crest origin, may cross the midline, and may present with metastatic or paraneoplastic features.
- Opsoclonus–myoclonus is another association listed.

cases.title: An adolescent with repeatedly elevated blood pressure
cases.vignette: A 14-year-old boy is found to have elevated blood pressure during two separate clinic visits. He is overweight and has a family history of hypertension. The clinician repeats the measurement using an appropriate cuff while the child is relaxed. Examination is directed toward renal, cardiovascular, endocrine and syndromic causes.

questions.stem: Which statement about blood pressure classification in children is correct ?

options.label: A
options.text: Blood pressure is interpreted using age, sex and height percentiles in children

options.label: C
options.text: Adult fixed cut-offs apply identically to most infants and children

options.label: D
options.text: Blood pressure does not vary with age or height

options.label: E
options.text: A single elevated reading typically proves chronic hypertension

questions.correctAnswerText: Blood pressure is interpreted using age, sex and height percentiles in children
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance uses percentile-based BP categories in children and includes age and height-related values. Accurate interpretation requires age-appropriate reference values and repeated measurements.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Pediatric BP interpretation is based on age, sex and height percentiles in the supplied material.
- B. Incorrect. Incorrect cuff size can distort the measured BP.
- C. Incorrect. Fixed adult thresholds cannot be applied uniformly to all children, particularly younger children.
- D. Incorrect. BP varies with age, sex and height.
- E. Incorrect. Elevated readings should be confirmed with appropriate technique and repeat measurements.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Use age-, sex- and height-appropriate BP standards.
- Repeat an abnormal reading with correct technique.
- clinical guidance categorizes normal BP below the 90th percentile, with higher categories based on percentile thresholds; adolescent thresholds are also provided.

questions.stem: Which technique is essential for accurate BP measurement in a child?

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the arm hanging below heart level

options.label: C
options.text: Use an appropriately sized cuff and ensure the child is relaxed, with arm and device at heart level

options.label: E
options.text: Use an adult cuff for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Use an appropriately sized cuff and ensure the child is relaxed, with arm and device at heart level
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance emphasizes the correct cuff size, a relaxed and comfortable child, and positioning the machine, heart and limb at the same level.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. BP should be measured on the exposed arm rather than through thick clothing.
- B. Incorrect. The arm should be at heart level.
- C. Correct. These are the measurement conditions described.
- D. Incorrect. Exercise can transiently raise BP and should not precede a resting measurement.
- E. Incorrect. Cuff size must match the child's arm.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Correct cuff size.
- Child relaxed and comfortable.
- Arm, heart and device at the same level.
- Repeat and confirm abnormal measurements.

questions.stem: Which statement best matches the distribution of primary and secondary hypertension in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: most pediatric hypertension is essential hypertension

options.label: B
options.text: Primary hypertension is more common in young children; secondary hypertension is rare

options.label: D
options.text: Hypertension in children is typically due to obesity

options.label: E
options.text: Primary hypertension is uncommon in pediatric patients in the sheet, while secondary hypertension is more common

questions.correctAnswerText: Primary hypertension is uncommon in pediatric patients in the sheet, while secondary hypertension is more common
questions.initialExplanation: The supplied clinical guidance describes primary hypertension as approximately 10% and secondary hypertension as approximately 90%, with primary hypertension more common in adolescents.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Secondary causes are important in childhood.
- B. Incorrect. This reverses the pattern described.
- C. Incorrect. Secondary hypertension is not restricted to neonates.
- D. Incorrect. Renal, endocrine, cardiac, CNS and medication-related causes are also listed.
- E. Correct. This matches the approximate proportions given.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The supplied clinical guidance: primary ≈10%, secondary ≈90%.
- Primary hypertension is more common in adolescents.
- In a younger child, actively look for secondary causes.

questions.stem: What is the most common category of secondary hypertension in children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Renal disease
questions.initialExplanation: Renal parenchymal disease and renovascular disease are the major secondary causes listed in the supplied clinical guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis is not a recognized major cause of pediatric hypertension.
- B. Incorrect. Otitis media is not a listed cause.
- C. Correct. Renal disease is emphasized as the most common category, including glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, CKD and renal vascular disease.
- D. Incorrect. GERD does not explain chronic hypertension.
- E. Incorrect. A skin infection does not represent the common secondary category.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Renal parenchymal disease is the commonest secondary cause.
- Consider GN, pyelonephritis, CKD, renal artery stenosis and renal vein thrombosis.
- Coarctation is an important cardiovascular cause.

questions.stem: Which endocrine conditions are listed as causes of secondary hypertension?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cushing syndrome, hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance Cushing syndrome, hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma among endocrine causes of secondary hypertension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Type 1 diabetes is not listed as the characteristic endocrine cause in this section.
- B. Incorrect. Vitamin D deficiency and rickets are not the listed causes.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism is not the endocrine group highlighted.
- D. Correct. All three are specifically listed.
- E. Incorrect. Iron deficiency anaemia does not represent the endocrine causes asked for.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Endocrine causes listed: Cushing syndrome, hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma.
- Also consider drugs such as steroids.
- Assess for clinical clues of endocrine disease during examination.

questions.stem: Which examination finding may suggest renovascular or renal disease as a cause of hypertension?
questions.correctAnswerText: Renal bruit on abdominal examination
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance includes abdominal examination for a renal bruit as part of the assessment of secondary hypertension. A bruit may suggest renovascular disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is an ocular feature of Alport syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Fixed wide splitting of S2 suggests ASD.
- C. Correct. A renal bruit is an important clue to renovascular pathology.
- D. Incorrect. This supports hydrocele.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests IgA vasculitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Examine general build, obesity, dysmorphic features, cardiovascular pulses, abdomen for renal bruit and genitalia when indicated.
- Consider Turner/Cushing features, coarctation and endocrine causes.
- A careful examination helps direct investigations.

questions.stem: Which initial investigation group is listed for a child with hypertension?

options.label: A
options.text: Urine VMA/HVA in each patient as the sole test

options.label: B
options.text: Renal biopsy in children in routine care before basic tests

options.label: E
options.text: Urea/electrolytes, urinalysis, renal ultrasound, echocardiography and Doppler as indicated

questions.correctAnswerText: Urea/electrolytes, urinalysis, renal ultrasound, echocardiography and Doppler as indicated
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance renal function and urine tests, renal ultrasound, echocardiography, Doppler studies, ABG, thyroid function and renal biopsy in selected cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. VMA/HVA are relevant to suspected neuroblastoma, not the sole investigation for all hypertension.
- B. Incorrect. Renal biopsy is reserved for selected cases after appropriate evaluation.
- C. Incorrect. These do not form the routine initial hypertension assessment.
- D. Incorrect. These assess allergy and respiratory function, not the main secondary hypertension causes.
- E. Correct. These are part of the work-up described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Initial assessment: U/E, urinalysis and renal imaging.
- Additional studies may include echo, Doppler, ABG, TFT, renin/aldosterone and selected renal biopsy.
- Tailor investigations to the suspected secondary cause.

questions.stem: Which management plan best matches the general approach to pediatric hypertension?

options.label: B
options.text: Weight control, exercise, salt restriction, indicated medication and treatment of the cause

questions.correctAnswerText: Weight control, exercise, salt restriction, indicated medication and treatment of the cause
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance general measures including weight reduction, increased physical activity and salt restriction, alongside medication classes such as ACE inhibitors, diuretics, hydralazine and calcium-channel blockers. Treating the underlying cause is essential.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Lifestyle measures are explicitly included.
- B. Correct. This combines the general and cause-directed measures described.
- C. Incorrect. Fluid restriction alone does not address most causes of pediatric hypertension.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics are indicated only for infection, not routine hypertension management.
- E. Incorrect. Nephrectomy is not routine hypertension treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lifestyle: weight control, activity and salt reduction.
- Drug classes listed: ACE inhibitors, diuretics, hydralazine and calcium-channel blockers.
- Treat the underlying cause, especially renal or cardiovascular disease.
- Drug choice depends on age, cause, renal function and specialist guidance.

cases.title: Repeated high blood-pressure readings
cases.vignette: A 12-year-old boy is found to have repeatedly elevated blood-pressure readings during clinic visits. He is overweight and has a family history of hypertension. The clinician repeats the measurement after the child rests and checks that the cuff fits correctly. Urinalysis and renal investigations are requested because renal disease is an important secondary cause in children.

questions.stem: For a child aged 1–13 years, which blood-pressure finding is most consistent with hypertension according to the threshold summarized on page 45 of clinical guidance?

options.label: B
options.text: A reading at or above the 95th percentile, or at least 130/80 mmHg if that is the lower threshold

options.label: D
options.text: A single reading above the 90th percentile typically establishes stage 2 hypertension

questions.correctAnswerText: A reading at or above the 95th percentile, or at least 130/80 mmHg if that is the lower threshold
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that in children aged 1–13 years, hypertension is at least the 95th percentile or at least 130/80 mmHg, whichever is lower. The child's age, sex and height are relevant to percentile interpretation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The 50th percentile is around the middle of the reference distribution.
- B. Correct. This matches the threshold stated on page 45.
- C. Incorrect. The 75th percentile is not the stated diagnostic threshold.
- D. Incorrect. The 90th percentile relates to elevated BP, not stage 2 hypertension.
- E. Incorrect. Below the 90th percentile is within the normal category in the summary table.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance classifies normal BP as below the 90th percentile.
- It uses age, sex and height centiles for children.
- clinical guidance separately states that in young people aged 13 years and above, hypertension is at least 130/80 mmHg.

questions.stem: The nurse obtains a high reading while the child is anxious and using an adult-sized cuff that is too small. What is the best next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Diagnose hypertension immediately without repeating the measurement

options.label: B
options.text: Measure BP while the child is standing and moving

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the measurement after the child is relaxed, using an appropriate cuff and correct arm positioning

options.label: D
options.text: Use the same cuff for children in routine care regardless of arm size

questions.correctAnswerText: Repeat the measurement after the child is relaxed, using an appropriate cuff and correct arm positioning
questions.initialExplanation: Accurate measurement requires an appropriate cuff, a relaxed and comfortable child, and positioning the machine, heart and limb at the same level.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A single poorly performed measurement should not establish the diagnosis.
- B. Incorrect. Movement and poor positioning reduce reliability.
- C. Correct. It follows the technique described.
- D. Incorrect. Cuff size must be appropriate for the child's arm.
- E. Incorrect. BP should be measured using correct standardized technique, not over clothing.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ensure correct cuff size.
- Allow the child to rest and relax.
- Keep the arm at heart level and use consistent technique.

questions.stem: In a child with newly confirmed hypertension, which category of secondary cause should be prioritized in the initial evaluation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Renal parenchymal or renovascular disease
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies renal disease as the most important secondary cause of childhood hypertension. Examples include glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, CKD, renal artery stenosis and renal vein thrombosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Renal causes are emphasized as the leading secondary category.
- B. Incorrect. Hydrocele is not a recognized cause of hypertension.
- C. Incorrect. Orthostatic proteinuria is usually benign and does not explain hypertension.
- D. Incorrect. Hypospadias is a congenital genital anomaly.
- E. Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis is not the key secondary cause described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical guidance secondary hypertension as more common in children than primary hypertension.
- Other secondary causes include endocrine disease, coarctation of the aorta, CNS disease and medications such as steroids.
- Primary hypertension is more common in adolescents and is associated with factors such as obesity and family history.

questions.stem: A child with hypertension has no obvious endocrine features. Which initial investigations are included 's work-up?

options.label: B
options.text: Brain MRI in children in routine care

options.label: D
options.text: Electrolytes/urea, urinalysis, renal ultrasound and selected cardiac/vascular assessment

options.label: E
options.text: No investigation is needed if the child is overweight

questions.correctAnswerText: Electrolytes/urea, urinalysis, renal ultrasound and selected cardiac/vascular assessment
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance urea/electrolytes and urinalysis, ultrasound, echocardiography and Doppler studies, with further tests such as ABG, thyroid function, renal biopsy, renin and aldosterone according to the case.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urine culture alone does not evaluate the broad renal and cardiovascular causes of hypertension.
- B. Incorrect. Brain MRI is not a routine first-line test for every child with hypertension.
- C. Incorrect. These tests do not address the main causes listed.
- D. Correct. This reflects the investigation set.
- E. Incorrect. Overweight may contribute to primary hypertension, but secondary causes still need consideration.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Initial assessment: electrolytes/urea, urinalysis and renal ultrasound.
- Additional tests may include echocardiography, Doppler, ABG, TFT, renal biopsy and plasma renin/aldosterone.

questions.stem: A child with persistent primary hypertension is overweight and has a high-salt diet. Which initial management package best matches clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete bed rest and no fluids

options.label: E
options.text: Weight reduction when needed, increased physical activity, salt restriction and medication when indicated

questions.correctAnswerText: Weight reduction when needed, increased physical activity, salt restriction and medication when indicated
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance general measures such as weight reduction, physical activity and salt restriction. Drug options listed include ACE inhibitors, diuretics, hydralazine and calcium-channel blockers, alongside treatment of any underlying cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bed rest and fluid deprivation are not the recommended lifestyle measures.
- B. Incorrect. Nephrectomy is not treatment for primary hypertension.
- C. Incorrect. Antibiotics are only used for an appropriate infection, not hypertension itself.
- D. Incorrect. Steroids are not routine antihypertensive therapy and may themselves contribute to hypertension.
- E. Correct. This reflects the lifestyle and medication options.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat the underlying cause when hypertension is secondary.
- Lifestyle management includes weight reduction, activity and salt restriction.
- Clinical guidance ACE inhibitors, diuretics, hydralazine and calcium-channel blockers as drug options.

cases.title: Loin pain and haematuria in a child
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old boy presents with intermittent severe loin pain radiating toward the groin and visible haematuria. He has a history of recurrent UTI. Urine culture grows Proteus. Imaging identifies a renal calculus. The clinician investigates the stone composition and looks for metabolic causes.

questions.stem: Which risk factors for childhood renal stones are listed?

options.label: D
options.text: UTI, structural urinary tract anomalies and metabolic abnormalities

questions.correctAnswerText: UTI, structural urinary tract anomalies and metabolic abnormalities
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies urinary infection, structural abnormalities of the urinary tract and metabolic disturbances as important predisposing factors for childhood renal stones.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are congenital genital/urethral conditions, not the principal stone risk categories.
- B. Incorrect. These are features of Alport syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Allergic diseases are not the stone risk group highlighted.
- D. Correct. These are the three categories listed.
- E. Incorrect. Hypertension may coexist with renal disease but is not one of the primary stone risk categories listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Renal stones are uncommon in childhood.
- Risk factors: UTI, urinary tract structural anomalies and metabolic abnormalities.
- Recurrent stones require evaluation for an underlying cause.

questions.stem: Which organism is particularly associated with infection-related phosphate stones?
questions.correctAnswerText: Proteus
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that phosphate stones are commonly associated with infection, especially Proteus. Proteus splits urea and alkalinizes urine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Adenovirus — Incorrect. It may cause haemorrhagic cystitis but is not the listed phosphate-stone organism.
- B. Mycoplasma — Incorrect. It is not the infection-related stone association stated.
- C. Proteus — Correct. Urease activity produces ammonia and raises urine pH, promoting phosphate/struvite stone formation.
- D. Candida — Incorrect. It is not the organism highlighted for phosphate stones.
- E. E. coli — Incorrect. It is the commonest UTI organism overall, but Proteus is specifically associated with infection-related phosphate stones.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Proteus → urease → ammonia → alkaline urine.
- Infection-related phosphate/struvite stones are associated with Proteus.
- Consider urine culture and pH in a child with suspected stones and UTI.

questions.stem: Which metabolic abnormality is identified as the most common metabolic abnormality associated with calcium-containing stones in children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Idiopathic hypercalciuria
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that calcium-containing stones may occur with idiopathic hypercalciuria, which it identifies as the most common metabolic abnormality.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Idiopathic hypercalciuria — Correct. This is specifically identified.
- B. Hypermagnesaemia — Incorrect. It is not the abnormality highlighted.
- C. Hypophosphataemia — Incorrect. It is not the most common metabolic abnormality listed for calcium stones.
- D. Hypocalciuria — Incorrect. Reduced urinary calcium is not the risk factor described.
- E. Low urinary urate — Incorrect. clinical guidance mentions increased urinary urate as a possible contributor, not low urate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Childhood renal stones are uncommon.
- Idiopathic hypercalciuria is highlighted as the most common metabolic abnormality for calcium stones.
- Increased urinary urate and oxalate may also contribute.

questions.stem: What is nephrocalcinosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Calcium deposition within the renal parenchyma

options.label: B
options.text: Fluid accumulation in the tunica vaginalis

options.label: E
options.text: Retrograde urine flow into the ureter

questions.correctAnswerText: Calcium deposition within the renal parenchyma
questions.initialExplanation: Nephrocalcinosis refers to deposition of calcium within renal parenchymal tissue, rather than a discrete calculus within the urinary collecting system.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the definition.
- B. Incorrect. This is hydrocele.
- C. Incorrect. Crescents are a histological feature of severe glomerular injury.
- D. Incorrect. This is hydroureter.
- E. Incorrect. This is VUR.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nephrocalcinosis = calcium deposition in renal parenchyma.
- Associations: hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, distal RTA and neonatal furosemide therapy.
- Distinguish nephrocalcinosis from a discrete renal stone.

questions.stem: Which condition is associated with nephrocalcinosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Distal renal tubular acidosis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria and distal RTA among causes/associations of nephrocalcinosis. It also notes neonatal furosemide therapy as a potential association.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Distal RTA is an association listed.
- B. Incorrect. Enuresis is a voiding disorder.
- C. Incorrect. Alport syndrome is a collagen IV disorder.
- D. Incorrect. Cystitis is a lower UTI and is not the association highlighted.
- E. Incorrect. Minimal change nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome, not nephrocalcinosis as a characteristic association.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nephrocalcinosis: hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, distal RTA and neonatal furosemide exposure.
- If nephrocalcinosis is found, investigate metabolic and tubular causes.

questions.stem: Which symptom combination may occur in a child with renal calculi?

options.label: B
options.text: Fixed wide splitting of S2 and cyanosis

options.label: C
options.text: Haematuria, loin or abdominal pain, UTI or passage of a stone

options.label: D
options.text: Painless scrotal swelling with positive transillumination

options.label: E
options.text: Isolated hearing loss and visual impairment

questions.correctAnswerText: Haematuria, loin or abdominal pain, UTI or passage of a stone
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance haematuria, loin or abdominal pain, UTI and passage of a stone as possible presentations of pediatric renal calculi.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests IgA vasculitis.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests a congenital cardiac lesion such as ASD with associated findings.
- C. Correct. These are the clinical features described.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests hydrocele.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests Alport syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider stones in a child with loin/abdominal pain and haematuria.
- UTI may coexist, particularly with infection-related stones.
- Ask about previous stones, family history, fluid intake and metabolic disease.

questions.stem: Which investigation set is most appropriate to identify metabolic risk factors for renal stones in a child?

options.label: B
options.text: Urine pH, calcium, phosphate, oxalate, cystine, uric acid, citrate/creatinine and renal function

questions.correctAnswerText: Urine pH, calcium, phosphate, oxalate, cystine, uric acid, citrate/creatinine and renal function
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance urinalysis and metabolic urine testing, including urine pH, calcium, phosphate, oxalate, cystine, uric acid, citrate and creatinine, together with blood renal function tests and imaging.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. VMA/HVA are used in neuroblastoma evaluation.
- B. Correct. This is the metabolic evaluation listed.
- C. Incorrect. These assess the heart, not renal stone chemistry.
- D. Incorrect. These do not assess urinary stone risk.
- E. Incorrect. ASO and C3 are used in selected glomerular disorders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Urine evaluation: pH, Ca, phosphate, oxalate, cystine, uric acid, citrate and creatinine.
- Blood tests: renal function and relevant metabolic studies.
- Imaging may include CT according to the supplied clinical guidance; modality choice should balance diagnostic need and radiation exposure.

questions.stem: Which general preventive measure is recommended for all children with renal stones?

options.label: A
options.text: Avoiding most dietary calcium in each patient

questions.correctAnswerText: High fluid intake
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance high fluid intake for all affected children. If a metabolic abnormality is identified, specific therapy may be possible.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Universal calcium restriction is not recommended by clinical guidance and may be harmful.
- B. Incorrect. Nephrectomy is not a preventive strategy for routine childhood stones.
- C. Incorrect. Dehydration increases urinary concentration and may promote stone formation.
- D. Correct. This is the general preventive measure stated.
- E. Incorrect. Fluid restriction increases concentration of urine.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- High fluid intake is recommended in all affected children.
- Treat the underlying metabolic abnormality when identified.
- Lithotripsy or surgery may be required for selected stones.

cases.title: Recurrent loin pain and haematuria
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child presents with intermittent loin pain, visible haematuria and one episode of urinary infection. Urine testing is requested, and the clinician asks about dietary fluid intake, family history and possible metabolic abnormalities. Imaging identifies echogenic foci with acoustic shadowing in the renal collecting system.

questions.stem: A child has calcium-containing renal stones, and metabolic testing reveals increased urinary calcium without another identified cause. Which abnormality is described as the most common metabolic risk factor?
questions.correctAnswerText: Idiopathic hypercalciuria
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies idiopathic hypercalciuria as the most common metabolic abnormality associated with calcium-containing stones.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Increased urinary calcium predisposes to calcium-containing calculi.
- B. Incorrect. clinical guidance also mentions increased urate excretion as a contributor, not low urate.
- C. Incorrect. Hyperoxaluria is a risk factor for calcium deposition, not low oxalate.
- D. Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia is unrelated to stone formation.
- E. Incorrect. Reduced urinary calcium does not explain calcium stone formation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Calcium-containing stones may be associated with idiopathic hypercalciuria and increased urinary urate or oxalate.
- Cystine and xanthine stones are described as rare.

questions.stem: A child with distal RTA develops calcium deposition within the renal parenchyma rather than a free stone in the collecting system. What is this called?
questions.correctAnswerText: Nephrocalcinosis
questions.initialExplanation: Nephrocalcinosis is calcium deposition within the renal parenchyma. clinical guidance links it with hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria and distal RTA, and also notes it may occur after neonatal furosemide therapy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hydronephrosis is dilatation of the collecting system.
- B. Incorrect. VUR is retrograde urine flow.
- C. Correct. This is the definition of nephrocalcinosis.
- D. Incorrect. Renal agenesis is absence of renal tissue.
- E. Incorrect. Renal vein thrombosis is a vascular complication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nephrocalcinosis is distinct from a discrete renal calculus.
- Consider hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, distal RTA and neonatal furosemide exposure.

questions.stem: Which advice should be included for all children with renal stones alongside cause-specific management?

options.label: D
options.text: Stop most dietary calcium without assessment

questions.correctAnswerText: Encourage high fluid intake
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance high fluid intake for all affected children. If a metabolic cause is found, specific treatment may also be possible.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Severe fluid restriction increases urinary concentration and is contrary to the advice.
- B. Correct. High fluid intake is recommended for all children with stones.
- C. Incorrect. Immobility does not prevent stone formation.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance does not recommend blanket calcium restriction.
- E. Incorrect. Corticosteroids are not routine stone therapy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Investigations may include urinalysis, urine pH, urinary calcium, phosphate, oxalate, cystine, uric acid, citrate and creatinine, blood renal function tests and CT imaging.
- Management may require lithotripsy or surgery for selected stones, plus high fluid intake and correction of the underlying metabolic cause.

topics.name: Renal Anatomy, Nephron and Glomerular Function

cases.title: A child undergoing assessment of renal function
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child is assessed because of recurrent urinary abnormalities. The clinician reviews the basic renal anatomy, the nephron and the filtration barrier before interpreting renal function. The family asks why the kidneys are important beyond producing urine.

questions.stem: Which structures are listed as being located mainly in the renal cortex?

options.label: A
options.text: the thin ascending limb of the loop of Henle

options.label: D
options.text: Glomeruli, proximal convoluted tubules and distal convoluted tubules

questions.correctAnswerText: Glomeruli, proximal convoluted tubules and distal convoluted tubules
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance the cortex as the outer renal zone containing glomeruli, PCT and DCT, as well as collecting ducts.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The loop of Henle is associated with the medulla.
- B. Incorrect. The renal pelvis and urethra are parts of the urine drainage pathway.
- C. Incorrect. The renal papilla is the apex of a renal pyramid in the medulla; calyces are part of the draining system.
- D. Correct. These structures are listed in the description of the renal cortex.
- E. Incorrect. The ureters and bladder are parts of the urinary tract outside the renal cortex.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cortex: glomeruli, PCT, DCT and collecting ducts.
- Medulla: loops of Henle and final portions of collecting ducts.
- The renal pyramids are medullary structures.

questions.stem: Which structure is specifically associated with the renal medulla?
questions.correctAnswerText: Loop of Henle
questions.initialExplanation: The medulla is the inner renal zone and contains the loops of Henle and final portions of the collecting ducts. It is arranged into renal pyramids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The renal artery supplies the kidney and is not a medullary nephron segment.
- B. Correct. The loop of Henle is a principal medullary structure.
- C. Incorrect. Bowman's capsule surrounds the glomerulus in the cortex.
- D. Incorrect. The PCT is a cortical structure.
- E. Incorrect. Glomeruli are located in the cortex.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Medulla: loop of Henle and terminal collecting ducts.
- Renal pyramids form the medullary architecture.
- The renal papilla is the apex of a renal pyramid.

questions.stem: What is the structural and functional unit of the kidney?
questions.correctAnswerText: Nephron
questions.initialExplanation: The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney. It includes a glomerular component and a tubular component.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The ureter transports urine to the bladder.
- B. Incorrect. The renal pelvis collects urine before it enters the ureter.
- C. Correct. The nephron performs filtration and subsequent tubular processing.
- D. Incorrect. A minor calyx collects urine from a renal papilla.
- E. Incorrect. The bladder stores urine.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nephron = glomerulus plus renal tubule.
- The tubule includes PCT, loop of Henle and DCT.
- Urine then drains through collecting ducts and the collecting system.

questions.stem: Which cells form the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule?
questions.correctAnswerText: Podocytes
questions.initialExplanation: The visceral layer of Bowman's capsule is formed by podocytes. Their foot processes lie on the glomerular basement membrane and leave filtration slits.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Urothelial cells line the renal pelvis, ureters and bladder.
- B. Incorrect. Transitional epithelium lines parts of the urinary collecting system.
- C. Incorrect. Hepatocytes are liver cells.
- D. Incorrect. Mesothelial cells line serous cavities.
- E. Correct. Podocytes are the specialized visceral epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bowman's capsule has parietal and visceral layers.
- The visceral layer consists of podocytes.
- Podocyte foot processes form filtration slits.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly describes the glomerular filtration barrier?

options.label: B
options.text: Fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocytes

options.label: C
options.text: Proximal tubular cells, collecting ducts and renal pelvis

questions.correctAnswerText: Fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocytes
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance three components of the filtration barrier: fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium, the capillary basement membrane and podocytes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are not the glomerular filtration layers.
- B. Correct. These are the three layers described.
- C. Incorrect. These are tubular or collecting-system structures rather than the filtration barrier.
- D. Incorrect. These are hepatic structures.
- E. Incorrect. These structures do not form the glomerular filtration barrier.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium + basement membrane + podocytes.
- The basement membrane contains type IV collagen and proteoglycans.
- Podocyte foot processes create filtration slits.

questions.stem: Why does the normal glomerular filtration barrier restrict the passage of many plasma proteins?

options.label: A
options.text: It actively pumps most proteins into the renal pelvis

options.label: B
options.text: It permits unrestricted passage of high-molecular-weight proteins

options.label: C
options.text: It is formed by collecting duct cells

options.label: E
options.text: It has size-selective and negatively charged properties

questions.correctAnswerText: It has size-selective and negatively charged properties
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance explains that the filtration barrier is size-selective and charge-selective. The negative charge helps repel negatively charged plasma proteins, while the structure limits passage of large molecules.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The barrier does not pump proteins into the renal pelvis.
- B. Incorrect. The barrier restricts rather than freely permits high-molecular-weight proteins.
- C. Incorrect. Collecting duct cells do not form the glomerular filtration barrier.
- D. Incorrect. The glomerular basement membrane is an essential component.
- E. Correct. Both size and charge selectivity help prevent protein loss in urine.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Size selectivity limits filtration of large molecules.
- Negative charges repel negatively charged proteins.
- Damage to the filtration barrier may result in proteinuria.

questions.stem: Which group contains functions of the kidneys recommended?

options.label: A
options.text: Fluid, electrolyte and acid-base regulation; waste excretion; vitamin D activation; erythropoietin production

options.label: B
options.text: Surfactant production, gas exchange and haemoglobin synthesis

options.label: C
options.text: Bile production, insulin secretion and bilirubin conjugation

options.label: D
options.text: Thyroxine synthesis, cortisol secretion and bile storage

questions.correctAnswerText: Fluid, electrolyte and acid-base regulation; waste excretion; vitamin D activation; erythropoietin production
questions.initialExplanation: The kidney maintains water, electrolyte and acid-base balance, excretes waste products, activates vitamin D and stimulates erythropoiesis through erythropoietin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. All these functions are included in the renal functions listed.
- B. Incorrect. Surfactant production and gas exchange are pulmonary functions.
- C. Incorrect. Bile production and bilirubin conjugation are hepatic functions; insulin is produced by pancreatic beta cells.
- D. Incorrect. Thyroxine and cortisol are produced by endocrine glands, not the kidney.
- E. Incorrect. These are not the principal renal functions listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Kidneys regulate fluid, electrolytes, blood pressure and acid-base balance.
- They excrete metabolic waste.
- They activate vitamin D and produce erythropoietin.

questions.stem: Which statement about glomerular filtration rate in early life is consistent with the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: GFR is highest at birth and falls to adult levels by 2 weeks

options.label: B
options.text: Adult GFR is normally reached before birth

options.label: C
options.text: GFR is low in newborns, especially preterm infants, and approaches the adult range by approximately 2 years

options.label: D
options.text: GFR is identical in preterm infants and adolescents

options.label: E
options.text: GFR does not change during childhood

questions.correctAnswerText: GFR is low in newborns, especially preterm infants, and approaches the adult range by approximately 2 years
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that GFR is low in newborns, particularly preterm infants, and increases gradually to the adult range by about 2 years of age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Clinical guidance a low neonatal GFR that increases with maturation.
- B. Incorrect. Adult-range GFR is reached after birth, not before birth.
- C. Correct. This is the developmental pattern described.
- D. Incorrect. GFR changes with age and maturation.
- E. Incorrect. GFR increases during early childhood.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal GFR is low, especially in preterm infants.
- Renal filtration matures progressively after birth.
- clinical guidance places attainment of the adult range at approximately 2 years.

cases.title: A school-age child with protein detected in urine
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child is found to have protein on a urine dipstick during a routine assessment. The child is otherwise well, has normal blood pressure, no oedema and normal renal function.

questions.stem: What is the definition of proteinuria used in the supplied nephrology clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Presence of white blood cells in the urine

options.label: B
options.text: Presence of red blood cells in the urine

options.label: C
options.text: Excretion of an abnormal amount of protein in the urine

options.label: E
options.text: Excretion of glucose in the urine

questions.correctAnswerText: Excretion of an abnormal amount of protein in the urine
questions.initialExplanation: Proteinuria is the excretion of an abnormal amount of protein in urine. Clinical guidance that normal urine may contain no protein or only trace amounts.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. White blood cells in urine indicate pyuria.
- B. Incorrect. Red blood cells in urine indicate haematuria.
- C. Correct. This matches the definition.
- D. Incorrect. Complete absence of urine production is anuria.
- E. Incorrect. Glucose in urine is glycosuria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Proteinuria = abnormal urinary protein excretion.
- Normal dipstick: negative or trace.
- Interpret a positive dipstick with the clinical context and quantitative assessment where indicated.

questions.stem: Which result is within the normal urinary protein limits listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Dipstick negative or trace
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance a negative or trace dipstick as the normal finding. It also gives a 24-hour urinary protein value below 150 mg/day and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio below 0.2 as reference limits.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Negative or trace is the normal dipstick result.
- B. Incorrect. +++ or more is listed in the heavy or nephrotic-range category.
- C. Incorrect. Persistent heavy proteinuria with oedema is not a normal finding.
- D. Incorrect. A ratio above 2 is listed in the nephrotic-range category.
- E. Incorrect. More than 3 g/day is listed in the heavy proteinuria range.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal dipstick: negative or trace.
- Clinical guidance normal 24-hour urinary protein as less than 150 mg/day.
- Clinical guidance a normal urine protein-to-creatinine ratio below 0.2.
- Confirm units and local laboratory reference ranges when interpreting an actual patient result.

questions.stem: A child has mild proteinuria during a febrile illness. The child has no oedema, hypertension or other renal symptoms, and the dipstick shows only + or ++. Which type of proteinuria is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Proteinuria due to renal vein thrombosis

options.label: E
options.text: Proteinuria due to advanced chronic kidney disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Transient proteinuria
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance transient proteinuria as common and self-limiting. It may occur with fever, exercise, heart failure, dehydration or seizures, often with only + or ++ protein on dipstick and no renal symptoms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Renal vein thrombosis is not the most likely explanation for this brief mild finding.
- B. Incorrect. Persistent proteinuria requires continued abnormal findings rather than a single result during fever.
- C. Correct. The clinical context and mild dipstick finding fit transient proteinuria.
- D. Incorrect. Nephrotic-range proteinuria is heavy protein loss and is not suggested by this mild transient pattern.
- E. Incorrect. The child has no clinical evidence of advanced CKD in this vignette.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Transient proteinuria: fever, exercise, heart failure, dehydration or seizures.
- It is commonly self-limiting.
- Clinical guidance reassurance without evaluation when the typical benign transient pattern is present.
- Recheck after the provoking illness or condition has resolved when clinically appropriate.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes orthostatic (postural) proteinuria?

options.label: A
options.text: Proteinuria is typically associated with gross haematuria

options.label: B
options.text: Proteinuria occurs during sleep and increases when supine

options.label: D
options.text: Proteinuria is defined by a positive urine culture

options.label: E
options.text: Proteinuria occurs in the upright position and decreases or disappears when supine

questions.correctAnswerText: Proteinuria occurs in the upright position and decreases or disappears when supine
questions.initialExplanation: Orthostatic proteinuria is posture-dependent. Protein appears in the urine during the upright part of the day and decreases or disappears during the supine position.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Gross haematuria is not required.
- B. Incorrect. This reverses the positional pattern described.
- C. Incorrect. clinical guidance highlights it as a common cause of proteinuria in school-age children.
- D. Incorrect. A positive urine culture indicates bacteriuria, not orthostatic proteinuria.
- E. Correct. This is the definition of orthostatic proteinuria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Orthostatic proteinuria: present upright, reduced or absent supine.
- It is a common cause of proteinuria in school-age children.
- The child typically has no renal manifestations, oedema or hypertension.

questions.stem: Which approach is described to help diagnose orthostatic proteinuria?

options.label: A
options.text: Obtain a single random urine culture

options.label: B
options.text: Measure serum amylase before and after meals

options.label: D
options.text: Perform a chest X-ray after exercise

options.label: E
options.text: Compare urine protein-to-creatinine ratios in early-morning supine and upright samples

questions.correctAnswerText: Compare urine protein-to-creatinine ratios in early-morning supine and upright samples
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance measuring the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio in a series of early-morning urine specimens collected in supine and upright positions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A urine culture evaluates infection and does not establish a posture-dependent protein pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Serum amylase is not used for this renal assessment.
- C. Incorrect. ECG does not assess urinary protein excretion.
- D. Incorrect. Chest X-ray does not diagnose orthostatic proteinuria.
- E. Correct. Comparing supine and upright samples demonstrates the posture-related change in protein excretion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Compare supine and upright urinary protein excretion.
- Use the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio.
- A single random dipstick cannot establish the orthostatic pattern.

questions.stem: Which combination is classified as heavy or nephrotic-range proteinuria in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Dipstick negative, 24-hour protein below 150 mg/day and ratio below 0.2

options.label: B
options.text: No protein on dipstick with normal renal function

options.label: C
options.text: Dipstick + or ++, 24-hour protein below 3 g/day and ratio 0.2–2

options.label: D
options.text: Protein detected after standing, with no supine proteinuria

options.label: E
options.text: Dipstick +++ or more, 24-hour protein above 3 g/day or above 40 mg/m²/day, and ratio above 2

questions.correctAnswerText: Dipstick +++ or more, 24-hour protein above 3 g/day or above 40 mg/m²/day, and ratio above 2
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance classifies heavy or nephrotic-range proteinuria using a dipstick of +++ or more, a 24-hour collection above 3 g/day or above 40 mg/m²/day, and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio above 2.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These values are within the normal limits listed.
- B. Incorrect. This is a normal rather than heavy protein excretion pattern.
- C. Incorrect. These values are listed in the non-heavy range.
- D. Incorrect. This describes the positional pattern of orthostatic proteinuria.
- E. Correct. This is the heavy or nephrotic-range pattern table.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Heavy/nephrotic range: dipstick +++ or more.
- 24-hour protein: above 3 g/day or above 40 mg/m²/day.
- Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio: above 2.
- Verify the reporting units and the original table before applying thresholds clinically.

questions.stem: Which result best matches the non-heavy (non-nephrotic-range) category?

options.label: A
options.text: Dipstick + or ++ and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.2–2

options.label: C
options.text: Dipstick +++ or more and ratio above 2

options.label: E
options.text: Dipstick negative or trace with ratio below 0.2

questions.correctAnswerText: Dipstick + or ++ and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.2–2
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance + or ++ on dipstick and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.2–2 in the non-heavy range.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the non-heavy range described.
- B. Incorrect. This describes a haematuria pattern and does not define the non-heavy protein range.
- C. Incorrect. These are heavy/nephrotic-range values.
- D. Incorrect. Anuria describes absent urine output, not proteinuria classification.
- E. Incorrect. These are normal or negative/trace values.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Non-heavy range: dipstick + or ++.
- Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio: 0.2–2.
- Interpret the amount of protein together with blood pressure, oedema, renal function and the clinical history.

questions.stem: A child continues to have protein detected on repeated urine testing after fever and dehydration have resolved. Which classification should now be considered rather than assuming a transient episode?
questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent proteinuria
questions.initialExplanation: Proteinuria that remains present on repeated testing after a transient provoking factor has resolved should be assessed as persistent proteinuria. clinical guidance classifies proteinuria by duration as transient or persistent.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Persistent proteinuria is the appropriate classification when repeated abnormal findings continue.
- B. Incorrect. Orthostatic proteinuria requires demonstration of the positional pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Sterile pyuria is white cells in urine with a negative culture.
- D. Incorrect. A transient episode should resolve after the provoking factor has passed.
- E. Incorrect. Haemoglobinuria is free haemoglobin in urine, not persistent urinary protein.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Proteinuria classification includes duration, amount and origin.
- Persistent proteinuria requires appropriate renal assessment rather than automatic reassurance.
- Consider blood pressure, oedema, renal function, urine microscopy and quantitative protein measurement.

cases.title: Protein in the daytime sample
cases.vignette: A healthy 11-year-old boy is referred after two school urine dipsticks show protein. He has no oedema, haematuria, urinary symptoms or recent illness. His blood pressure, serum creatinine and examination are normal. A urine sample collected immediately after waking is negative for protein, while a sample obtained after several hours upright is positive.

questions.stem: Which explanation best fits the difference between the morning and daytime urine samples?
questions.correctAnswerText: Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria
questions.initialExplanation: Protein appears when the child is upright but disappears or markedly decreases in the supine, early-morning sample. This is the characteristic pattern of orthostatic proteinuria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Persistent glomerulonephritis — Incorrect. Persistent glomerular disease would not be expected to produce this isolated posture-dependent pattern with otherwise normal findings.
- B. Nephrotic syndrome — Incorrect. This would usually produce heavy, persistent proteinuria and often oedema or hypoalbuminaemia.
- C. Orthostatic proteinuria — Correct. Protein excretion occurs during the upright position and decreases or disappears while supine.
- D. Pyelonephritis — Incorrect. Fever, systemic illness, urinary symptoms or inflammatory urine findings would be expected.
- E. Renal tubular acidosis — Incorrect. It causes acid–base and tubular abnormalities, not isolated postural proteinuria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Orthostatic proteinuria is common in school-age children.
- Blood pressure, renal function and examination are usually normal.
- Compare early-morning supine urine with a sample obtained after the child has been upright.

questions.stem: Which finding would most strongly support reassurance rather than an extensive renal investigation in a child with a single episode of mild proteinuria during a febrile illness?

options.label: A
options.text: Proteinuria that disappears after the fever resolves, with no renal symptoms

options.label: E
options.text: Persistent proteinuria in repeated early-morning samples

questions.correctAnswerText: Proteinuria that disappears after the fever resolves, with no renal symptoms
questions.initialExplanation: Transient proteinuria may occur with fever, exercise, dehydration, heart failure or seizures. It is usually self-limiting and does not require a full renal evaluation when it resolves and there are no concerning findings.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. A temporary mild finding during fever that resolves is consistent with transient proteinuria.
- B. Incorrect. Heavy proteinuria with oedema requires assessment for nephrotic syndrome.
- C. Incorrect. Hypertension and impaired renal function are warning signs.
- D. Incorrect. Gross haematuria and red-cell casts suggest glomerular disease.
- E. Incorrect. Persistent early-morning proteinuria is not the typical benign orthostatic pattern and requires further assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Transient causes: fever, exercise, heart failure, dehydration and seizures.
- Clinical guidance transient proteinuria as usually mild (+ or ++), benign and self-limiting.

questions.stem: A child has a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.12 and a negative-to-trace dipstick result. How should this result be interpreted using clinical guidance's reference values?
questions.correctAnswerText: Within the stated normal range
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance gives a normal urine protein-to-creatinine ratio below 0.2 and a dipstick result of negative or trace.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Nephrotic-range proteinuria is associated with a much higher ratio.
- B. Incorrect. The given result does not indicate heavy protein loss.
- C. Incorrect. Steroid resistance is a treatment-response category and cannot be diagnosed from this result.
- D. Correct. Both the ratio and dipstick result fall within the reference values.
- E. Incorrect. The result does not establish tubular protein loss.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal 24-hour urinary protein: less than 150 mg/day.
- Normal urine protein-to-creatinine ratio: less than 0.2.
- Normal dipstick: negative or trace.

questions.stem: Which combination best represents nephrotic-range protein loss in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Dipstick negative, ratio below 0.2 and less than 150 mg/day

options.label: E
options.text: Dipstick +++ or more, ratio above 2 and more than 40 mg/m²/day

questions.correctAnswerText: Dipstick +++ or more, ratio above 2 and more than 40 mg/m²/day
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies +++ or more on dipstick, a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio above 2 and urinary protein above 40 mg/m²/day as nephrotic-range findings.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are normal-range values.
- B. Incorrect. These values fall within the non-nephrotic range.
- C. Incorrect. Trace protein alone does not meet the heavy-proteinuria threshold.
- D. Incorrect. Haematuria is not a measurement of protein excretion.
- E. Correct. All three findings indicate heavy/nephrotic-range proteinuria.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Non-nephrotic range: dipstick + or ++, ratio 0.2–2 and 4–40 mg/m²/day.
- Nephrotic range: dipstick +++ or more, ratio above 2 and more than 40 mg/m²/day.

topics.name: Estimating Glomerular Filtration Rate in Children

cases.title: Estimating renal filtration in a growing child
cases.vignette: A child with a renal disorder has serum creatinine measured during follow-up. The clinician explains that renal filtration changes with age and that height and serum creatinine are used in the paediatric Schwartz estimate.

questions.stem: Which combination of variables is used in the Schwartz formula for estimating GFR in children, as presented?

options.label: A
options.text: Blood pressure multiplied by haemoglobin, divided by height

options.label: B
options.text: Weight multiplied by serum sodium, divided by blood urea

options.label: C
options.text: Serum albumin multiplied by urine glucose, divided by body surface area

options.label: D
options.text: Urine volume multiplied by serum potassium, divided by age

options.label: E
options.text: Height multiplied by an age-related constant, divided by serum creatinine

questions.correctAnswerText: Height multiplied by an age-related constant, divided by serum creatinine
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance presents the Schwartz estimate as height multiplied by a constant (K), divided by serum creatinine. The value of K varies with age in the supplied table.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Blood pressure and haemoglobin are not components of the equation.
- B. Incorrect. Weight, sodium and urea are not the variables in the formula presented.
- C. Incorrect. Albumin and urine glucose are not the variables in the Schwartz estimate.
- D. Incorrect. Urine volume and potassium are not used in the Schwartz equation.
- E. Correct. Height, an age-related constant and serum creatinine are the variables shown.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Schwartz estimate: height × K / serum creatinine.
- Clinical guidance age-dependent K values.
- Check the original laboratory units and local equation convention before calculating an actual GFR; OCR extraction may misread units and constants.

cases.title: Topic Questions (No Shared Case Text in Source)

questions.stem: Which statement best defines a vaccine?

options.label: A
options.text: A preparation used to treat established viral infection

options.label: B
options.text: An antibiotic that directly kills bacteria in the bloodstream

options.label: C
options.text: A substance that stimulates the body's immune response

options.label: D
options.text: A substance that suppresses most immune responses

options.label: E
options.text: A product that provides immediate passive antibodies in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: A substance that stimulates the body's immune response
questions.initialExplanation: The source defines a vaccine as a substance that stimulates the body's immune response. Vaccines are used to induce active immunity and reduce the risk or severity of infectious disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vaccines are primarily preventive immunizing agents, not treatment for established viral illness.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics treat susceptible bacterial infections; they are not vaccines.
- C. Correct. This matches the definition in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Vaccination stimulates an antigen-specific immune response rather than suppressing immunity.
- E. Incorrect. Passive immunization provides ready-made antibodies; it is different from active vaccination.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vaccine = substance that stimulates the immune response.
- Active immunization stimulates the recipient's own immune response.
- Do not confuse vaccines with immunoglobulin or other passive antibody preparations.

questions.stem: Which group contains only live attenuated vaccines listed?

options.label: A
options.text: IPV, rabies, hepatitis A and injectable pertussis

options.label: B
options.text: MMR, BCG, oral polio (Sabin), varicella and rotavirus

options.label: C
options.text: Diphtheria toxoid, tetanus toxoid and pneumococcal polysaccharide

options.label: D
options.text: Hepatitis B recombinant vaccine and HPV recombinant vaccine

options.label: E
options.text: Inactivated pertussis, cholera and plague vaccines

questions.correctAnswerText: MMR, BCG, oral polio (Sabin), varicella and rotavirus
questions.initialExplanation: Live attenuated vaccines contain weakened organisms that can replicate in the host and stimulate immunity without causing the full disease in an immunocompetent recipient. The source lists MMR, BCG, Sabin OPV, varicella, rotavirus, yellow fever, intranasal influenza and typhoid among this group.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are examples of killed/inactivated vaccines.
- B. Correct. All five are listed in the live attenuated group.
- C. Incorrect. Diphtheria and tetanus are toxoid vaccines; pneumococcal vaccine is a subunit/conjugate vaccine.
- D. Incorrect. Hepatitis B and HPV are listed as recombinant vaccines.
- E. Incorrect. These are examples of inactivated vaccines, not live attenuated vaccines.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Live attenuated examples: MMR, BCG, OPV/Sabin, varicella, rotavirus, yellow fever, intranasal influenza and typhoid (as listed).
- Live organisms replicate in the host.
- Live vaccines require attention to immunodeficiency, immunosuppressive therapy and storage/handling.

questions.stem: A child is due for an inactivated polio vaccine. Which property distinguishes IPV from oral Sabin vaccine?

options.label: A
options.text: IPV is a toxoid made from detoxified bacterial toxin

options.label: B
options.text: IPV contains a live weakened virus that replicates in the intestine

options.label: C
options.text: IPV contains inactivated virus and cannot replicate in the host

options.label: D
options.text: IPV is a recombinant yeast-derived hepatitis antigen

options.label: E
options.text: IPV contains capsular polysaccharide linked to a carrier protein

questions.correctAnswerText: IPV contains inactivated virus and cannot replicate in the host
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance classifies IPV (Salk) as an inactivated polio vaccine given intramuscularly. OPV (Sabin) is live attenuated and given orally.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes a toxoid vaccine, such as diphtheria or tetanus.
- B. Incorrect. This describes live oral polio vaccine (OPV/Sabin).
- C. Correct. IPV is inactivated and cannot replicate in the host.
- D. Incorrect. This describes a recombinant vaccine concept, not IPV.
- E. Incorrect. This describes a conjugated polysaccharide vaccine.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- OPV/Sabin: live attenuated, oral.
- IPV/Salk: inactivated, intramuscular.
- The source notes IPV is included in Hexa and Penta combinations.

questions.stem: A vaccine is prepared by detoxifying a bacterial exotoxin and using it to stimulate protective antibodies. Which vaccine type is this?
questions.correctAnswerText: Toxoid vaccine
questions.initialExplanation: Toxoid vaccines are prepared from toxins that have been detoxified. clinical guidance gives diphtheria and tetanus as examples and describes toxoid vaccines as effective and safe immunizing agents.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Conjugate vaccines link a polysaccharide antigen to a carrier protein.
- B. Incorrect. Recombinant vaccines use cloned genes for selected antigens.
- C. Incorrect. Live attenuated vaccines contain weakened organisms.
- D. Incorrect. Inactivated whole-virus vaccines contain killed virus rather than detoxified toxin.
- E. Correct. Detoxified exotoxin is a toxoid.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Toxoid = detoxified toxin.
- Examples in the source: diphtheria and tetanus.
- Toxoid vaccines induce antitoxin immunity.

questions.stem: A child receives a vaccine made by linking a bacterial capsular polysaccharide to a carrier protein to improve immunogenicity. Which vaccine principle is being used?
questions.correctAnswerText: Conjugated vaccine
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes a conjugate vaccine as a special type of subunit vaccine in which a polysaccharide is linked to a carrier protein to enhance the immune response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Passive immunization supplies ready-made antibodies rather than stimulating active immunity.
- B. Incorrect. Live attenuated vaccines use weakened organisms.
- C. Incorrect. Toxoid vaccines use detoxified exotoxins.
- D. Incorrect. Inactivated whole-cell vaccines use killed organisms.
- E. Correct. Linking the polysaccharide to a carrier protein improves the immune response.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Conjugate vaccine = polysaccharide linked to carrier protein.
- The source gives meningococcal and pneumococcal vaccines as examples.
- Conjugation improves the immunogenicity of polysaccharide antigens.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched with the vaccine technology described?

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatitis B - recombinant vaccine; Diphtheria - toxoid vaccine

options.label: B
options.text: Hepatitis B - live attenuated; Diphtheria - recombinant vaccine

options.label: E
options.text: MMR - killed vaccine; Rabies - live attenuated

questions.correctAnswerText: Hepatitis B - recombinant vaccine; Diphtheria - toxoid vaccine
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance hepatitis B and HPV vaccines as recombinant vaccines and diphtheria/tetanus vaccines as toxoids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Both vaccine types are matched correctly.
- B. Incorrect. Hepatitis B is listed as recombinant, while diphtheria is a toxoid.
- C. Incorrect. OPV is live attenuated; tetanus is a toxoid.
- D. Incorrect. BCG is live attenuated, and HPV is recombinant.
- E. Incorrect. MMR is live attenuated and rabies is listed as inactivated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Recombinant examples: hepatitis B and HPV.
- Toxoid examples: diphtheria and tetanus.
- Combination vaccines include MMR, DPT, DT and Hexa in the source.
- Polyvalent vaccines include more than one strain/serotype of the same species.

cases.title: A newborn attends the clinic for the first routine vaccines
cases.vignette: A healthy newborn is brought to the vaccination clinic shortly after delivery. The parent asks which vaccines are due at birth and how they are administered.

questions.stem: According to the routine schedule table, which vaccines are due at birth?
questions.correctAnswerText: BCG, OPV and hepatitis B
questions.initialExplanation: The routine Libya schedule table lists BCG, OPV and hepatitis B at birth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the three vaccines listed at birth.
- B. Incorrect. MMR, meningococcal and PCV are scheduled later.
- C. Incorrect. Tdap and HPV are adolescent vaccines in the table.
- D. Incorrect. Hexa, rotavirus and PCV are scheduled from 2 months.
- E. Incorrect. Penta and MMR are later infant doses; varicella appears at 15 months and 6 years in the schedule.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Birth schedule: BCG + OPV + HepB.
- Do not confuse the birth OPV dose with the later 9-month OPV dose.
- Use the routine schedule table when answering schedule-specific questions.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant attends for routine immunization. Which group is listed in the schedule?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hexa, rotavirus and PCV
questions.initialExplanation: The 2-month visit in the routine table includes Hexa (DPT + HepB + Hib + IPV), rotavirus and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. All three are listed at 2 months.
- B. Incorrect. BCG and the initial OPV/HepB are listed at birth; Tdap is at 15 years.
- C. Incorrect. Tetra and HPV are later childhood/adolescent vaccines.
- D. Incorrect. These are later vaccines.
- E. Incorrect. Penta is listed at 18 months; MMR at 12 and 18 months.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- At 2 months: Hexa + Rota + PCV.
- Hexa = DPT + HepB + Hib + IPV.
- The same three-vaccine group is listed again at 4 months.

questions.stem: Which routine vaccines are listed at both the 4-month and 6-month visits in the schedule table?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hexa and rotavirus
questions.initialExplanation: The schedule table lists Hexa and rotavirus at both 4 and 6 months. PCV is also listed at 4 months, but it is not shown in the 6-month row of the table.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. MMR and varicella are later vaccines.
- B. Incorrect. BCG and hepatitis B are listed at birth.
- C. Incorrect. These are later childhood/adolescent vaccines.
- D. Correct. Hexa and rotavirus appear at both visits.
- E. Incorrect. Hepatitis A and HPV are later.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 4 months: Hexa + Rota + PCV.
- 6 months: Hexa + Rota in the table.
- Schedule questions should be answered from the relevant row, not by assuming every earlier vaccine repeats.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant attends for immunization. Which pair is listed in the routine schedule?
