questions.correctAnswerText: Meningococcal vaccine and OPV
questions.initialExplanation: The 9-month row lists meningococcal vaccine (ACYW135) and OPV.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Penta is at 18 months and Tdap at 15 years.
- B. Incorrect. MMR and PCV are listed at 12 months.
- C. Incorrect. Hexa and rotavirus are listed at 2, 4 and 6 months.
- D. Correct. These are the vaccines listed at 9 months.
- E. Incorrect. Hepatitis A and varicella are listed at 15 months.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 9 months: meningococcal ACYW135 + OPV.
- OPV is oral; meningococcal vaccine is listed as an injection.
- A later meningococcal dose is listed at 12 months.

questions.stem: Which group correctly represents the routine 12-month vaccines in the schedule table?
questions.correctAnswerText: Meningococcal ACYW135, MMR and PCV
questions.initialExplanation: The 12-month row lists meningococcal vaccine, MMR and pneumococcal vaccine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are birth vaccines.
- B. Correct. These three are listed at 12 months.
- C. Incorrect. These are early infant vaccines.
- D. Incorrect. Varicella and hepatitis A are listed at 15 months; Tdap at 15 years.
- E. Incorrect. Penta is at 18 months; HPV at 12 years.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 12 months: meningococcal + MMR + PCV.
- MMR is listed again at 18 months.
- PCV appears at 2, 4 and 12 months in the routine schedule.

questions.stem: Which pair is listed at 15 months in the routine schedule?
questions.correctAnswerText: Chickenpox (varicella) and hepatitis A
questions.initialExplanation: The schedule table lists chickenpox vaccine and hepatitis A vaccine at 15 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hexa and rotavirus are earlier infant vaccines.
- B. Incorrect. Tetra is at 6 years and HPV at 12 years.
- C. Incorrect. MMR and meningococcal are listed at 12 months; MMR also at 18 months.
- D. Correct. Both appear in the 15-month row.
- E. Incorrect. These are listed at birth.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 15 months: varicella + hepatitis A.
- Hepatitis A booster interval is described separately on page 10.
- Varicella appears again at 6 years in the routine table.

questions.stem: Which schedule statement is correct for later childhood and adolescence according to the table?

options.label: A
options.text: At 6 years: Tetra and chickenpox; at 12 years: meningococcal and HPV; at 15 years: Tdap

options.label: B
options.text: At 6 years: BCG; at 12 years: Penta; at 15 years: varicella

options.label: C
options.text: At 6 years: HepA and MMR; at 12 years: BCG; at 15 years: OPV

options.label: D
options.text: At 6 years: MMR; at 12 years: HepB; at 15 years: influenza

options.label: E
options.text: At 6 years: Hexa; at 12 years: rotavirus; at 15 years: PCV

questions.correctAnswerText: At 6 years: Tetra and chickenpox; at 12 years: meningococcal and HPV; at 15 years: Tdap
questions.initialExplanation: These are the later-age vaccines listed in the routine schedule table.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the 6-, 12- and 15-year rows.
- B. Incorrect. These are not the listed later-age groups.
- C. Incorrect. These pairings do not match the schedule.
- D. Incorrect. The table lists more than one vaccine at 6 and 12 years and specifically lists Tdap at 15 years.
- E. Incorrect. These vaccines are scheduled at different ages.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- 6 years: Tetra (DPT + IPV) + chickenpox.
- 12 years: meningococcal ACYW135 + HPV.
- 15 years: Tdap.
- Tetra and Penta are different combinations in the source.

cases.title: Why does one vaccine need one dose and another needs a series
cases.vignette: A primary care center is running the routine infant and toddler immunization session. Parents and a trainee nurse ask a series of questions about how different vaccines are built and why their schedules differ.

questions.stem: A mother brings her 2-month-old daughter for the first Hexa, PCV and rotavirus visit. She remembers that her 4-year-old son received BCG as a single injection at birth, and she asks why the baby will need three doses of Hexa and later boosters to be protected. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Hexa is a live attenuated vaccine, so each dose must be repeated to replace the organisms that the host rapidly clears from the body after injection

options.label: B
options.text: BCG is an inactivated vaccine, and inactivated vaccines give lifelong immunity after a single injection, so one dose is typically enough

options.label: C
options.text: Intradermal vaccines typically protect after a single dose, whereas intramuscular vaccines not usually do, whatever kind of antigen they contain

options.label: D
options.text: BCG is live and multiplies in the host, giving a larger antigenic dose than injected, whereas Hexa's non-replicating antigens need repeated doses as titers may fall

options.label: E
options.text: Combination vaccines such as Hexa need repeated doses because mixing several antigens in one syringe cancels out their immune effect

questions.correctAnswerText: BCG is live and multiplies in the host, giving a larger antigenic dose than injected, whereas Hexa's non-replicating antigens need repeated doses as titers may fall
questions.initialExplanation: Live attenuated vaccine organisms multiply in the host, so the antigenic dose the immune system sees is larger than what was injected, and one dose is usually enough (oral vaccines are the exception). Killed/inactivated and other non-replicating antigens cannot multiply, so they usually need several doses, and antibody titers may diminish with time.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical reasoning here is to ask "does the antigen replicate in the host?" before asking how many doses are needed. The mother compares a live vaccine (BCG) with a multi-antigen vaccine whose components cannot replicate.

- A. Incorrect. Hexa is DPT + hepatitis B + Hib + IPV. None of these is a live replicating vaccine, so the idea that organisms must be "replaced" after being cleared reverses the real mechanism.
- B. Incorrect. BCG is listed among the live attenuated vaccines. Killed/inactivated vaccines are the ones that generally need multiple doses and whose titers can wane.
- C. Incorrect. The number of doses follows the nature of the antigen (replicating or not), not the route. Note also that clinical guidance excepts oral live vaccines from the "one dose" rule, so even live vaccines are not always single-dose.
- D. Correct. This links BCG (live, replicates, larger antigenic dose, usually one dose) with Hexa's non-replicating antigens (multiple doses, titers may diminish, hence boosters later in the schedule).
- E. Incorrect. clinical guidance gives the purpose of combination vaccines as simplifying administration, reducing cost and minimizing the number of contacts with the health system. It does not state that antigens cancel each other.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Live attenuated: replicate in the host, larger antigenic dose than injected, carry all major and minor antigenic components, severe reactions are possible, fragile (careful storage), usually one dose except oral vaccines.
- Killed/inactivated: killed by heat or chemicals, cannot replicate, generally less effective than live vaccines, antibody titers may diminish with time, usually safe, usually need multiple doses.
- This difference explains the primary series plus boosters used for DPT-containing vaccines in the schedule.

questions.stem: At the 9-month visit an infant receives the meningococcal vaccine (ACYW135). A trainee tells the parents that this vaccine, and the 13-valent pneumococcal vaccine the baby received earlier, are both "combination vaccines, just like Hexa". The supervising pediatrician corrects her. Which statement is the most accurate correction?

options.label: A
options.text: They are polyvalent, not combination, vaccines: each covers several strains of one species and uses polysaccharide antigens linked to a carrier protein

options.label: B
options.text: They are combination vaccines, because each one protects against several different diseases with a single injection given to the infant at one visit

options.label: C
options.text: They are live attenuated polyvalent vaccines, which is why they need especially careful storage and handling in the cold chain system

options.label: D
options.text: They are recombinant vaccines produced by cloning selected antigen genes into yeast cells, in the same way as the hepatitis B vaccine

options.label: E
options.text: They are toxoid vaccines made from detoxified bacterial exotoxins that stimulate antitoxin antibodies, as diphtheria and tetanus vaccines do

questions.correctAnswerText: They are polyvalent, not combination, vaccines: each covers several strains of one species and uses polysaccharide antigens linked to a carrier protein
questions.initialExplanation: A combination vaccine joins different antigens (different diseases) in one product, as Hexa does. Meningococcal ACYW135 and PCV13 are polyvalent, because each covers several groups or serotypes of one species, and they are conjugated polysaccharide (subunit) vaccines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The trainee's error is confusing "many antigens in one syringe" with "many strains of the same organism". The Hexa example (DPT + HepB + Hib + IPV) contains different diseases; the meningococcal vaccine contains groups A, C, Y and W135 of one species, and PCV13 contains 13 serotypes of Streptococcus pneumoniae.

- A. Correct. It separates polyvalent from combination and adds the subunit/conjugation principle: bacterial polysaccharide antigens give antibody with less functional activity, and conjugation to a carrier protein improves immunogenicity.
- B. Incorrect. This describes combination vaccines (Hexa, MMR, DPT, DT). Each of these two vaccines targets one organism, not several diseases.
- C. Incorrect. Both are given intramuscularly and are not in the live attenuated list; polyvalent describes strain coverage, not viability.
- D. Incorrect. The recombinant examples are hepatitis B and HPV vaccines.
- E. Incorrect. Toxoid vaccines (diphtheria, tetanus) are made from detoxified exotoxin, which is unrelated to capsular or cell-wall polysaccharides.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Combination vaccine = different antigens in one product (MMR, DPT, DT, Hexa). Reasons: simplify administration, reduce costs, minimize contacts with the health system.
- Polyvalent vaccine = more than one strain of the same species (OPV, rotavirus, meningococcal A/C/Y/W135, PCV with 13 serotypes).
- Plain polysaccharide antigens produce antibody with less functional activity; conjugation to a carrier protein improves immunogenicity.

source.raw: Pediatric Vaccination sheet - Page 3 (Subunit vaccines; Combination vaccines; Polyvalent vaccine; Conjugated vaccine); Page 4 (Hexa composition; meningococcal vaccine in the schedule).

cases.title: A school-entry immunization review
cases.vignette: A school health clinic reviews the immunization records of children entering primary school and children with pertussis-like illness. The team uses the routine schedule table and the DPT/pertussis section together.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy attends for school-entry immunization. His card shows every dose given on time: BCG, OPV and hepatitis B at birth; Hexa at 2, 4 and 6 months; Penta together with MMR at 18 months. Today he is due for Tetra and the second varicella dose. His mother asks whether he will still need any diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis-containing injection later, and why Tetra does not include hepatitis B. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Today's Tetra is his third booster, so no further pertussis-containing dose of any kind will be needed after today

options.label: B
options.text: Today's Tetra is his first booster, because the 18-month Penta counted as the third primary dose of his primary series

options.label: C
options.text: Today's Tetra is his second booster and contains DPT, Hib and hepatitis B components, exactly like the Hexa he received in infancy

options.label: D
options.text: Today's Tetra is his second booster and replaces Tdap, so no DPT-containing vaccine will be due at 15 years of age

options.label: E
options.text: Today's Tetra is his second booster and contains DPT and IPV (hepatitis B series already complete); Tdap is still due at 15 years

questions.correctAnswerText: Today's Tetra is his second booster and contains DPT and IPV (hepatitis B series already complete); Tdap is still due at 15 years
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance DPT as "3 doses and 3 boosters". In the Libya schedule the three primary doses are the Hexa doses at 2, 4 and 6 months, and the three boosters are Penta (18 months), Tetra (6 years) and Tdap (15 years). Tetra is DPT + IPV only.
questions.detailedExplanation:
To answer, build the child's timeline: primary series = Hexa x3; booster 1 = Penta at 18 months; booster 2 = Tetra today; booster 3 = Tdap at 15 years. Then compare the composition of each product.

- A. Incorrect. Tdap at 15 years is a separate booster listed in the schedule, so today's dose is the second booster, not the third.
- B. Incorrect. The 18-month Penta is a booster after the three primary Hexa doses.
- C. Incorrect. Hexa = DPT + HepB + Hib + IPV; Penta = DPT + Hib + IPV; Tetra = DPT + IPV only. Tetra has no Hib or hepatitis B component.
- D. Incorrect. The 15-year visit lists Tdap, so a further DPT-type booster remains.
- E. Correct. The hepatitis B series is already four doses (birth dose plus three Hexa doses), and Tetra contains only DPT and IPV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DPT: 3 primary doses + 3 boosters, mapped to Hexa (2, 4, 6 months), Penta (18 months), Tetra (6 years) and Tdap (15 years).
- Hexa = DPT + HepB + Hib + IPV; Penta = DPT + Hib + IPV; Tetra = DPT + IPV. Penta lacks HepB; Tetra lacks both HepB and Hib.
- Hepatitis B: birth dose + Hexa doses at 2, 4, 6 months = 4 doses.

source.raw: Pediatric Vaccination sheet - Page 4 (routine schedule table and combination compositions); Page 7 (DPT: 3 doses and 3 boosters; replaced by Hexa); Page 8 (hepatitis B: 4 doses in total).

cases.title: A child has a mild cold on the day of vaccination
cases.vignette: A 14-month-old child is brought for scheduled vaccination. The child has mild rhinorrhoea but is active, feeding normally and has no significant fever. The parent asks whether vaccination must be postponed because the child is unwell.

questions.stem: Which condition is specifically listed as not being a contraindication to vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Severe generalized reaction to the preceding dose of the same vaccine

options.label: B
options.text: Pregnancy before a live attenuated vaccine

options.label: C
options.text: Severe acute febrile illness requiring medical treatment

options.label: E
options.text: Known severe immunodeficiency before a live attenuated vaccine

questions.correctAnswerText: Mild common cold
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists a mild common cold as a condition that is not a contraindication to vaccination. It also lists prematurity, breastfeeding, mild local reaction to a previous dose, family history of allergy/eczema/asthma and antibiotic treatment as conditions that are not contraindications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Severe local or general reaction to a preceding dose is listed among contraindications to routine active immunization.
- B. Incorrect. Pregnancy is listed as a contraindication to live attenuated vaccines.
- C. Incorrect. Acute febrile illness requiring medical treatment is listed as a reason to defer routine active immunization.
- D. Correct. Mild common cold is explicitly listed as not a contraindication.
- E. Incorrect. Immunodeficiency is a contraindication to live attenuated vaccines.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mild common cold is not a contraindication.
- Prematurity, breastfeeding and a family history of atopy are not contraindications in the source.
- Distinguish a mild intercurrent illness from significant acute illness.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed as a contraindication to routine active immunization in the general section of clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Mild local reaction to a previous dose

options.label: D
options.text: Acute febrile illness with malaise and symptoms requiring medical treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Acute febrile illness with malaise and symptoms requiring medical treatment
questions.initialExplanation: The source's general contraindications section lists acute febrile illness, malaise, cough, diarrhea or other symptoms requiring medical treatment, and a severe local or general reaction to a preceding dose of the same vaccine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A mild local reaction is specifically listed as not a contraindication.
- B. Incorrect. Family history of allergy, eczema or asthma is not a contraindication.
- C. Incorrect. Prematurity and IUGR are not contraindications.
- D. Correct. This matches the general contraindication listed.
- E. Incorrect. Breastfeeding is listed as not a contraindication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- General deferral criteria include significant acute illness requiring medical treatment.
- Severe reaction to a previous dose is a separate concern.
- Mild illness should not be confused with significant febrile illness.

questions.stem: A child with a significant cellular immunodeficiency is due for MMR and varicella vaccines. Which principle applies?

options.label: B
options.text: most live vaccines should be given at double dose

options.label: C
options.text: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in immunodeficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Live vaccines are safe during chemotherapy

options.label: E
options.text: Immunodeficiency is a contraindication to inactivated vaccines

questions.correctAnswerText: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in immunodeficiency
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists humoral, cellular or combined immunodeficiency (primary or secondary, including HIV) as a contraindication to live attenuated vaccines. It also lists malignancy, immunosuppressive treatment, pregnancy and very severe protein-energy malnutrition.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The restriction is not limited to toxoid vaccines.
- B. Incorrect. Increasing the dose does not make a live vaccine safe in immunodeficiency.
- C. Correct. This is the stated principle in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Chemotherapy/immunosuppressive treatment is listed as a contraindication to live attenuated vaccines.
- E. Incorrect. The source specifically identifies live attenuated vaccines as the concern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Live attenuated vaccines require assessment of immune status.
- Clinical guidance primary/secondary immunodeficiency, malignancy and immunosuppressive treatment.
- Pregnancy is also listed as a contraindication to live attenuated vaccines.
- Check the vaccine-specific information and treating specialist advice in clinical practice.

questions.stem: Which group contains only conditions clinical guidance identifies as not being contraindications?

options.label: A
options.text: Severe anaphylaxis to a previous dose, acute febrile illness and cellular immunodeficiency

options.label: C
options.text: Mild common cold, mild local reaction to a previous dose, breastfeeding and prematurity

options.label: D
options.text: Severe generalized reaction and uncontrolled neurological disease

options.label: E
options.text: Severe acute illness and known anaphylaxis to a vaccine component

questions.correctAnswerText: Mild common cold, mild local reaction to a previous dose, breastfeeding and prematurity
questions.initialExplanation: The source explicitly lists mild common cold, mild local reaction to a previous dose, family history of allergy/eczema/asthma, antibiotic course, prematurity/IUGR, breastfeeding, congenital heart disease/chronic chest disease, Down syndrome and family history of SIDS as not contraindications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are significant contraindications/precautions in the source.
- B. Incorrect. These are contraindications to live attenuated vaccines.
- C. Correct. All four are listed as not contraindications.
- D. Incorrect. Severe reaction and progressive neurological disease are listed as contraindications for relevant vaccines.
- E. Incorrect. Severe acute illness and anaphylaxis are important contraindications.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- False contraindications in the source include mild cold, prematurity, breastfeeding and family history of atopy.
- A child should not miss vaccination for minor conditions listed as non-contraindications.
- Distinguish vaccine-specific contraindications from general precautions.

cases.title: A morning clinic for children due for live vaccines
cases.vignette: A pediatric clinic reviews several children who are due for live attenuated vaccines. For each, the physician must decide whether the history is a true contraindication or only a false one.

questions.stem: Five children are reviewed on the same morning for MMR. Which child can receive the vaccine today?

options.label: A
options.text: A 5-year-old girl with acute lymphoblastic leukemia in remission, clinically well, whose last chemotherapy cycle ended 3 months ago

options.label: B
options.text: A 7-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome, afebrile, who has been receiving large daily doses of prednisolone continuously for the last 3 months

options.label: C
options.text: A 14-month-old with mild-to-moderate undernutrition and mild coryza, finishing oral antibiotics for otitis media; he is afebrile, and his father has asthma

options.label: D
options.text: A 4-year-old boy who had a bone marrow transplant 4 months ago and is now clinically well with no current infection

options.label: E
options.text: An 18-month-old girl with very severe protein-energy malnutrition who is afebrile and has no other acute illness at present

questions.correctAnswerText: A 14-month-old with mild-to-moderate undernutrition and mild coryza, finishing oral antibiotics for otitis media; he is afebrile, and his father has asthma
questions.initialExplanation: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in immunodeficiency, malignancy, immunosuppression (bone marrow transplant, chemotherapy or radiotherapy within 6 months, large prolonged corticosteroid doses), pregnancy and very severe protein-energy malnutrition. A mild cold, an antibiotic course and a family history of asthma are not contraindications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Each option hides one item from the live-vaccine contraindication list; only option C contains items that clinical guidance explicitly says are not contraindications.

- A. Incorrect. Chemotherapy within the last 6 months is a listed contraindication, and leukemia is a listed malignant condition.
- B. Incorrect. A large, prolonged corticosteroid dose is a listed immunosuppressant contraindication.
- C. Correct. Mild respiratory symptoms, an antibiotic course and a family history of asthma are listed as non-contraindications. Protein-energy malnutrition counts only if it is very severe, and this child is mild-to-moderate.
- D. Incorrect. Bone marrow transplantation within the last 6 months is a listed contraindication.
- E. Incorrect. Severe protein-energy malnutrition is listed as a contraindication only when very severe, which describes this child.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Contraindications to live vaccines: humoral, cellular or combined immunodeficiency (primary or secondary, e.g., HIV); leukemia and Hodgkin disease; BM transplant, chemotherapy or radiotherapy within 6 months; large prolonged corticosteroid dose; pregnancy; protein-energy malnutrition only if very severe.
- Not contraindications: mild cold, mild local reaction to a previous dose, family history of allergy/eczema/asthma, antibiotic course, prematurity/IUGR, breastfeeding.
- Do not withhold vaccines for false contraindications, and do not give live vaccines inside the 6-month window after chemotherapy or transplant.

source.raw: Pediatric Vaccination sheet - Page 5 (Contraindication to live attenuated vaccines; Conditions which are not contraindications).

questions.stem: A 12-month-old infant with HIV infection is clinically stable and asymptomatic on antiretroviral therapy (ART). He missed BCG at birth because the diagnosis was made at 2 months. Today the mother asks whether he can receive MMR and the BCG he missed. Which plan is consistent with clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Give MMR, because HIV on ART is the stated exception, but not BCG, which is contraindicated in HIV infection even when asymptomatic

options.label: B
options.text: Give both BCG and MMR today, since the infant is clinically well and has no symptoms or signs of HIV-related disease

options.label: C
options.text: Withhold both vaccines, because each live vaccine is contraindicated in each HIV-infected child without any exception

options.label: D
options.text: Give BCG but withhold MMR, because BCG is the live vaccine that the sheet permits in HIV-infected children

options.label: E
options.text: Give BCG after a negative tuberculin test, because a negative Mantoux overrides the HIV contraindication, and withhold MMR

questions.correctAnswerText: Give MMR, because HIV on ART is the stated exception, but not BCG, which is contraindicated in HIV infection even when asymptomatic
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance immunocompromise as a contraindication to MMR "except HIV on ART", whereas for BCG it lists HIV infection, symptomatic or asymptomatic, as a contraindication.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Two live vaccines are being compared for the same child, and clinical guidance treats HIV differently for each. The trap is to apply the "asymptomatic means safe" reasoning to both vaccines, or the "immunocompromised means no live vaccine" reasoning to both.

- A. Correct. MMR has an explicit exception for HIV on ART; BCG has an explicit contraindication that includes asymptomatic infection.
- B. Incorrect. BCG is contraindicated in HIV whether symptomatic or asymptomatic. Disseminated BCG disease is a recognized complication in immunodeficient infants.
- C. Incorrect. MMR carries a specific exception for HIV on ART, so a blanket ban is not what Clinical guidance for MMR.
- D. Incorrect. This reverses clinical guidance: BCG is the one with the HIV contraindication.
- E. Incorrect. A negative tuberculin test is relevant to TB exposure (a positive test is itself a BCG contraindication), but it does not cancel the HIV contraindication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MMR: immunocompromised are contraindicated except HIV on ART.
- BCG: HIV infection (symptomatic or asymptomatic) is a contraindication; a positive Mantoux is also a contraindication.
- Disseminated BCG infection is a recognized complication in infants with immunodeficiency.

source.raw: Pediatric Vaccination sheet - Page 5 (BCG contraindications and complications); Page 8 (MMR contraindications).

cases.title: Allergy and antibody history before the 12-month visit
cases.vignette: At the 12-month visit (MMR, meningococcal, PCV) several toddlers have histories that need careful interpretation before MMR is given.

questions.stem: A 12-month-old boy attends for MMR, meningococcal and PCV. His mother reports that 2 months ago, minutes after eating scrambled egg for the first time, he developed lip swelling, generalized urticaria and wheezing and needed emergency treatment. He is afebrile, immunologically normal, has no known neomycin allergy, and has had no recent immunoglobulin. What is the most appropriate plan for MMR?

options.label: A
options.text: Cancel MMR permanently, because egg anaphylaxis is an absolute contraindication with no alternative approach

options.label: B
options.text: Give MMR immediately without further assessment, because egg allergy not usually affects MMR

options.label: C
options.text: Replace MMR with BCG, because BCG gives equivalent protection against measles

options.label: D
options.text: Perform a skin test first, and vaccinate after the skin test rather than giving the vaccine directly

options.label: E
options.text: Give MMR intradermally instead of subcutaneously, because the intradermal route prevents anaphylaxis

questions.correctAnswerText: Perform a skin test first, and vaccinate after the skin test rather than giving the vaccine directly
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance anaphylactic reaction to egg ingestion as a consideration for MMR, with vaccination after a skin test. Other contraindications (pregnancy, neomycin anaphylaxis, recent immunoglobulin, immunocompromise) are not present in this child.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The history (lip swelling, urticaria and wheeze within minutes of egg) is a convincing anaphylactic reaction. The question tests the "next best step" rather than the diagnosis.

- A. Incorrect. clinical guidance does not describe permanent exclusion; it describes vaccination after a skin test.
- B. Incorrect. Giving the vaccine directly ignores the specific precaution.
- C. Incorrect. BCG is a TB vaccine and gives no protection against measles, mumps or rubella.
- D. Correct. It follows clinical guidance's instruction: vaccinate after a skin test.
- E. Incorrect. The MMR route is subcutaneous. Intradermal administration is the BCG route, and no route is described as preventing anaphylaxis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MMR contraindications/precautions: pregnancy (risk of fetal damage), anaphylaxis to egg ingestion (vaccinated after skin test), anaphylactic allergy to neomycin, immunoglobulin within 3 months, immunocompromise except HIV on ART.
- MMR: 2 doses at 12 and 18 months, SC route.
- General safety principle (not stated ): vaccinate where anaphylaxis can be managed.

source.raw: Pediatric Vaccination sheet - Page 8 (MMR: schedule, route and contraindications).

questions.stem: An 11-month-old girl developed generalized urticaria, lip swelling and stridor minutes after receiving neomycin-containing ear drops. Her mother asks which of the upcoming routine vaccines need to be reconsidered because of this history. Which answer is consistent with clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: BCG and OPV, because live vaccines are the ones affected by an antibiotic allergy

options.label: B
options.text: MMR (12 and 18 months) and pertussis-containing vaccines such as Penta at 18 months

options.label: C
options.text: PCV and the meningococcal vaccine, because they are given at the next visit

options.label: D
options.text: the hepatitis A and varicella vaccines at 15 months, because these are given after the 12-month visit

options.label: E
options.text: None, because anaphylaxis to an antibiotic is not usually a reason to change any vaccine in the routine schedule

questions.correctAnswerText: MMR (12 and 18 months) and pertussis-containing vaccines such as Penta at 18 months
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance anaphylactic allergy to neomycin as a contraindication to MMR (the vaccine contains neomycin), and lists anaphylaxis to neomycin, streptomycin and polymyxin in the contraindications column for pertussis-containing vaccines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The approach is to identify the antigen-independent contraindication (a specific drug allergy) and search clinical guidance for every vaccine that lists it.

- A. Incorrect. BCG and OPV are not the vaccines for which neomycin anaphylaxis is listed.
- B. Correct. MMR lists neomycin anaphylaxis explicitly; the DPT/pertussis table lists anaphylaxis to neomycin, streptomycin and polymyxin. The next pertussis-containing doses are Penta (18 months), Tetra (6 years) and Tdap (15 years).
- C. Incorrect. Nothing ties PCV or the meningococcal vaccine to neomycin allergy.
- D. Incorrect. Hepatitis A and varicella vaccines are not the vaccines clinical guidance links to neomycin anaphylaxis, and this option leaves out MMR and the pertussis-containing vaccines that are.
- E. Incorrect. Anaphylaxis to specific antibiotics is listed as a contraindication for particular vaccines.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neomycin anaphylaxis: contraindication to MMR (the vaccine contains neomycin).
- Pertussis/DPT contraindications also include anaphylaxis to neomycin, streptomycin and polymyxin, previous post-vaccination anaphylaxis, uncontrolled convulsions, progressive neurological illness and non-minor acute febrile illness.
- Always ask about drug allergies, not only previous vaccine reactions.

source.raw: Pediatric Vaccination sheet - Page 7 (Pertussis contraindication table); Page 8 (MMR contraindications).

cases.title: A newborn is scheduled for BCG vaccination
cases.vignette: A newborn is brought for BCG vaccination. The nurse prepares the vaccine for intradermal administration in the upper arm. The parent asks about the expected local reaction and what would be considered a complication.

questions.stem: Which route and site are described for BCG administration?

options.label: A
options.text: Intradermal injection in the left upper arm over the deltoid region

options.label: C
options.text: Intramuscular injection in the gluteal region

questions.correctAnswerText: Intradermal injection in the left upper arm over the deltoid region
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance BCG as a live attenuated vaccine given intradermally, usually soon after birth, in the left upper arm over the deltoid insertion area.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the route and site described.
- B. Incorrect. The source specifies intradermal administration in the upper arm.
- C. Incorrect. BCG is not administered intramuscularly in the gluteal region.
- D. Incorrect. BCG is not an intravenous vaccine.
- E. Incorrect. Oral administration is used for OPV and rotavirus, not BCG.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- BCG = live attenuated vaccine.
- Route: intradermal.
- Site: left upper arm over deltoid insertion region.
- The routine schedule table specifies neonatal BCG at birth.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed as a contraindication to BCG in the vaccine-specific section?

options.label: C
options.text: HIV infection, whether symptomatic or asymptomatic

questions.correctAnswerText: HIV infection, whether symptomatic or asymptomatic
questions.initialExplanation: The BCG section lists a positive tuberculin test and HIV infection (symptomatic or asymptomatic) as contraindications, in addition to the general contraindications to live attenuated vaccines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Breastfeeding is listed as not a contraindication.
- B. Incorrect. Family history of allergy/eczema/asthma is not a contraindication.
- C. Correct. This is explicitly listed in the BCG-specific section.
- D. Incorrect. Prematurity/IUGR is listed as not a contraindication to vaccination generally.
- E. Incorrect. Mild common cold is listed as not a contraindication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- BCG is live attenuated.
- Clinical guidance tuberculin positivity and HIV infection as BCG contraindications.
- Assess immune status before administering a live vaccine.

questions.stem: A child develops marked regional lymph node enlargement with a cold abscess and sinus after BCG vaccination. Which complication is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Suppurative BCG lymphadenitis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance regional suppurative lymphadenitis, cold abscess and tuberculous sinus among BCG complications. It also notes BCG-oma when the vaccine is given subcutaneously and disseminated BCG infection in immunocompromised infants.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Regional suppurative lymphadenitis with cold abscess/sinus is a recognized BCG complication listed.
- B. Incorrect. Anaphylaxis is an immediate allergic reaction and is not the described local BCG complication.
- C. Incorrect. This is not a recognized complication described for BCG.
- D. Incorrect. Intussusception is not listed as a BCG complication.
- E. Incorrect. Vaccine-associated paralytic polio is associated with OPV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- BCG local effects include papule/ulcer and scar formation.
- Complications include regional suppurative lymphadenitis and cold abscess.
- Disseminated BCG infection is a concern in immunocompromised infants.
- Subcutaneous administration may cause BCG-oma.

questions.stem: A parent is worried because the child has no visible BCG scar. Which statement is supported by clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: BCG should be repeated in the same arm without assessment

options.label: B
options.text: Absence of scar proves severe immunodeficiency

options.label: C
options.text: Absence of a scar does not necessarily mean that the child failed to respond to BCG

options.label: D
options.text: children in routine care without a scar must immediately receive multiple booster doses

options.label: E
options.text: A BCG scar must appear within 24 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Absence of a scar does not necessarily mean that the child failed to respond to BCG
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that a scar appears in most, but not all, vaccinated individuals. It states that absence of a visible reaction does not itself prove lack of response. It describes tuberculin testing and a possible repeat dose if the test is negative.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Clinical guidance assessment and, if indicated, a second dose in the right arm.
- B. Incorrect. Absence of a scar alone does not diagnose immunodeficiency.
- C. Correct. This is the specific caution in the source.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance does not recommend multiple automatic boosters.
- E. Incorrect. BCG reactions evolve over weeks, not within 24 hours.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- A visible BCG scar is common but not universal.
- No scar alone does not establish vaccine failure.
- The source describes a tuberculin skin test before considering revaccination.
- The source specifies that a second dose, if given, is placed in the right arm.

cases.title: A family affected by tuberculosis
cases.vignette: A child vaccinated with BCG is seen in a family where an adult has confirmed pulmonary TB, and a younger infant has no visible BCG scar.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. His wife brings their 3-year-old son, who received BCG at birth and has a typical scar, and says: "My husband was vaccinated as a child and still developed lung TB, so BCG must be useless for our son too." Which statement should the pediatrician make?

options.label: A
options.text: BCG gives complete protection against most forms of TB, so the husband's illness cannot be tuberculosis at most and must be something else

options.label: B
options.text: BCG protects against pulmonary TB in adults and gives no protection to young children against TB meningitis at most

options.label: C
options.text: BCG is about 70-80% effective against severe forms such as TB meningitis in children, but less effective against respiratory disease

options.label: D
options.text: BCG is effective against respiratory disease if it is repeated each 5 years, given in the same arm each time

options.label: E
options.text: A visible BCG scar proves lifelong protection against respiratory TB, so the child needs no further consideration at most

questions.correctAnswerText: BCG is about 70-80% effective against severe forms such as TB meningitis in children, but less effective against respiratory disease
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance gives BCG efficacy as 70-80% against the most severe forms of TB (TB meningitis in children) and notes it is less effective against respiratory disease, which is more common in adults.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The father's pulmonary TB does not contradict the vaccine's purpose. BCG is aimed at preventing severe childhood forms, and its weaker effect on respiratory disease is exactly what Clinical guidance.

- A. Incorrect. Clinical guidance partial efficacy and a weaker effect on respiratory disease.
- B. Incorrect. This reverses clinical guidance: the stronger effect is against severe childhood forms such as TB meningitis.
- C. Correct. It matches the efficacy statement and explains the father's case.
- D. Incorrect. No 5-year repetition schedule is described; BCG is given once soon after birth, with a second dose considered only in the specific no-scar situation.
- E. Incorrect. The scar reflects the local reaction, not a guarantee of protection against respiratory TB. clinical guidance also notes that a scar does not appear in everyone.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- BCG: 70-80% effective against the most severe forms of TB (TB meningitis in children).
- Less effective in preventing respiratory disease, which is more common in adults.
- One dose soon after birth, intradermal, left upper arm over the deltoid insertion.

source.raw: Pediatric Vaccination sheet - Page 5 (BCG: dose, site and efficacy).

questions.stem: A 4-month-old girl received BCG intradermally in the left upper arm at birth. There is no scar at the site. She has no immunodeficiency and is afebrile. A tuberculin skin test performed today is negative. Which plan is consistent with clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Give a second BCG dose in the right arm, and advise that no other vaccine be given in that arm for 3 months

options.label: B
options.text: Do not repeat BCG, because absence of a scar is normal and the tuberculin result has no bearing on the decision

options.label: C
options.text: Give the second BCG dose subcutaneously in the left arm, because this route gives a stronger response

options.label: D
options.text: Give BCG boosters at monthly intervals until a scar appears, regardless of the tuberculin result

options.label: E
options.text: Repeat BCG in the right arm and give the next intramuscular vaccines in the same arm on the same day

questions.correctAnswerText: Give a second BCG dose in the right arm, and advise that no other vaccine be given in that arm for 3 months
questions.initialExplanation: A scar appears in most but not all vaccinated infants, so absence of a scar does not prove non-response. clinical guidance advises a tuberculin skin test; if negative, a second BCG dose is given in the right arm, with advice not to have any vaccination in that arm for 3 months after BCG.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The sequence is: no scar (not itself diagnostic) -> tuberculin test -> negative -> second dose in the right arm -> arm precaution. clinical guidance gives the 3-month advice without stating the reason, so it should be remembered as written.

- A. Correct. This follows the sequence.
- B. Incorrect. The tuberculin result is exactly what decides repeat vaccination, and a negative test leads to a second dose.
- C. Incorrect. Subcutaneous BCG risks BCG-oma; the route is intradermal.
- D. Incorrect. Clinical guidance a single second dose, not repeated boosters.
- E. Incorrect. clinical guidance advises no vaccination in the arm used for BCG for 3 months.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- A BCG scar appears in most but not all vaccinated people; its absence does not by itself mean non-response.
- Tuberculin skin test first; if negative, give a second BCG dose in the right arm (it is not necessary to inspect this scar).
- Avoid any other vaccination in the arm used for BCG for 3 months.
- Wrong route (subcutaneous) may cause BCG-oma.

source.raw: Pediatric Vaccination sheet - Pages 5-6 (BCG: no-scar management; complications).

cases.title: A household includes an immunocompromised child
cases.vignette: A healthy infant is due for oral polio vaccine. A sibling at home has a congenital immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: Which statement about OPV is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a conjugate vaccine given intradermally

options.label: B
options.text: It is an inactivated vaccine given intramuscularly

options.label: D
options.text: It is a recombinant vaccine given subcutaneously

options.label: E
options.text: It is a live attenuated vaccine given orally

questions.correctAnswerText: It is a live attenuated vaccine given orally
questions.initialExplanation: OPV (Sabin) is described as a live attenuated polio vaccine given by the oral route. The source notes that it can support herd immunity through cross-infection but may rarely cause vaccine-associated paralytic polio.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. OPV is not a conjugate vaccine.
- B. Incorrect. This describes IPV (Salk).
- C. Incorrect. Toxoid vaccines are used for diphtheria and tetanus.
- D. Incorrect. OPV is not recombinant and is not given subcutaneously.
- E. Correct. This is the description of OPV in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- OPV/Sabin = live attenuated, oral.
- IPV/Salk = inactivated, intramuscular.
- OPV may cause vaccine-associated paralytic polio.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes IPV?

options.label: A
options.text: It is administered intradermally at birth

options.label: B
options.text: It is live attenuated and administered orally

options.label: C
options.text: It is contraindicated in most healthy infants

options.label: D
options.text: It is an inactivated polio vaccine given intramuscularly and included in Hexa/Penta combinations

questions.correctAnswerText: It is an inactivated polio vaccine given intramuscularly and included in Hexa/Penta combinations
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes IPV (Salk) as an inactivated polio vaccine administered intramuscularly and included in the Hexa or Penta combination vaccines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The source describes IPV as intramuscular, not intradermal.
- B. Incorrect. This describes OPV.
- C. Incorrect. IPV is part of the routine combination vaccines in the schedule.
- D. Correct. This is the vaccine type, route and combination use described.
- E. Incorrect. IPV is not a toxoid.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IPV = inactivated polio vaccine.
- Route: IM.
- Included in Hexa and Penta combinations.
- OPV is the oral live attenuated alternative.

questions.stem: Why does clinical guidance discuss adding IPV to OPV-only schedules?

options.label: A
options.text: Because IPV is used to prevent diphtheria

options.label: B
options.text: Because OPV cannot induce any immunity

options.label: C
options.text: To reduce the risk associated with vaccine-associated paralytic polio and maintain protection

options.label: E
options.text: Because IPV is a live vaccine and spreads by cross-infection

questions.correctAnswerText: To reduce the risk associated with vaccine-associated paralytic polio and maintain protection
questions.initialExplanation: The source notes that WHO no longer recommends an OPV-only schedule and that countries using OPV-only schedules should add at least one IPV dose. It relates this to vaccine-associated paralytic polio and risk of transmission from neighbouring countries.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. IPV protects against poliovirus, not diphtheria.
- B. Incorrect. OPV induces immunity and has been used to support herd immunity.
- C. Correct. This reflects the explanation provided.
- D. Incorrect. IPV is a preventive vaccine, not treatment for established poliomyelitis.
- E. Incorrect. IPV is inactivated and does not replicate or spread by cross-infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- OPV is live attenuated and carries a risk of vaccine-associated paralytic polio.
- IPV is inactivated and is added to an OPV schedule in the source's discussion.
- IPV is incorporated into Hexa/Penta combinations.

questions.stem: Which situation is specifically highlighted as a reason not to give OPV?

options.label: B
options.text: The infant has a mild common cold

options.label: C
options.text: A sibling has a family history of eczema

options.label: D
options.text: The infant is premature but otherwise stable

questions.correctAnswerText: A household contact is immunocompromised
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that OPV should not be given to household contacts of immunocompromised individuals or to subsequent siblings of a child with congenital immunodeficiency until the younger child is shown to be normal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is specifically mentioned in the OPV contraindication section.
- B. Incorrect. Mild common cold is not a contraindication to vaccination generally.
- C. Incorrect. Family history of eczema is not a contraindication.
- D. Incorrect. Prematurity alone is not a contraindication in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Breastfeeding is not a contraindication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- OPV is live attenuated.
- Avoid OPV in immunocompromised recipients and relevant household contacts.
- The source advises delaying OPV during immunosuppressive therapy until at least 3 months after stopping treatment.

cases.title: A child developed a severe neurological event after a previous DPT dose
cases.vignette: A child is brought for the next scheduled DPT-containing vaccine. The parent reports a severe reaction after a previous dose and asks whether the next dose can be administered. The clinician reviews contraindications and the difference between whole-cell and acellular pertussis vaccines.

questions.stem: Which history is listed as a contraindication to DPT?

options.label: E
options.text: Severe reaction to a previous DPT dose

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe reaction to a previous DPT dose
questions.initialExplanation: The DPT section lists acute febrile illness, evolving or suspected neurological disease and severe reaction to a prior DPT dose as contraindications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotic treatment is listed as not a contraindication.
- B. Incorrect. Family history of epilepsy is listed as not a contraindication in the pertussis table.
- C. Incorrect. Stable CP is listed as not a contraindication in the pertussis table.
- D. Incorrect. A mild local reaction is not the severe reaction described.
- E. Correct. Severe reaction to a previous DPT dose is specifically listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DPT contraindications listed: acute febrile illness, evolving/suspected neurological disease and severe prior reaction.
- Do not confuse stable neurological conditions with progressive/evolving neurological illness.
- Assess the exact nature of the previous reaction.

questions.stem: Which adverse effects are described as common after pertussis-containing vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Severe chronic hepatitis in each recipient

options.label: B
options.text: Progressive renal failure and nephrotic syndrome

options.label: E
options.text: Injection-site pain/redness/swelling, fever, drowsiness and reduced appetite or vomiting

questions.correctAnswerText: Injection-site pain/redness/swelling, fever, drowsiness and reduced appetite or vomiting
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance local pain, redness and swelling, fever, drowsiness, anorexia and/or vomiting as common side effects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Chronic hepatitis is not listed as a common adverse effect.
- B. Incorrect. These are not common pertussis vaccine adverse effects.
- C. Incorrect. Permanent paralysis is not the expected common response.
- D. Incorrect. Disseminated TB is associated with BCG complications in immunocompromised individuals, not DPT.
- E. Correct. These are the listed common adverse effects.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common effects are usually local/systemic and self-limited.
- The source also mentions rare convulsions or encephalopathy.
- A common mild reaction should be distinguished from a severe contraindicating reaction.

questions.stem: A child cannot tolerate the whole-cell pertussis preparation because of adverse effects. Which alternative is described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acellular pertussis vaccine (Tdap)
questions.initialExplanation: The source states that the acellular pertussis vaccine (Tdap) is used for those who cannot tolerate the whole-cell preparation and has fewer side effects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hepatitis A vaccine prevents hepatitis A.
- B. Correct. Tdap is the acellular pertussis alternative described.
- C. Incorrect. MMR protects against measles, mumps and rubella.
- D. Incorrect. OPV prevents poliomyelitis.
- E. Incorrect. BCG prevents severe forms of tuberculosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Whole-cell pertussis preparation is described with DTP.
- Acellular pertussis vaccine (Tdap) is the alternative for those who cannot tolerate whole-cell vaccine.
- The source notes fewer side effects with the acellular preparation.

questions.stem: Which history is listed as not being a contraindication to pertussis vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Anaphylaxis to a vaccine component listed in the sheet

questions.correctAnswerText: Stable cerebral palsy
questions.initialExplanation: The pertussis table lists stable CP, family history of epilepsy, antibiotic treatment and previous febrile convulsion as not contraindications, while uncontrolled convulsions and progressive neurological illness are contraindications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The source lists anaphylaxis to specified vaccine components as a contraindication.
- B. Incorrect. Previous post-vaccination anaphylaxis is a contraindication.
- C. Incorrect. Uncontrolled convulsions are listed as a contraindication.
- D. Correct. Stable CP is explicitly listed as not a contraindication.
- E. Incorrect. Progressive neurological illness is listed as a contraindication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stable CP is not the same as progressive neurological disease.
- Uncontrolled convulsions are a contraindication in the pertussis table.
- Family history of epilepsy alone is not a contraindication.

cases.title: A school-entry immunization review
cases.vignette: A school health clinic reviews the immunization records of children entering primary school and children with pertussis-like illness. The team uses the routine schedule table and the DPT/pertussis section together.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy has had a 12-day paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting and no fever. PCR is positive for Bordetella pertussis. His illness is mild, with no apnea or cyanosis, and he is improving. His card shows all pertussis-containing doses were given on schedule (Hexa x3, Penta at 18 months, Tetra at 6 years). His father says, "He had every injection, so the vaccine was useless." Which response is the most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: A fully vaccinated child cannot develop pertussis, so the positive PCR must be a false result and the diagnosis is wrong

options.label: B
options.text: Pertussis in a vaccinated person tends to be mild and short, and titers after killed vaccines may wane, so a Tdap booster is scheduled at 15 years

options.label: C
options.text: Vaccination typically makes pertussis more severe than in unvaccinated children, so the vaccine should be withheld from his younger siblings

options.label: D
options.text: A mild course proves that the boy received a single dose of a pertussis-containing vaccine rather than the full series

options.label: E
options.text: Pertussis-containing vaccines not usually lose their effect over time, so a breakthrough case can mean that the vials used were faulty

questions.correctAnswerText: Pertussis in a vaccinated person tends to be mild and short, and titers after killed vaccines may wane, so a Tdap booster is scheduled at 15 years
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that pertussis in a vaccinated person is mild and of short duration, and that killed/inactivated vaccines may lose antibody titers with time. A mild breakthrough illness does not mean the vaccine was useless.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The key clinical idea is that a vaccine can modify disease without guaranteeing that infection never occurs. Here the child had the full series, his illness is mild and self-limited in course, and a booster is already planned in the schedule.

- A. Incorrect. clinical guidance does not claim complete protection; it describes the disease in vaccinated people as mild and short.
- B. Correct. It combines the mild/short course in the vaccinated with waning titers after killed vaccines, and it points to the Tdap booster at 15 years.
- C. Incorrect. Nothing suggests vaccination worsens pertussis; the contraindications are about specific severe reactions, not about disease severity.
- D. Incorrect. A mild course is expected in vaccinated people and does not indicate under-vaccination.
- E. Incorrect. Killed vaccines are described as having titers that may diminish; clinical guidance does not support the idea of lifelong protection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pertussis in a vaccinated person is mild and of short duration.
- Killed/inactivated vaccines: antibody titers may diminish with time, so boosters are used.
- Tdap (acellular) is the booster listed at 15 years in the schedule.

source.raw: Pediatric Vaccination sheet - Page 2 (killed/inactivated vaccines: titers may diminish); Page 4 (Tdap at 15 years); Page 7 (Pertussis: whole-cell DTP, mild disease in the vaccinated; acellular Tdap).

cases.title: A newborn is delivered by a mother who is HBsAg-positive
cases.vignette: A newborn is delivered to a mother known to be hepatitis B surface antigen-positive. The infant is clinically well. The neonatal team prepares immediate prophylaxis and explains that active vaccination and passive immunization are both required.

questions.stem: What should the infant receive on the day of birth?

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG)

questions.correctAnswerText: Hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG)
questions.initialExplanation: The source states that infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers should receive both hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG on the day of birth, at the same time but in separate thighs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Both active and passive prophylaxis are recommended.
- B. Incorrect. These vaccines are not the immediate prophylaxis for maternal hepatitis B exposure.
- C. Incorrect. BCG and varicella do not provide hepatitis B prophylaxis.
- D. Incorrect. PCV and meningococcal vaccines do not prevent hepatitis B infection.
- E. Incorrect. OPV and rotavirus do not prevent vertical HBV transmission.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HBsAg-positive mother: give HepB vaccine + HBIG at birth.
- Administer at the same time but in separate thighs.
- This is an urgent newborn prophylaxis scenario.

questions.stem: What HBIG dose is stated in the source for the exposed newborn?
questions.correctAnswerText: 100 IU IM
questions.initialExplanation: The source specifies HBIG 100 IU given by intramuscular injection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Intradermal 0.05 mL is listed for neonatal BCG in the routine table.
- B. Incorrect. Two oral drops are used for OPV/rotavirus contexts, not HBIG.
- C. Incorrect. The source specifies IM administration for HBIG.
- D. Incorrect. Oral 0.5 mL is not the HBIG route or dose.
- E. Correct. This is the HBIG dose and route stated on page 8.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HBIG is passive immunization.
- The source lists 100 IU IM.
- Hepatitis B vaccine is active immunization and is given separately from HBIG.

questions.stem: After birth prophylaxis, which hepatitis B vaccine schedule is stated for the infant born to an HBsAg-positive mother?

options.label: B
options.text: Three doses at birth, 9 and 12 years

options.label: C
options.text: No further doses are needed after HBIG

options.label: E
options.text: Three subsequent doses at 2, 4 and 6 months, giving four total doses including the birth dose

questions.correctAnswerText: Three subsequent doses at 2, 4 and 6 months, giving four total doses including the birth dose
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers receive the birth dose plus three subsequent doses at 2, 4 and 6 months, for a total of four hepatitis B vaccine doses.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These ages are not the hepatitis B schedule in this scenario.
- B. Incorrect. The subsequent doses are at 2, 4 and 6 months.
- C. Incorrect. HBIG is passive prophylaxis and does not replace the vaccine series.
- D. Incorrect. A single dose at 12 months is not the described schedule.
- E. Correct. This is the exact sequence stated on page 8.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Birth: HepB vaccine + HBIG for infant of HBsAg-positive mother.
- Subsequent HepB doses: 2, 4 and 6 months in the source.
- Total: four vaccine doses including birth dose.

questions.stem: A preterm infant weighs less than 2000 g and is born to an HBsAg-negative mother. Which timing is described?

options.label: A
options.text: Do not vaccinate the infant at most

options.label: B
options.text: Give one hepatitis B dose at 12 months

options.label: C
options.text: Give HBIG and vaccine immediately because the mother is HBsAg-negative

options.label: D
options.text: Delay the first hepatitis B dose until age 1 month or hospital discharge, then complete doses at 2, 4 and 6 months

options.label: E
options.text: Replace hepatitis B vaccine with BCG

questions.correctAnswerText: Delay the first hepatitis B dose until age 1 month or hospital discharge, then complete doses at 2, 4 and 6 months
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that if maternal HBsAg is negative and the preterm infant weighs less than 2000 g, the first hepatitis B dose is delayed until age 1 month or hospital discharge, followed by the schedule at 2, 4 and 6 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The infant still requires hepatitis B immunization.
- B. Incorrect. One dose at 12 months is not the schedule described.
- C. Incorrect. Clinical guidance HBIG plus vaccine at birth for infants of HBsAg-positive mothers.
- D. Correct. This is the schedule described for this specific group.
- E. Incorrect. BCG does not replace hepatitis B vaccine.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Maternal HBsAg status changes newborn hepatitis B management.
- Preterm infant <2000 g with HBsAg-negative mother: delay first dose to 1 month or discharge as stated.
- Do not mix this pathway with the pathway for an HBsAg-positive mother.

cases.title: A toddler develops fever and rash after MMR
cases.vignette: A toddler receives MMR at the routine 12-month visit. About 8 days later the child develops mild fever and a rash but remains clinically well. The parent worries that the child has developed measles.

questions.stem: Which explanation best fits the timing and presentation described in the MMR section?

options.label: A
options.text: A typical immediate anaphylactic reaction beginning 8 days later

options.label: B
options.text: A possible mild vaccine-related fever and rash occurring 7-10 days after vaccination

questions.correctAnswerText: A possible mild vaccine-related fever and rash occurring 7-10 days after vaccination
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance fever and rash, or a mild form of the disease, 7-10 days after MMR as possible side effects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Anaphylaxis is an immediate hypersensitivity reaction, not a delayed rash after 8 days.
- B. Correct. The timing and mild presentation match the adverse effect described.
- C. Incorrect. This is not a typical MMR adverse effect in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Disseminated BCG infection is a rare BCG complication in immunocompromised individuals.
- E. Incorrect. Vaccine-associated paralytic polio is associated with OPV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MMR side effects may include soreness/erythema and fever/rash 7-10 days later.
- A mild delayed reaction is different from immediate anaphylaxis.
- Assess severity and clinical status rather than assuming vaccine failure.

questions.stem: Which schedule and route are listed for MMR in the vaccine-specific section?

options.label: A
options.text: Two doses at 12 and 18 months, subcutaneous route

options.label: C
options.text: Two doses at 6 and 12 years, intramuscular route

options.label: E
options.text: Three oral doses at 2, 4 and 6 months

questions.correctAnswerText: Two doses at 12 and 18 months, subcutaneous route
questions.initialExplanation: The MMR section lists two doses at 12 and 18 months and a subcutaneous route.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the schedule and route stated in the MMR section.
- B. Incorrect. Tdap is listed at 15 years.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the MMR schedule in the source.
- D. Incorrect. BCG is the intradermal vaccine at birth.
- E. Incorrect. The oral 2, 4 and 6 month schedule relates to rotavirus, with IPV/Hexa also given in that period.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MMR: 12 and 18 months.
- Route in the MMR section: SC.
- MMR is live attenuated.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed as a contraindication to MMR?

options.label: A
options.text: Immunoglobulin administration within the previous 3 months

questions.correctAnswerText: Immunoglobulin administration within the previous 3 months
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance immunoglobulin within 3 months as a contraindication/precaution because it can blunt the immune response. It also lists pregnancy, anaphylaxis to neomycin, specified egg-allergy precautions and immunocompromise (with an exception noted for HIV on ART).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. The source gives the 3-month interval because antibody-containing products can blunt the immune response.
- B. Incorrect. Mild common cold is listed as not a contraindication to vaccination generally.
- C. Incorrect. Breastfeeding is not a contraindication.
- D. Incorrect. Prematurity is listed as not a contraindication.
- E. Incorrect. Congenital heart disease is not listed as a general contraindication.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MMR is live attenuated.
- Clinical guidance recent immunoglobulin administration as a concern because of reduced immune response.
- Other listed contraindications include pregnancy, severe allergy to neomycin and immunocompromise (with the source's stated exception).

cases.title: Allergy and antibody history before the 12-month visit
cases.vignette: At the 12-month visit (MMR, meningococcal, PCV) several toddlers have histories that need careful interpretation before MMR is given.

questions.stem: A 12-month-old boy, born to an HBsAg-positive mother, received hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG 100 IU IM at birth in separate thighs and later completed four doses of hepatitis B vaccine. Today he is due for MMR, meningococcal vaccine and PCV. His mother worries that "the antibodies he was given at birth" will block the measles vaccine. What is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: Delay MMR until 18 months, because HBIG given in the newborn period blocks live vaccines for the first two years of life

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat HBIG today so that MMR can be given under antibody cover, since the first HBIG dose was given at birth

options.label: C
options.text: Give MMR at double dose to overcome the interference from HBIG, then repeat the dose at 18 months as scheduled

options.label: D
options.text: Replace MMR with inactivated vaccines for life, because he received an immunoglobulin product as a newborn infant

options.label: E
options.text: Proceed with MMR; immunoglobulin interferes when given within the previous 3 months, and HBIG was given about 12 months ago

questions.correctAnswerText: Proceed with MMR; immunoglobulin interferes when given within the previous 3 months, and HBIG was given about 12 months ago
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance immunoglobulin within 3 months as a contraindication to MMR because of a blunted immune response. HBIG was given at birth, about 12 months before today's visit, so the 3-month window has long passed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This question links two separate sections of clinical guidance (neonatal HBV prophylaxis and MMR contraindications) and tests whether the student applies the time window rather than the mere history of receiving immunoglobulin.

- A. Incorrect. clinical guidance gives a 3-month window, not 2 years.
- B. Incorrect. Repeating immunoglobulin would create the interference the 3-month rule warns about.
- C. Incorrect. Doubling the dose is not a solution described for any live vaccine problem.
- D. Incorrect. There is no need to replace MMR; the contraindication has expired.
- E. Correct. The interval since HBIG is far longer than 3 months.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MMR: contraindicated if immunoglobulin was given within the last 3 months (blunted immune response).
- HBsAg-positive mother: HepB vaccine + HBIG 100 IU IM on the day of birth in separate thighs, then HepB vaccine at 2, 4, 6 months (4 doses).
- The key is the interval since immunoglobulin, not whether immunoglobulin was ever given.

source.raw: Pediatric Vaccination sheet - Page 8 (Hepatitis B: infant of HBsAg-positive mother; MMR contraindications).

cases.title: An infant attends for oral rotavirus and pneumococcal immunization
cases.vignette: A 2-month-old infant is due for routine oral rotavirus vaccine and intramuscular PCV. The parent asks about the rotavirus product schedule and the diseases prevented by pneumococcal vaccine.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes rotavirus vaccine?

options.label: A
options.text: It is an inactivated vaccine given intradermally

options.label: B
options.text: It is a recombinant vaccine given subcutaneously

options.label: C
options.text: It is a live attenuated vaccine given orally

options.label: D
options.text: It is a polysaccharide vaccine given intravenously

options.label: E

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is due for the second varicella dose. His mother reports that 9 days after the first dose at 15 months he had a low-grade fever and a brief rash, with pain and redness at the injection site, all of which resolved without treatment. He had no breathing difficulty or swelling of the face. He has no immunodeficiency, no lymphopenia, and is not receiving immunosuppressive therapy. What is the appropriate decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Cancel the second dose, because fever and rash after the first dose indicate that he developed anaphylaxis

options.label: B
options.text: Give the second dose, because fever, rash and local pain or redness are listed adverse reactions, not contraindications

options.label: C
options.text: Skip the second dose, because the rash proves that he developed wild chickenpox and is now permanently immune

options.label: D
options.text: Postpone the second dose until age 15 years, when it can be given together with the Tdap booster at that visit

options.label: E
options.text: Give the second dose after first administering varicella immunoglobulin to prevent a more severe reaction

questions.correctAnswerText: Give the second dose, because fever, rash and local pain or redness are listed adverse reactions, not contraindications
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance fever, rash and local pain or redness as adverse reactions to varicella vaccine, and lists anaphylaxis after a previous dose, lymphopenia, immunodeficiency and immunosuppressive therapy as contraindications. This boy's history fits the first list.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The task is to separate an expected adverse reaction from a contraindicating reaction. Anaphylaxis would involve airway or circulatory features; the mother describes none.

- A. Incorrect. Anaphylaxis after a previous dose is a contraindication, but this history lacks respiratory difficulty or facial swelling.
- B. Correct. The reactions described are listed adverse reactions, and none of the listed contraindications are present.
- C. Incorrect. clinical guidance does not support the idea that a vaccine rash replaces the second scheduled dose.
- D. Incorrect. The routine schedule lists the second dose at 6 years, and Tdap is a separate vaccine.
- E. Incorrect. Immunoglobulin is not part of the varicella vaccination process.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Varicella vaccine: 0.5 mL SC or IM; site anterolateral thigh or upper arm; doses at 15 months and 6 years.
- Adverse reactions: fever, rash, local pain or redness.
- Contraindications: anaphylaxis after a previous dose, lymphopenia, immunodeficiency, immunosuppressive therapy.
- Storage: 2-8 degrees C, protect from light, use within 30 minutes of reconstitution.
