- E. Grunting â€” Correct. The mechanism and clinical significance match clinical guidance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Grunting is an expiratory sound and a sign of respiratory distress.
- It may occur in bronchiolitis, pneumonia and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
- Stertor is low-pitched and often sounds like nasal congestion.

questions.stem: Which respiratory rate indicates tachypnoea in an infant aged 2 months to 1 year?
questions.correctAnswerText: More than 50 breaths/min
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance defines tachypnoea in infants aged 2 months to 1 year as a respiratory rate above 50 breaths/min.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. >60/min â€” Incorrect. This is the threshold listed for neonates.
- B. >80/min â€” Incorrect. This is far above the stated threshold.
- C. >30/min â€” Incorrect. This is below the infant threshold.
- D. >40/min â€” Incorrect. This is not the threshold given for this age group.
- E. >50/min â€” Correct. This is the infant threshold.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonate: >60/min.
- Infant (2 monthsâ€“1 year): >50/min.
- 1â€“5 years: >40/min.
- School-age child: >30/min in the source table.
- Interpret RR with age, fever, activity and the overall clinical picture.

questions.stem: A child has tachypnoea and nasal flaring but no chest recession. Which grade of respiratory distress is described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Grade I â€” mild
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance grades respiratory distress by the progression of signs. Grade I is tachypnoea with nasal flaring; recession is added in Grade II.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Grade II includes recession.
- B. Incorrect. Grade III includes grunting in addition to earlier signs.
- C. Correct. Tachypnoea plus nasal flaring corresponds to mild Grade I distress.
- D. Incorrect. Grade IV includes cyanosis and disturbed consciousness.
- E. Incorrect. Tachypnoea and nasal flaring are signs of increased work of breathing.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Grade I: tachypnoea + nasal flaring.
- Grade II: + recession.
- Grade III: + grunting.
- Grade IV: + cyanosis and disturbed conscious level.

questions.stem: A child has severe breathlessness. Which statement about the possible causes is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Breathlessness typically originates from the lungs

options.label: B
options.text: Consider airway, lung or pleural disease and extrapulmonary causes such as heart failure, anaemia or metabolic acidosis

options.label: E
options.text: Heart failure is excluded when cough is present

questions.correctAnswerText: Consider airway, lung or pleural disease and extrapulmonary causes such as heart failure, anaemia or metabolic acidosis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance classifies causes of breathlessness into airway obstruction, lung parenchymal disease, pleural disease and extra-pulmonary causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Breathlessness is not exclusively pulmonary.
- B. Correct. This is the classification given.
- C. Incorrect. Metabolic acidosis may cause compensatory tachypnoea/deep breathing rather than isolated wheeze.
- D. Incorrect. Anaemia can cause breathlessness because oxygen-carrying capacity is reduced.
- E. Incorrect. Heart failure can cause cough and breathlessness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Airway: asthma.
- Parenchyma: pneumonia.
- Pleura: pneumothorax.
- Extra-pulmonary: heart failure, anaemia and metabolic acidosis.
- Do not assume every tachypnoeic child has a primary respiratory disorder.

cases.title: â€” Nasal discharge and low-grade fever
cases.vignette: A 2-year-old child presents with nasal congestion, clear-to-mucopurulent nasal discharge and low-grade fever. The child is active, drinking adequately and has no focal chest findings. Symptoms began three days ago.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Common cold (coryza)
questions.initialExplanation: Clear or mucopurulent nasal discharge, nasal blockage and low-grade fever in a well child are typical of the common cold.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bacterial sinusitis usually follows a URI and is more likely with persistent or worsening symptoms, focal facial pain or swelling.
- B. Incorrect. Pneumonia usually produces lower respiratory features such as tachypnoea, fever, chest signs or increased work of breathing.
- C. Incorrect. AOM is associated with otalgia or infant irritability and a bulging, inflamed tympanic membrane.
- D. Correct. This is the commonest childhood respiratory infection.
- E. Incorrect. Epiglottitis presents abruptly with high fever, drooling, dysphagia and a toxic appearance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common cold is the commonest childhood infection.
- Typical features: nasal discharge, nasal blockage and low-grade fever.
- Most cases are viral and self-limiting.

questions.stem: Which pathogen group causes most common colds in children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Viruses
questions.initialExplanation: The common cold is usually viral. Clinical guidance rhinoviruses, coronaviruses and RSV among common pathogens.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Group A streptococci â€” Incorrect. This is a bacterial cause of some pharyngitis.
- B. Fungi â€” Incorrect. They are not typical causes of uncomplicated coryza.
- C. Viruses â€” Correct. Viral pathogens account for the common cold.
- D. Mycobacteria â€” Incorrect. TB is a cause of chronic respiratory disease, not the common cold.
- E. Helminths â€” Incorrect. They do not cause the common cold.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rhinoviruses have many serotypes.
- Coronavirus and RSV are also listed.
- Most childhood respiratory infections are viral.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate treatment for an uncomplicated common cold?

options.label: D
options.text: Systemic corticosteroids for children in routine care

options.label: E
options.text: Paracetamol if needed and increased fluid intake

questions.correctAnswerText: Paracetamol if needed and increased fluid intake
questions.initialExplanation: The common cold is self-limiting. Treatment is supportive, including antipyretic/analgesic treatment when needed and adequate fluids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Chest physiotherapy is not routine treatment for an uncomplicated common cold.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics have no role in uncomplicated viral coryza.
- C. Incorrect. Nebulized adrenaline is used in selected severe upper-airway obstruction such as croup, not coryza.
- D. Incorrect. Steroids are not routine treatment for an uncomplicated common cold.
- E. Correct. This is the supportive treatment described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common cold: self-limiting; no antibiotics.
- Use symptomatic treatment and fluids.
- Clinical guidance that antitussives, vitamin C and decongestants have no role in routine management.

questions.stem: A child remains coughy for 3 weeks after a common cold but is otherwise improving. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Cough may persist for up to 4 weeks after a common cold

options.label: B
options.text: A persistent cough excludes a preceding viral illness

options.label: C
options.text: children in routine care needs antibiotics

options.label: D
options.text: The child must have cystic fibrosis

options.label: E
options.text: Persistent cough at 3 weeks typically proves bacterial pneumonia

questions.correctAnswerText: Cough may persist for up to 4 weeks after a common cold
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that cough can persist for up to four weeks after a common cold. The child's overall clinical state and any red flags should guide reassessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is specifically stated.
- B. Incorrect. A viral illness may be followed by a lingering cough.
- C. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not indicated for a post-viral cough without evidence of bacterial disease.
- D. Incorrect. CF is one of many causes of chronic cough, but a resolving post-viral cough does not establish it.
- E. Incorrect. Duration alone does not diagnose bacterial pneumonia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Post-cold cough may last up to 4 weeks.
- Daily cough longer than 4 weeks meets clinical guidance's chronic cough definition and requires broader assessment.
- Look for red flags such as respiratory distress, persistent fever, haemoptysis or poor growth.

cases.title: Why a blocked nose matters in a young infant

questions.stem: A 3-week-old term infant is brought with a 2-day history of marked nasal blockage and clear nasal discharge. He repeatedly stops sucking during feeds to breathe. His respiratory rate is 62/min with mild subcostal recession, SpO2 is 97% in air and the chest is clear. Which statement best explains why a simple blocked nose causes this degree of distress at his age?

options.label: A
options.text: The right main bronchus is wider and straighter, so nasal secretions are readily aspirated into the lungs

options.label: B
options.text: The lower airways dilate during inspiration, so nasal secretions are drawn straight into the bronchioles

options.label: C
options.text: Newborns and young infants are obligatory nasal breathers with small airways, so nasal blockage markedly raises the work of breathing

options.label: D
options.text: Eustachian tube dysfunction transmits the nasal obstruction to the middle ear and causes reflex tachypnoea

options.label: E
options.text: Adenoid hypertrophy obstructs the airway at the level of the vocal cords in the first month of life

questions.correctAnswerText: Newborns and young infants are obligatory nasal breathers with small airways, so nasal blockage markedly raises the work of breathing
questions.initialExplanation: Newborns and young infants breathe mainly through the nose and have small airways, so even a common cold can cause feeding difficulty and respiratory distress.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The wider, straighter right main bronchus explains why inhaled foreign bodies lodge on the right. It does not explain distress from nasal blockage when the chest is clear.
- B. Incorrect. The lower airways do dilate in inspiration, but secretions are not "drawn" into the bronchioles. A clear chest and normal saturation point to an upper-airway (nasal) problem.
- C. Correct. Obligatory nasal breathing plus small, still-growing airways means that nasal obstruction in an infant behaves like a significant airway obstruction.
- D. Incorrect. Eustachian tube anatomy predisposes infants to acute otitis media, not to tachypnoea.
- E. Incorrect. The adenoids lie in the nasopharynx. Adenoid hypertrophy causes snoring or sleep apnoea in older children; it does not obstruct the vocal cords.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Newborns and infants are obligatory nasal breathers.
- Smaller airways and growing lungs mean that the younger the child, the more severe the respiratory disease, especially lower respiratory infection.
- The common cold is the commonest childhood infection, is usually viral, and is treated supportively.
- The right main bronchus is wider and straighter, which is why foreign bodies commonly lodge there.

cases.title: â€” Fever and sore throat in a school-age child
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, dysphagia, tender enlarged cervical lymph nodes and headache. The child is clinically stable and can drink fluids.

questions.stem: Which cause is most common in childhood pharyngitis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Viral infection
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies viral causes, including adenovirus, rhinovirus, enterovirus and EBV, as common. GAS is less common and is rare under 3 years of age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Viral infection â€” Correct. Viral causes are common in childhood pharyngitis.
- B. GAS â€” Incorrect. It is an important bacterial cause but is less common than viral disease.
- C. Candida â€” Incorrect. Oral candidiasis may affect the mouth but is not the common cause of acute tonsillopharyngitis.
- D. Meningococcus â€” Incorrect. It is not a typical cause of uncomplicated pharyngitis.
- E. TB â€” Incorrect. TB is not the common cause of acute sore throat.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral causes are common.
- GAS is a bacterial cause and is uncommon below 3 years.
- Clinical assessment alone may not reliably distinguish viral from bacterial disease.

questions.stem: Which statement about distinguishing viral from bacterial pharyngitis is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is not possible to distinguish them reliably on clinical features alone; a clinical score may help

options.label: B
options.text: each sore throat is caused by GAS

options.label: C
options.text: Clinical findings typically distinguish the two reliably

options.label: D
options.text: A low-grade fever proves viral disease

questions.correctAnswerText: It is not possible to distinguish them reliably on clinical features alone; a clinical score may help
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that it is not possible to reliably distinguish viral and bacterial causes clinically, although Centor criteria or a clinical score may help guide assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the teaching point.
- B. Incorrect. Viral disease is more common.
- C. Incorrect. Clinical appearances overlap.
- D. Incorrect. Fever intensity alone is not a definitive diagnostic test.
- E. Incorrect. Tonsillar enlargement can occur with viral and bacterial infections.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral and GAS pharyngitis overlap clinically.
- Centor criteria/score may help stratify the likelihood of GAS.
- Microbiological testing should be used according to local guidance where appropriate.

questions.stem: When is penicillin indicated in the treatment approach described by clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: For confirmed streptococcal infection, with a 10-day course stated in the sheet

options.label: D
options.text: For children in routine care with a sore throat

options.label: E
options.text: For infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV

questions.correctAnswerText: For confirmed streptococcal infection, with a 10-day course stated in the sheet
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance symptomatic treatment for uncomplicated disease and penicillin for streptococcal infection, with a 10-day course.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the antibiotic indication and duration stated in the source clinical guidance.
- B. Incorrect. Cough does not establish GAS infection.
- C. Incorrect. Coryza is usually viral and does not require penicillin.
- D. Incorrect. Routine antibiotics for every sore throat would expose children with viral illness to unnecessary treatment.
- E. Incorrect. Penicillin is not used to treat EBV infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Symptomatic treatment: antipyretic/analgesia and fluids.
- Penicillin is used for streptococcal infection in the source clinical guidance.
- Antibiotic choice and duration must follow local pediatric guidance.

questions.stem: A child with infectious mononucleosis is mistakenly prescribed amoxicillin for tonsillitis and develops a widespread maculopapular rash. Which statement best explains the association?

options.label: A
options.text: The rash confirms anaphylaxis in each case

options.label: B
options.text: The rash proves the child has measles

options.label: C
options.text: Amoxicillin may cause a widespread maculopapular rash in EBV-associated tonsillitis

options.label: D
options.text: The rash is the defining feature of bacterial tracheitis

questions.correctAnswerText: Amoxicillin may cause a widespread maculopapular rash in EBV-associated tonsillitis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance warns that amoxicillin is best avoided when infectious mononucleosis is suspected because it may cause a widespread maculopapular rash.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A maculopapular rash does not automatically mean anaphylaxis; assess for immediate hypersensitivity features.
- B. Incorrect. The rash is not diagnostic of measles.
- C. Correct. This is the association highlighted in the source.
- D. Incorrect. It is unrelated to bacterial tracheitis.
- E. Incorrect. Amoxicillin may provoke the rash rather than prevent it.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- EBV infectious mononucleosis can present with tonsillopharyngitis.
- Avoid amoxicillin when EBV is suspected because of the characteristic widespread rash association.
- Distinguish a delayed maculopapular eruption from immediate anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: Which is an indication for tonsillectomy listed?

options.label: A
options.text: A single uncomplicated viral sore throat

questions.correctAnswerText: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance peritonsillar abscess, obstructive sleep apnoea and frequent tonsillitis as indications for tonsillectomy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. One uncomplicated viral episode is not an indication.
- B. Correct. Quinsy is specifically listed.
- C. Incorrect. Coryza is unrelated to the surgical indication.
- D. Incorrect. A short-duration cough is not an indication.
- E. Incorrect. Common cold does not require tonsillectomy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Indications: quinsy, obstructive sleep apnoea and recurrent/frequent tonsillitis.
- Recurrent tonsillitis thresholds: â‰¥7 episodes in 1 year, â‰¥5/year for 2 years or â‰¥3/year for 3 years.
- Apply current ENT guidance and assess the clinical history carefully.

topics.name: Acute Otitis Media (AOM) and Otitis Media with Effusion (OME)

cases.title: â€” Fever and ear pain in a toddler
cases.vignette: A 16-month-old boy presents with fever, irritability and poor feeding. He has been waking frequently at night and pulling at his right ear. Otoscopy shows a congested, bulging tympanic membrane with loss of the normal light reflex. There is no evidence of mastoid swelling.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acute otitis media
questions.initialExplanation: Fever and ear symptoms with a bulging, congested tympanic membrane and loss of the normal light reflex are characteristic of AOM.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sinusitis causes nasal, facial and respiratory symptoms rather than a bulging tympanic membrane.
- B. Incorrect. Otitis externa affects the external auditory canal and typically causes canal tenderness/discharge.
- C. Incorrect. Mastoiditis is a complication and may cause mastoid tenderness/swelling and protrusion of the pinna.
- D. Incorrect. Otosclerosis is not an acute febrile middle-ear infection.
- E. Correct. The clinical presentation and otoscopic finding fit AOM.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- AOM = suppurative infection of the middle ear cavity.
- Bulging, congested tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex is a key finding.
- Fever in an infant/young child should prompt examination of the tympanic membranes.

questions.stem: Which organism is listed as the most common bacterial cause of AOM?
questions.correctAnswerText: Streptococcus pneumoniae
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance Streptococcus pneumoniae as the most common bacterial pathogen, followed by non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. TB is not a typical AOM pathogen.
- B. Incorrect. Candida is not a common bacterial cause of AOM.
- C. Correct. clinical guidance gives pneumococcus as the commonest bacterial cause.
- D. Incorrect. Pertussis causes whooping cough, not typical AOM.
- E. Incorrect. Pseudomonas is not the commonest routine cause in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common bacterial causes: S. pneumoniae, non-typeable H. influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis.
- RSV and rhinovirus are listed as viral causes.
- Pneumococcal vaccination reduces disease burden.

questions.stem: Which age group represents the peak incidence of AOM?
questions.correctAnswerText: 6â€“24 months
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies 6â€“24 months as the peak age range for AOM.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. It is common in infants and young children, but not limited to neonates.
- B. Incorrect. AOM can occur in older children but this is not the peak.
- C. Incorrect. This is older than the peak age.
- D. Correct. This is the age range specified.
- E. Incorrect. AOM is common in childhood, not primarily an elderly condition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Peak age: 6â€“24 months.
- Boys are affected more often.
- Infant Eustachian tubes are shorter, more horizontal and function less effectively.

questions.stem: Which factor is protective against AOM?
questions.correctAnswerText: Breastfeeding
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance bottle feeding as a risk factor and breastfeeding as protective.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Tobacco smoke exposure increases risk.
- B. Incorrect. Cleft palate is a craniofacial risk factor.
- C. Incorrect. Bottle feeding is listed as a risk factor.
- D. Incorrect. Pacifier use is listed as a risk factor.
- E. Correct. Breastfeeding is specifically identified as protective.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Risk factors: young age, bottle feeding, cleft palate, Down syndrome, smoke exposure, pacifier use and immunodeficiency.
- Breastfeeding is protective.
- Eustachian tube anatomy contributes to susceptibility in young children.

questions.stem: Which investigation is central to the diagnosis of AOM?

options.label: A
options.text: Otoscopy showing a congested, bulging tympanic membrane

questions.correctAnswerText: Otoscopy showing a congested, bulging tympanic membrane
questions.initialExplanation: AOM is diagnosed using history and otoscopic examination. Pneumatic otoscopy assesses tympanic membrane mobility and may help distinguish AOM from middle-ear effusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Otoscopy is the key diagnostic assessment.
- B. Incorrect. EEG assesses cerebral electrical activity.
- C. Incorrect. Renal ultrasound is unrelated.
- D. Incorrect. Chest X-ray does not diagnose middle-ear infection.
- E. Incorrect. Abdominal CT is not relevant to AOM diagnosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- History + otoscopy.
- Bulging/congested TM and loss of normal light reflex.
- Pneumatic otoscopy assesses TM movement.
- Assess both ears in febrile infants and young children.

questions.stem: Which antibiotic is listed as the drug of choice when antibiotics are indicated for AOM?
questions.correctAnswerText: Amoxicillin
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies amoxicillin as the drug of choice when antibiotic treatment is indicated. Many cases resolve spontaneously, and analgesia/antipyretics are important.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Metronidazole targets anaerobic organisms and is not routine first-line AOM treatment.
- B. Correct. Amoxicillin is the listed first-line antibiotic.
- C. Incorrect. Rifampicin is not the routine drug of choice for AOM.
- D. Incorrect. Acyclovir is antiviral therapy.
- E. Incorrect. Fluconazole is antifungal therapy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- AOM often resolves spontaneously.
- Analgesia/antipyretics are important.
- Amoxicillin is listed as DOC when antibiotics are indicated.
- The source OCR dose should be checked against the original PDF/local guidance before prescribing.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has persistent middle-ear fluid and conductive hearing loss after recurrent AOM. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.text: Sensorineural hearing loss due to Alport syndrome

questions.correctAnswerText: Otitis media with effusion (glue ear)
questions.initialExplanation: Recurrent AOM may lead to otitis media with effusion, in which fluid persists in the middle ear. It is a common cause of conductive hearing loss in children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Epiglottitis causes acute upper-airway obstruction.
- B. Incorrect. Otitis externa affects the external canal.
- C. Incorrect. Croup is an upper-airway viral illness with barking cough and stridor.
- D. Correct. Persistent middle-ear fluid with conductive hearing loss is typical of OME.
- E. Incorrect. Alport syndrome causes sensorineural hearing loss, not middle-ear fluid.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- OME = fluid in the middle ear without the acute suppurative features of AOM.
- It is a common cause of conductive hearing loss.
- Persistent hearing impairment may affect speech and learning.

questions.stem: What is the management approach for uncomplicated OME described?

options.label: B
options.text: No assessment of hearing is needed

options.label: D
options.text: Routine mastoidectomy for children in routine care

options.label: E
options.text: Watchful waiting for 3 months; if not improved, ENT review and possible myringotomy with grommet insertion

questions.correctAnswerText: Watchful waiting for 3 months; if not improved, ENT review and possible myringotomy with grommet insertion
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance watchful waiting for three months, with ENT referral and possible myringotomy with grommet insertion if the effusion does not resolve.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Prolonged IV antibiotics are not routine management for uncomplicated OME.
- B. Incorrect. Hearing assessment is important because persistent conductive hearing loss can affect speech and learning.
- C. Incorrect. Tracheostomy is an airway intervention and unrelated.
- D. Incorrect. Mastoidectomy is not routine treatment for OME.
- E. Correct. This is the management sequence.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- OME often resolves spontaneously.
- Watchful waiting for 3 months is recommended.
- Persistent effusion/hearing impairment â†’ ENT review; may need myringotomy and grommet tube.
- Complications include conductive hearing loss and speech/learning difficulties.

cases.title: Ear and sinus infections: presentation, advice and complications

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy has had fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting and two loose stools for 24 hours. He has mild coryza, a respiratory rate of 38/min, clear and equal breath sounds and a flat anterior fontanelle, and he is consolable between cries. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat as gastroenteritis with oral rehydration and reassure, because vomiting and diarrhoea exclude an ear source

options.label: B
options.text: Examine both tympanic membranes with an otoscope, because fever with irritability, vomiting and diarrhoea may be due to AOM

options.label: C
options.text: Request a chest X-ray, because irritability and poor feeding in an infant are signs of lower respiratory disease

options.label: D
options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics for presumed sepsis without further examination

options.label: E
options.text: Start nebulised salbutamol, because poor feeding in an infant means bronchiolitis

questions.correctAnswerText: Examine both tympanic membranes with an otoscope, because fever with irritability, vomiting and diarrhoea may be due to AOM
questions.initialExplanation: Infants with AOM often have non-specific features such as fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting or diarrhoea. clinical guidance advises examining the tympanic membranes of every febrile infant or young child.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vomiting and diarrhoea are listed features of AOM in infants and do not exclude an ear source.
- B. Correct. Otoscopy (a congested, bulging membrane with loss of the light reflex) is the key diagnostic step.
- C. Incorrect. The respiratory rate is normal for age and the chest is clear, so there is no evidence of lower respiratory disease.
- D. Incorrect. The child is consolable with a flat fontanelle. A simple, treatable source should be sought first.
- E. Incorrect. There is no wheeze or respiratory distress to suggest bronchiolitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infants with AOM: fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhoea and ear discharge. Older children: fever, otalgia and otorrhoea.
- Examine the tympanic membranes of every febrile infant or young child.
- Diagnosis = history + otoscopy (congested, bulging membrane, lost light reflex, sometimes perforation). Pneumatic otoscopy tests membrane movement.
- Peak age is 6–24 months, and the Eustachian tube in infants is short, horizontal and functions poorly.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy is diagnosed with AOM on day 2 of illness. He is drinking well and has no complications. His mother asks for a decongestant, an antihistamine and ear drops "to protect his hearing", and wants antibiotics for the same reason. Which advice is consistent with clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain; decongestants, antihistamines and ear drops add no benefit, and antibiotics have not been shown to reduce hearing loss

options.label: B
options.text: A decongestant and an antihistamine, because they shorten the illness and prevent glue ear; antibiotics are unnecessary

options.label: C
options.text: Antibiotic ear drops, because local medication is the main treatment and systemic antibiotics are not usually used

options.label: D
options.text: Amoxicillin, because it has been shown to reduce hearing loss, together with a decongestant for the Eustachian tube

options.label: E
options.text: No analgesia, because pain relief masks complications, with immediate referral for grommet insertion

questions.correctAnswerText: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain; decongestants, antihistamines and ear drops add no benefit, and antibiotics have not been shown to reduce hearing loss
questions.initialExplanation: AOM usually resolves spontaneously. Analgesia and antipyretics are the mainstay. Decongestants, antihistamines and ear drops are not beneficial, and antibiotics only marginally shorten pain without proven protection against hearing loss.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the treatment statements.
- B. Incorrect. Neither decongestants nor antihistamines are beneficial in AOM.
- C. Incorrect. Clinical guidance there is no role for local ear drops in the treatment of AOM.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics have not been shown to reduce the risk of hearing loss, and decongestants are not beneficial.
- E. Incorrect. Analgesia and antipyretics are part of treatment. Grommets are for persistent effusion (glue ear) after watchful waiting, not for acute AOM.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat pain and fever with paracetamol or ibuprofen.
- Amoxicillin is the drug of choice when antibiotics are indicated (clinical guidance gives 80–90 mg/kg/day; verify doses against the original and local guidance).
- Antibiotics marginally shorten pain and do not reduce hearing loss. Decongestants, antihistamines and ear drops are not beneficial.
- Complications: recurrent otitis media with effusion, conductive hearing loss with speech and learning problems, acute mastoiditis, meningitis and dural venous thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl finished amoxicillin for AOM 10 days ago. She now has high fever, repeated vomiting, severe headache, marked irritability, neck stiffness and dislike of light. There is no swelling or tenderness behind the ear. Which complication of AOM should be suspected?

options.label: A
options.text: Otitis media with effusion, because it commonly causes high fever and severe headache

options.label: B
options.text: Conductive hearing loss, because it explains vomiting and dislike of light

options.label: C
options.text: Acute mastoiditis, because it presents with headache and no signs behind the ear

options.label: D
options.text: Meningitis, with dural venous thrombosis as a related intracranial complication

options.label: E
options.text: Recurrent AOM, because each recurrence produces neck stiffness

questions.correctAnswerText: Meningitis, with dural venous thrombosis as a related intracranial complication
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, vomiting, severe headache, neck stiffness and photophobia after AOM indicate an intracranial complication. Clinical guidance meningitis and dural venous thrombosis among the complications of AOM.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Glue ear causes conductive hearing loss and is typically not febrile with severe headache and neck stiffness.
- B. Incorrect. Hearing loss is a consequence of effusion. It does not explain a systemic illness with meningeal signs.
- C. Incorrect. Mastoiditis is a complication of AOM, but it shows as a mastoid swelling and tenderness, which are absent here.
- D. Correct. The meningeal picture is explained by an intracranial spread of middle-ear infection.
- E. Incorrect. Recurrence of AOM does not by itself explain meningeal signs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Complications of AOM: recurrent OME (glue ear), conductive hearing loss with speech and learning difficulties, acute mastoiditis, meningitis and dural vein thrombosis.
- OME is the commonest cause of conductive hearing loss in children (common at 2–7 years), usually resolves spontaneously, and is managed by watchful waiting for 3 months, then ENT review and possible grommets.
- Always look for red-flag signs: persistent fever, severe headache, vomiting and meningism.

source.raw: Respiratory sheet — Page 9 (Complications of AOM; OME; mastoiditis).

cases.title: â€” Fever, headache and facial tenderness after a URI
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child develops fever, headache, cough and mucopurulent nasal discharge after an upper respiratory tract infection. There is pain and tenderness over the cheek, suggesting maxillary sinus involvement. The clinician assesses for orbital and intracranial complications.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sinusitis
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, headache, cough and mucopurulent discharge following a URI, with cheek pain/tenderness, are consistent with sinusitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. FBA typically follows a choking episode and causes sudden cough or unilateral wheeze.
- B. Incorrect. Bronchiolitis affects the lower airways and causes wheeze/respiratory distress.
- C. Incorrect. AOM is diagnosed by middle-ear symptoms and otoscopic findings.
- D. Incorrect. Croup causes barking cough, hoarseness and stridor.
- E. Correct. This matches the symptoms described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sinusitis often follows an upper respiratory infection.
- Symptoms: fever, headache, cough, nasal discharge and facial tenderness.
- Maxillary sinusitis may cause cheek pain/swelling/tenderness.

questions.stem: Which organisms are listed among bacterial causes of sinusitis?

options.label: E
options.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Staphylococcus aureus

questions.correctAnswerText: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Staphylococcus aureus
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance viral rhinovirus and bacterial organisms including pneumococcus, Hib and Staphylococcus aureus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are urinary pathogens and not the organisms listed for sinusitis.
- B. Incorrect. These are viral respiratory pathogens, not bacterial causes.
- C. Incorrect. Fungal causes are not listed as routine pediatric sinusitis pathogens.
- D. Incorrect. These are parasitic pathogens.
- E. Correct. These are the bacterial pathogens listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral: rhinovirus is listed.
- Bacterial: S. pneumoniae, Hib and S. aureus.
- Sinusitis may follow an initial viral URI.

questions.stem: Which sinus is present at birth?

options.label: B
options.text: most paranasal sinuses are fully developed at birth

questions.correctAnswerText: Maxillary and ethmoid sinuses
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are present at birth, while sphenoid and frontal sinuses develop later.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Frontal sinuses develop later, beginning around 7 years.
- B. Incorrect. Sinus pneumatization occurs at different ages.
- C. Incorrect. Both develop later, not at birth.
- D. Correct. These are the sinuses present at birth.
- E. Incorrect. Sphenoid sinuses begin developing at approximately 2â€“3 years.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Maxillary and ethmoid: present at birth.
- Sphenoid: begins at 2â€“3 years and completes around 5 years.
- Frontal: begins around 7 years and completes around 12 years.
- Frontal sinusitis is uncommon in the first decade.

questions.stem: Which is a serious complication of pediatric sinusitis listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Orbital cellulitis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance orbital cellulitis as a complication of sinusitis, along with dural sinus thrombosis, meningitis and frontal bone osteomyelitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Nephrocalcinosis is a renal condition.
- B. Correct. Orbital cellulitis is an important complication, especially from ethmoid sinus infection.
- C. Incorrect. Hypospadias is a congenital urethral abnormality.
- D. Incorrect. Hydrocele is a scrotal fluid collection.
- E. Incorrect. Coarctation is a congenital aortic lesion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Complications: orbital cellulitis, dural sinus thrombosis, meningitis and frontal osteomyelitis.
- Look for eye swelling, pain with eye movement, visual symptoms, severe headache or neurological signs.
- Complication red flags require urgent assessment.

questions.stem: Which imaging options are listed for assessment of sinusitis in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: D
options.text: Plain sinus X-ray and CT scan of the paranasal sinuses

questions.correctAnswerText: Plain sinus X-ray and CT scan of the paranasal sinuses
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance plain X-ray of the paranasal sinuses and CT scan, with sinus aspiration and culture in selected situations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Abdominal CT does not assess the paranasal sinuses.
- B. Incorrect. Neurological investigations are not the sinus imaging listed.
- C. Incorrect. These assess cardiac disease.
- D. Correct. These are the imaging options mentioned in the source.
- E. Incorrect. These are renal/urinary investigations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Imaging in the source: plain X-ray and CT paranasal sinuses.
- Sinus aspiration/culture may be used in selected cases.
- Investigation should be guided by severity, atypical features and complications.

cases.title: Ear and sinus infections: presentation, advice and complications

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with known asthma has had 10 days of fever, purulent nasal discharge, cough and cheek tenderness after a cold. His asthma control has worsened, with more night cough. His mother asks whether the sinuses above the eyes (the frontal sinuses) are involved. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Frontal sinusitis is the commonest form at this age because the frontal sinuses are fully formed at birth

options.label: B
options.text: The worsening asthma is unrelated, because sinusitis cannot influence the lower airways

options.label: C
options.text: Maxillary or ethmoid involvement is more likely, because frontal sinuses start developing around 7 years, and sinusitis can exacerbate asthma

options.label: D
options.text: Sphenoid sinusitis is impossible at this age, because the sphenoid sinuses do not form until adolescence

options.label: E
options.text: The illness is typically viral, so antibiotics and imaging have no role at any stage

questions.correctAnswerText: Maxillary or ethmoid involvement is more likely, because frontal sinuses start developing around 7 years, and sinusitis can exacerbate asthma
questions.initialExplanation: Maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are present at birth, the sphenoid begins at 2–3 years, and the frontal begins at about 7 years. Sinusitis is also listed as a cause of asthma exacerbation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Frontal sinuses begin to develop at about 7 years and complete by 12. Frontal sinusitis is uncommon in the first decade.
- B. Incorrect. Exacerbation of bronchial asthma is a listed complication of sinusitis.
- C. Correct. It combines the sinus development timeline with the asthma link.
- D. Incorrect. The sphenoid sinuses begin at 2–3 years and are complete by 5 years.
- E. Incorrect. Bacterial causes (S. pneumoniae, Hib, S. aureus) are listed. Treatment includes analgesia and antibiotics, and plain X-ray or CT can be used.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sinus development: maxillary and ethmoid at birth; sphenoid 2–3 years (complete by 5); frontal from 7 years (complete by 12).
- Complications of sinusitis: orbital cellulitis, dural sinus thrombosis and meningitis, frontal bone osteomyelitis, and exacerbation of bronchial asthma.
- Features: fever, headache, cough, mucopurulent or watery discharge, and cheek pain, swelling and tenderness with maxillary involvement.

source.raw: Respiratory sheet — Page 10 (Sinusitis: complications; key points on sinus pneumatization).

topics.name: Stridor and Chronic Upper Airway Disorders

cases.title: â€” Inspiratory stridor from the first weeks of life
cases.vignette: A 6-week-old infant is brought because of noisy breathing that began shortly after birth. The sound is inspiratory and becomes louder when the infant cries, feeds or lies supine. It improves when the infant is prone. The infant is otherwise thriving, has normal oxygen saturation and has no significant respiratory distress. Flexible laryngoscopy shows an omega-shaped epiglottis and supraglottic collapse during inspiration.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Laryngomalacia
questions.initialExplanation: Laryngomalacia is the commonest cause of congenital and chronic stridor in infancy. The soft supraglottic structures collapse inward during inspiration, causing inspiratory stridor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Foreign body aspiration â€” Incorrect. It usually follows a sudden choking episode and causes abrupt cough, wheeze or stridor.
- B. Laryngomalacia â€” Correct. Onset in early infancy, inspiratory noise, positional variation and an omega-shaped epiglottis strongly support this diagnosis.
- C. Bacterial tracheitis â€” Incorrect. It is an acute infectious upper-airway emergency with high fever and a toxic child.
- D. Subglottic stenosis â€” Incorrect. It can cause biphasic stridor and may be congenital or acquired, but the positional inspiratory pattern and laryngoscopy favour laryngomalacia.
- E. Acute epiglottitis â€” Incorrect. It presents abruptly with high fever, drooling, dysphagia and a toxic appearance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Laryngomalacia is the commonest cause of chronic congenital stridor in infancy.
- Soft supraglottic structures collapse during inspiration.
- Many infants thrive and have normal oxygen saturation.

questions.stem: Which factor typically worsens the stridor of laryngomalacia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Supine positioning
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that laryngomalacia-related stridor commonly becomes louder with crying, URTI and lying supine, and improves in the prone position.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Prone positioning â€” Incorrect. Clinical guidance improvement in this position; however, sleep positioning must still follow safe-sleep guidance.
- B. Quiet sleep â€” Incorrect. Crying and agitation are more typical aggravating factors.
- C. Head elevation â€” Incorrect. This is not the positional feature described.
- D. Sitting upright â€” Incorrect. It is not listed as the characteristic aggravating position.
- E. Supine positioning â€” Correct. This is a typical aggravating position in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Worsens with crying, URTI and supine position.
- Improves when prone in the clinical description.
- Do not confuse positional symptom relief with safe infant sleep recommendations.

questions.stem: Which investigation is described as useful to confirm laryngomalacia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Flexible laryngoscopy
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance diagnosis by history and examination, supported by flexible laryngoscopy, which may demonstrate the characteristic omega-shaped epiglottis and inspiratory supraglottic collapse.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Flexible laryngoscopy directly evaluates the larynx and supports the diagnosis.
- B. Incorrect. Spirometry is not feasible or appropriate in a young infant in this context.
- C. Incorrect. Bronchial challenge testing is used in selected asthma assessments, not laryngomalacia.
- D. Incorrect. Renal ultrasound does not assess the upper airway.
- E. Incorrect. CT abdomen is unrelated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Diagnosis: compatible history/examination plus flexible laryngoscopy.
- Typical laryngoscopy description: omega-shaped epiglottis.
- Assess growth, feeding, oxygenation and severity.

questions.stem: What is the usual natural history of uncomplicated laryngomalacia described?

options.label: A
options.text: It usually worsens progressively into adulthood

options.label: D
options.text: It requires routine antibiotics for several months

options.label: E
options.text: It is self-limiting and improves spontaneously by about 18â€“24 months

questions.correctAnswerText: It is self-limiting and improves spontaneously by about 18â€“24 months
questions.initialExplanation: Most uncomplicated cases improve as the laryngeal structures mature. Clinical guidance spontaneous improvement by approximately 18â€“24 months and reassurance of parents.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is not the usual natural history described.
- B. Incorrect. Tracheostomy is not routine treatment for uncomplicated laryngomalacia.
- C. Incorrect. The case described often has normal oxygen saturation and good growth.
- D. Incorrect. Laryngomalacia is a structural dynamic airway condition, not a bacterial infection.
- E. Correct. This is the time course given in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Usually self-limiting.
- Many infants thrive with normal oxygen saturation.
- Reassure and monitor; severe feeding, growth or respiratory compromise requires specialist assessment.

questions.stem: A newborn has stridor from birth due to a congenital membrane between the vocal cords. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Laryngeal web
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance a laryngeal web as a congenital membrane covered by connective tissue between the vocal cords, producing stridor from birth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the anatomical description and timing.
- B. Incorrect. Laryngomalacia is due to dynamic supraglottic collapse during inspiration.
- C. Incorrect. Bronchiolitis causes lower-airway wheeze and respiratory distress.
- D. Incorrect. Pleural effusion produces reduced chest movement and stony dullness, not congenital stridor.
- E. Incorrect. Croup is an acute viral illness, usually in infants and young children after a URI prodrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Laryngeal web: congenital connective-tissue membrane between vocal cords.
- Stridor is present at birth.
- Treatment listed: laryngoscopic ablation.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes subglottic stenosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Collapse of supraglottic tissues during expiration

options.label: B
options.text: Narrowing below the vocal cords, causing inspiratory and expiratory stridor

options.label: E
options.text: Infection of the alveoli by RSV

questions.correctAnswerText: Narrowing below the vocal cords, causing inspiratory and expiratory stridor
questions.initialExplanation: Subglottic stenosis is narrowing of the airway below the vocal cords. Clinical guidance that it may be congenital or acquired, including after cuffed endotracheal tube use, and may cause biphasic stridor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dynamic supraglottic collapse during inspiration describes laryngomalacia.
- B. Correct. This is the definition and characteristic sound described.
- C. Incorrect. This is epiglottitis.
- D. Incorrect. This is pleural effusion.
- E. Incorrect. RSV bronchiolitis affects bronchioles.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Subglottic stenosis: narrowing below vocal cords.
- May be congenital or acquired after intubation.
- Stridor may be inspiratory and expiratory.
- Bronchoscopy is used for diagnosis; treatment depends on severity and may include surgery or tracheostomy.

questions.stem: A child has stridor, dysphagia and recurrent apnoea due to compression of both trachea and oesophagus by an abnormal aortic arch. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Vascular ring
questions.initialExplanation: A vascular ring is a congenital anomaly of the aortic arch and great vessels that can encircle or compress the trachea and oesophagus. Double aortic arch is the commonest type.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Croup causes laryngotracheal mucosal inflammation and barking cough.
- B. Incorrect. Epiglottitis is an acute infectious airway emergency.
- C. Correct. Airway and oesophageal compression explains stridor, wheeze, apnoea, cyanosis and dysphagia.
- D. Incorrect. Laryngomalacia causes dynamic supraglottic collapse and does not compress the oesophagus.
- E. Incorrect. Bronchiolitis is a lower-airway viral infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vascular ring: congenital aortic arch/great-vessel anomaly.
- Double aortic arch is highlighted as the commonest form.
- May compress trachea and oesophagus â†’ stridor, apnoea, wheeze, cyanosis and dysphagia.
- Assessment may include chest X-ray, barium swallow, echocardiography and angiography; treatment is surgical.

cases.title: â€” Barking cough and inspiratory stridor at night
cases.vignette: A 20-month-old child develops rhinorrhoea and low-grade fever for two days, followed by a barking cough, hoarse voice and harsh inspiratory stridor. Symptoms are worse at night. The child is not toxic and can drink. The clinician assesses severity and decides whether home care or hospital treatment is required.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis)
questions.initialExplanation: A URI prodrome followed by barking cough, hoarseness and harsh inspiratory stridor, often worse at night, is typical of viral croup.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bronchiolitis typically affects infants and causes wheeze and lower respiratory distress.
- B. Correct. The gradual onset and classic barking cough/stridor pattern support viral croup.
- C. Incorrect. FBA usually follows a choking episode with abrupt cough or wheeze.
- D. Incorrect. Bacterial tracheitis usually causes high fever and a toxic child, with stridor and only mild cough.
- E. Incorrect. Epiglottitis usually has sudden onset, high fever, drooling, severe dysphagia, a toxic appearance and little or no cough.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Croup = laryngotracheobronchitis.
- Commonest cause of acute stridor in children.
- Gradual URI prodrome â†’ barking/brassy cough, hoarseness and harsh stridor.

questions.stem: Which virus is the commonest cause of viral croup in the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Parainfluenza virus
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies parainfluenza virus types 1, 2 and 3 as the commonest causes of viral croup. Other listed viruses include RSV, influenza, metapneumovirus and adenovirus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Adenovirus is another possible viral cause.
- B. Correct. Parainfluenza is the most common cause in the source.
- C. Incorrect. EBV is listed as a cause of pharyngitis, not the commonest cause of croup.
- D. Incorrect. RSV may cause croup but is not the commonest listed cause.
- E. Incorrect. Rhinovirus is associated with common cold and other respiratory illness, but is not the leading croup cause stated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Parainfluenza types 1â€“3 are the commonest viral croup causes.
- Most cases occur between 6 months and 6 years; peak age is 1â€“2 years.
- Croup is common in autumn and early winter.

questions.stem: What causes the airway narrowing in viral croup?

options.label: A
options.text: A foreign body acting as a ball valve in a main bronchus

options.label: C
options.text: Laryngotracheal mucosal inflammation and oedema with increased secretions

options.label: D
options.text: A congenital membrane between the vocal cords

questions.correctAnswerText: Laryngotracheal mucosal inflammation and oedema with increased secretions
questions.initialExplanation: Viral inflammation produces mucosal oedema and increased secretions in the larynx and trachea. Because the pediatric upper airway is narrow, relatively small swelling can cause significant obstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A ball-valve foreign body causes unilateral air trapping in the bronchial tree.
- B. Incorrect. Alveolar septal destruction is not the mechanism of croup.
- C. Correct. This is the pathophysiology described.
- D. Incorrect. This describes a laryngeal web.
- E. Incorrect. Pleural fluid causes lung compression and reduced expansion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Larynx/trachea inflammation â†’ oedema + secretions â†’ narrowed upper airway.
- The smaller airway calibre in young children increases the effect of swelling.
- Symptoms may worsen at night.

questions.stem: A child with suspected upper airway obstruction is brought to the emergency department. Which action should be avoided?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeatedly examining the throat using a tongue depressor

options.label: C
options.text: Keeping the child calm with a caregiver

options.label: E
options.text: Avoiding unnecessary investigations that delay airway management

questions.correctAnswerText: Repeatedly examining the throat using a tongue depressor
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance warns against using a tongue depressor to examine the throat in a child with suspected upper-airway obstruction, because agitation or airway manipulation may worsen obstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Throat examination with a spatula/tongue depressor should be avoided in this setting.
- B. Incorrect. Airway management is the priority.
- C. Incorrect. Keeping the child calm is encouraged.
- D. Incorrect. Avoiding a flat position is recommended in suspected upper-airway obstruction.
- E. Incorrect. Unnecessary investigations should not delay stabilization.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Keep the child calm, ideally with a caregiver.
- Do not force the child supine.
- Do not examine the throat with a tongue depressor if significant upper-airway obstruction is suspected.
- Prioritize airway management over non-essential investigations.

questions.stem: Which clinical feature is used to classify severe croup?

options.label: A
options.text: Barking cough without stridor or distress

options.label: E
options.text: Normal breathing with normal oxygen saturation

questions.correctAnswerText: Stridor at rest
questions.initialExplanation: The severity table distinguishes mild croup, with cough mainly and no respiratory distress, from moderate croup, with cough and stridor, and severe croup, with stridor at rest and severe respiratory distress signs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is closer to mild croup.
- B. Incorrect. Stridor when crying is less severe than stridor at rest.
- C. Incorrect. Rhinorrhoea alone is an upper respiratory symptom.
- D. Correct. Stridor at rest is the defining severity feature 's table.
- E. Incorrect. This does not indicate severe croup.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mild: cough mainly, no signs of respiratory distress.
- Moderate: cough + stridor, moderate distress.
- Severe: stridor at rest, severe distress, restlessness/dusky appearance and low saturation.
- Very severe cases may require airway intervention.

questions.stem: Which treatment is used for moderate or severe croup?

options.label: B
options.text: Routine oral antibiotics for each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Dexamethasone or nebulized budesonide
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance corticosteroids to reduce severity and duration of croup, including a single dose of oral/injected dexamethasone or nebulized budesonide.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pancreatic enzymes are used in cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Viral croup does not routinely require antibiotics.
- C. Correct. Corticosteroids are the anti-inflammatory treatment described.
- D. Incorrect. Diuretics do not treat laryngotracheal oedema.
- E. Incorrect. Antituberculous therapy is not used for typical viral croup.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Corticosteroids reduce severity and duration.
- Clinical guidance dexamethasone or nebulized budesonide.
- Mild cases may be managed at home with observation and clear return precautions.

questions.stem: A child with severe croup receives nebulized adrenaline and rapidly improves. Why must the child remain under observation for several hours?

options.label: A
options.text: Improvement may be transient because adrenaline has a short duration of action, with possible rebound of symptoms

options.label: B
options.text: Observation is required to monitor renal function

options.label: C
options.text: Adrenaline typically causes delayed bacterial pneumonia

options.label: D
options.text: Adrenaline causes permanent paralysis of the vocal cords

options.label: E
options.text: Adrenaline causes immediate permanent resolution of the infection

questions.correctAnswerText: Improvement may be transient because adrenaline has a short duration of action, with possible rebound of symptoms
questions.initialExplanation: Nebulized adrenaline can rapidly reduce upper-airway mucosal oedema, but the effect is temporary. Clinical guidance observation for approximately 3â€“4 hours to detect recurrence as the drug effect wears off.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Temporary improvement may be followed by recurrence of stridor and distress.
- B. Incorrect. The key concern is recurrence of airway symptoms, not renal function.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the reason for observation.
- D. Incorrect. Vocal cord paralysis is not the expected adverse effect described.
- E. Incorrect. Adrenaline does not eradicate the viral infection or guarantee permanent resolution.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nebulized adrenaline gives rapid but transient improvement.
- Observe for about 3â€“4 hours after treatment as stated.
- Continue to assess work of breathing, stridor at rest and oxygenation.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes spasmodic croup from typical viral croup?

options.label: A
options.text: Spasmodic croup is a lower-airway bacterial infection

options.label: B
options.text: Spasmodic croup is typically caused by Hib

options.label: C
options.text: Spasmodic croup not usually causes stridor

options.label: D
options.text: Spasmodic croup is often recurrent, may be associated with atopy and lacks the usual coryzal/fever prodrome

options.label: E
options.text: Spasmodic croup typically presents with drooling and toxic appearance

questions.correctAnswerText: Spasmodic croup is often recurrent, may be associated with atopy and lacks the usual coryzal/fever prodrome
questions.initialExplanation: The source compares viral croup, usually associated with a viral prodrome, with spasmodic croup, which may recur, be linked with allergy/atopy and have no preceding coryza or fever.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Spasmodic croup is an upper-airway syndrome, not a lower-airway bacterial infection.
- B. Incorrect. Hib is the commonest cause of acute epiglottitis, not spasmodic croup.
- C. Incorrect. It may produce the same croup-like barking cough and stridor.
- D. Correct. This is the comparison.
- E. Incorrect. Drooling and toxic appearance suggest epiglottitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral croup: viral prodrome, coryza and low-grade fever.
- Spasmodic croup: recurrent attacks, possible atopy, often no fever/coryza.
- Treatment approaches are similar.

cases.title: Croup and epiglottitis: imaging, disposition, counselling and confirmation

questions.stem: At 2 a.m., a 9-month-old girl is brought with a barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor when she cries, with mild subcostal recession; she is comfortable at rest. Oxygen saturation is normal and she is drinking. The family lives 45 minutes from the nearest hospital and has no transport. Which decision best fits clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Manage at home with warm moist air alone, because moist air is the main treatment and there is no stridor at rest

options.label: B
options.text: Give a single dose of dexamethasone and admit for observation, because age under 12 months, night-time and distance from hospital most favour admission

options.label: C
options.text: Discharge with oral antibiotics, because croup at this age is usually bacterial

options.label: D
options.text: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor to exclude epiglottitis before any decision

options.label: E
options.text: Send for an urgent lateral neck X-ray and blood cultures before giving any treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Give a single dose of dexamethasone and admit for observation, because age under 12 months, night-time and distance from hospital most favour admission
questions.initialExplanation: She has moderate croup (cough plus stridor with some distress). Steroids are indicated, and clinical guidance says the decision between home and hospital depends on severity, time of day, access to hospital and age, with children under 12 months needing admission more often because of their narrow airway.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Warm moist air is not beneficial, and the other factors favour admission.
- B. Correct. Steroid treatment plus admission applies the four decision factors listed.
- C. Incorrect. Viral croup (parainfluenza) does not need antibiotics.
- D. Incorrect. Examining the throat with a tongue depressor is contraindicated in suspected upper-airway obstruction.
- E. Incorrect. Imaging and blood tests should not delay treatment, and cultures are not part of croup management.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Severity: mild = cough mainly; moderate = cough + stridor with moderate distress; severe = stridor at rest with severe distress, restlessness or dusky colour, low SpO2.
- Home vs hospital depends on severity, time of day, ease of access to hospital and age (under 12 months have a narrower airway).
- Steroid (dexamethasone single dose or nebulised budesonide) for mild to severe; nebulised adrenaline (racemic epinephrine) for severe, with 3–4 hours of observation.
- Intubation is very rarely needed in viral croup.

questions.stem: The parents of a 2-year-old recovering from viral croup ask three questions: whether steaming the bathroom or warm mist would have shortened the illness, how long recovery usually takes, and whether a vaccine can prevent it. Which answer is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Warm moist air is the most effective treatment; recovery takes about 3 weeks; a parainfluenza vaccine is routinely given

options.label: B
options.text: Warm moist air works when combined with antibiotics; recovery takes about 4 weeks; a vaccine is given at 2 months

options.label: C
options.text: Humidified air replaces corticosteroids; recovery takes about 10 days; a vaccine is available if requested

options.label: D
options.text: Warm moist air has not been shown to help; recovery usually occurs in 2–5 days; there is no vaccine for the parainfluenza viruses

options.label: E
options.text: Warm moist air prevents viral pneumonia, which affects most children; recovery takes 1 day; a vaccine exists

questions.correctAnswerText: Warm moist air has not been shown to help; recovery usually occurs in 2–5 days; there is no vaccine for the parainfluenza viruses
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance marks inhalation of warm moist air as not beneficial, gives an excellent prognosis with recovery in 2–5 days, and states there is no vaccine against parainfluenza viruses.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Moist air is not beneficial, and no parainfluenza vaccine exists.
- B. Incorrect. Moist air does not need antibiotics to "work", and the recovery time is much shorter than 4 weeks.
- C. Incorrect. Humidified air does not replace steroids, which reduce severity and duration.
- D. Correct. It matches all three points.
- E. Incorrect. Viral pneumonia is an uncommon complication (about 2%), not a feature in most children.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Complication: viral pneumonia (about 2%).
- Prognosis: excellent; recovery usually in 2–5 days.
- Prevention: no vaccine for parainfluenza viruses.
- Parents should watch the child at home for signs of increasing severity.

cases.title: â€” A toxic child with drooling and tripod posture
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old child is brought with sudden onset of high fever, severe throat discomfort and difficulty swallowing. The child is toxic, exhausted and drooling, with a muffled â€œhot potatoâ€‌ voice. The child sits leaning forward with the mouth open and jaw thrust forward. Stridor is present but softer than expected, and there is little cough.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acute epiglottitis
questions.initialExplanation: Sudden onset, high fever, toxic appearance, drooling, severe dysphagia, muffled voice and tripod posture are classic features of acute epiglottitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Acute epiglottitis â€” Correct. The clinical pattern suggests a swollen epiglottis and impending airway obstruction.
- B. Bronchiolitis â€” Incorrect. It causes lower-airway wheeze, cough and respiratory distress, especially in infants.
- C. Asthma â€” Incorrect. It causes episodic expiratory wheeze, cough and breathlessness.
- D. Viral croup â€” Incorrect. It usually has a gradual URI prodrome, barking cough, hoarseness and harsh stridor.
- E. Laryngomalacia â€” Incorrect. It causes chronic inspiratory stridor beginning in early infancy, often with positional variation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Epiglottitis: abrupt onset, toxic child, high fever, drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice and tripod posture.
- Stridor may be soft/whispering and cough absent or slight.
- It is a medical emergency because of sudden complete airway obstruction risk.

questions.stem: Which organism is identified as the commonest cause of acute epiglottitis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Haemophilus influenzae type b
questions.initialExplanation: Hib is the commonest cause listed. The condition has become much rarer following Hib immunization.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. RSV is a major cause of bronchiolitis.
- B. Incorrect. Rhinovirus commonly causes coryza.
- C. Incorrect. Mycoplasma is associated with atypical pneumonia.
- D. Incorrect. Parainfluenza is the commonest cause of viral croup.
- E. Correct. Hib is the commonest cause identified.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hib is the classic organism in pediatric epiglottitis.
- Other organisms listed include group A/C streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus.
- Hib vaccination has markedly reduced incidence.

questions.stem: Which action is contraindicated when epiglottitis is suspected?

options.label: C
options.text: Attempting to visualize the epiglottis with a tongue depressor in the emergency room

questions.correctAnswerText: Attempting to visualize the epiglottis with a tongue depressor in the emergency room
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance explicitly warns that attempting to examine the throat with a tongue depressor may provoke laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Calm handling is essential.
- B. Incorrect. Oxygen is part of breathing support.
- C. Correct. This can trigger sudden total airway obstruction and must be avoided.
- D. Incorrect. Controlled airway planning is central to management.
- E. Incorrect. Early involvement of anesthesia, ENT and pediatric teams is appropriate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Suspected epiglottitis: do not use a tongue depressor to inspect the throat.
- Avoid unnecessary agitation and procedures.
- Secure airway in a controlled setting with experienced teams.

questions.stem: What is the appropriate initial management priority for a child with suspected acute epiglottitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Perform repeated throat swabs at the bedside

options.label: B
options.text: Secure and maintain a patent airway, with urgent ICU and specialist support

options.label: D
options.text: Send the child alone for a lateral neck X-ray before any clinical action

questions.correctAnswerText: Secure and maintain a patent airway, with urgent ICU and specialist support
questions.initialExplanation: Epiglottitis is an airway emergency. clinical guidance prioritizes airway protection, oxygenation, IV access/fluids, IV antibiotics and direct ICU admission with anesthesia, ENT and pediatric teams.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bedside throat manipulation can precipitate obstruction.
- B. Correct. Airway stabilization is the first priority.
- C. Incorrect. A toxic child with drooling and dysphagia should not be discharged.
- D. Incorrect. Imaging must not delay airway management and may be unsafe in an unstable child.
- E. Incorrect. Bronchodilators do not treat epiglottic swelling due to bacterial infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- A: secure airway (intubation; rarely urgent tracheostomy).
- B: oxygen.
- C: IV access/fluids and IV third-generation cephalosporin after appropriate cultures when feasible.
- Admit to ICU and involve anesthesia, ENT and pediatrics.
- Steroids and adrenaline are listed as ineffective for acute epiglottitis.

questions.stem: Which comparison best distinguishes epiglottitis from viral croup?

options.label: A
options.text: Epiglottitis: recurrent attacks without fever; croup: toxic child with drooling

options.label: B
options.text: Epiglottitis: abrupt onset, toxic appearance, drooling and muffled voice; croup: gradual onset after coryza with barking cough and hoarseness

options.label: C
options.text: Epiglottitis: chronic inspiratory stridor since birth; croup: wheeze since infancy

options.label: D
options.text: Epiglottitis: low fever and barking cough; croup: high fever and no cough

options.label: E
options.text: Both typically present with identical cough and voice changes

questions.correctAnswerText: Epiglottitis: abrupt onset, toxic appearance, drooling and muffled voice; croup: gradual onset after coryza with barking cough and hoarseness
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance's comparison table highlights abrupt onset, high fever, toxicity, drooling and soft stridor in epiglottitis, versus gradual onset, coryza, barking cough, hoarseness and harsh stridor in croup.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. It reverses the typical patterns.
- B. Correct. This is the key clinical distinction.
- C. Incorrect. This describes laryngomalacia for epiglottitis and does not describe croup.
- D. Incorrect. The fever and cough patterns are reversed.
- E. Incorrect. The onset, cough, voice and drooling patterns differ.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Epiglottitis: toxic, drooling, dysphagia, tripod and muffled voice.
- Croup: barking cough, hoarse voice, harsh stridor and URI prodrome.
- Do not attempt routine throat examination in suspected epiglottitis.

questions.stem: Which preventive intervention has reduced the incidence of acute epiglottitis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hib vaccination
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that Hib vaccination at 2, 4 and 6 months has led to a major reduction in acute epiglottitis. Rifampicin prophylaxis for close contacts is also mentioned.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Hib immunization is the key prevention measure listed.
- B. Incorrect. BCG protects against selected forms of tuberculosis.
- C. Incorrect. RSV monoclonal antibody is used for prevention in selected high-risk infants with respect to RSV disease.
- D. Incorrect. Influenza vaccination prevents influenza, not Hib epiglottitis.
- E. Incorrect. Polio vaccination prevents poliomyelitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hib vaccine: prevention of Hib epiglottitis.
- The source lists doses at 2, 4 and 6 months.
- Rifampicin prophylaxis is mentioned for close contacts.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child is febrile and toxic with stridor and a mild barking cough. There is no drooling or tripod posture. The child deteriorated after a viral URTI. Which diagnosis should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bacterial tracheitis
questions.initialExplanation: Bacterial tracheitis is a rare but serious infectious cause of upper-airway obstruction. Clinical guidance high fever, toxic appearance, stridor and mild cough, sometimes after a viral URI.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Asthma causes lower-airway expiratory wheeze.
- B. Incorrect. Viral croup generally causes a less toxic child and a characteristic gradual prodrome.
- C. Incorrect. Pleural effusion causes reduced chest expansion, stony dullness and reduced air entry.
- D. Correct. The toxic febrile child with stridor and a mild barking cough is consistent with bacterial tracheitis.
- E. Incorrect. Laryngomalacia is chronic congenital stridor in infancy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bacterial tracheitis is rare but serious.
- Clinical guidance Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae as causes.
- May follow viral URTI.
- Investigations include CBC, CRP and tracheal secretion culture.

questions.stem: Which set of organisms is listed as a cause of bacterial tracheitis in the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae as bacterial tracheitis pathogens.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These organisms are named in the bacterial tracheitis section.
- B. Incorrect. These are viruses associated with respiratory infections and croup/bronchiolitis, not the bacterial pathogens listed.
- C. Incorrect. These fungi are not the causes highlighted.
- D. Incorrect. These are urinary pathogens.
- E. Incorrect. Hib is the classic epiglottitis organism; Mycoplasma is associated with atypical pneumonia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bacterial tracheitis: S. aureus and S. pneumoniae.
- High fever and toxic appearance distinguish it from uncomplicated viral croup.
- Airway assessment and microbiological evaluation are important.

cases.title: Croup and epiglottitis: imaging, disposition, counselling and confirmation

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl, whose family declined the Hib vaccine, has a temperature of 39.4 °C and appears toxic. She is drooling, sitting forward with her mouth open, and has a muffled voice with soft stridor. The team is deciding how to investigate and confirm the diagnosis. Which plan agrees with clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Send CBC and blood culture (neutrophilia and Hib growth expected), avoid a lateral neck film, and inspect the epiglottis by laryngoscopy in the operating room under general anaesthesia, where a cherry-red swollen epiglottis is expected

options.label: B
options.text: Inspect the throat with a tongue depressor in the emergency room to see a cherry-red epiglottis, then request a lateral neck film to confirm the thumb sign

options.label: C
options.text: Send her to radiology for a lateral neck X-ray and secure the airway if no thumb sign is seen

options.label: D
options.text: Take a throat swab in the emergency room and start oral penicillin, with review in 24 hours

options.label: E
options.text: Arrange a lumbar puncture and CT of the neck before making any airway plan

questions.correctAnswerText: Send CBC and blood culture (neutrophilia and Hib growth expected), avoid a lateral neck film, and inspect the epiglottis by laryngoscopy in the operating room under general anaesthesia, where a cherry-red swollen epiglottis is expected
questions.initialExplanation: Epiglottitis is an airway emergency, so the child goes to ICU with anaesthesia and ENT support. The supportive tests are CBC (neutrophilia) and blood culture (Hib), and direct inspection is done only in the operating room under general anaesthesia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. It matches the investigation plan.
- B. Incorrect. A tongue depressor can provoke laryngospasm and total airway obstruction. It is contraindicated.
- C. Incorrect. The lateral neck film (thumb sign) is not done in suspected epiglottitis, and waiting for it delays airway control.
- D. Incorrect. Throat manipulation is unsafe, and oral penicillin is not the treatment. IV third-generation cephalosporin is used.
- E. Incorrect. Neither lumbar puncture nor CT is part of the plan, and both delay airway management.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Epiglottitis: CBC shows raised WBC mainly neutrophils; blood culture is positive for Hib; direct laryngoscopy only in the operating room under GA.
- Management: airway first (intubation; rarely urgent tracheostomy), oxygen, IV fluids, IV third-generation cephalosporin, direct ICU admission with anaesthesia, ENT and paediatric teams.
- Steroids and adrenaline are ineffective. Prevention: Hib vaccine at 2, 4 and 6 months; rifampicin prophylaxis for close contacts.
- Features: abrupt onset, toxic, fever above 38.5 °C, drooling, muffled voice, soft stridor, little or no cough, tripod position, age 2–7 years.
