cases.title: â€” An infant with coryza followed by wheeze
cases.vignette: A 5-month-old infant develops rhinorrhoea and low-grade fever. Over the next two days, the infant develops cough, bilateral wheeze, tachypnoea, subcostal recession and poor feeding. On auscultation there is prolonged expiration, bilateral rhonchi and fine end-inspiratory crackles. The liver edge is palpable below the costal margin, but there is no primary hepatic disease.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acute bronchiolitis
questions.initialExplanation: A young infant with a coryzal prodrome followed by cough, bilateral wheeze, tachypnoea and feeding difficulty has a typical presentation of acute bronchiolitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Epiglottitis causes abrupt upper-airway symptoms with drooling, dysphagia and toxicity.
- B. Incorrect. CF can cause recurrent respiratory infections and poor growth, but this acute first episode following coryza is more typical of bronchiolitis.
- C. Incorrect. Sinusitis causes nasal/facial symptoms rather than diffuse bronchiolar wheeze in an infant.
- D. Incorrect. FBA usually follows a sudden choking episode and may cause unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry.
- E. Correct. The age, viral prodrome and diffuse lower-airway signs are characteristic.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bronchiolitis is a common serious respiratory infection in infancy.
- Typical sequence: coryza for a few days, then cough, wheeze, breathlessness and poor feeding.
- Apnoea may be an early or prominent feature in young infants.

questions.stem: Which virus accounts for the majority of bronchiolitis cases in the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: RSV
questions.initialExplanation: Respiratory syncytial virus is identified as the main pathogen, accounting for approximately 80% of cases in the supplied clinical guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. RSV is the predominant pathogen in the source.
- B. Incorrect. Rhinovirus is among other possible bronchiolitis pathogens but is not the predominant one in the source.
- C. Incorrect. Parainfluenza is the commonest cause of viral croup.
- D. Incorrect. EBV is associated with infectious mononucleosis and pharyngitis.
- E. Incorrect. Influenza may cause lower respiratory infection but is not the commonest cause listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- RSV types A and B are described.
- Incubation period: 2â€“6 days.
- Other pathogens include rhinovirus, adenovirus, influenza, human metapneumovirus and occasionally Mycoplasma.
- Co-infection may cause more severe disease.

questions.stem: Which age group represents the peak incidence of bronchiolitis?
questions.correctAnswerText: 3â€“6 months
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance bronchiolitis as occurring in children younger than 2 years, with a peak incidence at 3â€“6 months. It is common in winter and early spring.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Neonates can be affected, but the peak is later in early infancy.
- B. Incorrect. This age group is beyond the typical bronchiolitis peak.
- C. Correct. This is the peak age stated.
- D. Incorrect. This is not a typical adult disease.
- E. Incorrect. Bronchiolitis is principally an illness of infancy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mainly affects children under 2 years.
- Peak age: 3â€“6 months.
- Season: winter and early spring.
- Slight male predominance is mentioned.

questions.stem: What is the principal pathophysiological mechanism producing wheeze and air trapping in bronchiolitis?

options.label: B
options.text: Fixed obstruction of the aortic arch

options.label: C
options.text: Destruction of alveoli by pancreatic enzymes

options.label: E
options.text: Bronchiolar inflammation, mucosal oedema and secretions narrow the small airways

questions.correctAnswerText: Bronchiolar inflammation, mucosal oedema and secretions narrow the small airways
questions.initialExplanation: Viral invasion of bronchiolar mucosa causes inflammation, oedema and exudate/secretions. Narrowed small airways lead to air trapping, hyperinflation and sometimes atelectasis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Vocal cord palsy produces upper-airway stridor rather than diffuse bronchiolar wheeze.
- B. Incorrect. Aortic arch abnormalities may compress the trachea but do not explain viral bronchiolar inflammation.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the pathogenesis of bronchiolitis.
- D. Incorrect. Pleural effusion compresses the lung from outside rather than causing bronchiolar mucosal oedema.
- E. Correct. This is the sequence described in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral infection â†’ bronchiolar inflammation â†’ oedema + secretions â†’ airway narrowing.
- Partial obstruction causes air trapping and hyperinflation.
- Complete small-airway obstruction may cause atelectasis.
- Hyperinflation may displace the diaphragm downward and make the liver palpable (pseudohepatomegaly).

questions.stem: Why may the liver edge be palpable in an infant with bronchiolitis despite no primary liver disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Pleural effusion pushes the liver upward

options.label: B
options.text: Hyperinflated lungs push the diaphragm downward

options.label: C
options.text: The infant has congenital biliary atresia

options.label: D
options.text: Hepatic failure causes the liver to enlarge in each case

options.label: E
options.text: RSV directly infects the liver and causes acute hepatitis

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyperinflated lungs push the diaphragm downward
questions.initialExplanation: Air trapping causes lung hyperinflation and downward displacement of the diaphragm. The liver may therefore be palpable lower than usual, producing pseudohepatomegaly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pleural effusion does not explain the typical downward displacement caused by hyperinflation.
- B. Correct. This is the mechanism illustrated in the bronchiolitis section.
- C. Incorrect. Biliary atresia causes conjugated jaundice and hepatobiliary disease, not this acute respiratory finding.
- D. Incorrect. Hepatic failure is not the expected explanation.
- E. Incorrect. Direct liver infection is not the mechanism described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bronchiolitis causes hyperinflation.
- Diaphragm is displaced downward.
- A palpable liver can be a mechanical effect rather than true hepatomegaly.

questions.stem: How is uncomplicated acute bronchiolitis usually diagnosed?

options.label: A
options.text: Mainly clinically from history and examination

options.label: B
options.text: Routine chest CT in each infant

options.label: C
options.text: Sweat chloride testing in each first episode of wheeze

options.label: E
options.text: Blood culture in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Mainly clinically from history and examination
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that bronchiolitis is diagnosed mainly clinically. Routine investigations, including chest X-ray and blood gases, are not recommended unless respiratory failure or another complication is suspected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Clinical diagnosis is the recommended approach in typical cases.
- B. Incorrect. CT is not a routine test for bronchiolitis.
- C. Incorrect. CF testing is considered with recurrent infection, poor growth or other compatible features, not automatically for every first wheezing episode.
- D. Incorrect. Bronchoscopy is not routinely required.
- E. Incorrect. Blood cultures are reserved for selected clinical indications.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Clinical diagnosis: typical infant age, coryzal prodrome, cough, wheeze and respiratory distress.
- CXR may be normal, hyperinflated or show patchy atelectasis.
- Viral PCR is not routine because it often does not change management.
- ABG is reserved for severe cases/concern about respiratory failure.

questions.stem: Which finding is an indication for hospital admission in acute bronchiolitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Persistent oxygen saturation below 92% in room air

options.label: B
options.text: Normal oxygen saturation and no respiratory distress

questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent oxygen saturation below 92% in room air
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance persistent saturation below 92%, severe respiratory distress, apnoea, poor feeding/dehydration, young age and high-risk comorbidity as admission indications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Persistent SpO2 below 92% in room air is explicitly listed.
- B. Incorrect. These are reassuring features.
- C. Incorrect. An isolated cough without other concerning signs does not meet the listed admission criteria.
- D. Incorrect. Bronchiolitis primarily affects infants; uncomplicated coryza at age 5 does not meet the admission criteria.
- E. Incorrect. Mild coryza with adequate feeding and no distress can usually be managed at home.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Admit for severe respiratory distress, grunting, cyanosis or apnoea.
- Poor feeding, dehydration or persistent SpO2 <92% are important indications.
- Consider admission for infants under 3â€“6 months and those with prematurity/VLBW, immunodeficiency, CHD or chronic lung disease/BPD.

questions.stem: Which treatment best represents routine management of acute bronchiolitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Routine antibiotics, systemic corticosteroids and bronchodilators for each infant

options.label: D
options.text: Supportive care with hydration, oxygen when needed and close observation

options.label: E
options.text: Nebulized adrenaline as first-line treatment for typical presentations

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive care with hydration, oxygen when needed and close observation
questions.initialExplanation: Treatment is supportive. clinical guidance emphasizes adequate hydration (oral, NG or IV according to need), oxygen when hypoxic, and monitoring of respiratory rate, distress, apnoea and oxygen saturation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is secondary bacterial infection; corticosteroids and bronchodilators are not routine.
- B. Incorrect. Ventilatory support is reserved for severe cases with respiratory failure or exhaustion.
- C. Incorrect. Physiotherapy has no routine role in acute bronchiolitis.
- D. Correct. This is the core management described.
- E. Incorrect. Nebulized adrenaline is associated with selected upper-airway obstruction such as croup, not routine bronchiolitis treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Supportive care: hydration + oxygen if indicated + monitoring.
- NGT feeding or IV fluids may be required when oral intake is inadequate.
- CPAP/BiPAP or mechanical ventilation may be required in ICU for severe disease.
- Antibiotics only if secondary bacterial infection is suspected/confirmed.

questions.stem: Which statement about bronchodilators and other specific treatments in bronchiolitis matches the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Corticosteroids and antihistamines have no benefit; antibiotics have no role unless secondary bacterial infection occurs

options.label: B
options.text: Hypertonic saline is mandatory in each case

options.label: D
options.text: Chest physiotherapy is essential in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Ribavirin is routinely used in most infants

questions.correctAnswerText: Corticosteroids and antihistamines have no benefit; antibiotics have no role unless secondary bacterial infection occurs
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that corticosteroids, antihistamines, antibiotics (unless bacterial infection), physiotherapy and hypertonic saline have no routine role. Ribavirin is not routinely used and is mentioned only for selected high-risk infants.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This reflects the specific statements in the source.
- B. Incorrect. Hypertonic saline is stated as having no routine role.
- C. Incorrect. Steroids are not routine therapy for bronchiolitis.
- D. Incorrect. Physiotherapy has no routine role in acute bronchiolitis.
- E. Incorrect. Ribavirin is not routinely used; the source restricts it to selected high-risk infants.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bronchodilators may be trialled only where local protocol/clinical context supports it; they are not a universal routine intervention.
- Steroids and antihistamines: no benefit in the source.
- Antibiotics: only for secondary bacterial infection.
- Ribavirin: not routine; selected high-risk infants only.
- Complications include apnoea, respiratory failure, dehydration, secondary infection and pneumothorax.

questions.stem: Which preventive statement about RSV bronchiolitis is correct ?

options.label: A
options.text: Hand hygiene and avoiding exposure to symptomatic people are important; the sheet also mentions palivizumab for selected high-risk infants

options.label: B
options.text: Routine monthly corticosteroid injections prevent RSV infection

options.label: C
options.text: Isolation is not usually useful because RSV is not contagious

options.label: D
options.text: A universally effective RSV vaccine is available for most infants in the sheet

options.label: E
options.text: Antibiotic prophylaxis is required for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Hand hygiene and avoiding exposure to symptomatic people are important; the sheet also mentions palivizumab for selected high-risk infants
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance emphasizes hand hygiene and avoiding contact with symptomatic individuals. It also lists monthly IM palivizumab for selected high-risk children, particularly preterm infants. The source states that no RSV vaccine is available; current prevention recommendations should be checked against up-to-date local guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the prevention measures described.
- B. Incorrect. Corticosteroids are not RSV prophylaxis.
- C. Incorrect. RSV is highly contagious.
- D. Incorrect. The source does not describe a universal vaccine for all infants.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not prevent viral RSV infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hand hygiene and contact precautions reduce transmission.
- The source mentions palivizumab for selected high-risk infants.
- Most cases recover within 1â€“2 weeks, but apnoea and respiratory failure are important complications.

cases.title: Not every breathless infant has bronchiolitis

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant was admitted 5 weeks ago with severe bronchiolitis due to adenovirus type 7. Since discharge he has had persistent cough, wheeze and tachypnoea that do not respond to bronchodilators. There is no history of choking, no steatorrhoea and his growth is normal. Which complication of bronchiolitis is most likely, and what chronic lung disease can it lead to?

options.label: A
options.text: Pneumothorax, which resolves spontaneously and leaves no chronic lung disease

options.label: B
options.text: Reinfection with RSV, which typically resolves within 1–2 weeks

options.label: C
options.text: Bronchiolitis obliterans, a recognised sequel of adenovirus types 3 and 7 that can also lead to bronchiectasis

options.label: D
options.text: Cystic fibrosis, because persistent wheeze after bronchiolitis is a direct complication of RSV

options.label: E
options.text: Missed foreign body aspiration, because bronchiolitis commonly hides a foreign body

questions.correctAnswerText: Bronchiolitis obliterans, a recognised sequel of adenovirus types 3 and 7 that can also lead to bronchiectasis
questions.initialExplanation: Bronchiolitis obliterans is a listed complication of bronchiolitis, linked to adenovirus 3 and 7. It also appears as an acquired cause of bronchiectasis and as a cause of persistent wheeze.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pneumothorax is an acute complication and would not explain weeks of persistent symptoms.
- B. Incorrect. Reinfection can occur, but it would not cause continuous symptoms unresponsive to bronchodilators after severe adenoviral illness.
- C. Correct. The adenovirus type, the persistent symptoms after severe bronchiolitis and the poor bronchodilator response fit this complication.
- D. Incorrect. CF is a genetic disease and not a complication of RSV or bronchiolitis. There is no malabsorption or poor growth here.
- E. Incorrect. There is no choking history or focal signs.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Complications of bronchiolitis: apnoea and respiratory failure, dehydration, secondary bacterial infection, pneumothorax, recurrence, and bronchiolitis obliterans (adenovirus 3 and 7).
- Bronchiolitis obliterans also appears as a cause of persistent wheeze and of bronchiectasis (acquired).
- Most bronchiolitis cases recover in 1–2 weeks, and mortality is about 1% from respiratory failure, apnoea and dehydration.

source.raw: Respiratory sheet — Page 21 (Bronchiolitis: complications and prognosis); Page 42 (Wheezy chest differential); Page 48 (Bronchiectasis: causes).

cases.title: â€” A febrile child with tachypnoea and focal chest signs
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old child presents with fever, cough, breathlessness and poor feeding. Respiratory rate is above the age-specific threshold. Examination reveals reduced movement on the right side, reduced chest expansion, increased tactile vocal fremitus, localized dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing and coarse end-inspiratory crackles. The clinician assesses severity, possible complications and the need for admission.

questions.stem: What is the most sensitive clinical sign of pneumonia highlighted?
questions.correctAnswerText: Tachypnoea
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies increased respiratory rate as the most sensitive clinical sign of pneumonia and advises measuring the respiratory rate in a febrile child.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Cyanosis is a serious sign of hypoxaemia but is not the most sensitive early sign.
- B. Incorrect. Haemoptysis may occur in selected complications but is not sensitive.
- C. Incorrect. Tracheal deviation suggests major volume or pressure displacement, not routine pneumonia.
- D. Incorrect. Clubbing may occur in chronic suppurative lung disease but is not the sensitive acute sign.
- E. Correct. Tachypnoea is the sensitive sign highlighted.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Always measure respiratory rate in a febrile child.
- Use age-specific tachypnoea thresholds.
- Tachypnoea is sensitive but not specific; it can also occur in heart failure, sepsis and metabolic disorders.

questions.stem: Which organism group is most common in pneumonia among infants and young children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Viruses
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists viruses, particularly RSV, as the most common causes in infants and young children, while bacterial causes become more prominent in children older than 5 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fungal pneumonia is considered in selected immunocompromised children, not as the commonest cause.
- B. Correct. Viruses are the commonest group in infants and young children.
- C. Incorrect. Mycoplasma is emphasized in school-age children.
- D. Incorrect. Group B streptococcus and Gram-negative organisms are listed for newborns.
- E. Incorrect. TB should be considered at all ages but is not the commonest routine cause.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Newborn: group B streptococci and Gram-negative enteric organisms.
- Infant/young child: viruses (especially RSV) common.
- Older child >5 years: bacteria including Mycoplasma, S. pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae.
- Consider TB at all ages when risk factors or chronic features are present.

questions.stem: Which pathogen is specifically associated with pneumonia in school-age children (5â€“15 years)?
questions.correctAnswerText: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance associates Mycoplasma pneumoniae with school-age children aged approximately 5â€“15 years, often with an insidious onset, cough and low-grade fever.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Proteus is a urinary pathogen and may be associated with infection-related urinary stones.
- B. Incorrect. Chlamydia trachomatis is associated with pneumonia in young infants, particularly in early infancy.
- C. Correct. This is the age association in the table.
- D. Incorrect. RSV is common in infants and young children, not the specific school-age pathogen asked for.
- E. Incorrect. Group B streptococcus is listed among neonatal pathogens.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mycoplasma pneumonia: often school-age, gradual/insidious onset and low-grade fever.
- May have extra-pulmonary manifestations involving skin, CNS, joints, heart and blood.
- Cold agglutinins may be positive.

questions.stem: Which finding is characteristic of staphylococcal pneumonia?

options.label: D
options.text: Rapid deterioration, severe fever and complications such as lung abscess, empyema or pneumatoceles

questions.correctAnswerText: Rapid deterioration, severe fever and complications such as lung abscess, empyema or pneumatoceles
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance staphylococcal pneumonia as potentially severe with sudden onset, high fever and rapid clinical deterioration. Lung abscess, pleural effusion/empyema and pneumatocele may occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This is more compatible with uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infection.
- B. Incorrect. This may suggest exercise-induced asthma.
- C. Incorrect. This is a renal symptom.
- D. Correct. This is the severe clinical pattern and complication profile described.
- E. Incorrect. These features suggest epiglottitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Staphylococcal pneumonia may be severe with rapid deterioration.
- Complications: lung abscess, pleural effusion/empyema and pneumatocele.
- Clinical guidance cloxacillin or vancomycin in the organism-specific treatment discussion; actual treatment follows culture and local protocols.

questions.stem: Which clinical finding is part of the classic examination pattern of lobar consolidation?

options.label: A
options.text: Stony dullness with tracheal shift away from the affected side in each uncomplicated case

options.label: C
options.text: Normal expansion and normal air entry in typical presentations

options.label: E
options.text: Localized dullness, increased tactile vocal fremitus, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles

questions.correctAnswerText: Localized dullness, increased tactile vocal fremitus, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles
questions.initialExplanation: Consolidated lung transmits vocal vibrations more effectively, leading to increased tactile vocal fremitus and vocal resonance, with dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stony dullness and contralateral tracheal shift suggest a large pleural effusion, not uncomplicated consolidation.
- B. Incorrect. Isolated wheeze without fever does not establish pneumonia.
- C. Incorrect. Focal examination findings may be present, although they can be absent in young children.
- D. Incorrect. Hyperresonance and reduced fremitus suggest increased air or reduced transmission, such as pneumothorax.
- E. Correct. These are the classical signs of consolidation described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Inspection: reduced movement on affected side.
- Palpation: reduced expansion, trachea often central, increased TVF.
- Percussion: localized dullness.
- Auscultation: reduced air entry, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles.
- Classic signs may be absent in young children.

questions.stem: Which statement about chest X-ray and blood tests in distinguishing viral from bacterial pneumonia is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Neither chest X-ray nor CBC/CRP reliably distinguishes viral from bacterial pneumonia on its own

options.label: C
options.text: A normal CBC proves viral pneumonia

options.label: D
options.text: A lobar opacity typically proves a single bacterial organism

options.label: E
options.text: They reliably distinguish viral from bacterial causes in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Neither chest X-ray nor CBC/CRP reliably distinguishes viral from bacterial pneumonia on its own
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance explicitly warns that chest X-ray and blood tests, including CBC and CRP, are not sufficiently reliable to differentiate viral from bacterial pneumonia in clinical practice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Clinical context, severity and microbiology when indicated are needed.
- B. Incorrect. Neutrophilia may support bacterial infection but does not identify a specific organism.
- C. Incorrect. A normal CBC does not definitively prove viral disease.
- D. Incorrect. Radiographic patterns suggest but do not prove a single pathogen.
- E. Incorrect. There is considerable overlap between viral and bacterial patterns.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral pneumonia may show lymphocyte predominance; bacterial pneumonia may show neutrophilia, but overlap exists.
- CXR patterns can suggest lobar, bronchopneumonia or interstitial disease.
- Do not use CXR/CBC/CRP alone to decide viral versus bacterial aetiology.

questions.stem: Which is an indication for hospital admission in a child with pneumonia?

options.label: A
options.text: Mild cough with normal feeding and oxygenation

options.label: B
options.text: Mild sore throat without chest signs

options.label: C
options.text: A normal respiratory rate in a well child

options.label: D
options.text: Severe respiratory distress, grunting or oxygen saturation below 92%

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe respiratory distress, grunting or oxygen saturation below 92%
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance severe respiratory distress, very high respiratory rate, grunting, feeding difficulty/dehydration, immunodeficiency, oxygen saturation below 92%, recurrent apnoea, young age, complications and failure of oral therapy as admission indications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Mild illness with adequate feeding and oxygenation may be managed at home.
- B. Incorrect. A sore throat without lower respiratory disease is not an admission criterion for pneumonia.
- C. Incorrect. This is reassuring rather than an admission criterion.
- D. Correct. These are explicit admission criteria.
- E. Incorrect. Coryza alone does not indicate admission for pneumonia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Admit for severe distress, hypoxaemia, grunting, apnoea or inability to feed.
- Consider very young age (<3â€“6 months), immunodeficiency and complications.
- Failure to respond to oral treatment is another reason to admit.

questions.stem: A child has pneumonia with a small sterile parapneumonic pleural effusion. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: each small sterile effusion requires immediate pneumonectomy

options.label: C
options.text: The child must have congenital heart disease

options.label: D
options.text: It may resolve with appropriate antibiotics, but empyema may require chest tube drainage

questions.correctAnswerText: It may resolve with appropriate antibiotics, but empyema may require chest tube drainage
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that sterile parapneumonic effusions often resolve with appropriate antibiotics, while progression to empyema may require drainage with a chest tube.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pneumonectomy is not routine management of a parapneumonic effusion.
- B. Incorrect. An effusion has multiple possible causes and does not prove TB.
- C. Incorrect. Congenital heart disease may cause transudative effusions but does not have to be present in parapneumonic effusion.
- D. Correct. This is the management point described.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics are appropriate for bacterial pneumonia and are adjusted to the clinical picture.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Parapneumonic effusion may resolve with treatment of pneumonia.
- Empyema requires drainage in selected cases.
- Complications include lung abscess, empyema, pneumatocele, pneumothorax, bronchopleural fistula and respiratory failure.

questions.stem: How does clinical guidance define recurrent pneumonia?

options.label: B
options.text: Two or more episodes in one year, or three or more episodes ever, with radiographic clearing between episodes

options.label: E
options.text: Any two cough episodes in a lifetime

questions.correctAnswerText: Two or more episodes in one year, or three or more episodes ever, with radiographic clearing between episodes
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance defines recurrent pneumonia as at least two episodes in one year or at least three episodes ever, with radiographic clearing of the infiltrates between episodes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Radiographic clearing between episodes is part of the definition.
- B. Correct. This is the definition given.
- C. Incorrect. Bilateral disease in one episode is not recurrent pneumonia.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotic use does not determine recurrence.
- E. Incorrect. Cough episodes alone do not meet the definition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Recurrent pneumonia = â‰¥2 episodes/year or â‰¥3 ever, with radiographic clearance between episodes.
- Same-site recurrence â†’ consider missed foreign body.
- Different-site recurrence â†’ consider immune deficiency, CF, ciliary dyskinesia, bronchiectasis, CHD, TEF, GERD and neuromuscular disorders.

questions.stem: A child has recurrent pneumonia repeatedly affecting the same lobe. Which underlying cause should be particularly suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: A missed foreign body aspiration
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance emphasizes that recurrent pneumonia in the same anatomical location should raise suspicion of an obstructing lesion, particularly a missed foreign body.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Epiglottitis is an acute upper-airway emergency.
- B. Correct. A retained foreign body can cause persistent obstruction, infection and recurrent consolidation in the same region.
- C. Incorrect. Atopy may contribute to asthma but does not specifically explain recurrent focal pneumonia in the same lobe.
- D. Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome increases infection risk but does not explain repeated same-lobe disease as specifically as obstruction.
- E. Incorrect. Hypertension does not cause recurrent focal infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Same-site recurrence: missed FBA until proven otherwise.
- Different-site recurrence: investigate systemic, immune, structural and aspiration causes.
- Persistent focal signs warrant imaging and specialist assessment.

questions.stem: A child develops chemical pneumonitis after accidental kerosene ingestion. Which management principle is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: Supportive oxygenation and hydration; antibiotics if secondary bacterial infection develops; gastric lavage is contraindicated

options.label: E
options.text: Routine gastric lavage followed by prophylactic antibiotics for most

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive oxygenation and hydration; antibiotics if secondary bacterial infection develops; gastric lavage is contraindicated
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance chemical pneumonitis following aspiration of gastric contents or hydrocarbons. Treatment is supportive, with good hydration and oxygenation; antibiotics are reserved for secondary bacterial infection. It specifically warns that gastric lavage is contraindicated after kerosene ingestion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Respiratory symptoms can evolve and observation is important.
- B. Correct. This is the management described in the source.
- C. Incorrect. Inducing vomiting increases the risk of further aspiration.
- D. Incorrect. Steroids are not routine treatment for chemical pneumonitis.
- E. Incorrect. Gastric lavage is contraindicated after kerosene ingestion because it increases aspiration risk; routine antibiotics are not indicated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Aspiration of gastric/chemical contents can cause chemical pneumonitis.
- Supportive management: hydration and oxygenation.
- Antibiotics only if secondary bacterial infection is suspected.
- Kerosene ingestion: gastric lavage is contraindicated.

cases.title: Choosing antibiotics by age and organism

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with lobar pneumonia is admitted with SpO2 of 90% in air, a respiratory rate of 55/min, mild dehydration and fever. His mother asks whether chest physiotherapy will speed recovery and whether the chest X-ray will need to be repeated. Which management plan matches clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Give oxygen, IV fluids, antipyretic and monitoring; no physiotherapy; repeat X-ray in 4–6 weeks if needed

options.label: B
options.text: Chest physiotherapy twice daily as essential treatment, with a repeat X-ray each 48 hours

options.label: C
options.text: Antibiotics alone, with oxygen withheld until cyanosis and no monitoring after admission

options.label: D
options.text: Nebulised hypertonic saline and DNase to loosen secretions, followed by daily bronchoscopy

options.label: E
options.text: Mandatory chest physiotherapy and CT chest in each case, with no follow-up X-ray

questions.correctAnswerText: Give oxygen, IV fluids, antipyretic and monitoring; no physiotherapy; repeat X-ray in 4–6 weeks if needed
questions.initialExplanation: Supportive care for pneumonia is oxygen for hypoxia, IV fluids when dehydrated or tachypnoeic, an antipyretic and monitoring. Physiotherapy has no proven role except in CF or bronchiectasis. clinical guidance also lists a repeat X-ray after 4–6 weeks to assess resolution.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. It matches the supportive and follow-up measures.
- B. Incorrect. Physiotherapy has no proven role in uncomplicated pneumonia, and X-rays every 48 hours are not recommended.
- C. Incorrect. Hypoxia (SpO2 below 92%) needs oxygen now, and RR, distress, apnoea and oximetry need monitoring.
- D. Incorrect. Hypertonic saline and DNase are mucolytic treatments used in CF, and daily bronchoscopy is not indicated.
- E. Incorrect. Physiotherapy is not mandatory, and CT is only needed in selected cases.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Supportive: humidified oxygen for hypoxia, IV fluids if dehydrated or high RR, antipyretic, monitoring of RR, distress signs, apnoea and pulse oximetry.
- Physiotherapy has no proven role except in CF or bronchiectasis.
- Chest X-ray is necessary if there is doubt about the diagnosis, is repeated after 4–6 weeks to assess resolution, and CT may be needed.
- Admission criteria: severe distress, grunting, feeding difficulty or dehydration, SpO2 below 92%, recurrent apnoea, immunodeficiency, complications, age under 3–6 months and no response to oral treatment.

cases.title: â€” Sudden cough after choking while eating
cases.vignette: A 20-month-old child suddenly develops violent coughing and choking while eating peanuts. The child later has persistent cough and unilateral wheeze. Examination shows reduced air entry on the right. Inspiratory and expiratory chest X-rays are obtained because the suspected object may not be radiopaque.

questions.stem: Which age group is most commonly affected by foreign body aspiration?

options.label: A
options.text: 6 monthsâ€“4 years, with a peak at 1â€“2 years

questions.correctAnswerText: 6 monthsâ€“4 years, with a peak at 1â€“2 years
questions.initialExplanation: Young children explore objects orally and have immature chewing and swallowing coordination. clinical guidance gives 6 monthsâ€“4 years as the common age range, with a peak at 1â€“2 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the age range listed.
- B. Incorrect. Neonates are not the typical age group.
- C. Incorrect. Adolescents are not the peak age group.
- D. Incorrect. This is not a typical pediatric aspiration age.
- E. Incorrect. School-age children can aspirate foreign bodies, but they are not the commonest group.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common age: 6 monthsâ€“4 years.
- Peak: 1â€“2 years.
- Peanuts are the commonest foreign body; popcorn, small toys and coins are also listed.

questions.stem: Which anatomical site is particularly common for an aspirated foreign body?
questions.correctAnswerText: Right main bronchus
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies the right main bronchus and larynx as common sites. The right main bronchus is relatively wider and more vertical.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Oesophageal foreign bodies are a different clinical problem.
- B. Incorrect. A foreign body typically lodges in a larger airway, not an alveolar duct.
- C. Incorrect. The left bronchial tree can be affected, but the right main bronchus is emphasized.
- D. Correct. This is one of the common sites listed.
- E. Incorrect. The pleural cavity is not an airway and is not the usual site.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Common sites: right main bronchus and larynx.
- Most common aspirated object: peanut.
- A laryngeal foreign body may cause acute stridor and airway obstruction.

questions.stem: A foreign body causes partial bronchial obstruction and acts as a ball valve. What is the expected effect?

options.label: A
options.text: The affected lung becomes smaller with mediastinal shift toward the opposite side

options.label: C
options.text: Air cannot enter or leave, typically causing immediate total collapse

options.label: E
options.text: Air enters during inspiration but is trapped during expiration, causing unilateral hyperinflation

questions.correctAnswerText: Air enters during inspiration but is trapped during expiration, causing unilateral hyperinflation
questions.initialExplanation: A partially obstructing foreign body may allow air to pass during inspiration but obstruct expiration. This creates air trapping and hyperinflation on the affected side.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Complete obstruction may cause collapse with mediastinal shift toward the affected side, not this partial obstruction pattern.
- B. Incorrect. The effect is generally localized to the affected side.
- C. Incorrect. Complete obstruction may cause collapse, but partial ball-valve obstruction produces air trapping.
- D. Incorrect. The mechanism does not directly produce pleural fluid.
- E. Correct. This is the ball-valve mechanism described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Partial obstruction â†’ ball-valve effect â†’ air trapping and hyperinflation.
- Complete obstruction â†’ distal collapse/atelectasis.
- Inspiratory and expiratory films may help demonstrate air trapping.

questions.stem: Which X-ray finding is expected with complete bronchial obstruction by a foreign body?

options.label: D
options.text: Pleural effusion with shift away from the affected side in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Collapse of the affected lung with mediastinal shift toward that side

questions.correctAnswerText: Collapse of the affected lung with mediastinal shift toward that side
questions.initialExplanation: Complete obstruction prevents ventilation distal to the foreign body, leading to lung collapse and volume loss. The mediastinum may be pulled toward the affected side.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Boot-shaped heart is associated with TOF.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the expected focal complete-obstruction pattern.
- C. Incorrect. Rib notching is associated with coarctation.
- D. Incorrect. A large pleural effusion may shift the mediastinum away, but this is not the mechanism of bronchial occlusion.
- E. Correct. This is the radiographic pattern described for complete obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Partial obstruction â†’ hyperinflation on the same side.
- Complete obstruction â†’ atelectasis/collapse and ipsilateral mediastinal shift.
- A normal X-ray does not exclude a radiolucent foreign body.

questions.stem: Which procedure is both diagnostic and therapeutic for an aspirated airway foreign body?
questions.correctAnswerText: Rigid bronchoscopy
questions.initialExplanation: Rigid bronchoscopy is identified as diagnostic and therapeutic. Definitive treatment is removal of the foreign body, generally by bronchoscopy with the appropriate specialist team.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Abdominal imaging is unrelated.
- B. Incorrect. Spirometry assesses lung function but cannot remove an aspirated object.
- C. Incorrect. Flexible laryngoscopy evaluates the larynx, not the main bronchial tree.
- D. Incorrect. Pleural aspiration removes pleural fluid and does not remove an airway foreign body.
- E. Correct. It allows airway inspection and foreign body removal.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Rigid bronchoscopy: diagnostic and therapeutic.
- Flexible bronchoscopy is described mainly as diagnostic.
- Definitive treatment is removal of the foreign body.
- Complications include complete airway obstruction, recurrent pneumonia, localized bronchiectasis and lung abscess.

questions.stem: An infant younger than 1 year has severe airway obstruction from choking. Which first-aid sequence is described?

options.label: D
options.text: Back blows and chest thrusts; avoid abdominal thrusts

questions.correctAnswerText: Back blows and chest thrusts; avoid abdominal thrusts
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance back blows and chest thrusts for infants, avoiding abdominal thrusts because of the risk of injury to the liver and spleen.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Blind finger sweeps can push an object deeper and are not recommended.
- B. Incorrect. Abdominal thrusts are avoided in infants.
- C. Incorrect. Giving fluids is unsafe in a choking infant.
- D. Correct. This is the infant first-aid approach described.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not relieve acute mechanical airway obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infant with severe choking: back blows and chest thrusts as described in the course clinical guidance.
- Older child: abdominal thrusts are described in the source.
- If the child becomes unconscious, start CPR according to current pediatric resuscitation training/protocol.
- Do not perform a blind finger sweep.

questions.stem: A child had a choking episode several weeks ago and now has persistent cough, unilateral wheeze and recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe. What is the best next step if FBA is suspected?

options.label: A
options.text: Arrange specialist airway assessment and bronchoscopy for diagnosis/removal

options.label: C
options.text: Treat repeated episodes with antibiotics indefinitely without investigation

options.label: D
options.text: Reassure because a delayed presentation excludes foreign body aspiration

questions.correctAnswerText: Arrange specialist airway assessment and bronchoscopy for diagnosis/removal
questions.initialExplanation: A missed foreign body can cause persistent cough, unilateral wheeze and recurrent pneumonia. Bronchoscopy is required to identify and remove the object.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This addresses the underlying obstruction and prevents ongoing damage.
- B. Incorrect. Asthma does not explain a preceding choking event and persistent focal findings as well as FBA.
- C. Incorrect. Repeated antibiotics without assessing the obstruction misses the cause.
- D. Incorrect. A missed foreign body may present weeks later with chronic symptoms and recurrent pneumonia.
- E. Incorrect. Steroids do not remove a mechanical obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sudden cough/choking is a key historical clue.
- Missed FBA may present later with chronic cough, wheeze and recurrent pneumonia.
- Same-site recurrent pneumonia should prompt consideration of a retained foreign body.

cases.title: â€” Recurrent wheeze triggered by exercise and allergens
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child has repeated episodes of cough, wheeze, breathlessness and chest tightness. Symptoms worsen at night and with exercise, cold air, dust mites and viral URTIs. The child is usually well between attacks. A family history of allergic rhinitis and eczema is present. Examination between episodes is normal.

questions.stem: Which definition best describes bronchial asthma in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Pleural inflammation causing restrictive lung disease

options.label: B
options.text: Acute bacterial infection of the bronchioles

options.label: C
options.text: Fixed obstruction due to a foreign body

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic inflammatory airway disease with airway hyperresponsiveness and reversible airflow obstruction

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic inflammatory airway disease with airway hyperresponsiveness and reversible airflow obstruction
questions.initialExplanation: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by bronchial hyperresponsiveness and variable, usually reversible, airflow obstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pleural inflammation causes a different respiratory physiology.
- B. Incorrect. This describes an infectious process, not chronic asthma.
- C. Incorrect. FBA causes mechanical obstruction and usually has a sudden onset.
- D. Correct. This is the definition.
- E. Incorrect. Alveolar destruction is not the defining feature of asthma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Asthma = chronic airway inflammation + hyperresponsiveness + reversible airflow obstruction.
- Symptoms are variable over time and intensity.
- Control is important to prevent exacerbations and airway remodelling.

questions.stem: Which pattern is typical of asthma symptoms?

options.label: C
options.text: Recurrent episodes with triggers and often normal periods between attacks

options.label: E
options.text: Continuous progressive breathlessness without symptom-free intervals

questions.correctAnswerText: Recurrent episodes with triggers and often normal periods between attacks
questions.initialExplanation: Asthma commonly causes episodic cough, wheeze and breathlessness in the presence of triggers, with children often asymptomatic between attacks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests infection such as pneumonia or bacterial tracheitis.
- B. Incorrect. This suggests FBA.
- C. Correct. This variability is characteristic of asthma.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests congenital upper-airway disease such as laryngomalacia.
- E. Incorrect. Continuous progressive symptoms suggest another chronic or severe process.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Symptoms: cough, wheeze, breathlessness and chest tightness.
- Nocturnal/early-morning symptoms are common.
- Cough may be the only symptom (cough-variant asthma).
- Examination may be completely normal between attacks.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a recognized asthma trigger in the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cold air and exercise
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance exercise, cold air, viral URTI, allergens, smoking, pollution, chemical irritants, strong smells, emotional factors and selected drugs as triggers.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sleep itself is not the trigger, although asthma symptoms often increase at night.
- B. Incorrect. Breastfeeding is not listed as an asthma trigger.
- C. Incorrect. Increased water intake is not a listed trigger.
- D. Incorrect. Dietary fibre is not a listed trigger.
- E. Correct. Cold air and exercise are recognized triggers.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Triggers: viral URTI, dust mites, pollens, moulds, pets, exercise, cold air, smoke, pollution, chemicals/perfumes, emotional stress and selected drugs (e.g. beta-blockers and aspirin).
- Ask about triggers and atopy at history-taking.

questions.stem: Which sequence best explains asthma pathophysiology?

options.label: A
options.text: Alveolar bacterial invasion without airway hyperresponsiveness

options.label: B
options.text: Pulmonary venous obstruction followed by pulmonary oedema

options.label: C
options.text: Pleural fibrosis followed by permanent lung collapse

options.label: D
options.text: Airway inflammation, oedema, mucus production and bronchoconstriction causing reversible narrowing

questions.correctAnswerText: Airway inflammation, oedema, mucus production and bronchoconstriction causing reversible narrowing
questions.initialExplanation: Asthma involves inflammatory cell infiltration and airway hyperresponsiveness. Oedema, excessive mucus and bronchoconstriction narrow the airways and produce wheeze, cough and breathlessness.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Asthma is not defined by bacterial invasion.
- B. Incorrect. Pulmonary venous obstruction is a different pathology.
- C. Incorrect. Pleural fibrosis is not the mechanism of asthma.
- D. Correct. This is the pathophysiological pathway.
- E. Incorrect. Tracheal cartilage destruction is not the mechanism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Inflammatory cells include eosinophils, mast cells and lymphocytes.
- Bronchoconstriction is relieved by bronchodilator (e.g. salbutamol).
- Airway inflammation responds to inhaled corticosteroids.
- Repeated uncontrolled inflammation may contribute to airway remodelling.

questions.stem: Which statement about asthma diagnosis in children younger than 5 years is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A single episode of wheeze proves asthma

options.label: C
options.text: Spirometry is mandatory in each infant

options.label: D
options.text: Chest X-ray is diagnostic in typical presentations

options.label: E
options.text: Diagnosis is mainly clinical because reliable spirometry may not be feasible

questions.correctAnswerText: Diagnosis is mainly clinical because reliable spirometry may not be feasible
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that asthma diagnosis is mainly clinical, particularly in children under 5 years. A compatible history of recurrent episodes, triggers, atopy and bronchodilator response supports the diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A single wheezing episode has a broad differential, including bronchiolitis and FBA.
- B. Incorrect. Examination can be normal between episodes.
- C. Incorrect. Spirometry is generally possible in older children, not mandatory in every infant.
- D. Incorrect. CXR is often normal and is not diagnostic of asthma.
- E. Correct. This matches the diagnostic approach.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Diagnosis under 5 years: mainly clinical.
- Recurrent variable symptoms and triggers support asthma.
- Improvement with bronchodilator supports reversible obstruction.
- Consider other causes of wheeze, particularly in a first episode or persistent focal symptoms.

questions.stem: In a child older than 5 years, which spirometric pattern supports obstructive airflow limitation?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced vital capacity alone proves asthma

options.label: C
options.text: Increased FEV1 with no change in airflow

questions.correctAnswerText: FEV1/FVC ratio below 80%
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance airflow limitation by a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio, with a value below 80% listed in its spirometry section.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Reduced vital capacity alone does not establish asthma.
- B. Correct. This is the threshold stated in the supplied clinical guidance.
- C. Incorrect. Increased FEV1 does not indicate obstruction.
- D. Incorrect. This is not an obstructive pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Spirometry can be normal between symptomatic periods.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Spirometry is usually feasible from around 5 years.
- The source lists FEV1/FVC <80% as evidence of airflow limitation.
- Normal testing between attacks does not always exclude asthma.

questions.stem: Which bronchodilator response supports asthma in the spirometry criteria presented?

options.label: A
options.text: Improvement in FEV1 of at least 12% after inhaled beta-agonist

options.label: C
options.text: Reduction in FEV1 of at least 12% after beta-agonist

options.label: E
options.text: Reduction in peak flow after exercise proves reversible obstruction

questions.correctAnswerText: Improvement in FEV1 of at least 12% after inhaled beta-agonist
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance an improvement in FEV1 of 12% or more after inhaled beta-agonist as a positive bronchodilator response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the response threshold stated in the source.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not used to demonstrate bronchodilator reversibility.
- C. Incorrect. A fall in FEV1 is not a positive bronchodilator response.
- D. Incorrect. No improvement does not demonstrate reversibility.
- E. Incorrect. Exercise challenge is assessed by a fall in FEV1 after exercise, but that is a different test.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bronchodilator reversibility: FEV1 improvement â‰¥12%.
- Exercise challenge: worsening/fall in FEV1 after exercise (threshold in the source â‰¥15%).
- PEF may show variability and help monitor response in children able to perform the test.

questions.stem: In which age group does clinical guidance describe peak expiratory flow monitoring as useful?

options.label: A
options.text: Children who cannot cooperate with a forced expiration

questions.correctAnswerText: Children older than 5 years
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance the peak expiratory flow meter as useful in children older than 5 years for diagnosis and monitoring treatment response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The child must be able to perform a forceful expiratory manoeuvre.
- B. Correct. This is the age guidance given in the source.
- C. Incorrect. Infants cannot reliably use a PEF meter.
- D. Incorrect. Neonates cannot reliably perform the required manoeuvre.
- E. Incorrect. It is also useful in children, not restricted to older adults.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PEF meter: usually useful in children >5 years.
- It is portable and suitable for serial measurements.
- Clinical guidance FEV1 below 80% and diurnal variation above 20% among supportive findings.

questions.stem: A child with asthma deteriorates rapidly. ABG initially shows low PaCO2 due to hyperventilation. Later, PaCO2 rises with hypoxia and acidosis. What does the later pattern suggest?
questions.correctAnswerText: Impending respiratory failure and fatigue
questions.initialExplanation: Early in an acute asthma attack, hyperventilation may lower CO2. A normalizing or rising CO2 in a severely distressed child, particularly with hypoxia and acidosis, may indicate fatigue and impending respiratory failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. In a deteriorating child, rising CO2 is not reassuring.
- B. Incorrect. Resolution of bronchospasm should improve ventilation rather than cause CO2 retention.
- C. Correct. Rising CO2 with hypoxia/acidosis is a late warning sign.
- D. Incorrect. A simple cold does not produce this severe gas-exchange pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Anxiety may cause hyperventilation and low CO2 but does not explain late hypoxia and acidosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early severe asthma: hyperventilation â†’ hypocapnia.
- Late deterioration: rising/normalizing CO2, hypoxia and acidosis â†’ fatigue/respiratory failure risk.
- ABG is reserved for rapid deterioration, life-threatening asthma or inability to maintain oxygenation.

questions.stem: Which feature indicates life-threatening asthma in the supplied severity table?

options.label: C
options.text: Silent chest, drowsiness or altered consciousness

questions.correctAnswerText: Silent chest, drowsiness or altered consciousness
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance silent chest, drowsiness, agitation/confusion, cyanosis, arrhythmia and low blood pressure among life-threatening features.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Being asymptomatic between episodes does not define an acute life-threatening attack.
- B. Incorrect. Mild wheeze without distress is not life-threatening.
- C. Correct. These indicate critically reduced airflow or severe physiological compromise.
- D. Incorrect. Peak flow above 80% is reassuring in the source classification.
- E. Incorrect. This is not a severe exacerbation pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Life-threatening signs: silent chest, drowsiness, confusion, cyanosis, arrhythmia and hypotension.
- Severe asthma may present with inability to speak or feed, exhaustion and markedly reduced air entry.
- A silent chest is a danger sign, not evidence that wheezing has resolved.

questions.stem: What is the initial treatment sequence for an acute severe asthma attack described?

options.label: A
options.text: Withhold bronchodilators until the chest X-ray is completed

options.label: C
options.text: Oxygen, repeated inhaled/nebulized salbutamol, add ipratropium when needed and give systemic corticosteroid

options.label: D
options.text: Immediate chest physiotherapy as the measure

questions.correctAnswerText: Oxygen, repeated inhaled/nebulized salbutamol, add ipratropium when needed and give systemic corticosteroid
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance assessment, high-flow oxygen, repeated short-acting beta-agonist (salbutamol), addition of ipratropium if response is inadequate, and systemic corticosteroids. Treatment should not be delayed for routine imaging.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bronchodilator and oxygen treatment should be started promptly; CXR is reserved for selected indications such as suspected pneumothorax, collapse or infection.
- B. Incorrect. Antihistamines and cough suppressants are not acute severe asthma treatment.
- C. Correct. This is the acute treatment sequence in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Physiotherapy is not the initial treatment for acute asthma.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics are only indicated when bacterial infection is suspected; they do not reverse bronchospasm.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Start with assessment and oxygen when hypoxic.
- Repeated SABA (salbutamol) is first-line bronchodilator therapy.
- Add nebulized ipratropium in severe or poorly responding attacks.
- Give systemic corticosteroid early.
- Escalate to PICU and consider IV therapies/ventilation if not responding.

questions.stem: Which intravenous agent is described as the usual first-line IV adjunct in severe asthma not responding to initial treatment?
questions.correctAnswerText: Magnesium sulphate
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that intravenous magnesium sulphate is usually the first-line IV agent in severe asthma not responding to initial inhaled treatment. It warns that profound hypotension may occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Desmopressin is an ADH analogue used in selected conditions.
- B. Incorrect. Penicillin treats selected bacterial infections, not bronchospasm.
- C. Incorrect. Rifampicin is an antimicrobial and is not used to treat acute asthma.
- D. Incorrect. Furosemide is a diuretic and is not the standard IV asthma adjunct.
- E. Correct. This is the IV adjunct identified in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IV magnesium sulphate is listed as first-line IV adjunct in the source.
- Monitor BP because hypotension may occur.
- IV salbutamol and aminophylline require close ECG/electrolyte monitoring; aminophylline commonly causes nausea/vomiting.
- IV salbutamol may cause tachycardia and lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: Which statement about antibiotics during an asthma exacerbation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: They are required in each asthma attack

options.label: B
options.text: They are indicated solely because sputum is present

options.label: D
options.text: They are given when there are clinical features of bacterial infection

questions.correctAnswerText: They are given when there are clinical features of bacterial infection
questions.initialExplanation: Asthma exacerbations are usually inflammatory/bronchospastic rather than bacterial infections. Clinical guidance that antibiotics are only indicated when clinical features of bacterial infection are present.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Routine antibiotics are not indicated for every asthma attack.
- B. Incorrect. Sputum alone does not establish bacterial infection.
- C. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not replace bronchodilators or anti-inflammatory treatment.
- D. Correct. This is the source teaching point.
- E. Incorrect. They do not prevent future asthma exacerbations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- No routine antibiotics for asthma exacerbation.
- Give antibiotics only if bacterial infection is clinically suspected/confirmed.
- Assess for pneumonia or another trigger if fever, focal chest findings or atypical deterioration is present.

questions.stem: Which inhaler delivery device is appropriate across pediatric age groups when used correctly, with a face mask for younger children?

options.label: A
options.text: Nebulizer is typically more efficient than an MDI with spacer

options.label: B
options.text: Dry powder inhaler in each infant

questions.correctAnswerText: Pressurized metered-dose inhaler with spacer
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that an MDI with spacer is suitable across age groups, using a face mask for children under approximately 2 years and a mouthpiece in older cooperative children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Clinical guidance MDI plus spacer as more efficient than a nebulizer in many situations.
- B. Incorrect. Dry powder inhalers require adequate inspiratory flow and are not suitable for every infant.
- C. Incorrect. Inhaled medications are central to asthma treatment.
- D. Incorrect. Breath-actuated devices require the child to trigger the device with an adequate inhalation.
- E. Correct. It improves lung deposition and reduces oropharyngeal deposition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- MDI + spacer: useful across pediatric ages.
- Younger child: spacer with face mask; older cooperative child: mouthpiece.
- Spacer improves delivery to lungs and reduces oropharyngeal/systemic adverse effects.
- Teach and re-check inhaler technique at every review.

questions.stem: Which device limitation is correctly described?

options.label: A
options.text: A spacer reduces drug deposition in the lungs

options.label: B
options.text: Dry powder inhalers require good inspiratory flow and may be less suitable during a severe attack

options.label: C
options.text: A face mask is not usually needed in young children

options.label: D
options.text: Nebulizers are typically more efficient than MDI with spacer

options.label: E
options.text: MDI with spacer cannot be used in children under 5 years

questions.correctAnswerText: Dry powder inhalers require good inspiratory flow and may be less suitable during a severe attack
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that dry powder inhalers require adequate inspiratory flow and are less suitable in severe asthma or during an acute attack.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A spacer increases drug delivery to the lungs and reduces oropharyngeal deposition.
- B. Correct. This is the device limitation stated.
- C. Incorrect. A face mask is often used for children too young to use a mouthpiece reliably.
- D. Incorrect. clinical guidance says nebulizers are less efficient than MDI plus spacer in many circumstances.
- E. Incorrect. MDI plus spacer can be used in young children, with an appropriate mask.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dry powder inhaler: needs adequate inspiratory flow.
- Nebulizer: may be used in acute asthma when oxygen is required, but is not inherently more efficient than MDI + spacer.
- Correct technique is essential to ensure effective delivery.

topics.name: Long-Term Asthma Control and Preschool Wheeze

cases.title: â€” Frequent reliever use and night-time symptoms
cases.vignette: An 8-year-old child with established asthma uses salbutamol on most days and wakes at night with cough and wheeze. Symptoms interfere with school and sport. The family is unsure which inhaler provides immediate relief and which prevents airway inflammation. The clinician reviews adherence, trigger exposure and inhaler technique before stepping up controller therapy.

questions.stem: Which medication is used as a rapid-relief inhaler for acute bronchoconstriction?
questions.correctAnswerText: Salbutamol
questions.initialExplanation: Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) that rapidly relaxes airway smooth muscle and is used as a reliever inhaler.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Budesonide is an inhaled corticosteroid used as a preventer.
- B. Incorrect. Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist used as controller/add-on therapy in selected children.
- C. Incorrect. Omalizumab is a specialist biologic therapy for selected severe allergic asthma.
- D. Incorrect. Beclometasone is also an inhaled corticosteroid preventer.
- E. Correct. Salbutamol is the rapid-acting bronchodilator listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SABA (e.g. salbutamol): reliever.
- Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS): anti-inflammatory preventer.
- Frequent SABA use suggests poor asthma control and need to review controller treatment.

questions.stem: Which class of medication is described as the most effective inhaled prophylactic treatment for asthma?
questions.correctAnswerText: Inhaled corticosteroids
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies inhaled corticosteroids as the most effective inhaled prophylactic treatment for asthma. They reduce airway inflammation and exacerbation risk.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Diuretics do not treat asthma inflammation.
- B. Incorrect. Antibiotics do not prevent asthma inflammation.
- C. Correct. ICS are the main preventer therapy listed.
- D. Incorrect. Mucolytics are used in selected chronic suppurative airway conditions, not as asthma controller therapy.
- E. Incorrect. Antihistamines may help allergic rhinitis but are not the most effective asthma preventer.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Low-dose ICS is a core preventer in the stepwise strategy.
- Review adherence and inhaler technique before escalating treatment.
- Preventer medication should be used regularly as prescribed, not only during symptoms.

questions.stem: Which statement about long-acting beta-2 agonists (LABA) is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: LABA should not be used without an inhaled corticosteroid

options.label: B
options.text: LABA is the preferred sole treatment for children in routine care

options.label: D
options.text: LABA replaces most reliever medication in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: LABA should not be used without an inhaled corticosteroid
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance salmeterol and formoterol as LABAs and states that they should not be used without an inhaled corticosteroid.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. LABA monotherapy is not the strategy described; it is combined with anti-inflammatory controller therapy.
- B. Incorrect. LABA alone is not appropriate controller therapy in asthma.
- C. Incorrect. LABAs are bronchodilators, not antibiotics.
- D. Incorrect. A reliever strategy is still required according to the child's prescribed plan.
- E. Incorrect. LABAs produce prolonged bronchodilation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LABA examples: salmeterol and formoterol.
- Clinical guidance not to use LABA without ICS.
- Combination ICS/LABA therapy is considered when asthma is not controlled at lower treatment steps.

questions.stem: Which drug is listed as a leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA)?
questions.correctAnswerText: Montelukast
questions.initialExplanation: Montelukast is the leukotriene receptor antagonist listed in the asthma treatment table and can be used as add-on/controller therapy in selected children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Montelukast is an LTRA.
- B. Incorrect. Prednisolone is a systemic corticosteroid.
- C. Incorrect. Theophylline is a methylxanthine.
- D. Incorrect. Ipratropium is an anticholinergic bronchodilator.
- E. Incorrect. Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LTRA: montelukast.
- SABA: salbutamol/terbutaline.
- LABA: salmeterol/formoterol.
- ICS: budesonide, beclometasone, fluticasone and mometasone.
- Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic window and notable adverse effects.

questions.stem: Which aspect should be checked before stepping up a child's asthma controller medication?

options.label: B
options.text: Adherence, inhaler technique, triggers and whether the diagnosis is correct

options.label: D
options.text: Routine CT chest in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Adherence, inhaler technique, triggers and whether the diagnosis is correct
questions.initialExplanation: Before increasing treatment, the clinician should confirm that the child is taking the prescribed medication correctly, using the device properly, avoiding relevant triggers and that the symptoms are actually due to asthma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Calcium level does not assess inhaler adherence or technique.
- B. Correct. These are essential parts of asthma review and education.
- C. Incorrect. Hair colour is unrelated to asthma control.
- D. Incorrect. CT is not routine asthma monitoring.
- E. Incorrect. Blood group does not determine controller treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Review diagnosis, adherence, device technique and trigger exposure.
- Provide an individualized asthma action plan.
- Arrange regular follow-up and assess school/activity impact.
- Explain the difference between reliever and preventer treatment.

questions.stem: Which pattern best describes mild intermittent asthma in the classification table supplied?

options.label: A
options.text: Symptoms each day with peak flow below 33%

options.label: B
options.text: Persistent symptoms with severe activity limitation

options.label: C
options.text: Symptoms on no more than 2 days per week, night waking no more than twice per month and FEV1/PEFR above 80%

options.label: D
options.text: Daily symptoms and night waking each night

options.label: E
options.text: Symptoms throughout the day and FEV1 below 60%

questions.correctAnswerText: Symptoms on no more than 2 days per week, night waking no more than twice per month and FEV1/PEFR above 80%
questions.initialExplanation: The source classifies mild intermittent asthma by infrequent daytime symptoms, infrequent night waking and near-normal lung function.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A peak flow below 33% is a life-threatening acute severity marker, not mild intermittent chronic asthma.
- B. Incorrect. Marked activity limitation suggests more severe persistent disease.
- C. Correct. This matches the mild intermittent row.
- D. Incorrect. Daily symptoms and frequent night waking indicate persistent disease.
- E. Incorrect. This is consistent with severe persistent disease in the table.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mild intermittent: symptoms â‰¤2 days/week, night waking â‰¤2 times/month, FEV1/PEFR >80%.
- Mild persistent: symptoms >2 days/week.
- Moderate persistent: daily symptoms with more frequent night waking.
- Severe persistent: symptoms throughout the day with marked activity limitation and lower lung function.

questions.stem: Which delivery device is described as suitable for a child who cannot coordinate actuation and inspiration reliably?

options.label: B
options.text: Pressurized MDI with spacer and an age-appropriate face mask

options.label: E
options.text: No inhaled therapy can be used

questions.correctAnswerText: Pressurized MDI with spacer and an age-appropriate face mask
questions.initialExplanation: A spacer reduces the need for precise hand-breath coordination. A face mask can be used for younger children who cannot seal their lips around a mouthpiece.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Dry powder inhalers require adequate inspiratory flow and coordination.
- B. Correct. This is the delivery system described for young children.
- C. Incorrect. Breath-actuated devices require the child to trigger the inhaler with inspiration.
- D. Incorrect. A spacer is useful for improving delivery and reducing coordination demands.
- E. Incorrect. Inhaled therapy can be effectively delivered using a suitable spacer/mask.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Under about 2 years: spacer with face mask.
- Older cooperative child: spacer with mouthpiece.
- Reassess technique at every asthma review.

questions.stem: Which symptom pattern in a preschool child is most consistent with viral episodic wheeze rather than multiple-trigger wheeze?

options.label: A
options.text: Wheeze triggered mainly by viral URTIs, with no symptoms between infections

options.label: B
options.text: Wheeze with eczema, food allergy and strong family history of atopy

options.label: C
options.text: Wheeze with dust, pets, cold air, exercise and viral infections

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent wheeze with chronic productive cough and clubbing

questions.correctAnswerText: Wheeze triggered mainly by viral URTIs, with no symptoms between infections
questions.initialExplanation: The source describes viral episodic wheezing as triggered by viral URTIs and often resolving by around 5 years as airway size increases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This matches the viral episodic pattern.
- B. Incorrect. Atopy and family history increase the likelihood of asthma/multiple-trigger wheeze.
- C. Incorrect. Multiple triggers including allergens, cold air and exercise suggest multiple-trigger wheeze.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests chronic suppurative lung disease such as CF or bronchiectasis.
- E. Incorrect. Sudden onset after choking suggests FBA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral episodic wheeze: triggered by viral URTIs.
- Multiple-trigger wheeze: viral infection plus cold air, dust, animal dander and exercise.
- Preschool wheeze is diagnostically challenging; evaluate atopy, family history and symptom pattern.

questions.stem: Which feature increases the likelihood that a preschool child with recurrent wheeze has asthma and may benefit from asthma treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal breathing without any wheezing episodes

options.label: B
options.text: Atopy, eczema, food allergy or family history of asthma

options.label: C
options.text: Sudden onset after choking with unilateral reduced air entry

options.label: D
options.text: A single isolated episode of wheeze during bronchiolitis

questions.correctAnswerText: Atopy, eczema, food allergy or family history of asthma
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance links multiple-trigger wheeze and a positive family/personal history of atopy with a greater likelihood of asthma and response to asthma therapy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Without symptoms, there is no basis to diagnose recurrent wheeze.
- B. Correct. These features increase the likelihood of an asthma phenotype.
- C. Incorrect. This suggests foreign body aspiration.
- D. Incorrect. One viral bronchiolitis episode does not establish asthma.
- E. Incorrect. This suggests an acute infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Personal atopy and family history of asthma support asthma in preschool wheeze.
- Viral episodic wheeze may resolve by about 5 years.
- Reassess the phenotype over time rather than labeling every preschool wheeze as asthma.

cases.title: â€” Recurrent chest infections, steatorrhoea and faltering growth
cases.vignette: A 3-year-old child has recurrent chest infections, chronic cough, loose bulky stools, poor weight gain and digital clubbing. The mother reports that the child's skin tastes unusually salty. The newborn history includes delayed passage of meconium.

questions.stem: Which inheritance pattern is associated with cystic fibrosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Autosomal recessive
questions.initialExplanation: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the CFTR gene.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. It is not Y-linked.
- B. Incorrect. CF is not an X-linked disorder.
- C. Incorrect. It is not a mitochondrial disorder.
- D. Incorrect. CF is not autosomal dominant.
- E. Correct. This is the inheritance pattern specified.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CF = autosomal recessive.
- CFTR gene is located on chromosome 7.
- clinical guidance identifies خ”F508 deletion as the commonest mutation.

questions.stem: What is the primary physiological role of the CFTR protein described?

options.label: C
options.text: Production of surfactant by type II pneumocytes

options.label: D
options.text: Regulation of chloride and sodium movement across epithelial membranes

questions.correctAnswerText: Regulation of chloride and sodium movement across epithelial membranes
questions.initialExplanation: CFTR regulates chloride and sodium transport across epithelial surfaces. Dysfunction leads to abnormal water movement and thick, viscous secretions in multiple organs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Immunoglobulin production is a B-cell function.
- B. Incorrect. CFTR is not an insulin-producing protein; CF may later cause CF-related diabetes due to pancreatic damage.
- C. Incorrect. Surfactant production is performed by type II pneumocytes.
- D. Correct. This is the transport function described.
- E. Incorrect. Haemoglobin determines oxygen transport.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CFTR defect â†’ abnormal chloride/sodium transport â†’ thick, viscous secretions.
- Major systems: lungs, pancreas, liver and intestine.
- Clinical guidance خ”F508 as the most common mutation.

questions.stem: Which neonatal gastrointestinal presentation is associated with cystic fibrosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Necrotizing enterocolitis as the defining feature

options.label: C
options.text: Meconium ileus with failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Meconium ileus with failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours
questions.initialExplanation: Thick, viscous meconium can obstruct the terminal ileum and cause meconium ileus. Clinical guidance delayed passage of meconium, vomiting and abdominal distension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Biliary atresia causes conjugated jaundice and pale stools.
- B. Incorrect. NEC is a separate neonatal intestinal disease.
- C. Correct. This is the neonatal presentation described.
- D. Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease is a separate congenital enteric disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious projectile vomiting, not meconium ileus.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Meconium ileus occurs in a proportion of neonates with CF (clinical guidance gives 10â€“20%).
- Failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours, vomiting and abdominal distension are clues.
- Salty-tasting skin may be noticed by caregivers.

questions.stem: Which gastrointestinal feature in a young child with CF suggests pancreatic exocrine insufficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute watery diarrhoea for one day

options.label: D
options.text: Steatorrhoea, malabsorption and failure to thrive

questions.correctAnswerText: Steatorrhoea, malabsorption and failure to thrive
questions.initialExplanation: Thick secretions obstruct pancreatic ducts, impairing delivery of digestive enzymes. This results in malabsorption, steatorrhoea and poor growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
