- A. Incorrect. Acute watery diarrhoea alone is nonspecific and does not demonstrate pancreatic insufficiency.
- B. Incorrect. Haematuria is a renal symptom.
- C. Incorrect. Drooling and dysphagia suggest upper-airway or swallowing pathology.
- D. Correct. This is the pancreatic exocrine picture described.
- E. Incorrect. This does not fit malabsorption and pancreatic insufficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency â†’ malabsorption and steatorrhoea.
- Leads to poor growth/failure to thrive.
- Management includes pancreatic enzyme replacement (e.g. Creon) and high-calorie nutrition.

questions.stem: Which organism is highlighted as a later respiratory pathogen in cystic fibrosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance distinguishes early respiratory pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenzae from later organisms including Pseudomonas and Burkholderia cepacia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Group B streptococcus is mainly a neonatal pathogen.
- B. Incorrect. M. leprae is unrelated.
- C. Correct. Pseudomonas is listed among later CF respiratory pathogens.
- D. Incorrect. Chlamydia trachomatis is associated with pneumonia in young infants.
- E. Incorrect. Pertussis may cause prolonged cough but is not the later CF pathogen asked for.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early CF respiratory infection: Staph aureus and H. influenzae.
- Later infection: Pseudomonas and Burkholderia cepacia.
- Chronic infection causes progressive lung damage and bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: Which investigation is described as the gold standard diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sweat chloride test
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies the sweat test as the gold standard. Sweat chloride is elevated because of abnormal CFTR-mediated salt transport in sweat ducts.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the gold-standard test stated.
- B. Incorrect. CXR may demonstrate pulmonary involvement but is not definitive.
- C. Incorrect. Stool testing may show malabsorption but does not confirm the CFTR disorder.
- D. Incorrect. CBC is nonspecific.
- E. Incorrect. Pulmonary function tests assess respiratory function but do not confirm CF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sweat chloride test: gold standard in the source.
- Newborn screening may use elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT).
- Genetic testing can identify CFTR mutations.
- Stool elastase helps assess pancreatic exocrine function.

questions.stem: A child aged over 6 months has a sweat chloride concentration of 72 mmol/L. How should this be interpreted using the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Indicative of cystic fibrosis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance classifies sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or higher as indicative of CF in children and adults; 40â€“59 mmol/L is intermediate and 0â€“39 mmol/L makes CF unlikely.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Sweat chloride is not an asthma diagnostic test.
- B. Incorrect. PCD is a separate inherited ciliary disorder.
- C. Correct. A result of 72 mmol/L is above the source's diagnostic threshold.
- D. Incorrect. The intermediate range is 40â€“59 mmol/L in the table.
- E. Incorrect. The value is not in the unlikely range.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sweat chloride â‰¥60 mmol/L: indicative of CF in the source table.
- 40â€“59 mmol/L: intermediate.
- 0â€“39 mmol/L: CF unlikely.
- Interpret the result alongside clinical findings and confirmatory testing/genetics according to specialist practice.

questions.stem: Which finding supports pancreatic insufficiency in a child with suspected CF?
questions.correctAnswerText: Low faecal elastase
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance stool examination for evidence of malabsorption, including low faecal elastase, which supports pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Low faecal elastase supports pancreatic exocrine dysfunction.
- B. Incorrect. Nitrite positivity supports bacterial UTI.
- C. Incorrect. Urinary calcium relates to renal metabolic assessment.
- D. Incorrect. Urinary VMA is used in neuroblastoma evaluation.
- E. Incorrect. ASO supports recent streptococcal infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Low faecal elastase supports pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
- LFTs assess hepatic involvement.
- Chest imaging and lung function assess pulmonary disease.
- Genetic testing can confirm pathogenic CFTR variants.

questions.stem: Which treatment combination addresses pulmonary and nutritional problems in CF as described?

options.label: C
options.text: Airway clearance, bronchodilators, antibiotics when indicated, nutrition, enzymes and fat-soluble vitamins

questions.correctAnswerText: Airway clearance, bronchodilators, antibiotics when indicated, nutrition, enzymes and fat-soluble vitamins
questions.initialExplanation: CF is multisystemic and requires multidisciplinary care. Clinical guidance airway clearance, bronchodilators, organism-directed antibiotics, mucolytics, high-calorie nutrition, pancreatic enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are renal interventions, not CF treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Steroids are not routine treatment for every CF patient.
- C. Correct. It addresses respiratory clearance/infection and pancreatic malabsorption.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics alone do not address airway clearance, malabsorption or nutritional deficiency.
- E. Incorrect. High-calorie nutrition is recommended; fluid restriction/low-calorie intake would be inappropriate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pulmonary: airway clearance/chest physiotherapy, bronchodilators, antibiotics and mucolytics (e.g. DNase/hypertonic saline in selected plans).
- Nutrition: high-calorie diet, pancreatic enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamins.
- Treat complications such as CF-related diabetes.
- clinical guidance identifies bilateral lung transplantation as an option for end-stage pulmonary disease.

questions.stem: Which complication may develop in an older child with CF due to progressive liver involvement?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance liver disease that may progress to cirrhosis and portal hypertension in older children with CF.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Hydrocele is a scrotal fluid collection.
- B. Correct. This is the hepatic complication listed.
- C. Incorrect. Nephrocalcinosis is not an inevitable CF complication.
- D. Incorrect. Coarctation is a congenital cardiac lesion.
- E. Incorrect. Epiglottitis is an acute upper-airway infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CF affects lungs, pancreas, intestine and liver.
- Liver involvement may progress to cirrhosis/portal hypertension.
- Other features include nasal polyps, sinusitis, clubbing, rectal prolapse, haemoptysis and pneumothorax.
- Male infertility may occur due to congenital absence of the vas deferens.

cases.title: â€” Chronic productive cough and recurrent pneumonia
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old child has a daily productive cough with large amounts of sputum, recurrent episodes of pneumonia and occasional haemoptysis. Examination reveals digital clubbing and coarse crackles. Previous chest X-rays were initially unrevealing, but high-resolution CT now demonstrates dilated, thick-walled bronchi with a characteristic honeycomb-like appearance.

questions.stem: What is the definition of bronchiectasis?

options.label: A
options.text: Abnormal irreversible dilatation of the bronchial tree

options.label: D
options.text: Fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity

questions.correctAnswerText: Abnormal irreversible dilatation of the bronchial tree
questions.initialExplanation: Bronchiectasis is permanent, abnormal dilatation of bronchi due to chronic airway inflammation and damage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the definition given.
- B. Incorrect. Alveolar haemorrhage is a different pulmonary process.
- C. Incorrect. This describes acute epiglottitis.
- D. Incorrect. This describes pleural effusion.
- E. Incorrect. Reversible airway narrowing is characteristic of asthma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bronchiectasis = abnormal, irreversible bronchial dilatation.
- Clinical clues: chronic productive cough, recurrent pneumonia, haemoptysis and clubbing.
- High-resolution CT is the diagnostic imaging test.

questions.stem: Which inherited condition is an important cause of bronchiectasis in childhood?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cystic fibrosis
questions.initialExplanation: CF is a major inherited cause of chronic suppurative airway disease and bronchiectasis. Primary ciliary dyskinesia and immunodeficiency are other important causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Marfan syndrome is a connective-tissue disorder.
- B. Incorrect. Turner syndrome is associated with conditions such as coarctation, not a typical bronchiectasis cause.
- C. Incorrect. Williams syndrome is associated with supravalvular aortic stenosis.
- D. Correct. CF causes thick secretions, recurrent infection and progressive airway damage.
- E. Incorrect. Alport syndrome is a hereditary renal, auditory and ocular disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Congenital/inherited causes listed: primary ciliary dyskinesia/Kartagener, CF, hypogammaglobulinaemia and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
- Acquired causes include severe measles, pertussis, TB, HIV, missed foreign body and bronchiolitis obliterans.
- Always search for the underlying cause in a child with bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: Which clinical combination is most typical of established bronchiectasis?

options.label: A
options.text: Sudden choking followed by complete recovery

options.label: B
options.text: Chronic productive cough, recurrent pneumonia, haemoptysis and clubbing

options.label: D
options.text: Isolated acute barking cough and stridor

options.label: E
options.text: Recurrent isolated nocturnal wheeze with normal growth

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic productive cough, recurrent pneumonia, haemoptysis and clubbing
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic airway infection and inflammation damage the bronchial wall, producing persistent sputum, recurrent infection and sometimes haemoptysis. Longstanding disease may cause clubbing and failure to thrive.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests a choking event and possible FBA.
- B. Correct. These are the clinical features described.
- C. Incorrect. This suggests pneumothorax or another acute pleural process.
- D. Incorrect. This suggests croup.
- E. Incorrect. This is more consistent with episodic asthma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chronic productive cough with large-volume sputum.
- Recurrent pneumonia and haemoptysis.
- Clubbing and poor growth may be present.
- Auscultation may reveal bilateral or unilateral crackles and reduced air entry.

questions.stem: Which imaging test is diagnostic for bronchiectasis in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: B
options.text: Plain chest X-ray in each early case

options.label: D
options.text: High-resolution CT scan of the chest

questions.correctAnswerText: High-resolution CT scan of the chest
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies HRCT as the diagnostic imaging modality. Early chest X-ray may be normal, while later disease may show a honeycomb appearance and bronchial wall thickening.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Echocardiography evaluates cardiac structure and function.
- B. Incorrect. Early CXR can be normal and is not the definitive test.
- C. Incorrect. Lateral neck X-ray is used in selected upper-airway problems, not bronchiectasis.
- D. Correct. HRCT directly demonstrates bronchial dilatation and wall changes.
- E. Incorrect. Barium swallow may investigate oesophageal compression or aspiration-related problems.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HRCT chest: diagnostic.
- CXR: may be normal early; honeycomb appearance may occur later.
- Sputum analysis helps identify infective organisms.

questions.stem: What is the main medical treatment approach for bronchiectasis?

options.label: E
options.text: Routine long-term systemic corticosteroids for each patient

questions.correctAnswerText: Antibiotics and chest physiotherapy/airway clearance
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies medical therapy as the main approach, especially antibiotics and chest physiotherapy to clear secretions and reduce infective burden.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bronchodilators may be used if there is associated airflow obstruction, but they do not replace airway clearance and infection management.
- B. Incorrect. Antihistamines do not treat chronic suppurative airway disease.
- C. Incorrect. Pleural drainage is used for selected pleural effusions/empyema, not routine bronchiectasis.
- D. Correct. This is the core management described.
- E. Incorrect. Systemic steroids are not the routine treatment for bronchiectasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat infections with appropriate antibiotics.
- Regular airway clearance/chest physiotherapy is important.
- Treat underlying causes such as CF, PCD or immunodeficiency.
- Severe localized disease or severe haemoptysis may require surgical resection.

questions.stem: Which complication may occur in longstanding bronchiectasis?

options.label: C
options.text: Nephrotic syndrome as the defining complication

options.label: E
options.text: Respiratory failure, severe haemoptysis and secondary amyloidosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Respiratory failure, severe haemoptysis and secondary amyloidosis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance recurrent pneumonia, empyema, lung abscess, respiratory failure, severe haemoptysis and amyloidosis as complications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Coarctation is a congenital cardiovascular lesion.
- B. Incorrect. Hydrocele is a scrotal fluid collection.
- C. Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome is a renal disorder.
- D. Incorrect. Epiglottitis is an acute upper-airway infection, not a complication of bronchiectasis.
- E. Correct. These are the complications described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Complications: recurrent infection, empyema, lung abscess, respiratory failure and severe haemoptysis.
- Secondary amyloidosis may occur in chronic suppurative disease.
- Surgery is reserved for selected advanced, localized or complicated cases.

topics.name: Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD) and Kartagener Syndrome

cases.title: â€” Neonatal respiratory distress, chronic sinusitis and situs inversus
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child has had chronic wet cough since infancy, recurrent pneumonia, chronic otitis media and recurrent sinusitis. Imaging reveals situs inversus. The parents report that a male relative has infertility.

questions.stem: What is the underlying defect in primary ciliary dyskinesia?

options.label: B
options.text: Congenital absence of the pulmonary artery

options.label: D
options.text: Destruction of alveolar macrophages by bacteria

questions.correctAnswerText: Impaired motility/function of respiratory cilia
questions.initialExplanation: PCD comprises inherited disorders in which ciliary function is impaired. Mucociliary clearance becomes ineffective, leading to chronic infection and airway damage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Surfactant deficiency is associated with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
- B. Incorrect. Pulmonary artery absence is a separate congenital cardiovascular anomaly.
- C. Incorrect. CF is due to abnormal CFTR function, not excessive CFTR activity as described.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the mechanism of PCD.
- E. Correct. This is the defining defect.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PCD is an inherited ciliary disorder.
- Clinical guidance autosomal recessive inheritance and an approximate frequency of 1:20,000.
- Impaired mucociliary clearance causes chronic respiratory infection and bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: Which combination is characteristic of Kartagener syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis and situs inversus

options.label: C
options.text: VSD, pulmonary stenosis and overriding aorta

questions.correctAnswerText: Bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis and situs inversus
questions.initialExplanation: Kartagener syndrome is a classic presentation of primary ciliary dyskinesia, with bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis and situs inversus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests an atopic phenotype associated with asthma.
- B. Correct. This is the classic triad.
- C. Incorrect. This describes the components of tetralogy of Fallot.
- D. Incorrect. This is the characteristic triad of Alport syndrome.
- E. Incorrect. This describes nephrotic syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Kartagener = bronchiectasis + chronic sinusitis + situs inversus.
- PCD may also cause chronic otitis media and neonatal respiratory distress.
- Not every child with PCD has situs inversus.

questions.stem: Which reproductive problem may occur in males with primary ciliary dyskinesia?

options.label: B
options.text: Congenital absence of the prostate in each patient

questions.correctAnswerText: Immotile sperm causing infertility
questions.initialExplanation: Sperm flagella share structural features with motile cilia. Impaired ciliary/flagellar function may cause sperm immotility and male infertility. clinical guidance also mentions female infertility due to fallopian tube ciliary dysfunction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The problem is impaired motility, not excessive motility.
- B. Incorrect. Congenital absence of the prostate is not the feature described.
- C. Correct. This is the genitourinary manifestation described.
- D. Incorrect. Torsion is not an expected universal PCD manifestation.
- E. Incorrect. Hypospadias is a separate congenital urethral abnormality.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Male: immotile sperm and infertility.
- Female: fallopian tube ciliary dysfunction may impair fertility.
- PCD may also be associated with situs inversus, asplenia, congenital heart disease and other orientation defects.

questions.stem: Which test is described as a screening test for primary ciliary dyskinesia?
questions.correctAnswerText: Nasal nitric oxide measurement
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists nasal nitric oxide as a screening test. Additional diagnostic assessment may include nasal ciliary sample analysis/electron microscopy and genetic testing.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. ASO supports recent streptococcal infection.
- B. Incorrect. PEF is used in asthma diagnosis/monitoring, not PCD screening.
- C. Incorrect. VMA/HVA are used in neuroblastoma assessment.
- D. Incorrect. Sweat chloride is used to investigate cystic fibrosis.
- E. Correct. Nasal nitric oxide is listed as a screening test.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Screening: nasal nitric oxide.
- Further evaluation: ciliary microscopy/electron microscopy, genetic testing and imaging.
- Imaging may include chest CT and sinus CT.

questions.stem: Which long-term management strategy is appropriate for PCD?

options.label: C
options.text: Airway clearance therapy, bronchodilators when indicated, antibiotics and ENT follow-up

options.label: E
options.text: No treatment because ciliary function typically returns spontaneously

questions.correctAnswerText: Airway clearance therapy, bronchodilators when indicated, antibiotics and ENT follow-up
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance management focused on airway clearance, treating infection, bronchodilator use where appropriate and ENT involvement for chronic ear/sinus disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Respiratory and ENT manifestations require ongoing care throughout childhood.
- B. Incorrect. Diuretics do not treat the underlying ciliary disorder.
- C. Correct. These measures address impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent infection.
- D. Incorrect. Nephrectomy is unrelated.
- E. Incorrect. PCD is inherited and does not spontaneously resolve.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Airway clearance is central.
- Treat respiratory infections with appropriate antibiotics.
- ENT assessment is important for chronic otitis media and sinusitis.
- Monitor bronchiectasis and lung function over time.

cases.title: â€” Breathlessness with reduced chest expansion and stony dullness
cases.vignette: A 10-year-old child presents with progressive breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain following pneumonia. Examination reveals reduced movement of the right hemithorax, reduced chest expansion, tracheal deviation to the left, reduced tactile vocal fremitus, stony dullness to percussion and markedly reduced air entry on the right. Chest X-ray shows homogeneous opacity occupying much of the right hemithorax with contralateral mediastinal shift.

questions.stem: What is the definition of pleural effusion?

options.label: B
options.text: Accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity

questions.correctAnswerText: Accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity
questions.initialExplanation: Pleural effusion is abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural space between the visceral and parietal pleura.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes bronchiectasis.
- B. Correct. This is the definition.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the definition of pleural effusion.
- D. Incorrect. This describes purulent airway disease, not pleural effusion.
- E. Incorrect. Air in the pleural cavity is pneumothorax.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pleural effusion = fluid in the pleural cavity.
- Causes may be transudative or exudative.
- Pneumothorax is air, not fluid, in the pleural space.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed as a cause of transudative pleural effusion?
questions.correctAnswerText: Congestive heart failure
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance nephrotic syndrome, liver cirrhosis, hypoproteinaemia and congestive heart failure as causes of transudative effusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. TB is listed as an exudative cause.
- B. Incorrect. Connective tissue disease such as SLE is listed among exudative causes.
- C. Incorrect. Ruptured lung abscess causes an inflammatory/exudative process.
- D. Incorrect. Pneumonia is listed as an exudative cause.
- E. Correct. CHF increases hydrostatic pressure and may cause a transudative effusion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Transudative causes: nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, hypoproteinaemia and CHF.
- Exudative causes: pneumonia, TB, ruptured lung abscess, tumors and CTD such as SLE.
- Identify and treat the underlying cause.

questions.stem: Which finding supports an exudative rather than transudative pleural effusion in the comparison table?

options.label: A
options.text: Low cell count and low specific gravity

options.label: B
options.text: Clear fluid with low protein and low LDH

options.label: D
options.text: High protein concentration and increased LDH

questions.correctAnswerText: High protein concentration and increased LDH
questions.initialExplanation: The source comparison describes exudative fluid as more turbid, with higher protein, more cells and higher LDH, whereas transudative fluid is clear with lower protein, low cell count and lower LDH.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Low cell count and low specific gravity are described for transudative fluid.
- B. Incorrect. This describes a transudative pattern.
- C. Incorrect. An abnormal pleural fluid profile is expected in an effusion.
- D. Correct. These findings support exudative effusion.
- E. Incorrect. Exudative fluid typically contains more cells.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Transudate: clear, low protein, low cell count, low specific gravity and lower LDH in the source table.
- Exudate: turbid, high protein, high cell count and higher LDH.
- standard guidance's numeric cut-offs are simplified; apply current pleural fluid criteria clinically.

questions.stem: Which combination of physical signs is most consistent with a large pleural effusion?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased fremitus, localized dullness and bronchial breathing

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced movement, reduced expansion, tracheal shift away, reduced fremitus, stony dullness and reduced/absent air entry

options.label: D
options.text: Diffuse bilateral wheeze with normal percussion

options.label: E
options.text: Hyperresonance with tracheal shift toward the affected side

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduced movement, reduced expansion, tracheal shift away, reduced fremitus, stony dullness and reduced/absent air entry
questions.initialExplanation: A large fluid collection reduces lung expansion and transmission of vocal vibrations, produces stony dullness and may push the mediastinum/trachea to the opposite side.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Increased fremitus and bronchial breathing are more consistent with consolidation.
- B. Incorrect. These findings suggest upper-airway obstruction/epiglottitis.
- C. Correct. This is the examination pattern described.
- D. Incorrect. Diffuse wheeze is more consistent with asthma or bronchiolitis.
- E. Incorrect. Hyperresonance suggests pneumothorax; shift toward may occur with volume loss/collapse.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Inspection: reduced movement on affected side.
- Palpation: reduced expansion and TVF; trachea may shift away if effusion is large.
- Percussion: stony dullness.
- Auscultation: reduced or absent air entry.

questions.stem: Which management approach is described for a clinically significant pleural effusion?

options.label: A
options.text: No treatment even when severe respiratory distress is present

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the underlying cause and perform thoracocentesis with or without chest tube drainage when indicated

options.label: C
options.text: Antibiotics for each transudative effusion regardless of cause

questions.correctAnswerText: Treat the underlying cause and perform thoracocentesis with or without chest tube drainage when indicated
questions.initialExplanation: Management depends on severity and cause. Clinical guidance treatment of the underlying cause and thoracocentesis, with chest tube drainage connected to an underwater seal when needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A large symptomatic effusion may cause significant respiratory compromise and requires intervention.
- B. Correct. This is the treatment approach given.
- C. Incorrect. Transudative effusions require treatment of the underlying hydrostatic/oncotic cause, not routine antibiotics.
- D. Incorrect. Lung transplantation is not treatment for ordinary pleural effusion.
- E. Incorrect. Bronchodilators do not remove pleural fluid.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat the underlying cause.
- Thoracocentesis may be diagnostic and therapeutic.
- Chest tube with underwater seal drainage may be needed for significant/recurrent or complicated effusion.
- Clinical severity and fluid characteristics guide the intervention.

topics.name: Integrated Respiratory Assessment and Childhood Infection Patterns

cases.title: A child with nocturnal noisy breathing
cases.vignette: A 6-year-old child is referred because of loud snoring during sleep, restless sleep and daytime tiredness. Examination shows enlarged tonsils and adenoids. The family reports that the child sometimes pauses breathing during sleep. The clinician distinguishes snoring/stertor from stridor and wheeze.

questions.stem: Which mechanism produces snoring?

options.label: B
options.text: Vibration of loose upper-airway tissues during sleep

options.label: C
options.text: Fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity

options.label: D
options.text: Expiration against a partially closed glottis

options.label: E
options.text: Turbulent flow through narrowed bronchioles during expiration

questions.correctAnswerText: Vibration of loose upper-airway tissues during sleep
questions.initialExplanation: Snoring is caused by vibration of relaxed or loose soft tissues in the upper airway during sleep. It may be associated with obesity, Down syndrome, adenoid hypertrophy and tonsillar hypertrophy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Alveolar collapse is atelectasis.
- B. Correct. This is the mechanism described in the source.
- C. Incorrect. This is pleural effusion.
- D. Incorrect. This is the mechanism of expiratory grunting.
- E. Incorrect. This describes wheeze due to lower-airway narrowing.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Snoring is generated by vibration of upper-airway soft tissue during sleep.
- Risk factors listed: obesity, Down syndrome, adenoid hypertrophy and tonsillar hypertrophy.
- Adenotonsillar hypertrophy may contribute to obstructive sleep apnoea.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes stertor from stridor?

options.label: A
options.text: Stridor is a low-pitched sound produced by pleural fluid

options.label: B
options.text: Both terms describe crackles caused by alveolar fluid

options.label: D
options.text: Stertor is low-pitched and arises from the nose/back of throat, whereas stridor is harsh and high-pitched from upper-airway narrowing

options.label: E
options.text: Stertor is typically expiratory wheeze from bronchioles

questions.correctAnswerText: Stertor is low-pitched and arises from the nose/back of throat, whereas stridor is harsh and high-pitched from upper-airway narrowing
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance stertor as a low-pitched sound from the nose or back of the throat, often resembling nasal congestion or snoring. Stridor is a harsh, high-pitched sound from partial upper-airway obstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pleural fluid causes reduced breath sounds and stony dullness, not stridor.
- B. Incorrect. Crackles are separate added lung sounds.
- C. Incorrect. Asthma produces lower-airway wheeze.
- D. Correct. This is the acoustic and anatomical distinction in the source.
- E. Incorrect. Expiratory wheeze is produced by narrowed lower airways.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stertor: low-pitched, nasal/pharyngeal, often resembles congestion.
- Stridor: harsh, high-pitched, upper-airway obstruction, mainly inspiratory.
- Wheeze: musical sound from narrowed lower airways, usually expiratory.

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of childhood respiratory infections are described as viral in the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.initialExplanation: The source states that approximately 80–90% of childhood respiratory infections are viral and that about 80% are upper respiratory tract infections.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Some respiratory infections are bacterial or caused by other organisms.
- B. Correct. This matches the epidemiological figure.
- C. Incorrect. This is not the estimate given.
- D. Incorrect. This is not the proportion stated.
- E. Incorrect. This is substantially below the estimate in the source.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Approximately 80% of childhood respiratory infections are URTIs.
- Approximately 80–90% are viral in the source.
- Infants and primary-school children may experience numerous respiratory infections each year.

cases.title: Why a blocked nose matters in a young infant

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy is admitted for the third time with a lower respiratory tract infection. He was born at 31 weeks, weighing 1.3 kg. His mother smoked throughout pregnancy, and the family of nine lives in a small overcrowded house. He was exclusively breastfed, his vaccinations are complete and an echocardiogram was normal. Which set of this child's background features corresponds to recognised risk factors for respiratory disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Male sex, prematurity/very low birth weight, maternal smoking in pregnancy and overcrowding

options.label: B
options.text: Exclusive breastfeeding, complete immunisation, normal cardiac anatomy and overcrowding

options.label: C
options.text: Male sex, complete immunisation, exclusive breastfeeding and a large house

options.label: D
options.text: Prematurity/very low birth weight, normal echocardiogram, exclusive breastfeeding and maternal smoking

options.label: E
options.text: Overcrowding, complete immunisation, normal cardiac anatomy and male sex

questions.correctAnswerText: Male sex, prematurity/very low birth weight, maternal smoking in pregnancy and overcrowding
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance male sex, prematurity or VLBW, maternal smoking during pregnancy and overcrowding among the risk factors for respiratory disease in children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. All four are listed risk factors.
- B. Incorrect. Only overcrowding is a listed risk factor. Breastfeeding, immunisation and normal cardiac anatomy are not risk factors.
- C. Incorrect. Male sex is a risk factor, but the other three items are not. A large house is not listed, whereas overcrowding and a large family are.
- D. Incorrect. Prematurity/VLBW and maternal smoking are risk factors, but a normal echocardiogram and breastfeeding are not. Congenital heart anomalies would be a risk factor, and this child does not have one.
- E. Incorrect. Overcrowding and male sex are listed; immunisation and normal cardiac anatomy are not.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Risk factors: poor socio-economic status and overcrowding, large family size, parental genetic predisposition and smoking (maternal during pregnancy), male sex, prematurity or VLBW, cystic fibrosis, congenital heart or lung anomalies, and (rarely) immune deficiency.
- Respiratory illness accounts for about 50% of illness in children under 5 years and about 30% of hospital admissions.
- About 80% of respiratory infections are upper respiratory tract infections, and 80–90% are viral.
- Pneumonia is the leading cause of death under 5 years in low- and middle-income countries.

source.raw: Respiratory sheet — Page 6 (Respiratory disorders and risk factors); Page 3 (anatomy figure); Page 22 (Pneumonia definition).

cases.title: Reading the cough and grading the distress

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had cough and fever for 2 days. His respiratory rate is 52/min. He has nasal flaring, subcostal and intercostal recession and an audible expiratory grunt. He is alert and not cyanosed. Which statement correctly describes his respiratory status?

options.label: A
options.text: He is not tachypnoeic, because the threshold for his age is more than 60 breaths/min

options.label: B
options.text: Grade II (moderate) distress, because grunting is a feature of grade IV

options.label: C
options.text: Grade I (mild) distress, because nasal flaring is present

options.label: D
options.text: Grade III (severe) distress, with a respiratory rate above the age threshold of 40/min

options.label: E
options.text: Grade IV (advanced) distress, because recession and grunting are both present

questions.correctAnswerText: Grade III (severe) distress, with a respiratory rate above the age threshold of 40/min
questions.initialExplanation: A rate of 52/min exceeds the 1–5-year threshold (>40/min). Tachypnoea, flaring and recession plus grunting make grade III. Grade IV additionally needs cyanosis and a disturbed conscious level.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. More than 60/min is the neonatal threshold. For a 1–5-year-old it is more than 40/min.
- B. Incorrect. Grade II has recession but no grunting. Grunting defines grade III.
- C. Incorrect. Grade I is only tachypnoea plus nasal flaring.
- D. Correct. Tachypnoea + flaring + recession + grunting = grade III, and the rate is above the age-specific threshold.
- E. Incorrect. Grade IV requires cyanosis and a disturbed conscious level, and he is alert and pink.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Tachypnoea thresholds: birth–2 months >60; 2 months–1 year >50; 1–5 years >40; school age >30.
- Grade I = tachypnoea + flaring; II = + recession; III = + grunting; IV = + cyanosis and disturbed conscious level.
- Recession can be subcostal, intercostal, suprasternal, and sternal in newborns. Grunting is expiratory against a partly closed glottis.
- Tachypnoea is sensitive but not specific, and it also occurs in heart failure, metabolic disorders and sepsis.

source.raw: Respiratory sheet — Pages 5–6 (Signs of respiratory distress; grades of RD).

cases.title: Not every breathless infant has bronchiolitis

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant presents with 2 days of rapid, deep breathing and poor feeding after several days of profuse watery diarrhoea. He has sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes. There is no coryza, fever or wheeze. Air entry is equal and the chest is clear, with no crackles and no recession. Which statement best explains his tachypnoea and the right approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Bronchiolitis, because tachypnoea in an infant is typically caused by RSV; give oxygen

options.label: B
options.text: Pneumonia, because tachypnoea is specific to lung parenchymal disease; start antibiotics

options.label: C
options.text: Foreign body aspiration, because deep breathing is its typical sign; request bronchoscopy

options.label: D
options.text: Pleural effusion, because tachypnoea occurs with pleural disease; request thoracocentesis

options.label: E
options.text: Metabolic acidosis from dehydration; tachypnoea is sensitive but not specific, so assess hydration and acid–base status instead of treating as bronchiolitis

questions.correctAnswerText: Metabolic acidosis from dehydration; tachypnoea is sensitive but not specific, so assess hydration and acid–base status instead of treating as bronchiolitis
questions.initialExplanation: A clear chest with no wheeze, crackles or recession and a history of fluid loss points to an extra-pulmonary cause of tachypnoea. Clinical guidance metabolic acidosis, heart failure, severe anaemia and sepsis among causes of tachypnoea and distress in infants.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bronchiolitis follows a coryzal illness and gives wheeze, crackles and recession. None of these is present.
- B. Incorrect. Tachypnoea is sensitive but not specific, and there are no focal chest signs or fever.
- C. Incorrect. Foreign body aspiration follows a choking episode and gives unilateral signs.
- D. Incorrect. Pleural effusion would give reduced movement, stony dullness and reduced air entry.
- E. Correct. The deep breathing with dehydration suggests compensatory tachypnoea from metabolic acidosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Causes of acute respiratory distress in an infant: bronchiolitis, viral episodic wheeze, pneumonia, heart failure, foreign body, anaphylaxis, pneumothorax or pleural effusion, metabolic acidosis and severe anaemia.
- Tachypnoea is one of the most sensitive signs of respiratory illness, but is not specific.
- Breathlessness may come from airway disease, parenchymal disease, pleural disease or extra-pulmonary disease (heart, blood, metabolic).

source.raw: Respiratory sheet — Page 19 (Causes of acute respiratory distress in an infant); Page 5 (Tachypnoea); Page 4 (Breathlessness).
source.pages: 19 (Causes of acute respiratory distress in an infant)

cases.title: An infant with a staccato cough and conjunctivitis
cases.vignette: A 2-month-old infant develops a gradually worsening cough. The infant is afebrile or has only minimal fever and has sticky conjunctival discharge. The cough is repetitive and staccato in character. CBC shows eosinophilia.

questions.stem: Which organism is associated with pneumonia in the first three months of life, staccato cough and conjunctivitis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Chlamydia trachomatis
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance associates Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia with young infants, particularly in the first three months, gradual onset, staccato cough and conjunctivitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pertussis causes paroxysmal whooping cough, not the specific infant pneumonia pattern described.
- B. Correct. The age, cough pattern and conjunctivitis match the source.
- C. Incorrect. Group B streptococcus is an important neonatal bacterial pathogen but does not describe this classic staccato/conjunctivitis picture.
- D. Incorrect. Mycoplasma is more commonly associated with school-age children.
- E. Incorrect. Staphylococcal pneumonia may cause severe rapid deterioration and pneumatoceles.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia: young infant, gradual onset, staccato cough and conjunctivitis.
- The source notes eosinophilia and serology among supportive investigations.
- Treatment is supportive plus an appropriate antibiotic such as a macrolide.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old has an insidious onset of cough and low-grade fever. The child develops erythema multiforme and haemolytic anaemia. Which organism is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
questions.initialExplanation: Mycoplasma pneumonia is associated with school-age children and may cause extrapulmonary manifestations affecting skin, CNS, joints, heart, blood and gastrointestinal system. Cold agglutinins may be present.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Proteus is a urinary pathogen and is associated with infection-related urinary stones.
- B. Incorrect. RSV is a common cause of bronchiolitis in infants.
- C. Correct. The age, insidious onset and extrapulmonary manifestations fit Mycoplasma.
- D. Incorrect. Hib is associated with epiglottitis and some bacterial respiratory infections.
- E. Incorrect. Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia is associated with young infants and staccato cough/conjunctivitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mycoplasma pneumonia: school-age child, gradual onset and low-grade fever.
- Extrapulmonary manifestations may include erythema multiforme/Stevens–Johnson syndrome, meningoencephalitis, Guillain–Barré, arthritis, myocarditis/pericarditis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and protein-losing enteropathy.
- Cold agglutinins may be positive; the source lists macrolides.

questions.stem: A child with severe dysphagia and neuromuscular weakness develops pneumonia after aspirating oropharyngeal contents. Which lung region is most commonly affected?

options.label: B
options.text: Both lung apices equally in each case

options.label: C
options.text: Right upper lobe, with a right apical opacity

questions.correctAnswerText: Right upper lobe, with a right apical opacity
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance that aspiration pneumonia usually affects the upper right lobe and may produce a right apical opacity on chest X-ray.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The source specifically highlights the upper right lobe.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the characteristic pattern described.
- C. Correct. This is the location described in the source.
- D. Incorrect. Aspiration affects the lower respiratory tract/lung parenchyma, not the pleural cavity alone.
- E. Incorrect. A pulmonary artery is a vessel, not the site of aspiration pneumonia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Aspiration pneumonia: inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric material into the lower airway.
- Chemical pneumonitis is inflammation caused by chemical contents such as gastric material.
- Risk factors: GERD, cleft palate, neuromuscular disorders/CP, Down syndrome and H-type TEF.
- Oil/kerosene ingestion in an infant is a serious aspiration risk; gastric lavage is contraindicated after kerosene ingestion.

questions.stem: A child has increased respiratory rate without lower chest indrawing. Which WHO-style acute respiratory illness category is described in the supplied clinical guidance?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pneumonia
questions.initialExplanation: The source's ARI classification describes increased respiratory rate without lower chest indrawing as pneumonia, managed at home with antibiotics in the table.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. No pneumonia is associated with normal respiratory rate and no lower chest indrawing.
- B. Incorrect. Respiratory failure is a separate critical clinical state.
- C. Incorrect. Severe pneumonia is associated with increased RR plus lower chest indrawing.
- D. Correct. Increased respiratory rate without lower chest indrawing is classified as pneumonia in the source table.
- E. Incorrect. Very severe pneumonia includes lower chest indrawing and danger signs such as cyanosis, convulsions, abnormal sleep/alertness or poor feeding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Normal RR, no lower chest indrawing → no pneumonia.
- Increased RR, no lower chest indrawing → pneumonia.
- Increased RR + lower chest indrawing → severe pneumonia.
- Increased RR + lower chest indrawing + danger signs → very severe pneumonia and urgent referral.

questions.stem: Which radiographic pattern is most commonly associated with interstitial pneumonia in the source?

options.label: B
options.text: A thumb sign in the lateral neck

options.label: D
options.text: Homogeneous opacity confined to one lobe

questions.correctAnswerText: Scattered bilateral perihilar pulmonary infiltrates
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance interstitial pneumonia as usually viral and showing scattered bilateral perihilar pulmonary infiltrates. Lobar pneumonia is more likely to show homogeneous opacity in one or more lobes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. This is the interstitial pattern stated in the source.
- B. Incorrect. Thumb sign is associated with epiglottitis.
- C. Incorrect. Rib notching is associated with coarctation of the aorta.
- D. Incorrect. This is the lobar pneumonia pattern.
- E. Incorrect. Boot-shaped heart is associated with tetralogy of Fallot.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Lobar pneumonia: homogeneous opacity in one or more lobes, usually bacterial in the source.
- Bronchopneumonia: scattered opacities in both lungs; may be viral or bacterial.
- Interstitial pneumonia: bilateral perihilar infiltrates, usually viral.
- Radiographic pattern suggests but does not definitively identify the organism.

cases.title: Choosing antibiotics by age and organism

questions.stem: A 10-day-old term neonate has fever, a respiratory rate of 72/min, grunting and subcostal recession. The delivery was vaginal. The chest X-ray shows bilateral patchy opacities. Which choice of likely organisms and initial treatment matches clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: RSV and rhinovirus; supportive care, with no antibiotics

options.label: B
options.text: Group B streptococci and Gram-negative enteric organisms such as E. coli; IV ampicillin plus gentamicin, or a third-generation cephalosporin

options.label: C
options.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae; an oral macrolide at home

options.label: D
options.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Hib; oral amoxicillin at home

options.label: E
options.text: Staphylococcus aureus; oral cloxacillin at home

questions.correctAnswerText: Group B streptococci and Gram-negative enteric organisms such as E. coli; IV ampicillin plus gentamicin, or a third-generation cephalosporin
questions.initialExplanation: Newborn pneumonia is caused by organisms from the maternal genital tract (group B streptococci, Gram-negative enterococci such as E. coli). clinical guidance gives IV ampicillin plus gentamicin, or a third-generation cephalosporin, for newborns.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Viruses predominate in infants and young children, not in the early neonatal period, and this neonate is severely ill.
- B. Correct. The organisms and regimen match the age-based table.
- C. Incorrect. Mycoplasma and Chlamydia pneumoniae are organisms of school-age children, and oral home treatment is unsafe in a neonate.
- D. Incorrect. Oral amoxicillin is for older infants and young children with mild-to-moderate disease.
- E. Incorrect. Staphylococcus can cause severe pneumonia, but it is not the only expected organism, and oral treatment is not appropriate.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Newborn: group B streptococci and Gram-negative enteric bacilli; IV ampicillin + gentamicin, or a third-generation cephalosporin.
- Older infant and young child: viruses (RSV) commonest; amoxicillin or co-amoxiclav (oral in mild to moderate cases).
- Over 5 years: amoxicillin and/or a macrolide (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin).
- Antibiotic choice depends on age, severity and chest X-ray. TB should be considered at all ages.

source.raw: Respiratory sheet — Page 23 (Pneumonia by age); Page 26 (Treatment: antibiotic choice).

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy has had 10 days of dry cough and low-grade fever. He is playing and eating normally, with few chest signs, but the chest X-ray shows extensive bilateral infiltrates and the cold agglutinin titre is positive. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: This is typical lobar pneumococcal pneumonia; give IV cloxacillin

options.label: B
options.text: This is Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia acquired at birth; no treatment is needed

options.label: C
options.text: This is bacterial pneumonia in which the X-ray is expected to look milder than the child; give amoxicillin alone

options.label: D
options.text: This is viral bronchiolitis; give no antibiotics and use nebulised adrenaline

options.label: E
options.text: This is Mycoplasma pneumonia, where the X-ray is often worse than the clinical picture ("walking pneumonia"); a macrolide is appropriate

questions.correctAnswerText: This is Mycoplasma pneumonia, where the X-ray is often worse than the clinical picture ("walking pneumonia"); a macrolide is appropriate
questions.initialExplanation: Insidious cough and low-grade fever in a school-age child, positive cold agglutinins and radiology worse than the clinical state are the pattern of Mycoplasma pneumonia, treated with a macrolide.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pneumococcal pneumonia presents more acutely, with a typical lobar pattern, and is treated with amoxicillin or co-amoxiclav. Cloxacillin is for staphylococcal disease.
- B. Incorrect. Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia occurs in the first 3 months of life.
- C. Incorrect. In Mycoplasma pneumonia the radiograph looks worse than the child, not milder, and a macrolide is used.
- D. Incorrect. Bronchiolitis is a disease of infants under 2 years, and adrenaline is not its treatment.
- E. Correct. All features match clinical guidance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mycoplasma: age 5–15 years, insidious onset, low-grade fever; chest X-ray worse than clinical findings (walking pneumonia); cold agglutinins (IgM); macrolides.
- Extra-pulmonary features: erythema multiforme/Stevens–Johnson syndrome, meningoencephalitis, Guillain–Barré syndrome, arthritis, myocarditis, pericarditis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and protein-losing enteropathy.
- Staphylococcus: sudden severe illness in infancy, complications (lung abscess, empyema, pneumatocele), cloxacillin or vancomycin.

source.raw: Respiratory sheet — Page 24 (Important types of bacterial pneumonia: Mycoplasma); Page 26 (Investigations for the causative organism).

topics.name: Additional Asthma and Cystic Fibrosis Integration

cases.title: A child with asthma and a neonate with salt loss
cases.vignette: A school-age child with asthma has persistent symptoms despite treatment, while a separate infant with suspected cystic fibrosis presents with dehydration and hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. The clinician reviews imaging indications in asthma and the extrapulmonary consequences of CFTR dysfunction.

questions.stem: In which situation does the source recommend chest X-ray in a child with asthma?

options.label: A
options.text: Suspected pneumonia, sudden deterioration, pneumothorax/lung collapse or before and after mechanical ventilation in PICU

options.label: B
options.text: children in routine care with a normal examination between attacks

questions.correctAnswerText: Suspected pneumonia, sudden deterioration, pneumothorax/lung collapse or before and after mechanical ventilation in PICU
questions.initialExplanation: Chest X-ray is not routine for uncomplicated asthma. Clinical guidance suspected pneumonia, sudden deterioration, suspected pneumothorax/lung collapse and assessment around mechanical ventilation in PICU as indications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are the indications described.
- B. Incorrect. Normal examination between attacks is common and does not justify routine CXR.
- C. Incorrect. Eczema is an atopic association, not an indication for chest imaging.
- D. Incorrect. Routine imaging is not necessary in every mild exacerbation.
- E. Incorrect. Routine follow-up is based on symptoms, control, lung function and technique rather than serial CXR.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CXR is often normal in asthma.
- Use when another diagnosis/complication is suspected, including pneumonia, pneumothorax or collapse.
- ABG is reserved for rapid deterioration, life-threatening asthma or inadequate oxygenation.

questions.stem: A neonate with CF develops dehydration, hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia and metabolic alkalosis. Which CF-related complication is described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pseudo-Bartter syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance pseudo-Bartter syndrome in CF, characterized by hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia and metabolic alkalosis, often associated with salt loss and dehydration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The case is linked to CF-related salt loss rather than an adrenal tumour.
- B. Incorrect. SIADH causes water retention and hyponatraemia, not the described salt-loss alkalosis.
- C. Incorrect. Distal RTA causes metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis.
- D. Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome causes proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema.
- E. Correct. This is the complication named in the CF neonatal section.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CF can cause salt loss in sweat and dehydration.
- Pseudo-Bartter pattern: hypokalaemia + hypochloraemia + metabolic alkalosis.
- Assess hydration and electrolytes in infants with suspected CF.

questions.stem: Which reproductive manifestation is associated with cystic fibrosis in males?

options.label: A
options.text: Infertility due to congenital absence of the vas deferens

options.label: B
options.text: Immotile sperm caused by primary ciliary dyskinesia in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Infertility due to congenital absence of the vas deferens
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance male infertility due to absence of the vas deferens as a genitourinary manifestation of CF.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens is associated with CF and obstructive infertility.
- B. Incorrect. Immotile sperm is associated with PCD due to flagellar dysfunction, not the specific CF mechanism in this question.
- C. Incorrect. Hypospadias is a congenital urethral meatal abnormality.
- D. Incorrect. Hydrocele is fluid in the tunica vaginalis.
- E. Incorrect. Torsion is unrelated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CF: male infertility due to absence of the vas deferens.
- PCD: male infertility due to impaired sperm flagellar motility.
- Distinguish the mechanism when comparing CF with PCD.

cases.title: Optimizing treatment in established cystic fibrosis
cases.vignette: A 7-year-old child with confirmed CF has recurrent pulmonary exacerbations, chronic thick airway secretions, pancreatic insufficiency and faltering growth. The family asks how treatment can address both the respiratory and nutritional problems and what may be required if lung disease progresses.

questions.stem: What is the central organizational principle of cystic fibrosis management?

options.label: A
options.text: Multidisciplinary care involving respiratory, nutritional and other specialist teams

options.label: B
options.text: Respiratory treatment by one clinician without nutritional assessment

options.label: C
options.text: Surgical treatment in each newly diagnosed infant

questions.correctAnswerText: Multidisciplinary care involving respiratory, nutritional and other specialist teams
questions.initialExplanation: CF is a multisystem disorder, so management requires a multidisciplinary team. Respiratory, gastrointestinal, nutritional and endocrine complications may all need attention.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. clinical guidance explicitly emphasizes a multidisciplinary team because CF affects several organ systems.
- B. Incorrect. Nutritional and pancreatic complications are common and require active assessment.
- C. Incorrect. Surgery is not required in every child; treatment is individualized.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics address selected infections but do not treat all aspects of CF.
- E. Incorrect. Regular review is necessary to monitor lung function, growth, nutrition and complications.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CF requires coordinated multidisciplinary care.
- Follow respiratory disease, growth, nutrition, pancreatic function, liver disease and diabetes.
- Management is long term and individualized.

questions.stem: Which intervention is a core component of routine pulmonary care in cystic fibrosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Daily bronchoscopy for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Chest physiotherapy and airway-clearance techniques
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance chest physiotherapy, including percussion, postural drainage and breathing exercises, as an important part of pulmonary care. It recommends regular airway clearance, at least twice daily in the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bronchoscopy is not a daily routine treatment.
- B. Incorrect. Bed rest does not clear airway secretions and may worsen deconditioning.
- C. Correct. Airway clearance helps mobilize thick secretions and supports pulmonary care.
- D. Incorrect. Routine fluid restriction is not part of CF respiratory management.
- E. Incorrect. Activity should be encouraged as tolerated; airway clearance and exercise can support respiratory health.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chest physiotherapy is a central treatment.
- Methods include chest percussion, postural drainage and breathing exercises.
- Clinical guidance regular sessions, at least twice daily.
- Airway clearance should be integrated into the child's daily routine.

questions.stem: A child with CF develops an acute pulmonary exacerbation. Which antibiotic approach is described in the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Antifungal treatment as the antimicrobial therapy

options.label: B
options.text: Lifelong IV antibiotics for each patient from diagnosis

options.label: C
options.text: No antibiotics even when bacterial infection is present

options.label: E
options.text: Oral antibiotics during well periods when indicated, with IV antibiotics for acute exacerbations

questions.correctAnswerText: Oral antibiotics during well periods when indicated, with IV antibiotics for acute exacerbations
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance oral antibiotics for selected treatment periods and IV antibiotics for acute exacerbations, with drug selection guided by the organisms and clinical situation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Antifungals do not replace antibacterial treatment when bacterial infection is present.
- B. Incorrect. clinical guidance does not recommend lifelong IV antibiotics for every patient.
- C. Incorrect. Bacterial airway infection is an important contributor to CF lung disease and may require antibiotics.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotic treatment is used before transplantation when clinically indicated.
- E. Correct. The source distinguishes oral treatment from IV therapy for more significant acute exacerbations.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early airway pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus and H. influenzae.
- Later pathogens include Pseudomonas and Burkholderia cepacia.
- IV antibiotics are used for acute exacerbations according to clinical and microbiological assessment.
- Do not assume every cough requires an identical antibiotic regimen.

questions.stem: Which statement about nebulized mucolytic therapy in CF is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: DNase or hypertonic saline may reduce secretion viscosity and are used before chest physiotherapy

options.label: B
options.text: They should be given after most physiotherapy has finished because they prevent secretion mobilization

options.label: C
options.text: They are contraindicated in each patient with CF

options.label: E
options.text: Mucolytics are used to treat pleural effusion

questions.correctAnswerText: DNase or hypertonic saline may reduce secretion viscosity and are used before chest physiotherapy
questions.initialExplanation: The source lists nebulized mucolytics such as DNase, hypertonic saline and acetylcysteine to reduce the viscosity of secretions. It describes administration before physiotherapy to facilitate clearance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Clinical guidance mucolytics before physiotherapy to assist secretion clearance.
- B. Incorrect. The source places mucolytic treatment before physiotherapy.
- C. Incorrect. clinical guidance includes these agents as treatment options in CF.
- D. Incorrect. Mucolytics complement rather than replace airway-clearance techniques.
- E. Incorrect. Mucolytics are included in CF pulmonary care, not pleural effusion management.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Nebulized DNase, hypertonic saline or acetylcysteine may be used.
- Their aim is to reduce secretion viscosity.
- Give before airway-clearance physiotherapy.
- Treatment should be individualized by the CF team.

questions.stem: A child with CF has pancreatic insufficiency, steatorrhoea and poor weight gain. Which combination best addresses the nutritional problem?

options.label: B
options.text: Low-calorie diet and avoidance of most dietary fat

options.label: D
options.text: High-calorie diet, pancreatic enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation

questions.correctAnswerText: High-calorie diet, pancreatic enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance high-calorie nutrition, pancreatic enzyme replacement such as Creon and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation for patients with pancreatic insufficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Fasting is not a nutritional treatment and can worsen nutritional compromise.
- B. Incorrect. A low-calorie diet worsens faltering growth, and routine complete fat avoidance is not recommended.
- C. Incorrect. Fluid restriction and iron alone do not treat pancreatic malabsorption.
- D. Correct. This addresses increased nutritional needs, impaired digestion and vitamin malabsorption.
- E. Incorrect. Antibiotics cannot correct exocrine pancreatic insufficiency or nutritional deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CF pancreatic insufficiency → malabsorption and steatorrhoea.
- High-calorie diet is recommended.
- Pancreatic enzyme replacement improves digestion.
- Supplement fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.stem: An older child with CF develops diabetes mellitus. Which treatment is specifically mentioned for CF-related diabetes?

options.label: D
options.text: Oral antibiotics as the sole treatment

questions.correctAnswerText: Insulin
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies diabetes as an endocrine complication of CF and lists insulin as treatment for this complication.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. Insulin is the treatment specified for CF-related diabetes in the source.
- B. Incorrect. Pancreatic enzymes treat exocrine insufficiency, not hyperglycaemia.
- C. Incorrect. Fluid restriction is not a treatment for CF-related diabetes.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics treat selected infections and do not treat diabetes.
- E. Incorrect. Bronchodilators treat reversible airway narrowing.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CF may cause endocrine pancreatic dysfunction and CF-related diabetes.
- Insulin is used to manage the diabetes described.
- Continue nutritional and respiratory care alongside diabetes management.

questions.stem: A patient with CF develops end-stage lung disease despite optimized medical care. Which option is identified as the therapeutic option for end-stage pulmonary disease?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bilateral lung transplantation
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies bilateral lung transplantation as the therapeutic option for end-stage CF lung disease. It does not replace the need to manage extrapulmonary disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pancreatic enzymes treat exocrine insufficiency and do not reverse advanced lung disease.
- B. Incorrect. Oxygen may be required in advanced respiratory disease; it should not be avoided when indicated.
- C. Incorrect. Antihistamines do not treat end-stage structural lung damage.
- D. Correct. Bilateral lung transplantation is described as the option for end-stage CF lung disease.
- E. Incorrect. Routine lobectomy is not recommended for every patient with CF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Optimize airway clearance, antimicrobial therapy and nutrition.
- CFTR modulators/gene-targeted treatments are mentioned in the source as improving outcomes in selected patients.
- Bilateral lung transplantation may be considered for end-stage pulmonary disease.
- Continue multidisciplinary care after lung transplantation.

cases.title: Recurrent respiratory symptoms with changing clinical clues
cases.vignette: A pediatric clinic reviews several children with recurrent respiratory symptoms. Some have episodic wheeze, others have chronic wet cough or recurrent infections, and one has a history of sudden choking. The task is to use the pattern of onset, associated symptoms, examination and targeted investigations to distinguish common respiratory conditions.

questions.stem: A toddler develops sudden coughing and wheeze while playing with small objects. Symptoms persist and air entry is reduced on one side. Which diagnosis must be actively excluded before labeling the child as having asthma?
questions.correctAnswerText: Foreign body aspiration
questions.initialExplanation: Sudden onset during play, persistent symptoms and unilateral reduced air entry are red flags for foreign body aspiration. A foreign body may be missed and later present with recurrent cough or pneumonia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Functional abdominal pain is unrelated to the respiratory presentation.
- B. Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain sudden unilateral lower-airway signs.
- C. Correct. The abrupt choking-type onset and focal examination findings strongly suggest an inhaled foreign body.
- D. Incorrect. Anaemia may cause fatigue or breathlessness but not sudden focal wheeze after choking.
- E. Incorrect. Coryza may cause cough but does not explain a choking episode and focal reduction in air entry.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sudden choking + persistent cough/wheeze + unilateral signs → consider foreign body aspiration.
- Obtain appropriate chest imaging, but a radiolucent object may not be visible.
- Rigid bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic.

questions.stem: Which clinical pattern most strongly supports asthma rather than a single inhaled foreign body?

options.label: A
options.text: One abrupt episode while eating peanuts

options.label: B
options.text: A visible foreign body in the right main bronchus

options.label: C
options.text: Recurrent trigger-related episodes, nocturnal symptoms and wellness between attacks

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent focal reduction in air entry after a choking event

options.label: E
options.text: Sudden choking followed by persistent unilateral wheeze

questions.correctAnswerText: Recurrent trigger-related episodes, nocturnal symptoms and wellness between attacks
questions.initialExplanation: Asthma is characterized by recurrent variable symptoms related to triggers, often with nocturnal worsening and symptom-free intervals. Sudden choking and persistent unilateral findings suggest foreign body aspiration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. An abrupt episode during eating should raise concern for aspiration.
- B. Incorrect. A visible foreign body establishes an alternative mechanical cause of obstruction.
- C. Correct. This is the typical episodic clinical pattern described for asthma.
- D. Incorrect. Persistent focal signs are atypical for uncomplicated asthma and suggest a localized lesion or foreign body.
- E. Incorrect. This is a classic history for foreign body aspiration.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Asthma: recurrent, variable, trigger-related and often nocturnal symptoms.
- Foreign body: sudden onset, choking, persistent focal signs.
- A normal examination between asthma attacks does not exclude asthma.

questions.stem: A child has recurrent chest infections, chronic wheeze, steatorrhoea, faltering growth and a salty taste to the skin. Which investigation should be prioritized to confirm the suspected underlying disorder?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sweat chloride test
questions.initialExplanation: The combination of respiratory disease, pancreatic malabsorption and salty skin suggests cystic fibrosis. clinical guidance identifies sweat chloride testing as the gold-standard diagnostic procedure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Echocardiography does not diagnose CFTR dysfunction.
- B. Incorrect. Peak flow may support assessment of airflow but cannot confirm CF.
- C. Correct. Sweat chloride is the key diagnostic test for CF in the supplied clinical guidance.
- D. Incorrect. Troponin evaluates myocardial injury.
- E. Incorrect. Tuberculin testing evaluates TB infection and does not confirm CF.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- CF clues: recurrent chest infection, steatorrhoea, faltering growth, clubbing and salty skin.
- Sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L is indicative in the supplied table.
- Low faecal elastase supports pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.

questions.stem: A child has chronic productive cough, large amounts of sputum, recurrent pneumonia and clubbing. Chest X-ray is not diagnostic, but clinical suspicion remains high. Which investigation is most appropriate?
questions.correctAnswerText: High-resolution CT chest
questions.initialExplanation: The clinical pattern suggests bronchiectasis. Clinical guidance that early chest X-ray may be normal and identifies HRCT chest as the diagnostic investigation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Bone age is used in growth assessment.
- B. Incorrect. Skin-prick testing identifies allergen sensitization but does not diagnose bronchiectasis.
- C. Incorrect. EEG evaluates cerebral electrical activity.
- D. Correct. HRCT demonstrates bronchial dilatation and is the diagnostic imaging test listed.
- E. Incorrect. Abdominal ultrasound does not assess the bronchial tree.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bronchiectasis: chronic productive cough, large sputum volume, recurrent infection and clubbing.
- Chest X-ray can be normal early.
- HRCT is diagnostic.
- Investigate an underlying cause such as CF, PCD or a missed foreign body.

questions.stem: A child has chronic wet cough from early life, recurrent otitis media, chronic sinusitis and situs inversus. Which underlying mechanism explains the respiratory disease?

options.label: D
options.text: Defective ciliary function with impaired mucociliary clearance

questions.correctAnswerText: Defective ciliary function with impaired mucociliary clearance
questions.initialExplanation: The features suggest primary ciliary dyskinesia/Kartagener syndrome. Defective ciliary function impairs clearance of mucus and pathogens, leading to recurrent respiratory infections and bronchiectasis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pleural effusion causes a different clinical and examination pattern.
- B. Incorrect. IgE-mediated airway inflammation may contribute to asthma/allergy but does not explain situs inversus and chronic ENT disease.
- C. Incorrect. Pancreatic enzyme deficiency is associated with CF but does not explain situs inversus.
- D. Correct. This is the underlying mechanism of primary ciliary dyskinesia.
- E. Incorrect. Surfactant dysfunction is not the mechanism described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PCD: impaired ciliary function and mucociliary clearance.
- Kartagener syndrome: situs inversus, chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis.
- Nasal nitric oxide is listed as a screening test.

questions.stem: A child has fever and breathlessness, reduced movement on one side, stony dullness and reduced air entry. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pleural effusion
questions.initialExplanation: Reduced chest movement, stony dullness and reduced air entry over one hemithorax are characteristic signs of pleural effusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Rhinitis affects the upper airway and does not cause unilateral pleural signs.
- B. Incorrect. Asthma usually causes bilateral variable airflow obstruction and wheeze.
- C. Correct. Pleural fluid reduces expansion and breath-sound transmission, causing stony dullness and reduced air entry.
- D. Incorrect. Cough-variant asthma does not produce stony dullness.
- E. Incorrect. Croup causes barking cough and inspiratory stridor.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pleural effusion: decreased movement, reduced expansion and tactile fremitus, stony dullness and reduced air entry.
- A large effusion may push the mediastinum away from the affected side.
- CXR and CT chest are listed investigations.

questions.stem: A child with acute severe asthma initially has a low PaCO2 due to hyperventilation. Later, the child becomes exhausted and the PaCO2 rises with hypoxia and acidosis. What does this change indicate?

options.label: B
options.text: Deterioration with possible impending respiratory failure

questions.correctAnswerText: Deterioration with possible impending respiratory failure
questions.initialExplanation: Early asthma commonly causes hypocapnia from hyperventilation. A rising or high PaCO2 in a severely distressed or exhausted child is concerning for inadequate ventilation and impending respiratory failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This describes acute deterioration, not stable long-term control.
- B. Correct. The transition from hypocapnia to hypercapnia with hypoxia/acidosis indicates worsening ventilation and fatigue.
- C. Incorrect. This is a dangerous progression, not a reassuring recovery pattern.
- D. Incorrect. Resolution should be accompanied by clinical improvement, not exhaustion and worsening gas exchange.
- E. Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not cause this ABG progression.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early acute asthma: hyperventilation and low PaCO2.
- Late deterioration: hypoxia, rising PaCO2 and acidosis.
- Exhaustion, altered consciousness or silent chest requires urgent escalation.

questions.stem: A child with asthma is repeatedly attending hospital and using the reliever inhaler on most days. Before simply increasing medication, which review is particularly important?

options.label: C
options.text: Ignore nocturnal symptoms if the child is growing normally

options.label: E
options.text: Check adherence, inhaler technique, trigger exposure and the current control plan

questions.correctAnswerText: Check adherence, inhaler technique, trigger exposure and the current control plan
questions.initialExplanation: The asthma clinical guidance emphasizes family education, trigger avoidance, correct inhaler technique, understanding reliever versus preventer medication and regular follow-up. Frequent reliever use or repeated exacerbations should prompt reassessment of these factors and overall control.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stopping controller therapy may worsen airway inflammation and increase exacerbation risk.
- B. Incorrect. Normal activity should be maintained with appropriate asthma control.
- C. Incorrect. Nocturnal symptoms are an important marker of poor control and should not be ignored.
- D. Incorrect. Antibiotics are not routine asthma treatment and are used only when bacterial infection is suspected.
- E. Correct. Poor technique, non-adherence and ongoing triggers can explain poor control and should be assessed before treatment is stepped up.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Reassess diagnosis, adherence, inhaler technique and trigger exposure.
- Review reliever use, night waking and activity limitation.
- Provide a personalized action plan and regular follow-up.
- The aim is normal activity and school performance with prevention of exacerbations.

cases.title: Reading the cough and grading the distress

questions.stem: Four children attend a paediatric clinic on the same day. (1) A 7-year-old has bouts of coughing whenever he runs during games. (2) A 10-year-old coughs mainly in the early morning, clears his throat often and feels mucus running down the back of his throat. (3) A 6-week-old afebrile infant has a repetitive staccato cough with sticky eyes. (4) A 3-year-old began coughing suddenly after choking on a peanut. Which option pairs each child with the most characteristic diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: (1) Croup; (2) Pertussis; (3) Chlamydia infection; (4) Foreign body aspiration

options.label: B
options.text: (1) Exercise-induced asthma; (2) Posterior nasal drip; (3) Pertussis; (4) Foreign body aspiration

options.label: C
options.text: (1) Exercise-induced asthma; (2) GERD; (3) Chlamydia infection; (4) Foreign body aspiration

options.label: D
options.text: (1) Foreign body aspiration; (2) Posterior nasal drip; (3) Chlamydia infection; (4) Exercise-induced asthma

options.label: E
options.text: (1) Exercise-induced asthma; (2) Posterior nasal drip; (3) Chlamydia infection; (4) Foreign body aspiration

questions.correctAnswerText: (1) Exercise-induced asthma; (2) Posterior nasal drip; (3) Chlamydia infection; (4) Foreign body aspiration
questions.initialExplanation: Each cough has a characteristic association: recurrent cough with exercise (exercise-induced asthma), early-morning cough (posterior nasal drip), staccato cough (Chlamydia) and sudden cough after choking (foreign body aspiration).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Croup gives a barking cough with stridor, and pertussis gives a spasmodic whooping cough. Neither matches children 1 and 2.
- B. Incorrect. Child 3 has a staccato cough with sticky eyes (Chlamydia), not whooping cough.
- C. Incorrect. GERD is a cause of chronic cough, but an early-morning cough with a mucus-down-the-throat sensation is the pattern of posterior nasal drip.
- D. Incorrect. The pairings of children 1 and 4 are swapped.
- E. Correct. All four pairings follow the cough-characteristics table.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Spasmodic whooping cough → pertussis; barking (brassy) cough → croup; staccato cough → Chlamydia infection.
- Sudden cough after a choking episode → foreign body aspiration.
- Night-time (nocturnal) cough → asthma; recurrent cough with exercise → exercise-induced asthma.
- Morning cough → sinusitis or allergic rhinitis; early-morning cough → posterior nasal drip.
- Chronic cough = daily cough for more than 4 weeks (4–6 weeks).

source.raw: Respiratory sheet — Page 4 (Symptoms and signs: cough characteristics); Page 24 (Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia).

topics.name: Acute and Chronic Stridor — Additional Differential Diagnosis
