cases.title: A child with stridor and possible upper-airway obstruction
cases.vignette: A young child is brought to the emergency department with noisy breathing. The sound is predominantly inspiratory. The clinician must first assess airway safety, then distinguish acute causes of stridor from congenital or progressive chronic causes.

questions.stem: A child presents with acute stridor and increased work of breathing. what is the most important initial management priority?

options.label: A
options.text: Obtain a routine outpatient spirometry test

options.label: B
options.text: Give oral fluids and discharge the child

options.label: C
options.text: Perform a prolonged throat examination with a tongue depressor

options.label: D
options.text: Delay assessment until a chest X-ray is available

questions.correctAnswerText: Maintain a patent airway
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance acute stridor as an emergency. The most important management step is to maintain airway patency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Spirometry is not the immediate priority in a child with acute stridor.
- B. Incorrect. Discharge is unsafe before the cause and severity of acute stridor have been assessed.
- C. Incorrect. Unnecessary manipulation of a potentially compromised upper airway may worsen obstruction.
- D. Incorrect. Imaging must not delay urgent airway management.
- E. Correct. Airway assessment and maintenance take priority in acute upper-airway obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute stridor is an airway emergency.
- Prioritize airway patency and urgent assessment.
- Do not delay airway management for non-essential investigations.

questions.stem: Which group contains causes of acute stridor recommended?

options.label: A
options.text: Nephrotic syndrome, cystitis and renal calculi

options.label: D
options.text: Croup, acute epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis and laryngeal foreign-body aspiration

options.label: E
options.text: Bronchiectasis, chronic kidney disease and hydrocele

questions.correctAnswerText: Croup, acute epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis and laryngeal foreign-body aspiration
questions.initialExplanation: The acute stridor list includes croup, acute epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis and foreign-body aspiration in the upper airway.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are renal or urinary disorders and do not form the acute stridor differential.
- B. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal disorders.
- C. Incorrect. These are cardiovascular disorders.
- D. Correct. All four are included among acute causes of stridor.
- E. Incorrect. These are not the acute upper-airway causes listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute stridor causes include croup, epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis and laryngeal foreign body.
- Other listed causes include laryngeal oedema, hypocalcaemia, corrosive injury and inhalational injury.
- Clinical urgency is determined by airway compromise, not simply by the name of the suspected disease.

questions.stem: Which combination contains non-infectious causes of acute stridor specifically listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Angioneurotic oedema, hypocalcaemia and corrosive or smoke-related inhalational injury

options.label: B
options.text: Coeliac disease, lactose intolerance and giardiasis

options.label: D
options.text: Cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis and primary ciliary dyskinesia

options.label: E
options.text: Nephrotic syndrome, Fanconi syndrome and renal tubular acidosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Angioneurotic oedema, hypocalcaemia and corrosive or smoke-related inhalational injury
questions.initialExplanation: The acute stridor differential includes laryngeal oedema, hypocalcaemia, corrosive ingestion and inhalation of smoke or hot fumes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. These are non-infectious acute causes included.
- B. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal disorders.
- C. Incorrect. These are congenital cardiac lesions.
- D. Incorrect. These are chronic respiratory diseases and do not represent the acute non-infectious list asked for.
- E. Incorrect. These are renal tubular or glomerular disorders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute non-infectious causes include angioneurotic oedema, hypocalcaemia, corrosive ingestion and inhalational injury.
- Ask about exposure to chemicals, smoke and hot fumes.
- Acute upper-airway swelling can progress rapidly and requires urgent airway assessment.

questions.stem: A febrile child develops acute stridor. Which of the following is included in the infectious causes of acute stridor listed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Retropharyngeal abscess
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance includes measles, diphtheria, glandular fever, retropharyngeal abscess and quinsy among infections that may cause acute stridor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Acute rheumatic fever is an inflammatory complication following streptococcal infection, not a listed acute stridor cause.
- B. Incorrect. Nephrocalcinosis is a renal condition.
- C. Correct. Retropharyngeal abscess is specifically included in the acute infectious differential.
- D. Incorrect. VUR is retrograde urine flow from the bladder into the upper urinary tract.
- E. Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes gastric outlet obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infectious causes listed: croup, epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, measles, diphtheria, glandular fever, retropharyngeal abscess and quinsy.
- A toxic child with stridor requires urgent assessment for serious upper-airway infection.

questions.stem: Which group contains chronic causes of stridor recommended?

options.label: C
options.text: Laryngomalacia, laryngeal web, vocal cord palsy and vascular ring

options.label: E
options.text: Acute bronchiolitis, pneumonia and pleural effusion

questions.correctAnswerText: Laryngomalacia, laryngeal web, vocal cord palsy and vascular ring
questions.initialExplanation: The chronic stridor list includes laryngomalacia, laryngeal web or haemangioma, vocal cord palsy, vascular ring and subglottic stenosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are congenital cardiac lesions.
- B. Incorrect. These are renal disorders.
- C. Correct. All four are listed chronic upper-airway causes.
- D. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal disorders.
- E. Incorrect. These are lower respiratory disorders and are not the chronic stridor group requested.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chronic stridor: laryngomalacia, laryngeal web/haemangioma, vocal cord palsy, vascular ring and subglottic stenosis.
- Differentiate chronic structural or compressive causes from acute inflammatory obstruction.
- A history beginning in early infancy may suggest a congenital airway abnormality.

questions.stem: A child has persistent stridor due to a lesion arising within the larynx. Which pair is specifically included among the chronic causes?
questions.correctAnswerText: Laryngeal web and laryngeal haemangioma
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include laryngeal web and haemangioma among causes of chronic stridor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are renal tumours or lesions.
- B. Incorrect. These are cardiovascular structural abnormalities.
- C. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal congenital or obstructive disorders.
- D. Correct. Both are chronic laryngeal causes listed.
- E. Incorrect. These are pleural disorders and do not represent chronic laryngeal lesions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chronic intrinsic laryngeal causes include web and haemangioma.
- Vocal cord palsy and subglottic stenosis are additional chronic causes.
- Persistent stridor warrants evaluation for an anatomical lesion.

questions.stem: A child has chronic stridor due to compression of the airway from outside. Which group of causes is listed?

options.label: D
options.text: Nephrotic syndrome, renal stones and hydrocele

options.label: E
options.text: Coeliac disease, giardiasis and food intolerance

questions.correctAnswerText: Goitre, lymphadenopathy and mediastinal mass
questions.initialExplanation: The chronic stridor section includes extrinsic compression from goitre, lymphadenopathy and mediastinal mass.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These may cause respiratory symptoms but do not constitute the external compression group in the chronic stridor list.
- B. Incorrect. These are upper respiratory or ENT infections, not the external compressive causes listed.
- C. Correct. All three are listed causes of external airway compression.
- D. Incorrect. These are renal or urological conditions.
- E. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal conditions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- External compression causes of chronic stridor: goitre, lymphadenopathy and mediastinal mass.
- A vascular ring is another important compressive cause.
- Consider both intrinsic airway lesions and extrinsic compression.

questions.stem: An infant has chronic stridor and swallowing difficulty. Imaging suggests compression of the trachea and oesophagus by an abnormal vascular structure. Which diagnosis best fits the chronic stridor differential?
questions.correctAnswerText: Vascular ring
questions.initialExplanation: A vascular ring can compress the trachea and oesophagus. It is listed among the chronic causes of stridor in the supplied clinical guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Pleural effusion produces pleural signs such as stony dullness and reduced air entry.
- B. Incorrect. Bronchiolitis is an acute lower-airway disease characterized by wheeze and respiratory distress.
- C. Incorrect. Viral episodic wheeze is a preschool wheezing pattern, not an extrinsic tracheo-oesophageal compression.
- D. Incorrect. Pneumonia causes parenchymal infection and does not explain vascular compression.
- E. Correct. A vascular ring can produce chronic airway and oesophageal compression.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vascular ring is a chronic compressive cause of stridor.
- It may cause both respiratory and feeding/swallowing symptoms.
- Consider structural compression when stridor is persistent or associated with dysphagia.

cases.title: Croup and epiglottitis: imaging, disposition, counselling and confirmation

questions.stem: Two children are seen in the emergency department. Child A is an 18-month-old with 2 days of coryza followed by a barking cough, hoarseness and harsh stridor when upset; an AP neck film taken for another reason shows a steeple sign. Child B is a 4-year-old with abrupt high fever, drooling and a muffled voice; a junior doctor asks for a lateral neck X-ray to look for a thumb sign before any intervention. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The steeple sign points to epiglottitis, and the thumb sign is the diagnostic sign of viral croup

options.label: B
options.text: Both children need a neck X-ray before any airway intervention in order to confirm the diagnosis

options.label: C
options.text: Child B should go to radiology first for a lateral neck film, because it is quick and safe in suspected epiglottitis

options.label: D
options.text: Child A cannot be diagnosed without an AP neck film, because croup has no recognised clinical picture

options.label: E
options.text: The steeple sign is linked to croup, which is diagnosed clinically, and the thumb sign to epiglottitis, but airway management must not wait for a neck film

questions.correctAnswerText: The steeple sign is linked to croup, which is diagnosed clinically, and the thumb sign to epiglottitis, but airway management must not wait for a neck film
questions.initialExplanation: Croup is a clinical diagnosis (steeple sign on AP neck view is the associated radiograph sign). The thumb sign of epiglottitis is seen on a lateral neck film, but Clinical guidance this is not done when epiglottitis is suspected, because the airway is the priority.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. The two signs are reversed. Steeple sign is linked to croup, and thumb sign to epiglottitis.
- B. Incorrect. In suspected upper-airway obstruction one should not lose time with unnecessary radiological requests.
- C. Incorrect. Sending a child with suspected epiglottitis for imaging delays airway control and is unsafe. The lateral film is not done in this setting.
- D. Incorrect. The diagnosis of croup is mainly clinical (history and examination).
- E. Correct. It matches clinical guidance: clinical diagnosis for croup and airway first for epiglottitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Croup: diagnosed mainly clinically; steeple sign on AP neck view.
- Epiglottitis: thumb sign on lateral neck X-ray, which is not performed in the suspected case.
- In suspected upper-airway obstruction: do not use a tongue depressor, do not lay the child flat, do not delay for blood tests or radiology, and keep the child calm (on the mother's lap).

source.raw: Respiratory sheet — Page 14 (Croup: diagnosis); Page 16 (Epiglottitis: diagnosis).

topics.name: Recurrent and Persistent Wheeze — Differential Diagnosis and Additional Asthma Therapy

cases.title: A preschool child with repeated wheezing episodes
cases.vignette: A preschool child has recurrent episodes of wheeze. Some episodes occur during viral upper respiratory infections, while others follow exposure to dust, cold air or exercise. The pattern of wheezing guides the differential diagnosis and the selection of additional asthma therapies in selected children.

questions.stem: Which group contains causes of a first episode of wheeze listed?

options.label: A
options.text: Pleural effusion, pneumothorax and pulmonary hypertension

options.label: B
options.text: Bronchial asthma, cystic fibrosis and bronchiolitis

options.label: C
options.text: Bronchiectasis, vascular ring and foreign-body aspiration

options.label: D
options.text: Coeliac disease, giardiasis and lactose intolerance

options.label: E
options.text: Nephrotic syndrome, HUS and renal tubular acidosis

questions.correctAnswerText: Bronchial asthma, cystic fibrosis and bronchiolitis
questions.initialExplanation: The differential table includes bronchial asthma, cystic fibrosis and bronchiolitis among causes of a first wheezing episode.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These conditions may cause breathlessness but are not the first-episode wheeze group in the table.
- B. Correct. These are included in the first-episode differential.
- C. Incorrect. These are among causes considered in recurrent or persistent wheeze, not the complete first-episode group requested.
- D. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal disorders.
- E. Incorrect. These are renal disorders.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- First-episode wheeze differential includes asthma, CF and bronchiolitis.
- Age, preceding viral symptoms, feeding history and examination help distinguish causes.
- Do not label every first wheeze as asthma without considering alternative diagnoses.

questions.stem: A child has repeated wheezing attacks over several months. Which group is included 's differential for recurrent attacks?

options.label: A
options.text: Asthma, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and bronchiectasis

options.label: D
options.text: Acute epiglottitis, croup and bacterial tracheitis

questions.correctAnswerText: Asthma, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and bronchiectasis
questions.initialExplanation: The wheeze differential table lists asthma, GERD and bronchiectasis among causes to consider in recurrent attacks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. All three are included in the recurrent-attack differential.
- B. Incorrect. These are congenital urological conditions.
- C. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal conditions.
- D. Incorrect. These are causes of stridor or acute upper-airway obstruction rather than the recurrent wheeze group requested.
- E. Incorrect. These are congenital cardiac lesions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Recurrent wheeze: consider asthma, GERD and bronchiectasis.
- A recurrent pattern requires assessment for underlying disease rather than repeated treatment of symptoms alone.
- Review growth, feeding-related symptoms, infection history and response to bronchodilator therapy.

questions.stem: A child has persistent wheeze between acute illnesses. Which group contains causes listed for persistent wheeze in the supplied differential table?

options.label: A
options.text: Nephrotic syndrome, PSGN and renal calculi

options.label: C
options.text: Foreign-body aspiration, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis and vascular ring

options.label: D
options.text: Acute viral croup, epiglottitis and tonsillitis

options.label: E
options.text: Coeliac disease, giardiasis and lactose intolerance

questions.correctAnswerText: Foreign-body aspiration, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis and vascular ring
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance foreign-body aspiration, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis and vascular ring among causes of persistent wheeze.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are renal conditions.
- B. Incorrect. These are cardiac conditions and do not form the persistent-wheeze list.
- C. Correct. All four conditions appear in the persistent-wheeze differential.
- D. Incorrect. These are acute upper-airway disorders.
- E. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal conditions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Persistent wheeze should prompt consideration of FBA, CF, bronchiectasis and vascular ring.
- A history of choking or unilateral findings is important when considering FBA.
- Persistent symptoms from early life may suggest an underlying structural or inherited disorder.

questions.stem: Which trigger pattern best describes viral episodic wheeze in a preschool child?

options.label: A
options.text: Wheeze that occurs during sleep with no preceding infection

options.label: D
options.text: Episodes triggered mainly by viral upper respiratory tract infections

options.label: E
options.text: Continuous wheeze caused by a fixed foreign body in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Episodes triggered mainly by viral upper respiratory tract infections
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance viral episodic wheeze as being triggered by viral URTIs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Nocturnal symptoms alone do not define viral episodic wheeze.
- B. Incorrect. Exercise is one possible trigger in asthma but does not define viral episodic wheeze.
- C. Incorrect. Feeding-related symptoms may suggest aspiration or GERD.
- D. Correct. Viral URTIs are the characteristic trigger.
- E. Incorrect. A fixed foreign body is an alternative cause of persistent or focal wheeze.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral episodic wheeze: triggered by viral URTIs.
- Clinical guidance that it often resolves by about 5 years as airway size increases.
- Distinguish it from multiple-trigger wheeze and assess for atopy and family history.

questions.stem: Which finding increases the likelihood that a preschool child has multiple-trigger wheeze rather than purely viral episodic wheeze?

options.label: A
options.text: A single episode of choking with persistent unilateral wheeze

options.label: B
options.text: Symptoms triggered by dust, cold air and exercise, with eczema or a family history of asthma

options.label: C
options.text: Wheeze during viral URTIs and no symptoms between infections

options.label: D
options.text: Stridor from birth with feeding difficulty

options.label: E
options.text: Isolated stony dullness over one hemithorax

questions.correctAnswerText: Symptoms triggered by dust, cold air and exercise, with eczema or a family history of asthma
questions.initialExplanation: Multiple-trigger wheeze may occur with several stimuli, including viral infections, cold air, dust, animal dander and exercise. Atopy, eczema, food allergy or a family history of asthma increases the likelihood of asthma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. This suggests foreign-body aspiration.
- B. Correct. Multiple triggers and atopic features fit the pattern described.
- C. Incorrect. This is more typical of viral episodic wheeze.
- D. Incorrect. Congenital stridor with feeding difficulty suggests an upper-airway or compressive disorder.
- E. Incorrect. Stony dullness suggests pleural effusion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Multiple-trigger wheeze: viral infections, cold air, dust, animal dander and exercise.
- Atopy, eczema, food allergy and family history increase the likelihood of asthma.
- Viral episodic wheeze is more closely linked to viral URTIs and often resolves with age.

questions.stem: Which asthma treatment is an injectable monoclonal antibody directed against IgE?
questions.correctAnswerText: Omalizumab
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance identifies omalizumab as an injectable monoclonal antibody that acts against IgE and is used as add-on therapy in selected patients.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Ipratropium is an anticholinergic bronchodilator.
- B. Correct. Omalizumab is the anti-IgE monoclonal antibody listed.
- C. Incorrect. Theophylline is a methylxanthine.
- D. Incorrect. Mepolizumab is directed against interleukin-5.
- E. Incorrect. Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Omalizumab: anti-IgE monoclonal antibody.
- It is listed as add-on treatment, not as a routine rescue inhaler.
- Specialist assessment is required for biologic therapy.

questions.stem: Which biologic therapy listed targets interleukin-5 (IL-5)?
questions.correctAnswerText: Mepolizumab
questions.initialExplanation: The asthma drug list includes mepolizumab as an anti-IL5 monoclonal antibody.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist.
- B. Incorrect. Omalizumab acts against IgE.
- C. Correct. Mepolizumab is the anti-IL5 therapy listed.
- D. Incorrect. Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist.
- E. Incorrect. Budesonide is an inhaled corticosteroid.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mepolizumab: anti-IL5 monoclonal antibody.
- Omalizumab: anti-IgE monoclonal antibody.
- Both are additional specialist therapies rather than first-line reliever medications.

questions.stem: A child has chronic wheeze despite treatment for presumed asthma. Which additional group of conditions is listed as a differential diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Nephrotic syndrome, Bartter syndrome and renal tubular acidosis

options.label: B
options.text: Pyloric stenosis, coeliac disease and intussusception

options.label: C
options.text: Otitis media, sinusitis and oral thrush

options.label: D
options.text: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia, bronchiolitis obliterans, tracheobronchomalacia and immunodeficiency

options.label: E
options.text: ASD, VSD and patent ductus arteriosus

questions.correctAnswerText: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia, bronchiolitis obliterans, tracheobronchomalacia and immunodeficiency
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance includes bronchopulmonary dysplasia, bronchiolitis obliterans, tracheobronchomalacia and immunodeficiency among additional causes of wheeze. It also lists recurrent anaphylaxis and chronic aspiration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are renal disorders.
- B. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal conditions.
- C. Incorrect. These are ENT or oral conditions and do not form the chronic wheeze group.
- D. Correct. These are all included in the additional differential for wheezy chest.
- E. Incorrect. These are cardiac lesions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Additional wheeze differentials: bronchopulmonary dysplasia, bronchiolitis obliterans, tracheobronchomalacia and immunodeficiency.
- clinical guidance also lists recurrent anaphylaxis and chronic aspiration.
- Persistent wheeze should trigger reconsideration of the diagnosis and a search for an underlying cause.

cases.title: A child with pneumonia and an abnormal chest radiograph
cases.vignette: A child admitted with pneumonia undergoes chest radiography because the clinical course is more severe than expected. The team reviews the radiographic patterns described and looks for complications such as pleural effusion and lung abscess.

questions.stem: According to the pneumonia section, what is an important role of chest X-ray in a child with suspected pneumonia?

options.label: A
options.text: It is required before assessing airway and breathing

options.label: B
options.text: It replaces history, examination and oxygen saturation assessment

options.label: C
options.text: It can help assess the lungs and identify complications such as lung abscess

options.label: D
options.text: It identifies the causative organism with certainty in each case

options.label: E
options.text: It reliably distinguishes viral from bacterial pneumonia in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: It can help assess the lungs and identify complications such as lung abscess
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance chest X-ray as an investigation for pneumonia and for identifying complications, including lung abscess.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. Stabilization and assessment of airway and breathing must not be delayed for imaging.
- B. Incorrect. Clinical assessment remains essential.
- C. Correct. Recognized features include assessment of the lungs and detection of complications as important roles.
- D. Incorrect. Chest radiography does not identify the organism with certainty.
- E. Incorrect. clinical guidance warns that chest X-ray and routine blood tests do not reliably distinguish viral from bacterial pneumonia by themselves.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chest X-ray may demonstrate pneumonia patterns and complications.
- Complications listed include pleural effusion, lung abscess and pneumatocele.
- Do not use the radiograph alone to determine viral versus bacterial aetiology.

questions.stem: A chest radiograph shows a meniscus-shaped upper border of pleural fluid. Which finding does this sign indicate?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pleural effusion
questions.initialExplanation: The meniscus sign is associated with pleural fluid and is included beside the pleural effusion image in the pneumonia radiology section of clinical guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. A normal thymic shadow is a normal mediastinal finding in young children.
- B. Incorrect. Pneumothorax is characterized by pleural air and a visible pleural line rather than a fluid meniscus.
- C. Incorrect. Lobar collapse produces volume loss and displacement of adjacent structures.
- D. Correct. A meniscus-shaped fluid level is a radiographic feature of pleural effusion.
- E. Incorrect. Asthma may cause hyperinflation but does not create a pleural fluid meniscus.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Meniscus sign: pleural effusion.
- Interpret chest radiographs together with examination findings such as reduced expansion, stony dullness and reduced air entry.
- A parapneumonic effusion may complicate pneumonia.

questions.stem: Which set contains the chest radiograph patterns explicitly illustrated in the pneumonia section of the supplied clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Ground-glass kidneys, renal scarring and nephrocalcinosis

options.label: B
options.text: Boot-shaped heart, snowman sign and rib notching

options.label: C
options.text: Bird-beak oesophagus, thumb sign and steeple sign

options.label: D
options.text: Double-bubble sign, corkscrew oesophagus and string sign

options.label: E
options.text: Right upper-lobe pneumonia, bronchopneumonia, interstitial pneumonia, pleural effusion and lung abscess

questions.correctAnswerText: Right upper-lobe pneumonia, bronchopneumonia, interstitial pneumonia, pleural effusion and lung abscess
questions.initialExplanation: The pneumonia radiology page illustrates upper right-lobar pneumonia, bronchopneumonia, interstitial pneumonia, pleural effusion and lung abscess. It also labels pneumatocele and the meniscus sign.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are renal imaging findings.
- B. Incorrect. These are cardiac radiographic associations.
- C. Incorrect. These signs belong to other conditions and are not the pneumonia pattern group requested.
- D. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal radiographic signs.
- E. Correct. These are the patterns and complications shown in the pneumonia section.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pneumonia patterns illustrated: lobar, bronchopneumonia and interstitial.
- Complications shown include pleural effusion and lung abscess.
- The page also labels pneumatocele and meniscus sign.

topics.name: Additional Infectious Stridor and Wheeze Differentials

cases.title: Reviewing less common causes of noisy breathing
cases.vignette: A child with noisy breathing is being assessed after repeated episodes.

questions.stem: Which group contains infectious causes of acute stridor specifically listed in the respiratory clinical guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Measles, diphtheria, glandular fever, retropharyngeal abscess and quinsy

options.label: B
options.text: Influenza, malaria, typhoid and urinary tract infection

options.label: C
options.text: Coeliac disease, giardiasis and inflammatory bowel disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Measles, diphtheria, glandular fever, retropharyngeal abscess and quinsy
questions.initialExplanation: The acute stridor page lists measles, diphtheria, glandular fever, retropharyngeal abscess and quinsy among infectious causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct. All five conditions are included in the infectious differential on page 11.
- B. Incorrect. This is not the infectious list provided for acute stridor.
- C. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal disorders.
- D. Incorrect. These are urinary or renal conditions.
- E. Incorrect. These conditions do not form the listed upper-airway stridor group.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infectious causes listed include measles, diphtheria, glandular fever, retropharyngeal abscess and quinsy.
- Croup, epiglottitis and bacterial tracheitis are also included among acute stridor causes.
- Acute stridor requires urgent airway assessment.

questions.stem: A child has recurrent wheeze despite treatment for asthma. Which pair is specifically included as additional causes of wheeze?
questions.correctAnswerText: Recurrent anaphylaxis and chronic aspiration
questions.initialExplanation: The wheezy-chest differential on page 42 includes recurrent anaphylaxis, for example in food allergy or cow's milk protein intolerance, and chronic aspiration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect. These are renal conditions and do not form the listed wheeze differential.
- B. Correct. Both are explicitly listed in the additional wheeze differential.
- C. Incorrect. These are ENT or dental conditions, not the listed causes of recurrent wheeze.
- D. Incorrect. These are congenital cardiovascular lesions.
- E. Incorrect. These are gastrointestinal conditions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Additional wheeze causes include recurrent anaphylaxis and chronic aspiration.
- clinical guidance gives food allergy and cow's milk protein intolerance as examples associated with recurrent anaphylaxis.
- Reassess the diagnosis when wheeze persists or does not respond as expected to asthma treatment.
